[THE COMPLETE WORKS OF SICARD.]

[Col. 0009]

NOTICE CONCERNING SICARD, BISHOP OF CREMONA

(Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. VII, p. 523, in the Preface to Sicard’s *Chronicle*)

Francis Arisius of Cremona, a most learned man joined to me by long-standing friendship, conservator of the orders in his native city and one who has deserved exceedingly well of that city, not only mentions Sicard, bishop of Cremona, but also lists his writings in his *Learned Cremona*, vol. I, under the year 1185. He lists Sicard’s books in the following order. The acts and death of Saint Homobonus, who flourished in Sicard’s own time through holiness of life and miracles, and who, through the agency of that bishop himself—as is stated in Sicard’s *Chronicle* under the year 1198—was enrolled among the saints by Pope Innocent III. Various books of chronicles, of which we shall speak below. A treatise on humility, for which Arisius cites as witness Fanusius of Campania, in his book *On the Illustrious Families of Italy*. Yet Fanusius’s book, preserved in the Ambrosian Library, has always seemed to me to have been composed by a pseudonymous—and certainly pseudographical—writer; I would therefore not readily rest upon its authority. Raphael of Volterra, moreover, before Arisius, informed us at the beginning of Book XXII of his *Commentaries* that Sicard had also compiled a history, or lives, of the Roman pontiffs. Finally, the *Mitrale*, or *Compendium concerning the Offices*, or *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, is attributed to Sicard. But if my conjecture has any weight, the *Mitrale*, undoubtedly composed by him, is perhaps nothing other than another of Sicard’s chronicles. [Note: [Col. 0009] Muratori said this without due consideration. See below Cardinal Mai’s Notice on Sicard’s *Mitrale*. EDITOR.] For Gualvaneus de la Flamma, when enumerating not all books but only the historical works he had used, mentions a *Mitrale of the Emperors* composed by Sicard, bishop of Cremona. As for the *Compendium concerning the Offices*, Antonio Possevino indicates it on Leland’s authority, and it is said to be preserved in the Vatican Library. Since this work is unknown to me, I shall add nothing further concerning it.

Yet I cannot pass over what Gerardus Johannes Vossius, a man of exceptional learning, says of our Sicard in Book II, chapter 53, of *On Latin Historians*. He observes that Raphael of Volterra includes our Sicard among those who transmitted the lives of Roman pontiffs, placing him immediately after Sigebert and Hugh of Fleury; and that Godfrey of Viterbo, who flourished in 1186, is placed after Sicard. Thus, Vossius says, if Volterra is to be trusted, Sicard must have lived around the year 1160. Certainly there is no ground for doubt that Sicard was alive in 1160, and lived in the very period in which the man of Viterbo flourished. But because Sicard lived until 1215, thus outliving Godfrey, Volterra would more fairly have assigned precedence to the man of Viterbo rather than to Sicard. Vossius continues that he wonders why Possevino, in mentioning so ancient an author as Sicard, nevertheless adds that this was that Sicard of Cremona to whom Lawrence Lauretus, a Carmelite, dedicated his *Scholia*, when Lauretus flourished about A.D. 1570. But Possevino, mentioning our Sicard, says: “to whose work Lawrence Lauretus left *Scholia*,” etc. That is, Lauretus did not present the *Scholia* to Sicard during his lifetime, but added them to Sicard’s book *On the Offices* long after Sicard had died; and thus there is no contradiction here.

In his *Chronicle*, under the year 1179, Sicard calls Offredus, bishop of Cremona, “my ordainer.” He then relates that in 1183 he was advanced to the rank of subdeacon by Lucius III. Under the year 1185 he adds: “In this year I, Sicard, compiler and scribe of the present work, was elected at Cremona, though unworthy, to the episcopal office.” In the following year, through his efforts, peace was restored between Emperor Frederick I and the citizens of Cremona. In 1187, moved by the entreaties and affection of those same citizens, he set out for Germany to obtain from the Emperor pardon for the rebuilding of Manfred’s castle. Under the year 1194 he writes that the castle of Jovisalta—now Genivolta—was begun by him and happily completed; and in 1199 he went as a pilgrim to Rome, on which occasion he obtained from Pope Innocent III the canonization of Blessed Homobonus, a citizen of Cremona who had died not long before. In 1203 he went to Armenia and remained there with Peter, cardinal and legate of the Apostolic See; and in the following year he proceeded to Constantinople, where, in the church of Saint Sophia, by order of that same legate, he celebrated a solemn ordination of clerics. You therefore see that Ughelli was mistaken in assigning Sicard’s journey to the East, in his catalogue of the bishops of Cremona, to the year 1209. Finally, after returning to his homeland, Sicard ended his life in 1215, as the records of Cremona attest. The following is noted in the Imperial codex: “In the year 1215, Bishop Sicard, compiler of this present work, died in the month of June.” I consider this certain concerning the year of our author’s death; but Arisius in *Learned Cremona*, Ughelli, and others, who state that Sicard departed this life on 26 January, cause me to doubt the month. Perhaps the person who once wrote the Vienna manuscript, finding *Jan.* there abbreviated for *Januarius* [January], carelessly read *Jun.*, that is, *Junius* [June]. Christopher Sandius, in his notes on Vossius’s *On Latin Historians*, having observed that Sicard had died at last in 1215, then adds: “How, then, could he have carried his *Chronicle* from the origin of the world to the year 1221, as Lambecius reports in vol. II of *On the Vienna Library*, p. 871?” Sandius asks this not without reason. But the words of the *Chronicle* itself cited by Lambecius now establish that Sicard did indeed depart this life in 1215; the few words that follow were added, as often happens, by another writer, who continued Sicard’s book for five years.

Here Gualvaneus de la Flamma must again be heard. In chapter 247 of the manuscript *Sheaf of Flowers*, he relates that in 1214 the Cremonese were routed in battle by the Milanese, adding: “And, according to Sicard, never had so enormous a loss been inflicted upon the people of Cremona.” Yet neither the Este nor the Vienna codex contains a word concerning this most dreadful battle; indeed, the narrative of both ends in the preceding year, 1213. What is to be said here? Did Gualvaneus possess a codex in which not Sicard, but some other person, had added the mention of this bloody battle? Or has the complete *Chronicle* of Sicard not been preserved for us? [Col. 0011] I remain uncertain, especially because I observe so great a dissimilarity between these two manuscript codices. Moreover, even the brief Annals of the Cremonese, which I shall publish below, make no mention under the year 1214 of this Milanese victory.

[*MITRALE*, OR COMPENDIUM CONCERNING ECCLESIASTICAL OFFICES.]

[Col. 0011]

ON SICARD’S *MITRALE*, OR TREATISE CONCERNING ECCLESIASTICAL OFFICES.

(Mai, *Roman Spicilegium*, vol. VI, p. 583, Preface to the Fragments from Sicard’s *Mitrale*.)

We have repeatedly seen cited in Bernard Gui’s *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs* the *Chronicle* of Sicard, bishop of Cremona, a contemporary of Pope Innocent III; Muratori finally published that *Chronicle* in the seventh volume of the *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, and in his preface listed other works of the learned bishop. Yet the great man twice stated there, incautiously, that he thought Sicard’s work called the *Mitrale* was nothing other than one of the chronicles written by Sicard. But others before Muratori had already explicitly named Sicard’s *Mitrale*, or *Compendium concerning the Offices*, so that *Mitrale* is called, as it were, “episcopal” or “pontifical,” because in that volume Sicard explains the liturgy of bishops and lesser priests. Indeed, in two Vatican codices this title is prefixed to the work; in one: “Here begins the *Mitrale concerning the Offices*, composed by Sychardus, bishop of Cremona”; in the other: “Here begins the book called the *Mitrale*, composed by Sicard, bishop of Cremona.” Here, too, we see the variation in spelling, *Sychardus* and *Sicardus*. Thus, having dismissed Muratori’s empty opinion or conjecture concerning the subject of the *Mitrale*, we shall describe this work itself, a truly excellent and hitherto unpublished one, somewhat more carefully. It consists of nine books, each having its own prologue. These are its titles or chapters.

(The sequence of chapters, which the most learned editor presents here by way of specimen, we relegate to the end of the work. EDITORS OF THE PATROLOGY.)

Here, therefore, we see the richest sources for liturgical study, which it is almost unworthy to keep any longer upon the shelves of manuscripts, as though in their native caverns. For if they are drawn forth, all who will hereafter treat ecclesiastical offices will immediately water their gardens from them; and not they alone, but also those who wish either to resolve their doubts or to illuminate Christian antiquities, and especially to know the origin, order, and practice of sacred offices on each day of the year. Trombellius already used several authorities from the third and sixth books of our Sicard, whom he read in a Bolognese codex, in his treatises *On Baptism*, vol. I, pp. 212, 221, 312. For my part, having gladly read Sicard’s work in a Vatican codex, I could scarcely restrain myself from committing the whole to print. It would indeed make a volume of moderate size; and, if adorned with suitable notes as well, would take the form of a substantial work. Both Vatican codices are folios, written densely in two columns: one is very complete and nearly of Sicard’s own age; the other is a century later and lacks a few things at its end. Yet, reflecting upon the brevity of life and upon the obstacles that often impede one’s purpose, so that readers may have something of Sicard from me without delay, I prepared a few extracts, chiefly concerning sacred buildings and ecclesiastical philology; and I trust that discerning persons will consider them valuable. (The Fragments follow.)

[Col. 0013]

THE *MITRALE*, OR COMPENDIUM CONCERNING ECCLESIASTICAL OFFICES, OF SICARD, BISHOP OF CREMONA.

(Now published for the first time according to a transcript preserved in the library of the Count de l’Escalopier.)

AUTHOR’S PROEM.

[Col. 0013A] A wealthy and prudent man who wishes to invite his dependents to dinner ought to build and adorn a dining hall and service rooms, prepare utensils, appoint servants, clothe them suitably, and finally assign each particular office to a particular servant. Thus that rich One, whom all things serve, in the beginning created heaven and earth, the sea, and all things in them [Note: [Col. 0013] Gen. 1]; and, after making the structure of the world together with the things of the world, he formed man from the mud of the earth, breathed into him the breath of life, and placed him in the paradise of delight, assigning for his food every tree pleasing to the sight and sweet for eating, except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil [Note: [Col. 0013] Gen. 2]. And when the end of all flesh had come before him, because the earth had been filled with iniquity, he commanded that, for preserving the seed of a second beginning, an ark be made for him from smooth and incorruptible wood, that food of every kind fit to be eaten be gathered into it for the sustenance of those about to enter [Col. 0013B] [Note: [Col. 0013] Gen. 6], and that Noah enter with his household [Note: [Col. 0013] Gen. 7].

Our Master also, when he was seen upon earth and lived among human beings [Note: [Col. 0013] Baruch 3], wishing to eat the Passover according to the Law with his brethren and disciples, said to them: “Go into the city, and you will meet a man carrying a jar of water; follow him wherever he enters, and tell the master of the house to assign you a guest room where the Master may eat the Passover with his disciples. He will show you a large furnished upper room; prepare it there” [Note: [Col. 0013] Mark 14; Luke 22]. Thus we also, though wholly unworthy and feeble imitators, yet intending to invite brethren and children to the cultivation of paradise, the sacrament of baptism, and the Supper of the Lord, which are to be celebrated in the Church, shall first treat of the Church, which is likened to paradise, the ark, and a great dining hall: of its construction, adornment, and utensils. Secondly, we shall treat of the institution, vestments, and bearing of its ministers; thirdly, of their offices; fourthly, of the order of the offices. We intend not merely to set these forth, but also to explain them exactly, adding the institutions of each and the reasons for their institution.

But in pursuing these reasons I may perhaps go beyond the minds of the authors; yet for this reason, as a swift and envious detractor will allege, I have not written harmfully. For Augustine says in the book *On Christian Doctrine* [Note: [Col. 0013] Book II, chapter 36]: “If anyone understands something in the Scriptures other than what he who wrote them understood, [Col. 0014B] he is neither harmfully deceived nor altogether lying, provided that, if he is deceived, he is deceived by an interpretation that builds up charity. He is like one who leaves the road by mistake but nevertheless travels through a field by which that road leads to its destination. If the road is visible, he must be corrected; if it is hidden, he must be taught not to leave the road, lest through a habit of straying he be forced to go crosswise or perversely.” Therefore, since I was not a counsellor in the authors’ undertaking, nor is it permitted to investigate their minds further, though it is permitted to go beyond them, I am pleased to range through these matters as well, provided that the excursion is useful for the building up of charity.

BOOK ONE. ON THE CONSTRUCTION, ADORNMENT, AND UTENSILS OF THE CHURCH.

[Col. 0013]

CHAPTER I. ON THE INSTITUTION OF THE CHURCH.

[Col. 0013C]

“In the churches bless God, the Lord, from the fountains of Israel” [Col. 0014C] [Note: [Col. 0013] Ps. 67]. Although the great God may everywhere—in the wilderness and in every place of his dominion [Note: [Col. 0013] Ps. 102]—be blessed and ought to be invoked, nevertheless at an appropriate time the faithful rightly run to the oratory as to a royal court, in order to hear the commands of the eternal King. They rightly hasten to the dining hall, that they may receive from the banquet of the fattened calf; they rightly hurry to the sanctuary, where, according to the Lord’s word, God may dwell in their midst. Nor is the institution of places of prayer new. The Lord commanded Moses on Mount Sinai to make a tabernacle wondrously fashioned from curtains. One part of it was holy, where the people sacrificed; the other was called the Holy of Holies, where the priests and Levites ministered [Note: [Col. 0015] Exod. 25, 40]. After it had been worn out by age, the Lord commanded a temple to be made, which Solomon built in peace, wonderful in workmanship and renowned throughout the world; it had two parts, like the tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0015] III Kings 8]. From both of these our material church received its form: in its front part [Col. 0015B] the people listen and pray, while in the sanctuary the clergy preach, sing joyfully, and minister.

Therefore, because of the diversity of its parts or the multiplicity of its places, the Prophet says, “in the churches,” not “in the church.” The tabernacle, because it was made for a journey, sometimes bears the type of the world, because this world passes away, and its desire [Note: [Col. 0015] I John 2]. Hence it consists of the four colors of its curtains, just as the world is composed of four elements. It was, indeed, as it were an elemental world; rather, whatever is in the world was represented within it. Therefore God in the tabernacle is God in this world, just as Christ, reddened with blood, is in the temple [Note: [Col. 0015] Heb. 13].

More explicitly, the tabernacle bears the type of the Church Militant, which has here no lasting city, but seeks the city to come. It is therefore called a tabernacle because tabernacles belong to soldiers. Thus the four colors of the curtains express four forms of righteousness in this warfare: in twisted fine linen is expressed the flesh resisting through chastity; in blue, the mind desiring heavenly things; in purple, the flesh subject to suffering; in twice-dyed scarlet, the mind shining forth through love of God and neighbour. Therefore God in the tabernacle is God among the faithful gathered in his name.

The first part of the tabernacle, called the holy place, in which the people sacrificed, is the active life, in which the people laboured in love of neighbour. The other part, called the Holy of Holies, where the Levites ministered, is the contemplative life, in which the sincere conduct of religious persons is devoted to the love and contemplation of God [Col. 0015D]. Therefore, in Holy Scripture there are three tabernacles: the first exists in figure only, as the tabernacle of Moses; the second in figure and truth, as the structure of the world; the third exists in truth alone, as the warfare of God’s people.

The tabernacle is transformed into the temple because one runs from warfare to triumph. For the temple built by Solomon, and possessed by the people in their homeland and in peace, signifies the temple of glory, constructed from living stones in the heavenly Jerusalem—that is, in the vision of peace—by the true peaceful Solomon, where the Church resounds with everlasting peace. Thus it is said [Note: [Col. 0015] III Kings 6] [Col. 0016A] that no hammer, axe, or any iron instrument was heard in the building of the temple; rather, everything was prepared outside Jerusalem, suitably fitted, and restored to its place, being joined either with mortar or with nails. For in the peace of eternal blessedness, faith is not to be tested by tribulations, nor life struck by any disturbance. But those who have been disciplined here are there fitted into their proper ranks by the glue of charity and by bonds.

And although this is that Jerusalem “whose participation is in the same” [Note: [Col. 0015] Ps. 121], yet the temple here too is divided into two, because the heavenly court is distinguished by the difference between angels and human beings. Nevertheless, the temple is sometimes used as a designation of the Church Militant. Thus it is read [Note: [Col. 0015] III Kings 7] that it had two columns before its doors, one called Firmness and the other Strength. The first signifies the ancient fathers, who through faith conquered kingdoms and practised righteousness. Joseph was a firm column, whom the harlot could not separate from righteousness [Note: [Col. 0015] Gen. 39]. The second signifies the later fathers—namely, the apostles and martyrs, witnesses of Christ—who could not be torn away from the truth by any assault of winds. Paul was a strong column, whom neither death nor life could separate from Christ’s charity [Note: [Col. 0015] Rom. 8].

It is also for this reason that the temple is said to have been built in seven years and dedicated in seven days [Note: [Col. 0015] III Kings 6, 8]. For as long as the present Church dwells in this life, which revolves through seven days, it is continually built whenever some are converted to faith, and continually dedicated while they are consecrated to the Lord through repentance and holy conduct [Col. 0016C]. Those two things together, therefore, designate the universal Church: the former, because it was on a journey, properly signifies the Church Militant; the latter, because it was in a time of peace, the Church Triumphant.

Our material church, however, just as it derives the origin of its form and institution from both, likewise draws its signification equally from each. Thus our material church signifies the universal Church. When you hear “universal,” understand the Church Militant, composed alike of Gentiles and Jews, and the Church Triumphant, to be gathered and already gathered from angels and human beings. Its body and choir therefore represent the Church Militant and the Church Triumphant; or, with regard to the Church Militant, they signify the two lives, active and contemplative, or the two churches of Gentiles and Jews; with regard to the Church Triumphant, the two assemblies of human beings and angels. The Prophet therefore rightly says in the plural, “in the churches,” as though in the congregation of the faithful converted from Jews and Gentiles. In it, we who have been converted from Bashan—that is, from the confusion of sins—bless God, to whom *latria* [worship] is due, and the Lord, to whom *dulia* [veneration] is due [Note: [Col. 0015] St Thomas, III Part, question 25, article 2]; we, I say, who have drunk from the fountains of Israel, that is, from the doctrine of the apostles, so that, in imitation of those whom Christ chose from Israel, you may preach, making them fountains of living water springing up to eternal life [Note: [Col. 0015] John 4].

CHAPTER II. ON THE FOUNDATION OF THE CHURCH.

[Col. 0017A]

The house of the Lord is well founded upon the firm rock [Note: [Col. 0017] Matt. 7]. The Church is founded upon the rock in this manner. Let a bishop sprinkle the prepared site of the foundation with holy water to drive away the phantasms of demons, or let a priest do so if a bishop cannot be present [Note: [Col. 0017] Ps. 131]. Let him place in the foundation a stone impressed with a cross, chanting the psalms, “Have mercy on me, O God” [Note: [Col. 0017] Ps. 50], and “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” [Note: [Col. 0017] Ps. 86], etc., together with fitting prayers and an oration such as: “Deign to send forth, Lord God almighty Father, your angel from heaven, that he may guard, cherish, visit, and defend this place and all who pray or will pray in it.” While saying and doing these things, the bishop should turn toward the east—namely, the rising of the equinoctial sun—not, as some do, toward the rising of the summer sun. Then let him erect the altar and celebrate Mass: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” [Note: [Col. 0017] I Cor. 3].

This is the rock upon which the Church is founded; hence: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” [Note: [Col. 0017] Matt. 16]. It is indeed a firm and stable foundation, which will yield neither to winds, nor to the force of a torrent, nor collapse through dripping water. O human being, enter into this rock and hide in the pit of the earth [Note: [Col. 0017] Isa. 2]; stand in the clefts of this rock [Note: [Col. 0017] Song 2], so that you may see the Lord’s back; follow this rock, that it may refresh you when thirsty [Note: [Col. 0017] Exod. 33]; strike your beak against this rock, that your youth may be renewed like an eagle’s [Col. 0017C] [Note: [Col. 0017] Ps. 102]. Upon this foundation is placed the foundation of the apostles and prophets, of which the Apostle says: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” [Note: [Col. 0017] Eph. 2]. Christ, therefore, is the foundation of foundations.

This building is directed toward the equinoctial east because the Church, which wars upon earth, ought to govern itself with equanimity in prosperity and adversity. Again, it turns toward the east both because in it the Sun of Righteousness is worshipped [Note: [Col. 0017] Mal. 4], and because he whose name is the East is adored, according to the words: “The East from on high has visited us” [Note: [Col. 0017] Zech. 6; Luke 1]; and because the paradise of delights lies in eastern regions [Note: [Col. 0017] Gen. 2], which the Church recalls through a multiplicity of meanings. This is the enclosed garden, the sealed fountain [Note: [Col. 0017] Song 4], where Adam was placed to cultivate and guard it; where were the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, the tree of life, the other fragrant trees, and the four rivers proceeding from one and the same spring [Note: [Col. 0017] Gen. 2].

In the garden are irrigation, nourishment, trees, and fruits; in the Church are baptism, anointing, faithful persons, and works—things hidden from the wise but revealed to little ones [Note: [Col. 0017] Matt. 11]. What do we understand by Adam, cultivator and guardian, but the priestly order? They are the labourers sent into the harvest [Note: [Col. 0017] Luke 10]; they are the watchmen who guard the city [Note: [Col. 0017] Song 3]. Of them, if they have eaten from the tree of disobedience, it is said: “See lest perhaps they take from the tree of life” [Note: [Col. 0017] Gen. 2]. On account of sin this tree, which had not previously been forbidden, is forbidden: that is, the body of Christ. “The tree planted beside the streams of the waters of life” [Note: [Col. 0017] Ps. 1], because whoever eats that flesh receives eternal life [Note: [Col. 0017] John 6]; “but whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” [Note: [Col. 0017] I Cor. 2].

By the other fragrant trees we understand the saints, one of whom said: “I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God” [Note: [Col. 0017] Ps. 51]. Of them he also says: “Your sons are like young olive trees around your table” [Note: [Col. 0017] Ps. 127]. The four rivers are the four Evangelists, drawing waters from the one breast of the Lord, by whom the world is irrigated and the Church made fruitful. Of them he says: [Col. 0018B] “The rivers lifted up their voices” [Note: [Col. 0017] Ps. 92]. Let us therefore worship this East toward the east, that we may be illuminated by the sun, visited by the East, enjoy the tree of life, and be watered by the rivers of paradise.

CHAPTER III. ON THE ALTAR.

Now may one of the seraphim fly to me and, taking a carbuncle from the altar, touch my lips [Note: [Col. 0017] Isa. 6]. May Christ, the greatest of angels, the Angel of Great Counsel [Note: [Col. 0017] Isa. 9], not reproach me, a sinner, for “taking my covenant in your mouth” [Note: [Col. 0017] Ps. 49]; but, taking from himself, the altar, the fire of charity—he from whom comes the fullness of every gift [Note: [Col. 0017] John 1]—may he touch my lips, so that they may not speak from the altar deceitful or empty things, but things approved by priestly men.

Thus Noah is read to have first constructed an altar [Note: [Col. 0017] Gen. 8]; then Abraham [Note: [Col. 0017] Gen. 12], Isaac [Note: [Col. 0017] Gen. 26], and Jacob to have built altars [Note: [Col. 0017] Gen. 33]. These are understood as nothing other than upright stones, upon which they slaughtered sacrifices. At times, indeed, fire descending from heaven consumed the sacrifice offered; hence Cain killed his brother [Note: [Col. 0017] Gen. 4], because the Lord looked with favor upon Abel and his sacrifice. For heavenly fire consumed Abel’s sacrifice, while Cain’s sacrifice remained untouched.

Observe that *altaria* [altars] and *arae* [altars/altars for sacrifice] are sometimes found without distinction. Yet this is the difference between an *altare* and an *ara*: *altare* is so called as though from *alta res* [a high thing], or *alta ara* [a high altar], upon which priests burned incense; while *ara* is so called as though from *area* [a level space], that is, “flat,” or from *ardor* [burning], because sacrifices burned upon it. Moses also made an altar from shittim wood, and likewise an altar of incense, which he overlaid with purest gold [Note: [Col. 0017] Exod. 25]. Solomon likewise made a golden altar [Note: [Col. 0017] III Kings 8]. From these ancient fathers the altars of later times took their beginning. They rise with four horns; some are of a single stone, while others are constructed from several.

The stones erected as altars, the golden altar, and our stone altars signify Christ, the stone cut from the mountain without hands [Note: [Col. 0017] Dan. 2], the square and stable stone, upon whom we heap the vows of our prayers—hence we conclude our prayers “through Jesus Christ our Lord.” Upon him we slaughter the lamb, calf, and kid, while we consecrate Christ’s innocence, works, and repentance. Upon him we consecrate the body of Christ, because, believing in him, we are refreshed from him; and with him, as many members, we become one body, and as many stones, one altar. He is golden because “in him are hidden all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God” [Note: [Col. 0019] Col. 2].

Altars and sacrificial altars also represent the cross of the Lord. Therefore the lamb, kid, and calf on the altar are Christ suspended on the cross, who, though innocent, bore our sins [Note: [Col. 0019] Isa. 53], subdued the earth of our flesh, and enriched it with the fruit of the seed of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0019B] The steps by which one ascends to the altar are the martyrs; because they poured out their blood for love of him, the Bride in the Song of Love called the ascent purple [Note: [Col. 0019] Song 3]. Or the altar signifies the heart of each faithful person, stone through the solidity of faith, gold through the endowment of wisdom.

By the steps we understand the virtues. The altar has fifteen steps, by which Solomon arranged for ascent into the temple; the Prophet continuously set these forth in fifteen psalms [Note: [Col. 0019] Ps. 73], and the blessed man has disposed the ascents in his heart. This is the ladder upon which Jacob saw angels ascending and descending [Note: [Col. 0019] Gen. 28]. The altar is also called the more secret place, according to the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0019] chapter 8]: “The Angel went out from the altar,” that is, Christ from the more secret place.

The altar made of shittim wood is the clean way of the righteous—firm and incorruptible—prepared for offering sacrifices of good works, where the flesh of animals is slaughtered, because they crucify their flesh with its vices and desires [Note: [Col. 0019] Gal. 4], and offer God a living sacrifice as an odor of sweetness [Note: [Col. 0019] Rom. 12]. The altar of incense, which was likewise made of shittim wood and overlaid with gold [Note: [Col. 0019] Exod. 30], is the manner of life of the perfect: firm in faith, shining in wisdom, eminent in the four virtues, devoted to prayer for receiving and nourishing the fire of charity, and prepared to offer libations of virtues. Let us therefore strive, brethren, that our altars may be able, through the altar, to attain unto the altar.

## Chapter IV. On the Parts of a Church

[Col. 0019D] “All your walls [shall be of] precious stones, and the towers of Jerusalem shall be built with gems” [Note: [Col. 0019] Tobit 13]. Thus the Church is built: it has a pavement with subterranean crypts; it rises high, long and broad, with four walls. Some churches, however, are formed in the shape of a cross, while others are made round, their walls built of stone and mortar, with certain slanting windows and doors. Within they contain screens and pulpits, columns with bases and capitals, beams, timbers and roof-tiles, spiral stairways and galleries with protective side-rails. Outside [Col. 0020A] are attached exedrae, cemeteries, towers, and cloisters.

The pavement, trodden beneath the feet, is the common people, by whose labours the Church is supported. The underground crypts are the hermits, indeed cultivators of a more hidden life. By the doctrines of the four Gospels, as by walls, it rises to the heights of virtue. Its length is long-suffering, which patiently endures adversity until it reaches its homeland; its breadth is charity, which, with the bosom of the mind enlarged, loves friends in God and enemies for God’s sake. Its height is hope of the future reward, which despises prosperity and adversity alike until it sees the good things of the Lord in the land of the living [Note: [Col. 0019] Ps. 26]. Churches formed in the shape of a cross show that we ought to be crucified to the world [Note: [Col. 0019] Gal. 6], or to follow the Crucified One, according to the saying: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and [Col. 0020B] take up his cross and follow me” [Note: [Col. 0019] Matt. 16]. Those made in the form of a circle signify the Church extended throughout the circuit of the world; hence: “Their words [have gone] to the ends of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0019] Ps. 18]. Or they signify that from the circle of the world we come to the circle of the crown of eternity.

Walls mortared from stones are communities of religious persons, strong in faith and action, united by the bond of charity and fortifying the weak by their prayers. Of these it is said: “All your walls, Jerusalem, [shall be of] precious stones” [Note: [Col. 0019] Tobit 13]; and elsewhere: “Let your walls, Jerusalem, be built” [Note: [Col. 0019] Ps. 50]. Therefore the stones in the four walls are people in communities established in the four quarters of the world, or learned in four [disciplines], or made firm in the four virtues. All are polished and squared, precious [Col. 0020C] and gem-like: that is, pure, steadfast, adorned with virtues, and arranged by the hand of the supreme Craftsman. They shine the more brightly the more fervently they burn with charity. Some support others, as the apostles do; some both support and are supported, as teachers do; some are supported as weak persons. The more differently they excel, the more humbly they raise the building higher. The cornerstone joins them all in the unity of faith [Note: [Col. 0019] Isa. 28], and charity’s bitumen binds them together.

Mortar likewise consists of lime, water, and sand. Lime is the fervour of charity; water is the Holy Spirit. Sand is mixed with these when spiritual persons take thought for earthly matters, without which life in this world cannot be lived. They are tossed by the waves of the age, yet by blows [they acquire] steadfastness, form a wall, and set before it the outer defence of patience. Hence: “Our city of strength is Zion; a wall and a bulwark shall be placed in it” [Col. 0020D] [Note: [Col. 0019] Isa. 26], in suffering. Or, by the walls we understand the Holy Scriptures, by which we exclude the importunity of heretics.

Windows, which exclude the storm and admit light, are teachers who withstand the whirlwind of heresies and pour the light of the Church into the faithful. Hence: “Behold, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows” [Note: [Col. 0019] Song 2]. Veiled by the wall of our mortality, he enlightened us from on high through the windows—that is, the apostles—[Col. 0021A] he who enlightens every person coming into this world [Note: [Col. 0021] John 1].

The glass of the windows, through which the sun’s ray is cast upon us, is the mind of teachers, which contemplates heavenly things “through a mirror, in an enigma”; or it is that through which the true Sun enters us as through a mirror, in an enigma [Note: [Col. 0021] 1 Cor. 13]. Observe that windows are sometimes splayed—that is, wider within—which Solomon devised [Note: [Col. 0021] 3 Kings 6]; for the teacher who beholds the splendour of heavenly contemplation, or the tomb, at times enlarges the bosom of his heart and prepares himself by diligent exercise to grasp greater things.

Or, by windows which, when shut, exclude the storm and, when opened, admit it, understand the five bodily senses. When restrained, they are the gate of life; when wanton, they are the doors of death. Thus Jeremiah says [Col. 0021B] [Note: [Col. 0021] ch. 9]: “Death enters through our windows.” They must also be narrowed outwardly lest they take in vanities, while inwardly they stand open to spiritual gifts [Note: [Col. 0021] Ambrose, in the hymn *Jam lucis*, 2]. Or understand the windows as the Holy Scriptures, which forbid harmful things and enlighten those dwelling in churches. These too are broader within, because their mystical sense is more ample and excels the literal sense.

The door of the church is Christ. Hence: “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” [Note: [Col. 0021] John 10]; and “No one goes to the Father except through Christ” [Note: [Col. 0021] John 14]. For a door (*ostium*) is said to derive from *obstare*, “to stand against,” or *ostendere*, “to show,” or from *hostes*, “enemies” (for doors are made to repel enemies and admit guests). He is the one who resists the proud and gives grace to the humble [Note: [Col. 0021] James 4]; by resisting through justice [Col. 0021C] he will keep unbelievers from the kingdom, and through his boundless mercy, showing and opening the entrance [Note: [Col. 0021] Mic. 2], he will bring the faithful into the kingdom. Doors are spoken of in the plural because the ways of the Lord are many: “Show me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths” [Note: [Col. 0021] Ps. 24]. Folding doors (*valvae*) are so called from turning; outer doors (*fores*) from leading out from within; gates (*portae*) from carrying. These are the apostles, by whose preaching we are carried to faith, and through faith to blessedness. Of them it is said: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the dwellings of Jacob” [Note: [Col. 0021] Ps. 86].

By the screens (*cancelli*), which are window-like lattices, we understand the prophets and other obscure teachers of the Church Militant. In them, because of the two commandments of charity, the little columns are sometimes doubled, just as [Col. 0021D] the apostles were sent out two by two to preach [Note: [Col. 0021] Luke 10]; or because they are the backs of those seated, [they signify] the different dwelling-places in the Father’s house [Note: [Col. 0021] John 14].

Or the screen, which is a low part of a palace, signifies how great humility ought to be in the clergy. For, as is read in Paralipomenon [Note: [Col. 0021] 2 Chron. 6], Solomon made a bronze platform and placed it in the middle of the basilica; he stood upon it and, stretching out his hands, spoke to God’s people. Ezra, however, made a wooden platform for speaking, and, standing upon it, rose above all the people [Note: [Col. 0021] Ezra 8]. From these [Col. 0022A] our pulpits took their origin, and, as some say, they are called *pulpita* as though “public [places].” Although we more often use stone ones, none is devoid of mystery.

The pulpit, therefore, is the life of the perfect. The bishop standing above signifies that, by right of a more perfect life, he should surpass the common people in understanding the sacraments, which, like bronze, do not decay with any lapse of time; or [he should surpass them] in the doctrines of the apostles, who were so resonant like bronze that “their sound went out into all the earth” [Note: [Col. 0021] Ps. 18]. He should also surpass them by imitation of the Lord’s Passion: denying himself, bearing the cross [Note: [Col. 0021] Matt. 16], and glorying in the cross of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0021] Gal. 6], because the Lord reigned from the wood. He should surpass them also in steadfastness of faith and show himself Christ’s vicar, he who is the cornerstone, in the midst between the two [Note: [Col. 0021] Eph. 2], just as [Col. 0022B] this man too is placed between clergy and people.

The columns that support the house are bishops, who sustain the fabric of the Church by word and life. Because of the resonance of divine speech they are called silver, as in the Song of Songs [Note: [Col. 0021] ch. 3]: “He made its columns of silver.” Though they are many in number, they are nevertheless said to be seven, according to the saying: “Wisdom built herself a house and cut out seven columns” [Note: [Col. 0021] Prov. 9], because they ought to be filled with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. “James and John,” the Apostle says, “seemed to be columns” [Note: [Col. 0021] Gal. 2]. The bases of the columns are apostolic men, supporting the universal fabric of the Church. The heads of the columns are the minds of bishops; for as our limbs are directed from the head, so [Col. 0022C] our words and deeds are directed from the mind. The capitals are the words of Holy Scripture, to the meditation and observance of which we submit.

The beams that join the house are secular rulers or preachers, who strengthen the Church’s unity: the latter by word, the former by deed, exterminating heretics and restraining schisms.

The timbers are preachers, of whom it is said: “The timbers of our houses are cedar” [Note: [Col. 0021] Song 1]. For preachers ought to be incorruptible in virtues, and by the fragrance of their preaching and life to drive away serpents, that is, demons.

The roof-tiles, which repel rain from the house, are soldiers who protect the Church from pagans and enemies. They are set upon and rest upon the timbers, because they strive alongside [Col. 0022D] preachers and obey them; hence through them they are raised on high.

The spiral stairways, whose model is taken from Solomon’s Temple [Note: [Col. 0021] 3 Kings 6], are hidden paths interwoven in the wall. By them we understand the secrets of each person’s thoughts, which only those ascending to heavenly things recognize, and not even they fully, because God alone does so. For although the door stands open—because the deeds of works and the confession of sacraments are open—God alone is the searcher of hearts [Note: [Col. 0021] 1 Kings 16; Ps. 93; Heb. 4].

The galleries established by Solomon for walking around the Temple [Col. 0023A] [Note: [Col. 0023] 3 Kings 6], which in the Gospel are called pinnacles [Note: [Col. 0023] Matt. 4], are the ranks of the Church Militant. Thus three galleries are recorded as having existed in Solomon’s Temple [Note: [Col. 0023] 3 Kings 6]: upper, middle, and lower, because of the three orders—virgins, continent persons, and married persons.

*Luricae*, or *luriculae*, are the sides made around the galleries: walls, screens, or any kind of barriers, so that teachers seated in the galleries and preaching to the people, according to the saying, “Preach upon the roofs” [Note: [Col. 0023] Matt. 10], may not slip down to the depths, as happened, we read, to Ahaziah, king of Samaria, who fell through the screens [Note: [Col. 0023] 1 Kings 4]. By these are signified the divine protections which help us—labouring in this world and striving upward according to our capacity—not to fail. Heretics and schismatics, of whom [Col. 0023B] Ahaziah was a figure, may seem at times to climb the summit of good conduct; yet, because they lack the binding structure of unity, deprived of the protections and defences of divine guardianship, they fall back to the lowest vices.

Reclining seats are also made in a church. By them we understand contemplative men, in whom God rests without offence; for those who contemplate the brightness of eternal life are compared to gold. Hence: “He made a reclining seat of gold” [Note: [Col. 0023] Song 3].

Exedrae are masonry arches situated in a cemetery; they are so called because they adhere outside. In Solomon’s porticoes there were three kinds of seats, as Isidore says: the chairs of teachers; the *synedrae*, seats of hearers, so called from sitting together; and the *exedrae* of assessors, where [Col. 0023C] the judge discussed a more secret matter with his assessors. Yet *exedra* is sometimes used for a bedchamber; hence the dead are buried in *exedrae*, as though in bedchambers.

A cemetery is the dormitory of the dead. For those dying in Christ are not called dead but sleeping. The dead are buried around a church for three reasons: that they may be commended to the Lord by the prayers of faithful people coming to church; that, as mother Church gave them birth for Christ through baptism when they were dead to the world, and nourished them with milk, so, when dead in the flesh, she may cherish them in her bosom and commend them to God by prayers; and that, as they are buried in the estate of Jesus Christ, so they may be his co-heirs in the kingdom of God.

Perhaps for this reason Abraham refused to bury his wife in Ephron’s field unless he paid a price [Note: [Col. 0023] Gen. 23], lest, if she had been buried in the estate [Col. 0023D] of an unbeliever, the father of unbelief should claim that he had some right in her. Perhaps for the same reason we ought not to build churches except on land reckoned as the estate of Jesus Christ.

Observe also that perhaps exedrae with stone tombs took their origin from the double cave; nor is this without mystery, since the soul sleeping must rest from worldly cares in the repose of action and devote itself to contemplation, entering “into the clefts of the rock” [Note: [Col. 0023] Isa. 2] and hiding itself in the pit of the earth. Or perhaps [they derive] from the mausoleums and pyramids of the gentiles, because whatever is bestowed upon the human body is not a safeguard of salvation but [Col. 0024A] a consolation of humanity.

No one ought to be buried in churches unless he is a person endowed with high rank, in view of merit or sacrament; but more will be said about these matters below in the treatise on the dead.

Towers are constructed in prominent places: in some places one, in others two, in others four—two at the front and two at the rear. A cross or a cock is placed upon them, and bells are hung in them. One tower is the life of preachers, or the preacher himself; and its pinnacle is the life, or the mind, that stretches upward. This is “the tower of David,” as is read in the Song of Songs [Note: [Col. 0023] ch. 4], “built with bulwarks on Mount Lebanon, which looks out toward Damascus: a thousand shields hang from it, and all the armour of the mighty.”

The life of preachers must be steadfast and impregnable [Col. 0024B] for defending the structures of faith and repelling the enemies’ missiles, since it is built by David—that is, by the strong hand and the desirable king. It must remain in the height of virtues, so as to look out toward Damascus, against enemies coming from afar. Damascus is the metropolis of Syria, which, even to the present day, has assailed and even captured Jerusalem. By it we understand a multitude of human beings or of wicked spirits, against whose snares one must be on guard. This life is fortified with bulwarks if the grace of miracles is added, or if it relies upon the unanswerable judgments of Scripture, with the shield of reason; it is armed with the weapons of action. It fortifies itself against heretics and strikes them down; from it examples of resistance and life [Col. 0024C] depend for us.

The two towers are the two laws; the four are the teaching of the four evangelists: Matthew and John in front, because they associated bodily with God; Luke and Mark behind, as disciples of the apostles. The Lord gave the Law of Moses on Mount Sinai [Note: [Col. 0023] Exod. 31]; he also taught the Gospel on a mountain [Note: [Col. 0023] Matt. 5], and on Tabor revealed its reward [Note: [Col. 0023] Matt. 17], indicating that through observance of his commandments we shall come from Zion to Tabor, from contemplation to comprehension.

Or the two towers and the four towers are preachers trained in these laws and doctrines, of whom it is said: “May peace be in your strength, and abundance in your towers” [Note: [Col. 0023] Ps. 121]. A cross is placed above, because the tongue of a preacher speaks in vain unless faith in the Mediator is present, and because one ought to glory only in the cross of the Lord [Col. 0024D] [Note: [Col. 0023] Gal. 6]. The cupola upon which it is placed, by its roundness, signifies that the Catholic faith must be preached inviolate.

A cock is placed above because the diligent preacher, through the teaching of each Law, ought to awaken sleepers at midnight to confess the Lord [Note: [Col. 0023] Ps. 118]. The night is the present age; those sleeping are persons lying in sin. The cock distinguishes the hours when it preaches distinctly and awakens them to rise from sins. It announces the light when it proclaims the future glory that will be revealed in us [Note: [Col. 0023] Rom. 8]. But first it beats itself with its wings when it chastises its body [Note: [Col. 0023] 1 Cor. 9], lest, while preaching, it be rejected [Col. 0025A] by others. It turns against the wind when, for God’s house, it sets itself as a wall against the proud and resists the devil as he comes. The iron rod set there is rectitude of speech, which ought to be in the preacher’s mouth [Note: [Col. 0025] (William Durand, *Rationale*, bk. I, under no. 42, cites this passage), no. 1].

The cloister took its beginning from the watches and guards of the Levites around the tabernacle, or from the court of the priests, or from Solomon’s portico adjoining the Temple. For the Lord commands Moses not to count the Levites with the common multitude, but to appoint them over the tabernacle of testimony, to carry and guard it.

In the tribe of Levi is signified the priestly order, which is not placed on the same level as the common multitude, but presides so as to stand out as an example, taking care of the material and militant Church, in which the Lord’s covenants are stored. [Col. 0025B] Its office is to govern the people and to teach them by word and deed to live honourably; it bears them on the shoulders of patience by compassion, counsel, and endurance of the ways of the weak, and keeps watch with pastoral care lest an entrance lie open to the enemy.

Solomon, however, made the court of the priests; he also made the portico [Note: [Col. 0025] 3 Kings 6], which represented the ancient fathers of the Church Militant, Abel and Enoch. In this portico the apostles remained together, rising unanimously for prayer; and they had one heart and one soul [Note: [Col. 0025] Acts 4]. This pattern is followed by regular canons and by monks who undertake a stricter promise, when, dwelling unanimously in the cloister, they rise to God’s service and, abandoning secular things, live a common life in all matters.

Moreover, as [Col. 0025C] the Temple signifies the Church Triumphant, so the cloister signifies the heavenly paradise, where there will be one and the same heart in love and will toward God. For as water mixed with wine does not differ from wine, so the will of the saints differs in no respect from God’s will. There they will possess all things in common, because what anyone has less of in himself, he will rejoice to possess in another; for God will be all in all [Note: [Col. 0025] 1 Cor. 15].

Therefore the diversity of workshops and offices in the cloister is the diversity of dwelling-places, with diversity of rewards in the kingdom; or it signifies the paradise of Eden. For as there are fruitful trees there, one the tree of life and another of the knowledge of good and evil [Note: [Col. 0025] Gen. 2], whose eating brought eternal death, so in the cloister there are books of Holy Scripture, which are to some “an aroma [Col. 0025D] from life unto life,” but to others “from death unto death” [Note: [Col. 0025] 2 Cor. 2].

Morally, however, the cloister is the contemplation of the soul, into which it withdraws when separated from the crowd of carnal thoughts and meditating only on heavenly things. Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, having gone out from this cloister to see the women of that region, was violated by Shechem son of Hamor, and his soul was joined to her [Note: [Col. 0025] Gen. 34]. She is the human mind: when, neglecting its own pursuits, it is occupied with worldly and alien activities, it is corrupted by the devil and joined to him through iniquity.

In this cloister there are four sides: contempt [Col. 0026A] of self, contempt of the world, love of neighbour, and love of God. Each side has its own row of columns: for example, contempt of self has humiliation of mind, affliction of the flesh, humble speech, and the like. The base of all the columns is patience. In this cloister, the diversity of workshops is the diversity of virtues; the hospital is compassion of mind.

Observe that a hospital receives differing names according to the different persons [it receives]: it is called a *xenodochium*, *nosocomium*, *orphanotrophium*, *ptochotrophium*, or *gerontotrophium* [printed *betrytrophium*, perhaps corrupt]. For holy fathers and religious emperors established certain places where pilgrims, orphans, old people, the sick, the weak, and the wounded might be received. Since we have compassion on them, the hospital signifies compassion of mind. The chapter-house is [Col. 0026B] the secret place of the heart; the refectory, the delight of holy meditation; the cellar, Holy Scripture; the dormitory, a pure conscience; the oratory, an unstained life; the garden of trees and herbs, an abundance of virtues; the well of living waters, the irrigation of dwellings, which here mitigates thirst and in the future wholly extinguishes it.

## Chapter V. On the Names of a Church

“My house shall be called a house of prayer” [Note: [Col. 0025] Matt. 21]. A building constructed from so many parts is distinguished by many authoritative names. It is called a house of prayer, or an oratory, because the people of the faithful come there to pray. As certain places [Col. 0026C] are assigned to necessary uses, such as a dormitory, so certain places are properly designated for prayer, such as a church and the oratories established by monks on their granges.

It is also called the house of God because God dwells in it. Thus Jacob says: “This is the house of God and the gate of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0025] Gen. 28]. Observe that the house of God is the Church Militant, the faithful soul, and the heavenly homeland. The house of the mind is conscience; the house of a human being is his household; the house of the devil is human faithlessness. Solomon says of God’s house: “Wisdom built herself a house” [Note: [Col. 0025] Prov. 9]; and David: “I rejoiced in the things said to me: ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord’” [Note: [Col. 0025] Ps. 121]. Of the house of the mind it is said: “Set your house in order” [Note: [Col. 0025] Isa. 38]; and: “Three things drive a man from his house: smoke, dripping, and a bad [Col. 0026D] wife” [Note: [Col. 0025] Prov. 19, 27]—that is, the sin of ignorance, of suggestion, and of one’s own concupiscence. Of a man’s house it is said that the Lord built houses for the midwives [Note: [Col. 0025] Exod. 1]. Of the devil’s house, the devil himself says: “I shall return to my house, from which I came out” [Note: [Col. 0025] Luke 11].

It is also called, by excellence, a house (*domus*) from *domate*, “roof,” because those dwelling in one house are under one roof. It is called a church (*ecclesia*), that is, a convocation, because it contains the true church—that is, the people convoked—by the figure called by grammarians metonymy, when the container [Col. 0027A] is put for the contained.

The synagogue was called a gathering because there the people were gathered under the rod of the Law like a flock of irrational cattle. But the church is called a convocation because it is summoned by love of the Holy Spirit into one faith, to God’s judgments, and to Christ’s banquet. As formerly the people assembled to hear judgments and again assembled to eat the Passover—whence the Apostle says: “When we assemble in one place, it is now no longer to eat the Lord’s supper” [Note: [Col. 0027] 1 Cor. 11]—so today it is called together to hear the punishments and rewards of the age to come and to receive the Lord’s body.

It is also called a basilica, as is found in Paralipomenon [Note: [Col. 0027] 2 Chron. 4, 6], that is, “royal,” because there service is rendered to the King of kings. For *basileus* is interpreted “king,” as though [from] *basis*, *kasa*, that is, “a column and support of the people”; whence the basilisk [Col. 0027B] is called king of serpents. It is also called *Kyriaca*, that is, “the Lord’s [house],” because there service is rendered to the Lord of lords. For *kyrios* means “Lord.” Hence *Kyrie eleison*: “Lord, have mercy.”

It is also called a hall (*aula*) because there the banquet of the eternal King is celebrated. Hence: “This place is terrible. This is the house of God and the gate of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0027] Gen. 28], and it shall be called the hall of God. It is called a monastery, that is, a solitary place or dwelling of solitaries; for *monos* means “alone” or “one,” whence monks are single and sad. It is called a cenobium, from *coenon*, “common,” because it is a common dwelling; hence those dwelling in it are called cenobites.

It is also called the sanctuary (*sanctum*), that is, “your firm place,” because it is founded upon the firm rock [Col. 0027C] [Note: [Col. 0027] Matt. 7; Luke 6], and because there was a firm structure there for God’s service. Hence: “The high priest entered the Holy Place once a year” [Note: [Col. 0027] Exod. 30; Lev. 16; Heb. 9]. It is also called the place of martyrs, where the bodies of martyrs lie, where they suffered, or where those gather who suffer for Christ’s name; regular canons today take their place.

The larger churches are called temples, that is, broad roofs, because the people are gathered there beneath the breadth of a single roof. Smaller chapels are named from goat skins, because noblemen had churches made from goat skins while travelling; or *capenum* is a house to which the poor flock for alms. Hence a chapel is the place where the poor in spirit are fed with the food of the daily word, and its custodians and ministers are called chaplains. [Col. 0027D] Therefore perhaps they are bound to use—not varied skins but goat skins—and not to be served but to serve [Note: [Col. 0027] Matt. 20]. Or perhaps chaplains are called from the cloak (*cappa*) of St Martin, because it was carried before the kings of the Franks in wars and battles.

Therefore, brothers, when we come together in church, let us by no means indulge bodily uses there, but devote ourselves to prayer, lest we make it a den of thieves [Note: [Col. 0027] Matt. 21]. It ought to be filled with the smoke of spices and the fragrances of ointments, by which health is bestowed here and healing obtained in the future.

## Chapter VI. On the Consecration of a Church

[Col. 0028A]

“Solomon kept a solemn feast, and all Israel with him before the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0027] 3 Kings 8]. Consecrating churches and altars is not a recent custom but an anciently authorized one. Jacob set up a stone as a pillar, pouring oil upon it [Note: [Col. 0027] Gen. 28]. Solomon likewise built the Temple and dedicated it to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0027] 3 Kings 6, 8]. From this the fathers of the New Testament took, as we said above, the example both of building churches and of consecrating those built.

This consecration accomplishes two things: it appropriates the material church itself to God, and indicates the espousal both of the Church and of the faithful soul. A house not yet consecrated is like a girl promised to a man, [Col. 0028B] yet neither endowed nor united to him in the intercourse of one flesh. But through consecration it receives a dowry and becomes the proper bride of Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0027] Eph. 5], whom it is sacrilege thereafter to violate by adultery; it ceases to be a brothel of demons.

If you seek an example, many are available; but that temple which was formerly called the Pantheon will suffice as an instance: it passed into the palace of the eternal King, in which he dwells by grace. For in the Temple the glory of the Lord visibly descended [Note: [Col. 0027] 3 Kings 8]. The unconsecrated house is gentile society, or a soul ignorant of divine knowledge. The consecration of a house is the union of Christ with the Church, or with the soul; and let us show this through each of the signs of dedication.

[Col. 0028C] First, the bishop performs a litany before the relics, in the place where they had been deposited on the preceding night, imploring God’s mercy and the saints’ help to perform worthily so arduous a sacrament of the Church. Then, before the doors of the church, he performs an exorcism of salt and water, saying, “O God, attend to my help” [Note: [Col. 0027] Ps. 69], and so forth, without *Alleluia*. We shall speak of these matters below.

This water seasoned with the wisdom of salt signifies baptism, which is seasoned with the wisdom of faith when the candidate for baptism is instructed concerning faith [Note: [Col. 0027] Matt. 3]. The Lord consecrated its font in Judaea. With this water alone the bishop sprinkles the church outside, going around it, and prays to God for its blessing. This threefold sprinkling and threefold prayer are patterned upon the three-day burial. Immersion in the font is the invocation of the Holy Trinity [Col. 0028D] in baptism, which the Lord commanded the apostles to perform among the nations throughout the circuit of the world, saying [Note: [Col. 0027] Matt. 28]: “Go, baptize them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”

Meanwhile twelve candles illuminate the church all around, because the twelve apostles enlightened the nations with the light of doctrine. The three responsories sung meanwhile are the joy of the three orders receiving faith, namely Noah, Daniel, and Job. Since at this invocation the grace of faith, hope, and charity is poured forth, sprinkling is therefore done at the foot, the middle, and the upper part of the wall [Col. 0029A]. While sprinkling, some bishops sprinkle the court also; others, before the church has been sprinkled, sprinkle the court with water previously blessed, as is found in the canons.

The canonical boundary of courts is thirty or forty paces, except for chapels contained within the circuit of castles. The court is Christ, through whom entrance into the heavenly Jerusalem lies open; he is sanctified in us [Note: [Col. 0029] Eph. 2], according to the saying: “Hallowed be your name” [Note: [Col. 0029] Matt. 6]. Thirty and forty signify the ministry of faith and repentance, which are necessary to the Church Militant.

This sprinkling is performed with an aspergillum made of hyssop, according to the saying: “You shall sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed” [Note: [Col. 0029] Ps. 50]. Hyssop is a low-growing herb, growing on a rock and useful for healing bodies; therefore it signifies humility, proceeding from the rock, Christ [Note: [Col. 0029] 1 Cor. 10], who said: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” [Note: [Col. 0029] Matt. 11]. For the water of baptism benefits none of the baptized unless it proceeds from the root of humility. But if humility is present, it drives away the swelling of pride, washes and cleanses a person so thoroughly that it makes him incomparably whiter than snow—or like snow [Note: [Col. 0029] Ps. 50]—according to Isaiah’s saying: “They shall be made white as snow” [Note: [Col. 0029] Isa. 1], so that a person may become the Lord’s garment. For whoever is baptized into Christ puts on Christ [Note: [Col. 0029] Gal. 3]: a snowy garment, [Col. 0029C] that is, without spot or wrinkle [Note: [Col. 0029] Eph. 5], as was represented in the Lord’s Transfiguration [Note: [Col. 0029] Matt. 17].

When the bishop comes before the church door, he strikes the lintel three times with his staff, saying: “Lift up your gates, O princes” [Note: [Col. 0029] Ps. 23]. This threefold striking is Christ’s threefold power in heaven, on earth, and in hell [Note: [Col. 0029] Phil. 2]. Thus he struck three times when he granted his Church the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth, and added that the gates of hell would not prevail against it [Note: [Col. 0029] Matt. 16]. Therefore he commands the gates of death to be lifted away and the eternal gates to be raised. The gates of death are vices; the gates of life are virtues and the sacraments of the Church.

Or he strikes three times when he rebuked the ungodly with harsh words, according to Isaiah: “He shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips [Col. 0029D] he shall slay the ungodly” [Note: [Col. 0029] Isa. 11]; and this threefoldly because he taught faith in the Trinity. By this striking the devil is driven out, signified by the fleeing deacon. Fittingly, one who belongs to this order performs the role of the other, because *deacon* means “minister”; while they are ministering spirits, according to the saying, “Thousands of thousands ministered to him” [Note: [Col. 0029] Dan. 7], and the Apostle: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for service?” [Note: [Col. 0029] Heb. 1].

If he is an archdeacon, he represents Lucifer, of whom Job says: “He is the beginning [Col. 0030A] of the ways of God” [Note: [Col. 0029] Job 40]. Hence he is clothed in precious garments, because “every precious stone was his covering” [Note: [Col. 0029] Ezek. 28]. This strong man, armed, guarded his court [Note: [Col. 0029] Luke 11] while he possessed the human world; but one stronger than he came upon him, expelled him, and distributed the spoils, when Christ conquered him through his Passion and freed the Church and the soul [Note: [Col. 0029] Heb. 2].

Nor is it said to him, “Open,” because he opens the hearts of the faithful to faith, but because the departure of vice brings about the entrance of virtues; and because, when the devil departs, the Church immediately opens to Christ the door of faith. Or the question of the one shut within is ignorance of sin; the opening of the door is the exclusion of transgression.

When the bishop enters, let him say three times, “Peace to this house” [Note: [Col. 0029] Luke 10], because Christ, entering the world, brought peace to people of good will [Note: [Col. 0029] Luke 2], reconciling them to the holy Trinity [Col. 0030B]. He enters with two or three others, so that “by the mouth of two or three witnesses the word” of consecration may stand [Note: [Col. 0029] 2 Cor. 13; Matt. 18]; or because the Lord, transfiguring himself for the Church, prayed in the presence of few [Note: [Col. 0029] Matt. 17]. Then the pontiff prostrates himself in prayer for the consecration of the church, because Christ humbled himself and prayed to the Father for the Church’s sanctification, saying: “Father, sanctify those whom thou hast given me” [Note: [Col. 0029] John 17]. The clergy, praying and chanting the litanies, signify the Apostles, who interceded with God for the sanctification of the Church and of souls. Rising, the pontiff does not greet the people with *The Lord be with you*, but invites them to prayer with *Let us bend the knee*, because unbelievers are not to be greeted but summoned to repentance [Col. 0030C], and those not yet sanctified are not to be applauded but prayed for.

After this he inscribes two alphabets on the pavement, by which we understand the knowledge of the two Testaments, or the understanding of sacred Scripture—namely, letter and spirit. The letters indeed are few; nevertheless, the whole fullness of knowledge is contained in them. This knowledge, therefore, must be written on the pavement of our breast, in the hearts of earthly people, so that through it we may be able to recognize the Lord and be raised toward heavenly things. Thus it is written from the left corner of the east to the right corner of the west. The left corner of the east is Judaea, in which Christ rises according to the flesh, yet is reckoned among those on the left because of its unbelief. The right corner of the west is the Gentile world [Col. 0030D], in which unbelief fell, and for which Christ, the sun of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0029] Mal. 4], sets and will prevail at the right hand. Therefore it is written from the left to the right corner in memory of that transfer concerning which it is said: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” [Note: [Col. 0029] Matt. 21].

The alphabet is also written from the right corner of the east to the left of the west. The right corner of the east is the primitive Church, in which the light of faith arose [Note: [Col. 0029] Ps. 96]; the left of the west is the remnant of Israel, who still incline to the left and will continue so to incline until the world’s setting [Col. 0031A]. Thus it is written from the right toward the left because, after the fullness of the Gentiles [Note: [Col. 0031] Rom. 11], Israel will be converted to the faith. The first alphabet is written in Greek and the second in Latin: the former is earlier and excels in wisdom; the latter follows and excels in power. Hebrew is not written, because it is silent in the Church. Both, however, are written with a staff, because all these things are accomplished through preachers.

They are written so as to meet in the middle of the pavement in the form of a cross: first, because the two Testaments teach faith in the Passion; and second, because the two peoples are saved in the mystery of the cross. Yet before this, if any bodies of unbelievers lie beneath the pavement, they must be removed, because they are neither holy nor shall be sanctified; Christ has not betrothed their souls with the ring of faith [Col. 0031B], nor will they pass, together with the bodies of the faithful, into the glorious union of the general body. They must either be removed or buried so much deeper in the earth that no trace of their tombs appears. For if we desire that the pavement of our breast be sprinkled with the hyssop of humility, cleansed with sacramental water, filled with spiritual knowledge, and saved by faith in the cross, it must be emptied of rubbish and every mortal contagion of sin, so that, made whiter than snow [Note: [Col. 0031] Ps. 50], we may put on Christ [Note: [Col. 0031] Rom. 13] and be presented to him as a virgin bride, chaste, without wrinkle or stain [Note: [Col. 0031] Eph. 5].

## CHAPTER VII. AGAIN, ON THE SAME SUBJECT

“Christ, acting as pontiff, entered the holy places through his own blood” [Col. 0031C; Note: [Col. 0031] Heb. 9]. Up to this point there has been, as it were, a prologue to the dedication; from here the dedication of the church begins. Therefore, in what follows, Christ’s Passion and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit are signified.

Accordingly, when the pontiff approaches the altar to bless the water, he says, “O God, make haste to help me” [Note: [Col. 0031] Ps. 69], and adds, “Glory be to the Father,” without *Alleluia*. This order must be observed in the blessing of this water, of the preceding water, and of that which Pope Alexander ordained to be blessed on Sundays: thus divine help is implored. And because this blessing is performed to render glory to the Trinity, the *Glory be* is also added. But because we are still being purified and have not yet obtained the effect of blessing, placed amid sighs, we refrain from *Alleluia*—that is, the praise owed to God for benefits received [Col. 0031D]. Hence it will be sung after the church’s consecration, because, the devil’s illusion having been expelled, God will be praised in it. So Christ, approaching the altar of the cross, invoked his Father’s aid and underwent death in order to make known the glory of the Trinity [Note: [Col. 0031] Matt. 27; Luke 23], although he sang *Alleluia* only after the Resurrection, through the manifest accomplishment of his work.

Then salt, ashes, and water are blessed and mixed together after the sign of the cross has been made; finally wine is added. Salt is God’s wisdom. Hence Elisha cast salt into the water, so that the waters were healed [Note: [Col. 0031] 2 Kings 2]; the Father sent his Son into this world [Col. 0032A] so that the world might be saved through him [Note: [Col. 0031] John 3]. Ashes are Christ’s human nature: this is the red heifer that was burned [Note: [Col. 0031] Num. 19]—that is, Christ’s flesh, reddened with blood and consumed by the fire of the Passion, by which we have been redeemed. Water signifies the people. Hence: “Many waters are many peoples” [Note: [Col. 0031] Rev. 17]. Therefore salt and ashes are mixed when “the Word became flesh” [Note: [Col. 0031] John 1]; they are mixed with the water through the sign of the cross when the people are saved in Christ’s Passion.

The addition of wine signifies either that the Godhead accomplishes this redemption, or that the sorrow of the Passion has been changed into the joy of the Resurrection; or it signifies that through this water we receive the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0031] John 16], of whom it is said: “He who believes in me, from his belly shall flow rivers of living water” [Note: [Col. 0031] John 7]. Salt, ashes, and wine are mixed [Col. 0032B], because those whom the Spirit washes are seasoned with wisdom, sprinkled with the dust of repentance, and made drunk with spiritual understanding. Thus the Church is washed without and within, so that whoever is to be saved may be born again of water and Spirit [Note: [Col. 0031] John 3]. Or: salt is the doctrine of faith; ashes, the remembrance of Christ’s Passion; wine mixed with water, divinity joined to humanity. Thus we are sanctified by the doctrine of faith and the remembrance of Christ’s Passion, so that we may be joined to our head, God and man.

Afterwards, with his thumb the pontiff makes crosses from this water on the altar, in the middle and at its four corners, and sprinkles the altar all around seven or three times. The altar here denotes the primitive Church, in whose midst he made the cross when [Col. 0032C] he underwent the Passion “in the midst of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0031] Ps. 73], namely, Jerusalem. He also signified the four corners when he saved the four regions of the world by the cross. He sprinkled the altar seven times when he commanded the Church in Jerusalem to be baptized, that it might receive the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0031] Acts 1]. Or it is sprinkled three times when it is baptized in the name of the holy Trinity, or when the Church is cleansed from sins of thought, speech, and deed. Hence, while the sprinkling is performed, *Have mercy on me, O God* is sung [Note: [Col. 0031] Ps. 50].

Then he sprinkles the church three times around its circuit from east to west, and once through its middle in the form of a cross, because Christ commanded all Judaea, or all nations, to be baptized in the name of the Trinity [Note: [Col. 0031] Matt. 28], and gave that baptism efficacy through the mystery of the Passion. That the sprinkling is done around the circuit signifies that the Lord [Col. 0032D], having care for his own, sends his angel “round about those who fear him” [Note: [Col. 0031] Ps. 33]. That it proceeds from east to west indicates that it began with the Jews [Note: [Col. 0031] Matt. 1 and Heb. 7], from whom the Lord arose and to whom our faith refers.

While these things are done, the psalms are sung: “I rejoiced when they said unto me” [Note: [Col. 0031] Ps. 121], etc.; “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered” [Note: [Col. 0031] Ps. 67], etc.; and “He who dwells in help” [Note: [Col. 0031] Ps. 90], etc. For when the Apostles preached the mystery of the Resurrection and the sacrament of baptism, the fury of enemies was dispersed and the house of the Lord firmly built—a house which we shall enter [Note: [Col. 0031] Matt. 7] and in whose aid [Col. 0033A] we now dwell [Note: [Col. 0033] Ps. 5], for which Christ prays, and, standing in the midst as mediator, daily intercedes with God the Father for us [Note: [Col. 0033] John 17].

Then he pours water at the base of the altar, indicating that from Jerusalem the very fountain of baptism sprang forth; or entrusting to God that which in so great a sacrament exceeds human powers. That the altar is afterwards wiped with a linen cloth signifies that, after the pattern of Christ’s Passion, the tribulation of the primitive Church is alleviated. For by linen, which grows from the earth and with labor is brought to whiteness, we understand Christ, who was born of a virgin [Note: [Col. 0033] Luke 1] and through the labor of the Passion reached the joy of the Resurrection.

## CHAPTER VIII. AGAIN, ON THE SAME SUBJECT

[Col. 0033B] “Let us therefore hasten to enter into that rest” [Note: [Col. 0033] Heb. 4], as participants in Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0033] Heb. 3]. When these things have been completed, the pontiff goes to the relics and, with procession, prayer, reverence, and great devotion, carries them to the place prepared for them by the deacon. So Christ, after preparing a place for us, receives the righteous—who in this present night keep themselves from evils with watchful mind—and leads them into the house of his Father [Note: [Col. 0033] John 14; Matt. 26]. Hence is sung: “Walk, saints of God; enter into the city of the Lord,” that is, the heavenly Jerusalem. For this is the new Church, in which the people shall worship the Lord forever.

This chant signifies there the joy of the angels receiving souls with rejoicing, accompanying them until they are received, according to their merits, into their due [Col. 0033C] dwelling places. Before the pontiff enters the church, he goes around it with the relics, so that they may be protectors of that church. The responsory concerning tithes is sung again; consequently the pontiff afterwards admonishes the people concerning tithes and offerings, the endowment, and lights.

Afterwards, he makes with chrism the sign of the cross on the lintel, by which it is indicated that we ought not be ashamed to bear on our foreheads the seal of the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. This is taken from the blood of the Paschal lamb, with which the doorposts were anointed by the Lord’s command [Note: [Col. 0033] Exod. 12]. The people accompany the entering pontiff, so that they may be governed by the protection of Christ and the saints; and therefore he intercedes as mediator for the faithful.

When he comes to the tomb to deposit the relics, let him stretch a veil [Col. 0033D] between the altar and the people, because the places or chambers of souls are hidden from mortal sight. Of them it is sung: “The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice in their chambers” [Note: [Col. 0033] Ps. 149]. Then he places chrism in the *confession*—that is, the reliquary chamber—at the four corners in the form of a cross, saying: “Let this tomb be sanctified in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”; that is, may these dwelling places be established for us forever through faith in Christ’s Passion, which you preached through the four quarters of the world. Then he places three portions of incense, as if to say: “And may that which you obtained for us from [Col. 0034A] the holy Trinity through your prayers be established anew.” Afterwards the relics are sealed in the tomb, and souls are placed in heaven. Hence, fittingly, while these things are done, the clergy sing, “In the heavenly kingdoms,” etc. The slab, secured with chrism and laid over it, is the protection of Jesus Christ. Hence it is sung: “We have received our dwelling beneath the altar of God.” This is the eternal rest which is strengthened for us by lime, that is, by the cement of charity.

## CHAPTER IX. AGAIN, ON THE SAME SUBJECT

“The Lord wrought salvation in the midst of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0033] Ps. 73]. For the pontiff who makes the cross with holy oil upon the altar, in the middle of the altar and at its four corners, is Christ, who poured out the Holy Spirit upon the primitive Church [Col. 0034B] through faith in the Passion, and through it extended the Church to the four quarters of the world. Three times is sung: “Jacob set up a stone as a pillar” [Note: [Col. 0033] Gen. 28].
