For that Church was a standard for the others, “because from Zion went forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0033] Isa. 2].

The altar is anointed three times—twice with holy oil and the third time with chrism—because the Church is distinguished by faith, hope, and charity, which is greater than the rest [Note: [Col. 0033] 1 Cor. 13]. While chrism is poured on it, this is sung: “Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a full field” [Note: [Col. 0033] Gen. 27]. This field is the Church, which blossoms with flowers, shines with virtues, and is fragrant with deeds; there are the roses of martyrs, the lilies of virgins, the violets of confessors; there are the green growth of beginners, the flower of those progressing, and the fruit of those attaining [Note: [Col. 0033] Matt. 13].

Then he makes [Col. 0034C] twelve crosses with chrism on the walls of the church, beginning from the right and proceeding to the left. This anointing is faith in the Passion, which through the Apostles passed from the Jews to the Gentiles; or rather, this anointing is the grace of the Holy Spirit, whose fullness, existing in Christ the head, descended upon the beard—the beard of Aaron [Note: [Col. 0033] Ps. 132]—that is, upon the Apostles, who preached the mystery of the cross through the four walls of the church, that is, through the four quarters of the world, and also added faith in the Trinity. Hence three crosses are fittingly impressed on each wall.

The frequent use of incense is the continual intercession before God the Father, on our behalf, of Christ priest and pontiff. To make the cross with incense is to show the Passion to the Father and intercede for us. To burn abundant incense in the middle of the altar and at its corners is to multiply prayers for the Jerusalem Church and the universal Church.

Afterwards the bishop anoints the face of the stone in the form of a cross, saying: “Confirm this, O God” [Col. 0034D; Note: [Col. 0033] Ps. 67], because Christ, or the Church itself, entreats the Father to confirm the redemption which he has wrought. Hence it is that the baptized are confirmed. This redemption began from the holy temple which is in Jerusalem, because the salvation of human nature began in the midst of the earth [Note: [Col. 0033] Ps. 73]; or it began from the temple, that is, Christ, in whom dwells [Col. 0035A] the fullness of divinity [Note: [Col. 0035] Col. 2]. And because the Trinity accomplishes this redemption, the *Glory be to the Father* is added, so that praise may be sung to the Trinity.

After this the vessels, vestments, and linens to be assigned to worship are blessed. For implements to be blessed is for our works to be referred to God; what implements are necessary we shall say below. The altar is then clothed. For the altar to be clothed is for the soul to be joined to an immortal and incorruptible body. Of this garment Christ himself says concerning himself: “Thou hast torn my sackcloth from me; thou hast clothed me with gladness” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 29]. Or the final blessing of the altar signifies that final blessing in which it is said: “Come, ye blessed of my Father” [Note: [Col. 0035] Matt. 25].

After this the church is adorned in many ways, as will be said below, and lights are kindled. Then [Col. 0035B] the works of the righteous will shine; then “the righteous shall shine and run to and fro like sparks among reeds” [Note: [Col. 0035] Wis. 3]. Then Mass is sung, for churches ought not to be consecrated without Mass. Then will be revealed the sacrament that was hidden even from the angels from the beginning [Note: [Col. 0035] Eph. 3]. The Introit is: “This place is terrible” [Note: [Col. 0035] Gen. 28]. For what is more terrible than that at which angels will fear and the righteous person will scarcely be saved [Note: [Col. 0035] 1 Pet. 4]?

Then the pontiff comes solemnly vested, and the chant is sung in joy. For then the Lord will be seen by us face to face in his glory [Note: [Col. 0035] 1 Cor. 13]. Observe that in sprinkling the basilica he uses only linen and lesser vestments; but when he approaches the mystery of the altar, he is adorned with precious pontifical vestments [Col. 0035C], recalling that the Levitical high priest expiated the sanctuary in linen garments and, after washing, offered a ram as a burnt offering in pontifical vestments. And because in those same linen garments he sent forth the goat after the expiation [Note: [Col. 0035] Lev. 16], certain persons also use simple linen vestments at the consecration of fonts and the immersion of catechumens, where their sins are transferred.

Or, by the altar we understand Christ, as by the Church we understand the bride. For he is the stone which Jacob set up as a pillar [Note: [Col. 0035] Gen. 28], because he stood as a sign to the peoples [Note: [Col. 0035] Isa. 11], the corner-stone [Note: [Col. 0035] Acts 4], “who made both one” [Note: [Col. 0035] Eph. 2]. He is the stone growing into a mountain [Note: [Col. 0035] Dan. 2], the rich mountain [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 67], anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 44]. Therefore altars are not anointed unless they are of stone.

He is also prefigured by the way-stone [Col. 0035D], because “he rejoiced as a giant to run his course” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 18], and, “He shall drink of the brook in the way” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 109]. Likewise, for similar reasons, the way-stone is sprinkled with salt, ashes, water, and wine, and, after fragrances have been applied, is confirmed with chrism.

Beside this altar—I mean the Christian altar—is a basin in which hands are washed. This is Christ’s mercy, by which people are cleansed from the filth of sins in baptism or repentance. The altar is approached by steps; these are, as we said before, the martyrs, or the virtues through which one comes to [Col. 0036A] the Lord. In these are relics, that is, the treasures of God’s wisdom and knowledge [Note: [Col. 0035] Col. 2]. For this is the ark of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0035] Deut. 10], in which were manna and the tablets of the covenant. Upon these we burn incense and oil when we plainly ascribe priesthood and kingship to him.

Upon the Christian altar are placed caskets: these are the Apostles and martyrs. Likewise vestments and altar-cloths signify confessors and virgins, or all the saints, concerning whom it is said: “With these thou shalt clothe thyself as with a garment” [Note: [Col. 0035] Isa. 49]. The Gospel-book is fittingly placed upon it, because the Gospel was issued by him and bears testimony to him. The cross is also raised over these for three reasons: that the sign of the king may be venerated in the royal house or city; that Christ’s Passion may be represented; and that the people may imitate Christ crucified by crucifying themselves [Col. 0036B] with their vices and desires [Note: [Col. 0035] Gal. 5]. Banners too are raised above altars so that Christ’s triumph may be continually remembered in the Church, through which we too may hope to triumph over the enemy.

## CHAPTER X. AGAIN, ON THE SAME SUBJECT, IN ITS MORAL SENSE

“The temple of God is holy, which temple ye are” [Note: [Col. 0035] 1 Cor. 3]. All these things are referred to the human being. For the church is washed outside; its door is struck by the bishop; the bishop enters; the alphabet is written on the ground; the church is illuminated; the altar is washed with salt, ashes, water, and wine; the church is sprinkled within; the Lord’s body and relics are deposited in the altar; incense and chrism are placed there; the altar is anointed with oil [Col. 0036C], repeatedly incensed, adorned with vestments, and upon it the sacrifice of praise is offered.

The human being is indeed the Church, as Paul says in the epistle of the day: “You are God’s building” [Note: [Col. 0035] ibid.]. Therefore, once baptized, the human being is pierced with compunction for three sins—namely, thought, speech, and action—and, when the door of faith is opened, Christ enters. Hence in the Gospel of the day: “Zacchaeus, I must stay in thy house today” [Note: [Col. 0035] Luke 19]. The Scripture of both Testaments is impressed upon the mind, and the mind is illuminated by the teaching of the twelve Apostles. The heart, which is in our body as the altar is in the temple, is seasoned with the salt of knowledge, sprinkled with the dust of repentance, washed by the saving water of the Holy Spirit, and made drunk with the wine of wisdom. Thus one who has been washed in the flesh is also washed in mind [Col. 0036D], so that he may say: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 83]. Therefore the words of the offertory are not irrationally repeated, namely, “Solomon did,” etc.

To place the Lord’s body and relics in the altar is to retain in memory the Lord’s commandments and the examples of the saints, so that it may be said: “I have hidden thy sayings in my heart, that I might not sin against thee” [Note: [Col. 0035] Ps. 118]. Incense and chrism are also placed in the altar when we devote ourselves to prayers, good repute, and good works. We anoint our altar with oil [Col. 0037A] when we do not forget mercy. The supreme priest, according to the order of Melchizedek [Note: [Col. 0037] Ps. 109], approaches the altar of our heart and anoints it when he says: “Be merciful, as your Father also is merciful” [Note: [Col. 0037] Luke 6]. That supreme pontiff abounded in this oil beyond his fellows [Note: [Col. 0037] Ps. 44] when he said: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” [Note: [Col. 0037] Luke 23].

Not only the heart but all the limbs ought to be anointed with this oil. For the hand, if it is not anointed and not opened to the needy, withers. Let us fumigate this our altar with prayers and adorn it with virtues, so that upon it we may be able to offer ourselves as a living sacrifice pleasing to God [Note: [Col. 0037] Rom. 12], so that we may be both the sacrifice of the temple and the temple of God.

## CHAPTER XI. ON THE RECONCILIATION OF A CHURCH

[Col. 0037B]

“Remove thy shoe from thy feet, for the place where thou standest is holy” [Note: [Col. 0037] Exod. 3; Josh. 5]. Since a church has been endowed in consecration to so great a Bridegroom with such solemnity, and its vessels assigned to divine worship, it is plainly a grave sin to violate it by dishonorable uses. Hence, when Belshazzar abused the vessels of the Lord, threatening writing appeared in the royal hall: *Mane, Thecel, Phares*—that is, “numbered, weighed, and divided” [Note: [Col. 0037] Dan. 5].

A church is violated by burning, homicide, adultery, the removal of its seal, or the moving of its principal altar. If it has been violated and is not reconciled—or, where appropriate, consecrated anew—it will be unclean and open to dogs. The form of reconciliation is this: first the pontiff prays before the doors [Col. 0037C] of the church; afterwards he enters the church with litanies and prays again; then he washes the church with blessed water mixed with salt, ashes, and wine, purifies the contaminated places, and thus performs the reconciliation with chants and prayers appointed for this purpose.

So too the human being, consecrated as God’s temple in baptism, is contaminated by the incitement of vices and by mortal sin [Note: [Col. 0037] 1 Cor. 3]. If through heresy he has lost the seal of faith, he too is violated. If he has also suffered diminution of the head—by which I mean the mind or the bishop—the whole body and people are weakened. Therefore it is necessary that one who can no longer be helped by baptism be renewed by the fountain of tears, that is, through repentance, and assisted by prayers. Otherwise God’s temple will return to being a brothel [Col. 0037D] of demons; the lodging of the Trinity, a prostitute’s den, where demons dance and sirens nest. But through prayers it returns to being God’s temple and the dwelling of the Holy Spirit; and one who has suffered shipwreck on the sea returns to the harbor of salvation.

Therefore a church must be guarded with great care, for it enjoys a threefold privilege: in persons, in things, and in place. Nothing concerning persons and things belongs to the present discussion. But the place itself must be guarded with such reverence that no one presumes there to celebrate love-feasts, spread beds, lead dances, commit assaults or thefts, drag a fugitive from it, or perpetrate any other desires [Col. 0038A] of the flesh. Nor should anyone presume, within the boundaries of churches, which extend thirty or forty paces, to break into houses.

For this is the holy—that is, secure—place concerning which the Lord said to Moses [Note: [Col. 0037] Exod. 3], and the angel to Joshua: “Remove thy shoe from thy feet, for the place where thou standest is holy” [Note: [Col. 0037] Josh. 5]. A shoe is made from the skins of dead animals. Therefore, to remove the shoe from one’s feet is to remove from one’s actions the bonds of mortal sins, which we ought to remove when entering God’s sanctuary, so that we may meditate upon the life of the angels, where there is rest without sleep, peace without war, repose without toil, and satiety without rest.

Whenever, therefore, we enter this place—especially when the heavenly mystery is celebrated, where the assembly [Col. 0038B] of angels is believed to be present—let us enter reverently before their sight, incline our faces to the ground, contemplate their joys, and remember that we are ashes [Note: [Col. 0037] Gen. 18; Job 30].

In church one should also abstain from superfluous words, according to the saying of Chrysostom: “When you are about to enter a royal court, you compose yourself in dress and bearing; entering here, where truly is a royal court, do you laugh? You do not know because you do not see—namely, that angels are present—because the house of God is full of incorporeal powers.” But the Apostle teaches what we ought to say: “Speaking to yourselves in psalms, hymns, and songs” [Note: [Col. 0037] Eph. 5].

Out of reverence for this same privilege, women rising after childbirth do not enter the church; nor do menstruating women, nor women joined to men [Col. 0038C], according to Roman custom. For the same reason solemn penitents are excluded: first, because while they endure punishment they remember their fault; and second, because in all these matters the mystery is understood that the unclean are utterly excluded from the heavenly temple. Otherwise, on the day on which they did or suffered one of the aforesaid things, they might enter in order to give thanks to God.

For this is the holy city, the blessed city Jerusalem, the city of God, concerning which: “Glorious things are spoken of thee, O city of God” [Note: [Col. 0037] Ps. 86]; and elsewhere: “I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven” [Note: [Col. 0037] Rev. 21]. It fights on earth but reigns in heaven. This is the glorious kingdom whose guardians on earth are the college of prelates, the companies of martyrs, and the assembly [Col. 0038D] of confessors and virgins; and this court is adorned by that unique jewel which has not been seen first, nor has any successor.

Yet since it also signifies the Church militant, I do not object if at times evil people are bodily mingled with good. For in Eden woman is formed from man, the tree of life and of knowledge is set forth [Note: [Col. 0037] Gen. 2], and the serpent too is found [Note: [Col. 0037] Gen. 3]. In Noah’s ark there are clean and unclean animals [Note: [Col. 0037] Gen. 7], having peace together in one place. Those who do not keep peace are not in the ark, though they may appear to be, and are found more savage than beasts. Outside the Church there is no place of refuge; yet not all who are now within it [Col. 0039A] will obtain the Father’s favor. For Ham received a curse in his sons [Note: [Col. 0039] Gen. 9]; in Abraham’s house the son of the handmaid is believed to have played with the son of the free woman [Note: [Col. 0039] Gen. 21]; in the womb of pregnant Rebecca the twins struggle [Note: [Col. 0039] Gen. 25], of whom the smooth one is loved and the hairy one rejected [Note: [Col. 0039] Gen. 27]. Often within the enclosure of the sealed garden the bitterness of wormwood is found.

At the Lord’s supper [Note: [Col. 0039] Matt. 26], and in Simon’s little boat, there was an Iscariot. In the fisherman’s net there are good and bad fish [Note: [Col. 0039] Matt. 8]; on the threshing floor, grain and chaff [Note: [Col. 0039] Matt. 13]. Likewise, in churches men pray together with women [Note: [Col. 0039] 1 Tim. 2], such that, according to the customs of some, women are on the northern side and men on the southern. For men signify those who are strong amid the temptations of this world and in faith, and fervent in charity; women signify those more fragile and lukewarm in good works.

[Col. 0039B] According to others, men are at the front and women at the rear. For the man is the head of the woman [Note: [Col. 0039] Eph. 5], and therefore her guide. That males should stand separately and females separately, we have learned from Bede to be derived from ancient custom. Hence Joseph and Mary left the child behind [Note: [Col. 0039] Luke 2], because each, not seeing him with himself or herself, thought that he was with the other. The reason for the separation is that the flesh of man and woman, if they come too near, is kindled to lust.

Wherever women have their place, they ought always, according to the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0039] 1 Cor. 11], to pray veiled, lest with loosened hair they entice the minds of young men, or grow proud because of the beauty of their hair; indeed, they should do so “because of the angels,” that is, the priests. For the priest [Col. 0039C] is judge and vicar of Jesus Christ; therefore before the priest a woman should veil herself, so that, conscious of original sin, which occurred through her, she may seem ashamed and by that very habit accuse herself before the judge. Accordingly Linus, by Peter’s command, ordained that a woman should enter church with veiled head. Although she may pray, she may not speak—that is, preach to peoples [Note: [Col. 0039] 1 Cor. 14].

Therefore a place does not save one whom the perversity of conscience condemns, just as dreadful places do not harm those who live devoutly. Nadab and Abihu are consumed by fire in the tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0039] Lev. 10]; Korah, Dathan, and Abiram are swallowed up before the tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0039] Num. 16]; Eli the priest perished in the holy place [Note: [Col. 0039] 1 Sam. 4]; Uzzah died beside the ark [Note: [Col. 0039] 2 Sam. 6]; Joab is killed beside the altar [Note: [Col. 0039] 1 Kings 2]; Uzziah is struck with leprosy in the temple [Note: [Col. 0039] 2 Chron. 26]. Conversely, Moses is delivered from [Col. 0039D] the river [Note: [Col. 0039] Exod. 2]; Joseph from the pit [Note: [Col. 0039] Gen. 37] and prison [Note: [Col. 0039] Gen. 40]; Job from the dung heap [Note: [Col. 0039] Job 2]; Jeremiah from the mud [Note: [Col. 0039] Jer. 38]; Daniel from the lions’ den [Note: [Col. 0039] Dan. 6]; and the three youths from the fiery furnace [Note: [Col. 0039] Dan. 3]. Finally, the devil fell from heaven [Note: [Col. 0039] Isa. 14], and man from paradise [Note: [Col. 0039] Gen. 3]; but the righteous are visited upon earth and raised from hell to heavenly things.

But although a place does not itself sanctify, nevertheless, because of reverence for the sacrament, it contributes greatly to sanctification. Therefore, because of this reverence, let us remove shoes from our feet [Col. 0040A], that we may deserve to be sanctified by the Lord in the holy place [Note: [Col. 0039] Exod. 3].

## CHAPTER XII. ON THE ORNAMENTATION OF THE CHURCH
“Lord, I have loved the beauty of thy house, and the place where thy glory dwells” [Note: [Col. 0039] Ps. 25].

Churches are adorned with carvings, paintings, and lathe-worked sculptures, taking their form from the tabernacle of Moses [Note: [Col. 0039] Exod. 25] or the temple of Solomon [Note: [Col. 0039] III Kings 6]. For Moses carved two cherubim; Solomon too carved them, and adorned both the walls with carvings, the lathe, and paintings. Such things are made not merely as ornaments of churches, but also as letters for the laity. For “whatever things were written,” or sculpted, “were written for our instruction” [Note: [Col. 0039] Rom. 15]: letters, I say, that recall things past, [Col. 0040B] indicate things present, and foretell things to come. They concern the past in histories and visions; the present in virtues and vices; and the future in punishments and rewards. Of these, if not every example, let us survey the more customary ones.

Thus the two cherubim in the tabernacle, facing one another and looking toward the mercy-seat, are the two Testaments, differing in nothing. For their faces would turn away from one another if what one promised the other denied. They look toward the mercy-seat when everything contained in them is referred to the service of the Creator. In our churches, however, the image of our Lord Jesus Christ is painted in many ways and for many reasons. Painted in the manger, it recalls his birth; painted in his mother’s lap, his childhood; painted or sculpted [Col. 0040C] upon the cross, his Passion.

Upon the cross, too, the sun and moon suffering eclipse are depicted; the thieves and the nails, pincers and wounds, lance, blood and water, inscription and crown, together with the purple garment: all these are emblems of the Passion. Painted in the ascent of the steps, it indicates the Ascension; painted upon a lofty throne, it indicates his present majesty and power, as though it were said: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to him” [Note: [Col. 0039] Matt. 28]. Thus is fulfilled the vision of Isaiah, who says: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up” [Note: [Col. 0039] Isa. 6]—that is, the Son of God reigning over the angels—according to that saying: “Thou who sittest upon the cherubim” [Note: [Col. 0039] Ps. 79].

At times, however, he is painted as Moses and Aaron [Note: [Col. 0039] Exod. 24], Nadab and Abihu saw him: namely, upon the mountain, and beneath his feet, as it were, a work of sapphire, and [Col. 0040D] like the sky when it is clear. Around him angels are sometimes painted with six wings, according to Isaiah, who says: “Seraphim stood above him; six wings to the one and six wings to the other: with two they covered his face, with two his feet, and with two they flew” [Note: [Col. 0039] Isa. 6].

I think that *seraphim* ought here to be written with an *m*, and that “two” is understood, because “to the one and to the other” follows. They stand over the Church as guardians; and, being fiery, they kindle it to the two commandments of love [Col. 0041A]. They are said to have wings because of the swift course of their guardianship. With these they cover the head and feet, and reveal the middle, because they conceal from us the first things and the last things.

Hence Isaiah says: “Declare to me the former things, and the latter things which shall be, and I shall say that ye are gods” [Note: [Col. 0041] Isa. 41]. But the middle things, made in six days and six ages [Note: [Col. 0041] Gen. 1], they reveal to us by representative or partial disclosure, because “we know in part and prophesy in part” [Note: [Col. 0041] I Cor. 13]. For although the invisible things of God are seen, however imperfectly understood, through the things that have been made [Note: [Col. 0041] Rom. 1], yet his eternity is incomprehensible, and we are not sufficient to perceive how he is Alpha and Omega.

At times the angel Michael is painted around him, trampling the dragon, according to John’s saying: “There was [Col. 0041B] war in heaven; Michael fought with the dragon” [Note: [Col. 0041] Apoc. 12]. I take this battle to mean the division among the angels, the confirmation of the good and the fall of the evil; or else the persecution of the faithful in the present Church.

At times the twenty-four elders are painted around him, according to the vision of the same writer, in white garments and with golden crowns [Note: [Col. 0041] Apoc. 4]. By them are signified the teachers of the Old and New Law. They are twelve on account of faith in the holy Trinity, which they proclaim through the four regions of the world; or twenty-four on account of the works and observance of the Gospels. They are clothed by innocence and crowned with the diadem of charity and wisdom. If lamps are added, the gifts of the Holy Spirit are represented; if a glassy sea, [Col. 0041C] baptism is indicated.

At times the four living creatures are painted around him, according to the vision of Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0041] ch. 1] and of the same John [Note: [Col. 0041] Apoc. 4]: the likeness of their faces was the face of a man, the face of a lion on the right, the face of an ox on the left, and the face of an eagle above the four of them. Each had four faces and four wings; their likeness was like coals, and their appearance like lamps. These are the four Evangelists; hence they are painted with books at their feet, because what they taught by word and writing they fulfilled in mind and deed.

Each has four faces, for the knowledge of the Incarnation of the Word possessed by one was possessed by all. Yet individual attributes belong to each severally. Although each relates his own material, each carries out his particular matter more distinctively. Thus Matthew, speaking of the humanity [Col. 0041D] of Christ—“The book of the generation of Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0041] Matt. 1]—receives the human figure and represents Christ as man, who, though he was God, was made man [Note: [Col. 0041] Phil. 2].

Mark, beginning with the preaching of John crying in the wilderness, bears the figure of a lion roaring in the wilderness. He also explains Christ’s resurrection more openly than the others, in which Christ is represented by the lion, which is born dead and is given life by its father’s voice on the third day. These are placed on the right, because Christ’s birth [Col. 0042A] and resurrection were the universal joy of all. Hence in the Psalm: “Joy comes in the morning” [Note: [Col. 0041] Ps. 29].

Luke is the calf, because he began with Zechariah the priest and treated Christ’s Passion and sacrifice more particularly. For the calf is an animal suitable for priestly sacrifices. Or he is compared to a calf because he has two horns, as though he contained the two Testaments, and the hoofs of four feet, as though the sum of the four Gospels. By this creature Christ too is represented, he who was sacrificed for us as a calf. Therefore Luke is placed on the left, because Christ’s death was grievous to the Apostles. Hence: “Weeping shall linger in the evening” [Note: [Col. 0041] ibid.]; and elsewhere: “You shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy” [Note: [Col. 0041] John 16].

John is the eagle, since, soaring to the heights, he says: “In the beginning was [Col. 0042B] the Word” [Note: [Col. 0041] John 1]. He too signifies Christ, whose youth is renewed like the eagle’s [Note: [Col. 0041] Ps. 102], when, rising from the dead, he flourishes and enters heaven. He is described as not beside but above the others, because he indicates the Ascension and proclaims the Word as being with God [Note: [Col. 0041] John 1]. Each flies with four wings when he raises his eyes to the Godhead and proclaims it throughout the four regions of the world.

John, however, assigns six wings to these living creatures, because through the visible things of this world, completed in six days [Note: [Col. 0041] Gen. 1], they came to know invisible things and glorified God as Lord [Note: [Col. 0041] Rom. 1]. Or the first wing was the natural law; the second, the Mosaic law; the third, the prophets; the fourth, the Gospel; the fifth, the institutions of the Apostles; the sixth, those of the doctors. By these the Church flies [Col. 0042C] when preachers receive from them the foundations of all preaching. According to John they are also full of eyes, on account of their complete knowledge of creation.

These are coals of fire [Note: [Col. 0041] Ps. 17, 139], desolating coals [Note: [Col. 0041] Ps. 119]. If you sit upon them, they will help you; if you touch them, you will be kindled by these coals, and with the holy you will be holy [Note: [Col. 0041] Ps. 17]. These are lamps gleaming with the light of good repute [Note: [Col. 0041] Matt. 25].

At times the Apostles are painted around him, or rather below him: they were witnesses in word and deed in Samaria and Judaea, and unto the uttermost part of the earth [Note: [Col. 0041] Acts 1]. At times divided tongues are painted above each of them, because by such tokens the Paraclete filled their hearts [Note: [Col. 0041] Acts 2]. At times they are painted long-haired, as Nazirites [Note: [Col. 0041] Num. 6], that is, holy persons. For the law of the Nazirites was [Col. 0042D] that during the time of their separation no razor should pass over their heads. They separated themselves from the common life of humankind, some for a time and some continually, as Samuel did [Note: [Col. 0041] I Kings 1].

At times John the Baptist is included, as an hermit; martyrs with their instruments of torture, as Lawrence on the gridiron and Stephen with stones; confessors with their insignia, as mitred bishops, hooded abbots, and doctors with books in their hands; virgins, according to the Gospel, with [Col. 0043A] lamps [Note: [Col. 0043] Matt. 25]. At times martyrs with palms and confessors with lilies are painted [Note: [Col. 0043] Apoc. 7]. For the palm signifies victory, and lilies chastity. A palm was given to victors so that, as the palm remains green, so their memory might flourish eternally. The palm grows upward from a narrow place; so martyrs, when they return from the contest, are rewarded in the heavenly capitol. Hence: “The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree” [Note: [Col. 0043] Ps. 91]. With the palm they came to kingdoms.

Observe that the Lord Jesus is always painted crowned, as though it were said: “Go forth and see King Solomon with the diadem with which his mother crowned him” [Note: [Col. 0043] Song 3]. Note that the Lord was crowned threefold by his mother: with a crown of mercy on the day of his conception. This crown is twofold, on account of natural and gratuitous gifts; therefore [Col. 0043B] it is also called a diadem, because a diadem is a double crown.

He was also crowned by his stepmother with a crown of misery on the day of his Passion [Note: [Col. 0043] Matt. 27]. This crown was of thorns, because he bore our sins [Note: [Col. 0043] I Pet. 2]. He was also crowned by the Father with a crown of glory on the day of his resurrection. Hence: “Thou hast crowned him, O Lord, with glory and honour” [Note: [Col. 0043] Ps. 8]. Finally, he will be crowned by his household with a crown of power on the day of the final revelation, when he shall come with the senators of the earth; surrounded by their host, he shall judge the world in equity [Note: [Col. 0043] Rom. 2; Ps. 95, 97].

Thus all saints are painted crowned, as though it were said: Daughters of Jerusalem, come and see the martyrs with the crowns with which the Lord crowned them. God willing, we shall set down this antiphon below. Here it suffices to say that we used the plural, “crowns,” because of [Col. 0043C] the openwork crown fastened to the rim of the table, and because of the aureole set above it [Note: [Col. 0043] Exod. 25].

The table is sacred Scripture; its rim is the doctrine of preachers; the openwork crown is eternal life, distinguished among the saints according to diversity of merits, because “star differs from star in glory” [Note: [Col. 0043] I Cor. 15]. The aureole is the general glorification of bodies, or the spiritual radiance of virgins. Observe that a crown of this kind is painted in the shape of a round shield, because the saints enjoy divine protection. Thus they sing joyfully: “Lord, thou hast crowned us as with a shield of thy good will” [Note: [Col. 0043] Ps. 5].

Observe also that Christ’s crown is distinguished from the crown of the saints by the figure of the cross, because by the banner of the cross he merited for himself the glorification of his flesh, and for us [Col. 0043D] liberation from captivity and the enjoyment of life.

At times Paradise and Hell are painted in churches, so that the former may attract us to delight in rewards and the latter may frighten us by the terror of torments. At times lilies are painted, at times a palm, so that by the lilies we may understand chastity, and by the palms victory. We also intermingle other flowers with fruits, to represent the fruit of good works springing from the roots of virtues.

Finally, the variety of carved reliefs—which in Greek are called *anaglypha*—and likewise of paintings signifies [Col. 0044A] the variety of virtues: “To one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge; to another faith; to another the grace of healings” [Note: [Col. 0043] I Cor. 12]. Charity also, joy, peace, patience, and long-suffering [Note: [Col. 0043] Gal. 5] are carvings of holy minds.

That virtues are painted in female form is because they soothe and nourish. Or, by carvings, also called ceiling-panels (*laquearia*), which serve for the beauty of the house, we understand the simpler servants of Christ, who adorn the Church not by doctrine but by virtues alone. Of them are the cypress ceiling-panels [Note: [Col. 0043] Song 1]; for they are of lofty and excellent fragrance and suitable for healing bodies.

Walls are worked with the lathe when the faithful are strong in ready resolve for the Lord’s service, saying: “I will bless the Lord at every time” [Note: [Col. 0043] Ps. 33], and: “My heart is ready, [Col. 0044B] O God, my heart is ready” [Note: [Col. 0043] Ps. 107]. They strive so greatly in virtues that no adversity turns them from their path. For lathe-work surpasses other arts in speed and preserves a rule that works without error. Thus the life of the saints is ready for divine services and is not shaken by any byways of error.

Observe that the sculptures seem to project and emerge from the walls, because, when virtues have entered such habitual practice among the faithful as to seem naturally implanted in them, they are exercised in the manifold works of those virtues.

Altars and churches are also adorned with cloths, curtains, silk fabrics, linen, figured tapestries, royal crowns, other images, and diverse marked characters. All these pertain to Christ’s miracles [Col. 0044C] or to future glory, which shall be revealed in us through the examples of the ancients and our merits—indeed, through the manifold and fruitful works of God’s grace [Note: [Col. 0043] Rom. 8].

Things adorned not outside but within pertain to the moral adornment of the bride, whose glory is from within in golden fringes [Note: [Col. 0043] Ps. 44], that is, in perseverance in good works. For though outwardly black with tribulations, she is inwardly beautiful through virtues [Note: [Col. 0043] Song 1]. Therefore white cloths or curtains signify purity; red, charity; green, contemplation; black, mortification of the flesh; many-coloured, the variety of virtues; linen, tribulation; silk, virginity. Thus through visible adornments we may be moved toward invisible ones [Note: [Col. 0043] Rom. 1] and seek with eager mind the glory laid up in [Col. 0044D] heaven [Note: [Col. 0043] II Tim. 4].

## CHAPTER XIII. ON THE UTENSILS OF THE CHURCH

“We have the treasure of the Lord in earthen vessels” [Note: [Col. 0043] II Cor. 4].

The vessels or utensils in the house of the Lord had their origin from Moses [Note: [Col. 0043] Exod. 25] or Solomon [Note: [Col. 0043] III Kings 7]. For Moses, at the Lord’s command, made an ark of setim wood, gilded within and without, with a golden crown, four rings, and two poles always placed in the rings. In it were put the tablets of the Testament. Above it he placed the mercy-seat and two cherubim, looking [Col. 0045A] toward the mercy-seat with faces turned toward it.

He also made a table of gilded setim wood with a rim, an openwork crown, and an aureole, with four feet, an equal number of rings, and two poles always in the rings. Upon it were placed twelve loaves. He made bowls, vinegar-cups, and drinking-cups; censers in which libations were offered. He also made a golden lampstand, a shaft and branches, cups and knobs, and lilies proceeding from it. He made lamps to be set upon the lampstand, with their snuffers and vessels. Our fathers also had cauldrons, pincers, forks, fire-pans, fire-receptacles, whips, small vessels, water-jars, mortars, basins, and baths. For moving camp, whose examples they imitated, they had trumpets [Note: [Col. 0045] Num. 10], [Col. 0045B] standards, and banners [Note: [Col. 0045] Num. 2].

The necessity and use of utensils follow the time and rite of sacrifices. Hence some claim for themselves things proper to the time of the Law, such as cauldrons and forks; others claim things peculiar to the time of grace, such as the cross and the chalice with its paten; others are common to both, such as censers and lampstands. Yet although the material use has passed away, let us seek the treasure of the Spirit, which remains and gives life [Note: [Col. 0045] II Cor. 3].

The ark of the Lord, therefore, made of setim wood—which is light, incorruptible, and like the white thorn—is the body of Christ, composed of most pure members, corrupted by no contagion of sin. For he came not in sinful flesh, but in the likeness of sinful flesh [Note: [Col. 0045] Rom. 8]. [Col. 0045C] Its length is the endurance of the Passion, which he taught by word and deed. Hence it was two cubits long. Its breadth is charity; its height, hope of future glorification. It is gilded within because of the Godhead, and without because of the radiance of holy works and miracles.

Or the ark of setim wood is the Church, built of the faithful. It contains a half-measure in every dimension, because “we know in part and we prophesy in part; but when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away” [Note: [Col. 0045] I Cor. 13]. It is gilded with wisdom and crowned with eternal life.

The four rings of both arks—that is, of the body of Christ and of the Church—are the four Evangelists through the four corners of the world, carrying the mystery of the Incarnation and the faith of the Church. Hence two are on the right side, Matthew [Col. 0045D] and John, who adhered to Christ during his preaching; and two on the left, Mark and Luke, who came to faith after the Lord’s Ascension.

The poles of both arks are strong teachers, endowed with wisdom, keeping the two commandments of charity, and carrying abroad by their preaching faith in the Incarnation and in the Church. They are always inserted into the rings, because those who preach heavenly things to others must never withdraw their mind from remembrance of sacred Scripture or their hands from observance of the commandments. Those who keep watch over the office of preaching should not depart from the study of reading, [Col. 0046A] so that when the ark must be carried, no delay may arise in inserting the poles. For it is shameful if a shepherd seeks to learn when a shepherd ought to resolve a question.

Therefore let us always cling to the rings of books, meditating upon the divine utterances [Note: [Col. 0045] Ps. 1], so that, when need arises, we may lift the ark and be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks us for a reason for the hope that is in us [Note: [Col. 0045] I Pet. 3].

In each ark are the tablets of the Testament: because in Christ are hidden the treasures of God’s wisdom and knowledge [Note: [Col. 0045] Col. 2], and in the Church are meditation upon God and the Gospel. In each is a golden urn of manna: because in Christ is the fullness of divinity [Note: [Col. 0045] ibid.], and in the Church faith in the Incarnation. In each is Aaron’s rod: because in Christ is the power of priesthood, which, cut off through death, flowered again on the morning of the Resurrection [Col. 0046B]; in the Church is participation in the kingdom. Hence: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” [Note: [Col. 0045] I Pet. 2]. Or it signifies the Blessed Virgin, who, though dry, bore a flower and, though inviolate, gave birth to the Saviour [Note: [Col. 0045] Isa. 11, 45].

Above each ark is the mercy-seat, namely a golden plate of the same measure as the ark. Appearing above it to Moses, the Lord was merciful to the people. Thus in Christ it signifies mercy, which triumphs over judgment [Note: [Col. 0045] Jas. 2], and all his works. Hence: “The Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works” [Note: [Col. 0045] Ps. 144]. In the Church it signifies divine grace, descending into the minds of the faithful from the Father of lights [Note: [Col. 0045] Jas. 1].

In each ark, the two cherubim above the mercy-seat [Col. 0046C] are the two Testaments, showing forth in fullness of knowledge the Incarnation of the Lord, his mercies [Note: [Col. 0045] Ps. 144], and the grace given us [Note: [Col. 0045] John 1]. They do this with faces turned toward the mercy-seat, because what one promises the other supplies concerning propitiation.

The table of setim wood is sacred Scripture, woven from the strong sayings of the Fathers. Its length is perseverance, preached in this verse: “From the morning watch until night, let Israel hope in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0045] Ps. 129]. Its breadth is charity, commanded in this verse: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart” [Note: [Col. 0045] Deut. 6; Matt. 22]. Its height is hope, suggested by this verse: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” [Note: [Col. 0045] Matt. 5].

The length of perseverance is two cubits, because of purity and action, or [Col. 0046D] conscience and reputation. The breadth of charity is one cubit, because charity is one and simple, by which we love the Lord, our neighbour, and our enemies, though differently. Jacob loved all his sons, but loved Joseph above the rest on account of his merit of innocence [Note: [Col. 0045] Gen. 37]. The height of hope is a cubit and a half, because the kingdom for which we wait and which we contemplate is one, but we see it through a glass darkly [Note: [Col. 0045] I Cor. 13].

The golden rim is the pure doctrine of preachers. The openwork crown, four fingers high, is eternal life promised by preachers, according to diversity of merits, if they keep [Col. 0047A] the doctrine of the four Gospels, which are written with the finger, or in which the finger of God is found [Note: [Col. 0047] Exod. 31; Deut. 9; Exod. 8; Luke 11]. The aureole is general glorification, or the radiance of virgins. The four feet of the table are the fourfold exposition of sacred Scripture; for it is expounded historically, allegorically, tropologically, and anagogically.

History is when an event is narrated in simple language, as when the people came from Egypt into the land of promise [Note: [Col. 0047] Exod. 12; Josh. 5]. It is called history from *historein*, “to see,” because it is the task of historians to explain deeds done according to the primary meaning of words.

Allegory is when the mysteries of the Church are signified by mystical words or things. By words: “A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall ascend from his root” [Note: [Col. 0047] Isa. 11]—that is, a virgin shall be born from the stock [Col. 0047B] of David, and Christ from the virgin. By things: the people freed from Egypt through the blood of the lamb [Note: [Col. 0047] Exod. 12] is the Church, redeemed from the power of the devil by the blood of Christ. Allegory is so called as though it were an alien utterance.

Tropology is moral discourse concerning the formation or correction of character. It is made through plain words, as: “Little children, let us not love in word or in tongue, but in deed and in truth” [Note: [Col. 0047] I John 3]; or figurative words, as: “Let thy garments be white at all times, and let oil not fail from thy head” [Note: [Col. 0047] Eccl. 9]. It is called tropology, “turned speech,” when what is said is turned to signify moral conduct.

Anagoge is speech leading upward, as concerning future rewards or the life to come. It is made by plain or mystical words. By plain words: “Blessed are the pure in heart, [Col. 0047C] for they shall see God” [Note: [Col. 0047] Matt. 5]. By mystical words: “Blessed are they who wash their robes, that they may have authority over the tree of life and may enter through the gates into the city” [Note: [Col. 0047] Apoc. 22]. That is: blessed are those who cleanse their thoughts [Note: [Col. 0047] Matt. 5] and works, so that they may see Christ, who is the way, the truth, and the life [Note: [Col. 0047] John 14], and may enter the kingdom through the teaching and examples of those who went before.

Observe that signification is twofold: real and verbal. Verbal signification occurs when things are signified through sounds by means of concepts; logic speaks of this [Note: [Col. 0047] Aristotle, *On Interpretation*, I]. Real signification occurs when one thing figures another. Verbal signification derives from human institution; real signification from divine institution. For as a human being indicates his will through speech, so God indicates his will through creatures and works. Verbal signification is either univocal or equivocal. Real signification [Col. 0047D] is deeper, because as many as are the properties, so many are the varieties of signification. Both are necessary in the feet of the table; and thus it is clear that knowledge of the arts contributes to the knowledge of the divine Scriptures.

For there are three arts, or branches, of philosophy: logic, ethics, and theory. Logic concerns words; ethics, morals; theory, things. Theory is divided into mathematics, physics, and theology. Mathematics speaks of visible forms, physics of visible natures, theology of divine things. [Col. 0048A] Therefore logic contributes to theology when Scripture is expounded through words; ethics contributes when it is applied to morals; theory contributes when the invisible things of God are perceived through the things that have been made [Note: [Col. 0047] Rom. 1].

The four rings at the corners are the four Gospel books spread through the four regions of the world. The two poles are preachers keeping the two commandments of charity, always in the rings—that is, adhering to evangelical teachings—as we said above concerning the poles of the ark. When they refer the words of sacred Scripture to faith and love of the Gospel, they carry the whole table of the Lord.

Upon it were placed the loaves of refreshment, because Scripture supplies the food of life for eternal joys and shows how they are reached. They are called loaves of presentation [Note: [Col. 0047] Lev. 24], because [Col. 0048B] words of consolation ought not to be lacking in the Church, but the word of salvation ought to lie open to all the faithful.

Upon it were placed vessels for libations, that is, for vows, such as bowls [Note: [Col. 0047] Exod. 37]. This variety of vessels signifies the variety of words adapted to the capacities of hearers, because not all things suit everyone. Hence the Apostle: “I gave you milk” [Note: [Col. 0047] I Cor. 3]; “but we speak wisdom among the perfect” [Note: [Col. 0047] I Cor. 2].

Thus ample preaching is signified by bowls; restrained expression by drinking-cups. Whoever more fully intoxicates his hearers offers a bowl; whoever communicates what he thinks in whatever measure gives a taste through a cup; whoever rebukes those subject to him offers a vinegar-cup; whoever stirs people to pray bears a censer. Sacred Scripture presents all these things to us: it refreshes us with food and drink, serving substantial matters and pouring out lighter ones. For it waters the little ones with milk [Col. 0048C] and feeds the strong with bread. Yet that which is set before us as food “has become to the Jews a snare, a recompense, and a stumbling-block” [Note: [Col. 0047] Ps. 68].

The censer is a vessel common to both Laws. As we said, it signifies either preaching about prayer, which stirs people to pray, or the Lord’s flesh. But if it is golden, it also signifies wisdom, because all treasures of wisdom and knowledge were hidden in him [Note: [Col. 0047] Col. 2]. Hence: “An angel stood beside the altar of the temple, having a golden censer in his hand” [Note: [Col. 0047] Apoc. 8]: that is, Christ rising again had his flesh in his power.

If it is silver, it also signifies that flesh as clean of every stain and gleaming with purity; if bronze, as fragile and mortal; if iron, the strength of him who rises again. If it has four [Col. 0048D] lines, it shows that it consists of the four elements, or is adorned with the four virtues—prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. The fifth line, dividing the parts, signifies the soul, which separated itself from the flesh in death during those three days.

But if it has three lines, it represents flesh, soul, and Word coming together in one person. The fourth, which separates the parts, is the power by which he laid down his soul for his sheep [Note: [Col. 0047] John 10]. If it is supported by only one line, it signifies that he alone is born of the Virgin [Note: [Col. 0047] Isa. 7; Matt. 1], or that he alone is [Col. 0049A] free among the dead [Note: [Col. 0049] Ps. 87]. The circle to which all these things are joined is the divinity, enclosed by no boundary, by which all these things are sustained and wrought.

Incense signifies the prayers which he poured out for us in the flesh [Note: [Col. 0049] Isa. 53]. Hence: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight” [Note: [Col. 0049] Ps. 140]. The fire is charity, by which he loved us so greatly that he heated and scorched that very flesh upon the altar of the cross [Note: [Col. 0049] John 15]. Hence: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” [Note: [Col. 0049] Ps. 21]. He brought the fragrant offering of prayers, sprinkled upon the nostrils of the Father; hence he answered: “I have glorified, and I shall glorify again” [Note: [Col. 0049] John 12].

Or by the fragrance we understand the good odour of Christ, which whoever wishes to live must convey into his heart. Or by the censer we understand the Apostles and preachers, who are to some “an odour of life unto life,” and to others [Col. 0049B] “an odour of death unto death” [Note: [Col. 0049] II Cor. 2]. Their sermons and prayers are like much incense and like the smoke of aromatics [Note: [Col. 0049] Apoc. 8]. Or the censer is the human heart; the fire, charity; the incense, prayer. As incense smells sweet and rises upward with fire in the censer, so prayer with charity in the heart gives fragrance surpassing every spice.

The lampstand also is a beaten-work vessel common to both Laws, although the ancient Fathers made it more splendidly. For Moses made a lampstand of the purest gold [Note: [Col. 0049] Exod. 25, 37]. This is Christ, “who enlightens every man coming into this world” [Note: [Col. 0049] John 1]. For he shone with the light of divinity and of his preaching, so that he might become the lampstand of the world, by whose light the sinner might recognize his own darkness. He was made of gold because of wisdom [Col. 0049C] and purity, and was beaten-work because of his endurance of the Passion; through it he was led to the grace of resurrection. Hence: “Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name” [Note: [Col. 0049] Phil. 2].

The shaft is the Church, which stands free amid adversities; or rather, the whole lampstand is the whole Christ, head and members [Note: [Col. 0049] Eph. 5]. For the Church too shows light to the erring, possesses the brightness of wisdom, is beaten with hammers, and is led from strength to strength [Note: [Col. 0049] Ps. 83]. The shaft is Christ, the head of the Church [Note: [Col. 0049] Eph. 5], the mediator of God and men [Note: [Col. 0049] I Tim. 2], from whom the whole body, being built together, grows into the increase of Christ.

The reeds (*calami*) are preachers, who gave the world a sweet sound, [Col. 0049D] that is, a new song; and all those who, obeying the Prophet’s saying, “Sing to the Lord a new song” [Note: [Col. 0049] Ps. 95, 97], resound in praises of the Creator. They are six because of the perfection of works [Note: [Col. 0049] Gen. 1]: three from one side and three from the other, because both those who went before and those who followed cried out, “Hosanna in the highest” [Note: [Col. 0049] Matt. 21], preaching faith in the divine Trinity.

For David, among those who went before, says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host” [Note: [Col. 0049] Ps. 32]. John, who followed, [Col. 0050A] added: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0049] I John 5]. Or, both before and after the Incarnation, there were three ranks in the Church: Noah, Daniel, and Job—that is, rulers, virgins or continent persons, and married persons. These are those who, according to the Gospel, are in the field, in the bed, and at the mill [Note: [Col. 0049] Matt. 24].

Cup-bowls are preachers, or hearers, who intoxicate or are intoxicated by the wine of knowledge. The little spheres signify the mobility of preachers and of all the elect: as a sphere rolls on every side, so neither adversity nor prosperity corrupts a preacher or any one of the elect; rather, he is strong amid adversities, humble amid prosperities, has no angle of fear, and raises no brow of pride. After the cups and little spheres lilies are formed [Col. 0050B], because after spiritual meditation and holy activity, variable according to the diversity of times, the green homeland follows, which blooms for holy souls with eternal flowers. For the Lord who has offered the cup of spiritual wisdom has shown the unhindered course of activity. Lest we run in vain [Note: [Col. 0049] Gal. 2.], he has opened to us the gate of the green homeland. There are on each branch three cups, little spheres together with them, and lilies; for every order has three periods, whether before the Incarnation or afterward: before it, the time before the Law, under the Law, and under the prophets; afterward, the first Church from Israel, the second from the Gentiles, and the third from the remainder. In each there are, have been, and will be those who thirst for the cups of grace as for bowls, are intoxicated, and intoxicate others; [Col. 0050C] who run in God’s way like little spheres; and who desire to behold the brightness and fragrance of perpetual light like lilies. Observe that all these proceed from the shaft, because “we have all received from his fullness” [Note: [Col. 0049] John 1]. Therefore, just as he says, “I am the vine and you are the branches” [Note: [Col. 0049] John 15], so he may say: I am the lampstand and you are the stems and cups. On the shaft itself are four cups, little spheres together with them, and lilies, because the four Gospels proclaim him as full of the grace of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0049] John 1], proclaim that “he rejoiced like a giant to run his course” [Note: [Col. 0049] Ps. 18], and that, glorified [Note: [Col. 0049] John 12], he sits at the Father’s right hand [Note: [Col. 0049] Ps. 109]. Nor is it without significance that each branch is furnished with cups, little spheres, and lilies, because holy preachers are sustained by the divine commands and [Col. 0050D] promises of the Lord.

“[He] made also seven lamps” [Note: [Col. 0049] Exod. 37]. The seven lamps are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which illuminate the darkness of our blindness in the night of this age. They are placed above the lampstand because upon Christ rested the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0049] Isa. 2]; by these he preached release to captives [Note: [Col. 0049] Isa. 61]. The snuffers are tongs for trimming the wicks. These are the divine words [Col. 0051A] by which we cut away the letter and reveal the shining Spirit. For certain things in the Law and the Gospel are to be observed both here and in the future, such as: “Love the Lord your God” [Note: [Col. 0051] Deut. 6; Matt. 22]. Certain things are for here, not for the future, such as: “Make for yourselves friends from unrighteous mammon” [Note: [Col. 0051] Luke 16]. Certain things are in the Law but not in the Gospel, such as “Keep the Sabbath day” [Note: [Col. 0051] Exod. 20] and the sacrificial rites, which, when observed in their own time, shone like wicks soaked in the oil of devotion and kindled by the fire of charity. But they are trimmed when the letter is taught to have ceased and the understanding of the Spirit is opened more brightly. Therefore it is said: “You shall eat the very oldest of old stores, and when new things arrive you shall throw away the old” [Note: [Col. 0051] Lev. 26].

The vessels in which the trimmed wicks are extinguished are the hearts of the faithful, which admit that observance of the Law has expired. Or the wicks [Col. 0051B] are the charisms of graces, and the vessels are the bodies or hearts of the saints. Thus the trimmed wicks shine more brightly in the saints, because, when the present uses of gifts have been removed, their uses will be clearer; or, when mortality has ended, “they shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0051] Matt. 13]. The plurality of lamps in the Church signifies the plurality of graces among the faithful. Or the lights are those by whose teaching the Church shines, like the sun and moon, to whom it is said: “You are the light of the world” [Note: [Col. 0051] Matt. 5]. But the single lamp is Christ, who enlightens every person coming into this world [Note: [Col. 0051] John 1].

Among modern people lamps are placed in crowns. Crowns, however, are hung in churches for three reasons: first, for ornament or usefulness; [Col. 0051C] second, to signify that those who remain in the unity of the Church, if they serve God devoutly, will receive the crown of life [Note: [Col. 0051] Jas. 1]; third, because the heavenly Jerusalem is recalled to our memory, after whose figure the crown seems to have been made. For it consists of gold, silver, bronze, iron, chains, and precious stones.

Gold signifies martyrs; silver, virgins; bronze, teachers; iron, the continent; precious stones, those resplendent with the five virtues. The chain is contemplation, which always raises them to the Lord. The highest circle is God, who contains and comprehends all things. Pots or cauldrons receiving ashes are the faithful who reflect devoutly upon the Lord’s Passion; for by the ashes of the heifer, by which the defiled person was sanctified [Note: [Col. 0051] Num. 19; Heb. 9], the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion is understood.

[Col. 0051D] Tongs, by whose double tooth the fire is arranged, are preachers, who instruct us from the harmonious pages of both Testaments and, harmonizing all things, kindle us to charity. Flesh-hooks or forks, by which meat was lifted from the cauldrons and brought for the nourishment of those to be refreshed, while some was left to be consumed by the fire, are preachers who handle Christ’s mysteries as the flesh of the saving victim: in part imitating them by works, in part refreshing others, but leaving to the Holy Spirit those things not within our capacity. Fire-pans, by which [Col. 0052A] fire was carried from the altar of burnt offerings to the altar of incense, are preachers who transfer the fire of charity into the hearts of the faithful through the examples of the saints; who turn the hearts of fathers toward their children [Note: [Col. 0051] Mal. 4]; and kindle them from strength to strength [Note: [Col. 0051] Ps. 83].

The receptacles for fire are the children themselves, who imitate the hearts of their fathers fervent in devotion and strive to kindle within themselves the flame of heavenly sacrifice which they behold in the minds of their neighbours. All the vessels were of bronze, because the hearts of the saints obey steadfastly and instruct with a clear voice.

*Scutiae* are vessels of equal width at the bottom and at the mouth, made for warming. They are teachers who do not hide the treasure of the heart but bring forth from it things new and old [Note: [Col. 0051] Matt. 13]. Nor do they put the lamp [Col. 0052B] under a bushel, but upon the lampstand, so that it may give light to those in God’s house [Note: [Col. 0051] Matt. 5], that they may receive the light and warmth of the Holy Spirit.

*Amulae* are vessels for offering wine. They are preachers sharply rebuking those subject to them; judges judging rigorously; or anyone intoxicated by the grace of the Holy Spirit and intoxicating others. Hydriae are vessels for water: they are teachers who have drunk the water of saving wisdom and are filled with living waters [Note: [Col. 0051] Sir. 15]. A little mortar is the labour of penitents, by which they mortify their flesh, chastise the body, and reduce it to servitude [Note: [Col. 0051] 1 Cor. 9], crushing it with the pestle of fear. Solomon made ten lavers [Note: [Col. 0051] 3 Kgs. 7], that is, basins, besides the molten sea, that is, the greater laver. Each of the ten [Col. 0052C] held forty baths, but the larger held two thousand. In the ten lavers burnt offerings were washed; in the larger, the priests washed themselves. The greater laver is baptism, which is called a sea in remembrance of the Red Sea. Hence: “Our fathers were all under the cloud; all crossed the sea; and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” [Note: [Col. 0051] 1 Cor. 10]. In this all priests—that is, the elect, members of the priest Jesus Christ—are washed, when through its power they are cleansed from the stains of sins. It held two thousand baths [Note: [Col. 0051] 3 Kgs. 7], while, washing both peoples, it conveyed them to the perfection of the squared ten: in the present life, to a steadfast conscience not bent from the state of uprightness by any temptation; in the future, to the ten of life, in which no reprobation is found.

[Col. 0052D] The ten lavers are the Ten Commandments, or the baptized who keep the Ten Commandments. Thus each held forty baths because of the observance of the Decalogue and the Gospels, in which sacrifices are cleansed—that is, spirits are contrited and hearts humbled—that they may make a sweet savour to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0051] Num. 28]. For: “A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit; a broken and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” [Note: [Col. 0051] Ps. 50]. The ancients used trumpets, as is read in Numbers [Note: [Col. 0051] ch. 10], to gather the multitude, to fight, and to rejoice on feast days, but with a diversity [Col. 0053A] of sounds. They were malleable and of silver, and their use was so powerful in jubilation that at their sound Jericho fell [Note: [Col. 0053] Josh. 6]. These are the two Testaments, or the preachers by whom the people are summoned to the battle-line of faith, stirred to repentance and tearful compunction, invited to offer praise to the Lord, summoned to Mount Zion, to the holy city Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0053] Isa. 2], to the great multitude of angels [Note: [Col. 0053] Heb. 12], and to God’s future judgment. Observe that trumpets are sounded alike in adversity and prosperity, because every time is suited to the word of God. Hence: “I will bless the Lord at every time; his praise shall always be in my mouth” [Note: [Col. 0053] Ps. 33]. Yet the speech of teachers must be moderated and varied according to the character of hearers and times: [Col. 0053B] for at one time one must teach, at another pray, and at another sing [Note: [Col. 0053] Eccl. 3]. When giving milk to the multitude [Note: [Col. 0053] 1 Cor. 3], we speak simply; but among the perfect we speak wisdom openly [Note: [Col. 0053] 1 Cor. 2]. Nevertheless, let all things be done for edification [Note: [Col. 0053] 1 Cor. 14].

For what benefit is obscurity in reading which does not edify the hearer? We speak for nothing if those for whose sake we speak do not understand us. Therefore let the teacher, above all, teach truth rather than words [Note: [Col. 0053] Ibid.]. It is a remarkable natural disposition to love truth in words, and not the words themselves. What use is a golden key if it does not open? What harm is an iron one if it opens? We seek nothing except that what is closed be opened and what is hidden revealed. Yet sound words should preferably be chosen, because the trumpets are silver—that is, shining in their intention of speech. If such words are unavailable, even corrupt ones may be used, provided that the matter is taught and learned soundly. But because patience proves a perfect work [Note: [Col. 0053] Jas. 1], they are malleable, so that they may be enlarged by the blows of tribulations. In place of trumpets we now have bells, to announce in the morning the Lord’s mercy and his truth through the night [Note: [Col. 0053] Ps. 91], so that, as they sound at the canonical hours, they may make hearers of divine praise attentive, teachable, and well disposed. Bells are bronze vessels discovered at Nola in Campania. Hence larger vessels are called *campanae*, from the region of Campania; smaller ones *nolae*, from the city of Nola. They have a striker with a fastening, a piece of wood with a rope; when the priest pulls it and it is pulled, the bell is struck by its sounding striker. Although trumpets and bells [Col. 0053D] differ in kind, they have the same meaning. Bells are preachers, vessels of the Holy Spirit, strong and resonant. For the hardness of the metal signifies strength of mind. Hence the Lord says: “I have made your forehead harder than their foreheads” [Note: [Col. 0053] Ezek. 3].

The iron striker is the tongue, or the steadfastness of discourse, which strikes on either side when it resounds with both Testaments. The fastening is modulation, by which the tongue is controlled; but the bond by which the bell is joined to the wood is charity, by which the preacher is bound to the wood of the cross, according to the saying: “Far be it from me [Col. 0054A] to glory except in the cross of our Lord” [Note: [Col. 0053] Gal. 6]. For the wood is Christ’s Passion, set in our head—that is, in the mind—proclaimed by the prophets and made known through the apostles.

The rope is sacred Scripture, joined together from many sayings; or it is the bond of charity, extended even to the ground—that is, to the weak; or the preacher’s humility, by which he condescends for others. Hence the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0053] 2 Cor. 5]: “Whether we are beside ourselves or whether we condescend, it is for you.” At its end is placed a ring, signifying perseverance or the crown of reward. The priest pulls the rope downward when he descends from contemplation to the active life; it is drawn upward when, taught by Scripture, he is raised into contemplation. Or he pulls it downward when he understands Scripture according to the letter, which kills [Note: [Col. 0053] 2 Cor. 3]; it is drawn upward [Col. 0054B] when he expounds it spiritually. Or, according to Gregory: he pulls downward and is drawn upward when in it he measures how far he lies fallen among evil things and how far he advances toward doing good. The priest should not disdain this work, but be an imitator of the sons of Aaron, of whom it is said: “The sons of Aaron shall sound the trumpets” [Note: [Col. 0053] Num. 10]. Whoever recognizes that he owes the duty of preaching must not hold back from setting the bells in motion. At the drawing of the rope the bell sounds and the people are gathered, because the preacher is heard in the exposition of sacred Scripture and the people are united in the unity of faith and charity. Therefore, as the bell rings, so the watchman of Jerusalem set upon the watchtower must not be silent, according to the saying: “You who remind the Lord, give him no silence” [Note: [Col. 0053] Isa. 62]. And because preachers abound more frequently in the time of grace, for that reason on feast days, which belong to grace, bells ring more tumultuously and sound longer, [so that] sleepers and drunkards—“for those who sleep sleep at night, and those who are drunk are drunk at night” [Note: [Col. 0053] 1 Thess. 5]—may be compelled to rise for God’s praises. Thus the evangelical preacher should imitate at least the threefold ringing on a solemn day—morning, evening, and that sounded at the beginning of Mass—so as to preach, in season and out of season, the lamentations [Note: [Col. 0053] Ezek. 2] of the present life, the song of the future, and the woe of Gehenna. You may wonder that preachers, as stated above, are called by so many names: they are necessary for many ministries.

The ancients used standards and banners [Note: [Col. 0053] Num. 2] when moving camp; each person proceeded [Col. 0054D] in the camp under his own standard. Standards are the individual properties found in body or mind. For example, although we are all alike, each nevertheless has his own distinction—in face, voice, stature, clothing, or posture. The same is true in the mind: one person is gentle, another proud. Perhaps as great as the diversity of bodily appearance is the diversity in souls. Hence Solomon says: As faces differ from faces, so do human hearts. From the conjunction of these things there proceeds, as some say, that unique property by which Peter is distinguished from Paul, and which is called, by a coined word, “Paul-ness” (*Paulitas*) [Col. 0055A]. As there are universal signs of this sort in a human being, so, I think, there are gratuitous ones, namely the exercises of virtues. The elements are the same among the Greeks and among us, but the signs are not the same; the virtues are the same in all as dispositions, but not the same in exercise. Hence Abraham is commended for faith [Note: [Col. 0055] Gen. 15], Moses for gentleness [Note: [Col. 0055] Num. 12], and David for humility [Note: [Col. 0055] 2 Kgs. 6]. According to these and similar signs, each proceeds from the warfare and race-course of the camp to the homeland and the prize of eternal things [Note: [Col. 0055] 1 Cor. 9]. Hence those eminent in knowledge pass to the cherubim; those nourished by the love of God alone pass to the seraphim; and so with the remaining dwelling places. For as there are divisions of graces, activities, and ministries in the present life [Note: [Col. 0055] 1 Cor. 12], so there are different dwelling places in the kingdom [Col. 0055B] of God [Note: [Col. 0055] John 14].

Our standard and banner is the mystery of the holy cross. Hence: “He who stands as a standard for the peoples” [Note: [Col. 0055] Isa. 11], that is, the grace of God. Likewise:

> The royal banners advance;  
> the mystery of the cross shines forth.

The sign of the holy cross is raised in churches so that the king’s standard may be venerated by soldiers in his own house, as though in a royal city. It is also raised so that Christ’s Passion may be set before us. It is also raised so that each person, crucifying his own flesh, may imitate Christ [Note: [Col. 0055] Gal. 5]. The triumphal cross of Christ is placed in the middle of the Church both so that we may see the sign of victory publicly and so that we may love our Redeemer from the middle of our heart, he who “paved the middle with love for the daughters of Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0055] Song 3]. We use a banner together with the cross on altars in memory of the trophy [Col. 0055C] of our Lord Jesus Christ, because the Lord reigned from the wood [Note: [Col. 0055] Ps. 95]. For when life dies upon the wood, it rises in love. For the strong man bound the strong [Note: [Col. 0055] Luke 11] and plundered his goods.

The name and origin of the cup are drawn from both the Old and the New Testament. Hence Jeremiah: “Babylon, a golden cup, intoxicating the whole earth” [Note: [Col. 0055] Jer. 51]; David: “A cup in the Lord’s hand, full of pure wine mixed with dregs” [Note: [Col. 0055] Ps. 74]; and elsewhere: “I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0055] Ps. 115]. In the Gospel the Lord says: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” [Note: [Col. 0055] Matt. 20]. Likewise: “Taking the cup, he gave thanks” [Note: [Col. 0055] Matt. 26].

The cup ought to be of gold, silver, or tin, but not of bronze or brass, since the strength of the wine would [Col. 0055D] cause verdigris and vomiting; not of glass, because, being breakable, it would threaten spillage; nor of wood, because its body is porous and spongy and would absorb the blood. Mystically, the cup is the spirit of wisdom [Note: [Col. 0055] Sir. 15], which has been given to us according to the measure of faith [Note: [Col. 0055] Rom. 12]. For we know in part [Note: [Col. 0055] 1 Cor. 13]. Hence: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and my cup” [Note: [Col. 0055] Ps. 15].

The cup is also the Old Testament, containing in itself the pure wine of spiritual understanding and moral precepts, mixed with the dregs of the letter and bodily sacraments. Hence: “A cup in the Lord’s hand, full of pure wine mixed with dregs.” Although “the Lord has poured it from this into that” [Note: [Col. 0055] Ps. 74], that is, from Jew to Gentile, nevertheless the dregs of the letter have not been emptied out, but sinners of the earth—the Jews and Ebionites—drink them. There is also the wisdom of the world or of the flesh. “The wisdom of the world is foolishness with God” [Note: [Col. 0055] 1 Cor. 1]; “the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God” [Note: [Col. 0055] Rom. 8]. The first counsels empty things; the second pleasant things. By the first, to be wise is to deceive; [Col. 0056B] by the second, to be wise is to be mad. Hence: “Babylon, a golden cup” [Note: [Col. 0055] Jer. 51].

The cup is also suffering, as though a pleasing draught. Hence: “They went rejoicing from the presence of the council” [Note: [Col. 0055] Acts 5], because they suffered insults for the name of Jesus Christ. Or it is a measured draught, for God is faithful and will not permit us to be tempted beyond what we are able [Note: [Col. 0055] 1 Cor. 10]. Here it says: “I will take the cup of salvation” [Note: [Col. 0055] Ps. 115]; there: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” [Note: [Col. 0055] Matt. 20]; and again: “Taking the cup, he gave thanks” [Note: [Col. 0055] Matt. 26]. If it is golden, it signifies the treasures of wisdom hidden in Christ [Note: [Col. 0055] Col. 2]; if silver, it denotes freedom from guilt; if of tin, it suggests the likeness of guilt and punishment. For tin lies between silver and [Col. 0056C] lead. Though Christ’s flesh was not lead—that is, the flesh of a sinner—it was nevertheless like sinful flesh [Note: [Col. 0055] Rom. 8]; and although it was not silver—that is, passible on account of its own guilt—it was nevertheless like flesh passible on account of ours. For “he himself bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows” [Note: [Col. 0055] Isa. 53].

Evangelical books also are not undeservedly adorned with gold, silver, and precious stones: in them shine the gold of wisdom, the silver of eloquence and miracles, and precious stones—these are the golden chains studded with silver, belonging to the bride [Note: [Col. 0055] Song 1]. Nor should anyone say: “These could have been sold and given to the poor” [Note: [Col. 0055] Matt. 26], for such a person resembles Judas and opposes the woman who anointed with ointment. We do this not because naked bodies delight the Lord less than golden ones, but [Col. 0056D] because, when people willingly offer to God what they love, we overcome avarice through divine worship. Moreover, these are moral offices of divine devotion and signs of future glory.

# BOOK TWO. ON THE INSTITUTION, VESTMENTS, AND HABIT OF THE MINISTERS OF THE CHURCH

[Col. 0055]

# PROLOGUE

[Col. 0055D]

The most high Author of the universe reserved for himself certain things specially from the totality of its parts: from places, venerable places; from persons, clerics, monks [Col. 0057A] and nuns; from things, tithes and offerings; from times, solemn days. We have spoken of places; in the following section let us discuss persons [Note: [Col. 0057] 3 Kgs. 9; Num. 3; Deut. 26; Exod. 20].

# CHAPTER ONE. ON THE INSTITUTION AND HABIT OF ECCLESIASTICAL PERSONS

“Let a person regard us in this way: as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God” [Note: [Col. 0057] 1 Cor. 4]. For a clearer understanding of ecclesiastical persons, it should be known that three famous sects are recorded: those of the Gentiles, Hebrews, and Christians. The first is called a *secta* from *secare*, “to cut,” because it cuts—that is, separates us from God; the second and third from *sectari*, “to follow,” for the former enlightens and the latter saves and frees.

[Col. 0057B] The rites of Gentiles and Hebrews have been converted into the rite of Christians, and this is “the change of the right hand of the Most High” [Note: [Col. 0057] Ps. 76]. Christian persons, both secular and ecclesiastical, are derived from those two sects, namely Hebrew and Gentile. For among the Gentiles there was a diversity of persons: some belonged to the people—that is, were laypersons (*laos* means “people”)—or were secular, such as monarch, emperor, king, patrician, prefect, senator, duke, margrave, count, governor, tribune, centurion, decurion, four-man official, three-man official, praetor, quaestor, and court gatekeeper; others were devoted to the cults of gods, such as archflamens and flamens, so called from the thread worn upon their heads, that is, priests of both sexes. Others were assigned to studies, such as comedians, tragedians, and historiographers.

Likewise among the Hebrews there were [Col. 0057C] secular persons, such as kings and leaders, and beneath them chiliarchs, hecatontarchs, pentacontarchs, and decarchs—that is, commanders of thousands, [hundreds], fifties, and tens. For *chile* means “a thousand,” *echas* “a hundred,” *penta* “fifty,” and *decas* “ten.” Moses appointed these at the counsel of Jethro, his father-in-law [Note: [Col. 0057] Exod. 18]. Those devoted to divine worship were the high priest, lesser priests, Levites, Nethinim, trimmers, exorcists, gatekeepers, singers, and *arditui* [uncertain term; Note: [Col. 0057] Exod. 28; Num. 18; 1 Chr. 6]. Moses also established these; David and Solomon, however, ordered some of them at the Lord’s command. Likewise among Christians there are many persons, who, so far as their names go, are almost the same as those among the Gentiles devoted to divine worship: clerics and monks.

Clerics are called from *cleros*, meaning “lot,” for in the Old Testament priests were chosen by lot [Note: [Col. 0057] Lev. 16], and Matthias was chosen by lot [Note: [Col. 0057] Acts 1]. For the Gentiles chose by lot one of their children for divine worship. Or clerics are so called because they receive the Lord’s lot—that is, inheritance—such as tithes, firstfruits, and offerings. For *cleros* also means “inheritance.” Or one is called a cleric because the Lord has chosen him as his lot, or because he himself has chosen the Lord, according to the saying: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” [Note: [Col. 0057] Ps. 15].
