Hence, at the [Col. 0058A] tonsure of clerics we use these words: “Therefore, whoever is the Lord’s portion, or has the Lord as his portion, should have nothing, as Jerome says, besides the Lord; but should so present himself that he may possess the Lord, or be possessed by the Lord; and then he shall receive blessing from the Lord and shall be the generation of those who seek the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0057] Ps. 23], as we are accustomed to say in the same tonsure.

Clerical tonsure took its beginning from the practice of the Nazirite, who, by the Law’s command, shaved his hair and burned it as a sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0057] Num. 6]. Nazirites are called “holy”; and thus they taught that ministers of the Church ought to be shorn, so that, with superfluous thoughts excluded from the mind and themselves inflamed with the fires of divine love, they may serve the Holy of Holies in holiness [Note: [Col. 0057] Luke 1]. Or, in another way, tonsure derives an occasion from the Law.

[Col. 0058B] The priests of the Law wore on the head a tiara—that is, a small cap of fine linen in the shape of a hemisphere [Note: [Col. 0057] Exod. 28]—while the king wore a crown. Thus the shaved part of the head signifies the tiara, and the circle of hair signifies the crown, so that we may understand and give thanks that God has established us as an elect race and royal priesthood [Note: [Col. 0057] 1 Pet. 2]. Or, again, it derives from the Law, where a crown four fingers high above the table, and above it a small crown, is commanded to be made [Note: [Col. 0057] Exod. 25]. Thus by the circle of hair a crown, and by the bald surface a little crown, is represented, so that we may hope that through the teaching of sacred Scripture, and especially of the four Gospels, we shall merit not only the sweetness of eternal life for the soul but also glorification for the body.

Or clerical tonsure and shaving, as we use them according to our custom, took their origin from Christ. [Col. 0058C] For Christ our king wore a crown of thorns [Note: [Col. 0057] Matt. 27; Mark 15; John 19] in order to remove the thorns and briers of our sins; and, about to offer himself upon the altar of the cross, he endured baldness. For among the ancients it was customary to shave the heads of captives whom they wished to crucify. Hence too the place where the Lord was crucified was called Calvary [Note: [Col. 0057] Ibid.]. And therefore he is called “made bald,” not because he was actually shaved, but because he suffered at Calvary. Hence he was prefigured by Korah, whose name means “bald,” by Elisha, to whom fools said, “Go up, baldhead” [Note: [Col. 0057] 4 Kgs. 2], and by Samson, whose head Delilah shaved [Note: [Col. 0057] Judg. 16]—that is, whom the Synagogue, devoid of understanding, crucified at Calvary. We, therefore, the sons of Korah, are made bald above when we are shorn; and thus through the circle of hair and the bare [Col. 0058D] surface of the shaving we recall Christ’s Passion, in which we ought to glory and which we ought to imitate.

The shaving is called a crown because Christ’s baldness was our victory. Hence: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0057] Gal. 6]. Yet this glory, what it shall be, has not yet appeared [Note: [Col. 0057] 1 John 3]; for it still bears a sign of sadness until sadness is turned into joy [Note: [Col. 0057] John 16]. Or it derives from Peter, as is found on Bede’s authority in his History of the English. He says that no tonsure ought to be embraced more than that [Col. 0059A] which he wore on his head, to whom the Lord said when he confessed him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church” [Note: [Col. 0059] Matt. 16]; and none more detestable than that worn by the one to whom Peter said, when he wished to purchase the grace of the Holy Spirit: “May your money perish with you” [Note: [Col. 0059] Acts 8].

For Peter, captured by Gentiles, had his beard shaved and his head made bald; but what they had done in mockery, he wished to be observed as a mystery: namely, either of the aforementioned divine Passion or of the moral meaning which ought also to be within us. For by the head the mind is understood, which is adorned with thoughts just as the head is adorned with hair. It ought to be shaved of superfluous thoughts by the razor of the fear of God, so that with the face of the heart laid bare it may be able to contemplate heavenly things. The circle of hair is the adornment [Col. 0059B] of virtues. The hairs are made equal in the circle because virtues are perfected in the concord of charity, so that the cleric may be strong in himself, wholly smooth and round; for among figures nothing agrees more with itself and is more harmonious from every side than a circle.

The upper part is shaved and the circle is left on the lower part so that reason may freely contemplate the things of God, while sensuality may be brought into harmony and, not dissenting from reason, may necessarily meditate on the things of the world. Hair must remain, because it is sometimes fitting to think about temporal matters without which life cannot be conducted, provided that they do not hinder the ears and eyes, lest secular thoughts draw the ears and eyes of the mind toward secular things, which are accustomed to choke [Col. 0059C] the word of the sower [Note: [Col. 0059] Luke 8]. Or we bear reproaches upon the head so that in this outward sign we may appear to await the crown of eternal life which God promised to those who love him [Note: [Col. 0059] Jas. 1].

We shave the beard so that we may appear as children; if we imitate their humility and innocence, we shall eat a meal with the Lord and enter the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 0059] Matt. 18], and shall be made equal to the angels, who always flourish again in youthful age. But during fasts we permit hair and beard to grow, so that we may represent the habit of penitents; or so that we may not condemn active thoughts which do not oppose God, such as building churches and similar things; or because, according to Gregory, by a life of great continence we signify presumptuous thoughts growing luxuriantly. Finally, there is no great need to inquire whence our form of tonsure [Col. 0059D] derived its origin, since we know that this practice has been rationally established. There are many things whose authors the present Church does not know, but which it approves by custom.

Clerics who are to be tonsured, or have just been tonsured, should wear copes and stoles in divine services, and albs, and sometimes woollen garments closed and slit. The cope seems derived from the chasuble; through it, therefore, as through the chasuble, we are admonished to remain in works of charity and to teach charity by word and example.

The stole, or cotta, or surplice, is a white garment formed in the shape of a cross. Its whiteness represents [Col. 0060A] purity, or rather the new glory of the saints and the angelic life; its form represents the aforesaid Passion. Note that on non-festal days we use black copes, in order that we may be like the black, raised fronds of palm trees, like a raven: that we may cleave to the head, direct our minds to heaven, and confess with humble conscience the blackness of our sins. On feast days we use white robes, signifying that we shall clothe the daily blackness of saving righteousness with the brightness of future joy. For the children of the Bridegroom cannot mourn while the Bridegroom is with them [Note: [Col. 0059] Matt. 9; Mark 2; Luke 5]. The garments are unseamed, white, reaching to the ankles, and loose, having one or two tongues. They are white because they signify purity of life; loose because they signify abundance of good works; ankle-length because they signify perseverance to the end. This [Col. 0060B] is Joseph’s ankle-length tunic [Note: [Col. 0059] Gen. 37], action completed at the end of life. Those who wish to please God in holiness and sanctification should use these garments.

The seamless tunic of the Lord is said [Note: [Col. 0059] John 19] to have had a tongue. The tongue of the garment is the teacher’s speech. If there are two, they signify the two Testaments, in which teachers ought to be skilled; or the two commandments of charity, that they may love the Lord and their neighbour [Note: [Col. 0059] Matt. 22]; or, in priests, the twofold power of binding and loosing [Note: [Col. 0059] Matt. 18; John 20].

A woollen tunic signifies the harshness of penance, or humility, or the virtue of patience. It ought to be circular and closed, not slit, lest the wind—that is, the vice of arrogance—creep in. Clerics ought not to bear arms, because they ought to fight not human beings but demons, [Col. 0060C] just as Moses fought Amalek not with weapons but with prayers [Note: [Col. 0059] Exod. 17.]; and just as the apostles taught us not to resist with arms, but rather to suffer injury [Note: [Col. 0059] Acts 5.]. Therefore we must not misuse lay clothing, just as laypeople may not usurp clerical office and therefore ought not to put on clerical garments. Lay clothing, however, ought to be close-fitting and slit, so that laypeople may be unencumbered for battle and protect the Church from heretics and pagans. Let us therefore observe this dress, so that we may appear not as laypeople but as ministers of the Lord—that is, as clerics.

Monks are called solitary and sorrowful, from *monos*, “one,” and *chaos*, interpreted as “sorrow.” When they receive the habit of humility, they bind themselves to obedience, chastity, a prescribed manner of dress, and renunciation of possessions. [Col. 0060D] These belong to the substance of the vow; the rest—fasting, the office, silence, and similar matters—are adjuncts. Thereupon we clothe them in the cowl, with prayers appointed for this purpose: that they may put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new [Note: [Col. 0059] Eph. 4.], who is created according to God.

The monks’ cowl derives from the apostles’ *collobia*, which were made in the form of a dalmatic and bore upon them the form of a cross, because they crucified themselves with their vices and desires [Note: [Col. 0059] Gal. 5.]. Its blackness is contempt for the world; its length, perseverance in goodness. Among nuns, however, the blackness of the garment signifies contempt for [Col. 0061A] the embrace of a man; the veil is a sign of modesty and of future honour. At weddings, maidens veil their heads: just as Rebekah veiled herself when she saw Isaac [Note: [Col. 0061] Gen. 24.], so the bride of Christ veils herself, in order that she may appear forbidden to all men. For this reason the crown of life is laid up for her [Note: [Col. 0061] II Tim. 4.].

With these garments the blessed Virgin is depicted, she who was mistress of both ways of life: of the active life, because she was married; of the contemplative life, because she was clothed in garments of low esteem. Hence on her feast the Gospel of Mary and Martha is read [Note: [Col. 0061] Luke 10.]. For widows too, a humble dress is contempt for the world. Under the name “monks” we understand converts, hermits, and hospitallers of both sexes. All take on the habit of humility, although not every one of the foregoing practices is observed by all.

That monks and nuns of certain orders wear white garments [Col. 0061B] derives, in the case of women, from blessed Cecilia, who, while she shone outwardly in her clothing, gleamed inwardly in chastity. For a white garment signifies a vow of virginity. In men it derives from the angels, who were seen at the Lord’s resurrection in white garments [Note: [Col. 0061] Mark 16.]; their whiteness signifies the splendour of future glorification.

## CHAPTER II. ON ORDERS

> “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob” [Note: [Col. 0061] Ps. 23].

Some ecclesiastical persons, therefore, have a simple status; others hold an office in God’s Church. For they possess either only the habit of religious life, as monks do; or an order, as [Col. 0061C] clerics do; or, together with a habit or order, a dignity, as abbots and bishops do. There are seven orders: doorkeeper, reader, exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, deacon, and priest. They are seven on account of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0061] Isa. 11.], by whose gift they perform their offices.

If you wish to assign individual gifts to the individual orders, beginning with fear, you will assign it to the doorkeepers; then, assigning each gift in turn to each order, you will fit wisdom to priests. These are the seven women in whom the Holy Spirit has his dwelling, and for each of whom he prepares her own banquet [Note: [Col. 0061] Isa. 4.].

When someone is advanced gradually through these grades, this sequence is generally to be observed: first they are called; second, instructed concerning their duties; third, ordained; fourth, blessed. [Col. 0061D] All these are matters of solemnity except ordination, which consists in words and things; these we shall treat as the substance of the sacrament.

Doorkeepers hold the place of gatekeepers or temple-wardens, who guarded the temple or sanctuary, as Samuel did [Note: [Col. 0061] I Sam. 2.]. Of them it is said in Chronicles: “At the four winds were the doorkeepers” [Note: [Col. 0061] I Chron. 9.]. When a doorkeeper is ordained, the bishop hands him the keys of the church, saying: “Act in such a way as one who must render an account to God for the things unlocked by these keys.” The keys, then, and these words are the substance of this sacrament. “Things” means the treasures and persons of the church. For [Col. 0062A] the doorkeeper must guard the books, bells, and everything within the church; he must hold the book for preachers and readers, ring the signal, close and open the church, receive the faithful, expel the excommunicated and unbelievers, admit and exclude catechumens, and bring into the bosom of their mother those penitents whom the bishop has reconciled.

Readers hold the place of singers who resounded Solomon’s songs, such as Asaph and Jeduthun. When they are ordained, the bishop hands them the book of prophecies, saying: “Receive it, and be a herald of God’s word; if you faithfully and humbly fulfil your office, you shall have a share with those who have ministered the word of God.” The book, therefore, and these words are the substance of this sacrament. Their office is to read distinctly, to pronounce the lessons in [Col. 0062B] church, and to preach to the people what the prophets foretold. The preliminary instruction that he read distinctly is thought to have been taken from Ezra, of whom it is said [Note: [Col. 0061] II Esdr. 8.] that he read the law distinctly and clearly to the assembled people. It is also his office to bless bread and all new fruits. Hence, in some regions it is customary for boys to bless tables and the readings of prelates.

Those are called, and formerly were called, exorcists who adjured demons and expelled them from possessed bodies, as Josephus relates concerning Eleazar the exorcist. When such a man is ordained, the bishop hands him a book of exorcisms, saying: “Receive it, commit it to memory, and have authority to lay your hand upon an energumen—whether baptized or catechumen.” The book, therefore, and these words are the substance of this sacrament.

An *energumen* means a possessed person: *en*, “in”; *erga*, “labour”; *menon*, “defect”; *noos*, “mind.” Hence an energumen is one so besieged by demons that he suffers a defect of mind. This occurs not only through bodily affliction, but also when someone, through sin, is a member of the devil and a dwelling-place of a demon. The exorcist’s duty, therefore, is to retain this exorcism by heart: “I adjure you, unclean spirit, by God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, to depart from this servant of God”; and by exorcisms—that is, adjurations—to prohibit demons from the bodies of catechumens, and to drive demons away from possessed persons, whether baptized or about to be baptized. Such men, therefore, ought to have a clean spirit, [Col. 0062D] since they must command unclean spirits.

Acolytes hold the place of wick-trimmers or lamp-tenders, who trimmed lamps and kindled lights [Note: [Col. 0061] Lev. 24.], such as Nadab and Abihu. When an acolyte is ordained, the bishop hands him a candlestick with a candle, saying: “Receive the candlestick with the candle, that you may know that you are appointed to kindle the lights.” He likewise hands him an empty wine-cruet, saying: “Receive the cruet for presenting wine, that is, the Eucharist of Christ’s blood.” These vessels, therefore, and these words are the substance of this sacrament.

*Acolyte* in Greek is called *ceroferarius* in Latin, “candle-bearer.” His duties include preparing the lights [Col. 0063A] in the sacristy; carrying candles and censers for adorning the altar and vesting the priest; clothing him with pallia and vestments; and supplying the subdeacon with wine and water for the Eucharist.

There follows the treatment of sacred orders, in which a more searching examination is required. The archdeacon presents the candidate; the bishop examines him. The archdeacon testifies; the people are put under adjuration; prayers are offered by the people for those to be consecrated. Then, in the prescribed order, they are called and instructed; afterwards they are ordained and blessed. And, as we have said, all are matters of solemnity except ordination, which consists in words and things, and these we shall discuss as the substance of the sacraments.

Those who are now called subdeacons were formerly called *nathinaei* [Note: [Col. 0063] I Chron. 6.], that is, “those who serve humbly,” [Col. 0063B] because they received the sacrifices from the people and supplied what was needed in the temple, as Nathanael did. Concerning them Ezra says: “Each dwelt in his own cities: the priests, Levites, and nathinaei” [Note: [Col. 0063] II Esdr. 11.]. They are called *hypodiacones* in Greek and subdeacons in Latin.

When he is ordained, he receives from the bishop an empty chalice and paten, and from the archdeacon a cruet with water, a basin, and a hand-towel. The bishop says to him: “See whose ministry is entrusted to you.” The latter articles are rightly received from the archdeacon, since subdeacons are consecrated to assist him. Afterwards the bishop gives him the maniple, saying: “Receive your maniple and fulfil your ministry; for God is able [Note: [Col. 0063] II Cor. 9.] to increase grace in you.” These vessels, therefore, and these words are the substance of this sacrament.

The bishop also gives [Col. 0063C] him a tunic, saying: “May the Lord clothe you with the tunic of gladness and the garment of joy.” This garment and these words pertain to solemnity, not substance, since the subdeacon’s ministry is performed without it. His duty, therefore, is to read the Epistle and minister to the deacon: namely, to give him the corporal cloth, carry the paten with the offerings, the chalice with wine, and the cruet with water; supply water to priests and Levites at the altar; and hold the hand-towel and water-basin. Therefore the rule of continence is imposed upon them, according to the saying, “Be clean, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0063] Isa. 52.]. And it appears that to this order first a garment—namely the *mapula*, as though a *manipula*—is given, by which penance is understood. Hence none but a penitent should approach the subdiaconate.

Those who are now called deacons—that is, ministers—were formerly called Levites, from Levi the son of Jacob; that is, “chosen,” because they were chosen to assist the priests, like Eleazar and Ithamar [Note: [Col. 0063] Num. 20.]. [Col. 0063D] This order was confirmed by the apostles, since they chose seven men full of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0063] Acts 6.]. These are the seven angels of the seven Churches [Note: [Col. 0063] Apoc. 8.], the seven golden lampstands [Note: [Col. 0063] Apoc. 1.], and likewise the seven thunders [Note: [Col. 0063] Apoc. 10.], because they preached the word of the Lord and enlightened the hearers whom they threatened.

When a deacon is ordained, the bishop lays his hands upon him. We wholly reject, therefore, the assertion that the bishop alone ought to lay on hands because deacons are consecrated not to priesthood but to ministry. Can one bishop pray more effectively by himself than several apostles? Those who lay on hands do not give the Spirit, but pray that he may come upon them. Since the use of all gifts is not in one person but in many, several rightly lay on hands, so that each may beseech the Lord to grant the ordinand a share in the Holy Spirit, after the example of Moses, from whose spirit the Lord gave to seventy men [Note: [Col. 0063] Num. 11.].

Afterward the bishop gives him a stole over the left shoulder, saying: “Receive the white stole from the hand of the Lord,” etc. Then, that he may understand himself to be Christ’s herald, he hands him the Gospel, saying: “Receive authority to read the Gospel in the church, both [Col. 0064B] for the living and for the dead, in the name of the Lord.” This object and these words are the substance of the sacrament. A dalmatic, if it is given to him, belongs to solemnity and not to substance.

Observe that the stole signifies obedience, or the Lord’s yoke expressed in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0063] Matt. 11.], and therefore it is given with the Gospel. It is laid upon the left shoulder alone, either because obedience to the Gospel is first undertaken in the active life; or because it teaches temporal matters to be subdued and spiritual things to be served; or because the deacon ought to keep his right hand free in order to run more readily to priestly ministry. For his duty is to guard the church and its furnishings, as Numbers says [Note: [Col. 0063] ch. 18.]: “And, when necessary, to carry the curtains and vessels.” Hence I think that the guardians ought to be deacons.

Again, [Col. 0064C] the deacon’s duty is to assist priests and minister in the Church’s sacraments: in baptism, chrism, paten, and chalice; to present offerings and arrange them upon the altar; distribute the blood; prepare the table; and carry the cross. Therefore he wears a dalmatic bearing the form of a cross, by which Christ’s passion is signified. He pronounces the prayers—that is, the litanies—recites the names of those to be ordained, catechumens, excommunicated persons, and successors, and reads the Gospel. For when the Lord preached the Gospel he was a minister; therefore the Gospel is assigned especially to the deacon, because “deacon” means minister.

Formerly the deacon read the lessons, when the Gospel had not yet been written; but after [Col. 0064D] it was established that the deacon should read the Gospel, it was added that the subdeacon should read the Epistles and lessons. Insofar as these are lower in dignity than the Gospel, so much lower is the subdeacon. The deacon himself, when necessary, also preaches and baptizes. He bids the people pray, saying: “Let us bend the knee.” He bids them attend to the Lord, saying: “Humble yourselves for the blessing,” or “Bow your heads to God.” He dismisses the people, saying: “Go, the dismissal has been made.” He exhorts them to cry out to the Lord; he announces solemn days and fasts.

Those now called presbyters were formerly called princes of the people, such as Korah, Dathan, and Abiram; or magistrates or teachers of the temple, such as Nicodemus [Note: [Col. 0063] John 3.] and [Col. 0065A] Gamaliel [Note: [Col. 0065] Acts 5.]. They are now called presbyters—that is, elders—not because of age but because of understanding. “The gray hairs of a person are understanding” [Note: [Col. 0065] Wis. 4.]. Or they are *presbyteri*, as though “providing a way,” because they furnish the people a way from the exile of this world to the homeland of the kingdom. Or they are priests, that is, sacred leaders, as Bede says, because they provide leadership to the people; or “givers of sacred things,” because they give sacraments to the people and sacrifices to God.

Priests are successors of the seventy men to whom the Lord imparted Moses’ spirit [Note: [Col. 0065] Num. 11.], and of the seventy-two disciples [Note: [Col. 0065] Luke 10.], just as bishops are representatives of Moses and the apostles. When a priest is ordained, he is to be approved by the testimony of deacons and priests concerning his character, his future conduct, and his obedience; then the blessing hand of the priests present is laid upon him.

[Col. 0065B] The laying on of hands signifies the exercise of works of the Holy Spirit. For by the head we understand the mind; by the fingers, the gifts of the Holy Spirit; and by the hand, works. Therefore a finger or hand is laid upon the head of one who, with a mind imbued with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, imitates Christ’s works. Hands are laid on by several priests for the reason previously stated in the case of the deacon. But since hands are laid on the deacon, why are hands laid on the priest again? I answer: because he is transferred from ministry to ministry and from work to work.

The bishop then folds his orarium over his right shoulder in the form of a cross upon his breast, saying: “Receive the yoke of the Lord; for his yoke is sweet and his burden light” [Note: [Col. 0065] Matt. 11.]. The stole is folded [Col. 0065C] from the left shoulder to the right, because obedience, beginning in the active life through love of neighbour, passes into the contemplative life through love of God. Or it is because a priest must be armed on the right and on the left with the weapons of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0065] II Cor. 6.], bearing the cross upon his breast when he imitates in mind the passion of Christ, whose minister he is.

What some add—“May the Lord clothe you with the stole of innocence”—refers to the primitive stole, which signified innocence and of which this is the substitute, as will be explained below. The stole now in use is the stole of obedience.

Thereupon the bishop clothes him in a chasuble, saying: “Receive the priestly garment,” by which charity is understood; for God is able [Note: [Col. 0065] II Cor. 9.] to increase in you charity and a perfect work. This is the wedding garment [Col. 0065D] without which priests will be cast into outer darkness [Note: [Col. 0065] Matt. 22.].

Afterwards the bishop anoints both his hands with chrism, saying: “Deign, O Lord, by this anointing and our blessing, to consecrate and sanctify these hands, that whatever they consecrate may be consecrated,” etc. The hands are anointed so that they may be clean for offering victims for sins, and so that priests may imitate in works of mercy the footprints of the crucified Christ, from the consecrated Lord they receive the power to consecrate.

[Col. 0066A] Afterwards the bishop gives him a paten with offerings and a chalice with wine, saying: “Receive authority to offer sacrifice to God and to celebrate Masses for the living and the dead in the name of the Lord.” The stole and chasuble, oil, chalice and paten together, and these words are the substance of this sacrament; all that precedes and follows belongs to solemnity. His duty is to bless persons and things, celebrate Mass, distribute the Lord’s body, meditate upon God’s law, teach, preach, pray, baptize, bind or absolve penitents, anoint the sick, and bury the dead. Great power, wondrous dignity, lofty and fearsome office!

Observe that priests and deacons are especially named by the people, because they are foremost in the service of the altar. Hence, according to Ambrose, [Col. 0066B] their ordination especially is celebrated around the altars, and the bishop prostrates himself before the altar for them. The others to be ordained are not ordained at the altar, because they are not appointed to altar ministries: some fulfil the office of readings, others attend to the lights, and others prepare necessary things below the deacon. Yet all seek the face [Note: [Col. 0065] Ps. 104.]—that is, the presence—of God, that they may be able to inherit among the firstborn, after the example of Jacob, who claimed for himself his brother’s birthright [Note: [Col. 0065] Gen. 27.].

## CHAPTER III. FURTHER MORAL INTERPRETATIONS OF THE ORDERS

> “Whoever serves me, let him follow me” [Note: [Col. 0065] John 12].

Jesus [Col. 0066C] Christ expressed all the above-mentioned orders both in word and deed, and showed in himself the figure of all of them. He was a doorkeeper when, having made a whip of cords, he overturned the money-changers’ tables and drove sellers and buyers from the temple [Note: [Col. 0065] John 2.]; likewise when he called himself the door [Note: [Col. 0065] John 10.], and rightly so, because no one goes to the Father except through him [Note: [Col. 0065] John 14.]. For he is the doorkeeper “who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens” [Note: [Col. 0065] Apoc. 3.].

He was a reader when, in the midst of the elders, he opened the book of Isaiah, saying: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to proclaim to the poor” [Note: [Col. 0065] Luke 4; Isa. 61.]. He was an exorcist when he set demoniacs free and touched the ears of the deaf man and the tongue of the mute man with saliva, saying: “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened” [Note: [Col. 0065] Mark 7.]. He testifies that he is an acolyte when he says: “I am the light of the world” [Note: [Col. 0065] John 8.]. He performed the office of subdeacon [Col. 0066D] when he girded himself with a linen cloth, washed the disciples’ feet, and dried them with the linen cloth [Note: [Col. 0065] John 13.].

He represented the office of deacon when he distributed to his disciples the sacrament of body and blood, or when he awakened those asleep for prayer, saying: “Watch and pray” [Note: [Col. 0065] Matt. 26.]. He expressed the office of priest when he changed bread into body and wine into blood, and when he offered himself upon the altar of the cross, priest and victim alike [Note: [Col. 0065] Matt. 27.]. Still glorious, he fulfils the office when, sitting at the Father’s right hand, he daily intercedes for us [Note: [Col. 0065] Heb. 1; Rom. 8.].

Since, therefore, the King of kings [Note: [Col. 0065] Apoc. 19.], the power of God and the wisdom of God [Col. 0067A] [Note: [Col. 0067] I Cor. 1.], whose power extends from sea to sea [Note: [Col. 0067] Ps. 71.], did not disdain to perform these offices, let no one, however noble, wise, rich, or powerful, disdain to minister in them. Let no office of any order seem lowly to one who aspires to the supreme pontificate; rather, when required, let him hasten eagerly outwardly to the offices, and lest he be found reprobate [Note: [Col. 0067] I Cor. 9.], let him fulfil morally in himself what he ministers to others by serving them.

Since the doorkeeper is the temple of God [Note: [Col. 0067] I Cor. 3.], he should open himself to virtues and to God, and close himself to vices and the devil, lest the way of life be obstructed and death enter through his windows [Note: [Col. 0067] Jer. 9.]. Everyone is also a spiritual doorkeeper when, through faith, he introduces the humble into the Church and reproves and expels the obstinate. For faith is the door through which we enter the sheepfold, because “the just lives by faith” [Note: [Col. 0067] Rom. 1.], [Col. 0067B] which the Apostle numbered among gifts of grace, saying: “To another, faith in the same Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0067] I Cor. 12.].

Let the reader fulfil in deeds the things that he declares to the people must be observed. Everyone is also a spiritual reader if he teaches some persons things conducive to life and, while teaching, “turns back the mouth of the turtledove toward the armpits” [Note: [Col. 0067] Lev. 5.], lest, while preaching to others, he incur the mark of reprobation. The Apostle included this ministry under the gift of knowledge; hence whoever is advanced to the grade of reader or preacher ought to be adorned with knowledge.

An exorcist commands demons authoritatively if he is not accused by the guilt of his conscience. Everyone is also a spiritual exorcist while by his prayers he frees others from the power of the demon and from the sickness of sins; the Apostle understood this gift [Col. 0067C] under the grace of healing. Just as the acolyte carries burning lamps in his hands [Note: [Col. 0067] Matt. 5.], so let his works shine before God and human beings. Everyone is also a spiritual acolyte when he supplies others with the light of good works, kindling in them the fire of charity by word or deed. We believe this gift belongs to prophecy. For prophets’ offices under the Lord are to foretell future things and explain the obscure meanings of Scripture, so that hearers may be enlightened and inflamed to love the Lord.

Subdeacons, while they receive clean vessels, should also receive the *mapula* and penance, so that they may present themselves clean for ministry and recognize themselves as vessels of the Lord. Everyone is also a spiritual subdeacon when by word or deed he washes away the faults of others. We may comprehend this gift [Col. 0067D] under the working of miracles or discernment of spirits.

Deacons, while they receive the stole, should recognize that they are bound to the law of the Lord, and through their free right hand know themselves to be unencumbered for ministering to the faithful. Everyone is also a spiritual deacon when he serves others in charity and teaches others by word or deed to pray. We may understand this gift under the interpretation of tongues.

Priests whose hands are anointed with chrism should restrain themselves from every impurity, so that they may worthily make the body of the Lord. Everyone is also a spiritual presbyter if he offers the sacrifice of a contrite spirit [Note: [Col. 0067] Ps. 50.] and if he offers [Col. 0068A] himself as a living sacrifice pleasing to God [Note: [Col. 0067] Rom. 12.]. For every saint is a priest, as Chrysostom says; we believe this should be ascribed to wisdom. Let us therefore minister to the Lord in these ways, that we may attain him.

## CHAPTER IV. ON DIGNITIES

> “You shall appoint them princes over all the earth” [Note: [Col. 0067] Ps. 44].

From what has been said, it is clear that orders derive their origin and examples from the Law; the institution of dignities likewise depends upon the Old Testament. At Jethro’s counsel, Moses established commanders of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens, who dealt with lesser matters and referred greater ones to Moses [Note: [Col. 0067] Exod. 18.]. Finally, seventy men were appointed, [Col. 0068B] who, receiving Moses’ spirit, were set over the people [Note: [Col. 0067] Num. 11.]. Their counterparts are the subdean and dean, sub-scholastic and scholastic, sub-chanter and chanter, treasurer, chief sacristan, keeper of treasures, *primicerius*, and steward or provost; archpriest and archdeacon; *vicedominus* and co-bishop; bishop, archbishop, primate, and patriarch.

Some nevertheless say that orders derive from the Law, while dignities take their form from pagan society. Thus the pope bears the likeness of a monarch, and the patriarch that of royal power. Accordingly, just as a king presides over three dukes, so a patriarch presides over three archbishops. Archbishops are compared to dukes, bishops to counts; hence certain archbishops are dukes and bishops are counts. [Col. 0068C] Co-bishops are compared to prefects, provosts to military tribunes, archpriests to centurions, and deans to decurions.

But whatever the source of the institution, it is clear that episcopal dignity presides over all. The dignity of bishops is divided into four: bishops, archbishops, primates, and patriarchs. “Bishop” is both a general and a particular name, and means “overseer”: for *epi* means “over,” and *scopos*, “one who looks,” because he sits on high as guardian of the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts [Note: [Col. 0067] Isa. 5.] and watches the conduct and life of every person. He is also called a watchman [Note: [Col. 0067] Ezek. 3.], because, placed as if on a watchtower, he watches for approaching enemies—the devil, the flesh, and the world, heretics and false brethren—and exhorts and strives to arm the citizens for resistance.

He is also called *praesul*, because he presides over counsel; and *antistes*, because, standing before others, he excels the people, or because he stands against them—for *anti* means “against”—since bishops confront heretics, so that shepherds may resist wolves and protect sheep. He is also called pontiff, as though “holy bridge,” for the bishop’s life ought to be a bridge for the people over the sea of this age to the homeland of paradise; or as one making a bridge, because by sound teaching he leads the people across the marshes of heresies to the courts of life. This is Aaron, the high priest in the Law.

When bishops are ordained, they are presented and examined on Saturday about their character and the state of their past life, while in the meantime a blessing is sought, in order that the holy [Col. 0069A] Trinity may be shown to preside over the ordination. In the morning they are examined concerning their future conversion, conduct, and faith. This examination derives from the constitution of the primitive Church because of persons suspected in faith, morals, or social condition.

Afterwards, two bishops hold the book of Gospels over his shoulders, as if praying and admonishing the ordinand that he should submit more than usual to the yoke and obey the Gospel. A third bishop pronounces the blessing. The presence of three bishops derives from the apostles, because James, the brother of the Lord, was ordained bishop of Jerusalem by Peter, James, and John. The reason is that so great a benefit may not seem to have been conferred secretly; moreover, “every word is established by the mouth of two or three witnesses” [Note: [Col. 0069] Deut. 17; Matt. 18; II Cor. 13.]. [Col. 0069B] Such men should therefore be summoned as rejoice in the ordinand’s progress and offer prayers for him.

Afterwards he anoints the head with chrism in the form of a cross, saying: “May your head be anointed and consecrated by heavenly blessing, in the pontifical order, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” In this anointing he is spiritually shown to be the representative of Jesus Christ, who was anointed with invisible oil [Note: [Col. 0069] Ps. 44; Heb. 1.], so that, as Christ was head of the universal Church [Note: [Col. 0069] Eph. 1 and 5; Col. 1.], this bishop may be head of the Church entrusted to him. Or, according to Gregory, oil upon the head is charity in the mind.

Then he anoints the hands in the form of a cross, saying: “May these hands be anointed with sanctified oil and the chrism of sanctification, as Samuel anointed David king and prophet [Note: [Col. 0069] I Sam. 16.], so may they be anointed and consecrated [Col. 0069C] in the name of God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit.” Afterwards he confirms the thumb; then gives the staff, then the ring, then the Gospel, so that the imposition upon the thumb may benefit all unto salvation; in the staff he may recognize the power of binding and loosing entrusted to him; in the ring he may fortify himself by integrity of faith. Likewise, with the staff of doctrine he will lead the flock to pasture; with the ring of faith he will entrust the hidden things of Scripture to the bride; in the Gospel he will know himself to be an apostle.

Each item is given with its proper words. Therefore the anointing of head and hands, confirmation of the thumb, delivery of staff and ring, and their respective words, are, in my opinion, the substance of this sacrament; the rest belongs to solemnity. Chrismal anointing began with the Law, where by the Lord’s command kings, priests, [Col. 0069D] and prophets are recorded as having been anointed [Note: [Col. 0069] I Sam. 10; Exod. 29; III Kings 19.]. For Leviticus says [Note: [Col. 0069] ch. 21.] concerning the pontiff: “Upon whose head the oil of anointing has been poured, and whose hands have been consecrated in the priesthood.”

The laying on of hands began with Isaac, who laid his hand upon Jacob while blessing him [Note: [Col. 0069] Gen. 27.]; and Moses laid his hand upon Joshua when he appointed him leader over the people [Note: [Col. 0069] Deut. 31.]. The Lord also laid his hand upon the apostles when he made them princes of the world [Note: [Col. 0069] Luke 24.]; and the apostles themselves, through laying on of hands, [Col. 0070A] gave the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0069] Acts 8.].

The consecrations of bishops ought to be celebrated on Sundays and at the third hour, for on such a day and at such an hour the apostles were consecrated by the Holy Spirit with invisible oil [Note: [Col. 0069] Acts 2.]. Oil gives light and heals wounds; so the Holy Spirit bestowed knowledge on the apostles and healed sins. Bishops are therefore anointed on this day and at this hour, that they may be taught that they receive the Holy Spirit given to the apostles. What Mass of consecration belongs to the pontifical order—the office of which plainly accords with consecration—let the diligent investigator determine.

The bishop’s office is to ordain priests and other ministers of the Church, veil virgins, confirm the baptized, consecrate chrism and oil, dedicate churches, excommunicate rebels, reconcile penitents, [Col. 0070B] and sanctify vestments and vessels. Observe that bishops too were formerly called presbyters, as many authorities demonstrate; but “presbyter” is a name of age, whereas “bishop” is a name of office. Afterwards, however, just as an archdeacon is chosen from deacons and a commander from an army, so one greater is selected from among priests. Thus the names were divided, so that the one who is greater in each city should be called bishop, as though [the representative of Christ. [Note: [Col. 0069] The passages enclosed here and below in brackets are presented as erased in the copy.]] [There is, however, one greater man chosen over the other priests, to whom the whole care of the Church belongs, so that the seeds of schisms may be removed from among them, lest anyone say, “I belong to Paul,” “I to Apollos” [Note: [Col. 0069] I Cor. 1.]. The aforesaid duties belong to him rather by custom, as Jerome [Col. 0070C] says, than by the truth of the Lord’s ordinance.]

An archbishop is called the chief of bishops; he is the same as a metropolitan, from the metropolis, the mother-city. He is Moses, who consecrated Aaron as pontiff with oil [Note: [Col. 0069] Exod. 29.]. There are also certain sees adorned with the title of primacy, from the firstfruits of conversion to the faith. Some of these, because primate and patriarch differ in name only and not in office, have claimed for themselves the title of patriarch, as Venice has done. A patriarch is called the father of the ark—that is, of the Church—or chief of the fathers.

[There are three of these, corresponding to three parts of the world: one in Asia, who held the episcopal see at Antioch; another at Alexandria, who held primacy in Africa; and a third in Europe, who holds the pontificate at Rome. Abraham, [Col. 0070D] Isaac, and Jacob prefigured them. These dignities were transferred elsewhere through favour or hostility: the Antiochene patriarchate to Jerusalem, the Alexandrian to Aquileia. For although Peter preached at Antioch and Mark at Alexandria, both places returned to the vomit of unbelief [Note: [Col. 0069] Prov. 26; II Pet. 2.] and were therefore deprived of patriarchal dignity. Jerusalem, however, is honoured because “from Zion went forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0069] Isa. 2.]. Aquileia likewise is honoured [Col. 0071A] because Mark first presided at Aquileia and afterwards at Alexandria. Concerning the Roman patriarchate, moreover, the ancients decided that, just as Augustus was held above kings, so the pope should be called by a special name above all bishops, and that the right and title of the patriarchate should be transferred to Constantinople.]

To archbishops, primates, and patriarchs, besides the aforesaid solemn consecration of bishops, are granted the insignia of a cross to be carried before them, so that they may recognize their duty to imitate the Crucified One. They are also granted the insignia of the pallium, that they may be crowned with the wreath of victory. Yet the pallium will be explained more fully below.

The office of archbishops is to consecrate bishops, that of patriarchs to consecrate archbishops, and that of both to assemble councils and restore rights that have fallen into abeyance. [Col. 0071B] The pope is called “Father of fathers”; he is also called universal, because he presides over the whole Church. He is also called apostolic, because he performs the office of the Prince of the Apostles. He is called supreme pontiff because he is the head of all pontiffs: as members proceed from a head, so all receive from his fullness; yet he calls them to share his solicitude, not the fullness of his power. He is Melchizedek, whose priesthood is not comparable with the others. [Note: [Col. 0071] Gen. 14; Heb. 7.] When a pope is ordained, his name is changed, because the Lord changed Peter’s name when placing him over the Church [Note: [Col. 0071] John 1.], and Paul was made Paul from Saul. [Note: [Col. 0071] Acts 9.] Seven candle-stands, as though representing the gifts of the Holy Spirit, precede him; to him [Col. 0071C] the keys are handed over, because Christ gave Peter the keys of the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 0071] Matt. 16.], so that he might know himself to be the gatekeeper of heaven. A red mantle is bestowed on him, by which charity or martyrdom is signified—martyrdom for which he must always be ready on behalf of the sheep. [Note: [Col. 0071] John 10.] His office is to order Masses and other offices, establish canons, consecrate the emperor, give pallia to patriarchs and archbishops and privileges to all religious persons, and govern the whole Church.

Abbots too are blessed in this manner. First, one is chosen by the community, confirmed by the bishop, and publicly announced in the ambo for the assent of all. Secondly, with the pontiff and the elect lying prostrate before the altar, the litanies and the Lord’s Prayer are performed. Thirdly, the pontiff alone rises and says over the elect the prayers and orations appointed [Col. 0071D] for this purpose. Finally, he hands him the Rule transmitted to us by the holy Fathers. Afterwards he gives him a staff, saying: “Receive the staff of the pastoral office, that in correcting vices you may be mercifully severe; and when you are angry, remember mercy.” [Note: [Col. 0071] Tob. 3.] The blessing of an abbess is similar, except that a special blessing is poured out over her. Virgins ought not to be veiled except on the days of Epiphany, in the white days of Easter, or on the feasts of the Apostles, unless they are prevented by grave illness. This is so that the Holy Spirit may seem to descend upon them as upon those simple as doves; and so that, through the apostles—who first handed down to the Church the practice of virginity—they may be consecrated to the Lord as brides, as though through bridegrooms’ friends; they who breathe forth the life and manner of living of the apostles, [Col. 0072A] indeed of angels also. The emperor too is consecrated—or rather anointed and crowned—following David, whom Samuel anointed king. [Note: [Col. 0071] 1 Sam. 16.] He is consecrated in this manner: first he pledges fidelity to the holy Roman Church; second, prayers are said over him; third, the bishop of Porto anoints his right arm and between his shoulders, reciting prayers. Fourth, the supreme pontiff places the diadem upon him, saying: “Receive the sign of glory, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” His office is to protect the Church of Christ, make laws, and preserve justice, so that he may attain eternal fullness.

## Chapter V. On Sacred Vestments

[Col. 0072B]

> “He shall make holy garments for Aaron and for his sons.” [Note: [Col. 0071] Exod. 28.]

The sacred vestments and the insignia of the aforesaid dignities must be treated more fully. Sacred vestments seem to have been taken from the old Law; for the Lord commanded Moses to make holy garments for Aaron and his sons, for glory and beauty. Yet some are taken from the holy apostles. Both these and those signify virtues, works of righteousness, or the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation. Since bishops wear all the garments worn by the other ministers, though not conversely, let us speak of the bishop’s vestments, so that particulars may be included under generalities.

[Col. 0072C] Thus silk stockings signify that purity and washing of the feet concerning which the Lord said: “He who has washed is wholly clean and has no need except to wash his feet.” [Note: [Col. 0071] John 13.] But because purity of heart is not sufficient without patience in persecution, red cloth wrappings follow, signifying martyrdom. Whoever has purity in heart and, should occasion require, patience in will may safely proceed to apostolic preaching, signified by the sandals. Sandals are called from the herb *sandaraca*, or from the vermilion (*sandaricus*) colour with which they are painted. They are a type of footwear by which the foot is partly covered below and partly left bare above, made from the skins of dead animals, white within and black or red without, woven with many threads and lines, adorned with gems, [Col. 0072D] and perhaps having four straps, or at least two for fastening: one over the foot and another rising from the heel.

Footwear did not begin with Aaron, who lived only in Judaea and therefore did not need it, but with the apostles, to whom it was said: “Go, teach all nations.” [Note: [Col. 0071] Matt. 28.] They therefore used this kind of footwear, which bishops also ought to use—but not priests—so that the variety of sandals may mark the variety of ministers. Bishops must travel through their parishes to govern the people; consequently they have sandals tied to their feet, lest they slip off. From this [Col. 0073A] one may understand how necessary it is for bishops to make firm the steps of the mind. Priests are to offer sacrifices at home; and therefore, since they walk securely, they have no fastening on their feet. The deacon has one, because it belongs to him to go in attendance.

Mystically, this is the preaching of the apostles: by the letter it is covered for carnal persons; by allegory it is uncovered for those seeking heavenly things; or it is partly bare and partly covered, because the preacher ought neither to conceal heavenly things nor to crave earthly ones in any way. He sets before them the examples of the saints who went before: their conscience, or life, was white in purity before God, black—that is, lowly in humility—before human beings; or red, that is, inflamed with charity. The many threads are many sayings. The three lines are Law, prophecy, and Gospel; [Col. 0073B] the outer lines signify the Law and prophecy, while the middle one signifies the Gospel. The two lines are folded back toward the middle because Law and prophecy are recapitulated in the Gospel. The gems are works of virtue. The four straps are the teaching of the Testaments, teaching us to rise from earthly things, not cling to them, and lift ourselves toward heavenly things. Or the straps, separated from the leather of the sandals, are the tongues of persons who give good testimony by their preaching, though separated from the manner of life of spiritual persons: for they must have a good testimony from those who are outside. [Note: [Col. 0073] 1 Tim. 3.] The fastening is the mystery of the Incarnation; the multiplication of fastenings is the superabundance of preaching. That it is loosened, but not wholly, indicates that we are not worthy—that is, not sufficient—[Col. 0073C] to untie the straps of Christ’s sandals. [Note: [Col. 0073] John 1; Luke 3.] That the sandals are whole in some places and pierced in others signifies that heavenly sacraments are to be revealed to some and hidden from others.

The shoulder-garment, called the *ephod*, upon which were two stones bearing the names of the twelve patriarchs [Note: [Col. 0073] Exod. 39.], is among us called the amice (*amictus*). It is a white garment covering the head, neck, and shoulders, and its two bands gird the breasts of the chest, so that one edge is visible and the other hidden. It is hope of heavenly things, for the sake of which we consecrate to the Lord purity of mind and the discipline of speech and action. The head is the workshop of the mind, the neck the instrument of speech, and the shoulders the bearers of burdens. Thus we cover the head with the clean amice when, for hope of heavenly things, [Col. 0073D] setting a guard upon our mouth [Note: [Col. 0073] Ps. 38.], we utter nothing but the Lord’s praises. We cover the shoulders when, for hope of heavenly things, bearing one another’s burdens [Note: [Col. 0073] Gal. 6.], we undertake active labours and assist our neighbours in their needs.

The two edges of the shoulder-garment are charity, or faith and action. When these are fulfilled in the breast, faith and charity are hidden in the heart, but action appears in the performance of works. The two ribbons or bands are fear of punishment and desire for life; for the hope of blessedness they keep evil thoughts from the priest’s breast. Or, generally, the shoulder-garment signifies the priestly burden by which we are bound to sympathize with our neighbours from the heart, provide for them in mind, and bear burdens on our shoulders. Or the amice at once bears the type of the shoulder-garment and the breastpiece: through the shoulder-garment it pertains to righteousness, through the breastpiece to wisdom, and therefore it covers breast and shoulders. Or by the amice understand discipline of speech, for it covers the neck, the organ of speech; the restraint of thoughts, for it girds the breast; and the covering of the eyes’ gaze.

The alb, called in the Law the tunic or the talar garment, and among the Greeks the *poderis* (foot-length robe), is a white garment descending to the ankles, with a hood and a tongue-shaped flap, narrow in the middle and spreading at the end through many joins. It is the purity of chastity, the discipline of the body, with which the whole life of the priest must be adorned, to the end and perseveringly, so that he may imitate the ministers of the eternal King—[Col. 0074B] namely, angels—in white garments. The hood is the profession of chastity. The flap is the power of the priestly tongue, which binds the obstinate and, by absolving, reconciles penitents. [Note: [Col. 0073] Matt. 16, 18.] This chastity is constricted by worldly pressures amid a crooked and perverse nation [Note: [Col. 0073] Phil. 2.], but is expanded in charity as virtues multiply. It restrains hands and arms lest they become wanton, knees lest they grow slack in the constancy of prayer, and shins and feet lest they run to evil. This garment was once narrow because people had received the spirit of servitude; now it is broad because we have received the spirit of adoption and freedom. [Note: [Col. 0073] Rom. 8.]

The belt, called in the Law and among the Greeks the *baltheus*, girds the loins and holds the alb in place lest it slip down [Col. 0074C] and impede the step. It is the guarding of the mind, fear of the Lord, or continence, which restrains the lust of the flesh. It is placed at the loins because lust rules there. Hence: “Let your loins be girded,” [Note: [Col. 0073] Luke 12,] and of the devil it is said: “His strength is in his loins.” [Note: [Col. 0073] Job 40.] To gird the loins, then, is to restrain lustful impulses. It prevents chastity from straying by devious paths and from impeding the course of good works.

The sub-belt, called the *perizoma* or the cincture (*succinctorium*), which hangs double from the belt, signifies prayer and fasting, by which chastity is strengthened and without which it is difficult to preserve. Or by the sub-belt we understand the zeal of one who has mercy; therefore it is double, because each person ought first to have mercy upon his own soul, and then mercifully distribute necessities to neighbours. [Col. 0074D]

Formerly the stole was a white garment reaching to the feet. The patriarchs used it before the Law; firstborn sons put it on when receiving their father’s blessing, and offered victims to the Lord as pontiffs. But after the alb began to be worn, it was changed into a collar, called both stole and *orarium*. By the first stole we understand the innocence that was in the first man; but when he lost it through sin [Note: [Col. 0073] Gen. 3.], it had to be recovered through the fatted calf. [Note: [Col. 0073] Luke 15.] Blessed are those who keep this stole from the stain of crimes, or wash it when stained [Col. 0075A] with tears, for their power shall be in the tree of life [Note: [Col. 0075] Rev. 22]—that is, in Christ, through whom they shall possess the glory they lost. Yet it remains for us, who fell through disobedience, to rise through obedience.

Appropriately, in order to recover the garment of innocence, we take up the collar of obedience; for by the stole now in use we understand obedience to the Gospel. The Gospel indeed is the Lord’s sweet yoke and light burden, of which the Lord says: “Take my yoke upon you.” [Note: [Col. 0075] Matt. 11.] Obedience is a strap. Therefore, when the priest subjects his neck to the straps, he indicates that he patiently obeys the evangelical yoke. Hence it is moved from the left shoulder to the right, because through obedience one passes from action to contemplation. It is called an *orarium* because, although priests may baptize, impose penance, and perform similar acts without the other priestly garments, [Col. 0075B] they may not do so without the *orarium*, except under the compulsion of extreme necessity. It extends to the knees, which bend, so that our humility may thereby be shown. Some understand by the stole endurance in adversity and prosperity, and by its length perseverance. That the stole is gathered with the belt indicates that virtues are united with virtues.

The tunic in the Old Testament [Note: [Col. 0075] Exod. 39.] was wholly hyacinth-blue. It had above a woven opening all around and, down to the feet, forms like pomegranates with bells interspersed. Jerome says that it is called the *subucula*, an under-tunic proper to the pontiff; through it is understood the heavenly manner of life of the perfect, for heaven has a hyacinth-blue colour. The Apostle was clothed with this tunic when he said: “Our manner of life is in heaven.” [Note: [Col. 0075] Phil. 3.] Or, as a stone of that colour changes its colour according to the condition of the air—for it is bright in clear weather and pale in cloud—so it is fitting for a bishop to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep. [Note: [Col. 0075] Rom. 12.] If it is of another colour, it has another meaning.

The woven, that is, firmly made, opening is the beginning of heavenly conduct, supported by the root of fear of the Lord; or it is the preacher’s steadfast confidence in preaching heavenly things. To extend this garment to the feet is to labour in good works to the end of life. By the pomegranates understand the life of the priest, who protects chastity and a will ready [Col. 0075D] for martyrdom by the single defence of charity. By the bells is signified his teaching; for he provokes against himself the wrath of the hidden Judge if he proceeds without the teaching of preaching. Thus the perfection of priestly conduct is contained in works and in the teaching of truth, according to the saying: “Jesus began to do and to teach.” [Note: [Col. 0075] Acts 1.]

The dalmatic is a garment named from the province of Dalmatia, where it was first invented. It is believed to have been derived from the seamless tunic of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0075] John 19.] and from the apostles’ *collobium*. A *collobium* is a sleeveless garment, as we see in monks’ cowls. [Col. 0076A] But blessed Sylvester changed the *collobium* into a dalmatic: he added loose sleeves and appointed it to be worn at sacrifices. It therefore bears the form of a cross, having two red or purple lines, before and behind, with fifteen fringes hanging on each side of both lines, that is, arranged in front and at the back. The left sleeve also has fringes, but the right does not.

By it is understood holy and undefiled religion [Note: [Col. 0075] Jas. 1.], such as a pontiff’s ought to be. Its two sleeves are like the wings of the pontiff’s protection. For as God’s wisdom gathers the chicks of the Church beneath the wings of grace and mercy [Note: [Col. 0075] Matt. 23.], so a pontiff ought by preaching to gather the faithful beneath the wings of the Old and New Law; spread himself over them by examples; and by prayers defend and protect them from birds—that is, demons. [Col. 0076B] The broadness of the sleeves is the cheerfulness of the pontiff in giving. Beneath the wing is the pierced side [uncertain reading], so that he may imitate Christ’s footsteps [Note: [Col. 0075] 1 Pet. 2.], who was pierced in the side by a lance. [Note: [Col. 0075] John 19.]

It is to be worn at Mass and when the Gospel is proclaimed, where Christ is made present and preached, because it bears the form of the cross. It bears that form both because Christ bore for us the instrument of the cross [Note: [Col. 0075] Phil. 2.] and because the pontiff ought to crucify himself with vices and desires. [Note: [Col. 0075] Gal. 5.] The scarlet lines before and behind are love of God and neighbour commanded in both Testaments. [Note: [Col. 0075] Deut. 6; Matt. 22.] The purple lines are faith in Christ’s blood, necessary in both peoples. The fringes are the commandments, effects, or exercises of love, or the words and works [Col. 0076C] of preaching. Thus there are fifteen in front and behind, because fifteen psalms in the Old Testament emerge like fifteen steps from the path of charity, and likewise fifteen branches grow from the tree of charity in the New Testament—for example:

> “Charity is patient, is kind; it is not envious, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices together with truth; it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never fails.” [Note: [Col. 0075] 1 Cor. 13.]

Some dalmatics have twenty-four fringes in front and as many behind, where the sevenfold Spirit is repeated eight times, filling the eight classes of those praising the Lord: kings and peoples, princes [Col. 0076D] and judges, young men and virgins, old and young. [Note: [Col. 0075] Ps. 148.] The line in the middle is the trunk of charity. The left side also has fringes because the active life is anxious and troubled about many things; but the right side has no fringes because the contemplative life has chosen the better part [Note: [Col. 0075] Luke 10.], namely the security of the present life and the repose of contemplation. With all these things the life of the pontiff ought to be adorned. The present life, understood by the left side, is hindered by more obstacles; the future life, understood by the right, will be constricted by no anxieties.

It is often white, varied with patterned work [Col. 0077A] because of purity and the variety of virtues, and adorned with gold embroidery, according to the saying: “The queen stood at your right hand in a golden garment, surrounded by variety.” [Note: [Col. 0077] Ps. 44.] Or by the dalmatic we understand the hidden reason of sublime things. Hence it is closed around the neck so that the breast is covered, because the reason of sublime mysteries is hidden from carnal persons. These two tunics—the tunic and the dalmatic—are not girded, because those led by the Spirit of God are not under the Law. [Note: [Col. 0077] Gal. 5.]

The chasuble, called as it were a little house (*parva casa*), is also called a *planeta*, from *plano*, “I wander,” because its wandering hem is raised over the arms. Observe that this garment is doubled upon the breast and between the shoulders, tripled over the arms, laid over the other vestments, and changed in colour according to the season. It is charity, the mother and house of virtues. As the whole person is covered by a house, so charity embraces the entire body of virtues, because “love is the fulfillment of the Law.” [Note: [Col. 0077] Rom. 13.] It is doubled on the breast because through charity good will and holy thought are brought forth. It is doubled between the shoulders because through it adversities are borne, both from neighbours and adversaries; or the doubling means that we must have charity in heart and work, within and without.

It is raised over the arms when charity performs good works: over the right when we do good to the household of faith [Note: [Col. 0077] Gal. 6.], and over the left when it extends even to enemies. It is thus tripled on the right when we assist faithful monks, clerics, and laypeople—or rather Noah, Job, and Daniel, that is, rulers, married persons, and the continent. [Col. 0077C] It is tripled on the left when we supply necessities to unbelievers: namely bad Christians, Jews, and pagans; or to hirelings, adulterers, and foolish virgins. [Note: [Col. 0077] Matt. 25.] It is placed over the other garments because it is proved more eminent than the other virtues. Thus the Apostle says: “I show you a still more excellent way.” [Note: [Col. 0077] 1 Cor. 12.] Or because “charity is the fulfillment of the Law”; [Note: [Col. 0077] Rom. 13.] for the whole Law and the prophets hang upon its commandments. [Note: [Col. 0077] Matt. 22.]

It changes colour according to the season: white is used at the Resurrection because angels appeared in white garments; [Note: [Col. 0077] John 20.] red at Pentecost because the Holy Spirit appeared to the apostles in tongues of fire. [Note: [Col. 0077] Acts 2.] The amice is attached to it at the upper part, because hope embraces charity as a mother. [Col. 0077D] A priest ought not remove the chasuble during his office, because, as the Lord commanded [Note: [Col. 0077] Lev. 21.], he may not go out from holy things. Or by the chasuble we understand the contemplative life; when we remove it at times, we thereby indicate that it is sometimes necessary, for the brethren’s sake, to yield to temporal necessities.

The breastpiece (*rationale*) is a garment taken from the Law, made of gold, hyacinth, and twisted fine linen; it was doubled and square, measuring one span on every side. Twelve stones were woven into it, bearing the engraved names [Col. 0078A] of the sons of Israel. [Note: [Col. 0077] Exod. 28.] Truth and teaching were inscribed upon it, and the pontiff bore all these things on his breast. Today gold and gems, fixed to the chasuble, are worn upon the pontiff’s breast. This garment signified reason or discernment, and therefore was called the breastpiece of judgment, because the ruler must distinguish good and evil by subtle examination; shine with the gold of wisdom, the hyacinth of heavenly hope, and the fine linen of bodily purity; be double, so that his judgment may please God and not be despised by human beings; and be square, so that he may appear adorned with the four virtues and tend toward him who measures heaven with a span [Note: [Col. 0077] Isa. 40.] and orders all things by weight, number, and measure. [Note: [Col. 0077] Wis. 11.]

In holiness he should imitate the twelve apostles, the faith of the patriarchs, and works of simplicity; shine in truth [Col. 0078B] and teaching; be adorned with the gems of virtues; and, when sacrificing, remember the whole people.

The *fanon*, also called the *sudarium* and *mapula*, as though “a little sheaf” (*manipula*), is taken not from Aaron but from the ancient Fathers. As is read in Bede’s Martyrology concerning Father Arsenius, he always carried a cloth in his bosom or hand to wipe away the flow of tears. With a cloth we wipe away sweat and the moisture of the eyes, nostrils, and saliva. Therefore by the cloth we understand penance, through which the stain of daily transgression is wiped away; or weariness of worldly living, of which it is said: “My soul has slumbered from weariness.” [Note: [Col. 0077] Ps. 118.] For the soul is weary from the consciousness of sins and bodily weakness. With it we wipe the forehead of conscience; through it we desire, with [Col. 0078C] the Apostle, to be dissolved [Note: [Col. 0077] Phil. 1.], saying: “Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from this body of death?” [Note: [Col. 0077] Rom. 7.] Hence *sudarium* is named from *sudor*, “sweat,” with which we wipe away sweat produced by bodily labour. Thus a cloth is said to have been upon the head of our Lord Jesus Christ. [Note: [Col. 0077] John 20.]

It is therefore worn upon the left arm, because only in the present age do we suffer weariness and correct our sins by penance. Or by the maniple we understand the future recompense of works. Hence in certain monasteries, whenever white vestments are used on feasts, they wear maniples, because in that life each will receive his own reward according to his own labour; [Note: [Col. 0077] 1 Cor. 3.] and: “They shall come, coming with exultation, carrying their sheaves.” [Note: [Col. 0077] Ps. 125.]

The mitre is taken from the Law. It is called *tiara*, [Col. 0078D] *cidaris*, *infula*, or cap; it is made of fine linen, adorned with gold and gems, has two horns, two tongues at the back, and fringes hanging below. It covers and crowns the head. It signifies the guarding of the five senses from the enticements of the world in obedience to God’s commandments, for the crown of life that God promised to those who love him. [Note: [Col. 0077] Jas. 1.] Or it signifies the Church, adorned with the fine linen of purity, the gold of wisdom, and shining gems of virtues; preaching the two Testaments, continually fulfilling the two commandments, yet enduring in the weak the hindrances of reproaches and anxieties. [Col. 0079A] It crowns Christ’s head when, clean by baptism and made white through the labours of good works, it imitates the Head for the crown of glory and rejoices in his dignity.

The use of gloves is derived from the apostles. By the hands, therefore, we understand actions; by the gloves, their concealment. [Note: [Col. 0079] Matt. 6.] As hands are sometimes covered by gloves and sometimes uncovered, so good works are hidden in order to avoid arrogance and at times made public to build up neighbours. [Note: [Col. 0079] Matt. 5.] They are seamless because a pontiff’s actions ought to accord with right faith.

The use of the ring is believed to have been taken from the Gospel, where he who was lost and found is clothed in the first robe and distinguished with a ring. [Note: [Col. 0079] Luke 15.] The ancients once used rings to seal letters. [Col. 0079B] Therefore the pontiff wears a ring because he must seal up the mysteries of Scripture and sacraments of the Church from the faithless, and reveal them to the humble. Again, rings were used as a sign of freedom. Therefore the pontiff wears a ring because he ought not be subject to anyone’s servile condition—for pontifical dignity frees one from servile condition—and because he should be a preacher of the spiritual freedom by which Christ freed us. [Note: [Col. 0079] Gal. 4.]

Again, a certain wise Proteus first made an iron ring as a sign of love and set a diamond in it; from this arose the custom of giving betrothal gifts to brides. For as iron masters all things, so love conquers all; and as a diamond is unbreakable, so love is invincible: “For love is strong as death.” [Note: [Col. 0079] Song 8.] Therefore he ordained that the ring be worn on the ring finger, in which a vein proceeds from the heart. Afterwards gold rings were substituted for iron ones, and gems for diamonds, because as gold surpasses other metals, so love surpasses all good things; and as gold is adorned by a gem, so love is adorned by the other virtues. The pontiff therefore wears a ring so that he may know himself to be Christ’s bride or the Church’s bridegroom, according to the saying: “For I have espoused you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ,” [Note: [Col. 0079] 2 Cor. 11.] for whom—or for which—he may lay down his life if necessary. [Note: [Col. 0079] John 10.]

Or, because the name and image of a king are engraved on a ring, by the ring we understand the creed of the Catholic faith. Hear the name: Lord Father, Lord Son, Lord Holy Spirit. See the image: such as is the Father, such is the Son, [Col. 0079D] such is the Holy Spirit. Therefore to wear a ring on the hand is to show faith in action.

The staff is taken from the Law and the Gospel. It is also called the shepherd’s rod, *sambuca*, crook (*pedum*), and ferule. By the Lord’s command Moses possessed a rod, with which he did fearful things in heaven, on earth, and in the sea: [Note: [Col. 0079] Exod. 4.] for he produced food from heaven, [Note: [Col. 0079] Exod. 16.] drink from the earth, [Note: [Col. 0079] Exod. 17.] and led the flock to a land flowing with milk and honey. In the Gospel too the Lord commanded the apostles, when going out to preach, to take a staff. [Note: [Col. 0079] Mark 6.]

This staff is made of bone and wood, joined by a crystal or gilded little sphere. The bone curves back at the top; [Col. 0080A] the wood below is sharpened with iron, though somewhat blunted; bone and wood are polished by carving. By the staff is understood the authority of teaching: the weak are supported with it, the unruly corrected, and wanderers drawn back to penance. Hence it is called a crook (*pedum*): a *pedum* is curved wood by which shepherds draw back the feet of animals. It is made of bone, that is, the hardness of the Law, and wood, that is, the gentleness of the Gospel; these two are encircled by the little sphere of the divinity of Jesus Christ. Or by the bone understand severity, by the wood the pontiff’s gentleness, which he joins in judgment through charity. For severity or mercy is greatly deficient if either is maintained without the other; therefore the iron is blunted because judgment is tempered by clemency.

The staff bends back [Col. 0080B] when the preacher’s mouth is turned toward the little she-ass of action, or when those who err are recalled to penance. It is sharpened below with iron when preaching is brought to its end through the Last Judgment. Sometimes a *cape* [sic] is placed in the bend, because eternal life is promised to those converted to the Lord. Sometimes there is written in the bend: “When you are angry, remember mercy”; [Note: [Col. 0079] Tob. 3.] lest anger over the flock’s fault disturb the eye of reason in the shepherd, but that by word and example he may call sinners back to the Redeemer’s mercy. Sometimes a human figure is written in the little sphere, so that the pontiff may remember himself to be human and not be puffed up because of the power conferred. Sometimes beside the iron is written: “Spare,” so that in correcting his subjects he may spare them, in order that, being merciful, he may obtain mercy from the merciful one. [Col. 0080C] [Note: [Col. 0079] Heb. 4.] Therefore the pontiff should understand that he must

> Spare the subjected and subdue the proud.  
> *(Vergil, Aeneid* VI.853*)

Hence it is said:

> The curved part draws the gentle; the sharp part pricks the rebellious.

And again:

> The curved part draws those whom the rod governs; the final part pricks.

All are polished by the art of carving, because all these things ought to adorn a pontiff according to the rule of holiness.

The pallium is a collar encircling in the form of a circle, with strips of wool—that is, woven from cheap material—hanging before and behind; it is double on the left and single on the right. Black crosses are laid upon it, [Col. 0080D] and three pins or small thorns are inserted. Clearly this garment is not for adornment but for spiritual signification. For it signifies imitation of Christ’s Passion, of which it is said: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me”; [Note: [Col. 0079] Matt. 16.] through this imitation we shall merit the crown of eternal life.

The two strips are the two Laws setting forth Christ’s Passion. This imitation is contemptible to human beings; its preachers too, in the present life, [Note: [Col. 0079] Rom. 7.] now serve the mind, now the flesh; now cling to heavenly things, now seek earthly necessities; now are broken by adversities, now lifted up by prosperity. But in the life to come there [Col. 0081A] will be neither doubleness, spot, nor wrinkle, [Note: [Col. 0081] Eph. 5.] but happiness without adversity and joy without sorrow. The crosses are contrition of heart and mortification of flesh. The three little thorns are faith, hope, and charity; or servile, initial, and filial fear, by which the pontiff is upheld lest he fall from his purpose of imitation.

Or, by the pallium hanging over bishops’ shoulders is signified the reverence owed to the Roman see. Hence the pallium is received only from the Apostolic See. For as the Father sent the Son and he obeyed him, [Note: [Col. 0081] John 8.] and as the Son sent the apostles and they obeyed the Lord, [Note: [Col. 0081] Matt. 12; Luke 10.], so, because the Apostolic One sent bishops, they obey the Apostolic One. Or understand by the pallium the discipline which he must put on, so that he may know how to shape himself to and accommodate the manners of his subjects. [Col. 0081B] Its two strips are the two Testaments, in which true discipline remains. And as the collar was given only to those who had competed lawfully, [Note: [Col. 0081] 2 Tim. 2.] so the pallium is given only to those who have deserved it by their conduct; and we, by keeping discipline, shall be crowned with the collar of victory, according to Solomon’s saying: “Grace shall be added to your head, and a collar to your neck.” [Note: [Col. 0081] Prov. 1.]

Some say that the pallium was instituted in place of the golden plate. [Note: [Col. 0081] Exod. 28.] I think rather that the mitre’s gold embroidery serves in place of the plate; or rather, the golden plate prefigured the sign of the cross made in the rite of confirmation. There is the ineffable majesty of the Name; here, the ineffable mystery of the cross. It hung over the pontiff’s forehead upon the tiara, and upon it [Col. 0081C] was inscribed the tetragrammaton, namely *He, Toth, He, Vau*, interpreted: “This one, the beginning of the Passion, of life.” For the pontiff represents Christ, who is the beginning of the life lost in Adam and restored to us by his Passion. The plate signifies the confidence of our profession; therefore it was worn on the forehead, and today we are marked on the forehead and confirmed with chrism, because we are not ashamed of Christ’s Passion.

The cope is believed to have been borrowed from the tunic; and thus, just as that is adorned with little bells [Note: [Col. 0081] Ibid.], so this one is distinguished by fringes. It has a hood, reaches down to the feet, and remains open in front.
