By it holy conduct is signified; by the fringes, which are below, labours and the cares of this world; by the hood, heavenly joy; [Col. 0081D] by its length to the feet, perseverance to the end. Its opening signifies that eternal life lies open to those who live holily; or, by the cope we understand the immortality of glorified bodies. Thus we do not put them on except at the greater feasts, looking toward the future resurrection, when the elect—who, upon laying aside the flesh, receive white robes in their souls—will receive two robes: both the rest of their souls and the glory of their bodies. These are represented by the straight copes, open in front and unsewn except for the necessary clasp alone, because bodies then made spiritual will no longer confine the soul by any narrowness. They are also adorned with fringes, because [Col. 0082A] nothing will then be lacking to our perfection; rather, what we now know in part, we shall then know as we ourselves are known [Note: [Col. 0081] I Cor. 13.]. Finally, it is noteworthy that our bishop puts on more than eight vestments, whereas Aaron is read to have had only eight; for our righteousness must abound more than that of the scribes and Pharisees if we are to enter the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 0081] Matt. 5.].

## CHAPTER VI. ON ROYAL INSIGNIA

“I will give the conqueror authority over the nations, and he shall rule them with a rod of iron; and I will give him the morning star” [Note: [Col. 0081] Rev. 2.]. Royal insignia are the sceptre, crown, diadem, and purple garment. The sceptre’s rod is the power of kingship; the crown, the circle of the world; the diadem, the prize [Col. 0082B] of the contest; and the purple, the flesh of the weak person. By the rod he is admonished to love justice [Note: [Col. 0081] Wis. 1.]; by the crown, to govern the world; by the diadem, to contend in the contest in such a way as to receive the eternal prize [Note: [Col. 0081] I Cor. 9.]; and by the purple, although he sees himself exalted so greatly, not to become proud, but to acknowledge himself weak, and, whoever thinks himself standing, to take heed lest he fall [Note: [Col. 0081] I Cor. 10.].

Moreover, it is said that a wallet is added, so that he may recognize himself as a pilgrim in this kingdom of his; and, since he has here no abiding city, may seek the one to come [Note: [Col. 0081] Heb. 13.]. Or it signifies that, just as he may ascend to the height of kingship, so he may also be able to descend to beggary, like Diocletian, who from being Augustus became a gardener. The remaining royal garments are the chief virtues, or the powers subject to him. A cross is also carried before kings, so that they may serve the Crucified King. The sword and spear signify that he should not [Col. 0082C] depart from justice in judgment.

The Roman populace used to render him now a trophy, now a triumph. A trophy is rejoicing over routed enemies, at which not palms but laurels—that is, garlands of laurel—were given, together with white togas. But those who had fought manfully in the contest received around their necks a torque, that is, a golden ring. A triumph is rejoicing over conquered enemies; and its ceremony was as follows. The emperor was clothed in the trabea, that is, a purple garment; crowned with a wreath, he was carried in a chariot drawn by snow-white horses to the Capitol amid praises, with senators going before, soldiers riding on either side, and the people following, all singing hymns composed in celebration of victory. Captured leaders [Col. 0082D] were led before the chariot, bound in golden chains; the captive crowd followed with hands tied behind their backs. Herds of camels and horses, and those carrying the spoils, followed afterwards. As he was thus led, the whole city was adorned with *allia* [materially uncertain reading; perhaps a kind of garland or decoration]. At last the spoils were divided, and palms and palm-patterned togas—that is, togas on which palms were depicted—were given to those who had captured men.

Hence those who come from Jerusalem carry palms in their hands, as a sign that they have served that King who, fighting with the devil at Jerusalem, proved victorious and entered heaven’s palace in triumph with the angels. There the righteous will flourish like palms [Note: [Col. 0081] Ps. 91.] and shine like stars [Note: [Col. 0081] Matt. 13.].

## CHAPTER VII. AGAIN, ON VESTMENTS

[Col. 0083A]

“I saw one like a Son of Man clothed in a long robe” [Note: [Col. 0083] Rev. 1.]. Moreover, following the example of the ancient Fathers [Note: [Col. 0083] Exod. 28.], priestly vestments, according to their arrangement, material, and colour, signify the four elements and the two hemispheres of heaven. For the golden plate placed above upon the bishop’s forehead indicated that all things beneath are governed by God’s wisdom; and the bishop, bearing the likeness of the Creator, is bound to exercise wise care for all those subject to him.

Allegorically, however, they are referred to Christ’s priesthood. For the priest bears the person of our head, namely the Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, by the bishop’s shoes we understand the mystery of the Incarnation. Hence, through the [Col. 0083B] variety of their colours, we understand the multiplicity of Christ’s virtues. Divinity came to us shod in these shoes. Of this footwear the Psalm says: “Over Idumaea I shall stretch out my shoe” [Note: [Col. 0083] Ps. 107.], that is, “I shall make my Incarnation known to the Gentiles.” John the Baptist confesses that he is unable to untie the straps of this shoe [Note: [Col. 0083] John 1.]. Thus, by each of the sandals we understand the ineffable union of divinity and humanity.

Christ covered his head with the amice when he hid divinity—which is the head, that is, the beginning without beginning—in the hiding-place of flesh. This is the mighty angel clothed in a cloud, said in Revelation to have descended from heaven [Note: [Col. 0083] Rev. 10.], and in Isaiah: “Behold, the Lord ascends upon a bright cloud” [Note: [Col. 0083] Isa. 19.]. And [Col. 0083C] it is fitting that the same thing is figured in the amice and sandals, since divinity was hidden in the flesh, while through his flesh its knowledge courses through the whole world.

Christ put on the alb when he taught by word and example the new life of innocence, and bestowed it on those reborn in baptism. The long robe is Christ’s flesh, or the Church; he fastened the tongue of this garment not below but above when he directed the teaching of innocence, the flesh, and the Church toward heavenly rather than earthly things. Christ wore the girdle when he admonished that loins should be girded, saying: “Let your loins be girded” [Note: [Col. 0083] Luke 12.]. This is the golden belt of which Revelation says [Note: [Col. 0083] Ch. 1.]: “I saw him girded at the breasts with a golden belt.”

By Christ’s stole we understand the obedience and servitude which he underwent for our salvation. For he is that Jacob [Col. 0083D] who, obedient to the command of his father, namely God, and the counsel of his mother, that is, the Holy Spirit, served Laban [Note: [Col. 0083] Gen. 27.], that is, the world, bearing its sins on submissive shoulders, in order that he might take Rachel and Leah in marriage [Note: [Col. 0083] Gen. 28.], that is, might receive the synagogue from the Jews and the Church from the Gentiles.

By the episcopal tunic and dalmatic we understand the lofty teaching of Christ and concerning Christ, which is not open to everyone but to the greater and more perfect [Note: [Col. 0083] I Cor. 2.]. The bishops possessed this teaching, to whom it was said: “Go up on a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion” [Note: [Col. 0083] Isa. 40.]. Christ Jesus’ seamless tunic signified it [Note: [Col. 0083] John 19.]. The Lord possessed it, [Col. 0084A] in whom all treasures of God’s wisdom and knowledge were hidden [Note: [Col. 0083] Col. 2.]; and he gave it to the apostles, saying: “I have made known to you everything that I heard from my Father” [Note: [Col. 0083] John 15.].

The two garments signify the two gifts of the Holy Spirit, namely wisdom and knowledge; and the *mapula* signifies works. The gloves signify the purity of Jesus Christ’s works. By the bishop’s ring is signified the gift of the Holy Spirit, with which the Son of God came down to the Church, rich and adorned. He distributes it to those who believe in him as he wills, giving to one a word of wisdom and to another a word of knowledge [Note: [Col. 0083] I Cor. 12]. The bishop imitates the divisions of gifts [Note: [Col. 0083] Ibid.] by conferring orders, appointing some as priests and others as deacons. Thus it is not without reason that a jeweled ring shines on his finger, through whose ministry [Col. 0084B] the splendid charisms of the Holy Spirit are given; or Christ wore a ring when he betrothed his bride with the pledge of integrity of faith.

By the chasuble the holy Church is signified. This is the garment of the true Aaron: upon whose hem the anointing oil descends from the head through the beard [Note: [Col. 0083] Ps. 132.]. In our head is the fullness of the Holy Spirit, which descends into the beard, that is, the apostles and other perfect persons, and thence into the whole Church, down to the hem of the garment, that is, the Church’s lowest members. This garment is one, whole, and closed on every side, signifying unity and integrity of faith. Yet, though one, through the outstretched form of the Crucified it is in some manner divided: its front part signifies the portion of the Church that preceded the Lord’s [Col. 0084C] Passion, and its back part that which followed it. The amice is put over it and placed about the mouth, because Christ’s humanity is understood to be the crown and glory of the Church.

The bishop’s pallium signifies the humility of Jesus Christ, who attributed authority not to himself but to the Father, saying: “As the Father sent me, so I send you” [Note: [Col. 0083] John 20.]. He obeyed the Father even unto the bitterness of death; therefore God exalted him, gave him the name above every name, and gave him authority in heaven and on earth [Note: [Col. 0083] Phil. 2]. This is represented by the staff; and he crowned him with glory and honour [Note: [Col. 0083] Ps. 8.]. Hence the bishop wears a mitre, and the supreme pontiff is crowned.

## CHAPTER VIII. ON VESTING THE MINISTERS

[Col. 0084D]

“Let your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let your saints rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0083] Ps. 131.]. Sacred vestments are not to be used except when we enter the Holy of Holies, nor are we to go out to the people wearing them. Stephen, a Roman by nation, so ordained. By this it is understood that not all consecrated or secret matters are to be entrusted to the people; for a homily ought to be such that it can be understood by the household subject to it. Likewise, one must not enter wearing polluted and everyday clothing, because one must approach the Lord’s sacrament with a clean conscience, and in that contemplation by which one is stripped of carnal [Col. 0085A] thought. Therefore Jerome says: “Divine worship has one dress in ministry, another in common use.”

But now let us necessarily continue our treatment of ministerial dress, clothing the Lord’s ministers in the aforementioned vestments so that they may come groomed and adorned to Christ’s table [Note: [Col. 0085] John 20.]. White vestments are accordingly granted to doorkeepers, readers, exorcists, and acolytes, that through purity of chastity they may imitate the angels, the Lord’s ministers, and may be joined to them, as it were in white garments, when their flesh has been made glorious and spiritual. Note that ministers of the altar use linen garments especially, because just as flax is brought to whiteness through many labours, so it is necessary to reach the glory of the kingdom through many tribulations [Note: [Col. 0085] Acts 14.]. Likewise, one must attain the beauty of chastity [Col. 0085B] through the labour of fasts and vigils.

They therefore put on the shoulder-garment, by which the head, neck, and those parts by which burdens are borne are covered, so that they may learn to restrain their mind, curb their tongue [Note: [Col. 0085] Jas. 1.], bear others’ burdens [Note: [Col. 0085] Gal. 6.], and thus minister what is necessary to Christ in his members [Note: [Col. 0085] Rom. 12.], while recalling the humanity of Christ clothed in a cloud by means of the amice.

They put on the ankle-length long robe, so that they may learn to put on bodily purity and chastity, and to serve God in it until life’s end. Then they gird their loins with a belt, so that, in fear of the Lord, they may learn to restrain carnal desires and keep their loins girded in accordance with Christ’s command [Note: [Col. 0085] Luke 12.]. The aforementioned vestments are granted also to subdeacons, and two are added: [Col. 0085C] the *subtile* and the towel. They wear the *subtile*, also called the close-fitting tunic, so that they may put on righteousness as a breastplate [Note: [Col. 0085] Eph. 6.]. They also carry a towel on the left arm, by which dirt is wiped from vessels and tears from eyes, so that they may learn in this present life to cleanse away the filth of vices and through penitence to mourn past evils. It is noteworthy that the subdeacons’ towel is made larger than the priestly *fanon*, because where the transgression is greater, a greater fruit of penitence is required.

Deacons are additionally granted the use of dalmatics and stoles, and, at certain times, chasubles. By the dalmatic they are to learn to live holily and religiously, to mortify fleshly desire, to love God and neighbour [Note: [Col. 0085] Matt. 22.], to keep the commandments of love which are before and behind—that is, in the Law and the Gospel—or to search out the hidden meaning [Col. 0085D] of lofty things. Therefore they use it only on feasts, because the disciples did not understand lofty things until after the Lord had been glorified [Note: [Col. 0085] Matt. 15.].

By the fringes of the left sleeve and the stole placed over the left shoulder, they are to learn to undertake the burdens of the active life and, with Stephen, to minister to widows and orphans [Note: [Col. 0085] Acts 6.]. In that the stole is girded at the loins, the deacon is invited to be strong and ready against the assaults of lust. By the chasuble he is to learn that he is a preacher who should burn with love and aspire to the contemplative life. [Col. 0086A] At times he girds it and lays it doubled over his shoulder: when he sets aside the work of preaching, prayer, reading, and meditation, he comes to the aid of neighbours in need and, because of the twofold love, undertakes labour for the brethren. He folds it over the right side when he refers all things to the highest good. Thus, when he puts on the chasuble, he represents Mary; when he girds it, he represents Martha in ministry [Note: [Col. 0085] Luke 10.].

Now let us hasten with these ministers to vest the bishop—yet we by speech, they by ministry. Priest of the most high God, vicar of Jesus Christ, consider what you say, what you do, what is placed around you, and understand the mysteries that they signify. First you chant the Psalms: “How beloved are thy tabernacles” [Note: [Col. 0085] Ps. 83.], in which you declare to the sons of Korah—that is, “the bald one,” namely Christ’s ministers made bald at Calvary—[Col. 0086B] that you long with inestimable desire for the house not made with hands [Note: [Col. 0085] II Cor. 5.], for which you both pray and declare yourself humble, saying: “I have chosen to be cast down in the house,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0085] Ps. 83.].

“Thou hast blessed, O Lord, thy land” [Note: [Col. 0085] Ps. 84.], in which you ask that mercy be shown; you give thanks for salvation—that is, for the grace of Christ invisibly manifested; and you show the sons of Korah what is to be done, through whom God the Father offered the means of returning to that house, when he turned away our captivity, remitted iniquity, softened wrath, and gave kindness.

“Incline, O Lord,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0085] Ps. 85.], in which Christ prays for his own. To grant us the things just mentioned, he sprang from the earth and was crucified on the cross. His prayer is our instruction; our [Col. 0086C] prayer is the abolition of sins.

“Her foundations are in the holy mountains” [Note: [Col. 0085] Ps. 86.], in which you commend the aforementioned house in many ways so as to draw the sons of Korah to it, as though saying: “O sons of Korah, take an example from me. For I hasten to enter that rest [Note: [Col. 0085] Heb. 4.]; and in order to enter, I pray and show humility. You too hasten, and you can do so, because the Father has set you free through the Son [Note: [Col. 0085] John 8.]; and, that you might arrive, the Son prayed to the Father [Note: [Col. 0085] John 17.]. You ought to hasten to it, because there will be everlasting joy there, of which glorious things were spoken in ancient times.”

Then, returning to yourself, you say: “I believed, therefore I spoke” [Note: [Col. 0085] Ps. 115.], where you promise to receive the Lord’s cup and offer a sacrifice of praise. But because you feel yourself unworthy—for no one in a mortal body is without sin—there follows the penitential supplication, [Col. 0086D] when you say: “Out of the depths I cried to thee, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0085] Ps. 129.], so that you may be like Jonah crying to him from the belly of the whale [Note: [Col. 0085] Jonah 2.], with whom are propitiation, mercy, and abundant redemption. You must therefore add prayers and supplications appropriate to your ministry, such as: “The ears of thy mercy,” etc.

Having said these things, take off your everyday clothes and put on clean, sacred ones, so that you may put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new, who was created according to God [Note: [Col. 0085] Eph. 4; Col. 3.]. The old man is Adam, whose oldness [Col. 0087A] consists in vices and sins. The new man is Christ, whose newness consists in virtues and good works. Then comb the hair of your head, so that you may learn to order the dispositions of your mind or to drive away superfluous thoughts. Next, if you wish, wash your hands and face with water, so that you may know to wash away carnal acts and the stains of the mind with tears of penitence, and may be among the innocent who boldly say: “Judge me, O Lord, for I,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0087] Ps. 25.], and later: “I shall wash my hands among the innocent” [Note: [Col. 0087] Ibid.]. Then dry them with a towel, understanding that after tears of contrition you must also wipe out sins through works of satisfaction.

As we said before, flax is brought to whiteness through labour; so the penitent person reaches perpetual glorification through satisfaction. These adornments of hair, face, and [Col. 0087B] hands are not pleasures of luxury; rather, we read that they were enjoined by the Lord on priests as a symbol [Note: [Col. 0087] Exod. 30, 38.]. The bronze basin, made from women’s mirrors, in which they washed themselves, is sacred Scripture, containing the clear life of the saints. In it we wash our life when, by the examples of saints, cleansing ourselves of the stains of vices and restraining the hair of our thoughts, we are transformed into the beauty of virtues.

After this, you are shod with sandals by the ministers, so that you may remember the Lord’s Incarnation and, after the example of the apostles, proceed shod for the preparation of the gospel of peace. Thus in the adornment of your feet you must remember: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim [Col. 0087C] good things” [Note: [Col. 0087] Isa. 52.]. These shoes are not for honour but for burden, not for resting but for undertaking the journey of preaching. Therefore persist in preaching in season and out of season; rebuke, entreat, and reprove with all patience [Note: [Col. 0087] II Tim. 4.]. Imitate the examples of those whose vestments you put on. And so that the Spirit of the Father may speak in you [Note: [Col. 0087] Matt. 10] and give you knowledge of speech as he gave it to the apostles [Note: [Col. 0087] Acts 2], when you are shod with sandals say the hymn, “Come, Creator Spirit,” and elsewhere, “Come, Holy Spirit,” and prayers to the Holy Spirit: “O God, who [the hearts of the faithful]”; another, “Be present with us, we beseech thee, O Lord”; another, “Our minds, which, O Lord, the Paraclete”; and another, “Grant, we beseech thee, almighty God, that the Spirit …”

Afterward cover your head, neck, [Col. 0087D] garment, and shoulders with the clean amice; bind your breast and throat, so that in whatever you grasp in mind, whatever burden you undertake, whatever you think, whatever you say, you do not violate faith in the Mediator, but refer all things spotless to the Lord in hope of heavenly things, fearing punishment and desiring glory. If therefore wicked thoughts should arise in your heart [Note: [Col. 0087] Luke 24.], let it feel the amice, the white garment, so that under hope of eternal blessedness, mindful of chastity and purity, it may not be corrupted by contamination from any fly, but may become a clean heart, receiving a right spirit renewed in the inward parts [Note: [Col. 0087] Ps. 50.]. But if at any time a thought needing correction should creep in, bind [Col. 0088A] your throat with the linen amice and “keep your tongue from evil” [Note: [Col. 0087] Ps. 35.], so that there may be a guard upon your mouth and a watch around your lips [Note: [Col. 0087] Ps. 140.]. Let the priest’s neck and breast always be bound by the amice; let his heart always be clean and his speech chaste. For the soul is corrupted by thoughts and falsehood, and commits fornication away from the Lord.

Then put on the white, ankle-length long robe, so that you may have in yourself enduring purity of flesh and chastity, love extended even to enemies [Note: [Col. 0087] Matt. 5.], and may understand the liberty of adoption as sons [Note: [Col. 0087] Rom. 8], by which the Son set us free [Note: [Col. 0087] John 8.]. Then gird your loins, learning that you must restrain the impulses of lust. It is noteworthy that you ought to bind breast and throat gently, but the loins firmly, because movements of the mind are not in your control. Elijah first shut heaven [Col. 0088B] while thinking himself the only prophet of the Lord left, though seven thousand men still remained who had not bent their knees before Baal [Note: [Col. 0087] III Kings 17–19.]. The tongue also sits on something naked and moist and slips easily. The chief of the apostles denied his Master at a servant-girl’s voice [Note: [Col. 0087] Matt. 26.].

But in matters of the loins, brother, do not be mistaken. God is not mocked [Note: [Col. 0087] Gal. 6.]. Do not call a fall of the flesh venial, as though it were a tax naturally due; do not call it an ungovernable beast. Rather, binding your loins, chastise your body and bring it into servitude [Note: [Col. 0087] I Cor. 9.]. And, that you may more effectively restrain the impulses of lust, let a double cincture hang from your belt: namely fasting and prayer. With these weapons the assault of lust and the spirit [Col. 0088C] of fornication are cast out. Hence the Lord says: “This kind is not cast out except by prayer and fasting” [Note: [Col. 0087] Matt. 17.].

Next place the stole upon your neck, as a sign of obedience: that you may obey the Gospel of the Crucified. Then put on the hyacinth-coloured tunic, that is, heavenly conduct; and over it put on the dalmatic, that is, holy religious life, or mortification of the flesh, or understanding of lofty things. Afterwards put on the gloves, so that you may avoid vain glory, according to: “Beware lest you do your righteousness before men in order to be seen by them” [Note: [Col. 0087] Matt. 6.]. At times, however, take off the gloves, so that you may invite your neighbours to good works [Note: [Col. 0087] Matt. 5], according to: “Let your light shine before men, so that, seeing your good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0087] Ibid.]. Therefore you put on gloves in order to display the purity [Col. 0088D] of your works.

Therefore restrain your hands from touching unclean skin, and not only from theft and robbery, but shake them free from every gift, lest, when you approach Christ’s table, he say to you: “Do not touch me” [Note: [Col. 0087] John 20.]. For your voice sounds like Jacob, but your hands are Esau’s [Note: [Col. 0087] Gen. 27.]. In addition, put on the ring, so that you may love the Bridegroom more than yourself, to whom you keep faith; and the bride as yourself, to whom you reveal secrets and preach the freedom by which the true Bridegroom, whose vicar you are, set you free [Note: [Col. 0087] John 8.].

Furthermore, put on the chasuble, the wedding garment [Note: [Col. 0087] Matt. 22], understanding by it [Col. 0089A] charity. Unless you possess it, you will be like sounding bronze and a clanging cymbal [Note: [Col. 0089] I Cor. 13]; you will be excluded from the wedding feast and cast into outer darkness [Note: [Col. 0089] Matt. 22]. You shall lift it over your arms and fold it in three through loving action toward all: namely rulers, virgins, and the continent.

A priest must never perform his office without the chasuble, because it is always fitting that he remain in charity’s bond. But because we all offend in many things [Note: [Col. 0089] Jas. 3], and no one lives long without sin, therefore place a towel on the left hand, so that, if you sin through frailty or ignorance, you may live in penitence and wash away sins with tears, as you go forth weeping and cast your seeds [Note: [Col. 0089] Ps. 125.]. Then place on the pallium, so that it may appear that you are an imitator of Jesus Christ, [Col. 0089B] who bore our infirmities [Note: [Col. 0089] Isa. 53.]. And, since you are the world’s offscouring [Note: [Col. 0089] I Cor. 4], despised by the world and crucified to the world, bear the burdens of those subject to you [Note: [Col. 0089] Gal. 6], setting before them examples of service and humility.

Finally receive the mitre, understanding that you must guard the five senses from worldly enticements, keep the commandments of the two Testaments, and fulfill the two precepts of charity, that you may deserve to receive the eternal crown. Other priests, however, like clerics in general, cover their heads with no ornament, although at feasts they may otherwise be adorned over their whole body. This is either because our joy is not yet complete [Note: [Col. 0089] I John 1]—for we rejoice not in present realities but in hope of future ones—or because we strive to behold God with unveiled face [Col. 0089C] [Note: [Col. 0089] I Cor. 13.].

When you have been adorned with these vestments, confidently receive the staff, that is, the authority of teaching. For just as the preaching of one whose life is despised is itself held in contempt, so the teaching of one whose life is adorned with so many virtues is feared and received by hearers. After this, tread upon the carpets, so that you may learn to despise earthly things and love heavenly things. Observe that you put on all these garments, or have them put on you by ministers serving you; either because angels assist you in putting on spiritual garments [Col. 0090A], or because you are the vicar of Jesus Christ, whom angels then ministered to and whom all things now serve [Note: [Col. 0089] Matt. 4.].

Observe also the notable order: first you must put off the old man with his acts and thoughts; once stripped, wash; once washed, clothe yourself. Clothe yourself in purity of mind, heart, speech, and flesh. So that these may not fall away, add fear, fasting, and prayer. So that they may advance in you, add heavenly conduct and holy religious life. So that they may advance also in others—that is, so that you may draw others—you make works manifest and reveal hidden things. But because, if you deliver your body to be burned, it profits you nothing if you do not possess charity [Note: [Col. 0089] I Cor. 13], you love God above yourself, your neighbour alongside yourself, and all else below yourself. But because one who touches pitch is defiled [Col. 0090B] by it [Note: [Col. 0089] Ecclus. 13], because one who has bathed all over needs only to wash his feet [Note: [Col. 0089] John 13], and because the time of your sojourn is prolonged [Note: [Col. 0089] Ps. 119], you mourn. But because death enters through the windows [Note: [Col. 0089] Jer. 9], you protect and guard the five senses. And because you are a shepherd, to whom it is said: “Feed my sheep” [Note: [Col. 0089] John 21], you receive the staff, by which to support yourself and correct the sheep.

Then let the cantor put on his own vestments, namely the cope, which is also suited to every order; hence it makes no difference to which order he belongs. By it he should understand that he must live holily. According to some, let him crown himself with a cap, so that he may know to exalt in praises God, who is the head of all; or to gain a crown through praises. According to certain customs, [Col. 0090C] let him carry tablets in his hand, so that he may praise not only with his voice but also with works. For when you sing with your voice, “Break your bread for the hungry” [Note: [Col. 0089] Isa. 58], let your hand accord with your voice, so that you yourself extend the bread. These tablets are of bone and signify love of God and neighbour, or perseverance in good works. But according to others, in some places he carries a staff, so that those whom he strives to arouse by voice to harmonious praises, he may endeavour to invite by works to angelic ones.

# BOOK THREE. ON THE OFFICES OF THE MINISTERS OF THE CHURCH

[Col. 0089]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0089D]

The bishop, adorned by ministers and together with ministers, proceeds from the sacristy into public view to celebrate the office of the Mass. Therefore, though we are insufficient to expound anything of our own concerning this, yet because “our sufficiency is from God” [Note: [Col. 0089] II Cor. 3], let us begin by casting our anchor upon its author [Note: [Col. 0089] Ps. 54; I Pet. 5.]. May the secretary of salvation, keeper of David’s key, who opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens [Note: [Col. 0089] Isa. 22; Rev. 3], lead us into this wine-cellar [Col. 0090D] [Note: [Col. 0089] Song 2], into this sanctuary of propitiation [Note: [Col. 0089] Lev. 25], so that we may attend to that mercy-seat toward which the two cherubim—that is, the two Testaments—turn their faces and look at one another.

## CHAPTER I. ON THE NAME, INSTITUTION, AND PARTS OF THE MASS

The name *missa* (“Mass”) is sometimes particular and sometimes collective. It is particular because it signifies Christ, who was sent by the Father into this world. [Col. 0091A] It also signifies the angel who is sent so that through his hands the offering may be carried to the Lord’s high altar. It is used collectively because sometimes the office from the Introit to the Offertory is called the Mass, and this is the Mass of the catechumens; sometimes only that office from the beginning of the sacrifice to *Ite missa est*, and this more truly, because then the offering is sent; sometimes that which is read in silence, perhaps because catechumens were then sent out; and sometimes only those words by which bread and wine are sent—that is, transubstantiated—into flesh and blood.

Most commonly, however, the whole office from the Introit to *Ite missa est* or *Benedicamus Domino* is called the Mass. This is for four reasons: because the priest is sent by the people to God to intercede, and the angel is sent by God to the people to grant a hearing; because in this office Christ’s sending from the Father’s bosom into the world for its redemption is represented, namely the Incarnation; and Christ’s sending from the world to the Father to be appeased, namely the Passion. Hence the conclusion: *Ite missa est*. Some say that *missa* is so called from dismissal, because the people are dismissed after the office has been celebrated.

The Lord Jesus, priest according to the order of Melchizedek [Note: [Col. 0091] Ps. 109], instituted the Mass when he changed bread and wine into body and blood, saying: “This is my body; this is my blood” [Note: [Col. 0091] Matt. 26]. Behold: the Lord instituted the Mass—that is, he established these words and gave them substantial life—by which bread is sent into body and wine is sent, that is, transubstantiated, into blood. [Col. 0091C] He also instituted the Mass and added the reason for its institution when he commanded that this be done in remembrance of him, saying [Note: [Col. 0091] Luke 22]: “Do this in remembrance of me.”

Thus, although the apostles enlarged it by deciding that over the bread and wine there should be added not only the words spoken by the Lord but also the Lord’s Prayer; and although later their successors, who loved the beauty of the house [Note: [Col. 0091] Ps. 25], added different things at different times; nevertheless both institution and addition are referred to that true high priest himself, who once entered the holy places by his own blood [Note: [Col. 0091] Heb. 7].

Moreover, among the things said, sung, or represented by gestures in the Mass, some commemorate things past, some demonstrate things present, and some foretell things future. According to some, the office of the Mass is divided into four parts: supplication down to the secret prayer; prayer down to the *Pater noster*, which has four parts—the secret, preface, canon, and the prayer so called; petition down to communion; and thanksgiving down to the end. According to others, it is divided into seven offices: the first begins with the procession; the second, with the Epistle; the third, with the Gospel; the fourth, with the Offertory; the fifth, with the preparation of the altar; the sixth, with the bishop’s blessing; [Col. 0092A] and the seventh, with the kiss of peace. In the first is figured Christ’s embassy; in the second, the Church’s rejoicing; in the third, the preaching of Christ or the apostles; in the fourth, the devotion of the hearers; in the fifth, Christ’s Passion; in the sixth, his descent into hell; and in the seventh, his resurrection.

Let us follow everything according to this latter division. Therefore this office, extending from the procession to the reading, is called the Introit, because it recalls to our minds Christ’s coming in the flesh and his bodily life on earth, until he ascended to the Father’s seat. Considering this carefully, let us treat the parts of the office in sequence.

## CHAPTER II. ON THE FIRST PART OF THE MASS
The Lord sent an envoy to the nations [Note: [Col. 0091] Obad. 5:1]. Moses prefigured this embassy [Note: [Col. 0091] Exod. 4 and following]: when he went down into Egypt, he was received by the elders and the people; he gathers the scattered, subdues Egypt by signs, frees from harsh slavery those oppressed by the tyrant, leads them out of Egypt, and brings them into the land of promise. Thus Christ, coming into this world, is received by angels and shepherds [Note: [Col. 0091] Luke 2]; he joins diverse walls together in one faith, subdues the world by miracles, frees those oppressed by the devil, leads them out of hell, and brings them into the homeland of paradise [Note: [Col. 0091] Eph. 2].

This embassy, too, which the prophets preached and the wise taught, is presented to us by the procession of the bishop, who bears the figure of Christ. For the pontiff, adorned, proceeds from the sacristy to the church, because Christ, more beautiful than the children of men [Col. 0092C] [Note: [Col. 0091] Ps. 44], proceeding from the Father’s repose, or from the Virgin’s womb, like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber [Note: [Col. 0091] Ps. 18], came into the world.

The order of the procession, according to the customs of some, is this. To the crash of bells, ringing in harmonious accord, seven acolytes with lights go before. These seven are followed by subdeacons with plenaries; after them come seven deacons; after these, twelve elders, accompanied by three acolytes with censers and incense; then comes a subdeacon with the Gospel. Thereupon the pontiff is attended on his right by a deacon and a priest; the crowd accompanies him in prayer.

The ringing bells signify the prophets, announcing beforehand Christ’s coming. The seven acolytes with lights were all those who, through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, ministered the light of knowledge to the faithful [Col. 0092D]. The seven subdeacons with plenaries are those who, through the same grace, taught that the fullness of divinity would dwell bodily in Christ [Note: [Col. 0091] Col. 2]. The seven deacons are, universally, all those who through that same grace possessed a spiritual—that is, evangelical—understanding of Christ. The twelve elders were all those who shone in the faith of the Holy Trinity, or in the works of the three and four virtues. The three acolytes carrying censers signify the three Magi, who offered gifts to Christ [Note: [Col. 0091] Matt. 2]. The single subdeacon carrying the Gospel signifies the Law.

Therefore he goes before [Col. 0093A] and carries the Gospel, because the Law preceded Christ’s coming and contains within itself the evangelical mystery of the Passion. Since this was obscure in the book of the Law before the Lamb opened the seven seals [Note: [Col. 0093] Rev. 5], he carries the Gospel closed. The Gospel is set before the pontiff because the way to Christ’s life is prepared through evangelical teaching. The bishop, who is borne or led by two persons, is Christ, who is preached to the world by the two Testaments through prophets and apostles. For the deacon at the right is the preacher of the Gospel, in which heavenly things are promised.

The priest and subdeacon are at the left: the prophetic herald and the lawgiver, who promised earthly things according to the letter. And because the lawgiver preceded the prophets, [Col. 0093B] the subdeacon goes before the priest. The crowd accompanies the pontiff to the church, and the people of the faithful follow Christ to heaven.

Observe that in this pontiff’s escort, in which he is, as it were, borne in a chariot, there are ten orders: namely doorkeepers, readers, exorcists, acolytes, subdeacons, deacons, priests, singers, laymen, males and females; because “the chariot of God is manifold by ten thousand” [Note: [Col. 0093] Ps. 67]. “Thousands” is said to suggest their perfection. Yet he especially brings with him deacons, subdeacons, and acolytes prepared for service, according to the saying: “Behold, I send to you prophets, wise men, and scribes” [Note: [Col. 0093] Matt. 23]. The prophets are the deacons, who announce from the Gospel the life to come; the wise men are the subdeacons, [Col. 0093C] who wisely arrange the vessels; the scribes are the acolytes, who kindle the hearts of the faithful from Scripture.

This same order of escort must also be observed in our preaching. For acolytes, subdeacons, and deacons are all preachers who prepare the Lord’s way [Note: [Col. 0093] Mal. 3] before the face of Jesus Christ. The acolyte with incense goes first, because Christ’s humility must necessarily be preached first; hence the Apostle says: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except our Lord Jesus Christ, and him crucified” [Note: [Col. 0093] 1 Cor. 2].

The candlesticks follow, so that the light of preachers may shine before human beings upon the foundation; those who carry them in their hands fulfill in deed what they preach in word. The subdeacon with the Gospel [Col. 0093D] follows, because “we speak wisdom among the perfect” to hearers who have been enlightened [Note: [Col. 0093] ibid.]. For perfection is contained in the Gospel, as in: “If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have and give to the poor” [Note: [Col. 0093] Matt. 19].

In all these matters the significance of the number is considered according to the subject of the preaching. If there is one acolyte, subdeacon, and deacon, they indicate those preachers who show that the commandment of love is one; hence the whole Law is fulfilled in one saying [Note: [Col. 0093] Gal. 5]. If there are two in any order, they represent those preachers who proclaim the two commandments of charity and the two Testaments. Thus Abraham [Col. 0094A] had two sons, one by a slave-woman and one by a free woman [Note: [Col. 0093] Gal. 4]. If there are three, they signify those who continually proclaim Scripture in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms. If there are four, they recall Amminadab’s chariot [Note: [Col. 0093] Song 6] and the four living creatures seen by Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0093] Ezek. 1]. If there are five, they indicate those who preach the Lord’s fivefold Passion. If there are six, they signify those who invite the nations to works of mercy. If there are seven, they signify those who form the nations by the gifts of sevenfold grace.

For preachers ought to teach their subjects all these matters and things concerning them [Note: [Col. 0093] Ps. 67], through which the vicar of Jesus Christ—and Christ himself—is led forth publicly, amid young women playing tambourines. The singers lead him forward, and the two choirs receive him with rejoicing, [Col. 0094B] singing the proper Introit with its verse and the *Gloria Patri*, which we repeat twice on non-festal days and three times on feast days.

Originally only the Epistle and Gospel were read before the sacrifice, and the office began with the reading. This custom is still retained on Holy Saturday and at Pentecost. But Pope Celestine established that psalms should be sung at the Introit.

To represent more fully the joy of Christ’s coming, Gregory composed tropes and antiphons to be sung melodically at the Introit in place of psalms. Hence the first verse, with the *Gloria*, is sung from that psalm which is especially appropriate to the day—and formerly the entire psalm, with the *Gloria*, was sung at the Introit. Thus the Introit is rarely [Col. 0094C] taken except from the Psalter. Or it is because the psaltery is struck from below and gives back its sound from above: therefore we begin Mass with the psaltery, because in it we hasten from the work of the Passion, which receives its blow below, to the higher sweetness of the Resurrection. The Nicene Synod, however, added the *Gloria Patri*, but Pope Damasus ordered it to be sung at Mass.

The singers who receive the approaching pontiff with the *Gloria Patri* are the angels who received Christ coming in glory in the highest. The two choirs singing praises are the two peoples, Jewish and Gentile, who came with praises to meet Christ as he came. The Introit is the praise of the Church from the Jews, and therefore contains three elements: antiphon, verse, and glory, for the three orders of faithful people belonging to the Hebrew tongue—namely [Col. 0094D] the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles. The antiphon is the praise of the patriarchs, the verse that of the prophets, and the glory that of the apostles. The repetition of the antiphon is the sameness and confirmation of preaching: as though what the patriarch long before prefigured in deeds, the prophet foretold, and the apostle proclaimed in the Gospel. To mark that conversion as well, solemn tropes are inserted. *Tropos* is Greek; in Latin, *conversio*, “turning.” These are the changeable praises at the Introit.

Meanwhile, while these things are sung by the choir, the bishop enters the sanctuary; therefore this first chant is called the Introit. Bowing before the altar, he says with the antiphon the psalm: [Col. 0095A] “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause” [Note: [Col. 0095] Ps. 42]. In it he asks to be separated from evils, lest he fail under afflictions; and he rejoices that he is about to enter the invisible altar, for whose sake he approaches the visible one.

Then, trusting in that consolation, “I said, ‘I will confess,’ and you forgave” [Note: [Col. 0095] Ps. 31], he makes confession in order to enter without stain. He confesses the kinds of individual sins: namely, that he has sinned in thought, speech, and deed, as the Apostle says: “We all offend in many things” [Note: [Col. 0095] Jas. 3]. He does not, however, name the particular instances of these kinds—such as murder or adultery—lest he sear the consciences of his hearers. Then, praying for those around him, he seeks pardon for them.

This is Christ, who, when he had come from the Father’s hidden place into the world, and, while the fathers’ sighs were multiplied, had proceeded from the virginal womb [Col. 0095B] to suffer for us, entered Jerusalem, bowed himself toward death, entrusted his cause against the deceitful and unjust man to God, and made confession to the Father, saying: “I confess to you, Father of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” [Note: [Col. 0095] Matt. 11]. He also prayed to the Father for his own [Note: [Col. 0095] John 16], and himself granting us pardon, bore our sins in his own body [Note: [Col. 0095] 1 Pet. 2].

After this he kisses the Gospel, then the ministers beside him, those at his right and left. For Christ came and suffered in order that, through the faith which the Gospel teaches, he might reconcile to God the Father the Church which formerly said, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0095] Song 1], [Note: [Col. 0095] 2 Cor. 5]; that he might join the two walls into one faith [Col. 0095C]; and, preaching peace to those far away and those near [Note: [Col. 0095] Eph. 2], coming from north and south [Note: [Col. 0095] Luke 13], might unite them in one bond of peace [Note: [Col. 0095] Eph. 4].

According to some, he also offers peace to the singers behind him, fulfilling the saying: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” [Note: [Col. 0095] John 14]. He gives it to those present and leaves it to those absent. This must be observed: before the kiss, *Gloria Patri* is not said, because faith in the Trinity was not manifest before the Lord bowed himself, reconciled us, and commanded that the Trinity be preached through the apostles [Note: [Col. 0095] Matt. 28]. Therefore, once the kiss has been given, the bishop indicates to the singer that he should say: “Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, as it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, unto ages of ages. Amen.”

See what the singer announces: namely, that the hearts of the fathers are turned [Col. 0095D] toward the children [Note: [Col. 0095] Mal. 4]. Abraham saw three and worshipped one [Note: [Col. 0095] Gen. 18]; so we too, his children, must believe in the Trinity in unity. Once the kiss has been given, the deacons pray again with the pontiff, as though saying: “Lord, teach us to pray” [Note: [Col. 0095] Matt. 6]. When, after the prayer, he has reached the altar, he kisses it in the middle.

After kissing the Gospel, he signs himself with the sign of the cross, as though saying: I have come here in order to be the vicar of the Crucified One, who came into the world to hang for our peace upon the altar of the cross and to stand in the midst by charity [Col. 0096A] [Note: [Col. 0095] Song 3]. I am not ashamed to proclaim the Crucified One in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0095] Rom. 1], who came to preach peace to us [Note: [Col. 0095] Eph. 2]. Or understand the altar as the Jews and the Gospel as the Gentiles believing the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0095] Acts 4]. Christ gave peace to both when he became the cornerstone [Note: [Col. 0095] Eph. 2].

Likewise, according to some, the deacons customarily kiss each side of the altar, two by two, because the Lord sent them out two by two to preach. To them he also said: “Into whatever house you enter, say: ‘Peace to this house’” [Note: [Col. 0095] Matt. 10; Luke 2]. They returned to Christ just as the deacons return to the bishop.

He censes the altar in the figure of the Angel who in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0095] ch. 8] stood at the altar with a golden censer. Hence: “The Angel stood beside the altar of the temple, holding a golden censer in his hand, from which the smoke of aromatics rose in the sight of the Lord” [Col. 0096B]. For Christ, the Angel of great counsel [Note: [Col. 0095] Isa. 9], offered to the Lord for us upon the altar of the cross his spotless flesh, full of the Holy Spirit, as an odor of sweetness [Note: [Col. 0095] Eph. 5].

The smoke of aromatics is the prayers of the saints, which, spread abroad through the ardor of charity from the Lord’s Passion, ascend to God the Father and lead us onward to the crown of eternity [Note: [Col. 0095] Heb. 7]. Therefore he censes in the form of a cross and a crown. If he censes the cross once, he recalls the single Passion; if he makes one circuit as a crown, the recompense of one denarius [Note: [Col. 0095] Matt. 20]; but if he does so three times, he recalls both the Trinity’s operation in the Passion and the glorification of the three orders. Therefore, while censing, he says: “Let my prayer, O Lord, be directed as incense in your sight; the lifting up of my hands, an evening sacrifice” [Note: [Col. 0095] Ps. 140].

[Col. 0096C] This is also why, while the censing takes place, the prayers—that is, *Kyrie eleison*—are sung by the Church. They are the true incenses, of which it is added: “And much incense was given to him” [Note: [Col. 0095] Rev. 8]. *Kyrie eleison* is Greek, which Pope Sylvester adopted from the Greeks, but Gregory ordered to be sung at Mass by the clergy, whereas formerly it was sung by the people.

Observe that Mass is celebrated in three languages: Hebrew because of the Law, Greek because of wisdom, and Latin because of empire; or because the title of Christ hanging on the cross was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin [Note: [Col. 0095] John 19]. Hebrew words are *Alleluia*, *Amen*, *Sabaoth*, and *Hosanna*. Greek are *Kyrie eleison* and *ymas*; the rest are Latin. *Kyrie eleison* means “Lord, have mercy.” Sometimes *ymas* is added, which means “upon us”; and the sense [Col. 0096D] of *Kyrie eleison ymas* is: “O divine Power, have mercy upon us”; *Christe eleison*: “O Christ, who redeemed us by your blood”; *Kyrie eleison*: “O Lord, who returned to equality with the Father”—as though it said: “You who are man and God, have mercy upon us.”

The Church repeats “Lord” three times for the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. It repeats “Christ” three times, and then “Lord” three times again, because he is God and man, through whom one comes to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This threefold repetition, however, will be explained elsewhere and below.

The Church repeats “have mercy” nine times [Col. 0097A], because through the mercy of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit it asks to be joined to the orders of angels; and this looks back to what precedes or belongs to what follows.

In relation to what precedes: the faithful have assembled as one through the office of singers, that is, preachers, to praise the Lord. Therefore, lest any presumption creep in, we say: *Kyrie eleison*: “We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done” [Note: [Col. 0097] Luke 17]. Again, lest vain illusion abase us because of the composition of the melodies, we say: *Kyrie eleison*.

In relation to what follows: the priest is about to pray for the people. Therefore, in order that by his prayer dead flies may be driven away [Note: [Col. 0097] Ecclus. 10], that his mind may be made serene, that he may speak worthily with God, and that even if he has not prayed in mind the Lord may not be angry in the future but have mercy, we put *Kyrie eleison* before [Col. 0097B] the prayer. For the same reason it is placed before the Lord’s Prayer in the other offices, such as the morning and evening synaxis; and it represents the praise of the Church from the Gentiles, which drew its primitive origin from the Greeks.

At this, when the choir is silent, the priest alone begins aloud, facing east: “Glory to God in the highest”; and the people receive it joyfully in song. For while all things held deep silence [Note: [Col. 0097] Wis. 18], Truth, escaping the hiding-place of the Law, sprang from the earth [Note: [Col. 0097] Ps. 84]. It alone gave peace with God and the angels to people of good will [Note: [Col. 0097] Luke 2], and restored the glory of angels [Note: [Col. 0097] John 14]. Therefore the people, after the manner of the angels, joyfully raise a clamor of praise to Christ himself, who is Truth.

Yet neither peace nor reconciliation, nor the restoration of angels, was accomplished at Christ’s very birth; rather, it is an anticipation. For when Christ was born, the lamp was already kindled, by which eternal Wisdom would find the lost drachma [Note: [Col. 0097] Luke 15]. But this chant is fittingly sung here, because the bishop is presently to move to the right side of the altar, signifying Jesus Christ’s passage from death to life. By that passage he joined the souls of the saints to the company of angels. Hence glory was given to God in the highest and peace on earth to human beings, because under the same Lord heavenly things are joined with earthly.

Or the priest alone begins because a single angel began this hymn at the Lord’s birth, and the host of the heavenly army sang it together in congratulation [Note: [Col. 0097] Luke 2]. The priest begins while turning [Col. 0097D] eastward, because the angel came from the east to Bethlehem; or because we customarily worship the Lord facing east.

Observe that here only the angelic hymn is: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will”; and formerly this alone was said at Mass. But Hilary added “We praise you,” and the rest which follows; appropriately he added matters of praise, so that it might be shown to be a hymn of praise. This is evident from the Gospel reading, where it says: “There came to be with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising [Col. 0098A] God and saying: ‘Glory to God in the highest’” [Note: [Col. 0097] ibid.], and all that they report—which Hilary instituted to be sung at Mass.

Some say that Telesphorus established it to be sung only at Mass on the night of the Lord’s Nativity, a Mass instituted by him for that very night, and that he added to it the words which follow the angels’ words. Symmachus, however, added that it should be sung on feast days. Some also say that it ought not to be sung at Mass except at the third hour, because then the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles and filled them with glory and exultation [Note: [Col. 0097] Acts 2]. Yet it is also to be sung on the Lord’s night, because it was first heard then; and on the Saturdays of Easter and Pentecost, because lost glory is restored to those baptized.

When this hymn has ended, the priest, about to pass to the right, turns toward the people and says: “The Lord be with you,” or “Peace be with you.” This greeting, “The Lord be with you,” is taken from the book of Ruth [Note: [Col. 0097] ch. 2], where Boaz is read to have said to the reapers of his field: “The Lord be with you.” It is taken more fittingly from Chronicles, where a priest said to King Asa and the people assembled with him for battle: [Col. 0098B] “Hear, King Asa, and all the people of Judah and Benjamin: The Lord be with you who are assembled to do his will” [Note: [Col. 0097] 2 Chron. 15].

The angel also greeted Gideon, saying: “The Lord is with you” [Note: [Col. 0097] Judg. 6]. This greeting belongs to lesser priests; the other, namely “Peace be with you,” which is taken from the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0097] Luke 24; John 29], belongs to bishops, both because they are more particularly vicars of Jesus Christ, [Col. 0098C] who used this greeting to the apostles after the Resurrection, and because the New Testament is more worthy than the Old.

For when the bond-document of peace between angels and human beings had been drawn up in his death, he rose from the dead [Note: [Col. 0097] Rom. 6] and proclaimed that very bond-document of peace, saying to his own: “Peace be with you.” Joseph’s steward also used this phrase to his brothers [Note: [Col. 0097] Gen. 43].

The people respond: “And with your spirit.” The people pray that the Lord may be with the priest’s spirit, enabling him to pray in spirit and in mind; for by the name “spirit” we also understand the mind. A person prays only with the mouth who merely pronounces words; one prays with mouth and spirit who pronounces the words and discerns their meaning [Note: [Col. 0097] 1 Cor. 14]; one prays with mouth, spirit, and mind who utters the words, discerns them, and refers them to God and heavenly things. This response is taken [Col. 0098D] from the Apostle, namely from the Second Epistle to Timothy, where it is said: “The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit” [Note: [Col. 0097] 2 Tim. 4].

These mutual greetings indicate that priest and people ought to have one disposition. Observe that, although the choir answers the priest, “With your spirit,” the priest never says to the people, “The Lord be with you” in the singular, as the angel did to Gideon, but “with you” in the plural. Thus Pope Soter established that no one should celebrate Mass unless at least three persons are present.

Then, turning to the altar, he prays, raising his hands in the manner of Moses [Note: [Col. 0097] Exod. 17], [Col. 0099A] or of the Savior hanging on the cross. As he prays and invites others to pray, he says: “Let us pray.” He gathers the universal Church into himself, or speaks as the representative of the whole body under the person of many. This was taken from antiquity: the ancients, after first saying “Let us pray,” would together add the prayer.

He prays on the right side because Christ passed from death to life [Note: [Col. 0099] Rom. 6], through which he will bring us back from exile to our homeland. Therefore some of the deacons stand behind the bishop, as if praying that they may follow him even unto death and with him pass over to eternal life. The greater part, however, remains at the right side of the altar and the lesser at the left, because the Church seeks both: temporal blessing and eternal blessing, as in: “May we so pass through temporal goods that we do not lose [Col. 0099B] eternal ones.”

This prayer signifies the blessing with which Christ, about to ascend into heaven, blessed his disciples [Note: [Col. 0099] Luke 24]. Observe that *oratio* (“prayer”) is named from *orando* (“by praying”), because the good things of body and soul, present and future, are prayed for. The priest prays that good things may be present and evils absent. It is also called the *collecta* because under it the people gather, and the people’s petitions are gathered into one, to be presented to the Lord through the priest.

Strictly speaking, however, a *collecta* is one recited in processions when the multitude has gathered, whether at city gates, road junctions, or before church doors. One prayer should be said, as one Epistle and one Gospel, because of the unity of faith: “one God, one faith, one baptism” [Note: [Col. 0099] Eph. 4]. Yet by the institutions of the Fathers, three, five, or seven are sometimes said. Beyond these numbers another number is, I do not say blameworthy, but extraordinary.

Three are said for the Holy Trinity, or because Christ prayed three times, saying: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” [Note: [Col. 0099] Matt. 26]. Five are said for the Lord’s fivefold Passion, completed in five wounds. Seven are said for the seven petitions of the Lord’s Prayer [Note: [Col. 0099] Matt. 6], a number which it is presumptuous to exceed; or for the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0099] Isa. 11]. Even numbers should not be said, because “God delights in an odd number.” Nevertheless Roman authority permits two if a feast occurs on a Sunday; it established two to be said at the Mass of the Nativity of the Lord and on the feast of All [Col. 0099D] Saints, and likewise four at the commemoration of the Innocents.

However many are said, only the first and last should be ended with the proper conclusion. Prayers are for the most part addressed to the Father and concluded through the Son in the Holy Spirit, as though saying: “O Father, hear through your Son, who wills and is able to do this: he wills because he lives, he is able because he reigns; he lives, I say, and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit.” He neither lives nor reigns as a tyrant, a spirit of wickedness, but lives and reigns as God, in the spirit of kindness. Every prayer is rightly concluded through the Son, because no one goes to the Father except through him [Note: [Col. 0099] John 14], and because he said: “If you ask the Father for anything in my name, [Col. 0100A] he will give it to you” [Note: [Col. 0099] ibid.]. For he is the mediator of God and human beings [Note: [Col. 0099] 1 Tim. 2], through whom we obtain benefits from the Father, just as through an intervening crystal we receive heavenly fire from the distant sun into material placed beneath it.

The form for concluding prayers is this. If the address is made to the Father and there is no explicit mention of the Son or Holy Spirit, it concludes: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, through all ages of ages.” But if there is mention of the Son, it concludes: “Through the same our Lord,” etc.; or “Who lives and reigns with you,” etc.; or “our Lord,” as in: “O God, who [of eternal salvation …]”; or “Jesus Christ,” as at the Lord’s Supper: “He himself [may render] to you.” If mention is made of the Holy Spirit, there is added: “In [Col. 0100B] the unity of the same Holy Spirit,” etc.

But if the prayer is addressed to the Son, it concludes: “Who live and reign with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit,” etc.; or “Who with the Father live and reign,” etc. If, however, the prayer is addressed to the Trinity, it is concluded without any distinction of persons: “Who lives and reigns, God, through all ages of ages,” as: “May the service of my servitude be pleasing to you, Holy Trinity,” and “Receive, Holy Trinity, this offering.” Or the speaker may turn the address toward himself or toward the people, saying: “May he himself deign to grant this”—as is likewise concluded in benedictional prayers, in which the address is directed toward the people.

A question is raised concerning Advent prayers, such as: “Stir up, Lord, your power and come.”

Answer: There are three comings: the first in flesh, [Col. 0100C] the second in the mind, the third in majesty. These prayers concern the second coming; therefore the address may be directed to the Father or to the Son. For he says: “I, the Son, and the Father will come to those who keep my commandments” [Note: [Col. 0099] John 14]. Or rather they pray concerning the first or third coming: the earlier fathers entreated God the Father to send the Son, or the Son to come for redemption. Modern people, however, ask the Father to send the Son, or the Son himself to come for judgment and recompense. Therefore in almost every Advent prayer the conclusion is: “Who [live] with you,” or “Who live,” or the address is also directed to the Trinity.

A question is raised concerning this prayer: “God, creator of all the faithful,” etc., since Christ is properly the redeemer.

I answer: the address is directed to the Father. For the whole Trinity is God, creator and redeemer of all. Indeed, “almighty,” “merciful,” “eternal,” and “everlasting,” although they are essential names, are nevertheless frequently used in prayers personally to signify the Father.

A question is also raised concerning those prayers in which the address is directed to the head of the Church, if such a prayer is found; for Christ is the head of the Church [Note: [Col. 0099] Eph. 5].

I answer: likewise, there the address is directed to the Father; for the whole Trinity is the head of the Church. In exorcismal prayers it is said: “Through him who is to come to judge the world,” etc.; as soon as the devil hears this, [Col. 0101A] he flees, fearing the judgment of fire. Some likewise wished this to be said in prayers for the dead, but usage in some places opposes it. “Through all ages of ages” is said because the ages follow one another: when some depart, others succeed.

The people answer the prayer: *Amen*. Since this is Hebrew, it means in Latin, according to Jerome, “be it done”; according to Aquila, “faithfully”; according to some, “truly.” Thus in the Gospel: “Amen,” that is, “faithfully” or “truly, I say to you” [Note: [Col. 0101] Matt. 5, etc.]. Christ is also called *Amen*, as in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0101] ch. 2]: “Thus says Amen, Christ, the faithful witness.” But in prayers it is taken to mean “be it done,” as if it said: “May what you pray for be done for us.”

After this the bishop sits, signifying Christ’s [Col. 0101B] Ascension and his seat at the Father’s right hand. Some sit with him, by whom Christ’s members are understood, now resting in peace; of them the Apostle says: “He made us sit in heavenly places in Christ” [Note: [Col. 0101] Eph. 2]. Or they signify those who will sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel [Note: [Col. 0101] Matt. 19]. Those who stand, however, signify Christ’s members still engaged in conflict. But the Lord, seated on high in heaven [Note: [Col. 0101] Acts 1; Heb. 1], guards his city [Note: [Col. 0101] Ps. 126]; and the vicar, seated in the more eminent place, watches over his people and, like a vine-dresser, guards his vineyard, so that he may render to each according to his works [Note: [Col. 0101] Matt. 16; Rom. 2].

While he sits, the candle stands are moved from their places in a single line, from the first up to the altar. This is the custom of certain churches, to indicate that [Col. 0101C] from Christ’s fullness we all receive [Note: [Col. 0101] John 1], in unity of spirit but with diversity of graces. “For there are diversities of graces, but the same Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0101] 1 Cor. 12]. For the Spirit, proceeding from the first candle stand—that is, from Christ—and reaching in turn as far as the altar—that is, the hearts of the elect—varies the gifts of graces among the members.

Remember that the acolytes set the candle stands upon the ground, because after carrying out the offices of preaching they acknowledge in humility that they are dust and ashes, as Abraham said: “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” [Note: [Col. 0101] Gen. 18]. The number of candle stands does not exceed seven, because the whole Church is illumined by sevenfold grace.

Or, in another sense from the beginning of this part: Christ’s [Col. 0101D] procession is his going forth from the Father; his bowing is his self-emptying. “For he bowed the heavens and came down” [Note: [Col. 0101] Ps. 17], when, taking the form of a servant, he emptied himself [Note: [Col. 0101] Phil. 2].

The Introit signifies the longing of the ancient fathers for the Lord’s coming; the verse, their prophecies; the repetition, their sighs; the *Gloria Patri*, their praises; the *Kyrie eleison*, their prayers multiplied to this end: that the grace of the Holy Trinity, through Christ’s coming, might join them ninefold to the distinct ranks of angels.

“Glory in the highest” [Col. 0102A] is, as we have said, the angels’ hymn concerning Christ’s Nativity; the praises and harmony of the choir are the shepherds’ congratulation. The greeting and prayer are Christ’s saving work for us. For the Lord’s whole life and all his action were prayer for us. This is the smoke of aromatics which rises in the Angel’s hand before the Lord [Note: [Col. 0101] Rev. 8]. For in the days of his flesh, as the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0101] Heb. 5], offering prayers and supplications to God, he was heard because of his reverence.

Therefore the priest prays because Christ prayed for us, commanded prayer, and taught it. He prays at the right because Christ taught the Jews, to whom he was sent by the Father; hence: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0101] Matt. 13]. Hence someone says: “The right signifies the Jews, the left the Gentiles.” And so, up to this point, all things [Col. 0102B] have been in chant and action. Thus the custom arose that no one sits in church until the reading, because the preceding office is assigned to rejoicing over Christ’s coming and works. Therefore the Roman order says that the pontiff should not sit until “Amen” has been said after the first prayer.

For the pontiff signifies Christ coming and acting; the others represent those who went before, followed, and came to meet him [Note: [Col. 0101] Matt. 21]. Whoever, therefore, wishes to accompany Christ or to receive Christ as he comes must not be sluggish, but must receive Christ as he comes: singing with the prophets who announce Christ beforehand, praying with Anna and Simeon who longed for Christ, and rejoicing with angels and shepherds who congratulated him as he came [Note: [Col. 0101] Luke 2]. Or let that person follow the Lord, singing with the children who cry: “Hosanna to the son of David!” [Note: [Col. 0101] Matt. 21]; weeping with Mary who says: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died” [Note: [Col. 0101] John 11]; [Col. 0102C] praying with the Canaanite woman who says: “Lord, have mercy on me; my daughter is grievously tormented” [Note: [Col. 0101] Matt. 15].

## CHAPTER III. ON THE SECOND PART OF THE MASS
“Zion heard and rejoiced” [Note: [Col. 0101] Psalm 96]. While the priest is seated, the reader recites the reading, the people sit around, and the choir resounds with chant. The priest sits at three points in the Mass: while the Epistle is read, while the gradual is sung, and while the Alleluia is sung; for the Lord is said to have sat in the Temple for three days [Note: [Col. 0101] Luke 2]. Or the priest sits once—that is, continuously. While he is seated these things are performed, because, while Christ sits at the right hand of the Father, the preacher sounds forth the Scriptures to the world, and the people obey.

[Col. 0102D] Observe that a *lectio* (“reading”) is so called from *legere*, “to read”: it ought to be read, not sung. An *epistola* (“epistle”) is said to derive from *epi*, “above,” and *stola*, “a sending”; because, as prophecies stand above the Law, so Epistles are sendings above the Gospel. Hence not only Epistles but prophecies are read in the place of Epistles. For both are Jeremiah’s rags [Note: [Col. 0101] Jer. 38]; both are the innkeeper’s disbursements [Note: [Col. 0101] Luke 10]; both are additional enactments to the laws—[Col. 0103A] the former to the old Law, the latter to the new.

The Epistle, then, takes the place of the Law and prophecies before the holy Gospel, performing the office of a herald. Thus the Law preceded the Gospel as a herald precedes a judge, fear charity, beginning perfection, action contemplation. Although it is often taken from apostolic writings, it nonetheless occupies the same rank as though it were always taken from the Law or from the proclamation of the prophets. It always signifies a preceding course, suggests the moral life and action, and differs from evangelical majesty as action differs from contemplation, a servant from his lord, a herald from a judge, and an envoy from the one who sent him. Therefore, while the Epistle is read, we sit without disrespect; but while we hear the Gospel, we stand reverently before the Lord, with downcast faces.

[Col. 0103B] The custom of sitting is taken from the Old Testament, as is read in Ezra [Note: [Col. 0103] 1 Esdras 10]. Yet some stand for the Epistles of Paul [Note: [Col. 0103] 2 Tim. 2], because he called his own preaching “the Gospel.” Or, spiritually, the Epistle signifies the preaching of John the Baptist, the Lord’s forerunner; or the teaching of the seventy-two disciples, to whom he said: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the labourers are few” [Note: [Col. 0103] Luke 10]. Or the reader signifies every learned scribe, who brings forth from his treasure things new and old [Note: [Col. 0103] Matt. 13]. Hence he recites readings from both Testaments. Or he signifies Christ, who, opening the scroll of Isaiah, read: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” [Note: [Col. 0103] Luke 4; Isa. 61].

Again, observe that, just as no one but a priest is permitted to celebrate Mass, and no one but a deacon to read the Gospel, so no one ought to read the Epistle [Col. 0103C] unless he holds the office of subdeacon. It belongs to that office to bear upon the left arm a maniple adorned with fringes. For if, in accordance with the proclamation of John the Baptist, this herald and his hearer fear the axe of judgment laid to the root of the tree, and bring forth worthy fruits of repentance [Note: [Col. 0103] Matt. 3], with perseverance in good works they will carry away sheaves of righteousness. Of these the Psalm says: “Those who come shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” [Note: [Col. 0103] Psalm 125]. Since the fringe of the maniple—and of every sacred vestment—is the last part of a garment, it signifies perseverance and the completion of good works.

After the Epistle, the choir resounds in chant with the gradual, tract, [Col. 0103D] Alleluia, together with verses, neumes, and sequences. The use of chants, as is read in Ezra, likewise derives from the Old Testament. Ambrose, Gregory, and Gelasius composed graduals, tracts, and Alleluias and appointed them to be sung at Mass. Jerome, however, says that the Alleluia was said at Mass, while the tract came from the Church of Jerusalem. Notker, abbot of Saint Gall, first composed sequences for the neumes of the Alleluia itself, and Pope Nicholas permitted them to be sung at Mass. Hermanus Contractus, the inventor of the astrolabe, also composed: “Almighty King,” “On This Day,” and “May the grace of the Holy [Col. 0104A] Spirit be present with us.”

It is called a *gradual* from the steps on which it is sung, or because it is sung step by step. It is also called a *responsory*, because it answers the preceding reading, or because the choir answers those who begin it, or because it answers the verse. A *verse* derives from “turning,” because it turns back to the responsory. A *tract* derives from “drawing out,” because it is sung in a drawn-out manner, and its verse turns back to it. *Alleluia* means “Praise God”: *allelu*, “praise,” and *ia*, one of the ten names of the Lord. From its verse we return to the Alleluia, and on returning we employ neumes.

There is, moreover, a difference between *neuma, neumæ* and *pneuma, pneumatis*: *neuma, neumæ* means a jubilus, whereas *pneuma, pneumatis* means the Holy Spirit. A *sequence* is so called because it follows the neume of the jubilus. It is called *sequentia, sequentiæ*, both here and in the Gospel; it is also called a prose, that is, an extended composition.

[Col. 0104B] As we understand John’s preaching through the Epistle, so through the gradual understand the preaching of the apostles, and through the Alleluia understand joy together with devotion and preaching. Some, however, understand the Old Testament by the reading and the New by the chant: for, as the New is sweeter than the Old, so chanting is sweeter than reading. More soundly, chants accompany the Epistles because the joy of the Church followed the preaching of preachers: praises and proclamations to God for the conversion of believers. By the gradual, conversion from the Jews is understood; by the verse, conversion from the Gentiles; and by the Alleluia, the joy of both in faith is represented. The sequence [Col. 0104C] signifies a song of victory. Hence it imitates the applause of victors with neumes. This exultation was prefigured by Miriam the timbrel-player, who sang of victory for the people after their deliverance, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0103] Exod. 15], with whom the people also rejoiced.

Morally understood, we still sing graduals today while we are delivered amid the laments of repentance and endeavour to go from strength to strength [Note: [Col. 0103] Psalm 83]. For this chant belongs to the lament of repentance and to the labour of those who act. Hence it is so grave that custom does not allow it to be rendered in very elevated voices. Hence, too, it is omitted from the office on the days of Pentecost, because then the blessed state of the Church in the Kingdom and at rest is prefigured. Hence also the singer [Col. 0104D] resembles one placed in the valley of weeping [Note: [Col. 0103] Psalm 84], who nevertheless has set ascents in his heart. By remaining on a step lower than the one who sings the Alleluia, he indicates the weeping of repentance, the degree of humility, and the beginning of ascent. Hence it is sung on steps and derives its name from steps, because penitents and those active in good works advance through the degrees of virtues while fulfilling by deeds what they have heard.

For hearers are nourished in the reading, but in the chant their hearts are ploughed, as it were, by the ploughshare of compunction. Music indeed has a certain natural power to move the mind, as [Col. 0105A] Boethius says. We sing the tract because we labour on this journey. We shall discuss tracts more fully below; but for the moment know that the difference between a responsory and a tract is the difference between a dove and a turtledove.

The responsory is likened to a dove, which flies and mourns in a flock and signifies the mourning of the active life. The tract, however, is compared to a turtledove, which flies and mourns alone and therefore denotes the mourning of the contemplative life. When we pray to the Father in secret [Note: [Col. 0105] Matt. 6], we offer a turtledove, like Moses, who ascended the mountain alone [Note: [Col. 0105] Exod. 24]. But when we say, “Come, let us worship and fall down before God” [Note: [Col. 0105] Psalm 94], we bring doves to the altar.

We sing Alleluia because on this journey we hasten toward angelic praises. [Col. 0105B] We sing the verse because, going thus, labouring and hastening, we return to the Lord. Therefore, while singing the verse, we turn toward the east. Observe that the Alleluia, first said in a restrained manner, represents the joy of present contemplation; but when repeated afterward with jubilation, it signifies eternal joy and the banquet alike of angels and blessed souls. Hence this Hebrew name remains foreign in the office, because that joy is foreign to this life and we are pilgrims away from the Lord [Note: [Col. 0105] 2 Cor. 5].

It is therefore fittingly sung after the gradual, because contemplation follows action; the song of joy follows the mourning of repentance; and the greatness of consolation follows the watering of delay. For “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” [Note: [Col. 0105] Matt. 5]; and “Those [Col. 0105C] who sow in tears shall reap in rejoicing” [Note: [Col. 0105] Psalm 125]. We also rejoice fittingly in the Alleluia, so that the mind may be drawn to that place where “the saints shall rejoice in glory and be glad in their dwelling places” [Note: [Col. 0105] Psalm 149]. This joy can neither be expressed in words nor wholly kept silent: it is not expressed because of its greatness, nor kept silent because of love.

We sing the sequence in jubilation because we shall see God with ineffable joy.
