Hence it has unusual and praise-flowing words, because that joy is unknown to mortals, where there is a dwelling “as of all who rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0105] Psalm 86]. Some churches render sequences in neumes without words, because where the hearts of each will lie open, each beholding the book of life, [Col. 0105D] there will be no need for the signification of words; or because words are insufficient to express it. Hence: “What voice, what tongue can recount the rewards that you prepare for your martyrs?” Who can describe what has not ascended into the heart of man [Note: [Col. 0105] 1 Cor. 2]? Hence Paul says that he saw things “which it is not permitted for a human being to speak” [Note: [Col. 0105] 2 Cor. 12]. Therefore, when a jubilus follows the Alleluia, a sequence is not necessary, nor conversely.

Among those who sing, some are singers who distribute the chants through the choir in a loud voice. These are the rulers of the Church, who praise God and invite others by word and example to praise [Col. 0106A] him. Others are boys, who sing the gradual on the steps. These are active children, ascending from strength to strength [Note: [Col. 0105] Psalm 83] through the degrees of charity. When the gradual begins, they invite others to compunction; when they sing the verse, returning to themselves, they attend to their thoughts; when they begin the gradual again, they show that they have fought the good fight [Note: [Col. 0105] 2 Tim. 4] and completed the course. At first they do not raise their voices high; afterward they sing the verse: “For whoever wishes to build a tower should first reckon the cost” [Note: [Col. 0105] Luke 13]. But in the repetition, no longer afraid, they raise the verse confidently in their voices.

Others are perfect men, who sing the Alleluia or tract from the pulpits. These are contemplatives, afflicting the flesh [Note: [Col. 0105] 1 Cor. 9] and going beyond themselves in mind [Note: [Col. 0105] 2 Cor. 5], whose citizenship [Col. 0106B] is in heaven [Note: [Col. 0105] Phil. 3]. Their life is not human but angelic. The sequence, however, is not sung by them alone: the choirs rejoice together, because eternal and ineffable jubilation will be shared by angels and human beings.

## CHAPTER IV. ON THE THIRD PART OF THE MASS

“Proclaiming the command of the Lord, he was established upon his holy mountain” [Note: [Col. 0105] Psalm 2]. Here the preaching of Christ and of the apostles is signified: “Jesus, seeing the crowd, went up the mountain; and opening his mouth, he taught them” [Note: [Col. 0105] Matt. 5]. Moses prefigured this preaching [Note: [Col. 0105] Exod. 24]: he ascended the mountain, received the tablets and the blessing, and set the commandments before the people.

We likewise represent this when the deacon asks the bishop for a blessing, and the bishop [Col. 0106C] blesses him. The deacon, and no one of another order, should read the Gospel, because “deacon” means “minister.” Christ, moreover, was a minister when he preached the Gospel. Hence: “I came not to be served but to serve” [Note: [Col. 0105] Matt. 20]. In blessing the deacon, the bishop says: “May the Lord be in your heart and on your lips.” The deacon should therefore see to it that his heart agrees with his lips, lest the priest’s prayer be fruitless. Accordingly, by the priest’s hands he is fortified with the sign of the cross, as though he were told: “When you preach, do not forget the Lord’s passion.”

For the deacon’s order is apostolic. The Lord blessed it when he gave them the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0105] John 20] and sent them to preach throughout [Col. 0106D] the world [Note: [Col. 0105] Mark 16]. The subdeacon does not receive this blessing, because God invisibly sent the lawgiver and the prophets, but, having become visible, visibly sent and taught the apostles and evangelists.

The deacon receives the Gospel from the altar, because the apostles received the Gospel from the altar when, preaching the Lord’s passion, they proclaimed the good news. Or the altar, upon which the Gospel has lain from the beginning until now, is Jerusalem, from which they received the evangelical Law; for “from Zion went forth the Law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0105] Isa. 2]. Thus, although God had been known only [Col. 0107A] in Judea [Note: [Col. 0107] Psalm 75], his name became wonderful throughout the whole earth [Note: [Col. 0107] Psalm 8]. Or the altar signifies the Jews, from whom the Kingdom of God is transferred and given to a nation producing its fruits [Note: [Col. 0107] Matt. 21].

The deacon bears the Gospel on his left arm, because the left side prefigures the present life in which the Gospel must be preached. For in the future, knowledge will be abolished [Note: [Col. 0107] 1 Cor. 13], that is, there will be no need for the teaching of masters. The subdeacon precedes the deacon with a cushion, because for everything read in the Gospel the Law offers a suitable testimony. Or the cushion is the pleasantness and sweetness of God’s commandments, of which the Prophet says: “In your sweetness, O God, you have prepared for the poor” [Note: [Col. 0107] Psalm 67]; and elsewhere: “How sweet are your words to my palate” [Note: [Col. 0107] Psalm 118]. Therefore, once the Gospel has been read, the Gospel-book is borne upon the cushion, [Col. 0107B] because the Church “obeyed at the hearing of the ear” [Note: [Col. 0107] Psalm 17] and sweetly received the word in her heart; her soul melted when her beloved spoke to her [Note: [Col. 0107] Song 5].

Two acolytes precede with candlesticks and candles, and one with a thurible. These are Moses and Elijah, between whom the Lord shone on the mountain like the sun [Note: [Col. 0107] Matt. 17]; or they are the apostles, whom the Lord sent out two by two to preach [Note: [Col. 0107] Matt. 10; Luke 10]. Sometimes, however—as on ferial days—only one acolyte with a candle precedes. This is John the Baptist, who was the lamp of the Word [Note: [Col. 0107] John 5] and preceded Christ’s first coming. Thus the two can signify Enoch and Elijah, who will precede the second coming [Note: [Col. 0107] Mal. 4].

The two candlesticks are the two commandments; the two candles are the Law and the prophecies. While [Col. 0107C] the Gospel is read, according to some, they are placed upon the floor, because the shadow of the Law and the riddles of the prophecies are understood, through the light of the Gospel, even by the humble. Immediately after the Gospel has been read, they are extinguished, because through evangelical teaching the Law and prophecy have wholly vanished in the letter; or because, when the truth of the Gospel is apprehended, all knowledge will be abolished [Note: [Col. 0107] 1 Cor. 13].

The one who bears the thurible, by preaching, draws forth the fragrance of the sweetness of the slight Passion [the phrase *suavitatis exiguae passionis* is materially uncertain]. By the smoke of the incense is signified the good reputation of the preacher, who ought to be “an aroma from life unto life” [Note: [Col. 0107] 2 Cor. 2], “the aroma of a full field which the Lord has blessed” [Note: [Col. 0107] Gen. 27]. The thurible precedes the Gospel because the good repute of works ought to precede the teaching of words. Hence: “Jesus began to do and to teach” [Note: [Col. 0107] Acts 1].

The deacon, [Col. 0107D] ascending the ambo from the southern side—that is, the place appointed above for words—and turning toward the south, first greets the people, saying: “The Lord be with you”; to which the people respond: “And with your spirit.” For Christ came from Bethlehem, which lies to the south, into Jerusalem. Hence it is said: “God shall come from the south” [Note: [Col. 0107] Hab. 3].

The deacon’s ascent signifies that the preacher ought to stand upon the mountain of virtues, according to: “Go up upon a high mountain” [Note: [Col. 0107] Isa. 40]; or because Christ preached on a high mountain [Col. 0108A] [Note: [Col. 0107] Matt. 5]; or because he said: “What you have heard in the ear, preach upon the housetops” [Note: [Col. 0107] Matt. 10]; or because he gave lofty commandments.

In the fact that the Gospel is read from a higher step than the Epistle, it is indicated that apostolic teaching is worthier than legal teaching, and evangelical teaching more excellent than apostolic teaching. That he turns toward the south to read the Gospel is because the Bridegroom rests at noon [Note: [Col. 0107] Song 1], and because the Church burns with love in every part; or because men used to stand on this side, to whom spiritual things should be sown. By men, spiritual persons are understood; and by the south the Holy Spirit is understood [Note: [Col. 0107] Song 4].

Some, however, turn toward the north, as an old custom prevails in nearly all churches, where the women are, who signify the carnal; and the north signifies the faithful. [Col. 0108B] The Gospel must be preached to the carnal and unbelieving, so that they may be converted to Christ. Or the deacon’s coming from the south means the Son of God’s assuming flesh through the operation of the Holy Spirit. To direct the sermon toward the north means to reveal salvation and secret mysteries to the Gentiles, who had withdrawn from the heat of the sun. Or it is read toward the north so that evangelical faith may be set against the north, from which every evil is opened [Note: [Col. 0107] Jer. 1], according to: “Resist him, steadfast in the faith” [Note: [Col. 0107] 1 Pet. 5].

This north wind is cold—that is, the devil, who freezes human hearts with the blasts of temptations and chills them from the love of God. Thus it is said to him: “Arise, north wind” [Note: [Col. 0107] Song 4], that is, “Depart.” But if the Gospel is to be read at the altar, it should be read on the left side, [Col. 0108C] for from this point there is a passage from right to left. This marks the passage of the apostles from the Jews to the Gentiles when the former rejected the word of God [Note: [Col. 0107] Acts 13]. For when Gideon’s fleece was dried, dew watered the threshing-floor [Note: [Col. 0107] Judg. 6]; and he who had first said, “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” [Note: [Col. 0107] Matt. 10], afterward added, “Go into all the world” [Note: [Col. 0107] Mark 16].

That the deacon, about to read the Gospel, first greets the people—although he has said nothing on the way after receiving the book from the altar—derives from the fact that the apostles greeted no one on the road. But when they entered any house in which they intended to preach, they first greeted those dwelling in it, by the Lord’s command, saying: “Peace to this house” [Note: [Col. 0107] Matt. 10; Luke 10]. By this greeting the deacon makes his hearers attentive to hear the word of the Lord; hence he turns toward them.

[Col. 0108D] The people, rendered attentive and well disposed, turn their hearts toward God and their faces toward the deacon, and say: “And with your spirit.” The people pray that the Lord may be with the preacher’s spirit, enabling him to preach rightly and to refer all things to God. When the deacon adds, “The continuation of the Holy Gospel,” he makes the hearers receptive. This is not because the majesty of the Gospel deigns to be subjected to the rules of rhetoricians, but because what eloquence attempts among human beings, Wisdom accomplishes in her Church.

The Gospel is called, in the pre-eminent sense, “good news” [Col. 0109A], from *eu*, “good,” and *angelus*, “messenger.” For it announces life after death, rest after labour, and a kingdom after servitude. Or, as some say, it derives from *Evan* and *Gelos*; but the sense is the same. Although other Scriptures announce good things, this Scripture—which the Lord himself preached with his own mouth—claims the name Gospel for itself.

The Gospels receive titles in two forms: either from the beginning, “The beginning of the Holy Gospel,” as in the openings of the evangelists; or “The continuation of the Holy Gospel.” It is called a continuation because it follows the beginning or what precedes. The people respond: “Glory to you, O Lord.” The Gospel treats of God’s glory and ours: namely, that he conquered the devil and, victorious, ascended to the glory of God the Father; that he redeemed us and [Col. 0109B] promised us greater things.

Therefore, when we hear mention of the Gospel, we turn toward the east and cry out in praise of the Creator: “Glory to you, O Lord,” as though saying: “May that which is preached in the Gospel, and which we believe and hope, benefit us, happen to us, and remain without end.” Henceforth “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name” belongs, and will belong, “glory” [Note: [Col. 0109] Psalm 113]. Thus the people glorify God, who sent us the Word of salvation and “worked redemption for his people” [Note: [Col. 0109] Luke 1], as is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “And they glorified God” [Note: [Col. 0109] Acts 11].

While these words are spoken, both the hearer and the speaker make the sign of the cross first with the thumb upon the forehead, second upon the mouth, and third upon the breast. The sign of the cross is made on the forehead because the forehead is the seat of modesty [Col. 0109C] and shame. Thus we call shameless people “brazen-faced,” as though without a forehead. By imprinting the sign of the cross upon our forehead, therefore, we show that we are not ashamed that our Lord was crucified—a reproach made against us by Jews and Gentiles. Hence the Apostle says: “We preach Christ our Lord crucified: a stumbling block indeed to Jews, and foolishness to Gentiles” [Note: [Col. 0109] 1 Cor. 1]. Nor ought we to be ashamed, because whoever is ashamed of the Son in this world, the Son will be ashamed of that person before the Father and the angels at the Judgment [Note: [Col. 0109] Luke 9].

By signing the mouth and breast, we indicate that we confess the crucified Lord with the mouth and believe in the heart. For “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made [Col. 0109D] unto salvation” [Note: [Col. 0109] Rom. 10]. Thus faith is understood in the sign on the breast, confession in the sign on the mouth, and action in the sign on the forehead, as though one said: “I sign myself on forehead, mouth, and breast, because I do not blush for Christ’s cross, but preach and believe it.”

The question is asked how we ought to sign ourselves: from left to right, or conversely. Some hold that the sign should be made from left to right, on the authority of Ambrose in the hymn *Come, Redeemer of the Nations* [Note: [Col. 0109] Ambrose, in the hymn *Veni, Redemptor gentium*]: “His coming forth from the Father, his course even to hell, his return even to the seat of God.” For Christ came from the Father into the world [Note: [Col. 0109] John 16], thence [Col. 0110A] to hell [Note: [Col. 0109] Eph. 4], and thence to the seat of God [Note: [Col. 0109] Acts and Heb. 1]. Thus, when one begins to make the sign, one starts with the upper part, which signifies the Father; descends to the lower, which signifies the world; and then moves from left to right: the left signifies hell, the right heaven. Christ, moreover, ascended from hell even to the heights of the heavens.

Others make the sign from right to left, because Christ, coming from the Father’s right hand, destroyed by the cross the devil, who is the left. Or the effect of the cross is applied to us: “God bowed the heavens and came down” [Note: [Col. 0109] Psalm 17], in order to teach us first to seek the Kingdom of God; and once it has been sought, temporal things too will be added to us [Note: [Col. 0109] Matt. 6]. Behold, then, the passage from right to left. He also came down in order to raise us from earth to heaven; and behold the passage from left [Col. 0110B] to right.

We sign the three places mentioned above with the thumb, and then encompass the same three with three fingers, because we refer our entire faith, confession, boldness, and action to the living and triune God.

Thereupon the deacon censes the book, signs it, and kisses the book at the sign, as though saying: “This is the book of God; this is the book of the Crucified One; this is the book of the Maker of Peace.” Some, however, first sign the book and afterward themselves, signing themselves only on forehead and breast, as though on both doorposts [Note: [Col. 0109] Exod. 12].

Afterward the deacon begins the Gospel, which has a threefold form of beginning: either through the beginning of the Gospel, as “In the beginning was the Word,” and likewise, “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ”; or through a definite determination of time, as “In the fifteenth year [Col. 0110C] of the reign,” etc.; or through “At that time,” where at least an unspecified time is meant. Its sense is: “At that time,” namely, the time of grace, of which it is said: “Behold, now is the acceptable time” [Note: [Col. 0109] 2 Cor. 6].

Observe that prophecies, Epistles, and Gospels begin or conclude through those expressions or clauses that occur in them most frequently. In prophecies, these phrases are repeated very often: “In those days,” and “Thus says the Lord Almighty.” In Paul’s Epistles, the phrases frequently recur: “Brothers,” and “in Christ Jesus our Lord.” In the Epistles of James and Peter, this expression is common: “Beloved.” In the Gospels, this phrase occurs more often: “At that time.”

The Gospels are read sometimes [Col. 0110D] according to history, as: “The shepherds spoke to one another” [Note: [Col. 0109] Luke 2], and “Mary Magdalene, Mary of James, and Salome” [Note: [Col. 0109] Mark 16]; sometimes according to allegory, as: “Jesus entered a certain village” [Note: [Col. 0109] Luke 10], in which Mary and Martha, Lazarus’s sisters, are mentioned. Since they signify the two lives, contemplative and active, it is read on the Assumption of blessed Mary, in whom the perfection of both lives is found. Sometimes it is read according to the person, as on the feast of Saint Thomas the Apostle: “Thomas, one of the twelve” [Note: [Col. 0109] John 20]; sometimes [Col. 0111A] according to a part, as on the feast of the Holy Cross: “There was a man of the Pharisees” [Note: [Col. 0111] John 3], because of this clause: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness” [Note: [Col. 0111] Num. 21], “so must the Son of Man be lifted up.” In this word the Passion and the raising up of the body upon the cross are signified. Sometimes it is read according to the whole, as: “After eight days were completed” [Note: [Col. 0111] Luke 2].

While the Gospel is read, it must be heard with the utmost reverence; no one may sit. Pope Anastasius decreed this. Staffs are to be put down from the hands, and coverings removed from the heads of men. When we forbid sitting, we permit neither lying down nor leaning, except in necessity. We must stand erect: the idle sit, sleepers lie down, the weak lean, and strong wrestlers stand.

[Col. 0111B] Therefore, to indicate that we are strong wrestlers of Jesus Christ in defence of the Gospel, let us stand erect while the Gospel is read, knowing that “our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers” [Note: [Col. 0111] Eph. 6]. To exclude every kind of leaning, staffs too are laid down, not only by the others but also by the singers.

The Law commanded [Note: [Col. 0111] Exod. 12] that those eating the lamb should have staffs in their hands. The singers represent this when they hold staffs at Mass, signifying that those who hasten toward their homeland need the food of the heavenly Lamb and staffs against enemies—that is, the sayings of Scripture against demons. In general, staffs signify legal observances; spiritually, the staffs of singers signify [Col. 0111C] the sayings of the Scriptures or the teachings of preachers. Therefore, through evangelical preaching we have laid aside legal observances in the present life; and in the future, when we apprehend evangelical truth, the tongues of teachers will be silenced, because knowledge will be abolished [Note: [Col. 0111] 1 Cor. 13].

Or we lay down staffs lest we seem to Judaize, like those who struck Christ’s head with a reed [Note: [Col. 0111] Mark 15]. Or to lay down the staff is, because of evangelical perfection, not to avenge injuries but to reserve vengeance for the Lord. Hence: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” [Note: [Col. 0111] Deut. 32; Rom. 12]. It is also not to put trust in princes or earthly supports, because “vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” [Note: [Col. 0111] Eccli. 12]. There is no need for human help while Christ is present with us and we hear his voice.

For similar reasons [Col. 0111D] coverings are removed from men’s heads: namely, that we may appear unlike the Jews who wove Christ’s head with a crown of thorns [Note: [Col. 0111] John 19]; or because present evangelical preaching has removed the coverings of the Law; or because the future apprehension of evangelical truth will remove the riddle and scales from our eyes [Note: [Col. 0111] Acts 9]. “Now we see God as through a mirror, in a riddle; but then we shall see face to face” [Note: [Col. 0111] 1 Cor. 13].

Or we uncover the head to indicate that we ought attentively to hear the word of the Lord. I have said “men,” because women ought not to hear with uncovered heads, on account of the shame of the forbidden fruit. Although [Col. 0112A] she may be a virgin, a mother, or any other woman, she should place some cloth upon her head if she has no veil [Note: [Col. 0111] 1 Cor. 11]. Even if a virgin takes delight in her hair, she ought not even to pray unless her hair is covered, as a sign of shame for the ancient transgression, of subjection, and of reverence toward the priest.

Once the Gospel has been read, everyone ought to say, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” or “Thanks be to God,” just as we say after other readings. For it is fitting to bless and give thanks to him who came to save us by this teaching. But it is better to say, “Amen,” as though saying, “What has been said is true.” This stands against the heresies or superstitions of some who, contradicting while the Gospel is read, say: “It is false.” Or “Amen” means, “May what the Lord promises in the Gospel be done for us.”

[Col. 0112B] After the Gospel, everyone ought also to fortify himself with the sign of the cross against the devil, who, once the Gospel has been read, immediately lies in wait lest the word take hold in us. We therefore strengthen ourselves with the sign of the cross, lest he snatch from the heart faith in the Passion and hope in the evangelical promise, confession from the mouth, boldness from the forehead or from action; and lest, through the tares of heresy, he corrupt in us the seed of right preaching [Note: [Col. 0111] Luke 8].

After signing himself, the deacon censes the book and kisses it, giving thanks to God, who taught us to pray and gave us peace.

After this, he carries incense to the bishop and the Gospel for kissing; for the apostles returned from preaching to Christ, giving thanks not to themselves but to him for the miracles and the progress of their preaching [Note: [Col. 0111] Luke 10], since it is certain that he taught us to pray [Note: [Col. 0111] Matt. 6] and gave us peace [Col. 0112C] [Note: [Col. 0111] John 14].

Then the bishop addresses the people. Some also preach before the Gospel, perhaps because of the bad custom of laypeople departing once the Gospel has been sung. Or rather, he suitably preaches both before and afterward, because he is to expound the Gospel to the people: he preaches beforehand so that, understanding what is to be read, they may listen more eagerly; afterward, so that, understanding what has been read, they may retain it in memory. Yet the Theologian preaches afterward, because Christ, after he became known to the people through the apostles, himself preached to the peoples in his own voice. Hence the bishop also preaches what Christ taught—namely repentance and similar matters.

After the sermon the clergy sing, “I believe in one God,” because the people affirm that they believe what the deacon has read [Col. 0112D] and the bishop has preached. This is the right order: the king calls, and the soldiers hasten. Yet it is not to be sung at every Mass, but on the feasts of those of whom some mention is made, and whose feast seems in some way to resound, in the Creed: Christmas, the Circumcision, Epiphany, Easter, the Ascension, Pentecost, the feast of All Saints and of each individual apostle; all feasts of the blessed Virgin; the day of the Lord’s Transfiguration; feasts of the Holy Cross; every Sunday; the feast of the Holy Trinity; and the Dedication of a church. On other feasts, not at all. It belongs most especially [Col. 0113A] to Easter and Pentecost, because the new offspring, instructed in the catechumenate, recites it in exultation.

There is doubt concerning the feast of blessed John the Baptist. Some say that it should be sung on his feast, either because Christ’s birth was mentioned at John’s birth, or because the Creed mentions the prophets, while he is more than a prophet [Note: [Col. 0113] Matt. 11]. Others say otherwise. There is also doubt concerning the proper feasts of particular oratories; and it is the custom of some not to omit it on the feast-day itself, but, if they celebrate its octave, to leave it unsung during the octave. This is the Creed of the Synod of Constantinople.

The Church now uses four Creeds: the Creed of Athanasius, composed against heretics, namely the Arians—“Whoever wishes to be saved”; likewise the Creed of Hilary, [Col. 0113B] composed in his book *On Synods*, and therefore read, wholly or in part, in synods; likewise the Apostles’ Creed—“I believe in God the Father Almighty”; and the Creed of the Synod of Constantinople, which the synod composed, but Pope Damasus instituted to be sung at Mass. While “And was made man” is sung in it, we bend the knee, because we worship Christ made man and crucified for us. While it is sung, the Gospel is borne with incense and is offered open by the subdeacon for each person to kiss, whereas previously it had been carried closed by the same minister. For the apostles bore Christ’s Word through the world [Note: [Col. 0113] Mark 16], became an aroma of life unto life [Note: [Col. 0113] 2 Cor. 2], and declared eternal peace; and thus [Col. 0113C] the evangelical faith, formerly closed within the Law, has now been opened and made manifest. It is offered especially to clerics, as though saying to them: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God” [Note: [Col. 0113] Luke 8].

When the Creed has been sung, each person signs himself, because it is an evangelical word. This is the “abbreviated Word” which the Lord accomplished upon earth, and, as is said elsewhere, which came upon the children of God [Note: [Col. 0113] Rom. 9]. In general, indeed, at all evangelical words we ought to impress the sign of the cross upon ourselves: as at the end of *Glory to God in the highest*; “I believe in one God”; “Holy, holy, holy”; the Lord’s Prayer; and at the end of *Blessed is he*, the *Magnificat*, and the *Nunc dimittis*—for the reason stated above, that one should make the sign at the end of the Gospels. Therefore, by the same reasoning, we ought to hear these standing, just as we hear the Gospel.

When the Creed has been sung—or before and while it is sung—in some places the people sing *Kyrie eleison*, “Lord, have mercy.” For after Christ and the apostles had instructed the people, and faith had been received, they gave praises to God [Note: [Col. 0113] Matt. 11], which perhaps are represented by the exceedingly sweet melody of the Creed. Or rather, lest the reproach be made: “We sang, and you did not dance,” the hearer of the Gospel, with a cheerful mind and a glad, dance-like voice, shows how well he has retained evangelical teaching.

## CHAPTER V. ON THE FOURTH PART OF THE MASS

“Thou shalt accept, O Lord, the sacrifice of righteousness, [Col. 0114A] offerings and whole burnt-offerings; and they shall lay calves upon thine altar” [Note: [Col. 0113] Ps. 50].

The fourth office is called the Offertory or Offering, and begins with “The Lord be with you” [Note: [Col. 0113] Ruth 2]. It is customary, when we have newly come among workmen, to greet them. Thus, according to some, when we pass from one office to another, we first offer a greeting. Hence some maintain that the second office begins with the greeting before the collect, the third with the Gospel greeting, the fourth here, the fifth with the greeting before the Preface, the sixth with the greeting of peace, and the seventh with the greeting before the completion.

The institution of this office derives its origin from Moses and Christ. For when Moses came down from the mountain, greeted the people, and prayed, the people came to meet him and offered gifts [Note: [Col. 0113] Exod. 35]. So too, when Christ came down from the mountain and, [Col. 0114B] according to the good custom of ancient tradition—as is credible—greeted the crowd and prayed for it, the crowd came to meet him with flowers [Note: [Col. 0113] Matt. 21]. Thus the bishop greets the people by “The Lord be with you,” praying that they may persevere firmly in the faith they have recited. When the people have answered the greeting, “And with thy spirit,” the priest immediately invites the people to pray, saying, “Let us pray.”

Among the Greeks the prayer follows here; among us, however, the people’s offering and the chant of those offering come first—as though the people say: “I believe, and I gladly demonstrate by the performance of a work the faith which I have confessed.” Observe that under the Law the people sometimes offered animals: from the herd, a bull-calf and a heifer; from the flock, a lamb and a kid, a sheep [Col. 0114C] and a goat; and from birds, a turtledove and a pigeon. This was called a *hostia*, because it was offered at the door of the tabernacle; or a *victima*, because the animal was bound. The pagans, however, called it *hostia* from enemies to be conquered, and *victima* from enemies already conquered. At other times they offered dry material, such as fine flour, bread, and incense; this was called an offering. At other times they offered liquid material, such as wine and oil; this was called a libation or offering. Although all these relate allegorically to Christ, they are nevertheless signs for us of present righteousness.

To offer a bull-calf is to practice righteousness manfully. To offer a heifer is to consecrate to the Lord the flesh that exalts itself. To offer a lamb and a sheep is to be innocent and simply abstain from evils. To offer a kid and a goat is humbly to repent of sins. In the turtledove [Col. 0114D] we offer chastity; in the dove, simplicity; in fine flour, wisdom; in bread, charity, or contemplation of God; in incense, prayer; in oil, mercy; in wine, the discipline of righteousness.

The people made offerings for seven reasons: namely, legal sacrifice and voluntary sacrifice; sacrifice for sin; sacrifice in thanksgiving; gifts; vows; and whole burnt-offerings. Legal sacrifice consists in tithes and firstfruits, or things which the Law commanded to be offered. Voluntary sacrifice is what is freely offered. A sacrifice for sin was offered for transgression of the Law’s command. A thanksgiving sacrifice was made, for example, on account of victory and triumph. Gifts were offered [Col. 0115A] for the adornment of the Temple; vows, on account of dangers from sickness or war. A holocaust—that is, a whole burnt-offering: for *holo* means “whole” and *cauma* “burning”—was offered when an entire lamb or bull-calf was burned upon the altar. It is said in Chronicles [Note: [Col. 0115] 2 Chron. 29] that the princes offered for vows, freewill offerings, sin, the kingdom, the sanctuary, and Judah.

The rite of the Synagogue passed into the religion of the Church, and the sacrifices of the carnal people were changed into the observance of the spiritual Christian people. Thus, as that people offered Moses, when he came down from the mountain, diverse gifts for making the tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0115] Exod. 35], so it offers diverse oblations to the bishop coming down from the pulpit: one offers gold, another silver, another something from other resources. He who offers gold [Col. 0115B] imitates the magi, who offered gold to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0115] Matt. 2]; he who offers silver follows those who put money into the treasury [Note: [Col. 0115] Mark 12; Luke 21]; he who offers something else joins those who, through Paul and Barnabas, sent necessities to the poor at Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0115] Rom. 15; Gal. 2].

Legal sacrifice is also offered in tithes and firstfruits, voluntary sacrifice in freewill offerings; sacrifice for sins when persons are redeemed by penances; thanksgiving sacrifice when something is offered in return for some grace bestowed; gifts when something is contributed toward church buildings or furnishings; vows when people fulfill what they vowed in dangers. Those offer a whole burnt-offering who leave the world and distribute their possessions to the poor.

And as the ancients, by decree of the Law, [Col. 0115C] assembled in Jerusalem and made offerings at certain solemnities—namely Easter, Pentecost, and the feast of Tabernacles [Note: [Col. 0115] Exod. 34]—so, by the institution of the holy Fathers, we are bound to offer according to our means at the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, Pentecost, and the feast of All Saints, so that priests may have sustenance from these offerings. For offerings ought to be applied to the needs of priests, or the poor, or another purpose belonging to the sacrament of the altar. Moreover, an offering should be made to purchase the Paschal candle, as the Gallican Church does. Contributions and joint collections should be made to buy lights; otherwise, as some say, people are not bound. But if they are made, they are voluntary offerings. Yet where burials are sold and payments are demanded for the ringing of bells, it is sin, as some say, as though the Church’s sacraments were being sold.

First, moreover, men should offer, who signify those strong in Christ—namely the martyrs, who suffered harsh things in the primitive Church and died as victims of Christ. Then women should offer, who signify the more frail—namely confessors, who in a time of peace offered to the Lord sacrifices of praise. While the people make their offerings in this manner, the clergy sing the offering or offertory, signifying the gladness of the offerers: “For God loves a cheerful giver” [Note: [Col. 0115] 2 Cor. 9]; or commemorating the joy [Col. 0116A] of the Israelite people offering gifts for the construction of the tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0115] Exod. 35], and likewise of Solomon’s Temple [Note: [Col. 0115] 2 Chron. 2]; or recalling the praises and acclamations of the children who, with psalms and flowers, came to meet Christ descending from the Mount of Olives and approaching the gibbet of the cross [Note: [Col. 0115] Matt. 21].

Or rather, it signifies the cry of the woman—that is, the Church—who in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0115] ch. 12] is read to be clothed with the sun, namely Christ, whom she put on in baptism; to have the moon beneath her feet, that is, to tread underfoot all mutable things; and to have on her head a crown of twelve stars, that is, to bear at her beginning the choir of the twelve apostles. Being with child, she cries out, suffering in labour to give birth. The offertory, by its grave and resounding [Col. 0116B] chant, imitates the cry of this woman in labour—that is, the saving suffering of the Lord. Stretched out in neumes and made fruitful with verses, however long its jubilant utterance, it is unable adequately to express what it signifies.

Once the offerings have been received, the priest—who, according to some, had thus far omitted preaching—also fittingly preaches here, warning the people to present themselves worthy of the coming immolation.

## CHAPTER VI. ON THE FIFTH PART OF THE MASS

“Christ entered once into the Holy Places” [Note: [Col. 0115] Heb. 9].

The priest, about to enter the altar to arrange the immolation, first washes his hands, because the Lord, before entering Jerusalem to suffer [Note: [Col. 0115] Luke 19], shed tears for love of us, as became known in the raising of Lazarus [Note: [Col. 0115] John 11]. [Col. 0116C] The earlier priests also washed themselves in the basin when about to sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0115] Exod. 30], which figured purity of works and our tears.

Besides these, the ministers also offer, signifying the faithful champions who, under Antichrist, amid diverse torments, will offer themselves to Christ as a living whole burnt-offering. But a linen cloth is first prepared upon the altar, so that, as it has been cleansed of earthly moisture and shines with its own brightness, so the mind of those offering may be cleansed from carnal desire and shine before God in simplicity.

Some, however, first offer and arrange the offerings on the altar, and first receive the people’s offerings, whom they refresh with the bread of God’s word. But this is, I think, an inverted order, due rather to sloth or ignorance than to the disciplined skill of any chastity. For the right order is that the word is first heard, [Col. 0116D] secondly expounded, thirdly believed, and fourthly put into execution. For faith is from hearing [Note: [Col. 0115] Rom. 10], and faith works through love [Note: [Col. 0115] Gal. 5].

The ministers offer bread, wine, and water. These are the earthly and material substance of this sacrifice; there is another, divine substance, concerning which we shall speak below. Melchizedek offered bread and wine [Note: [Col. 0115] Gen. 14], and Christ also offered them to the disciples at supper [Note: [Col. 0115] Matt. 26]; but there it was the figure of the body, here the substance of truth. For he gave his own body, taken from the Virgin, into which we believe the bread is transubstantiated.

This sacrament [Col. 0117A] is therefore made from bread because Christ calls himself bread, saying: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven” [Note: [Col. 0117] John 6], of which it is said: “Man ate the bread of angels” [Note: [Col. 0117] Ps. 77]. Or it is because, just as bread is made from many grains, so Christ’s particular body consists of many members, and his general body, which is the Church, of many faithful persons [Note: [Col. 0117] Eph. and Col. 1].

The grains are beaten out of their husks by flails; once dried, they are crushed between two stones. When flour has been made from them, water is sprinkled on it and it is kneaded. Then, having been made into bread, it is put into an oven; once baked, it turns white. Thus Christ’s members—or Christ himself, the noble grain, of whom it is said, “Unless a grain of wheat falls,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0117] John 12]—was separated from the husk, that is, the company of the apostles, by swords and clubs; dried by reproaches; scourged by Jews and [Col. 0117B] Gentiles as though by two stones; separated as through a sieve from rejected Barabbas; sprinkled with his own blood; nailed to the cross; and, baked by the fire of suffering, transformed into the brightness of immortality [Note: [Col. 0117] Matt. 26, 27, and 28].

The faithful likewise are beaten from the husk of their old life by the flail of preaching; dried by repentance; struck by the doctrine of the two laws; sifted when they are separated from unbelievers; sprinkled with the water of baptism; kneaded together by the bond of charity [Note: [Col. 0117] Col. 3]; baked in the furnace of tribulation; bathed in the brightness of innocence; and re-formed in God’s image [Note: [Col. 0117] 2 Cor. 3]. This is the sacrament.

It is made from wine because Christ made himself the vine, saying: “I am the true vine” [Note: [Col. 0117] John 15]; or because, [Col. 0117C] as wine is made from many grapes, so Christ’s particular body consists of many members, and his general body, which is the Church, of many faithful persons. Grapes are pressed between two pieces of wood in the winepress and are expressed into wine. Thus Christ’s members—or Christ himself—was pressed between the two timbers of the cross, from whose side blood was shed [Note: [Col. 0117] John 19]. The faithful too are trodden in tribulations and the pressures of the world; and, shedding their blood for Christ, they themselves are incorporated through suffering.

This sacrament, as Pope Alexander decreed, is made with water, because water came forth from Christ’s side [Note: [Col. 0117] ibid.]; or because “many waters” are many peoples [Note: [Col. 0117] Rev. 17]. Therefore, by water’s being mixed with wine, it is understood that the people are redeemed by Christ’s blood, or that they have been redeemed by the blood of the Passion and the water of baptism. [Col. 0117D] Whether one is transubstantiated without the other, and into what water is transubstantiated—if they are transubstantiated, how this occurs—let us for the present leave to investigating theologians, whom the labour of inquiry harasses, since we have also treated these matters diligently elsewhere, both on the Decrees and in disputations of theology. Yet we know that neither is the people saved without blood, nor is this mystery performed except for the people’s sake.

This sacramental bread passes into flesh, and the wine into [Col. 0118A] blood; because the Paschal Lamb, slain for us [Note: [Col. 0117] Exod. 12], redeemed our flesh from death, and, shedding his blood, laid down his life for us [Note: [Col. 0117] John 10], and purified from sins our soul, which dwells in the blood [Note: [Col. 0117] Lev. 17]. Observe that, although there are two species, there are not two sacrifices. For the unity of the Word brings about the unity of the sacrifice. This is the cloak with which Noah’s sons covered him [Note: [Col. 0117] Gen. 9], by which Christians cover Christ’s drunkenness—that is, his Passion—under the sacrifice.

Whether this bread should be unleavened or leavened is a question because of the importunity of the Greeks. For they say: “The Blessed Virgin was pregnant by the Holy Spirit; rightly, therefore, we signify the Lord’s incarnation by leavened bread, because of the swelling of the virgin womb.” I reply: We do not offer the Virgin’s womb [Col. 0118B] in sacrifice, nor do we believe a womb necessary for transubstantiation, but faith and God’s Word. For one who works with his hands and speaks the word but does not believe is an ass pricking up its ears at a lyre without understanding the melody of the song. Therefore, one who eats visible bread and, by unbelief, drives out the invisible, kills Christ; for he separates life from what gives life and rends, as though dead, the body of the sacrifice. Therefore he is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0117] 1 Cor. 11].

This is spiritual life, represented for us in the sacrifice without animal life, as the sun’s light without heat is represented in the work of the moon. Again the Greek says: “To offer unleavened bread is to Judaize. If, therefore, you insist on observing this Latin figure, you Judaize in the other matters also, in circumcision and sacrifices.” I reply: Unleavened bread indeed signifies that “we should feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” [Note: [Col. 0117] 1 Cor. 5]. Yet this figure of so necessary a matter is not to be cast aside. For we have not abandoned all the significant observances of the Law; some are still actually celebrated, so that what they signify may be brought before our minds opportunely and importunately. For we use a temple, altar, lampstand, censer, oil, the full moon at Easter, and similar things; yet we are not judged to Judaize in them.

The Latin proves that unleavened bread should be offered because the Lord, fulfilling the Law, blessed, broke, and gave unleavened bread to his disciples, saying: “Do this in remembrance of me” [Note: [Col. 0117] Matt. 26]. Under the Law, moreover, [Col. 0118D] leaven was not to be offered, according to: “Thou shalt not sacrifice the bread of my victim upon leaven” [Note: [Col. 0117] Exod. 23]; and elsewhere: “For seven days ye shall eat unleavened bread” [Note: [Col. 0117] Exod. 12; Deut. 16]. Hence Paul says: “Let us feast, not with the leaven of malice, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” [Note: [Col. 0117] 1 Cor. 5], so that between Christ, who took flesh without sin from the sinful mass—as unleavened bread from leaven—and the Christian people, figured by water, there may be no malice or corruption, just as in unleavened bread there is no foreign mixture between the wheat and the water.

[Col. 0119A] This bread is formed in the shape of a denarius, both because Christ, the bread of life [Note: [Col. 0119] John 6], was betrayed for denarii [Note: [Col. 0119] Matt. 26], and because the same denarius is to be given as a reward to those labouring in the vineyard [Note: [Col. 0119] Matt. 20]. On this bread the image and name of the emperor are often written, because through this bread we are re-formed into God’s image [Note: [Col. 0119] 2 Cor. 3], and our names are written in the Book of Life [Note: [Col. 0119] Luke 10].

This bread is to be formed and baked by priests, and placed upon the table, after the pattern of the breads which were also called the bread of presentation and the priests’ bread [Note: [Col. 0119] Exod. 25; Lev. 24]. Though Christ once redeemed believers by his death [Note: [Col. 0119] Heb. 9], the Church nevertheless necessarily repeats this sacrament daily for these reasons: those labouring in the vineyard are daily refreshed by it [Note: [Col. 0119] Matt. 20]; neophytes are incorporated through it; and the memory of Christ’s Passion [Col. 0119B] is daily impressed upon the minds of the faithful for imitation. Therefore it is called daily bread. For just as formerly his presence in flesh capable of dying was necessary, so now his presence in the sacrament, by which he may be eaten, is necessary; for it is said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” [Note: [Col. 0119] John 6].

The ministers must offer in the following order.

First, the washed priest, clothed in sacred vestments, enters the sanctuary and comes to the consecrated altar. This is Christ, who entered the great furnished upper room with his disciples to dine [Note: [Col. 0119] Luke 22]. Observe that Pope Zachary decreed, out of reverence [Col. 0119C] for the sacrament, that no one should approach the altar with a staff, that no one should do so with covered head, and that no one should celebrate Mass without consecrated priestly vestments or except on a consecrated altar.

Afterward the deacon spreads the corporal on the altar. The subdeacon carries the chalice in his left hand, the paten in his right, and the corporal above them; one of the singers carries the offering with the *fanon*, and wine with an ampulla. Another presents water to be mixed with the wine; finally the archdeacon, pouring water into the chalice, offers it to the bishop. This is the custom of certain churches: the subdeacon is Christ; the chalice, the Passion; the paten, the cross; the left hand, the present life; the right, the future; the corporal, the Church; one singer signifies the Jewish people, the other the Gentile people; the ampulla, devotion; [Col. 0119D] the offering, the body; the wine, the blood; the water signifies the Church; the archdeacon, Christ; and the bishop, God the Father.

Thus the subdeacon carries the chalice in his left hand because Christ drank from the torrent on the way [Note: [Col. 0119] Ps. 109], that is, endured the Passion in the present life. He carries the paten in his right because he attained glory: for this reason God exalted him [Note: [Col. 0119] Phil. 2]. The corporal is placed above them, because the Church never ceases to imitate his Passion; for the corporal is whitened by much labour, and the Church is conformed to Christ through many tribulations [Note: [Col. 0119] Acts 14]. Our Christ, the subdeacon, [Col. 0120A] also carried the paten with the chalice when he bore the cross together with the Passion [Note: [Col. 0119] John 19].

The first singer offers the offering with the *fanon* and wine with the ampulla, because the primitive Church received from the Jews faith in the Passion within devotion of mind. Observe that the offering is presented not in bare hands but with a white *fanon*, because Christ’s body is worthily received only by those who have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires [Note: [Col. 0119] Gal. 5]. The other singer offers water, and the deacon mixes it with wine and offers it to the bishop. This is the Gentile world, which offered its multitude, which Christ in his Passion offered to God the Father.

Our order, however, is this: the subdeacon offers the chalice and paten with bread and wine to the deacon; the deacon carries the offerings in his hands to the priest, [Col. 0120B] or—as is done among the more careful—arranges everything upon the altar itself. For the Law, signified by the subdeacon, only prefigured this sacrifice of our salvation in Melchizedek [Note: [Col. 0119] Gen. 14]; but through the evangelical tradition, signified by the deacon, it came to the altar, that is, to the Church’s solemn rite.

That the bishop alone mixes water with wine signifies that Christ alone redeemed the peoples by blood [Note: [Col. 0119] Rev. 5; Isa. 53]. That the priest places the offerings on the altar, upon the cross made in the altar’s consecration with chrism, is Christ affixing his flesh to the cross. That the deacon puts the chalice with wine and the water on the right-hand side signifies that the Gospel teaches blood and water to have flowed from Christ’s right side [Col. 0120C] [Note: [Col. 0119] John 19].

That the deacon lays out the corporal signifies that the Gospel fully describes Christ—or Christ’s body, indeed his whole humanity. For the corporal signifies Christ’s body: just as the corporal is made from pure linen and, through much labour, is turned white, so Christ’s body passed from the Virgin’s womb through many tribulations into the glory of the resurrection [Note: [Col. 0119] Matt. 20]. Or it signifies that body’s tribulation, purity, and glory. Or it signifies Christ himself: for just as the corporal is folded so that neither its beginning nor its end appears, so his divinity lacks a beginning and has no end; and just as the corporal is joined to the offering and placed on the altar, so flesh, joined to divinity, is fastened to the cross. Or it signifies the shroud in which we read that the Lord’s body was wrapped [Col. 0120D] [Note: [Col. 0119] Matt. 27]. Therefore Sylvester decreed that the sacrifice of the altar should be celebrated only on a linen cloth.

He who places two corporals signifies the two linen cloths with which Joseph wrapped the Lord’s body, prepared with spices [Note: [Col. 0119] ibid.]; or, by one that is multiplied, Christ’s manifold humanity—that is, his humanity declared in many ways—and, by the other, its manifold labour.

When the priest censes the sacrifice, he asks that the prayer made over the Lord’s Passion may rise to the ears of the Divinity [Note: [Col. 0119] Ps. 140] as a sweet savour. Or it signifies [Col. 0121A] that Christ, offered for us, was to the Father a sweet savour [Note: [Col. 0121] Eph. 5]. In this he recalls that the priest, entering the tabernacle, offered incense to the Lord, which the Lord prohibited from being offered for human use [Note: [Col. 0121] Exod. 30]. Hence, after blessed incense has been offered over the altar, if the censer is taken down to the people, other incense without a blessing must be added and offered to people. Hence also the fragrance of blessed incense is not given in church to the bridegroom and bride.

Then the priest, bowing before the altar, prays and says, “Receive, etc.” For Christ, bending himself to the disciples’ feet after handing over the sacrament at supper, prayed to the Father [Note: [Col. 0121] John 13; Matt. 26]. Then, turning to the people, he says, “Pray, brethren,” because Christ instructed the apostles to pray [Note: [Col. 0121] ibid.]. The priest urges them [Col. 0121B] to pray so that the sacrifice may be acceptable to the Lord. Accordingly, from this point we should attend to prayers and psalms.

Some say that before he says “Pray,” he ought to say silently during this turning, “The Lord be with you,” maintaining that this turning signifies that private appearance in which the Lord appeared to Mary Magdalene after the Resurrection [Note: [Col. 0121] John 20]. Subsequently he recites the Secret over the offerings, because Christ, having withdrawn at length from the apostles on the Mount of Olives, prayed in secret, saying: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” [Note: [Col. 0121] Matt. 26]. The priest prays for the acceptance of the victim, something he had previously warned the people to do.

This silence also signifies and recalls the sacrifice hidden in the sacrifices of the Fathers: Abel [Note: [Col. 0121] Gen. 4], Isaac [Note: [Col. 0121] Gen. 22], the Paschal lamb [Note: [Col. 0121] Exod. 12], the red heifer [Note: [Col. 0121] Num. 19], and the scapegoat [Note: [Col. 0121] Lev. 16]; or it signifies Christ’s hiding-place before the Passion. For our Lord no longer walked openly among the Jews when they were planning to kill him, but went away to the region near the desert, to a city called Ephraim [Note: [Col. 0121] John 11]. In this he prefigured that he would go away into the region of the Gentiles by the feet of those proclaiming the Gospel. And he likewise hid himself in Jerusalem. Hence the lamb to be sacrificed on the fourteenth moon was kept enclosed from the tenth moon [Note: [Col. 0121] Exod. 12].

Therefore the priest prays in this silence and prepares the holy sacrifice, because our Lord meditated in his hiding-place upon the saving mystery of the Passion. But since, at the approaching Passover, the Lord then walked openly—especially when he raised Lazarus [Note: [Col. 0121] John 11]—[Col. 0121D] the priest raises his voice and concludes the Secret aloud: “For ever and ever.” To this the people answer aloud: “Amen,” which means “let it be,” the word used by the Lord in the world’s creation when he said: “Let there be light” [Note: [Col. 0121] Gen. 1]. It is as though the people say: “I confess that by the Word through which the world was created, it has also been re-created.”

Here, according to some, the fifth office begins, in which we are reminded of the time when Christ went up into the great furnished upper room at supper and there gave thanks to God [Note: [Col. 0121] Matt. 26]. According to John [Note: [Col. 0121] John 17], he sang a hymn [Col. 0122A]. Therefore, by “The Lord be with you,” we understand the prayer he made for his disciples [Note: [Col. 0121] Mark 14]. By “Lift up your hearts,” we recall the ascent into the upper room; or by “The Lord be with you,” we desire the present King of heaven, who may make us such that he may deign to hold among us that banquet in which, lifting our hearts on high above his head, we may be able, with the woman bearing ointment, to pour out an alabaster flask of costly pure nard ointment [Note: [Col. 0121] Mark 14]—that is, to confess the divinity of the Son with the ointment of Catholic confession. For by “Lift up your hearts,” we rise to confess the Son’s divinity.

Cyprian says: We say “Lift up your hearts” so that all carnal awareness may depart, and the mind may think of nothing except that alone for which it prays; that it may shut its breast against the adversary and stand open to God alone, and not permit God’s enemy to approach it in the time of prayer. Or by “Lift up your hearts,” we invoke the ministry of angels, that they may receive our vows and carry them to God; or we raise ourselves to angelic harmonies, and for that reason sing with a pleasing voice. By “Let us give thanks,” we recall Christ’s thanksgivings and invite the people to give thanks to God the Father through the Son, through whom we are redeemed and admitted with the angels to praise.

Whence follows the Preface, that is, the preliminary utterance and preparation of the ensuing Canon, which prepares our minds for Christ’s mystery. At the beginning of this written Preface, the form of the letter V is placed sacramentally: for V signifies Christ’s humanity, [Col. 0122C] while D signifies his divinity. The former opens on one side and closes on the other, because Christ’s humanity is visibly from his mother but invisibly from the Holy Spirit—“the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie” [Note: [Col. 0121] John 1]. This letter O, however, is enclosed by a circular ring, because the Divinity is eternal and without beginning or end; the point of the cross in its midst is Christ’s Passion. This figure is therefore placed at the beginning of the Preface, because by the mystery of the union and of the Lord’s Passion human beings are reconciled to angels, and human things are joined to divine things in the proclamation of the Savior. For in every Preface human beings and angels join together to sing praises to the King. Thus they are sung in a high and pleasing voice, because the praises of angels are represented.

And note that Gelasius composed the Prefaces [Col. 0122D] in polished language; but, whereas the Prefaces had formerly been innumerable, he ordained that only nine be sung: namely, those of the Nativity, Epiphany, the Fast, the Cross or Passion, Resurrection, Ascension, the coming of the Holy Spirit, the Trinity, and the Apostles. Urban added a tenth Preface, of blessed Mary. There is also an eleventh, namely the daily Preface, into which others are inserted: some after “it is fitting and salutary,” others after “eternal God,” and others after “our Lord.”

In all of them the address is directed to the Father, to whom majesty is attributed [Col. 0123A] because of his authority. The angels praise him—in the designation “angels,” archangels too are understood; the dominions adore him; the powers, among which the principalities are also understood, tremble in wonder; the heavens, that is, the thrones and powers of heaven, rejoice; the seraphim, among whom the cherubim too are understood, celebrate with shared exultation. Note that seraph and cherub, as Jerome says, are singular and masculine in gender; their plural ending is cherubim. This does not mean that God’s ministers have sex, but that words, according to the character of the language, are called by different genders. Greek usage, however, writes cherubim and seraphim in the neuter gender. With them we join our voices, saying in a suppliant confession of praise: “Holy, holy, holy.”

[Col. 0123B] It is repeated three times because the Trinity is praised together. “Lord God” is uttered once and in the singular, because unity is adored. “Sabaoth,” that is, “of angelic hosts,” who give thanks to the Creator for his benefits, saying, “Heaven and earth are full of thy glory.” Yet heaven is full in actuality, while earth is full in hope; but then earth also will be full in actuality, when this is fulfilled: “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth” [Note: [Col. 0123] Matt. 6].

Thus far is the hymn of the angels, taken from Isaiah, who saw seraphim crying: “Holy, holy, holy, the Lord of hosts! The whole earth is full of thy glory” [Note: [Col. 0123] Isa. 6]. He foresaw the time of glory. For in the time of the Law God was known in Judaea [Note: [Col. 0123] Ps. 75]; but in the time of grace, those will come from east and west who [Col. 0123C] “will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” [Note: [Col. 0123] Matt. 8].

“Hosanna in the highest. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Hosanna in the highest.” This is taken from the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0123] Matt. 21]. Therefore, when it is sung, we make the sign of the cross upon ourselves. For here we also represent the joyful cry of the children meeting the Lord with flowers, and we give thanks to Christ for the benefit of our redemption: he triumphed through the cross and makes us triumph [Note: [Col. 0123] Col. 2]. It is the hymn of human beings adoring Christ’s humanity, rejoicing in the redemption of the human race, and saying: *Hosanna*, as though *hosi anna*, that is, “save, I beseech thee”; for *anna* among the Hebrews is an interjection of entreaty. But if the whole word is *Hosianna*, why do we say *Hosanna*? I answer: either we corrupt it in ignorance, or knowingly [Col. 0123D] contract it by synaloepha, as we customarily do in meters: “Save, I pray, O Lord who dwellest in the highest.”

Hosanna is repeated in order that we may be numbered among the angels in body and soul. Pope Sixtus ordered this hymn to be sung at Mass. Observe also that in this harmony of angels and human beings, we sometimes use organs and musical instruments. This derives from David [Note: [Col. 0123] I Chron. 15] and Solomon [Note: [Col. 0123] II Chron. 5], who instituted the resounding of hymns in God’s sacrifice with organs and other musical instruments, and the acclamation of praises by the people. Nevertheless, just as the heart [Col. 0124A] is greater than the body, so we confess to the Lord more devoutly with the heart than with the body. Our singers are trumpet and psaltery, harp and drum; choir, strings and organ; finally, our well-sounding cymbals, as is sufficiently explained at the end of the Psalter.

At this point Christ’s Passion is represented sometimes by gestures and sometimes by words. For the deacon and subdeacon walk behind the bishop, which figures the flight of the apostles, who fled during Christ’s Passion [Note: [Col. 0123] Matt. 26]. But those who stand behind the altar looking toward the bishop signify the women who, standing at a distance, saw his Passion [Note: [Col. 0123] Matt. 27]. All, both those standing behind and those looking upon the bishop’s face, bow themselves, reverencing the divine majesty and the Lord’s incarnation, which are introduced [Col. 0124B] by the song of angels and human beings. For the angelic order, saying, “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth,” introduces the divine majesty; the human order, saying, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” signifies his coming in the flesh.

Or the bowing signifies the disciples’ dismay at Christ’s death: they did not dare to raise themselves or confess that they were his disciples [Note: [Col. 0123] John 20]. They therefore remain bowed until it is said, “Deliver us from evil.” For it was vain for them to rise before the light [Note: [Col. 0123] Ps. 126], that is, to glory in Christ before the Resurrection, through which they were freed from every tribulation. Thus this is the seventh petition, and seven is the number of universality.

[Col. 0124C] After this the priest kisses the feet of Majesty, makes the sign of the cross upon his forehead, and, bowing himself, says, “Thee therefore”; thereby indicating that they should approach the mystery of the cross reverently. In some books the Majesty of the Father and the cross of the Crucified are depicted, so that we may as it were see him whom we invoke as present, and that the Passion being represented may be impressed upon the eyes of the heart; in some, however, only one of the two is depicted. Some priests first kiss the feet of Majesty and then those of the Crucified, according to the order of the Canon; others first those of the Crucified and then those of Majesty, because through the Son one comes to the Father [Note: [Col. 0123] John 14].

*Canon* is Greek; in Latin it is called a “rule,” because the consecration of the sacrament is regularly performed through it. It is also called an “action,” because in it our cause is transacted with God. It is said silently for several reasons. [Col. 0124D] First, because God attends not to the cry of the mouth but of the heart; hence he said even to Moses, “Why dost thou cry to me?” [Note: [Col. 0123] Exod. 14], although Moses himself was silent. For when we speak to God in thought, a resounding voice is unnecessary. Hence the Lord says, “Enter into thy chamber and pray to thy Father” [Note: [Col. 0123] Matt. 6]; and the Prophet says, “Be pierced with compunction in your chambers” [Note: [Col. 0123] Ps. 4]. Thus the praying Publican deserved to be heard, which the shouting Pharisee could not obtain [Note: [Col. 0123] Luke 18]. Nevertheless, we utter words so that we may not appear utterly ignorant of what we ought to ask or intend.

Another reason is that we may not grow weary through a long recitation, [Col. 0125A] or prevent the people from praying, who, as stated above, are then obliged to pray. Or it is lest the words of so great a mystery be cheapened by everyday use, and lest they become known to laypeople who would misuse them in unsuitable places—[as is related of shepherds: on a certain day, when they had placed bread and wine upon a stone and pronounced these words over them, the bread was suddenly changed into flesh and the wine into blood; divine vengeance struck them when fire was sent from heaven]. Therefore it is commanded under anathema in a synodal decree that no one say the Canon unless clothed in sacred vestments, with the book, at the altar, and over the sacrifice.

Or it is to signify that human reason cannot possibly comprehend so great a mystery fully; therefore it is said in a secret [Col. 0125B] voice. Or by this is represented how the priest of old entered the Holy of Holies, the secret place of secrets [Note: [Col. 0125] Exod. 30]. Again, it is performed secretly because this offering belongs to the priest alone. Therefore let the priest say, “Thee therefore.” Observe that the Canon begins with tau, T, which expresses the form of the cross; therefore the Crucified is customarily depicted upon it, so that the Passion, whose sign lies before the eyes, may be impressed also upon the heart’s eyes of the priest, who addresses the Father as though present. Thus he says, “Thee,” and the priest bows himself down to the altar, because here begins the mystery of Christ’s Passion, he who in obedience to the Father bowed himself down to the altar of the cross [Note: [Col. 0125] Phil. 2]. And behold the high priest who entered the Holy of Holies once a year [Note: [Col. 0125] Heb. 9]; [Col. 0125C] behold Christ, who entered once, having obtained eternal redemption.

“Most merciful Father,” that is, “making the mind bright”: for *clemens* is said as though *clara mens*, “bright mind.” The mind becomes bright when it senses God as propitious. Hence this sacrament ought not to be celebrated without light; for light signifies the Holy Spirit, who consecrates this sacrament and enlightens those who receive it worthily. Light also signifies joy, and this sacrament gives us eternal joy.

“We beseech thee”: here he kisses the altar in reverence for the Passion. “Bless these gifts”: concerning the three signs made over these and the others that follow, we shall treat here generally. We therefore make crosses, which have four angles, over the sacrifice, because while Christ hung upon [Col. 0125D] the cross he redeemed the four regions of the world. We arrange them in six orders: either because of the perfection of the number six, attributed to Christ’s body; or because it is whole and perfect; or because through his Passion the world was redeemed—a world completed in six days and distinguished by six ages.

Observe that in nearly every order the signs are arranged in an odd number, because Christ’s body, remaining one, is not divided. For we either make three crosses and express faith in the holy Trinity, or five and denote the fivefold Passion of the Lord [Col. 0126A].

In the first order we make three crosses when we say, “These gifts, these offerings, these holy sacrifices.” Here we indicate the time before the Law, distinguished by three intervals: from Adam to Noah, then to Abraham, and then to Moses. In these ages the righteous prefigured Christ in their sacrifices: Abel in the lamb [Note: [Col. 0125] Gen. 4], Melchizedek in bread and wine [Note: [Col. 0125] Gen. 14], Abraham in his son [Note: [Col. 0125] Gen. 22].

In the second order we make five crosses, saying, “Blessed, enrolled, ratified, body, and blood.” Here we express the time of the Law, which is distinguished by five books and in each of which Christ’s Passion is denoted; or which was governed by five persons, namely judge, king, prince, prophet, and priest [Note: [Col. 0125] Hos. 13], in whose persons Christ is prefigured. For what is Joshua [Col. 0126B] conquering by stratagem the king of the city of Ai [Note: [Col. 0125] Josh. 8], if not Christ overcoming the devil’s pride through weakness? What is David in the cave [Note: [Col. 0125] I Sam. 22], if not Christ in the tomb? What is Zerubbabel, born in confusion [Note: [Col. 0125] I Ezra 2], if not Christ born in the flesh? What is Elijah’s sitting by the brook Cherith [Note: [Col. 0125] III Kings 17], if not that the Lord drank from the torrent of the Passion on Calvary [Note: [Col. 0125] Ps. 109]? What is Jesus clothed in filthy garments [Note: [Col. 0125] Matt. 27; Zech. 3], if not Christ who took a foreign woman as wife?

In the third order, taking bread and wine into our hands, we make two crosses, one over the bread and the other over the chalice, saying, “Who on the day before,” etc. Here we indicate the time of the Supper and the time of grace, in which the two walls are joined in the cornerstone [Note: [Col. 0125] Eph. 2], [Col. 0126C] or the giant of twofold substance is crucified [Note: [Col. 0125] Ps. 18].

In the fourth order we make five crosses, saying, “A pure victim, a holy victim, an immaculate victim, the holy bread of eternal life, and the chalice of everlasting salvation.” Here we signify that Christ received five wounds in the flesh and redeemed five ages.

In the fifth order we make three crosses, saying, “Thou sanctifiest, enlivenest, blessest,” etc. Here we represent the primitive Church, which received faith in the Trinity.

In the sixth order we make five crosses with the offering: four over the chalice, saying, “Through him, and with him, and in him, is unto thee, God the almighty Father”; and a fifth at the side of the chalice, saying, “In the unity of the Holy Spirit.” Here we note the manner of the Lord’s Passion: he bore four wounds [Col. 0126D] in hands and feet, and a fifth in his side.

From what precedes it is clear that we make twenty-three signs. Since they are made with three fingers because of faith in the Trinity, if you multiply them by three, you will have sixty-nine. If to these you add the three signs made with the offering over the chalice while saying, “The peace of the Lord be always with you,” they become seventy-two: namely, the seventy-two languages scattered through pride, gathered through Christ’s humility, redeemed by his Passion, and joined to him by his body and blood.

It seems to Augustine that, if the cross were made over the bread and [Col. 0127A] wine only once, it could suffice, because the Lord was crucified once [Note: [Col. 0127] I Pet. 3]. Now let us return to the text.

“These gifts,” with reference to the bread, in which are flour and water; “these offerings,” with reference to the wine, in which are wine and water; “these holy sacrifices,” with reference to both, unblemished—that is, without stain—like the spotless Paschal Lamb [Note: [Col. 0127] Exod. 12], because it signifies Christ, who is without spot or wrinkle. Or we mark these three words with three crosses because we give thanks to the triune God, who grants us to receive the cup of salvation and call upon the Lord’s name [Note: [Col. 0127] Ps. 115], who gives us a gift and received an offering from us as a sacrifice.

For the same sacrifices are gifts and offerings: gifts, because they were given to us by him for our sustenance; offerings, because they are offered by us to him [Col. 0127B] for his praise. A gift is given by a superior; an offering, by an inferior; they are sacrifices in order to be sacrificed. Or, according to Augustine: we offer gifts when we give ourselves to him; offerings when we remember his benefits; unblemished sacrifices when we render him humility and praises.

“First of all, which we offer unto thee.” Observe that the prayer of the Canon is divided into five; hence it concludes five times, “Through Christ our Lord,” because the prayer of the faithful is heard through the Lord’s fivefold Passion. First we offer for the Catholic Church. Behold the priest of the Law, who, on entering the Holy of Holies, prayed [Note: [Col. 0127] Heb. 5 and 9]; behold Christ, who before his Passion prayed, glorified himself, and preserved his disciples [Note: [Col. 0127] John 16], [Col. 0127C] and who still intercedes daily for us [Note: [Col. 0127] Rom. 8]. Thus the priest pours forth prayers for himself and for the whole Church, which consists of prelates and subjects; hence there follows concerning the prelates:

“Together with thy servant, our Pope.” What some add concerning the bishop and king is a new tradition. “And all orthodox worshipers of the Catholic and apostolic faith.” Here schismatics and heretics are excluded, since they are neither orthodox—that is, of right faith—nor Catholic—that is, universal. After this there is added concerning the subjects: “Remember, O Lord, thy servants and handmaids, whose faith is known and whose devotion is manifest to thee.” For this reason catechumens, who have not received the sacraments of faith, are excluded at the beginning of the Canon. For it is written: “A stranger shall not eat of them, [Col. 0127D] because they are holy” [Note: [Col. 0127] Exod. 29; Lev. 22]. Therefore we admit to the eating of the Lamb only those joined to our household: every member of the household of faith, from prince to commoner, from apostle to tax collector.

“For whom we offer” in act, or “who offer unto thee” in devotion. “For themselves” is an exegesis, that is, an explanation, of what follows: “for the redemption of their souls, for the hope of their salvation and well-being.” “In communion with.” The prayer concludes with commemoration of the blessed Virgin, the apostles, and the martyrs: both in order to represent the priest of the Law, who bore the names of the fathers on his vestments [Note: [Col. 0127] Exod. 28], and Christ, who knows in mind and [Col. 0128A] deed the names of his sheep [Note: [Col. 0127] John 10]; and in order that they may be fortified by the aid of divine protection through the prayers and merits of these saints.

The holy Mother of God is commemorated in this sacrifice because the true victim proceeded from a virginal womb. The apostles likewise, because they proved Christ’s Passion by the testimony of word and blood. Peter, Andrew, and Philip were crucified; Paul, James, Matthew, and Bartholomew were beheaded; James, Simon, and Thaddaeus were killed; John was tortured with poison; Thomas was pierced through. The martyrs are also added because Christ’s Passion is confirmed by their sufferings. Some were supreme pontiffs, such as Linus; some bishops, such as Cyprian of Carthage; some deacons, such as Lawrence; some soldiers, such as Chrysogonus; John and Paul; some physicians, such as Cosmas [Col. 0128B] and Damian: because all ranks or orders have borne witness to the Lord’s Passion. Perhaps confessors ought not to be named here, because martyrs are properly “witnesses.” Some, however, add here the names of their own patrons.

“This offering of our service,” etc. In this second prayer he prays for himself and those serving under him, that the Lord, appeased, may receive their offering, which he presents to the Lord by means of a demonstrative pronoun. “And dispose our days,” etc. Gregory added this so that no one might consider himself secure here; rather, “let him who stands take heed lest he fall” [Note: [Col. 0127] I Cor. 10].

“This offering”: here he approaches the consecration of the Lord, saying, “This offering,” that is, the earthly material destined for the body of thy Son—thou, [Col. 0128C] O God, we beseech thee, “in all things,” that is, with all thought, all life, and all understanding, deign to make it “blessed,” that is, filled with the Holy Spirit; “enrolled,” that is, assigned to the Divinity; “ratified,” that is, established in truth so as to suffice for salvation; “reasonable,” in our faith; “acceptable,” in our devotion.

Behold Abigail, the wife of a foolish man, who prevented David from shedding blood and defiling his own hand. David blessed her, saying: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, and blessed be thy speech, and blessed be thou, who hast prevented me from going to bloodshed and from avenging myself with my own hand” [Note: [Col. 0127] I Sam. 25]. She is the Church, once the devil’s wife, which by the offering of this present sacrifice comes before Christ in his agony and begs for peace, lest he so avenge himself upon her that she perish with her husband in eternal [Col. 0128D] damnation. David fulfills this offering and prayer: “blessed,” when he blesses her speech; “enrolled,” when it is not erased by any offering; “ratified,” when the sentence of remission is not violated.

“Who, on the day before he suffered, took bread, blessed it, broke it, gave it to his disciples, and said: Take and eat; this is my body” [Note: [Col. 0127] Matt. 26]. We enact in dramatic gestures what the text says. Some maintain that “he blessed” with a blessing unknown to us, other than the one now used, “This is my body.” Others say that he blessed with the same blessing, and therefore alter the text thus: “He blessed,” saying, [Col. 0129A] “This is my body,” and afterwards broke it and gave it to his disciples, saying, “Take and eat.” This is a repetition of the words. Nor should it be understood that they ministered to themselves the body received from the Lord’s hand; rather, he who consecrated also ministered it himself.

If, when he blessed, he made the sign of the cross, those who were present know; especially since the banner of the holy cross had not yet been raised. And just as elsewhere it is said of the five loaves [Note: [Col. 0129] John 6], “He blessed”—that is, he poured into them the grace of multiplication—so here too we should understand “He blessed” to mean that he poured in the grace of transubstantiation, so that the bread might be transubstantiated into flesh. He filled it with the Holy Spirit, or showed it already filled, and thus broke it, thereby showing that he was to submit himself to death.

Observe that at the utterance of these words, [Col. 0129B] “This is my body,” the bread is divinely transubstantiated into flesh. For the divine material substance of this sacrifice is the Word which, joined to the element, effects the sacrament; just as the Word joined to flesh makes the man Christ. Indeed, “God is wonderful in his works” [Note: [Col. 0129] Ps. 71, 138]; but it is more wonderful to create all things from nothing than to transubstantiate a creature. Nature herself teaches: water is refined into fire; and a man changes warm wine into cold vinegar. Yet we do not say this because we wish to prove this matter by human reasoning. Logic does not rise to this; mathematics does not investigate it; physics fails in it. Sense occupies the first region, imagination the second, reason the third.
