Those ladies are accustomed to play in these matters, [Col. 0129C] but faith is superior to them: it has no merit when human reason supplies proof. [Note: [Col. 0129] Gregory, Homily 26.] Therefore let no one dispute this; let arguments cease where faith is sought. Let that which cannot be examined without danger be sought humbly; let that which cannot be possessed without reward be believed firmly. Understanding, however, transcends faith, when the saints no longer see in a mirror but face to face [Note: [Col. 0129] I Cor. 13].

“Taking this excellent chalice”: here it is in mystery, but not in metal; here it is in figure, but the other was in material reality. For both this chalice and that which Christ held in his hands signify, and signified, drunkenness—that is, the Lord’s Passion. Behold our David, who appears mad to King Achish [Note: [Col. 0129] I Sam. 21], who carries himself in his hands [Col. 0129D] when, holding bread and wine, he says, “This is my body; this is my blood.” Drool flows from his mouth when he is thought to utter childish things, saying: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” [Note: [Col. 0129] John 6]. Hanging on the cross, he beat the drum and struck at the door—that is, the closed hearts of the Jews.

That the priest elevates the bread signifies that it is food more excellent than all others. Likewise concerning the drink: “Giving thanks,” for our salvation, because we have been justified not by merits but by grace [Note: [Col. 0129] Rom. 3]. “He blessed,” etc.: do not expound what has already been expounded [Col. 0130A].

“Take and drink. O happy drunkenness! O saving fullness! The more abundantly and worthily it is received, the more it deigns to grant sobriety of mind. Judas drank, but did not quench the thirst of eternal fire, because he received the mystery of Jesus Christ unworthily [Note: [Col. 0129] John 13].” Observe that each disciple received the chalice in such a way that the Lord gave drink to each one. Thus the priest here sets down the chalice but does not leave it, saying, “This is the chalice of my blood” [Note: [Col. 0129] Matt. 20], that is, containing blood, or signifying by blood the Passion.

Observe that the Passion is called a chalice either from a hot drink, or because it is drunk in measure. “For God is faithful, who does not permit us to be afflicted beyond what we are able to bear” [Note: [Col. 0129] I Cor. 10]. “Of the new and eternal testament”: understand, “the confirmer.” Holy Scripture [Col. 0130B] is called a testament, as though the declaration of a dead person’s mind, because it contains bequests and trusts promised to us. The Old Testament indeed promised temporal things: “I will give you a land flowing with milk and honey” [Note: [Col. 0129] Lev. 20]. But in the New Testament Christ, through his blood and death, bequeathed eternal life to us as an inheritance.

It is called the New Testament because new blood is poured out for our redemption; formerly the blood of an irrational animal was poured out, not that of an innocent man [Note: [Col. 0129] Heb. 9]. It is called eternal because it will not be changed into another testament, as the Old was changed into the New. “The mystery of faith,” because one thing is seen and another understood: the appearance of bread and wine is perceived, but Christ’s body and blood are believed. *Mysterium* is Greek; in Latin, “secret.” [Col. 0130C] We are commanded to believe this; we do not dare to scrutinize it.

“Which shall be effectively poured out for you apostles and for many,” not for all. For it suffices for all, but has effect only for the elect, who are Christ’s body through the union of love. What is cleansed from guilt by baptism is freed from punishment by the blood. This is the benefit of this sacrament: by its help it becomes possible for the body, which is earth, to ascend to heaven. “For no one ascends to heaven except the Son of Man” [Note: [Col. 0129] John 3]. To him, as to the head, are attached the members of the body: all who through faith in this sacrament are made children of God. Thus the one body, the head with its members, ascends into heaven.

The Truth himself declares the purpose of so great a body in the following words, saying: “As often as [Col. 0130D] you do these things, you shall do them in remembrance of me”: in remembrance of me, who bore infirmities for you [Note: [Col. 0129] Isa. 53], underwent the cross [Note: [Col. 0129] John 19], rose again [Note: [Col. 0129] Mark 16], and ascended into heaven [Note: [Col. 0129] Acts 1].

And now the two fingers are joined together, either in reverence for the sacrament or as a sign that the priest approaches first—that is, that the Son obeys the Father. Hence follows the response of priest and people: “Mindful of so blessed a Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension.” The Church especially commemorates these three because the first wounds our love, the second strengthens faith, and the third gladdens hope.

“From thy gifts and things given.” Gifts [Col. 0131A] are in the eternal reality; things given are in temporal action. We offer a pure victim, namely the body; a holy victim, namely the blood; an immaculate victim, with reference to both. Or: a pure victim, that is, separated from other victims; a holy victim, that is, sanctifying; an immaculate victim, that is, cleansing from stains.

Morally, we offer a pure victim, a holy victim, and an immaculate victim when we offer a sacrifice “from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” [Note: [Col. 0131] I Tim. 1]. It follows: “the holy bread of eternal life.” This is Christ, on whom, having finally fed, we shall be eternally satisfied; “the chalice of perpetual salvation,” by tasting which we shall obtain salvation forever. The five crosses made between these words are the five seals of the Beloved [Note: [Col. 0131] Song 8], the five wounds of the Living One, the clefts of the rock [Col. 0131B] in which the immaculate dove nests [Note: [Col. 0131] Song 2].

Having prayed over the victim to be transubstantiated, transubstantiated it, and offered it transubstantiated to the Father, he now prays for its acceptance: that God may accept it after the pattern of ancient sacrifices and bring it into the sight of the divine majesty, so that through its intercession with the Father and through our reception of it, we may be filled with the blessing of heavenly grace.

“As thou didst deign to accept”: this concerns likeness, not degree. For this sacrifice is much more acceptable to God than that offered by Abel [Note: [Col. 0131] Gen. 4], by Abraham [Note: [Col. 0131] Gen. 22], or by Melchizedek [Note: [Col. 0131] Gen. 14], because reality is more powerful than shadow, truth than figure. We seek likeness itself rather [Col. 0131C] than an equal degree of acceptance.

We resemble Abel if we offer rightly and divide rightly. Since Cain did not do this, he sinned. For he offered rightly, because he offered to God, to whom he owed it; but he divided badly, because, withdrawing his heart from God, he kept himself for himself. Abel, however, subjected himself to the Lord; therefore the Lord looked upon Abel and his offerings. We also resemble Abraham when we offer God the son Isaac, that is, a cheerful will, and obey cheerfully. We likewise resemble Melchizedek when, without testing by human reason, we firmly believe that under the appearances of bread and wine we receive the flesh and blood of Jesus Christ.

Therefore let us divide rightly with Abel, cheerfully with Abraham, spiritually with Melchizedek, offering ourselves as a sacrifice of innocence, obedience, and justice; laying aside the ram-like arrogance of the spirit, stripping off bull-like ferocity, and slaying goat-like lust, according to the saying: “I will offer thee marrowy burnt offerings with the incense of rams; I will offer thee bulls with goats” [Note: [Col. 0131] Ps. 65]. Thus the Lord will accept our sacrifice as he accepted Abel’s gifts, Abraham’s sacrifice, and Melchizedek’s sacrifice and immaculate victim.

These things, I say, are morally applied to us; allegorically, however, they refer to Christ. For example, “thy righteous servant Abel”: in the lamb which he offered, and in himself, who, innocent, died when he was [Col. 0132A] thirty years old, he prefigured that immaculate victim of Christ. “Our patriarch Abraham”: this patriarch, the chief of fathers, is God the Father. For as Abraham offered Isaac but sacrificed the ram, so God handed over his only-begotten Son for us [Note: [Col. 0131] Rom. 8], while his divinity remained unharmed when his flesh was sacrificed. Melchizedek is here read to have been without father and mother, and is said to have sacrificed in bread and wine [Note: [Col. 0131] Heb. 7]. By him the Son of God is rightly understood, who is King Sadoch, King of righteousness, justly rewarding the righteous and justly condemning the unjust; who is without mother in heaven and without father on earth; who offered himself under the appearances of bread and wine to his disciples [Note: [Col. 0131] Matt. 26]. And Pope Leo added to the Canon, “a holy sacrifice, an immaculate victim.”

[Col. 0132B] By the priest’s subsequent bowing, the death of Christ is understood, which was prefigured and represented in the foregoing sacrifices: Christ “bowed his head and gave up the spirit” [Note: [Col. 0131] John 19]. Observe that according to some, during the Canon the deacon washes his hands, signifying that Pilate washed himself when he declared himself clean from Christ’s blood [Note: [Col. 0131] Matt. 27]; or that our filthy works are cleansed by Christ’s Passion; or that no unclean person should proceed to receive the sacraments of faith.

“Command these things to be borne by the hands of thy holy Angel to thy altar on high.” This Angel is the Angel of great counsel, that Counselor [Note: [Col. 0131] Isa. 9] by whose counsel the Father created and re-created the world [Note: [Col. 0131] Prov. 8]. The high altar in the sight of God is Christ crucified, seated at the Father’s right hand. Therefore the Angel bears these sacraments [Col. 0132C] to the high altar in the sight of God when, showing his scars, he intercedes with the Father for us [Note: [Col. 0131] Rom. 8], who perform these sacraments.

Where it is said elsewhere, “Command this to be borne, to be joined to the body of Christ,” it is understood thus: command that what this signifies, that is, the Church Militant, be joined to the Church Triumphant. Or, disharmony is a thing’s being alienated from its own appearance; therefore we ask that the enigma [Note: [Col. 0131] I Cor. 13] of the wayfarer be done away with and that, for us who have attained, the body be revealed in its proper appearance.

“That as many as,” etc. That the priest kisses the altar three times here signifies his giving thanks to the Trinity, which through the Lord’s Passion reconciled the human race to itself [Note: [Col. 0131] II Cor. 5]. At “body and blood,” some make the sign twice here, because the giant of twofold substance is crucified; others do not make it at all.

“We may receive”: according to the primitive Church, either in sacrament and reality, or in reality alone, according to the saying, “Believe, and thou hast eaten” [Note: [Col. 0131] Augustine]. “Every blessing.” Here the priest signs himself, that he may merit to receive the blessing and be filled with heavenly glory.

Remember also, O Lord, your servants, both men and women. Here the Church prays for the dead who rest in Christ, that these sacraments may benefit them; here you may note whatever names you wish [but not on the Lord’s Day, as some say, because souls are believed then to have rest in observance of the Lord’s Day]. And fittingly this remembrance is inserted for those who have departed [Col. 0133A], “who die in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0133] Rev. 14]. For the remembrance of the Lord’s death is completed, and our death follows: Christ went before, and we follow in his footsteps [Note: [Col. 0133] I Pet. 2]. “To us also sinners”: here we pray for penitents, and we interrupt the silence with a slightly audible voice and strike our breasts, recalling the thief’s confession and petition, namely: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” [Note: [Col. 0133] Luke 23], and the promise of the merciful God: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” [Note: [Col. 0133] ibid.]. The striking of the breast is a sign of repentance and mourning. Some refer this elevation to the centurion [Note: [Col. 0133] Matt. 8]. By “with John,” some understand John the Baptist; others Mark, who was also called John [Note: [Col. 0133] Acts 4]. Note that eight men [Col. 0133B] and seven women are counted here, because through this sacrifice the seven charisms of graces and the eight beatitudes are joined in us; likewise, the diversity of sexes and ranks is contained here. For among the evangelists and bishops is John, who is also called Mark, who was bishop of Alexandria; among deacons, Stephen the first martyr; among apostles, Matthias; among the seventy disciples, Barnabas; among patriarchs, Ignatius; among apostolic men, Alexander; among presbyters, Marcellinus; among exorcists, Peter; among the married, Felicity and Perpetua; among virgins, Agatha and all the rest, since all confirmed this sacrifice by their blood. Behold, the twofold commemoration of the saints recalls the *logion* and the ephod, on which the legal [Col. 0133C] high priest bore the names of the fathers [Note: [Col. 0133] Exod. 28].

“Through whom you create all these . . . good things”: you create them, that they may exist; you sanctify them by assigning them to yourself; you make them alive by animating them; you bless them, that they may be useful; you grant them, that they may benefit us. Here the sign of the cross is made three times, because the Lord’s passion is consummated. Accordingly, the corporal is removed, because the veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom [Note: [Col. 0133] Matt. 27]; and whatever had been concealed concerning the Passion is now revealed. Hence, after receiving the vinegar, he said: “It is finished” [Note: [Col. 0133] John 19]. When, again, three signs are made over the uncovered chalice with the host, at the words “Through him, and with him, and in him,” the confession of the centurion is recalled, who said: “Truly this man was the Son of God” [Note: [Col. 0133] Luke 23]. For when he saw the miracles accompanying the revealed Passion, through the Son, who was the victim, he recognized the Father and understood the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0133D] Likewise, the two crosses made with the same host at the side of the chalice, at the words, “To you, God the almighty Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit,” signify the blood and water which flowed from the side of the suffering one [Note: [Col. 0133] John 19]; or they signify him crucified for the two peoples. And all these things, consummated in the head, transfer their benefit to the members. Hence “all good things” is said in the plural; the spiritual body too is shown and indicated in the plural on account of the plurality of its members, as though saying: Through Christ you create us. Some add “wonderful” [*mirifica*], [Col. 0134A] and indeed this wondrous making, common to all through creation, becomes particular through grace, and the earthly human being becomes heavenly. You sanctify in baptism; you make alive in the Word, as in the food of life; you bless in the increase of grace; and you grant us eternal life after death. Through him, creating us; with him, re-creating us; and in him, raising us to glory, is all honour and glory to you, God the almighty Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit.

Here we touch the chalice with the host, indicating that the world’s redemption was effected in the Lord’s Passion. Therefore, since there are four quarters of the world, some touch four parts of the chalice. “For ever and ever.” Up to this point was the canon, that is, the rule; to add or subtract anything from it belongs not to devotion but to presumption. Its conclusion, [Col. 0134B] namely “for ever and ever,” is raised in a loud voice: both because the Lord gave up his spirit with a loud voice, and because the centurion cried, “Truly this man was the Son of God” [Note: [Col. 0133] Luke 23]; because the women mourned, weeping for the Lord; and in order to represent the legal priest’s going outside to wash his garments—that is, to pray publicly for the peoples—and so that the people, knowing the end of the canon, may answer, “Amen,” affirming what the presbyter has done and obtaining what he has prayed for. When the priest says, “For ever and ever,” the deacon raises the chalice; according to some, he covers part of it with the *fanon*, then places it on the altar, and covers the offering and chalice with the corporal. This signifies Joseph of Arimathea, [Col. 0134C] who received the Lord’s body from the cross, veiled his face with a cloth, wrapped it in a clean shroud, laid it in the tomb, and concealed it with a stone [Note: [Col. 0133] John 19; Matt. 27; Mark 15].

The priest who raises the offering represents Nicodemus [Note: [Col. 0133] John 19], and this elevation represents Christ’s deposition from the cross; the setting down represents his placement in the tomb. The deacon who kisses the priest’s shoulder indicates that Joseph, when laying down the body, kissed it—something represented in certain burials; or he indicates that we cannot see God except “through a mirror in an enigma” [Note: [Col. 0133] I Cor. 13]. The priest likewise kisses the host, indicating either that Nicodemus did the same as Joseph, or rather that our reconciliation was accomplished through the Lord’s Passion [Note: [Col. 0133] Rom. 5].

Let us pray. From this point we ought especially to pray [Col. 0134D] prostrate until the end of the *Pater noster* on weekdays, but standing on feast days. “Admonished by saving precepts”: the three following sections—namely, “Admonished,” the *Pater noster*, and “Deliver us”—signify the three days of the Lord’s burial. Therefore we use these alone on Good Friday; and this is the preface, or introductory appeal, to the Lord’s Prayer. He calls them precepts and a divine institution, because the Lord both instituted this prayer and commanded the apostles to pray in this manner.

Our Father. Blessed Gregory established that the Lord’s Prayer should be said at Mass, maintaining that it was unfitting [Col. 0135A] for a prayer composed by some scholastic to be said over the Eucharist while omitting the prayer which the Lord himself dictated and which the apostles were accustomed to say. Having received this practice from the Greeks, he wished it to differ in this respect: among the Greeks it is said by all the people, whereas among us it is sung by the priest alone. This prayer is sung aloud so that those about to communicate may forgive one another their offences, as it contains, lest they approach the Lord’s table unworthily [Note: [Col. 0135] I Cor. 11].

Or it is not said silently because it is from the Gospel. Yet an objection is made, because the Lord said of this prayer: “When you pray, enter into your chamber, and, having shut the door, pray to your Father” [Note: [Col. 0135] Matt. 6]. But he does not mean a door enclosing a hidden house, but the secret place of the heart: that is, we should shut our breast against evil thought [Col. 0135B] with the mystical key of faith, and, our lips being closed, should speak with an incorrupt mind. The Lord used to be called the Father of the ancients, as of servants; but now he is Father through grace, a word of freedom and great confidence. For what will he deny to children who ask perseveringly and worthily [Note: [Col. 0135] Luke 11], he who has already granted that he is Father? Having cast them out of the kingdom as useless servants [Note: [Col. 0135] Matt. 21], the Son grants an inheritance to those whom he refreshes with the bread of angels [Note: [Col. 0135] Ps. 77] and the flesh of the fatted calf [Note: [Col. 0135] Luke 15]. “Our,” because this is common to all: let no one say “my,” which belongs to Christ alone, who is Son by nature; we, however, are sons by the grace of adoption. Therefore nobles should not be proud, since we are children of the same Father. Let the rich claim nothing for themselves, since we are brothers and co-heirs [Note: [Col. 0135] Eph. 3]. [Col. 0135C] “Who are in heaven,” that is, in secret places, in angels, in saints, and spiritually through grace. “Hallowed be your name.” This prayer contains seven petitions, which we have heard only the apostles say over this sacrament. The first is: “Hallowed be your name.” The name which we ask to be hallowed is “Father,” by which we are relatively called children of God. We ask that it be hallowed in us, so that we may imitate the Father’s holiness and the Father’s name may be displayed in his children by conduct and life. Therefore we must live in such a way that we may be children and brothers of Christ [Note: [Col. 0135] Rom. 8]; for one is not a son who degenerates from his will and does not tend toward him in faith. Or “hallowed” means confirmed in us, so that he may not cease to be our Father nor we his children, and so that we who are sanctified in baptism may persevere [Col. 0135D] in what we have begun to be. Or “Hallowed be your name” means: as it is holy, may it become known to us, so that we may think nothing holier. It is similar to “May God be glorified in us” [Note: [Col. 0135] John 17], and magnified.

The second petition is: “May your kingdom come,” that is, may the Church come to you, in which you reign, of which it is said: “The kingdom of heaven is like” [Note: [Col. 0135] Matt. 13] a net cast into the sea; or may the kingdom of heaven come to us, which you promised us when you said: “Receive the kingdom prepared for you” [Note: [Col. 0135] Matt. 25]. Or, “May your kingdom come”: [Col. 0136A] God’s kingdom always exists, but may it come to us—that is, may it be revealed to us—that you reign in the saints and the saints reign in you, because we shall be unable to remain ignorant when the Lord comes to judge.

The third is: “May your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.” God’s will is always done, but we ask that the freedom of our will and action may accord with the divine will: as in angels, so in human beings; as in the righteous, so in sinners; as in Christ, so in the Church; as in the mind, so in the body—so that spirit and flesh may be one spiritual human being, whose heart and flesh rejoice in the living God [Note: [Col. 0135] Ps. 83], who lives not for himself but for you. Or the will is the observance of the commandments. These three petitions will be fulfilled more perfectly in the future; meanwhile, we pray in part that they may afterwards be fulfilled more perfectly in us.

[Col. 0136B] “Our daily,” or familiar, bread; another reading, “supersubstantial,” or excellent. It is called *supersubstantialis* in Latin, ἐπιούσιον (*epiousion*) in Greek, *segulla* in Hebrew. Our bread is God, our refuge and strength [Note: [Col. 0135] Ps. 45], whom we need daily, who is above all substances, and whom we ask to be given to us, because in him we live. Or our bread is the word of God or God’s commandments, which are necessary to us daily [Note: [Col. 0135] Exod. 10], because “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” [Note: [Col. 0135] Deut. 8; Matt. 4]; we ask that this be given to us because we are refreshed by it. Or our bread is Christ’s body, of our own humanity, which we need daily because we sin daily; of it it is said: “The bread which I shall give you, [Col. 0136C] is my flesh for the life of the world” [Note: [Col. 0135] John 6]. We ask that it be given to us because we are renewed in it. Therefore, since we are entangled in sins, we ask that we may be worthy of heavenly food.

“Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” He calls sins, faults, and offences “debts,” by which we offend God; and thus we are held liable as debtors. We ask that these be forgiven us, so that we may return free to our homeland—but on this condition and guarantee: “As we forgive our debtors,” that is, those who have offended us, and who therefore must make satisfaction to us. Otherwise there is no fruit of prayer, because the Lord says: “Unless you forgive people, neither will your Father forgive you” [Note: [Col. 0135] Matt. 6, 18].

“And do not lead us into diabolical temptation.” God tempts in order to test [Note: [Col. 0135] Gen. 22; Wis. 3], and a human being tests in order to learn [Note: [Col. 0135] Dan. 1], while the devil tempts in order to deceive [Note: [Col. 0135] Matt. 4]. But does God lead us into this deception? No: rather, he abandons us and permits us to be tempted. But is temptation not useful for the crown [Note: [Col. 0135] Jas. 1]? It is, because where the struggle is greater, there the crown is greater. Therefore we ask that he not lead us into temptation—that is, that by abandoning us he may not allow us to be conquered and fall in temptation. “But deliver us.” Observe that in all the petitions which concern us, one person prays for all: “give us,” “forgive us,” “do not lead us,” “deliver us,” because God is the God of peace and concord, and so he willed that one should pray for all [Col. 0137A] [Note: [Col. 0137] I Cor. 14; Rom. 15], just as he himself bore all in his one self; so that with one mouth, like the three children [Note: [Col. 0137] Dan. 3], we may bless the Lord. There follows, “from evil”: from guilt, from temporal punishment, and from eternal punishment. Once this is accomplished, nothing remains to be feared or prayed for. Behold, the seventh petition is the end of the prayer and the end of our persecution. Observe that while these seven petitions are said, the deacons stand bowed, awaiting communion; in this they signify the apostles, who, after the Lord’s death [Note: [Col. 0137] Luke 24], waited seven weeks for the confirmation of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0137] Acts 2]. The subdeacons, however, remain still, because the women were silent on the Sabbath, which is the seventh day [Note: [Col. 0137] Luke 23].

The embolism follows, that is, an addition: for it adds the repetition [Col. 0137B] and exposition of the final petition. That petition says, “Deliver us from evil.” This adds from what evils—past, present, and future—and then the transition is made to the prayer in which the Church reverently prays for peace to be given. The Ambrosian Church does this openly, the Roman Church silently; and the brief silence looks to the Sabbath, on which the Lord rested in the tomb. Likewise, the Lord’s Prayer with its petitions is set down as a sign of that seventh day, on which the apostles laboured [Note: [Col. 0137] Mark 6]: they laboured in prayer that they might be delivered from evils. “Deliver us”: behold, the repetition and exposition of the final petition, with the Blessed [one] interceding; behold the transition, in which, to obtain the grace of peace, the mother of Solomon—that is, of the peaceful man—is invoked, and Michael, the messenger of peace, and the Baptist, [Col. 0137C] herald of peace, and three apostles, witnesses of peace. More persons of peace are not counted here, because “every word is established by the mouth of three witnesses” [Note: [Col. 0137] Deut. 19; Matt. 18]. Once the embolism is finished, it is not concluded with “Through the Lord,” for this is the custom of prefaces and embolisms; instead, the prayer “Grant peace” is continued with it.

Here the paten is presented to the presbyter. Customs concerning its custody vary. In some places the acolyte and subdeacon hold it, the former covered and the latter uncovered; for sacred vessels are to be handled only by ordained clerics. But among us the subdeacon has kept it from “*Te igitur*” until now. Since it is called from *patere*, “to lie open,” it signifies the hearts of the holy women, whom the subdeacon represents, hearts open through the breadth of charity in Christ’s service as they came [Col. 0137D] to anoint the Lord’s body with spices [Note: [Col. 0137] Mark 16]. Therefore, by the subdeacon’s handing the paten to the deacon, it is recalled that the women, believing broadly in Christ’s resurrection, announced it to the apostles, who finally offered the Lord the breadth of their faith. Or understand Nicodemus through the subdeacon [Note: [Col. 0137] John 19], who also believed openly and rendered service to the Saviour. Grant, I say, peace of heart, that we may be free from sin; grant peace in time, that we may be secure from every disturbance, for disturbance harms the weak. And behold how much more plainly is unfolded the evils [Col. 0138A] from which we pray to be delivered.

Observe that, after kissing the paten, the priest makes the sign of the cross over himself in each of the two final clauses, because through the cross, this sacrifice, and its fragrance, he declares all things in heaven and on earth reconciled [Note: [Col. 0137] Col. 1]. The offering is broken because at supper the Lord blessed and broke the bread [Note: [Col. 0137] Matt. 26]. Both that breaking and this signify the breaking of his body on the cross, or the breaking of bread in which he was recognized after the resurrection [Note: [Col. 0137] Luke 24]; or the diversity of Christ’s body—namely, walking, resting, and sitting—of whose three parts we shall speak below. The pope does not break the offering, but bites a part from it and puts the remainder into the chalice, because Christ bit hell [Note: [Col. 0137] Hos. 13] and sent those taken from it into paradise [Note: [Col. 0137] Ps. 67]. It is concluded aloud, “For ever and ever,” so that the people, desiring [Col. 0138B] peace, may respond, “Amen”; or the elevation of the voice which follows signifies the good news of the Lord’s resurrection, through which we shall receive eternal joy and brightness.

## Chapter VII. On the Sixth Part of the Mass

“I will abundantly bless widow Zion” [Note: [Col. 0137] Ps. 131].

Through the Lord’s death and in his death, the faithful soul received the blessing. Accordingly, in the office concerning death, the deacon invites the people to humble themselves; the bishop blesses them with a threefold blessing and, fourth, confirms it by saying that he himself may deign to prepare it; fifth, he concludes the blessing and invokes the peace of the Almighty. Jacob prefigured these blessings when, [Col. 0138C] dying, he blessed his sons [Note: [Col. 0137] Gen. 49]. Moses also, about to die, enriched the children of Israel with blessings [Note: [Col. 0137] Deut. 33]. Thus Christ, dying, bestowed the blessing of his word upon the disciples, showing that those whom he had loved before he loved also to the end [Note: [Col. 0137] John 13]. So too, descending to the lower regions, he blessed those sitting in darkness; when he led them out and brought them into the Father’s storehouse, he assigned them everlasting peace. This the bishop represents when, after the representation of death, he blesses the people five times and adds: “And may his peace always be with you.”

He blessed five times because God first blessed human beings, saying: “Increase and multiply” [Note: [Col. 0137] Gen. 1]. Second, after the flood, he said the same thing [Note: [Col. 0137] Gen. 9]. Third, he blessed when he promised the patriarchs blessing through Christ’s sending [Note: [Col. 0137] Gen. 22], and foreshadowed it among judges [Col. 0138D] and kings, rulers, prophets, and priests. Fourth, he blessed when he sent his Son, who, descending and ascending, blessed and confirmed the blessing through the Holy Spirit. Fifth, he will bless, saying: “Come, blessed of my Father” [Note: [Col. 0137] Matt. 25]. Some assert quite reasonably that this office is not one of the seven offices of the Mass, since the Roman Church does not find these blessings and consequently does not use them. Whoever does find them, however, rightly places them where Christ is believed to have descended to hell: namely, [Col. 0139A] next before the resurrection, when, having brought captives out of prison, he granted them eternal blessing.

## Chapter VIII. On the Seventh Part of the Mass

“I will satisfy her poor with bread” [Note: [Col. 0139] Ps. 131].

Returning to the sacrifice, the bishop, seeing the people’s disposition in their answer “Amen” and their desire for peace, says: “And may his peace always be with you.” The priest says: “May the peace of the Lord always be with you.”

He prays for that peace which surpasses all understanding [Note: [Col. 0139] Phil. 4]. Observe that the deacon who removes the corporal and holds the chalice signifies him who removed the stone and the linen cloth and guarded the tomb [Note: [Col. 0139] Matt. 28; John 20]. As he says this, the priest or bishop makes the sign of the cross three times over the chalice with the particle [Col. 0139B] and drops it into the chalice, because, all things in heaven and earth having been reconciled, the soul of Jesus Christ returned to the body. Some drop it in before saying “The peace of the Lord,” and this too is not without mystery, since after the resurrection it became manifest that peace was given to people of good will [Note: [Col. 0139] Luke 2]. In return, the people answer, “And with your spirit”; and, joyfully wishing that through the Lamb’s mercy that peace may be given to us and that the body of the peace-maker may be worthily received by us, they sing: “Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us; and grant us peace”—for granting repentance unto the remission of sins and making peace between God, human beings, and angels. He did all these things. Hence “Have mercy on us” and “Grant us peace” are sung; Pope Sergius decreed that they be sung by clergy and [Col. 0139C] people during communion. Christ is called a lamb because of innocence; or from *agnus*, understood as “merciful,” because he redeemed us by mercy alone; or from *agnoscendo*, “recognizing,” because, hanging on the cross [Note: [Col. 0139] Luke 23; John 19], he recognized the Father by obeying, knew his mother by commending her to the virgin, and recognized the human race by redeeming it. We therefore ask that he, the innocent one who redeemed us by his Passion, may have mercy on us as we represent it, and that he who suffered in order to make peace may grant us peace, the peaceful king. For he is the Lamb slain by predestination from the foundation of the world [Note: [Col. 0139] Rev. 13]. He is the paschal lamb, through whom the people are delivered from the slavery of the Egyptians [Note: [Col. 0139] Exod. 12]. “Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us”: this is taken from the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0139] John 1], and is repeated three times because of the threefold [Col. 0139D] knowledge mentioned above. Or it is sung then because Christ’s body is understood in three ways: walking on earth, resting in the tomb, and seated in heaven. “Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us.” Observe that “have mercy on us” is said twice, and on the third occasion, “Grant us peace,” which is taken from the Old Testament [Note: [Col. 0139] Joel 2], where a similar form is found. For they cried: “Spare, Lord, spare your people”; and afterwards varied it: “Do not give your inheritance to reproach.” And rightly “have mercy on us” is said twice and “grant us peace” once, because in [Col. 0140A] this double life—of action and contemplation—we need mercy; in the other life, however, eternal peace will be granted us. At the Lord’s Supper, however, some say “Have mercy on us” three times. In the Mass for the dead, “Grant them rest” is said, and it ought to be said intermittently and intermingled with the prayer. Once the body and blood have been commingled, through which we apprehend the Lord’s resurrection, the priest grants peace to the people. Joshua prefigured this [Note: [Col. 0139] Josh. 13 and below], when, after overcoming his enemies, he possessed the land, divided it by lot, and possessed it in peace. Thus Christ, rising again after overcoming the devil, gave peace and gifts to human beings [Note: [Col. 0139] Luke 24; John 20]. The bishop represents this resurrection and the deeds of the risen one: when he mixes the third particle with the blood and puts it into the chalice, he indicates that Christ’s soul [Col. 0140B] returned to his body.

After this, as Pope Honorius decreed, he offers peace to the people, because by rising Christ gave peace to the human race. When about to give peace, according to some he receives the kiss of peace from the Eucharist itself; according to others, from the tomb, or the altar, or the book. He passes it, according to some, to the subdeacon, deacon, or cantor; according to others, to the archpriest. The archpriest, who had been on the pontiff’s left, goes to receive it at his right; through him is signified the Gentile people, which became first in faith and foremost in peace, passing from the left of unbelief to the right of faith and eternity. Through him peace descends to the people, but first to men and afterwards to women, because man is the head of woman [Note: [Col. 0139] I Cor. 11; Eph. 5]. Yet men [Col. 0140C] and women should not kiss one another, on account of lust; for that reason they are separated not only from a carnal kiss but even by physical position. Therefore kisses should be exchanged mutually by persons whom no stimulation of sexual desire excites.

The people kiss one another for three reasons. First, they rejoice that by their Lord’s death they have merited his grace and concord with the angels. Second, since we are children of God the Father [Note: [Col. 0139] Rom. 8] and of Mother Church, we are brothers in Christ [Note: [Col. 0139] Matt. 23], and therefore are to be refreshed by one bread, as by an inheritance [Note: [Col. 0139] I Cor. 10]. Third, in a kiss flesh is joined to flesh and spirit to spirit; and we who are joined by descent of the flesh from Adam are also bound together by the bond of charity. Therefore those who kiss while hating one another imitate the kiss of Judas the betrayer. After the kisses, the Eucharist is received, [Col. 0140D] as though it were said: whoever is not in unity is not a participant in his body. The priest communicates first, receiving the body from the altar himself, with no one ministering to him, because Christ will accomplish the restoration of our bodies through no one’s ministry; but he receives the blood from the deacon’s hand, because he restores the redemption of souls through the ministry of human beings. Thus, the vicar of Jesus Christ who communicates takes a part for himself, just as Christ, when he broke bread for the disciples at Emmaus, kept a part for himself and distributed parts to Luke and Cleopas [Note: [Col. 0139] Luke 24]. So too the priest divides it to the deacon and [Col. 0141A] subdeacon. “And afterwards he ate part of a broiled fish and a honeycomb, and gave the remains to the disciples” [Note: [Col. 0141] ibid.]. Therefore, after the deacon and subdeacon have communicated, let the brethren approach, that they too may receive a portion of holy communion.

Observe that the offering is divided into three parts, just as formerly the legal fine flour was offered in broken pieces: one is received by the priest; one is sometimes reserved on the altar in a pyx for the sick as viaticum; the third is put into the chalice. The first is the mystical body, that is, the Church walking upon earth; the second is likewise the mystical body sleeping in burial until the day of judgment; the third is the personal body resumed in glory. Or the part mingled with the blood signifies the Church militant on earth, while the others signify those in purgatory [Col. 0141B] and those who triumph in heaven. Or the threefold fragments signify the victim of the Holy Trinity, and the particle joined to the blood indicates the person of the Son. Beware, however: although the offering, or even Christ’s body in the sacrament, is thus broken and distributed to many, nevertheless Christ remains whole and entire in heaven, and each person receives him whole and entire in the sacrament. Nor does it pass into bodily nourishment except spiritually; for its power satisfies the inner human being, who, being satisfied, gladdens the outer person. Observe that, although he is received whole, common usage nevertheless says that the body alone is received, because a thing is designated according to what is seen—or this is merely a manner of speaking. Some say that one ought to refrain from spitting after receiving the sacrifice. [Col. 0141C] Indeed, it ought to be received with great reverence and guarded with prudent caution. Yet “the spiritual person judges all things, and is himself judged by no one” [Note: [Col. 0141] I Cor. 2]. “All things are clean to the clean” [Note: [Col. 0141] Rom. 14; Tit. 1]. Spittle is natural and proceeds without sin. The discharge of spittle benefits health. It is permissible to do for health what Christ did for our salvation. For the Lord made mud from spittle and anointed the eyes of the man born blind [Note: [Col. 0141] John 9]. Let the person who is thus careful not to cast out bread or wine with the spittle take care that not one word of those which the Lord has spoken slips and falls from his heart, for they too are spirit and life [Note: [Col. 0141] John 6]. But I do not refrain from spitting if phlegmatic moisture is abundant, because I trust in the Lord that flesh and blood pass into spiritual refreshment of soul and body. Nor do I inquire whether what has been received [Col. 0141D] goes out with superfluities or flows through the veins. But, believing devoutly, if anything of the lamb remains, I leave it, according to the Law [Note: [Col. 0141] Exod. 12], to be burned—that is, I entrust it to the Holy Spirit.

Afterwards the people communicate, because Christ ate not only with the few apostles [Note: [Col. 0141] Matt. 26; Luke 24], but also, when about to ascend, with the multitude of disciples. Let each communicate rarely or daily, according as he believes it better to do. For Zacchaeus received him joyfully into his house [Note: [Col. 0141] Luke 19]. The centurion said: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” [Note: [Col. 0141] Matt. 8]. We do not explain the prayers used when giving peace [Col. 0142A] and communicating, both because they need no exposition and because different persons say more or fewer of them. Meanwhile, the communion chant is sung, signifying the joyful and reciprocal exchange of the apostles concerning the resurrection, such as: “The Lord has truly risen” [Note: [Col. 0141] Luke 24], and what they recounted—how they recognized him in the breaking of bread. Or it is sung so that we may share in God’s grace with the righteous. Communion is thanksgiving, according to: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they shall praise the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0141] Ps. 21].

The greeting follows: “The Lord be with you.” Those who deny that the blessings constitute the sixth office reasonably make this the final office, for this greeting signifies the blessing with which the Lord, when about to ascend, [Col. 0142B] blessed the disciples [Note: [Col. 0141] Luke 24]. The prayer called the post-communion follows, in which the priest prays for those who have approached Eucharistic communion. It ought to be one prayer, or as many in number as there were collects; and it signifies the prayer of our head, namely our Lord Jesus Christ, who daily intercedes for us with the Father [Note: [Col. 0141] Rom. 8]. The priest’s moving to the right side of the altar signifies Christ’s return to the Jews at the end of the age: for when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, Israel will be converted to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0141] Rom. 11]. The final greeting follows: “The Lord be with you,” signifying eternal life.

Note that the priest greets the people seven times in the Mass, because the mystery of the Mass relates to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0142C]. In the first greeting is understood the spirit of wisdom, because wisdom entered this world in order to save us [Note: [Col. 0141] I Tim. 1]. In the second, the spirit of understanding, for he preached in order to teach us. In the third, the spirit of counsel: by God’s secret counsel he offered himself to the Passion in order to redeem us. In the fourth, the spirit of fortitude, because, hanging on the cross, he overcame the devil in order to deliver us. In the fifth, the spirit of knowledge, because, rising again, he greeted the disciples and opened their understanding in order to instruct us [Note: [Col. 0141] Luke 24]. In the sixth, the spirit of piety, because by mercy alone he raised human nature above the stars in order to exalt us. In the seventh, the spirit of fear, because the angels will fear when he comes for judgment in order to glorify us. Yet he turns to the people only five times. First, he greets them before [Col. 0142D] the collect; second, before the Gospel; third, before the offertory; fourth, before the sacrifice; fifth, before the kiss of peace; sixth, after communion; seventh, after the completion, that is, the final prayer. At the greeting before the sacrifice, he does not turn, because he holds the sacrifice in his hands. At the others he turns toward the people: those whom we greet, we present our face to. He turns to the people five times because he is read to have appeared five times after the resurrection.

The conclusion follows: “Go, the dismissal is made.” The Mass ends in three ways. On solemnities when “We praise you, God” and “Glory to God in the highest” are sung, it ends [Col. 0143A] with “Go, the dismissal is made.” Its sense is: Go after Christ and follow him. We must not sit down, but hasten toward our homeland, because the victim has been sent to appease God the Father, through whom hell was shattered. Oh, that when we hear this our mind may tend thither where the victim has gone, so that, where the body is, there too the eagles may be gathered [Note: [Col. 0143] Matt. 24; Luke 17]; that we may be there in desire, where the Desired of all nations [Note: [Col. 0143] Hag. 2] awaits us with his trophy, he who thus pleads to the Father for us: “I will that where I am, there also may be my servant” [Note: [Col. 0143] John 12 and 17]. Or “Go, the dismissal is made” means: the lamb has been sacrificed and entrance into paradise preserved; follow him, mortifying our flesh with its vices and desires [Note: [Col. 0143] Gal. 5; Col. 3]. Because the saying is directed to those present, the priest or deacon, when saying it, turns his face [Col. 0143B] toward the people. The people answer: “Thanks be to God.” This is taken from the people’s departure from Egypt, once they had received leave by Pharaoh’s permission, when they gave thanks to God [Note: [Col. 0143] Exod. 12]. Or from the one who, after receiving leave from Cyrus, returned from Babylonian captivity to Jerusalem and gave thanks to God [Note: [Col. 0143] I Ezra 1]. So let us, for the benefits received in our redemption, give thanks to the Redeemer, who ascended to the Father’s right hand [Note: [Col. 0143] Eph. 4; Heb. 1] and daily intercedes for us with the Father [Note: [Col. 0143] Rom. 8].

Accordingly, after the Ascension the preaching apostles said: “Give thanks; pray without ceasing” [Note: [Col. 0143] 1 Thess. 2 and 5]. They too returned to Jerusalem, blessing the Lord [Note: [Col. 0143] Luke 24]; so, having received the blessing, we shall go to our homeland, where we shall remain always in thanksgiving [Col. 0143C]. In the first Mass of the Nativity, however, according to some, “Ite, missa est” [“Go, the dismissal is made”] ought not to be said, lest the people seem to have leave to depart when they must be kept for another Mass. On other days the service ends with “Let us bless the Lord,” and this is taken from the Apostle, or from the Psalms, or from the hymn of the three youths, where it is said: “Let us bless the Father and the Son” [Note: [Col. 0143] Dan. 3]. In the Mass for the dead it customarily ends with “May they rest in peace”; and these prayers are, as it were, congratulatory interjections. When the conclusion is made by “Let us bless the Lord” or “May they rest in peace,” the priest or deacon should turn his face eastward and his mind toward the Lord.

The priest’s blessing after Mass signifies the blessing which Christ gave his disciples after the Resurrection [Col. 0143D; Note: [Col. 0143] Luke 24], or which the Holy Spirit brought to the faithful on the day of Pentecost, or by which the Church will enter gloriously into the bridegroom’s chamber. Such final blessings are taken from ancient custom; for the patriarch Jacob blessed his sons at the end of his life [Note: [Col. 0143] Gen. 49]; so Moses blessed the people of God before his death [Note: [Col. 0143] Deut. 33]; so the Lord blessed his disciples before the Ascension [Note: [Col. 0143] Luke 24]. Hence it is that when we part company, we seek a blessing for escort or protection. Or they are taken from the fact that the Lord commanded blessings to be given on Mount Gerizim over those who observed the Law, and, conversely, curses on Ebal over transgressors [Col. 0144A; Note: [Col. 0143] Deut. 27 and 28]: from those blessings we derive blessings, and from the curses, excommunications.

The Council of Toledo ordained that the hymn of the three youths should be sung after Mass, and subjected those who neglected it to anathema. We say it because we ought to give thanks to the Lord for all his benefits, whom we shall praise for ever and ever. After Mass we distribute to the people blessed bread, a substitute for holy communion. For in the primitive Church all who were present at Mass communicated, because the Lord said to the Apostles, “Drink from this, all of you” [Note: [Col. 0143] Matt. 26], and they all drank from the cup. They offered a large loaf, as the Greeks still do, sufficient for all; but [Col. 0144B] after the Church had increased in number but, because of the carnal-minded, diminished in holiness, it was decreed that they should communicate only on Sundays. But because afterward the love of many grew cold [Note: [Col. 0143] Matt. 24], and communicants thereby received judgment upon themselves [Note: [Col. 0143] 1 Cor. 11], it was instituted that they should communicate three times a year: at the Nativity, Easter, and Pentecost—and would that they might communicate worthily even once!

Against this falling away from the first institution there is therefore a threefold remedy. The first is the kiss of peace; and therefore in the Gallican Church it is given at every Mass except that for the dead. The second is blessed bread, called *eulogia*; and because this ought not to be given during Lent on account of abstinence, a third remedy was instituted: namely, the prayer over the people [Col. 0144C], which is announced: “Bow your heads to God.” When all these things have been duly performed, the priest and the others return to their own places. In the corporal left upon the altar, the priest returning to his own place is Christ, who, his embassy accomplished, ascended into the glory of the Father. The faithful too return when, released from the exile of prison, they are delivered into the liberty of glory [Note: [Col. 0143] Rom. 8]. The corporal upon the altar is the purity of chastity in the priest, or the Church in Christ.

## CHAPTER IX. A BRIEF RECAPITULATION OF THE MASS

“Thou hast judged, O Lord, my cause” [Note: [Col. 0143] Lam. 3]. No one doubts that the Mass is representative of battle, representing the conflict of a certain battle and the triumph of victory. It represents for us a threefold battle: one prefiguring, two prefigured [Col. 0144D]; one in the head, the other in the members. The prefiguring battle was when Moses overthrew Amalek [Note: [Col. 0143] Exod. 17], Joshua conquered seven peoples [Note: [Col. 0143] Josh. 6 and following], and David overcame Goliath, Saul, and the Philistines [Note: [Col. 0143] 1 Kings 17]. The battle prefigured in the head is this: Christ, fighting with the devil, overcame him and despoiled hell [Note: [Col. 0143] Col. 2]. That prefigured in the members is this: we are attacked not only by the world, but by the flesh and the devil; for “our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers” [Note: [Col. 0143] Eph. 6].

Therefore, while celebrating Mass, the priest should briefly and swiftly keep in mind, from what he does and what is done around him [Col. 0145A], the prefiguring things that came before, the things prefigured that have been fulfilled in the head, and what must be fulfilled by us in our conduct. When we make a procession with banners, relics, books, candles, and censers, let us recall Moses, who by signs and wonders led the people from Egypt through the wilderness to the promised land [Note: [Col. 0145] Exod. 7 and following]. There the people were armed; here the clergy wear sacred vestments. There was the ark; here, the reliquary chest. There were the tablets of the Covenant from Mount Sinai; here, the book of the Gospel from the altar. There was the pillar of fire; here, the burning candle. There was the rod; here, the king’s sceptre or the bishop’s staff. There were Moses and Aaron; here, king and bishop, or the bishop representing both: in the staff, the king; in the mitre, the pontiff.

Let us recall also Joshua, who marched around Jericho [Col. 0145B; Note: [Col. 0145] Josh. 6]; it fell, and the people gained the kingdom. There was the blast of trumpets; here, the ringing of bells. Let us recall David [Note: [Col. 0145] 2 Kings 6] and Solomon [Note: [Col. 0145] 3 Kings 8], who brought back the ark of God with hymns and songs and placed it in the Temple. Let us be mindful of Jesus Christ, who came from the bosom of the Father into the world [Note: [Col. 0145] John 8; 1 Tim. 1]; from the manger to the Temple [Note: [Col. 0145] Luke 2]; from Bethany to Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0145] John 12]; from Jerusalem to the mount [Note: [Col. 0145] Matt. 27; John 19]. Let us desire to return from the world to our homeland, as it were from one Church to another—from the Church militant to the Church triumphant—following the cross, that is, the footsteps of the Crucified, and crucifying ourselves with our vices and desires [Note: [Col. 0145] Gal. 5].

Following the footsteps of the saints and the precepts of the Gospels, let us put on the breastplate of righteousness, the belt of continence, the shield of faith, and the helmet [Col. 0145C] of eternal salvation [Note: [Col. 0145] Eph. 6]. Hence the priest, about to fight against the spiritual powers of wickedness in the heavenly places, is clothed in sacred vestments as though in armour: taking sandals for greaves, lest any dust cling to his feet; the amice for a helmet; the alb for a breastplate; the girdle for a bow; the subgirdle for a quiver; the stole for a spear; the *mapula* or maniple for a club; the chasuble for a shield; and the book for a sword. Thus armed, he proceeds to the altar on behalf of all; by confession he renounces the devil and accuses himself, because “the wise man at the beginning of his speech is his own accuser” [Note: [Col. 0145] Prov. 18]. By prayers and chants he challenges the devil; as he folds the chasuble over his shoulder, he prepares the sword against the enemy. When the Epistle is read in the voice of the herald, the emperor’s edicts are issued. The singer is the trumpeter; the precentors, who direct the choir, are the commanders who prepare the army for battle [Col. 0145D]; when they grow weary, others assist them. The chant of the sequence is the applause of victory. When the Gospel is read, the adversary is wounded, or the army, scattered after victory, is gathered together; when the bishop preaches it, the emperor, praising the victors, addresses them. The offerings are spoils distributed to the victors. The offertory chant is the triumph presented to the emperor.

But when the people again become slack through negligence, the Philistine rises up against Israel. Hence a duel is appointed between Goliath and David [Note: [Col. 0145] 1 Kings 17]. This is the sluggish [Col. 0146A] soul, or the human race, to which the devil declares war; but it is conquered by Christ, who fights for us. For he is the true David, strong in hand and desirable in appearance, whom the Father sends to battle; who fed the sheep, who overcame the bear and the lion [Note: [Col. 0145] Ibid.]; who carried the staff against the Philistine when he bore the cross against the devil.

Again, the Mass imitates a kind of judicial proceeding; hence the canon is called an *actio* [legal action], for an *actio* is a cause pleaded publicly before judges. In the Mass, indeed, our case is tried before God the judge. The oratory is the praetorium; God is judge; the devil is accuser; the priest is advocate and defender. For he is Moses, who pleaded the people’s cause before the Lord [Note: [Col. 0145] Exod. 32]. Through his advocacy the deceit of the informer is refuted; our innocence is established [Col. 0146B] and acquitted, or the anger of the judge is appeased and guilt is forgiven through mercy.

Again, the Mass represents to the people the actions of tragedies. For our tragic actor, when he says, “Pray,” recalls Christ, who admonished the Apostles to pray [Note: [Col. 0145] Matt. 26].

By the secret prayer he signifies Christ, who, like a voiceless lamb, went to sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0145] Isa. 53]. The spreading of the hands is Christ’s stretching forth upon the cross; the silence of the canon, the silence of the Passion; the kiss of peace, the joy of the Resurrection. Briefly and summarily, we conclude that the things celebrated in the office of Mass up to the secret prayer refer to those things read concerning Christ and his deeds up to Palm Sunday. For the introit to the assembly refers to the ancient prophets; [Col. 0146C] *Kyrie eleison* [“Lord, have mercy”] to those who were around Christ’s coming; *Gloria* to the song of the angels; the greeting and collect to the coming of the Saviour, who came for this purpose, that he might save us [Note: [Col. 0145] John 3; 1 Tim. 1]; the Epistle to John’s preaching [Note: [Col. 0145] Matt. 3]; the gradual to the calling of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0145] Matt. 4]; *alleluia* to the joy of their hearts; the Gospel to the Lord’s preaching; the Creed to the conversion of the people; and the offertory to that people’s devotion.

What follows now refers to what is read concerning Christ up to the Ascension. Bread signifies the body, wine the blood; likewise the chalice signifies the body, because wine is in the chalice and blood is in the body. The corporal signifies purity of body. The paten signifies the breadth of faith and charity; or otherwise, as is contained in these verses:

> [Col. 0146D] The altar is the cross; the chalice, the tomb; the paten, the stone;  
> White linen performs the office of the shroud.

The water is the people: therefore, as water is joined to wine, so the Church is joined to Christ. The secret prayer is Christ’s concealment [Note: [Col. 0145] John 11]. The backward station of the subdeacons and deacons signifies the flight of the disciples [Note: [Col. 0145] Matt. 26]. The priest’s bowing is Christ’s death [Note: [Col. 0145] Matt. 27]. Finally, from *Te igitur* [“Thee, therefore”] up to *nobis quoque peccatoribus* [“to us also sinners”], some things refer to the prayer which the Lord made on the mount [Note: [Col. 0145] Matt. 5], and some to the Passion which he underwent on the cross. From *ipso nobis* [“from him to us”] up to the mingling of body and blood belongs [Col. 0147A] to the burial. Thus the lifting of the chalice from the altar is the removal of the body from the cross, and its being placed again upon the altar is its placement in the tomb. The mingling, however, belongs to the Resurrection. The breaking of the offering corresponds to the breaking which the Lord performed at Emmaus [Note: [Col. 0147] Luke 24]. The greeting corresponds to what he said to the Apostles: “Peace to you” [Note: [Col. 0147] Ibid.]. The final greeting is the blessing given to the Apostles as they were sent forth at the Lord’s Ascension, or the eternal greeting.

Know also that formerly the Apostles did not sing Mass with so much ceremony or solemnity, but merely read beforehand the Epistle and Gospel and consecrated with the Lord’s words and the Lord’s Prayer; but holy Fathers and apostolic men added the solemnities which we have set forth above.

[Col. 0147B] It is not useless now to inquire at what hour, and how often, Mass should be celebrated. Accordingly, Mass is regularly celebrated at three hours: the third, sixth, and ninth. At the third, as Telesphorus instituted and Gregory approved, because then the Lord was crucified amid the cries of the Jews’ tongues: “Crucify him” [Note: [Col. 0147] John 19]. Then too he was scourged by the soldiers. At the sixth, because then he was sacrificed and crucified by the hands. At the ninth, because then he breathed his last. The third is sung on feast days, the sixth on ordinary days, and the ninth on fast days. Yet on the Ember Saturdays it should be celebrated very late because of the sacred orders, which belong to Sunday. On the Saturdays of Easter and Pentecost it should also be sung late, as is evident from the blessing of the candle [Col. 0147C], where it says, “This night,” and from the collect where it says, “O God, who hast made this most sacred night.” This is either because on that night the Lord rose again, or because of the women’s visit to the Lord’s tomb [Note: [Col. 0147] John 20].

At the Nativity of the Lord the first Mass is sung by night. That Mass is sung very early in the morning is a matter of custom, not rule, but is due to necessity. Pope Leo entered Mass at dawn; I do not know whether from convenience, reason, or solely by the authority of apostolic usage. Perhaps those who, through necessity, anticipate the third hour, or who offer after the ninth through divine love lest a day pass for them without sacrifice, may be excused with the disciples who plucked ears of grain on the Sabbath [Note: [Col. 0147] Matt. 12], and with David, who ate the loaves of presentation [Note: [Col. 0147] 1 Kings 21]. Or perhaps it is after the ninth in order to avoid gluttony; or because at Mass we commemorate the Passion, death and burial, Resurrection and Ascension. Therefore it is sung at so many different hours: at the third he is scourged, at the sixth he is sacrificed, at the ninth he dies, after the ninth he is buried, in the morning [Col. 0148B] he rises, and he ascends to heaven.

A priest ought to celebrate Mass once a day, because Christ willed once to be sacrificed for us [Note: [Col. 0147] Rom. 6; 1 Pet. 3]. Yet if necessity compels, as when two feasts coincide, two Masses—or three, as some maintain—may be celebrated: both because this is lawfully done at the Nativity, and because Christ’s Passion is threefold. For he suffered from the tongues of those insulting him, the hands of those striking him, and the nails of those crucifying him. He too was sacrificed figuratively in the actions of the patriarchs, offered sacrificially in the words of the prophets, and really offered by the Father and by himself [Note: [Col. 0147] Rom. 8]. Yet it is read that Pope Leo often celebrated Mass seven times, and sometimes nine times, on the same day. Therefore, as it is permissible for a priest to celebrate Mass several times, so it is permissible for a religious layperson to communicate several times in a day [Col. 0148C]. Neither, however, is to be sought after, because familiarity breeds contempt, and contempt brings judgment upon the eater; whereas discretion and devotion produce grace, which the Eucharist denotes both by its effect and by the etymology of its name.

# BOOK FOUR. ON THE OFFICES OF THE CHURCH

[Col. 0147]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0147D]

It is fitting for those harassed by the labour of the offices to investigate what an office is and whence it takes its name. An office, as Isidore says, is the appropriate action of each person according to the laws and customs of the city, or the institutions of one’s profession; for the institutions of monks are one thing, those of canons another. But, as Jerome says, *officium* is so called as though from *efficium* [accomplishment], because each person ought to accomplish his office; or because in it those things are to be done which benefit everyone and harm no one.

Some offices are general, to be observed throughout the whole year, such as Matins and the seven hours; some are special, according to the diversity of seasons and the intervals between solemnities. For some are sung in Lent, others in Advent [Col. 0148D], others at Easter, and others at the Nativity. Let us first treat of the general ones. Generally, we say that nothing should be sung unless it has been canonized by the supreme pontiff. For in the primitive Church different persons sang different things at their own will; yet they observed the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer. Later, when heresies had sprung up, the Emperor Theodosius, who uprooted heresies, asked Pope Damasus to entrust the ordering of the ecclesiastical office to a Catholic man. He therefore entrusted it to Jerome the priest, skilled in three languages—Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—who had lived at Rome under seven apostolic men. At that time, however, he was living at Bethlehem with Paula and Eustochium. He therefore arranged the Psalms, Epistles, and Gospels, and [Col. 0149A] for the most part all the nocturnal and diurnal offices except the chant. Pope Damasus canonized this work and commanded it to be observed in all Churches. Gelasius and Gregory added prayers and chants and fitted them to the readings and Gospels. Treating, then, of these offices, let us begin with the office of the night, so that we may come forth from darkness into light, and not the reverse.

## CHAPTER I. ON FERIAL NOCTURNS

“At midnight I arose to give thanks unto thee” [Note: [Col. 0149] Ps. 118]. Rising by night, keeping vigil, praising, praying to, and worshipping God are supported by no lack of examples and reasons. For David says: “At midnight I arose to give thanks unto thee”; and elsewhere: “I prevented the untimely night” [Note: [Col. 0149] Ibid.], or, according to another reading, “in the early time,” which, Augustine asserts, is the same thing. For the ancients called *tempestivum* [timely] that which was suitable, deriving the word from *tempus* [time] or *tempestas* [season], in the sense in which historians say *ea tempestate*, that is, “at that time”; hence they call *intempestivum* unsuitable. Similarly, immaturity is an unripe time, that is, an unsuitable one. That is, the night is unsuitable for activities; yet the Lord spent the night in prayer [Note: [Col. 0149] Luke 6]. And Paul and Silas sang psalms in prison at midnight [Note: [Col. 0149] Acts 16]. There is also the reason that we read that the Lord struck the sleeping Egyptians and delivered the wakeful Hebrews [Note: [Col. 0149] Exod. 12].

Likewise, Christ was born at midnight and on the Lord’s night; the angels praised him by singing “Glory,” and wakeful shepherds [Col. 0149C] worshipped him [Note: [Col. 0149] Luke 2]. Likewise, he was seized for us at night [Note: [Col. 0149] Matt. 26]. Likewise, at midnight and on the Lord’s night he bit hell [Note: [Col. 0149] Hos. 13]; and, like Samson [Note: [Col. 0149] Judg. 16], besieged by the Philistines, he rose from the dead at midnight after breaking the gates of hell. Likewise, he will then come to judge, like the destroying angel into Egypt. Hence: “At midnight a cry was made” [Note: [Col. 0149] Matt. 25]. Therefore we keep watch in vigils, so that, when he returns from the wedding, we may reach the way of freedom. Likewise, we imitate in shadow the angelic vigils, of which we shall speak below, and by nocturnal watchings we avoid the devil’s snares.

For these reasons, then, rising at night when we hear the bells, we run to church, just as an army, hearing the blast of trumpets, runs to military service. Thus the soldiers of the highest King, coming to the royal court [Col. 0149D] and entering it, bow toward the altar, because, like soldiers, we worship the King. For we are soldiers of the eternal King, to whom we ought always to be present in the readiness of spiritual warfare. Bowing toward the altar, we make a threefold prayer, saying the *Pater noster* three times and directing our speech to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. When we speak to the Father, we present ourselves at the middle of the altar—our heart’s intention and the posture of our body—to the Lord, on account of the Father’s power and our own perseverance. When we speak to the Son, [Col. 0150A] we turn toward the left side of the altar, because of his emptying of himself [Note: [Col. 0149] Phil. 2] and the offence of our fall. When we speak to the Holy Spirit, we pass to the right of the altar, because of his kindness and our attainment of grace.

Meanwhile the second bell sounds. The first bell, called the *squillus*, signifies Paul preaching keenly; the second, Barnabas joined to him [Note: [Col. 0149] Acts 13]. When we ring the third in turn, we indicate that, when the Jews rejected the word of God, the Apostles turned to the Gentiles, whom they instructed in the faith of the Trinity and imbued with the teachings of the four Gospels [Note: [Col. 0149] Ibid.]. Hence some ring four times. Some have particular prayers for these things, directing speech to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0150B] Having made the threefold prayer, we begin the gradual psalms. There are fifteen of them, signified by the fifteen steps of Solomon, by which one ascended to the Temple of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0149] 2 Chron. 9], and by the other fifteen of Ezekiel, by which he was seen to ascend into the city of God [Note: [Col. 0149] Ezek. 40, 43]. The number fifteen consists of seven and eight. Therefore we sing fifteen psalms, showing that we ought to observe the commandments of both Testaments. In the first five *Gloria Patri* we do not use it when praying for the dead, because through the five senses of the body we have committed sins which we ought to impute not to God but to ourselves, praying that life may not on that account be denied us, but that eternal rest may be granted through God’s mercy. In the following [Col. 0150C] ten psalms we implore God’s mercy for ourselves and our neighbours; and we add *Gloria Patri*, because, in being freed from the chain of sins, in seeking thee with all our heart, and in observing thy Decalogue, we offer glory: “Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory” [Note: [Col. 0149] Ps. 113].

After these things, we seek from the King permission to speak, so that we may announce his praises, saying: “O Lord, thou wilt open my lips, and my mouth shall declare thy praise” [Note: [Col. 0149] Ps. 50]. When we went to sleep at night, we fortified mouth and breast with the sign of the cross, as with the Lord’s seal; and therefore we ask from him whose seal it is permission to unseal our lips.

But why does man say to God, “O Lord, thou wilt open my lips” [Note: [Col. 0149] Ps. 80], when God says to man, “Open thy mouth, [Col. 0150D] and I will fill it” [Note: [Col. 0149] Ps. 126]? The answer is that free will is indicated here; there, its weakness without grace is manifested. But because one watches in vain unless the Lord guards the city, we therefore implore divine help, saying: “O God, attend unto my help; O Lord, make haste to help me” [Note: [Col. 0149] Ps. 69]. Observe that, while the night of sin reigned, lips closed to God’s praises were silent; now the sinner rises. But because “praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner” [Note: [Col. 0149] Ecclus. 15], he asks God to open his mouth, and, that he may praise more perfectly, he implores divine help.

And observe that the dignity of all the hours [Col. 0151A] is to be revered, since we refer both their beginning and their end to the Lord. For at the beginning we invoke the Lord’s aid, and at the end we give thanks to God. Having obtained permission to speak and implored the King’s help, in order to win the King’s goodwill we begin with the praises stated above, saying: “Glory be to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, as it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, unto ages of ages. Amen.” Jerome devised this verse and ordained that it should be said at the end of the Psalms. And because some are slow to come to the King’s proclamations or to military service, therefore, as a herald is sent through the city to summon soldiers, so the singer begins the invitatory and, inviting the brethren, adds: “Come.”

Consider that the invitatory begins on a low note and afterward rises, because the Church first praises and prays to God for herself in secret, as though with the door shut [Col. 0151B; Note: [Col. 0151] Matt. 6], then openly for others, in order that fervour may kindle her neighbours. When we sing the hymn together, we indicate that all the soldiers have assembled, after the invitation, for the King’s praises, in accord with the saying: “Zion heard and rejoiced” [Note: [Col. 0151] Ps. 96]. A hymn is praise of God with song; we sing it standing, so that by the uprightness of our bodies we may signify that we direct our minds to the Lord. For unless the mind accords with the tongue, it is certain that, however loud the voice may be, it does not please God.

Then we begin the nocturns. Observe that *nocturna nocturnae* is said of the hour, and *nocturni nocturnorum* [Col. 0151C] of the office. Or *nocturna nocturnae* is said of the collection of psalms before the readings; *nocturni nocturnorum*, of the psalms, readings, and responsories; and *nocturnae nocturnarum*, of the seasons. On ordinary days we customarily celebrate one nocturn, but on solemnities three. On ordinary days we commemorate the servitude of our exile; on solemn days, our deliverance. Since therefore we were first children of wrath and afterward children of grace [Note: [Col. 0151] Eph. 2], let us first treat of the office of ordinary days and afterward of the office of feasts, so that we may be able to pass from wrath to grace, from night to day, and from servitude to freedom. For the one by whom a person is overcome makes him his servant; the devil conquered the human race and subjected it to dreadful [Col. 0151D] servitude [Note: [Col. 0151] 2 Pet. 2].

Therefore, that we may be freed from this, we labour at divine offices during the nocturnal hours. But because we lament that our servitude extends through six ages, we regularly celebrate the same office on the six nights of the week. In it we sing twelve psalms with six antiphons, three readings, and as many responsories. Formerly psalms were sung in various numbers: some sang fifty, others more, others fewer. Hence, when the Fathers assembled to determine the number, by angelic revelation the number twelve was instituted. We assign twelve hours to the night, and for each one we sing a psalm to God [Col. 0152A], so that from blindness of mind and from the pestilence that walks in the darkness of the twelve hours [Note: [Col. 0151] Ps. 90], through God’s mercy we may attain the light of eternity.

Or there are twelve months of the year in which we serve the devil or the world. There are twelve Apostles, by whose teaching we are set free. Therefore we sing twelve psalms, that from servitude we may be granted freedom through apostolic teaching. Observe that a psalm was called a melody produced by the sounding of ten strings, from *psallere*, “to touch”; but now a psalm is praise of God, signifying good action. Therefore, while we sing them, we ought to stand, to show that we are ready for the exercise of good work in the cause of ourselves and our brethren. We join psalms in pairs, showing that neither our praises [Col. 0152B] nor our works have value without charity, which consists in love of God and neighbour [Note: [Col. 0151] Matt. 22]. According to the custom of the Gallican Church, we end two psalms with one *Gloria*, because our praises are accepted unto the glory of the Trinity when they consist in the bond of charity.

The choir sings the psalms antiphonally. *Chorus* takes its name from *choraea* [dance], or from *corona* [crown], or from *concordia* [harmony]. Formerly, standing around altars in the form of a crown, they sang harmoniously; but Flavianus and Theodorus instituted alternate psalmody. Thus the two choirs of singers signify angels and the spirits of the righteous, praising the Lord as if by reciprocal will and exhorting one another [Col. 0152C] to good action.

The six antiphons are the six ages in which good action and love of God and neighbour are necessary; or the six antiphons are the six works of mercy: feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, clothing the naked, receiving the stranger, visiting the sick, and redeeming the imprisoned [Note: [Col. 0151] Matt. 25]. If we observe these, we shall pass from the darkness of this night or death to true light and eternal life. Or charity, or devotion of mind, is understood through the antiphon. Therefore they are alternated, because charity exists between at least two persons; and the psalms are sung alternately under one antiphon, that is, burdens are borne under one bond of love [Note: [Col. 0151] Gal. 6]. For example, one reads and another sows; at harvest time the reader offers doctrine to the sower, and the sower bread to the reader. Thus [Col. 0152D] the unity of harmony and the arrangement of ordered concord signify the unity of a well-ordered city, so that the deaf may grasp it by sight and the blind understand it by hearing. Hence too antiphons are intermingled with psalms, because “faith works through love” [Note: [Col. 0151] Gal. 7].

Therefore an antiphon is called a reciprocal voice, as though a counter-sound, from *anti* and *phonas*, because the psalm is intoned according to the melody of the antiphon, and the hand works according as it is stirred by the little spark of charity. An antiphon is a song interspersed among divine praises for the refreshing of souls; and indeed nothing refreshes souls more from the heats of vices than charity [Col. 0153A]. Nothing more invites them to the proclamations of heavenly things. Ignatius of Antioch heard the choir of angels singing this chant alternately in heaven; he therefore taught his own church to sing alternately, and from him the whole Church received the practice of alternation.

The antiphon is begun before the psalm by one person and ended by all, because God first loved us, and we ought to respond to his love [Note: [Col. 0153] 1 John 4]. Likewise, it is begun before the psalm and sung in full after the psalm, because our praise or works then please God if, having begun in devotion, they end in the fullness of love; or because charity is begun here and will be made perfect in the world to come. The *neuma* at the end signifies the ineffable joy of the righteous: the devotion of minds through love or preaching, the amplitude of faith, the execution of works, the uplifting of hope, and the expansion of charity [Col. 0153B].

We read three lessons because the Lord set three watches, saying: “If he comes in the first, second, or third watch and finds them so, blessed are those servants” [Note: [Col. 0153] Luke 12].
