These three watches signify three ages: childhood, youth, and old age. In them, lest we be deceived by the devil, we are bound to watch well and praise the Lord. Or by the three readings we signify the teachings of the elect in the three periods of time. With them we sing responsories at intervals, indicating that whatever the elect taught in the three periods and whatever we do in the three ages, we refer to God and the Trinity, and glorify the Trinity in [Col. 0153C] faith, hope, and charity.

Therefore they are called responsories, from responding, because they indicate that we ought to answer in deeds the holy admonitions of God set forth in the readings, lest we be like the children playing in the marketplace and saying: “We sang, and you did not dance; we mourned, and you did not lament” [Note: [Col. 0153] Matt. 11]. Hence the responsories correspond to the readings in subject matter, as we sing sorrowful things in response to sorrowful things and joyful things to joyful things. For example, when the reader, like John [Note: [Col. 0153] Matt. 3], neither eating nor drinking, preaches repentance or the lamentation of the Lord’s Passion, we too weep in response; and when the reader, like the Son eating and drinking, sets before us the joy of the kingdom, we likewise sing psalms in response. Yet in some circumstances this is done differently.

Observe that when we modulate our voices, we sometimes indicate lamentation and sometimes represent joy. Low, high, and very high voices signify the three orders of human life: namely, married persons, the continent, and virgins, who will be rewarded with thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold fruit [Col. 0153D; Note: [Col. 0153] Matt. 13]. Or they correspond to Solomon’s three books: beginners, those making progress, and the perfect. Or a responsory is so called because, to the choir singing the responsory, the verse is answered by one person; it is also called a verse because he turns back to the responsory so that the whole responsory, or at least a part of it, may be repeated. This resolves the musical question concerning the verse of the second tone, which ends in C although the second tone always ends in D: we say that there is no ending there, but in the repetition of the responsory. Ambrose first composed this chant, and from him the whole Church received the form.

We conclude and end all these things with the *Gloria*, because we refer all things to the faith and glory of the Trinity. Observe that the choir’s harmonious following of a single leader in the responsory confirms what the Apostle says: that we should all say the same thing and that there should be no schisms among us [Col. 0154A; Note: [Col. 0153] 1 Cor. 1].

## CHAPTER II. ON FESTIVAL NOCTURNS
> “If in the first, second, and third watch the Lord [Col. 0154B] finds his servants watching, blessed are those servants” [Note: [Col. 0153] Luke 12].

On solemn days, however, such as Sundays and others, we divide the night office into three nocturns, imitating the watches of the heavenly Jerusalem, which “is built as a city” [Note: [Col. 0153] Ps. 121], and is guarded by the watches of angels: three groups distinguish three groups, while thrice three sing in harmony to the Trinity. So too we, who make our way toward that city—and are therefore called by its name, Jerusalem, because we bear its shadow—celebrate three nocturns on Sunday, the day on which we have merited the fellowship of angels; or we imitate the three interrupted watches of the primitive Church, which rose three times in the night to confess the Lord; so that, after three nocturns had been completed with three psalms, at dawn, [Col. 0154C] when the bells had been rung, it sang *Te Deum laudamus* and the Lauds. This custom of three watches was taken from a besieged city, where three watches guard against the enemy’s ambushes. The devil attacks our city, namely the Church, and especially lies in wait for it at night.

For night is suited to sins; therefore we ought to keep watch more attentively at night, so that we may avoid the snares of the hidden enemy. But later, when charity grew cold and people became too sluggish to rise so often, it was ordained that they should rise at midnight and sing the three nocturns continuously. The three nocturns also commemorate the Church’s warfare, which has served and serves in the camp of the Lord under three periods: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace.

Each period [Col. 0154D] has three divisions. The period before the Law is divided from Adam to Noah, from Noah to Abraham, and from Abraham to Moses. In the first division Abel, Enos, Enoch, and Lamech kept watch; this is indicated in four psalms. Abel sings: “Blessed is the man” [Note: [Col. 0153] Gen. 4], “who, like a tree planted beside streams of water,” yielded “the fruit of righteousness in its season” [Note: [Col. 0153] Ps. 1], when he died in preserving righteousness. Enos sings: “Why have they raged?” [Note: [Col. 0153] Ps. 2], he who served the Lord in fear [Note: [Col. 0153] Gen. 4], when he called upon the Lord’s name. Enoch sings: “O Lord, how many are they” [Note: [Col. 0153] Ps. 3] [Note: [Col. 0153] Gen. 5], whom the Lord [Col. 0155A] received when he translated him into paradise. Lamech sings: “O Lord, not in thy wrath” [Note: [Col. 0155] Ps. 6] [Note: [Col. 0155] Gen. 5], whom the Lord heard when he gave him such a son as saved the human race from God’s wrath in the ark. These are four psalms sung under one *Gloria*, according to the custom of some, just as they are concluded under one antiphon; because those fathers flourished in the four virtues, worshipped the Trinity, and exalted it with praises.

In the second division of the first period Noah, Shem, Eber, and Terah kept watch, as the following psalms suggest. Noah sings: “O Lord my God” [Note: [Col. 0155] Ps. 7] [Note: [Col. 0155] Gen. 6 and 7], whom the Lord found righteous in that generation and therefore saved from the pursuing waters. Shem sings: “O Lord, our Lord” [Note: [Col. 0155] Ps. 8] [Note: [Col. 0155] Gen. 9], whom the Lord [Col. 0155B] crowned with glory and honour when his father’s blessing raised him above his brothers. Eber sings: “I will confess thee” [Note: [Col. 0155] Ps. 9] [Note: [Col. 0155] Gen. 11], who proclaimed God’s wonders when he destroyed the city of the giants. Terah sings: “In the Lord I trust” [Note: [Col. 0155] Ps. 10] [Note: [Col. 0155] Gen. 11], who, established in Ur of the Chaldeans, trusts in the Lord, though fire and sulphur became the portion of his cup. These too are four psalms concluded under one *Gloria* and antiphon, for the reason already given.

In the third division of the first period Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph kept watch, as the following psalms declare. Abraham sings: “Save me” [Note: [Col. 0155] Ps. 11] [Note: [Col. 0155] Gen. 12], whom the Lord saved, in whose time the holy man failed because the world served idolatry. Isaac sings: “How long?” [Note: [Col. 0155] Ps. 12] [Col. 0155C] [Note: [Col. 0155] Gen. 22], upon whose sacrifice the Lord looked favourably. Jacob sings: “The fool hath said” [Note: [Col. 0155] Ps. 13] [Note: [Col. 0155] Gen. 28], for whom the Lord was hope. Hence it is said there: “Jacob shall rejoice; Israel shall be glad.” Joseph sings: “O Lord, who shall dwell?” [Note: [Col. 0155] Ps. 14] [Note: [Col. 0155] Gen. 39], who was without stain when he refused adultery. These also are four psalms, concluded under one *Gloria* and antiphon for the same reason. Or, through these twelve psalms we commit to memory the number of the patriarchs, who possessed faith in the Holy Trinity through the exercise of the four virtues; therefore groups of four psalms are contained under three *Glorias*. No psalm is separated from the others, because, as Augustine says, whoever has one virtue has them all.

After the psalms comes the verse, because it is fitting that one who has laboured [Col. 0155D] should turn toward rest. Therefore he who stood while singing the psalms should now sit for the reading. Hence it is called a *verse* (*versus*) from turning (*vertere*), because the choir turns toward the east, or because it turns from the psalms to the reading. It is sung by boys, that we may understand that our services please God if they are performed in innocence. Observe, moreover, that the verse is a sharp exclamation, an awakening of minds, lest we grow sluggish in the work begun. At times it arouses us to prayer, lest flies spoil the sweetness of the ointment [Note: [Col. 0155] Eccles. 10]; at times to reading, lest we become dull [Col. 0156A] through the security of sitting. For it is known that we sit during the reading; sitting pertains to security, and security gives rise to negligence. At times it pertains to the hymn, so that we may be watchful and attentive to Christ’s praises. Therefore it sometimes precedes prayer, sometimes reading, sometimes a hymn, as with the *Magnificat* and *Benedictus*. In this office the verse precedes the readings; in others it follows them. By this variety the weary mind is refreshed, as reading succeeds prayer and prayer succeeds reading.

The first verse, “I remembered in the night” [Note: [Col. 0155] Ps. 118], and likewise the second, “At midnight,” indicate the time of the nocturn. Yet whatever lies between the first and the last is called the middle; thus, even if we did not rise at the very midpoint, we are not to be charged with falsehood. Nevertheless, some, unwilling to seem to lie through laziness in sleep, [Col. 0156B] alter the verse and use another, namely: “For thou makest my lamp to shine” [Note: [Col. 0155] Ps. 17]. The third verse, “Be exalted, O Lord, in thy strength” [Note: [Col. 0155] Ps. 20], indicates the character of the office and promises a song of virtues belonging to the New Testament.

By the Lord’s Prayer, which is said secretly, is understood the king’s secret counsel, if we continue the comparison proposed. This prayer is said here so that by it the devil’s temptations may be driven away. For when the devil perceives that we intend to read matters pertaining to moral instruction, or containing the saints’ victories over him, he attacks us more fiercely. Hence we rely upon the Lord’s Prayer, lest we succumb [Col. 0156C] to temptation. Because this prayer is said silently, so that it may be grasped more attentively—or because we speak to God—the final part is concluded aloud, namely: “And lead us not into temptation,” so that it may be clear for what purpose the prayer is said: namely, that the reader may not be carried away by a delusive temptation, and the hearer may not be defrauded of understanding and profit from the reading.

Or we precede the readings with prayers, beseeching the Lord of the harvest “to send labourers into his harvest” [Note: [Col. 0155] Luke 10], and to open our heart in his law and commandments [Note: [Col. 0155] 2 Macc. 1], lest the seed of God’s word which we are about to hear be eaten by birds, choked by thorns, or grow upon rock where it has no moisture [Note: [Col. 0155] Luke 8]. The verse after the prayer is a command after counsel. Remember that the following verse is always to be announced, [Col. 0156D] except before the Gospel, where “Hear us, O Christ” is said. Some, however, announce no verse.

The alternation of readers represents the succession of envoys. When they say, “Command, lord, a blessing,” they request leave to depart; when they are blessed, leave is given. This indicates that no one ought to read in church unless he has been granted permission, and no one ought to preach unless sent: “For how shall they preach unless they be sent?” [Note: [Col. 0155] Rom. 10]. The reading itself is the execution of the entrusted embassy; “But thou, O Lord” is the envoy’s return, [Col. 0157A] where the imploring of mercy indicates that the office of embassy or preaching itself cannot be performed without the dust of some fault, however slight. Hence Augustine says: the word of preaching is heard more safely than it is spoken, for the preacher walks on earth. It is difficult for the feet of one who walks on earth not to be soiled by some dust; and difficult for a preacher, when he perceives that he has preached well, not to be lifted up in a spirit of pride.

When we give thanks to God, it is not in response to the reader’s prayers but pertains to the reading just given. We give thanks because he deigns to break for us the bread of his teaching, lest we perish through hunger for hearing the word of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0157] Amos 8]. At readings at whose end “But thou, O Lord” is not said—namely, the chapters of the regular hours, [Col. 0157B] in which God’s word is sown—“Thanks be to God” is answered by custom. Observe that, just as in the Church there are two orders, the wise and the unwise [Note: [Col. 0157] Rom. 1], so there are two kinds of readings. In the readings read at Mass, the wise are instructed; in those recited at night, the unwise are educated. Hence they are expounded.

Observe again that there are four ways of ending readings: either with “But thou, O Lord”; or, when prophecies are read, with “Thus saith the Lord: Turn unto me, and thou shalt be saved”; or, when the *Lamentations of Jeremiah* are read, with “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, turn to the Lord thy God”; [Col. 0157C] or simply, as in the Office of the Dead. Some, however, use a special conclusion even there. Or the readings represent the preaching of those Fathers, and the responsories signify their life, by which their preaching is answered.

The time of the Law is divided from Moses to David, from David to the Babylonian captivity, and from the Babylonian captivity to Christ. In the first division of this time priests kept watch, such as Aaron, when he taught; in the second, judges, such as Gideon, when he judged; in the third, kings, such as Solomon, when he governed the people. This is indicated in the following psalms. “Preserve me” [Note: [Col. 0157] Ps. 15] represents priests, whose inheritance and cup the Lord was. “Hear, O Lord, my righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0157] Ps. 16] signifies judges, whose [Col. 0157D] judgement proceeded from the countenance of the Almighty. “I will love thee, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0157] Ps. 17] indicates kings, whom the Lord established over the nations [Note: [Col. 0157] Ps. 44]. To each of these three psalms are given a *Gloria* and an antiphon, because each of the aforesaid orders worshipped the Trinity and exalted it in praises. The following readings are their preaching; the responsories, their works and thanksgivings.

The period of grace is divided into the time of apostolic preaching, the time of persecution, and the time of peace. In the first the apostles kept watch; in the second, martyrs; in the third, confessors. This is clearly indicated in the following psalms: [Col. 0158A] “The heavens declare the glory of God” represents the apostles, because “their sound has gone forth into all the earth” [Note: [Col. 0157] Ps. 18]. “May he hear thee” declares the martyrs, because he protected them “in the day of their tribulation” [Note: [Col. 0157] Ps. 19]. “O Lord, in thy strength” indicates the confessors, who were not deprived of the desire of their lips [Note: [Col. 0157] Ps. 20].

This time of peace began with King Constantine, who rejoiced in God’s strength concerning Christ’s salvation and exulted greatly when he assembled the Council of Nicaea. In the first hour of this period Paul sang, saying: “To the King of the ages, immortal and invisible, to God alone be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen” [Note: [Col. 0157] 1 Tim. 1]. In the second, Lawrence, saying: “I give thee thanks, Lord, because I have deserved to enter thy gate.” In the third, Gregory, who by musical art [Col. 0158B] arranged the divine office. We observe the first watch of this vigil when we preach; the second when we endure tribulations patiently; the third when we devote ourselves to contemplation.

But because “sorrow takes possession of the end of joy” [Note: [Col. 0157] Prov. 14], the final verses of the final psalm touch briefly upon the times of Antichrist, who shall be a furnace of fire in the time of his countenance; the Lord shall trouble him, and fire shall devour him with his accomplices [Note: [Col. 0157] Ps. 20]. Afterwards the elect shall sing forever and exult in the Lord’s powers [Note: [Col. 0157] ibid.]. To each of these three psalms likewise a *Gloria* and antiphon are given, because Christians flourish in faith and hope, worship the Trinity in charity, and extol its majesty with praise. The readings are the teachings [Col. 0158C] of the faithful; the responsories, the life which ought to answer to teaching. All these are sung on Sunday night, because all those mentioned above are saved in Christ’s resurrection.

Observe that at the third watch the Gospel is recited, because it was preached in the time of grace. Hence the etymology of *responsory* is mistaken here: responsories do not answer the Gospel readings by deriving from the histories; nor likewise does that which is sung concerning the Trinity in summer time.

The same applies to the vigils of saints, in which the readings are changed because of the vigils, but the responsories are not changed. It should also be known that at the third watch *Alleluia* is repeated in the antiphons. At saints’ solemnities likewise we celebrate three nocturns or vigils, [Col. 0158D] and in each sing three psalms, three verses, three readings, and three responsories. Thus there are nine psalms, nine verses, nine readings, and nine responsories. The number three and the number nine signify the same thing in all respects. We celebrate all these things in order to show that the saints, through faith in the Holy Trinity, are joined to the nine orders of angels; and so that through these offices we may please the Trinity so greatly that we may be joined to those same orders.

Or, the three psalms, three verses, three readings, and three responsories in the three nocturns make thirty-six. We therefore celebrate them so that, through [Col. 0159A] faith in the Holy Trinity, observance of the ten commandments, and performance of the six works, we may deserve to be crowned with the saints in heaven. Or, through the three nocturns, both on Sundays and on saints’ feasts—which pertain to present grace—we understand the three watches, according to the Gospel teaching: “If in the first, second, and third watch the Lord finds his servants watching, blessed are those servants” [Note: [Col. 0159] Luke 12].

The multiplicity of readings signifies the multitude of preachers in the time of grace, just as their scarcity on ordinary weekdays signifies their rarity in the time of the Law. For as a cock, in the deep night, ordinarily gives fewer cries, but as the joy of day approaches sings more frequently, so before the Lord’s incarnation, when the people walked in darkness [Note: [Col. 0159] Isa. 9], heralds were few [Col. 0159B] and labourers few [Note: [Col. 0159] Luke 10]; but in the time of fullness [Note: [Col. 0159] Gal. 4], and on the day of salvation [Note: [Col. 0159] 2 Cor. 6], all bear twin offspring, and none among them is barren [Note: [Col. 0159] Song 4]. Yet the reason why at Easter we use only three readings is another matter, as we shall say below.

Further, the hymn which Augustine and Ambrose devised, namely *Te Deum laudamus*, which follows all the foregoing and is sung aloud, signifies the woman’s joy over the drachma which she found after lighting a lamp [Note: [Col. 0159] Luke 15]. Hence, according to some, lights are then lit. The fact that the ending, “Day by day,” and the rest which follows are sung more loudly, and that bells are then rung, signifies the summoning of the neighbours and their rejoicing with her over the [Col. 0159C] recovered drachma. Or the hymn just mentioned represents the future joy and gladness [Note: [Col. 0159] Rev. 14] which the Church, resting from her labours, will attain on the day of judgement.

## CHAPTER III. ON THE SEVEN CANONICAL HOURS

> “Seven times a day I have spoken praise to thee” [Note: [Col. 0159] Ps. 118].

The people returned from Babylon, following Ezra’s teaching [Note: [Col. 0159] 2 Esdr. 9], praised God four times at night and four times by day: four times at night, namely at Vespers, Compline, Nocturns, and Matins; four times by day, namely at Prime, Terce, Sext, and None. We likewise sing by the number four, that we may offer the Lord every element of our body. Again, we confess the Lord eight times, that we may attain the eighth day. But the Prophet says that the Lord is to be praised “at midnight [Col. 0159D] and seven times in the day” [Note: [Col. 0159] Ps. 118]; in this work we follow his authority and its mystery.

The daily office, then, is divided into seven canonical hours: Lauds, Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline. For we speak the Lord’s praises seven times a day because of the seven ages of the world, or of a human being, or the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, or the seven mysteries of Jesus Christ. Every day represents the whole duration of this world, which is divided into seven intervals. Thus morning praise recalls the time in which the first parents praised God in paradise. Prime recalls that in which Abel lived; Terce, Noah; Sext, Abraham; None, the prophets; the apostles are signified in Vespers; and the last righteous in Compline.

A day also represents the life of every individual person, which varies through seven ages. Therefore by Matins we commemorate infancy; by Prime, childhood; by Terce, adolescence; by Sext, youth; by None, old age; by Vespers, advanced old age; and by Compline, life’s end. Thus “seven times” means always: since by speaking the Lord’s praise seven times a day, we indicate that the whole time of the world and the whole life of a human being must be referred to God. So blessed Nicholas, by not taking his mother’s breast on Wednesday and Friday, [Col. 0160B] referred his infancy to the Lord.

Or we praise the Lord seven times as we render tribute and thanksgiving for every benefit bestowed upon us by God. For the number seven is the number of universality. We also confess the Lord seven times a day because through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit we emerge from the darkness of vices and the devil’s slavery, represented by the night office, to the sun of righteousness; and are delivered into freedom, represented by the day office.

Below we shall explain the seven mysteries of Jesus Christ displayed to us in the flesh, which provide reasons for confessing the Lord seven times. Let no one, then, dare omit these seven hours unless he wishes to be ungrateful to the Holy Spirit [Col. 0160C] and to appear empty before the Lord [Note: [Col. 0159] Deut. 16]. For we read that the apostles observed these hours. Thus Peter and John went up to the temple at the ninth hour of prayer [Note: [Col. 0159] Acts 3]. Again, Peter, wishing to eat at the sixth hour, went up to the upper room to pray [Note: [Col. 0159] Acts 10].

Since therefore we ought to confess the Lord seven times a day, while there are twelve hours of daylight [Note: [Col. 0159] John 11], we include the other five under these seven: under Prime, the first; under the second, the second; under Terce, the third; under the fourth, the fourth; under Sext, the sixth; under the seventh, the seventh; under the eighth, the eighth; under None, the ninth; under the tenth, the tenth; under Vespers, the eleventh; and under Compline, the twelfth. Why, then, do we celebrate the office at these hours of the day rather than at others? The reason must be sought.

Matins is so called from morning (*mane*), and morning from the Manes. According to the pagans, the Manes are infernal gods, who were said to hold the day shut up throughout the night and to send it forth upon the earth in the morning. Hence *mane* also means “good,” because nothing in this life seems better than light. Morning praise is therefore sung to God, as it were, for the light granted us, since he has led us back from the darkness of error to the way of truth.

Again, we confess the Lord at this time because at such an hour God created the world and the morning stars [Note: [Col. 0159] Job 38], namely the angels, who immediately rejoiced to their Creator with their sweet harmony. We imitate them when singing at this hour, and may be called evening stars, [Col. 0161A] because we follow Christ, the sun setting for us [Note: [Col. 0161] Mal. 4; Luke 4], so that through him in the resurrection [Note: [Col. 0161] Mark 16], as at sunrise, we may reach the morning stars.

Again, at this hour the Lord led his people through the sea and killed the Egyptians in the sea, as is read in Exodus [Note: [Col. 0161] ch. 14]. At this hour, therefore, we give thanks to God, who through baptismal grace freed us from Pharaoh’s dominion in order to bring us to the promised land. Again, some hold that at this hour the righteous will awaken from the sleep of death, passing from the night of the world to the light.

Or at this hour, as at the others, we follow the mysteries of Jesus Christ. He was seized by night, mocked in the morning, and had mercy upon Peter [Note: [Col. 0161] Matt. 26]; at the first hour he was delivered to the Gentiles; at the third he was scourged [Col. 0161B] and crucified by a cry [Note: [Col. 0161] Matt. 27]; at the sixth he was fastened to the cross, and then darkness came over all the earth [Note: [Col. 0161] ibid.]; at the ninth he died, and then the thief was saved, the veil of the Temple was torn, and his side pierced; at the eleventh he was taken down from the cross; at the twelfth he was buried [Note: [Col. 0161] John 19].

Again, during the night he despoiled hell; in the morning he rose; at the first hour he appeared to Mary; at the third he met the two women returning from the tomb [Note: [Col. 0161] Mark 16]; at the sixth, James; at the ninth, Peter; at Vespers he opened the Scriptures to the two walking to Emmaus and, lodging with them, made himself known in the breaking of bread [Note: [Col. 0161] Luke 24]. At Compline he said to the apostles, “Peace be unto you,” and ate with them [Note: [Col. 0161] ibid.].

Again, after Peter had laboured all night fishing, Christ stood on the shore in the morning and filled the net with fish [Note: [Col. 0161] John 21]. At Prime [Col. 0161C] he ate with the seven disciples, said to them, “Children, have ye any food?” and entrusted his sheep to Peter [Note: [Col. 0161] ibid.]. At Terce the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles [Note: [Col. 0161] Acts 2]. At Sext, on the day of the Ascension, he reclined at table with the disciples. At None he ascended into heaven while they watched [Note: [Col. 0161] Mark 16]. At Vespers he came to save the world [Note: [Col. 0161] Acts 1]. At the end he will come to render recompense; he who also, at Vespers before the Passion, had supped with the disciples [Note: [Col. 0161] Matt. 26], washed their feet, and delivered his body to them [Note: [Col. 0161] John 13]. At Compline he had prayed for them in Gethsemane [Note: [Col. 0161] Matt. 26].

Therefore, because we have in writing these mysteries concerning Jesus Christ which occurred at these hours, we observe these, and no other, canonical hours: Matins, that with Peter we may flee to tears [Note: [Col. 0161] ibid.] and rise with the Lord [Note: [Col. 0161] Mark 16]; Prime, that we may be [Col. 0161D] those who seek first the kingdom of God [Note: [Col. 0161] Matt. 6] and offer him the first fruits of our works [Note: [Col. 0161] Lev. 27]—him who, delivered to the Gentiles, suffered for our offences and rose for our justification [Note: [Col. 0161] Rom. 4]—so that the sun of righteousness may rise upon us [Note: [Col. 0161] Mal. 4], and, justified [Note: [Col. 0161] Rom. 5] and joined to sevenfold grace, we may feast with him at the honeyed and eternal banquet [Note: [Col. 0161] 1 Cor. 5].

Terce, that we may imitate the patience of Christ when scourged, and be baptized in the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0162A] Sext, that, lifted up from the earth, he may draw us to himself and rescue us from the darkness descending upon the earth [Note: [Col. 0161] John 12; Exod. 10]. None, that we may die to the world, be saved with the thief [Note: [Col. 0161] Luke 23], behold with unveiled face the glory of God [Note: [Col. 0161] 2 Cor. 3], be redeemed by blood and washed by water, and at last be raised above the stars. Vespers, that we may recall the king’s evening sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0161] Exod. 29; Num. 28], which prefigured the new sacrifice instituted at evening; that we may be buried with Christ [Note: [Col. 0161] Rom. 6; Col. 2], be established as heirs by the testament, be taught humility by the washing of feet [Note: [Col. 0161] John 13], and be kindled to hospitality toward the poor by the bond and fire of charity, and enlightened to understand the Scriptures. Compline, that his sweat, prayer, rest, and peaceful greeting may bear fruit in us.

## CHAPTER IV. ON MORNING LAUDS ON WEEKDAYS

[Col. 0162B]

> “In the morning I slew all the sinners of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ps. 100].

The time before the nocturn signifies our life in sins. The nocturnal office signifies the service of our exile; morning praise, the aid of repentance, through which we make our way toward the joy of light and freedom.

Therefore, at weekday Matins we say first the psalm *Miserere mei, Deus*—“Have mercy upon me, O God” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ps. 50]. Converted Jews used this psalm frequently, and the Church uses it frequently now, because it summons us to repentance, through which there is a resurrection from the death of the soul. For just as [Col. 0162C] at Sunday Matins “The Lord reigneth” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ps. 92] is sung for Christ’s resurrection from bodily death, so on weekdays “Have mercy upon me, O God” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ps. 50] is sung for the resurrection of the faithful from the death of souls, as they emerge from darkness into light.

Therefore in the second psalm, which changes with each weekday, mention is made of morning or light: in *Verba mea*, “In the morning I will stand before thee” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ps. 5]; in *Judica me*, “Send forth thy light” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ps. 42]; in *Te decet*, “Thou shalt delight the goings forth of the morning and evening” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ps. 64]; in *Domine, refugium*, “May it flourish in the morning” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ps. 89]; in *Domine, exaudi*, “Make me hear thy mercy in the morning” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ps. 142]; in *Bonum est confiteri Domino*, “To declare thy mercy in the morning” [Note: [Col. 0161] Ps. 91].

These psalms are not without reason ordered thus at morning Lauds, so that in them the order of Christian [Col. 0162D] conversion may be marked. For *Verba mea* is the voice of the primitive Church called to the Lord’s inheritance; *Judica me* is its voice entering among the Gentiles; *Te decet* is sung as a figure of the Gentile world receiving faith; *Domine, refugium* is the voice of the Jew returning to right understanding; *Domine, exaudi* is the voice of that same Jew praying against Antichrist’s persecution; *Bonum est* is the voice of the Church resting in the Lord. A discerning reader may draw this from the titles and senses of the psalms themselves [Col. 0163A].

Since remission of sins and acquisition of the kingdom of heaven occur through charity [Note: [Col. 0163] 1 Pet. 4], two psalms follow, namely *Deus, Deus meus* [Note: [Col. 0163] Ps. 62] and *Deus, misereatur nostri* [Note: [Col. 0163] Ps. 66], which concern love of God and neighbour. The first concerns love of God, as it says: “My soul thirsted for thee” [Note: [Col. 0163] Ps. 62]; the second concerns love of neighbour, as it says: “May we know thy salvation among all nations” [Note: [Col. 0163] Ps. 66]. Therefore they are sung under one *Gloria*, because love of God and neighbour so accompany each other that in Christian profession neither is possessed without the other. Or they are sung under one *Gloria* because one person of Christ is venerated in them. Or they are continued under one *Gloria* because faith and action are understood in them: “faith without works [Col. 0163B] is dead” [Note: [Col. 0163] Jas. 2]; through these two we shall attain freedom and glory.

Since the performance of work is proof of love, six songs of victory are added for the six days, through which the six works of mercy are understood. On Monday, saying “I will give thanks,” we sing with Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0163] ch. 12], because as he overcame an unbelieving people, so we have overcome vices. On Tuesday we rejoice with Hezekiah, saying “I said” [Note: [Col. 0163] Isa. 38], because as he escaped bodily death, so we have escaped the death of the soul; hence it is added there: “The living, the living shall give thanks to thee” [Note: [Col. 0163] ibid.]. On Wednesday, saying “My heart rejoiced,” we exult with Hannah [Note: [Col. 0163] 1 Sam. 2], because as she overcame her rival, so we have overcome the flesh. On Thursday, saying “Let us sing” [Note: [Col. 0163] Exod. 15], we rejoice with the people [Col. 0163C] of Israel, because as they escaped the Egyptians through Moses, so we escape the devil and demons through Christ. On Friday, saying “O Lord, I have heard,” we rejoice with Habakkuk [Note: [Col. 0163] ch. 3], because as he [overcame] Babylon, so we have escaped the confusion of sins. On Saturday, saying “Hear,” we rejoice with Moses [Note: [Col. 0163] Deut. 32], because as his people entered the promised land after their enemies had been overcome, so we, after overcoming vices, shall attain the promised forgiveness, freedom, and joy.

They may also be adapted to the successive stages of the time of grace. Monday recalls the period in which the banner of the cross was first raised, as the wording of the preceding psalm, *Verba mea*, and of the following canticle, *Confitebor*, makes plain when it says: “Make known [Col. 0163D] his works among the peoples” [Note: [Col. 0163] Isa. 12]. Tuesday signifies the period in which emperors persecuted the Church. Therefore, lamenting, it says, “Judge me, O God”; and thus the canticle of Hezekiah is read, who was weakened by bodily illness. Wednesday indicates the period in which the Church was exalted above its enemies. Therefore it rejoices with those delivered from Babylon, saying *Te decet*, and sings with Hannah, who was freed from Peninnah’s oppression. Thursday indicates the period in which Moses’ people will enter the faith. Therefore the psalm is sung which is entitled “A prayer of Moses,” [Col. 0164A] and his canticle is added. Friday celebrates the Saviour’s Passion. Therefore the psalm is sung which is subtitled, “Of David himself, when his son Absalom persecuted him,” that is, Judas. Thus the canticle too says: “Horns are in his hands” [Note: [Col. 0163] Hab. 3]. Saturday is celebrated in memory of the elect who will be at the end of the world, as is gathered from the psalm’s title—namely, “A psalm, a song, for the Sabbath day”—and from the canticle given to the children of Israel after the toil of their journey.

Or let the six be adapted to the ages. On the second day the Lord divided the waters from the waters [Note: [Col. 0163] Gen. 1]. In the second age the Flood occurred [Note: [Col. 0163] Gen. 7]; both signified baptism. Christ also is believed to have been baptized on the second day. Therefore on the second day the canticle concerning baptism is rightly read, where it says: “You shall draw waters [Col. 0164B] with joy from the springs of the Saviour” [Note: [Col. 0163] Isa. 12], where the faithful are separated from the unbelieving.

In the third age Isaac is delivered from death [Note: [Col. 0163] Gen. 22]. Therefore on the third day the canticle of Hezekiah is rightly read, to whom the Lord added fifteen years of life. So too, if we remain in the faith of the Trinity, through observance of the Decalogue and faith in the five-part Passion, he will take away death from us and grant eternal life. In the fourth age Hannah was made fruitful; therefore on the fourth day Hannah’s canticle is read. Thus the Church has been chosen through the four Gospels, and the Synagogue rejected. In the fifth age the people were freed from Babylonian captivity [Note: [Col. 0163] 1 Esdr. 1]; therefore on the fifth day Moses’ canticle concerning the people’s deliverance from Pharaoh’s hands is read. In the sixth age the Lord was crucified; [Col. 0164C] therefore on the sixth day the canticle concerning his Passion is read, where it says: “Horns are in his hands” [Note: [Col. 0163] Isa. 12]. On the Sabbath the Lord rested from every work that he had accomplished [Note: [Col. 0163] Gen. 2], and lay in the tomb [Note: [Col. 0163] Matt. 27].

Therefore on Saturday is read the canticle that was given to the children of Israel after the labour of the journey, when they had entered the promised land. Observe the difference between a psalm and a canticle: a psalm signifies action; a canticle, praise arising from action. There follows: “Praise the Lord from the heavens” [Note: [Col. 0163] Ps. 148]. There are three psalms in which we commemorate triumph over the world, the flesh, and the devil; and, because while we are on the way instruction and consolation are necessary to us if so great a freedom and glory is to be revealed in us [Note: [Col. 0163] Rom. 8], the priest, in the person of the Lord, adds the chapter: [Col. 0164D] “Keep watch” [Note: [Col. 0163] I Cor. 15]. Or, “the night has gone before,” where he exhorts us to persevere in faith and to apply ourselves to works of mercy: to cast off the works of darkness and put on the armour of light [Note: [Col. 0163] Rom. 13]; and he consoles us by the promise of glory. It is called a chapter because it is taken from the heads of the epistles. Although it is a reading, it is nevertheless read without “Bid, Lord, a blessing,” and without the priestly blessing, because it belongs properly to the priest to read it; and prelates of the Church ought not to ask permission, but to grant it. Nor does he say, “But thou,” because the priest is perfect, so that he does not easily succumb to the devil’s suggestions [Col. 0165A]; yet in some places it is pronounced by subordinates.

Observe also that in the nocturnal office we devote ourselves more copiously to readings than in the daytime office, because we more willingly lend them our ears. Again observe that in readings of this kind the author is not named, as in the readings of the Mass, because those diligent in the offices recognize the author from the reading. But laypeople assemble for Mass, and the author is unknown to them. When at Matins there is sometimes prefixed, “A sermon of such-and-such a saint,” this is done as a precaution, lest an erroneous author be presented in the midst; and because often the author is not recognized from the reading.

Then follows the hymn, by which is indicated the joy we have over freedom; but lest we seem ungrateful for the benefit, we acknowledge the benefit [Col. 0165B] in the verse, “Filled.” Afterwards we give thanks to our deliverer and burst forth into his praise, saying aloud: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0165] Luke 1]. Why? Because he visited us when we were placed in misery, redeemed us, freed us from the hand of enemies, gave us knowledge of salvation in the remission of sins through the bowels of mercy, enlightened us, and directed us into the way of peace.

Observe that at only three hours we say three Gospel canticles: at dawn the *Benedictus* is sung, because there true light is announced; at evening, the *Magnificat*, because at the end of the world, as it says there, “God will scatter the proud and exalt the humble” [Note: [Col. 0165] ibid.]; at Compline, the *Nunc dimittis*, because after judgement the saints will reign in peace. The antiphon signifies the devotion [Col. 0165C] which we ought to have in the praises of the Redeemer.

“May the Lord be with you”: teacher and disciples pray for one another and exchange greetings. Its meaning is: May the Lord receive your praise and reward you with the reward of life. “And with thy spirit”: namely, since you are about to pray for us. The Lord will not hear prayers unless they proceed from a good heart; may he who is without whom there is nothing good be with thy spirit. But the priest, judging himself not sufficient through his own goodness, adds: “Let us pray,” as though saying: Pray with me, that we may more quickly obtain what we ask. The prayer he says signifies the pardon which the Lord has promised; “Amen,” namely: May that for which you prayed be done for us. Again he says, “May the Lord be with you.” This repeated greeting is an affectionate prayer that they may persevere in the grace obtained [Col. 0165D]. At last it is concluded: “Let us bless the Lord.” “Thanks be to God,” by which it is signified that until the end of life we ought, in rendering thanks for his benefits, to bless God.

“Let us bless” is said by boys, to show that unless through repentance we become as little children, we cannot worthily praise God [Note: [Col. 0165] Matt. 18]; or to indicate that our praise is childish, that is, insufficient. For when we speak of God, we utter and praise him, stammering as we can, yet we are insufficient; because God’s surpassing excellence exceeds our speech and [Col. 0166A] understanding: “For man approaches unto a deep heart, and God shall be exalted” [Note: [Col. 0165] Ps. 63]. Then follow the suffrages of the saints, because as long as we live we are placed as it were on slippery ground and are attacked by demons; therefore we always need the saints’ intercessions.

## CHAPTER V. ON MATINS PRAISES ON FESTIVAL DAYS

“At Matins, O Lord, I will meditate upon thee” [Note: [Col. 0165] Ps. 62].

The time before the nocturnal office signifies the time of death before the Law, in which people were silent from the praises of God. The time of the nocturnal office signifies the time of the Law given to Moses. The time of Matins praise signifies the time of grace, from the resurrection until the end of the world, during which we are bound to praise God: for the goods of nature [Col. 0166B] which he bestowed on us at this hour by creating us; for the goods of grace which he gave us at this hour by rising again; for the goods of glory which he will give us at this hour by raising us again. Therefore this entire office is full of praises. By the verse the priest rouses the hearers to these praises, and finally implores divine help; afterwards the choir, hastening towards the same help, glorifies God in the highest Trinity.

Thereupon, except during Lent, we begin with the psalm “The Lord hath reigned” [Note: [Col. 0165] Ps. 92]. There are eight psalms because there are eight orders of the elect saved through the water of baptism, just as eight souls were in the ark, in the water of the flood [Note: [Col. 0165] Gen. 6; I Pet. 3]. For the first order is that of the primitive Church living among the Jewish people; the second is [Col. 0166C] that same Church passing to the Gentiles; the third is that of the believing Gentiles; the fourth, that of the repentant Jew; the fifth will be that of those afflicted by Antichrist; the sixth, seventh, and eighth will be those enjoying Christ after Antichrist. These are said to be three because they will be gathered from Asia, Africa, and Europe. Since they will praise the Lord together [Note: [Col. 0165] Isa. 52], three psalms of praise are sung under one antiphon and one *Gloria*.

Thus in all these psalms we set forth the shadow of the Law and the truth of grace. The shadow: because after delivering the people from Egypt, the Lord reigned over them, gave the Law, and clothed himself in splendour in the tabernacle. The truth: because after redeeming his people, Christ rose from death, reigned, and put on the splendour of immortality [Note: [Col. 0165] Ps. 92; Rom. 6]. Hence the primitive Church raises praises, [Col. 0166D] saying: “The Lord hath reigned.” This psalm is rightly sung in the praises because it contains Christ’s praises and seven subjects of praise, as is expounded on that psalm itself.

“Make a joyful noise” [Note: [Col. 0165] Ps. 99]: here we show the shadow, because the people of God entered the gates—that is, the promised land—and rejoiced and served the Lord. The truth: because the Gentile people received the faith; all the earth rejoices in Christ, and the Gentiles serve in gladness.

“O God, my God” [Note: [Col. 0165] Ps. 62]: this psalm indicates the shadow of King Solomon and others rejoicing in the Lord. To it, “May God have mercy on us” [Note: [Col. 0165] Ps. 66] is joined without an intervening *Gloria* [Col. 0167A], because the kingdom of Judah and the kingdom of Israel are united in one Law. It also indicates the time of grace, when, persecution having been calmed, the Gentile Church meditates upon the Lord and the mouth of heretics is stopped. For this psalm is sung in the person of the Gentiles, and is therefore entitled, “A psalm of David, when he was in the wilderness of Idumaea.” By Idumaea the Gentiles are understood. “May God have mercy” is joined to it under one *Gloria*, because the Jewish people will be united with it in one faith.

“Bless ye” indicates the time when Nebuchadnezzar put the three boys into the furnace of fire [Note: [Col. 0167] Dan. 3], and that time when Antichrist will roast the three sons of Noah in the furnace of tribulation. Therefore it is sung without *Alleluia* and *Gloria*: without *Alleluia*, because then every praise of the Church will be restrained; or without *Gloria*, because in it we recall the Trinity, saying [Col. 0167B]: “Let us bless the Father and the Son with the Holy Spirit.”

Observe that this hymn has three divisions. In the first, the higher creatures are invited to praise the Creator: namely, those above heaven, those in heaven, and those in the air. In the second, earthly creatures and those moving in the waters are invited. In the third, human beings, spirits, and souls are invited, that with every creature we may bless the Lord; because, just as the three boys escaped Nebuchadnezzar’s furnace of fire, so we have escaped the devil and the fire of hell.

This canticle is well suited to the Lord’s Day and to every festival day, because on the first day the Lord created all things [Note: [Col. 0167] Gen. 1], and afterwards renewed them through his resurrection [Col. 0167C]. Therefore on that day and on the festivals which imitate the Lord’s resurrection this canticle is read, in which God’s creatures are invited to praise the Creator.

Some, however, say that Christ’s passion is brought to our remembrance in this canticle, because Nebuchadnezzar is the devil, the attendants are the Jews, the furnace of fire is the altar of the cross, and the three boys are Christ, in whom are three pure things: divinity, flesh, and soul; or from whom come three sacraments: spirit, blood, and water [Note: [Col. 0167] I John 5].

“Praise the Lord from the heavens” [Note: [Col. 0167] Ps. 148]. It proclaims that time of the shadow when the people returned from Babylon [Note: [Col. 0167] I Esdras 1] and built the Temple, and also that time of grace in which, Antichrist having been killed, the whole Church will praise God. Therefore three psalms are sung under one *Gloria*, because Christians, Gentiles, and Jews; or Noah, Job, and Daniel; or those gathered [Col. 0167D] from the three parts of the world—Asia, Africa, and Europe—will meet in one religion, praise, and kinship; or because in these praises we extol him who is three and one.

The chapter is, according to the foregoing shadow, Ezra’s preaching; the hymn, the people’s rejoicing over their return and the dedication of the Temple. Or the chapter is the angel’s promise when he promised a son to Zacharias [Note: [Col. 0167] Luke 1], and the hymn is rejoicing over Christ’s birth and resurrection. Or the chapter is an exhortation to those of the present time not to fail in battle, and the hymn is the Church’s exultation over victory against Antichrist. Or the chapter is [Col. 0168A] the last trumpet [Note: [Col. 0167] I Cor. 15], and the hymn eternal praise.

By the following verse, namely, “The Lord hath reigned,” it is indicated that after the resurrection authority in heaven and on earth was established for Christ [Note: [Col. 0167] Matt. 28]. By this he reigns in the present Church and will reign in the triumphant Church for ever. The custom of saying a versicle at all the hours arose from the ark: when it was placed in the tabernacle, it was said, “Return, O Lord, unto the multitude of the children of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0167] Num. 10]. Hence we say verses in prayer, that he may return to us and that our minds may return to the Lord; hence it took its name from return.

Here at Nocturns it is said before the reading, to stir the mind to hear the word of the Lord. At [Col. 0168B] the other hours it is said after the reading, so that the Lord’s teaching may not be neglected during the interval between the hours.

Through the canticle *Benedictus* [Note: [Col. 0167] Luke 1], which is sung at the dawning of the day, is signified Christ’s first coming, in which he visited and redeemed his people and enlightened those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death [Note: [Col. 0167] Isa. 9]. Or it signifies the second coming, in which he will illuminate with everlasting brightness the Church which long sat in the darkness of this world, after the psalms, readings, hymn, verse, and antiphon—that is, after good works, teaching, praises, conversion, and devotion of minds—when we shall serve the Lord without fear, in holiness and righteousness all the days of our life.

Meanwhile the altar is censed. The censer is the heart, the fire charity, [Col. 0168C] the incense prayer, which is then directed to the Lord when our heart is kindled with the fire of charity through the word of the Gospel and expanded in faith in the Passion. Hence, while censing, the priest says: “Let my prayer be directed, O Lord, as incense in thy sight” [Note: [Col. 0167] Ps. 140]. The censing fittingly follows the psalms and reading, because one who acts well and teaches others gives forth a good fragrance and offers others an example of good action. The prayer is that final blessing: “Come, ye blessed of my Father” [Note: [Col. 0167] Matt. 25]. “Let us bless the Lord” is the final and ineffable praise. Therefore, words often being laid aside, we rejoice with neumes. Observe that the praises on Sundays, Easter days, and saints’ festivals are the same, because they represent the joys of Christ’s resurrection [Col. 0168D] and of our own; through faith in the resurrection the saints already receive certain joys, which they will obtain more fully in the twofold robe.

## CHAPTER VI. ON PRIME

“The householder went out early in the morning to hire labourers for his vineyard” [Note: [Col. 0167] Matt. 20].

Let us now deal with Prime and the remaining hours, in which we imitate shepherds and labourers; for at these hours also the householder hired labourers for his vineyard. Therefore psalmody takes its name from these hours and not from others, [Col. 0169A] and is celebrated at them.

The priest, therefore, is the shepherd of the sheep; the flock is the people; the pastures are God’s commandments; many beasts are hostile to the flock. For on one side, “the roaring lion goes about seeking whom he may devour” [Note: [Col. 0169] I Pet. 5]; on another, the dragon kills wanderers with poison; on another, the wolf snatches them away; on another, the bear attacks. Therefore the shepherd, who has care for the sheep [Note: [Col. 0169] John 10], says: “O God, make speed to help me” [Note: [Col. 0169] Ps. 69]. Observe that this versicle is said first at all the hours and is taken from the Old Testament. For the ark was daily surrounded by enemies. Thus when Moses raised and carried it, he said: “Arise, O Lord, and let thine enemies be scattered, and let those who hate thee flee before thy face” [Note: [Col. 0169] Num. 10; Ps. 67].

The Church too suffers persecution within and without; therefore we implore divine [Col. 0169B] aid, saying: “O God, make speed to help me.” Likewise at all the hours there is said first: “Glory be to the Father,” that we may glorify the Trinity [Note: [Col. 0169] John 15], without whom we can do nothing [Note: [Col. 0169] Ambrose, on the hymn *Jam lucis*]. Thus the sheep invoke and glorify the supreme Shepherd, and subsequently in the hymn implore him to guard them in their daytime actions from harmful things.

Five psalms follow, so that they may divinely fortify the labourers’ five senses during the day. Or there are three, contained under three *Glorias*, because the Trinity is glorified in our works. Saying, “O God, in thy name” [Note: [Col. 0169] Ps. 53], they set out on their journey; and because “strangers have risen up” [Note: [Col. 0169] ibid.], they ask him by his power to scatter their enemies and deliver the sheep from every tribulation, just as David was delivered from the Ziphites [Note: [Col. 0169] I Sam. 23]. For David sang this psalm when the Ziphites wished to hand him over [Col. 0169C] to Saul. “Ziphites” means “flourishing ones”; these are the limbs of the devil, who seduce us by prosperity. Therefore, since the devil lays many snares for us, we sing this psalm at earliest dawn in order to avoid his cunning.

In “Blessed are the undefiled” [Note: [Col. 0169] Ps. 118], and the following octonaries, pastures are set before the sheep: the Law of the Lord, commandments, ordinances, and testimonies. This psalm treats of morals, because one whom God has freed from bonds and prison ought to stand before God with good conduct and all devotion.

On Sundays, however, and especially from Septuagesima until Easter, we say nine psalms, so that with the nine orders of angels we may praise the Trinity in the joy of the resurrection. [Col. 0169D] In the first five, “O God, my God” [Note: [Col. 0169] Ps. 21] and what follows, Christ’s Passion is sung, because through the merit of his fivefold Passion Christ came to the glory of the resurrection; and we too should hope for this if we wish to imitate him [Note: [Col. 0169] Heb. 2; Rom. 6]. The following four indicate that in the four parts of the world we ought to praise God through the teaching of the four Gospels.

In “Save me, O God, by thy name” [Note: [Col. 0169] Ps. 53], we ask for the removal of error. In “Give thanks unto the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0169] Ps. 117], we are exhorted to confession of praise. In “Blessed” [Note: [Col. 0169] Ps. 118], to the practice of praise. In “Reward” [Note: [Col. 0169] ibid.], to [Col. 0170A] meditation on the commandments. But because faith is the foundation of the commandments and “the victory that overcomes the world” [Note: [Col. 0169] I John 5], because all else is fruitless without faith [Note: [Col. 0169] Heb. 11], because a labourer without faith cultivates the vineyard in vain, and a shepherd without faith guards the sheepfold in vain, there follows the Creed of faith, namely, *Quicunque vult* [“Whoever wishes”], which Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, published at the request of the Emperor Theodosius, to eradicate the growing unbelief of heretics and spread the Catholic faith. The Church ordained that it should be sung at Prime every day, because then the people most fully gather at church; or because faith is the beginning of salvation. Some nevertheless omit it on days on which they sing at Mass, “I believe in one God.”

[Col. 0170B] But this is rather a matter of fastidiousness and sloth than of reason, because in *Quicunque vult* the people are taught the faith by their shepherds, while in “I believe in one God” each person, as one taught, professes his own faith. Athanasius, moreover, in this Creed describes the two principal parts of faith: concerning the Trinity and the incarnation of the Word. But he begins with the free choice of man, saying: “Whoever wishes to be saved.” For no one believes unless willing; although a person can do other things unwillingly, he cannot believe unless willing. “Before all things it is necessary that he hold the Catholic faith.” For this is the foundation of all good things. This—

> Prime seeks the field beneath the doubtful lot of battle,

—but because the name “faith” could cause confusion, he specifies it by saying “Catholic,” which is called Catholic or universal both on account of the universal precepts of the rules, as Boethius says, by which the authority of the Christian religion is understood, and because its worship has spread almost through all the regions of the world. For *catholicon* in Greek is called *universale* in Latin, “universal.” Not every faith, indeed, makes one a Christian. Taken generally, faith is the apprehension of the truth of any thing with the mind’s assent. Of apprehensions, one is of invisible things and another of visible things. Again, of apprehensions of invisible things, one is of things perceived by reason, another of things above reason, such as that God is three [Col. 0170D] and one, incarnate, born of a Virgin, suffered, and the like.

The first two have no merit, because they derive their beginning from human reason; for a faith to which human reason supplies proof has no merit. Only the third makes one a Christian: “which, unless each person keeps it”—by himself, as an adult and one possessing discernment; or through another, as one not capable of knowledge—“whole,” without the contagion of heretical depravity, “and inviolate,” without violation by schismatics, “without doubt he shall perish eternally.” For “without faith it is impossible to please God” [Note: [Col. 0169] ibid.]; and where the cause is absent, the effect is absent also. Faith is the cause of human salvation [Note: [Col. 0171] Eph. 2]; therefore, where it fails, salvation cannot be.

“But the Catholic faith is this: that we worship one God in Trinity and Trinity in Unity, neither confounding the persons nor dividing the substance.” Let us treat first of unity, and afterwards of the distinction of persons.

There are several kinds of unity. One is integral, which consists of parts, as a body does. Another is formal, deriving its origin from form, as an idol. Another is of nature, as you and I are one. Another is of will, as “that they may be one with us” [Note: [Col. 0171] John 17]. Another is principal, or singular, or solitary, or simple. It is principal because it is first; singular or solitary because it is alone. For nothing is found which is both several and singularly one [Col. 0171B] except in the Trinity. It is simple because it receives neither a folding of parts nor a folding of properties.

And to show that this unity is to be understood according to simplicity, he adds: “Such as the Father is, such is the Son, and such is the Holy Spirit”; that is, whatever is predicated substantially of the Father is likewise said of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. He then supplies examples from six names: uncreated, immeasurable, eternal, almighty, God, and Lord. These are said of each person and of all, not in the plural but in the singular and collectively; for example: “The Father uncreated, the Son uncreated, and the Holy Spirit uncreated; and yet not three uncreated, but one uncreated”; and similarly concerning the rest.

[Col. 0171C] Observe that some of these things are said negatively and some affirmatively of God: “uncreated,” namely, not created; “immeasurable,” that is, without measure; “eternal,” without beginning and end. He is called “almighty,” not because he can do whatever he wishes to do, but because he can do whatever he wishes to be done. Or “almighty” means principally mighty. For there are three powers: the first, God; the second, an angel; the third, a human being. Or he is almighty by causation, that is, the one from whom all power comes, just as he is called every good thing by causation. God is the Creator’s proper name and pertains to the worship of divinity; it is derived from the Greek *Theos*.

Observe that it is sometimes used personally, as in “God begot God,” that is, the Father begot the Son, and both are God. “Lord,” as Augustine says, is not a matter of nature but of power; but here it is according as it is said from lordship, because “Lord is his name” [Note: [Col. 0171] Ps. 67]. Yet according as it is said from ruling, it indicates a relation: “For as Christian truth compels us to confess each person severally to be God and Lord, so Catholic religion forbids us to call them three gods or lords.” It is as though he said that these essential names are said of all, not plurally but singularly and collectively.

Observe what Christian truth is. To make this clearer, consider philosophical truth. Philosophical truth is the nature or knowledge of a thing; for [Col. 0172A] humanity is the truth of a human being, according to which someone is a true human being. But Christian truth understands God as great without quantity, good without quality, everlasting without time, wholly everywhere without place, present without position, and making mutable things without mutability.

Likewise philosophical truth holds that, if the Father is great and the Son is great, the Father and Son are great. But Christian truth calls the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit not three great beings, but each one great and the three one great being. This is one of the universal rules from which, as we said according to Boethius, the Catholic faith takes its name.

Concerning the distinction of persons, Athanasius says: “The person of the Father is one, the person of the Son another, and the person of the Holy Spirit another.” Grammatically, “person” means everything spoken about in discourse; poetically, it means a mask, as in “the inventor of an honourable character”; and it means condition or fortune, as in: “God does not accept the person of a man” [Note: [Col. 0171] Gal. 2], that is, he does not regard the condition or fortune of the person. According to Boethius, a person is an individual substance of a rational nature.

In theology, therefore, to be a person is to be distinct through a relative property. For personal properties, such as fatherhood, sonship, and procession, are relations: fatherhood is the Father’s relation to the Son, sonship the Son’s relation to the Father, and procession the Spirit’s relation to both. Thus to be Father, to be Son, and to be Holy Spirit is not to be something, but to be in relation to something. Hence Augustine: When the Father [Col. 0172C] is Father, he is not that by which he is—that is, he is not the divine substance itself by the relation by which he is Father. Fatherhood is in the Father, and it itself is the Father; and so with the others. Hence, in the persons there is property, and in the essence unity.

“The Father is made by none, neither created nor begotten.” When it is said “by none,” authority is shown. The difference between “made” and “created” is the same as that between making and creating: to make is to produce something from pre-existing matter; to create is from nothing.

Observe that God’s operation is fourfold: one is eternal, three are temporal. The eternal operation is that by which he begot the Son before all ages; according to this operation he is called Father or begetter. The first temporal operation is that by which he created from nothing *hyle*, or chaos—that is, the confused matter of the elements—according to [Col. 0172D] which operation he is called Creator. The second temporal operation is that by which he distinguished that matter through the works of the six days [Note: [Col. 0171] Gen. 1], according to which he is called founder or maker. The third temporal operation is that by which he continues created species through succession, according to which he is called sower and author.

“The Son is of the Father alone, not made nor created, but begotten. The Holy Spirit is of the Father and the Son, not made nor created nor begotten, but proceeding.” Human speech is insufficient to assign the difference between the Son’s generation and the Holy Spirit’s procession, except that the Son proceeds from the Father in such a manner as to be Son; the Spirit, however, does not so proceed that he can be called Son. Therefore there is one Father, not [Col. 0173A] three fathers; one Son, not three sons; one Holy Spirit, not three holy spirits.

Observe that when “one God” is said, a multitude of gods is excluded; when “three persons” is said, singularity is excluded. Hence Augustine: He who said that God is three persons did not intend diversity, but did not intend singularity. “In this Trinity nothing is before or after, nothing greater or less,” in power. Authority, however, is ascribed to the Father, who proceeds from none. “But all three persons are coeternal with each other”; therefore none is earlier in time; “and coequal”; therefore none is lesser. Here Arius is indicated, who taught that the Son is less than the Father. Thus in every respect, as has already been said, unity in Trinity and Trinity in unity are to be worshipped. “Therefore he who wishes to be saved must thus think concerning the Trinity” [Col. 0173B]: behold the sum and conclusion of what precedes. We worship unity in Trinity, and conversely, when we say, believe, and adore that three are one, and conversely.

“But it is necessary for eternal salvation that he also faithfully believe the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Here the incarnation of the Word is treated. For just as faith in divinity is required for salvation, so also is faith in humanity, because no one could be saved without faith in the Mediator [Note: [Col. 0173] Acts 4].

There were three laws: the law of nature, the law of the letter, and the law of grace. The law of nature consists in reason and will; in both, humanity was weak, because reason was dim-sighted in contemplating the good and will failed in desiring the good. The law of the letter gave counsel but [Col. 0173C] not help; it warned the affection but did not move it; it did not take sins away, but increased them by forbidding them. For:

> We always strive toward what is forbidden, and desire what is denied.  
> [Note: [Col. 0173] Ovid, *Amores* III.4.17.]

And the Apostle: “The law entered in, and the offence abounded” [Note: [Col. 0173] Rom. 5]. Therefore the law of grace was necessary, which brings those two laws to effect. For without the eye-salve of grace, the eye is bleary [Note: [Col. 0173] Rev. 3], both that of nature and that of the letter. Therefore Wisdom spat upon the ground and anointed the eyes of the man blind from birth [Note: [Col. 0173] John 9].

This is Christ, who, as the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0173] I Cor. 1], is for us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption: wisdom, by giving us reason; righteousness, by delivering us from the enemy’s hand; sanctification, by forgiving sins; redemption, by [Col. 0173D] suffering for us. This is God’s power and God’s wisdom, which built itself a dwelling in the womb and came forth from the virginal womb, and raised seven pillars [Note: [Col. 0173] Prov. 9]: namely, wisdom concerning invisible things, understanding of visible things, knowledge of moral things, piety in showing mercy, counsel in helping, fortitude in delivering, and fear of the Lord in loving chastely. For Christ’s soul was fully adorned with these virtues from the very hour of creation and incarnation, so that it could make progress in nothing.

What is meant by “he advanced in wisdom and age” [Note: [Col. 0173] Luke 2] must be understood by us. Jesus and Christ are two names, not of the same kind: for Jesus is the name [Col. 0174A] of the person, as Peter is; but Christ is the name of a sacrament, as priest and prophet are. These names were customarily written not in letters but by abbreviations, so that the character of the writing might suggest the character of the nature: just as the divine nature is incomprehensible, so the name applied to signify it is written in abbreviated letters. The natures of created things are sometimes comprehended, and therefore their names are fully written out in letters. Or [this is so] because we are not able to unfasten the strap of that person’s sandal [Note: [Col. 0173] John 1]. “God is from the substance of the Father,” that is, from the Father’s substance—namely, from the Father as substance—so that generation is referred to the person, not to the essence, which neither begets nor is begotten. “Begotten before the ages”: this is said improperly, for “before” properly [Col. 0174B] signifies time; but time did not exist before the world, and began to exist with the world. Hence it is thus defined: time is the motion and duration of mutable things. Therefore, if anyone asks whether God existed before the world, the question is faulty: for the Creator does not precede the creature by a quantity of time, which “before” signifies, but by simplicity of nature. “Man is born from the substance of his mother in the world”: the preposition *ex* (“from”) is understood substantially, materially, potentially, and partially: substantially, as in “begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages”; materially, as in “born from the substance of his mother in the world”; potentially, as in “conceived from the Holy Spirit”; partially, as in “subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh” [Col. 0174C]; and similarly the preposition *de* (“from”), as in “from the Father,” “from the mother,” and “from the Holy Spirit.”

“Perfect God, perfect man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh; equal to the Father according to divinity, less than the Father according to humanity. Although he is God and man, he is nevertheless not two, but one Christ; one, however, not by conversion of divinity into flesh, but by the assumption of humanity into God.” Observe that there are two ways of joining things: by apposition and by composition—something grammarians also teach concerning prepositions. They say that a preposition is joined by apposition when, in that apposition, it passes into no compound with anything; but it is joined by composition when some compound is formed from it and the word to which it is attached. For example, in both respects: [Col. 0174D] “The fool said in his heart” [Note: [Col. 0173] Psalm 52].

It is similar among the natures of things. Things are joined by apposition when nothing is composed from them of which the things joined are predicated; for example, Abraham was added to his fathers, whence a company results, of which the things added are not predicated. But things are joined by composition in two ways: by mixture and without mixture. They are joined by mixture when one is converted into, or rather mingled with, another, as wine and water; for whichever of these becomes predominant mingles the other with itself. They are joined without mixture when something is so composed from different substances [Col. 0175A] that the properties and natures of the components are predicated of the composite, as a human being consists of spirit and body, and one rightly says that a human being is alive because of the soul and white because of the body. One likewise says that a human being is rational because of the soul and corporeal because of the body. This union of divinity with humanity, some say, occurs by composition without mixture, because Christ is God and man, where there is neither mixture nor conversion. Hence it is rightly said: not by conversion of divinity into flesh, but by assumption of humanity into God. Conversion changes a substance; assumption exalts it.

[According to others, the account of the Incarnation must be taken not according to composition but according to habitus, or condition. Hence when it is said, [Col. 0175B] “God is man,” “God was made man,” “God began to be man,” a condition is predicated; for he was made humanized (*humanatus*), and assumed man, or rather those things which belong to man. Hence, as for the words that follow, “One altogether, not by confusion of substance, but in unity of person,” they say that the preposition *in* does not indicate composition, but the simplicity of the person: for just as he was simple before, so also afterward. Human nature was not assumed as part of the being of that person, nor was it one person with the Word; rather, it is in unity of person—that is, it did not increase the number or magnitude of the person. Some omit *in*, saying: “But unity of person.” Others say that this person, Christ, consists of God and man, namely soul and flesh, and thus of three substances, yet not as though of [Col. 0175C] parts. Hence, when it is said, “God is man,” nature—namely humanity—is predicated.]

“For as the rational soul and flesh are one man, so God and man are one Christ.” [It seems one ought to have said: “A rational soul and flesh are one man.” For just as the singularity of the thing posited requires the singularity of the verb, as Sicard writes, so the plurality of the things posited requires the plurality of the verb, as in “Peter and Paul had gone up to the Temple.” The singular number, therefore, is put for the plural.]

See that this likeness does not correspond to the thing demonstrated in a complete comparison. For flesh and soul are constitutive parts of a human being, and the destruction of one of them entails the destruction of the whole; [Col. 0175D] but this is not so in Christ, God and man. For God existed before God was man, and therefore the assumed man is not a constitutive part of the person. Thus, just as soul and flesh are not several human beings, so God and man are not several Christs. “Who suffered for our salvation”: hence, “like a bird he was led to slaughter” [Note: [Col. 0175] Isaiah 53]. He is the high priest at whose death, under the ancient Law, captives were set free and returned to their inheritances [Note: [Col. 0175] Numbers 35]. For Christ’s death removed God’s sword from before Paradise [Note: [Col. 0175] Genesis 3]. He is the serpent; those who look upon him are freed from the bites of serpents [Note: [Col. 0175] Numbers 21; John 3]. “He descended into hell,” [Col. 0176A] according to: “I was counted among those descending into the pit” [Note: [Col. 0175] Psalm 87].—“On the third day he rose from the dead.” Hence Hosea: “After two days he will revive us, and on the third day he will raise us up” [Note: [Col. 0175] Hosea 6].—“He ascended into heaven” [Note: [Col. 0175] Psalm 67; Ephesians 4], according to: “Christ ascending on high.” There are three heavens: the aerial, where the bird flies; the ethereal, where the stars shine; and the empyrean, where angels praise God. “He sits at the right hand of God the Father Almighty.” Hence the Father says to the Son: “Sit at my right hand” [Note: [Col. 0175] Psalm 109]. By the name “right hand” is signified not a location or the spatial delimitation of divinity, but the blessedness of human happiness. In that empyrean heaven, in that blessedness, the assumed man has been placed above every angelic dignity. “From there he will come to judge the living and the dead; at whose coming all human beings must rise with their bodies [Col. 0176B] and render an account of their own deeds.” This rendering of account will not occur through the expression of words, but by the testimony of conscience: when our deeds, good and evil, are recalled to memory, it will be clear to each person whether he is worthy of love or hatred [Note: [Col. 0175] Ecclesiastes 9], life or punishment.

“And those who have done good will go into eternal life.” Whoever is there will at last possess complete perfection in body and soul. There are seven things in which complete perfection consists. Three belong to the soul: knowledge, justice, and joy. For, as philosophers say, three powers naturally belong to the human mind: reason, the concupiscible faculty, and the irascible faculty; and each of these, in this state of misery, has two things associated with it, namely a habit and a privation. Thus around reason [Col. 0176C] are knowledge and ignorance; around the concupiscible faculty, justice and injustice; around the irascible faculty, joy and sadness. But in the state of glory our rational faculty will be filled with knowledge, the concupiscible with justice, and the irascible with joy. The soul will therefore possess perfect knowledge, justice, and joy, because every virtue will be there without impediment or opposition.

Four things belong to the body: immortality, impassibility, agility, and beauty. As the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0175] I Corinthians 15], the body will be spiritual, not by losing the truth of its bodily substance, but by not needing food, as a spirit does not. It will therefore be immortal, because it will die no more, nor will death any longer have dominion over it [Note: [Col. 0175] Romans 6]. It will be impassible, because it will thereafter be troubled by no suffering. [Col. 0176D] Let us explain more deeply, saying that in the state of creation humanity had the ability to sin and the ability not to sin; the ability to suffer or die, and the ability not to suffer and not to die. In the state of corruption, it has the ability to sin, the inability not to sin; the ability to suffer and die, and the inability not to suffer and not to die. Understand “the inability not to sin” thus: inability to be without sin, namely without the cause of sin; by “cause” we mean concupiscence; or inability to remain long without sin. In the state of glorification it will have the ability not to sin, the ability not to suffer, and not to die; and the inability to suffer and the inability to die. Therefore the body will be immortal and [Col. 0177A] impassible. It will also be agile, because it will accompany the swiftness of thought in all things. It will also be most beautiful, because it will shine like the sun in the kingdom of the Father [Note: [Col. 0177] Matthew 13]. Thus the human being will put off, in both parts, a double garment of shame [Note: [Col. 0177] Psalm 108], and will put on the robe of twofold glorification.

“But those who [do] evil [go] into eternal fire.” The wretched are tormented in hell by nine kinds of punishments because by their deeds they do not deserve to be associated with the nine orders of angels. The first is unquenchable fire: even if the whole sea flowed into it, it would not be extinguished. Of this it is said here: “Those who have done evil will go into eternal fire.” The second is intolerably cold water, in which even if a fiery mountain were cast, it would be wholly turned to ice. Of these two it is said: “They shall pass from snowy waters to excessive heat” [Note: [Col. 0177] Job 24]. The third is the immortal worm, of which it is said: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” [Note: [Col. 0177] Isaiah 66]. The fourth is outer darkness, of which the Gospel says: “They are cast into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” [Note: [Col. 0177] Matthew 25]. The fifth is a putrid and unceasing stench, of which John says: “The devil was cast into the lake of sulphur” [Note: [Col. 0177] Revelation 20]. The sixth is the shame of sinners, because all the hidden things of darkness will be revealed to everyone [Note: [Col. 0177] I Corinthians 4]. Hence John says: “The books were opened” [Note: [Col. 0177] Daniel 7; Revelation 20]. The seventh is the dreadful sight of demons; hence Job: “dreadful things shall come upon him” [Note: [Col. 0177] Job 20].
