The eighth is a diversity of scourges corresponding to the diversity of crimes. Hence John says: “It was judged [Col. 0177C] of each according to their works” [Note: [Col. 0177] Revelation 20]. The ninth is the miserable cry of those weeping and wailing, because all tribes of the earth shall mourn over themselves [Note: [Col. 0177] Matthew 24; Revelation 11]. For it is fitting that one who here burned with the fire of concupiscence should there burn lamentably; that one who was stiffened by the cold of malice should there gnash; that one consumed by envy should be gnawed by the worm of conscience; that one who hates light should not rejoice in light; that one who rotted in the stench of lust should smell stench; that one who despised uncovering sins should uncover them; that one who refused to see God should see demons; that one who presented his members to serve iniquity should receive, member by member, retribution for iniquity [Note: [Col. 0177] Romans 6]; and that one who refused to rejoice with those rejoicing should weep with those weeping [Note: [Col. 0177] Romans 12].

“This is the catholic faith, which unless each person believes faithfully and firmly, he cannot be saved.” Faith is called [Col. 0177D] the virtue by which one believes, and this is proper usage. Faith is also called the effect or act of faith, namely belief itself, and this is improper usage. It is also called the thing believed, and this likewise is improper usage. Of the first kind there are three virtues: faith, hope, and charity. Of the second: “Your faith has saved you” [Note: [Col. 0177] Luke 7, 8], that is, the act; for it is not the virtue but the act that is reckoned as merit. Of the third: “This is the catholic faith.” In the chapter, the shepherd consoles the sheep [Note: [Col. 0177] John 10], and the master of the household the workers [Note: [Col. 0177] Matthew 20], lest they fail in heat and labor, as though saying: Act manfully in the Lord’s name, [Col. 0178A] because “everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” [Note: [Col. 0177] Romans 10]. Therefore they gladly give thanks and, with Peter, confess and invoke Christ, Son of the living God, saying: “Christ, Son of the living God, have mercy on us” [Note: [Col. 0177] Matthew 16]. Some, however, do not say the chapter reading or the responsory, because by the former they understand the shepherd’s work, who ought first to work himself, so that in the other Hours he may be able to exhort others to work.

Therefore, after the psalms they immediately say: “Arise, O Christ, help us” [Note: [Col. 0177] Psalm 43], turning toward the east. It is for this reason called a verse (*versus*), and its sense is: “Arise,” that is, make us arise, just as the saying of Moses, whose place he holds, was understood: “Return, O Lord, to the multitude of the children of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0177] Numbers 10], that is, make us return. The prayers that follow, namely *Kyrie eleison*—“Lord, have mercy”—[Col. 0178B] are said for three reasons: to cut off superfluous thoughts; to obtain mercy for the wandering sheep and the weary workers; and to seek help against temptations, so that in the Lord’s Prayer we may invoke the Father more confidently. But *Kyrie eleison* is said three times, *Christe eleison*—“Christ, have mercy”—three times, and then *Kyrie eleison* three times again, or once each in the individual [invocations], on account of the three states of divinity. He speaks of three states because of us, not because of God, “with whom there is no change or shadow of variation” [Note: [Col. 0177] James 1]. The first was before the Nativity, in which he was worshiped as three and one, and called Lord, because “Lord is his name” [Note: [Col. 0177] Psalm 67]. The second was in humanity. Therefore Christ is invoked, who, though he is “the way, the truth, and the life” [Note: [Col. 0177] John 14], is nevertheless one person; and again, is one in such a way that he is not separated [Col. 0178C] from the substance of the Trinity. The third is in glorification, where he is more clearly known and worshiped as three and one, and is called Lord.

The Lord’s Prayer is said privately, because in it we speak to God, who searches not only words but also reins and hearts [Note: [Col. 0177] Psalm 7]. Or it is done so that we may take it up with greater diligence. In it we ask seven things: that we may be freed from seven vices, enriched with seven gifts, and attain the proclamations of the seven beatitudes. But the conclusion is spoken aloud, so that all may affirm it. Through the two following verses, “My soul shall live” and “I have gone astray like a sheep that is lost” [Note: [Col. 0177] Psalm 118], it is clear that the subject is wandering sheep—that is, penitents—whom the shepherd leads to the fold [Note: [Col. 0177] John 10]. But because faith is the way for one returning, and [Col. 0178D] is like a traveler’s shield against the enemy’s snares [Note: [Col. 0177] Ephesians 6], the Apostles’ Creed follows, namely, “I believe in God the Father”; with God’s favor, we shall set out its exposition in the treatise on the Scrutinies. Confession is joined to it because, after confession, venial sins are forgiven—sins without which the present life is not lived by sheep and workers. Prayers for the worker himself who speaks, for shepherds, for kings, for the people, for the living and the dead; “Have mercy on me, O God” [Note: [Col. 0177] Psalm 50], for penitents; and the prayer for those standing by [Col. 0179A] are multiplied, because by such fruits dust is shaken from the workers’ feet, sheep are freed from pestilential pastures, and penitents are reconciled to the Lord. For the same reason, the seven penitential psalms and the litanies are sung in Lent.

But observe that the priest, who first prayed prostrate and now rises and standing prays to the supreme Master of the Household, signifies Christ, who first lived on earth [Note: [Col. 0179] Baruch 3], prayed for sinners [Note: [Col. 0179] Isaiah 53], and afterward, rising [Note: [Col. 0179] Matthew 28] and ascending into heaven, intercedes for us [Note: [Col. 0179] Romans 8], which pertains to our salvation. Therefore the greeting precedes and follows. For when the Lord rose, he greeted the disciples, saying, “Peace to you” [Note: [Col. 0179] Luke 24]; and after his intercession he will greet [them], because he will grant eternal salvation. “Let us bless [Col. 0179B] the Lord” signifies the blessing with which Christ blessed the disciples after the Resurrection [Note: [Col. 0179] ibid.]; hence they themselves gave thanks. Or it is the final praise which will be in glory, with thanksgiving.

Finally, because shepherds are accustomed to drive their flocks to other pastures and to mix salt with the fodder so that it may taste better, so the prelate leads the brethren into the chapter house. There, by the fodder of salt, the examples of the saints are set before them in the Martyrology; and by the verse, “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” [Note: [Col. 0179] Psalm 115], they are invited to patience and prayer. In “Holy Mary,” etc., the assistance of the saints is sought. Then, because varying adversaries arise in different places, the shepherd asks divine help three times against the snares of the devil, [Col. 0179C] the flesh, and the world, when he says, “O God, make haste to help me” [Note: [Col. 0179] Psalm 69]. Then all together pray and ask mercy, saying, *Kyrie eleison*, “Lord, have mercy,” and “Deliver us from evil”; saying “Our Father,” and [asking] love of good works, saying: “Look, O Lord, upon your servants for good” [Note: [Col. 0179] Psalm 89]. Thereupon the shepherd, as more solicitous both for himself and the sheep, asks that they be directed, sanctified, and kept in the law of the Lord, saying: “Direct and sanctify, rule and govern.” Finally, those especially who live in monasteries are refreshed by the fodder of reading and preaching, being occupied at every hour in God’s service and always eager to be satisfied by the food of Scripture. To deal with the office and order belongs to the following [section]; to provide pastures and sayings for the sheep follows thereafter. By “Our help is in the name of the Lord” and “Bless [us],” [Col. 0179D] the sheep are dismissed to the pastures and the workers to hasten to cultivate the vineyard [Note: [Col. 0179] Matthew 20], so that at the evening of the world they may be able to receive the denarius of recompense.

## CHAPTER VII. ON TERCE, SEXT, AND NONE

Daniel bent his knees and prayed three times a day, as is read in his book [Note: [Col. 0179] Daniel 6]; by these three times, according to Jerome, Terce, Sext, and None are understood. After Daniel, Ezra four times a day confessed to the Lord with the people [Note: [Col. 0179] II Esdras 9]: that is, according to Bede, at the first, third, [Col. 0180A] sixth, and ninth hours. At Sext also, in the time of grace, when Peter wished to eat, he went up to the upper room to pray [Note: [Col. 0179] Acts 10]; and at None Peter and John were going to the Temple [Note: [Col. 0179] Acts 3]. Therefore Terce, Sext, and None are adorned with a solemn office by the authority of the ancients.

Accordingly, at the beginning of these three Hours, as usual, we implore divine help, which must be done in every good work. Then the Trinity is glorified and God is praised in a hymn; afterwards three psalms are sung, because the Trinity is venerated in our works. Again, at Prime, Terce, Sext, and None we sing by octonaries, because we feed the flock and cultivate the vineyard well when we attend to the eight beatitudes, which we combine if we keep the two commandments of charity. Observe that we make eleven [Col. 0180B] combinations, in order to correct the number eleven of our transgression; or so that for whatever hour of the day in which we have sinned, we may offer the Lord a pair, of the Law and charity: for the first [hour], “Blessed”; for the second, “Reward”; for the third, “Set the Law”; for the fourth, “Remember”; for the fifth, “You have done goodness”; for the sixth, “It has failed”; for the seventh, “How I have loved”; for the eighth, “I have hated the wicked”; for the ninth, “Wonders”;” for the tenth, “I cried”; for the eleventh, “Princes” [Note: [Col. 0179] Psalm 118]. It is noteworthy that in every octonary something concerning the law of the Lord is mentioned, because by it the vineyard is cultivated and the denarius of eternity acquired [Note: [Col. 0179] Matthew 20].

Again, at the psalms in the four Hours, the *Gloria* is sung twelve times, so that for every hour in which we have sinned we may render glory to God [Col. 0180C] for the remission of sins. Yet in the three Hours—Terce, Sext, and None—a threefold state is indicated: those fighting, those advancing, and those becoming weary. At Terce, those fighting say: “I shall answer a word to those reproaching me” [Note: [Col. 0179] Psalm 118]. At Sext, those advancing add: “All day long it is my meditation” [Note: [Col. 0179] ibid.]. At None, those becoming weary say: “Tribulations and distresses have found me” [Note: [Col. 0179] ibid.]. By the antiphons we express charity, under which we conclude the psalms, if through it we commend our works to the Lord, according to: “Let all your works be done in charity” [Note: [Col. 0179] I Corinthians 16]. The chapter reading is the good shepherd’s exhortation to work. The response is the cheerful reply of the workers. The verse, which shows that we turn our minds toward the Lord, is the fruit of good work. [Col. 0180D] The prayer is the shepherd’s commendation of the workers. “Let us bless the Lord” and “Thanks be to God” are the workers’ thanksgiving to the shepherd.

This order is taken from those who, according to Ezra [Note: [Col. 0179] II Esdras 4], performed the work on the walls while others defended the workers with arms. So also at these Hours we now sing psalms: the psalm signifies the work of those whom the leader instructs by reading and fortifies by prayer. Or it is taken from the threefold kind of musicians. For music is made either by the striking of fingers, as on the psaltery and similar instruments; or by singing, as in the voice; or by blowing, as in the sound of a trumpet. Of the first it is said: “Praise him on [Col. 0181A] psaltery and harp” [Note: [Col. 0181] Psalm 150]; of the second: “Sing psalms with a shout” [Note: [Col. 0181] Psalm 32]; of the third: “Praise him with the sound of a trumpet” [Note: [Col. 0181] Psalm 150]. When we say psalms, we fulfill the first kind of music; when we read, we practice the second; when we sing, we delight in the third kind, stretching ourselves so far toward higher things that in the responsory we come to the glory of the Trinity.

Or rather, it is taken from the Apostle, who says: “Be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms, hymns, and songs” [Note: [Col. 0181] Ephesians 5]. Psalms pertain to work, hymns to praise, and songs to evangelical exultation; hence glory is joined to them, because nowhere is so great glory given to God as in the assembly of saints and angels. At these Hours prayers are also inserted on weekdays, which [Col. 0181B] are reasonably omitted on feasts. For on weekdays we mourn our pilgrimage; therefore we employ entreaties, prayers, and petitions, for ourselves and for all in common: “I said, O Lord, have mercy on me” [Note: [Col. 0181] Psalm 40], etc. But on feasts we recall both our resurrection and the Lord’s. And since we have no enduring city here [Note: [Col. 0181] Hebrews 13], we seek the heavenly Jerusalem that is to come; there misery will have no place, and therefore mercy will not be implored for the miserable.

## CHAPTER VIII. ON THE EVENING SYNAXIS

“Let evening prayer rise to you, O Lord!” Here too, as we said concerning the other Hours, we implore divine help [Col. 0181C] and ascribe glory to the Trinity. Afterwards we sing psalms five times, on account of the five wounds of Christ, who offered himself for us as a sacrifice at the evening of the world; this the patriarchs before the Law and the prophets under the Law prefigured, when they offered sacrifices to the Lord at evening [Note: [Col. 0181] Ephesians 5; Hebrews 9]. Or we sing psalms five times so that the sins of the five senses may be forgiven us; for the same reason we strike our breast with five fingers [Note: [Col. 0181] Exodus 29; Numbers 28]. For this signifies the weeping of those upon whom the sun of justice has set [Note: [Col. 0181] Jeremiah 15; Amos 8]. Or we sing psalms five times because we await a reward for the labor of the five senses: for at this Hour the day is closed, the end of works comes, and the beginning of rewards follows.

The psalms are sung according to the subject of the day. Thus, on Sunday night, when by his resurrection [Col. 0181D] Christ conquered the lion, “Blessed be the Lord my God” is sung [Note: [Col. 0181] Psalm 143], which contains David’s victory over Goliath [Note: [Col. 0181] I Kings 17]. The others sound forth praises. Observe that the evening and morning offices excel the other Hours in the number of psalm-singing forms, because in the sixfold distinction of works only evening and morning are mentioned [Note: [Col. 0181] Genesis 1]. The antiquity of the morning and evening office is also commended in the Old Law [Note: [Col. 0181] Exodus 29; Numbers 28; IV Kings 16]. The antiphon is the song of the soul, the virtue of love, sung between the psalms so that the works [Col. 0182A] of the body may be done in charity.

The chapter reading of the master of the household follows, by which he rouses the workers to rise for the Lord who is coming. “Thanks be to God” is the voice of the laborers’ joyful gratitude. In the chapter reading that follows the psalms, the character of the coming day is indicated; for the exposition of punishments or the manifestation of rewards accompanies works. Thus, when dividing the offices in the chapter reading, by what precedes we signify labor and by what follows reward. Therefore what precedes consists in psalms, and what follows in hymns and songs. Or, by what precedes we understand the present night, in which we labor greatly; by what follows, the day of future exaltation, because night precedes and day will draw near [Note: [Col. 0181] Romans 13]. Before the glorious night, from the beginning of the world day preceded night [Note: [Col. 0181] Genesis 1], [Col. 0182B] signifying that from the day of Paradise humanity had descended to the night of hell. But on the night of the Resurrection, which was common to both days, a reversal occurred, so that night should precede day, signifying that through Christ’s Resurrection, after the death of the flesh, we shall pass from the depths of dark night to the brightness of everlasting light.

This is why at Vespers we begin the office of the following day: because the evening synaxis is the first office, according to Ezra’s custom, in the fourfold night division. Hence the evening office is named after the evening star, which rises at the beginning of night. Therefore at that time they ought to celebrate this office according to Ezra’s custom. After the chapter reading, some add [Col. 0182C] a responsory, so that the cheerfulness of the workers may answer the master of the household’s summons; and they say that this should be done at all the Hours except Morning Lauds, where it would seem superfluous to delight in responsories, since they are joined to the night watches. Others append a verse joined to the chapter reading, because, just as a responsory excludes the Canticle of Zachariah, so it also excludes the Canticle of the Blessed Mary. The hymn that follows is the workers’ exultation in their progress. The verse is the mutual stirring or exhortation of those same workers. Or the hymn is a song of victory; the verse, a knocking at the door of glory.

Observe that a verse ought to indicate either the state of the time or the state of the office. The verse of Prime indicates the state of the time, namely: “Arise, O Christ, help us” [Note: [Col. 0181] Psalm 43]; [Col. 0182D] when it says “arise,” the beginning of work is indicated. Similarly, in the verse of Terce, “Be my helper; do not forsake me” [Note: [Col. 0181] Psalm 26], the words “do not forsake me” mark the state of battle. Likewise, in the verse of Sext, “The Lord rules me and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture he has set me” [Note: [Col. 0181] Psalm 22], the state of advancement and perfection is signified. In the verse of None, “Cleanse me, O Lord, from my hidden sins, and spare your servant from those of others” [Note: [Col. 0181] Psalm 18], the state of love growing cold is demonstrated. The verses [Col. 0183A] sung in the Passion and Resurrection likewise indicate the state of the time; but the evening verses indicate the state of the office, as: “Let evening prayer,” etc. From these words it is inferred that evening prayer is performed.

We customarily use the Canticle of the Blessed Mary, namely the *Magnificat*, at Vespers for three reasons: that we may recall the Lord’s Incarnation; that, recalling the Virgin’s deeds, we may merit her intercession by our prayers; and that we may follow examples of her chastity. The *Magnificat* [Note: [Col. 0183] Luke 1] is used at Vespers because the Virgin bore the Lord at the evening of the world. This canticle is the exultation of the workers, whose spirit exults in the Lord, because he who is mighty has done great things for them, whose mercy is unto the ages [Note: [Col. 0183] ibid.]. To represent this exultation, lamps are lit [Col. 0183B] at Vespers; or they are principally lit for this canticle because it is from the Gospel; or so that we, belonging to the number of maidens and the five prudent [virgins], may run with the lamps of good works into the fragrance of the perfumes [Note: [Col. 0183] Song of Songs 1] of the Blessed Virgin, entering with her into the joy of our Lord [Note: [Col. 0183] Matthew 25]. Since works do not shine in lamps unless they have been formed by charity, the canticle is therefore concluded under an antiphon.

Meanwhile, the altar is incensed by the priest, who takes Aaron’s place, for the reason we stated above concerning the *Benedictus*. Prayers also are added on weekdays and omitted on feasts, for the reason previously given above concerning the other Hours. The prayer is the Lord’s final blessing of the workers. [Col. 0183C] That prayers are said at the end is taken from the Acts of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0183] Acts 20], who, when they were parting, prayed on their knees. These final prayers are called *collects*, a name drawn from Leviticus [Note: [Col. 0183] ch. 23]: the Feast of Tabernacles (*scenopegia*), the last of the legal festivals, is called a “collection,” because there the gathering of fruits took place, which prefigured the future gathering of our works, when it will be said: “Behold the human being, and all his works with him” [Note: [Col. 0183] Ecclesiastes 11]. These collects are [so called] for the reason stated above in the treatise on the Mass. “Let us bless the Lord” is final praise and ineffable exultation. “Thanks be to God” is thanksgiving for the course completed. [Col. 0183D]

## CHAPTER IX. ON CONFERENCES AND COMPLINE.

> “In peace, in the selfsame state, I shall sleep and rest” [Col. 0183D] [Note: [Col. 0183] Ps. 4].

The conference (*collatio*) derives its origin from the holy Fathers, who used to assemble in the evening and confer about the Scriptures, like workmen conversing together for refreshment. Therefore, in our conferences we read the Lives of the Fathers and similar works, which serve more for delight than for honour; and, if a doubt arises, we may lawfully question those who are more learned than ourselves. It is called Compline (*completorium*) because our works are completed, as also the daily use of food, drink, and common speech. Hence it is customary for monks, after Compline, to fortify the barriers of their mouths; and it signifies [Col. 0184A] the end of the present life. When the number of the elect has been completed, God will complete the joy of His saints. Hence, because “the Lord judges the ends of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0183] 1 Sam. 2], we begin with “Convert us, O God of our salvation” [Note: [Col. 0183] Ps. 84], praying that He may turn us from evil and turn away His wrath from us; and, because our merits are insufficient, we ask for His help, saying: “O God, make haste to help me” [Note: [Col. 0183] Ps. 69].

We say four psalms to appease the Lord, because the body, which consists of four elements, is dissolved in death; and we commend it to the Lord. The first three speak of death or of the Lord’s Passion, and therefore we use them at the Compline of our life. We sing “When I called,” that we may sleep “in peace, in the selfsame state” [Note: [Col. 0183] Ps. 4], that is, immutably. We add “In thee, O Lord, have I hoped” [Note: [Col. 0183] Ps. 30], [Col. 0184B] so that, with Christ, we may commend our spirit into the Father’s hands [Note: [Col. 0183] Luke 23]. Thus we take the end of the psalm at the verse which the Lord uttered while expiring on the cross. It is the sixth verse, because Christ died in the sixth age; and may we likewise sleep in that age, so that our limbs rest while our heart keeps watch toward the Lord—as the flesh rested in the tomb while the divinity kept watch.

We add, “He who dwells in the aid of the Most High,” that we may be delivered from four temptations: namely, from the terror by night, the arrow flying by day, the business that walks in darkness, the assault, and the noonday demon [Note: [Col. 0183] Ps. 90], that is, the demon rushing upon us. The first is slight and hidden; the second, slight and manifest; the third, grave and hidden; the fourth, grave and manifest. In the fourth [Col. 0184C] place we conclude the psalms with “Behold now, bless the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0183] Ps. 133], so that after death, in the house of the Lord, we may both be blessed by the Lord and bless the Lord.

In the hymn, chapter, and verse, we ask victory over nocturnal illusions, and pray to be guarded “as the pupil of the eye” [Note: [Col. 0183] Ps. 16]; or we ask victory over the snares of the devil, the flesh, and the world; or over the four thoughts mentioned above, that in Christ, who conquered death, the world, and the devil, we may triumph [Note: [Col. 0183] Heb. 2; John 16; Luke 11; Col. 2]. Thus the verse, “Keep us, O Lord, as the pupil of the eye,” indicates the condition of the time and office: namely, the Saviour’s protection amid the dangers of the night.

Observe that, according to some, in this office the chapter precedes the hymn, as at Vespers and the other Hours, so that the hymn may be joined to the Gospel [Col. 0184D] which is here said. According to others, the hymn precedes the chapter, through an inversion of the practice of the other Hours: for at the other Hours the hymn precedes the psalm, but here the psalm precedes the hymn, in order that what is found in the psalm titles may be fulfilled: “a psalm of a song” and “a song of a psalm.” Again, the fact that the chapter precedes the hymn, and the hymn the chapter, follows the practice of a good speaker, in whose mouth praises now precede exhortation, now exhortation praises.

It is also noteworthy that, whereas the other Hours have seven parts—namely [Col. 0185A] the verse with the *Gloria*, the hymn, psalm, reading, chant, prayers, and prayer—at the three offices of Matins, Vespers, and Compline an eighth is added: namely, the evangelical canticle. For these three Hours belong to the eighth, that is, to the Lord’s Resurrection: He rose in the morning; in the evening He manifested Himself to the disciples; at Compline He said to the disciples, “Peace be unto you” [Note: [Col. 0185] Luke 24]. Therefore, at these three Hours the hymn, which is an expression of joy, follows the psalms, so that it may be joined to the Gospel of grace.

The Gospel of this office is the Canticle of Simeon, namely, “Now thou dismissest” [Note: [Col. 0185] Luke 2], in which we ask for eternal peace: so that, as Simeon, desiring to depart after seeing Christ, asked to be dismissed, so we too, after the light of faith, may attain the splendour of sight, where [Col. 0185B] there shall be eternal peace. We also add the prayers and the Lord’s Prayer, that we may be protected from enemies who lie in wait in darkness and at the heel of life [Note: [Col. 0185] Gen. 3].

Observe, too, that at Prime and Compline we do not omit the Apostles’ Creed, because we begin and end all our works in the name in whom we believe. Likewise, at both offices we add confession and “Have mercy upon me, O God” [Note: [Col. 0185] Ps. 50], so that whatever we have sinned by night or transgressed by day we may wash away by confession and repentance, fulfilling the saying: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved” [Note: [Col. 0185] Jas. 5]. We also have in view the ancient ordinance that the priest offered an *assarium* of flour on the day [Col. 0185C] of his service, half in the morning and half in the afternoon [Note: [Col. 0185] Lev. 6].

But our sacrifice is a humbled spirit [Note: [Col. 0185] Ps. 50]; and likewise we refer both offices to God alone, after the manner of first-fruits and tithes [Note: [Col. 0185] Deut. 12]. Therefore they are not changed for an approaching feast, except for that of Christ, who is God [Note: [Col. 0185] Rom. 9]—as some say in the Paschal season—and of the Blessed Virgin, to confirm that He is both Son of God and Son of Man. The prayers signify humility, which is always necessary: at the beginning, to signify which the service is begun in a humble voice, and at the end. Therefore the prayers are placed at the end. The final prayer is the final blessing. “Let us bless the Lord”; “Thanks be to God”: this is final and ineffable praise, and thanksgiving for the completed course.

[Col. 0185D] Finally, this point concerning the office is not to be neglected: according to some, the nocturnal office recalls the period from Adam to Noah; Matins, that from Noah to Abraham; Prime, that from Abraham to Moses; Terce, that from Moses to David; Sext, that from David to the coming of Christ; None, that from the first coming to the second, when the Lord will come to judge. By Vespers they understand the Sabbath of souls, in which they shall rest from their labours [Note: [Col. 0185] Rev. 14]; by Compline, that time of great solemnity in which the elect will come to receive the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0185] Matt. 25], and the joy of the saints will be completed, [Col. 0186A] struggle will cease, and eternal peace will follow. May the bridegroom grant the bride to sleep and rest immutably in that peace [Note: [Col. 0185] Song 3].

## CHAPTER X. ON THE MONASTIC OFFICE

> “Keep thy feasts, O Judah, and perform thy vows” [Note: [Col. 0185] Nahum 1; Ps. 75].

Nahum addresses those who confess, commanding them to fulfil the vows which they have vowed of their own will. For making a vow belongs to the will, but fulfilling vows to necessity; a vow is a conception of the mind confirmed by the deliberation of the soul. The monk’s continuous vows are obedience, the wearing of the habit, renunciation of possessions, fasting, silence, and the regular office. Setting aside the rest, we intend to treat of this office.

Thus blessed Benedict arranged the office differently from the canons; nor was it [Col. 0186B] rejected by the Church, but it was confirmed by blessed Gregory, who said: “The holy man could not give otherwise than he lived.” He therefore says once, “O God, make haste to help me” [Note: [Col. 0185] Ps. 69], and afterwards three times, “O Lord, thou shalt open my lips” [Note: [Col. 0185] Ps. 50], out of reverence for the Unity and the Trinity. Thereafter comes the psalm “O Lord, how are they multiplied,” because, according to some, it says therein concerning sleep: “I slept and fell asleep” [Note: [Col. 0185] Ps. 3]. Then, by the invitatory and “Come,” he invites them to come to church. Accordingly the Ambrosian hymn follows.

We have spoken above concerning hymns. Yet we think it should here be added that the ancient Fathers also sang hymns [Note: [Col. 0185] Ps. 64], as did David and the three youths in the furnace [Note: [Col. 0185] Dan. 3]. We also have the example of the Lord Himself and the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0185] Matt. 26]. Since [Col. 0186C] blessed Ambrose is known to have flourished in these hymns, they are called Ambrosian, either because they were composed by him, or because in his time they first began to be celebrated most widely in the Church.

To this he added seven psalms with their antiphons and four readings with an equal number of responsories in the first nocturn, and the same number in the second. The number six signifies the active life, in which we ought to perform the six works of mercy if we wish to attain the perfection of the contemplative life [Note: [Col. 0185] Matt. 25]. This is signified by the number four of readings and responsories, on account of the four Gospels; or both are figured by the number eight, on account of the eight beatitudes [Note: [Col. 0185] Matt. 5]. In the third nocturn, this man venerable in life ordained that three canticles should be sung in praise of the Trinity, from [Col. 0186D] whom we believe and hope that the perfection of both lives is given to us.

When this is sung with *Alleluia*, which is a heavenly song, it indicates either that the praise of a human voice is insufficient for the praise of the Trinity, or that through the praises of the Trinity we shall attain the song of heavenly joy. Then the four readings from the Gospel which follow indicate that praisers of the Trinity, through the teaching of the four Gospels, are distinguished, fortified, and instructed by four virtues. By the four responsories which follow is understood the gladness of those who praise.

[Col. 0187A] Observe that canons employ nine readings, whereas monks use twelve. For the number nine is square—namely, a quadrilateral with equal sides throughout—and is fitting for preachers, whose word and work ought to be weighed proportionally in an equal balance. The number twelve, however, consists of unequal sides, because three times four, or four times three, makes twelve; and it is fitting for monks, who, after the example of Jacob [Note: [Col. 0187] Gen. 32], wrestle with God and limp on one foot, because they work less and meditate more.

Again, the number four of that holy order signifies the square stability of the same order: the chariots of Amminadab [Note: [Col. 0187] Song 6], that is, the fourfold sense of Scripture—historical, allegorical, tropological, and anagogical—in which that holy order [Col. 0187B] meditates more than others. But lest, while doing this, they should ascribe the good to themselves rather than attribute all to God and call themselves unprofitable servants [Note: [Col. 0187] Luke 17], they add: “We praise thee, O God.”

After this the Gospel is read, which signifies the number ten, namely eternal life, which will be rendered at the end to those who praise worthily. Therefore it is sung solemnly and with honour. It is followed by *Amen*, that is, “May what we believe and hope from the Gospel be done for us.” By the hymn sung at the end, namely “Praise is fitting for thee,” is understood the final rejoicing, when, having received the denarius, the saints shall exult in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0187] Ps. 149]. Therefore it is sung with great delight and is called a hymn; for, as we say, a hymn is praise [Col. 0187C] of God with song.

At Matins, blessed Benedict instituted nearly the same number and the same psalms, hymns, and canticles, on ferial as on festal days, as we explained above, and with the same signification. He changed this only: he wished “God be merciful unto us” [Note: [Col. 0187] Ps. 66] to be sung first, directly and without an antiphon. This may be because Matins are sung at dawn, when the darkness is failing, while it says here: “May he cause his face to shine upon us” [Note: [Col. 0187] Ibid.]. Or it may be because this office belongs to the Lord’s Resurrection, through which we have received grace and blessing.

What follows—“Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy great mercy” [Note: [Col. 0187] Ps. 50]—the psalm, or Jubilee, recalls remission, both on account of the number of the psalms and of the penitential humility which it contains. [Col. 0187D] Again, the monastic order has this distinctive practice: at Matins and Vespers it says the Lord’s Prayer aloud, for the sake of the simple and the crafty. Some do not understand it or forget it; others, bearing the thorn of hatred in their hearts, hate a brother and do not wish to say, “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” [Note: [Col. 0187] Matt. 6]. They are therefore compelled to say this publicly, that they may be cleansed from that vice. It is said at Matins, that is, at the end of the day, so that no one may allow night or day to pass without reconciliation with his brother.

At the other Hours he did not direct that it be said aloud, because it often happens that one brother is angry with another [Col. 0188A] and is stirred by a sudden impulse of rage. Although he does not immediately restrain his mind, he must be waited for until he can grant pardon; for it is enough if “the sun does not go down upon his anger” [Note: [Col. 0187] Eph. 4].

The number three of psalms at Prime, Terce, Sext, None, and Compline signifies faith in the Holy Trinity, to whom daily works are to be referred. The number four of psalms at Vespers either directs us to the heavenly square, or to the four cardinal virtues, about whose hinges it is fitting that our works should turn.

Observe also that it is not without mystery that monks turn their whole bodies from east to west, signifying that God is to be worshipped everywhere, because He is present everywhere. Or, rather, it signifies that with rational motion we must proceed from the rising of our birth to the setting of death, just as the firmament naturally turns from east to west. The Church beyond the mountains likewise signifies this when, at “Glory be to the Father,” it bows toward the east, and, adding “as it was,” turns toward the west. This is a kind of devotion; and that master ordained that devotion be shown in the offices. For if we believe that God is present everywhere, we should then especially believe Him present when we stand at the divine work in body and mind; nor should we doubt the presence of angels.

Therefore, brothers, “serve the Lord in fear” [Note: [Col. 0187] Ps. 2]: serve in psalms and readings; exult in hymns and jubilations. “And trembling” [Col. 0188C] is added to fear, so that the service may not be negligent, nor the exultation sluggish. In psalms, sing with melody, that minds may more readily be bent toward compunction, and that those not pierced by words may be moved by the sweetness of modulation. For, as we know by experience, the weak soul is more ardently moved through song to an affection of piety.

In readings, let them be pronounced, for in them there is no small edification for hearers. Thus, although when psalmody is sung all should sing, and when prayer is offered all should pray, yet when a reading is read, silence must be kept and all must listen. Therefore if anyone arrives, let him adore God with bowed head, sign his forehead with the cross, and give his ear to the reading, lest under the pretext of prayer he lose the fruit of the reading being read [Col. 0188D] to him. For he will not always have it, whereas the opportunity of praying will always be ready at hand.

In prayers, let devotion be present. If one ought to speak in a subdued voice to a secular ruler, who is ashes and a worm, with how much greater devotion ought one to supplicate the Lord, who is the Creator of all? Let prayer also be brief, for “in much speaking sin will not be wanting” [Note: [Col. 0187] Prov. 10]; therefore the Lord says, “When praying, do not speak much” [Note: [Col. 0187] Matt. 6]. Hence also the Greek custom is to pray frequently, but briefly. Observe that in private prayer we ought to remain prostrate until we suppress our various thoughts, as [Col. 0189A] Gregory says. In an assembly, however, prayer should be brief, and at the signal one should rise from prayer.

Observe also that when the priest has said the prayer aloud, one ought not to pray in other words, but to attend inwardly to that prayer, so as to answer, once it has been said: *Amen*. Again, the brethren ought to remain prostrate until the words “in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God” are spoken, except at Compline, at which we remain prostrate until the words “The blessing of God the Father Almighty, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

Then we rise to answer: *Amen*. Moreover, let prayer be pure, proceeding from purity of heart and bringing forth the compunction of tears, from the upper and lower spring [Note: [Col. 0189] John 15]. For, as Gregory says, truly to pray is to utter bitter groans in compunction, not carefully composed words. Let it also be persevering, [Col. 0190A] because “whoever perseveres unto the end shall be saved” [Note: [Col. 0189] Matt. 24]. Let it also accord with works, so that the mouth of the turtledove may be turned toward the armpit [Note: [Col. 0189] Lev. 1].

But in hymns one should exult, so that there may be praise of God with song [Note: [Col. 0189] Ps. 68]. For if there is praise but it is not of God, it is not a hymn; and if there is praise of God but it is not sung, properly speaking it is not a hymn, although it may be so called in a broad sense: “When they had sung a hymn, they went out unto the Mount of Olives” [Note: [Col. 0189] Matt. 26]. One should likewise exult to the Lord with a voice of jubilation [Note: [Col. 0189] Ps. 46], but in such a way that the mind accords with the voice. This must also be understood of the rest: let us sing psalms with the spirit and also with the mind [Note: [Col. 0189] 1 Cor. 14]; let us sing psalms wisely to the Lord—that is, with heart and mouth—desiring that not so much our voices as our meaning and words may please human beings and God. Amen.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0189]

## PROLOGUE. ON THE MULTIPLICITY OF BOOKS AND THE VARIETY OF TIMES

[Col. 0189B]

Having run through the general matters, let us pursue the particular matters concerning the concord and differences of the offices. But because concord arises from the multiplicity of books, and diversity of offices from the variety of times, let us first set forth useful matters concerning the plurality of books and the variety of times.

Since the ecclesiastical office consists in reading and song, there are two kinds of ecclesiastical books. Some are books for reading, others for singing. The reading books are the Bible, passionary, legendary, homiliary, sermon-book, epistolary, Gospel-book, collectary, and [Col. 0189C] ordinal.

The Bible is so called from *biblos*, meaning “book”; or from *biblos*, because formerly writing was done on papyrus, and *theca*, meaning a receptacle, a term equivalent both to a bookcase, where books are stored, and to the great volume containing both Testaments. The Old Testament is divided into three parts: history, prophecy, and hagiographa. History contains twenty-one volumes: namely, the Pentateuch, called *Torah*, that is, “law.” These are the five books of Moses: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy. The Hebrews swear upon these, just as we do upon the Gospels, as though those were more sacred among them and these among us. Two books, Joshua and Judges, are added to the Pentateuch, and it is called the Heptateuch. Then follows the book of Ruth and the four divisions of Kings. [Col. 0189D] After these follow two books of Chronicles, two of Ezra, two of Maccabees, and the books of Tobit, Judith, and Esther. These are twenty-one because they teach that the Decalogue is to be observed in unity of faith, with body and mind.

The Prophets are sixteen: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, Ezekiel, and the twelve prophets. They are sixteen because they teach that the ten commandments must be fulfilled through six works. Next follow the hagiographa: namely, the book of Psalms, Job, the three books of Solomon—Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs—and the books of Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus. These are seven, because they teach that eternal life is to be attained through the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

[Tobit, the Maccabees, Wisdom, Philo—that is, “Love righteousness”—and the book of Jehu son of Sirach, “All wisdom is from the Lord God,” which is called Ecclesiasticus, are nevertheless said to be apocryphal. The Church does not authenticate these four apocryphal books, because their authors are unknown. For two express Solomon’s thought, and we believe Ezra composed the other two—Ezra who restored the library burned by the Babylonians [Col. 0190C].]

The books of the New Testament follow: the four Evangelists, the fourteen Epistles of Paul, the Apocalypse, the seven Catholic Epistles, and the Acts of the Apostles. The books of the two Testaments are nearly seventy-two, set against the seventy-two languages of the proud, so that the seventy-two languages may be converted to the Lord.

The passionary is the book containing the passions of the martyrs; the legendary, that containing the lives of confessors; the homiliary, that containing expositions of the Gospels; the sermon-book, the book of winter and summer sermons; the epistolary and Gospel-book are portions of the Bible; the collectary is the book of collects, just as the hymnary is the book of hymns; and the ordinal contains exorcisms, while the benedictionary contains [Col. 0190D] blessings.

There are three books for singing: the antiphonary, gradual, and troper. The antiphonary received its name from the more important element, namely the antiphons, though verses and responsories are also found in it. For it is read in the *Tripartite History* that blessed Ignatius heard angels singing antiphons; therefore he instituted antiphons with psalms to be sung in choir, as though in a dance, and for this reason they are called antiphons: for as responsories answer to the history, so antiphons answer to psalmody. Blessed Gregory arranged and compiled the antiphonary by piecing together excerpts.

The gradual is so called from the steps, because on feast-days one ascends the steps and sings there at the ambo. On non-festal days it is sung before the steps of the altar. The troper or tropary is the book containing tropes, *Kyrie eleison*, together with proses and sequences. It is called from *trophos*, meaning “turning,” because it turns toward the introit; hence a *trophium* is also called a girdle, which is turned from navel to navel.

The variety of times arises from the varied states of the human condition. As the solar year passes through the succession of four seasons—winter, in which seeds are cast; spring, in which seeds come forth and grow into ears; summer, in which harvests whiten and are cut with the sickle; autumn, in which grain is separated from chaff, the chaff is burned, and the grain stored in barns—so too the great year of this present life, lasting from the beginning of the world to the end of the age, is measured by a fourfold succession.

The first was the time of deviation, from Adam to Moses, in which all turned aside from the worship of God, became useless together, and “there was none that did good, no, not one” [Note: [Col. 0191] Ps. 13]. For they served the creature rather than the Creator [Note: [Col. 0191] Rom. 1]. The second was the time of recall, from Moses to Christ, in which they were recalled through the Law [Col. 0191C] and the Prophets, and instructed concerning Christ’s coming, the avoidance of sin, and the love of the one God. The third was the time of reconciliation, from the Lord’s Nativity to His Ascension, in which divine things are reconciled to human, because “there was glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will” [Note: [Col. 0191] Luke 2]. The fourth is the time of our pilgrimage, from the Lord’s Ascension to the consummation of the age.

The first is compared to night, the second to morning, the third to midday, and the fourth to evening. Thus man enters in sin, but, having strayed, is recalled in baptism; he advances in work, but departs and is completed in death. Seeing these times of the great year, the Church uses a praiseworthy variety of offices in accordance with the variety of times. For in Advent she recalls the time [Col. 0191D] of recall; from Septuagesima to the octave of Easter, the time of deviation; in the Paschal days to the octave of Pentecost, the time of reconciliation; from the octave of Pentecost to Advent, the time of pilgrimage.

Therefore, following the arrangement of the books in this artificial order, we shall make four divisions in the offices according to the four times. For in this season the Church begins the offices of her spiritual warfare, because it presents, as we have said, the figure of recall. In this it retains the subject-matter, though it does not follow the order: for it was not fitting that she, who desired to avoid error and find the physician, should begin with the time [Col. 0192A] of deviation.

## CHAPTER ONE. THE FIRST SUNDAY OF ADVENT

“Looking from afar, behold, I see the power of God coming.”

We celebrate the Lord’s Advent for a twofold reason, for the Lord’s Advent is twofold. The first was in humility; the second will be in majesty. For the Lord, who is everywhere through the invisible presence of His majesty, is said to come—that is, to come to us—when, by assuming that which is visible, He makes Himself visible to the sight of our flesh. This occurred when “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” [Note: [Col. 0191] John 1]; and the [second] will occur when [Col. 0192B] we see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven [Note: [Col. 0191] Luke 21].

Therefore, the period preceding the Lord’s Nativity is called Advent because it commemorates partly those things belonging to the first advent, such as “Behold, a virgin shall conceive” [Note: [Col. 0191] Isa. 7]; partly those belonging to the second, such as “Behold, in the clouds of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0191] Dan. 7]; and partly those which appear to concern both, such as “Let the heavens rejoice and let the earth exult” [Note: [Col. 0191] Ps. 95].

Of those matters belonging to the first advent, some are bridal songs of the Virgin; others concern the archangel Gabriel as bridegroom’s friend; others are proclamations of the Forerunner; others are rattling announcements of the Saviour as He sets out; others are rejoicings of converted gentile nations. For the bridegroom’s friend announced, “The Virgin has conceived” [Note: [Col. 0191] Luke 1]; the Forerunner pointed with his finger [Note: [Col. 0191] John 1]; the Saviour came; the gentile world believed. Let the discerning reader observe in the service books which items belong [Col. 0192C] to the one or the other of these matters.

In certain service books, such as the lectionary and Gospel-book, five weeks are marked, on account of the five ages of the preceding world, in which the proclamation of the coming Saviour went before and in which were elect those who believed, hoped for, and loved the Lord’s Advent. But in others, namely the antiphonary and gradual only, four are designated, on account of the Law, Psalms, prophecies, and books of the gentiles, in all of which the Lord’s Advent was prefigured. Or the reader warns one, in order to receive Christ, to cleanse the dwelling-place of the body, compacted from the material of four elements. Or the reader warns active persons, through Christ’s Advent, to be led from the land of the north. Thus in Jeremiah: “The Lord brought forth [Col. 0192D] the seed of Israel from the land of the north” [Note: [Col. 0191] Jer. 23, 31], that is, from sins. These are the five thousand men who followed God and were fed with five loaves, of whom the Gospel speaks [Note: [Col. 0191] John 6].

The singer, however, stirs up persons to a loftier manner of life and cheers the contemplative, who are borne in the four chariots of Amminadab [Note: [Col. 0191] Song 6]. These are the four thousand men fed with seven loaves [Note: [Col. 0191] Mark 8], that is, nourished with sevenfold grace. The reason for this difference, I think, is that at the entrance of the tabernacle there were five columns, but before the Holy of Holies four [Note: [Col. 0191] Exod. 26, 27]. For beginners are chastened by the rod of the Law, while the perfect are strengthened by [Col. 0193A] grace. To represent the joy of their minds, the chants are renewed. To them the evening verse says:

> “Drop down dew, ye heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Saviour” [Note: [Col. 0193] Isa. 45].

For they are the heavens who distil subtle matters concerning Christ’s Incarnation, such as “The Word was made flesh” [Note: [Col. 0193] John 1]. They are the clouds which rain down more tangible matters, such as “Joseph betrothed Mary” [Note: [Col. 0193] Matt. 1]. To these same persons the morning verse also says:

> “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God” [Note: [Col. 0193] Isa. 40].

To prepare the way is to do and preach repentance; to make the paths straight is, after the commandments, to observe the counsels. Yet three weeks are often observed in Advent, on account of the three times—before the Law, under the Law, and under grace—of whose course we shall discuss more fully below.

The beginning of Advent must always be celebrated on a Sunday: not before the fifth day before the Kalends of December [27 November], nor after the third day before the Nones of that month [3 December]; but wherever Sunday falls within these seven days, there the Lord’s Advent is to be celebrated. But now let us attend to the nocturnal and daily offices.

> “Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar, and his brightness fills the whole earth” [Note: [Col. 0193] Isa. 30].

This is interpreted in Isaiah concerning the second Advent, but may be understood in the same way concerning the first. “Behold,” a demonstrative word of time, suggests brevity. “The name of the Lord” is the Son of the Father Himself; hence: “Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory” [Note: [Col. 0193] Ps. 113]. “He comes from afar,” because He comes from heaven to earth [Note: [Col. 0193] John 3, 16], from the Father’s bosom into the Virgin’s womb. “And his brightness,” that is, His teaching or renown, fills the whole [Col. 0193C] earth, because He is fragrant with the finest perfumes, as poured-out oil is poured forth [Note: [Col. 0193] Song 1], whose fragrance fills the whole house [Note: [Col. 0193] John 12].

> “Hear the word of the Lord, O nations, proclaim it in the islands that are far away, and say” [Note: [Col. 0193] Jer. 31]: “Behold, our Saviour shall come, and now do not fear” [Note: [Col. 0193] Isa. 62].

Jeremiah invites the nations to be converted to faith in the Mediator, because “there is no other in whom we must be saved” [Note: [Col. 0193] Acts 4]. He calls this Mediator the Word, because, just as the intention of the mind is expressed through a word, so the Father is known through the Son [Note: [Col. 0193] Matt. 11]. This is the Word in which and through which all things were made [Note: [Col. 0193] John 1], of whom the Psalmist says: “My heart has uttered a good word” [Note: [Col. 0193] Ps. 44].

There is an inspired word, such as human understanding; there is an indicated word, such as divine worship; and there is an uttered word, such as God made man. [Col. 0193D] Hear this word of the Lord, by which the heavens were established [Note: [Col. 0193] Ps. 32], and proclaim it to the ends of the earth [Note: [Col. 0193] Ps. 21]. For all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord. And say: “Behold, our Saviour shall come,” as though He shall come to us, because the Lord shall make known His salvation; in the sight of the nations He shall reveal His righteousness [Note: [Col. 0193] Ps. 97]. Therefore do not fear, but “come unto him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be confounded” [Note: [Col. 0193] Ps. 33].

> “Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, thy King [Col. 0194A] comes to thee meek, to save thee” [Note: [Col. 0193] Isa. 62; Zech. 9].

Isaiah directs this speech to the watchers on the walls, the sentinels who guard the city, the guardians of the daughter of Zion—that is, to the teachers of the Church—so that they may say: “Daughter of Zion, behold, thy King comes meekly”; that is, so that they may announce to believers and to those who look toward God the first Advent of the Saviour, who comes in meekness for salvation.

> “The wilderness shall rejoice, and the solitary place shall exult, and it shall flourish as the lily” [Note: [Col. 0193] Isa. 35].

Isaiah prophesies concerning the conversion of the gentile world, which before the Saviour’s Advent had been deserted by God: a wilderness on the way without Christ, who is “the way, the truth, and the life” [Note: [Col. 0193] John 14]; a solitary place without law and without a teacher. But through and after His Advent it shall rejoice in mind, exult in body, and flourish in the fragrance of good repute like the lily. Hence: “As the lily among thorns, so is my beloved [Col. 0194B] among the daughters” [Note: [Col. 0193] Song 2]. For amid a crooked and perverse nation [Note: [Col. 0193] Phil. 2], the Church dwells red in martyrs, white in confessors, green in virgins, and fragrant in doctors.

### “In the latter days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be on the summit of the mountains”  
[Note: [Col. 0193] Isa. 2.]

Isaiah speaks of Christ’s pre-eminence, saying: “In the latter days,” of which Jacob says [Note: [Col. 0193] Gen. 49.], “that I may tell you what shall happen to you in the latter days”; that is, in the time of fullness, in the fullness of time, namely in the final age. The mountain of the house of the Lord is the head of God’s Church, whom, as though a stone cut from a mountain without hands, Daniel saw grow into a great mountain [Note: [Col. 0193] Dan. 2.]. He was prepared by God, predestined; according to his humanity, chosen beforehand by grace alone [Note: [Col. 0193] Rom. 1.]. “It shall be on the summit of the mountains,” that is, protecting all [Col. 0194C] above them and instilling into them from the fullness [Note: [Col. 0193] John 1.] of his fountain. These mountains are the angels and all the saints, of whom it is said: “The mountains are round about him” [Note: [Col. 0193] Ps. 124].

The angel Gabriel spoke to Mary, saying: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with thee; blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb” [Note: [Col. 0193] Luke 1.]. Luke gives the angel’s name so that, from the interpretation of the name itself, you may recognize what ministry he had come to perform. Gabriel is called “strength of God,” because he announces him who came to overcome the devil [Note: [Col. 0193] Heb. 2.]. He spoke to Mary, “star of the sea,” who bore light to those tossed upon the sea of this world; or “lady of the sea,” who carried the Lord of the whole world: “Hail, full of grace.” Through Eve death entered the world; through you, salvation and life. Hence, fittingly, the greeting [Col. 0194D] of salvation is opposed to the name Eve. That grace was emptied; but you are full of a threefold grace: because you offered the gift of virginity to the Lord; because you deserved to enjoy the sight and conversation of an angel; because you brought forth for the world the author of all grace.

For “the Lord is with thee”: in your soul through love; in your womb through the incarnation; in your aid through the bestowal of virtues. “Blessed art thou among women,” because, beyond the precedent of womanly condition, you are virgin, mother, and *Theotokos*—God-bearer. “Blessed is the fruit of thy womb,” of whom the Prophet foretold: [Col. 0195A] “Of the fruit of thy womb I will set upon thy throne” [Note: [Col. 0195] Ps. 131.].

Mary said, as you suppose: “What sort of greeting is this? For my soul is troubled, and because I am to bear a King who will not violate the enclosure of my virginity.” From Luke is taken the reply of blessed Mary, who, in the manner of a virgin, is troubled by the sight of a male; in the manner of human frailty, by the angelic vision and unfamiliar greeting; and she marvels at the new manner of conceiving. Hence she adds: “How shall this be done in me?”

“Behold, the Lord shall come, whom John preached as about to come with glory.” This is taken from Matthew. For John says of Christ, as is read in Matthew: “He who is to come after me is mightier than I” [Note: [Col. 0195] Matt. 3.]. Although Christ had already come into the world, John nevertheless preached [Col. 0195B] that he was to come, because he was to come to preach and to baptize. Hence follows: “He shall baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire” [Note: [Col. 0195] Ibid.]: with the Spirit of sanctification in the present, and with the fire of purgation in the future. He was also at last to come with glory in order to judge, because “the Father has given all judgment to the Son” [Note: [Col. 0195] John 5.]. Therefore, “whose winnowing-fan is in his hand” [Note: [Col. 0195] Matt. 3.]—that is, judgment is in his power—we await our Lord and Savior, who gives salvation to our body and confirms his brightness in us.

The Apostle says this [Note: [Col. 0195] Phil. 2.] to the Philippians in the person of the ancient and modern Fathers. The ancient Fathers awaited the Messiah to redeem them; we too await him to judge; and both await him to save. They awaited him for the salvation [Col. 0195C] of souls; we, for the healing of bodies. Salvation properly belongs to the soul; health, to the body. Now is the time of salvation, which the ancients awaited. Thus the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the day of salvation” [Note: [Col. 0195] II Cor. 6.]. In the future there will be the time of bodily health, which we await, when this mortal thing shall put on immortality and this corruptible thing incorruption [Note: [Col. 0195] I Cor. 15.], when our Savior shall refashion the body of our lowliness, made like the body of his brightness [Note: [Col. 0195] Phil. 3.]. Yet either term is used for the other. Thus: “who gives salvation to our body and confirms his brightness in us.” At the first coming he confirmed in us the brightness of doctrine or grace; in the future he will confirm the brightness of glory.

### “Remove the stones that are in the way”  
[Note: [Col. 0195] Jer. 50.]

For our Lord shall come with salvation. By comparison with bodies, he provides us with a remedy for souls. So long as harmful humors are in the body, it is useless to add nourishment; for the more you feed impure bodies, the more you injure them. When iron is in a wound, it is not the time to apply a poultice; and unless a vessel is clean, whatever you pour into it turns sour. Likewise, “wisdom shall not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins” [Note: [Col. 0195] Wis. 1.]; rather, the departure of vice makes the entry of virtues possible.

Therefore, cast stones out of the streets: remove the hardness of vices from the breadth of your hearts. [Col. 0196A] If they are in the course of your deeds, remove them; do not leave one stone upon another [Note: [Col. 0195] Luke 19.]. For our Lord shall come with salvation; therefore, “do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” [Note: [Col. 0195] Matt. 3.].

### “Looking from afar, behold, I see the power of God coming, and a cloud covering the whole earth,” etc.

That responsory is not Gregorian, but was added and compiled by some monk. The rest was compiled by Gregory. Therefore this should not precede those, except that the Church’s usage has prevailed so strongly.

This responsory is sung in the person of John the Baptist, or of the Bride, saying: “Looking from afar”—namely from earth to heaven—“I see the power of God coming.” Although power is properly assigned to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and goodness to the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0196B] here understand “power” as the Son of God, to whom “all power is given in heaven and on earth” [Note: [Col. 0195] Matt. 28.], and who is “the Lord mighty in battle” [Note: [Col. 0195] Ps. 23.]. To him the prophet says: “Gird thy sword upon thy thigh, O most mighty one” [Note: [Col. 0195] Ps. 44.]. He came when he showed himself visible.

“And a cloud covering the whole earth.” This cloud is God’s mercy, which affords refreshment against the heat of vices. Moses entered it when he ascended to receive the Law [Note: [Col. 0195] Exod. 20.]. Peter understood it when, seeing the Lord, Moses, and Elijah in the bright cloud, he said: “Let us make three tabernacles here” [Note: [Col. 0195] Matt. 17.]. It appeared in the Temple after the dedication [Note: [Col. 0195] II Chron. 7.]. It led the people into the wilderness and protected them from fire [Note: [Col. 0195] Exod. 14.]. It is the power of the Most High which overshadowed the Virgin [Col. 0196C] [Note: [Col. 0195] Luke 1.], and which covers the whole earth, because “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0195] Ps. 32], and because “he makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil” [Note: [Col. 0195] Matt. 6.].

Or by “cloud” he means unbelief or ignorance. For man was ignorant of God, of himself, of his native land, and that concupiscence is sin. This cloud covered the whole earth, because “all have turned aside; together they have become useless” [Note: [Col. 0195] Ps. 13], and “from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there was no soundness in them” [Note: [Col. 0195] Isa. 1.].

### “Go to meet him, and say: Tell us whether thou art he who is to reign over the people Israel.”

John said similar things to his disciples: “Prepare the way of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0195] John 1.]; and, through his disciples, to Christ: “Art thou he that is to come, or do we await another?” [Note: [Col. 0195] Matt. 11.] Or these are the Bride’s words to the young women: “Go to meet [Col. 0196D] the Bridegroom” [Note: [Col. 0195] Song 5; Matt. 25.].

The way of God to us is faith, or mercy; for our way to him is charity. The prophet marked both, saying: “My God, his way is undefiled” [Note: [Col. 0195] Ps. 17], namely faith; “he has made my way spotless,” namely charity. Go therefore by the way of charity, and say: “Tell us,” etc. Reveal to us, through Scripture, through eternal inspiration, more and more through thy presence, whether thou art the Messiah promised in the Law, and whether thou art to reign over the people Israel—the people [Col. 0197A] whom thou hast prepared for thy vision—so that it may be said to thee: “Deliver Israel, O God, from all his tribulations” [Note: [Col. 0197] Ps. 24.].

And because Law, psalmody, and prophecy foretold this coming of the Savior—or rather, because the Fathers before the Law foresaw this coming, the Fathers under the Law desired it, and the Fathers of grace preached it—three verses consequently follow, through which the Fathers of the three periods are understood. Therefore the Baptist, or the Church, says: You Fathers before the Law, “all ye earth-born, and sons of men, both rich and poor together,” go to meet him [Note: [Col. 0197] Ps. 48], etc.

He calls the wicked “earth-born,” since they belong to Adam’s portion, formed from earth, and pursue earthly things. He calls the good “sons of men,” since they belong to the portion of the second Adam, the Son of Man. He then calls rich those whom he had called earth-born, and poor those whom he had called sons of men. [Col. 0197B] Therefore, all of you—that is, every one of you—earth-born, rich in malice; and sons of men, poor in spirit [Note: [Col. 0197] Matt. 5], who are together as one: in one sheepfold, lambs and kids; in one net, good and bad fish [Note: [Col. 0197] Matt. 13]; in one womb, Jacob and Esau [Note: [Col. 0197] Gen. 25]; in one ark, Shem, Ham, and Japheth; in one threshing-floor, grain and chaff [Note: [Col. 0197] Gen. 7]. Go to meet him: let you wicked begin through entering in, and let you good advance through progress.

You Fathers under the Law likewise say: “Give ear, thou that rulest Israel, thou that leadest Joseph like a sheep”: tell us, etc. Thou that rulest Israel—the Jewish people who see God—through the teaching of the Law; thou that leadest from strength to strength [Note: [Col. 0197] Ps. 83], leading Joseph like an innocent sheep—the Gentile people increased through the grain that died [Note: [Col. 0197] John 12]—give ear; [Col. 0197C] pour upon us the light of thy mercy. And tell us, etc.

You Fathers under grace also say: “Lift up your gates, O princes; and be lifted up, O everlasting gates, and there shall enter” [Note: [Col. 0197] Ps. 23] he who is to reign, etc. O princes and powers of this air, and O offspring of vipers [Note: [Col. 0197] Matt. 3], remove the gates of death—the vices by which the devil enters hearts. And, O everlasting gates—the virtues leading to eternity—rise up against vices, and through you the King of glory, who is to reign in the people Israel, shall enter and dwell.

Note that at the third verse there is no response, “Tell us,” because the Fathers of the New Testament were assured of Christ’s coming; the Fathers of grace are certain of the King of glory’s entrance. But because faith in the incarnation [Col. 0197D] never was, is not, and never will be sufficient without faith in the most holy Trinity, there is therefore added: “Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.” And because he who came in humility will also come in majesty [Note: [Col. 0197] Matt. 25], the responsory is repeated anew. In the repetition, however, understand “cloud” literally: “For he shall come in the clouds of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0197] Dan. 7; Luke 21; Acts 1]. As the cloud received him, so cloud and darkness shall be round about him [Note: [Col. 0197] Ps. 96]. Or, briefly, the three verses with one *Gloria* represent that the Fathers understood God as three and one; [Col. 0198A] hence Abraham saw three and worshipped one [Note: [Col. 0197] Gen. 18].

### “I beheld in the vision of the night, and behold, in the clouds of heaven the Son of Man came; and there was given to him a kingdom and honor, and every people, tribe, and tongue shall serve him”  
[Note: [Col. 0197] Dan. 7.]

Daniel, burning with heavenly desires—and thus deserved to be called “a man of desires” [Note: [Col. 0197] Dan. 10]—having received understanding through an angel, disclosed by these words the unsearchable riches of the mystery hidden from the ages: that is, the mystery of the incarnation of the Word, who in the beginning was with the Father [Note: [Col. 0197] John 1]. He says: “I beheld in a vision,” or vision, “of the night.”

There are three kinds of vision: night-vision, day-vision, and vision of light. Night-vision belongs to the time before grace; day-vision to the time under grace; luminous vision to glory. The patriarchs and prophets saw in night-vision, for “all our Fathers were under the cloud” [Note: [Col. 0197] I Cor. 10]. For [Col. 0198B] “to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” [Note: [Col. 0197] Isa. 53.] Moses’ face was veiled, and a veil hung in the middle of the Temple [Note: [Col. 0197] Exod. 34; II Cor. 3; Exod. 26]. Therefore Daniel here too beheld in night-vision.

The apostles saw in day-vision, to whom the humanity of our Savior appeared [Note: [Col. 0197] Titus 3], by whom he was seen upon earth and conversed with them [Note: [Col. 0197] Bar. 3]: Emmanuel [Note: [Col. 0197] Isa. 7], that is, “God with us”—with us by participation in form, by the likeness of sinful flesh, and by dwelling among us [Note: [Col. 0197] Rom. 8]. In luminous vision the sons of God shall see face to face [Note: [Col. 0197] I Cor. 13], when the strap of the sandal shall be loosed [Note: [Col. 0197] John 17], when, according to Zechariah [Note: [Col. 0197] Zech. 14], there shall be neither day nor night, but only light: for the succession of night and day shall cease, and light shall continue without interruption.

Truth itself suggests this distinction of visions in the Gospel, saying: “Abraham rejoiced [Col. 0198C] to see my day; he saw it and was glad” [Note: [Col. 0197] John 8]. Again: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it” [Note: [Col. 0197] Luke 10]—supply, “as you see it.” For they saw in night, you in day; they in figure, you in truth.

“And behold, in the clouds of heaven the Son of Man came.” The clouds of heaven are the flesh of the Word: not drawn from heaven, but heavenly, because formed by the operation of the Holy Spirit. Of this Isaiah says: “The Lord rides upon a light cloud” [Note: [Col. 0197] Isa. 19]. It is a cloud because it gives refreshment against the heat of vices; it is light because it is free from guilt. In this cloud the Son of Man came, as Daniel’s account continues, unto the Ancient of Days, that is, unto equality with the Father.

Thus, “being in the form of God, he did not think it robbery to be equal with God” [Note: [Col. 0197] Phil. 2]. “And there was given [Col. 0198D] to him a kingdom and honor,” namely “the name that is above every name” [Note: [Col. 0197] Ibid.], which was given from eternity but manifested in time. A thing is said then to come about when it becomes known. Thus: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” [Note: [Col. 0197] Matt. 28]. “And every people, tribe, and tongue shall serve him”; for, as Isaiah says: “Every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall swear by the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0197] Isa. 45].

“His power is an everlasting power, which shall not be taken away, [Col. 0199A] and his kingdom one which shall not be corrupted.” For there shall be no end of his kingdom.

### “The angel Gabriel was sent to Mary, a virgin betrothed to Joseph.”

By these words Luke [Note: [Col. 0199] Ch. 1.] sets forth the order of the Annunciation. The Savior wished to be born of one betrothed, so that the order of generation might be established through a man; so that the mother might not, as an adulteress, be stoned; so that the virgin might have both the comfort of a husband and a witness to her integrity; and so that the devil might remain ignorant of the mystery of the incarnation.

### “Hail, Mary, full of grace.”

By these words the same Luke adds the manner of conception, saying: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee.” He shall come upon thee, I say, protecting thee and cleansing thee from every defilement; and then the power of the Most High, namely the Word of God, shall overshadow thee, taking flesh from thee [Col. 0199B]. A shadow is customarily formed by a body placed before light. The Virgin’s soul could not contain the fullness of divinity; and therefore the Power overshadowed the Virgin, making a shadow when the incomprehensible light of divinity assumed in her a body of humanity.

“For that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God.” We, conceived in sin [Note: [Col. 0199] Ps. 50], are by nature children of wrath [Note: [Col. 0199] Eph. 2], though we can be sanctified by grace. But Christ, who was not tithed in Abraham’s loins [Note: [Col. 0199] Heb. 7], was not conceived from male seed; therefore he is rightly born holy and called Son of God.

“How shall this be done in me, since I know not a man?” The Virgin had read: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive” [Note: [Col. 0199] Isa. 7]. Therefore she did not doubt that a virgin would give birth, for she knew the prophecy [Col. 0199C] must be fulfilled; but because she had not read or heard how it would happen, she asked how it was to be fulfilled. This is the mystery hidden from the saints, not foretold by the prophets, reserved for the angel [Note: [Col. 0199] Col. 1], as though she said: “How shall I conceive, who have resolved always to remain in virginity?” Taken interrogatively, it consists of two words; taken admiratively, it is one word.

Note the order. In the first responsory divinity is adored; in the second humanity is honored; in the third and fourth, the manner in which divinity was incarnate is shown. This incarnation is confirmed by the Apostle, who said, “We await a Savior” [Note: [Col. 0199] Phil. 3]; strengthened by the prophets, who say, “Hear the word of the Lord. Behold, a Virgin shall conceive” [Note: [Col. 0199] Isa. 7]; and proved by the Law, where Moses says: “I beseech thee, Lord, send whom thou wilt send” [Col. 0199D] [Note: [Col. 0199] Exod. 4]. And because he came, therefore “let the heavens rejoice and let the earth exult” [Note: [Col. 0199] Ps. 95].

### “We await a Savior.”

This saying of the Apostle has especial reference to the second coming. “Hear the word of the Lord” has been explained above; for we shall pass over what has been explained, but, if any ambiguity appears in what has not been explained, we shall not omit it.

### “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Wonderful, God, Mighty”  
[Note: [Col. 0199] Isa. 7–9.]

The Jews say [Col. 0200A] that here the word “virgin” does not mean integrity, but age—that is, a young woman. But on this interpretation there would be no sign, nor would Isaiah’s meaning be made clear. For when Ahaz had despaired of the liberation of his city and nation, the Lord said through Isaiah: “Ask for thyself a sign from the Lord, either in the depth of hell or in the height above” [Note: [Col. 0199] Ibid.]. It is as though he said: “Do you wish the earth to be split open or heaven opened?”

Moses received a sign from earth when he sent signs and wonders in the midst of the land of Egypt, upon Pharaoh and his servants: frogs, locusts, gnats, and the like [Note: [Col. 0199] Exod. 8]. He received signs also from heaven, such as hail and three days’ darkness [Note: [Col. 0199] Exod. 9]. Saul received one from the depth of hell when Samuel was raised [Note: [Col. 0199] I Sam. 28]. Hezekiah received one from heaven when the sun went back ten lines [Note: [Col. 0199] II Kings 20; Isa. 38]. And when Ahaz replied, “I will not ask, [Col. 0200B] nor will I tempt the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0199] Isa. 7], he heard: “Behold”—as though, “I show you”—“a Virgin shall conceive and bear a son; ‘the Word was made flesh’” [Note: [Col. 0199] John 1], the sign of our deliverance and salvation. “And his name shall be called,” etc. We shall speak more fully below concerning Christ’s names.

“He shall sit for ever upon the throne of David and upon his kingdom”: that is, upon the humble, as David was humble. For the humble are Christ’s throne, as he says: “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, save upon the humble and quiet?” [Note: [Col. 0199] Isa. 66.] They are Christ’s kingdom, which he shall hand over to God the Father [Note: [Col. 0199] I Cor. 15].

“I beseech thee, Lord, send whom thou wilt send; and behold the affliction of thy people” [Note: [Col. 0199] Exod. 4]. As thou hast spoken, come and deliver us from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea [Note: [Col. 0199] Ps. 106]. When the Lord had said to [Col. 0200C] Moses: “I have seen the affliction of my people in Egypt; I have come down to deliver them from the hand of the Egyptians” [Note: [Col. 0199] Exod. 3], “Come, and I will send thee, that thou mayest bring the children of Israel out of Egypt,” Moses said: “I beseech thee, Lord, send whom thou wilt send”—namely, thy Son—to deliver thy people.

“See the affliction of thy people”: how greatly it is afflicted in Egypt, that is, in the world, by Pharaoh, namely the devil; in the mud of lust and the bricks of avarice. “As thou hast spoken,” saying, “I have come down to deliver,” so come and deliver us who dwell from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and the sea [Note: [Col. 0199] Ps. 106], that is, the south. Or all this concerns the second coming: send thy Son to judge; look upon us to show mercy; come to deliver; from the rising of the sun, etc., because they shall come from east and west, north and south, and shall recline [Col. 0200D] with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob [Note: [Col. 0199] Matt. 8; Luke 13].

### “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall raise up for David a righteous Branch; and a King shall reign and be wise, and shall execute judgment and justice upon earth. And this is the name by which they shall call him: The Lord our Righteous One. In those days Judah shall be saved and Israel shall dwell securely.”

Jeremiah says these things [Note: [Col. 0199] Ch. 23.], which are understood particularly of the first coming.

“Strengthen the weary hands, and strengthen the weak knees; take courage in your minds, you who are faint-hearted; do not fear,” says [Col. 0201A] the Lord, “for I come to break the yoke of your captivity. Behold, the Lord Ruler shall come with power” [Note: [Col. 0201] Isa. 35.].

Isaiah exhorts them that heart and flesh may exult in the living God [Note: [Col. 0201] Ps. 83], saying: you whose hands have been loosened from good works and wearied by the burdens of sins, be strengthened in faith; you whose weak knees limp through diverse worships of idols, be strengthened in hope; and you faint-hearted, be strengthened in charity.
