Do not fear the devil’s snares, the adversities of the world, or those who kill the body; but fear him who can destroy body and soul in Gehenna [Note: [Col. 0201] Matt. 10], namely the Lord Ruler, who shall come with power to break the yoke of our captivity.

### “Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth exult”  
[Note: [Col. 0201] Ps. 95.]

The heavens are the greater and heavenly persons, such as preachers who declare [Col. 0201B] God’s glory [Note: [Col. 0201] Ps. 18], or angels. The earth consists of the lesser and earthly persons, such as hearers watered by the clouds of heaven. “Cry aloud, ye mountains, in praise, for our God shall come and have mercy upon his poor. In his days justice shall arise, and abundance of peace” [Note: [Col. 0201] Isa. 49; Ps. 85].

The mountains are those in whom Zion is founded, and upon whom the Bridegroom leaps. All are invited to praise because he comes with provision for the poor. By “poor” he means the nations without the Law. He also comes with justice and abundance of peace. Note that the responsory is from Isaiah while the verse is taken from a prophet, a kind of compilation from diverse places that you will often find in the antiphonary.

“Lift up thine eyes, O Jerusalem, and see the power of the King. Behold, the Savior comes to save thee from bondage” [Note: [Col. 0201] Isa. 62]. “Lift up thine eyes round about” [Note: [Col. 0201] Isa. 49, 60], and see the mighty King. [Col. 0201C] Isaiah exhorts the Church, or the soul, to raise the eyes of the mind and behold through understanding the mighty King, because he comes to free her from the bondage of sin, punishment, and the devil.

“Let the mountains break forth in joy and the hills in righteousness, for the light of the world comes with power. From Zion shall go forth the Law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.” These things are taken from Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0201] Ch. 2.], who invites greater and lesser persons to gladness and to the observance of justice, according as the Lord commanded it to be observed in Jerusalem, or as the primitive Church taught and observed it—the Church which was Zion through contemplation and Jerusalem through the vision of peace.

The morning praises signify both comings. [Col. 0201D] The first: “In that day,” when, according to Joel’s prophecy [Note: [Col. 0201] Ch. 3], the mountains—the Apostles—dripped the sweetness of preaching, and the hills—the doctors—flowed with the milk and honey of doctrine for lesser and greater persons. Then, according to Zechariah [Note: [Col. 0201] Ch. 9], Zion—that is, the Church from the Jews—rejoiced, and Jerusalem—that is, the Church from the Gentiles—exulted. Then all, that is, persons of every kind thirsting for salvation and knowledge, came, according to Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0201] Ch. 55], to the waters of baptism and doctrine.

The second: “Behold, the Lord shall come, and all his saints with him.” Enoch said this, as Jude [Note: [Col. 0201] v. 14.] asserts: “Behold, the Lord shall come with [Col. 0202A] his holy thousands to execute judgment against all.” “Behold, a great prophet shall come, and he shall renew Jerusalem by giving a new law and establishing new commandments.”

These responsories with their verses are sung at the Hours. Certain weekday antiphons are gathered from the prophetic books, and others from the Gospel. We have explained some above; others, because of their plainness, we leave for the reader to explain. The daytime office of the first Sunday signifies the Savior’s first coming.

Before all else, this general point must not be omitted: the holy Gospel is the chief of all that is said in the office of the Mass. For just as the head stands above the other members and the other members serve it, so the Gospel stands above the whole office of the Mass, [Col. 0202B] and all that is sung and read there agrees with it in spiritual meaning. For example, on this first Sunday of the Lord’s Advent the Gospel is read: “When the Lord drew near to Jerusalem, he sent two of his disciples to loose the tethered she-ass and bring her to him, so that he might sit gently upon her when loosed and lead her back to Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0201] Matt. 21]. Or it is read because of that clause: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” Or because the event described there is well suited to the season.

For this is why the Lord came—that is, came to us in the flesh: that, taking pity on the she-ass, namely the human race bound by the devil with the chains of sins, he might free her; rest upon her when loosed; and lead her back by the paths of his saving riding into the heavenly Jerusalem, whence she had been led away captive [Col. 0202C]. But because she is not led back unless she lifts up her soul to the Lord, at the Introit she sings: “To thee have I lifted up my soul, O my God” [Note: [Col. 0201] Ps. 24]. This is the voice of the human race, bound by the chains of original sin and idolatry, desiring to return to its heavenly fatherland. It is as though it said: “In the time of my wandering I lifted up my hands and my heart to the works of my hands, saying to wood or stone: ‘Thou art my God’” [Note: [Col. 0201] Jer. 2]. “But now, in the time of my healing and renewal, to thee have I lifted up my soul, because thou truly art my God, and therefore I trust in thee” [Note: [Col. 0201] Ps. 24].

Hence: “I shall not be put to shame, nor shall my enemies mock me” [Note: [Col. 0201] Ibid.], namely, may the demons who have long held me bound by the chains of sins neither confound me—and so it shall be. “For all who await thee shall not be confounded” [Col. 0202D] [Note: [Col. 0201] Ibid.]. And because I have lifted up my soul to thee in order to come to thee, therefore: “Show me thy ways, O Lord, and teach me thy paths” [Note: [Col. 0201] Ibid.], that is, thy commandments and counsels.

And because one often passes from the way to wandering, Paul teaches in the Epistle which ways are to be followed and which avoided, saying: “Knowing that now is the hour for us to rise from sleep” [Note: [Col. 0201] Rom. 13]. The way is to rise from sleep, put on the armor of light, and walk honestly [Note: [Col. 0201] Ibid.]. Wandering is to be sluggish in the night, work the works of darkness, and take delight in revellings and similar things. The Epistle concludes: “Put on [Col. 0203A] the Lord Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0203] Ibid.], which is the same as saying to the she-ass: “Receive the King as thy rider.” But because it depends not on him who wills or runs, but on God who shows mercy [Note: [Col. 0203] Rom. 9], the Alleluia adds: “Show us thy mercy, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0203] Ps. 84].

The Gradual and Offertory repeat the Introit, and this repetition is made so that he who stands may see that he does not fall [Note: [Col. 0203] I Cor. 10]. “Blessed is the man who is always fearful” [Note: [Col. 0203] Prov. 28]. Behold, a person has lifted up his soul to the Lord, has learned the Lord’s ways, has risen from sleep, and, like the she-ass, has received the rider. Yet it may happen that the soul declines toward earthly things, fails to know the ways, and the sleep of the mind steals upon it, so that the offended rider wishes to change his vehicle. Therefore the Gradual repeats: “All who await thee,” etc.; and, “Thy ways,” etc. The Offertory continues: “To thee have I lifted up,” etc. [Col. 0203B] It also adds: “Direct me in thy truth” [Note: [Col. 0203] Ps. 24].

### Communion: “The Lord shall give goodness”  
[Note: [Col. 0203] Ps. 84.]

Today’s singer, that is, the human race, consoles itself, seeing through the Prophet’s mouth that, by the goodness of the Holy Spirit, our earth—that is, the blessed Virgin in conceiving—“shall yield her fruit” [Note: [Col. 0203] Ibid.], namely God and man. Through him it shall be freed from the bonds of sins and led back to its fatherland.

The prayers plainly look to the first coming. Accordingly, the station is at Saint Peter’s, for he is the first of the Apostles sent to loose the she-ass. Paul was his companion at Rome, so that, just as those two were sent in Jerusalem to loose the beast of burden, these men were sent to Rome, that they might make the capital of the world, freed [Col. 0203C] from sins, into the vehicle of Jesus Christ.

Note that blessed Gregory arranged the stations, in which he expounded twenty Gospel homilies at various times. Other homilies, when his stomach was weak, he entrusted to others to deliver. Some churches, however, read the Gospel: “There shall be signs in the sun and moon” [Note: [Col. 0203] Luke 21], which pertains to the Savior’s second coming. There it is said: “The kingdom of God is near.” The Epistle is fitted to this, where it says: “Our salvation is nearer” [Note: [Col. 0203] Rom. 13]. And because thy kingdom, O Lord, is near, therefore the singer—the old man, or John the Baptist, as some say—says: “To thee have I lifted up my soul, O my God”; and therefore: “Show me thy ways,” and “Show me thy mercy” [Note: [Col. 0203] Ps. 84]. And, as though assured concerning mercy, he concludes: “The Lord shall give [Col. 0203D] goodness,” that is, good affection; and “our earth,” namely the flesh, “shall yield her fruit,” that is, good works. The prayers may likewise suitably be adapted to the second coming.

On Wednesday and Friday, Gospels are read concerning John’s manner of life and preaching. His preaching partly pertains to the second coming, as in: “Offspring of vipers, who taught you to flee from the wrath to come?” [Note: [Col. 0203] Matt. 3.] Again: “The axe is laid to the root of the tree” [Note: [Col. 0203] Ibid.]. Again: “His winnowing-fan is in his hand” [Note: [Col. 0203] Ibid.]. The Epistle is therefore matched to these: “Give thanks” [Note: [Col. 0203] I Thess. 5], where the faith of the Thessalonians and the future judgment are treated.

It partly pertains to the first coming, as: “One mightier than I comes.” Hence is taken the morning antiphon: “One mightier comes after me, whose sandal-strap I am not worthy,” that is, not sufficient, “to loose” [Note: [Col. 0203] Matt. 3]—that is, to disclose the sacrament of the incarnation.

Here certain general matters concerning the whole Advent must be added. Throughout Advent the whole of Isaiah is read, because he not only prophesies but also proclaims as Gospel the Savior’s first and second comings. The reader should omit, however, what is read at Christmas: “The people of the Gentiles, at the first time” [Note: [Col. 0203] Isa. 9]; “Comfort ye” [Note: [Col. 0203] Isa. 40]; “Arise” [Note: [Col. 0203] Isa. 52]; and what is read at Epiphany: “Arise, be enlightened” [Note: [Col. 0203] Isa. 60]. For these concern Christ already born; the rest concern him who is to be born.

Yet in the fasts of the four [Col. 0204B] seasons and on the vigil, Isaiah is not read, because they have their own readings and offices. Likewise, throughout Advent the songs of gladness are silenced: *Te Deum laudamus*, *Gloria in excelsis*, and *Ite missa est*, because the righteous before Christ’s coming were held in the sorrow of hell. Or this is done so that the grace of the New Testament may be recognized as superior to that of the Old.

Or *Te Deum laudamus* is silenced so that it may be resumed more festively on the feast day with greater joy, for what is rare is more precious. Thus in Samuel:

“And the word of the Lord was precious” [Note: [Col. 0203] 1 Sam. 3], because it was rare, or because he whom we await was not yet present; for speech is directed to one who is present. *Glory in the highest* is omitted for similar reasons. Or, thirdly [Col. 0204C], so that it may be sung as though newly on the day on which it first began through the angels. *Ite missa est* is omitted so that the people, who must be continually instructed, may not be dismissed.

Beware of those who simply assert that these three invariably accompany one another in alternation. Although they often do, they do not always do so. For on the Chair of Blessed Peter, even if it falls in Lent, according to some, *Te Deum laudamus* is sung while the others are omitted, because we customarily use this chant for enthroning bishops in their sees. And on this day Peter was enthroned in the chair of Antioch. Moreover, *Gloria in excelsis* and *Ite missa est* are said at the Lord’s Supper if a bishop is present and celebrates the office of the oil; but *Te Deum laudamus* is omitted. Moreover, *Gloria in excelsis* is sung at the night Mass of the Nativity [Col. 0204D]; yet, according to some, *Ite missa est* is not to be said until the third Mass, so that the people may know that they are still to hear a third Mass.

But *Alleluia* is not omitted in Advent, because of the ancient fathers’ firm hope in Christ’s incarnation and our certainty concerning future glorification. Likewise, throughout Advent garments of rejoicing are laid aside: the subdeacon does not wear a tunic, nor does the deacon wear a dalmatic. For the Law, signified by the subdeacon, lacked the adornment of the Gospel before the Lord’s incarnation; and the brightness of the Gospel, signified by the deacon, [Col. 0205A] had not yet appeared. Or this is because he had not yet come who was to clothe us with the garment of innocence and immortality. Or it is so that these garments may be assumed with greater eagerness on the feast, since everything rare is dear.

They do, however, wear the chasuble, the priestly garment—not in order to read or minister in it; rather, those about to read or administer take it off, professing that it is not their proper garment, but that they receive it on loan out of reverence for some feast. Or it represents charity; and therefore the deacon, when reading the Gospel, folds it over his shoulder, because a preacher ought in charity to bear both his own burdens and those of another [Note: [Col. 0205] Gal. 6], to gird his own loins [Note: [Col. 0205] Luke 12], and to have burning lamps in his hands for his own people [Note: [Col. 0205] Luke 11]. Or the practice was derived from the ancient priests, who, while sacrificing, threw the ends of their girdle over the left shoulder.

[Col. 0205B] Likewise, throughout Advent, according to some, the Hours of the Blessed Virgin are kept silent, because her whole office belongs to her praise. Similarly, special suffrages of the saints are omitted, as some say, both in the collects of the Mass and at Vespers and the other Hours, because every day a general commemoration of all saints is made by this antiphon: “Behold, the Lord will come, and all his saints with him,” and by this prayer: “Cleanse our consciences,” etc., which, some say, is always to be said at Matins and Vespers after *Benedicamus Domino*, though others say before it—but beware. For if it is said, “We beseech you, Lord, cleanse our consciences by visiting them, so that Jesus Christ our Lord, when he comes with all his saints, may find in us a dwelling prepared for himself,” [Col. 0205C] it pertains to the advent in the mind. For there are three advents: in the flesh, in the mind, and in majesty.

Observe also that from the first Sunday of Advent until Epiphany weddings should not be celebrated. Indeed, a husband ought even to abstain from the marriage-bed unless the marital debt is demanded, because during Advent one should devote oneself to prayer and to the sacred solemnities together with their weekdays. Yet some are troubled that we said “until Epiphany,” wondering whether this prohibition extends to the Octave. Some say that it would extend thus, were it not that the Lord honored marriage both by his presence and by a miracle. It is sounder to hold that it does extend, just as the office concerning the conversion of water into wine is deferred until the Sunday which follows the Octave of Epiphany. [Note: [Col. 0205] This extension has now been abolished by decree of the Council of Trent; hence the prohibition is extended inclusively to the third day of Epiphany.]

[Col. 0205D] A similar reason underlies the prohibition during the three weeks before the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist: namely, that people may devote themselves more freely to prayer. For the Church had instituted two Lents besides the greater one: one before the Lord’s Nativity and another before the birth of Blessed John, during which prayers, fasts, and almsgiving were to occupy them. But owing to human frailty the two were reduced to one; and that one likewise was divided into the three weeks of Advent, except where an interruption is made for the reason stated above. During these weeks one must devote oneself without interruption to fasts, [Col. 0206A] almsgiving, and prayer, and therefore abstain from weddings.

Thus Advent is celebrated partly in affliction, when we fast, because we do not yet possess what we hope for at the second Advent; and partly in joy, when we say *Alleluia*, because through the first Advent we have been assured of what we hope for at the second. Thus we fast on account of the delay affecting both ourselves and the ancients. But we rejoice, as in the week of Pentecost, because of the certainty of future blessedness.

## CHAPTER II. THE SECOND SUNDAY OF ADVENT

“Your salvation, Jerusalem, will come quickly.” This office for the second week is drawn partly from the prophetic books and partly from the Gospels. Its responsories [Col. 0206B] and antiphons alike concern both advents. Let this suffice concerning it. For it was enough to provide, in the readings of the first office, a model of exposition; to undertake an exposition of them all would produce a work excessively long and full, and would generate weariness.

It is noteworthy that the chant is renewed each week, because of the joy of those who make progress, who advance from virtue to virtue, that they may see the God of gods in Zion [Note: [Col. 0205] Ps. 83]. The second daytime office signifies the Savior’s advent, in which the Gospel is read [Note: [Col. 0205] Luke 21]: “There will be signs in sun and moon.” After the signs that will precede the glorious advent have been set forth, it adds: “Then they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven.” Thereupon follows the cry of the child of an exiled people, of an exiled mother, lamenting the absence of [Col. 0206C] the father whom he has not yet seen: “When these things begin to happen, lift up your heads, because your redemption draws near”; and below: “The kingdom of God is near.”

To him as he weeps—because his sojourn in misery is prolonged [Note: [Col. 0205] Ps. 119]—his compassionate mother, gladdening and consoling him, sounds in the Introit with the prophetic trumpet: “People of Zion, behold, the Lord will come to save the nations, and he will make heard the glory of his voice” [Note: [Col. 0205] Isa. 30], namely this voice: “Come, blessed of my Father” [Note: [Col. 0205] Matt. 25]. But because without prayer there is no consolation of the mind, only a sign of crafty betrayal, it therefore adds: “Give heed, O shepherd of Israel, who lead Joseph like a sheep” [Note: [Col. 0205] Ps. 79], and the collect adds: “Stir up, O Lord.”

The following Epistle agrees with this consolation, namely: “Whatever things were written” [Col. 0206D]—which invites us to patience and to the consolation of the Scriptures, so that through them we may have hope in those things promised by the ancient fathers [Note: [Col. 0205] Rom. 15], namely the salvation of the nations and the joy of the saints. The Gradual, “Out of Zion comes the splendor of his beauty” [Note: [Col. 0205] Ps. 49], sings that he is manifestly to come, whose beauty is from Zion—that is, salvation is from the Jews—and announces him to those saints who are to be gathered at the right hand, because they established the New Testament upon sacrifices.

Having heard his mother’s consolation [Col. 0207A] concerning the father’s coming, the salvation of his own people, and his companion’s joy, the son rejoices in the *Alleluia*, saying: “I rejoiced at the things said to me: ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord.’ Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0207] Ps. 121]. Afterwards, assured through the Gospel where it says, “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” [Note: [Col. 0207] Matt. 24], he says more confidently at the Offertory: “O God, when you turn, you will give us life” [Note: [Col. 0207] Ps. 84].

The Communion, “Jerusalem, arise” [Note: [Col. 0207] Baruch 5], concludes the central meaning of this office: it exhorts the exiled Jerusalem—that is, the present Church—to endure patiently the exile of this life. In enduring, let it arise; in arising, let it stand on high; standing, let it see the joy that will come to it from the Lord. To arise and stand is what the Gospel calls lifting up one’s heads; this is what the collect concludes: [Col. 0207B] to despise earthly things and love heavenly ones. Therefore the station is fittingly held on this day at Jerusalem, for whose heart’s consolation the entire office is ordered; or because in the *Alleluia* is sung, “Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem.”

Some read the Gospel, “When John had heard” [Note: [Col. 0207] Matt. 11], which concerns the second Advent because John asks, “Are you he who is to come, or are we to await another?” To him the Lord replies: “Behold, I came to redeem, and I shall come again to save; this you may infer from the signs, because the blind see” [Note: [Col. 0207] ibid.; Isa. 35], etc. On Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday the Gospels are read concerning Christ’s testimony about John, and John’s testimony about Christ and his advent, of which the Epistle speaks: “Be patient” [Note: [Col. 0207] Jas. 5].

## CHAPTER III. THE THIRD SUNDAY OF ADVENT

[Col. 0207C]

“Behold, the Lord will appear” [Note: [Col. 0207] Rev. 14]. In this office also the materials are compiled partly from prophecy and partly from the Gospel. Both antiphons and responsories concern what is common to both advents. But the daytime office pertains especially to the joy of preachers, who teach others concerning the Lord’s advent. Therefore the Gospel is read concerning that famous preacher, John the Baptist: “The Jews sent” [Note: [Col. 0207] John 1], or “When he had heard”—John who pointed out the Lord with his finger and proclaimed his coming. The Lord denied that he was a man clothed in soft garments and announced, by prophetic utterance, that in office or merits he was an angel, saying: “Behold, I send my angel” [Note: [Col. 0207] Matt. 11; Mal. 3].

Who should not blush to weep when, through the office [Col. 0207D] of preaching, he deserves to be called by the title of angel? Rather, rejoice. The Apostle sings in the Introit: “Let your moderation be known to all men” [Note: [Col. 0207] Phil. 4]. If they shut their eyes and refuse to see it shining before them, be anxious about nothing; for the Lord is near, because he will thrust your light even upon those unwilling to see it. Only let your petitions be made known to God. For that single witness will prevail against all detractors: he who will turn away Jacob’s captivity [Note: [Col. 0207] Ps. 84], who will fill you with peace [Col. 0208A] surpassing all understanding [Note: [Col. 0207] Rom. 15].

Having heard consolation concerning the Lord’s Advent, the ruler of the Church prays in the collect, “Incline your ear,” that by his visitation he may illuminate the darkness we suffer when we are falsely judged. And in the Epistle he exhorts his subjects: “Let a man so account of us” [Note: [Col. 0207] 1 Cor. 4], so that they may think nothing but good of their teachers and judge nothing before the time. Even if whisperers do not cease to judge, he consoles himself, saying: “It is a very small matter to me that I should be judged by you or by a human day” [Note: [Col. 0207] ibid.].

But because the burden of detractors is heavy, in the Gradual and *Alleluia* he calls upon him who sits above the cherubim [Note: [Col. 0207] Ps. 79]—that is, who possesses fullness of knowledge—to stir up his power, come, and give heed: to illuminate the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of hearts [Note: [Col. 0207] 1 Cor. 4]; to turn away captivity [Col. 0208B] [Note: [Col. 0207] Ps. 13]; and to forgive iniquity [Note: [Col. 0207] Ps. 84]. Since this will undoubtedly happen, the ruler at the Offertory confidently uses the past for the future, saying: “You have blessed, Lord, your land” [Note: [Col. 0207] ibid.].

The Communion, “Say to the faint-hearted” [Note: [Col. 0207] Isa. 35], is the conclusion of this office’s central message: rulers are exhorted that, though made faint-hearted by the dishonor of detraction, they may nevertheless be strengthened through the conscience of the heart and devotion of mind, and may trust in the Savior’s advent—as is afterwards requested in the Postcommunion. This office, established concerning the rulers of the Church, accords with the station at Saint Peter, who held primacy as ruler.

On the Wednesday of this third week the fast of the winter season is instituted. Among the weekdays, Wednesday and Friday are assigned to fasts [Col. 0208C] because they are especially distinguished above the others by remembrance of the Lord’s Passion. For on Wednesday the Lord was sold by Judas, but on Friday he was crucified by the Jews. Hence also every week has its proper readings from the Gospels and Epistles.

Thus the fasts of the Four Seasons began under the Law, concerning which Zechariah says [Note: [Col. 0207] Zech. 8]: “The fast of the fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and tenth [month] shall be turned for the house of Judah and Jerusalem into festive days of joy.” As Jerome says on Zechariah, they instituted these fasts in those months because of various calamities that occurred to them at those times; nor is this without mystery. For as there are four elements of the body and four seasons of the year, each divided into three months [Col. 0208D], so we fast four times in the year for three days: the three days corresponding to the three months, while we offer to the Lord one day of each month, contented with wholesome restraints [*contentatiis*, sic], that he may grant us a tranquil life, protect the body’s four elements, and by fasting wear down and chastise wanton bodies. Or we fast three times four, that we may offer to the Lord the firstfruits of our days.

This winter fast is more solemn than the fasts of the other seasons, having a fuller office and pertaining to the Savior’s advent. Thus, while [Col. 0209A] the flesh is afflicted by fasting, the soul is delighted by testimonies of its redemption from sacred reading or the Church’s song. Indeed, it pertains to the Savior’s advent in such a way that it pertains to his temple, the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit—the Blessed Virgin, I mean—in whom God dwelt for nine months and deigned to become man.

For the Gospel reads: “The angel was sent” [Note: [Col. 0209] Luke 1]. It recounts the announcement of the bridal friend, the virgin’s consent, and the Lord’s Incarnation, which had previously been proclaimed by prophetic trumpets. Hence the prophet sings beforehand in the Introit: “Drop down dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One” [Note: [Col. 0209] Isa. 45]. He says “drop dew” and “rain,” because the Word descended into the chamber of the believing virgin as rain descends upon the fleece [Note: [Col. 0209] Judg. 6; Ps. 71]. By “heavens” and “clouds” he meant angels and prophets, who declare the glory of God [Note: [Col. 0209] Ps. 18].

In the prophetic [Col. 0209B] reading, “It shall be in the last days” [Note: [Col. 0209] Isa. 2], he speaks of the mountain of the Lord, which grew from a small stone into a mountain [Note: [Col. 0209] Dan. 2], which will reign in the house of Jacob. Hence the Gradual fittingly follows: “Lift up; the King of glory shall enter,” and: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?” [Note: [Col. 0209] Ps. 23].

In the Epistle reading, “The Lord spoke to Ahaz: Ask a sign for yourself from the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0209] Isa. 7], he manifestly speaks of the Blessed Virgin. The Gradual is fittingly joined to it: “The Lord is near to all who call upon him” [Note: [Col. 0209] Ps. 144], as though saying: “Ask, because he is near.” And lest any doubt steal in, the Offertory adds, “Be strengthened”; another Offertory, according to some, is “Hail Mary.” The Communion, “Behold, a virgin,” is taken from the Gospel; and therefore today’s station at Saint Mary is fitting.

[Col. 0209C] On Friday the Gospel is read: “Rising up” [Note: [Col. 0209] Luke 1], and the Epistle reading: “A rod shall come forth” [Note: [Col. 0209] Isa. 11], which are manifestly understood of the Lord’s advent and the Blessed Virgin. Since he was in the immaculate Virgin, he was near. Therefore in the Introit the Church sings beforehand: “Be near, O Lord,” and “Blessed are the immaculate” [Note: [Col. 0209] Ps. 118]. The Gradual, “Show us, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0209] Ps. 84], and the Offertory, “You, O God,” or according to others, “Hear, O Israel,” look to the first advent. Since the heavens proclaimed it [Note: [Col. 0209] Ps. 18]—that is, the apostles preached it—and since they will judge with the Lord at the second advent [Note: [Col. 0209] Matt. 19], today’s station is therefore at the Holy Apostles. Of them it is said in the Virgin’s canticle, mentioned in the Gospel: “He has cast down the mighty”—that is, the proud scribes and Pharisees—[Col. 0209D] “and exalted the humble” [Note: [Col. 0209] Luke 1], that is, the apostles. And in the Communion: “Behold, the Lord will come, and all his saints with him” [Note: [Col. 0209] Jude 14].

The following Saturday, and all Saturdays of the Four Seasons, are called Saturdays of the twelve readings, although only six are read. This derives from an ancient Roman custom. Since the Roman Church comprised both Greeks and Latins, each reading was recited in both languages, because if recited in only one language it was not understood by the peoples of both languages; or this was done to signify the unanimity of the two peoples. [Col. 0210A] It is said that this is still done in the Eastern Church. Thus, since each is read twice, the doubled six are counted as twelve—not on account of twelve different readings or passages.

But if two readings are read on Wednesday and six on Saturday, why is Friday left impoverished with one? It would seem better for this ninefold set to be divided among the three days, three by three. Yet this is not without reason. For it is established that ordinations be celebrated on the Saturdays of the Four Seasons. Those to be ordained on Saturday are selected on the preceding Wednesday. They are selected on Wednesday because in the fourth age Levites were assigned by David [Note: [Col. 0209] 2 Sam. 6] and Solomon [Note: [Col. 0209] 3 Kgs. 8] to ministries of the Temple.

Those selected must be examined in the pages of both Testaments. Therefore two readings are read [Col. 0210B]. The first has a descending tone and signifies the first Testament, which promised earthly things, as: “I will give you a land flowing with milk and honey” [Note: [Col. 0209] Num. 14]; hence we bend the knees toward the earth. The second has an ascending tone and signifies the second—that is, the New Testament—which promises heavenly, eternal, and exalted things, as: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0209] Matt. 5].

For although these two Testaments seem on the surface of the letter to promise two different things, in the Spirit they promise the one thing of which it is said: “But one thing is necessary” [Note: [Col. 0209] Luke 10]. They direct us toward that one and eternal thing of which it is said: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of [Col. 0210C] my life” [Note: [Col. 0209] Ps. 26]. Therefore, on Friday, on which we were created, only one reading is read and it is sung in a high tone.

But because one arrives at that one thing only through works of mercy, six readings are read on Saturday. Or, two readings are read on Wednesday because in the fourth age the observance of Law and prophecy was commanded. The knees are bent once, because both in Law and prophecy worship of one God is commanded. On Friday one reading is recited because in the sixth age Law and prophecy are fulfilled in evangelical unity. There *Flectamus genua* (“Let us bend the knees”) is said, because Christ the Lawgiver is worshipped.

Or, although two readings are recited on Wednesday for the reasons stated, according to the progress of the fast three ought to be recited on Friday [Col. 0210D] and four on Saturday. But two are transferred from Friday to Saturday. With one remaining on Friday, six are recited on Saturday, so that an abundance of the sacred office to be performed may be reserved for those to be ordained. They are instructed both in fasting and enlisted as recruits in sacred warfare. Four of these readings are divided among the first four orders so that after each prayer one order follows; after each order has been conferred, one reading with its responsory follows, as though it were said: “The Church prays for you who are to be ordained, and these orders are given you for reading and chanting. Go, therefore, to read and sing.”

But see that what you read and chant with your mouths you believe with your hearts, and what you believe with your hearts you prove by your works. See that you abound in the four virtues, so that you may belong to the four orders which bless the Lord, to whom the Psalmist says: “House of Israel, bless the Lord; House of Aaron, bless the Lord; House of Levi, bless the Lord; you who fear the Lord, bless the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0211] Ps. 113; Ps. 134].

Whatever the origin of the four preceding readings and responsories, the fifth reading, “The angel of the Lord came down,” together with the preceding prayer and following hymn, is not changed either on this Saturday or on the other Saturdays of the Four Seasons. It is always read continuously in the fifth place [Col. 0211B] and concerns fasting. For just as heavenly grace aided the children cast by the Babylonian king into the furnace, and made the middle of the furnace like a wind blowing with dew [Note: [Col. 0211] Dan. 3], so the urgency of fasts and prayers frees those cast down by the king of confusion, the devil, through the incentives of lust. “For this kind of demons is not cast out except by prayer and fasting” [Note: [Col. 0211] Matt. 17].

Once delivered, they are bound to praise the Lord and, lest they appear ungrateful for benefits, to magnify him with songs. Or these things concern the sacrament of the following sacred orders. For, because the furnace tests a potter’s vessels [Note: [Col. 0211] Sir. 27], and because the Apostle says: “Let these first be tested, and then let them minister” [Note: [Col. 0211] 1 Tim. 3], the prophecy of the furnace is placed before the sacred orders. For just as the children were tested in the furnace [Col. 0211C] of fire, so those to be ordained to sacred offices are tested in the furnace of tribulation. Hence blessings follow, because after testing they are crowned.

The following prayer also pertains to this: “O God, who [to] the three children...” After the order of subdeacon is conferred, the Epistle is assigned to the newly made subdeacon. At the prayers over the prophecies we bend the knees, but by no means at the Epistle. Some, however, never bend the knees at “The angel of the Lord,” lest they seem to worship Nebuchadnezzar’s statue.

Afterwards the order of the diaconate is conferred, so that the Gospel may be assigned to the newly made deacon. Then priests are ordained, so that the recruits may enter the altar with the ordainer, standing on either side and making the signs along with him who makes them. Some, however, confer sacred orders between the reading “The angel of the Lord” and the Epistle [Col. 0211D], so that after consecration they may set before the consecrated men the Epistle and Gospel, after the manner of a good shepherd who, when sending his son, teaches him what and how he is to act. By the Epistle they are admonished to preserve the blessing they have received; by the Gospel it is said to them: “Go, teach all nations” [Note: [Col. 0211] Matt. 28].

Some, after conferring the subdiaconate before the Epistle for the reason stated, immediately after it confer the diaconate and priesthood. Once these have been conferred, they burst into the joyful cry, “Praise,” because these orders especially are invited to praises. These orders are chiefly conferred about the Gospel because [Col. 0212A] Moses and Aaron ordained Levites for the ministry of the tabernacle, and Christ sent seventy-two ordained disciples to preach.

It is also noteworthy that orders are especially conferred at the Four Seasons, which are the firstfruits of the days, so that those to be ordained may know themselves to be leaders of the Church; that they may be adorned with the four virtues; and that they may be admonished to serve Christ and the Church under the four Gospels. In spring, that they may flower in virtues; in summer, that they may burn with charity; in autumn, that they may gather the fruit of good works; and in winter, that they may preserve the harvest in the granary and enjoy it in the Lord.

They are also conferred in Lent, so that they may wither from vices; amid fasts, by those who are fasting and upon those who are fasting, that they may imitate the apostles. When the apostles appointed Paul and Barnabas [Col. 0212B] to evangelize the nations [Note: [Col. 0211] Acts 13], and established presbyters through the churches, they laid hands on them while fasting and praying [Note: [Col. 0211] Acts 14], commending them to the Lord in whom they had believed. Thus they may understand with how great devotion, on the part of both givers and recipients, the sacrament of this blessing ought to be conferred.

It is celebrated on Saturday because, among all days, the Lord especially sanctified the Sabbath [Note: [Col. 0211] Gen. 2]. By this we understand that the ordained ought to cease not only from servile work but also from vices [Note: [Col. 0211] Exod. 20]. Yet today, although it occurs on Saturday, it ought to be assigned to the Lord’s Day. Therefore ordination should be celebrated on its eve, from which it takes its beginning, and may fittingly be extended to the morning of the Lord’s Day, provided the fast is continued. [Col. 0212C] The mysteries of priestly blessings are fittingly celebrated on this day, on which the charisms of graces were bestowed.

For on this day the Lord rose again; on this day, as it is said, he “breathed on the apostles, saying: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them’” [Note: [Col. 0211] John 20]. On this day the promised Spirit came. Hence we rightly direct the priestly blessing to this day, so that with the risen Lord we may walk in newness of life [Note: [Col. 0211] Rom. 6], and with the apostles may joyfully sing: “Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful”—namely, those ordained.

That ordination is celebrated on the Saturday of Mid-Lent and on Holy Saturday, as is found in the canons, perhaps refers to the rites and office of those days, so that, just as neophytes were then called to baptism, [Col. 0212D] so they may be called to the sacrament of this character. This solemn observance of the aforesaid days must be observed only for sacred orders. Lesser orders, however, bishops may confer on notable days. But no bishop, except the Roman pontiff, may promote anyone to the subdiaconate or beyond except on the days specified above. Therefore Scottish bishops are rebuked who promoted their subjects to sacred orders at church dedications.

Peter, first and chief among the apostles, instituted ordinations of this kind; after Christ, the supreme pontificate of the Church was entrusted to him. Therefore [Col. 0213A] both on this Saturday and on the other Saturdays of the Four Seasons the station is fittingly held at Saint Peter’s.

Let us now return to the central meaning of the office, which concerns both advents, as was evident in the preceding readings—except the fifth—and responsories; and as is also clear in the Epistle, “We beseech you” [Note: [Col. 0213] 2 Thess. 2], which deals with the son of iniquity, whom the Lord will destroy by the brightness of his advent. The Tract accompanies the Epistle, lest the ordained man be raised up in pride, but rather be humbled to mourning for himself and others.

The Gospel, “In the fifteenth year,” belongs to the Advent, where it says: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” [Note: [Col. 0213] Luke 3]. That the Offertory, “Rejoice, daughter” [Note: [Col. 0213] Zech. 9], and the Communion, “He rejoiced as a giant” [Note: [Col. 0213] Ps. 18], likewise belong to it is evident to everyone [Col. 0213B] without ambiguity.

Nor should this be passed over in silence: this Saturday must always precede the Lord’s vigil, both because each day has its own office and because Saturday concerns the Advent, whereas the vigil does not, but concerns the Nativity and belongs to the season of joy. This is evident from Gregory’s arrangement itself, for he assigned as the final Advent antiphons to the Gospel: “The days were fulfilled” and “Behold, all things were fulfilled” [Note: [Col. 0213] Luke 2].

Therefore, since Advent should regularly have at least twenty-one days—that is, three complete weeks besides the Lord’s vigil—and since it always begins on a Sunday, if Christmas falls on Sunday Advent must be extended through four weeks. If it falls on Monday [Col. 0213C], fasting will take place on Saturday both for the fast of the Four Seasons and for the vigil; and on Sunday the office of the vigil will be celebrated, while *Alleluia* will be sung because of Advent or the Lord’s Day.

Observe that we understand the three weeks of Advent as three periods of the fathers. The first were before the Law; as a grain cast into the earth is remote from fruit, so they, far removed from the Lord, cry in the Introit: “To you have I lifted up [my soul]” [Note: [Col. 0213] Ps. 24]. The second were under the Law; instructed by the Law’s teaching and thus drawing nearer to the light, they are called the people of Zion in the Introit. The third were the prophets, especially those whom that Nativity found, such as Simeon; because the Redeemer was near to them, it is said in the Introit of the Mass: “Rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0213] Phil. 4].

Some say that the office of the first Sunday [Col. 0213D] concerns the calling of the Jews; the second, the calling of the nations—hence it says there, “to save the nations”; and the third, the calling of both peoples—hence here it says, “Rejoice, rejoice.” It is sung on the first Sunday in the person of John; on the second, in the person of the prophets; on the third, in the person of the apostles; and on the following fourth, in the person of teachers—again speaking of the calling of the nations and exhorting them to persevere in the grace conferred, so that from the grace of hope they may come to the glory of sight.

## CHAPTER IV. THE FOURTH SUNDAY OF ADVENT
Blow the trumpet in Zion [Note: [Col. 0213] Joel 2]. In this history also, compiled for the Fourth Sunday [Col. 0214A] partly from the Prophets and partly from the Gospel, the matters common to both Advents are sung, and especially the calling of the Gentiles through Christ’s coming is declared. Thus, in the person of the Apostles or doctors, it is said: “Blow the trumpet; call the Gentiles”; while in the Gradual: “The Lord is near.” This Sunday was formerly entitled “vacant,” either because it has no office of its own but borrows another’s, namely *Rorate*, and this because the Apostolic See was occupied with the ordinations of the preceding day—for ordinations were often customarily celebrated by the Apostolic See in December—or because it exceeds the number of Advent days, namely twenty-one, which ought not to have been counted among the Sundays of Advent but called vacant; or rather because the station of this day is assigned, as is read, to no saint [Col. 0214B], and rightly so. For today the Gospel is read: “The Jews sent,” in which John says: “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal” [Note: [Col. 0213] John 1]. If, therefore, John—than whom none greater has arisen among those born of women [Note: [Col. 0213] Matt. 11]—is not sufficient to lay bare the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation (“For who shall declare his generation?” [Note: [Col. 0213] Isa. 53]), namely how the Word is embodied, how it is made alive, endowed with a soul, how the Alpha is conceived: to which saint may this mystery be entrusted, so that this office may be celebrated before him at its fitting station?

Moreover, if the offices are properly considered, they seem to accord with the virtues or merits of those saints at whose solemn stations they are appointed. Thus, at St Peter’s, who possesses the primacy of binding and loosing [Note: [Col. 0213] Matt. 16], the station is celebrated when the loosing of the she-ass is proclaimed to us in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0213] Matt. 21]; thus, when scrutinies are held or catechumens are signed, recourse is had to the teacher of the Gentiles. Therefore this Sunday is vacant, not because its office is unauthentic or because it lacks a proper office, but because it is reasonably excepted from the most orderly arrangement of stations: for it has a subject inaccessible to investigation by any saint, bestowed upon all, yet administered by the Holy Spirit alone, who, in the bridal chamber of the Virgin’s womb, alone was mediator, alone privy, and the sole master of the feast of the heavenly marriage.

In that womb, seeing that divinity would be shod, the Gentile world, according to certain modern writers, cries out to it in the Introit [Col. 0214D], saying: “Remember us, O Lord, in the favour shown to thy people” [Note: [Col. 0213] Ps. 105]; that is, in the Son, in whom alone thou wast well pleased beyond the thousands of the people, who was thine from the beginning of the world. It then rejoices with others in the Epistle, saying: “Rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0213] Phil. 4]. In view likewise of the Virgin’s womb it sings in the Gradual that the Lord is near and that his coming is swift; in the Alleluia: “Come, Lord”; in the Offertory: “Be strengthened”; in the Communion: “Behold, a Virgin.” These are well known: in them it longs, consoles itself, and concludes the ground of its consolation.

And observe that the week next before the Nativity is rightly called the Preparation; in its history is sung “Cry aloud with strength,” which belongs not, as simple people suppose, [Col. 0215A] to the four Ember Days, but to the Lord’s approaching Nativity. Hence it is sung with six matutinal lauds: because through six ages the ancients prepared themselves for the Advent, and we too are prepared for the Second Advent through the six works of mercy. Nevertheless, we customarily sing, on the eighth day beforehand, the ferial antiphons written for the feast of St Thomas; and it is fitting that the chants be renewed before the approaching Nativity. For just as the minds of subjects are more and more stirred to care in receiving their superior by many, increasingly frequent, and new messengers, so through the renewal of chants we are more strongly aroused that we may be a dwelling worthy of the coming Lord.

Yet the whole of Advent may also be called Preparation. Hence at the beginning it is read: “Let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armour of light,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0215] Rom. 13]. All these are marks of preparation.

In this week seven antiphons of the second tone are sung, each in order on its own day, until the Nativity. They are of the second tone because they are directed to Christ, who became a giant of twofold substance; and there are seven because upon him rested the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0215] Isa. 11]. Through these seven gifts he ministered to us the grace of his Incarnation. For he is the Wisdom through which the Father made all things [Note: [Col. 0215] Ps. 103], who came in the spirit of wisdom to teach us the way of prudence. He is Adonai, [Col. 0215C] who declared his name to Moses [Note: [Col. 0215] Exod. 6], who gave him the law on Sinai [Note: [Col. 0215] Exod. 31], and who came in the spirit of understanding to redeem us. He is the root of Jesse [Note: [Col. 0215] Isa. 11], who stood upon the gibbet of the cross as a sign for the peoples, who came in the spirit of counsel to free us. He is the key of David, who opens and none shuts, who shuts and none opens [Note: [Col. 0215] Isa. 22; Rev. 3], the storehouses of Paradise and hell; he came in the spirit of might to bring us out from the prisons of hell.

He is the rising sun, the sun of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0215] Zech. 6; Mal. 4], who came in the spirit of knowledge to enlighten us. He is the king of the Gentiles, the cornerstone [Note: [Col. 0215] Isa. 28], who came to save us in the spirit of piety. He is Emmanuel, “God with us” [Note: [Col. 0215] Isa. 7], who came through the spirit of fear to save us and gave us the gift of love.

All these antiphons begin with *O*, used rather as an exclamation of wonder than as a vocative. [Col. 0215D] Or there are seven because they are sung in representation of the ancient fathers, who, observing the sevenfold number, awaited the Lord’s Advent; hence “Come” is said in them all. They are sung at Vespers because the Lord came in the evening of the world. He is Elijah, who in the evening eats flesh and in the morning bread [Note: [Col. 0215] 3 Kings 17]: that is, our Lord, who in the last age of the world assumed flesh and, rising at dawn, passed into the bread of angels [Note: [Col. 0215] Ps.]. If, according to some, nine are sung, one is added for the Virgin who conceived and another for the angel who entered in to the Virgin [Note: [Col. 0215] Luke 1]. If there are twelve, the twelve prophets who preached Christ’s Advent are represented—the Advent whose witness the twelve Apostles confirmed—from which twelve tribes, and from them twelve thousand, are sealed and saved [Note: [Col. 0215] Rev. 7].

## Chapter V. On the Vigil of the Lord’s Nativity

“Today you shall know that the Lord will come, and in the morning you shall see his glory” [Note: [Col. 0215] Exod. 16].

This day is called the Vigil of the Lord’s Nativity. Vigils began with the shepherds. By ancient custom, two nocturnal offices were held on the chief feasts: one only at the beginning of the night, by the pontiff with his chaplains, without the *Venite*; the other at midnight, as is still observed by some [Col. 0216B] on solemn occasions. The people who had come to the feast kept watch throughout the night in praises. But after mockers turned the praiseworthy institution into a jest and devoted themselves to shameful songs, dances, and fornications, vigils were forbidden; and days devoted to fasting retained the old name of vigils. Among these, the Lord’s Vigil is the most celebrated and principal, possessing its own nocturnal as well as diurnal office.

Over the *Venite* is sung: “Today you shall know that the Lord will come, and in the morning you shall see his glory.” This is taken from Exodus with a slight alteration. For when the Lord had said to the children of Israel, “Behold, I shall rain down bread for you from heaven,” Moses and Aaron said to them: “In the evening you shall know [Col. 0216C] that the Lord has brought you out of the land of Egypt, and in the morning you shall see his glory” [Note: [Col. 0215] Ibid.]. For quail came down upon the camp in the evening, and manna in the morning. The quail was Christ’s flesh; the manna was a figure of God’s Word [Note: [Col. 0215] 1 Cor. 10], the living bread that came down from heaven [Note: [Col. 0215] John 6]. We received flesh in the evening and the Word in the morning, when at the end of the ages “the Word was made flesh” [Note: [Col. 0215] John 1]. This is at the ends of the ages and, although it is more plausibly called evening, it is also called morning, because in him, as in a time of grace, the sun of righteousness shone upon us [Note: [Col. 0215] Mal. 4], and a new morning restored to believers the New Testament, the new light of knowledge.

Therefore, “Today you shall know, and in the morning you shall see his glory”: that is, in the time of grace you shall know by experience the Word incarnate. Thus this was said to them that they might prepare themselves [Col. 0216D] to eat the Lord’s flesh. Or it is said spiritually to those who were present at the Savior’s birth and deserved to receive the true manna. Or, more truly, this brief clause pertains on the one hand to the Nativity and on the other to the Resurrection: “Today,” that is, in the present life, “you shall know that the Lord will come,” that is, the living bread that came down from heaven [Note: [Col. 0215] John 6]; “and in the morning,” that is, in the glory of the Resurrection, you shall see not only his humanity but also the glory of his divinity.

At Lauds: “Judah and Jerusalem, do not be afraid; [Col. 0217A] tomorrow you shall go forth, and the Lord shall be with you.” This frequent and most celebrated oracle of divine consolation directs us to the history in Paralipomenon. When Jehoshaphat was king, the children of Ammon and Moab, together with the inhabitants of Mount Seir, assembled against Judah. All Judah came together in Jerusalem and in the Temple of the Lord to pray before him; and, while they stood before the Lord with their wives and children and cried aloud to the Lord, Jahaziel son of Zechariah, a Levite, cried out from the midst of the multitude in the Spirit of the Lord, saying: “O Judah and Jerusalem, do not be afraid; tomorrow you shall go forth, and the Lord shall be with you” [Note: [Col. 0217] 2 Chron. 20].

Ammon is interpreted “a troubled people,” Moab “from the father,” and Seir “hairy.” These are the vices that trouble and embitter human beings, proceeding from the devil [Col. 0217B], which had gathered for our entrance, and there was no one to help until the Samaritan came in the flesh, dressed the wounded man’s wounds, and entrusted him to the innkeeper [Note: [Col. 0217] Luke 10]. The saying is therefore addressed to those who, before the Lord’s Nativity, were held under the devil’s power or imprisoned in the confines of hell: “O Judah and Jerusalem”—that is, those confessing and desiring peace—“do not be afraid. Tomorrow,” that is, soon, “you shall go forth, and the Lord shall be with you.” Being like you, he will dwell in you.

Morally: O active persons, for whom confession of sins is necessary, and O contemplative persons, for whom the vision of peace is an object of desire, “do not fear those who kill the body” [Note: [Col. 0217] Matt. 10]. “Tomorrow,” that is, soon, you shall go forth from this body of death [Note: [Col. 0217] Rom. 7], “and the Lord shall be with you.” Therefore desire “to be dissolved and to be with Christ” [Note: [Col. 0217] Phil. 1].

From these two clauses, namely, “Today you shall know that the Lord will come,” and “Judah and Jerusalem, do not be afraid,” almost all the remainder of the nocturnal office is woven. Know concerning it that, on whatever weekday the Lord’s Vigil falls, it takes that day’s ferial psalms with their antiphons and canticle; but if it falls on a Sunday, it has six responsories from the history “Blow the trumpet,” and three from the Vigil itself, with their Lauds. Today also, and until the Athanasian Creed at the nocturnal office of Epiphany, according to the custom of some, it is kept silent.

The purpose of the diurnal office is evidently to show not only that Christ was born, but also of whom, why, and how great he was born. He was born, as is said in Paul’s Epistle [Note: [Col. 0217] Rom. 1] and in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0217] Matt. 1], [Col. 0217D] being of David’s seed, from Mary betrothed to Joseph. For today Mary’s betrothal is read, so that it may be known that she was betrothed to one person, namely Joseph, and made fruitful by another, namely the Holy Spirit. He was born in order to save the people and wipe away the iniquity of the earth: today in hope through the sacraments of grace, tomorrow in reality through the revelation of glory. These things are clear in the Introit and Gradual, “Today you shall know,” and the Alleluia. On the following day some have the Alleluia, “Hail, Mary”; nevertheless, the Alleluia is not sung in vigils because of the observance of the fast [Col. 0218A], unless it falls on a Sunday, for then it is not omitted because of the Lord’s Resurrection. The same is also clear in the Communion, “It shall be revealed.” But because his Incarnation was to be the dispersion of the Jews, the verse “Thou who rulest” is therefore added in the Gradual, in which prayer is made for them. How great he is is shown by the psalm sung at the Introit, namely: “The earth is the Lord’s” [Note: [Col. 0217] Ps. 22]. From it is also taken the Offertory: “Lift up your gates.”

Observe that this Vigil has its own collect, and therefore it ought to be said at Vespers. This, according to some, is to be generally observed in every vigil: if it has its own collect in the Mass, it should also be said at Vespers; if it has no proper collect, the collect of the following feast should be said at Vespers.

At Vespers of the Nativity Vigil, the psalms [Col. 0218B] sung are, according to some: “Praise the Lord, ye children” [Note: [Col. 0217] Ps. 112]; “Praise the Lord, all ye nations” [Note: [Col. 0217] Ps. 116]; “Praise the Lord, O my soul” [Note: [Col. 0217] Ps. 145]; “Praise the Lord, for he is good” [Note: [Col. 0217] Ps. 146]; and “Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0217] Ps. 147], in which we are invited to praise.

According to others, however, they are: “Praise the Lord, ye children” [Note: [Col. 0217] Ps. 112]; “Those who trust” [Note: [Col. 0217] Ps. 124]; “When the Lord turned again” [Note: [Col. 0217] Ps. 125]; “Remember” [Note: [Col. 0217] Ps. 131]; and “Blessed be the Lord my God” [Note: [Col. 0217] Ps. 143]. And rightly so: for the first invites the devout continually to praise and proclaim the Lord; the second exhorts them to trust in the Lord. In the following three the reason is given why praise should be pressed forward and trust placed in the Lord: namely, because he turned our captivity [Note: [Col. 0217] Jer. 1] and magnified himself with us [Note: [Col. 0217] Ps. 125]; because he fulfilled his promises when he placed the fruit of David’s womb upon his throne [Note: [Col. 0217] Luke 1; Ps. 131]; because he bent [Col. 0218C] the heavens and came down [Note: [Col. 0217] Ps. 17]; and because at last he will send out his hand from on high [Note: [Col. 0217] Ps. 143], to deliver us from many waters and from alien sons.

## Chapter VI. On the Lord’s Nativity

“A child is born to us” [Note: [Col. 0217] Isa. 9].

The Lord wished to be born at the end of the year in order to show that he was coming in the last age of the world. He was conceived on Friday and born on Sunday; crucified on Friday and raised on Sunday, so that he who had lost the human being formed on the sixth day might free him on Friday, and he who, coming on Sunday as the dawn from on high [Note: [Col. 0217] Luke 1], might enlighten us. This rule is confirmed by the concurrent [letter] of that year, if you trace it backwards [materially uncertain OCR: *v. illius anni*].

He was also born by night, according to the saying: “While all things held the midst of silence, and night was running its course, the almighty word of the Lord came from the royal thrones” [Note: [Col. 0217] Wis. 18]. Hence we rise at midnight to announce the Nativity, because we believe that then the Virgin gave birth and sang to the child *profescennines*—that is, the little songs which nurses make for children—“Glory to God in the highest” [Note: [Col. 0217] Luke 2]. Nor is this without mystery. For he was born at night in order to signify that he came hidden beneath the flesh, or to show that he came to enlighten [Col. 0219A] our night, since “upon those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, light has risen” [Note: [Col. 0219] Isa. 9]. Hence, from his Nativity the days lengthen, because those who believe in him are called to the light of eternity.

The nocturnal offices are therefore rightly celebrated; and, according to ancient custom, two nocturnal offices are assigned to the Lord’s Nativity. One, in which the antiphons “The Lord is as though poured out” and the responsories “Today to us,” together with others, are sung; the other, in which the antiphons “Lord, be exalted in the sun” and the responsories “Behold the Lamb of God” are sung. But this latter is reserved for the Octave.

Let us now attend first to: “Come, Christ is born to us; come, let us adore.” This is sung in the person of the angels, by whom the shepherds—or rather the whole people—are invited to adore the newborn Lord [Col. 0219B]. Invited, therefore, to these rejoicings, we rejoice with him and sing psalms in three divisions.

In the first, Christ’s eternal and ineffable begetting is treated; in the second, Christ’s Incarnation; in the third, the praises of the Bridegroom and Bride. In three lessons we bear witness to him by Isaiah’s oracles, for Isaiah described Christ’s Incarnation not so much prophetically as evangelically. In three responsories we rejoice with the angels; these represent for us all things in heaven and on earth [Note: [Col. 0219] Eph. 1] restored through Christ’s Nativity. In the first, in which the host of angels rejoices, the restoration of heavenly things is sung. In the second, in which true peace comes down, [Col. 0219C] the reparation of earthly things is sung. In the third, in which it is said that he entered our region, the liberation of those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death is recalled [Note: [Col. 0219] Isa. 9]. Since the Trinity works all these things, therefore, according to some, a *Gloria* follows each individual one; or, according to others, after these three.

Because the fabric of the world is ineffably created by the Word of God [Note: [Col. 0219] Gen. 1; Ps. 32], a jubilation is therefore made at “the fabric of the world.” Again, because he is believed ineffably to have come forth from the Virgin “as a bridegroom from his chamber” [Note: [Col. 0219] Ps. 18], a chant is therefore sounded at *tamquam* (“as”). Again, because he is proclaimed ineffably coequal with the Father and Holy Spirit, jubilation therefore exults at “Glory be to the Father.” And because he is Alpha and Omega [Note: [Col. 0219] Rev. 1], it is therefore modulated on A and O.

In the second nocturn we read lessons from expositions, and we rejoice in singing with the shepherds, while recalling their devotion: we sing that they hastened to Bethlehem and found Christ in the manger [Note: [Col. 0219] Luke 2]. In the third nocturn the first antiphon, “He shall call upon me,” is set in the sixth differentia and introduces, in the seventh place, the psalm: “I will sing for ever of the mercies of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0219] Ps. 88], because the mercy of him is sung who came with sevenfold grace to redeem the one who had been created and fallen on the seventh day [Note: [Col. 0219] Gen. 1–2].

In that same nocturn *Alleluia* occurs frequently in the antiphons, because joy came to [Col. 0220A] the world in the third age, that is, the age of grace. In it we read the Gospels: two concern the temporal birth; in the third, the giant of twofold substance is declared. Observe that we divide the number nine through the three nocturns, so as to understand that the fathers of the three ages are joined to the nine orders of angels. Therefore *Alleluia* is silent in the first two, because the fathers joined to them were murmuring within the confines of hell; but in the third it occurs frequently, because the fathers passing over in our own age are immediately joined to the angels.

The triad in the first nocturn consists of the three fathers of the first age: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The triad in the second: lawgiver, psalmist, and prophet. The triad in the third: people from the three parts of the world, or the primitive Church, the Church of the Gentiles, and the final conversion of the remnant [Col. 0220B]. All these arrive at the fellowship of angelic society through good works, evangelical teaching, and faith in the Holy Trinity [Note: [Col. 0219] Rom. 11].

Women customarily visit women in childbirth and bring gifts to mother and child. We imitate them in the responsories of the three nocturns, when we salute now Christ, now the Virgin, or, as though offering gifts to each, applaud each. Observe that in the first nocturn the prophets, in the second the doctors, and in the third the Evangelists are read, because prophecy concerning Christ’s Incarnation came first; the expositor, like a shepherd, unfolded what was obscure; and the Evangelist made it clear.

Observe also that, according to some, three cloths are customarily laid upon the altar before the nocturns, and one is removed at each nocturn [Col. 0220C]. The first is black, for the time before the Law; the second somewhat whitish, for the time of the Law; the third richly red, for the time of grace. When the third is removed, the lights of the Church are more fully kindled.

After this, Matthew’s Gospel is sung: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0219] Matt. 1]. Jacob, sleeping at night, saw a ladder, with the Lord leaning upon it and angels descending and ascending on it [Note: [Col. 0219] Gen. 28]. What is Jacob’s ladder except Christ’s genealogy, upon which the Lord leans when he is placed through Joseph on the lowest rung? The angels descending and ascending are all the elect, who first humble themselves to receive faith in Christ’s Incarnation and afterward are raised to behold his glory. For, having become human, God first cries in a cradle and is baptized in the Jordan’s water; [Col. 0220D] afterward he shines with heavenly miracles [Note: [Col. 0219] Matt. 3]. By the first he teaches us to humble ourselves by the example of his humility [Note: [Col. 0219] Phil. 2]; by the second he instructs us that the humble are raised to understand the glory of his divinity.

Matthew and Luke seem to indicate both this descent and ascent when they describe Christ’s genealogy: the one descending, the other ascending. Or Matthew [Note: [Col. 0219] ch. 1] counts downward because he describes Christ’s humanity, through which he came down to us. Luke [Note: [Col. 0219] ch. 3] recounts upward, because, beginning from the baptized Christ, he ascends to God, showing the effect [Col. 0221A] of baptism: that the baptized become children of God. Jacob saw the ladder while sleeping in the night; therefore we read this genealogy in the deep night, sleeping not with bodily sleep but in contemplation of heavenly things, according to the saying: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” [Note: [Col. 0221] Song 5].

Observe that this genealogy begins from David and Abraham and ends with Joseph. Promises were made to these three. To Abraham it was said: “In thy seed shall all nations be blessed” [Note: [Col. 0221] Gen. 22], a promise signifying a human being. To David: “Of the fruit of thy womb I will set upon thy throne” [Note: [Col. 0221] Ps. 131], a promise signifying a human being and king. To Joseph: “She shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins” [Note: [Col. 0221] Matt. 1], a promise [Col. 0221B] declaring a human being and God.

And just as one comes to the Jordan through forty-two stations [Note: [Col. 0221] Josh. 3], and from there to the promised land, so through forty-two fathers one comes to the Virgin, the Savior’s mother. In the middle, however, the Evangelist placed Rahab the harlot and Ruth the Moabitess, indicating that Christ had come not only for the Jews but also for the Gentiles; as the Prophet also foretold: “I shall remember Rahab and Babylon, those who know me” [Note: [Col. 0221] Ps. 86], that is, the broad extent of the confused nations. For Rahab means “breadth,” Babylon “confusion.”

Awaking from sleep, Jacob broke out into confession of the Lord, saying: “Truly the Lord is in this place” [Note: [Col. 0221] Gen. 28]. And we, when the genealogy has been sung, resound in God’s praises, saying: [Col. 0221C] “We praise thee, O God”; in this we also rejoice over the lost drachma, which the woman found after lighting a lamp [Note: [Col. 0221] Luke 15]. Rising from sleep, Jacob set up a stone as a memorial, pouring oil upon it [Note: [Col. 0221] Gen. 28]. And we, after singing the genealogy and the confession of praise, celebrate the solemnities of the Mass, where we raise up the cornerstone [Note: [Col. 0221] Eph. 2] and pour out the oil of confession and devotion.

After the Communion has been sung, we insert the matutinal lauds before the final collect concludes. In them four psalms pertain to the present state. In the first, “The Lord reigns” [Note: [Col. 0221] Ps. 92], we praise the beauty and splendour of the King; in the second, “Make a joyful noise” [Note: [Col. 0221] Ps. 99], we in turn invite ourselves to praise; in the third, as though thirsting in the desert of Idumea, we say: [Col. 0221D] “O God, my God” [Note: [Col. 0221] Ps. 62]; in the fourth we ask for the rain of mercy, saying: “May God have mercy” [Note: [Col. 0221] Ps. 66]. Then we exhort the creatures to praise the Lord, saying: “Bless” [Note: [Col. 0221] Dan. 3].

The three that follow, namely “Praise the Lord from the heavens” [Note: [Col. 0221] Ps. 148], “Sing” [Note: [Col. 0221] Ps. 149; printed *159*], and “Praise the Lord in his holy places” [Note: [Col. 0221] Ps. 150; printed *10*], pertain to the future state, in which, together with the angels, we shall praise the Lord without end or interruption. With these psalms the Church, as it were, leads a dance, while the Bride sings to her deliverer in the matutinal praises, which the priest concludes with the collect of the Mass. Although this arrangement seems to be made for the festal splendour, the Mass nevertheless precedes the Lauds for this reason: the eternal begetting, of which the Mass speaks, existed before any creature existed that could praise God. One collect ends both Lauds and Mass, because Christ’s Incarnation must be referred to him from whom comes the eternal generation. And this first Mass should end not with *Ite, missa est* (“Go, the dismissal is made”), but with *Benedicamus Domino* (“Let us bless the Lord”), lest the people be dismissed from the office.

Some, when the nocturn has ended, immediately begin “We praise thee, O God,” thereby representing the hour in which Christ was born; at once they add the Mass with “Glory to God in the highest,” representing the joy of the angels. Then they add “The book of the generation,” representing the joy of human beings. But our Church, after the nine responsories, celebrates the Mass; when it is finished, it adds the Gospel, “The book of the generation,” and after the Gospel, “We praise thee, O God,” because the generation of divinity preceded the generation of humanity, knowledge of both of which was for us a source of praise.

Let us now pursue the offices of the Masses. Three Masses are celebrated on the Lord’s Nativity, according to the institution of Pope Telesphorus, who wished Mass to be celebrated at night in order to show that he who is born at night is the same as he who is sacrificed on the altar, and in remembrance of the angels who sang that night the hymn of angels: “Glory to God in the highest” [Note: [Col. 0221] Luke 2]. The author of the office wished another to be celebrated in the morning, in order that the entrance of the new Light into the world might be shown; [Col. 0222C] and because the Father sanctified him from the beginning of his conception, sacrifice is offered at the beginning of light, or because of the shepherds’ visit to the Lord’s manger, where they found fodder [Note: [Col. 0221] Ibid.], by which the souls of saints are daily refreshed. Again, the third Mass is celebrated at the third hour, that the due order of Mass may be kept.

These three Masses signify three ages. It is certain that the three ages of the world are saved through this unique Nativity. By the Mass celebrated at night is understood the time before the Law, wrapped in the darkness of ignorance; therefore it is sung at night, and in it is read: “The people of the Gentiles who walked in darkness” [Note: [Col. 0221] Isa. 9]. By the Mass sung at dawn is expressed the time of the Law, in which the light of faith is shown to the world through the Scriptures; therefore [Col. 0222D] it is sung at dawn, and in it is said: “A light shall shine.” By the third Mass, celebrated in daylight at the third hour, is denoted the day of salvation and the time of grace, in which Christ is born; therefore it is sung in the day, and in it is said: “A child is born to us” [Note: [Col. 0221] Isa. 9].

This is what is said in Leviticus [Note: [Col. 0221] ch. 26]: “You shall eat the very old things of old, and when new things come in, you shall cast away the old.” The very old is the natural law; the old, the Mosaic law; the new, the evangelical law. The natural law taught the understanding of God; hence the first Mass speaks of eternal generation. The Mosaic law promised that the Lord would be born.

[Col. 0223A] Hence in the second Mass it is said: “A light shall shine.” The evangelical law proclaims him born. Hence in the third Mass it is said: “A child is born to us.” Thus it has been written in verse:

> In the Nativity, observe what the solemnities  
> Of the most sacred Mass signify and why they are celebrated:  
> The first in night, the following under light, the last in full light.  
> Sacred things were under Noah, under the Temple, under Christ:  
> Night, dawn, day; shadow, figure, God.

The first Mass pertains to the generation which is from the secret—that is, the substance—of the Father, which is from the Father without a mother; therefore it is sung at night: “For who shall declare his generation?” [Note: [Col. 0223] Isa. 53.] Or because all who lived before the Law almost entirely failed to know it. Therefore there is also sung in it: “Today I have begotten you before the morning star.” [Note: [Col. 0223] Ps. 109.] The second pertains to that generation [Col. 0223B] which is from the womb of a virgin, which is from a mother without a father. Therefore it is sung at daybreak, because the people of the Law had a half-complete knowledge of it; and therefore there is sung in it: “Light shall shine upon us today, because the Lord has been born to us.” The third pertains to both, as is clear from its Gospel. For where it says, “In the beginning was the Word,” the eternal generation is signified; where it adds, “And the Word was made flesh” [Note: [Col. 0223] John 1.], the temporal generation is shown. Therefore it is sung in daylight, because those under grace came more fully to know the divinity through the temporal Nativity, since through knowledge of the Son one comes to the Father. [Note: [Col. 0223] John 14.]

Thus the office of the first Mass commemorates the divine Nativity in nearly all its parts, as in the introit: “The Lord said to me: [Col. 0223C] You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” [Note: [Col. 0223] Ps. 2.] That is, “I have begotten you eternally.” For “today,” as blessed Augustine maintains, signifies the present; and in eternity nothing is past, as though it had ceased to be, nor future, as though it were not yet, but only present: since whatever is eternal always is. Therefore “I have begotten you today” is to be understood there in a divine sense.

The same is sung in the gradual, Alleluia, and Communion, and what is set forth in the introit is repeated. But how do these parts suit their head, namely, the Gospel which recounts the birth from the Virgin? Yet when it says there, “Mary brought forth her firstborn son” [Note: [Col. 0223] Luke 2.], it plainly fits the foregoing subject, because we do not refer “firstborn” to Mary, but affirm that he was begotten first—that is, before [Col. 0223D] every creature. Or because this divinity came to us shod, and through this footwear we came to know the divinity. Therefore the prayers, lessons, Gospel, and offertory plainly commemorate the birth from the Virgin.

Hence some say that the intention of the whole office can be referred to the temporal Nativity, explaining it thus: “Today,” namely on this day, “before the morning star,” that is, the morning star, “I have begotten you”—that is, I have brought about your generation. And what is said in the Gospel, “Mary bore a son,” namely the firstborn, means one after whom, or before whom, there is none.

[Col. 0224A] The office of the second Mass wholly accords with the words of the shepherds, who say, as is read in the Gospel: “Let us go as far as Bethlehem and see this Word which has come to pass.” [Note: [Col. 0223] Ibid.] Rejoicing, they say in the introit: “Light shall shine.” But the half-taught grammarian says: Why do they not say, “Light shines; the star has risen from Jacob”? [Note: [Col. 0223] Num. 24.] Yet “Light shall shine” is more fittingly said, because the sky reddens at dawn, shines at the third hour, burns at the sixth, and grows warm in the evening. Or “Light shall shine” is spoken in the person of the Law, which promised beforehand the temporal Nativity to the ancient fathers; and it follows: “The Lord has reigned; he is clothed with beauty,” [Note: [Col. 0223] Ps. 92.] with that beauty with which his mother crowned him. [Note: [Col. 0223] Song 3.]

This is his humanity: the adornment of mercy, the diadem of loving-kindness, the beauty of charity. And in the gradual they add: [Col. 0224B] “Blessed is he who comes”; and in the Alleluia: “The Lord has reigned.” In the offertory they then state who he is and how great he is, saying: “For God has established the world of the earth.” [Note: [Col. 0223] Ps. 92.] And because the first wall is from the Hebrews, the firstfruits—that is, the shepherds—speak to them in the Communion: “Rejoice, daughter of Zion.” [Note: [Col. 0223] Isa. 12.] The Church from the Hebrews is called the Daughter of Zion, because in Zion, which was also Jerusalem, were the Temple and the Holy of Holies.

In both Masses the station ought to have been at Saint Mary’s, because true salvation came to us from her womb; but another consideration intervenes, so that the procession goes to Saint Anastasia, who on this day passed to the Lord through martyrdom. Therefore in the second Mass the second prayer is said for Saint Anastasia.

The office of the third Mass proclaims the wonders [Col. 0224C] of the Word of God, which was in the beginning and begins to be flesh, as is read in the Gospel. [Note: [Col. 0223] John 1.] This Word is the child who, according to the prophet, “has been born to us,” [Note: [Col. 0223] Isa. 9.] as we sing in the introit. And this is the new song of which the Prophet says: “Sing to the Lord a new song”; [Note: [Col. 0223] Ps. 97.] and Jeremiah: “The Lord will make a new thing upon the earth.” [Note: [Col. 0223] Jer. 31.] This is that arm of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0223] Ps. 97.] which, according to this day’s prophetic lesson, the Lord prepared before the eyes of the nations.
