This is the speech which, according to the apostolic lesson, the Father spoke in the Son—he who in many ways formerly spoke to the fathers in the prophets. [Note: [Col. 0223] Heb. 1.]

And note that both at the vigil and in the three Masses of today’s feast, two lessons are read consecutively: the first from the prophet Isaiah, the second from the Apostle, because [Col. 0224D] Christ is born for the joining of two peoples in one wall; or because the column of the apostles is founded upon the base of the prophets; or because the active and contemplative are saved through this Nativity in one faith; or because his Nativity is preached harmoniously through prophets and apostles, and more clearly through the former and the latter—that is, through both Testaments. These are the two cherubim who cover the propitiatory and, with faces turned toward it, look upon the propitiatory. [Note: [Col. 0223] Exod. 25.]

By the propitiatory the incarnate Lord is figured, of whom John says: “He is the propitiation [Col. 0225A] for our sins.” [Note: [Col. 0225] 1 John 2.] Therefore, when they do not disagree but harmoniously recount the mystery of the Incarnation—the former foretelling it, the latter preserving it—they direct the face of their intention toward the propitiatory and look upon one another in turn. This Word is also that saving one of whom there is immediately sung in the gradual: “They have seen.” [Note: [Col. 0225] Ps. 97.]

This is the great light which descended into the Virgin’s womb: “Which enlightens every person coming into this world.” [Note: [Col. 0225] John 1.] And note that the neumes sung in the *Kyrie eleison* or the Alleluia are more often jubilated on E or A, so that through these vowels we may signify the spiritual joy restored to us in the Virgin’s childbirth. In her, the name Eva was transformed, when the angel said: “Ave Maria.” [Note: [Col. 0225] Luke 1.] *Ave*, indeed, is a word of joy; Eva, [Col. 0225B] of grief, which those who are born express by lamenting, “E” or “A.”

Finally, this is that rich and mighty one spoken of in the offertory: “Yours are the heavens, and yours is the earth; you have humbled the proud.” [Note: [Col. 0225] Ps. 88.] But did he humble the proud today, when he did not know how to call [anyone] father or mother? I answer: he humbled him causally, according to: “Hasten, strip away the spoils; hurry to plunder.” [Note: [Col. 0225] Isa. 8.] In the Communion it is concluded concerning the same one, who is salvation, that “all the ends of the earth have seen.” [Note: [Col. 0225] Ps. 97.] And because blessed Peter saw and confessed this before the others, the Father who is in heaven revealing it to him, [Note: [Col. 0225] Matt. 16.] therefore the station is at Saint Peter’s.

This should not be passed over in silence: from today until the octave of the Epiphany, at Prime, Terce, Sext, and None we always say responsories [Col. 0225C] and their verses with Alleluia, to represent the height of joy which came in the time of grace. The Vespers of the Nativity of the Lord should likewise first be sung in full each day. Afterwards the *Magnificat* is sung with the antiphon and collect of the following feast of blessed Stephen and of the others. Some, however, say the entire second Vespers; others only the antiphon and collect. This is a privilege of these Vespers: whereas the other offices are changed for an intervening feast, these Vespers are not changed. And there is something singular in this, because the Lord came in the evening—that is, in the last age of the world—to save at least the remnant of the human race.

## CHAPTER VII. ON THE OCTAVE OF THE LORD

[Col. 0225D] “After eight days were completed, so that the child might be circumcised, his name was called Jesus.” [Note: [Col. 0225] Luke 2.]

On the day of the Nativity two feasts coincide: that of the woman giving birth and that of the birth—that is, of mother and son. But because of the celebration of the Son, we could not solemnize the Mother fully. We therefore reserved her solemnities for the octave, signifying that if we serve Christ in this life, we shall rejoice in the glorification of the Church, which Mary figures, in the octave—that is, in the future life. Therefore the nocturnal office pertains in large part to the Virgin who gave birth; and for this reason two Masses [Col. 0226A] are celebrated: the first of the Mother, “Your countenance”; [Note: [Col. 0225] Ps. 44.] the other of the Son, “A child has been born to us.” [Note: [Col. 0225] Isa. 9.] If anyone wishes to omit one of them, let him not omit the one which concerns the Virgin, so that he says the prayer, “O God, who [of eternal salvation …].” This is to be said from the Circumcision until the Epiphany, and from the Octave of the Epiphany until the Purification.

On this day, however, a threefold solemnity is indicated: of the Octave, circumcision, and imposition of the name, as is read in the Gospel: “After eight days were completed.” [Note: [Col. 0225] Luke 2.] The three matters are commemorated. The first solemnity is assigned to the Ogdoad—that is, the eighth day—and because the following days are adorned with the names of octaves, discourse on octaves may appropriately proceed more fully.

The book of Leviticus indicates that the eighth day is to be celebrated, saying: [Col. 0226B] “The eighth day shall be most solemn and most holy.” [Note: [Col. 0225] Lev. 23.] Octaves are celebrated for different and particular reasons. For example, the Octave of the Nativity is celebrated to render an account of the first day: on the day of the Nativity we honored Christ’s coming to us; on the Octave we honor humankind’s coming to Christ. He came to us so that we might go to him, and this is clearly recognized from the antiphons. There it is said: “The woman who gave birth bore a king.” Here: “O wondrous exchange!” By the word “exchange” it is understood that one thing is given and another received. Christ gave us his divinity and received our humanity. What he gave is honored at the Nativity; what he received is honored on the octave day. The members joined to the head rejoice together [Col. 0226C] in the present feast. So also in the other antiphons: in those the Nativity is treated; in these, the joining of the members which was effected through the Nativity.

That antiphon, “The wondrous mystery of man,” declares the assumption when it says, “they are renewed.” Behold the new exchange of natures: God becomes human and the human being God—yet so that what he was remained, and he assumed what he was not, suffering neither the mixture which Sabellius asserted nor the division which Arius barked out.

For a similar reason the Octave of the Epiphany is celebrated. For at the Epiphany it is sung that the Lord was baptized; at the Octave the reason is given why he was baptized, namely, so that we might be baptized, so that through our washing we might be cleansed from sins. This is declared by the antiphons themselves: “The old man.” Here [Col. 0226D] the question arises why the Octave of the Passion is not celebrated on the same ground of reasoning. For just as Christ, who is the sun of righteousness, [Note: [Col. 0225] Mal. 4.] was born not for himself but so that light might appear to our minds, which were in darkness; [Note: [Col. 0225] Isa. 9; Luke 1.] and just as he was baptized not for himself but to wash away our sins; [Note: [Col. 0225] Rom. 6.] so he died not for himself but so that we might die to sin, through which he might free us from death. [Note: [Col. 0225] Heb. 2.]

I answer: because an approaching feast of joy overshadows and abolishes the commemoration of sorrow. Yet even if a reason is given why they are not observed, it need not be demanded in every similar case why these are observed. For he was also circumcised bodily so that we might be circumcised spiritually; [Note: [Col. 0227] Luke 2.] he fasted so that we might fast; [Note: [Col. 0227] Matt. 4.] he washed feet so that we might be washed. [Note: [Col. 0227] John 12.] Yet we do not celebrate octaves for these or similar things.

But the octaves of saints, such as Stephen and others, are celebrated for a different reason. On their birthdays, indeed, we honor the receptacles of their souls; on their octaves, the resurrection of their bodies. Hence the titles of the Psalms say, “For the octave.”

And note: octaves of certain saints are celebrated, lest this mystery remain hidden; but not of all, lest it become cheapened. And if we cannot celebrate the feasts of all saints, how much less their octaves? Again, the octave of the Paschal solemnity has a different reason: although it possesses the mystery of the octave, the octave is added on account of the eight beatitudes, which will be received in that solemn octave. [Col. 0227B] Again, the Octave of Pentecost has a different reason, being celebrated so that the completion of the works of the Holy Spirit may be declared.

Finally, there is a general rationale for all octaves: the octave returns to the beginning, as Augustine maintains concerning the beatitudes. The same day is both first and eighth, namely Sunday. Therefore the Lord’s resurrection is said to have occurred on the octave—that is, on Sunday. Consequently the celebration of octaves is observed so that we may return to the first state of innocence. In remembrance of this innocence, Circumcision was performed on the eighth day, so that the mind might be circumcised from every fleshly contagion.

[Col. 0227C] Let the discussion now turn to circumcision and the imposition of the name. Rightly, on the eighth day, is the solemnity of circumcision and the imposition of the name Jesus celebrated. For just as on the day of the Nativity it is shown how Christ came to us to save us, namely through the Incarnation, so on the octave it is shown how we shall come to him to be saved by him, namely through circumcision.

Concerning circumcision, it should be known that the Lord commanded it to Abraham as a sign of obedience, righteousness, faith, and the distinguishing of the people. [Note: [Col. 0227] Gen. 17; Rom. 4.] It was performed on the eighth day with a stone knife on the organ of lust, in which the first-created man felt the shame of disobedience. It signified that in the octave of grace every corruption of sin is taken away through faith in Christ, [Note: [Col. 0227] Rom. 6.] and in the octave of glory [Col. 0227D] through Christ even every corruption of punishment is wholly abolished. [Note: [Col. 0227] Rom. 8.]

Hence subdeacons, young and strong, celebrate this feast, signifying that in the octave of those who rise again there will be no feeble age: neither old age, nor decrepitude, nor helpless childhood; but all “shall attain to a perfect man,” [Note: [Col. 0227] Eph. 4.] when “this mortal shall put on immortality and this corruptible incorruption.” [Note: [Col. 0227] 1 Cor. 15.] Its effect was the abolition of original sin. Why, then, did Christ, who was the spotless [Col. 0228A] lamb, [Note: [Col. 0227] Isa. 53; John 1.] having neither spot nor wrinkle, [Note: [Col. 0227] Eph. 5.] “who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth,” [Note: [Col. 0227] 1 Pet. 2.] why, I say, did he will to be circumcised, having nothing in himself that ought to be cut away?

I answer: just as he willed to be presented in the Temple, [Note: [Col. 0227] Luke 2.] baptized, [Note: [Col. 0227] Matt. 3.] and feast on the Paschal lamb with his disciples, [Note: [Col. 0227] Matt. 26.] so he willed to be circumcised in body—not for himself, but for us. First, lest the Jews be offended against him, saying, “This is not the Messiah promised in the Law, because he does not live according to the Law”—he who later said of himself: “I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it.” [Note: [Col. 0227] Matt. 5.]

Second, because of the figure: for carnal circumcision figures the present spiritual circumcision, which is by grace, and the future one, which will be in glory. Nor did he give us an example [Col. 0228B] of being circumcised bodily—as though, “Be circumcised; Christ will profit you nothing” [Note: [Col. 0227] Gal. 5.]—but invited us spiritually to spiritual circumcision, that is, renewal of life. The Spirit invites us to this through Jeremiah, saying: “Make new land for yourselves.” [Note: [Col. 0227] Jer. 4.]

And perhaps not without hidden reason this solemnity of renewal coincides with the new year of the Gentiles: for then we shall celebrate the new year, augured by a gift and under a good omen, if we have been renewed in mind and spirit. [Note: [Col. 0227] Eph. 4.] Finally, he changed carnal circumcision by establishing the baptism which followed it.

Third, because of propriety: it is more fitting to be washed with water than to be mutilated in body; because of usefulness, because it is more universal. For whereas only males were circumcised, both males [Col. 0228C] and females are baptized; and because it is more effective, since circumcision cleansed only from original sin, while baptism cleanses from every sin and opens the entrance to paradise.

Concerning Christ’s names, it should be known that some are said of Christ relatively, or as it were relatively, such as shepherd, [Note: [Col. 0227] John 10.] bridegroom, [Note: [Col. 0227] Ps. 18.] and mediator; [Note: [Col. 0227] 1 Tim. 2.] others are said non-relatively, such as human being. [Note: [Col. 0227] John 1.] Again, some are said of Christ figuratively, such as lamb, sheep, [Note: [Col. 0227] Isa. 53.] calf, [Note: [Col. 0227] Luke 15.] serpent, [Note: [Col. 0227] Num. 21; John 3.] ram, [Note: [Col. 0227] Gen. 22.] lion, [Note: [Col. 0227] Rev. 5.] and worm. [Note: [Col. 0227] Ps. 21.]

Again, some which are appellative by institution are appropriated to him by the prerogative of privilege, such as Christ, which is called *Christos* in Greek, *Messias* in Hebrew, and “Anointed” in Latin. “God anointed him with the oil of gladness above his companions.” [Note: [Col. 0227] Ps. 44.] This name is “oil poured out”; therefore the young women loved [Col. 0228D] him. [Note: [Col. 0227] Song 1.] Since this name is Greek, it is written in Greek abbreviation thus: ΧΡΣ. For the Greeks put Χ for *chi*; P for *r*; and c for *s*. But if it is written with *s*, it takes a Latin ending. Therefore, if it is written in the full form, it should be represented with aspiration thus: *Christus*.

Jesus, however, is properly the proper name of that person, imposed upon him by the angel on the day of conception and by human beings on the day of circumcision. It is called *Jesus* [Note: [Col. 0227] Luke 1 and 2.] in Hebrew, *sōtēr* in Greek, and “Savior” in Latin. Hence the angel said to Joseph: “You shall call his name Jesus, for he himself shall save his people from their sins.” [Note: [Col. 0229] Matt. 1.] Porphyry the philosopher, skilled in Greek and Latin, wrote this name *Jesus* in Latin, but in Greek with eta (Η), which the Greeks pronounce as long *i*. Hence some pronounce it *Gisus*. Latin writers, however, use it for long *e*; therefore it seems more correct to write it JHC by Greek abbreviation than JHS by Latin aspiration.

He is also called Alpha and Omega, that is, Beginning and End. [Note: [Col. 0229] Rev. 1.] He is also called Emmanuel, [Note: [Col. 0229] Isa. 7.] which is interpreted “God with us.” For he is with us by the presence of his majesty. He is further called Way, Truth, and Life: [Note: [Col. 0229] John 14.] way in example or precept, truth in promise, life in reward. Concerning these names you will find abundant material [Col. 0229B] in that sequence, *Alma chorus*.

*Sabaoth*, that is, God of hosts; [Note: [Col. 0229] Isa. 5.] *Adonai*, [Note: [Col. 0229] Exod. 6.] which is “Lord”; *Athanatos*, that is, “immortal”; *Kyrios*, that is, “Lord”; *Theos*, that is, “God”; *Pantocrator*, that is, “almighty”; *Homoousios*, that is, “of the same essence”—these are names of God, not only of the person of Christ.

Furthermore, according to Isaiah, [Note: [Col. 0229] Chap. 9.] Christ is called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace: Wonderful in the Incarnation—for what is more wonderful than that “the Word was made flesh”? [Note: [Col. 0229] John 1.] Counselor in complete knowledge of things: this is the Angel of great counsel, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God,” [Note: [Col. 0229] Col. 2.] to whom every heart lies open and every will [Col. 0229C] speaks. God in the creation of things: for this is the child who created the stars; indeed, all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. [Note: [Col. 0229] John 1.] Mighty in the ordering of things: for this is Wisdom, which “reaches from end to end mightily,” [Note: [Col. 0229] Wis. 8.] and orders all things by weight, number, and measure. [Note: [Col. 0229] Wis. 11.]

He is called Father of the age to come in the repayment of merits: for this is the householder who will settle accounts with his servants, and will say to the one who has proved faithful in what was entrusted: “Enter into the joy of your Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0229] Matt. 25.] He is called Prince of Peace either because he was mediator of God, human beings, and angels, [Note: [Col. 0229] 1 Tim. 2.] or because he grants that peace which surpasses all understanding, [Note: [Col. 0229] Phil. 4.] of whose “peace there shall be no end.” [Note: [Col. 0229] Isa. 7.]

Christ is also called by the ineffable name Tetragrammaton, that is, of four [Col. 0229D] letters: *Jo, He, vau, He*, which among us are *I, e, u, he*. Thus the name is *Jeuhe*. It is called ineffable not because it cannot be spoken, but because God ought not to be invoked by this name except in difficult matters; or because its meaning cannot be sufficiently explained. Its interpretation is as follows: *Iod*, “beginning”; *he*, “this one”; *vau*, “of the passion of life”—as if, “This one is the beginning of life through passion.” In Greek fashion the genitive is used for the ablative: *passionis*, “of passion,” for *passione*, “through passion.” But we cannot sufficiently perceive how our life depends upon his death.

What we said about the Gentiles celebrating the new year today [Col. 0230A] is to be understood of the Romans. For the Arabs begin after the summer solstice, whereas the Hebrews begin in March. Understand “year” also in its usual sense. There is a solar year: the sun’s single circuit through the zodiac, from which, through four years, the accumulation of quarter-days produces one day and makes the fourth year leap-year. There is a lunar year: the moon’s twelve circuits through the zodiac; when this falls short of the solar year by eleven days, threefold accumulation of these produces an embolismic year. There is also the usual year, which today begins according to human usage. There is the emergent year, beginning on any given day. There is the natural year, when the moon is placed beneath the sun, whence the sun suffers eclipse. There is the great year, when all the stars return to their proper place and [Col. 0230B] order. Among the Greeks there is the Olympiad, so called from the Olympic contest, which was observed from the fourth year to the fourth. Among the Romans there is the lustral year, a period of five years called a *lustrum*, because, after the censuses had been paid, they offered sacrifice and purified the city. Among the same people there is the indictional year, which contains three periods of five years. Among the Hebrews there is the Jubilee year, that is, of remission, celebrated when seven weeks of years have been completed. Among Christian pilgrims there is the year of kindness and grace, in which Christ came and redeemed us by kindness alone. Among the holy comprehensors there is the year of eternity and glory, in which “the saints shall rejoice in glory” [Note: [Col. 0229] Ps. 149.] without end.

[Col. 0230C] The philosophers divided the solar year into four seasons—spring, summer, autumn, and winter—and into twelve months. A month is the period in which the moon makes one circuit through the zodiac. The Gentiles gave months names: some from gods, some from causes, some from numbers. Thus they called January from an idol—and indeed from the idol—because they named it after two-faced Janus, on whose first day they celebrated the rites of Janus. But more truly January is named from a thing, because it is established as the gate and beginning of the year.

February is named from an idol, namely from *Februus*, that is, Pluto; or from a thing, from fevers; or from *februo, -as*, “I purify,” because on its first day the city was purified. They called March thus in honor of Romulus, whom they believed to be the son of Mars, and so it is named [Col. 0230D] from an idol. But it is named from a thing, from males, because at that time living creatures desire males. April is called as it were *aperilis*, because the bud then opens into flower, and so it is named from a thing; but from an idol it is called from *Aphros*, which is Venus, as it were *Aphrilis*. May is named from Maia, Mercury’s mother. June is named from Juno; but more truly May is named from elders and June from younger people, because what the elders prescribed in May, the young carried out in June. July is named from Julius Caesar; August from the august Octavian. For previously July was called Quintilis and August Sextilis. September, October, November, and December [Col. 0231A] received their names from numbers and the rains of the air.

They also divided the months into Kalends, Nones, and Ides. The Kalends are so called from *colendo*, “worshipping,” because the beginnings of months were observed; or rather from *calon*, “good.” And know that among the Egyptians the beginnings of months were announced beforehand. Therefore “the tenth day before the Kalends,” and similarly the rest, is found. The Nones are so called from *nundinae*, and the Ides means the division of the month.

The months also contain four weeks. A week is called from the Greek word *hebdomos*, which is interpreted in Latin as “seventh,” because it is completed in a course of seven days. A day is a space of twenty-four hours and has two parts, day and night. Day is the sun’s presence above the earth, and it has three parts: morning, midday, and late day. Night is the sun’s absence above the earth, and it has seven parts: [Col. 0231B] twilight, so called as if from *creperum*, “uncertain”; evening, so called from the rising of the star having this name; *conticinium*, when all things are silent; *intempestum*, that is, the unsuitable time, when it is not fitting to do anything; cockcrow, from the crowing of the cock; morning, from the star or from dawn; and pre-dawn, from light, that is, the time that is daybreak.

Those, however, who say there are four [parts] include twilight and evening under *conticinium*, and understand morning within pre-dawn. These four parts are called watches, a term taken from shepherds or the sentries of camps, which the Lord in the Gospel called by other names: evening, midnight, cockcrow, and morning. [Col. 0231C]

The Gentiles assigned names to the days from the planets, naming the first day after the sun, which is ruler and governor of all the stars, just as this day is first of all days; the second after the moon; the third after Mars; the fourth after Mercury; the fifth after Jupiter; the sixth after Venus; and the seventh after Saturn. They assigned individual hours to each planet, so that whichever planet occurs first after twenty-four [hours] claims the name of that day. Thus this is the order of the planets: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, and Moon. From these the philosophers derived the names of days, because they held that each contributed something in human beings: slowness from Saturn, moderation from Jupiter, [Col. 0231D] ardor from Mars, spirit from the sun, pleasure from Venus, eloquence from Mercury, and body from the moon.

Among the Hebrews they say: first [day] of the Sabbath, second of the Sabbath, third of the Sabbath, fourth of the Sabbath, fifth of the Sabbath, sixth of the Sabbath, Sabbath. The meaning is: “first of the Sabbath,” that is, first from the Sabbath; and similarly for the others. We, however, call the days *feriae*, either because *feriari* is said as though from *fari*, “to speak”—for in the creation of the world, on each day, the Lord said: “Let there be light” [Note: [Col. 0231] Gen. 1.]—or because *feriari* means “to call”; and it is derived from the Gentiles, who called festival days *feriae*. But we call every day *feriae*, either because we celebrate the solemnities of Mass on each day, or because every day we are bound to cease from sins. [Col. 0232A]

Therefore the day on which the Lord rose is called the Lord’s Day; the same is called the first *feria*, that is, the first day on which one ought to keep holiday—that is, refrain from sins. Likewise with the others. Or the Sabbath was formerly considered a holiday; therefore Sunday is called the first *feria*, that is, first after the *feria*, just as first after the Sabbath. Christian religion, however, has preserved the name Sabbath from Hebrew truth.

And note that there are sidereal days, in which the stars move and people are barred from navigation. There are campaign days, of which [it is written] in the Book of Kings: “at the time when kings customarily go forth to war.” [Note: [Col. 0231] 2 Sam. 11.] There are intercalary days, which we know to be additional to the twelve months. There are dog days, in which the Dog Star burns the lands. There are solstitial days, in which [Col. 0232B] the sun seems to stand still. There are equinoctial days, in which days are equal to nights. There are lawful days, on which laws are spoken; unlawful days, their opposites; feast days, that is, festive days, such as the days of unleavened bread; [Note: [Col. 0231] Matt. 26.] and ordinary days, as it were far from feasts.

There are evil days, whence the Apostle says: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil”; [Note: [Col. 0231] Eph. 5.] because on them people are afflicted more than usual. Conversely, there are good days. There are Egyptian days, on which Egypt is believed to have been struck, or whose observance was invented by the Egyptians. There is also the day of salvation, on which the Lord came to save. There is the day of judgment, or the day of the Lord, [Note: [Col. 0231] 2 Cor. 6.] on which he will come to judge. [Note: [Col. 0231] 2 Pet. 2.]

The days in which we live are ours, because in them we contend according to free choice; [Col. 0232C] but the day of judgment is not ours but the Lord’s day, [Note: [Col. 0231] 1 Thess. 2.] because he will reward us according to his own judgment. It will be a day of joy for the good, but of calamity and misery for the wicked. [Note: [Col. 0231] Zeph. 1.] A day has twenty-four hours, and an hour four points. These too are full of mysteries.

For we worship two-faced Janus when we mourn past sins and guard ourselves against those that follow; when, forgetting what is behind, we stretch ourselves forward with the Apostle. [Note: [Col. 0231] Phil. 3.] The general year is Christ, whose members are the four seasons, namely the four Evangelists. The twelve months are the Apostles; the weeks, each possessing the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; the days, each attaining by faith in the Trinity to the eight beatitudes; the hours, each fragrant with four virtues. Or by the entire year [Col. 0232D] we understand the whole time of this present life; by the four seasons, the four states of the Church militant: the state of peace, tyrannical persecution, heretical depravity, and feigned familiarity. These are the four horses—white, red, black, and pale—of which John speaks in the Apocalypse. [Note: [Col. 0231] Rev. 6.]

Each state contains three dimensions, shining in the elect as seven lamps: [Note: [Col. 0231] Rev. 4.] beginning, middle, and end. It also contains day and night, that is, prosperity and adversity. In both there were twelve prophets and twelve apostles, and likewise all teachers of the Old and New Law, who are called the twenty-four; [Note: [Col. 0231] Rev. 5.] or because they proclaim faith in the Holy Trinity through the four regions of the world; or because they perform the six works of the fourfold Gospel. All these are supported by the points of the four virtues.

Or the year is the warfare of a human life upon earth. [Note: [Col. 0233] Job 7.] The four seasons are the four ages: adolescence, youth, old age, and decrepitude; or the four virtues, in which we ought to serve the Holy Trinity, be fragrant with three virtues, and abound in seven gifts in prosperity and adversity, so that through the quaternity of virtues we may attain the senary of works, and through the ternary of virtues the octonary of beatitudes.

## CHAPTER VIII. SUNDAY AROUND THE OCTAVE
While all things kept the midst of silence, and night in [Col. 0233B] its course had reached the middle of its way, your almighty Word came from royal thrones [Note: [Col. 0233] Wis. 18.]. There are three silences: the first before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third shall be in glory. The first was ignorance of sickness; the second, despair of healing; the third, the attainment of health. For before the Law man did not recognize his disease, and therefore, being silent, did not seek a remedy; and this is the first silence. But when the Law entered in [Note: [Col. 0233] Rom. 5.], the sick man recognized his disease and sought to be healed through the works of the Law [Note: [Col. 0233] John 5.]; but, realizing that no one can be justified through the Law [Note: [Col. 0233] Gal. 3, 5.], wearied by prolonged cries and despairing of salvation, he was silent again. Nor was man alone silent, but also all things: namely, men, angels, and the elements, which had previously borne testimony to Christ about to be born, [Col. 0233C] whether through voices or through signs. This is the second silence: while all things kept it, night in its course had reached the middle of its way.

Night is understood in a threefold sense: the devil, the passing course of this present life, and sin. There are likewise three ways: the first to heaven, the second to hell, the third the course of the present life. Or the middle way is the human race, or the human spirit, intermediate between the spirit which dies and is clothed in flesh, and the Spirit which neither dies nor is clothed in flesh. The devil possessed the whole human race and, in his course, was drawing it toward the abyss of perdition. The present life too is night: its first stage is from non-being to being through generation; its last, from being to non-being through corruption; its middle, from one mode of being to another [Col. 0233D] through change. For the course of the present life is that upon which we enter by being born, traverse by living, and leave by dying. In this course that night had reached the middle of its way, when death drew down to the lower regions all whom it found in the course of this present life. The night of sin too, beginning with original sin and running through actual sins, had reached the middle of its way when, as transgression of the natural and written Law followed, sin had come to its greatest increase: when “death reigned from Adam unto Moses” [Note: [Col. 0233] Rom. 5.] and indeed persisted until the coming of the Lord.

Therefore, when every hope of recovered [Col. 0234A] salvation had perished and night was carrying all things away with it, the almighty Word is sent to deliver them, so that the gift of divine grace may be the more highly commended. Moses, God’s servant, uttered many words and sent forth many powerless utterances, unable to accomplish what they promised; but the Word of the Father is one and unique, because “God has spoken once” [Note: [Col. 0233] Ps. 61.], and he himself is almighty. For he not only “spoke, and they were made” [Note: [Col. 0233] Ps. 32.], but “did whatsoever he willed” [Note: [Col. 0233] Ps. 113.]. This Word came. But whence did he come, and whither? From royal thrones—from the Father’s assent, from equality of majesty—to flesh, to the cross, to death; from the light of heaven to the darkness of hell.

Thus coming, he interrupted silence: for he spoke peace, gave grace, set forth mercy, and promised pardon. Therefore [Col. 0234B] the sick began to hasten to the physician and, with purity of faith and confession of truth, loudly to demand the remedy. This Word still speaks, while daily accomplishing in his own people what he promised; the sick man still asks that he may receive health through grace. But when complete health has come, there will be nothing further to request, according to the words: “In that day you shall ask the Father nothing” [Note: [Col. 0233] John 16.]; and then there will be the third silence, that of consummation.

The Office is the voice of the primitive Church, in which it recalls the Lord’s Nativity. It proclaims its fruit in the Epistle, *As long as* [Note: [Col. 0233] Gal. 4.], because we have passed from servitude to the adoption of sons; and it commends him according to wisdom, as in the Gospel: [Col. 0234C] *Joseph was* [Note: [Col. 0233] Luke 2.], where it is said: “The child grew and was strengthened, full of wisdom; and the grace of God was with him.” According to power, as in the Alleluia, *The Lord has reigned* [Note: [Col. 0233] Ps. 92.], and the Offertory, *For God has established* [Note: [Col. 0233] Ibid.]; according to beauty, as in the Gradual, *Beautiful in form* [Note: [Col. 0233] Ps. 44.]. In the Communion, however, *Take the child* [Note: [Col. 0233] Matt. 2.], the time of flight is marked, when the Lord descended into Egypt; and mystically it refers to the adoption of the Gentiles, since the Lord passed from Judaea to the Gentiles in order to adopt them as heirs.

Observe that if the Nativity of the Lord, or the solemnity of Saint Stephen, Saint John, or the Innocents falls on a Sunday, this Office shall be sung after the Octave of the Lord; but otherwise it is sung within the Octave. Hence, if Sunday falls within the octaves of the saints, [Col. 0234D] this Sunday Office shall be sung, and only a commemoration of the octave shall be made. Accordingly, some say that, just as the Office of Christmas Day is the joy of the Gentiles who have seen God’s salvation, so today’s Office is the proclamation of the Jews who are to be recalled at the end of the age. For the wild olive ought not to boast against the branches of the good olive [Note: [Col. 0233] Rom. 11.], nor should the younger brother be angry with the elder [Note: [Col. 0233] Luke 15.]; rather, amid the feasting, he should entreat the father to come out and bring him in, softened by gentle exhortations. For he who is now set for a fall shall be set for resurrection in Israel, as is said in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0233] Luke 2.].

Then will be fulfilled what the Apostle [Col. 0235A] says in the Epistle: that God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the Law, in order that he might redeem those who were under the Law [Note: [Col. 0235] Gal. 4.]. Then the little child who was under the elements [Note: [Col. 0235] Ibid.], that is, under the literal sense, shall be an heir and obtain the throne of the kingdom. But now the Lord is in Egypt [Note: [Col. 0235] Matt. 2.], that is, among the Gentiles, who formerly served under Pharaoh, namely the devil. Yet then through faith he shall return from Egypt into the land of Israel—that is, to the Jews—when the remnant shall be saved [Note: [Col. 0235] Isa. 10, and Rom. 9.]. This return is treated in the Gospel, *Herod having died* [Note: [Col. 0235] Matt. 2.], which is read at the vigil of Epiphany. That vigil borrows its entire Office, except for the Gospel, from the Mass of dawn: *Light shall shine*, because at Epiphany, the glorious and beatific manifestation of the Lord, in which the Lord shall appear as he is [Note: [Col. 0235] I John 3.], the saints shall shine in [Col. 0235B] God [Note: [Col. 0235] Matt. 13.], and God shall shine in them.

It is asked whether this day is to be fasted; and indeed it seems that it is, since an Office is assigned to it and the Alleluia is omitted in the Office, unless it is Sunday.

## CHAPTER IX. ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

We celebrate a day adorned by three miracles. Today the star led the Magi to the manger. For when the Lord had been born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: “Where is he that is born King of the Jews? For we have seen his star in the East, and have come to worship him” [Note: [Col. 0235] Matt. 2.].

Zoroaster, a king, invented the magical art. Balaam, who prophesied of Christ, saying, “A star shall arise out of Jacob, and [Col. 0235C] a man shall rise out of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0235] Num. 24.], sprang from his seed. From this lineage came these three Magi, who came to worship the Lord with gifts—gold, frankincense, and myrrh. The Magi were called mathematicians, that is, persons skilled in the stars. These three were the first fruits of the Gentiles, whom the Lord chose to worship him, in order to signify the conversion of the Gentiles from the three parts of the world—Asia, Africa, and Europe—and from the three sons of Noah. They offered three gifts, believing him king in gold, God in incense, and mortal in myrrh. Or by the three gifts we understand natural philosophy, ethics, and logic; or history, tropology, and allegory; or wisdom of faith, prayer, and good works.

They came, led by the star, on the twelfth day after the Nativity, signifying that the Gentiles were to be drawn to faith in Christ [Col. 0235D] “with the word cooperating” [Note: [Col. 0235] Mark 16.] through the twelve apostles. But if they first saw the star on the day of the Nativity, how could they have arrived so quickly from regions so remote? Some answer that they saw it before the Nativity; others, that they came on dromedaries. A dromedary is an animal smaller than a camel but swifter than it; for it runs in one day as much as a horse in three days. It is therefore said to derive from δρόμος (*dromos*), “running,” and ἀρετή (*aretē*), “strength” or “excellence.”

It is asked what became of the star after it had fulfilled its office. Some answer that it fell into a well and still appears to certain persons, but only to virgins; [Col. 0236A] others, that it was dissolved into its primordial matter. With respect to this miracle, the solemnity is called Epiphany, from ἐπί (*epi*), “above,” and φάσις (*phasis*), “appearance.”

Today Christ, “when he was beginning to be about thirty years old” [Note: [Col. 0235] Luke 3.], was baptized in the Jordan by John for three reasons: that he might fulfil all righteousness [Note: [Col. 0235] Matt. 3.], approve John’s ministry, and impart to the waters a regenerative power. He therefore chose to be baptized in his thirtieth year and afterward to preach, because a preacher ought first to be strong and pure in himself and then preach to others. This age is also fitting for a preacher. He is baptized in the Jordan as a sign of humility, and by John as a sign of God’s grace. For Jordan means “descent,” and John is interpreted “the grace of God,” because God’s grace is conferred upon those humbled in baptism.

[Col. 0236B] In this baptism the Trinity appeared: the Father in a voice, the Son in flesh, and the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove. Accordingly, from this miracle the solemnity is called Theophany, from Θεός (*Theos*), “God.” Today, when the year had come full circle, the Lord changed water into wine at the wedding of the chief steward [Note: [Col. 0235] John 2.]; in accordance with this miracle, the solemnity is called Bethphany, from *beth*, “house.” Bede says in his commentary on Luke that the Lord performed a fourth miracle on the same day, when the year had come full circle: namely, the feeding with loaves. Accordingly, the solemnity is called Phagiphany, from φαγεῖν (*phagein*), “to eat.” But the Church does not celebrate this, as being, so to speak, unauthentic.

It is asked, concerning the first three miracles, which should be preferred to which. The Greeks say [Col. 0236C] that baptism is to be preferred to the others, and for this reason today celebrate the sacrament of baptism more frequently and solemnly; in their canons the Roman Church opposes them. First, because Christ’s baptism and ours differ in character; and then because “all we who were baptized in Christ were baptized into his death,” not into his baptism: “For we were buried with him by baptism into death” [Note: [Col. 0235] Rom. 6.]. Thus, after he had risen from the dead, he gave the apostles authority and a form for baptizing, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0235] Matt. 28.]. Although he could have instructed them about this before his Passion, he did not wish to do so, signifying that the grace of regeneration began from his resurrection, and that the regenerative power of the waters flowed [Col. 0236D] from his side.

That miracle, therefore, in which he was worshipped by the Magi, unquestionably Gentiles, is more eminent; it affords the hearts of the Gentiles great matter for spiritual joys. For by taking them up, “our peace made both one” [Note: [Col. 0235] Eph. 2.]. What could be fuller of a heavenly miracle than that the Magi were taught not by Scripture, not by a human teacher, not by an angel, but by the oracle of the Holy Spirit alone through a star? What is worthier of heavenly instruction? What could be more fitting than to confess him king by gold, Lord by frankincense, and mortal by myrrh?

From these three miracles, and especially from the first, is composed the Office of this day, [Col. 0237A] both nocturnal and diurnal. At its beginning the nocturnal Office differs from the usual practice. For *Come, let us exult in the Lord* [Note: [Col. 0237] Ps. 94.] is not sung, first because kings come to worship the Lord [Note: [Col. 0237] Matt. 2.] without having been invited. Hence immediately after *Lord, thou wilt open my lips* [Note: [Col. 0237] Ps. 50.], *Bring unto the Lord* [Note: [Col. 0237] Ps. 28.] is said, as though suddenly. According to our custom, the antiphon containing the theme of the following Office—namely, the three miracles—is sung.

Nor do we sing *Come* or the invitatory, lest we seem to imitate Herod. For he invited the chief priests and scribes of the people and asked them where Christ should be born; he said to the Magi: “When you have found him, report to me, that I too may come and worship him” [Note: [Col. 0237] Matt. 2.]. He said this not in order to worship Christ, [Col. 0237B] but to destroy him. For a similar reason, during the three days before Easter we give the kiss of peace to no one, lest we seem like Judas the traitor.

Perhaps also the antiphon is reserved for the sixth hour because of the Gentiles, who came to faith in Christ in the sixth age of the world; or to signify that Christ, to whom the psalm invites us, came in the fullness of time [Note: [Col. 0237] Gal. 4.], for six signifies perfection. It should be noted that Alleluia is not placed in the antiphons of the earlier nocturns, because they are assigned to the old state.

The first nocturn touches upon the time of the natural Law, in which Abraham offered a ram [Note: [Col. 0237] Gen. 22.] and men invited one another to sing psalms and worship the Lord. The second touches upon the time of the Mosaic Law, in which [Col. 0237C] the prophets foresaw the Gentiles coming to worship the Lord. The third belongs to the New Testament, which begins with baptism. Therefore it has at its head the antiphon *The river’s stream*, with the psalm *Our God* [Note: [Col. 0237] Ps. 45.]; this is an inverted and unusual ordering of psalms, though the psalm properly occupies the seventh place, because it relates to the sevenfold Spirit of grace bestowed through the power of baptism. The following antiphons with their psalms likewise indicate the New Testament; and these three psalms show the agitation of the Gentiles against the apostles’ preaching, the overthrow of idols, and the conversion of believers.

We have said this according to the custom of some. We, however, place *The river’s stream*, with its psalm, in the first [Col. 0237D] nocturn, and *Come* in the third, preserving the proper, natural, and customary order of the psalms. This is also fitting, because the Gentiles came to faith in the time of grace. Observe also that there is an ascent in the antiphons: the first pericope contains priests, the second kings, and the third reaches as far as angels. Alleluia occurs frequently in the third nocturn, because in the third age the redeemed Church rejoices. After the third nocturn follows the Gospel concerning Christ’s baptism and genealogy [Note: [Col. 0237] Luke 3.].

Notice that two Gospels concerning Christ’s genealogy are read at night: one at the Nativity, the other today, because both [Col. 0238A] generations of Christ were in night, that is, obscure and not understood by earlier minds. One is carnal, the other spiritual. In the carnal genealogy we count downward, and *begat* is used, expressing carnal and temporal succession. In the spiritual genealogy we ascend, and *who was* is used, followed by *son*, to indicate adoption in spiritual generation. Why Matthew descends and Luke ascends has been discussed above; or Luke counts upward because it is proper to priests to lead the people from lower things to higher. When the Gospel has been read, rejoicing in Christ’s generation, we resound aloud, *We praise thee, O God*. The diurnal Office, however, wholly concerns what we have said to be the chief and principal miracle: the first fruits of the Gentiles [Col. 0238B] and the gifts of the Magi.

Therefore holy Church, chosen from among the Gentiles, rejoicing in the beginning of her calling, offers God a noble proclamation of praise for her salvation, saying: *Behold, he has come*. This is taken from Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0237] Chap. 3.], though it is not found there in this continuous form. For singers were permitted, after the manner of bees, which compose a single sweetness of honey from diverse flowers, to compose for God a song of gladness from various places in Scripture; a mixture of good things is more pleasing. *Behold*: it is openly manifest that the Lord, Lord by nature and ruler in effect, has come. He has come to us—that is, he assumed flesh. Or, to allude to the present day: he came to us, that is, he who lay hidden in the flesh appeared to be God through many signs, so that through [Col. 0238C] the star and the gifts, through the Father’s voice and the Spirit in the dove, the remaining things might be manifest.

Observe that it is customary on this day to announce the Lord’s Easter in these words: “Your charity knows, dearest brethren, that, with the mercy of Christ’s assent, you ought to celebrate the Lord’s Easter on such a day.” It is announced beforehand because it is not celebrated like other feasts. Other feasts are observed annually on fixed dates and follow the sun and stars. The sun represents Christ, who is the Sun of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0237] Mal. 4.], while stars signify the saints, according to the Apostle: “Star differs from star in glory” [Note: [Col. 0237] I Cor. 15.]. Therefore, just as the sun and stars seem immutable to our sight, so Christ’s Nativity and the natal days of the saints are celebrated without change.

The Easter solemnity, however, by the Lord’s command follows the moon, [Col. 0238D] as shall be explained below; and the moon often appears to men’s sight to wax and wane. Again, it does not occur on the same date each year. For if today is the fourteenth, when the year has gone around and eleven days have been added, today will be the twenty-fifth; and in the third year, when eleven more are added and thirty taken away, today will be the sixth. Again, Easter is celebrated only on Sunday; but the day that is Sunday will in the next year be called Monday. Thus that solemnity varies, and its variation causes the variation of Septuagesima, Sexagesima, Ascension, and Pentecost. For the intervening days should be neither more nor fewer in number, [Col. 0239A] as we shall teach below, between Septuagesima and Easter, Easter and Ascension, and Easter and Pentecost.

Thus that solemnity must necessarily be announced beforehand, so that we may know during what period after the feast of Epiphany to sing the history *O Lord, rebuke me not in thine anger* [Note: [Col. 0239] Ps. 6.], and when Septuagesima ought to begin. On the Sunday falling within the Octave, according to our custom, the lessons are of Sunday; at the *Benedictus*, the antiphon *Son*; at the *Magnificat*, the antiphon *Child*; the Introit *On the high throne*, the Epistle *I beseech you*, the Gospel *When he was*, and the prayer *Vows*. After the commemoration of Epiphany, the remaining Hours are said of Epiphany. But their rationale and course will be set forth below.

On the Octave of Epiphany there is rejoicing over baptism, [Col. 0239B] namely the second Epiphany miracle, as in the antiphon *The old man* and the other following chants, which were translated from Greek into Latin. Therefore the idiom has a more solemn character in their composition. They are in the seventh tone, because they concern baptism, in which the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit operates; and they are eight in number, for the sake of the true Octave, to which the Baptist leads through the mystery and merit of baptism. The Office is deferred to the Octave because it takes the place of circumcision, which was celebrated on the eighth day; and the invitatory is sung on this day because, when the apostles preached, people were invited to baptism. The third miracle, namely the changing of water into wine, is reserved for the Sunday following the Octave. [Col. 0239C] Hence arises the judgment that it was not permissible before the eighth day, but is permissible only from this point onward to celebrate the sacrament of marriage.

## CHAPTER X. ON THE OFFICES AFTER THE FIRST SUNDAY OF EPIPHANY

“O Lord, rebuke me not in thine anger, neither chasten me in thy fury” [Note: [Col. 0239] Ps. 6, 37.]. This history, used from the Octave of Epiphany until Septuagesima, is plainly taken from the Psalms, both in Sunday and weekday antiphons and responsories. For in the preceding solemnities we have fallen into worldly joy and indulged in feasts and wanton songs. Therefore we employ, in the responsories and antiphons, psalms inviting us to repentance, and recite the Epistles of Paul, which in some manner instruct us toward repentance [Col. 0239D]. Hence, on the day following the Octave, we set the Epistles and weekday chants; or because, as prophecy follows the Law, so apostolic Scripture follows the Gospel.

Since we undergo this repentance in the hope of joy, we therefore sing psalms joyfully and chant Alleluia; this we multiply in the final Office at Vespers, because those who repent worthily pass from this life to rest and receive the immeasurable, everlasting joy of the angels. But we shall speak more fully of this below.

The diurnal Offices have another consideration, for they concern the apparition—that is, the manifestation of divinity. For just as from Christmas Day to Epiphany the humanity of the Saviour appeared from the Offices [Note: [Col. 0239] Tit. 3.], so in the three Sunday Offices that follow, his divinity shines forth. Thus on the first Sunday is read the Gospel: *When Jesus was twelve years old*, in which, by saying, “Did you not know that I must be in the things that are my Father’s?” [Note: [Col. 0239] Luke 2.], he plainly declares himself to be God—the one whom thousands upon thousands of angels serve [Note: [Col. 0239] Dan. 7.]. Therefore *Upon the high throne* is sung, [Col. 0240A] where it is said that a multitude of angels worships him; they praise him in the Gradual; and likewise in the Alleluia and Offertory they invite the earth, saying: “Sing joyfully to God, all the earth” [Note: [Col. 0239] Ps. 99.]. But because praise of the Saviour does not sit well upon the lips of a sinner [Note: [Col. 0239] Ecclus. 15.], the Apostle accordingly exhorts and entreats them to holiness of life in the Epistle [Col. 0240B]. The Communion corresponds to the Gospel.

On the second Sunday is read the Gospel which says that the Lord, invited to a wedding, changed water into wine [Note: [Col. 0239] John 2.]; this was a great indication of his divinity. For God alone can change nature and restore our corruptible nature to glory. Therefore let all the earth worship him, sing psalms [Note: [Col. 0239] Ps. 65.], rejoice, confess, and praise; and let it invite the angels to praise, as appears in the Introit, Gradual, Alleluia, and Offertory. The Communion corresponds to the Gospel.

On the third Sunday is read the Gospel, *When he had come down* [Note: [Col. 0239] Matt. 8.], in which, by saying, “I will; be cleansed,” he shows the goodness and power of his divinity. Hence the cleansed leper, like [Col. 0240C] a chorus-leader, invites angels and men alike to worship God, saying in the Introit, “Worship the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0239] Ps. 95.], and in the Gradual, “The nations shall fear” [Note: [Col. 0239] Ps. 101.]; and he gives the reason in the Alleluia and Offertory, saying, “The right hand of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0239] Ps. 117.]. The Communion corresponds to the Gospel.

See how clearly divinity appears in the three Sunday Offices. They are three because for three years the Lord preached and declared his divinity through miracles. These three Offices intimate to us Christ’s benefits bestowed to gladden our hearts; therefore in the Offertories we sing, “Rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0239] Ps. 65.]. For we ought to rejoice because he leads us out of the prisons of hell and delivers us from the lowest hell [Note: [Col. 0239] Ps. 85.]; or because in the first of these three years, that is, immediately after baptism and temptation, [Col. 0240D] angels came and ministered to him [Note: [Col. 0239] Matt. 4.].

Therefore, immediately after Epiphany, on the Sunday occurring before the Octave, *Upon the high throne* is sung as the Introit and the Gospel is read: *When Jesus was twelve years old* [Note: [Col. 0239] Luke 2.]. It is suitably fitting that on the Sunday nearest after the twelfth day of the Nativity, the event known to have occurred in the twelfth year should be read; and, if necessary, it should be repeated even on the following Sunday. Our custom, nevertheless, prevails: if the date of Septuagesima is delayed, only the Epiphany Office is said on the Sunday within the Octave. But if Epiphany falls on the Sunday after the Octave, the Sunday Office is omitted.

[Col. 0241A] Since in the second year he shone more manifestly through miracles, on the second Sunday the Epistle in which gifts of grace are written is read [Note: [Col. 0241] Rom. 12.], and the Gospel concerning the beginning of the Lord’s signs is recited [Note: [Col. 0241] John 2.]. This is also fitting because the miracle is said to have been performed in the second year after baptism; and because it figures the change of letter into spirit, earth into heaven, and corruption into incorruption, all the earth is summoned to worship God in the rejoicing of the Introit.

It is nevertheless said that Augustus Caesar, for the glory of the Roman Empire, issued an edict that someone should come to Rome from every city of the world, bringing thence as much earth as his fist could hold, so that it might thereby be established that all were subject to the Roman Empire. [Col. 0241B] This was done. From that earth there arose a little hill upon which a church was afterward built and dedicated on this Sunday. Therefore at its dedication is sung: “Let all the earth worship thee” [Note: [Col. 0241] Ps. 65.].

And because in the third year he redeemed us by his Passion, through which he healed both peoples of eternal infirmity [Note: [Col. 0241] Isa. 53.], the Gospel concerning the healed sick man and leper is read [Note: [Col. 0241] Matt. 8.]. Therefore there is a doubling of words in the chants: “Sion has rejoiced, and the daughters of Judah have exulted” [Note: [Col. 0241] Ps. 96.]; and in the Gradual: “The nations shall fear . . . and kings” [Note: [Col. 0241] Ps. 101.]; and in the Alleluia and Offertory: “The right hand of the Lord, the right hand of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0241] Ps. 117.]. Through the healing of both peoples, moreover, the number of angels was increased. Therefore they are invited to praise in the Introit, where it is said: [Col. 0241C] “Worship” [Note: [Col. 0241] Ps. 96.].

But because a corrupt humour is not healed unless the swelling of pride is removed, the Epistle therefore commands us, after the example of Christ suffering and not striking back, not to render evil for evil [Note: [Col. 0241] Rom. 12.]. Some add a fourth Sunday and a fourth Gospel, in which, when Christ enters the boat, the sea is troubled and he, sleeping, is awakened by his disciples [Note: [Col. 0241] Matt. 8.], because, according to some, he ascended the cross in the fourth year after baptism; the devil stirred up the crowd of Jews; Christ fell asleep in the sleep of death; and on the third day he rose for the benefit of his own.

Nor should the opinion of those who assign the entire period from Christmas to the Purification to [Col. 0241D] the Saviour’s infancy be passed over in silence. Therefore, they say, commemorations of saints, especially those concerning the cross, should not be made, lest the objection be raised: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk” [Note: [Col. 0241] Exod. 23, and Deut. 14.]. Therefore, in the nocturnal vigils the New Testament is read, on account of the present life of the same man Christ, which these days signify; and Paul, the great herald of holy newness, comes into the hands of the Gentiles. Comparing new grace with the old Law, he humbled the law of works and raised up the law of faith with the palm of righteousness.

This is, as it were, a Lent of Christ, consisting of two perfect [Col. 0242A] numbers: doubled six and twenty-eight. The doubleness of six signifies the twofold perfect humanity of body and soul; the unity of the greater perfect number signifies the unity of divinity. Therefore, as there is rejoicing over the manifestation of humanity during twelve days, so there is rejoicing over the manifestation of divinity during twenty-eight. We celebrate this Lent in joy, because Christ’s incarnation was the joy of angels and men.

After this Lent follows Hypapante—that is, the Presentation of the Lord—by which we are stirred to our own presentation to God the Father. The forty days, therefore, show the present state of the Church, in which we labour through the four parts of the world to fulfil the Decalogue: that is, “to live justly and piously in this world, awaiting the blessed hope and the glory of the kingdom of the great God” [Note: [Col. 0241] Tit. 2.]. At that presentation [Col. 0242B] the Lord shall appear glorious to us. Therefore in these days the verse is sung: “For the Lord has built Sion, and he shall be seen in his glory” [Note: [Col. 0241] Ps. 101.]. Hence too around Hypapante the Introit “Worship” is fittingly sung [Note: [Col. 0241] Ps. 96.], because then it will be manifest to us face to face that the choir of angels worships the Lord.

## CHAPTER XI. ON THE HYPAPANTE OF THE LORD

“After the days of Mary’s purification were fulfilled” [Note: [Col. 0241] Luke 2.], etc. There were two commandments in the Law, one concerning the woman who had given birth, the other concerning the child born. Concerning the mother: if a woman bore a male, she was to refrain, as though unclean, from entering the Temple for forty days [Col. 0242C] [Note: [Col. 0241] Lev. 12.], because a child conceived in impurity is said to remain unformed for forty days in the womb. But if she bore a female, she was to double the period. For menstrual blood, which accompanies childbirth, is considered so unclean that, as Solinus says, crops wither and herbs die at its touch.

But why is the period doubled for a female? **SOLUTION:** because the curse upon female offspring is double. For she had Adam’s curse, and in addition: “In sorrow you shall bring forth” [Note: [Col. 0241] Gen. 3.]. Or because, as the science of physicians says, females remain unformed in conception twice as long as males.

When the days of purification had passed, the woman who had given birth offered a dove or a turtledove for the sin connected with childbirth. For a son or daughter she offered a yearling lamb as a burnt offering; and she who could not procure a lamb offered [Col. 0242D] two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one as a burnt offering for the child and the other for her own sin. This signified that, whether one had produced strong or weak works, one offered for them a lamb—that is, the riches of an innocent life—or a dove and a turtledove—that is, simplicity and chastity; or action and contemplation; but always, for the sins of both, the abundant watering of compunction.

The Virgin was obliged to observe these things, not because she needed purification or because her Son needed sanctification, but lest she seem to dissolve the Law. The present solemnity is therefore twofold, concerning [Col. 0243A] the woman giving birth and the child born—that is, mother and son. With regard to the mother it is called Purification; with regard to the Son, Hypapante, which means “meeting,” because, as is read in today’s Gospel, Simeon met the Lord when he was presented in the Temple by his parents [Note: [Col. 0243] Luke 2.]. Indeed, according to Malachi, the Lord, the ruler, came into the Temple [Note: [Col. 0243] Mal. 3.].

For Simeon, a just and God-fearing man, had received the answer from the Holy Spirit that he should not see death until he had seen the Christ of the Lord. Thus he took him into his arms and said: “Now dost thou dismiss thy servant, O Lord, in peace” [Note: [Col. 0243] Luke 2.]. But Anna, coming up, gave thanks to the Lord, awaiting the redemption of Israel [Note: [Col. 0243] Ibid.]. Therefore the nocturnal and diurnal Office alike is celebrated prophetically and evangelically concerning the queen, the king, Anna, and Simeon.

[Col. 0243B] But this must not be passed over in silence: on this day we customarily make a solemn procession with candles, as though visibly going to meet the Lord with Anna and Simeon. For to carry lights in our hands is, with Simeon, to confess and believe that Christ is prepared before the face of all peoples, “a light for the revelation of the Gentiles” [Note: [Col. 0243] Ibid.], which “enlightens every person coming into this world” [Note: [Col. 0243] John 1.]; and since we cannot visibly carry him, we carry in our hands his visible sign, fittingly corresponding to him.

For by the wax we understand Christ’s humanity: just as bees produce wax together with virgin honey by their work—for they are not dissolved by any lust nor joined in any intercourse—so [Col. 0243C] the blessed Virgin gave birth to Christ, God and man, without injury to the integrity of her womb. By the wick his mortality is expressed; by the fire, his divinity. Some [Col. 0244A] understand the divinity by the wick, and by the flame of the fire the gifts of the Holy Spirit, by which he was enkindled above his fellows [Note: [Col. 0243] Ps. 44; Heb. 1.].

Therefore, forty days later, at the feast of the Virgin, we carry candles in our hands as a figure of Christ, so that, with the five prudent virgins, our lamps of good works kindled, we may go to meet Christ the bridegroom [Note: [Col. 0243] Matt. 25.], carrying our sheaves [Note: [Col. 0243] Ps. 125.]; and, through the blessed Virgin, may be able to enter the heavenly city for the wedding and, cleansed by Christ’s mercy after the fortyfold discipline of penitence and the observance of the Decalogue and evangelical teaching, to be presented in the heavenly temple.

Those who sing before the chancel in the procession itself, “He received an answer,” signify the prophets foretelling both the Lord’s birth and mercy. The melody of those responding [Col. 0244B] is the joy of those receiving this mercy of God. Therefore, holding them in our hands, let us say: “We have received your mercy, O God” [Note: [Col. 0243] Ps. 47.].

Women likewise imitate the blessed Virgin in this: after childbirth, when forty days have passed, they enter the church, signifying that, if they have imitated the Virgin, after the present life they will enter eternal life. Observe also that the Gentiles at the beginning of this month purified the city walls and consecrated them to Februus, that is, Pluto; Pope Sergius changed that purification into the present procession. Observe also that the Purification has no octave, because it belongs to the rite of the old law and not to the New Testament, signifying that during the fortyfold course [Col. 0244C] of life we should so purify ourselves by the fortyfold course of penitence that we may be able to stand in the heavenly sanctuary.

## BOOK SIX

[Col. 0243]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0243D]

In an inverted order, the Church sets before us the error and deviation of the human race. As we treated above, it was not fitting to begin, after the first work of the special treatise, in which we dealt with recall, with that from which the physician sought to call us back; yet the obligation of the natural order presses upon the mind, and the ear itches to demand it. Therefore, in this second part of the special treatise, it is worthwhile to set forth chapters concerning this very deviation of the human race.

## CHAPTER ONE. ON SEPTUAGESIMA SUNDAY

“They surrounded me with the groans of death” [Note: [Col. 0243] Ps. 17.]. This Sunday is called Septuagesima because here begins the seventy days, which begin today and end on the Saturday of Easter week. This Septuagesima [Col. 0244D] both recalls past things and signifies present things.

For it recalls the period of seventy years during which Israel was under Babylonian servitude. For it is written [Note: [Col. 0243] 4 Kings 25.] that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, destroyed Jerusalem by force of arms, led the people captive, and afflicted them with hard labours for seventy years. Hence Jeremiah says: “They shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years” [Note: [Col. 0243] Jer. 25.]. Yet after sixty years had passed, Cyrus, who was also called Christ, subdued the Babylonian kingdom and granted the people leave to return [Note: [Col. 0243] 1 Esdras 1; Isa. 45.]. Thus one part returned with Zerubbabel to their homeland and joyfully rebuilt the temple at Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0243] 1 Esdras 2.], while another part remained in captivity until the completion of the seventy years. When these were completed, they returned happily under Darius and Ahasuerus, and then had a double joy.

Mystically, Nebuchadnezzar is the devil, Babylon the world, and Jerusalem [Col. 0245A] paradise. Nebuchadnezzar carried the people captive from Jerusalem into Babylon when the devil seduced the human race from paradise into the confusion and exile of this world [Note: [Col. 0245] Gen. 3.], where it is afflicted for seventy years. Or this is because the present life turns through the course of seven days; or because it is contained within seven thousand years. From the beginning of the world to the Lord’s Ascension we reckon six thousand years; from then onward, whatever time follows until the end of the age we comprehend within the seventh millennium, whose end God alone knows.

Behold two periods of seventy years, one historical and the other mystical. The present seventy days celebrated by the Church represents both: it recalls the historical one and signifies and figures the mystical one. For just as the children of Israel in that [Col. 0245B] captivity laid aside their instruments, saying, “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” [Note: [Col. 0245] Ps. 136.], concerning whom Jeremiah says, “I will take from them the voice of joy and gladness, the voice of bridegroom and bride” [Note: [Col. 0245] Jer. 7.], so we too ought not to rejoice but to mourn in the present life. This we represent during this season when we lay aside signs of joy in chants, garments, and food.

In chant, for example, we set aside Alleluia. The reason is that Alleluia signifies not just any praise, but that glory of which the Psalm says: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp; I will arise at dawn” [Note: [Col. 0245] Ps. 56.]. The glory of the Father is the Son, who assumed the harp of our humanity; broken in the Passion, he refashioned it into a psaltery through the Resurrection. [Col. 0245C] The prophets desired to see this and did not see it [Note: [Col. 0245] Luke 10.]. The bridegroom too has departed and withdrawn from us [Note: [Col. 0245] Song 6.]. Therefore, as we recall the condition of the Church not yet redeemed and lament our sojourn [Note: [Col. 0245] Ps. 119.], we rightly lay aside Alleluia.

Some bury it on Saturday at Sext, some at None, some at Vespers, some at Matins, some on the first Sunday day. This variety arises from varying ways of reckoning the beginning of the day. For some begin the day at midday, some at None, some at evening, some at midnight, and some at dawn. The Church, however, begins it at Vespers, because “the night has passed, and the day has drawn near” [Note: [Col. 0245] Rom. 13.]. Therefore Alleluia is more rightly set aside at Vespers; and Pope Alexander II decreed this, so that its repetition might refer to the end of the penitential season preceding [Col. 0245D] it, since angelic praise will follow, as we said above; or so that its laying aside might be assigned to the mourning which follows.

Hence some churches lay aside Alleluia with great rejoicing, while others do so with groaning and sighing. The former represent future restoration; the latter, expulsion from paradise [Note: [Col. 0245] Gen. 3.]. Thus, in bidding Alleluia farewell, we show it the same attentions as those departing from us: we kiss their neck and mouth, forehead and eyes. In place of the Alleluia laid aside, at the beginning of the Hours the Church uses: “Praise to you, Lord, King of eternal glory.” Not because these are equivalent: the former [Col. 0246A] is an angelic utterance, the latter human; the former Hebrew and therefore worthier, the latter Latin and therefore less worthy. In antiphons and responsories we use: “For ever.” At Mass, in place of Alleluia, we say the Tract.

No substitution is made in the Hebrew language, which, as Jerome says in his commentary on Isaiah, is richer than Greek; nor is one made in Greek, which is richer than Latin. But Latin, poorer than all the others, is substituted for Alleluia, in order to signify the poverty of the present life.

Likewise, we omit joyful chants, such as *Te Deum laudamus*, except, according to some, when it is sung on the Chair of Blessed Peter, because it is the hymn of those being enthroned, and on that day Peter was enthroned upon the see of Antioch. Likewise, we omit joyful chants such as *Gloria in excelsis*, except [Col. 0246B] at the Lord’s Supper, if a bishop is present and celebrates Mass, because of reverence for the oil. And rightly do we fall silent concerning *Te Deum laudamus* and *Gloria in excelsis*: because, as sinners by right, we represent sinners, “the praises of the Saviour” do not sound fittingly in the mouth of a sinner [Note: [Col. 0245] Ecclus. 15.]; or because, as we have said, the condition of the Church not yet redeemed through Christ is represented. These chants pertain especially to Christ.

And observe that the Church’s chant is threefold: one of sorrow, as in this season; another of joy, as at Easter; and a third of consummated glory, as on the day of Pentecost. In garments we omit joy: for just as those Israelites laid aside their wedding garments, so we also [Col. 0246C] ought in this season to lay aside the dalmatic and the subdiaconal garments, which are likewise solemn garments, and put on ordinary mournful dress. In food also we represent sorrow, both because we are afflicted by fasts and because we do not use delicacies.

That we ought indeed to fast is shown by Zechariah, who says: “When you fasted during those seventy years, did you fast a fast for me?” [Note: [Col. 0245] Zech. 7.] Therefore the Greeks sanctify the coming week by fasting. Let us then fast at least from friendship with this world. Yet just as they were freed in the sixtieth year from Babylonian servitude through Cyrus, so we were redeemed from the devil’s servitude by Christ in the sixth age of the world, and through the remission of baptism the robe of innocence was restored to us [Note: [Col. 0245] Luke 15.]. Therefore on Holy Saturday [Col. 0246D] we sing one Alleluia, already rejoicing in the hope of eternal rest and recovery of our homeland.

And just as one part returned home with Zerubbabel, while another remained in captivity [Note: [Col. 0245] 1 Esdras 2.], so one part of the faithful dead rose with Christ [Note: [Col. 0245] Matt. 27; 1 Thess. 4.], while another remained in the consolation of expectation. Likewise, one part of the living attained to the grace of faith, while another persisted in unbelief. But those who returned to Jerusalem, though they had joy, were nevertheless not free from anxiety for wives and children, companions and provision. So we too labour and groan in the present Church, and [Col. 0247A] bear a certain burden of care for the body [Note: [Col. 0247] Rom. 8; 2 Cor. 5.]. Therefore on Saturday and during the week we sing the Gradual after Alleluia.

When the seventieth year was completed, all returned, and therefore they doubled their joy. Hence on the Saturday of the newly baptized we double Alleluia, signifying that, when the time of our exile is ended, captivity will be released and the robe will be doubled.

Morally, every person is generated in paradise through the water of baptism; after baptism, through sins, he is taken captive into Babylon. There, when converted through the seven-day cycle, he performs the sevenfold course in the mourning of penitence, so that on the day of resurrection he may return joyfully to the heavenly Jerusalem. Observe that Alleluia is laid aside on Saturday in descending order, begun on Saturday, and doubled on Saturday: because in Adam’s fall—when he was in great [Col. 0247B] rest—we lost joy; but we recover it for souls in rest, and finally shall double it for bodies in the resurrection.

It is also noteworthy that Septuagesima begins in sorrow and ends in joy, through which it signifies penitence; for such is the nature of penitential psalms. Again, it has one part in sorrow and one half-completed part in joy, because those who pass through with penitence receive the blessedness of souls, or at least a certain expectation in purgatory. Again, for sixty days we represent the widowhood of the Church, namely up to Holy Wednesday; then for three days, the mortification of our flesh, up to holy Easter; then for six days, works of mercy, which, if we do them after baptism, enable us to obtain on Saturday [Col. 0247C] rest and the double robe of joy.

Again, it begins on Sunday and ends on Saturday, because our captivity began with departure from the dwelling-place of paradise and will endure until future rest; or because we who withdrew from our Lord through sin shall return through mercy to rest. Further, it begins in February in accordance with Zechariah, who says in the eleventh month, Shebat: “In the second year of Darius the word of the Lord came to him” [Note: [Col. 0247] Zech. 1.]. In our language *Shebat* is translated “rod”; it conveys severity and correction, because during this season of Septuagesima we ought to correct and amend ourselves for the sins through which we were taken captive by the devil. Again, it extends through ten weeks, because through the Decalogue one comes to [Col. 0247D] joy.

Therefore, because during Septuagesima we signify the time of deviation and guilt and recall our present captivity, we begin Genesis, and read the Heptateuch and Ruth until Palm Sunday. There the error and deviation of the human race and its expulsion are marked—an expulsion which we also sing mournfully and weep as we sing. Indeed, we follow the ancient history in which the miseries of the old life are recounted: Adam’s expulsion [Note: [Col. 0247] Gen. 3.], Noah’s flood [Note: [Col. 0247] Gen. 7.], and Abraham’s departure [Note: [Col. 0247] Gen. 12.].

At Matins Lauds, “The Lord has reigned” [Note: [Col. 0247] Ps. 92.] is omitted, because it is a psalm of joy and instructs the perfect. Instead we say, “Have mercy on me, O God” [Note: [Col. 0247] Ps. 50.] and “Give praise” [Note: [Col. 0247] Ps. 117.], because through penitence one comes to the confession of praise, and through fear to hope. For the first psalm impresses upon us fear of the punishment of sins; but because through contrition confidence to approach the Lord is born in us, we therefore praise God and say to one another: “Give praise.” Of these two, namely fear and hope, Moses says: “You shall not take the lower and upper millstone as a pledge” [Note: [Col. 0247] Deut. 24.], that is, from the sinner, who is a debtor, fear and hope.

At Prime, however, “O God, in your name” [Note: [Col. 0247] Ps. 21.] is sung with what follows, and “The Lord has reigned” [Note: [Col. 0247] Ps. 92.], lest anything from the Psalter be omitted; thus the whole Psalter is read in the week, although formerly it was all read on individual days. For this reason [Col. 0248B] “Give praise” is also said [Note: [Col. 0247] Ps. 117.], or in order that children may be instructed to know how to give praise to the Lord amid palm branches [Note: [Col. 0247] Matt. 21.]. For this psalm properly belongs to that day because of this verse: “O Lord, save me; O Lord, make me prosper. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0247] Ps. 117.].

What is sung at Mass—“The groans of death surrounded me”—is the voice of the primitive Church mourning in Abel, the proto-martyr and precentor, whose blood cried from the ground to the Lord, who opened its mouth and received him from the hand of Cain, his brother [Note: [Col. 0247] Gen. 4.]. Hence the station is at Saint Lawrence, whose precious death [Note: [Col. 0247] Ps. 115.] cried to heaven by a new and unheard-of kind of passion and was heard throughout the whole world. Hence in the Roman Church he is pre-eminent among the martyrs.

It is also the voice [Col. 0248C] of the human race groaning because it has lost joy and gladness and found tribulation and sorrow [Note: [Col. 0247] Ps. 114.]. For sick humanity, descending from Jerusalem to Jericho, fell among robbers, was stripped, wounded, and left half dead [Note: [Col. 0247] Luke 10.]. Driven from the felicity of paradise and from the face of its Creator, it says weeping: “The groans of death surrounded me.” But because it received a divine oracle concerning the recovery of salvation, when the Lord said to the serpent: “I will put enmities between you and the woman, between your seed and her seed; you shall lie in wait for her heel, and she shall crush your head” [Note: [Col. 0247] Gen. 3.], for in such words the victory of the Redeemer is promised. Though he is the seed of the woman alone, he so [Col. 0248D] exercised enmity against the serpent as to crush its head, plunder its vessels, and take all power from it [Note: [Col. 0247] Luke 11.].
