Therefore it adds: “In my tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he heard my voice from his holy temple” [Note: [Col. 0247] Ps. 17.]. By prophetic usage, because of excessive certainty, the past is put for the future. Therefore it promises love to the Redeemer, adding: “I will love you” [Note: [Col. 0247] Ibid.].

But because a long road remained from Adam to Christ’s birth—for seventy-seven generations are counted in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0247] Luke 3.]—the epistle concerning the long race-course is read: “Do you not know that those who run in the stadium …” [Col. 0249A] [Note: [Col. 0249] 1 Cor. 9.]. Here we are invited to battle, because “our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers” [Note: [Col. 0249] Eph. 6.], and are instructed in the discipline of military service: namely, to abstain from what hinders combat, so that as victors we may receive the prize and be crowned with the wreath of victory.

And because this race-course is distinguished by six ages, and because those hired in the morning bore the burden and heat while murmuring because those who came last entered first, the Gospel concerning the six ages and the murmurers is read [Note: [Col. 0249] Matt. 20.]. Yet the long-suffering comfort themselves in hope, saying in the Gradual, “Helper” [Note: [Col. 0249] Ps. 9.]; and, recognizing themselves to be in the depths of sins, after Jonah’s example they cry, groan, and pray [Note: [Col. 0249] Jonah 2.], saying in the Tract: “Out of the depths” [Note: [Col. 0249] Ps. 129.].

Observe that nearly all [Col. 0249B] authentic Tracts are composed in grave tones, and all indicate, through their mournful chant and weighty sounds, the weeping and sorrow of the saints living in this present life, whether in the active or contemplative life. Hence they are called *tracts*, either because they are sung in a drawn-out manner on account of their gravity, or because the saints, sighing, draw a groan from the depths of the breast. For although at times they rejoice, either in the benefit of grace already received or in the hope of glory yet to be received—whence they sometimes burst into melodies and words of joy—nevertheless, while dwelling in the valley of tears, especially when the Church represents our sojourn, they pour out tears beside the rivers of Babylon [Note: [Col. 0249] Ps. 136.] for their own transgressions and those of others. From their proximity to the Babylonian river, they see some sprinkled by it and others already carried downward, submerged by the river’s rapacity.

But present weeping sometimes arises from the upper watering-place and sometimes from the lower one [Note: [Col. 0249] Josh. 15.]: now because of the delay of heavenly blessedness, whence, “Alas for me, because my sojourn has been prolonged” [Note: [Col. 0249] Ps. 119.]; now because of the stains of the present life, whence, “I mingled my cup with weeping” [Note: [Col. 0249] Ps. 101.]. Therefore, although Tracts have grave tones, their words sometimes express joy, as “Praise” [Note: [Col. 0249] Ps. 146.], and sometimes represent sorrow, as “Out of the depths” [Note: [Col. 0249] Ps. 129.]. Or, because the Tract is sung in a drawn-out manner and sounds sweetly in the ears, it signifies that we should persevere with the Apostle in long-suffering and gentleness [Note: [Col. 0249] 2 Cor. 6.].

In the Offertory, “It is good” [Note: [Col. 0249] Ps. 91.], the one who is sick but awaits redemption now confesses and praises God; now he is troubled and wonders that the good labour while the wicked flourish [Note: [Col. 0249] Ps. 72.], adding: “How magnified” [Note: [Col. 0249] Ps. 103.]; now he predicts the destruction of sinners and the future exaltation of the good through Christ the unicorn. The Communion, “Enlighten” [Note: [Col. 0249] Ps. 32.], is the voice of the servant stripped of the glory of God’s countenance, who, placed in darkness, prays that the wall of enmity may be broken down [Note: [Col. 0249] Eph. 2.], so that, irradiated by the beam of the true sun, he may not be put to shame. Or all the official mourning signifies the disposition to which we ought to be bound, namely that through [Col. 0250A] mourning and humility we may attain to the Lord’s Passion.

## CHAPTER II. SEXAGESIMA SUNDAY

“Arise, why do you sleep, Lord? Arise, and do not reject us utterly” [Note: [Col. 0249] Ps. 43.]. This Sunday is called Sexagesima because here begins the sixty days, which begin today and end on the Wednesday of Easter week, when “Come, blessed ones” is sung [Note: [Col. 0249] Matt. 23.].

The number sixty signifies widowhood, because it enters the enclosure of continence; just as thirty signifies marriage, because it kisses itself with caressing fingers. Therefore this Sexagesima signifies the time of the Church’s widowhood: namely, the time in which it was widowed through the death—that is, the fall—of the first-created man, or through the bridegroom’s absence, [Col. 0250B] since he is absent from sinners by grace and from wayfarers by the presence of his humanity. For although Christ is present to us according to divinity, as in the saying, “I shall be with you until the consummation of the age” [Note: [Col. 0249] Matt. 28.], nevertheless he is absent inasmuch as he went abroad [Note: [Col. 0249] Matt. 25.]. It is called Sexagesima from six times ten.

For remedy and consolation, six works of mercy and the ten precepts of the Decalogue have been given in the present life, so that the Church may exercise itself in them and through their observance deserve to have the door of its bridegroom opened to it. Whoever observes these will deserve to hear, “Come, blessed ones,” which is sung on the last day of Sexagesima. Or the number six is perfect in its parts, while ten, when counted, signifies the reward [Col. 0250C] of works [Note: [Col. 0249] Matt. 20.]. Therefore whoever seeks reward through ten—that is, through the perfection of works—will receive the kingdom promised on Wednesday.

The nocturnal office of this day is the same history sung in Septuagesima, concerning the fall of the first human being, through whom the Church is widowed and becomes a pilgrim. In the daytime office, however, it laments exile and implores God for liberation, saying: “Arise, why do you sleep, Lord?” [Note: [Col. 0249] Isa. 59.]. It speaks doubtfully because sins separate God and humanity. “For our soul has been humbled in the dust, and our belly has clung to the ground”; but “arise and redeem us for your name’s sake,” not for our merit. For you deigned to redeem us; we are not worthy to receive it.

The manner [Col. 0250D] and effect of this liberation are expressed in the daytime office. Its manner is that it was to be accomplished through him who, taking the form of a servant, went forth [Note: [Col. 0249] Phil. 2.] to sow his seed, as is read in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0249] Luke 8.]. And because he was to sow through tillers, namely the apostles, one of whom was the vessel of election [Note: [Col. 0249] Acts 9.], a seed-scatterer who sowed more than the others, through whom the Gentiles came to know grace [Note: [Col. 0249] Acts 17; 1 Cor. 15.], the station is therefore at Saint Paul; and for this reason he is mentioned in the collect, where it says: “God, who perceives that we subsist by no strength of our own.” For we have sold ourselves under sin [Col. 0251A] [Note: [Col. 0251] Rom. 7.], and there is in us no power to pay [Note: [Col. 0251] Matt. 18.]; therefore we pray that the Lord may intervene to pay. For this reason Paul’s labours and dangers are also enumerated in the epistle [Note: [Col. 0251] 2 Cor. 11.]: “You gladly endure …”

Observe that the office is often arranged according to its station, as today: because the station is at Saint Paul, Paul’s labours are treated in the prayer and epistle. Similarly, in view of the station, mention is made of the martyrs Cosmas and Damian on Thursday, and of Susanna on the Saturday before mid-Lent.

Again, Paul, a good athlete, expresses in the epistle the means of escape, encouraging us to despise foolish masters who reduce us to slavery and devour us. The effect is expressed in the Gradual and Tract: because the sowing of the word was to some “an odour of life unto life,” and to others [Col. 0251B] “an odour of death unto death” [Note: [Col. 0251] 2 Cor. 2.]. For some were made like a wheel and chaff before the face of the wind [Note: [Col. 0251] Ps. 82.]; others knew God’s name and were moved to penitence, so as to flee from the face of the bow [Note: [Col. 0251] Ps. 59.], namely judgment, and that the elect might be delivered. After the earth has been shaken, the seed is introduced, as follows in the Gospel. Observe that in Septuagesima the vineyard is cultivated, while in Sexagesima the field is sown.

The Offertory, “Make perfect my steps” [Note: [Col. 0251] Ps. 16.], accords with the Gospel. We must fear lest the seed of God’s word, cast beside the way, be snatched away by birds—that is, unclean spirits—or choked by the cares and riches of this world, or wither in us because it lacks honour, that is, the richness of charity; and lest thus our steps be not made perfect. Therefore let [Col. 0251C] each one of us pray, and let us all pray, that the Lord may perfect our steps, make his mercies wonderful over us, guard the seed as the pupil of the eye lest it be choked by thorns, protect it beneath the shadow of his wings lest it be dried by the heat of the sun, and rescue it from the wicked one lest it be taken away from our hearts [Note: [Col. 0251] Ibid.]. Thus may good soil bear fruit and, bringing forth fruit in patience, say: “I shall appear in your sight with righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0251] Ps. 42.]. Thus in the Communion is sung: “I shall enter unto the altar of God” [Note: [Col. 0251] Ibid.]. Since we are earth, we shall not rise to the heavenly granaries unless we are borne by the word of God; but by it we shall be raised up, carrying sheaves [Note: [Col. 0251] Ps. 125.] of righteousness, making God glad—our youth in the vigour of eternal springtime.

## CHAPTER III. QUINQUAGESIMA SUNDAY

[Col. 0251D] “Be to me a protecting God and a house of refuge, that you may save me” [Note: [Col. 0251] Ps. 30.]. This Sunday is called Quinquagesima because here begins the fifty days, which begin today and end on holy Easter Day. For just as there were three returns of that people—the first under Zerubbabel, the second and third under Ezra [Note: [Col. 0251] 1 Esdras 2 and below]—so it was fitting that we, lamenting our sins and imploring mercy for them, should make three terminations: namely, return triumphantly to glory on Saturday, on Wednesday, and at Easter.

[Col. 0252A] Therefore this Quinquagesima signifies the time of remission. For the fiftieth year was called the year of jubilee in the old law [Note: [Col. 0251] Lev. 25; Num. 36.], that is, of remission or penitence; and the fiftieth psalm, “Have mercy on me, O God,” is a psalm of remission and penitence, which we use especially in this season. It is called Quinquagesima from five times ten and contains seven complete weeks. The number five therefore signifies Christ’s five wounds or the five operations of human sense; ten signifies the ten precepts of the Decalogue; and seven, the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. If, then, we firmly believe the Lord’s Passion and through outward observance fulfill the Decalogue in the Holy Spirit, we shall obtain remission from the Lord and come to the blessed and glorious resurrection.

Or we spend fifty [Col. 0252B] days in penitence so that in the following fifty days, namely from Easter to Pentecost, which we shall spend in joy, we may not pass them without deserving to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit on Pentecost Day. In this day’s nocturnal office, the Flood is read and sung, because penitence is designated by it. For just as the Flood extends through three times fifty days, so penitence is imposed for thought, words, and deeds. And it should be observed that first the punishment of the Flood is sung, then Abraham’s obedience, and finally the Gospel antiphons concerning the blind man receiving sight are added; because whoever has washed himself from the filth of sins through penitence and obeyed God’s commands will rejoice to be enlightened by Christ.

[Col. 0252C] The daytime office, however, takes its foundation from the blind man, namely the human race. For as is read in the Gospel: when the Lord approached Jericho, a blind man sat begging by the roadside and said, “Son of David, have mercy on me,” although he was rebuked by the crowds. The Lord said to him: “Receive sight; your faith has made you whole” [Note: [Col. 0251] Luke 18.]. This blind man is the human race, once ignorant of God, of itself, and of its native land, and ignorant that concupiscence is sin [Note: [Col. 0251] Rom. 7.]. Although it was hindered by the crowds of invisible enemies, nevertheless, anticipating the coming of illumination, it asks from the one in whom it hoped, at the Introit, for protection, a refuge, guidance on the way, salvation, and deliverance, saying: “Be to me a protecting God and a place of refuge” [Note: [Col. 0251] Ps. 30.].

The people returning used lamentation, flight, and prayers [Note: [Col. 0251] 1 Esdras 3 and below]. So we also, [Col. 0252D] returning through penitence, now mourn, saying “They surrounded me” [Note: [Col. 0251] Ps. 17.] and “Arise” [Note: [Col. 0251] Ps. 43.]; now flee and pray, saying, “Be to me a protecting God and a place of refuge” [Note: [Col. 0251] Ps. 30.]. Here we also indicate that we are on campaign: in Septuagesima we mourned, in Sexagesima we doubted, and now we trust in protection.

The epistle accords with the Gospel not merely in the words, “Now we see through a glass, in an enigma” [Note: [Col. 0251] 1 Cor. 13.], but because it points out a more excellent way, namely charity. [Col. 0253A] This is what makes saving faith operative; this is the eye of the heart. Whoever lacks it is blind, walks in darkness, and does not know where he goes [Note: [Col. 0253] John 12.]. For when the Lord began to enlighten the human race [Note: [Col. 0253] Luke 1.], he first anointed its eyes with this eye-salve [Note: [Col. 0253] Rev. 3.], saying: “You shall love the Lord your God” [Note: [Col. 0253] Matt. 22.]. In this epistle are set forth the necessary provisions of our warfare: faith, hope, and charity—these three.

In the Gradual we render thanks to the conqueror in the warfare, for the certain hope of triumph, saying: “You are God, who do wonders.” And because there are two peoples of the human race, and both are enlightened through Christ and share in triumph, it says: “You have made known your strength among the nations,” and adds: “You have delivered the children of Israel and Joseph” [Note: [Col. 0253] Ps. 76.]. Therefore in the Tract [Col. 0253B] the whole earth is invited to proclaim the enlightener and conqueror, when it says: “Make a joyful noise” [Note: [Col. 0253] Ps. 99.], as if to say: “Come to him, and be enlightened” [Note: [Col. 0253] Ps. 33.]; “Serve the Lord who made us” [Note: [Col. 0253] Ps. 99.], not him to whom we sold ourselves [Note: [Col. 0253] Rom. 6 and 7.].

Therefore in the Gospel the blind man doubles his petition, saying: “Son of David, have mercy on me” [Note: [Col. 0253] Luke 18.]. Therefore in the Offertory he doubles his thanks for the illumination of both peoples, saying: “Blessed are you, O Lord; blessed are you, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0253] Ps. 118.]; and in different words asks ever more earnestly for a double illumination, saying: “Teach me your justifications; teach me your justifications” [Note: [Col. 0253] Ibid.]. Or he says “justifications” twice because of the way of the testimonies of truth and of the commandments.

But because it is not enough to have reached the way and received the illumination of knowledge [Col. 0253C] unless we cast off the works of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0253] Gal. 5.], we are fittingly frightened by the example of those concerning whom we say in the Communion, “They ate” [Note: [Col. 0253] Ps. 77.]. And because in the great body of this blind man the chief, Peter, was enlightened, when the Son of God said to him: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood …” [Note: [Col. 0253] Matt. 16.], this station is appropriately assigned to him.

And note the rationally ordered sequence of the Gospels: in Septuagesima we cultivate the vineyard; in Sexagesima we sow the seed; in Quinquagesima we gather the fruit of light in the blind man who receives sight.

## CHAPTER IV. AT THE BEGINNING OF THE FAST
“Return to me with all your heart, in fasting, weeping, and mourning; rend your hearts, not your garments” [Note: [Col. 0253] Joel 2]. This day is called the Head of the Fast [Col. 0253D]; for on this Wednesday the Lenten fast begins. Excluding the six Sundays, thirty-six days remained for fasting. Hence Saint Gregory indicates to us only thirty-six days of abstinence. Perhaps these four had not yet been added, though they had to be added to complete the forty-day fast; and rightly, beginning on Wednesday, we continue forty-six days in abstinence. For we read that Solomon built the Temple of the Lord in the fourth age [Note: [Col. 0253] 3 Kings 6]; therefore our fasts begin on Wednesday, so that [Col. 0254A] at Easter we may be the Temple of God. Or we begin fasting on Wednesday because we have learned that Christ began his fast on that same day, having been baptized on Wednesday and begun his fast on the same day as his baptism. Or because four is a number made perfect by the equality of its sides. Hence fortitude occupies fourth place among the virtues, and this name “strong” is fourth among the names of Christ. Therefore catechumens are summoned on the same weekday, as are those to be ordained; and, just as the Temple is said to have been built in forty-six years, so the present fast is continued in abstinence for forty-six days.

Thus in the Gospel: “This Temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise [Col. 0254B] it up in three days?” [Note: [Col. 0253] John 2]. If anyone says that only forty-five years are reckoned from the first year of Cyrus, in which construction of the Temple began, to the sixth year of Darius, in which Ezra records that it was completed, let him know that, according to Josephus, its more distinguished portions were completed in the forty-sixth year. The Temple of Christ’s body too is believed to have been built in forty-six years, because the Virgin was twelve years old when she bore the Only-Begotten, who, according to some, drank the cup of death in his thirty-fourth year. Hence the name Adam, compounded from four elements, fittingly belongs to him. The letters of his name—whose body is made from the four elements—are likewise not without reason taken from the four quarters of the world: Anatole, meaning east; Dytis, meaning west; Arctos, meaning [Col. 0254C] north; and Mesembria, meaning south. By alphabetical calculation these amount to the same number: for in Greek numerical notation A signifies one, D four, again A one, and M forty; joined together, they make forty-six. Therefore we observe forty-six days in abstinence, so that we who, in a carnal manner, have been scattered through the four parts of the world by our first parent may, afflicted by that number, be conformed to the body of the second Adam, so as to deserve worthily to receive him at holy Easter. Or because an embryo lies unformed in the womb for forty-six days, we devote ourselves for that many days to fasting and prayer, that we may reform our unformed state in the Lord. Therefore, having until now been on campaign, we now begin battle with holy fasts [Col. 0254D]. Hence in the collect: “Grant, we beseech you, O Lord, that we may begin the safeguards of Christian warfare with holy fasts.”

And because the Lenten fast begins today according to ecclesiastical institution, chants and readings concerning fasting abound in the night and day office, especially those taken from the Epistle, “Return” [Note: [Col. 0253] Joel 2], and the Gospel, “When you fast” [Note: [Col. 0253] Matthew 6]. But fasting is fruitless without contrition of heart, an outpouring of tears, distribution of alms, vigils, and prayer—all of which are [Col. 0255A] fruits of repentance and weapons for our battle. Therefore some of these are included in the night and day offices: in the introit, “You have mercy” [Note: [Col. 0255] Wisdom 11]; in the gradual, “Have mercy on me” [Note: [Col. 0255] Psalm 56]; and in the tract, “O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0255] Psalm 102]. Observe that we use this tract until the Passion, on the second Wednesday and Friday, so that on the days assigned to stricter fasting we may remember our repentance once begun and unite prayer with fasting. The offertory, “I will exalt you” [Note: [Col. 0255] Psalm 29], is thanksgiving for forgiveness obtained; the communion, “He who meditates” [Note: [Col. 0255] Psalm 1], exhorts others to meditation upon the Law. It agrees with the Gospel, because to meditate upon the Law is to lay up treasure in heaven [Note: [Col. 0255] Matthew 6]. This Mass is to be sung at None, and Vespers is to follow immediately, as in Lent. In this Mass, and on every Sunday until the Passion [Col. 0255B] of the Lord, the preface “Who by bodily fasting” is to be said. Some, however, use the daily preface on Sundays, since those days are exempt from strict fasting.

Nor should it pass unnoticed that the Samaritan who recognized his suffering [Note: [Col. 0255] Luke 17], saying, “They surrounded me” [Note: [Col. 0255] Psalm 17], and therefore repeated his prayers, saying, “Arise” [Note: [Col. 0255] Psalm 43], and “Be” [Note: [Col. 0255] Psalm 30], seeing that he could not be cured without the poultice of repentance, today puts on the ash of humility and the haircloth of austerity by the medicine of salvation; for ashes and haircloth are the weapons of penitents. Today, indeed, we impose ashes upon our heads, recalling what was said to Adam: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” [Note: [Col. 0255] Genesis 3]. By this same attire we confess that we are neither gods nor from heaven—though we wished to be gods [Note: [Col. 0255] ibid.]—[Col. 0255C] but human beings, whose origin is from the earth; and we likewise recall Job’s ash and cinders [Note: [Col. 0255] Job 30]. Today we put on haircloth, recalling the loincloth of the first-formed man [Note: [Col. 0255] Genesis 3], recalling the repentance of the Ninevites [Note: [Col. 0255] Jonah 3], and recalling John’s clothing [Note: [Col. 0255] Matthew 3]. Today we bare our feet, representing Adam’s nakedness [Note: [Col. 0255] Genesis 3] and signifying that we need the adornment of grace. Today we make a procession, indicating that we strive to return to our homeland; but because we know that enemies stand against us on the way [Note: [Col. 0255] Exodus 13], we endeavor, armed with virtues, to go forth to battle “against the spiritual forces of wickedness” [Note: [Col. 0255] Ephesians 6]. Today also, recalling the day of our expulsion from Paradise, we expel sinners from the Church; and upon those expelled we impose seven years’ penance, [Col. 0255D] or another term in proportion to the magnitude of their crimes, because the human race, fallen in Adam, was condemned by God’s judgment to this exile of seven thousand years. Miriam likewise was outside the camp for seven days with leprosy [Note: [Col. 0255] Numbers 12]. We also impose exile because Cain, under God’s manifest vengeance, became a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth [Note: [Col. 0255] Genesis 4]; while the penitential prison begins with Joseph [Note: [Col. 0255] Genesis 39]. Both in prison and in exile they grow their hair and beard; [Col. 0256A] the Church took its example for this unkemptness from Joseph [Note: [Col. 0255] Genesis 41] or David [Note: [Col. 0255] 1 Kings 21]. In this exile they carry a staff as a sign of correction, through which one returns to the grace of communion. This staff is a cubit long, because “with the measure with which they have measured, it shall be measured back to them” [Note: [Col. 0255] Matthew 7 and Mark 4]. You will find the form of expulsion in the Council of Agde; the canons concerning penance are in the penitential book.

On Thursday the Epistle concerning Hezekiah is read [Note: [Col. 0255] Isaiah 38], and the Gospel concerning the centurion’s servant [Note: [Col. 0255] Matthew 8]. To the former the Lord added days; to the latter he restored health. By these we are admonished to cast our thought upon the Lord [Note: [Col. 0255] Psalm 54], to cry to him, to believe in him [Note: [Col. 0255] John 14], and to pray to him perseveringly [Note: [Col. 0255] Luke 11]. On Friday the Epistle, “Cry aloud” [Note: [Col. 0255] Isaiah 58], and the Gospel, “You have heard” [Note: [Col. 0255] Matthew 5], are read. In both, God’s testimonies, [Col. 0256B] which fleshly people understood carnally, are expounded spiritually. For the Epistle says that one must not fast for quarrels and disputes; the Gospel says that we ought not to love, give alms, or pray in order to be seen by people. Thus both discourage us from vainglory and invite us to spiritual understanding and works of mercy, lest we perish from the way [Note: [Col. 0255] Psalm 2], but obtain forgiveness from the Lord. On Saturday the Epistle is read: “If you remove” [Note: [Col. 0255] Isaiah 58], where light and rest are promised us; and the Gospel: “When evening came” [Note: [Col. 0255] Mark 6], where the Apostles come from the conflict of the sea to the harbour of safety, and from the darkness of ignorance to knowledge of the Saviour. Although this Saturday has an Epistle [Col. 0256C] and Gospel like certain days throughout the yearly cycle, it has no office in the chants, because, according to some, it had not yet been assigned to the solemn fast. But today let us fast, that we may reach the Sabbath.

## Chapter V. The First Sunday of Lent

“He shall call upon me, and I will hear him; I will deliver him and glorify him; with length of days I will satisfy him” [Note: [Col. 0255] Psalm 90]. This Sunday is called Quadragesima, because here begins the forty days, beginning here and ending at the Lord’s Supper. Through these forty days of penance we recall the forty years in which we know that the people returned from Egypt to their homeland. For it is read that the children [Col. 0256D] of Israel served under Pharaoh in Egypt for a long time [Note: [Col. 0255] Exodus 12], but, freed through Moses, crossed the wilderness for forty years [Note: [Col. 0255] Numbers 14], receiving food from heaven [Note: [Col. 0255] Exodus 16] and drink from the hardest rock [Note: [Col. 0255] Exodus 17], and thus finally came to a land flowing with milk and honey [Note: [Col. 0255] Joshua 5]. Mystically, as Augustine says, this number is a sacrament of this laborious time in which we fight against the devil. For time runs in fourfold divisions, and the world is bounded by four regions. [Col. 0257A] Therefore we, who served under the devil for a long time in this world but have been freed through Christ, upon whose body we feed and whose blood we drink [Note: [Col. 0257] 1 Corinthians 10], must return to the land flowing with milk and honey—that is, to Paradise—through observance of the Ten Commandments and the four Gospels, which multiplied make forty. Thus, in celebrating this Lent, we recall those forty years and signify our return to our homeland.

But because, after leaving Egypt, they entered the Promised Land through forty-two stations [Note: [Col. 0257] Joshua 5] and immediately celebrated the Passover, we add two days after forty-two days and celebrate the Lord’s Passover; and we rejoice on the day which the Lord has made [Note: [Col. 0257] Psalm 117]. Whoever therefore hastens to the homeland [Note: [Col. 0257] Hebrews 4] should strive [Col. 0257B] to complete this number. The genealogy of the Lord is likewise described by Matthew in the same number [Note: [Col. 0257] Matthew 1], Jechoniah being counted twice. Whoever, then, desires through baptism to come to Christ should arrive by the sacrament of that number, as Jerome says: the number by which the Lord came from the patriarch to the Virgin, as though to the Jordan, flowing with a full stream and overflowing with the graces of the Holy Spirit.

Of these forty-two days, six Sundays are excepted from fasting. For by the forty-six weeks we understand the whole time of this life; or because by multiplication the reckoning rises to fifty; or because it is a time of affliction, while life is varied by the six ages of the world or of the human being. Although afflictions exist universally in every one of them, we nevertheless had some consolation: [Col. 0257C] in the first, Adam delighted in Paradise [Note: [Col. 0257] Genesis 2]; in the second, Noah was comforted amid the flood [Note: [Col. 0257] Genesis 8]; in the third, Joseph delivered Israel from famine [Note: [Col. 0257] Genesis 42 and following]; in the fourth, Solomon reigned in peace [Note: [Col. 0257] 3 Kings 5]; in the fifth, we returned from Babylon [Note: [Col. 0257] 1 Ezra 1]; in the sixth, we rejoiced at the presence of the Bridegroom [Note: [Col. 0257] Matthew 9]. Or, although we sin at every age of our lives—whence also in every week of this time we sing while mourning and mourn while singing, and afflict by fasting the flesh that incites sins—yet through the six works of mercy we correct sins and deserve forgiveness of sins; therefore we end the affliction of fasting on six Sundays. Or perhaps, in remembrance of the Sunday resurrection and in hope of our own resurrection, we receive this small consolation [Col. 0257D] amid our weeping.

Thus, with six days excepted from fasting out of the forty-two, only thirty-six remain for fasting. These are a tenth of our 365 days; for it was fitting that, as we give tithes from other things, we should also pay a tenth from our days, that by this tenth of days we may correct whatever we have done against God’s commandments at other times. Hence perhaps this season should more properly be called a tithe than a forty-day fast. But as the Hebrews gave a tenth of their goods to God the supreme King [Note: [Col. 0257] Leviticus 27], so the pagans [Col. 0258A] paid a fortieth of their goods to their gods and kings—a fortieth which Venetians still exact in maritime customs duties. Therefore perhaps, from the custom of the pagans, we call this season not a “tithe” but a “forty-day fast.”

Yet to this tithe, consisting of thirty-six fasting days, four preceding days are added: in remembrance of four things which we mourn as having incurred—namely, that we were expelled from Paradise because of food; that we were condemned to beastly food; that we are afflicted by these punishments; and that we are to be more severely afflicted in Tartarus. Or they are added for an understanding of the four orders which we shall see at the future judgment. The first will be those judging: these are the perfect. The second, those to be judged by judgment: these are married persons. The third is that of the condemned: these are unbelievers. The fourth is that of those to be condemned: [Col. 0258B] these are believers empty of good works. Or rather, morally speaking, we fast these four days in order to amend whatever we have committed against the observance of the four Gospels through the wantonness of the four elements, in the four seasons of the year, or in the four courses of the day; or in order that we may sustain ourselves in fasting by the four virtues, so that the soul, which dies by the four deaths of thought, speech, action, habitual practice, or impenitence, may be raised by their aid. Thus this fast is more truly called a forty-day fast, in which we are bound to amend whatever we sin against the Law and Gospel; or we offer the number ten to God four times, so that for our daily sins we may observe our discipline mindfully and more devoutly.

[Col. 0258C] As Augustine says, daily and yearly cycles are completed by the number four. For the day passes through morning, noon, evening, and night hours; the year slips by through spring, summer, autumn, and winter months. In all these we are drawn away from love of eternal things; therefore by the number four we understand our daily excess in sins. But ten contains the whole of our discipline. For, as Augustine likewise asserts, knowledge of Creator and creature signifies what pertains to the instruction of humankind: knowledge and discipline consist in the creature’s serving the Creator. The Creator is God, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things [Note: [Col. 0257] Deuteronomy 32]. Therefore the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is worshipped here [Col. 0258D] by the mind that loves him with all its heart, all its soul, and all its understanding [Note: [Col. 0257] Matthew 22].

These are three; the body, formed from four elements, is subject to the mind for governance. Therefore to fast for forty days is to multiply this ten by four: that is, to establish it in us temporally and, through this ten—that is, through the service which the creature owes the Creator—to amend temporal sins. Or we fast for forty days, anticipating with prayers that in the following forty days, namely from Easter to the Ascension, [Col. 0259A] which we shall spend in joy, we may not transgress, but may be able to follow our Head into heaven. Or we fast forty days so that we may be reconciled to God by the same number through which we departed from him; for by the number four—of body or year, world or day—we violated the commandments of the Decalogue. By this number the Ninevites repented [Note: [Col. 0259] Jonah 2]; this span shall be given to those who apostatize under Antichrist; these are the priests’ curtains in the court of the forty-cubit tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0259] Exodus 26, 36].

Or rather, we fast for forty days so as to deserve knowledge of the Law and Prophets, and above all imitation of and grace from our Lord Jesus Christ. Moses fasted for forty days to receive the Law [Note: [Col. 0259] Exodus 34], and likewise Elijah [Note: [Col. 0259] 3 Kings 19]; Daniel too fasted for three weeks [Note: [Col. 0259] Daniel 10]. Our Lord [Col. 0259B] fasted for forty days without food immediately after baptism, when he was tempted by the devil in the wilderness [Note: [Col. 0259] Matthew 4]. Those men fasted for merit, but the Lord fasted for instruction; he also fasted as an example. Hence some observe only one forty-day fast. More commonly, three are observed, because, as the Hebrews hand down, Moses fasted upon ascending to the Lord three times; or rather because three persons are recorded as fasting forty-day periods: Moses, Elijah, and the Lord. But the Lord, whom we ought to imitate, fasted immediately after baptism.

Why did the Church institute fasting not immediately after Epiphany, but before Easter? Answer. First: because Christ’s resurrection follows his Passion. [Col. 0259C] Therefore we fast before Easter, praying that, as we suffer with him through affliction of the flesh, we may rise with him in glory [Note: [Col. 0259] Romans 6]. It is like a sick person who suffers more severely when approaching health. Second: because at this time the children of Israel entered the Promised Land [Note: [Col. 0259] Joshua 5], or returned from Babylon and immediately celebrated Passover. Therefore we fast so that, our labour completed, we may rise with Christ and pass from this life to eternal life. Third: because in spring, by the natural movement of heat and moisture, all living things are driven to lust; therefore we fast at this time so that, chastising our beast, we may reduce it to slavery [Note: [Col. 0259] 1 Corinthians 9] and restrain it from the assault of lust. For these reasons, then, the Church instituted this Lenten fast.

But [Col. 0259D] because clergy, as they precede the people in rank, ought also to precede them in holiness, Pope Telesphorus added a seventh week, calling this season Quinquagesima, “the fiftieth,” which is not without mystery. For just as by six weeks we understand six works of mercy, so by seven weeks are signified the seven ways in which sins are forgiven: through baptism, martyrdom, almsgiving, forgiveness, preaching, charity, and repentance. As time went on, because by the permission of certain pontiffs food was eaten twice on Saturday, lest nature be weakened by the fast [Col. 0260A] of Friday, they added an eighth week in compensation for the Saturdays of this season, calling it Sexagesima, “the sixtieth.” Finally, because of reverence for the Lord’s Ascension, the holy Fathers established that Thursday should be observed as a festival like Sunday; hence even now we are provided for more liberally on that day. For those Thursdays they added a ninth week, and thus instituted Septuagesima, “the seventieth,” consecrating the whole according to the Greeks by fasting, concerning whom we have discussed sufficiently at length above.

Let us now return to Lent. Since this season is customarily and rightly assigned to repentance, and the fruits of repentance are fasting, vigils, and other afflictions of the flesh; bodily and spiritual almsgiving and other works of mercy; prayer and supplication and other forms [Col. 0260B] of contemplation; weeping and tears and other signs of contrition—the Church therefore reads and sings abundantly, in the day and night offices, on this day and the following days, of these and similar matters pertaining to repentance. It should be noted that, because fasting begins, the order of the biblical histories is interrupted: in Septuagesima and Sexagesima there was singing about Adam, and in Quinquagesima about Noah and Abraham. On this first Sunday material concerning the fruits of repentance is inserted; on the second, it concerns Jacob; on the third, Joseph; and on the fourth, Moses will be sung about. Today’s day office, however, strongly exhorts those about to fight against the devil through fasting to engage in battle.

It is the custom of a commander about to fight to set before recruits who are to fight what reward awaits those who fight rightly, with what caution and with what weapons they should proceed, whose examples they should follow, and whose help they should await. [Col. 0260C] The Gospel declares the cause and the precaution; all these matters are gathered from the present office. But I leave their collection to the reader. Indeed, already part of the battle is accomplished, because he whom we invoked as protector says: “He shall call upon me, and I will hear him” [Note: [Col. 0259] Psalm 90]; and in the Epistle: “In an acceptable time I heard you, and in a day of salvation I helped you” [Note: [Col. 0259] 2 Corinthians 6]. In the gradual angels guard us [Note: [Col. 0259] Psalm 90]; in the tract we are surrounded by the shield of truth [Note: [Col. 0259] ibid.]; in the Gospel we press toward triumph, saying to the enemy: “Get behind me, Satan” [Note: [Col. 0259] Matthew 4]. Observe that from this day the Church frequently uses the Psalm “He who dwells,” because it is engaged during these days in a great contest. This Psalm instructs [Col. 0260D] those engaged in contest who place their hope in the Lord and ask his help.

Again, from this day until Good Friday, crosses are covered and a veil is hung before the altar. This is believed to derive from the Old Law. For under the Law a veil, woven with marvellous workmanship and spread out in beautiful variety, was hung between the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies; through it the Ark was veiled from the people [Note: [Col. 0259] Exodus 26]. This veil was rent at the Lord’s Passion [Note: [Col. 0259] Matthew 27], that is, heaven, which divides bodily from spiritual things and by which Christ and that heavenly city are hidden from us; afterwards, it will be rolled up like a book [Note: [Col. 0259] Isaiah 34], [Col. 0261A] and gathered like a tent [Note: [Col. 0261] Numbers 9], and then the face of the Lord will be revealed [Note: [Col. 0261] 1 Corinthians 13 and 2 Corinthians 3]. Or this is the sword which stood before the gate of Paradise [Note: [Col. 0261] Genesis 3], which was removed at the Lord’s Passion. Or rather, it is the letter of the Law, namely its carnal observance, signified also by the veil laid over Moses’ face, which remains over the hearts of the Jews to this present day [Note: [Col. 0261] Exodus 34 and 2 Corinthians 3]. Therefore they do not see Moses’ glorious face, that is, the spiritual understanding of the Law. This is the “darkness of waters in the clouds of the air” [Note: [Col. 0261] Psalm 17], that is, an obscure meaning in the Prophets.

Since, then, this season signifies the time of wandering and guilt, especially of those who preceded the Lord’s coming and had a veil before their eyes, therefore, just as in these days the Old [Col. 0261B] Testament is read, in which the letter contains an obscure teaching concerning the Lord’s incarnation, Passion, resurrection, and the glory of the kingdom to come, so crosses are covered and concealed, and veils are suspended and hang. But because even then there were animals that chewed the cud and divided the hoof, and oxen that ploughed [Note: [Col. 0261] Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14]—that is, people discerning the mysteries of the Scriptures and understanding them spiritually—therefore a few priests enter beyond the veil, to whom “it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God” [Note: [Col. 0261] Luke 8].

These veils are removed at the Lord’s Passion: both because the veil of the Temple was rent [Note: [Col. 0261] Matthew 27], because the fiery sword was removed, because heaven is opened, and because the book sealed with seven seals is opened [Note: [Col. 0261] Revelation 6]. It was opened more clearly in Christ’s resurrection, when he opened the minds of the Apostles [Col. 0261C] and explained the Scriptures to them [Note: [Col. 0261] Luke 24]; it will be opened most clearly at our resurrection, when heavenly glory is unveiled to us. Today’s station is at the Lateran, built in honour of the Saviour and of John, greater than a prophet, because today’s office prophetically resounds with the blessedness of our Saviour, who above all and for all walked upon asp and basilisk and trampled lion and dragon [Note: [Col. 0261] Psalm 90].

On Monday the Gospel is read [Note: [Col. 0261] Matthew 25], in which the Son of Man is shown coming in his majesty and separating the nations set before him, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats: placing the sheep on the right and the goats on the left, saying to the former, “Come,” and thundering to the latter, “Depart.” [Col. 0261D] This prophetic utterance anticipates the same sense in the Epistle, where the Lord says: “Behold, I shall seek my sheep and lead them out into their own land, and feed them upon the mountains of Israel, by the streams, in settled places, in rich pastures” [Note: [Col. 0261] Ezekiel 34]. What is set down in the Epistle is nothing other than the kingdom of which the Gospel says: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the origin of the world.” Likewise, in order that we may be counted among the sheep and deserve to receive this kingdom, let our eyes be toward the Lord [Col. 0262A] our God, and let us pray that he may have mercy on us [Note: [Col. 0261] Psalm 122], look upon his servants, hear their prayers, and grant us understanding, so that we may not fear the thousands of people surrounding us [Note: [Col. 0261] Psalm 3].

Nor should it pass unnoticed that, because we have a command to pray for kings and all who are set in high places [Note: [Col. 0261] 1 Timothy 2], and for those who labour in afflictions and the furnace of fire, we offer prayers on this day, and only every third day, lest the people be wearied by tedium. In order that we may humble ourselves under the mighty hand of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0261] 1 Peter 5], on this day and all following days, at the appointed prayers, in place of the first prayer at the beginning of the whole office, we say, “Let us bend the knee.” Observe that we prostrate ourselves upon the ground for many reasons: [Col. 0262B] first, because in worshipping Christ we believe that he descended to earth and put on flesh from the earth; second, because we recall that although we were created in Paradise almost angelic, our bodies, because of our fall, lie among brute animals and the soul is weighed down by bodily mass [Note: [Col. 0261] Wisdom 9]; third, that by the act itself we may confess that we are sinners and cling to earthly desires, as we press face to earth and soul to pavement [Note: [Col. 0261] Psalm 118]; fourth, that we may signify contrition and shame of heart, because we do not dare to lift our eyes to God [Note: [Col. 0261] Luke 18]; fifth, because we were taken from dust [Note: [Col. 0261] Genesis 2 and 3]; sixth, because we do not raise ourselves; seventh, because we see where we are and why we fall; and eighth, because every knee bends to Christ [Note: [Col. 0261] Philippians 2]. Therefore we indicate this. Hence not only one knee but both [Col. 0262C] are to be bent, lest we seem like the Jews [Note: [Col. 0261] Matthew 27], or in order to mark this distinction between dulia, veneration, and latria, worship.

This rite, however, took its origin from the pagans, who, when giving honour to kings, worship them with bent knee; or rather from Abraham himself, who fell to the ground and worshipped the Lord [Note: [Col. 0261] Genesis 17], whom the Prophets imitated, and the Apostle, saying: “I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0261] Ephesians 3]. In private prayers, when for the reasons stated we cast ourselves upon the ground, at times we pray with bent knees and uplifted face, as if saying, “Draw me after you” [Note: [Col. 0261] Song of Songs 1]; at times we pray “standing,” as though rejoicing that “we shall go into the house of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0261] Psalm 121]. In the first we express [Col. 0262D] our condition, in the second our desire, and in the third our hope. Thus on this day and the following days the prayer over the people is said, which stands in place of holy communion.

Formerly all communicated, and the deacon invited those about to communicate to bend the knee. But now, because many receive the Lord’s body unworthily, we use prayer in place of communion; while the deacon, as formerly, performs his office and says: “Humble your heads before God” [Note: [Col. 0261] 1 Corinthians 11]. For “whoever humbles himself [Col. 0263A] shall be exalted” [Note: [Col. 0263] Matthew 23]; and whoever is blessed by these good acts shall be enrolled among the eternal blessedness. In this prayer the priest entrusts Christ’s soldiers to battle against the ancient enemy and the enemy’s snares. Therefore, through the minister, he arms them with the weapons of humility, saying, “Humble your heads before God,” and then finally pours over them the protection of his blessing. This is especially done in Lent, when our adversary goes about anxiously seeking someone to devour [Note: [Col. 0263] 1 Peter 5]. In the first collect we bend the knees in petition for righteousness, which is necessary in the present life; in the final prayer we rest in thanksgiving for the daily denarius of the life to come [Note: [Col. 0263] Matthew 20]. We shall do this throughout all Lent, except on Sundays and at festal Masses until [Col. 0263B] the Lord’s Supper.

On Tuesday the Gospel is read [Note: [Col. 0263] Matthew 21] concerning those buying and selling in the Temple, whom the Lord powerfully expelled and reproved by word. Leaving his accusers, he went to Bethany—that is, to the house of obedience—namely to the Gentiles, who became obedient at the hearing of the ear [Note: [Col. 0263] Psalm 17]. Accordingly the prophetic reading appropriately begins: “Seek the Lord while he may be found” [Note: [Col. 0263] Isaiah 55]. It speaks to the accusing Jews, that they should seek him while he is near, because the time will come when he will not be near them: namely, when he has gone over to Bethany, that is, to the Gentiles. And what follows—“it shall prosper in those things for which I sent it”—agrees with the Gospel in that he powerfully and successfully [Col. 0263C] expelled the sellers, overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves. The remaining chants in the introit, gradual, offertory, and communion are prayers, consolations, and thanksgivings of those who seek the Lord.

On Wednesday the solemnity of fasting is doubled; hence the bodies of penitents who fast more severely are dried up. In such bodies the unclean spirit does not dwell, as the Gospel says: it walks through dry places seeking rest and finds none [Note: [Col. 0263] Matthew 12], because it loathes bodies dried by fasting. Therefore, to make fasting more gladly desired, examples are set before us of Moses [Note: [Col. 0263] Exodus 24] and Elijah [Note: [Col. 0263] 3 Kings 19], each of whom is said in the respective readings to have fasted forty days and forty nights. Therefore, because the fast is doubled, two [Col. 0263D] verses are placed in the gradual. Observe that at the first prayer we say, “Let us bend the knee,” but at the second, “The Lord be with you,” and not “Let us bend the knee”; this is said to be in remembrance of the two Testaments. The texts sung in the introit, gradual, tract, offertory, and communion are consolations and prayers: that those who fast may be delivered from tribulations, and that enemies may not rule over those afflicted by fasting.

On Thursday, the Gospel is read [Note: [Col. 0263] John 8] in which Jews boasting that they are Abraham’s children are convicted [Col. 0264A] of not being Abraham’s children, because they do not do his works, but do the works of their father the devil. Or, as is customary in certain places, the Gospel is read [Note: [Col. 0263] Luke 16] concerning the rich man tormented in the lower world, who calls upon and begs Abraham, but is not heard as a son. In agreement with these is the prophetic passage prefixed in the Epistle: if a just man begets a son who sheds blood and commits every detestable act, the father himself shall live in his righteousness; but his son, who has committed iniquity, shall die by death [Note: [Col. 0263] Ezekiel 18]. The remaining texts in the introit, gradual, and offertory are praises and prayers of the just person. The communion, “The bread which I shall give” [Note: [Col. 0263] John 6], declares from what the just person lives: namely, from Christ’s flesh.

Observe that Thursdays formerly did not have their own propers, but were furnished with offices from summer Sundays; [Col. 0264B] and their Gospels were established not concerning fasts but concerning the rich man and Lazarus, and the raising of the widow’s son. For formerly, as we said above, people did not fast, but kept them festally as Sundays. Later, however, Gregory the Younger added them to the Lenten fast and furnished them with offices. Hence the variety of Epistles and Gospels found on Thursdays.

On Friday the Gospel is read in which the grace of baptism is signified, by which the youthfulness of the soul is renewed like that of an eagle [Note: [Col. 0263] Ps. 102], its life is redeemed from destruction, and it is crowned with mercy and compassions. For the pool [Note: [Col. 0263] John 5] signifies either the Jewish people or the Blessed Virgin, into whom the Angel of Great Counsel descended [Col. 0264C] [Note: [Col. 0263] Isa. 9], when, taking the form of a servant, he emptied himself [Note: [Col. 0263] Phil. 2]. The stirring of the water signifies the disturbance of the Jews; the healing of one, the conversion of the nations, who come together in the unity of faith and humbly descend into the sacrament of baptism. To this corresponds the prophetic reading, where it is said: “If the wicked man turns away from his wickedness and does judgment and justice, he shall live in life and shall not die” [Note: [Col. 0263] Ezek. 18]. But he shall be healed from his long-standing infirmity. In the introit and gradual the sick man descending into the water prays; in the offertory and communion he gives thanks for his deliverance and reproves the unbelieving Jews for their obstinacy.

For those ordained on Saturday, and for the other ministers of Christ’s altar, this Gospel is suitably read: “Jesus took Peter, James, and John and led them up a high mountain” [Note: [Col. 0263] Matt. 17]. For priests [Col. 0264D] and the other ministers of the altar, when they are advanced to so great a ministry, ascend as it were with the Lord onto a very high mountain, so that with unveiled face they may behold his radiant countenance [Note: [Col. 0263] II Cor. 3], understand what Moses and Elijah—that is, the Law and the Prophets—speak with him or concerning him, and proclaim Catholic faith and moral teaching to the people below. Thus the apostolic reading is fittingly set before it: “We beseech you, brethren, rebuke the unruly, comfort the faint-hearted” [Note: [Col. 0263] I Thess. 5]; for this is the office of those who have been ordained for this purpose, that they may be shepherds of souls. [Col. 0265A] The canticle, “Blessed art thou” [Note: [Col. 0265] Dan. 3], and the tract, “Praise” [Note: [Col. 0265] Ps. 116], are the praises of the ordained; the remainder are prayers, either for them or for penitents generally. Hence they do not forget to bend the knee at the prayers following the prophecies. Some say that, out of reverence for the apostolic reading read today, we do not bow our heads at the prayer over the people.

## Chapter VI. The Second Sunday in Lent

“Jesus went out and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon; and behold, a Canaanite woman, coming out from those borders, cried out, saying: Lord, have mercy on me, Son of David” [Note: [Col. 0265] Matt. 15].

This Sunday was anciently entitled the “Sunday without [an office],” not because it lacks every office, but because it lacks one particular office. [Col. 0265B] For it does not lack the nocturnal office, the epistle, or the Gospel, but only the daytime chant. Therefore it ought to be entitled “Sunday without [an office]” neither in the antiphonary, the epistolary, nor the Gospel-book, but only in the gradual. The nocturnal office returns to the histories, where Jacob is sung of: he fed his father, supplanted his brother [Note: [Col. 0265] Gen. 27], saw a ladder, erected a stone, and poured oil upon it [Note: [Col. 0265] Gen. 28]; he saw God and wrestled with the angel [Note: [Col. 0265] Gen. 32]. All these things apply to penitents who overthrow vices.

The daytime office, like the others, takes its foundation from the Gospel, where the Canaanite woman is read of, whose daughter was tormented by a demon. The Canaanite woman is mother Church; the daughter is the sinful soul. The Church, preserving faith in simplicity, patience in humility, and constancy in steadfastness, prays for every sinful soul [Col. 0265C] that it may be given the power to resist sin and that sanctification may be established within it. Of this the Apostle says in the Epistle: “This is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from fornication; that each one of you know how to possess his vessel in sanctification” [Note: [Col. 0265] I Thess. 4].

The remaining chants in the introit, gradual, tract, offertory, and communion are the cries of the Canaanite woman, taken from elsewhere. For while the Roman pontiff was occupied with conferring orders—which he began on Saturday evening and conferred on Sunday—he was unable to arrange the office. Therefore it is inscribed “Sunday without [an office],” and its office was received from elsewhere. It is received, however, from the day of fasting, because the passions of evil desire [Note: [Col. 0265] Ibid.], signified by the demon, [Col. 0265D] are the very things for whose expulsion the woman prays in the Gospel: “They are not cast out except by prayer and fasting” [Note: [Col. 0265] Matt. 17].

On Monday the Gospel is read: “I go away, and you shall seek me, and you shall die in your sin” [Note: [Col. 0265] John 8]. Here he indicates that he will pass over to the nations and abandon the Jews because of the sin of unbelief. Daniel, foreseeing this, laments it with tearful complaint [Note: [Col. 0265] ch. 9], and asks that the Lord turn away his fury and anger and show his face over the desolated sanctuary. The chants in the introit, gradual, offertory, and communion [Col. 0266A] are prayers, consolations, and praises of converted heathendom and of the converted nations, to whom the Lord has granted understanding [Note: [Col. 0265] Ps. 15].

On Tuesday the Gospel is read concerning the arrogance of the Scribes and Pharisees, who sat upon Moses’ seat, saying but not doing. At last he strikes them with the conclusion: “Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” [Note: [Col. 0265] Matt. 23]. For these proud men were to be removed from the teaching office of the knowledge of God, while humble teachers from the nations were to receive even their seat. This is also signified by the widow of Zarephath [Note: [Col. 0265] III Kings 17], of whom the preceding reading speaks. Elijah went to her, though there were many widows in Israel. To those who magnified their fringes and remained in the pride of barrenness it is said: [Col. 0266B] “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruit” [Note: [Col. 0265] Matt. 21]; and elsewhere: “I will command my clouds”—that is, the preachers—“not to rain rain upon it” [Note: [Col. 0265] Isa. 5].

But the widow of Zarephath received the Lord in the hospitality of faith, gathered the two sticks of the cross, and made the ash-bread of penitence. By the merit of her humility, neither flour failed in the jar nor oil in the flask, because she possesses knowledge of the Law and observes the spiritual understanding of the Gospel. Thus the woman of Zarephath displays her affection toward Christ in the introit, saying: “My heart said to thee” [Note: [Col. 0265] Ps. 26]; in the gradual she consoles and exhorts herself, saying: “Cast thy thought” [Note: [Col. 0265] Ps. 54]; in the offertory she seeks mercy [Note: [Col. 0265] Ps. 50]; and in the communion [Col. 0266C] she promises, as though secure, that she will recount his wonders [Note: [Col. 0265] Ps. 9].

On Wednesday the Gospel is read in which the Lord, revealing his passion to the disciples, says: “Behold, we go up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man shall be delivered up” [Note: [Col. 0265] Matt. 20]. That passion was the redemption of the human race; hence at the end it concludes: “The Son of Man shall come to give his soul as a redemption for many” [Note: [Col. 0265] Ibid.]. Thus Esther’s prayer is suitably placed first: she prays to the Lord for the inheritance which he redeemed. The history from which this prayer is taken also fits the Passion well, because just as Haman prepared a cross for Mordecai and was caught upon it [Note: [Col. 0265] Esth. 13], so the devil prepared one for Christ and was deceived upon it.

Therefore Esther prays in the introit: “Do not forsake me” [Note: [Col. 0265] Ps. 37]; and in the gradual: “Save thy people” [Note: [Col. 0265] Ps. 27]. Then, as if secure concerning salvation, [Col. 0266D] she adds in the offertory: “Unto thee, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0265] Ps. 24], and concludes in the communion: “The Lord is just” [Note: [Col. 0265] Ps. 10]. Or rather, these are the words of the suffering Christ, who says in the gradual verse, “I shall be like those who go down into the pit.” Therefore, hanging upon the cross [Note: [Col. 0265] Matt. 27], he asks help for himself and his own, trusting in the Father’s justice and grace.

On Thursday the Gospel is read in which the Lord teaches that trust should be placed not in human testimony but in that of God alone. Speaking of himself according to the weakness of the flesh, he says: “If I bear testimony concerning myself, [Col. 0267A] my testimony is not true”; and below: “I do not receive testimony from man”; and again: “I have testimony greater than John’s” [Note: [Col. 0267] John 5]. The preceding reading from Jeremiah corresponds to this [Note: [Col. 0267] ch. 17]: “Cursed is he who trusts in man”; and likewise: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord.” Therefore the one who trusts prays in the introit, gradual, and offertory in the person of Moses, in which the words are repeated because he often interceded with the Lord for the people [Note: [Col. 0267] Exod. 32]. The communion, “He who eats,” shows what benefit comes to the one who trusts: namely, that he abides in Christ and Christ in him [Note: [Col. 0267] John 6]. This communion would suit the Saturday before Palm Sunday well.

On Friday the Gospel is read about the householder who leased his vineyard to husbandmen; they killed not only the servants [Col. 0267B] but also his own heir, saying: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance” [Note: [Col. 0267] Matt. 21]. The reading set before it concerning Joseph corresponds to this parable; his brothers said of him: “Behold, the dreamer comes; come, let us kill him” [Note: [Col. 0267] Gen. 37]. The heir and Joseph bear the type of the Lord, who was sold, handed over to death [Note: [Col. 0267] Matt. 26], and buried [Note: [Col. 0267] Matt. 27]. Thus he was cast out from his vineyard and, like a useless stone, rejected by the builders [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 117]; with him the kingdom of God passed to the nations producing its fruit, just as Joseph, transferred from his own people to strangers, fed the Egyptians. Since he loved justice and escaped many plots, both from his brothers and from others [Note: [Col. 0267] Gen. 39 and following], he therefore sings in the introit: “But I shall appear in justice” [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 16]; and in the [Col. 0267C] gradual: “To the Lord when I was troubled” [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 119]; in the offertory: “O Lord, to my aid” [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 39]; and in the communion: “Thou, O Lord, shalt preserve” [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 11].

On Saturday, both in the Gospel, where there is read [Note: [Col. 0267] Luke 15] of the man who had two sons, and in the epistle, where Jacob and Esau are read of [Note: [Col. 0267] Gen. 27], the signification of two peoples is contained: the Jewish people and the Gentile people. The former, namely the Jewish people in respect of the worship of the one God, is tortured by envy when the father receives the repentance of the younger, that is, the Gentile people. It stands outside, though it ought rather to rejoice, because its brother “was dead and has come to life; was lost and has been found” [Note: [Col. 0267] Luke 15]. For as we sing in the introit: “The law of the Lord is without blemish, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to little ones” [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 18]. Indeed, [Col. 0267D] the epistle which precedes agrees well with the Gospel. There the younger brother feasts with his father, while the elder remains outside in the field; so, while Jacob offers the meal and, by the counsel of Rebecca—who signifies the Holy Spirit—hastens toward the blessing, Esau is occupied outside in hunting. For the Jewish people, held fast by earthly perceptions and carnal observances, loses spiritual grace.

But the Gentile, converted to repentance, glories and sings in the introit in the law of the Lord; in the gradual, he confesses to [Col. 0268A] and praises the Lord [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 91]; in the offertory, he asks that his eyes may be enlightened, lest he sleep or his enemy prevail over him [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 12]. Notice that, reasonably, in the second week of Lent the Gospel is read about the prodigal son returning to his father, because the Gentile people return to the worship of the Creator through the teaching of the Law and the Gospel; and every penitent is reconciled to the Lord through faith and works, or through the two commandments of charity.

## Chapter VII. The Third Sunday in Lent

“My eyes are ever toward the Lord, because he shall pluck my feet from the snare” [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 24].

The nocturnal office of this third Sunday follows the order of the history. [Col. 0268B] For since on the preceding Sunday Jacob was sung of, on this one Joseph is sung of: sold by his brothers [Note: [Col. 0267] Gen. 37], he enriched his brothers during the famine [Note: [Col. 0267] Gen. 42 and following]. Christ, crucified by the Jews, redeemed the human race by his death and, in redeeming it, freed it from the devil. This is read in today’s Gospel, upon which the daytime office is founded: “Jesus was casting out a demon, and it was mute” [Note: [Col. 0267] Luke 11], and according to another Evangelist [Note: [Col. 0267] Matt. 9], deaf as well. That is, the human race, bound under the devil’s power, was mute and deaf to speak and hear the words of God. But when one stronger than the strong man armed came upon him and plundered his vessels, casting out the prince of this world [Note: [Col. 0267] John 12], the deaf man heard and the mute man proclaimed the Word of God.

Therefore he who had been mute now [Col. 0268C] speaks eloquently and joyfully in the introit: “My eyes are ever toward the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 24]. Lest he fail again, he implores, adding: “Look upon me” [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 9]; and in the gradual: “Arise, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 122]. Then the voice of one formerly mute, now rich in speech, whose mouth Wisdom opened, doubles its prayers and, with a fitting comparison, entreats in the tract: “To thee I lifted up” [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 18]. In the offertory, now eloquent, he proclaims the Lord’s righteous judgments: the demon had departed from one who humbled himself, but the unclean spirit had returned to the proud Jewish people. In the communion, made an orator from being mute, he rejoices because, “as the sparrow finds a house for itself and the turtle-dove a nest” [Note: [Col. 0267] Ps. 83]. But lest we restore strength to the enemy so that he may take with him seven spirits more wicked than himself, which may enter and dwell in us [Note: [Col. 0267] Luke 11], let us hear Paul, the eminent soldier of that stronger one, who teaches in the Epistle that we should be imitators of God as most dear children, and that there should be no fornication or uncleanness among us [Note: [Col. 0267] Eph. 5].

Let us follow Lawrence in martyrdom, at whose church the station is celebrated today, just as he cast the strong man armed—that is, the devil—out of his court, which was Rome. Hence Prudentius, speaking in the person of the martyr:

> Depart, adulterous Jupiter,  
> Forgetful of thy sister’s violation,  
> Leave Rome free. [Col. 0269A]

Thus, extinguishing the flames of vices, let us triumph over the devil.

On Monday the Lord indicates in the Gospel that he will pass over to the nations when he says: “No prophet is accepted in his own country” [Note: [Col. 0269] Luke 4], as though saying: “Because you do not honor me, I shall pass to those who will honor me.” Likewise, when he adds that Elijah did not go to the widows of Israel but only to the widow of Zarephath [Note: [Col. 0269] III Kings 17], and that Elisha healed not the lepers of Israel but only Naaman the Syrian [Note: [Col. 0269] IV Kings 5]. Further, in that they drove him out of the city and led him to the brow of the mountain upon which their city was built, in order to cast him down, while he himself passed through their midst and went away, salvation is signified as passing away from them. For when, from the brow of pride in which [Col. 0269B] they dwelt together, they wished to cast him into the depth of oblivion, he went with his feet—that is, with his holy preachings—through their midst to the nations.

Thus the reading about Naaman the Syrian [Note: [Col. 0269] IV Kings 5] is fittingly placed before this Gospel. Elisha signifies Christ; Naaman the leper signifies the Gentile people, idolatrous and unclean, which comes to Christ in faith. But Christ did not go to him bodily; rather, he gave him the command: “Go and wash seven times in the Jordan.” This is what he said to the apostles: “Going into all the world, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0269] Mark 16; Matt. 28]. The leper is washed seven times because in baptism the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit works, through which we are reborn and, receiving remission of sins, [Col. 0269C] are restored like little children to newness of innocence. The remaining chants in the introit, gradual, offertory, and communion are the prayers, consolations, and thanksgivings of Naaman the Syrian—that is, of the Gentile people—offered to Christ, who gave from Zion salvation to Israel and turned back the captivity of his people [Note: [Col. 0269] Ps. 13].

On Tuesday the work of mercy is commended in the Gospel, the Lord saying: “If thy brother sin against thee, rebuke him”; and below: “Forgive one who sins against thee, I say not seven times, but up to seventy times seven” [Note: [Col. 0269] Matt. 18]. Rebuking and forgiving are works of mercy. Thus the reading concerning the multiplied oil of the woman is fittingly placed before it. A certain woman, whose husband had died, cried out to Elisha because her creditor was trying to reduce her sons to slavery. Elisha commanded her [Col. 0269D] to borrow empty vessels, close the doors, and pour in oil; once it had been multiplied, she was to pay the creditor and live on what remained [Note: [Col. 0269] IV Kings 4].

She is the Church, which generates children in baptism. When the understanding of sound knowledge has died, the wicked devil, a usurious creditor, seeks to drag them into the slavery of eternal death in payment for the money of ruinous pleasure and wicked action. But Christ, having given pastors the power of binding and loosing, as is read in today’s Gospel, commands them to close the doors and pour oil into empty vessels: namely, [Col. 0270A] to correct sinners privately, fill those empty of knowledge, and mercifully forgive them—not merely seven times but seventy times seven, that is, in every kind of transgression. Indeed, the oil often overflows, as in the case of Mary Magdalene [Note: [Col. 0269] Luke 7]. But whoever is not anointed with the oil of pardon should be as a heathen and a publican [Note: [Col. 0269] Matt. 18] and be cut by the more severe cautery of penitence.

Therefore the woman praying for her sons says in the introit: “I cried out” [Note: [Col. 0269] Ps. 16]; in the gradual: “From hidden sins” [Note: [Col. 0269] Ps. 18]. Then, her prayers heard, she gives thanks in the offertory: “The right hand of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0269] Ps. 117]; and teaches in the communion what sort of persons they ought to show themselves to be who desire the oil of mercy: “Those who desire to rest upon the mountain, let them enter without stain and work justice” [Note: [Col. 0269] Ps. 14].

On Wednesday the Gospel is read [Note: [Col. 0269] Matt. 15] in which the Lord, when the Pharisees accuse him because the Lord’s disciples transgress the traditions of the elders, rebukes them in return and prudently turns the spearpoint of the accusation back upon its authors: namely, that because of human traditions they transgress God’s commandments, especially this one: “Honor thy father and thy mother” [Note: [Col. 0269] Exod. 20]. Therefore the reading is fittingly prefaced in which it begins with honor for one’s father and the other commandments of God follow. Likewise, what is said in the Gospel—“This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me”—is what is set before it in the reading: “And the people stood afar off” [Note: [Col. 0269] Ibid.]. Likewise, in the Gospel the disciples come to Jesus and are taught; in the Epistle Moses comes near to the darkness in which God was and is instructed. The chants in the introit, gradual, offertory, and communion are the prayers and thanksgivings of Moses [Col. 0270C] or of the Lord’s disciples.

On Thursday the Gospel is read in which the Lord exhorts the crowds coming to him in order to make him king—because they had eaten his loaves and were filled—saying: “Work not for the food which perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life.” He had rebuked them, saying: “You came to me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves” [Note: [Col. 0269] John 6]. In this he strikes at priests who come to the altar not because they delight in contemplating the mysteries but because they seek tithes and offerings.

The preceding reading from Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 0269] ch. 7] suitably corresponds, where the Lord promises that he will dwell with them and thus, as it were, be their king, if they have worked for such food [Col. 0270D] that they do not commit calumny, do not shed innocent blood, make their ways good, and judge rightly between man and man [Note: [Col. 0269] Ps. 77]. “The salvation of the people” is the voice of the Lord consoling the people. The gradual, offertory, and communion are the voices of a people confident in the grace of its king. Today the station is at Saints Cosmas and Damian; therefore they are mentioned in the collect.

On Friday the Gospel is read that Jesus, weary from the journey, sat at the sixth hour upon the well [Col. 0271A] and spoke with the Samaritan woman, who had come to draw water [Note: [Col. 0271] John 4]. The mystery is well known: the Lord, having come to us in the sixth age, was wearied unto death by the journey and sat upon the well; that is, he surpassed the depth of human wisdom. He taught the Samaritan woman, namely the Church of another people, which drew dead water from cisterns—that is, from the obscure teachings of philosophers, which could not satisfy and from which whoever drank would thirst again—that she should drink from the water which he himself would give, namely the Holy Spirit; whoever drank from it would never thirst.

The reading about the children of Israel saying to Moses, “Give us water” [Note: [Col. 0271] Num. 20], is suitably placed before this. Although Moses was distrustful, he struck the rock twice with the rod, and very abundant waters came forth. Moses signifies [Col. 0271B] the unbelieving Jewish people; the thirsty people, the human race; and the rock, Christ [Note: [Col. 0271] I Cor. 10]. Moses struck him twice when he hung him upon the two timbers of the cross [Note: [Col. 0271] John 19]; after the striking, the water of the Holy Spirit overflowed. Thus Jesus, weary and struck by the rod, prays for the people and consoles himself and his own in the introit, “Deal with me” [Note: [Col. 0271] Ps. 85]; in the gradual, “He hoped in God” [Note: [Col. 0271] Ps. 27]; in the offertory, “Give heed” [Note: [Col. 0271] Ps. 5]; and in the communion, “Whoever shall drink” [Note: [Col. 0271] John 4].

On Saturday the Gospel is read [Note: [Col. 0271] John 8] concerning the woman caught in adultery. The Scribes and Pharisees tested the Lord concerning her sentence: whether, for mercy’s sake, he would set himself against the justice of the Law, or, for justice’s sake, set aside mercy. Gentleness meets them with justice in such a manner that, when the accusers depart—withdrawn by their cauterized conscience—only misery and mercy remain. [Col. 0271C] The reading from Daniel is appropriately placed before this Gospel, although Jerome says it is not found in the Hebrew, where Susanna is read of as delivered by God’s aid from the false accusation of adultery [Note: [Col. 0271] Dan. 13]. She escaped by mercy; the other woman, however, escaped stoning by justice. In this office, therefore, truth and mercy meet one another [Note: [Col. 0271] Ps. 84] under the same protection of compassion, in persons of the same sex but under unlike causes.

Each woman therefore prays in the introit, saying: “Words” [Note: [Col. 0271] Ps. 5], and in the offertory: “Steps” [Note: [Col. 0271] Ps. 18]; in the gradual she consoles herself [Note: [Col. 0271] Ps. 22]; the communion is taken from the Gospel. At the compline of this Saturday the antiphon “In the midst of life” is sung, because the middle week of Lent now begins. Those who sing it on the preceding Thursday, however, reckon the number of days afflicted by fasting.

We have therefore judged that it should be explained briefly for scholarly persons. “In the midst of life” is Christ, for he is the mediator of God and men [Note: [Col. 0271] I Tim. 2]; he is “the way, the truth, and the life” [Note: [Col. 0271] John 14]; he is holy, he is God, he is mighty [Note: [Col. 0271] Dan. 9], he is merciful and Savior [Note: [Col. 0271] Isa. 9]. Thus the address is directed to Christ: “O middle of life,” that is, “O Christ.” Or the middle life is the Holy Trinity, which is life in itself and a middle life to us—that is, sufficient and common life—and the address is directed to it: [Col. 0272A] “O middle of life,” namely, “O Holy Trinity.” Therefore the phrase is subdivided: “Holy God, holy mighty one, holy merciful one”; that is, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, from whom, through whom, and in whom we are saved, and who therefore is called Savior and Trinity. Yet, to whomever we direct the address, we seek help because we are in death amid the miseries of this present life, and ask that he not deliver us to the bitterness of eternal death.

Or: “O Lord, we who exist in the middle life are in death.” The first life was the life of justice and innocence in which man was created; the second was the life of sin and misery into which man fell; the third will be the life of immortality and glory to which man will be restored. We, therefore, are in the middle life and are in death, because the life of sin—the middle life—is death to the life [Col. 0272B] of justice; and therefore we seek a helper. Or: “O faithful one, [you who are] in the middle of life,” that is, despise temporal things, whether good or evil, which are common to all, because we are in death; and therefore, O Lord, we ask thee as our helper.

## Chapter VIII. The Fourth Sunday in Lent

“Rejoice, Jerusalem, and assemble together, all you who love her” [Note: [Col. 0271] Isa. 66].

Every science possesses its own idiom of speaking, writing, and signifying. Just as it is customary for theologians to pass over the oppositions of numbers, so they signify the same thing equally by numbers of the same designation or expression. For example, the six works of mercy are signified by six, sixty, six hundred, and six thousand. Yet completeness increases with the addition of the enlarged decade. Therefore the Church commemorates the seventy years of Babylonian captivity not only through seventy days, as we have said above, but also through seven Sundays. It calls the first of them Septuagesima, since it is the seventh from this final Sunday; the sixth Sexagesima; and the fifth Quinquagesima.
