Since, therefore, the people sat in that seventy-year captivity and wept beside the rivers of Babylon [Note: [Col. 0271] Ps. 136], and at the end, when Cyrus permitted it, went out rejoicing and entered Jerusalem in gladness [Note: [Col. 0271] I Esdras 1], therefore, after on the first Sunday the captive people had wept, saying, “They surrounded me” [Note: [Col. 0271] Ps. 17], on the second had prayed, saying, “Arise, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0271] Ps. 43], on the third likewise had prayed, saying, “Be thou unto me” [Note: [Col. 0271] Ps. 30], and on the fourth had received consolation, [Col. 0272D] the Lord saying, “He shall call upon me, and I shall hear him” [Note: [Col. 0271] Ps. 90], and after on the fifth it had again persisted in prayer, saying, “Remember” [Note: [Col. 0271] Ps. 24], while on the sixth, Darius granting permission, it received consolation concerning its return and therefore said, “My eyes” [Note: [Col. 0271] Ibid.], in this week, as though entering Jerusalem joyfully at the end of Septuagesima, it exults, saying: “Rejoice, Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0271] Isa. 66].

The Church also represents the sevenfold course of the present life, which revolves in the cycle of seven days or, as we said, is contained within seven thousand years—or rather, the seven ages by which the world itself is distinguished—through seven Sundays, just as it does through seventy days. The first age is from Adam to Noah; the second, from Noah to Abraham, or, according to some, to Moses; the third, from Moses to David; the fourth, from David to the Babylonian migration; the fifth, from the Babylonian migration to the Lord’s coming; the sixth, to the end of the age; and the seventh likewise to that same end. For they run concurrently: the former in those who are awake and laboring, the latter in those asleep and at rest, where the souls of the elect rest joyfully between the breasts of their mother, the heavenly Jerusalem.

Of these ages the Lord says: “In six tribulations thou shalt be delivered, and in the seventh evil shall not touch thee” [Note: [Col. 0273] Job 5]. By the six tribulations he means [Col. 0273B] all the afflictions of the six ages, the six winds which strike us from six sides: from the front, the suggestion of demons; from behind, the pleasant recollection of past sins; from below, the enticement of the flesh; from above, the consent of reason; from the right, prosperity; and from the left, adversity. Whoever is delivered from all these is delivered through the Lord. Hence: “Many are the tribulations of the just, and from all these the Lord delivered them” [Note: [Col. 0273] Ps. 33]. We are delivered in death, which is the boundary of life leading to life; from this point, in the seventh age, souls shall rest from their labors [Note: [Col. 0273] Rev. 14].

That the seven Sundays represent these seven ages is shown by their offices. In the first of them, as in the infancy of the world, man cries out after being cast down from blessed delight; in it Abel, the first martyr, is killed, and his blood cried from the earth to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0273] Gen. 4]. Therefore the Church cries out in his voice, as though in that of a precentor: “The groans of death surrounded me” [Note: [Col. 0273] Ps. 17]. And because through many ages and long periods it must labor in groans of this kind and bear the burden of the day and heat [Note: [Col. 0273] Matt. 20], the epistle concerning the long race is read [Note: [Col. 0273] I Cor. 9], and the Gospel concerns the ages.

On the second Sunday, as in the childhood of the world, man conceives hope of his reconciliation from the Lord’s saying to Noah: “I will establish my covenant with you” [Note: [Col. 0273] Gen. 7]. The Church implores the hastening of this covenant or reconciliation in the voice of Noah, as though of a precentor, saying: “Arise, why sleepest thou, [Col. 0273D] O Lord?” [Note: [Col. 0273] Ps. 43]. The manner and effect of this reconciliation are set forth in the Gospel and elsewhere, as we have taught above.

On the third Sunday, as in the adolescence of the world, man conceives his deliverance because the Lord led the children of Israel out of Egyptian bondage through Moses and Aaron [Note: [Col. 0273] Exod. 12]. The Church prays for the hastening of his protection and deliverance in the voice of Moses, as though of a precentor: “Be thou unto me a God who protects” [Note: [Col. 0273] Ps. 30]. See how, when the Lord sent Moses to the people, performed wonders before [Col. 0274A] them, and gave them the commandments of life [Note: [Col. 0273] Exod. 20], from then on that great blind man—that is, the human race—began to receive sight. He is read of in today’s Gospel and is thus rebuked by the crowd while asking light from the Lord [Note: [Col. 0273] Luke 18], just as the children of Israel were oppressed by the Egyptians when they asked leave to go a three-day journey in order to sacrifice to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0273] Exod. 5].

The fourth Sunday signifies the Church’s youth, in which it is crowned with the diadem of kings and adorned with the wisdom of prophets, in whose hands Christ is likened [Note: [Col. 0273] Hos. 13]. For David, outstanding among kings and prophets, is chosen [Note: [Col. 0273] I Kings 16]. His name is interpreted “strong of hand and desirable in appearance”; he prefigured Christ by his name, by his victories, and proclaimed him in psalms and songs. For as David overcame Goliath [Note: [Col. 0273] I Kings 17] and the lion, so Christ overcame the devil, [Col. 0274B] walking upon the asp and basilisk. Hence today’s office is celebrated in chants with David’s voice as precentor [Note: [Col. 0273] Ps. 90], and in the Gospel Christ’s victory is set forth [Note: [Col. 0273] Matt. 4].

The fifth Sunday signifies the old age of the Church, in which its natural heat began to fail. For when the temple was destroyed and the people were carried captive to Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar [Note: [Col. 0273] IV Kings 25], the captive Church had neither altar nor temple, but hung its instruments upon the willows [Note: [Col. 0273] Ps. 136]. Thus it is not without reason that this Sunday lacks its own office and has none except one borrowed from another weekday. That captivity signifies the captivity of the sinful soul, which is repelled only by fasting and prayer [Note: [Col. 0273] Matt. 17]. Therefore the Church, as though in the voice of Daniel crying out in that captivity [Note: [Col. 0273] Dan. 9], [Col. 0274C] borrows an office from the fast, wholly characterized by sorrow; and through the Canaanite woman’s daughter tormented by a demon, the same captivity of souls is understood. Therefore the Gospel concerning her is read [Note: [Col. 0273] Matt. 15].

The Sixth Sunday signifies the old age of the Church, namely the end-times, when the Son of God came into the world and freed the human race from the devil’s power. Therefore, lest it be forgetful and ungrateful for the benefit received, it rejoices and says: “My eyes are ever toward the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0273] Ps. 24]. Thus the Gospel concerning the man freed from a demon is fittingly read [Note: [Col. 0273] Luke 11].

This seventh and final Sunday signifies the sabbath of the world, in which the souls of the saints rest, having laid aside the burden of the flesh; and, like victors after wars who have put down their arms, they rejoice in leisure, rewarded each with a single robe and awaiting two robes in glory [Col. 0274D]. There the Jerusalem above, which is free and is our mother [Note: [Col. 0273] Gal. 4], rejoices; keeping festival for the number of children returning from pilgrimage, she pours forth the stored feast and, nursing from her breasts, presses out the delights of maternal consolation. Hence whatever is sung today at nocturns concerns the liberation of the people from Egypt—that is, the liberation of the soul from this body of death [Note: [Col. 0273] Rom. 7]. What is sung in the daytime office concerns the joy and fullness of the heavenly Jerusalem.

[Col. 0275A] For the feeding with five loaves and two fish, recounted in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0275] John 6], signifies the eternal satisfaction which begins here and is completed in the world to come. For now, through what we receive from the books of Moses, the Psalms, and the Prophets, we know in part [Note: [Col. 0275] 1 Cor. 13]. But then Jesus, who went across the Sea of Galilee—that is, “rising from the dead” [Note: [Col. 0275] Rom. 6]—passed through all the world’s bitterness; he will satisfy with a great banquet all the multitude coming to him and all the children of the heavenly Jerusalem, when they have been weaned. Abraham prefigured this when, on the day of Isaac’s weaning—the only son of the free woman—he made a great feast [Note: [Col. 0275] Gen. 21].

Therefore the address of the Holy Spirit comforts all the saints who are to be satisfied at this feast, saying: “Rejoice, Jerusalem”; and observe that [Col. 0275B] words of joy are multiplied, because we are freed from manifold tribulations and summoned to manifold joys: “And hold an assembly, all you who love her,” because you shall be satisfied, because you shall go “into the house of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0275] Ps. 121], where there will be peace and abundance. This is sung in the gradual; when we have reached it, what follows in the tract will be fulfilled: “He who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved for ever” [Note: [Col. 0275] Ps. 124]. In the offertory, all those feasting at that table are invited to praise [Note: [Col. 0275] Ps. 138]. But lest anyone understand this of Palestinian Jerusalem, the communion specifies that what has been said concerns Jerusalem which has not yet been built but is still being built as a city [Note: [Col. 0275] Ps. 121] from living stones, into which ascend [Col. 0275C] tribes, the tribes of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0275] ibid.], royal tribes and priestly tribes.

The church itself to which today’s station is assigned also signifies by its name the holy heavenly city, Jerusalem. For it is called Holy Jerusalem so that, for citizens of heaven making their pilgrimage in this world—who have here no abiding city but seek the city to come [Note: [Col. 0275] Heb. 13]—the very name may awaken remembrance of the heavenly city, and that they may greet it from afar as pilgrims [Note: [Col. 0275] Heb. 11]. Yet the rationale of this station differs from that of the Second Sunday of Advent: that is an announcement of future blessedness, whereas this is, as it were, a contemplation of present blessedness. Hence we celebrate more festively, because it is the feast of our hope.

On this day the Christian emperor is crowned, so that he may meditate upon the crown of the heavenly Jerusalem [Col. 0275D]. On this day the Roman pontiff bears in his own hands a golden rose full of balsam, not for temporal delight but for spiritual signification. This flower signifies that flower which speaks of itself, saying: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” [Note: [Col. 0275] Song 2]. It is golden because he is “King of kings and Lord of lords” [Note: [Col. 0275] Rev. 19]; its redness appeared in the tokens of the Passion [Note: [Col. 0275] Isa. 63], and its fragrance in the glory of the Resurrection.

On this day likewise, by the authority of the Roman rite, two collects are said, as on the Annunciation of the Lord, so that we seem to discharge, as it were, a double feast [Col. 0276A]. If anyone objects, “Why is this not observed on the chief feasts, such as the Nativity of the Lord and similar days?” I answer: because they are extended through octaves and are not confined to the observance of one day.

Others distinguish the offices from Septuagesima differently, nor does the subject-matter of the words fail them. They say that one pilgrimage of the people is read of in Egypt [Note: [Col. 0275] Gen. 46; Exod. 1], and one captivity in Babylon [Note: [Col. 0275] 4 Kings 25]. By both are signified our pilgrimage and captivity in this world. Two returns of God’s people are also recorded: one from under Pharaoh, through the Red Sea and the wilderness, to the promised land [Note: [Col. 0275] Exod. 12]; the other from Babylon to Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0275] 1 Ezra 1]. By these are signified our returns: the first from under the devil’s power, through baptism and penitence, to [Col. 0276B] the Church; the second from this world’s confusion to the enjoyment of eternal peace. Captivity and pilgrimage, as stated above, are extended through the number seven. Hence they are denoted by four weeks.

Thus in all nocturnal and daytime offices, whatever is read or sung is either the voice of pilgrims grieving over their pilgrimage; or the voice of captives groaning over their captivity; or the voice of those returning from darkness to light, from unbelief to faith; or the voice of those returning from mourning to joy, from the world to heaven. More often, indeed, the nocturns are the voice of pilgrims, the morning praises of captives, and the Mass office of those returning. [Col. 0276C] Let the diligent reader attend to which voice belongs where.

By what means our return occurs is expressed in the two following Sundays of the Passion: namely, through the Lord’s Passion. For there are two of our returns, or two passions of the Lord: one in himself; the other, that which he suffers in his body. Hence: “Saul, why do you persecute me?” [Note: [Col. 0275] Acts 9]. The Sunday of the Resurrection will immediately follow, in which our return shall be completed.

On Monday is read the Gospel in which, when the Pharisees ask Jesus what sign he shows and by what authority he drives the money-changers from the temple, he answers: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” [Note: [Col. 0275] John 2], speaking of the temple of his body. He does not command it, but foretells it. Then follows: “He himself [Col. 0276D] did not entrust himself to them” [Note: [Col. 0275] ibid.].

The reading concerning the two harlots who disputed before Solomon over the living son is rightly set before this Gospel. To the one who said, “Let it be neither mine nor yours, but divided” [Note: [Col. 0275] 3 Kings 3], King Solomon did not restore the living child. These women bear the type of the Synagogue and the Church. The Synagogue bore a son, whom it crushed while sleeping: this is Christ, whom it bore in the flesh and, according to his humanity, hung upon the cross. The Church likewise had a son, whom it preserved unharmed: this is Christ, whom it conceived and bore in the womb of faith, and whose divinity it did not doubt [Col. 0277A] to be living.

These are the two goats, one of which is slaughtered and the other sent away [Note: [Col. 0277] Lev. 16]. These are the ram and Isaac [Note: [Col. 0277] Gen. 22]: as it were two sons, yet not two Christs, but one by identity of person—the giant of twofold substance—whom the Synagogue neither conceived nor bore in the womb of faith, but desired to be slain and still desires that his memory be extinguished. But the true Solomon did not entrust the child, namely himself, to the Synagogue; rather, he passed into the faith of the Church, as if saying to the apostles: “Give her the living child; for she is our mother” [Note: [Col. 0277] 3 Kings 3]. She, therefore, is the one who prays in the introit, gradual, and communion, and who in the offertory invites the whole earth to make joyful noise [Note: [Col. 0277] Ps. 99].

On Tuesday is read the Gospel in which he rebukes [Col. 0277B] the Jews for transgressing the Law of Moses, saying: “Did not Moses give you the Law, and yet none of you keeps the Law?” [Note: [Col. 0277] John 7]. Therefore that prayer of Moses ought not to intercede for them: namely, “Let your anger cease, and be merciful concerning the wickedness of your people” [Note: [Col. 0277] Exod. 32]. He then rebukes them for homicide, adding: “Why do you seek to kill me?” Accordingly, the reading in which the Lord says to Moses is fittingly set before this Gospel: “Go down from the mountain, because your people has sinned. Leave me, that my wrath may grow hot against them and that I may destroy them.” To this Moses replies: “Why, Lord, does your wrath grow hot?” etc. [Note: [Col. 0277] ibid.].

This prayer prevailed for them until the time when they crucified the Son of God, as the Lord had promised Moses, saying: “I have forgiven according to your word. Nevertheless, on the day of vengeance I shall visit upon them this sin also” [Col. 0277C] [Note: [Col. 0277] ibid.]. What is placed in the introit and gradual consists of Moses’ prayers; what is in the offertory and communion consists of his consolations.

On Wednesday begin the sacraments proper to the new Church, namely the scrutinies. We have said that the children of Israel returned from the Babylonian captivity in the seventieth year [Note: [Col. 0277] 1 Ezra 1]. On their return they had uncertain priests. Therefore Ezra and the other wise men carefully searched the genealogies and separated Jews from Gentiles and priests from Jews [Note: [Col. 0277] 1 Ezra 2, 8]. Likewise we begin the scrutinies not in any of the preceding weeks, but only in this week, which signifies the end of that seventy, so that we may separate believers from unbelievers, whom we renew [Col. 0277D] from water and Spirit at the most holy solemnity of our redemption.

For it was the Church’s custom to celebrate the sacrament of our regeneration at no other time unless danger of death threatened. Hence: “All of us who have been baptized into Christ have been baptized into his death” [Note: [Col. 0277] Rom. 6]; and, as he rose from the dead, so we should walk in newness of spirit [Note: [Col. 0277] ibid.]. Therefore all the offspring of the Church, whom it had begotten throughout the year by the nourishment of the divine word, gave in their names on this day. They were to be examined lest any root of bitterness should be present [Note: [Col. 0277] Heb. 12], [Col. 0278A] as among heretics, lest holy things be given them before Christian faith had fixed roots in their minds [Note: [Col. 0277] Matt. 7]. Thus, after their names had been given, each of them heard the rule of faith during the following days up to the solemnity of Easter; and so, nourished and growing great at the full moon—that is, in baptism—rendering the Creed to Christ in full faith, he died with Christ and rose again.

For this reason he was called a *catechumen*, interpreted “one hearing” or “one instructed,” because he was instructed both in the faith necessary for baptism and in the conduct of life to be observed after baptism. Hence *catechization* means instruction, and *scrutiny* comes from searching. But before the net is filled with a multitude of fish [Note: [Col. 0277] Matt. 13], because it was dangerous to defer so great a multitude owing to occasions of death, [Col. 0278B] especially in the case of infants, whose tender life is cut short by a slight cause, it seemed expedient—permission having been granted for baptism to be administered generally—to forestall every danger; yet the solemnity of baptism, at least for some, was reserved for the Lord’s Resurrection because of the resemblance.

The scrutiny is begun on Wednesday rather than another day for five reasons. First, because, as on the fourth day the stars were created and joined to the sun and moon [Note: [Col. 0277] Gen. 1], so today believers are conceived, who are joined to Christ the sun and the Church the moon. Second, because in the fourth age of the world the Christian empire took its beginning from the promise, when the Lord swore to David: “Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne” [Note: [Col. 0277] Ps. 131:8; 2 Kings 7].

Therefore [Col. 0278C] Christian religion rightly begins on the fourth day and in the fourth week, which represents the youthful age of humankind. This is suited to the steering of empire and signifies the royal age, renewed by the promise of Christ’s kingdom, concerning which kingdom the angel said to the Virgin: “He shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever” [Note: [Col. 0277] Luke 1]. Third, because, as in the fourth age Solomon built the temple for the Lord [Note: [Col. 0277] 3 Kings 7], so now those to be baptized are prepared on this Wednesday for the temple of the Lord. Fourth, because, as on Wednesday the Lord was betrayed by Judas in order to die for the redemption of the Church, so on Wednesday the Church is catechized, so that it may avoid no dangers in acquiring Christ. Fifth, because the lamb was kept and prepared for fourteen days, and was sacrificed at the fifteenth moon [Col. 0278D] [Note: [Col. 0277] Exod. 12].

It is fitting, therefore, that the Church’s new offspring, being prepared to die with Christ, should through fifteen days of fasting be spiritually fed and match the age of the moon, which signifies it. For if the scrutinies were celebrated on Friday, which is the fifteenth [day] of the Passion, only thirteen days would remain for preparation in fasting, because fasting is not permitted on the two intervening Sundays. Thus, while the scrutinies begin on Wednesday and the following [Col. 0279A] fifteen days are devoted to instruction in faith, discipline of morals, and fasting, the new Church—fair as the moon [Note: [Col. 0279] Song 6], full of faith, dying with Christ and rising with him—is joined to him in baptism.

Although the scrutinies, as we have said, are observed for fifteen days, they are celebrated only seven times, so that when the catechumens are completed through the number seven, the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit may be given to them. The scrutinies are celebrated in this order. When the children come to the church door, their names are written by the acolyte. Afterwards they are called by name into the church and the males are placed to the right, the females to the left. Those who seek faith come to the door, for faith is the Church’s door. Their names are written in heaven [Note: [Col. 0279] Luke 10], and those acting manfully [Note: [Col. 0279] Ps. 26] [Col. 0279B] shall stand at the right in judgment, whereas those living effeminately shall stand at the left [Note: [Col. 0279] Matt. 25].

Then the exorcist, to whom this office properly belongs, asks whether they renounce the devil, his works, and his pomps. For every human being born in original sin is by right subject to the devil’s lordship; believers escape his claim when they submit themselves to Christ’s yoke [Note: [Col. 0279] Matt. 11]. Some works of the devil are committed by an operation of the spirit, others by an operation of the body: of the spirit are pride, anger, and the like; of the body, fornication, drunkenness, and the like. The devil’s pomps are spectacles, dances, games, wantonness, and, to state it briefly, every empty and superfluous honor.

They are then questioned concerning faith in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, without which no one is said to please God [Note: [Col. 0279] Heb. 11]. [Col. 0279C] Next the devil is blown out, so that they may become a dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit. The sign of the cross is impressed upon their foreheads as a seal, so that the house of God may be fortified against demons. Seeing this sign, the devil trembles and flees, remembering that by it he was conquered. The cross is impressed upon the forehead so that they may be reminded not to be ashamed of Christ crucified. Afterwards, through prayers, they are received into the Church’s unity; through the taste of salt they are seasoned with the teaching of wisdom.

Then the devil is driven away through exorcisms; therefore “Accursed one” is repeated three times, because the devil is manfully opposed through faith in the Trinity. Males are exorcized separately toward the south, females separately toward the north, because greater things are to be offered to those who understand more, and lesser things [Col. 0279D] to those who grasp less and are cold. That the nostrils and ears are touched with saliva signifies the petition that teaching, which flows from the Most High [Note: [Col. 0279] Sir. 24], may enter through their ears and smell sweet to them.

They are brought in and sent out by the doorkeeper, because through Christ, who is the door [Note: [Col. 0279] John 10], they shall be brought by the Holy Spirit into the wine-cellar of heaven [Note: [Col. 0279] Song 2], or shut out by the opposing sword [Note: [Col. 0279] Gen. 3]. They are enlightened by the acolyte, who is the kindler of lights, so that, when the darkness of sins has fled and the blindness of error has been driven away, they may be illumined by the light of understanding. The deacon reads the Gospel over them, because evangelical teaching [Col. 0280A] is set before them. On the final day, however, the openings of four Gospels are read to them, because from the four quarters of the world they come to the sacraments of faith [Note: [Col. 0279] Luke 13].

That one male and one female are brought into the sanctuary by the acolytes signifies that persons of both sexes are converted to evangelical faith. The Apostles’ Creed and the Lord’s Prayer are recited and expounded over males and females in Greek and Latin, wherever either language has been marked as belonging to the Church, so that every tongue may confess the Lord [Note: [Col. 0279] Phil. 2], and so that all wisdom and all power may be referred to the Lord. For the Greeks excelled in wisdom and the Romans in power. We have set forth above, in the treatise on the Mass, an exposition of the Lord’s Prayer.

Here, however, let us briefly expound the Apostles’ Creed [Col. 0280B], in which we confess the Father as Creator of all things; in which we also join the Son, equal in power, who is proclaimed as conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin; who is said to have suffered, been crucified, died, and been buried; who is known to have descended to hell and risen on the third day; who is believed to have ascended into heaven and to sit at the Father’s right hand; and who is expected to come to judge the living and the dead.

In this same Creed the Holy Spirit is likewise added without distinction of deity, the same as the Father and the Son. In it the holy catholic Church is named; and therein are taught the communion of saints, the remission of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and the attainment of eternal life. The words of this Creed are indeed few, arranged not by the speech of human wisdom but by true divine reason [Col. 0280C]. Yet its mysteries are great, foreseen long beforehand through the prophets and declared through the apostles. Hence it is called a *symbol*, “a common morsel” or “a contribution,” because in it twelve articles are set forth as secrets and contributed by the apostles; it is called a *symbol*, “a common bite” or “a contribution,” and we propose to distinguish them and strengthen them by Old Testament authorities.

“I believe in God the Father almighty, Creator of heaven and earth.” As Augustine says, it is one thing to believe God, another to believe that God exists, and another to believe in God. To believe God is to believe true what he says; the wicked also do this, and we believe a human being, but not in a human being. To believe that God exists is to believe that he himself is God; even demons do this [Col. 0280D]. To believe in God is, by believing, to love; by believing, to go into him; and by believing, to cleave to him. This only the good do.

Therefore one who says, “I believe in God,” lies if he does not love God—unless you say that the Church speaks in his person, or that he is speaking not of what he is, but of what he ought to be. In saying “God” in the singular, he avoids a plurality of gods. Hence: “Hear, Israel: your God is one” [Note: [Col. 0279] Deut. 6]; and the Apostle: “One God, one faith, and one baptism” [Note: [Col. 0279] Eph. 4].

In saying “Father,” he begins to distinguish the persons, concerning whom Isaiah says: “Who has weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers?” [Note: [Col. 0279] Isa. 40]. And elsewhere: “The Seraphim cried, ‘Holy, holy, [Col. 0281A] holy’” [Note: [Col. 0281] Isa. 6]. And the Lord: “Baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0281] Matt. 28]. And John the Evangelist: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0281] 1 John 5].

The Father is the first person in the Trinity, not in time but in authority. The word that follows, “almighty,” is an essential name, as we have declared in the Athanasian Creed. Therefore we refer it, not without reason, either to the substantive “God” or to the relative “Father,” saying: “I believe in God almighty,” or “in the Father almighty.” The same applies to what follows, “Creator of heaven and earth.” Here the heretic is refuted who asserts one creator of heaven and another of earth; one of heavenly things and another of earthly things; one of bodies and another of souls. Against such persons David says: [Col. 0281B] “In the beginning you, Lord, founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands” [Note: [Col. 0281] Ps. 101]; and the Apostle: “In him all things were created, in heaven and on earth” [Note: [Col. 0281] Col. 1].

“And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.” Behold the second person in the Trinity. This is Jesus, who saved his people from their sins [Note: [Col. 0281] Matt. 1]. This is the Father’s only Son, of whom David says: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” [Note: [Col. 0281] Ps. 2]; and the Apostle: “God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the Law” [Note: [Col. 0281] Gal. 4]. This is our Lord because he created us and bought us, slaves of another master, at the price of blood. Some join “only” to “our Lord.”

“Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of [Col. 0281C] the Virgin Mary.” Behold the first mystery of Christ, namely the Incarnation: as though it said, he who, though God, became man—not from male seed, but conceived through the operation of the Holy Spirit; “born of the Virgin Mary.” Hence Isaiah: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” [Note: [Col. 0281] Isa. 7]; and the angel in the Gospel: “Hail, Mary, full of grace; the Lord is with you,” and below: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” [Note: [Col. 0281] Luke 1].

“Suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried.” Behold the second seal in Christ’s humiliation, namely the Passion. Its time is described: “under Pontius Pilate”; its manner is added: “crucified”; its end is concluded: “died and was buried.” Hence, lamenting, he says through the mouth of David and Jeremiah: “They pierced my hands and my feet, and counted all my bones” [Note: [Col. 0281] Ps. 21; Jer. 18]. Concerning death, the prophet says: “From the Lord came the escape from death” [Note: [Col. 0281] Ps. 67].

Concerning the tomb, Isaiah says: “His tomb shall be glorious” [Note: [Col. 0281] Isa. 11]. These things are manifest in the Gospel.

“He descended into hell; on the third day he rose from the dead.” Behold the third mystery, namely the Resurrection. But first is stated the descent into hell, and from it the dead are liberated. Hence in Hosea: “From the hand of death I shall free them; from death I shall redeem them. I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O hell” [Note: [Col. 0281] Hos. 13]. [Col. 0282A] This is the strong man of the Gospel, who bound the strong man and plundered his goods [Note: [Col. 0281] Luke 11]. This is he who says in the Psalm: “I slept and was in a deep sleep, and rose again, because the Lord sustained me” [Note: [Col. 0281] Ps. 3]; who, when the Father says, “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” [Note: [Col. 0281] Ps. 56], answers in a brief utterance: “I shall arise at dawn” [Note: [Col. 0281] ibid.]. Women and men give testimony in the Gospel to his resurrection [Note: [Col. 0281] Matt. 28; Mark 16; Luke 24; John 20].

“He ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty.” Behold the fourth mystery, namely the Ascension. For, as David says, he ascended: “Above the cherubim he rode and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds” [Col. 0282B] [Note: [Col. 0281] Ps. 17]; and: “He prepared his throne in heaven, and his kingdom shall rule over all” [Note: [Col. 0281] Ps. 102]. To him the Father says: “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” [Note: [Col. 0281] Ps. 109]. And lest visual testimony to the Ascension also be absent, Luke says: “While the disciples watched, he was raised up, and a cloud received him from their eyes” [Note: [Col. 0281] Acts 1].

“From there he shall come to judge men and the dead.” Behold the fifth seal, not yet opened. For the King shall come openly, to whom the Father has given judgment [Note: [Col. 0281] John 5]. And as David says: “He shall prepare his throne for judgment and shall judge the peoples in righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0281] Ps. 9; Ps. 97]; and elsewhere: “God shall come openly, our God, and shall not keep silence” [Note: [Col. 0281] Ps. 49]. And Luke: “Thus he shall come as you saw him going into heaven” [Note: [Col. 0281] Acts 1]. And Micah: “The Lord has a judgment [Col. 0282C] with his people” [Note: [Col. 0281] Mic. 6].

“I believe in the Holy Spirit.” Behold the third person in the Trinity, namely the Holy Spirit, of whom Moses says: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” [Note: [Col. 0281] Gen. 1]; and David: “The Spirit blew, and the waters shall flow” [Note: [Col. 0281] Ps. 147]; and the Lord in the Gospel: “The Spirit, who proceeds from the Father” [Note: [Col. 0281] John 15], “shall teach you all things” [Note: [Col. 0281] John 14]. For he teaches, he sanctifies, he unites, and he forgives sins. Through him one obtains resurrection unto glory; through him one obtains eternal life.

What follows, “the holy catholic Church,” may therefore be joined thus: “I believe in the Holy Spirit, [and that] the holy catholic Church”—that is, that the Church of the faithful is sanctified through the Holy Spirit. Likewise with what follows: “I believe in the Holy Spirit, [and] the communion of saints”—namely, that through the Holy Spirit saints are united in the bond of charity. And: “I believe in the Holy Spirit, [and] the remission of sins”—that is, that sins are remitted through the Spirit. Likewise: “I believe in the Holy Spirit, [and] the resurrection of the flesh and life everlasting”—that is, that through the Holy Spirit the flesh shall attain glory and the soul eternal life.

Or thus: “I believe in the holy catholic Church.” Yet, as Augustine maintains, we do not say that we believe *in* the Church as we believe in [Col. 0283A] God. We believe the Church, while living in the Church we tend toward God; and we profess with the firmest faith that what follows derives from it: namely, the communion of saints, remission of sins, resurrection of the flesh, and life everlasting.

Accordingly, join it thus: “I believe [the] holy catholic Church, [and] the communion of saints”: that is, through the faith which I have while existing in the holy and universal Church, I attain the communion of saints—that is, concord and union. For as there is one Shepherd, so there is one fold [Note: [Col. 0283] John 10]; as there is one God, so there is one faith and one baptism [Note: [Col. 0283] Eph. 4]. Or, “I receive the communion of saints,” that is, the bread of blessing, of which it is said: “Believe, and you have eaten” [Note: [Col. 0283] St Augustine].

Likewise with what follows: “I believe [the] holy Church, [and] remission”: that is, through the faith which I have while existing in the holy and universal Church, I obtain remission of sins—that is, the healing of leprosy, concerning which it is said in the Law [Note: [Col. 0283] Lev. 14] and the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0283] Matt. 8]: when Miriam, Aaron’s sister, had been outside the camp for seven days, she was cleansed of leprosy [Note: [Col. 0283] Num. 12]; Naaman the Syrian, washed seven times in the Jordan, was cured of leprosy [Note: [Col. 0283] 4 Kings 5]; likewise the Lord cleansed ten lepers, but only one gave glory to God [Note: [Col. 0283] Luke 17]. Of Magdalene also it is said: “Many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much” [Note: [Col. 0283] Luke 7]. And the Lord says to the paralytic: “Son, your sins are forgiven you” [Note: [Col. 0283] Matt. 9]. It follows:

“I believe [the] holy catholic Church, [and] the resurrection of the flesh”: that is, through the faith which I have while existing [Col. 0283C] in the Church, I obtain the resurrection of the flesh, concerning which Job says: “I believe that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise again, and in my flesh I shall see God my Savior” [Note: [Col. 0283] Job 19]. Hence also in the Gospel: “The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob is not God of the dead but of the living” [Note: [Col. 0283] Matt. 22]; and the Apostle: “We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed” [Note: [Col. 0283] 1 Cor. 15].

What follows should likewise be joined: “I believe [the] holy catholic Church, [and] life everlasting”: that is, through the faith which I have in the Church, I shall obtain eternal life. This is the land of the living, concerning which David says: “I believe that I shall see the Lord’s good things in the land of the living” [Note: [Col. 0283] Ps. 26]. Eternal life, moreover, is to see God the Father and Jesus Christ whom he sent [Note: [Col. 0283] John 17].

[Col. 0283D] When these matters have thus been completed, the neophytes are dismissed from the church, because it is not fitting that those who have not been regenerated should either be reckoned among God’s children or be present at Christ’s mysteries. Some dismiss catechumens before the Gospel, but I do not approve, since the Gospel ought to be preached to them, as the apostles preached it to the first-fruits of the Gentiles. But they ought not to be present at the sacrifice: both because the priest prays for those standing around, whose faith is known and whose devotion is recognized, whereas these are still called unbelievers; and because what is consecrated is offered to them.

Observe that, before this Wednesday, [Col. 0284A] on Sunday or Monday, the scrutiny of this Wednesday must be announced to the people in these words:

> Beloved brethren, know that the day of scrutiny is near, on which our elect are to be instructed by God. Therefore deign to assemble with attentive devotion on the following Wednesday about the ninth hour, so that we may be able to perform without fault the heavenly mystery by which the devil and his pomp are destroyed and the gate of the heavenly kingdom is opened.

Likewise, on Wednesday, when the solemnities of the Masses have ended, the priest announces that they are to return for the scrutiny on the following Saturday; and he announces thus again and again until the seven scrutinies are completed.

Let us now continue with the office of this day’s Mass. [Col. 0284B] The Gospel concerning the man blind from birth is read [Note: [Col. 0283] John 9]. He is the human race, which, following the prince of darkness, lost its eyes in the first parent [Note: [Col. 0283] Gen. 3], and therefore is called blind from birth. For him the Lord spat upon the ground, made mud, and anointed his eyes, saying: “Go to the pool of Siloam and wash.” Therefore he went, washed, and saw [Note: [Col. 0283] John 9].

The spittle which descends from the head signifies Christ’s divinity—the Word which the Father uttered [Note: [Col. 0283] Ps. 44]. The Father is the head. When he sent the Son, the Father spat the Word upon the earth, which every wind shook, and in the Virgin’s womb joined him in one person to the dust of our nature. Therefore the mud from spittle and dust is Christ from divinity and humanity. His faith is proclaimed to the blind man; his eyes are anointed with the mud [Col. 0284C] which the Lord made; and, when catechized—that is, instructed by the word of preaching—he is sent to the pool and washed in the font of baptism.

And observe that the pool of Siloam is called “of the Sent One”: that is, of the Holy Spirit, who, sent from the Father and the Son, works especially there. Every element of the office depends upon this Gospel; for example: “When I have been sanctified among you, I will gather you from all lands and pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements” [Note: [Col. 0283] Ezek. 36]. The Lord is sanctified in catechumens when they hear and believe that he is holy. Clean water, namely the Holy Spirit, is poured upon them; through him the visible water cleanses. Once cleansed, they live so as to bear witness that he is holy, by whose command they themselves [Col. 0284D] are holy.

The same is read in the first lesson, with the addition: “I will take away the stony heart from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.” Catechumens have a heart of flesh—that is, a soft heart—when they receive from Scripture or discipline the teaching of faith. This teaching is not received by the stony hearts of the Jews, which are broken; in their type the first tablets were broken [Note: [Col. 0283] Exod. 32], whereas in the type of the Gentiles other tablets were cut [Note: [Col. 0283] Exod. 34]. The other reading also, “Wash yourselves and be clean” [Note: [Col. 0283] Isa. 1], similarly concerns catechumens who are to be baptized.

Two readings are read, because the catechumens [Col. 0285A] must be instructed in the practice of the twofold love, or in the teaching of both Testaments, or concerning faith and morals. Hence the first reading treats of faith, the second of morals; for, as Augustine says, those to be baptized must be taught not only what they ought to believe, but also how they may rescue themselves from this corrupt age. To preach Christ is not merely to state what must be believed concerning Christ, but what must be observed by one who approaches the structure of Christ’s body. And as there are two readings, so also there are two collects; but we bend the knee at only one, because we invite the catechumens to the unity of faith. Likewise there are two graduals sounding in the same sense; for this is the voice of the Church catechizing her new offspring: “Come, children; hear me: I will teach you the fear of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0285] Ps. 33]; and that other: “Blessed is the nation,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0285] Ps. 32]. Nor without reason does the present office accumulate an increase of readings, collects, and graduals, so that an increase of spiritual children may have an increase of nourishment. In the offertory are the proclamations of the blind man—that is, of the human race, or of the Christian people—praising God for his illumination and inviting others to praise [Note: [Col. 0285] Ps. 65]. The communion is the confession of the same blind man, saying, “Mud” [Note: [Col. 0285] Josh. 9], and it is repeated, because the blind man gave the Jews this answer twice, or because God enlightened the human race in two peoples. For when the Jews had cast him out, unwilling to hear anything about the mud, he did not cease to confess the mud—that is, the Lord’s incarnation—saying: “He made mud,” [Col. 0285C] etc. Hence follows that beatitude of which the Lord says: “Blessed are you when people hate you and persecute you” [Note: [Col. 0285] Matt. 5].

It must not be passed over in silence that, wherever the scrutinies are performed, special collects are said for the catechumens: “Almighty, everlasting God, thy Church.” Likewise, “[the collect] ‘of healing,’ etc.” Today’s station at Saint Paul’s is celebrated not without reason: both because he was the catechist of the whole world, namely the Teacher of the Gentiles [Note: [Col. 0285] 1 Tim. 9], and because he himself was catechized in a wondrous manner [Note: [Col. 0285] Acts 2]. For he did not learn the Gospel from a human being, but by the miraculous revelation of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0285] Gal. 1]. He too is not altogether unlike the blind man of the Gospel. Blind in soul from birth, and blind in body for three days, he came to the pool of saving baptism and [Col. 0285D] saw both in soul and body; and while the Jews contended against him and cast him out of their synagogue, he preached the mud—that is, the Lord’s incarnation.

On Thursday, the Gospel is read in which the Lord says: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” [Note: [Col. 0285] John 5]. He adds what is to be understood by this working: “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son gives life to whom he will.” Here, as Augustine says, the present resurrection is treated of, which occurs through faith, by which a person passes from the death of falsehood to the life of truth, from the death of iniquity to the life of righteousness. To this Gospel [Col. 0286A] is rightly prefixed the reading concerning the son of the Shunammite, whom the boy sent by Elisha with the staff did not raise; finally Elisha came, bent himself over the boy, walked to and fro, and the boy yawned seven times and opened his eyes [Note: [Col. 0285] 4 Kings 4]. This raising of the boy is the raising through faith of the human race. To raise it, the Lord sent a boy with a staff—that is, Moses with the sting of the Law, which said: “If anyone does this or that, let him die the death.” Yet he could not raise the dead, because, as Paul testifies, the Law brought no one to perfection [Note: [Col. 0285] Heb. 7]. Returning toward the house, Elisha bent himself over the boy when he took the form of a servant [Note: [Col. 0285] Phil. 2]; he walked about when he preached, or when he passed from Judaea to the Gentiles. Thus the boy yawned seven times and opened his eyes, [Col. 0286B] because the person dead in sins, receiving the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, lives by faith in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0285] Rom. 1], and so revives by the spirit of love, whom the rod of fear does not correct. The remaining items sung in the introit, gradual, offertory, and communion are consolations and prayers for one who has been raised.

On Friday, the Gospel is read concerning Lazarus, whom the Lord loved [Note: [Col. 0285] John 11]. He bears the type of every believer who, although he is the Lord’s friend through faith, nevertheless dies to him through wicked action, buried in the tomb of an evil conscience and stinking through the stain of disgrace; at last, shaken by the Lord’s hidden inspiration and by great fear of the coming judgment, as though by the Saviour’s great cry, he springs back to life [Col. 0286C] through repentance. When the tomb of conscience has been opened by confession, he is released from the bonds of sins. Observe that this Gospel is always read on the day which is the fifteenth from the Lord’s Passion, because Lazarus is known to have been raised on this day. From this Gospel is taken the responsory, “The Jews came together,” which is sung today. Fittingly prefixed to it is the reading concerning the dead son of the woman of Zarephath, whom Elijah raised, placing him upon the bed and stretching himself over him three times [Note: [Col. 0285] 3 Kings 17]. This woman is the Church, which receives Christ by faith into the lodging of the heart; her son is any believer, who dies when he commits a sin deserving death. Elijah’s bed signifies the catholic Church, in which alone souls revive when, through faith in [Col. 0286D] the Trinity, they rise from the death of sins. The rest are praises, confessions, and consolations of anyone raised from sins.

On Saturday the Gospel is read: “I am the light of the world” [Note: [Col. 0285] John 8], where the Lord bears witness concerning himself and proves from the Law that this must necessarily be granted. Corresponding to it is the prefixed reading in which he says: “Behold, I have given him as a witness to the peoples, a leader and teacher to the nations” [Note: [Col. 0285] Isa. 55; now in the missal not the reading mentioned here, but another from Isa. 49]. Observe that two readings are read on this Saturday for the reasons set out above for Wednesday. For on this day the scrutiny and also [Col. 0287A] ordinations are celebrated; therefore, because of the increase of children, it is fitting that the nourishment of spiritual food should increase. Rightly, then, the Church’s voice is prefixed in the introit: “You who thirst, come to the waters” [Note: [Col. 0287] Isa. 55]. Here catechumens are called to baptism, and those to be ordained to the sacrament of order; both are called to light and to the intoxication of wisdom. This water of wisdom agrees with the Gospel light, because he who is the light of the world is also the Lord’s wisdom, the same source of life and light from light. The remaining items said in the gradual, offertory, and communion are consolations for the catechumens, or also for him whose testimony the Jews disputed.

## CHAPTER IX. PASSION SUNDAY

[Col. 0287B] “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause” [Note: [Col. 0287] Ps. 42]. After the most orderly arrangement of seven Sundays, by which, as has been said, the seven ages of the world are figured, all of which have been redeemed by the Passion, the celebration of the Sunday of the Passion itself begins. As though a long funeral procession had gone before, the very victim of our salvation follows, setting before our eyes the wounds which he suffered for us and the emblems of death. This celebration of the Passion begins at the end of Saturday, that is, with the evening preceding the light of this Sunday. For Lazarus having been raised on the preceding Friday, certain persons from Bethany went to the Pharisees and reported the miracle; many of them had gone up to Jerusalem to sanctify themselves [Note: [Col. 0287] John 11]. It was the Jews’ custom, by command of the Law, to sanctify themselves [Col. 0287C] before Passover, and to begin that sanctification on the first day of the first month, on which the tabernacle had been dedicated and on which they were commanded to choose the lamb for sacrifice. Therefore, since that Friday was the new moon—that is, the first day of the month [Note: [Col. 0287] Exod. 12]—many Jews, chief priests, and Pharisees had gathered for sanctification. On hearing of the sign, immediately, as John says—that is, on Saturday—“they gathered a council against Jesus, and from that day they planned to kill him; and thereafter Jesus did not walk openly among them” [Note: [Col. 0287] John 11], because his hour had not yet come. Therefore, on the evening of Saturday, as though after the hour of that council, the Church begins a public mourning, suffering with her Lord as members with the head; and [Col. 0287D] from then on, mourning, she recites the royal banner, the mystery of the cross, the vinegar, gall, and reed, the nails and spear that pierced the body, the day of the Passion, the prayers of the sufferer, the mockery of the enemies, and their plots.

These and similar things she laments in Vespers and the nocturnal offices, gathered from the authoritative Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments. Therefore we too in a certain way withdraw, while we suppress voices of joy. For we omit the *Gloria Patri* in the responsories and in the introit at Mass; likewise at the *Venite*, where the repetition of the invitatory is customarily altered so that it is repeated from the middle at the first verse and from the beginning at the second. The *Gloria* is suppressed because that verse pertains to the praise of the Trinity, whereas the second person of the Trinity is remembered as having undergone the Passion. Thus the whole Trinity is dishonoured; and also because “the Lord no longer walked openly.” Therefore we in some measure restrain the voice of his praise and glory, passing it over with a little silence—though not entirely, since it is not omitted at the end of psalms. The mourning ought to be more moderate, because the Lamb was not handed over into the hands of slaughterers immediately after the council had been held. Jeremiah is frequently read in the nocturnal vigils, both because by his words and sufferings he signified the Lord’s Passion and did not give way in tribulations—although the Jews maintain otherwise, namely that he was stoned by the people [Col. 0288B] going down into Egypt—and because he prefigured Israel’s blindness in the capture of Zedekiah, whose sons were killed by the king of Babylon and who was then deprived of his eyes [Note: [Col. 0287] 4 Kings 25]. For the Jewish people was taken captive in its pride; after its sons had been slain—that is, the carnal works of the Law, in which no life-giving grace of God remained—the devil tore out its eyes, so that those who see might become blind [Note: [Col. 0287] Luke 8]: “Their eyes were darkened, that they may not see, and their back is forever bent” [Note: [Col. 0287] Ps. 68]. Also, through the type of that captivity which then occurred, Jeremiah lamented with tearful laments the future rejection of the Jewish people.

We observe the foregoing while celebrating the Lord’s Passion for two weeks: both on account of the two Testaments, one of which announces the Lord about to suffer and the other the Lord having suffered; because he suffered for two peoples; because he is foreshadowed in the acts of the patriarchs and foretold in the words of the prophets [Note: [Col. 0287] Hos. 13]; or because those who before the Law and under the Law were inglorious and murmuring were in hell, and were reconciled through Christ in the time of grace, which is signified by the third week, namely the Paschal week. Let us now pursue the daily office of the Mass. Since the Gospel says, “Jesus hid himself and went out of the Temple” [Note: [Col. 0287] John 8], it is plainly indicated that the Temple and all the Jews’ holy things were to be abandoned by the Lord because of their pride, according to: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you” [Note: [Col. 0287] Matt. 21], and Josephus’s saying: “Let us depart from these [Col. 0288D] dwellings.” The same is declared in the Epistle: a better high priest, a more perfect tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0287] Heb. 9], and a more effective sacrifice are substituted [Note: [Col. 0287] Lev. 26], when the old things are cast aside as the new arrive. The introit, “Judge me, O God” [Note: [Col. 0287] Ps. 42], and the gradual, “Deliver me” [Note: [Col. 0287] Ps. 142], are the voices of the Lord going out from the Temple and praying according to his humanity, that his cause—that is, his righteousness, that is, the faith of the Gospel—may be distinguished by manifest separation from the justifications of the Law. This also came about when the Temple was destroyed and sacrifices abolished. For if the power of the Jewish kingdom and the worship of the old Temple had remained, they would have been a greater impediment [Col. 0289A] to Christian faith, because carnal people could not easily have discerned the emptiness of the old priesthood if it had been supported by temporal prosperity and glory. For as the children of Israel crossed the Jordan under Joshua’s leadership after Moses’ death [Note: [Col. 0289] Josh. 3], so, after the old priesthood has been destroyed, we pass to Christ’s saving baptism.

In the tract he gives the reason why he went out from the Temple: “They have often fought against me from my youth” [Note: [Col. 0289] Ps. 128]; namely, from the blood of righteous Abel they prolonged their iniquity by persistently killing my own [Note: [Col. 0289] Matt. 23], even to myself, of whom they said: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him” [Note: [Col. 0289] Matt. 21]. In the offertory, “I will confess” [Note: [Col. 0289] Ps. 118], he asks the reward of obedience, having become obedient unto death [Note: [Col. 0289] Phil. 2], when according to his humanity he adds: “Reward thy servant, and I shall live”—that is, I shall rise again—[Col. 0289B] “and then I shall keep,” that is, I shall cause to be kept, “thy words” [Note: [Col. 0289] Ps. 118]. The communion, “This is my body” [Note: [Col. 0289] 1 Cor. 11], is the voice of the new high priest going out from the Temple, entering once into the holy place by his own blood [Note: [Col. 0289] Heb. 9], and pouring it out for the three orders, namely for Noah, Job, and Daniel. Hence it is repeated three times. Since Peter was the first heir of this priesthood, the first high priest after Christ in rank and time, who followed him when he said, “Follow me” [Note: [Col. 0289] John 21], being led, girded with a like death, where he did not wish to go [Note: [Col. 0289] Ibid.], the station is rightly celebrated at his church in today’s office.

On Monday the Gospel is read in which the Lord says: “You will seek me and will not find me; and where I am, you cannot come” [Note: [Col. 0289] John 7], because the wall of unbelief stands in the way. By these words he threatened that he would pass to the Gentiles. Hence they too, divining this, said: “Will he go into the dispersion of the Gentiles?” [Note: [Col. 0289] Ibid.] Fittingly prefixed to this Gospel is the reading concerning the prophet Jonah, who was sent to preach to the great city of Nineveh. Fleeing in the waves of the sea toward Tarshish, he was swallowed by a sea-monster, was vomited forth alive on the third day, and only then did Nineveh, terrified by his preaching, repent for three days [Note: [Col. 0289] Jonah 3]. Jonah means “dove”: he is Christ, sent by God the Father for the salvation of the world. When he did not wish to go bodily to the Gentile people, he remained among the waves and tumults of the persecuting Jews; death swallowed him, but on the third day he rose. At his preaching through the apostles, while the world is washed by the threefold immersion of baptism, it is saved from the punishment of three days. The rest are prayers of the praying Ninevites and confessions of the King of glory.

On Tuesday the Gospel is read in which it is said that Jesus walked in Galilee, for he did not wish to walk in Judaea because the Jews sought to kill him; and below, when he had gone up privately into Judaea for the feast day, the Jews sought him, saying: “Where is he?” [Note: [Col. 0289] John 7] Corresponding to this Gospel is the prefixed reading concerning Daniel, although [Col. 0290A] it is not found in the Hebrew, which says that the assembled Babylonians said to the king: “Hand Daniel over to us, who destroyed Bel and killed the dragon” [Note: [Col. 0289] Dan. 14]. The Babylonians gathered together and sought Daniel from the king; the Jews gathered together and sought Christ. They sent Daniel into the lions’ den; these sent Christ to the altar, from which he descended into the tomb. Daniel escaped the lions’ bites; Christ rose from the dead. There the king confessed that Daniel’s God was great; here Babylon believed and became faithful, according to Peter’s words: “The Church which is gathered in Babylon greets you” [Note: [Col. 0289] 1 Pet. 5]. The rest are Daniel’s consolations, or Christ’s prayers.

On Wednesday the Gospel is read in which the Lord testified not only that he was the Christ whom they sought, but also that he was God, saying, when the Jews asked whether he was the Christ: “I speak to you, and you do not believe”; and below: “I and the Father are one” [Note: [Col. 0289] John 10]. Let Arius hear “one”; let Sabellius hear that he did not say “one person.” Therefore the reading is rightly prefixed in which the Lord testifies to a stiff-necked people through various commandments that he is the Lord God, saying: “I am your God” [Note: [Col. 0289] Lev. 19]. Thus these rebels, children of rebels, violent persons and children of violent persons, having stiff necks, deserved to be made far from the promise, just as those people were overthrown in the wilderness [Note: [Col. 0289] Exod. 32; Acts 7]. The rest are words of Christ escaping his enemies’ plots and praying to and exalting the Father [Note: [Col. 0289] 1 Cor. 10].

On Thursday the Gospel is read where it is said that, although some wished to seize Jesus, [Col. 0290C] no one laid a hand on him. The chief priests said to the officers: “Why have you not brought him?” The officers answered: “Never has a man spoken as this man speaks.” And below Nicodemus says: “Does your law judge a man unless it first hears what he does?” But those jealous chief priests, quarrelling among themselves, returned home, each to his own house [Note: [Col. 0289] John 7]. For they believe neither the works nor even their own witnesses; in order to cast a shadow over Scripture and not hear anything praiseworthy concerning him, they stop their ears and hide. Because of the guilt of rejecting Christians, they deserve the punishment of exile; indeed, they are exiled and were exiled, as their fathers were exiled in Daniel’s time. But because the remnant [Col. 0290D] of Israel shall be saved [Note: [Col. 0289] Isa. 10; Rom. 9], therefore, as the three children [Note: [Col. 0289] Dan. 3] prayed for those fathers, so do we pray for the remnant. The prayer of the three children contains the prayer; the rest are voices of a people confessing its crimes and longing for grace. Observe that the Gospel is aptly read on this day where it says, “They returned, each to his own house,” and the offertory is sung: “In the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments” [Note: [Col. 0289] Dan. 3], because after this day no Gospel is read in which the Lord is reported publicly [Col. 0291A] to have preached to the Jews. Behold, then, that instrument of divinity is hung upon those willows—that is, the fruitless people of Babylon [Note: [Col. 0291] Ps. 136].

On Friday the Gospel is read: “The chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council against Jesus and said: What shall we do? For this man performs many signs. If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him.” They advanced as if reasonable the cause of their concern, saying: “The Romans will come and take away our place and nation” [Note: [Col. 0291] John 11]. For they were under the Romans’ authority, because the sceptre had already been taken from Judah and the ruler from his thigh [Note: [Col. 0291] Gen. 49], and they had Pilate as governor of Roman power. Therefore they alleged as the cause of their concern that, if he were called king, they themselves would be condemned for treason against the Roman Empire. But because they so feared frost, snow came upon them [Note: [Col. 0291] Job 6], and they were crushed with a double crushing [Note: [Col. 0291] Jer. 17]. For they lost both place and nation [Note: [Col. 0291] John 11], and, blotted out from the book of the living, they are written in the earth. Hence Jeremiah’s reading concerning the double crushing of those who forsook the Lord for temporal things is prefixed. The rest are words of the Lord, the Mediator, praying according to his humanity amid his enemies’ plots.

Saturday is vacant, because the lord pope gives alms. On this Saturday the Lord came to Bethany, reclined in Simon’s house, Martha ministered, Mary anointed Jesus’ feet with precious ointment, and the house was filled with the fragrance [Note: [Col. 0291] John 12]. In these things three matters are commended to us: obedience, almsgiving, and good repute. For if we are obedient, the Lord comes to us and rests in us; if we assist the poor, we minister with Martha; but we anoint with Mary when we devote ourselves to the pursuit of virtues. Or, in this celebrated mystery there is especially commended the fragrant work of almsgiving. For Mary bore the type of the Church; the Lord’s feet are the poor and infirm, who, though they are the lowliest parts, are nevertheless his members through the union and unity of faith. The woman anoints the Lord’s feet and wipes them with her hair flowing from the body whenever the rich, who are in the Church, cherish poor believers with the kindness of mercy and supply their need from what is abundant to themselves. Augustine says that this ointment [Col. 0291D] was righteousness, and therefore it was a pound. Anoint Jesus’ feet, then, by living justly; follow his footsteps; wipe them with your hair, by bestowing your surplus upon the poor. Therefore, that the lord pope may offer the Lord a supper celebrated with Martha ministering, or with Mary anointing his feet and wiping them with her hair, he gives alms on this Saturday, so that he may offer Christ’s members what devout women offered to the head, and thus the house may be filled with the fragrance of ointment—that is, the world or the Church with good repute—so that a precious example for our imitation may be left to us. On this day he also celebrates the *mandatum* [foot-washing rite], since in the Lord’s supper, because of the greatness of the [Col. 0292A] office, he cannot do this. Thus, with the lord pope occupied with the Lord’s feet and the *mandatum*, this Saturday is rightly free from the office. Nevertheless, the Gospel concerning Judas’s betrayal is assigned to it; fittingly prefixed is Jeremiah’s reading where it says: “Come, let us devise plans against the Just One” [Note: [Col. 0291] Jer. 18].

## CHAPTER X. PALM SUNDAY

“Lord, do not keep thy help far from me” [Note: [Col. 0291] Ps. 21].

It is noteworthy and worthy of admiration that the Lord created and re-created the world, as it were, in the same course. For just as, when he was about to create man and all other things for man’s sake, he began on Sunday, worked for six days, created man on the sixth day, and rested from all work on the Sabbath [Note: [Col. 0291] Gen. 2], so, when about to re-create man, he began [Col. 0292B] on Sunday, entering Jerusalem and entering it on each successive day; on Friday he redeemed man by suffering on the cross, and on Saturday he rested sleeping in the tomb. Therefore, just as on this first day he said, “Let there be light” [Note: [Col. 0291] Gen. 1], beginning the work of creation with light, so on the same day, with light or splendour, he enters upon this work of the saving Passion. For on this day he enters Jerusalem to suffer [Note: [Col. 0291] Matt. 21], which accords not only with the beginnings of the world but also with the command of the Law. For it was then the tenth day of the moon, concerning which the Lord said to Moses: “On the tenth day of the first month let each take a lamb for his family and household; and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of the same month, and the whole assembly [Col. 0292C] of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it at evening” [Note: [Col. 0291] Exod. 12]. As Bede says: “A harmony of the Old and New Testaments is found not only in events but also in times. For as the lamb to be sacrificed is brought into the house on the tenth day, so Christ, about to suffer, enters Jerusalem. For he is the true Lamb who took away the sins of the world [Note: [Col. 0291] John 1], who on this tenth day offers himself to the Passion by entering Jerusalem. And as he was about to enter, as is read in today’s Gospel, he sent two disciples ahead to bring a tethered ass and a colt with her. When they brought them, they placed their garments upon them and made him sit upon them. A very great crowd spread their garments in the way; others, however, cut branches from the trees; and those going before and those following cried: Hosanna to the Son [Col. 0292D] of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0291] Matt. 21].

Mystically: “Thy riding, O Lord, is salvation” [Note: [Col. 0291] Hab. 3]. For by these things you signified that, about to ascend the Mount of Olives—that is, to the right hand of the Father, who is “the Father of mercies and God of all consolation” [Note: [Col. 0291] 2 Cor. 1]—you would send the apostles, who, having received the power of binding and loosing [Note: [Col. 0291] John 20], would release the ass and the colt—that is, the Jewish and Gentile people—from the burdens of sins; and that, having brought the human race to you through faith, sitting upon it (for “the soul of a just person is God’s seat” [Note: [Col. 0291] St Gregory, Homily 33]), you would save it by sitting upon it and lead it into the heavenly Jerusalem, where angels, bearing palms and [Col. 0293A] olive branches—the emblems of peace and victory—would come to meet it with praises. In representation of this glorious reception on Sunday, the Church today celebrates a procession with branches and flowers, bearing olives and palms in its hands. If it has no olives, it carries other branches and flowers, especially those green with enduring freshness; and it also signifies morally that, when we make the procession, we receive Christ coming to us. We go out to meet him with children if we preserve innocence; we bear olives if we devote ourselves to works of mercy; we carry palms if we gain victory over vices and the devil; we bear green flowers and branches if we are adorned with virtues; we spread garments if we mortify the flesh; we gather branches if we imitate the footsteps of the saints.

[Col. 0293B] That the Church goes out from the city, rejoicing as it proceeds to the cross and the heights, recalls the Hebrew children going toward the Mount of Olives, and indicates that “far be it from us to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0293] Gal. 6]. Far be it also from us to hope in any worldly glory, however great. Those who meet the pontiff outside the city, stationed beside the cross, with his attendants, and enter the city with him while he goes before the people, do this more exactly. Perhaps in this procession we also recall the procession of the children of Israel, who on this day crossed the Jordan dryshod and entered the promised land in triumph [Note: [Col. 0293] Josh. 3]. This procession must not be reckoned among the other Sunday processions. For this is a proclamation of the Passion; the others are significative and commemorative of the Sunday resurrection or ascension, of which we shall speak below. Hence those act more correctly who begin the procession before the third hour on Sunday and celebrate that of this day with palms after the third hour. Indeed, Zechariah’s reading and John’s Gospel are prefixed to our procession, because there the Sunday procession is prophesied and here its history is set forth.

In the tract the children are invited to proclamations; but the Passion is read at Mass [Note: [Col. 0293] Matt. 26–27], because the Lord, entering Jerusalem, is exposed to the cup of the Passion; or because “mourning occupies the end of joy” [Note: [Col. 0293] Prov. 14], and therefore after the joy of the procession follows the reading of the Passion; or because the Lord joined to that exultation [Col. 0293D] the lament for Jerusalem’s destruction [Note: [Col. 0293] Luke 19], and because, hanging on the cross, he said: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” [Note: [Col. 0293] Matt. 27]. It is certain that the whole twenty-first psalm is written in his person; therefore almost all of it is sung in his person in today’s office. First, in the introit, “Lord, do not keep [thy help] far away,” he prays the Father not to remove help—that is, the resurrection—but to deliver his humility from the unicorns, that is, from those of singular pride. In the tract he uses the words of the same psalm more extensively. The Epistle is fittingly prefixed to the Passion, where it says that Christ became obedient unto death, even death [Col. 0294A] on a cross [Note: [Col. 0293] Phil. 2]. The question is asked why the gradual is sung on this day, since it seems in no way to suit his person; for “My feet were almost moved” [Note: [Col. 0293] Ps. 72] does not suit Christ’s person. But the psalm from which it is taken is a correction of those who praised God only in prosperity. Christ abolishes such praises, confirming us by his Passion so that we may not be scandalized when we see the wicked prosper and the good brought low.

For what righteous person, seeing Justice itself crucified, would not patiently endure if the sword or rod of adversity struck him? Yet a part of the gradual is appropriately applied to Christ’s person when it says: “Thou hast held,” etc. For the Father led him according to his will and handed him over into the enemies’ hands. In the offertory there are plain words of Christ suffering and emblems of the Passion, taken from the sixty-eighth psalm, which throughout is composed in the person of the Saviour praying in the agony of the Passion. Observe that on this day, and on Tuesday and Wednesday, before the Passion it is said: “The Lord be with you,” but not “Glory to thee, O Lord.” Yet our custom is before no Passion to say “The Lord be with you,” nor “Glory to thee, O Lord,” nor to kiss the book, nor to incense, nor even to sign ourselves or the book. But when the passage is reached, “On the following day” [Note: [Col. 0293] Matt. 27], etc., incense is offered, the book is kissed, the sign of the cross is made upon the foreheads, and the communion from the Passion is taken; it is repeated twice, either because the Lord prayed thus more than once, or because he suffered for two peoples. And [Col. 0294C] observe that this week is called Major because it has a longer and greater office. It is also called Painful because then we ought to punish our sins; and Holy because the ungodly are justified in it, during which we use the preface of the Cross.

Monday, the second day of the world’s creation, was less adorned than the other days. For when the Lord said, “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters” [Note: [Col. 0293] Gen. 1], it was not added: “And God saw that it was good” [Note: [Col. 0293] Ibid.]. Although this is indeed added in the Septuagint interpreters, it is not found in the Hebrew truth; in this the number two is discredited, because it is the first to depart from unity and signifies division. Thus on it the waters’ division was made. Therefore it is not surprising if this second day, [Col. 0294D] which corresponds to that one, as we have said, is less adorned than the others in its office with the purple emblems of the Lord’s death. Nevertheless, this day’s Gospel contains that Jesus came to Jerusalem and, when the Gentiles wished to see him [Note: [Col. 0293] John 12] as their salvation—of whom Jacob said, “He shall be the expectation of the Gentiles” [Note: [Col. 0293] Gen. 49]—he called himself a grain of wheat [Note: [Col. 0293] John 12], to be put to death by the Jews’ unbelief but multiplied by the Gentiles’ faith. Further on he added: “If I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself.” He said this, signifying by what death he would die [Note: [Col. 0293] Ibid.]. Therefore, because he came to Jerusalem and delivered his life into the hands of those who sought him, [Col. 0295A] the reading of Isaiah is fittingly prefixed, speaking in the Lord’s person: “I did not turn back; I gave my body to those striking me” [Note: [Col. 0295] Isa. 50]. The rest are prayers of one about to suffer, by which he asks that his assailants be overcome and that he himself be delivered.

On Tuesday the Passion is preceded by Jeremiah’s reading, speaking in the Lord’s person: “I was like a lamb carried to the sacrifice,” and below: “They devised plans against me, saying: Let us put wood into his bread” [Note: [Col. 0295] Jer. 11]. During these days, when the Lord taught in the Temple and returned by night to the Mount of Olives, these were their plans. For proud Haman sought in his house how to destroy Mordecai [Note: [Col. 0295] Esth. 5]; he is the devil, seeking in the Jews’ hearts how to kill Jesus. This wood [Col. 0295B] is the Lord’s cross: a stumbling-block to Jews, foolishness to the wise [Note: [Col. 0295] 1 Cor. 1], but glory to us. Hence in the introit: “But it is fitting for us to glory in the cross of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0295] Gal. 6]. The rest are the words of Christ in agony and praying for the glory of the resurrection.

On the Fourth Day, the visible sun was formed for the light of the world [Note: [Col. 0295] Gen. 1.], and the Sun of righteousness was sold for our salvation [Note: [Col. 0295] Mal. 4.]. For on this day the Jews agreed to give money to the traitor, who promised to deliver the Savior to them [Note: [Col. 0295] Matt. 26.]. Therefore, because on this weekday the Church was deprived of her head, throughout the whole annual cycle it takes second place after Friday in the observance of penitential fasts. For this reason the Passion is also read on this day [Note: [Col. 0295] Luke 22–23], where the Lord is said to have prayed while in agony. Therefore, lest anyone presume to stand proudly upright [Col. 0295C], when he bent his knees for us, it is sung beforehand at the Introit: “At the name of the Lord every knee shall bend” [Note: [Col. 0295] Phil. 2.], because from these words we are bound to pray for persecutors. The Roman order directs that on this day the genuflections and prayers be made which we customarily recite on Friday.

Observe, too, that this antiphon—though this is rare—is taken from the Apostle; and the compiler of the office interrupts it at “Every tongue shall confess,” because the Jewish tongue is silent. Then two readings follow, and at each one “Let us bend the knee” is said. These are readings from Isaiah, who quite plainly suggests the transaction of the seller when he says: “Behold, his reward is with him” [Note: [Col. 0295] Isa. 62–63.]. Yet he also describes the appearance of the sufferer, saying in the first reading: “Who is this who comes from Edom,” that is, from the bloody [Col. 0295D] or earthly Jews, “with garments dyed,” that is, with the members of the body, which are the garments of divinity, taking on the purple of blood, “from Bozrah?” Bozrah is a city in Moab and is interpreted “strong”; figuratively, it is Jerusalem, which the Lord had formerly strengthened by his aid, but whose people, having become Moabites—that is, people of the devil as father [Note: [Col. 0295] Isa. 63.]—dyed the king’s garments with the purple of blood.

And when he had answered, “I who speak righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0295] John 8.], he is asked again: “Why then is your clothing red, and your garments like those of one treading in a winepress?” [Note: [Col. 0295] Isa. 53.] As though to say: Why are you bloodied by the pressure [Col. 0296A] of the cross, if you speak righteousness? But he replies: “I have trodden the winepress alone” [Note: [Col. 0295] Ibid.], for all, that all might be set free. In the second reading likewise he is portrayed in the same form in which the Evangelist presents him in the Passion, where “he has neither beauty nor comeliness” [Note: [Col. 0295] Ibid.], and below: “Like a sheep he shall be led to slaughter.” Two readings are read because Christ is delivered up for two peoples. At each, knees are bent, because he is worshipped by each people, and because at his name those in heaven and on earth bend the knee [Note: [Col. 0295] Phil.].

After the first reading the gradual is sung; after the second, the tract. Both are the prayer of Christ’s person when he was troubled. The tract has five verses because of Christ’s five wounds. And [Col. 0296B] note that here occurs what is also found on Good Friday and on the Ember Saturdays: namely, that the tract immediately follows the Epistle. On other days the Epistle is followed either by the gradual or by the Alleluia, lest the musician rebuke us, saying: “We sang, and you did not dance; we lamented, and you did not mourn” [Note: [Col. 0295] Matt. 11.]. The Alleluia is sung in greeting; the gradual is added for penitential mourning.
