But because that musician is taken from us—for today he is sold and on Good Friday he is crucified—the tract is joined to the Epistle to signify greater grief.

That the tract signifies greater grief than the gradual is indicated by this: it is never sung together with the Alleluia, except for a special reason on Holy Saturday, where two readings [Col. 0296C] are read because Christ, who underwent death for our soul and body, is now assigned to death. For Christ died for both. Hence Ambrose: “The flesh of Christ was given for the salvation of the body, and his blood was poured out for our soul.” In the first reading the death of the soul is recalled; therefore one verse follows, because one human being has only one soul. In the second, the death of the body is recalled; therefore the tract with five verses follows, to signify the number five of the bodily senses, through whose windows death enters [Note: [Col. 0295] Jer. 9.]. Once the Passion has been read, the prayer is repeated in the Offertory. In the Communion, however, are the voices and words of one weeping, and yet consoling Zion, for whom he suffers, with mercy [Note: [Col. 0295] Ps. 101.].

## CHAPTER XI. GENERAL MATTERS CONCERNING THE THREE DAYS

[Col. 0296D]

“As Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights” [Note: [Col. 0295] Matt. 12.], so the Church represents the obsequies of the Lord’s death, lasting three days, in great sorrow for three days. And, by an unusual order because of the disordered hearts of the Jews, she celebrates her office beginning on Thursday, for two reasons: either because the shameful bargain of the Jewish betrayal had already occurred, or because she wished to celebrate the obsequies of the dead Christ for seventy-two hours. Thus she could express the grief of the seventy-two [Col. 0297A] disciples; but the night of the Lord’s resurrection ought to be made bright with the joys of victory. Therefore the mourning of death had to begin beforehand on the night of Thursday.

Accordingly, on these three days—that is, during the seventy-two hours of Thursday, Friday, and Saturday—the following emblems of sorrow are set before human ears and eyes: neither the night vigils nor the daytime hours have their customary beginning and ending. For at the night vigils there are omitted: “O God, come to my assistance,” the hymn, the Gloria at the end of the psalms, “Bid, lord,” and “But you, O Lord” in the lessons. The first three of these lessons are read more as lamentation than as reading. A candle is extinguished with each psalm; in some places twelve, in others twenty-four [Col. 0297B], and in others seventy-two lights are set out. When these have been extinguished, at the Benedictus [Note: [Col. 0297] Luke 1.] a sound like a crackling voice is made; then mournful laments are sung through the *Kyrie eleison*. Thus the vigil is ended with the *Pater noster*, “Have mercy on me, O God” [Note: [Col. 0297] Ps. 50.], and an unusual conclusion; and the remaining five Hours lack their customary beginning and ending.

As evening approaches—that is, at the end of Thursday—greater incentives to sorrow follow: the altars are stripped, washed with wine, the bells fall silent, wooden clappers are struck, and sorrowful silence swallows up every regular Hour except the night vigils. We know the practice; let us seek its mysteries.

Therefore we take away the beginning and ending of the regular Hours [Col. 0297C] because Christ, who is “Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” [Note: [Col. 0297] Rev. 1.], has been taken from us and delivered into the hands of the wicked. Thus we cut off the heads of the praises of our joy—that is, of the regular Hours—because we have been deprived of our head; and we entirely omit their endings also, such as “Through our Lord,” “Let us bless the Lord,” and “Glory be to the Father.” In this we represent an ancient custom of the Church. For Jerome established this practice and wrote to Damasus: “Likewise, we pass over the *Te Deum laudamus* in silence.” For how shall we ask him to attend to our aid when we see him deprived of his own aid? How shall we exult in him when we see him seized, scourged, and hanging upon the cross?

Or we do not sing the invitatory in order to avoid [Col. 0297D] “the assembly of evildoers” [Note: [Col. 0297] Ps. 63.], who took counsel against Jesus [Note: [Col. 0297] John 11.]. How shall we sing to him glory and a hymn of praise while he has become “the reproach of the nations and the rejection of the people” [Note: [Col. 0297] Ps. 21.]? For if his resurrection is his glory, according to the words, “Arise, my glory” [Note: [Col. 0297] Ps. 56.], then his death and burial are his humiliation.

Likewise, how can “Bid, lord,” and “But you, O Lord,” blessing or mercy, be requested when the merciful shepherd fails and the rams are scattered [Note: [Col. 0297] Zech. 13; Matt. 26.]? Or those going forth to preach are understood by “Bid, lord,” and those returning from preaching by “But you, O Lord.” [Col. 0298A] Therefore, because on these days no one was being sent by Christ or returning to him, neither is said.

Nine lessons are said by canons and monks: the first three are lamentations from the prophet Jeremiah, recited not so much by reading as by mourning [Note: [Col. 0297] Lam. 1.], because, as King Josiah was mourned by Jeremiah, so our king is mourned by the Church. They are marked by the Hebrew alphabet: *Aleph* means “doctrine”; *beth*, “house”; *gimel*, “fullness”; *daleth*, “of tablets.” This is the first connection, in which it is said that the doctrine of the Church, which is the house of God [Note: [Col. 0297] I Tim. 3.], is in the fullness of the Scriptures. *He*: “this”; *vau*: “and”; *zain* and *heth*: “life.” This is the second connection, in which it is said that this doctrine which we have mentioned is the life by which we live. *Teth*: “good”; *jod*: “beginning.” This is the third [Col. 0298B] connection, in which it is said that it is good to begin by knowing the Lord through the Scriptures, as through a mirror, at least in an enigma [Note: [Col. 0297] I Cor. 13.]. *Caph*: “hand”; *lamed*: “heart and discipline.” This is the fourth connection, in which it is said that the discipline of the heart is rightly required, because we can do nothing unless we have recognized what must be done. *Mem*: “from these things”; *nun*: “everlasting”; *sammech*: “help.” This is the fifth connection, in which it is said that from the Scriptures we have everlasting help. *Hain*: “eyes”; *pe*: “has erred”; *zadi*: “righteousness and consolation for minds”; *cof*: “look”; *ress*: “head”; *se*: “over the wound”; *tau*: “sign,” or “consummation.” This is the seventh connection, in which there is also a mystical understanding concerning the Lord: it is said, “Look: in Scripture [Col. 0298C] is contained our head, from whom we have healing for wounds and shall attain consummation, that is, eternal life.”

Three further lessons from the Psalmist and three further lessons from the Apostle follow, so that it may be clear that he whom the prophets foresaw to be slain, the apostles teach to have been slain. Notice also that there are nine psalms, nine lessons, and nine responsories, arranged in three nocturns, because three kinds of people are distinguished by the field, the mill, and the one bed [Note: [Col. 0297] Luke 17.], and are believed to have existed in three periods: those of the patriarchs, of the Law, and of the prophets; and to have descended to hell. The Lord joined to action, knowledge, and joy the nine orders of angels. Psalms belong to action; lessons to knowledge of God’s works; [Col. 0298D] responsories to exultation.

Thus the Savior’s obsequies are celebrated so as to seem to differ only in a small point from the obsequies of other dead persons. The extinguishing of the candles that follows is especially proper to these obsequies. For these Tenebrae, celebrated over three nights, signify the darkness that covered the face of the earth for three hours, from the sixth hour to the ninth, while the sun hung upon the cross [Note: [Col. 0297] Matt. 27.]. Therefore the light is extinguished on three nights, because the true Sun lay in the tomb for three days. Twelve lights are extinguished when the twelve apostles are scattered, according to the saying: [Col. 0299A] “I shall strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” [Note: [Col. 0299] Zech. 13.].

By the twenty-four lights, according to some, we likewise understand the apostles. They are the twelve night-hours—that is, those who illumined the Church, who preached the Lord of glory in the night of this age. Hence on festal nights twenty-four Glorias are sung: for example, the first at “O God, come to my assistance”; the second at “Come”; the third at the hymn; nine at the psalms; three at the responsories; again one at the *Te Deum*; again one at “O God, come to my assistance”; five more at the psalms; one at the hymn; and finally one at the *Benedictus*. When counted, these make twenty-four Glorias, as it were so many hours. All these Glorias we omit because the Sun of righteousness has been extinguished; and therefore [Col. 0299B] we extinguish the lights that many times.

By the seventy-two lights we understand the seventy-two disciples, whose scandalized grief we represent; likewise, as stated above, we understand the seventy-two hours spent in mourning. Or the many lights which we find burning when we rise for Matins signify the saints who, shining by prophetic speech, announced the rising Sun of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0299] Mal. 4.] as stars going before him, and whom the Jews killed. Thus the extinguishing of the candles signifies the blinding of the Jewish people, who killed the prophets and stoned those sent to them [Note: [Col. 0299] Matt. 23], and finally, when the Lord of the prophets had been killed, fell into the darkness of unbelief.

In the fact that individual lights are extinguished at the psalms is signified [Col. 0299C] that the prophets were individually killed by them, each having fulfilled the ministry of his prophecy. The last light to be extinguished, which is larger than the others according to some, signifies Christ, who was the Lord of the prophets. According to others it is not larger than the rest, and likewise signifies Christ, who was considered as one of the prophets [Note: [Col. 0299] Matt. 16.]. This is extinguished last because after him no prophet arose among them; rather, when extinguished, he left them in the darkness of their unbelief. It is extinguished at the Gospel canticle because Christ, preaching the Gospel, is to be killed.

Observe that the offices of the shepherd, such as the chapter, are omitted because the shepherds had been scattered. Yet the verse, which is the office of lesser persons, is not omitted because the disciples appeared less known. Hence this three-day office [Col. 0299D] is celebrated especially by lesser persons, in the figure of the lesser disciples and of the women who followed the Lord. The outcry at the *Benedictus* [Note: [Col. 0299] Luke 1.] in the darkness is the din of Judas the traitor and the greeting of the blind disciple: “Hail, Rabbi” [Note: [Col. 0299] Matt. 26.]; the clamour and trembling of the singers are the tumult of those pursuing the Lord and mockingly worshipping him. Or they signify the laments of the holy women who followed the Lord, who are said for that reason to have lamented “[uncertain: … teeth against the tomb]” [Note: [Col. 0299] Matt. 27.].

According to the custom of some, moreover, [Col. 0300A] the order of the singers is this. The cantors before the altar sing: “Kyrie eleison, Christe eleison, Lord, have mercy”; the choir responds, and the people cry out likewise. The cantors sing: “Christ the Lord became obedient for us”; the choir and people respond likewise. The cantors sing: “Christ, the Lord who suffered”; the choir and people likewise. The cantors sing: “Christ, the Lord”; but the choir and people always respond: “Kyrie eleison, Lord, have mercy.” Yet this, because Life dies on the wood for us, is said only on Friday.

The prayer and the other things that follow in silence in the darkness signify that the apostles trembled in secret. Afterwards a new fire is produced from stone or crystal because through Christ our mediator the Holy Spirit is poured into us [Col. 0300B]. It is rekindled for our benefit and because of our weakness, since we cannot be without light; otherwise, after the first extinguishing it ought to remain extinguished until the Resurrection.

The altar signifies Christ; for as it stands above the temple, so Christ stands above his body, “which is the Church” [Note: [Col. 0299] Col. 1.]. Hence: “You shall make me an altar of earth” [Note: [Col. 0299] Exod. 20.]. To make an altar of earth is to believe or hope for his incarnation; and upon it we also offer a gift and make our deeds firm by faith in the Lord’s incarnation.

When, therefore, we see the altar bare, we recall that prophetic saying: “Behold, we saw him, and he has neither beauty nor [Col. 0300C] comeliness; and we considered him despised and the last of men” [Note: [Col. 0299] Isa. 53.]. This occurred in the Passion, for before that he was beautiful, “fair in form beyond the sons of men” [Note: [Col. 0299] Ps. 44.]. Or the stripping of the altar is the stripping of Christ, who was stripped at the column and on the cross, when the soldiers divided his garments among themselves [Note: [Col. 0299] Matt. 27.], made four shares, and cast lots for his tunic [Note: [Col. 0299] John 19.].

Or the bare altar signifies Christ abandoned by the apostles. Hence: “Those who were near me stood afar off” [Note: [Col. 0299] Ps. 37.]; and in the Gospel: “Leaving him, they all fled” [Note: [Col. 0299] Matt. 26.], for they are the altar’s garments. Or the garments signify Christ stripped of the glory of divinity. Hence: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” [Note: [Col. 0299] Matt. 27.] The flesh about to die cries out because of the separation of divinity—that is, because it did not afford its customary [Col. 0300D] aid. This is Noah, who planted a vineyard, drank, became drunk, and was stripped naked [Note: [Col. 0299] Gen. 9.]. Christ is he in whom we find rest for our souls [Note: [Col. 0299] Matt. 2.], who nurtured the Jewish people and was made drunk by its bitterness when he was overcome by the sleep of death; and then he appeared stripped of the glory of divinity.

The altars are washed with wine and water to signify that blood and water flowed from Christ’s side [Note: [Col. 0299] John 19.], or to show that he was baptized not with John’s baptism but with his own baptism, namely of water and the Holy Spirit. They are washed with penitential psalmody or [Col. 0301A] with a chant pertaining to the Passion. The rough wine-and-oil cloths with which they are washed signify the scourges by which his most sacred breast was beaten.

Observe that on Thursday itself, when the hour has already turned toward evening, the altars are stripped, but only on Good Friday are they washed; and this agrees better with reason. The bells fall silent. By them we understand the apostles, who, instructed by the fire of charity, abiding in the protection of the God of heaven [Note: [Col. 0301] Ps. 90.] as in a land of strength, with reason suspended within, were not silent in preaching God’s name. But in the Passion they not only fell silent but even fled [Note: [Col. 0301] Matt. 26.] and denied the truth. Therefore we do not command the bells to be silent until the evening on which the Lord was betrayed, when all the disciples fled [Col. 0301B], except John, who was known to the high priest [Note: [Col. 0301] John 18.].

Our custom, however, is to ring the bells until Prime on Thursday and no later. By the sound of the wooden clapper we understand terror; therefore the clapper is struck, because the Jews inspired great fear in the apostles. Or, by wood striking wood—that is, a hammer suspended on the board—we understand Christ, who is “the tree planted beside streams of waters” [Note: [Col. 0301] Ps. 1.], who hung on the wood of the cross. Therefore wood alone is struck because he alone trod the winepress [Note: [Col. 0301] Isa. 63.]. Or in the use of wood the Savior’s taking of humanity is suggested, for its sound is humbler than that of bronze. An ancient custom of the Church is denoted. Hence the Eastern Church still retains the use of wooden instruments, not [Col. 0301C] because of a lack of bronze, but because of their antiquity.

The silence of the Hours signifies that silence of the apostles when they no longer went about preaching in villages and cities, but, after a hymn had been sung, went out with Jesus to the Mount of Olives. When the Lord said, “Behold, he who will betray me draws near” [Note: [Col. 0301] Matt. 26.], they dozed from sorrow and fell silent from praises. Hence silence begins at Compline. But if sorrowful silence opens the daytime Hours, why does melody adorn the night vigils? I answer: in the daytime Hours we signify the present reality of the Lord’s Passion. In the night vigils, however, we designate earlier times, in which the prophets foretold that same future Passion. Since they were killed without being silent, therefore, while we utter their voices, [Col. 0301D] the candles are extinguished, as stated above.

## CHAPTER XII. ON THE LORD’S SUPPER

“Take for yourself, Moses, the finest spices and oil from olives” [Note: [Col. 0301] Exod. 30.].

Just as on the first weekday, when the race of our creation arose from waters [Note: [Col. 0301] Gen. 1.], part is returned to the deep and part is lifted into the air, so that beings sprung from one stock are carried to different places; so too on Thursday of this week, which is that of our re-creation, the sacraments of one and the same salvation partly cast us down into sorrow and partly raise us to joy. Therefore today’s offices are celebrated [Col. 0302A] in a diverse worship or habit—that is, of sorrow and of joy. The causes of sorrow have indeed been explained above; now let us pursue the causes of joy.

For today penitents are absolved, and those expelled from the Church at the beginning of Lent are today received into the bosom of their mother, for several reasons. First, because, as we said above, on this day fish are separated from birds: fish are left in low and moist places, but birds are lifted to the heavens [Note: [Col. 0301] Ibid.]. Fish are sinners, but birds are the innocent or penitents. Or because John the Baptist preached repentance at the end of the fifth age [Note: [Col. 0301] Matt. 3.], and Christ at the end of the fifth age, who afterwards cancelled the bond of the human race [Note: [Col. 0301] Col. 2.]. Therefore the Church established that penitents should be released on Thursday. Or because the Lord was seized [Col. 0302B] and bound today [Note: [Col. 0301] Matt. 26.], those who are bound are released today. For why is mercy bound except to release wretched repentant sinners? As the Apostle says: “Christ died for the ungodly” [Note: [Col. 0301] Rom. 5.]. Or because today the Lord washed the disciples’ feet [Note: [Col. 0301] John 13.], the reconciliation of penitents takes place today, for the washing of feet denotes remission of sins.

The form of reconciliation is this. The bishop goes out to the open doors of the Church, where penitents lie prostrate on the ground, and in Christ’s stead calls them to the fear of the Lord, saying: “Come, come, come, children; hear me: I will teach you the fear of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0301] Ps. 33.]. That this is Christ’s voice is proved by the title of the psalm from which it is taken, which is as follows: “A psalm of David, when he changed [Col. 0302C] his countenance before Abimelech, and was carried in his hands, and Abimelech dismissed him” [Note: [Col. 0301] I Kings 21.]. Abimelech is interpreted “the kingdom of my Father,” by whom we understand the Jews, before whom the true David changed his countenance—that is, the rite of sacrifice—and was carried in his hands when he gave bread and wine to his disciples, saying: “This is my body, and this is my blood” [Note: [Col. 0301] Matt. 26.]. This was indeed done today. Therefore, when the bishop, the vicar of Jesus Christ, says “Come,” he invites penitents to the banquet of the body and blood; consequently he prays for them, bends the knee, admonishes them, and, reconciling them, brings them into the Church.

It is noteworthy that the doors stand open on every side, so that you may understand that neither from the south nor from the north—that is, neither the righteous nor sinners—are to be forbidden to approach mercy [Col. 0302D]; and they remain open from Easter, because in the octave of our resurrection there will be no reproach of sins for the elect. Note also that, once received, they cut off the hair and beard which they had let grow and put on clean clothing, taking their example from Joseph, who, brought out of prison, was shaved, washed, and adorned with garments [Note: [Col. 0301] Gen. 41.]. By this likewise it is suggested that, laying aside the multitude of sins, they put on the garments of virtues.

Today chrism is made and consecrated. There are three sacred kinds of anointing: oil of the sick, chrism oil, and oil of catechumens. The Lord could have poured his grace into believers without visible signs; for he could have saved the ancients without circumcision and those of later times without oil and water. For he saved Abel and Noah, who did not experience the knife of circumcision; he saved the Innocents [Note: [Col. 0303] Matt. 2.], who poured out their blood for Christ without water and oil. He also saves one who, hastening faithfully to the sacrament, is overtaken by death, who is deprived not of the reality of the sacrament but of its sacramental form.

But he preferred these things to be observed: both so that ministers might not be idle but exercise themselves; so that humility might be proved; and so that, from visible things, “his invisible things, understood through the things that are made from the creation of the world, may be seen—his everlasting power also and divinity” [Note: [Col. 0303] Rom. 1.]. Explaining this, [Col. 0303B] Augustine says in the twenty-fourth psalm: visible oil is in the sign, invisible oil is in the sacrament, and spiritual oil is within. Just as visible oil drives away ailments, refreshes and illuminates the limbs, so invisible grace, which is figured by oil and poured in through anointing, drives away vices, strengthens virtues, and illumines with the rays of the true Sun. Hence, according to Augustine, to despise these things after their institution is a mortal sin.

The Lord instituted the sign of circumcision for the ancients and for us the water of baptism. The apostles instituted the oil of the sick; hence in the Gospel: “They anointed the sick with oil, and they were healed” [Note: [Col. 0303] Mark 6.]. Apostolic men instituted the oil of chrism and of catechumens; hence that oil was mentioned first, because the teaching of the apostles is earlier and more venerable [Col. 0303C] than that of apostolic men.

The oil of the sick is that by which the sick are anointed, as James says: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him call the priests, that they may pray over him and anoint him with holy oil” [Note: [Col. 0303] Jas. 5.]. Some say that this anointing can be performed by one priest, but ought not to be if more can be present. The blessing of this oil is rightly said at that point in the Canon where we customarily bless grapes, namely where the prayer ends: “Grant admittance, we beseech thee, O giver of pardon, through Christ our Lord.” For it has no office of its own: that is, it has neither the words of salutation at the beginning, such as “The Lord be with you,” nor “Let us pray,” nor is it concluded at the end, as other prayers are, with “Through our Lord.” Rather, when the exorcism and blessing [Col. 0303D] are finished, there immediately follows: “Through whom, O Lord, you always create all these good things,” and so forth. This is because it is not an office in itself but an embolism of the preceding office, namely of the prayer “To us also, sinners,” just as “Deliver us, we beseech thee” is an embolism of the preceding Lord’s Prayer.

Reasonably, the blessing of this oil of the sick is joined to that prayer in which prayer is made for penitents and for those departing this life. Again, reasonably, oil for the dying is made where the Lord’s death is consummated, so that, as Christ’s death destroyed the author of death, so the grace conferred on the dying through anointing may destroy sins, which are the cause [Col. 0304A] of death [Note: [Col. 0303] Heb. 2.].

That this oil is offered by the people is taken from Exodus [Note: [Col. 0303] ch. 27.], where it is said: “Command the children of Israel to offer you oil from olive trees.” This signifies that earthly administration ought to support spiritual ministry, according to the saying: “If we sow spiritual things for you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?” [Note: [Col. 0303] I Cor. 9.] When it is offered, it is a simple liquid; but by blessing it becomes a sacrament, which is blessed not only by the bishop but also by priests. Hence this sacrament was instituted by Christ for his disciples; or it derives from the ancient custom by which, in the primitive Church, priests together with the bishop used to consecrate Christ’s body with words and hands—perhaps as a testimony or for the instruction of younger men, as those newly ordained do today with [Col. 0304B] their ordainer.

That the Holy Spirit the Paraclete is named only in the blessing of this oil—for example, “Send the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, from heaven”—is not without reason. To make this clear, let us see what the Spirit accomplishes in each case. The oil of catechumens, which may fittingly be called exorcismal oil, commands the devil to depart from the catechumen, who is still regarded as dead. Chrism oil sanctifies one living from the dead. The oil of the sick gives healing to the wounded. Pain follows sickness, consolation follows pain; and *Paraclete* is interpreted “Comforter.” But one who is dead does not suffer pain, because he does not feel, and therefore consolation does not follow. One who is sanctified, however, has no pain and therefore does not need consolation.

The principal oil [Col. 0304C] called chrism is made from the purest balm and oil. *Chrisma* in Greek is called *unctio* in Latin, “anointing”; hence *Christus*, that is, “Anointed One.” Chrism had its beginning in the Old Testament, where the Lord commanded Moses to make chrism, saying: “Take for yourself the finest spices and oil, with which he was to dedicate the tabernacle and the ark of testimony, and anoint Aaron and his sons and kings” [Note: [Col. 0303] Exod. 30.]. But Moses is not read to have been anointed with natural oil [Note: [Col. 0303] Ps. 44.], but only with spiritual anointing, like Christ.

Hence we dedicate churches with chrismal anointing, consecrate chalices, and anoint bishops and kings. And because all of us are bound to shine with the oil of good works and mercy, to give forth fragrance from the balm of faith [Col. 0304D], and also to be members of Christ the king and supreme priest—so that we may govern ourselves by good morals and offer sacrifice to the Lord—therefore every person is also anointed with this chrismal anointing twice: by a simple priest on the crown of the head, and by a bishop on the forehead. It is done twice because the Spirit which it signifies was given twice: when Christ breathed upon the apostles and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0303] John 20.], and when he sent the Paraclete from heaven [Note: [Col. 0303] Acts 2.].

Observe that episcopal confirmation does for one baptized what a guardian does for a ward. For what benefit is it if someone grants a great inheritance to his son unless he himself, or the law, or the ruler provides that child with a guardian? The Paraclete is for those regenerated [Col. 0305A] in Christ a comforter, guardian, and protector. Prompted by the devil, they could, like children, lose their property—that is, the benefit of baptism—if they did not have this guardian.

Chrism, therefore, is the sign of the Holy Spirit, whom it appropriately pleased to signify by this substance. Oil surpasses other liquids in lightness and brightness, as seafarers’ skill proves. Balm excels in fragrance, as the testimony of practitioners confirms. So the Spirit illuminates the one whom he fills, lifts him from the waves of sins, and emits a fragrance of sweetness in the one in whom he makes his breathing-place. Balm and oil are rightly mixed in chrism because oil signifies life and balm doctrine. In every person anointed with chrism and filled with sevenfold grace, life ought to accord with doctrine. They are connected, as appears in the gifts themselves: wisdom belongs to life; understanding and counsel to doctrine; fortitude to life; knowledge likewise to doctrine; piety to life.

Or understand mercy by oil and the reputation and renown of good virtues by balm. For our works ought to shine before God and human beings, so that those who see them may glorify our Father who is in heaven [Note: [Col. 0305] Matt. 5.]. Again, oil refreshes weary limbs and balm makes them fragrant; it refreshes when, by forgiving sins, it grants strength for works, and it inspires that strength in others through the balm of a good fragrance. Or by chrism we understand Christ. Hence his name is “oil poured out” [Note: [Col. 0305] Song 1.]: being Light from Light, he has enlightened us; being the cornerstone [Note: [Col. 0305] Eph. 2.], he has reconciled both walls [Col. 0305C]; he bore in himself the ailments and wounds of sins [Note: [Col. 0305] Isa. 53.]; he “flew, flew upon the wings of the winds” [Note: [Col. 0305] Ps. 17.]; and in the fragrance of his ointments we run [Note: [Col. 0305] Song 1.].

Holy oil too took its beginning from the Law, by which only kings and priests were anointed; but today, since we are bound to govern ourselves and to offer ourselves in sacrifice, we are all anointed with it on the shoulders and on the breast: on the shoulders, that we may be strong to bear the burdens of the Law; on the breast, that we may understand his commandments. The consecration of each oil—namely chrism, which is therefore called “principal,” because at its anointing the Holy Spirit is bestowed chiefly, and holy oil—has its proper rite. [Col. 0305D] For each is first exorcised; then, at “The Lord be with you” and “Lift up your hearts,” the blessing begins and is concluded through our Lord. But in the exorcism of the holy oil it concludes: “Who is to come”; for this concerns driving the devil away from one who is still dead. Hearing of the coming judgment, in which he knows that he is to be condemned, the devil is more readily put to flight, because he is shaken by terror of it. But in the exorcism of the chrismal oil it concludes: “Who lives and reigns”; for it concerns those who have risen and live with Christ.

Over the vessel of each oil the bishop breathes three times; by the breath which proceeds publicly from his lung and organ [Col. 0306A] and covers the vessel, he indicates that the third Person, namely the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son, dwells in the body of the Lord. For the vessel with chrism signifies the body together with divinity; or the threefold act of breathing signifies the Trinity, as is said in the blessing. This anointing makes our faces glad and serene; by our faces let us understand the manifestation of works. Both are consecrated in that part of the canon where peace is given, because we are anointed for this purpose: that peace may reign in us. For unless we are peaceable toward God and human beings, we shall by no means deserve to be filled with the gifts of the Holy Spirit through the anointing of chrism. For, as Isidore says, the olive tree is a distinguished tree of peace; its fruit is called the olive, and its juice oil.

Both are also [Col. 0306B] offered, greeted, and brought back with a similar solemnity. The form of the solemnity is this: after the episcopal blessings have been said, “And may his peace be always with you.” Before the *Agnus Dei* is said, the pontiff alone communicates; and when he has communicated, he sits down and awaits the vessels, which are carried in this solemn order. Two acolytes with lights go first; then two crosses, between which an acolyte carries the vessel of chrism that is to be used. Afterward two thurifers follow, between whom an acolyte carries the vessel of oil for the catechumens that is to be used. The vessel with oil signifies humanity filled with the Holy Spirit. Therefore the two lights, two crosses, and two censers are the Law and the Prophets, which foretold Christ [Col. 0306C] as suffering and yet as God. Then the Gospel follows, because the Gospel that follows confirms what the Law and the Prophets foretold. Finally twelve presbyters follow, two by two. These are witnesses of the mystery of chrism: the apostles, sent out two by two as fellow-workers in the office of preaching [Note: [Col. 0305] Luke 10.], and witnesses of our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0305] I Cor. 3.]. Their chant, namely *O Redeemer*, signifies the apostles’ preaching and prayer [Note: [Col. 0305] Luke 24; Acts 1.]. That the vessel is brought to the altar through each rank indicates that the Lord, in his body before the Passion, fulfilled the offices of six ranks.

Some, however, observe another order: an acolyte goes first with a light; two presbyters follow, one with incense and the other with a cross, and between them a deacon with the Gospel. Then follow [Col. 0306D] acolytes with the vessels; four carry a pallium over them; finally all are led on by two who follow with chanting. These represent the former shadow and the truth. The acolyte with the light signifies the angel in the pillar of fire, who went before the people journeying toward their homeland [Note: [Col. 0305] Exod. 13.]. The presbyter with incense is Aaron in his priestly office; the other with the cross is Joshua with the sceptre; the deacon with the Gospel is Moses with the Decalogue; the pallium is the tabernacle or the pillar of cloud. But in the pattern of truth, he who goes before with the light is John the Baptist [Note: [Col. 0305] Matt. 3.]. The deacon is Christ, between Moses and Elijah [Note: [Col. 0305] Matt. 17.]; [Col. 0307A] the pallium is the bright cloud that overshadowed them; the two singers are preachers announcing to the peoples the two commandments of charity.

According to the Roman order, however, the vessels are carried on the left arm, because Christ lived in this present life; and before they come to the altar, one half is covered with a linen cloth and the other half left uncovered, because before the Passion Christ was at one time hidden—as when he fled into Egypt [Note: [Col. 0307] Matt. 2.], when he was sought among his relatives, and when he was subject to his parents [Note: [Col. 0307] Luke 2.]—and at another time openly showed himself—as when he preached beyond what belongs to a mere human being, saying, “I and the Father are one” [Note: [Col. 0307] John 10.], and when he performed miracles in which he displayed the power of his divinity. But when, blessed at the altar, they depart from the bishop’s hand, they are greeted visibly and uncovered, because Christ from the altar [Col. 0307B] of the cross offered his presence to those whom he wished to be witnesses of his resurrection. To others, however, they are carried for greeting invisible and covered, because Christ, ascending into heaven, became invisible to human beings; although they do not see him, they nevertheless greet him daily in veneration. Therefore the clean linen cloth is his flesh, or his spotless manner of life. It is greeted five times by the bishop, that thanks may be given for the five wounds.

When these things have been done, the choir says, *Agnus Dei*, and the communion; then the presbyters and the others who are to communicate receive communion.

Then the old chrism and oil are burned in lamps, and the new are distributed through the presbyters. These three anointings are made from the same liquid, because, although [Col. 0307C] there are distinctions of operations, nevertheless it is the same Spirit who works all things in all [Note: [Col. 0307] I Cor. 12.]. These three anointings are rightly consecrated on this day, because today the lamb was sacrificed at evening, and the two doorposts and lintel of the houses in which it was to be eaten were smeared with its blood, so that, seeing this sign, the destroyer of Egypt [Note: [Col. 0307] Exod. 12.] might pass untouched over the houses of the sacred meal. By this it was prefigured that, if the sign of the cross is impressed upon our foreheads by the anointing of chrism, as though by the blood of Christ—whose name is interpreted “Anointed”—the devil may have no power to harm in the houses of our souls. Rightly, therefore, on the day on which that figurative act was performed, what it signified is solemnly celebrated.

But you will say: “It follows, then, that on this night children should be confirmed, that is, marked on their foreheads with [Col. 0307D] sacred chrism?” I answer: Holy Church dedicated the day on which the Lord suffered to mourning, and reserved the joy of solemnity and feast for the third day, on which the Lord rose, so that only then, for the recovered salvation of souls accomplished on the sixth day, and for the future resurrection of bodies granted us on the eighth, we may celebrate the feast of the Paschal Lamb, saying: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. Therefore let us feast” [Note: [Col. 0307] I Cor. 5.]. Therefore, having received that by which we ought to mark the doorposts of our foreheads, we abstain from the marking itself until the Paschal feast, so that then, passing from under Pharaoh through the Red Sea [Col. 0308A] and marking our houses against the destroyer, we may celebrate the Paschal feast.

But you will say: “Why, then, is the anointing of chrism not deferred until Saturday?” I answer: Because from this Thursday until Saturday evening we abstain from the solemnities of Mass. Yet chrism may lawfully be consecrated only amid the solemnities of Mass; but baptism ought to be celebrated before Mass, as we shall say below. Or the anointing is celebrated on Thursday because Christ was anointed in the fifth age; for he came in the fifth, who consecrated with blood in the sixth. Of his anointing Daniel says: “Let the Holy of Holies be anointed” [Note: [Col. 0307] Dan. 9.]; and Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he sent me to proclaim to the meek, that I might heal” [Note: [Col. 0307] Isa. 61.]; and [Col. 0308B] David: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” [Note: [Col. 0307] Ps. 44.]. His anointing began at that time when “the Word was made flesh” [Note: [Col. 0307] John 1.], when the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily in him [Note: [Col. 0307] Col. 2.]. It was completed, however, when at baptism the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove [Note: [Col. 0307] Matt. 3.]. Therefore the anointing made today for anointing is reserved until baptism, in order that we may signify that the Spirit visibly descended upon the Lord in baptism and that we receive the Holy Spirit in baptism. From these things it is evident that confirmation ought to take place on Saturday evening immediately after baptism, so that the Paschal feast may afterward be celebrated; and indeed I think that the mystery of confirmation ought at least to be begun for a few persons [Col. 0308C].

Today, while the Lord was dining with his disciples, he washed their feet during the meal; for he rose from supper and washed them, and after the washing reclined again [Note: [Col. 0307] John 13.]. Therefore, when John says that these things happened “when supper had been made,” it is understood as prepared, not consumed. In washing the feet he gave us an example of humility and signified a mystery: “For,” he says, “I have given you an example, that as I have done, so you also should do” [Note: [Col. 0307] Ibid.]. How, when we are dust and ashes [Note: [Col. 0307] Gen. 18.], are we not ashamed to raise our necks proudly, when the maker of the human creature deigned to bend himself down to his disciples’ footsteps? He displayed this example of humility as he was about to die, so that it might cling more firmly to the minds of those whom he named his heirs.

Mystically, he rose from supper—that is, from the banquet of paternal glory—when he came forth from the Father’s reclining place. He laid aside his [Col. 0308D] garments when he emptied himself [Note: [Col. 0307] Phil. 2.]; he girded himself with a linen cloth when he took the form of a servant [Note: [Col. 0307] Ibid.]; he put water into a basin, with which he washed the disciples’ feet, when he poured out his blood for the remission of sins, by which our feet—that is, our actions—are washed. For although we have been washed in baptism through faith, nevertheless, if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves [Note: [Col. 0307] I John 1.]. For in our subsequent life we tread the earth. Hence Peter, although he had been washed and was clean, nevertheless heard: “Unless I wash you, you shall have no part with me” [Note: [Col. 0307] John 13.]. He washes our feet daily when he intercedes for us [Note: [Col. 0307] Rom. 8.]. To signify this, today the pavements of the church are washed. [Col. 0309A] For the washing of pavements is a sign of the washing of feet, and the washing of feet is a sign of the remission of sins.

But before this meaning of the Gospel washing, the epistle *Convenientibus* is fittingly placed, in which it is shown how we are washed by this sacrament: namely, if, when eating and drinking, we do not eat and drink unworthily [Note: [Col. 0309] I Cor. 11.]. Committing that powerful example of humility to memory as heirs and sons, we celebrate the *mandatum* this evening in accordance with his example, in a twofold manner. The first is that of prelates toward their subjects; the second, that of all persons toward the poor. It is clear that prelates need both authority and humility. The Lord exercised authority when, having made a scourge of cords, he drove the money-changers from the temple [Note: [Col. 0309] John 2; Matt. 21.]. The Lord enjoined this upon the first-created human being, that he should rule [Col. 0309B] over the beasts of the earth [Note: [Col. 0309] Gen. 1.].

If, therefore, subjects are like beasts, prelates should employ staff and rod. The Lord exercised humility when he washed the disciples’ feet, saying: “Let the greatest among you become the servant” [Note: [Col. 0309] Luke 22.]. And when he had washed their feet, he delivered to them a most splendid discourse, in which he earnestly promises the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0309] John 13.]. Therefore we too, after the disciples’ feet have been washed, read or hear the same discourse, signifying that the grace of the Holy Spirit is bestowed only upon those who have been washed and made clean. The Lord prefigured the second *mandatum* on the preceding Sabbath, when he came to Bethany, and Mary anointed Jesus’ feet, wiped them with her hair, and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment [Note: [Col. 0309] John 12.]. To anoint feet is to sustain the poor with alms; [Col. 0309C] to wipe them with hair is to restore them with superfluities: this is the figure of this commandment. It fittingly came first; for we ought so to wash feet with the ointment of alms that we ourselves may be washed by the Lord. This is the order of the commandment: first we eat bread and feed the poor from it; then, rising from the table, we wash the feet of the poor; when this has been done, we return to the table and eat again, refreshing others and being refreshed.

But the objection is made that it is commanded under anathema that the fast not be broken for this reason on this day. I answer: this is not breaking the fast, but interrupting supper after the Lord’s example. Hence the prepared table is not removed. From this arose the canonical custom that, when they celebrate the *mandatum*, they first bring the poor into the monastic workrooms [Col. 0309D] and have them recline at the feast, and sufficiently refresh them. Assuredly Christ is received in them into Bethany—that is, into the house of obedience—in which the Lord dines with Mary, who, rising from supper, washed Jesus’ feet. Thus the poor feast—or rather, the Lord in the poor—when the daughter of contemplation pours upon them a pound of ointment: that is, an intention of almsgiving sweetly fragrant before the Lord.

Today likewise, while the Lord was dining with his disciples, after the typical lamb he gave them his body and blood [Note: [Col. 0309] Matt. 26.], bringing the Old Testament to its end [Col. 0310A] and beginning the New. This was fittingly done at the end of the fifth day, as the sixth day approached, because at the end of the fifth age and the beginning of the sixth the Law ended and the Gospel took its beginning. Now is fulfilled in him what was formerly signified in the same person, when, as the Jews wished to stone him, he went out of the temple and hid himself from them [Note: [Col. 0309] John 8.]. For then he went out when he abandoned their sacrifices; then he hid himself when he instituted the rite of the new sacrifice, in which he could not be recognized by the carnal-minded.

Therefore, because the true pontiff today instituted the true and new sacrifice, and, about to die, wrote the New Testament in his blood for his heirs, the Mass exults amid the sorrowful hours as the sun sometimes shines red amid clouds. For in the midst of sorrow, the Mass alone receives a solemn [Col. 0310B] chant and the glad vesture of ministers, lest any beauty be lacking to the holy sacrifice on the day of its institution. For this day is more solemn than every other solemnity, apart from the solemnities of the Trinity. All ministers who are able ought to wear solemn vestments, not only because of the solemnity of the new sacrifice, but also because penitents recover the lost garments of holiness. Songs of gladness and glory are also sung, such as *Gloria in excelsis Deo*, not only because of the solemnity of the Eucharist, but also because the angelic choir rejoices at the reconciliation of penitents and the anointing of believers, through which peace is granted to people of good will [Note: [Col. 0309] Luke 2.]. Hence, according to our custom, peace is given; but according to others, at the third *Agnus [Col. 0310C] Dei* “Grant us peace” is not said, but “Have mercy upon us,” and peace is not given, because Judas on this night betrayed with a kiss of peace [Note: [Col. 0309] Matt. 26.] him who is true peace and made the two one [Note: [Col. 0309] Eph. 2.].

But *Gloria in excelsis* and the other solemn observances are to be observed only by bishops, who alone have the fullness of power in today’s sacraments. Nevertheless, neither “Let us bend the knee” nor the prayer over the people is to be pronounced by others. The office of the Mass contains the sum and mystery of our redemption. For the Gospel is read concerning the washing of feet [Note: [Col. 0309] John 13.], the epistle concerning Christ’s body and blood [Note: [Col. 0309] I Cor. 11.], the introit concerning the cross [Note: [Col. 0309] Gal. 6.], the gradual concerning death [Note: [Col. 0309] Phil. 2.], and the offertory concerning the resurrection [Note: [Col. 0309] Ps. 117.]. For all these, according to the mystical sense, depend upon the Gospel, which is the head of the office.

For Christ, as we said before, to rise from supper is to come from the Father’s reclining place; [Col. 0310D] to lay aside garments is to empty himself [Note: [Col. 0309] Phil. 2.]; to gird himself with a linen cloth is to take the form of a servant [Note: [Col. 0309] Ibid.]; to put water into a basin is to pour out his blood; to wash feet is to remit sins; to wipe with linen is to cleanse by faith in the Passion; to resume garments is to put on the garment of glorious flesh. To recline again is to ascend and sit at the right hand of God [Note: [Col. 0309] Heb. 1.]; the offertory pertains to this. To teach the disciples is to send them the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0309] Acts 2.]. Nevertheless, [Col. 0311A] because they did not yet believe perfectly, the *Credo* is not said. The communion is taken from the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0311] John 13.].

Behold, briefly, the sum of human redemption, which was sufficient for all. This is addressed in the prayer *Deus a quo*, and Judas is mentioned, concerning two kinds of penitents: one kind making progress, such as the confessing thief, who deserved to hear: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” [Note: [Col. 0311] Luke 23.]; and the other not making progress, such as the contemptuous thief and Judas the betrayer, who hanged himself with a noose [Note: [Col. 0311] Matt. 27.]. This redemption was also accomplished in the evening of the world, that is, in the sixth age of the world. Therefore the evening Mass assembly is continued in the sixfold number of psalms, and both offices are ended under a single prayer, through *Ite missa est*, if a bishop is present, or through *Benedicamus Domino*, because of the evening conclusion: [Col. 0311B] May the Redeemer grant us, through the sacraments, to attain the perfect effect of redemption.

## CHAPTER XIII. ON PARASCEVE.

“Go forth, daughters of Zion, and behold King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him” [Note: [Col. 0311] Cant. 3.]. As on the sixth day God formed man from the mud of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life [Note: [Col. 0311] Gen. 2.], so in the sixth age and on the sixth weekday he restored the disfigured one, redeemed the one held captive by the devil’s power, when, crucified for us and not for himself, he bore our infirmities and himself carried our sorrows [Note: [Col. 0311] Isa. 53.]. And this is that Friday which claimed for itself, by antonomasia, the name Parasceve. *Parasceve* [Col. 0311C] means “preparation.” Every Friday was called *Parasceve* by Jews dispersed among Greeks, because on Thursday they prepared the things that would be necessary on the Sabbath, according to what had been commanded them concerning manna [Note: [Col. 0311] Exod. 16.]: namely, “On the sixth day you shall gather from it double,” because on the Sabbath it was not lawful to prepare food, just as neither to gather manna. Those, however, who live among Romans more commonly call this day “pure supper.”

But this Friday retained the name Parasceve with a certain special propriety, because on this day the Lord offered to us and for us that manna of sweetness which suffices for us unto the Sabbath of eternity. Concerning this day it is asked whether it ought to be observed in joy and gladness, or rather in sadness. For it seems that it should be celebrated with solemn joys, [Col. 0311D] since it is the beginning of our salvation. Again, if the passions of holy martyrs, through which they passed over to the glory of immortality, are adorned with festive honors—and rightly, because “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” [Note: [Col. 0311] Ps. 115.]—it seems that this Passion ought to be venerated with a more excellent celebration, because the King of saints opened paradise to the saints, saying to the criminal: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” [Note: [Col. 0311] Luke 23.]; by it the captivity of the world was redeemed, the barriers of hell broken, and the gate of heaven opened. Again, the Apostle says that one ought to glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0311] Gal. 6.].

[Col. 0312A] I answer: the saints fly at once to the kingdom after martyrdom, but Christ descended into hell. Hence, although some things invite us to exult, other things nevertheless darken our exultation: authority and consciousness of guilt. For from Gospel authority we have learned that on this day we should grieve and leave joy to the Jews. For when the Lord had said, “A little while and you shall not see me, and again a little while and you shall see me,” he immediately added: “The world shall rejoice, but you shall grieve” [Note: [Col. 0311] John 16.]. Again, to the women following him and weeping, he said: “Do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves and your children” [Note: [Col. 0311] Luke 23.]. Therefore consciousness of our guilt opposes joy, because we, rebellious servants, committed the deed for which that Lord is scourged: “For he paid [Col. 0312B] what he did not take” [Note: [Col. 0311] Ps. 68.].

The joy of so great a salvation, necessary redemption, captivity rescued, and opening of heaven’s gate—of which we have spoken—must therefore be deferred; it must be deferred, I say, until the third day, on which the conqueror rose, and then, for the redemption of souls accomplished on this day and the resurrection of bodies established on that day, the Church’s solemnity may be doubled for the twofold gift. But on this day let it represent sadness; let everyone walk with bowed head, because of consciousness of guilt. Let us take off the sandals from our feet with Moses, that we may hear Christ saying from the midst of the bush: “I have surely seen the affliction of my people, and have heard their groaning, and have come down to deliver [Col. 0312C] them” [Note: [Col. 0311] Exod. 3.]. Let no one greet another. Hence on this day neither “The Lord be with you” nor a kiss is to be given, because Judas betrayed the Lord with a greeting and a kiss of peace [Note: [Col. 0311] Matt. 26; Luke 22.].

From morning until the ninth hour let us keep a deep silence friendly to mourning, together with solitude for meditation, recalling the Savior’s struggle and reproaches. For Moses also says: “The Lord will fight for you, and you shall be silent” [Note: [Col. 0311] Exod. 14.]. But at the ninth hour, because the Lord, about to die, cried: “Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit” [Note: [Col. 0311] Luke 23.], and the centurion said: “Truly this was the Son of God” [Note: [Col. 0311] Matt. 27.], and “Joseph and Nicodemus received the body and wrapped it in linen cloths with spices” [Note: [Col. 0311] John 19.]; because these and the other disciples were permitted to draw near and to restrain their laments, after the persecutors had withdrawn, sated by the divine spectacle [Col. 0312D] or frightened by the miracles—at this ninth hour, I say, let us assemble as for a funeral.

When None has been sung, let us offer funeral lamentation in this order. First, two lessons are read, because Christ suffered for two peoples, namely Hebrew and Gentile, or for the salvation, as stated above, of body and soul. Know that this order is ancient and taken from the custom of the primitive Church, which did not wholly reject Judaism, which read on its Sabbaths one lesson from the Law and another from the Prophets. They are read [Col. 0313A] without a title, because the head of the Church is taken away from us. The first is taken from Hosea’s prophecy [Note: [Col. 0313] Hos. 6.], the second from the Law [Note: [Col. 0313] Exod. 12.], because the Passion of Christ was foretold by the Prophets [Note: [Col. 0313] Hab. 3.] and prefigured by the Law. These are the two living creatures between whom he is known; these are Moses and Elijah, between whom he is transfigured [Note: [Col. 0313] Matt. 17.]. The first is an announcement of the resurrection, where it says: “After two days he will revive us, and on the third day he will raise us up.” In the second the manner of the Passion is expressed, where it says: “The whole multitude shall sacrifice him at evening.”

Two tracts are sung between the readings; one tract follows each lesson, which accords with mourning. For a tract is plainly a chant of mourners, and therefore the tract is prolonged: we mourn [Col. 0313B] for sins that we commit, for punishments that we suffer, and for our prolonged sojourning [Note: [Col. 0313] Ps. 119.]. A gradual is not sung with the tract, as on Wednesday, but two tracts, to express greater mourning. The first tract rouses us to trembling, Habakkuk saying: “Lord, I heard your report and was afraid” [Note: [Col. 0313] Hab. 3.]. For if Habakkuk, seeing the horns of the cross in Christ’s hands, was terrified, what shall we do when we see his strength in the clouds of heaven? This tract has four verses, signifying the four horns of the cross, upon which Christ, composed of four elements, is fastened between two thieves; hence in one of the verses it is sung: “He is crucified between the two living creatures.” Or the human being, composed of the same four elements, is redeemed and called to faith from the four regions [Col. 0313C] of the world. To arouse the human being more strongly to fear, in many churches it is sung in such a way that after each verse the tract is repeated alternately, now from the beginning, now from the middle.

The second tract instructs us to pray in a time of tribulation, through the voice of David singing against Goliath and saying: “Deliver me, Lord, from the evil man” [Note: [Col. 0313] Ps. 139; I Kings 17.]. For our David, Christ, today defeated the great Goliath, that is, the devil. This tract has ten verses, because through our transgression of the Decalogue Goliath took us captive, and by today’s Passion the Lord delivered us from his power. Some churches, however, today omit the tract “He who dwells in the help” [Note: [Col. 0313] Ps. 90.], although it was formerly sung, because Christ was first, namely in the fast, secretly tempted by the devil [Col. 0313D] as by a dragon [Note: [Col. 0313] Matt. 3.], and second was harshly afflicted in the Passion by the same devil as by a lion. This is noted in the verse: “You shall walk upon the asp and basilisk, and shall trample the lion and dragon” [Note: [Col. 0313] Ps. 90.]; or because in the sequence of this psalm we are taught to imitate Christ’s Passion. But the custom prevailed that “Deliver me, Lord” [Note: [Col. 0313] Ps. 139.] should be sung, because the contest of the Passion is expressed there.

Afterward the Passion according to John is read, but without “The Lord be with you,” [Col. 0314A] because of Judas’s greeting; and, according to some, without a title, because we suffer the removal of the head. The Passion according to John is read today for two reasons [Note: [Col. 0313] John 18.]: because he wrote last after the others, and because he was present at the Passion. Known to the high priest, he came boldly while the others fled, and stood by the cross with the Lord’s mother and his mother’s sister. When the Lord saw him, he commended his mother to him as to a son, and him to his mother as to a son [Note: [Col. 0313] John 19.]. Rightly, therefore, on the day on which the Passion is represented to our eyes, the testimony is read [Note: [Col. 0313] Ibid.] of him who saw and bore witness, and we know that his testimony is true.

Let us now consider what the Lord suffered, because he wished not only what he did, but also what he suffered, [Col. 0314B] to contribute to our edification. Therefore, by the thorny crown which they placed upon his head [Note: [Col. 0313] Ibid.], is signified what had been prophesied concerning him: namely, “He himself bore our sins” [Note: [Col. 0313] Isa. 53.]. For thorns signify sins, which prick and tear the soul; on account of sins they are also said to have been inflicted upon our earth: “The earth shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” [Note: [Col. 0313] Gen. 3.]. Behold, daughters of Zion, see King Solomon in the thorny diadem with which his mother, the Synagogue, crowned him [Note: [Col. 0313] Cant. 3.], on the day of his espousal and the day of his heart’s gladness. That is, on this day on which, in the gladness of his heart, he brought forth the first elements of the bride who was to be born to him, namely the Church.

By the purple garment [Note: [Col. 0313] John 19.] with which they clothed him we understand his mortality; by the scarlet garment [Note: [Col. 0313] Matt. 27.], charity. For scarlet is of fiery [Col. 0314C] heat; but in the priestly garment it is commanded to be taken twice dyed [Note: [Col. 0313] Exod. 28.], on account of love for God and neighbor. The Lord, however, because of his exceeding charity by which he loved us, put on the garment of mortality [Note: [Col. 0313] Eph. 2.] and drank the cup of the Passion. In that his face was veiled, struck with fists, and beaten with slaps [Note: [Col. 0313] Matt. 26; John 18.], we understand the veil of the Jews, who even to the present day [Note: [Col. 0313] II Cor. 3.] strike him with fists in their streets and slap him with curses. In patiently enduring the things mentioned, he gave us an example of humility.

Afterward they crucified him: the cross, which had been figured in many ways in the Old Testament. It was said to the angel striking Egypt: “Wherever you find T, Tau, written, do not kill the firstborn” [Note: [Col. 0313] Exod. 12.]. For all are condemned [Col. 0314D] who are not saved through faith in the Mediator. Moses also raised up the bronze serpent in the desert, and all who looked upon it were saved from the bite of serpents [Note: [Col. 0313] Num. 21.]. The bronze serpent has the likeness of a serpent, yet is not a real serpent; so Christ had the likeness of sinful flesh, yet it was not sinful [Note: [Col. 0313] Rom. 8.].

The form of the cross is four-part, either because by his Passion he healed the four elements corrupted in us; or because he drew to himself people from the four regions of the world, according to [Col. 0315A] the saying: “If I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” [Note: [Col. 0315] John 12.]. And Sedulius says:

> Thus the four quarters of the squared world are gathered.

Or this four-sidedness pertains to mortality, for it has length, breadth, height, and depth. The depth is the point driven into the earth; the length extends from there to the arms; the breadth is in the outstretching; the height or loftiness runs from the arms to the head. Depth signifies faith, which is placed in the foundation [Note: [Col. 0315] Heb. 5.]; height, hope, which is laid up in heaven; breadth, charity, which extends even to the left—that is, to enemies [Note: [Col. 0315] Matt. 5.]; length, perseverance [Note: [Col. 0315] Matt. 10.], which is enclosed by faith.

Some say that the four woods, the four kinds of timber, were in the Lord’s cross: namely the base, the upright, [Col. 0315B] the crossbeam, and the board which Pilate had added in order that the title’s inscription might be made. But when the soldiers had crucified the Lord [Note: [Col. 0315] Matt. 27.], they divided his garments among themselves and cast lots for the tunic [Note: [Col. 0315] John 19, and Ps. 21.]. This is represented by two subdeacons or deacons removing the two cloths placed upon the altar. Or the removal of the cloths signifies the flight of the apostles, who were like Christ’s garments. For Peter denied him [Note: [Col. 0315] Matt. 26.], and John fled naked [Note: [Col. 0315] John 18.]. The seamless garment is not divided [Note: [Col. 0315] John 19.]; it signifies the unity of the Church and the truth of the Catholic faith, which could not be torn by schismatics.

Notice that there are four layings aside of Christ’s garments. At supper he laid them aside and resumed them [Note: [Col. 0315] John 13.]. At the pillar and before Herod he is said to have been stripped [Col. 0315C] and reclothed [Note: [Col. 0315] John 19.]. At the cross, however, he was stripped and not reclothed [Note: [Col. 0315] Matt. 27.]. The first pertains to the apostles, whom he shortly resumed; the second pertains to penitents, whom he continually resumes; the third pertains to the remnant, whom he will resume at the end; but the fourth pertains to perverse baptized persons, who are not resumed but will be eternally damned.

At the sixth hour the Lord was crucified, and “there was darkness from the sixth hour until the ninth” [Note: [Col. 0315] Matt. 27]. Hence among some the fire is extinguished at the sixth hour and relit at the ninth. Because the sun hid its light at the sixth hour and restored it at the ninth, we represent these three hours of darkness by the darkness of three days, as stated above. “Go forth, daughters of Zion” [Note: [Col. 0315] Song 3], from these darknesses—or rather from those signified by them, namely the blindness of minds which still [Col. 0315D] covers the face of the Jews.

While the Lord hung upon the cross, they offered him vinegar mixed with gall when he thirsted [Note: [Col. 0315] Matt. 27], of which “when he had tasted it, he would not drink” [Note: [Col. 0315] ibid.]. The Lord thirsted for the salvation of the human race; but the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts, from which he expected it to bear grapes, “produced wild grapes” [Note: [Col. 0315] Isa. 5], and mixed the bitterness of death into its drink. Having tasted this a little—that is, for three days—he was no longer willing to drink of the fruit of that vine [Note: [Col. 0315] Matt. 26]. “For, having risen from the dead, he dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” [Note: [Col. 0315] Rom. 6]. Therefore, by the rejected bitterness of vinegar we understand the rejection of the Jewish people.

By the reed, moreover, we understand his soul. This is the rod turned into a serpent [Note: [Col. 0315] Exod. 7], so that it might swallow up the serpents of the Egyptians. For Christ’s soul, in some manner descending into death—which entered the world through the serpent—swallowed up the deaths of sinners [Note: [Col. 0315] 1 Cor. 13], and likewise returned into a rod, that is, into its former power. That the Lord’s legs were not broken [Note: [Col. 0315] John 19] signifies that all his ways are inviolable; for as powers are understood through bones, so his ways are understood through his legs. Hence in the Song of Songs: “His legs are marble pillars, founded upon bases of gold” [Note: [Col. 0315] Song 5], that is, his fair paths established upon the wisdom of divinity. Therefore neither his bones nor his legs are broken, because his powers and ways are not violated.

[Col. 0316B] “One of the soldiers pierced his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came forth” [Note: [Col. 0315] John 19]. This is the ark of the Lord, that is, the humanity of the Saviour, which has in its side a window—that is, the wound of the lance [Note: [Col. 0315] Gen. 6].

Observe that the outpouring of Jesus Christ’s blood was fivefold: first at the circumcision, second in the sweat, third in the scourging, fourth in the crucifixion, fifth in the piercing by the lance. But upon the cross a fivefold outpouring of blood is found. Hence the canon of the Mass is divided into five parts. Yet it was fitting that the side be pierced with a lance, though it was not fitting that his legs be broken: just as Eve, the companion, was formed from the rib of the sleeping man [Note: [Col. 0315] Gen. 2], so from the side of the dead man the Church, his sister and bride, ought to be born—she who [Col. 0316C] is redeemed by blood and washed by water [Note: [Col. 0315] Eph. 5]. Hence: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0315] John 3]. Indeed, the sacrament of this water took its beginning from this miracle.

The Lord, therefore, was baptized in his Passion. Of this baptism he speaks to the sons of Zebedee: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink? Or be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” [Note: [Col. 0315] Mark 10]. By the names of cup and baptism he denotes the Passion of martyrdom. And elsewhere: “I have a baptism with which to be baptized; and how I am constrained until it is accomplished!” [Note: [Col. 0315] Luke 12]. By this baptism he washed away the defilements of his mortality, of which it is read in Zechariah: “Jesus was clothed in filthy garments” [Note: [Col. 0315] Zech. 3]—that is, the defilements of our weakness. Hence: “He himself bore our infirmities” [Note: [Col. 0315] Isa. 53].

[Col. 0316D] Once the Passion has been read, prayers are said for all, because although we suffer persecutions from enemies, we must nevertheless always return to prayer; or because Christ is crucified for all and offered himself for all upon the altar of the cross; or because, standing at the altar, he prayed for all, according to the saying: “An angel stood beside the altar of the temple, holding a golden censer in his hand” [Note: [Col. 0315] Rev. 8]. Today he stood at the altar for us and kindled the censer of prayer. For he prayed for himself, saying: “Father, glorify thy Son” [Note: [Col. 0315] John 17]; and for [Note: [Col. 0317] [This note appears at the foot of columns 317 and 318, but callout number (28) has not been printed in the text.] 1 Cor. 1.] [Col. 0317A] his own, saying: “I pray for those whom thou hast given me” [Note: [Col. 0317] John 17]; and for those who were to believe in him, saying: “I pray not for these only, but for those also who will believe in me” [Note: [Col. 0317] ibid.].

Rightly, then, although we ought faithfully to pray at every time for every state of the Church, on this solemn day we especially offer prayers for those known to us and also for all outsiders—for Gentiles and Jews, schismatics and heretics—according to the saying: “And much incense was given to him” [Note: [Col. 0317] Rev. 8]. This is also because the Lord, hanging upon the cross, prayed by chanting this psalm: “My God, my God, look upon me” [Note: [Col. 0317] Matt. 27; Ps. 21], and some believe that he continued as far as “In thee, O Lord, have I hoped”; and when he came to this verse [Note: [Col. 0317] ibid.], “Into thy hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit,” he gave up the spirit [Note: [Col. 0317] Luke 23; Ps. 30].

[Col. 0317B] Therefore we too customarily pray after the Passion. For it is customary on other days to say prayers before the Gospel, but today we multiply prayers after the Gospel Passion. Again, it is the Church’s practice to say “The Lord be with you” before prayers; this is the priest’s proper utterance and office. But it is not prefixed to these prayers, because our Priest and Lord is slain. At each prayer we bend the knee, showing that all nations bend their knees to Christ, or that by the posture of the body we may show the devotion of the mind.

For the Jews, however, we do not bend the knee, to avoid their mockery, since they bent their knees before God in derision [Note: [Col. 0317] Matt. 27]; or because the blindness which happened to Israel [Note: [Col. 0317] Rom. 8] can be driven away by no prayer until the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in [Col. 0317C] [Note: [Col. 0317] ibid.]. Therefore one ought not pray urgently for them, and hence we do not bend the knee. Nevertheless prayer must be made for both, since it shall come to pass that he who was lifted up on the cross will draw all things to himself [Note: [Col. 0317] John 12].

Take care that the texts preceding the genuflections are not prayers, but prefaces and exhortations, all beginning with *Oremus* (“Let us pray”), in which it is shown for whom we are able to pray in the prayers that follow. Hence “Amen” is answered only at the end of the following prayers.

The Jews brought three accusations against the Lord: namely, that he had forbidden tribute [Note: [Col. 0317] Luke 23]; that he had made himself king [Note: [Col. 0317] John 19]; and that he had called himself the Son of God [Note: [Col. 0317] ibid.]. Against these three accusations the Saviour sets before them three accusations drawn from Micah, namely: “My people”; “Because I brought [you out]”; “What more ought I to have done?” [Note: [Col. 0317] Mic. 6]. Here he reproaches them with his benefits: deliverance from Egypt, guidance in the wilderness, and introduction into an excellent land. It is as though he said: You accuse me of forbidding tribute; rather, you ought to give thanks, because I delivered you from the slavery of Egypt. You accuse me of making myself king; rather, you ought to give thanks, because I fed you royally in the wilderness. You accuse me because I said that I am the Son of God; rather, you ought to give thanks, because I bestowed upon you a land flowing with milk and [Col. 0318A] honey.

They also inflicted three mockeries upon him. The first was when, after covering his face, they struck him with fists [Note: [Col. 0317] Matt. 26]; the second, when the soldiers bent their knees and worshipped him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews” [Note: [Col. 0317] Matt. 27]. This is attributed to the Jews because they gave the order. The third was when they said to him as he hung upon the cross: “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God” [Note: [Col. 0317] ibid.].

Against these three mockeries we set three acts of adoration: *Agios*, *Sanctus*, and this in two languages, Greek and Latin; for the third, Hebrew, is silent. Or there are the three antiphons—“My people,” “because I brought [you out],” “what more ought I to have done?”—which differ little or not at all in sense and are alike in words and melody. They signify the threefold inscription of the title which was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” [Note: [Col. 0317] John 19].

Whether the beginning of the title was written in the three languages is unknown, but the conclusion, “King of the Jews,” is certain. In Hebrew: *Malchos Judaeorum* (“king of the Jews”); in Greek: *basileos exomosoleon* (“king of those who confess,” reading uncertain); in Latin: “king of those who confess.” Because the Jews denied this, saying: “Do not write, ‘King of the Jews’; but, ‘He said, I am King of the Jews’” [Note: [Col. 0317] ibid.], the matter is accordingly asserted in those antiphons from its effect: namely, that as their king he brought them out of Egypt, led them through the wilderness, and brought them into a good land.

That which was written in the title, “Jesus,” is concluded in each antiphon by “Saviour”; that which was “Nazarene” is answered at each by *Agios*, *Sanctus* (“Holy”); and because the title was written in three languages, the response is made in two—Greek and Latin—which adore what was written. Hebrew [Col. 0318C], however, contradicted it and still blasphemes.

Therefore deacons or priests clothed in white, chanting the aforesaid antiphons, carry the cross to the place where Greek and Latin are answered and it is devoutly adored. For the crucified Lord passed from the unbelief of the Jews to the confession and devotion of the Gentiles, being carried by the innocent apostles and sung of by them—that is, with all their strength confessing and preaching the reproach of the cross—though at times, wearied by the burden of persecutions, they rest a little. Hence, those carrying the cross now proceed, now, as weary men, stand still.

Then they remove the veil, joyfully crying: “Behold the wood of the cross.” This is the veil which was upon the face of Moses [Note: [Col. 0317] Exod. 34; 2 Cor. 3]. This is that by which the Lord [Col. 0318D] hid himself from the Jews [Note: [Col. 0317] John 8], which was revealed when the veil of the Temple was torn [Note: [Col. 0317] Matt. 27]; and which the Lord also revealed when he hung upon the cross. Therefore he said: “It is accomplished” [Note: [Col. 0317] John 19]. For before the Passion all the sacraments of the Christian faith and the entire teaching of the law lay hidden beneath the letter; but in the Passion all things were revealed. Then the banners of the King come forth, which were formerly hidden; then the Lord also revealed them when he opened the meaning of the Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0317] Luke 24].

This is the wood by which bitter waters are made sweet [Note: [Col. 0317] Exod. 15]. They signified the law, [Col. 0319A] which commanded this bitterness: “eye for eye,” and the like [Note: [Col. 0319] Exod. 21]. But they are made sweet when the wood of the Lord’s Passion and the sayings of the Gospel are set forth: “If anyone strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other also” [Note: [Col. 0319] Matt. 5].

The unveiled cross is greeted, because through the cross salvation is restored to humanity; and as it was mocked by unbelieving Jews, so now it is adored by the faithful. But since the Lord was honoured upon an ass [Note: [Col. 0319] Matt. 21] and dishonoured upon the cross, why do we adore the cross and not the ass? I answer: the honour upon the ass was earthly, and salvation did not proceed from it; but the reproach upon the cross was our salvation. This is David’s sword, by which he killed Goliath [Note: [Col. 0319] 1 Sam. 17], which was preserved for a long time and held in honour. So the cross by which the devil is killed is [honoured,] adored, [that is, greeted with reverence,] and kissed, [and this kind of adoration is called *dulia*, which is also owed to creatures. There is another kind called *latria*, by which God alone is to be adored.]

When we kiss the cross, moreover, we prostrate ourselves upon the earth, so that humility of mind may be shown by the posture of the body; and because, just as Christ humbled himself before the Father for us unto death [Note: [Col. 0319] Phil. 2], so we who imitate his death ought to humble ourselves. Concerning this worship of the cross Sedulius says:

> Let no one be ignorant that the form of the cross is to be venerated.

Augustine says concerning the manner of prostration: “If someone humbles himself so as to plant his knees, he still has a further degree to which he may humble himself. Whoever humbles himself so that his belly cleaves to the ground has no further degree to which he may humble himself.” [Col. 0319C] While we adore the cross, we chant its praises and proclamations, namely the antiphons and hymns: *Crucem tuam* (“Thy cross”); *Crux fidelis* (“Faithful cross”); *Pange, lingua* (“Sing, O tongue”).

When these things have been duly completed, let the priest put on his chasuble and approach the altar. Then, in the customary manner, let the subdeacon, or two priests, bring to the altar the body of the Lord that was reserved on the preceding day.

It seems reasonable that the body of the Lord should be consecrated on this day, and that from then until the day of the Sabbath, lulled into continuous silence, we should abstain from the ministry of the sacred altar. For on this day Christ was sacrificed; on the Sabbath he rested in the tomb; and the disciples spent the whole following night in sorrow, until the women, at dawn, reported what they had heard and seen [Note: [Col. 0319] Luke 24], when they began to breathe again in joy.

I answer: On the day before he suffered, our Lord took bread and a cup, blessed them, and gave them to his disciples, saying: “This is my body; this is my cup.” Then he was sacrificed in his own hands; and concerning this sacrifice he added: “Do this in remembrance of me” [Note: [Col. 0319] Matt. 26; 1 Cor. 11]. Thus, from this sacrifice—which must not be omitted, since it is firmly commanded—Friday is the second day, on which he rests as though in a tomb. The Sabbath is the third, on which he rises as though from death.
