Moreover, because the Lord rose during that part of the night which grows light on the first day of the Sabbath [Note: [Col. 0319] Matt. 28], he drew that night powerfully away from the silence or sorrow required by the repose of the tomb [Col. 0320A] and inseparably illuminated it with the radiance of joy. Therefore the three days of the Lord’s death, which could not be completed when reckoned from his being slain by the Jews, are shifted to the time when he was sacrificed in his own hands. A principal indication of this is that on the night of the Supper we celebrate vigils with the lights extinguished. Thus on Thursday, as though it were Friday, double manna is gathered [Note: [Col. 0319] Exod. 16], because on this day, as though it were the Sabbath, it is not found.

Or, Christ’s body is not consecrated today because today he is truly sacrificed for us, and when the reality has come, the figure ought to cease; or because the true priest was taken away today, for he descended into hell; or because the victim has been removed from Christ’s hands and from ours. Therefore friends should not sacrifice while enemies slaughter him; or because the veil of the Temple was torn [Note: [Col. 0319] Matt. 27] and the altar destroyed [Note: [Col. 0319] 1 Macc. 4]; or because Moses says: “You shall be silent, and another shall fight for you” [Note: [Col. 0319] Exod. 14], namely Christ; “for he trod the winepress alone” [Note: [Col. 0319] Isa. 63].

Since, then, the body of the Lord is not to be consecrated on this day, it must be reserved for this day for three reasons. First, for the sick, lest anyone die without viaticum; second, for religious persons, who communicate during these three days; third, in order to fulfil the office. The species of wine, however, is not reserved for three reasons. First, because through negligence it might easily be spilled; second, because at supper the Lord said: “From now on I shall not drink of this fruit of the vine until I drink it in the kingdom of my Father” [Col. 0320C] [Note: [Col. 0319] Matt. 26]; third, because by bread we understand the New Testament, by wine the Old. To signify this, when the Lord had drunk, he said: “It is accomplished” [Note: [Col. 0319] John 19]; the cup is finished and the bread is preserved, because the law has an end [Note: [Col. 0319] Lev. 26] and the Gospel has a beginning [Note: [Col. 0319] 2 Cor. 5]: for when new things come, old things have passed away.

When two priests have brought the body of the Lord to the altar, the officiating priest, having placed it upon the corporal and set the chalice there, as is customary, with wine placed in the chalice, says: “Let us pray. Instructed by saving precepts.” It is established that this place is in the canon, where, with the chalice raised together with the body of the Lord, “For ever and ever” is said, followed by this preface: “Instructed by saving precepts.” Meanwhile the chalice is covered, in which is represented for us that the body of the Lord, taken down from the cross, is buried [Col. 0320D]. Hence by the two priests who bring the body to the altar we represent Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, who took the body to bury it [Note: [Col. 0319] John 19].

Three sections of the canon are said over the body once it has been placed there: “Instructed,” “Our Father,” and “Deliver us, we beseech thee,” because, as we shall say below, the buried Lord is hidden for three days. From what has been said it follows that the Lord’s Prayer alone is not sufficient for consecrating the Eucharist.

For if it were sufficient, it would not be necessary to preserve the body of the Lord [Col. 0321A] until the present day. In this manner the apostles celebrated Mass: when they were first about to celebrate Mass and consecrate, they uttered these words alone: “This is my body; this is my blood.” But afterward they added the Lord’s Prayer, and this is the custom of the apostles represented here. Blessed Gregory, Gelasius, and Celestine, however, added other things.

When the words “For ever and ever” have been reached, the priest, as usual, breaks the host. After it has been broken, he does not say, “The peace of the Lord be always with you,” because the kisses of those present do not follow. Likewise, when placing the third portion in the chalice, he does not say, “May this most holy mingling of the body and blood of the Lord,” for the blood is not present. Hence it is asked whether wine is consecrated by contact. I answer: it is not consecrated, but sanctified. There is a difference between something consecrated and something sanctified. To consecrate is to transubstantiate by consecration; “to sanctify” is similarly used, but loosely. To be sanctified is, through contact with a sacred thing, to become worthy of reverence.

Thereafter *Agnus Dei* is omitted, because he who is seen to fail in agony does not appear to be one who should be invoked. Let the priest communicate in silence, and all ought to communicate. Hence the communion chant is not sung; but while we are silent, that blood which we receive cries out from our mouth to the Lord for us. For we are that earth which opened its mouth and drank Abel’s blood [Note: [Col. 0321] Gen. 4], that is, Christ’s blood, which Cain—that is, the Jewish people—shed. [Col. 0321C] Hence he became a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth [Note: [Col. 0321] ibid.], according to the saying: “Scatter them in thy power” [Note: [Col. 0321] Ps. 58]. He became accursed with that curse: “His blood be upon us” [Note: [Col. 0321] Matt. 27].

After communion, let the evening psalms be chanted in the number six, and under one collect, “Look upon us, O Lord,” let the entire office—that is, Mass and Vespers—be ended. When this is done, let the cross be returned to its place. In some places it is customary for the choir to say psalms before it, and for the bishop or his vicar to do so until the hour at which the Lord rose. Once the office has been celebrated, we take refreshment with only one dish, because on this day the Lord incorporated into himself only one person, namely the thief to whom he said: “Today thou shalt be with me in paradise” [Note: [Col. 0321] Luke 23].

## Chapter XIV. On Holy Saturday

[Col. 0321D]

“Put on the new man, who is created according to God” [Note: [Col. 0321] Eph. 4]. Just as God, after completing the works of the world’s creation on the sixth day, rested on the seventh from all the work that he had done [Note: [Col. 0321] Gen. 2], so, after the works of re-creation had been completed in the sixth age, according to what the Lord said while hanging upon the cross, “It is accomplished” [Note: [Col. 0321] John 19], he rested in the seventh age. For when his soul departed from the body’s capacity for suffering, he was in some manner at rest. Likewise, as the creation of man was made on Friday and he rested on the next day, so, after man’s re-creation was accomplished on the same Friday, the Lord slept in the tomb [Col. 0322A].

Therefore this day is called Sabbath, which means “rest”; and, by antonomasia, Holy Sabbath, because of the rest of Jesus Christ, in whose death we have been sanctified; or because of the baptismal font blessed today, in which the new offspring of the Church is unquestionably sanctified. Toward the evening of this night, which grows light on the first day of the Sabbath [Note: [Col. 0321] Matt. 28], the solemnity of the office begins and is continued, as it were, throughout the whole night until daylight, so that this may be fulfilled: “Night is my illumination in my delights, and the night shall be illuminated as the day” [Note: [Col. 0321] Ps. 138].

For this day shines illuminated in our delights for three reasons: because of the redemption of souls, which, although it was restored by the Lord’s death on the day of Preparation, has its joy and gladness transferred to this night [Col. 0322B] for the reason already given; because of the resurrection of bodies, which, when the Lord rises, is hoped to occur on the first day of the Sabbath—therefore we keep vigil and, keeping vigil, sing to him as he rises; and because of the sacrament of baptism, which is celebrated today, since it took its beginning from those causes and grants us their fruit.

For on this day the office for catechumens is celebrated, so that catechumens, buried with Christ through baptism into death, may rise with him [Note: [Col. 0321] Rom. 6]. This night, then, is called Pascha, which means “passing over,” because the Lord passed from the world to the Father, from death to life. We too pass over—“for Christ, our Pascha, has been sacrificed” [Note: [Col. 0321] 1 Cor. 5]—from the enemy to the Father, from darkness to light, from guilt to grace, from punishment to [Col. 0322C] glory, from battle to victory.

This night is celebrated at the full moon; the moon borrows the brightness of its light from the sun. The moon is the Church; the sun, Christ, who, while he sets, is slain. But by his setting the Church is illuminated with the fullness of grace. This night is celebrated after the equinox, when day overcomes night, because after ignorance knowledge of God is extended; and where iniquity abounded, grace abounded yet more [Note: [Col. 0321] Rom. 5]. This night is celebrated in spring, when, after winter’s harshness, flowers bloom and birds sing, because, once the frost of unbelief had been driven away, the world flowered with the beauty of virtues, and the sound of the apostles went out into all the earth [Note: [Col. 0321] Ps. 18].

This night is common to both reckonings of the day. For until now the day naturally preceded the night, signifying the fall of the first Adam, who descended from light into [Col. 0322D] darkness; but henceforth the night artificially precedes the day, indicating the restoration of the second Adam, who restored us from darkness to light. This night ends the forty-day period of affliction and begins the fifty-day period of release, because through the resurrection we shall pass from the servitude of captivity to the jubilee of freedom. This night mediates between the seventh and eighth, the alpha and omega of the other Testament. Now let us proceed with the office and its order.

At the beginning of the office, every fire in the church ought to be extinguished, and a new fire should be struck from a stone, by steel striking it, or kindled by crystal set before the sun, and nourished with brushwood. The old fire signifies the old law, whose figures were fulfilled in Christ’s death and therefore ought to cease as though extinguished. But the new fire is struck from the stone—that is, Christ, who is the cornerstone [Note: [Col. 0323] Eph. 2]—who, struck by the blow of the cross, poured out the Holy Spirit upon us; or from crystal placed between the sun and the tinder, that is, Christ, who was mediator between God and our weakness [Note: [Col. 0323] 1 Tim. 2], and who, as he testifies, came to cast fire upon the earth [Note: [Col. 0323] Luke 12].

The new fire is struck when, through his Passion and resurrection, the Holy Spirit is poured into us. The same Christ, who is the true vine [Note: [Col. 0323] John 15], supplies it with fuel. It is no empty religious observance to proceed in solemn procession for the blessing of this fire: “Let us go forth,” says the Apostle, “to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach” [Note: [Col. 0323] Heb. 13]. Therefore, as we proceed to that fire, we ought to remember that we must go out to him whom the Jews cast outside the camp. We bless it with the cross and water, that we may signify that we have been washed by the power of his Passion, through which we receive the Holy Spirit.

Observe that, as fire is extinguished on each of these days—the Lord’s Supper, the Preparation, and Holy Saturday—so, some say, a new fire is kindled in remembrance of the Passion, as said above. With the fire solemnly blessed, the deacon goes out to the doors of the church, saying three times, “The Light of Christ,” to which the choir responds, “Thanks be to God.”

Then, coming into the choir, he blesses the Paschal candle. Zosimus, the twenty-eighth pontiff of the Roman Church, instituted the blessing of the candle so that Christ might be visibly [Col. 0323C] recalled to memory. According to Augustine, Christ is to be recalled to memory in all things. From the sweetness of his blessing the praises of the Lord’s resurrection begin. For the renewed and illuminated candle signifies Christ, who rose from the dead in glorified flesh, appeared as true God, and truly displayed in himself the splendour of divinity. With the joy of his love he made serene the sorrow of the disciples—indeed, of the whole world—which had been saddened by the extinguishing of the lamps, that is, the prophets, and of the greater lamp, that is, the Passion of the Saviour.

The mother bee brought forth its wax without intercourse, because the Virgin Mary conceived and bore Christ’s flesh [Note: [Col. 0323] Isa. 7] and, bringing forth God in the flesh as honey in wax, remained inviolate. Therefore, since Christ is signified by the candle, the year from the Lord’s Incarnation is fittingly inscribed immediately afterward; or because Christ is the greatest year, ancient and full of days [Note: [Col. 0323] Dan. 7], in whom is the fullness of every good thing [Note: [Col. 0323] John 1; Col. 2], as in a year is the fertility of fruits. Its twelve months are the apostles, its days the faithful, and its hours baptized children. The indiction and epact are likewise inscribed, because human actions and the succession of times are ordered through Christ’s governance. Observe also that an indiction is a period of fifteen years, and each of these is called an *aera*; *aera* means the tribute paid every year.

[Col. 0324A] The deacon blesses the candle, not the priest or bishop, because the proclamation of Christ’s resurrection was made known to the apostles by the lesser sex, namely women [Note: [Col. 0323] Luke 24], not to women by the apostles. For since a woman, sent by the devil, offered death to the man [Note: [Col. 0323] Gen. 3], fittingly that same sex, sent by the risen Christ, proclaimed life to the male sex.

As he approaches to bless it, he carries with him small pieces of incense, so as to offer and fix them into the little cross engraved upon the candle. For those women bought spices in order to come and anoint Jesus after his crucifixion [Note: [Col. 0323] Mark 16]. In blessing it, he says: *Exsultet* (“Let [it] rejoice”). When afterward he greets the people, he makes them well-disposed and attentive, saying: “The Lord be with you.”

In the lighting of the pillar, we know the praises of this pillar, which glowing fire kindles in honour of the Lord [Col. 0324B]. Here it is indicated that the same thing is represented by the candle as was prefigured by the pillar which went before the children of Israel [Note: [Col. 0323] Exod. 13]. The pillar of cloud bore the figure of humanity, but the pillar of fire of divinity. As Jerome says, the pillar was granted to the children of Israel at the third station, after the eating of the lamb; it went before the people to the Red Sea and through the desert, until they crossed the Jordan and entered the land of promise.

Hence, according to some, the candle is blessed on the third day after the Lord’s Supper, before baptism, and is carried before the neophytes to the baptistery and in the offices until the octave of the solemnity, or before the bishop, who is the head of the people. The pillar did three things for the people: it shaded them from the sun, protected them from the enemy, and gave light [Col. 0324C] in the night. Thus Christ shades against the heat of vices, protects from the suggestions of demons, and enlightens every person coming into this world [Note: [Col. 0323] John 1], until he brings that person to the kingdom of heaven—“offering,” etc.

“The glowing fire kindles it”: this is the divinity which gave life again to the humanity lying in the tomb, that is, united the soul to the body; or the new fire prefigured his new teaching, who says: “I give you a new commandment” [Note: [Col. 0323] John 13], or the new glory displayed in the resurrection. It continues: “Though divided into parts, it nevertheless knows no loss of its borrowed light.” From the same fire all the small candles in the church are lighted from the consecrated candle. For the Lord sent fire upon the earth [Note: [Col. 0323] Luke 12], and what did he will except that it should burn intensely? “And of his fullness we have all received” [Note: [Col. 0323] John 1]. Also, standing among the disciples on the day he rose, he said to them: “Receive the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0323] John 20]. The two smaller candles represent the apostles, sent out two by two to the office of preaching [Note: [Col. 0323] Luke 10]; or the prophets and apostles; or all the teachers of the Church, burning with twofold love, or shining forth both in word and deed.

If there is only one smaller candle, it signifies the order of the apostles, of whom, just as he had said of himself, “I am the light of the world” [Note: [Col. 0323] John 8], so he added concerning them: “You are the light of the world” [Note: [Col. 0323] Matt. 5]. Both go before the catechumens [Col. 0325A], because Christ enlightened the Church through himself and through the apostles.

When offering incense, he says: “Receive, holy Father, this evening sacrifice of incense.” The evening sacrifice of the law signified that the Lord was to be sacrificed in the evening of the world. Therefore, when the cross is engraved, the image of the crucified one is signified. “Which,” etc.

The blessed candle is distributed to the people on the octave of Easter, according to the custom of some, for fumigating houses; because at the final resurrection Christ will be bestowed upon the faithful as their reward. To signify this more expressly, the Romans make lambs from wax mixed with oil; for in the wax lamb the Lamb prefigured and sacrificed at Passover is recalled to memory, into which Saint Gregory poured oil, [Col. 0325B] when he disclosed the mysteries of the Paschal Lamb.

There follows the baptism which we celebrate today; for on this night one stronger, coming upon the strong man, bound him [Note: [Col. 0325] Luke 11.] and restored the spoils to paradise. Likewise: “For as many of us as were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life.” [Note: [Col. 0325] Rom. 6.] Christ’s death was the abolition of our death [Note: [Col. 0325] Heb. 2.], but Christ’s death was single, whereas ours is twofold. For through Christ’s one death we obtain in baptism the abolition of that death which receives in baptism the likeness of Christ’s death: this is the death of the soul, which saving grace immediately [Col. 0325C] drives away. But it has reserved the other death, that of the body, for the judgment of justice; yet even this mortal element shall be swallowed up. And it was fitting that, just as the death of the soul had been the cause of bodily death, so the justification of the spirit should become the cause of the body’s glorious transformation.

The Lord instituted baptism when he brought forth blood and water from his side; later he confirmed it by an authoritative ordinance, saying: “Unless a person is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.” [Note: [Col. 0325] John 3.] The Lord was baptized in his Passion; hence: “I have a baptism to be baptized with,” [Note: [Col. 0325] Luke 12.] and, “How I am constrained until it is accomplished”; in it he poured forth a river of blood and water, washed his whole body, which is the Church [Note: [Col. 0325] Eph. 5.], and made it whiter than snow. [Note: [Col. 0325] Ps. 50.] Thus the Church is born from Christ’s side, [Col. 0325D] just as Eve was fashioned from Adam’s side. [Note: [Col. 0325] Gen. 2.]

That, therefore, was the universal baptism of Abraham and of the others, and of the thief hanging on the cross. [Note: [Col. 0325] Luke 23.] But we read that Paul was baptized [Note: [Col. 0325] Acts 9.], because he was not yet in the body of the universal Church but in the synagogue of Satan. Augustine could not discover whether the other apostles had been baptized with water, as he says in the letter which he writes to Seleucianus. Some say that they were baptized with water when the Lord washed their feet. [Note: [Col. 0325] John 13.] Others do not doubt that they were baptized with water, in the form of John or of Christ [Note: [Col. 0325] John 4.], through whose ministry Christ baptized others. For they baptized others [Col. 0326A] before the Passion, as some think, in John’s form; after the resurrection, in the Savior’s form, who said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” [Note: [Col. 0325] Matt. 28.] This is the substantial form of the sacrament; the rest belongs to its solemnity, in which the devil is adjured and, as it were, condemned by judicial sentence. We shall proceed through these matters in the order in which they are read.

Thus, in certain churches twenty-four readings are read: twelve in Greek, because of the authority of the Seventy Interpreters, whose authority flourished in Greece; and in Latin, because of the authority of Jerome, whose translation prevailed in Italy. Hence, although there are twenty-four readings, there are nevertheless only twelve readings in sense, which are read in Greek and Latin [Col. 0326B] because of the diversity of the hearers, as we said previously when speaking of the Ember Saturdays.

Twelve are read because the catechumens to be baptized are instructed in the teaching of the twelve apostles. They are instructed by the variety of two days, namely Wednesday and today, so that if anything they learned on the Wednesday after mid-Lent has perhaps slipped away through forgetfulness, or if some have been absent, they may now be instructed more perfectly and fully. Or they are instructed by these twofold variations of two days, not so that they may understand the doctrine itself to vary, but, according to Bede, so that they may know that the present life consists in faith and action.

In certain churches, however, only six readings are read, because [Col. 0326C] the catechumens are invited to works of mercy. However many are read, the titles are omitted: either because Christ our head [Note: [Col. 0325] Eph. 1.] has not yet been restored to us; or, rather, because those being baptized, to whom the office belongs, are held in ignorance of the Scriptures. Since they do not understand Scripture, it is not expedient for the authors to be named to them. For titles are recited in the readings so that the authors of heavenly doctrine may be known as citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, and so that wise hearers, through love of the sweet name of their fellow citizens, may understand the reading more eagerly. Therefore, because the neophytes do not know those citizens who sing there, the titles of the readings are not pronounced.

For this reason they are also read at night and without tone: because the unlearned and simple catechumens are instructed in them. Or, for this reason, [Col. 0326D] titles are withheld from the twelve readings read to catechumens because the neophytes have not yet been sealed among the twelve thousand. [Note: [Col. 0325] Rev. 9.]

The readings bear the type of Eliezer, Abraham’s servant, who, by his master’s command, after Sarah had died, brought Rebecca to Isaac as his wife. He found her at a fountain, gave her bracelets and earrings to adorn her face, and without delay she left her father’s house and hastened joyfully to the bridegroom. [Note: [Col. 0325] Gen. 24.] The priests of the Ancient of Days, delegates of God the Father, coming to the font of baptism, offer to the new people, who are to be joined to Christ our laughter or joy, by reading the lessons, the ornaments of faith and doctrine for their ears; they put on bracelets [Col. 0327A] when they work obediently. They are joined to Isaac when, forgetting their people and their father’s house [Note: [Col. 0327] Ps. 44.], they are united to Christ through love. And these things occur after Sarah has died, because the synagogue which bore him, choked by blood when it said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children,” [Note: [Col. 0327] Matt. 27.] while the Church, the bride from among the Gentiles, hastened on.

The first reading, namely, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” is suited to those being baptized because it says: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters,” and below: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” [Note: [Col. 0327] Gen. 1.] “In the image” is insofar as he is rational; “in the likeness” insofar as he is good. For image concerns natural endowments, but likeness gratuitous ones. A human being could not lack the image, [Col. 0327B] but lost the likeness through sin. In order to recover it, the Spirit of the Lord is borne over the water of baptism. Therefore this reading is read because it suggests a mention of the Trinity and displays the power of the Holy Spirit. It is also suited to those being baptized because of the distinction of the days and their works.

Just as in the beginning God created heaven and earth, so now in Baptism he creates a new offspring of the Church; he divides waters from waters, the spiritual from the carnal; and from the waters he brings forth fish and birds [Note: [Col. 0327] Ibid.]: that is, those who swim amid worldly cares and those “whose citizenship is in heaven.” [Note: [Col. 0327] Phil. 3.] Their earth, that is, their flesh, produces for some green grass, fruit-bearing plants, and trees of virtues; for others it sprouts thorns and briars of vices. Yet over all, in the firmament of Scripture, the sun, moon, and the other [Col. 0327C] lights preside [Note: [Col. 0327] Gen. 1.]: namely, the greater and lesser teachers, who shine upon good and evil [Note: [Col. 0327] Matt. 5.], wise and unwise. [Note: [Col. 0327] Rom. 1.] And just as afterward he created humanity and finally rested [Note: [Col. 0327] Gen. 2.], so in baptism he re-creates and regenerates, and gives rest here from guilt; but we await the future rest, which shall be more fully free at once from guilt and punishment.

The second reading, namely, “When Noah was five hundred years old,” [Note: [Col. 0327] Gen. 5, 6.] is suited to the sacrament of baptism in this respect: it speaks of the inundation of the Flood, in which, just as sinners perish and the righteous are saved, so in baptism sins are blotted out and souls are set free.

The third, namely, “God tested Abraham,” [Note: [Col. 0327] Gen. 22.] approaches baptism in this respect, because it declares that Isaac is [Col. 0327D] to be sacrificed. He is Christ, in whose death we are baptized [Note: [Col. 0327] Rom. 6.] and in whom we receive blessing.

In the fourth reading, the event is a clear figure of baptism. For Moses represents the priest, [Note: [Col. 0327] Exod. 14.] the Red Sea baptism, the candle the pillar, the catechumens the Egyptians, and those already baptized the Hebrews. Hence the hymn of victory immediately follows in their voice: “Let us sing.” For it must be sung, because in the death of our Lamb the firstborn of the Egyptians die, and in the Red Sea the Egyptians [Col. 0328A] are submerged; that is, original and actual sins are utterly swallowed up in baptism by the reddening blood of Christ.

The fifth reading likewise, namely, “This is the inheritance,” [Note: [Col. 0327] Isa. 54.] plainly proclaims baptism, where it says: “All who thirst, come to the waters.” [Note: [Col. 0327] Isa. 55.]

The sixth, namely, “Hear, Israel,” [Note: [Col. 0327] Bar. 3.] indicates the Incarnation, saying: “He was seen on earth and conversed with men.” [Note: [Col. 0327] Ezek. 37.]

The seventh, namely, “It came to pass upon me,” [Note: [Col. 0327] Isa. 4.] intimates our resurrection.

The eighth, namely, “Seven women shall take hold of one man,” [Note: [Col. 0327] Ibid.] suggests the seven gifts bestowed in the sacrament of baptism. It also contains the union of Christ and the Church, which was made in [Col. 0328B] the Savior’s Incarnation and will be more fully accomplished in the resurrection. Therefore those two readings precede it. The Church is also united to Christ in the sacrament of the washing; hence it is added here: “If he shall wash away the filth of the daughters of Zion.” [Note: [Col. 0327] Ibid.] Therefore the hymn follows: “A vineyard has been made for the beloved.” For “the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel.” [Note: [Col. 0327] Isa. 5.]

The ninth, namely, “The Lord said to Moses,” [Note: [Col. 0327] Exod. 12.] commands the sacrifice of the Paschal lamb, that is, Christ, by whose blood we are redeemed and by whose water we are washed.

The tenth, namely, “The word came to pass,” [Note: [Col. 0327] John 3.] likewise plainly declares the Lord’s Passion, which was the origin of baptism.

The eleventh also suits those reborn, namely, “Moses wrote,” [Note: [Col. 0327] Deut. 31.] where he sets God’s law before those reborn [Col. 0328C] and promises heavenly things in the hymn. [Note: [Col. 0327] Deut. 32.] Therefore the hymn follows: “Give ear.”

The twelfth, namely, “Nebuchadnezzar,” also declares baptism, in which the Holy Spirit consumes sins just as the angel extinguished the flame of the furnace. [Note: [Col. 0327] Dan. 3.] Hence the catechumens joyfully resound with the hymn “As the deer”: [Note: [Col. 0327] Ps. 41.] for they desire the fountain of life.

Those who read four readings use these: “In the beginning”; “It came to pass in the watch”; “Seven women shall take hold”; and “This is the inheritance,” or “Moses wrote.” These four are read today because the four classes of believers—namely, the simple, the understanding, the advanced, and the wise—are instructed in four ways: through history, allegory, tropology, and anagogy. [Col. 0328D] For today a fourfold table is set before our neophytes.

The first reading teaches the simple concerning their formation, where it says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” [Note: [Col. 0327] Gen. 1.] and likewise, “He created them male and female.” Hence the priest prays that he may restore in the catechumens the image which he created in human beings.

The second reading instructs the understanding concerning the manner of restoration through allegory, saying that the Egyptians were submerged in the sea [Note: [Col. 0327] Exod. 14.] and the Hebrews set free, signifying that demons and sins [Col. 0329A] are submerged and souls are set free in baptism. Thus, in the person of the Hebrews and of those set free from vices in the font, the hymn of victory follows: “Let us sing.” Afterwards the priest prays that, just as they were freed from the Egyptians, so these may be freed from demons.

The third reading teaches the advanced through tropology, where it says that the filth of the daughters of Zion is to be washed away in the spirit of judgment, and the blood of Jerusalem in the spirit of burning, [Note: [Col. 0329] Isa. 4.] because tears wash away what is light, while the harshness of penance washes away what is grave; and all these things are washed in the font through the sevenfold Spirit. These are the seven women who took hold of the one man. The hymn “The Vineyard” follows this, because eternal joy accompanies good conduct; and this hymn pertains to the Synagogue, which will be joined to the man when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered. [Col. 0329B] [Note: [Col. 0329] Rom. 11.] Thereafter the priest prays that after present things they may receive eternal goods.

The fourth reading raises the wise to heavenly things through anagogy, while it promises the eternal inheritance. [Note: [Col. 0329] Isa. 54, 55.] Two hymns follow it, because in that inheritance those baptized will rejoice in body and soul; or because two things are joined in the reading, namely the conduct of the present life and the inheritance of the future, concerning which the Prophet says: “His soul shall abide among good things, and his seed shall inherit the earth.” [Note: [Col. 0329] Ps. 26.] Therefore the words of the reading and of the hymns agree. There it says, “All who thirst”; here, “My soul has thirsted.” [Note: [Col. 0329] Ps. 41.] There, “David faithful”; [Note: [Col. 0329] 1 Sam. 22.] here, “God faithful.” [Note: [Col. 0329] Deut. 32.] There, “The rain came down”; [Note: [Col. 0329] Isa. 55.] here, “My words descend like dew.” [Note: [Col. 0329] Ps. 132.] But after the hymn [Col. 0329C] “Give ear, O heaven,” the priest prays that the promise of inheritance may be firm. After the other hymn, “As the deer,” he prays again that the catechumens may thirst for the fountain of life.

The hymns follow the readings in the person of the catechumens, because the catechumens are to be among the number of the one hundred and forty-four thousand who sing the new hymn, [Note: [Col. 0329] Rev. 14.] or rather, who exult because they are freed from the burdens of the Egyptians. But because, as long as we are in the body, this exultation ought to be in trembling and in laborious mortification of the flesh, we render the song in tracts, which belong to mourners and signify the present exile.

Likewise, the first reading relates the human fall, and hence no hymn follows it: for fallen humanity, in ignorance, did not sing thanks to God, but [Col. 0329D] became mute and deaf. Therefore the person to be baptized is told *ephpheta*, that is, “to open.” [Note: [Col. 0329] Mark 7.]

The next three readings concern the three times of the world: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. In these, the sacrament of baptism is proposed as necessary for the restoration of the fallen. Hence in the second reading, concerning those to whom the Law had not yet been given, it is said: “All were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea.” [Note: [Col. 0329] 1 Cor. 10.] In the third, concerning those who were under the Law, it is said: “If the Lord shall wash away the filth of the daughters of Zion.” [Note: [Col. 0329] Isa. 4.] In the fourth, “All who thirst” [Note: [Col. 0329] Isa. 55.] invites them to drink water from the fountains of the Savior, who said [Col. 0330A] to the Samaritan woman: “Whoever drinks the water which I shall give shall become in him a fountain of living water springing up into eternal life.” [Note: [Col. 0329] John 4.]

Therefore, because they recognized the remedy of baptism in each age, a hymn is sung after each of the three readings, and a fourth is concluded without a preceding reading, so that the neophytes may make recompense for the silence of the first: those who had been silent concerning the fall, now made certain of restoration, may double their joys. Or they do not await further instruction, because they joyfully hasten to the washing: “As the deer longs for fountains of water.” [Note: [Col. 0329] Ps. 41.]

It should be known that, whatever the order, there are four hymns corresponding to the four points, as was said above of the readings. They are called hymns because they are sung, or because in authoritative books they are named hymns. For of the first it is said, [Col. 0330B] “Moses sang a song to the Lord”; [Note: [Col. 0329] Exod. 15.] of the second, “I shall sing to my beloved a song of my kinsman”; [Note: [Col. 0329] Isa. 5.] of the third, “Moses wrote a song”; [Note: [Col. 0329] Deut. 31.] and of the fourth this is said in the preface of the hymn.

It is noteworthy that, however many readings there may be, the prayers following always look back to the preceding readings and tracts; and the order is reversed. Ordinarily, first the priest prays, second the reader reads, and then the singer chants in response. But here, first there is a reading, so that the doctrine of faith may be set before the neophytes. Second, it is sung in their person, so that the devotion and joyfulness of those to be baptized may be recognized. When these are recognized, the priest confidently prays that their devotion may not fail but may receive increase. And, just as the titles are suppressed in the readings, [Col. 0330C] so for the same reason “The Lord be with you” is omitted from the prayers.

While the readings are being read, the twelvefold number of the litanies is completed by three groups of four clergy, praying that the doctrine of the apostles, endowed with faith in the Trinity and the four virtues, may take hold in those being baptized. Or they are made in groups of seven, to obtain sevenfold grace, and in groups of five, to obtain the guarding of the five senses. And because we are not sufficient of ourselves to obtain this, we seek the intercessions of the saints.

But this must not be passed over in silence: in the readings and litanies the old men go before and the young men follow, either because the old servant brought Rebecca for young Isaac to take her, [Note: [Col. 0329] Gen. 24.] or because in baptism the Church becomes young and is renewed, [Col. 0330D] as our youth is renewed like the eagle’s. [Note: [Col. 0329] Ps. 102.]

When these things have been duly completed, we solemnly approach the fonts, as in processions, singing these verses: “King of the saints.” Fonts ought not to be outside the Church, because she is the mother from whom new offspring is generated. Baptism is called an anointing or a washing.

Noah prefigured baptism in the Flood; [Note: [Col. 0329] Gen. 7.] Moses, in the Red Sea; [Note: [Col. 0329] Exod. 14.] Solomon, in the Bronze Sea. [Note: [Col. 0329] 1 Kings 7.] John displayed it by his office; [Note: [Col. 0329] Matt. 3.] the Lord confirmed it by baptism, consecrated it by his Passion, and commanded it by his mandate. [Note: [Col. 0329] John 19; Matt. 28.] The bishop or priest prays to God the Father and through [Col. 0331A] Jesus Christ invokes the Holy Spirit. Therefore he first reads in the manner of a prayer; but afterward, rejoicing that the Holy Spirit has come, he gives thanks and sings in the manner of a preface.

The consecration of the font is accomplished in the name of the holy Trinity, and especially by invocation of the Holy Spirit. For the holy Trinity so divided its works that the Father created humanity, the Son redeemed it, and the Holy Spirit, illuminating, regenerated it, and, regenerating it, illuminated it; yet the works of the Trinity are indivisible. The priest invokes the Spirit of adoption to sanctify and make the water fruitful. When he divides the water with his hand in the form of a cross, he recalls that Moses sweetened the water by the touch of wood; [Note: [Col. 0331] Exod. 15.] and that water prefigured baptism, while the wood prefigured the cross.

[Col. 0331B] By breathing across it, he signifies the expulsion of unclean spirits. Thus it is said: “Let the unclean spirit depart,” in which the Lord’s word is fulfilled: “The prince of this world shall be cast out.” [Note: [Col. 0331] John 12.] By breathing upward three times he indicates that this is done in the invocation of the holy Trinity. Once the devil has departed, the water is fortified with the seal of the cross when it is said, “May this be holy,” so that it may be free from the assault of the adversary and he may no longer have a place to return. Again, to the same effect, it is fortified by invocation of the holy Trinity when there follows, “May it be a living fountain.”

By the threefold manual division, indeed, we understand the threefold operation of the holy Trinity, as the very adjectives in the prayer prove: for “living fountain” refers to the Father; “regenerating water” to the Son; and “purifying wave” [Col. 0331C] to the Holy Spirit. For just as the Trinity was present at Christ’s baptism [Note: [Col. 0331] Matt. 3.]—the Father in the voice, the Son in the person, the Holy Spirit in the dove—so our blessing also ought to be made by invocation of the Trinity. Therefore, when it is said, “Through the living God,” the Father is indicated; then the Son, when “Through Jesus Christ” follows; then the Holy Spirit, when “The power of your Spirit” is added.

Observe that in this sequence of blessing miracles performed in water are set forth: that at the beginning of creation “the Spirit was borne over the waters”; [Note: [Col. 0331] Gen. 1.] that in the Flood [Note: [Col. 0331] Gen. 7.] the crimes of a guilty world were cleansed by water; that in the beginning water was separated from dry land; [Note: [Col. 0331] Gen. 1.] and that at a feast it was changed into wine. [Note: [Col. 0331] John 2.] Thus, just as then the waters miraculously obeyed the Lord’s [Col. 0331D] commands, so now, beyond the natural cleansing which they can provide for washing bodies, may they also be miraculously effective for purifying minds.

The change in the voice signifies the coming of the Holy Spirit, or rather a certain humble preparation of the mind for obtaining the Holy Spirit’s coming into the water. Then the priest invites him in a loud and joyful voice, saying: “May he descend into this.” Hence, when we immediately put the candles into the water, we do not doubt that the Holy Spirit descends into the water. On this account only one candle is put in, for there was one pillar: bright by night, a little cloud by day. [Col. 0332A] [Note: [Col. 0331] Exod. 13.] This is Christ, who came so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind. [Note: [Col. 0331] John 9.]

But two, as it were, are read. For just as a lighted candle recalls the pillar of fire and signifies the person of the Son, so an extinguished candle recalls the pillar of cloud and the person of the Holy Spirit. Hence, according to some, two candles are reasonably placed in the water. A candle lit from a candle signifies that the apostles—the Israelite pillars filled with the Holy Spirit—were enlightened by Christ. Some, however, defer lighting both candles of the neophytes until the lamps of the church are lit. Or the two candles signify love of God and love of neighbor: the one turned to the right signifies love of God, and the one turned to the left love of neighbor.

Through the mingling of chrism and water [Col. 0332B] we signify the union of Christ and the Church. Then let the children be baptized, after they have first been questioned concerning faith and whether they renounce Satan, his works, and his pomps, so that confession of the mouth may be made for their salvation. [Note: [Col. 0331] Rom. 10.]

Observe that this office has been rehearsed in the scrutiny, but it is perhaps repeated because some were absent, or because through negligence they lost what they had received. And as the first guest is expelled by renunciation, the second enters through confession. Because of this repetition of renunciation and confession, it is entitled in the sacramentary, “On the Saturday of Easter, for those rendering back”; for they render back what they received in the scrutinies.

Then they are anointed with oil on the breast and between the shoulders, that they may be strengthened in faith [Col. 0332C] and action: faith by the breast, action by the shoulders; by these two a person is saved. Or it is so that, secure in mind and body, they may renounce the works of the devil, spiritual and carnal. Or they are anointed on the breast so that they may be capable of understanding God’s word, and on the shoulders so that they may be strong enough to bear the Lord’s yoke. [Note: [Col. 0331] Matt. 11.]

Afterward they are baptized with these words: “I baptize you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” And because they are baptized in the name of the Trinity, they are immersed three times: either that through faith in the holy Trinity they may be delivered from the three deaths—of thought, speech, and action—or that they may be freed from the three transgressions, namely those against the natural law, the Mosaic law, and the Gospel; or that they may be conformed to Christ’s threefold death, [Col. 0332D] because we have been baptized into his death. [Note: [Col. 0331] Rom. 6.]

The immersion is to be performed in this manner. First, with the face straight toward the water and the head turned toward the east. Second, with the head turned toward the north. Third, with the head turned toward the south, so that a cross may be formed in the immersion. For the person baptized is crucified to the world and fastened to Christ’s cross. [Note: [Col. 0331] Gal. 2, 6.]

Children receive a name in baptism because baptism takes the place of circumcision, in which the Hebrews give names to children, since Abraham’s name was changed at the time of circumcision: for whereas he had formerly been called Abram, [Note: [Col. 0331] Gen. 17.] he was afterward called Abraham. When the priest has lifted the child [Col. 0333A] from the font, let the godparents receive him; and while they hold him in their hands, let the priest anoint the crown of his head with chrism. In this he is, as it were, betrothed, and the Holy Spirit is given to him as a pledge (*arrhabo*). Pope Sylvester instituted this. [Note: [Col. 0333] William Durand cites this passage in the *Rationale*, book I, chapter 8, no. 10.]

For when the Church’s bosom was enlarged and bishops could not attend everyone through confirmation, it was instituted, lest they should perish without chrismal anointing, that priests should anoint them on the crown of the head, above the brain, where the seat of wisdom is. What is given here is the Spirit as a pledge; but in the subsequent confirmation, performed by the bishop, he is given for strength and increase of grace. If the person dies, grace gives an increase of glory proportionate to the grace received. Nevertheless, we believe that a person is saved by baptism alone even without anointing; but star differs from [Col. 0333B] star in glory. [Note: [Col. 0333] 1 Cor. 15.]

The priest uses these words in anointing: “Almighty God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has regenerated you from water and the Holy Spirit, and who has given you forgiveness of all sins, may he himself anoint you with the chrism of salvation unto eternal life.” The bishop, when confirming, uses similar words, saying: “Almighty, everlasting God, who have deigned to regenerate this your servant, or this your handmaid, from water and the Holy Spirit, and who have given him forgiveness of all sins, send upon him your sevenfold Paraclete Spirit from heaven.”

The bishop prays for those to be confirmed, drawing this from the Acts of the Apostles, where it is said: “When the apostles who were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received [Col. 0333C] the Word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When they had come, they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit. Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.” [Note: [Col. 0333] Acts 8.] From this it is inferred that bishops ought to go where there are people upon whom hands must be laid. And when they have come there, they should pray for them, saying: “Send upon them your sevenfold Spirit, your Holy Spirit the Paraclete, from heaven.” For, as Augustine says, none of the disciples gave them the Holy Spirit; rather, they prayed that he might come upon those on whom they laid hands.

Why he called him the sevenfold Spirit he explains next: “the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety”; and, “he filled him with the spirit of the fear of the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0333] Isa. 11.] The Prophet, [Col. 0333D] as Gregory says, spoke of Christ, who descended from the heavenly places to the lowest; but we, who strive from earthly things toward heavenly things, ought to number these stages in ascending order, so that we may arrive from fear at wisdom. “The fear of the Lord, therefore, is the beginning of wisdom.” [Note: [Col. 0333] Ps. 110.] This is the first stage of ascent.

But no fear is before the eyes of the Almighty which is not raised to piety: one who does not pity one’s neighbor and does not share in that neighbor’s tribulations does not possess it. Therefore the second stage is piety. But because piety sometimes consists in disordered or lax mercy—if, for example, it spares what ought not to be spared—it spares temporal punishment but builds up for Gehenna. Therefore the third stage is knowledge, which teaches what it ought to punish from justice and what it ought to remit from mercy. But what if one knows what ought to be done, yet lacks the power of acting rightly? Let knowledge therefore increase into the fourth stage, that of fortitude, [Col. 0334A] so that it may not tremble with fear but defend the good it perceives. But if fortitude is not prudent and is insufficiently watchful concerning vices, it falls by its very presumption. Let it therefore rise to the fifth stage, namely counsel, that it may foresee how to guard itself. But counsel is absent where understanding is lacking. Let us therefore rise to the sixth stage, namely understanding. But what if understanding is alert with great keenness? Let us rise to the seventh stage, namely wisdom, [Col. 0334B] so that wisdom may maturely moderate what understanding has discovered acutely. For wisdom pertains to life, just as knowledge pertains to teaching.

There follows: “I seal him with the sign of the cross, being propitiated unto eternal life.” I seal him, I say, so that he may not lose the Spirit. When this prayer is completed, as the Roman booklet says, the bishop shall make the cross with his thumb and chrism upon the foreheads of each person, saying: “I sign you with the sign of the cross; I confirm you with the chrism of salvation, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.”

Both priest and bishop anoint with the sign of the cross to show the sign by which we have been redeemed. We show it to the destroyer in the present, so that he may pass over our houses, [Note: [Col. 0333] Exod. 12.] and we shall show it to the Lord [Col. 0334C] in the future, so that he may number us among the redeemed. Therefore this sign is placed on the foreheads by bishops, both because what is fixed on the forehead seems more secure, and because there the high priest wore the golden plate with the ineffable name. [Note: [Col. 0333] Exod. 28.]

Chrismal anointing pertains to life and doctrine, the two things which, as we said, are joined in the seven gifts. The anointing is made with the thumb because in the consecration of a bishop he is spiritually consecrated for this purpose, or because every good gift descends from the Father of lights. [Note: [Col. 0333] Jas. 1.]

Bede, in his commentary on the Acts of the Apostles, [Note: [Col. 0333] Chapter 8.] proves from them that this laying on of hands is to be performed by bishops alone, as follows: Philip was one of the seven deacons; for if he had been an apostle, he could have laid hands on them so that they might receive [Col. 0334D] the Holy Spirit. For this belongs to bishops alone.

The bishop greets the anointed person, saying: “Peace be with you.” For this manner of greeting belongs to the new person, who has been created according to God in holiness and truth. [Note: [Col. 0333] Eph. 4.] This anointing is to be preserved for seven days and not washed off, because through this anointing the Holy Spirit comes to his guest in seven gifts; for his coming is also observed for the same number of days by his first guests. Or because the course of the present life is understood through the number seven. Let the anointing not be washed off for seven days, so that what Solomon says may be fulfilled in us: “At all times [Col. 0335A] let your garments be white, and let oil not fail from your head.” [Note: [Col. 0335] Eccl. 9.]

The baptized person is crowned with a mitre and clothed in a white garment, because he becomes a member of Christ the king and priest: through the mitre we understand the king’s crown, and through the white garment the priestly dignity. Or by the white garment we signify the robe of innocence, which we lost in the first parent but receive through Christ in baptism. “Clothed in white robes,” as the Apocalypse says, [Note: [Col. 0335] Chapter 4.] and likewise: “Blessed are those who wash their robes, that they may have authority in the book of life.” [Note: [Col. 0335] Rev. 22.]

This white garment is made of linen in the likeness of a cope. According to some, it has sewn upon it a red-edged fringe, representing the cord which Rahab let down through the window, [Note: [Col. 0335] Josh. 2, 6.] by whose sign she and all her house were saved. It signifies [Col. 0335B] the Passion of the Lord, which is the source of the baptism that saves.

According to some, shoes are also given to those being baptized; they are emblems of the Lord’s death, so that, following the example of Him who died for us, the baptized person may put his flesh to death with its vices and desires [Note: [Col. 0335] Gal. 5.]. Behold the younger son, namely the Gentile people, who had consumed his substance in luxurious living and fed the pigs of strangers in a far country, now returns; for him the father kills the fatted calf and gives a ring—that is, the seal of faith [Note: [Col. 0335] Luke 15.]—the faith which, as he professes to believe it, he is clearly shown to have inscribed on the tablets of his heart. The Father also clothes him with the first robe, according to the saying: “All of you who have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” [Note: [Col. 0335] Jer. 31; Heb. 8:10.]. These are the garments without which one who enters the king’s banquet will hear [Col. 0335C] the terrible voice: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” [Note: [Col. 0335] Matt. 22.]

It should be noted that, since the priest raises all from baptism, he is the father of all and is bound to teach all; thus Mark is said to have been Peter’s son. But because he could not attend to all and discharge the duties owed, he entrusts them to the care of sponsors or *competentes*. They are called *competentes* as though seeking baptism or faith together with the child; they are to make promises on their behalf and teach them the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, which all Christians are obliged to know, either in Latin or in their native language. Whoever does not know these is shown not to be a Christian. And when they have taught them these things, they must guard them as far as they can [Col. 0335D] lest they stray from faith or righteousness, being sureties for their faith and destined to answer for all their transgressions on the Day of Judgment.

Nor should it be doubted that one person is saved through another’s faith, or that catechumens are freed from demons through the confession of believers; for we read that the daughter of the Syrophoenician woman was freed from an unclean spirit through her mother’s confession [Note: [Col. 0335] Matt. 15.]. Augustine shows the reason for this, saying: “That someone may be regenerated through another’s ministry is effected by the one Spirit by whom the person presented is regenerated. For it is not written, ‘Unless one is born again from the will of parents or the faith of those presenting him,’ but ‘from water and the Holy Spirit’ [Note: [Col. 0335] John 3.]. Therefore the powerful sacrament of water, and the Spirit working within, accomplish the benefit of grace.”

The number of sponsors is as follows: one may suffice for all the sacraments; but because every word is established by the mouth of two or three witnesses [Note: [Col. 0335] Matt. 18.], there should be at most three, so that carnal union may be prevented through spiritual kinship [Note: [Col. 0335] By the Council of Trent only one is now admitted, or at most two, or one man and one woman.]. Some say that four kinds of persons should be barred from sponsorship: monks or nuns; unbelievers; half-believers, such as those not confirmed; likewise, a husband and wife together, unless they have made a vow of chastity. Relatives too are barred by some [Note: [Col. 0335] This impediment has now been removed by the said council.], since it is fitting that the love of charity be extended through baptism.

[Col. 0336B] Note that baptism is canonically administered twice in the year, and only on the Sabbath, which is interpreted “rest,” because eternal rest is bestowed through baptism [Note: [Col. 0335] This is to be understood of solemn baptism.]. Therefore let us celebrate baptism on the Paschal Sabbath, that we may be buried with Christ in his death; and on the Sabbath of Pentecost, that we may be worthy to receive the Holy Spirit in baptism. But let no one except a priest presume to baptize, because the canons forbid it. Yet something is often found outside the canons: those constrained by the necessity of illness, persecution, siege, or shipwreck may be baptized at any time and by anyone, even a layperson, provided they are baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and with simple water. If they survive, some maintain that afterward they should be catechized by a [Col. 0336C] priest. Whatever be the case concerning catechesis, they should be anointed with chrism on the forehead by a bishop.

For the apostles too baptized in this simplicity, namely in pools and springs, and solely in the name of the Trinity, whether expressed explicitly or implicitly—for example, in the name of Christ. But Clement, following Peter’s teaching, added the anointing with chrism and oil. Leo, Damasus, and Ambrose added other ceremonies, such as exorcisms and the like. It is not an idle question whether one may baptize in beer or mead, oil, wine, or another liquid. Some answer that it is permitted only in pure water. Further, if the water is muddy, or if it is lye, some say that baptism may be performed. But when another liquid—namely wine, oil, or some other liquid, such as “blavae” or “gomi” [uncertain readings]—mixed with water predominates over the water itself, baptism cannot be performed. Nor does it take place if immersion is not done together with the words—that is, if the words are said before or after, rather than while the person is immersed.

One is baptized in water because it is found more abundantly; because we read that the Spirit brooded over it in the beginning [Note: [Col. 0335] Gen. 1.]; and because it washes away filth, suppresses thirst, reflects an image, and extinguishes fire. Thus in baptism we are washed from the filth of sins, given drink from the fountain of life, restored to the lost image, and thereby the fire of punishments is extinguished. But the Gospel’s words, “He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit [Col. 0337A] and with fire” [Note: [Col. 0337] Matt. 3.], are understood as the spirit of sanctification and the fire of present tribulation; or of future purification; or as the fire of ardor by which the apostles were inflamed on the day of Pentecost [Note: [Col. 0337] Acts 2.]. We too are inflamed by the laying on of hands; this fire consumes wood, hay, and stubble [Note: [Col. 0337] 1 Cor. 3.], for our God is a consuming fire [Note: [Col. 0337] Deut. 4.], and it grants the warmth of eternal life and the light by which we may see things hidden from mortal eyes.

This canonical solemnity of baptism is celebrated at the ninth hour, because Christ is read to have expired at that hour [Note: [Col. 0337] Matt. 27.], and we were baptized into his death [Note: [Col. 0337] Rom. 6.]. At this hour also the angel came to Cornelius, announcing baptism to him [Note: [Col. 0337] Acts 10.]; at this hour the sheet full of animals appeared to Peter. Once the neophytes have been baptized, the lamps of the church and their candles should immediately be [Col. 0337B] lit, so that, with the lamps of good works, the children of the Church illuminated through Christ may reverently meet Christ. The neophytes’ candles ought not to have been lit before the Holy Spirit had purified their hearts. We customarily defer this illumination until the Office of the Mass, either because we believe that they are illuminated through the bishop’s laying on of hands, or because it is celebrated at night—which, just as it was illumined by the glory of the Resurrection, should likewise be illuminated by candlelight.

When the solemnity of baptism has been completed, according to some the bells are rung, and there is a procession to the fonts with a threefold litany. Observe that litanies are carried out around the baptistery both before and after baptism, because we read in the Apocalypse: “There was a rainbow around [Col. 0337C] the throne” [Note: [Col. 0337] Rev. 4.]. The rainbow signifies the intercessions of the saints, and the throne the Church, for which the saints preceding Christ’s advent and those following it have prayed and do pray most devoutly. This litany is made around the fonts as far as “Saint John, pray for us,” because he was the first baptizer. Then they return likewise with the threefold litany as far as “All saints, pray for us,” to show that all the saints pray for the baptized son, who was dead and has come to life, was lost and has been found [Note: [Col. 0337] Luke 15.], that he may share in the sacrament of baptism in the true faith of the Trinity, or that he may love with all his heart, all his mind, and all his strength the Lord whom he has confessed [Note: [Col. 0337] Matt. 22.].

Once baptism has been celebrated, priests may celebrate Mass, because at once the banquet of the evening sacrifice is prepared [Note: [Col. 0337] Ps. 140.], and for the son who has been found the fatted [Col. 0337D] calf is added [Note: [Col. 0337] Luke 15.]. This is Christ, who is called the calf because he was sacrificed for us, and therefore “fattened” because he is filled with the fullness of divinity [Note: [Col. 0337] Col. 2.]. The elder son, that is, the Jewish people, does not wish to attend this banquet, but stands outside and finds fault. Yet the Father will go out to him and urge him to enter the feast, when the remnant of Israel is converted and saved [Note: [Col. 0337] Rom. 11.].

Meanwhile the joy of the father’s house, that is, of the present Church, is not complete. For although the Jewish people have always hated the salvation of the Gentiles, the Church of Christians nonetheless grieves that its salvation should become an occasion of stumbling to its brother. Therefore certain ornaments [Col. 0338A] are omitted in so festive an Office: the introit, gradual, offertory, *Agnus Dei*, and communion. Or the introit is suppressed because our Head is still among the dead and has not yet been restored to us. Or the ancient custom is represented, when Masses had no introit. Thus this Office begins with *Kyrie eleison*, that joy over those reborn may be expressed; and remember that this was the custom of beginning Mass before Pope Celestine. *Gloria in excelsis Deo* follows because peace is granted in baptism to people of good will [Note: [Col. 0337] Luke 2.]. Hence the angels rejoice, because the tenth order of angels will be restored from among them. That *Gloria in excelsis* is a song of angels none doubts; with them the choir rejoices, harmonies resound, and the bells [Col. 0338B] ring out—until now, according to some, they had been silent.

There follows, “The Lord be with you,” not “Peace be with you,” and then the prayer is said: “O God, who makest this most sacred night …” Here it is established that this Mass should be celebrated either at night, or at least at sunset. Nor, as Jerome says, may the people awaiting Christ’s coming be dismissed before midnight, as will be said below: “And celebrate the feast-day in dense throngs unto the horn of the altar” [Note: [Col. 0337] Ps. 117.]. Nor should Mass be celebrated on this Saturday any more than in the preceding service, since the apostles are known to have kept silence and sorrowed on these days. It is similar on the Saturdays of ordinations: for the Mass on this day, as on those days, is not [Col. 0338C] of Saturday but belongs to Sunday.

Thereafter Paul addresses those reborn, saying: “If you have risen with Christ” [Note: [Col. 0337] Col. 3.]. Those who are baptized—that is, into the likeness of his death—also rise together in Christ, in whom their life is hidden and with whom they shall appear in glory. To represent this, the ministers of the altar put on solemn garments, or to display the robe of innocence of those reborn. The gradual is not sung because the baptized have not yet advanced by works in the virtues; or because Cyrus gave permission to return [Note: [Col. 0337] 1 Esd. 1.], and therefore without delay they burst into the voice of confession and praise, saying, “Alleluia, Alleluia.” What has been silent from Septuagesima is now restored, because, just as the hope of liberty was offered through Cyrus to the captives, so in baptism [Col. 0338D] and Christ’s Resurrection the joy of future life is promised to us. This Alleluia is the angels’ rejoicing over the baptized, who have obtained the Lord’s mercy.

Hence follows: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures for ever” [Note: [Col. 0337] Ps. 117.]. John in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0337] ch. 19.] shows that Alleluia is the song of angels, saying: “I heard, as it were, the voice of many trumpets in heaven, saying: Alleluia.” Or it is the rejoicing of the universal resurrection, for this psalm properly belongs to the day of Resurrection, where it says: “This is the day which [Col. 0339A] the Lord has made.”

But because great anxiety remained for those recalled from Babylonian captivity, and a great labor of good works remains for those reborn who have risen in the first resurrection [Note: [Col. 0339] Rev. 20.], so that they may have a share in the second resurrection—in which labor there remain fear and weeping, because of the danger of Gehenna, present sinfulness, and desire for eternal life—therefore after the Alleluia, which signifies joy in hope, follows the tract, which signifies mourning over sins and exile from the kingdom. For just as humanity passed from the joys of Paradise to the sadness of the world, from rest to sweat, so those reborn pass from the joy of remission to the wilderness of labor and to the tears of the upper and lower spring. It is not fitting to rejoice here without weeping, and this order is reversed and unusual.

[Col. 0339B] We do not customarily sing Alleluia with tracts but with graduals; and even then we put the gradual first and afterward add Alleluia, as on the following day. But here Alleluia precedes the tract because of the joy of those returning; in other cases the gradual comes first because of the progress of those advancing. Or Alleluia is put first in memory of Adam’s former state, and the tract follows in memory of his subsequent state. Or the Alleluia of the neophytes signifies their preceding purification, and the tract their subsequent defilement. Or Alleluia, a Hebrew word, precedes in dignity for those being instructed, because this language first praised God.

Up to this point the sacrifice concerned the neophytes, and the words of the Office were directed to them; but afterward the Resurrection is recalled to mind. For the Gospel [Col. 0339C] reads [Note: [Col. 0339] Matt. 28.] of the anxiety of the women seeking the Lord. Before this Gospel no light is carried, because the hour at which the Lord rose had not yet come, but he remained hidden amid the darkness of hell; or because the women believed him only mortal and went secretly to the tomb; or because of the blindness of those ignorant that he could rise. Incense, however, is carried, because the women bought spices in order to anoint Jesus when they came.

“I believe in one God” follows and is used frequently throughout the ensuing week, whereby those reborn affirm that they are tending toward God and most firmly believe the things said of Christ in the Gospel. The offertory, however, is not sung because the women, bringing spices in obedience to the commandment of the law, came silently and secretly to the tomb [Note: [Col. 0339] Luke 23.]. The Preface, “It is truly meet at all times …,” is plainly concerned with the Lord’s Resurrection; therefore it is sung both in this Mass and on the following days until the Ascension, except that here it says, “Especially on this most holy night”; tomorrow and within the octave it will say, “Especially on this most holy day”; after the octave it says, “It is truly meet at all times … but especially to proclaim thy glory more gloriously in this …”

“Holy, holy, holy” is not omitted, because the angels did not omit praise of the risen Lord but announced the Resurrection to the women. In the Canon [Col. 0340A] also, when “In communion with” is said, there is added: “And celebrating this most sacred night,” where the aforesaid alteration is likewise made. There also mention is made of those reborn, when it says: “This oblation, then, of our service, and also of all thy household, which we offer thee also for those whom thou hast deigned to regenerate by water and the Holy Spirit.”

The *Agnus Dei* is not sung because the apostles and women kept silent and believed that he was not the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world. Some, however, say three times, “Lamb of God, have mercy upon us.” “Grant us peace” is not to be said, nor is the peace to be given, either to avoid the kiss of the betrayer, or because Christ, who is our true peace [Note: [Col. 0339] Eph. 2.], had not yet announced peace, since he had not yet risen. Hence [Col. 0340B] on the day of Resurrection he said to the apostles: “Peace be with you” [Note: [Col. 0339] Luke 24.]. Perhaps for this reason the form of greeting by the bishop at the beginning of this Mass is deferred, that the people may receive the new greeting more affectionately on the day of its origin. Our custom, however, according to some, is that the peace is given for the same reason that *Gloria in excelsis Deo* is sung.

Here candles are lit because the baptized receive light through the Lamb who takes away sins [Note: [Col. 0339] John 1.], the darkness, as it were, of the world. Nor is the Communion sung, perhaps because the baptized do not communicate until the following day, or because the Vespers that follow take its place. Yet, although the singers are silent, the priest nonetheless performs his office, because while the women and apostles feared and doubted the Resurrection, the Lord worked [Col. 0340C] our salvation [Note: [Col. 0339] Ps. 75.].

After communion, Vespers are sung in place of the Communion as follows: the antiphon “Alleluia,” with the single and very brief psalm, “Praise the Lord, all nations” [Note: [Col. 0339] Ps. 116.]; and the antiphon of Vespers with the Gospel hymn, “My soul magnifies” [Note: [Col. 0339] Luke 1.], both without “Glory be to the Father and to the Son,” because the Son is not yet glorious. These Vespers are sung so briefly lest the neophytes, who are not yet accustomed to hear the Office, be wearied. Finally, the Mass is concluded with the prayer.

Vespers are sung before the prayer of the Mass lest, once Mass were finished, the people should seem to have permission to depart; or the entire Office is completed in one prayer because the sacrament of baptism is consummated in Christ’s Passion [Col. 0340D]; or this day ends in Mass, not in Vespers, so that Christ, who redeemed us by death, may be praised without end—he who is blessed for ever.

## CHAPTER XV. ON THE PASCHAL SOLEMNITY

“I have risen, and I am still with thee” [Note: [Col. 0339] Ps. 138.]. Today’s solemnity is called either the Resurrection of the Lord or Pascha. It is called Resurrection because on this day the Lord rose. But the question is asked whether the Lord rose in the night, or at what hour he rose. I reply, according to Jerome, Ambrose, and Greek tradition, that he chose the time of night.

For this is Samson, who, besieged by his enemies, carried off the gates by night and ascended to the summit of the mountain [Col. 0341A] [Note: [Col. 0341] Judg. 16.]. Samson means “their sun.” This is Christ, the Sun of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0341] Mal. 4.], who, besieged by guards and weapons, rising from the sleep of death in the middle of the night, took away from the gates of hell the right of death and ascended to the right hand of the Father. By rising at night he also intimates to us that at the Second Coming he will come like a thief in the night [Note: [Col. 0341] 1 Thess. 5.], as happened in the days of Noah and Lot [Note: [Col. 0341] Matt. 24.], when, while all were selling and buying, planting and building, sudden destruction came upon them. Thus he signified to us that we must always be ready; for just as he rose while people rested, so “at an hour when you do not expect him the Son of Man will come” [Note: [Col. 0341] Luke 12.].

And this is why, as stated above, [Col. 0341B] the people may not be dismissed until midnight, so that the Lord when he comes may find them watching. For just as the women did not give their eyes to sleep, but counted night as day, desire as light, and the moon as the sun, and, setting out in the evening, came to the tomb at dawn, while it was still dark, carrying spices [Note: [Col. 0341] John 20.], so faithful souls, watchful in mind and bearing the fragrances of virtues, hasten to Him who will come like a thief for judgment.

Some nevertheless say that he remained dead for forty hours, so that he might restore to life the four quarters of the world, dead under the Decalogue of the law. For there are two nights of his death—he who banished our two deaths—and one day that illumined the darkness. Augustine seems to agree with this, saying, “The Lord rose at dawn.” The Church also agrees, celebrating Matins at that same hour in honor of the Resurrection. There are forty hours: four evening hours of the Preparation, and thirty-six of two nights and one day. Yet whatever hour he rose, it is certain that he rose on this day, which, reckoned from the day of death, is by synecdoche the third day.

His death lasted three days, that he might blot out the sins of the three times, expending a single day of death for each time; or that he might obtain for us the propitiation of the undivided Trinity. Hence we are baptized with three immersions in the name of the Trinity. This is the three-day journey of the Hebrews, concerning which: “We shall go a journey of three days and sacrifice to our God” [Note: [Col. 0341] Exod. 5.]. Abraham [Col. 0341D] too, setting out to sacrifice Isaac, reached on the third day the place God had told him of [Note: [Col. 0341] Gen. 22.]. This is the triduum of which the Lord says: “Today and tomorrow I cast out demons and perform healings; on the third day I am consummated” [Note: [Col. 0341] Luke 13.].

The first day is that of penitence, on which he suffered; the second, of righteousness, on which he slept; the third, of recompense, on which he rose. Penitence torments, righteousness gives peace, recompense brings joy. These three days are signified by the three fifties of the Psalms; thus the first ends in penitence: “Have mercy [Col. 0342A] on me, O God” [Note: [Col. 0341] Ps. 50.]; the second in righteousness: “I will sing of mercy and judgment unto thee, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0341] Ps. 100.]; and the third in praise: “Let every spirit praise the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0341] Ps. 150.]. The Church represents these three days through the vigils, feasts, and octaves of saints.

The Lord also walked upon the earth for thirty-three years, in which he made the number three twofold: one part tenfold, the other within the bounds of a single unit. If, then, the number three is notable among philosophers because, after unity, it is the first of numbers that admit no division, it is still more notable among theologians, both because of the undivided Trinity and because of Christ’s earthly life, death, rest, and Resurrection.

He rose on this day, which is the first of the world and, returning to the beginning, the eighth—of which mention is made in [Col. 0342B] Chronicles [Note: [Col. 0341] 2 Chron. 7.] and in the titles of the Psalms. Just as the seven ages of the world precede this eighth, six of those ages being for wayfarers and one for sleepers, so seven days of our restoration precede this day. Likewise, just as seven Sundays from *Circumdederunt* to *Laetare Jerusalem* have preceded, as though with the memory of the Sunday of the Passion interposed, this Sunday follows as a representation of the eighth age. In it, just as the eighth is the same as the first, humanity will be restored to that same state for which it was created; indeed, it will be repaired to a dignity above that of its original creation and will attain the most blessed immortality of body and soul.

Perhaps this is signified by the eighth beatitude, which returns to the beginning—that is, to the first—because the reward of both is the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 0341] Matt. 5.]. Circumcision also signified this eighth, for the law commanded it on the eighth day [Note: [Col. 0341] Gen. 17; Lev. 12.]. The octaves of the saints, whose heavenly birthdays we observe, have the same reference; for we do not doubt that, having departed from their bodies, they receive the first robe, namely everlasting blessedness. We add octaves because they have been received into glorious immortality.

He rose on this day, which was the seventeenth of the first month. The first month among the Hebrews is Nisan, that is, April; they reckon the months by the course of the moon repeated twelve or thirteen times. There are two kinds of year: the common and the embolismic. The common year has twelve lunations; the embolismic thirteen. He rose in the first month, on a growing day, [Col. 0342D] because through his Resurrection the darkness of death began to diminish and the day of life began to increase, and because he is Light from Light, through whom one comes to the day of eternal light. He rose on the seventeenth day of the moon, so that through observance of the Decalogue he might bring us to the eternal rest of the Sabbath. Therefore he rose when the moon seeks the heights, to signify that the Church ought safely to seek things above and ascend the temples of heaven. He rose in the third week of the moon, thereby signifying that the third era, namely that of grace, had arrived.

Hence, although we always celebrate this solemnity in the April lunation and at the full moon by the Lord’s command, we celebrate it sometimes in our April and sometimes in March. But when we establish it after twelve lunations, it is indicated that through the ten commandments of the law and the two commandments of charity we shall attain the glory of the Resurrection. When we observe it after thirteen lunations, it is indicated that through the Decalogue and faith in the Trinity we shall attain the glory of eternity. Note that, whereas the Jews have a fixed Paschal term on the fourteenth moon, we celebrate the Lord’s Day on the following Sunday: both, as Augustine says, that our feast may differ from the Jewish feast, and because by an angel’s command we are instructed to celebrate this feast on Sunday.

This solemnity [Col. 0343B] is called *Pascha*.
