It is a noun of the first declension and neuter gender, a feature found in only three Greek nouns: *Pascha*, *manna*, and *mammona*; or it is of the third declension, so that it is called *Pascha, paschatis*, as one says *phantasma, phantasmatis*. *Phase* is Hebrew; *Pascha* Greek; in Latin, “passage” or “crossing.” In naming this solemnity we use Greek, not Hebrew, although Hebrew is more dignified, lest we seem to Judaize. Again, we use Greek rather than Latin because of its authority: in ancient Italy Greek possessed such authority that feasts and dignities were called by Greek names—feasts such as Pascha, Pentecost, Epiphany, and Hypapante; dignities such as bishop, archbishop, and apostolic.

Or, according to Augustine, the name *Pascha* was fashioned by divine disposition from Greek *paschein*, meaning “to suffer,” and Hebrew *phase*, interpreted “passage.” These two meanings suitably meet in the name, because in the Lord’s Passion was his passage. Therefore, from the day when the Lamb was enclosed for sacrifice—that is, from Palm Sunday until the octave of Pascha—the whole period is called Pascha. Yet according to popular custom, Palm Sunday is called “Flowering Pascha,” Friday *Phase*, and today Pascha.

Pascha is understood historically, allegorically, tropologically, and anagogically. Historically, when Passover is read to have been celebrated, the destroying angel passed through Egypt and killed the firstborn in those houses whose doorposts he did not find smeared with the lamb’s blood in the form of Tau [Col. 0343D] [Note: [Col. 0343] Exod. 12.]. Then too the people of Israel passed, that is, went out, from Egypt, and on the third day crossed the Red Sea [Note: [Col. 0343] Exod. 14.]. Allegorically, the Church passes through baptism from unbelief to faith. Tropologically, the soul must pass through confession and contrition from vice to virtue. Anagogically, Christ passed from mortality to immortality, from death to life, from hell’s confines to the joys of paradise, so that he might cause us to pass from this world’s misery to eternal joys.

This solemnity, by whatever name it is called, is the solemnity of solemnities. Just as “Holy of holies” and “Song of songs” are said because they surpass [Col. 0344A] other holy things and songs, so it is called the solemnity of solemnities because the nobility of this solemnity surpasses all other solemnities. Therefore every emblem of joy is displayed. The church is cleansed and adorned—in its walls, choir, altar, and ministers. On the walls curtains and wholly silk hangings are stretched; in the choir, backs of seats, carpets, and bench-coverings are arranged. The veil that was before the cross is either raised high, removed, or placed behind the altar, because things formerly hidden are now manifest.

The altar too is adorned with its ornaments: banners; crosses, which according to some signify the victory of Jesus Christ; Gospel-books; phylacteries—that is, vessels of silver, gold, ivory, any metal, or precious stone—in which relics are deposited. This was established against Helvidius, who mocked the faithful because they preserved the ashes of saints. Against him the Church ordained that they should be kept honorably, as it were the Ten Commandments, namely in precious vessels bearing a similar name. For a *phylactery*, *phylacterii*, is the little sheet upon which the Pharisees carried the Ten Commandments, and it is said to derive from *phylaxe*, “to keep,” and *Thorath*, “law”; hence the Gospel says: “They enlarge their phylacteries and magnify their fringes” [Note: [Col. 0343] Matt. 23.]. A phylactery is a vessel in which saints’ relics are placed, and is said to derive from *phylaxe*, “to keep,” and *teron*, “end,” because something from the extremities, such as a tooth, a finger, or something similar, is preserved.

The altar is vested in precious cloths. In some churches three-colored veils are placed upon it: black, whitish, and red, to signify three periods. Black signifies the time before the law and is removed when the first lesson and its responsory end. Whitish, signifying the time under the law, is removed at the second lesson; red, signifying Christ’s Passion, at the third. This adornment of the church, so great and of such a kind, spiritually signifies the adornment of our own temple.

The ministers also, for the beauty of this solemnity, wash beforehand in baths, shave their beards and crowns—that is, their tonsures—and cut their hair; they lay aside black garments and put on white. Although these are done for beauty, they are also referred to the spiritual person. For we are not washed for pleasure but for signification. By outward washing we signify purification of the soul. The shaving of hairs, which are superfluities of the stomach, is the laying aside of superfluities. To cut the hair above the ears is to prepare the five bodily senses for service to the Lord. To bare the sole is to remove what lies between us and God. To take off the black garment is to lay aside the harshness of penitence; to put on white garments is steadfastly to await the robe of immortality. Or by white garments we signify the robe of innocence of those reborn, or represent today’s appearance of the angels [Note: [Col. 0343] Mark 16.].

Behold, in a church so gloriously adorned, ministers so fittingly [Col. 0345A] arrayed come to the Office. Celebrating the nocturnal Office, they use three psalms to represent the works of the three days which the Lord promised [Note: [Col. 0345] Luke 13.]: namely, to cast out demons, perform healings, and be consummated on the third day. Of the first the first antiphon says, “My counsel is not with the ungodly,” and the psalm, “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly” [Note: [Col. 0345] Ps. 1.]. Of the second, the second says, “He has given me the nations,” and the psalm, “I will give thee the nations” [Note: [Col. 0345] Ps. 2.]. Of the third, the third antiphon with its psalm says, “I slept” [Note: [Col. 0345] Ps. 3.]. The first separates from the ungodly; the second joins us to the Head; the third causes us to rise through justification.

In the exorcized, the first casts out the devil by renunciation; in them the second performs healing through faith; the third justifies them through the laying on [Col. 0345B] of hands. Therefore we use these three psalms to signify these three things granted to us: renunciation of the devil, union with the Head, and justification of minds. Or they signify that, by works of faith, hope, and charity, the works of darkness are repelled from us: namely, the devil’s suggestion, the flesh’s delight, and the mind’s consent. Or they represent the three-day burial which preceded the Resurrection by day. Or rather, the three psalms signify the three periods; the three antiphons are sung, in which patriarchs, prophets, and apostles are signified; three lessons are read because law, psalms, and prophecies profess the Lord’s Resurrection; three responsories follow because the three orders, Noah, Job, and Daniel, are saved by Christ’s Resurrection.

After each responsory, *Gloria Patri* is added in some churches, because the Trinity is praised by all orders. In others, however, only one *Gloria* is continued through the three responsories, according to the general custom. Or we everywhere employ the number three because of the sacrament of baptism, celebrated in the name of three Persons. Or few lessons are used because of the few preachers present at that time. For the apostles were few in number, silent from fear of the Jews, saddened by the Lord’s death, and almost beside themselves at the news of the Resurrection [Note: [Col. 0345] John 20; Luke 24.]. Some wish to retain this small number until Pentecost, when they became more numerous preachers and more fervent through the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0345] Acts 2.]. Others, attending rather to the solemnity, retain the full and solemn number, because even if the apostles were silent, the speech of angels and the Lord’s frequent appearances were not lacking.

When the third responsory has been sung with the *Gloria*, we proceed from the choir with candles and solemnity to some place where we arrange an imaginary sepulchre. There persons are introduced representing the women and the two disciples John and Peter, who came to the Lord’s tomb seeking him; and certain other persons represent the angels, who declared that Christ had risen from the dead [Note: [Col. 0345] John 20.]. [Col. 0346A] In the persons of these angels the following portion of the second responsory may fittingly be sung: “Do not be afraid,” and the remainder to the end of the responsory. Then they return to the choir, as though reporting to the brethren what they had seen and heard; in their persons that responsory, “Rejoice together,” is suitably sung, without a verse. If anyone has verses composed concerning this representation, though they are not authentic, we do not disapprove of them. Then the choir, having heard of Christ’s resurrection, bursts forth in a loud voice, singing: “We praise thee, O God.” Some perform this representation before beginning Matins; but this is its proper place, because the *Te Deum laudamus* expresses the hour at which the Lord rose. Our priest, however, censes the cross before Matins [Col. 0346B], sprinkles it with blessed water, and three times says aloud before the altar: “Christ our Lord has risen from the dead”; and the choir responds: “Thanks be to God.” Afterwards follows the antiphon, “Christ rising”; the versicle, “Say among the nations”; and the prayer, “Look upon [us].”

Afterwards the cross is to be placed in its own place, while the antiphon “Above all things” is sung; then Matins Lauds are to be sung. That the psalms sung at Matins Lauds pertain to the resurrection has been made clear by the preceding discussion. At Prime, however, some say the entire psalm, “Give thanks to the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0345] Psalm 117], because it pertains especially to the resurrection; others say only the verse, “This is the day.” We also use this verse at this and the other hours [Col. 0346C] as a chapter, because we signify that life in which teaching will be needed by no one [Note: [Col. 0345] Jer. 31; Heb. 8], but all, being taught, shall rejoice and exult. “Whosoever will” is not said, because this time signifies the octave, where there will be no faith—which shall be done away—but the reality which shall be apprehended. For the same reason the shorter Creed is omitted at Prime, namely, “I believe in God,” because “when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away” [Note: [Col. 0345] I Cor. 13]. The intercessions also are omitted, because where there will be no misery, mercy need not be sought; where there will be no temptation, it will not be necessary to say, “Deliver us from evil.”

That a procession is held on this day is derived from the authority of the Gospel: the angels say to the women, “Go, tell the disciples, for he will go before [Col. 0346D] you into Galilee” [Note: [Col. 0345] Mark 16]; and the Lord says to them, “Tell my brethren to go into Galilee; there they shall see me” [Note: [Col. 0345] Matt. 28]. Galilee is called “transmigration”; to go into Galilee was to pass from the Jews to the Gentiles. Concerning this migration he later said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0345] Ibid.]. To signify this migration, today we make a solemn procession; and to signify baptism, we sprinkle ourselves and the places with blessed water. Yet it is not blessed today, nor at Pentecost, because it is taken from the font for reservation before [Col. 0347A] chrism is poured in and before anyone is immersed. Nor do we sprinkle in order to be rebaptized, but in order to invoke the grace of the divine Name in remembrance of baptism.

Water also signifies purity of life; and the lights which go before in the procession signify good works, so that the Gospel saying may be fulfilled in us: “Let your loins be girded and lamps burning in your hands” [Note: [Col. 0347] Luke 12]. The cross likewise goes before, so that we may crucify the flesh with its vices and desires [Note: [Col. 0347] Gal. 5]. During the sprinkling we sing “I saw water,” which is taken from Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0347] ch. 47]. The Lord showed him a city built upon a mountain and sloping southward, in which was a wonderful temple. The city is the Church, of which it is said: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” [Note: [Col. 0347] Matt. 5]. The temple [Col. 0347B] is Christ’s body, concerning which he says: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” [Note: [Col. 0347] John 2]. The water proceeding from the temple is the font of baptism proceeding from Christ’s side [Note: [Col. 0347] John 19].

But if he was pierced on the left side, why is it said here that it came forth from the right side? I answer: Christ has two sides, right and left. The right is his divinity; the left, his humanity. It therefore came forth from the right side, because from Christ’s divine nature proceeds the Holy Spirit, the invisible water; he grants saving power to the visible water which flowed from the left side—that is, from his pierced humanity. Rightly, then, in this procession we sing this in praise of that river, by whose flooding we came to life through Christ’s death. [Col. 0347C]

This procession is celebrated in the following order: crosses go before, and banners, which are the insignia of Jesus Christ’s victory. Then white-clad priests go before, exulting in praises of the resurrection, while the following people await with such expectation, through distinct and unhurried stations, that that prophetic saying may seem to be fulfilled bodily: “You shall go out with gladness and be led forth with joy” [Note: [Col. 0347] Isa. 55]. “For the mountains and hills shall leap with joy while awaiting you.” In this procession nothing from the old history is to resound; only those things are to be sung which proclaim the glory of the Gospel. Among these especially admitted is: “With great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection of Jesus” [Note: [Col. 0347] Acts 4], because, as we have said, migration into Galilee is the apostles’ preaching.

When the middle [Col. 0347D] of the church is reached, with people of both sexes standing around, the choir should with all its strength burst into a voice of exultation, singing the antiphon “The angel sat,” which expresses what the apostles taught—namely, that Christ lives. It must be sung with all strength and offered to the hearing of those standing around, because “their sound went forth into all the earth” [Note: [Col. 0347] Psalm 18]. Or today’s procession recalls to us that the King of glory migrated with the army of the redeemed from the prison-houses of hell to the heavenly kingdoms.

And observe that on this day, as the apostolic [figure] proceeds, tow is kindled above his head, which is quickly reduced to ashes, so that he may remember [Col. 0348A] that he himself must be reduced to ashes, his adornment turned into dust, and that the glory of the world will likewise pass away in a moment. From today’s procession all Sunday processions have derived their origin. In them too the head is followed by the members, and only matters from the New Testament are to be sung. But during sprinkling after Pentecost the antiphon “Thou shalt sprinkle me, O Lord” is to be said, which the prophet foretold concerning faith in the Passion and the humility of baptism [Note: [Col. 0347] Psalm 50].

Know also that the sprinkling of salt and water took its beginning from Elisha, who, mixing salt with water, cleansed its defect of barrenness [Note: [Col. 0347] IV Kings 2]. In remembrance of this, and also of the legal sprinkling performed with the blood of the lamb, we are sprinkled, so that through faith in the true blood we may be delivered and made stronger in good works [Note: [Col. 0347] Exod. 24; Heb. 9]. In processions of this kind, held throughout the year on Sundays, we ought more frequently to salute the Virgin and sing something that pertains especially to her. Hence the custom has grown up that monasteries should have an oratory of the Virgin, whom at the first station we salute according to the primary custom.

Although it is said that the risen Christ first appeared to Magdalene [Note: [Col. 0347] Mark 16], it is more truly believed that he appeared before all others to his Mother. Yet it did not belong to the Evangelists to say this: their office was to introduce witnesses of the resurrection, whereas it was not fitting to introduce the Mother as a witness for her Son. For if the words of unrelated women seemed madness [Note: [Col. 0347] Luke 24], how much more would they have thought that his mother was mad through love for her Son? [Col. 0348C] It is therefore more truly believed that the risen Son appeared first to his Mother; but she, as she had done from the beginning, “kept all these words, pondering them in her heart” [Note: [Col. 0347] Luke 2]. If this were not believed because it is attested by none of the Evangelists’ testimonies, it would follow that after the resurrection he did not appear to his Mother at all, since no one explains where or when. But far be it that such a Son should have dishonoured his Mother by so harsh a neglect!

The Roman Church does not think so. On the first day of Easter it holds its station at Blessed Mary’s, as though setting forth Jerusalem—that is, the Virgin—who saw peace before others at the beginning of her joy [Note: [Col. 0347] Psalm 136]. Therefore, just as on the first day the service is assigned to St Mary, so in her honour the first station in Sunday processions is appointed there, so that, extolling her in praises and hastening to her oratory, we may seem to say with the Bridegroom: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of incense” [Note: [Col. 0347] Song 4]. The mountain is the Blessed Virgin Mary, from whom the stone cut without hands is hewn [Note: [Col. 0347] Dan. 2], and that stone is joined to the plants of mortification and prayer. The Son goes to her by appearing, and we go to her by worshipping. That we go from the choir to some altar and there make a station signifies that souls shall go to Christ and sing in harmony among the companies of angels.

Let us now proceed with the office of the Mass, which directs its attention to that day of eternity, whose entrance God opened through [Col. 0349A] his Only-begotten Son after death had been conquered. He who answered the Father saying, “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp,” with “I will arise at dawn” [Note: [Col. 0349] Psalm 56], because he rose first, the firstfruits of those who sleep [Note: [Col. 0349] I Cor. 15]—the precentor sends forth the first note through the mouths of the prophets, saying to the Father: “I have risen, and am still with thee” [Note: [Col. 0349] Psalm 138].

Through the resurrection of this head the entrance of paradise lies open, as the first prayer shows. Though this is a feast of praise, a priestly prayer is nevertheless added amid the praises. Praise has joy; prayer has groaning. Something has been promised us, but we do not yet possess it. Because he who promised is true, we rejoice; because we do not possess it, we groan; and we pray in order that we may possess it. Paul invites and instructs the neophytes in the newness of this song [Note: [Col. 0349] I Cor. 5], that, having purged out in baptism [Col. 0349B] the old leaven, they may so preserve the newness of the dough that they attain to the newness of resurrection.

The gradual, “This is the day” [Note: [Col. 0349] Psalm 117], since it is the lament of those being delivered, does not seem fittingly sung on that day on which eternal joy is represented. But why it is sung during this week we explained above when discussing Septuagesima. Here we add that the gradual is sung because of the baptized, since they have undertaken the toil of warfare, in order to attain the Alleluia of eternal joy. Great and grievous toil remains for them if they are to have a share in the second resurrection; and the gradual is sung for six days, because of the number six of works. Thereafter Alleluia is continued; but because in this labour we have hope of future joy and the joy of present righteousness, [Col. 0349C] therefore, although the chant is solemn, its words bid us exult—both in it and in its verses, which are distributed throughout the whole week.

There is the day of time, whence: “Today, if you hear his voice” [Note: [Col. 0349] Psalm 94], that is, if you hear it during the time in which you live; and there is the day of eternity, whence: “One day in thy courts is better than thousands” [Note: [Col. 0349] Psalm 83]. Today’s feast begins this day; therefore it is rightly said demonstratively, “This is the day,” and “Today the Lord rose.” But while this day is at dawn, or in its ascent, it is called the day of salvation and grace. When it is at noon, it will be called the day of eternity and glory. It will know no decline; therefore this solemnity has no Vespers: Alleluia. “Our Pasch”—as though it said, “Praise the Lord”—“for Christ our Pasch has been sacrificed” [Note: [Col. 0349] I Cor. 5].

The Gospel according to Mark is read [Note: [Col. 0349] ch. 16], both because it bears the figure of the Lion, so that it might proclaim the roar of the rising Lion, and because it describes a young angel clothed in a white robe. In this is indicated the youthfulness of the baptized, which shall be renewed like the eagle’s [Note: [Col. 0349] Psalm 75] and shall be without spot or wrinkle [Note: [Col. 0349] Eph. 5]. The offertory, “The earth trembled” [Note: [Col. 0349] Psalm 75], is spoken either of the earthquake that occurred when the Lord rose, or of that day when he will make judgment heard—namely: “Come, ye blessed,” and “Depart, ye cursed” [Note: [Col. 0349] Matt. 25]. Then the earth trembled—that is, the impious shall be terrified—[Col. 0350A] because “the powers of heaven shall also be moved” [Note: [Col. 0349] Luke 21], and the earth shall rest, that is, the impious shall cease to do harm.

The communion, like the Alleluia, is taken from the epistle [Note: [Col. 0349] I Cor. 5]. Some say that “I have risen” is the Bridegroom’s voice to the bride, consoling her in the present time concerning his death, to whom the bride replies: “Thou hast placed.” The remaining words are the harmony of angels and human beings rejoicing in Christ’s resurrection; or it is the voice of the human race, which fell in Adam and rose through Christ.

Observe that the sacrifice of this day is twofold: evening and morning. The evening sacrifice was celebrated in the night; the morning sacrifice in the day, because today’s solemnity has a twofold cause: the redemption of souls, prepared on the evening of Parasceve by Christ’s death; and the resurrection of bodies, confirmed on the first [Col. 0350B] day of the Sabbath when Christ rose. Observe also that on this day the Lamb is blessed; according to the Roman order, it is to be blessed not at the altar but at the table.

At the canonical hours, from today until the octave of Pentecost, we always say Alleluia with the responsories and their verses. Finally, although all the aforesaid canonical hours bear the marks of newness, the evening synaxis—that is, gathering—is distinguished above the rest by the brightness of this feast. We do not begin it with “O God, come to my aid,” because in that life we shall not need help as we do here. Rather, it begins with *Kyrie eleison*, because baptism at the evening hour of Easter Saturday began with *Kyrie eleison* and was celebrated in the name of the Trinity. Therefore, at the same hour and in the same words, throughout this whole week the Holy Trinity is adored in the joy of festal regeneration. [Col. 0350C]

Or it begins with *Kyrie eleison* so that, as an office not existing independently, it may be contained within the office of the Mass. For, as we have said, this day has no Vespers, because eternity knows no decline. Three psalms are said under one Alleluia, because through faith in the Trinity one comes to the eternal Alleluia, that is, joy; or these three psalms suit the resurrection of Jesus Christ, which occurred on the third day. As the chapter there follows “This is the day,” as at the other hours, because there teaching will not be needed, but exultation; or in order to mark the solicitude of the baptized, who are still pilgrims and labouring, because they do not yet possess [Col. 0350D] joy except in hope, by which they will attain the Alleluia of reality. In place of the hymn follows Alleluia, which is the proper hymn of those citizens.

After the *Magnificat* with its antiphon, and after the prayer has been said, they proceed to salute the cross, through which and in which we have obtained the redemption of souls.

Then they proceed with jubilation to the font, where two psalms are sung, because by a twofold love one reaches the font of life. These psalms also suit the baptized and baptism. They suit the baptized in “Praise the Lord, ye children” [Note: [Col. 0349] Psalm 112], which is sung around the fonts [Col. 0351A] and is an exhortation to praise addressed to the neophytes, who have become children—that is, pure from vices. For them Mother Church exults at the fonts in praise of that grace through which she deserved to become what she heard in the song of love: “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters” [Note: [Col. 0351] Song 4].

Afterwards they proceed to the oratory of St Andrew with the psalm, “When Israel went forth” [Note: [Col. 0351] Psalm 113], which suits baptism when it says: “What aileth thee, O sea, that thou fleddest?” [Note: [Col. 0351] Ibid.]. They go to St Andrew because “the mountain leaped like a ram” [Note: [Col. 0351] Ibid.]; Gregory was spiritually devoted to him, and therefore built a church for him.

By going solemnly in procession to the font for seven days, we recall the passage of Israel through the Red Sea [Note: [Col. 0351] Exod. 14]. Israel remained by the shore for seven days and came each day to [Col. 0351B] the shore, singing to the Lord the song of Moses. Or this signifies the passage through the Jordan, performed in order; or the evening processions of this week signify the return from Babylonian captivity [Note: [Col. 0351] I Esdr. 1]. For this is the week of those returning, who at the end of their captivity shall return to the Lord. Thus Vespers are completed with a threefold station, just as baptism here is celebrated in the name of the Trinity.

Those who have no fonts should not go out, but should say five psalms continuously and, after the collect of the day, add a collect of the cross. These same Vespers are repeated every day, because the entire week is reckoned as one and the same day. It is also noteworthy that from Easter until after Pentecost we do not bend the knee, but pray standing, so that we may profess the freedom which the Lord acquired for us by rising. [Col. 0351C] For the women too did not fall down at the angelic vision, but merely bowed their faces [Note: [Col. 0351] Luke 24]. We likewise omit the intercessions, because there will be no supplication of the wretched, but only praise of the blessed; similarly on Sundays and feasts, on which our resurrection and fellowship with angels are represented.

But this is the practice among canons; among certain monks the practice concerning the intercessions is otherwise, as it is concerning readings and stations. For they neither restrict themselves to three readings, nor, although they have no fonts, dispense with the solemnities of the fonts, nor delight in evening stations. These are pontifical traditions and pertain to the shepherds of the people.

[Col. 0351D] All Christians ought freely to assemble for the aforesaid offices of this day, to acclaim the glory of the resurrection which shall be revealed in us [Note: [Col. 0351] Rom. 8]. This solemnity, therefore, is the Christians’ jubilee, in which those at discord are reconciled, offences are forgiven, those who have sinned are restored to communion, and debts are not exacted. Workshops are not to be opened, wares are not to be displayed, except those without which a meal cannot be provided. Captives are to be released; shepherds and servants are not to be compelled to service, so that they may enjoy liberty and delight in the feast of future joy.

Hence in the cloisters of certain churches even bishops [Col. 0352A] with their clergy employ “December liberty,” descending even to the game of dancing or ball, although not playing is more praiseworthy. It is called December liberty because in December, among the Gentiles, shepherds, male servants, and maidservants were granted a certain liberty by their masters, and their masters feasted with them at tables set together.

Observe that paganism instituted dances for the applause of idols, so that people might praise their gods with their voices and serve them with their whole bodies, wishing also by them to figure something of mystery in their own manner. For by circling they understood the revolution of the firmament; by joining hands, the union of the heavens; by the melodies of singers, the harmonies of the planets; by bodily gestures, the movements of signs or planets; and by clapping [Col. 0352B] hands and stamping feet, the crashes of thunder. But what they rendered to their idols, worshippers of the one God have turned to his praises. For it is read that the people, after coming forth from the Red Sea, led a dance, and that Mary sang before them with a timbrel [Note: [Col. 0351] Exod. 15]; David danced with all his strength before the ark and sang psalms with a harp [Note: [Col. 0351] II Kings 6]; and Solomon appointed singers around the altar, who are said to have rendered songs with voice, trumpet, cymbals, organs, and other musical instruments [Note: [Col. 0351] II Chron. 5].

But since this solemnity signifies that octave which follows the sevenfold course of this life, why does it have octaves, when its celebration is extended not merely through eight days but even until Pentecost? The answer is that the future resurrection [Col. 0352C] was signified by circumcision, commanded on the eighth day [Note: [Col. 0351] Gen. 17]. To true circumcision correspond eight beatitudes [Note: [Col. 0351] Matt. 5], of which the eighth returns to the first, so that, as it were upon the Lord’s harp—of which it is said, “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” [Note: [Col. 0351] Psalm 56]—the heavenly diapason may sound. Therefore, to represent these beatitudes, we celebrate the octaves of the Lord’s resurrection with solemn offices lasting eight days. This resurrection is both the cause and the sign of our future circumcision.

Augustine, in his book *On Christian Doctrine*, adapts these beatitudes to the seven spirits, omitting the last because it returns to the first. “Fear,” he says, “produces poverty,” that is, humility: for while we fear eternal death, we fasten the movements of pride to the wood of the cross [Col. 0352D]. Piety produces meekness: while we worship God—which is the office of *theosebia*, “worship of God”—we become gentle and submit ourselves to Holy Scripture. Knowledge produces mourning: for “he who increases knowledge increases sorrow” [Note: [Col. 0351] Eccl. 1]. Fortitude produces endurance in adversities, so that we may always hunger and thirst for righteousness [Note: [Col. 0351] Matt. 5]. Counsel produces mercy, when one has mercy upon another who would wish another to have mercy upon himself. Understanding cleanses the eye of the mind, so that the pure in heart may see God [Note: [Col. 0351] Ibid.]. Wisdom makes peace in the breast, so that one may attain the peace of eternity. Behold how, by stages, one comes from fear to wisdom. Hence: “The fear [Col. 0353A] of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” [Note: [Col. 0353] Psalm 110].

Therefore baptismal offices are celebrated for seven days, either because the baptized are enriched by the sevenfold Spirit, or because the entire course of time itself revolves in a sevenfold number of days. Since faith, hope, and charity are especially necessary for them, we use three psalms at Matins; but thereafter they are multiplied, so that good habits of diverse works may be accumulated. Or we celebrate an office of one colour for seven days, so that we may refer the whole course of our life to the death and resurrection of the Lord. For as day represents the resurrection, so night represents the Lord’s death. The Lord rose on one day, yet for seven days we say, “On this day especially,” and “This is the day.” Christ’s death was one, prolonged through three days, [Col. 0353B] yet through seven nights we say three psalms and three readings.

He sings three psalms at night who holds himself in mind to be buried with Christ and dead to sin, who does not commit sin [Note: [Col. 0353] Rom. 6]. He sings “This is the day” for seven days who perseveres in justification. Let us now adapt the offices of individual days to these spirits and beatitudes.

Thus the office of Sunday itself, the Resurrection, pertains to fear, by which we fear the dreadful sentence of the Judge. For when the King and Judge of all says to the Father, “I have risen, and am still with thee” [Note: [Col. 0353] Psalm 138], in reproach of his enemies who say, “When shall he die and his name perish?” [Note: [Col. 0353] Psalm 40], then there will be great fear and trembling. Hence also, in the offertory: “The earth trembled” [Note: [Col. 0353] Psalm 75]. Here the spirit and foundation of fear is laid, [Col. 0353C] upon which one builds firmly. For it is the first of the seven steps by which, according to Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0353] ch. 40], one ascends to the eastern gate.

But one may ask why, beginning with fear, we end in wisdom, whereas Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0353] ch. 11] began with wisdom and descended to fear. But Isaiah, in saying this, described the Saviour and descended from what is highest. We, however, seek to rise from earthly to heavenly things; therefore we must count the steps in ascending order, so that we may arrive from fear at wisdom. And because this spirit, as we have said, produces humility, the station is at St Mary’s, who was queen of the humble, whence she says: “He hath regarded the humility of his handmaiden” [Note: [Col. 0353] Luke 1].

[Col. 0353D] On Monday the Gospel is read [Note: [Col. 0353] Luke 24] concerning the two disciples going to Emmaus, to whom the Lord opened the Scriptures of Moses and all the prophets. Corresponding to it is the reading from the Acts of the Apostles, where it is said: “To him all the prophets bear witness” [Note: [Col. 0353] Acts 10]. In this Gospel the Lord proves that his Passion was necessary for the human race. By pretending to go farther, he showed himself to them in body as he was in their minds; and by this example strangers are to be constrained [to stay], and bread is to be blessed in the Church. For him whom they did not recognize in the exposition of Scripture, [Col. 0354A] they recognized in the breaking of bread, because not hearers but doers of the law shall be justified [Note: [Col. 0353] Rom. 2], and truth is understood better by doing than by hearing.

Observe that although the Gospel concerning the Lord’s appearance is read today, this appearance occurred not today but yesterday. For ten appearances of Christ after the resurrection are found in the Gospels: five on the very day, and five afterwards. Moreover, the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0353] I Cor. 15] that he appeared to James and to five hundred brethren at once. Some say that on that first day he also appeared to his Mother, to James, who had vowed not to eat, and to Joseph, who was imprisoned on his account.

From the Gospel are taken the Alleluia, “Morning,” and the offertory, “The angel,” because it says there that the women saw visions of angels, who say [Col. 0354B] that he lives; likewise the communion, “He has risen,” because it says: “The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon.” This office, therefore, pertains to piety, in which the remembrance of the Scriptures is contained; and through piety one comes to meekness. To the meek, moreover, is promised that land of which it is said: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” [Note: [Col. 0353] Matt. 5]—the land, namely, flowing with milk and honey. Hence also in the introit: “The Lord has brought you into a land flowing with milk and honey” [Note: [Col. 0353] Exod. 13]. These are the words of Moses leading the people from Egypt after the eating of the lamb. He brought them in, I say, in hope; but he also brought them in reality into that land which Caleb gave to his daughter Achsah [Note: [Col. 0353] Josh. 15], watered by the upper and lower springs. The lower spring is fear; the upper, love. For Caleb, whose name is interpreted as “heart,” gives [Col. 0354C] devotion to the soul together with fear and love.

Today’s station is at St Peter’s, either because, as the Virgin was an example to the humble, so Peter was an example to the meek; or because God gave him both springs in more abundant grace: the lower, when after his threefold denial he wept bitterly [Note: [Col. 0353] Matt. 26]; the upper, when the risen Lord appeared to Simon, as is read in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0353] Luke 24] and sung in the communion.

On Tuesday the Gospel, “Jesus stood” [Note: [Col. 0353] Ibid.], is read. It says that with these words, “Peace be unto you,” the Lord greeted the apostles; and “may it be” or “it is” is understood. For this was his first utterance to the disciples after the resurrection. Therefore his vicar uses it when he first turns toward the people; but, to show that he is one of us, [Col. 0354D] afterwards he says, “The Lord be with you.”

There also he proved his resurrection in many ways: through sight; through touch, when he showed himself tangible and displayed the scars, which he retained principally for three reasons: to prove the resurrection, to intercede for us, and to reproach the faithless. Again, through taste, because he ate with the disciples. The food he took is believed in this act to have been dissolved, as water is consumed by fire or by a ray of the sun. He ate a portion of broiled fish and a honeycomb. He himself is the fish caught [Col. 0355A] in the waters of the human race by the net of death. He is the honeycomb—that is, honey in wax: divinity in human nature. We eat him when we believe him to be such.

He also eats the broiled fish and honeycomb when he incorporates into eternal rest us who have been roasted for Christ in the furnace of tribulation, yet have not departed from love of inward sweetness, where we shall be joined to true sweetness. Again, he proves the same thing through hearing when he expounds the Scriptures. This pertains to knowledge; hence in the introit the blessed men are said to have drunk the water of wisdom [Note: [Col. 0355] Ecclus. 15], while the Lord thunders from heaven. In the offertory, “And the Most High gave his voice” [Note: [Col. 0355] Psalm 17], fountains of waters are remembered as having appeared. In the communion, those who have risen with Christ are commanded to seek and set their minds on things above [Note: [Col. 0355] Col. 3].

Furthermore, in [Col. 0355B] the Gospel the disciples’ understanding is opened to understand the Scriptures. The understanding of Scriptures is indeed an effective cause of lamentation and mourning. As one walking through the midst of the slain is pricked, at least a little, by restraining laughter, so one who reads in the Scriptures of slain prophets and the Lord of the prophets is bitten, at least a little, by sorrow. The more a person understands his own sins, the more he bursts forth into mourning and the lamentations of repentance. This mourning produced by knowledge is not mourning for the dead, which comes by the common law of nature, but repentance. Hence when the Lord opened to the disciples their understanding of the Scriptures, he added: “Repentance and remission of sins must be preached among all nations” [Col. 0355C] [Note: [Col. 0355] Luke 24]. Although, then, these days should be devoted to joys, let us put away unsuitable merriment, and let us not eat the flesh of the lamb without wild lettuces [Note: [Col. 0355] Exod. 12], because “Blessed are those who mourn” [Note: [Col. 0355] Matt. 5].

It is noteworthy that, whereas all the gradual verses of this week are taken from Psalm 117, today’s is taken from Psalm 106, because that psalm exhorts the faithful to praise God, who through knowledge of himself redeemed and delivered them from a fourfold temptation: because he delivered them from their necessities—that is, from unbelief; because he delivered them from their necessities—that is, from evil habit; because he delivered them from weariness in good action; and because he brought them out from the wiles of heretical assault. The Alleluia, “It was necessary,” is taken from the Gospel.

Today’s station is at St Paul’s, [Col. 0355D] either because with singular grace the Lord opened to him the understanding of the Scriptures, as he himself testifies: “I received my Gospel neither from myself nor from man, but through the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0355] Gal. 1]; or because through him was especially fulfilled what is read in today’s Gospel, namely, that repentance must be preached among all nations. Therefore his preaching also is read in today’s reading from the Acts of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0355] ch. 13].

Observe that these three days are to be kept more solemnly as holidays. On the following days men may perform rural work, but women may not spin, because rural work is more necessary; dancing, however, is never permitted. For Gregory says: “It is better to dig and plough than to lead dances.” Hence those individual days have proper responsories, while the rest have borrowed ones. According to some, certain places have proper ones as far as Thursday. It is also noteworthy, though it may provoke laughter, that it is not devoid of mystery that in certain regions on Monday women beat men, while on this Tuesday men beat women. By this it is indicated that they ought to correct one another, lest either demand from the other the marital debt during these days. For Pope Julian ordered abstinence from embraces at least for three days before communion and three afterwards. This was taken from David, who, when he and his young men were about to receive the loaves of proposition, said to Abimelech: “We have kept ourselves from women since yesterday and the day before yesterday” [Note: [Col. 0355] I Kings 21].

[Col. 0356B] On Wednesday the Gospel is read in which it is said that, when morning had come, he stood on the shore of the sea, saying to the disciples who were fishing: “Cast the net on the right side of the boat.” They cast it and drew in one hundred and fifty-three fish. Then he invited those seven disciples who were fishing to a meal, saying, “Come, dine”; and he gave them bread and broiled fish [Note: [Col. 0355] John 21.]. The sea is the day of judgment, on which, when the night of this age has passed, the Lord will no longer appear amid the waves of the age, but will stand firm upon the solid ground of eternity. The one hundred and fifty-three fish found on the right side of the boat and drawn to shore are those perfected in faith in the Trinity, to be gathered on the right hand at the end of the age. The seven disciples reclining with the Lord are the Church illuminated by the sevenfold Spirit, which, having received its bodies, will recline with the Lord at the eternal banquet, where [Col. 0356C] it will feast not with old leaven, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth [Note: [Col. 0355] 1 Cor. 5.], and will eat neither a serpent instead of a fish nor a stone instead of bread [Note: [Col. 0355] Luke 11.], but the true bread and broiled fish—that is, it will know Christ to be God and a man who suffered. This is that fullness of which it is said: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” [Note: [Col. 0355] Matt. 5.]. Therefore, what is said in the Gospel, “Come, dine,” is what is sung in the introit: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” [Note: [Col. 0355] Matt. 25.]. For this kingdom is the eternal meal, where there will be great fish, but one upon the coals—not of suffering but of love—of whom Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0355] ch. 31.] says: “The Lord, whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem.”

[Col. 0356D] Observe also that the kingdom is reasonably promised us by Christ on Wednesday, because David and Solomon reigned in the fourth age, and in their hands Christ’s kingdom is signified more particularly and fully. And because Peter drew the aforesaid net to land—for the Church was entrusted to him, and it was especially said to him, “Feed my sheep” [Note: [Col. 0355] John 21.]—therefore his preaching from the Acts of the Apostles is taken for the Epistle [Note: [Col. 0355] Acts 3.]. The offertory, too, belongs to this fullness: “He opened the gates of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0355] Ps. 77.], namely, the prophets who foretold, the angels who announced, Mary who bore him, the apostles who preached, and the doctors who expounded. Through all these [Col. 0357A] the Lord rained manna into the mouths of needy souls, that is, the word of God or the sacrament of the body, so that they might not fail on the way as they journey to their homeland, where they will eat the bread of angels.

The gradual verse, “The right hand of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0357] Ps. 117.], accords with the Gospel saying, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat”; or rather, it is the voice of the man standing on the shore, that is, in eternity, and saying: “The right hand of the Lord has wrought strength” [Note: [Col. 0357] ibid.], because the power of the Word united to me made me conquer death. Therefore “the right hand of the Lord has exalted me” [Note: [Col. 0357] ibid.], that is, has made me worthy of praise. Thus he repeats, “The right hand of the Lord has wrought strength,” in order to show the quality of the resurrection, namely, that it is eternal. Hence follows: “I shall not die, but live” [Note: [Col. 0357] ibid.]. In this sense we sing with the Apostle, in the Alleluia and the Communion, of Christ’s resurrection [Note: [Col. 0357] Luke 24; Rom. 6.]. [Col. 0357B] These things belong to fortitude; and because Lawrence was a broiled fish, strong in hunger and hungering in strength, the station is held today at Saint Lawrence.

On Thursday the Gospel relates that Mary, who had been a sinner in the city and had washed the Lord’s feet while the Pharisee murmured [Note: [Col. 0357] Luke 7.], stood outside the tomb weeping; and, after speaking with the angels, she turned back and saw Jesus, and, having first been called, called him “Master.” Jesus said to her: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” [Note: [Col. 0357] John 20.]. She is the Church from the Gentiles, which, abandoning its errors, ran to the fountain of grace while the Jewish people looked on with envy. She stood outside because she had not entered into the knowledge of the Law and the Prophets, [Col. 0357C] like the centurion [Note: [Col. 0357] Acts 10.] and the eunuch, who did not understand when he read Isaiah; so also many others sought and nevertheless stood outside [Note: [Col. 0357] Acts 8.]. Thus we read that some said to Philip: “We wish to see Jesus” [Note: [Col. 0357] John 12.], but truth did not shine upon them before the Ascension.

Hence follows, “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father; but go to my brethren and say to them, ‘I ascend,’” and so forth. It is as though he said to the Church: “You will not touch me through faith before the Ascension, but afterwards you will come to me in faith through the preaching of my brethren.” Then will be fulfilled what Hosea says: “I will call ‘not my people,’ ‘my people’; and ‘not having obtained mercy,’ ‘having obtained mercy’” [Note: [Col. 0357] Hos. 2; Rom. 9.].

Today’s office proceeds from the mystical sense of this Gospel. For the Gentile Church is that mute man, and [Col. 0357D] those infants unable to speak of God, of whom it is sung in the introit: “The victorious hand” [Note: [Col. 0357] Wis. 10.], and so forth. Hence in the collect: “O God, who [hast united] the diversity of the nations,” and so forth. [Note: [Col. 0357] John 20.] What is signified in the Gospel by the sinful woman is signified in the Epistle by the Ethiopian [Note: [Col. 0357] Acts 8.]: for each signifies the Gentile Church to be justified, which is joined to the Jewish people through the cornerstone, of whom it is said in the gradual verse: “This is the shining stone, and it has shone upon us” [Note: [Col. 0357] Ps. 117.], as is sung in the Alleluia.

Therefore [Col. 0358A] the day of solemnity is called in the offertory: “This is a great and splendid day, day from day, light from light, on which we came out of the land of Egypt and were led into a land flowing with milk and honey” [Note: [Col. 0357] Exod. 13.]. On it the Ethiopian put off his blackness [Note: [Col. 0357] Jer. 13.], and Mary the blindness of her sloth [Note: [Col. 0357] Luke 7.]; and we, the people of acquisition, are commanded in the Communion to proclaim her virtues, “because he called us out of darkness into his marvelous light” [Note: [Col. 0357] 1 Pet. 2.]. This office, therefore, pertains to counsel and mercy. For it was the great counsel of the sinful woman to wash his feet with tears, that she might obtain mercy. And because the Lord’s brethren spoken of in the Gospel are the apostles, through whom all these things were fulfilled—namely, the mouth of the mute man opened and the eloquent speech of infants—the station is held at the Holy Apostles.

[Col. 0358B] On Friday it is read in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0357] Matt. 28.] that the disciples went into Galilee, saw the Lord, and received the formula of baptism, namely, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, which the Lord enjoined in these words: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

“Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you.” Here it should be noted that the hearer must first be catechized—that is, taught concerning the faith; secondly, baptized; and thirdly, instructed in the Lord’s commandments. Therefore the scrutinies precede baptism. Galilee is interpreted “migration,” which suitably applies to the baptized, who pass from the oldness of life to newness [Note: [Col. 0357] Rom. 6.]. This migration was prefigured in the crossing of the Red Sea [Note: [Col. 0357] Exod. 14.]. Therefore [Col. 0358C] it is sung in the introit, “The Lord led them out,” and so forth [Note: [Col. 0357] Ps. 77.], and in the offertory: “This day shall be a memorial to you,” namely, the day on which you cross the sea [Note: [Col. 0357] Exod. 12; Lev. 23.]. It was also prefigured in Noah [Note: [Col. 0357] Gen. 7.]. Therefore the Epistle of Peter is read concerning him: “Christ once” [Note: [Col. 0357] 1 Pet. 3.]. For just as Noah, whose name means “rest,” guided the ark over the waves of the flood, so Christ, the true rest, guides the Church over the wave of baptism.

The gradual verse, preserving its order—“The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” [Note: [Col. 0357] Ps. 117.]—together with the Communion expresses the glory and honor with which the Lord was crowned through suffering, saying in the Gospel: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” [Note: [Col. 0357] Matt. 28.]. This office, therefore, pertains to purity of heart; for in baptism [Col. 0358D] body and soul are washed. And because the vision of God is promised to pure hearts, as there: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” [Note: [Col. 0357] Matt. 5.]; and because through purity one attains understanding, it is fittingly said in the Gospel that those who had migrated saw God, and seeing him adored him. This occurred upon a mountain, namely at Nazareth, and, as Jerome says, in Mary’s house. Therefore today’s station is at Saint Mary’s.

On Saturday the Gospel is read [Note: [Col. 0357] John 20.] which says that Peter and [Col. 0359A] John ran to the tomb. And although John ran ahead, Peter, following him, entered first, and then John. These are the two peoples: Peter signifies the Gentiles, who came later to knowledge of the Passion but nevertheless were among the first to believe. John signifies the Synagogue, which heard earlier of the Lord’s Passion in the Law and the Prophets, but was not yet willing to believe in one who had died. Yet it will believe, when the remnant of Israel is saved [Note: [Col. 0359] Rom. 11.].

Of these two peoples, namely the believing and unbelieving, Peter speaks in today’s Epistle: “Putting away” [Note: [Col. 0359] 1 Pet. 2.]. Of the believer it is said in the introit: “The Lord led forth his people” [Note: [Col. 0359] Ps. 104.]. The Lord brought Israel out of Egypt with gold and silver; but when they murmured in the desert, they perished [Note: [Col. 0359] Num. 21; 1 Cor. 10.]. He brought those who did not murmur [Col. 0359B] out of the desert into the land of promise [Note: [Col. 0359] Josh. 4.], with a voice of exultation. For these same persons we omit the gradual and double the Alleluia, because the neophytes who were laboring now praise God in voice and deed. The Alleluia also applies to them: “Praise the Lord, children” [Note: [Col. 0359] Ps. 112.]; for that entire psalm is directed toward the election of the Gentiles, as is proved by its ending: “Who makes the barren woman dwell in a house” [Note: [Col. 0359] Ps. 112.].

What is sung in the offertory also suits the same children: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0359] Ps. 117.]. For the children sang this verse when they met the Lord coming to his Passion [Note: [Col. 0359] Matt. 21.]. The words that follow, “We have blessed you from the house of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0359] Ps. 117.], Mother Church added, saying to her children: “We have blessed you,” that is, “we who are the household of the Lord have sealed you by baptism,” because “[Col. 0359C] God the Lord has shone upon us” [Note: [Col. 0359] ibid.]. The following verse, “This is the day,” concerns the joy of believers. The other verse, “The stone which the builders rejected,” concerns the rebuke of the Jews. The Communion also applies to these same believers: “All who [have been baptized] into Christ” [Note: [Col. 0359] Gal. 3.], and so forth.

This office, therefore, pertains to the peacemakers, who shall be called sons of God [Note: [Col. 0359] Matt. 5.]; for the Lord gave “to those who believe in his name” “power to become sons of God” [Note: [Col. 0359] John 1.], to whom wisdom is given for their enjoyment. The maternal prerogative of the Lateran church requires that, since baptism was begun there on Holy Saturday of Easter, it should today be concluded in the same church, which is the apostolic see, built by Constantine in honor of the Holy Savior and John the Baptist. [And observe that the name “at the Lateran” accuses the ancient disgrace of filthy Nero, who, having used evil potions, hid there and vomited frogs; but where iniquity abounded, grace abounded still more [Note: [Col. 0359] Rom. 5.]. For now the Church is there the mother of the Roman Empire.]

This Church, which gave birth to them on Holy Saturday, spiritually circumcises them on this eighth day by the rock: the rock is, to unbelievers, a stone of stumbling and rock of offense, but to believers it is honor and the head of the corner [Note: [Col. 0359] 1 Pet. 2.]. This circumcision is not carnal but spiritual, concerning which Peter says in today’s Epistle: “Putting away all malice,” [Col. 0360A] and so forth [Note: [Col. 0359] ibid.]. This is Zipporah, Moses’ wife, who circumcised her sons, saying to Moses: “You are a bridegroom of blood to me” [Note: [Col. 0359] Exod. 4.]. Moses is Christ. Zipporah, the foreign woman, is Mother Church taken from the Gentiles; lest Moses be killed in his sons, she circumcises the sons, whose blood touches Moses’ feet, that is, his footsteps. For Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps [Note: [Col. 0359] 1 Pet. 2.]. To him the Church says, “You are a bridegroom of blood to me,” as though saying: “In betrothing yourself to me, or me to yourself, you poured out your blood as dowry for me. Therefore I too will crucify my flesh with its vices and desires [Note: [Col. 0359] Gal. 5.], and, should occasion require it, will repay in kind with my own blood.”

Observe that this week is called *In albis*, “in white garments,” because the baptized formerly wore white clothing on these days [Col. 0360B] from the day of baptism until the present day, to signify, as we have said, the robe of innocence. It ought to be worn for eight days, so that in this present sevenfold period we may preserve purity of body, and in the eighth attain glorification in rest. For by these garments we indicate both what we ought to be in the present life—namely, pure—and what sort of bodies we shall at last receive. These garments are customarily double, because the saints will possess double things [Note: [Col. 0359] Isa. 61.], namely blessedness and glorification.

Their laying them aside on Saturday signifies that they will find rest at the departure from life; and when they have been washed again, not others but the same take them up, because souls will receive not foreign bodies but those which they governed in this life. Throughout this entire week the baptized are brought to [Col. 0360C] church to be fed with the Savior’s body, after the example of the children of Israel, who, after crossing the sea, were nourished with manna before entering the promised land. As a pillar went before them [Note: [Col. 0359] Exod. 16.], so a candle goes before these.

Observe that these eight days represent the whole Christian life. The day of baptism represents the entry of faith, on which the baptized sing one Alleluia together, because they wash their robe in the blood of the Lamb [Note: [Col. 0359] Rev. 7.]; but the tract follows because they are still pilgrims. Yet that tract is one of praise, because “the ordinances of the Lord are songs to him in the place of pilgrimage” [Note: [Col. 0359] Ps. 118.]. Or it represents the life of the old Adam, who was in a state of joy; therefore the Alleluia is sung. But this joy was not everlasting, and therefore [Col. 0360D] the tract follows.

The following six days, on which the gradual and Alleluia are sung, represent the whole present life, either because of the six works or because of the six ages of humankind. In them one labors in action and contemplation, and in the sweat of his face a man eats bread [Note: [Col. 0359] Gen. 3.]; but the Alleluia is sung after the gradual, because labor and sorrow will be turned into joy [Note: [Col. 0359] John 16.]. Almost all the gradual verses are taken from the psalm *Confitemini* (“Give thanks”) [Note: [Col. 0359] Ps. 117.], because this psalm speaks of eternal joy.

But this Saturday signifies the future life, in which the Alleluia is doubled on account of [Col. 0361A] Christ’s and our resurrection, or on account of the two robes which body and soul will put on, or because joy will then be everlasting [Note: [Col. 0361] Isa. 61.]. Since it is joy, there is one Alleluia; since it is everlasting, a second Alleluia is sung. Today Septuagesima ends, which above we compared to the Babylonian captivity [Note: [Col. 0361] 2 Kings 25.], and which we may also compare to the children of Israel, who, while in Egyptian slavery [Note: [Col. 0361] Exod. 2.], wept, saying: “They surrounded me” [Note: [Col. 0361] Ps. 17.]; “Arise” [Note: [Col. 0361] Ps. 43.]; “Be [a refuge]” [Note: [Col. 0361] Ps. 30.].

The office of Wednesday, that is, the beginning of the fast, is as though it were said to Moses, “Take off the sandals from your feet.” The office of Lent is like the contest of Pharaoh and Moses, that God’s people might be freed [Note: [Col. 0361] Exod. 3.]. Baptism is the Red Sea [Note: [Col. 0361] Exod. 7 and below]. The journey through the desert under leaders is the bringing of the neophytes [Col. 0361B] through this week under priests and godparents; and so at last, on this Saturday, they arrive at the promised land. Therefore the Alleluia is frequent, and this frequency continues from this Saturday until the Saturday after Pentecost.

These are the fifty days of the yearly jubilee, that is, a time full of jubilation, signifying the future life, in which Alleluia will be sung by all through every street of Jerusalem. Just as [Col. 0362A] the preceding period signifies the present life, so this one signifies future exultation. Hence in the former we devote ourselves to fasts and prayers; in this one we relax the fasts and give ourselves to praises. The first was prefigured by Christ’s Passion, the second by his Resurrection; or, as the former signifies action, so this one signifies contemplation. We shall discuss the fiftieth year more fully at Pentecost.

At today’s Vespers the ferial psalms are said with Alleluia. Observe that in ancient books the yearly Easter is noted, which is called the anniversary: for formerly those baptized at the preceding Easter solemnly commemorated the day of their regeneration in the following year, calling to mind their second birth, of which the Lord said to Nicodemus: “Unless one is born again of water and the [Col. 0362B] Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0361] John 3.], and so forth. Nicodemus represents those who believe, or have received faith, but do not yet act faithfully. Such are the neophytes, who solemnize through this Gospel. Perhaps this was taken from the Gentile people, which, while born into misery, observed its birthday [Note: [Col. 0361B] Corrupt passage.]. Much more should that day be celebrated on which we are regenerated to grace, that we may reign in glory.

# BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0361]

# PROLOGUE

[Col. 0361C]

Old Adam, transgressor of the commandment, turned aside from the way of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0361] Gen. 3.]; but the merciful Lord, who does not forget to show mercy [Note: [Col. 0361] Ps. 76.], recalled the wanderer through messengers. For the son returning home, the Father killed the fatted calf, gave him a robe and a ring [Note: [Col. 0361] Luke 15.], and although he had consumed the portion of grace given to him, nevertheless reconciled him to an eternal inheritance. The Church, celebrating solemnly, celebrates this reconciliation in the following liturgical section.

# CHAPTER ONE. SUNDAY IN THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

“Like newborn infants, desire the rational milk without deceit” [Note: [Col. 0361] 1 Pet. 2.].

Today’s office belongs to the eighth beatitude, namely: “Blessed are [Col. 0361D] those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0361] Matt. 5.]. Since this returns to the first head and is the same as the first, almost the same office is sung. Yet it differs a little, because one cause of the same blessedness is marked in the first and another in this last beatitude: there humility is indicated when it says, “Blessed are the poor in spirit” [Note: [Col. 0361] ibid.]; but here martyrdom, when it says, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution” [Note: [Col. 0361] ibid.].

Of this martyrdom the Gospel says [Note: [Col. 0361] John 20.] that, when the doors were shut and the disciples remained within for fear of the Jews, [Col. 0362C] the Lord stood in their midst and announced peace to them. By the disciples shut in we understand all who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake [Note: [Col. 0361] Matt. 5.], who do not dare to come into public because of the rage of persecutors, just as the disciples did not dare because of fear of the Jews.

John speaks of the same martyrdom in the Epistle [Note: [Col. 0361] 1 John 5.], saying, “All that is born,” and: “There are three that bear witness on earth: the spirit, the water, and the blood.” By these three witnesses—namely, the Holy Spirit, the water of baptism, and the martyrdom of Christ’s blood—our faith is confirmed, and the kingdom is adjudged to those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake. The Alleluia, “After eight days,” pertains to the same martyrdom. But the introit, “Like newborn infants,” is to be sung through the following days of the week [Col. 0362D]; this also suits the Gospel according to another saying which the Lord uttered in the Gospel concerning future believers: “Blessed,” he says, “are those who have not seen and have believed” [Note: [Col. 0361] John 20.]. Here faith is commended by the Lord; but lest we think faith alone sufficient for us, a rule of life is set before us in the introit, that we may draw the milk of doctrine from the breasts of the Savior [Note: [Col. 0361] Isa. 12.], or of Mother Church, without which faith is dead [Note: [Col. 0361] Jas. 2.].

The final portion of the preceding Epistle agrees with this statement: “He who believes in the Son of God has the testimony of God in himself” [Note: [Col. 0361] 1 John 5.]. Likewise the Communion: [Col. 0363A] “Put forth your hand,” and so forth, whose plain sense builds up our faith; but if we look inwardly, by Thomas we understand the remnant of Israel, which will not believe until the thing appears, Enoch and Elijah having come beforehand. But ours is a more praiseworthy faith, because we have obeyed by the hearing of the ear [Note: [Col. 0363] Ps. 17.]. Let us therefore believe in this manner, and live as believers, that we may obtain blessedness.

# CHAPTER II. THE FIRST SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

“The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0363] Ps. 32.].

On this Sunday councils are celebrated, in which a model is set forth for the shepherds of souls to follow. Therefore, through today’s office, a model and example are placed before them: a model, that they may be merciful, [Col. 0363B] whence the introit: “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord”; and that they may be steadfast in the word of God, whence follows: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm.” The example is Christ, “who suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps,” as is read in the Epistle [Note: [Col. 0363] 1 Pet. 2.]; he was the good shepherd, knowing his sheep and laying down his life for his sheep, as is read in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0363] John 10.].

The other parts of the office depend upon this: “Alleluia. I am the good Shepherd”; similarly, the Communion. The offertory, however, “God, my God, I watch for you from the dawn” [Note: [Col. 0363] Ps. 62.], also agrees with the Gospel, because this psalm has the title: “A psalm of David, when he was in the wilderness of Idumea.” The wilderness is the Jews, who abandoned God and were abandoned by God. [Col. 0363C] They are likewise Idumeans, that is, earthly or blood-stained people, who shed the blood of the prophets [Note: [Col. 0363] Matt. 21, 23.] and of the Lord. In this wilderness Christ, the good Shepherd, laid down his life for his sheep, giving us an example that, for the guarding of the flock, we may watch toward God and not toward payment, lift up our hands, and, when the wolf comes, not flee but lay down our lives for the sheep, lest we be counted thieves or hirelings.

Observe that before the Resurrection the Law and the Prophets were read; after the Resurrection, however, the Apocalypse and the Catholic Epistles, which are the apostles’ writings, are read and sung with jubilant chants. For the Law and the Prophets foretold Christ’s Passion and Resurrection, but the apostles announced and testified to them as already accomplished. Therefore that responsory is sung: “With great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection” [Note: [Col. 0363] Acts 4.].

[Col. 0363D] And observe that according to the Roman order, nine lessons are always read on Sundays; although the Council of Mainz instituted that only three should be read from Easter until Pentecost, so that the service might be sung by day, because in the future the Trinity will be comprehended and the saints will serve the Lord in light. The Apocalypse is also read and sung for good reason, because it recounts the vision of Christ and discourse with angels. In that life which the Paschal season signifies, souls will rejoice in the vision of the Trinity and the fellowship of angels [Col. 0364A].

The Apocalypse is read with the history *Dignus* for fifteen days; afterwards the Epistles are read with the history *Si oblitus*, until the Ascension, with sermons and homilies also added. What is said in a certain responsory—“The people in Israel sang Alleluia, and the whole multitude of Jacob sang lawfully, and David himself [Note: [Col. 0363] 2 Sam. 6; 1 Chron. 15.] struck the harp with the singers in the house of the Lord”—refers to the fact that, after Saul’s kingdom had been destroyed, that is, the dominion of death, the ark—that is, the Savior’s humanity, in which are the manna, that is, the Word, and the tablets of testimony, that is, the hidden treasures of God’s wisdom and knowledge [Note: [Col. 0363] Col. 2.]—is brought into Jerusalem and placed in the tabernacle, that it may enjoy the eternal vision of peace and be gloriously exalted to equality with the Father.

[Col. 0364B] Since above, in the times of the Lord’s infancy, we said that Paul ought to be read, but now the writings of the other apostles, it is evident that throughout every time in which the Lord’s presence is commemorated, whether before the Passion or after it, the heralds of the New Testament fittingly speak, so that the sons of consolation may drink the strengthening milk as though from the bridegroom’s breasts. For these writings are breasts [Note: [Col. 0363] Isa. 66.], of which it is said: “Your breasts are better than wine” [Note: [Col. 0363] Song 4.]. May the Lord, whose mercy fills the earth [Note: [Col. 0363] Ps. 32.], thus refresh us from them, so that we may all receive from his fullness [Note: [Col. 0363] John 1.].

# CHAPTER III. THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

“Make a joyful noise to God, all the earth” [Note: [Col. 0363] Ps. 65.].

This Sunday and those that follow until the Ascension [Col. 0364C] pertain to the joy of the Resurrection, which the Lord at supper promised would come after the sorrow of the Passion. The Lord showed these two things, namely sorrow and joy, in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0363] John 16.], “A little while,” and so forth, through the comparison of a woman giving birth. Peter also suggests them in the Epistle [Note: [Col. 0363] 1 Pet. 2.], “I beseech [you],” through abstinence and glorification. For in abstinence there is labor, like that of a woman in labor; in glorification, when God is glorified in our works, there is joy, like that occasioned by a man born into the world. For just as, when a woman has given birth, she no longer remembers the anguish because of joy that a human being has been born into the world, so those who slandered us glorify God from our works on the day of visitation.

This was prefigured in Tamar [Note: [Col. 0363] Gen. 38.], who, after she had conceived by [Col. 0364D] Judah and had been accused of fornication before Judah, produced the ring, bracelet, and staff, saying: “I have conceived by the man to whom these things belong.” Tamar, who covered her face, is the Church ashamed of its former errors. She sat on the road by which Judah went to the washing, to shear sheep; that is, she met Christ coming to baptism, just as the deer longs for springs of water [Note: [Col. 0363] Ps. 41.]. When she conceived faith from Christ, and received that same faith as a ring, works of faith as a bracelet, and justification as a staff, she is accused by Gentiles and Jews [Col. 0365A] of having committed fornication with falsehood and been polluted by error. But through the aforesaid pledges she proves that she conceived by the true God, with whom she will be glorified on the day of visitation.

The introit, “Make a joyful noise to God,” pertains to this joy. For this psalm also bears the title: “Unto the end, a song of the resurrection.” The offertory also pertains to it: “Praise the Lord, O my soul”; for this psalm too is entitled “from Alleluia,” and what is said in its verse—“The Lord raises up the crushed; the Lord releases the bound” [Note: [Col. 0365] Ps. 145.]—is the rejoicing of those whose sorrow has been turned into joy.

# CHAPTER IV. THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

“Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done marvelous things” [Note: [Col. 0365] Ps. 97.].

On this Sunday the Gospel is read: “I go [Col. 0365B] to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’ But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart. Yet it is expedient for you that I go away, because if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send him to you” [Note: [Col. 0365] John 16.]. Many refer these words to the Ascension, thinking that he then departed for the first time, but they are mistaken. For, as Luke says [Note: [Col. 0365] ch. 24.], when he ascended, the disciples returned to Jerusalem with great joy; but here it says, “Sorrow has filled your heart,” and below, “The world will rejoice, but you will be sorrowful.”

Likewise they are mistaken because, on the day on which he rose, he breathed upon the apostles, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” [Note: [Col. 0365] John 20.]; [Col. 0365C] but here it says, “If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you.” Therefore this is not understood of the journey of the Ascension but of the Passion. For in death he passed from the world to the Father; indeed, he spoke these words on the night in which he was to be betrayed. Hence Passover is interpreted “passage” in reference to this. Thus, concerning this passage, he says, “I go to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’” These words are equivalent to: “I have trodden the winepress alone; I looked around, and there was no helper” [Note: [Col. 0365] Isa. 63.].

After this passage, the Paraclete was certainly given, namely the Holy Spirit, the Comforter, for the remission of all sins. This would not occur unless one man paid Adam’s debt for all. For, as John testifies [Note: [Col. 0365] John 7.], the Spirit had not yet been given, because Christ had not yet been glorified; [Col. 0365D] nor have we received reconciliation in any other way than through blood, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Without the shedding of blood there is no remission” [Note: [Col. 0365] Heb. 9.]. Therefore, “If I do not go away,” that is, if I have not died, “the Paraclete will not come,” that is, remission of sins will not occur. This is equivalent to: “Unless the grain of wheat has died,” [Note: [Col. 0365] John 12.], and so forth.

Likewise, when he says: “I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” [Note: [Col. 0365] John 14.], it is understood no better than of what he asked on the cross, where he was heard because of his reverence [Note: [Col. 0365] Heb. 5.]. Yet because, by the Ascension, the apostles were assured of the [Col. 0366A] Lord’s power and awaited on the mountain the promised Spirit, we rightly sing and read beside it how, when about to die, he promised that Spirit, and, when about to ascend to heaven, promised him again, so that we may know his death to be the effective cause of the gift.

What follows in the Gospel, “When he comes, he will convict the world of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment,” understand thus: of the sin of unbelief, which they possess; of the righteousness, which they do not possess; and of the judgment, which they do not fear. The reading “Every good gift” [Note: [Col. 0365] Jas. 1.] is fittingly placed before this Gospel, for the promised Paraclete is the best gift and perfect present. Through this gift we put off the old man and put on the new. This is to sing a new song [Note: [Col. 0365] Col. 3.]. Therefore in the introit we sing “Sing,” and in the offertory “Make a joyful noise” [Note: [Col. 0365] Ps. 97.], [Col. 0366B] because this gift is the cause of eternal jubilation. The Alleluia, “It is expedient that I go,” and the Communion, “When the Paraclete, our Comforter, comes,” are taken from the Gospel.

# CHAPTER V. THE FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF EASTER
“Announce the voice of joy, and let it be heard” [Note: [Col. 0365] Ps. 65]. On this Sunday the Gospel is read: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you; ask and you shall receive, that your joy may be full” [Note: [Col. 0365] John 16]. The Lord spoke these words at the end of his discourse concerning the glory of the Ascension, in which the disciples were assured of the Savior’s omnipotence; for, as John says, “we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, and he himself is the propitiation for sins” [Note: [Col. 0365] 1 John 2].

[Col. 0366C] Therefore this Gospel is prefixed in connection with the Ascension. But, lest we ask for dishonorable things, the tongue must be restrained; therefore the Epistle is read: “Be doers,” where it is added: “If anyone thinks himself religious while not restraining his tongue, that person’s religion is vain” [Note: [Col. 0365] Jas. 1]. But to those who, as is read at the end, keep themselves undefiled from this world, it is said: “Ask, and you shall receive,” just as Elijah said to Elisha: “Ask of me what you wish me to do for you before I am taken from you.” And he said: “I pray that your spirit may become double in me” [Note: [Col. 0365] 4 Kings 2].

For Elijah is Christ, the chariot of Israel and its driver: as the driver, he governs the Church by the word of doctrine; and as the chariot, he conveys it to heaven by the vehicle of divinity. Elisha here is any apostolic man, in whom the spirit of Christ is made double. For Christ walked gently among human beings, whence the Holy Spirit appeared over him in the form of a dove [Note: [Col. 0365] Matt. 39, probably 3]. Yet that same Spirit makes apostolic men, as cause or time requires, sometimes gentle and sometimes fervent in zeal. For toward those subject to them they come now with a rod, now in a spirit of gentleness [Note: [Col. 0365] 1 Cor. 4].

But when it is said, “Ask and you shall receive,” understand that the petition ought to be devout and persevering: devout, indeed, so that it may be expedient; persevering, so that it may not fail. The joy promised in the Gospel is the gladness which we are exhorted to announce as far as [Col. 0367A] the ends of the earth in the Introit. It is also the benefit for which the nations are invited to bless in the Offertory [Note: [Col. 0367] Ps. 65]. It is also that salvation [Note: [Col. 0367] Ps. 95] which they are commanded to announce in the Communion, through which they will deserve to receive full joy.

## CHAPTER VI. ON THE LITANIES

“He heard my voice from your holy temple” [Note: [Col. 0367] Ps. 17]. Mindful of that evangelical promise, namely, “Ask and you shall receive” [Note: [Col. 0367] John 16], Saint Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, placing firm hope in it, instituted litanies in this week.
