To discuss these more fully, it should be known that *litany* is Greek, and in Latin is called *supplicatio*, “supplication,” because in the litanies we entreat the Lord to defend us from every adversity and [Col. 0367B] sudden death, and we ask the saints to intercede for us with the Lord.

There are two litanies, the Major and the Minor. The Major is celebrated on the feast of Blessed Mark, and is called “Major” both because of the authority of its founder and because of the authority of its place. For the Apostolic See instituted it at Rome. Paul, monk of Monte Cassino and historian of the Lombards, describes the causes of this institution as follows. In the time of Pope Pelagius there was such a flooding of waters throughout Italy that the waters rose to the upper windows of Nero’s temple—a marvel. Then through the Tiber flowed a multitude of serpents, among which was an enormous dragon. Their breath corrupted the air, and from this arose [Col. 0367C] a plague of the groin, by which people died everywhere and suddenly. Since nearly the entire Roman people was being destroyed by it, Pope Pelagius commanded everyone to fast and to make a procession; but during that very procession he died, along with seventy others. Gregory I, called the Great, succeeded him and commanded that this litany be observed throughout the world. It is therefore called the Gregorian or Roman Litany.

The Minor Litany is so called in comparison with the former, because of the lesser authority of both its founder and its place. Blessed Mamertus instituted it at Vienne. For in his time earthquakes frequently occurred around Vienne, and houses and churches collapsed. Also, on Easter Saturday, while Mamertus himself was celebrating the divine office, the palace of that city was burned by fire sent from heaven [Col. 0367D]. Moreover, beasts—wolves and wild boars—fought against people in bands not only in villages but even in cities, and devoured them.

Because of these plagues Saint Mamertus proclaimed a three-day procession and a three-day fast. In likeness to the Ninevites [Note: [Col. 0367] John 3], a three-day fast is proclaimed according to customary practice; or because of the three parts of the world, Asia, Africa, and Europe; or because of the three orders of the Church, namely Noah, Job, and Daniel, all of whom need repentance. He chose the three days between the promise already mentioned—“Ask and you shall receive”—and Ascension Sunday, [Col. 0368A] so that, as he delivered the Ninevites from the overthrow of their city, he may likewise rescue us from calamities; and, as one about to ascend into heaven, may hear the petition based on that promise and finally grant us also to ascend into heaven [Note: [Col. 0367] John 16].

Both the Apostolic See in its litanies and the bishop in his chose the spring season, because then the fruits of the earth are in blossom and tender growth, and therefore are easily spoiled by unfavorable weather. That God may avert this, we offer prayers and litanies. Hence some explain the bread, fish, and egg, of which the Gospel speaks [Note: [Col. 0367] Luke 11], as these three things: the fruit of the earth, the fruit of the waters, and the fruit of animals. Morally, however, understand faith by the fish, hope by the egg, and charity by the bread. These are to be sought at this time, so that, rising from vices and strengthened by these [Col. 0368B] virtues, we may be able to climb to heaven with the Lord.

Again, he chose a season of war, in which the Church asks that he who destroyed the counsel of Ahithophel [Note: [Col. 0367] Esth. 7] may destroy the plans of those who devise battles all day long [Note: [Col. 0367] Ps. 139] and violate peace in the Church. Although the commendable custom of the three-day fast, instituted by Blessed Mamertus, was observed only in the Gallican Church, it was finally canonized at Rome, and thus what had been particular became universal.

It is notable that these three-day litanies are older than the Major Litany. For these were instituted in the time of Emperor Zeno, whereas that one was instituted in the time of Maurice; chronology records which preceded the other. In all litanies the following order ought to be observed, and formerly was observed: clerics in the first place; cloistered persons, such as monks and canons, in the second; nuns in the third; boys in the fourth; laypeople in the fifth; widows in the sixth; married women in the seventh. But at Rome, by Gregory’s institution, the order is designated thus: male clerics, monks and nuns, married women, widows, boys; let those of each group proceed from its respective church. But what we cannot supply in the number of persons, we supply in the number of litanies: for we ought to say the litany seven times before laying aside the insignia.

In all litanies these insignia are carried: crosses and banners. The Church received their use from Constantine, who, when he had seen the sign of the cross in a dream and had been told, “Conquer by this,” ordered the cross to be displayed on military standards. That the greater cross [Col. 0368D] is taken from the altar by the cross-bearer recalls that Simon of Cyrene bore it from Christ’s shoulders [Note: [Col. 0367] Matt. 27].

In some churches it is customary also to carry a dragon on the first two days before the cross and banner, with a long inflated tail; but on the third day, after the cross and banners, with its tail lowered. This is the devil, who deceives us, or desires to deceive us, through the three periods: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. During the first two he was, as it were, lord of the world; therefore he is called prince or god of this world. Hence on the first two days he goes before with inflated tail. But in the time of grace he was conquered by Christ [Col. 0369A] and does not dare to reign openly, but secretly seduces people; hence on the final day he follows with lowered tail.

For these reasons he is now called a lion, now a dragon. He was a lion in bringing about Christ’s crucifixion; a dragon in tempting him; and he will also be a lion in the time of Antichrist, concerning whom John says in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0369] Luke 10; ch. 12]: “I saw Satan fall from heaven like lightning, and he drew with him a third part of the stars.” By these stars we understand human beings: the first portion, the perfect; the second, the imperfect; the third, the reprobate, who are the devil’s tail.

In all litanies one must fast with Lenten food—not by divine authority of Scripture, but by the ordinances of the elders, which must be kept as law. In all, one must also walk in penitential and mournful dress, as though representing [Col. 0369B] the women who followed the Lord in lamentation [Note: [Col. 0369] Luke 23]. For on account of impending dangers, according to the Lord’s command, we must weep over ourselves and our children. In all, every person—men and women, even male and female servants—must abstain from servile work and attend the procession until it ends, so that, just as all have sinned, so all may supplicate for pardon; all may lift hearts together with hands to God—that is, raise the earnestness of prayer together with the merit of good works.

Finally, all litanies are celebrated with the same office. By the Gospel parable we are admonished to persevere, knocking at the door of the friend, namely Christ, whose children are with him in bed; for after the labor of the Passion he rests with his own on the bed of completed glory [Col. 0369C]. From this friend we ask three loaves, that is, understanding of the Holy Trinity, so that the other friend—that is, our friend, who had strayed into desiring temporal things and returns to the way leading to the homeland—may be refreshed by heavenly nourishment through contemplating things above.

But in order that we may attain the understanding of the Trinity, we ask with threefold insistence: we ask by praying, seek by living rightly, and knock by persevering. And we ask three things, namely faith, hope, and charity, which we receive through the fish, egg, and bread. Against these the Lord sets three things: the serpent, the scorpion, and the stone, which are unbelief, looking backward and remembering past things, and hardness of heart—that is, the harshness of hatreds [Col. 0369D].

The Epistle [Note: [Col. 0369] James 5] also suitably encourages the one knocking at the friend’s door to perseverance, offering Elijah’s example so that we may argue by analogy that the friend can be overcome by the persistence of knocking. Do not be troubled that an example is proposed from the righteous man, where it says: “The continual prayer of a righteous man is very powerful.” For the Apostle James was speaking to sinners when he said: “Confess your sins to one another” [Note: [Col. 0369] ibid.]. Confessing sins is the beginning of righteousness: “For the righteous person is his own accuser at the beginning” [Note: [Col. 0369] Prov. 18], that is, he begins to be justified by [Col. 0370A] accusing himself. Therefore James calls righteous the sinner justified by his self-accusation.

The first prayer teaches what one ought to ask, namely that we may be fortified against every adversity. One assured, as it were, that prayers have been heard sings in the Introit, “He heard” [Note: [Col. 0369] Ps. 17], and in the Offertory, “He confesses exceedingly to the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0369] Ps. 108], that is, with persistence, because of which the Gospel friend rises and gives his friend as many loaves as he needs. He invites the rest to the same confession in the Alleluia: “Give thanks” [Note: [Col. 0369] Pss. 106 and 117]. The Communion, “Ask and you shall receive,” is taken from the Gospel.

Finally, this should generally be observed concerning processions: as Christ’s embassy into the world for us is represented in the Mass, so in our processions our return [Col. 0370B] to our homeland is signified; and in almost every respect the solemnity of our processions follows the departure of the people from Egypt. For as that people was rescued through Moses from Pharaoh’s hands [Note: [Col. 0369] Exod. 12], so God’s people are freed through Christ from the lion’s mouth. As the tablets of the covenant are received from the mountain [Note: [Col. 0369] Exod. 31; 34], so the book of the Gospel is taken from the altar. A pillar of fire went before them [Note: [Col. 0369] Exod. 13], and the light of a candle goes before us. Standards were borne before their companies, and crosses and banners are carried before us. The Levites carried the tabernacle of the covenant [Note: [Col. 0369] Num. 2], while our subdeacons and deacons carry Gospel-books and caskets. The ark of the covenant was carried by priests; among us, a shrine or bier containing relics is carried by presbyters. Aaron, the high priest, followed in his ornaments; among us, the mitred bishop follows.

[Col. 0370C] Among them was Moses with a rod; among us, the king with a sceptre, or the bishop with a *sambuca* [a staff or liturgical instrument]. There was the blast of trumpets; here, the sound of bells. There, the people were armed; here, adorned with virtues. There, the people were sprinkled with blood [Note: [Col. 0369] Exod. 24]; here, with blessed water and salt. Thirsting Amalek met them [Note: [Col. 0369] Exod. 17]; a crowd of demons, always lying in wait for our life, meets us. Joshua emerges victorious [Note: [Col. 0369] Josh. 6], and our Jesus has obtained victory for us.

When we proceed toward a church, we then draw near, as it were, to the land of promise. When we enter the church singing, we arrive joyfully, as it were, at our homeland. When, with bells being rung, we carry the bier around churches, we encircle Jericho as it were with the ark, with the sound of trumpets, and with the people’s shout [Col. 0370D]. Jericho falls and is destroyed when concupiscence is conquered within us. David and Solomon also instructed us regarding processions, when David carried the Ark of the Lord into the tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0369] 2 Kings 6] and Solomon into the Temple [Note: [Col. 0369] 3 Kings 8], with hymns and songs, and placed it beneath the wings of the cherubim. Thus Christ’s humanity, ascending, enters heaven and is perpetually adored by angels.

## CHAPTER VII. ON THE VIGIL OF THE ASCENSION

“All nations, clap your hands” [Note: [Col. 0369] Ps. 46]. On the Vigil of the Ascension [Col. 0371A] of the Lord the Gospel is read: “Jesus, lifting his eyes to heaven, said: ‘Father, the hour has come and now is; glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you’” [Note: [Col. 0371] John 17]. This is read now because what he prayed when about to suffer became known to human beings when he ascended; or because it concludes: “I come to you,” in which he prays for those whom the Father gave him, that they may be one in the Father—that is, mutually united in heart. Hence the Epistle precedes: “Of the multitude of believers” [Note: [Col. 0371] Acts 4].

Nothing could more fittingly be prefixed in the Introit concerning this union, namely of human beings with God and with one another. For in hands is understood work, in clapping joy, and in the joining of hands the sharing of charity. We are therefore commanded to clap our hands so that whatever we do may all be done in cheerfulness and charity. Or this Introit belongs, together with the Alleluia, “He ascended,” and the Offertory, “He opened the gates of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0371] Ps. 77], to the coming solemnity of the Ascension. The Communion is taken from the Gospel.

Some not unfittingly refer the aforesaid offices of Easter week, through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, to those reborn through baptism. Thus one reborn by the breath of the spirit of wisdom may say: “I have risen” [Note: [Col. 0371] Ps. 138]—I who had fallen through Adam have now risen from the death of the soul. The Gospel [Note: [Col. 0371] Mark 16] declares by what he has risen, namely through the Lord’s resurrection. The spirit of understanding teaches what he has thereby acquired, saying: “He brought you into the land” [Note: [Col. 0371] Exod. 13], namely, the Church; and the spirit of counsel further adds: “He gave them to drink the water of wisdom” [Note: [Col. 0371] Ecclus. 15]. The spirit [Col. 0371C] of fortitude declares what he ought thereafter to acquire, saying: “Come, blessed of my Father” [Note: [Col. 0371] Matt. 25]. The spirit of knowledge teaches that he ought to praise God for these accumulated benefits, saying: “Victorious” [Note: [Col. 0371] Wis. 10]. The spirit of piety indicates what the resurrection has brought to those reborn, saying: “The Lord brought them out in hope” [Note: [Col. 0371] Ps. 77]; and the spirit of fear further adds: “The Lord brought out his people” [Note: [Col. 0371] Ps. 104].

For all these benefits conferred on humanity in baptism, angels rejoice; human beings give thanks to the Lord, urge one another to Christ’s praises, render thanks, rejoice, recall the benefits and the causes of the benefits, and confidently aspire to greater things. The remaining parts of the offices of the above-mentioned week are occupied with these things. Observe that here the order of the gifts changes. And note that in the offices of this week Alleluia is placed four times with the four Introits, and three times with the three others [Col. 0371D], because the Holy Trinity is praised from the four parts of the world, both for Christ’s resurrection and for the reception of human beings.

On the first Sunday, “Like newborn children” [Note: [Col. 0371] 1 Pet. 2], the baptized are admonished by their mother to live innocently as infants and to desire the milk of Holy Scripture, so that they may maintain in conduct and life the Paschal sacrament gained through Christ’s resurrection, conquer the world, triumph with Christ, and obtain joy in [Col. 0372A] body and soul together. For this reason Alleluia is doubled: either because they have escaped death and have deserved to possess hope of life; or because of action and contemplation; or because of the joy of preachers and converts.

On the second Sunday, namely, “The mercy of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0371] Ps. 32], the baptized, now instructed, sing aloud Christ’s mercy and preach the Trinity. For in “mercy” they proclaim the Spirit, in “word” the Son, and in “God” the Father. They put first the Spirit by whom they have been sanctified; then the Son by whom they have been redeemed; then the Father to whom they have been reconciled. And because they sing of the Trinity, they rejoice with Alleluia three times.

On the third Sunday, “Rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0371] Ps. 65], the baptized invite the whole world to God’s praise and sound forth the Trinity, understanding the Father in “God,” the Son in “name,” and the Holy Spirit in “praise.” And because they are strengthened in the faith of the Trinity by the two commandments of charity, they first sing Alleluia twice, then three times.

On the fourth Sunday, “Sing” [Note: [Col. 0371] Ps. 97], the baptized again invite the converted nations to God’s praise and commemorate the Trinity: they understand the Father in “the Lord,” the Son through “wonders,” and the Holy Spirit through “righteousness.” And because the nations received the faith of the Trinity from the four quarters of the world, they conclude the Trinity with the fourth Alleluia.

On the fifth Sunday, “The voice of joy” [Note: [Col. 0371] Ps. 65], the baptized again proclaim their deliverer to the nations, singing the Trinity through Alleluia set three times [Col. 0372C]. And, as this contains the earnestness of those preaching, so in the Offertory, “He heard” [Note: [Col. 0371] Ps. 6], is understood the concern of those turning from error; and in the Offertory, “All nations” [Note: [Col. 0371] Ps. 71], the applause of those who will ascend to heaven.

## CHAPTER VIII. ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

“Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” [Note: [Col. 0371] Matt. 24]. As we believe that our Redeemer has ascended into heaven, we raise our wavering hope and dwell in mind among heavenly things. For by the certainty of hope we already possess the thing which we rejoice that he has attained, and which, God being favorable, we shall now possess in reality though we possess it in hope. Hence some of the things sung at the Ascension are a narration of the Ascension as accomplished [Col. 0372D], such as “After the Passion” [Note: [Col. 0371] Acts 1], “All beauty,” “Ascending” [Note: [Col. 0371] Ps. 65], and “God ascended” [Note: [Col. 0371] Ps. 46]. Some are the Bridegroom’s consolation of the bride, such as “Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid” [Note: [Col. 0371] John 14], “It is time that I return” [Note: [Col. 0371] Job 12], and “If I do not go away” [Note: [Col. 0371] John 14]. Some are the bride’s congratulations to the Bridegroom, such as the responsory “Be exalted, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0371] Ps. 20] and “You make the cloud” [Note: [Col. 0371] Ps. 103]. In the narration hope is conceived; in the consolation it is raised; in the congratulations it is assured [Col. 0373A], or delighted.

Likewise, in the daytime office the Ascension is narrated in the Epistle [Note: [Col. 0373] Acts 1], and in the Gospel, where it is said that the Lord was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God [Note: [Col. 0373] Mark 16], that is, in equality with the Father; and in the Alleluia, “The Lord in Sinai” [Note: [Col. 0373] Ps. 67]. The Bridegroom consoles in the other Alleluia: “I will not leave you” [Note: [Col. 0373] John 14]. The bride offers congratulations in the Communion, saying: “Sing to God, who ascends above the heaven of heaven toward the east” [Note: [Col. 0373] Ps. 67]—that is, as far as the Word rationally united to himself, which is not said to have risen or to be about to rise, but is “the Rising One” [Note: [Col. 0373] Zech. 3, 6], because the Son always proceeds from the Father [Note: [Col. 0373] John 15]. Or “above the heaven of heaven toward the east” means above the firmament of heaven toward the eastern region.

What is sung in the Introit and Offertory, “Men of Galilee” [Note: [Col. 0373] Acts 1], is taken from the Epistle. In that passage the angels rebuke the pride of those who pierced [Note: [Col. 0373] Zech. 12; John 19], the worldly wisdom of those who did not know [Note: [Col. 0373] 1 Cor. 1], and the sloth of those who did not return the talents entrusted to them with due profit; and they stir the desire of those who waited too long for the Lord’s coming [Note: [Col. 0373] Matt. 25]. For this entire office consists in eager expectation and joy.

Observe that on this day the procession must not be neglected: by it we commemorate that the Lord proceeded with his disciples from Jerusalem to the Mount of Olives [Note: [Col. 0373] Matt. 28], or represent that we ought to follow him to the place into which he entered [Note: [Col. 0373] Acts 1], and by the same way, namely the way of obedience, on account of which God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every [Col. 0373C] name [Note: [Col. 0373] Phil. 2]. He represented this when he led them out to Bethany [Note: [Col. 0373] Luke 24], which is interpreted “obedience.” Hence, in the procession some sing responsories pertaining to that leading out, such as “The Lord brought out.”

Since therefore on this day we reasonably hold a procession, it is nevertheless still more fitting that it be celebrated not, as on Easter Day or other Sundays, before Terce is said, but after Terce has been sung. On Easter and Sundays water is blessed in memory and veneration of baptism. Therefore these rites precede Terce, at which the Holy Spirit descended upon the disciples [Note: [Col. 0373] Acts 2], so that, as we are first baptized and afterward receive the Holy Spirit, we first sprinkle ourselves and our places with blessed water, and afterward sing the memorial of the Holy Spirit’s coming, namely Terce. Why the memory of baptism is renewed on Sundays has been explained above.

But on this day, after Terce has been sung, the procession is celebrated; likewise all the others which are solemnly celebrated with a blessing of water, both so that they may be joined to the office of Mass and because no one follows him unless sanctified by the Holy Spirit [Col. 0373D]. Observe also that the primitive Church observed Thursday in memory of the Ascension, just as it observed Sunday in memory of the Resurrection. Then, on Thursday [Col. 0374A], the procession was made, commemorating today’s procession. But when the solemnities of saints multiplied, the Thursday solemnity was removed and the procession transferred to Sunday.

As we enter church and return to church, we recall the apostles returning to Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0373] Luke 24; Acts 1]. But though they were without Christ, we are nevertheless with the cross of the Crucified One, for he said: “I will be with you until the consummation of the age” [Note: [Col. 0373] Matt. 28].

## CHAPTER IX. THE SUNDAY AFTER THE ASCENSION

“Hear, O Lord, my voice with which I cried to you” [Note: [Col. 0373] Ps. 26]. After the first anointing which the apostles had received in Christ’s death, when he breathed on them and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0373] John 20], they awaited the second [Col. 0374B] which the Lord had promised when he said: “If I go away, I will send the Paraclete to you” [Note: [Col. 0373] John 16].

Therefore, while waiting, they sing in the Introit: “Hear.” This is again taken from Psalm 26, “The Lord is my illumination,” whose title is: “A psalm of David, unto the end, before he was anointed.” For it treats there of David’s threefold anointing [Note: [Col. 0373] 1 Kings 16]. First, he was anointed as a sign of his future kingship; second, as king over the tribe of Judah [Note: [Col. 0373] 2 Kings 2]; third, over all Israel [Note: [Col. 0373] 2 Kings 5]. We too sing the same because we await the third anointing. The first anointing is in baptism; the second in confirmation, or in the confession of repentance; the third will be in the resurrection.

Or, the first was in the apostles, the second in the Jews, and the third in [Col. 0374C] the Gentiles. For the ointment which descended upon Aaron’s beard [Note: [Col. 0373] Ps. 132], that is, upon the apostles, who were bearded—that is, perfect and fully mature men—and who were Aaron, that is, men of the mountain, namely Christ, who was the mountain on the summit of mountains [Note: [Col. 0373] Isa. 2]: that ointment, I say, descended to the edge of the garment, that is, to the chosen Jews near to the apostles, clothing the Lord; and it descended as the dew of Hermon upon Mount Zion—that is, exalted grace inundates the Gentiles who contemplate God.

And because the apostles, as we have said, while waiting were in the Temple, praying, praising, and blessing God [Note: [Col. 0373] Luke 24; Acts 1], we too in our waiting are invited to prayer in the Epistle, “Be prudent” [Note: [Col. 0373] 1 Pet. 4], and urged to praises in the Offertory, “Praise the Lord, O my soul” [Note: [Col. 0373] Ps. 145]. The Gospel [Note: [Col. 0373] John 15, 16] declares what was the effect [Col. 0374D] of that apostolic anointing: “When he comes,” where it says, “You will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.”

Observe that for the aforesaid reason—namely, because the apostles were awaiting being clothed with power from on high—this week is called the week of expectation. During it some customarily fast and devote themselves to prayer until Pentecost, because the apostles are read to have fasted during this period. But Master Gilbert proves that one ought not to fast, because it belongs to the Paschal season [Col. 0375A] and to the fifty days of Pentecost. Jerome, Ambrose, and Augustine likewise say that between Easter and Pentecost fasts ought not to be proclaimed as obligatory. By voluntary choice we may at any time abstain from receiving food, but it ought not to be obligatory. Hence Ambrose: “During these fifty days the Church knows no fasting, just as on the Sunday on which the Lord rose.” For these days are to be celebrated as a kind of Easter and Sunday; during them, as Bede says, one should devote oneself to more abundant feasts and heavenly hymns, because of reverence for the Lord’s resurrection [Note: [Col. 0375] Luke 24], remembrance of the Lord’s meal with the disciples, and hope of immortal glory. Nevertheless, penitents are excluded from this exemption. Gregory also excepted the litanies.

It is also notable [Col. 0375B] that the octave of Ascension Sunday, which ought to end on Thursday, must be prolonged further. For although the Sunday office operates on Thursday, nevertheless in the nocturnal offices of Friday and Saturday the invitatory and responsories concerning the Ascension are sung. Yet we say the nocturnal psalms with three lessons and omit *Te Deum laudamus*—but why, when the apostles were praising God [Note: [Col. 0375] ibid.]? Do not be surprised, since you find the same from the Nativity of the Lord until Epiphany; indeed the entire Paschal season contains the same thing, because it represents one and the same octave.

Nor is it without mystery, because the apostles, while waiting, deserved to receive the Paraclete in the mystery of the number ten through the observance of the Ten Commandments [Col. 0375C] [Note: [Col. 0375] Matt. 20]. We too, while waiting, shall receive the denarius of eternal life through the same observance. During these ten days the Acts of the Apostles are to be read; whoever follows them will receive the Holy Spirit and earn the denarius.

## CHAPTER X. ON THE VIGIL OF PENTECOST

“Come, Holy Spirit.” The solemnity of the coming of the Holy Spirit must be venerated, both because of the Person, who is equal to the Father and the Son, and because of its purpose. For the Spirit came in order that, before the rulers of the earth, he might defend in God’s court by advocacy the inheritance bequeathed by the Father’s testament and written out in the Son’s blood, against Jews, heretics, pagans, false [Col. 0375D] brothers, and demons. For he himself pleads for us with unutterable groanings [Note: [Col. 0375] Rom. 8].

Baptism appointed on Saturday now prefigures the coming. For baptism is solemnly celebrated on this Saturday: both so that those born after Easter, or prevented by necessities, may be baptized; because Peter baptized three thousand on this day [Note: [Col. 0375] Acts 2]; because the Son conquered the strong man by the finger of God [Note: [Col. 0375] Luke 11], and therefore the same work is represented through the same mystery, when the finger comes and the Son rises; because the first generation effected by baptism is the work of the Holy Spirit; and because, as today he descended upon the apostles [Note: [Col. 0375] Acts 2]—a descent which the Lord called baptism [Col. 0376A], saying, “But you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0375] Acts 1]—so in baptism he descends, though invisibly, upon those being baptized.

But someone will say: then baptism ought to be celebrated on Sunday and at the third hour. Indeed, this sacrament belongs to that day and that hour; but it is placed on Saturday either because of Christ’s death or because through this sacrament we obtain rest, although at other times it is sometimes celebrated because of the contingencies of this shifting world. And indeed our baptism more closely resembles the baptism of the apostles than that of Christ. For Christ was baptized not for his own sake, but for ours, that he might provide us with an example. The apostles, however, were baptized for the washing away of their own sins, and so are we for ours. But they were first baptized in water, then [Col. 0376B] by the Spirit on earth, and finally by the Spirit from heaven. We, however, when the bishop is present, are baptized at once and receive the Holy Spirit through confirmation. If we ever do otherwise, nevertheless we should without doubt refer everything to that day and hour.

The office of baptism has been set forth above. This, however, is notable: only four lessons are read today. At the Vigil of Easter the first was: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” [Note: [Col. 0375] Gen. 1]; but here the first is: “God tested Abraham” [Note: [Col. 0375] Gen. 22]. These two lessons recall for us two fathers, one carnal and one spiritual. From Adam we all received the beginning of carnal generation; but from Abraham the beginning of spiritual generation. The former destroyed us all through disobedience [Note: [Col. 0375] Gen. 3]. Therefore after [Col. 0376C] that first lesson no canticle follows, because through Adam we are born for mourning. The latter gained blessing for his seed through obedience [Note: [Col. 0375] Gen. 22]. Therefore after this first lesson a canticle follows, because through Abraham’s faith we hasten toward joy.

Some nevertheless say that no tract ought to follow, because Abraham sang no canticle for the promise made to him, since he had no companion with whom to sing: he was alone, a worshipper of God and a stranger in a foreign land. This lesson fittingly accords with the present day, because in the outpouring of the Holy Spirit the blessing was given to the Gentiles, concerning which the Lord said to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” [Note: [Col. 0375] Gen. 12 and 22]. The prayer beginning, “O God, who [of] thy servant Abraham,” fittingly agrees with this.

The second [Col. 0376D] lesson, “Moses wrote” [Note: [Col. 0375] Deut. 31], declares the Law given, which was given today and signifies the new Law poured out into the hearts of believers [Note: [Col. 0375] Jer. 31; Heb. 8 and 10]. Hence a canticle follows, in which eternal joy is promised anew.

The third lesson, “Seven women shall lay hold” [Note: [Col. 0375] Isa. 4], etc., declares the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which form each person into a man of good character. Hence a canticle follows, because joy accompanies good morals.

The fourth reading, “Hear, O Israel” [Note: [Col. 0375] Baruch 3], indicates the virtues accompanying the gifts—wisdom, prudence, light, and peace. Hence a canticle follows, because for these gifts and within them we shall rejoice eternally. The first reading resounds with [Col. 0377A] history, the second with allegory, the third with tropology, and the fourth with anagogy. Observe the difference between the Paschal readings and these Pentecostal ones: it is the difference between Adam and Abraham. There is recalled the jeopardy of the human race, even to destruction, through Adam’s disobedience; here, the restoration of the human race, even to salvation, through Abraham’s obedience. In all these readings the titles are left unspoken, because the authors of Scripture are still unknown to the catechumens. The remaining matters concerning baptism are set forth in the preceding teaching. But now the office of the Mass is to be traced out.

From this Saturday until the following one there are seven offices, all concerning the majesty and operation of the Holy Spirit and the instruction of those baptized. One day has no proper office, but borrows its office from Sunday or from the Thursday of Easter. This Mass begins with *Kyrie eleison*, so that the Church’s joy over the reborn may be declared; because angels rejoice over them, *Gloria in excelsis Deo* is added—or because the apostles, before receiving the Spirit, were praising and blessing God [Note: [Col. 0377] Acts 1]. Today’s reading, “It came to pass while Apollos...,” commends the unique dignity of Christ’s baptism: those baptized with John’s baptism were baptized with Christ’s baptism [Note: [Col. 0377] Acts 19]. It also proclaims the power and grace of the Holy Spirit, by which he caused the baptized to speak in diverse languages [Note: [Col. 0377] Acts 8, 10]. *Alleluia* is sung in remembrance of primitive innocence; but because that innocence was not everlasting, as we said before, it is changed into a tract.

[Col. 0377C] In the Gospel that Spirit and his operation are promised; that is, knowledge of the Trinity is intimated. When it says there, “He will give you another Paraclete” [Note: [Col. 0377] John 14], “another” means another in person and another in operation. For the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another. For although through the Son all things have being, life, sensation, discernment, and understanding, through the Holy Spirit they have well-being, holy life, right perception, prudent discernment, and wise understanding. “I believe in one God” must not be omitted, because, since this Creed is derived from the Creed of the Apostles, it indicates the faith which they possess.

The offertory, “Send forth” [Note: [Col. 0377] Psalm 103], plainly concerns the operation of the Spirit, because through him the Lord is blessed, and through him heaven is stretched out like a skin—that is, Scripture [Col. 0377D] is expounded so that almost nothing remains hidden. Likewise the communion, “On the last day,” concerns the same operation of the Spirit, who causes rivers, like living waters, to flow from the believer’s belly [Note: [Col. 0377] John 7], that is, an abundance of saving doctrine. And, as some maintain, this Mass should conclude with *Benedicamus Domino*.

At Vespers, according to the custom of certain churches, these psalms are sung together: “Praise the Lord, for he is good” [Note: [Col. 0377] Psalm 45]; the psalm “Praise the Lord, O my soul” [Note: [Col. 0377] Psalm 46]; and “Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0377] Psalm 47], because in these psalms the praises of God seem to sound forth more strongly. [Col. 0378A] For where the Spirit breathes, the instrument invites praise.

## CHAPTER XI. ON PENTECOST.

“The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world” [Note: [Col. 0377] Wisdom 1].

The ancient people celebrated three solemn feasts: namely, Passover, because God delivered them from Egyptian bondage and from the stroke of the angel [Note: [Col. 0377] Exodus 12]; Pentecost, because then they received the Law [Note: [Col. 0377] Exodus 19]; and Scenopegia—that is, the pitching of tabernacles—in September [Note: [Col. 0377] Leviticus 23]. These feasts, which were extended over seven days, were called principal feasts; and the Sabbath occurring within them was called “Sabbath of sabbaths,” that is, Sabbath of feasts. They added other feasts for other events, such as the *Encaenia*, namely, the dedication of the Temple.

We, however, have retained only two of them, [Col. 0378B] namely Passover and Pentecost, but for different reasons. They celebrated Passover because they passed out of Egyptian servitude; we celebrate Passover because we have been redeemed through Christ. They celebrated Pentecost because they received the Law; we celebrate it because we have received the Holy Spirit. They received a carnal law, written on tablets of stone, to signify the hardness of the people [Note: [Col. 0377] Jeremiah 31]; but we have received spiritual understanding, written in human hearts by God’s finger.

And Pentecost means “fiftieth”: for the Law was given on the mountain of God, Horeb or Choreb or Sinai, which are the same, on the fiftieth day after the immolation of the Paschal lamb. The lamb was sacrificed on the fourteenth day of April; the Law [Col. 0378C] was given on the fourth day of the third month, though it is said to have been given on the third day. For Scripture says [Note: [Col. 0377] Exodus 19]: “The third day had now arrived and dawned, and thunder began to be heard.” On the third day the Lord descended upon the mountain to give the Law; Moses went up to God and, coming down, related everything to the people; then, ascending again in the morning, he received the two written tablets. Take care to count only thirty days in the second month. Thus, according to the moon, sixteen in the first month, thirty in the second, and four in the third make fifty.

But observe that not every fifty is called Pentecost. There is a fifty of days, a fifty of years, a fifty of psalms, a fifty of persons, and a fifty of denarii.

The fifty of days is threefold. One extends [Col. 0378D] from “Be unto me, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0377] Psalm 30] to Easter; the second from Easter to Pentecost; the third from Saturday in Albis to the Saturday after Pentecost. The first is of penitence and affliction; the second, of joy and exultation; the third, of glory and glorification. For it represents the octave of the double robe. Therefore *Alleluia* is doubled during it.

The fifty of years was the jubilee year [Note: [Col. 0377] Leviticus 25, 27], in which freedom was restored to those who desired it. The fifty of psalms is threefold and signifies the three states of Christian religion: the first is that of penitence, [Col. 0379A] the second of righteousness, and the third of the praise of eternal life. Thus the first ends in “Have mercy on me, O God” [Note: [Col. 0379] Psalm 50]; the second in “Mercy and judgment” [Note: [Col. 0379] Psalm 100]; the third in “Let every spirit praise the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0379] Psalm 150]. These are the 150 psalms; the days of the Flood were equally numerous [Note: [Col. 0379] Genesis 8]. We sing them, therefore, that we may be delivered from the Flood and from every danger.

Concerning the fifty persons, Abraham asked the Lord: “If there are fifty righteous persons there, will you spare them?” [Note: [Col. 0379] Genesis 18]. Concerning the fifty denarii, the Gospel speaks of two debtors, one of whom owed five hundred denarii and the other fifty [Note: [Col. 0379] Luke 7]. But these do not concern us at present. For only the fiftieth day from Easter is called Pentecost, in the customary term—from *pente*, “five,” and *coste*, “ten”—because those who labor in the Lord’s vineyard through the [Col. 0379B] five bodily senses will be filled with the Spirit and will deserve in the future to receive the denarius of eternal recompense [Note: [Col. 0379] Matthew 20].

This number arises from seven taken seven times, with unity added. For there are seven weeks from Easter to this day: both because on this day the sevenfold grace is given, and because by the merits of sevenfold grace, through the sevenfold course of this life, one comes to that one thing of which it is said: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this will I seek” [Note: [Col. 0379] Psalm 26]. For when seven thousand years have been completed, through the sevenfold Spirit we shall attain the same joy.

Observe also that the ancients observed the seventh day as the Sabbath; the seventh week as Pentecost; the seventh [Col. 0379C] month as September; the seventh year as jubilee; and the seventh year of the seventh decade—that is, the sixty-seventh year. They observed this last only once, when they were granted leave to return from Babylonian captivity [Note: [Col. 0379] II Chronicles 36].

This number also arises from forty, multiplied by its parts, which contains the perfection of good works, or from ten added, which does not contain the recompense for those same works. And fittingly one comes from the state of contrition and penitence to the state of remission and glory, and from perfection of works to recompense. Recall that, just as by the Law’s command they offered sheaves of ears of grain at Passover [Note: [Col. 0379] Leviticus 23], so at Pentecost they offered two loaves of first-fruits. Therefore, from the day on which the Lord rose and offered his body as it were a sheaf [Col. 0379D] of new fruits, let us observe the fiftieth day, on which we received the Holy Spirit, and offer two loaves, giving thanks for the Law then given on stones and for grace poured out in our hearts [Note: [Col. 0379] Romans 5]. Let us celebrate on the fiftieth day after seven weeks, representing the jubilee, so that after the circle of this life we may reach the year of eternity, in which we shall not labor but recover the ancient possession which we lost by sinning.

On this day three antiphons are appointed: “There came suddenly” [Note: [Col. 0379] Acts 2], “Strengthen” [Note: [Col. 0379] Psalm 67], and “Send forth the Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0379] Psalm 103]. Compared [Col. 0380A] with the three Paschal antiphons—“I am” [Note: [Col. 0379] Psalm 1], “I asked” [Note: [Col. 0379] Psalm 2], and “I slept” [Note: [Col. 0379] Psalm 3]—they signify a more abundant perfection. For it is greater to be filled with a mighty spirit [Note: [Col. 0379] Acts 2], which shakes off the dust from one’s feet, than not to be reckoned with the ungodly; greater to be strengthened than to be numbered among the inheritance; greater for the face of the earth to be renewed than to rise from sins [Note: [Col. 0379] Matthew 10].

Some wish nine readings to be read, as on other Sundays; but it is canonical to read only three, because of the sacrament of baptism celebrated in the name of the three Persons; or because of the Lord’s three-day burial, into which we are buried in baptism [Note: [Col. 0379] Romans 6]; or because the power of miracles is one work of the indivisible Trinity; or because of faith, hope, and charity, which [Col. 0380B] every Christian ought to possess from the beginning of understanding.

Both the nocturnal and the daytime office proclaim today’s miracle, which is more clearly declared in the epistle when it says: “When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, all the disciples were together in the same place, and suddenly there came a sound from heaven” [Note: [Col. 0379] Acts 2]. This signified him who was to go into all the earth, concerning whom “the sound of the apostles went forth into all the earth” [Note: [Col. 0379] Psalm 18]. It continues: “as of a rushing mighty spirit.” He came in a mighty spirit because, just as a strong wind casts dust from the face of the earth, so the Spirit’s advent drives every earthly thing from the human heart. It continues: “and it came to pass that divided tongues, as of fire, appeared to them.” He is given in fire [Col. 0380C] in order to make them fervent in the love of charity. The force of fire consumes one material, such as wood, but refreshes and cherishes another, such as our bodies; so the fire of the Holy Spirit consumed the rust of sins and warmed souls to love of God and neighbor. He is given in tongues so as to make them eloquent in every kind of speech.

Therefore, filled with the Holy Spirit, they began to speak in diverse languages as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance: either they spoke in all languages, or, while speaking their own—that is, Hebrew—language, they were understood by all as though speaking each person’s native tongue; and they themselves likewise understood everyone’s languages as though they were their own. He is given at the third hour because the Holy Trinity is commanded to be preached. Thus the Holy Spirit gave eloquence, and gave knowledge and doctrine of all things; hence in the [Col. 0380D] Gospel: “He will teach you all things” [Note: [Col. 0379] John 14]; and in the introit: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world” [Note: [Col. 0379] Wisdom 1]. There God’s power is preached: he alone is everywhere and alone fills all things. For unless he were everywhere, he would not have been at once among the apostles separated by a great space of lands, nor would he be present at the consecration of diverse fonts.

Or, he filled the whole world when he made the apostles drunk, whose sound went forth into all the earth [Note: [Col. 0379] Psalm 18]. Since the earthly globe is divided into four regions, *Alleluia* is therefore sung four times. The double *Alleluia* sung after the epistle either signifies, as we have often said, joy to be doubled; or the Spirit given twice [Col. 0381A] to the apostles, namely from earth and from heaven; or that they sing with spirit and mind [Note: [Col. 0381] I Corinthians 14]; or the conversion of two peoples.

And he who contains all things has knowledge of speech: that is, he knows with what mind each person speaks; or he has knowledge of all things through which and concerning which the human voice can vary; or “knowledge of speech” means that he possesses the speech of knowledge—that is, he causes us to possess it—so that the things the apostles uttered by his inspiration they pronounced with understanding.

The offertory, “Strengthen” [Note: [Col. 0381] Psalm 67], suits this day. For it is agreed that faith had been given to the apostles, but it was weak in them. Thus Peter denied at the voice of a maidservant [Note: [Col. 0381] Matthew 26]. Today the Lord strengthened it in them, and we ask that it may be strengthened in us: “From thy holy temple which is in Jerusalem, kings shall offer [Col. 0381B] gifts unto thee”—that is, the Church of the apostles, who are the foundations of the Church; for “salvation is from the Jews” [Note: [Col. 0381] John 4].

The communion, “There came,” is taken from the epistle [Note: [Col. 0381] Acts 2]. Observe that this feast is celebrated for seven days, either because of the mystery of the present life, or because of the Sabbath-rest of souls, or because through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit full joys are bestowed on bodies and souls. Hence the last seven psalms are entitled from “Praises,” because eternal joys are bestowed through the operation of sevenfold grace. In them three readings are read daily, so that seven brothers may care for three sisters [Note: [Col. 0381] Job 1, 42], that is, the seven gifts may care for the three virtues—faith, hope, and charity—as Gregory explains in the *Morals*. For the offices of these days are adapted to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Yesterday’s office, therefore, and today’s, concern wisdom and understanding, as is clear from what precedes. [Col. 0381C]

On Monday the office concerns the calling of the gentiles, for whose salvation God sent his only-begotten Son into this world, that the world might be saved through him, as today’s Gospel testifies [Note: [Col. 0381] John 3]. The Holy Spirit accomplished this salvation. For while Peter was speaking, the Holy Spirit fell upon the gentiles, as today’s epistle testifies [Note: [Col. 0381] Acts 10]. To bring this salvation to completion, as is sung in the introit, “The Lord fed them with the fat of wheat and satisfied them with honey from the rock” [Note: [Col. 0381] Psalm 80]: the divine word is wheat, whose chaff is the Jews, while the gentiles are satisfied by its fat [Note: [Col. 0381] John 12]. Or the wheat is Christ, whose fat is the Holy Spirit, by whom the faithful [Col. 0381D] are satisfied with honey from the rock—that is, with doctrine proceeding from Christ, in whom are all the treasures of God’s wisdom and knowledge [Note: [Col. 0381] Colossians 2].

Here too *Alleluia* is sung four times because of God’s promises; remember to explain it in this way in what follows as well. To complete that same salvation, as is sung in the offertory, “The Lord thundered from heaven” [Note: [Col. 0381] Psalm 17], when suddenly a sound came from heaven [Note: [Col. 0381] Acts 2], “and the fountains of waters appeared” [Note: [Col. 0381] Psalm 17]—that is, through the apostles the veils of Scripture were disclosed. All this was done by the Spirit at work. Hence it follows in the communion: “The Holy Spirit will teach you whatever [Col. 0382A] I have said” [Note: [Col. 0381] John 14].

Observe that the calling of the gentiles was deferred for a time. Hence: “Do not go into the way of the gentiles” [Note: [Col. 0381] Matthew 10]. Yet in due time it was finally commanded: “Go, baptizing all nations” [Note: [Col. 0381] Matthew 28]. For he did not preach personally to the gentiles, but through the apostles. Thus Isaac did not command his younger son Jacob to offer him food so that he might receive the blessing; nevertheless, through Rebekah’s action he received the primacy of the blessing [Note: [Col. 0381] Genesis 27]. Since these things occurred by God’s hidden judgment, the Apostle cries: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” [Note: [Col. 0381] Romans 9; Romans 11]. Therefore today’s office concerns counsel. And it should be known that solemnities are to be observed throughout the week—*Gloria in Excelsis*, the Creed, *Ite missa est*, *Te Deum*, and *Alleluia*—both that we may rejoice together in the salvation of the baptized [Col. 0382B] and that we may prefigure the fullness of future joy.

Tuesday’s office contains a commendation of the apostles and their successors. They are the gatekeepers of whom the Gospel speaks [Note: [Col. 0381] John 10], who open the door of faith to the sheep. For it is certain that grace is received, and the Church entered, only through the door of apostolic faith. They lay hands on the baptized, and, as the epistle says, those baptized accordingly receive the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0381] Acts 8]. Their voice is in the introit: “Receive the joy of glory.” Since through twofold love we attain faith in the Trinity, *Alleluia* is therefore sung five times. The meaning is: “Receive the joy of glory,” namely the Holy Spirit, who will glorify and make you glorious, [Col. 0382C] so that each may be able to say of himself what is said in the communion: “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father, he will glorify me” [Note: [Col. 0381] John 15, 16]. He will also, as is sung in the offertory, “open the gates of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0381] Psalm 77], that is, the Scriptures of the apostles. And because they attacked, and attack, heresiarchs in a spirit of fortitude, today’s office therefore concerns fortitude. They rightly say that those who make the Spirit the gatekeeper do not speak inappropriately; for through Christ, the door, he introduces one to the Father.

Wednesday, by its office, proclaims knowledge, which is a gift of the Holy Spirit, who illuminated the saints so greatly that from the five books of Moses and the Scriptures of a few prophets there grew an abundance of books. Foreseeing this, [Col. 0382D] Daniel said: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” [Note: [Col. 0381] Daniel 12]. The Gospel mystically intimates this to us [Note: [Col. 0381] John 6] in the five loaves and two fish, which, just as they were multiplied among the mouths of those eating, so the Law and Prophets were multiplied among the studies of those handling them.

Of this Spirit Wisdom says in the first reading: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world” [Note: [Col. 0381] Wisdom 1]; and Isaiah in the second: “...where I shall pour water upon the thirsty,” and below, “I shall pour out the Holy Spirit upon thy seed” [Note: [Col. 0381] Isaiah 44]. Observe that two readings are read, because two peoples [Col. 0383A] are converted to the faith, or because those to be ordained are instructed in the page of each Testament; to them bread—that is, sacred Scripture—is set forth in the Gospel. The preceding introit accords with this: “O God, when thou didst go forth” [Note: [Col. 0383] Psalm 77].

For through knowledge God went forth, that is, became known; and because, by meditating on sacred expositions, they expounded the Scriptures, the offertory is sung: “I meditated upon thy commandments” [Note: [Col. 0383] Psalm 118]. And because they say the same thing and there are no schisms among them, the communion fittingly adds: “My peace” [Note: [Col. 0383] I Corinthians 1; John 14].

Observe that today’s Ember fast does not detract from the solemnity of the Holy Spirit, but rather illustrates it. For the delights of the Holy Spirit imply a distaste for carnal delights; and because, when the bridegroom was taken away, the apostles had to fast, as the Lord foretold, when [Col. 0383B] “the bridegroom shall be taken from them, then they shall fast” [Note: [Col. 0383] Matthew 9], they began voluntarily to fast when filled with the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0383] Acts 13, 14]. Therefore, on the preceding Monday some begin the summer Lent; but others, more soundly, judge that today’s fast is the beginning of this Lenten period. Some set its end at the feast of Saint John, whether it has six weeks or not. Others include Saint John’s feast and, fasting until they have completed six weeks, continue without a fixed end. Jerome approves this Lent as one of choice rather than necessity, saying: “We keep one Lent; they keep three, as though three saviors had suffered,” [Col. 0383C] not that it is forbidden to fast throughout the year except at Pentecost, but that it is one thing to offer a gift from necessity and another from free choice. Jerome said this against Montanus the heretic, who decreed that his followers should fast three Lents.

Thursday has no proper office, but borrows one from Sunday, so that from Saturday to Saturday there may be only seven offices assigned to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Yet some not unfittingly assign a gift even to this borrowed office, beginning this assignment not with Saturday but with Sunday. They assign the spirit of wisdom to Sunday; understanding to Monday; counsel to Tuesday; fortitude to Wednesday; and to this Thursday [Col. 0383D] they assign the spirit of knowledge, which gives the ability to search the deep things, as is sung in the *Alleluia*: “The Spirit searches all things.”

On Friday the Gospel treats of the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue [Note: [Col. 0383] Matthew 9], who is raised after the healing of the woman with the flow of blood. This signifies that operation of the Holy Spirit by which the synagogue, now dead, will revive through piety after the fullness of the gentiles has entered into the same piety [Note: [Col. 0383] Romans 11]. Fittingly before it comes that prophetic reading: “Rejoice, daughters of Zion, in God, who has given you the early and the latter rain” [Note: [Col. 0383] Joel 2]. This is Gospel doctrine, bestowed on us through the apostles, already [Col. 0384A] preached and still to be preached in the last times. It adds: “And you shall eat and be satisfied with food,” namely spiritual food, of which the introit says: “Let my mouth be filled with thy praise” [Note: [Col. 0383] Psalm 70]. Hence he commanded that food be given to the girl who had been raised. For, refreshed inwardly, she will say what we sing in the offertory: “Bless the Lord, O my soul” [Note: [Col. 0383] Psalm 102]. Then will be universally fulfilled what is sung in the communion: “The Spirit breathes where he wills” [Note: [Col. 0383] John 3], first going to the Jews, secondly to the gentiles, afterward returning to the Jews; for “no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0383] I Corinthians 12].

On Saturday the office figures the concord of the two peoples, namely Jew and gentile. These are the two blind men of whom the Gospel says [Note: [Col. 0383] Matthew 9] that they were [Col. 0384B] enlightened by Christ. Paul speaks of this concord in the epistle addressed to Jews and gentiles, saying [Note: [Col. 0383] Romans 5]: “Being justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.” But since peace or concord cannot be true except through charity, the introit therefore begins: “The charity of God has been poured forth” [Note: [Col. 0383] ibid.]. In it *Alleluia* is said three times, because faith in the Trinity is attained through the services of charity.

Not only the remaining parts of the office, but also the readings pertaining to the fast, attest the operation and grace of the Holy Spirit: the first, “I will pour out of my Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0383] Joel 2]; and the second, “He spoke” [Note: [Col. 0383] Leviticus 23], where it says: “You shall count seven weeks until the day after the completion of the seventh week.” [Col. 0384C] Understand this to refer to the present feast, formerly called the Feast of Weeks. And because, after the gentiles have entered, the remnant will be saved [Note: [Col. 0383] Romans 11], therefore, while they now weep and await the bridegroom, the Lord says to them: “For I will not leave you orphans” [Note: [Col. 0383] John 14], which we sing in the communion.

Since this concord will occur at the approach of the Day of Judgment—which will be a cause of fear even to the elect—this office therefore concerns fear; or because fear introduces charity, though charity casts fear out [Note: [Col. 0383] John 4]. Observe that in the order of these offices we count downward, but in the order of the Paschal offices, according to Augustine, upward: because by these the descent of the Holy Spirit to us is signified, while by those our ascent to him is signified.

Take care, because besides these offices pertaining to the fast, which we have explained for Wednesday, Friday, and this Saturday, there are other readings and Gospels found on the same days which perhaps seem to draw nearer to the solemnity. Yet both these and those sound forth the grace and operation of the Spirit. Hence some not unfittingly celebrate two Masses: one at the third hour for the feast, with *Gloria in excelsis Deo* and the Creed; the other at the ninth hour for the fast, without *Gloria in excelsis Deo*. In the latter clerics are to be ordained, who are fittingly ordained in this week, that they may deserve to receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

And [Col. 0385A] remember that the fifty days end on this day. Therefore *Alleluia* is frequently sung today, *Alleluia* is sung in place of graduals, and knees are not bent, for it belongs to the octave. This is a general rule: whenever the day’s matter is drawn from the time of grace, or the day is referred to an octave, we do not bend the knee; but standing in prayer, we profess the grace bestowed upon us and the glory to be bestowed, so that, although formerly we were bent slaves, we may now walk upright with the yoke broken—as on Sundays, saints’ feasts, and Paschal days.

Yet we may incline our heads, to imitate the devout women at the tomb [Note: [Col. 0385] Luke 34; probably Luke 24]. Nor should it be passed over in silence that there are four states of the Church: the first is of sin; the second, of sin [Col. 0385B] and punishment; the third, of punishment and grace; the fourth, of grace and glory.

The Church represents the first in Septuagesima, and therefore omits *Te Deum* and *Alleluia*, because “beautiful praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” [Note: [Col. 0385] Ecclesiasticus 15], and omits *Gloria in excelsis Deo*, because a wall of enmity has been placed between God and human beings [Note: [Col. 0385] Isaiah 59]. It represents the second in Advent, and therefore the aforesaid chants are likewise omitted, except *Alleluia*, because the Law given taught people to understand and praise God. It represents the third in the summer season; therefore, because of grace received, these are sung on feast days, but because of punishment they are omitted on weekdays, except *Alleluia*, [Col. 0386A] which is also frequently used every day, because hope in the future resurrection is not weakened. It represents the fourth between Easter and Pentecost; therefore the aforementioned chants of joy are used and multiplied daily.

But because we do not yet possess the glory for which we wait [Note: [Col. 0385] Romans 8], we omit *Te Deum laudamus* and *Gloria in excelsis* on weekdays. On Sundays, on which we represent the resurrection as it were doubly, namely in view both of the season and of the day, we sing two *Alleluia*s because of the double robe; but on weekdays only one, because before the resurrection the soul alone enjoys blessedness. On saints’ feasts we sing two, either because of the octave or because of rest and full enjoyment.

Nor should it disturb you that the Church represents not the proper but the reversed order, since “the last shall be first and the first last” [Note: [Col. 0385] Matthew 20]. Thus the variety of days and of human states assumes a variety of offices: some are celebrated with a responsory alone; others with *Alleluia* alone; others with *Alleluia* and responsory; others with responsory and tract; others with *Alleluia* and tract, as on Holy Saturday. For human actions are not alike: at times people mourn and labor, at times rejoice and devote themselves to contemplation [Note: [Col. 0385] Ecclesiastes 3]. The responsory signifies action; *Alleluia*, contemplation; the tract, mourning; and *Alleluia*, joy.

# BOOK EIGHTH.

[Col. 0385]

## PROLOGUE.

[Col. 0385C]

Although we have been called away from the byway by the proclamation of Scripture, and redeemed by the Lord’s precious blood, we are nevertheless still wayfarers, drinking from the torrent on the way [Note: [Col. 0385] Psalm 109], journeying abroad [Note: [Col. 0385] Matthew 25], and absent from the Lord [Note: [Col. 0385] II Corinthians 5]. The Church represents this pilgrimage in the Sundays following until Advent.

## CHAPTER ONE. SUNDAY IN THE OCTAVE OF PENTECOST, WHICH IS THE FIRST SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST.

“O Lord, I have hoped in thy mercy; my heart has rejoiced in thy salvation” [Note: [Col. 0385] Psalm 12].

There is a threefold variation concerning this Sunday, which is the first after Pentecost. Some sing of the Trinity, others of the Octaves, [Col. 0385D] and others begin the history, “Prepare,” or “God, the hearer of all.” Those who sing of the Trinity offer this reason: after the coming of the Holy Spirit, the faith and confession of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit at once began to be preached and celebrated in baptism. For before the resurrection the distinction of the Trinity was not made known. After the resurrection the rule was given: “Going into all the world, teach [Col. 0386C] all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0385] Matthew 28]. Now this was first put into effect, when on the very day of Pentecost three thousand people were converted.

Therefore the office of the Trinity rightly follows immediately after the Spirit’s coming, so that after receiving baptism and receiving the Spirit, we may enact in deeds the faith we proclaim with our voices. Thus the entire nocturnal and daytime office of the Trinity breathes forth the holy Trinity. In it is read the Gospel, “There was a man of the Pharisees” [Note: [Col. 0385] John 3], in which the remedy of baptism is commended, conferred through invocation of the Trinity. The preceding reading from the Apocalypse accords with it [Note: [Col. 0385] chapter 4]: “I saw a door,” where it says, “a sea of glass like crystal.” For the sea signifies baptism. There too it continues: [Col. 0386D] “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth,” where the unity of the Trinity is indicated.

[The Offices of the Trinity were devised by Alcuin; for in the time of Attila, who scourged the Christians and destroyed almost all the volumes of the Christian profession, Alcuin, Charlemagne’s master, composed a history of the Trinity—namely responsories and antiphons, a Mass, and a sequence. He also made a history of Saint [Col. 0387A] Stephen. He offered both to Pope Alexander, who rejected that concerning the Holy Trinity, saying: “Just as there is no special office of the Unity, so there ought not to be one of the Trinity, especially since every Sunday is a feast of Unity and Trinity.” At length, when the Arian heresy had arisen, the faith of the Trinity was almost extinguished; but Hilary, Eusebius, and Ambrose resisted it. Gregory the Great therefore consented, for this reason, that we should sing special chants concerning the Trinity and build up the Church thereby, although similar observances concerning the Unity are not made. For many doubted concerning the Trinity who in no way erred in confessing the Unity. Hence there is a diversity of custom concerning the history of the Trinity. Some do not use it, following Alexander’s rejection. Others use it [Col. 0387B] and, singing it on this first Sunday, follow Alcuin’s original institution. Others place it on the last Sunday, following Gregory’s final approval.]

Those, however, who celebrate the octave use the same Epistle and the Gospel already mentioned, because of the sacrament of baptism, observing everything else as on the solemn day. They celebrate the octave to signify the perfection or completion of the works of the Holy Spirit. During seven days the works of the sevenfold grace are represented; on the eighth, their completion is declared. And because the octave returns to its beginning, they observe everything as on the feast day, from Vespers to Vespers, including the Vespers themselves and the three nocturnal psalms. Augustine says of these octaves: “As new people, we celebrate the observance [Col. 0387C] of the octave days. Although the baptism of the newly baptized is performed on Saturday, it nevertheless pertains to that baptism which the apostles received on the day of Pentecost [Note: [Col. 0387] Acts 2.], whose eighth day is the following Sunday.”

Those who appoint the history *Prepare*—as we are accustomed to do in our own church—act better, because they follow the Roman Church, recalling the history of our pilgrimage and returning to it. For through Septuagesima we signified the expulsion of humankind from the homeland of Paradise; through Lent, the people’s servitude under Pharaoh; through Easter, the immolation of the lamb; through the forty paschal days, the forty years in the wilderness; through the Rogation Days, the entry into the Promised Land; through the seven days of Pentecost, [Col. 0387D] during which the seven gifts are distributed, the division of the land given to them. Therefore, through the period which follows from today, we signify the people’s affliction and government under judges and kings.

Accordingly, the four Books of Kings are placed in the readers’ hands: the first of these was written by Samuel, the second by Nathan, the third and fourth by Nehemiah; and also the two books of Chronicles, written by the sages of the Synagogue. And because Samuel was the greatest of the judges, and David himself and his son were the greatest of kings, the sayings and deeds of these men are especially celebrated in the history. Or these books are read because, as they fought, so we too, having received the Spirit, must fight. *Prepare* [Col. 0388A] is the voice of Samuel [Note: [Col. 0387] 1 Sam. 7.]. *God the Hearer* is the voice of King David [Note: [Col. 0387] 1 Sam. 17.]. This history is to be used until the Kalends of August.

Thus David, while he is afflicted by Saul and his servants and compelled to go among the nations, distrusts his own strength and places confidence in God’s help. He says in the Introit: “Lord, I have hoped in your mercy” [Note: [Col. 0387] Ps. 12.]; and in the Collect: “O God of those who hope in you” [Note: [Col. 0387] Ps. 40.]. Likewise, in the Gradual he prays, “I said” [Note: [Col. 0387] Ps. 5.]; in the Alleluia, “My words” [Note: [Col. 0387] ibid.]; and in the Offertory, “Attend” [Note: [Col. 0387] Ps. 9.], pleading for deliverance from his troubles. In the Communion he gives thanks for benefits bestowed, saying, “I shall recount.” In the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0387] Luke 16.], the character of each is expressed: Saul is understood in the rich man, and David in poor Lazarus, who rebukes the rich man for failing to show the charity through which David acquired the royal throne; this charity is commended in the Epistle [Col. 0388B] when it says, “God is charity” [Note: [Col. 0387] 1 John 4.].

Mystically, Lazarus the beggar is the Christian people. While still Gentile, they fled to the faith of the Trinity and desired to be refreshed by the inward meaning of the Law, as though by crumbs falling from the rich table of the Jewish people. This Lazarus is afflicted by Jews, unbelievers, heretics, and wicked Catholics—all of whom are clothed in purple and feast splendidly. For the Jews, purple is the nobility of the flesh, in which they gloried, saying: “We are children of Abraham” [Note: [Col. 0387] John 8.]; their feast is the Mosaic Law. For Gentiles and wicked Catholics, purple is secular wealth; their feast, philosophical writings or fleshly desires. For heretics, purple is the pretence of good works; their feast is corruptible [Col. 0388C] discourse. But the Christian people, humbly confessing their sins, despising earthly things and seeking heavenly ones, are cast aside as ulcerous—despised in this life by those just named. Yet “whoever loses his life here shall find it” [Note: [Col. 0387] John 12.].

Therefore the voice of this beggar is: “Lord, in your …” Like today’s singer, he places confidence in God’s mercy in the Introit; and in the Epistle he gives the reason, because God is charity, who first loved us and sent his Son as the propitiation for our sins, and who invites persecutors to charity, adding: “Let us love God” [Note: [Col. 0387] John 4.]. And still more devoutly he prays in the Gradual, Alleluia, and Offertory.

In the Communion and at the end of the Introit, he promises to render acts of thanksgiving. On Monday, although churches differ in their custom concerning this Sunday, [Col. 0388D] all nevertheless agree that during the week the responsories and antiphons of the aforesaid history, *Prepare*, are sung, and the Books of Kings are read. In the daily offices, however, the Roman Church repeats the Sunday throughout the whole week, except that on Wednesday and Friday special Epistles and Gospels are appointed.

At one time, before the Sunday office had been arranged, when heresy was spreading, lest the divine office should perish, they sang on Monday of the Trinity; on Tuesday, of charity; on Wednesday, of wisdom; on Thursday, of the Holy Spirit; on Friday, of the angels; on Saturday, of the Lord’s cross; and on the Sabbath, of blessed Mary. But afterward, what had been done under the pressure of necessity [Col. 0389A] ceased. When the Sunday office had been arranged, it was decreed that Monday should have its own office, namely of the Trinity; Tuesday, of the angels, because then they were first created in gratuitous goods. For then light was divided from darkness [Note: [Col. 0389] Gen. 1.], that is, the good angels from the evil; because then the evil fell, while the good were confirmed. Yet on Monday they were created in natural goods; and it is also sung for another reason, namely, that we may obtain the angels’ assistance for the departed. On the same day a Mass for the dead is sung because, as some say, those who are in purgatory have relief on Monday and immediately return to punishments on Tuesday. In order that aid may be given to their labours, a Mass for the dead is sung.

It was also instituted that Wednesday [Col. 0389B] should be a fast-day, and on that day the Mass of Sunday ought to be sung; on Friday, that of the Cross; and on the seventh day, that of the Blessed Virgin. This began because long ago, in a certain church at Constantinople, there was an image of the Blessed Virgin, before which hung a veil covering the whole image. On Friday after Vespers this veil withdrew from the image, with no one moving it but by God’s miracle, as though it were borne up into heaven, so that the people could fully behold the image. Once Vespers had been celebrated on the Sabbath, it descended before the same *icon*, that is, image, and remained there until Friday. When this miracle had been seen, it was decreed that on that day an office of Blessed Mary should always be sung in the Church.

Or this is so because she is our gate to [Col. 0389C] the kingdom of heaven, which was figured by the Lord’s Day. Therefore we solemnize the seventh day in her honour, which precedes the Lord’s Day; or so that the solemnity of the Mother may be joined to the solemnity of the Son, and so that the day on which God rested from his work [Note: [Col. 0389] Gen. 2.] may be kept more festively.

At the request of Archbishop Boniface, Alcuin, Charlemagne’s master, instituted a Mass of the Trinity on Sunday; of Wisdom on Monday; of the Holy Spirit on Tuesday; of Charity on Wednesday; of Angels on Thursday; of the Cross on Friday; and of Saint Mary on the Sabbath. Some celebrate the Angels on Monday; others a Mass for the dead; on Tuesday, one for sins or peace; on Thursday, one for tribulation; on Friday, as stated above, one of the Cross; and on the Sabbath, one of the Virgin, and so forth, as stated above. Some always celebrate her Mass [Col. 0389D] with more solemn observance, namely with *Glory to God in the highest*, and *We praise you, O God* is said at Matins of that Virgin. If other Masses are sung, prayers from the matters mentioned above are inserted, so that their patronage may be experienced through their intercessions.

## CHAPTER II. THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

“The Lord became my protector and brought me forth into a broad place” [Note: [Col. 0389] Ps. 17.]. Having received the kingdom, David made a great supper, of which the Gospel says: “He invited many, friends and enemies” [Note: [Col. 0389] Luke 14.]. But when the enemies, who [Col. 0390A] had been supporters of Saul, refused to come, he speaks to those who had come, saying in the Epistle: “Do not be surprised if the world hates you” [Note: [Col. 0389] 1 John 3.]. Here too today he cuts short the oracles in the Introit, saying: “The Lord became my protector.” And in the remaining chants, now he gives thanks to God, who bestowed so many good things upon him [Note: [Col. 0389] Ps. 12.], now he prays that God may rescue him from his enemies [Note: [Col. 0389] Pss. 6, 7.].

Mystically, David is Christ, who prepared the supper of faith and invites many. They excuse themselves, preferring secular things to spiritual; in speech they profess humility, but in action pride. For when they are told, “Leave the world; follow the Lord: ‘Sell all that you have and give to the poor; take up the cross and follow me’” [Note: [Col. 0389] Luke 18; Matt. 16.], one replies, “I bought an estate”; another, “I bought five yoke of oxen” [Note: [Col. 0389] Luke 14.]; another, “I have married a wife.” For [Col. 0390B] preoccupation with earthly things, delight in the five senses, and pleasure of the flesh prevent them from approaching the supper of Jesus Christ. But he compels others to enter, namely the poor in spirit [Note: [Col. 0389] Matt. 5.]. To those reclining at table he says what is read in the Epistle: “Do not be surprised if the world hates you”; and below: “Little children, let us not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth” [Note: [Col. 0389] 1 John 3.].

Therefore the choir of those reclining at table, refreshed by fullness, rejoices in the Introit, saying: “The Lord became …”; and afterward it gives thanks and worships. Note that we often omit the Sunday Alleluias, because they are arranged differently in different Graduals. The diligent reader should therefore observe these matters and carefully assign them to the complete sets of offices. This, however, must be added: [Col. 0390C] on Sundays we sing the Alleluia of the Trinity, *What the Father is like*, so that, joyfully professing the faith, we may attain the vision.

## CHAPTER III. THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

“Look upon me and have mercy upon me, for I am alone and poor” [Note: [Col. 0389] Ps. 24.]. When David reigned and flourished in prosperity, he committed adultery and murder [Note: [Col. 0389] 2 Sam. 11.]; but when the prophet rebuked him, he repented. He is the sheep that was lost and found. By David we understand any penitent person, whom the Lord consoles in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0389] Luke 15.], saying: “He who has lost a sheep or a drachma rejoices when he has found it”; and: “There is joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance.” [Col. 0390D] Here is indicated how great God’s concern is for the conversion of sinners, and how great the angels’ rejoicing is over those converted. Peter likewise consoles and admonishes them in the Epistle, saying: “Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God”; and below: “God has care for us”; and again: “He himself will perfect, strengthen, and establish you” [Note: [Col. 0389] 1 Pet. 5].

Let this penitent therefore place all his anxiety upon God, as is said here: “Let him cast his thought” [Note: [Col. 0389] Ps. 54.]; as is sung in the Gradual: “Let him fix his hope” [Note: [Col. 0389] Ps. 9.]; and as is added in the Offertory: “Let them hope in you” [Note: [Col. 0389] Ps. 24.]. This penitent prays in the Introit: “Look upon me” [Note: [Col. 0389] Ps. 16.]; and in the Communion: “I cried.” Note that this office [Col. 0391A] is sung around the feast of Saint John the Baptist, because he is read to have called the people to repentance [Note: [Col. 0391] Matt. 3.].

## CHAPTER IV. THE FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

“The Lord is my light and my salvation: whom shall I fear?” [Note: [Col. 0391] Ps. 26.]. After the sin of adultery and murder, David was so afflicted by his son Absalom, by God’s judgment [Note: [Col. 0391] 2 Sam. 11.], that he was driven from the royal throne [Note: [Col. 0391] 2 Sam. 15.]. He is the hypocrite who judges others, seeing the speck in his brother’s eye but not considering the beam in his own [Note: [Col. 0391] Matt. 7; Luke 5.]. By him, therefore, we figure any hypocrite reigning over others and suffering afflictions [Note: [Col. 0391] Job 34.].

To such a one the Lord says in the Gospel: “Be merciful, as your heavenly Father is merciful”; and below: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged”; and again: “The blind [Col. 0391B] cannot lead the blind”; and: “Cast the beam out of your own eye” [Note: [Col. 0391] Luke 6.].
