Paul likewise says to him in the Epistle, for endurance of suffering: “I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not comparable to the future glory which shall be revealed in us” [Note: [Col. 0391] Rom. 8.]. At last, afflicted by sufferings, chastened in conduct, and humbled in the eye of his heart, he rejoices in the Introit, saying: “The Lord is my light” [Note: [Col. 0391] Pss. 88; 12.]. He prays in the Gradual and Offertory, and rejoices in the Communion that the Lord has been his helper and deliverer [Note: [Col. 0391] Ps. 17.], attributing this not to himself but to the Lord.

## CHAPTER V. THE FIFTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

“Hear, O Lord, my voice with which I cried to you” [Note: [Col. 0391] Ps. 26.]. [Col. 0391C] After the scourges, David receives back the kingdom with rejoicing, and it is promised to his son. He is the Christian people, shaken by the hammers of persecutors; he is the little boat beaten by waves [Note: [Col. 0391] Matt. 8.]. He is the net which seems to break because of the multitude of fish, as is read in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0391] Luke 5.]. The fish are the carnal and the heretics, who not only press upon the Church but, insofar as they can, even break the net of faith.

The Apostle invites these fish to the works of the Spirit and to the bond of unity, saying in the Epistle: “Be all of one mind in prayer” [Note: [Col. 0391] 1 Pet. 3.]. Placed amid these dangers, the Church prays in the Introit, “Hear” [Note: [Col. 0391] Ps. 26.], and in the Gradual, “Protector” [Note: [Col. 0391] Ps. 83.]. Because she is sometimes restored to calm and eternal peace is promised her for consolation, she therefore gives thanks in the Offertory to him who [Col. 0391D] bestowed understanding upon her [Note: [Col. 0391] Ps. 15.]; and in the Communion, “One thing have I asked of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0391] Ps. 29.], she confirms her purpose in unity of faith, so that she may attain unity of hope.

Note that this office is sung around the feast of Blessed James. For, as is said in the Gospel, “Leaving the nets, he followed the Lord and became a fisher of men” [Note: [Col. 0391] Matt. 24.], a supplanter of vices in deed and in name.

## CHAPTER VI. THE SIXTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

[Col. 0392A]

“The Lord is the strength of his people” [Note: [Col. 0391] Ps. 22.]. As David dies, he gives thanks to God for conquered enemies. And, like a good master of a household, he blesses Solomon who has been anointed, and Solomon’s people [Note: [Col. 0391] 1 Kings 1.]. This is the Church, which instructs her children, begotten in baptism and confirmed by chrism, toward perfection. In the Gospel she says: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0391] Matt. 5.]. She instructs them toward newness of life and imitation of Christ, saying in the Epistle: “All of us who were baptized in Christ were baptized into his death”; and below: “Let us walk in newness of life” [Note: [Col. 0391] Rom. 5.]. She exhorts in the Introit, because the Lord is strength [Note: [Col. 0391] Ps. 17.]; but the instructed son [Col. 0392B] prays in the Gradual, “Turn” [Note: [Col. 0391] Ps. 89.], and in the Offertory, “Perfect” [Note: [Col. 0391] Ps. 16.], and promises to offer himself to the Lord in the Communion, “I shall go round” [Note: [Col. 0391] Ps. 26.], so that his righteousness may abound in the Lord.

## CHAPTER VII. THE SEVENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

“Clap your hands, all nations” [Note: [Col. 0391] Ps. 46.]. When David died, peaceful Solomon succeeded him. With wars silenced under his rule, the people rejoiced in the praise of God [Note: [Col. 0391] 1 Kings 5.]. Therefore on this Sunday the books of Wisdom are put into the readers’ hands: namely, Solomon’s works—Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs; the Book of Wisdom, composed by Philo; and Ecclesiasticus, issued by Jesus son of Sirach. Yet, because of their style, they are attributed to Solomon [Col. 0392C] as well. The history begins here, and these books are to be used until the Kalends of September.

Or we now use works of wisdom because this month is hot and signifies the heat of vices, in which we must live wisely, as in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation [Note: [Col. 0391] Phil. 2.]. Or because this month—August—is the sixth, and was called Sextilis before Augustus Caesar; and our true Solomon came in the sixth age, he who made both one [Note: [Col. 0391] Eph. 2.], who was the power of God and the wisdom of God, and who taught us to live and teach wisely [Note: [Col. 0391] 1 Cor. 1.]. This is Christ, King of kings [Note: [Col. 0391] Rev. 19.], who, with seven loaves and a few little fishes, as is read in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0391] Mark 8.], satisfied those who had come from afar and had remained with him three days. These are those who turn to the Lord from idolatry and, [Col. 0392D] possessing faith in the Trinity, hunger and thirst for righteousness [Note: [Col. 0391] Matt. 5.]. Those who previously served uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity now serve righteousness unto sanctification, as is read in the Epistle [Note: [Col. 0391] Rom. 6.]: “Humanly speaking,” etc.

The peaceful King invites those refreshed to clap their hands in the Introit, “All nations” [Note: [Col. 0391] Ps. 64.]; and in the Gradual, “Come, children” [Note: [Col. 0391] Ps. 33.], he calls them to the fear of God. They, offering themselves to the Lord as a holocaust [Note: [Col. 0391] Dan. 3.], [Col. 0393A] pray in the Offertory and Communion. Here it should be noted that whenever the history changes, the responsory from the history must be sung at Saturday Vespers, and likewise the ninth responsory at Matins must be from the history. On the other Sundays, at Saturday Vespers we customarily sing, “Fear God”; at Matins, the new responsory of the Trinity, so that we may confess her through whom we are saved.

## CHAPTER VIII. THE EIGHTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

“We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple” [Note: [Col. 0393] Ps. 47.]. Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem, adorned it with gold and gems, and established in it the worship of God in splendid order through the ministries of priests [Note: [Col. 0393] 1 Kings 6.]. This temple is the Church, which is built up when [Col. 0393B] its faith is strengthened by the destruction of heresies, concerning which the Gospel says: “Beware of false prophets” [Note: [Col. 0393] Matt. 7.]. Although this can be understood of hypocrites and false Christians, it applies particularly to heretics, who, because they are not led by the Spirit of God, are not children of God, as the Epistle says: “We are debtors” [Note: [Col. 0393] Rom. 8.]. For those to whom the Spirit bears witness are children of God. Joyfully they cry out in the Introit, “We have received” [Note: [Col. 0393] Ps. 47.]; pray in the Gradual, “Be” [Note: [Col. 0393] Ps. 30.]; and terrify heretics in the Offertory, “The people” [Note: [Col. 0393] Ps. 17.]. They also draw them in through the Communion, “Taste” [Note: [Col. 0393] Ps. 33.].

The temple is also the Blessed Virgin Mary, in whom we have truly received God’s mercy. Hence this office is fittingly sung around her feast, since she is the temple of the Lord [Col. 0393C] and sanctuary of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER IX. THE NINTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

“Behold, God helps me, and the Lord is the upholder of my soul” [Note: [Col. 0393] Ps. 53.]. After the seventh year, the temple is dedicated [Note: [Col. 0393] 1 Kings 8.]; therefore, after seven days, this Sunday is marked by an office concerning the same matter. At this dedication gifts are offered, the ark is brought in, and God is praised. This dedication of the temple is the strengthening of faith accomplished through the sevenfold Spirit. Once faith has been strengthened, ecclesiastical laws are established and debts are collected, as is said in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0393] Luke 16.], in which the master praised the steward of iniquity, who, mindful of his master’s anger, dealt mercifully with his debtors. This is any overseer of souls who, mindful of his own [Col. 0393D] frailty—by which he has either sinned, could have sinned, or may yet sin—mercifully imposes penance on those confessing sins.

The Epistle corresponds to this [Note: [Col. 0393] 1 Cor. 10.]: “Let us not be …,” where it says: “Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall,” as this steward saw, who confesses God’s remission as a benefit bestowed and gives thanks in the Introit, saying: “Seek first the kingdom of God” [Note: [Col. 0393] Matt. 6.].

## CHAPTER X. THE TENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

“When I cried to the Lord, he heard [Col. 0394A] my voice” [Note: [Col. 0393] Ps. 54.]. Once the temple had been dedicated, the Lord appeared to Solomon [Note: [Col. 0393] 1 Kings 9.]. By this it became known that the Lord had heard Solomon’s prayers. For when faith was strengthened, the Lord shone forth through many miracles; and as Solomon rejected the reprobate Levites [the reading *levitas* is uncertain] and chose the approved, so the Lord, as is read in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0393] Matt. 21.], “cast out those buying and selling from the temple”; and, as the Epistle says [Note: [Col. 0393] 1 Cor. 12.], chose those among whom he distributed gifts of the Spirit.

To one is given the word of wisdom [Note: [Col. 0393] ibid.], as to Dioscorus and Ignatius, who instituted alternating choirs singing psalms after the manner of angels. To another, the word of knowledge [Note: [Col. 0393] ibid.], as to Athanasius, who distinguished the faith into articles. To another, faith [Note: [Col. 0393] ibid.], as to Peter, upon which rock the Church is founded [Note: [Col. 0393] Matt. 16.]. To another, the grace of healings [Note: [Col. 0393] 1 Cor. 12.], as to Anthony, who healed many. To another, the working of miracles [Col. 0394B] [Note: [Col. 0393] ibid.], as to Martin, who shone with miracles. To another, prophecy [Note: [Col. 0393] ibid.], as to John the Hermit. To another, discernment of spirits [Note: [Col. 0393] ibid.], as to Macarius. To another, kinds of tongues [Note: [Col. 0393] ibid.], as to Jerome. To another, interpretation of utterances [Note: [Col. 0393] ibid.], as to Ambrose.

When these understand that their prayers have been heard by the Lord, they rejoice in the Introit, “When I cried” [Note: [Col. 0393] Ps. 54.], and in the Alleluia, “To you praise is due” [Note: [Col. 0393] Ps. 64.]. It should be noted here that almost wherever *Jerusalem* is written in chant, the neume is prolonged, so that the rejoicing of the heavenly Jerusalem may be figured. The same applies whenever we mark an Alleluia with two verses, so that we may rejoice in the twofold robe. They pray in the Gradual, “Guard” [Note: [Col. 0393] Ps. 16.], and in the Offertory, “To you” [Note: [Col. 0393] Ps. 24.]. Their sacrifice is accepted; hence in the Communion: “You will accept sacrifice” [Note: [Col. 0393] Ps. 50.].

Note, [Col. 0394C] moreover, that this Gospel [Note: [Col. 0393] Luke 19.], in which the destruction of Jerusalem is foretold, is read in August because the city is found to have been destroyed in this month first by Nebuchadnezzar and afterward by the Romans. May the Lord establish our city, hear our voices, and distribute the gifts of the Spirit to us.

## CHAPTER XI. THE ELEVENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

“God is in his holy place; God, who makes those of one manner dwell in a house” [Note: [Col. 0393] Ps. 67.]. The queen of Sheba came to Jerusalem to see the temple and hear the wisdom of Solomon [Note: [Col. 0393] 1 Kings 10.]. She prayed in the temple and offered gold and gems. She is the Church, which comes from Gentile custom and the paths of error to Jerusalem—that is, to the vision of peace—to hear the wisdom of Christ, the peaceful [Col. 0394D] king, and offers to wisdom the gold and gems of natural virtues. She recognizes that she was long a sinner, and therefore humbles herself under the parable of the publican and says: “God, be merciful to me a sinner.” Of her the Lord concludes in the Gospel: “Whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” [Note: [Col. 0393] Luke 18.].

The Epistle of the humble and peaceable Paul corresponds to her, in which he says of himself: “I am the least of the apostles” [Note: [Col. 0393] 1 Cor. 15.]. This humble person praises the Lord and gives thanks in the Introit, “God is in his holy place” [Note: [Col. 0393] Ps. 67.], in the Gradual, and in the Offertory. Having offered the gifts mentioned above [Col. 0395A], this person invites others, especially the Pharisee who had offered tithes, to offer likewise, in the Communion: “Honour” [Note: [Col. 0395] Prov. 3.]. At this time, this Communion is fittingly sung when barns are filled with crops and cellars with wine, with which the Lord is devoutly honoured.

## CHAPTER XII. THE TWELFTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

“Attend to my help, O God” [Note: [Col. 0395] Ps. 69.]. When Solomon died, the kingdom was divided [Note: [Col. 0395] 1 Kings 12.]. Therefore the September history is divided in two. The first part is fixed in one history; the other varies because the kingdom of Judah was established in David’s family, while the kingdom of Israel was occupied by many rulers. Hence a history is compiled concerning those righteous persons who were mixed among the Gentiles: Job, Tobit, Judith, and Esther. These works too are put [Col. 0395B] into the readers’ hands. Thus in the first week of September Job is read, which he himself wrote, with the responsories *If Good Things*. In the second, the book of Tobit, which he himself composed. In the third, Judith, which Achior issued. In the fourth, the book of Esther, composed by Mordecai—or rather by Ezra. Ezra’s book is also recited after these works; and with these are sung the responsories: *I Ask*, *Adonai*, *Lord*. In these times Elijah prophesied, who bore the type of Christ.

So, after Constantine’s death, the Church is divided. One part is Catholic; the other is separated through many schisms. From these the Catholic Church endured many adversities for the Lord, like those persons whose works are now read. Among Catholics some are perfect and some imperfect. The perfect are preachers, fit ministers [Col. 0395C] and fellow workers of God. They say in the Epistle [Note: [Col. 0395] 2 Cor. 3.]: “We have such confidence,” etc. These bring the imperfect and the alien, the deaf and mute, to the grace of Jesus Christ, as is read in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0395] Mark 7.]. Those are deaf and mute who become deaf to hearing commandments and mute in proclaiming praises.

Thus the voice of the perfect is: “Attend to my help, O God” [Note: [Col. 0395] Ps. 69.]. They implore God’s assistance that they may be able to resist heretics, correct them, and bring them to God’s grace. Or it is the voice of imperfect persons making progress, who implore God’s help in order that they may progress. In the Gradual, “I shall bless” [Note: [Col. 0395] Ps. 33.], and the Alleluia, “Lord, a refuge” [Note: [Col. 0395] Ps. 89.], it is indeed the voice of the perfect giving thanks that the former at times refrain from persecution [Col. 0395D] and that the latter are making progress. And because Moses was one of those who offered themselves for their subjects’ sins, therefore the Offertory sings: “Moses prayed” [Note: [Col. 0395] Exod. 32.]. These perfect persons are that land which, filled with the fruit of works—that is, with the gifts of the Holy Spirit—brings forth grass for beasts, that is, instruction for people. Hence in the Communion: “From the fruit” [Note: [Col. 0395] Ps. 103.]. Note that Job and Moses are rightly sung together, because they are found to have been contemporaries, through whose example we are invited to patience and gentleness.

## CHAPTER XIII. THE THIRTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

[Col. 0396A]

“Look, O Lord, upon your covenant” [Note: [Col. 0395] Ps. 73.]. Elisha was Elijah’s disciple. Through his merits a multitude of enemies is put to flight and a city is freed from danger [Note: [Col. 0395] 2 Kings 3.]. He is the Samaritan of whom the Gospel speaks [Note: [Col. 0395] Luke 10.], who delivered the man fallen among robbers—that is, the human race, which neither Law nor prophet could reconcile. Taking our lowliness upon himself, he poured the oil of mercy and the wine of justice upon the wounds of sins; bearing our sins upon the beast of his body, he brought him—that is, the wounded human race—as far as the inn of the Church. And he entrusted him to the innkeepers, that is, to the apostles and their successors. For neither priest nor Levite could heal him, because the Law led no one [Col. 0396B] to perfection; whence in the Epistle [Note: [Col. 0395] Heb. 7; Gal. 3.]: “To Abraham …” It is demonstrated there that justification does not come from the Law, because then all things were under sin.

Therefore this is the voice of the people to be delivered and of the infirm human race asking the Samaritan for healing: “Look”; likewise in the Gradual, “Look and arise” [Note: [Col. 0395] Ps. 73.]; and similarly in the Offertory, “In you, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0395] Ps. 30.]. The Communion, “Bread from heaven” [Note: [Col. 0395] Wis. 16.], which is taken from the Book of Wisdom, is the thanksgiving of one set free.

## CHAPTER XIV. THE FOURTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTECOST

“Our protector, behold, O God, and look upon the face of your Christ” [Note: [Col. 0395] Ps. 83.]. God had bestowed many benefits upon many kings of Jerusalem and Judah. Hezekiah alone, warned by Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0395] ch. 38.] to set his house in order, rendered [Col. 0396C] thanks for the benefits he had received. He is the one of the ten lepers of whom the Gospel speaks [Note: [Col. 0395] Luke 17.]: though all were cleansed, only one was found to give glory to God. Therefore those who did not give thanks are told in the Epistle [Note: [Col. 0395] Gal. 5.]: “Walk in the Spirit, and you shall not fulfil the desires of the flesh.”

That one man, who signifies the unity of the Church, prays in the Introit: “Protector,” where it says: “One day in your courts is better than thousands” [Note: [Col. 0395] Ps. 83.]; that is, it is better to think the same thing with one heart and one soul than to produce schisms. He gives thanks in the Gradual, “It is good” [Note: [Col. 0395] Ps. 117.], and invites others to the same in the Offertory, “The angel sends” [Note: [Col. 0395] Ps. 33.]. This Offertory is aptly sung together with Tobit, since his son too is delivered through an angel’s service. Where it says, “Taste and see” [Note: [Col. 0395] ibid.], what is to be tasted is sung in the Communion: “The bread which I shall give” [Note: [Col. 0395] John 6.].

On Wednesday the Gospel is read [Note: [Col. 0395] Mark 9.] concerning the deaf and mute man whom the apostles could not heal, because that kind of demon is cast out only by prayer and fasting; this fittingly corresponds to the day. For today is the fast of the Ember Days. Therefore two readings are read, so that those to be ordained may be instructed in the two commandments of charity, or the two laws: the first concerning the treader of grapes, appropriate to the season [Note: [Col. 0395] Amos 9.]; the second, namely from Ezra, is suitable [Col. 0397A] for those to be ordained [Note: [Col. 0397] 2 Ezra 8.]. To them it is said in the Introit: “Rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0397] Ps. 80.]. In the Offertory they promise to meditate [Note: [Col. 0397] Ps. 118.]. The Communion, “Eat rich foods” [Note: [Col. 0397] 2 Ezra 8.], is taken from the second reading.

On Friday, today’s office expresses the repentance of those to be ordained. Hence in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0397] Luke 5.]: “It came to pass,” the paralytic’s sins are forgiven. And in the reading from Hosea they are instructed toward conversion [Note: [Col. 0397] Hos. 14.]; and in the Introit, “Let [him] rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0397] Ps. 104.], they are invited to seek the Lord. The Gradual and Communion are prayers of the elect. The Offertory is their consolation.

The office of Saturday likewise pertains to the instruction of those to be ordained. In the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0397] Luke 13] they are warned that their teaching must not be barren, like the unfruitful fig tree, nor their life entangled in earthly things, like the bent-over woman. In the Epistle [Note: [Col. 0397] Heb. 9], moreover, where the first and second tabernacles are discussed, they are warned to serve in the tabernacle of the Church militant in such a way that they may be presented to the Lord in the tabernacle triumphant. In the readings this September fast is prescribed, and the reason for its institution and its usefulness are set forth. The remaining texts are exhortations, prayers, and consolations for those to be ordained. The Communion, namely, “In the seventh month,” is taken from the reading of Leviticus [Note: [Col. 0397] ch. 23]. Clerical ordination fittingly takes place in this month, since the feast of Tabernacles was celebrated in it. Those ordained are ministers of the Church, appointed in God’s tabernacle through sevenfold grace and in seven grades. Therefore ordination is celebrated in the third week; [Col. 0397C] because it was instituted by the apostles in the third age, that is, the age of grace. Yet formerly another reason was assigned by the wise.

For in former times fasts were appointed in the first week of March, the second of June, the third of September, and the fourth of December, in order to imitate the beginning-points of the four fourteen-generation divisions in the genealogy of Jesus Christ. For when someone is ordained, he is in a certain manner generated so as to belong to Christ. Thus Abraham is the first person of the first fourteen-generation division, from whom the ordination of the first week of March is derived. David is the first person of the second fourteen-generation division, from whom the ordination of the second week of June is derived. Jeconiah begins the third, from whom the ordination in the third week of September is derived. Finally Christ stands in the fourth place, from whom the ordination in the fourth week of December is derived. These ordinations are [Col. 0397D] derived from these persons rather than others, either because they were the greater figures in the genealogy, or because of the meanings of their names. For Abraham means “father of many nations”; David, “strong”; Jeconiah, “preparation of the Lord.”

Thus those who are ordained ought to be fathers, strong men, prepared for the Gospel of Jesus Christ. Or, just as there are fourteen generations from person to person, so fourteen weeks are found from ordination to ordination, so that those to be ordained may be skilled in both the discipline of the Decalogue and that of the Gospel. [Col. 0398A] Now, however, the fasts are arranged differently for the reasons already given: the universal fast, in the first week of Lent; the summer fast, in the week of Pentecost; the autumn fast, as before, in the third week of September—so that it always begins on the Wednesday of the third week; and the winter fast always ends on the Saturday before the Lord’s vigil.

And remember that the above-written fasts of the Four Seasons must be observed inviolably and altered for no voluntary reason. First, so that we may beseech the Lord for those being ordained anywhere. (For although ordination is not celebrated today in this church, nevertheless, when other clerics are ordained, we must fast and pray for them, because they are our brothers and united in one household [Note: [Col. 0397] Ps. 67].) Secondly, so that the unity of the Church may not be torn apart by the differing practices [Col. 0398B] of people—which would indeed happen if one person feasted while another fasted. Again, remember that the popes, down to Simplicius, always celebrated ordinations in December, so as to join those to be ordained to the genealogy of Jesus Christ; but Simplicius added ordinations to be conferred in February, so as to incorporate those to be ordained more closely into the body of Jesus Christ.

## CHAPTER XV. THE FIFTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTOST

“Incline, O Lord, thy ear unto me” [Note: [Col. 0397] Ps. 85]. To King Josiah Jeremiah prophesied the destruction of Jerusalem and the captivity of the people, because he had turned himself to concern for earthly things and had abandoned God’s law and justice [Note: [Col. 0397] 4 Kings 22, 23]. Josiah gathered the people [Col. 0398C] and commanded that the neglected law be observed. But even now there are those who hope in the uncertainty of riches, being more anxious about food and clothing than about the kingdom of God [Note: [Col. 0397] 1 Tim. 6]. To them the great Josiah says in the Gospel: “Do not be anxious about what you shall eat or what you shall wear. Seek first the kingdom of God and his justice, and all these things shall be added unto you” [Note: [Col. 0397] Matt. 6].

Paul addresses the same persons in the Epistle [Note: [Col. 0397] Gal. 5]: “If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit. Let us not become desirous of vain glory.” Thus, whoever sows from the flesh shall reap corruption. Therefore the voice in the Introit—“Incline” [Note: [Col. 0397] Ps. 85]—and in the Gradual—“It is good” [Note: [Col. 0397] Ps. 91]—and in the Offertory—“Waiting” [Note: [Col. 0397] Ps. 39]—is the voice of those who faithfully embrace Josiah’s commands. The Communion declares the food of the kingdom to be sought and the fruit we pursue [Col. 0398D] because we abide in God.

## CHAPTER XVI. THE SIXTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTOST

“Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I have cried to thee all day” [Note: [Col. 0397] Ps. 85]. After Josiah’s death, Jerusalem is destroyed, and the people are carried captive and oppressed [Note: [Col. 0397] 4 Kings 23, 24]. Therefore in this month of October the history of the Maccabees is read, and is sung: “May he open” [Note: [Col. 0397] 2 Macc. 1], concerning those who were heavily oppressed by their adversaries. Simon the high priest published its first part; another part, his son John; and the later part, a certain rustic but learned Jew.

These captives signify the Church militant, in which are leaders and followers, teachers and disciples, perfect and imperfect. The evangelical widow signifies teachers [Note: [Col. 0399] Luke 7]; she is a widow because, being militant, she is not with her triumphant Spouse. Her son dies when disciples are separated from the body of the Church for any offence; they are raised again when grace is infused. Thus she prays in the Gospel for her son’s resurrection, that is, for the infusion of grace. And in the Epistle [Note: [Col. 0399] Eph. 3] she exhorts them not to fail in tribulations, and for this purpose bends her knees. She likewise prays in the Introit, “Have mercy” [Note: [Col. 0399] Ps. 85], and in the Offertory, “O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0399] Ps. 70]. The Gradual refers to what is said in the Gospel: “Fear seized them all” [Note: [Col. 0399] Ps. 101]. The Communion, “O Lord, I will remember” [Note: [Col. 0399] Ps. 70], is an act of thanksgiving.

Or this month of October, [Col. 0399B] as some say, signifies the octave. Therefore, just as the Jews, when their battles were ended and the Temple restored, blessed the Lord in hymns and confessions [Note: [Col. 0399] 2 Macc. 10], so on the octave of the great feast the saints shall rejoice more festively [Note: [Col. 0399] John 7; Ps. 149].

## CHAPTER XVII. THE SEVENTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTOST

“Righteous art thou, O Lord, and upright is thy judgment” [Note: [Col. 0399] Ps. 118]. Daniel, set in captivity, interpreted the king’s dreams [Note: [Col. 0399] Dan. 2]. He rescued Susanna from death [Note: [Col. 0399] Dan. 13]. God himself delivered him from the lions’ den [Note: [Col. 0399] Dan. 14]. He is an example for what is read in the Gospel: “When he entered” [Note: [Col. 0399] Luke 14]. For, sitting in the lowest place, he deserved to go up; and when he humbled himself, he deserved to be exalted. In Paul’s Epistle he invites others to humility, saying: [Col. 0399C] “I beseech you, I who am a prisoner in the Lord, that you walk worthily of the calling wherewith you were called, with all humility and gentleness” [Note: [Col. 0399] Eph. 4]. That is, follow the example of him who called you, who was in the midst of his disciples “as one who serves” [Note: [Col. 0399] Luke 22], and who said to them: “Learn of me, for I am meek and humble of heart” [Note: [Col. 0399] Matt. 11].

The Introit, “Righteous art thou, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0399] Ps. 118], praises that Gospel saying: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” [Note: [Col. 0399] Luke 14]. The Gradual, “Blessed is the nation” [Note: [Col. 0399] Ps. 32], contains the universal blessedness of those who have humbled themselves and endured the Lord’s scourges patiently. The Offertory plainly sets forth Daniel’s example, when it says, “I prayed” [Note: [Col. 0399] Dan. 9]; in its verse an angel is mentioned, which is quite fitting, since [Col. 0399D] this office is sung about the dedication of Saint Michael. In the Communion Daniel exhorts his fellow captives—or any humble man, his fellow guests—to render their vows to the Lord and to humble themselves before “him who takes away the spirit of princes” [Note: [Col. 0399] Ps. 75], that is, of the proud, saying: “Give this humble man place” [Note: [Col. 0399] Luke 14].

## CHAPTER XVIII. THE EIGHTEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTOST

“Give peace, O Lord, to those who wait for thee, that thy prophets [Col. 0400A] may be found faithful” [Note: [Col. 0399] Ecclus. 36]. The aforementioned Daniel [Note: [Col. 0399] ch. 9], set in servitude, prayed for the people’s freedom. An angel appeared to him and foretold both that the people would be released and that Christ would be born. Therefore the great Daniel warns those returning from the captivity of sins in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0399] Matt. 22], “They came,” lest they forget to observe the law of Moses in its two commandments. Or, according to others, in another Gospel [Note: [Col. 0399] Matt. 23], he warns them that, if they sit upon the chair and preach well, they should not live badly.

In the Epistle [Note: [Col. 0399] 1 Cor. 1], Paul gives thanks for the captives’ return, the remission of sins, and the bestowal of gifts. The Introit, then, is Daniel’s voice, beseeching peace for the returning people; he rejoices in the Gradual, “I was glad” [Note: [Col. 0399] Ps. 121], because the people who are to enter the house of the Lord are foretold. In the [Col. 0400B] Offertory and Communion he invites and exhorts the returning people, after Moses’ example, to erect altars and offer sacrifices [Note: [Col. 0399] Exod. 40; Ps. 95].

## CHAPTER XIX. THE NINETEENTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTOST

“I am the salvation of the people, says the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0399] 1 Esdr. 1, 2]. When seventy years had passed, Cyrus permitted the people to depart. Zerubbabel and the priests proclaim God’s words to that people and strengthen them for their return. Thus our Cyrus, as is read in today’s Gospel, said to the healed paralytic: “Rise, take up thy bed, and go into thine house” [Note: [Col. 0399] Matt. 9]. But first, as the Epistle says [Note: [Col. 0399] Eph. 4], you must put on the new man, so that you may be able to return to your house.

He therefore who freed the people from captivity and healed the paralytic from his infirmity [Col. 0400C] truly sings in the Introit: “Salvation,” etc. But the liberated people and the healed paralytic direct prayer and the lifting up of hands to him in the Gradual, saying: “Let [my prayer] be directed” [Note: [Col. 0399] Ps. 140]. He also strengthens the feet formerly enfeebled, in the Offertory: “If I shall walk,” to walk “in the midst of tribulations” [Note: [Col. 0399] Ps. 137]; and in the Communion: “Thou hast commanded” [Note: [Col. 0399] Ps. 118], for the keeping of the ordinances.

## CHAPTER XX. THE TWENTIETH SUNDAY AFTER PENTOST

“All that thou hast done to us, O Lord, thou hast done in true judgment” [Note: [Col. 0399] Dan. 3]. After the return from captivity, Jerusalem is rebuilt and the Temple restored through Zechariah and Haggai, Ezra and Malachi [Note: [Col. 0399] passim], through whom the coming of the Lord is foretold. Therefore, in this month of November until the Lord’s Advent, the history of the prophets is sung: “I saw the Lord”; and in the hands of readers come the writings of the prophets—Ezekiel, Daniel, and the Twelve Prophets—the book of whom was published either by themselves or by the elders of the synagogue.

That bodily captivity signifies our spiritual captivity. Return from captivity is the remission of sins. Therefore the King of the prophets, wishing to restore the heavenly [Col. 0401A] Jerusalem, made a wedding-feast for his Son and, as is read in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0401] Matt. 22], invited many to the heavenly banquet. Note that three marriages are mentioned in the Gospel.

Of the first it is said: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who was a king, who made a marriage for his son” [Note: [Col. 0401] ibid.]. This Son is Christ, who joined human nature to himself; the bridal chamber was the womb of the Virgin. Thus, “like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ps. 18], he invited men to these nuptials before the Law through the patriarchs, and then under the Law through the prophets.

Of the second it is said [Note: [Col. 0401] Luke 12]: “Be ye like men waiting for their lord when he shall return from the wedding.” This lord is Christ, the new man, who in ascending joined angelic nature to himself. To these nuptials he summoned the Gentiles through the apostles [Col. 0401B].

Of the third it is said: “The virgins who were prepared entered with him to the wedding” [Note: [Col. 0401] Matt. 25]. Here the bridegroom is Christ, who after judgment will join the Church to himself and place her in the bridal chamber of glory. We are invited to these daily through the prelates of the Church. The Church celebrates the first at Christ’s Nativity, the second at the Ascension, and the third at the Resurrection. Christ will take his bride and bring her from the Babylon of the world into the wine-cellar of Paradise [Note: [Col. 0401] Song 1]. These are the nuptials that may be understood here.

For when a man entered not having a wedding garment, he was cast into the outer darkness [Note: [Col. 0401] Matt. 22]; but the others, clothed in wedding garments, are united with the Lord. These are the living stones from which the walls of Jerusalem are built [Col. 0401C] [Note: [Col. 0401] 1 Pet. 2; Ps. 50]. Therefore, lest we return to a similar captivity and be excluded from the wedding, Paul warns us in the preceding Epistle: “See therefore that you walk carefully, not as unwise men, but as wise” [Note: [Col. 0401] Eph. 5].

The Introit, “All that thou hast done” [Note: [Col. 0401] Dan. 3], is Daniel’s voice, recalling the past captivity and attributing it to God’s judgment upon the people’s merits. Similarly, in the Offertory, “By the rivers” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ps. 136], we lament that captivity; but in the Gradual, “The eyes of all” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ps. 144], we give thanks. In the Communion, “Remember the word” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ps. 118], we ask that the nuptials promised in hope may be received in reality.

## CHAPTER XXI. THE TWENTY-FIRST SUNDAY AFTER PENTOST

“In thy will, O Lord, all things are established” [Note: [Col. 0401] Esther 13]. [Col. 0401D] Though returned from captivity and having built the city, the people are nevertheless attacked by the surrounding enemies [Note: [Col. 0401] 1 Esdr. 4 and following]. For when a person, set in conflict between virtues and vices, has begun at times to flourish in holy virtues, and his wife has grown like a fruitful vine along the sides of his house—that is, of the Church—and his children like young olive plants around his table [Note: [Col. 0401] Ps. 127], suddenly the tempter shakes the house of steadfastness and destroys the works of virtue.

The fever in the Gospel, which nearly extinguished the royal official’s son [Note: [Col. 0401] John 4], signifies the shock or danger of this warfare [Col. 0402A]. The preceding Epistle [Note: [Col. 0401] Eph. 6] strengthens this combatant and equips him with spiritual arms, saying: “Be strengthened.” Therefore the voice of the combatant is: “In thy will” [Note: [Col. 0401] Esther 13], and in the Gradual: “O Lord, thou hast been our refuge” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ps. 89], and in the Communion: “In thy salvation” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ps. 118], where he either attributes victory to God, or prays, or gives thanks.

But in the Offertory, “There was a man” [Note: [Col. 0401] Job 1], the example of a strong combatant is proposed. What is read historically in Job is understood morally in the human person. Here it should be noted that the words in the Offertory are not repeated, but are, as it were, ridiculously doubled in the verses. This is because words are interrupted in one who is sick and trying to speak, and what is frequently begun is scarcely completed. In the verses Job speaks while sick; but in [Col. 0402B] the Offertory the writer, not sick, speaks of Job in the third person, whose patience is commended to us as an example.

## CHAPTER XXII. THE TWENTY-SECOND SUNDAY AFTER PENTOST

“If thou shalt observe iniquities, O Lord, O Lord, who shall endure?” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ps. 129]. God’s people are still afflicted, as they deserve because of their sins. This bodily affliction signifies the spiritual affliction which has existed from the beginning of the world, exists now, and shall exist until the end of the age. It will increase in the times of Antichrist, when the love of many shall grow cold [Note: [Col. 0401] Matt. 24], when the king comes to settle accounts with his servants and delivers the servant to the torturers until he pays [Col. 0402C] the whole debt, as today’s Gospel teaches [Note: [Col. 0401] Matt. 18].

For each of us to obtain remission of this debt, we must pray that love may not grow cold, but, as today’s Epistle says, may “abound more and more in all knowledge” [Note: [Col. 0401] Phil. 1]. Therefore, whoever considers the greatness of his own debt says in the Introit: “If [thou shalt observe] iniquities” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ps. 129]. Considering the usefulness of love, which both prevents sin and remits sins committed, he says in the Gradual: “Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” [Note: [Col. 0401] Ps. 132]. This dwelling together is ointment—that is, the remission of sins—which descends from Christ the head onto the beard, that is, onto the apostles, and to the edge, that is, onto us. The wicked servant of the Gospel did not have this ointment, because he did not remit his fellow servant’s debt.

In the Offertory, “Remember,” [Col. 0402D] taken from Esther’s prayer [Note: [Col. 0401] ch. 14], we are admonished to pray that our words may please in the sight of the King who settled accounts with his servants—namely, these words: “Forgive us our debts” [Note: [Col. 0401] Matt. 6]. But these words will not please in the Prince’s sight unless we forgive “our debtors also.” What is sung in the Communion, “I say,” is taken from Gospel authority, where the sinner is understood as a debtor who has compassion on a debtor, over whose conversion there is joy in heaven [Note: [Col. 0401] Luke 15].

## CHAPTER XXIII. THE TWENTY-THIRD SUNDAY AFTER PENTOST

[Col. 0403A]

“The Lord says: I think thoughts of peace, and not of affliction” [Note: [Col. 0403] Jer. 29]. At last the people were so pressed by afflictions that they were compelled to pay tribute to Caesar. This foreshadowed the time when Antichrist will bring the whole people under his service. Thus the Gospel is read in which the question is proposed whether it is lawful to give tribute to Caesar or not [Note: [Col. 0403] Matt. 22]. There we are warned to follow him in whose image we were created. He not only made our soul in his own image, but, as the Epistle says, “will transform the body of our lowliness to be conformed to the body of his glory” [Note: [Col. 0403] Phil. 3].

And because at that time the remnant of Israel shall be saved [Note: [Col. 0403] Rom. 11], the Lord declares in the Introit what had been prophesied concerning them [Col. 0403B], namely: “I think thoughts of peace, and not of affliction; you shall call upon me, and I will hear you, and I will bring back your captivity from all places” [Note: [Col. 0403] Jer. 29]. They respond in the Gradual: “Thou hast delivered us” [Note: [Col. 0403] Ps. 43], and in the Offertory: “Out of the depths” [Note: [Col. 0403] Ps. 129]. In the Communion the Lord again assures them of salvation, saying: “Amen, I say to you” [Note: [Col. 0403] Mark 11].

## CHAPTER XXIV. THE TWENTY-FOURTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTOST

There follows another Sunday, on which the Gospel concerning the ruler’s daughter and the woman with the issue of blood is read [Note: [Col. 0403] Matt. 9]. The ruler’s daughter is the synagogue; the woman with the issue of blood is the Church of the Gentiles. Salvation is promised first to the former, but given first to the latter. At length what was promised is bestowed upon the former; for the Church of the Gentiles precedes the Jews in receiving the salvation [Col. 0403C] prepared for them. But when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel shall be saved [Note: [Col. 0403] Rom. 11]. For this to be fulfilled, Paul prays in the Epistle, saying: “We do not cease praying for you” [Note: [Col. 0403] Col. 1].

Note that this Sunday has no proper chanted office: either because the Church shall be harassed by the persecutions of Antichrist and therefore keeps its instruments silent; or because the preceding office is most fittingly adapted to this Gospel; or because this Sunday frequently occurs in surplus, and therefore lacks its own office.

## CHAPTER XXV. THE TWENTY-FIFTH SUNDAY AFTER PENTOST

There follows yet another Sunday, adorned with its own reading and Gospel. In it is read the Gospel of the five loaves by which the Lord fed five thousand persons [Col. 0403D] [Note: [Col. 0403] John 6]. This also seems fittingly to concern that time in which Judaea shall be filled with spiritual understanding of Moses’ five books. Then that prophetic saying of Jeremiah shall be fulfilled: “Behold, days are coming,” where it is said: “In those days Israel shall be saved” [Note: [Col. 0403] Jer. 23].

The preceding chanted office also accords with this reading. For as the reading says, “The Lord lives, who brought out and brought back the seed of the house of Israel from the northern land and from all lands” [Note: [Col. 0403] ibid.], so the Introit sings: “I will bring back your captivity from all places” [Note: [Col. 0403] Jer. 29]. Therefore, released from the captivity by which they are now held, they offer thanksgiving in the Gradual, “Thou hast delivered us” [Col. 0404A] [Note: [Col. 0403] Ps. 43]; in the Offertory, “Out of the depths” [Note: [Col. 0403] Ps. 129], they offer prayer for this purpose; and in the Communion, “Amen, I say to you” [Note: [Col. 0403] Mark 11], they receive assurance that their petition is granted.

Finally, it is noteworthy that we have made an excursus through Old Testament history in the Sundays from David to the Lord’s Advent, and have compared it with the course of the running Church, from the advent of humility to that of final majesty. Therefore on this last Sunday, which concludes the others, an office is fittingly placed that may pertain to both comings of the Lord: the prophecy of Jeremiah, “Behold, days are coming, and I will raise up” [Note: [Col. 0403] Jer. 23]—behold the first advent; “In those days Judah shall be saved” [Note: [Col. 0403] ibid.]—behold the second.

Likewise, the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0403] John 6] rightly concerns the five loaves, because after five thousand years the bread of angels was given us in the first advent [Note: [Col. 0403] Ps. 77]. From this point five Sundays are also counted to the day on which the bread born in the manger shall be proclaimed [Note: [Col. 0403] Luke 2]. It is our custom to appoint this Epistle and Gospel, with the office, for Trinity Sunday; but during the week they are treated as on other ferial days. This Gospel is fittingly read near the feast of Saint Andrew, because it contains mention of him.

Nor should this be passed over in silence: although we have referred the summer nocturnal readings to that sequence of time extending from David to the Lord’s Advent, we may fittingly refer them also [Col. 0404C] to the sequence that began with the primitive Church. For just as David succeeded Saul, as is first read in the first books of Kings [Note: [Col. 0403] 1 Kings 16], so the worship of the one God succeeded the worship of demons. And just as David’s kingdom was divided into schisms through Rehoboam and Jeroboam, as is read in the following books [Note: [Col. 0403] 3 Kings 12], so the madness of heretics divides the Church. Then follow Solomon’s books, because after the struggles with heretics the talents of holy teachers shone in the Church. Afterward follows the book of Job, which treats of his persecutions and consolations, because although the Church flourishes in peace, the temptations of spiritual enemies are not lacking. The more hidden their combat, the more difficult it is; but the victory gained will be more glorious.

[Col. 0404D] It should also be added that we may adapt the individual months to former times. For January, in which the new year begins, signifies the time after the Flood, when the world is renewed. February, in which the alleluia is laid aside, indicates the time in which the diversity of tongues is confounded. March, in which Lent is most often celebrated, denotes the time in which God’s people were afflicted in Egypt. April, in which Easter is observed, shows the time in which the people were freed from Pharaoh. May, in which Pentecost is celebrated [Col. 0405A], recalls the time in which the people rejoice in the land of promise. June and July, in which the history of Kings is read, commemorate the reigns of Saul and David. August, in which the Book of Wisdom is recited, signifies the reign of wise Solomon.

The remaining four months denote the principal kingdoms: Babylon, in the East; Persia, in the South; Greece, in the North; and Rome, in the West. Thus the history of Job, read for two weeks in September, represents the eastern kingdom. Hence it says: “That man was great among all the easterners” [Note: [Col. 0405] Job 1]. It is read for two weeks because that kingdom endured two annual weeks, that is, twice seven hundred years. For so many years are found from the time of Ninus, with whom the kingdom of Babylon began, until Cyrus king of the Persians, in whom it failed. In the remaining part of September the Persian kingdom is indicated. Therefore two histories are read, because kings were then chosen sometimes from the Persians and sometimes from the Medes. The history of the Maccabees, read in October, signifies the Greek kingdom, under which the Maccabees were afflicted. November and December, in which prophecies are read, signify the Roman kingdom, in which Christ’s religion flourishes. The prophecies speak chiefly of Christ, whose nativity is at the end of the year, just as the Roman kingdom is at the end of the world.

# BOOK IX. On the Feasts of the Saints, and First Those from Advent until the Nativity of the Lord

[Col. 0405]

[Col. 0405B] “The saints rejoice in glory, exulting in their dwellings” [Note: [Col. 0405] Ps. 149]. Once wayfarers, they have become possessors [Note: [Col. 0405] 1 Cor. 13]. Once strangers [Note: [Col. 0405] 1 Pet. 2], they have become kings of the household [Note: [Col. 0405] Eph. 2]. The Church rejoices in their rejoicing when she celebrates their heavenly birthdays. But since they shall multiply in the house of the Lord like the cedar of Lebanon [Note: [Col. 0405] Ps. 91], let us at least bring forward a few words concerning a few.

Concerning those feasts of saints which occur in Advent, this should, according to some, be generally observed: although during Advent the Church does not use subdiaconal tunics and dalmatics, and omits *Te Deum laudamus*, *Gloria in excelsis*, and *Ite missa est*, nevertheless at the feasts of Saint Andrew and Saint Thomas she does not omit the aforesaid praises and signs of glorification, but fittingly celebrates them everywhere with solemnity. This is not so at the other feasts of saints, except where the dedication of a church is celebrated or commemorated, or the feast of that saint whose name the church itself bears.

On these feasts, therefore—those of Saint Andrew and Saint Thomas, church dedications, and feasts proper to particular churches—the Mass of the feast, with the aforesaid solemnities, is celebrated at the third hour, or in the morning. The same is to be observed at other feasts of nine lessons, though without the solemnities. But at the ninth hour the Mass of the fast is to be sung.

Nor should this be passed over in silence: if Saint Andrew’s feast falls on a Sunday, since Advent according to the rule begins on that same day, the feast is transferred to Monday, [Col. 0405D] because that Sunday is privileged. The same applies in similar cases, as we shall say below. The rule for the beginning of Advent is this: “Remember [the day] nearest to Andrew’s feast.” Or thus: “Whatever [weekday] lies nearest to Andrew’s feast designates the first weekday of the Lord’s Advent.” We have stated another rule when we treated of the Lord’s Advent. Thus the feast of Blessed Andrew sometimes precedes Advent and sometimes falls within Advent.

## CHAPTER I. ON SAINT ANDREW

Asian presbyters, disciples of Andrew himself, wrote the passion of Blessed Andrew, saying that he discoursed on the mystery of the Cross and the sacrifice of the altar. In Achaia he gained many people; at last, under the proconsul Aegeas, he underwent the punishment of the cross. Hanging upon it for two days, he ceased neither to praise God nor to preach to the people. Therefore the people demanded him from the proconsul, saying: “Grant us the righteous man. [Col. 0406C] Restore to us the holy man.” Finally, when he had given thanks to God and expired upon the cross, Maximilla embalmed his body with spices and buried it.

From this legend and from his calling, which is contained in the Gospel—“Jesus walking beside the sea” [Note: [Col. 0405] Matt. 4]—his history is compiled.

## CHAPTER II. ON SAINT NICHOLAS

The Argolic doctors committed to writing, for remembrance, the life of Blessed Nicholas and the miracles performed during his life. They say that, born of an illustrious family, he was filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother’s womb, or from his childhood years; that he freed three virgins from the shameful commerce of their father; that he was advanced to the supreme priesthood by divine revelation; that he aided sailors suffering shipwreck [Col. 0406D]; that he multiplied grain; that he exposed Diana’s deceit by inflammable oil; and that he freed some from capital sentence and others from prison.

Oil, a remedy for various [Col. 0407A] ailments, sweats from his tomb. When a substitute bishop had been installed and he was deprived of his see, it ceased to flow; when he was restored, it flowed again. With how many miracles Nicholas shone after his death, neither writing suffices to record nor any eloquence could express. From this legend, therefore, today’s history is compiled.

## CHAPTER III. ON SAINT LUCY

Blessed Lucy was interceding at the tomb of the blessed virgin Agatha for her mother, who suffered from an issue of blood. Blessed Agatha said to her in a dream: “My sister Lucy, why do you ask from me what you yourself can immediately grant through yourself?” And below: “As through me the city of the Catanese is exalted by Christ, so through you the city of Syracuse shall be adorned.” And from that hour her mother was healed [Col. 0407B].

Afterward, when she had distributed her patrimony to the poor, her betrothed accused her before the consul Paschasius. When he invited her to sacrifice to demons, she, instructed by the words of the Gospel and the Apostle, steadfastly resisted him to his face. Therefore it is fittingly sung in the daytime office: “Thou hast loved justice” [Note: [Col. 0407] Ps. 44], and “Grace is poured forth” [Note: [Col. 0407] ibid.]. Paschasius therefore handed her over to pimps to be violated and to fire to be burned. But the pimps are defeated and the fire is extinguished. Finally the virgin Lucy is pierced through the entrails with a sword and dies. From this legend today’s history is compiled.

## CHAPTER IV. ON SAINT THOMAS

The legend of Blessed Thomas, and anything found in responsories or antiphons drawn from it, is counted among the apocrypha [Col. 0407C].

## CHAPTER V. ON THE FEASTS FROM THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD UNTIL SEPTUAGESIMA

Concerning the feasts from the Lord’s Nativity until Septuagesima, this rule is to be observed: on the feast of Saint Stephen and on all other feasts that occur or can occur, both Matins and the remaining Hours are to be sung from the feast, except for Vespers belonging to the Lord’s Nativity. When the texts of the Nativity have been sung at these Vespers, the antiphon, with versicle and collect, is to be sung when the *Magnificat* is added with the antiphon.

## CHAPTER VI. ON SAINT STEPHEN

[Col. 0407D]

Stephen’s passion is believed to have been accomplished in August—on the day, that is, on which his discovery is celebrated. And the discovery took place on the present day. But because the feast of his passion is more worthy than the feast of his discovery, it is transferred to the season of the Lord’s Nativity. Or this is because his basilica was dedicated on this day; or because Stephen is the protomartyr, the first after the Lord’s Ascension to suffer martyrdom for Christ, namely in that same year as the Lord’s Passion. This is to be born in heaven. Christ’s Nativity has bestowed such a birth upon us. It was fitting, therefore, that Stephen’s Nativity [Col. 0408A] should be joined to the Lord’s Nativity, so that it might be marked that the one follows from the other. Hence one reads: “Yesterday Christ was born on earth, so that today Stephen might be born in heaven.” From this saying it is inferred that the deaths of saints are called their nativities or birthdays, because then they are born into the fellowship of angels.

His history was composed by Alcuin, Charlemagne’s chaplain. He took the nocturnal antiphons from the Psalms to which they are ascribed; the rest is more plainly drawn from the Acts of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0407] Acts 6 and 7], beginning with the passage: “Stephen, full of grace,” etc. Alleluia is frequently used in the versicles, either because of the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity or because of joy at Stephen’s fellowship and the assembly of angels. On this day the Gospel is read [Note: [Col. 0407] Matt. 23] concerning the killing of the prophets, in which it is said: “From the blood of righteous Abel” [Col. 0408B]; for just as he was the protomartyr in the Old Testament, so this man was in the New. Or because it says there: “You stone those who are sent to you”; and Stephen is read to have been stoned [Note: [Col. 0407] Acts 7]. Or because it says there: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” which suits the approaching Nativity.

His feast, since he was the outstanding one among deacons, ought to be celebrated by deacons, provided that they do not usurp the office of the priesthood, as they foolishly do in some places by giving blessings over the lessons.

## CHAPTER VII. ON BLESSED JOHN THE EVANGELIST

The Nativity, or Passing, of blessed John the Evangelist did not occur today. Rather, when he was ninety-nine years old, in the forty-fourth year after the Lord’s Passion [Col. 0408C], he departed from the way of this world on the Nativity of blessed John the Baptist. Therefore, because that feast is greater—the one of whom no greater has arisen among those born of women [Note: [Col. 0407] Matt. 11], and at whose birth the angel foretold joy [Note: [Col. 0407] Luke 1]—this man’s feast is transferred to the day on which he is said to have been invested with the mitre at Ephesus.

This was also fitting for the reason that the Bridegroom, who is ruddy and white [Note: [Col. 0407] Song 5], should have two companions: Stephen, ruddy through martyrdom, and John, white through virginity. This man reclined upon the Lord’s breast at supper [Note: [Col. 0407] John 13]; to him Christ entrusted the Virgin to a virgin [Note: [Col. 0407] John 19]. He bore witness to Christ [Note: [Col. 0407] John 21]. He composed the Apocalypse. He was banished into exile and cast into a vat of oil. At last he ended old age in peace. Therefore the Lord said: “Thus I will have him remain; what is that to you?” [Note: [Col. 0407] Ibid.]

Some say that, after he had celebrated Mass, he descended into a tomb and vanished from the eyes of those standing around. Since earth bubbles up from its depths, they add that he lives beneath the earth and that the earth bubbles from his breath. Others say that he was translated into heaven. Thus today’s history is assembled partly from the Gospel and partly from his tribulation. In its final responsory, namely *In medio Ecclesiae* (“In the midst of the Church”), taken from the book of Wisdom [Note: [Col. 0407] Sirach 15], where the spirit of understanding is treated, a jubilus is sung, because through the spirit of understanding he spoke concerning the ineffable Word of God.

Since, having received light, he offered God the sacrifice of virginity, Mass is sung at the beginning of light; and what is sung and read in both Masses plainly appears to pertain to him. Since he was both priest and bishop, priests and bishops should especially celebrate his feast.

## CHAPTER VIII. ON THE HOLY INNOCENTS

The passion of the Innocents did not immediately follow on the fourth day, but after the turning of the year. For in the first year Herod awaited the Magi and, having been accused, went to Rome. Returning and seeing that he had been mocked by the Magi, on the fourth day of the second year he killed children two years old and under [Note: [Col. 0409] Matt. 2]. *Bimatus*, in Greek, is called in Latin a year or a two-year period. For he feared lest the child, whom the stars serve [Col. 0409B], might transform his appearance above or below the age in question.

Then was fulfilled that passage of Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 0409] ch. 31]: “A voice was heard in Ramah, that is, in the heights: Rachel weeping for her children”—namely, the women of Bethlehem, near which Rachel was buried [Note: [Col. 0409] Gen. 35]. “She would not be comforted,” that is, she grieved inconsolably, because they are not, that is, they had ceased to be.

The nocturnal antiphons of today’s history are taken from the Psalms; the rest is plainly gathered from the Gospel or the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0409] ch. 14]. The statement that they are one hundred and forty-four thousand gives a finite number, because God comprehends all under a definite number. But the number also contains the mystery of the perfect Trinity proclaimed through the four quarters of the world. For three multiplied by four makes twelve; again twelve by four makes forty-eight; and forty-eight by four makes one hundred and forty-four [Col. 0409C].

The words, “I saw beneath God’s altar the souls of those slain” [Note: [Col. 0409] Rev. 6], should be understood thus: John saw the souls of the slain beneath the altar, that is, humbled beneath their head, or hidden away, because no one here perceives how they are there. On this day festive vestments are removed, such as the dalmatic and tunicle, and songs of joy are silenced, such as *Te Deum laudamus*, *Gloria*, *Alleluia* at Mass, and *Ite missa est*, because they descended into the lower regions. Or this is because in these little ones are understood the little ones of the Church, who suffer death through heretics: for Herod is a changeable heretic. Or it is done to represent maternal sorrow [Col. 0409D]. These observances are to be maintained unless the feast falls on a Sunday. For then no chant is omitted, because of joy in future glorification.

Yet we say *Gloria Patri*, and in the nocturnal office we also frequently use *Alleluia*, because, although they descended to the lower regions, we do not doubt that through Christ’s resurrection they have been assumed into joy. Hence some sing *Laus tibi* (“Praise to you”) instead of *Alleluia* at Mass; others sing *Cantemus eia* (“Let us sing, eia!”). What is sung and read in the Mass plainly pertains to the Innocents and requires no exposition. Innocent boys should celebrate the feast of the Innocents, provided that they do not usurp an office not due to them.

## CHAPTER IX. FELIX ON THE PINCIAN

[Col. 0410A]

Felix “on the Pincian” takes his title from the place. For the Pincian is a place near the city where the body of the confessor Felix is happily honoured, while his soul is more happily crowned in heaven.

## CHAPTER X. MARIUS, MARTHA, AUDIFAX, AND HABACUC

Roman presbyters wrote the passion of the blessed martyrs Marius, Martha, Audifax, and Habacuc: when, at the command of Claudius, the hands of Marius and of his sons Audifax and Habacuc were cut off, Martha gathered the blood of her husband and sons and anointed her face with it. At last the father and sons were beheaded and afterwards half-burned; Martha was drowned in a well [Col. 0410B] and fell asleep in the Lord. From these events the antiphons for today’s feast are gathered.

## CHAPTER XI. THE HOLY FABIAN AND SEBASTIAN

The feast of the blessed martyrs Fabian and Sebastian is commemorated under a double collect; at Mass and in both offices one collect is concluded “through the Lord.” The nocturnal office, which pertains only to Saint Sebastian, is undoubtedly derived from his life and passion. Although he had been acceptable to the emperors, by their command he was shot with arrows and beaten until he was exhausted. His body was first cast into a sewer, then placed by a certain matron near the resting-place of the Apostles.

## CHAPTER XII. SAINT AGNES

[Col. 0410C]

Saint Ambrose wrote the passion of blessed Agnes, saying that she was cast into flames. When these were extinguished by prayer, she ended her life struck by the sword. The sung history is clearly borrowed from this passion. Because the prefect’s son loved her, the introit is rightly sung on her feast: “Sinners waited for me” [Note: [Col. 0409] Ps. 118].

It should not be passed over in unprofitable silence that this feast has no octave. Hence one should not write “the octave of Agnes,” but “the second feast of Agnes,” so that it may not be understood as an octave but as a repeated solemnity, on account of the miracle that occurred on that day, when she appeared to her parents [Col. 0410D] saying: “Do not mourn me as dead, but rejoice with me, because I have received a dwelling with these virgins.” The office is celebrated as on the principal feast.

## CHAPTER XIII. ON FEASTS FROM SEPTUAGESIMA UNTIL EASTER

According to some, this rule is to be observed concerning feasts from Septuagesima until the day of the Resurrection: on the feasts of the Purification, the Chair of Saint Peter, Saint Matthias, the Annunciation, a Dedication, the special patron saint, and the anniversary Easter, chants of praise such as *Te Deum*, *Gloria in excelsis*, and *Ite missa est* are not to be suppressed. Rather, everything [Col. 0411A] is to be sung as at other times, except *Alleluia*. One Mass of the feast and another of the Lenten fast are to be celebrated, as in the fast—that is, with litanies and genuflections.

## CHAPTER XIV. ON SAINT BLAISE

Blessed Blaise, a physician, healed not only sick people but also sick animals. When he had at last become a bishop and was imprisoned, a certain woman brought him food with a candle. He told the woman that every year, on the day of his death, she should offer a candle in his commemoration, and that God would free her from illnesses and adversities and grant her abundance of temporal goods. And so it happened. From this arose the custom that numerous vows are directed to him for various [Col. 0411B] illnesses of people and beasts of burden, and that vows are paid in his honour with candles.

## CHAPTER XV. ON SAINT AGATHA

The passion of blessed Agatha provides us with the sung history. After slaps, the rack, and tortures; after the cutting off and healing of her breasts; and after being rolled on coals, she was finally perfected in prison. At her head in the tomb a tablet was visibly placed through angelic ministry, on which was written: “A holy, willing mind; honour to God; and deliverance for her native city.” Hence the custom arose of holding a procession through villages with a tablet bearing her image [Col. 0411C].

## CHAPTER XVI. ON THE CHAIR OF SAINT PETER

We celebrate the Chair of blessed Peter because he was installed as bishop in the see of Antioch. Hence, although *Gloria in excelsis* and *Ite missa est* may perhaps be silenced according to some, we ought nevertheless not omit *Te Deum laudamus*, because we are accustomed to sing it at the election of pontiffs. In the nocturnal office, therefore, we sing the history proper to blessed Peter. In the daytime office we celebrate him with the episcopal office, namely *Statuit* (“He established”) [Note: [Col. 0411] Sirach 45]. We commemorate his seat so that through him we may prepare for ourselves a seat in heaven. On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, he is recorded in the Martyrology as having first sat in the Roman see.

## CHAPTER XVII. ON SAINT MATTHIAS

[Col. 0411D]

Blessed Matthias, chosen by lot for the apostleship [Note: [Col. 0411] Acts 1], as he deserved the fellowship of the Apostles, so too received an office of like solemnity. He was one of the seventy disciples, chosen by lot by the Apostles in place of Judas Iscariot. Therefore *Matthias* means “given.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. ON THE ANNUNCIATION OF THE VIRGIN

Against celebrating the Annunciation of the Lord it is customarily objected that *Gloria in excelsis*, which is the chant of the Nativity; *Ite missa est*, which belongs to the Resurrection [Col. 0412A]; and *Te Deum laudamus*, which belongs to the finding of the drachma [Note: [Col. 0411] Luke 15], ought not to be sung on it, because the Lord had not yet brought these things to pass in human affairs. But those who contend for celebration reply that this feast is the source and beginning of Christ’s feasts; and that, although the aforesaid marvels had not yet occurred in actuality or time, in hope they preceded them.

If this feast falls on Passion Sunday or Palm Sunday, it is moved to Monday; for this is the general rule concerning privileged Sundays. If it falls in the three days before Easter, it is anticipated on the Saturday before Palm Sunday; some, however, transfer it to the octave. Likewise, if it falls on Easter Day, it may fittingly be celebrated within the week [Col. 0412B], in which the history compiled concerning the Advent is sung.

## CHAPTER XIX. ON FEASTS FROM THE RESURRECTION UNTIL THE OCTAVE OF PENTECOST

Concerning feasts from the Resurrection until the octave of Pentecost, this general rule is to be observed: on every feast of saints the history *Beatus vir* (“Blessed is the man”) is sung [Note: [Col. 0411] Ps. 111]. It is used for apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins; it is frequently used for one saint and for many. For this one Blessed Man is Christ, according to Tyconius’s rule: head and members. He is the martyr of whom it is said in the antiphon, “Daughters” [Note: [Col. 0411] Song 3], whom—the head, that is—the Lord crowned [Col. 0412C] with the robe of immortality in this season of solemnity and joy [Note: [Col. 0411] Ps. 8]; the members he will crown later, in the time that this season signifies, which will be the time of eternity and glory.

He is the one who speaks in the office now frequently used. In this season we frequently use identical offices for saints’ feasts because, in the reality signified, the wage of all will be the same [Note: [Col. 0411] Matt. 20], and because then we shall be glorified as one with Christ, who is now glorified in time.

Another rule is that on a feast of three lessons only one *Alleluia* is sung, and on a feast of nine lessons two are sung: one concerning the Resurrection, which is not repeated, and the other concerning the feast. But it is asked why the feast is not celebrated of those who are believed to have risen with Christ and ascended into heaven. Thus in the Gospel: “Many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose with Christ” [Col. 0412D; Note: [Col. 0411] Matt. 27; cf. Matt. 27:52]. The answer is: their death ought not to be solemnized, because they descended to the lower regions; indeed, we ought to solemnize their glorification. But we cannot do this because of the authority of a greater matter; rather, we distribute their feasts across other times, namely when we dedicate their churches. Hence in some parts of the world there has arisen the not blameworthy custom of building and consecrating churches in memory of the saints of the Old Testament: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, David, Daniel, and others.

## CHAPTER XX. ON SAINT MARK

[Col. 0413A]

On the feast of Saint Mark the Greater Litanies to Saint Peter are observed, concerning which we have spoken.

## CHAPTER XXI. THE HOLY PHILIP AND JAMES

On the Kalends of May the passion of Philip and James the Less is celebrated. He was called “the Less,” not by age but by calling, a custom that the Church still observes today in receiving brothers. This James was called the brother of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0413] Gal. 1] because he resembled him in face, or because they were blood relatives. The Jews customarily called brothers those connected by blood on either side. The Lord Jesus and James were sons of two sisters who had married two brothers, Joseph and Alphaeus [Col. 0413B]. Jesus was thought to be the son of Joseph; James was the son of Alphaeus [Note: [Col. 0413] Luke 3].

This James was bishop of Jerusalem and, after the Lord’s Passover, first celebrated Mass in Jerusalem. While he preached the name of Christ, he was thrown by the Jews from the pinnacle of the Temple onto fullers’ clubs. The antiphons assigned to them are taken from the words of the Gospel. Note that in the primitive Church not only the feasts of these men but also those of all the Apostles were celebrated on this day. Thus it is found in ancient plenaries. Since the individual Apostles did not have separate solemnities, it was decreed that on the day of these men’s passion the solemnity of all the Apostles should be celebrated, because [Col. 0413C] this season most aptly accords with the joys of each. For it signifies the octave, when God will be all in all [Note: [Col. 0413] 1 Cor. 15], and the good of one will be the joy of all.

## CHAPTER XXII. ON THE HOLY CROSS

Emperor Constantine conquered a multitude of barbarians by the sign of the cross. His mother Helena found the wood of the cross on Calvary through a certain Jew named Judas. At first only the Church of Jerusalem celebrated the day of its discovery. But Pope Eusebius later commanded it to be celebrated everywhere. On the same day is the feast of the martyrs Alexander, Eventius, and Theodulus. Therefore the office is mixed at Matins.

This Judas, formerly a Jew, converted to the faith [Col. 0413D], became bishop of Jerusalem, and, after a change of name, was called Cyriacus; Julian the Apostate killed him. [This Julian, a magician from childhood, once summoned a multitude of demons by his invocations. He made the sign of the cross, and they all vanished. When Julian was a monk, he took three pots of gold from a certain woman, who, concealing her gold beneath ashes, entrusted it to that pretender to religion. He stole it and returned only the ashes. Fleeing with it to Rome, he first obtained the consulship and later the empire. Therefore, wishing to rule by magical art and to have demons favourable to serving him, he remembered that at the sign of the cross they had utterly vanished as though in hatred [Col. 0414A], and so killed Judas, the discoverer of the cross, the bishop Cyriacus after his name had been changed.

But another Cyriacus avenged this Cyriacus. When Julian threatened destruction to a certain monastery and the brothers were greatly afraid, the abbot saw in a vision one night that the Blessed Virgin entered the monastery and commanded a certain soldier named Cyriacus, who had been buried seven days, to avenge her against Julian. He therefore seized the weapons hung in the church, mounted a horse still in the stable, and crossed over to Julian’s enemies. The following day the abbot disclosed the vision to the monks. Investigating everything more carefully, they found neither the soldier in the tomb, nor the weapons in the church, nor the horse in the stable. On the third day, when Julian was fighting his enemies [Col. 0414B], he was killed by the aforesaid dead man. On the following night, by the abbot’s command, he returned to the tomb and restored the horse and weapons to their places. Julian was buried at Constantinople, and an unbearable stench rises from his tomb.]

## CHAPTER XXIII. ON SAINT JOHN BEFORE THE LATIN GATE

The feast of John before the Latin Gate is the feast of blessed John the Evangelist, whom Domitian placed in a vat of boiling oil before the Latin Gate, as it was formerly called. But blessed John suffered no injury in it, divine grace protecting him. Yet in intention he was a martyr, and he fulfilled the Gospel saying: “You shall drink my cup” [Col. 0414C; Note: [Col. 0413] Matt. 20]. Therefore the Church decreed that his steadfastness should be remembered and this martyrdom of will celebrated as though he had suffered martyrdom in fact. After this Domitian banished him to the island of Patmos, where he saw the Apocalypse.

## CHAPTER XXIV. FEAST OF SAINT MARY AT THE MARTYRS

The feast of Saint Mary at the Martyrs is the dedication of the church of Saint Mary in honour of her and of all martyrs. Since the individual idols of the Romans could not have individual temples, the Romans built a common temple, which they called the Pantheon. Boniface, having cast out the idols, dedicated it in honour of the Blessed Virgin and all martyrs. At that time, no festive commemoration of confessors was yet observed [Col. 0414D]. He therefore decreed that on this day, namely the third day before the Ides of May, the feast of martyrs should be celebrated, just as the feast of Apostles was celebrated on the Kalends. But Gregory VII transferred both feasts—the commemoration of Apostles and of Martyrs—to the day of the Kalends of November.

## CHAPTER XXV. ON SAINT MICHAEL

The feast of Saint Michael’s victory derives its origin from this: when barbarians were ravaging Apulia, Christians proclaimed a three-day fast and implored the aid of Saint Michael. By his protection the enemies turned their backs and the Christians won victory [Col. 0415A]. Therefore it was decreed that, in honour of Saint Michael, the commemoration of this victory should be celebrated yearly on the eighth day before the Ides of May.

## CHAPTER XXVI. ON FEASTS FROM THE OCTAVE OF PENTECOST UNTIL THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

Concerning feasts from the octave of Pentecost until the Advent of the Lord, this rule must be observed: one must consider whether Sundays will be lacking or will be abundant up to Advent. If they would be lacking, feasts occurring on them are to be transferred to Mondays; otherwise they may lawfully be celebrated on those Sundays, except for privileged Sundays.

## CHAPTER XXVII. THE HOLY MARCELLINUS AND PETER

[Col. 0415B]

The passion of Marcellinus and Peter supplies the sung antiphons concerning them. For Peter the exorcist, imprisoned, freed the demon-possessed daughter of Arthemius and Candida; Marcellinus the priest, his companion, baptized them.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. THE HOLY GERVASIUS AND PROTASIUS

On the feast of the blessed Gervasius and Protasius, the introit is sung: “The Lord will speak peace to his people” [Note: [Col. 0415] Ps. 84], because peace between the Romans and Lombards was made on that day. The offices of saints partly suit the saints themselves and partly the events that occurred on their days.

## CHAPTER XXIX. ON SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

[Col. 0415C]

The Nativity of blessed John the Baptist has a vigil and solemnity, but not an octave. It was formerly customary that on saints’ feasts people should come to church with their wives and daughters and keep watch there through the night with lights. This is still observed in some places according to ancient custom. But because it often happened at these vigils that virgins were corrupted and greater opportunity was afforded for evil practices, it was instituted, as we have said, that vigils should be changed into fasts. Yet the old name remains everywhere: they are called vigils, not fasts.

This solemnity of the Nativity, however, contains both because of its reverence: fasting and keeping watch through the night [Col. 0415D]. But since blessed John was conceived in sin, why is his Nativity celebrated? I answer: there are two births, the first in the womb, the second from the womb; the first is conception, the second delivery. He was indeed conceived in sin, but sanctified in the womb, according to the saying: “Before you came forth from the womb I sanctified you” [Note: [Col. 0415] Jer. 1]. Although this is said of Jeremiah, it is understood of both. Therefore his Nativity is celebrated.

But how was he sanctified when he said, “I ought to be baptized by you” [Note: [Col. 0415] Matt. 3], that is, cleansed from sin? I answer: he said this in the person of the Church. Therefore this Nativity is celebrated because of history and because of allegory. Because of history [Col. 0416A], since the angel foretold it and added: “Many will rejoice at his birth” [Note: [Col. 0415] Luke 1]. Moreover, a barren woman bore a child, an old man begot one, the mother prophesied, the father was struck dumb, and finally blessed God. Because of allegory, because he prefigured the rising of glory: the herald preceded the Judge in annunciation, birth, preaching, death, and descent into the lower regions.

The office of this solemnity is therefore partly from the Old Testament and partly from the New, because John was the end of the Old and the beginning of the New Testament. He was the cornerstone between the Old and New Testaments. Hence one Mass is sung at dawn because he was the end of night: “The Law and the Prophets were until John” [Note: [Col. 0415] Luke 16]; and he was the beginning of day. For his birth was the dawn of Christ’s Nativity, as it were the rising of the sun. Or the sacrifice is offered at the beginning of light because, from the beginning of light, he offered the sacrifice of abstinence [Col. 0416B]. Another Mass is sung in daytime, according to the custom of other solemnities.

Note that on this feast *Alleluia* is not to be frequently used, although at other times it is sometimes used, either because John signifies the Law or because his Nativity was before the Lord’s Resurrection.
