Some nevertheless perform the office without *Alleluia* at the beginning of night, because of the figure of the Law, and afterwards repeat the office with *Alleluia* in the middle of the night, ending it at the beginning of light because of the remembrance of the Lord’s Resurrection and our future glorification.

## CHAPTER XXX. THE HOLY JOHN AND PAUL

[Col. 0416C]

The passion of John and Paul was described by a certain Terentianus. These two were household disciples, or rather eunuchs, of Constantia, daughter of Constantine and Helena. They converted Gallicanus, Constantia’s betrothed. At last they were beheaded under the emperor Julian by Terentianus, who afterwards repented of his crime and joined the faith of the Christians. The sung antiphons are compiled from this legend.

## CHAPTER XXXI. THE APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL

The passion of the Apostles Peter and Paul was carried out on the same day and under the same ruler, namely Nero, although some think otherwise. Yet although the identity of ruler and day joins them, a difference of punishments intervened because of Roman civic status: Peter was crucified and Paul was beheaded. This punishment seemed to involve less disgrace, for he was “a Roman citizen,” as is read in the Acts of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0415] ch. 22]. Their bodies were joined in the same burial.

But afterwards, as the Christian religion grew and Christians had built a separate church for each Apostle, they wished to separate their bodies but did not know whose bones were whose. As they prayed, the response was that the larger bones would be those of the preacher, the smaller those of the fisherman; and thus they were separated from one another and placed in their own churches. Others say that Pope Sylvester, wishing to consecrate the churches [Col. 0417A], weighed both the large and small bones in a balance with the greatest reverence, and placed one half in one church and the other half in the other.

Since their passion was carried out on the same day, their solemnity ought to have been celebrated on the same day. But blessed Gregory instituted that on that day Peter’s solemnity should be celebrated more particularly, and Paul’s commemoration on the following day: because Peter’s church was dedicated on that day; because he is greater in rank; because he was earlier in conversion and, according to some, in passion; and because he held primacy at Rome. When Paul is found in some places to be greater, and elsewhere equal, this should be understood thus: he is greater in preaching, lesser in rank, equal in holiness of life.

This feast has a vigil, solemnity, and octave: a vigil, that we may suffer with him with whom we seek to reign [Note: [Col. 0417] Rom. 8; 2 Tim. 2]; a solemnity, that we may rejoice in their first robe [Col. 0417B]; an octave, that we may certainly rejoice in the future second robe. For, considering that the saints already possess the beginning of blessedness and that its end, namely consummation, is extended to the octave of the resurrection, we rightly continue the day of solemnity through the eighth day.

At Peter’s solemnity, therefore, the history is compiled partly from the Gospel, partly from the Acts of the Apostles, and partly from his passion or miracles. At the commemoration of Saint Paul, however, the history is sung chiefly from words gathered from Paul himself; its antiphons are marked by verses because he is believed to have laboured more than the others in preaching [Note: [Col. 0417] 1 Cor. 15]. Within the octave, not individual but common offices for both are sung [Col. 0417C], such as: “Behold, I send you” [Note: [Col. 0417] Matt. 10].

## CHAPTER XXXII. ON THE FEAST OF THE DIVISION OF PETER AND PAUL

Different people seem to hold different opinions about the feast of the division of the Apostles. Some say it concerns that division which occurred at Jerusalem after twelve years, when they were separated to preach to the Gentiles. Others say it concerns the aforesaid division of Peter’s and Paul’s bones, which took place on the Nones, or on the eighth day before the Ides, of July. At this feast the great sequence “The heavens declare” is sung [Note: [Col. 0417] Ps. 18], and this Gospel is read [Note: [Col. 0417] Mark 16]: “While they were reclining.” It is the Gospel of the Ascension. Some begin at the end: “The Lord Jesus, after he had spoken,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0417] Ibid.]

## CHAPTER XXXIII. THE SEVEN BROTHERS

[Col. 0417D]

The seven brothers, sons of Saint Felicity, who through various punishments attained the kingdom of eternal blessedness.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. ON THE TRANSLATION OF SAINT BENEDICT

On the Translation of Saint Benedict. After his monastery had been devastated by the Gentiles, as he had foretold, his body was translated into Gaul and worthily buried there.

## CHAPTER XXXV. ON SAINT JAMES THE GREATER

[Col. 0418A]

Blessed James the Greater, brother of John the Evangelist and son of Zebedee [Note: [Col. 0417] Matt. 4], was sent to preach to the Spaniards. But since they would not hear the word, he returned to Jerusalem and found those whom he had converted wandering astray because Hermogenes and Philetus were performing miracles by magical art. The Apostle confronted them and converted them to the faith. Herod beheaded him with the sword [Note: [Col. 0417] Acts 12].

Hermogenes, Philetus, and three other disciples placed his body in a ship. Entering the sea without a helmsman, they entrusted the place of burial to divine Providence. At last they arrived in Spain, in the kingdom of Lupa. She was a queen so called both in name and by the merit of her life. The disciples said to her: “The Lord Jesus Christ has sent the body of his disciple to you, that you may at least receive him dead whom you refused to receive alive.” When Lupa committed them to the executioner and he cast them into prison, they left the prison and eventually converted the executioner and his city to the faith.

Hearing this, Lupa grieved and deceitfully provided untamed oxen to carry the Apostle’s body. But, when the sign of the cross had been made, they became gentle. The disciples then placed the body upon a living stone; the stone gave way, and the very laying-down of the body fitted a sarcophagus to it without human labour. They carried this stone with the body, without anyone guiding it, to the middle of Lupa’s palace. Therefore the astonished queen was converted to the faith [Col. 0418C], and a church was dedicated from her palace.

Thus the feast of blessed James, which is the eighth day before the Kalends of August, is the feast of this dedication, not of his passion, since he suffered around Easter, as that epistle indicates: “Herod sent forth” [Note: [Col. 0417] Ibid.]. This feast therefore has neither vigil nor fast.

> Let no one henceforth be uncertain concerning the two Jameses.  
> This one was born of Alphaeus, the other of Zebedee.  
> Remember that the one you heard first is called the brother of Christ.  
> We read that he first possessed the see of Jerusalem;  
> his solemn feast is commonly on the Kalends of May.  
> The Greater—that is, this one—was brother of the Apocalyptist;  
> he celebrates his birthday seven days before the end of July.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. SAINT PETER IN CHAINS

[Col. 0418D]

The feast of Saint Peter in Chains was instituted as follows. Theosebia, wife of the emperor Theodosius, journeying to Jerusalem, saw at Alexandria a feast celebrated on the Kalends of August for the triumph won over Cleopatra and Mark Antony. She was deeply grieved that such honour should be shown to a condemned pagan. Arriving in Jerusalem, she acquired the chains with which Peter had been bound under Herod. On returning to Rome she presented them to the Apostolic See, which ordered other chains, with which Peter had been bound under Nero, to be brought. On touching one another, they were miraculously joined so completely as if they had always been one and the same [Col. 0419A].

Theodosius therefore built a church in honour of blessed Peter and placed the chains there. It was dedicated on the Kalends of August, so that the solemnity of the Fisherman might overshadow the solemnity of the emperor, and Peter’s chain extinguish Augustus’s torque.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. ON THE DISCOVERY OF SAINT STEPHEN

We have said that the discovery of Saint Stephen occurred on the day on which his passion is celebrated, and conversely; but the transfer was made for the aforesaid reasons. It should also be known that in his discovery God performed many miracles. Therefore, on the day when the discovery is celebrated, a sermon about the miracles should be presented to the people. We customarily sing the history, except for the responsory *Hesterna die Dominus* (“Yesterday the Lord”).

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. ON THE TRANSFIGURATION OF THE LORD

[Col. 0419B]

We celebrate the Lord’s Transfiguration on the day of Saint Sixtus, not because it occurred on that day, but because it was made known by the Apostles. The Lord was transfigured about the beginning of spring, when he commanded the disciples who had seen it not to tell anyone until he had risen from the dead [Note: [Col. 0419] Matt. 17]. They therefore concealed it completely until this day. Since this Transfiguration pertains to the state which the faithful will possess after the resurrection, on this day blood is made from new wine, if it can be found, signifying the saying of the Gospel: “Henceforth I shall not drink [Col. 0419C] of this fruit of the vine until I drink it new in the kingdom of my Father” [Note: [Col. 0419] Matt. 26]. [If it cannot be found, at least a little juice of ripe grape should be pressed into the chalice, or bunches of grapes should be blessed, from which the people may receive communion.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. ON SAINT LAWRENCE
Laurence and Vincent, kinsmen, were brought to Rome from Spain by blessed Sixtus. Vincent returned to Spain and there ended his life by martyrdom. Laurence remained at Rome, where he endured most grievous torments, as is contained in his legend, from which the chant-history is compiled. Saint Laurence has two privileges: alone among the martyrs he had a vigil, which we above called a fast. The second is an octave: he alone, namely, and Saint Stephen have an octave among the martyrs, as Martin has among the confessors. The third privilege is in the repetitions of antiphons, as we said above concerning Saint Paul; but Paul has repetitions because of the excellence of his preaching, whereas Laurence has them because of the excellence of his suffering. For although some saints endured either greater or equally severe torments, the Church does not preserve them so universally and with such authority: both because of the dignity of the place—for he suffered at Rome—and because of his own distinction. As Laurence followed Sixtus, so Hippolytus followed Laurence; concerning whose sufferings the Church exults in antiphons.

## CHAPTER XL. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF SAINT MARY

The passing of the blessed Virgin is pre-eminently called the Assumption: she was first assumed in soul and afterwards, as is devoutly believed, assumed in body. Elizabeth, a religious woman of Saxony, says that it was revealed to her that, forty days after the assumption of her soul, she was assumed in body.

Observe that there are five authoritative feasts of the blessed Virgin: the first is the Nativity; the second, the Annunciation; the third, the Birth; the fourth, the Purification; the fifth, the Assumption. Yet the second and third belong more properly to the Lord. Among the others that pertain especially to the Virgin, this is the greater. For as a rule it is true of every saint that the feast of his or her passing is greater than another feast concerning that saint, because he or she passes from misery to life—except in a special case, as with John the Baptist. Therefore this feast of the Virgin alone has a fast and an octave, in which certain things are said that we use at the dedications of churches. The readings, too, are taken from the Song of Love, and likewise the antiphons and responsories, because she bears the figure of the Church. For as blessed Mary is mother, virgin, and bride, so too the Church, mother of the saints, bears the name of virginity and bride: virginity, that is, of mind and faith, which surpasses bodily virginity. Hence: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” [Note: [Col. 0419] 2 Cor. 11.].

Half of this song is to be read up to the octave; the other half is to be reserved for the Nativity of the same Virgin [Col. 0420C]. It is therefore fitting that the books of Solomon be read around this feast. The sermon of Jerome, “You compel me, Paula and Eustochium,” is read by some in church, but it was composed to be read in chapter and at table. At Mass the Gospel is read [Note: [Col. 0419] Luke 10.] concerning Martha and Mary Magdalene, according to the allegory. For the blessed Virgin was a little fortress, because she fortified herself well against the devil; she was Martha, because none was better in active life; she was Mary, because none was better in contemplation. Of her contemplation it is said: “Mary kept all these words in her heart” [Note: [Col. 0419] Luke 2.].

Observe that there are four Gospels concerning blessed Mary. One is “The angel was sent” [Note: [Col. 0419] Luke 1.], which ought not to be said except in Advent and at the Annunciation. The others may be said whenever a special Mass for her is to be sung; for example, “She stood before the cross,” where it is said [Note: [Col. 0419] John 19.] that the Virgin is entrusted to a virgin. Note that herbs are blessed on this day, because, “as a lily among thorns,” so she is among daughters [Note: [Col. 0419] Song 2.].

## CHAPTER XLI. ON THE BEHEADING OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

Blessed John the Baptist was beheaded around Passover. His disciples buried his body without its head in the city of Sebaste, where the Lord worked many miracles. Therefore a very great multitude of Christians flocked there, and Julian the Apostate caused his bones to be scattered through the fields. But when the miracles did not cease, they gathered the bones, burned them, and scattered the ashes to the wind. Yet that finger with which he pointed out the Lord, saying, “Behold the Lamb of God” [Note: [Col. 0421] John 1.], could not be burned, or was secretly removed by the faithful. For certain believers who were among the pagans preserved what they were able to conceal.

Thus this feast, which the Church celebrates, concerns the gathering and burning of the bones, as though of one already dead according to martyrdom. Or, when blessed Thecla had brought the aforesaid finger among the Alps and built a church, it was dedicated, and this is the feast of its dedication. Or the head was buried at Jerusalem, which blessed John revealed to two Eastern monks who had come to venerate Jerusalem. They found it near Herod’s dwelling on the Kalends of March [1 March; Col. 0421B]. But afterwards it was placed by others, through a lake, in a certain obscure cave in the city of Emesa, until it was again revealed to the presbyter Marcellus and raised up by the bishop of that city on the fourth day before the Kalends of September [29 August]. From that time the Beheading began to be celebrated in that city, on the day, I suppose, on which the head was raised; and the chant-history is sung, compiled from antiphons and responsories, including antiphons that contain the cause of the beheading.

## CHAPTER XLII. ON SAINT FELIX AND ADAUCTUS

When blessed Felix was being led to martyrdom, a certain man came up and said to the executioners, “I too am a Christian.” The executioners said to him, “Then you too shall go with him.” Since his name was unknown, he was called Adauctus, “the Added One” [Col. 0421C]; others call him Audactus.

## CHAPTER XLIII. ON THE CONCEPTION AND NATIVITY OF SAINT MARY

Some at one time celebrated the Conception of the blessed Virgin, and perhaps some still celebrate it, because of a revelation made to a certain abbot during a shipwreck. But it is not authoritative; indeed, it seems to some that it should be forbidden, since they say that she was conceived in sin.

The Nativity too was formerly not customarily celebrated. But a religious man heard angels solemnizing in heaven on this night for many years. When he asked the reason, it was revealed to him that the angels rejoiced because the blessed Virgin had been born on that night. The pope confirmed this and ordered the feast to be celebrated [Col. 0421D]. It has neither fast nor octave. In it the chant-history on the praises of the blessed Virgin is sung, and the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0421] Matt. 1.] is read: “The book of the generation.”

Here it is asked why the genealogy of Joseph rather than Mary is reckoned. I answer: either because Joseph and Mary were of the same tribe, and tribal genealogy is reckoned through men rather than women; or because he preferred to be called the son of a craftsman [Note: [Col. 0421] Matt. 13.] rather than have his mother stoned. And in truth he is the son of that craftsman who made the dawn and the sun [Note: [Col. 0421] Ps. 73].

## CHAPTER XLIV. ON THE EXALTATION OF THE HOLY CROSS

The Exaltation of the Holy Cross is celebrated because Cosroes, king of the Persians, invading Jerusalem, profaned the holiest places and carried off with him the wood of the Lord’s cross. [Seated on his throne, he placed it at his right hand in the place of a son; a cock at his left, in the place of the Holy Spirit; and ordered himself to be called father.] On hearing this, Heraclius, the Roman emperor, took vengeance. Declaring war against the Persians, he defeated Cosroes. When he afterwards carried the Lord’s cross to Jerusalem, the gates closed of themselves, and a voice was heard from heaven: the King of kings had not entered Jerusalem in this manner, but humble and riding upon an ass [Note: [Col. 0421] Matt. 21.]. Hearing this, the emperor humbled himself; the gates opened of their own accord, and the emperor entered the city barefoot. Since miracles were then performed through the cross, he exalted the cross and, with the consent of the bishops, established the day of the Exaltation as solemn in his empire for times to come [Col. 0422B].

The feast of the Finding, however, is greater than the feast of the Exaltation. The former was instituted by Pope Eusebius; the latter by Heraclius. Yet Pope Sergius, long afterwards, found in the treasury of Saint Peter a silver casket, and in it a cross made from a large portion of the saving wood, adorned with precious stones. Placed in the basilica of the Saviour, it is venerated by the people on the day of the Exaltation, on which the feast of the martyrs is also celebrated; consequently the office is combined.

## CHAPTER XLV. ON THE DEDICATION OF SAINT MICHAEL

Why the Dedication of Saint Michael is celebrated is explained in his history. But why, although it is the feast of all angels, in whose praise rejoicing is made from the Apocalypse, is it assigned more particularly to Michael? I answer: because he is the one sent into Egypt [Note: [Col. 0421] Exod. 12.], who inflicted those plagues, divided the Red Sea [Note: [Col. 0421] Exod. 14.], led his people through the desert, and brought them into the land of promise [Note: [Col. 0421] Exod. 15.]. He is the overseer of Paradise and guardian of souls; therefore we ought especially to venerate him. And Michael is the name of one angel; or rather, whenever anyone is sent to accomplish something great and wonderful, he is called Michael [Col. 0422C].

## CHAPTER XLVI. ON SAINT REMIGIUS

Blessed Remigius anointed the first king of the Gauls and converted the Frankish people to the faith. Among his other miracles he raised a girl from death. Therefore he is called the pope of the Franks, and is held in such veneration in France that his feast eclipses that of Saint Michael [Col. 0422D].

## CHAPTER XLVII. ON SAINT LUKE

Blessed Luke, a Syrian by nation, disciple of blessed Paul, patriarch of Antioch, was a preacher in Bithynia, where he ended his life by his own death rather than martyrdom. He composed two volumes, the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles. Taught especially by blessed Paul [Col. 0423A], he also learned from others what he taught, preached, and wrote.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. OF THE APOSTLES SIMON AND JUDE

Simon and Jude are also said to have been brothers of the Lord. Anne and Hismeria were sisters. Elizabeth, the mother of John the Baptist [Note: [Col. 0423] Luke 1.], son of Zechariah, was born of Hismeria. Anne bore the blessed Virgin by Joachim, and she married Joseph. After Joachim died, Anne married Cleophas, brother of Joseph, Mary’s husband, and bore another Mary. This Mary married Alphaeus, by whom she had James the Less, Simon, Jude, who is called Thaddaeus, and Joseph Barsabbas, who was surnamed Justus, lest he be believed to have been rejected from the apostleship on account of injustice [Col. 0423B]. After Cleophas died, Anne married Salome and had a third Mary, who married Zebedee; by her he fathered James the Greater [Note: [Col. 0423] Matt. 4.] and John the Evangelist.

Hence these verses concerning the line of the blessed Virgin:

> Anne is said to have borne three Marys,  
> Who married men: Joseph, Alphaeus, and Zebedee. Likewise,  
> Anne bore you, Virgin Mary, to her husband Joachim,  
> From whom came forth the true Wisdom without seed.  
> Afterwards, by Cleophas she bore you, virgin sister,  
> Who bears to Alphaeus Simon, James the Less,  
> Joseph Barsabbas, and Jude named Thaddaeus.  
> When this man too had died, she was joined to a certain Salome,  
> From whom the mother of Zebedee’s sons was born.

Observe that “brothers” is understood in Holy Scripture in several ways: by nature, nation, kinship, similarity, and religion. By nature, as Jacob and Esau [Note: [Col. 0423] Gen. 25.]; by nation, as all Jews. Hence, “If you buy your brother,” and: “Set one of your brothers over you as ruler, whom God has chosen” [Note: [Col. 0423] Deut. 17.]. By kinship, as: “Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside seeking you” [Note: [Col. 0423] Matt. 12.]. By similarity, as James, brother of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0423] Gal. 1.]. By religion, as: “Go, tell my brothers” [Note: [Col. 0423] John 20.]; and: “Behold how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” [Note: [Col. 0423] Ps. 132.].

## CHAPTER XLIX. ON THE FEAST OF ALL SAINTS [Note: [Col. 0423] See above, ch. 24.]

We have touched briefly above upon the feast of All Saints. Yet this should be added: this feast has a fast, which ought not to be changed, as some do because of Saint Quentin. The office of this feast varies according to the different classes of saints. For the first responsory is, according to some, of the Holy Trinity; in second place, of blessed Mary; third, of the angels; fourth, of the prophets; fifth, of the apostles; sixth, of the martyrs; seventh, of the confessors; eighth, of the virgins; ninth, jointly of all the blessed. Others place first one concerning unity: “I saw the Lord sitting” [Note: [Col. 0423] Acts 7.], and second one concerning the Trinity. The epistle concerning the number of those sealed [Note: [Col. 0423] Rev. 7.] and the Gospel concerning the number of the beatitudes [Note: [Col. 0423] Matt. 5.] are well suited to this feast.

## CHAPTER L. ON THE EXEQUIES OF THE DEAD

[Col. 0424A]

The commemoration of the dead follows the feast of All Saints. There are three successive days assigned to three mysteries. The vigil of All Saints is a day of affliction; the solemnity is a day of exultation; today, however, is a day of prayer. On the first, we afflict ourselves by fasting, recalling the misery of the present life. On the second, we rejoice with the blessedness of the saints, rendering thanks to the Lord. On the third, we pray for those detained in purgatory, obtaining for them by prayers now a milder punishment, now full absolution. Their office was first instituted by the apostles, but from an early origin, as Isidore testifies in the book *On Ecclesiastical Offices* [Col. 0424B], it was enlarged and arranged more fully. Augustine speaks of it in the *Enchiridion*. By “early origin” we mean the time after the apostles, in ecclesiastical offices. This office took its beginning from the old Law.

For after Jacob died, his sons mourned seventy days in Egypt and seven at Arad [Note: [Col. 0423] Gen. 50.]. After Moses died, the people mourned thirty days [Note: [Col. 0423] Deut. 34.]. Hence the Church today observes the seventh and thirtieth day for the dead. The seventh day, that they may attain the sabbath-rest of souls, or that the totality of their sins may be forgiven; for seven is the number of totality, because it comprises the whole human being. The soul has three powers—reason, desire, and anger—while the body has four elements, or four humours. Or, when we observe the seventh day, we intercede for sins committed in mind and body. Therefore Solomon says: “The mourning for a dead son is seven days” [Note: [Col. 0423] Ecclus. 22.]. The thirtieth consists of three tens.

We therefore perform these observances for the dead, that through keeping the Ten Commandments they may attain enjoyment of the Holy Trinity; or that by prayers what they sinned against in faith in the Trinity and in the work of the Decalogue may be amended. Some, however, celebrate the office of the dead for three days, in accordance with: “Whoever touches the corpse of a human being shall be sprinkled with this water on the third day” [Note: [Col. 0423] Num. 19.]. And in the Book of Wisdom: “Make mourning for a man according to his merit, for one day or two, because of slander” [Col. 0424D; Note: [Col. 0423] Ecclus. 38.], understand: besides the day of death.

We celebrate three days, that they may be members of Christ, who lay in the heart of the earth in a burial of three days; or that the dead may be forgiven sins committed in thought, word, and deed, or sins committed against the Holy Trinity; or for spirit, soul, and body. Some observe a ninth day, that, freed from punishments, they may be joined to the nine orders of angels. Yet this is not approved but forbidden, since it seems to have been introduced from the pagans, who mourned their dead for nine days and deposited the ashes on the ninth day. They called that period *novemdiale*, that is, mourning or an office of nine days [Col. 0425A].

Some add the fortieth and fiftieth day, that through the affliction of penitence they may attain jubilation. For forty is the number of penitence, because of the fortyfold affliction of the people and the forty days of Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0425] Matt. 4.]; and because, when its constituent parts are added, it produces fifty, which signifies the jubilee and the year of remission. For through contrition and affliction one comes to the remission of sins, to the eighth age, in which there will be remission and complete freedom. Or they observe the fortieth and fiftieth day so that, through the prayers of the living, whatever sins they committed in transgressing the Ten Commandments, the four Gospels, and the five senses may be forgiven them.

It is better, however, that we assign the three-day observance to the dead and the forty-day observance to the living [Col. 0425B]. Hence we impose Lenten penances for sins, because people sin in the body’s fourfold constitution and against the Decalogue of commandments. The hundredth day should, by this reckoning, be observed so that the dead may pass from left to right, from military service to triumph, from earth to heaven, from misery to glory, from death to life. Some interpret these periods more generously, so that the preceding days, on which we ought to be free from occupations, are not excluded by them; but although commemoration of the dead should be made on every day until the aforesaid periods, the offices are performed more solemnly at the stated periods.

The universal Church observes the anniversary, that from years of calamity one may attain the year of eternity. As we celebrate saints’ anniversaries for their honour and our benefit, so we celebrate those of the departed for their benefit and our devotion, hoping that they will someday pass into the fellowship of the saints [Col. 0425C].

Whatever day we assign to mourning, in these exequies, after the pattern of Christ’s three-day burial, the chants of Christ’s praise and joy are omitted: “Lord, you will open my lips” [Note: [Col. 0425] Ps. 50.], “O God, incline to my aid” [Note: [Col. 0425] Ps. 69.], “Come, let us exult” [Note: [Col. 0425] Ps. 94.], “Glory be to the Father,” “Command, Lord,” “Blessed,” “But you,” “We praise you, O God,” “Let us bless,” “Thanks be to God,” and “Go, the Mass is ended.” We omit joy because mourning and joy, sorrow and gladness, neither suit one another well nor dwell in one place. We suppress praises because we do not know whither the dead have passed [Col. 0425D], and therefore do not know whether we ought to praise the Lord for justice or for mercy. We omit joy because we entered this world sorrowful and depart more sorrowful still.

In the vigils of the dead there are three kinds of readings: from Job; from the Book of Wisdom, beginning there with “It is better to go to a house of mourning than to a house of feasting” [Note: [Col. 0425] Rev. 14.]; and besides this, from a sermon of Augustine that he composed on the dead. Some also read from the Psalms. Wherever the readings are taken from, they are to end thus: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0425] Eccl. 7.], as in Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0425] Isa. 45.], “Turn to me and be saved”; and in Jeremiah, “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, turn to the Lord your God” [Col. 0426A; Note: [Col. 0425] Jer. 4.].

We use the psalm *Te decet* [“Praise is due to you”; Note: [Col. 0425] Ps. 64.] in the exequies of the dead because it treats of the Israelites’ return from captivity to the promised land; likewise these persons pass from the misery of captivity to eternal life. At Mass incense should neither be carried through the choir nor offered—that is, the altar should not be incensed—but only around the body. For in the Law it was forbidden [Note: [Col. 0425] Lev. 5.] that the oil of joy [Note: [Col. 0425] Ps. 44.] and sweet-smelling incense be offered for sins; rather, mourning and contrition of mind were required. The exequies of the dead are celebrated because of their departures, and death is the first punishment of sin; for the same reason they ought not to be celebrated with oil, because Origen says that sacrifice for sin is not offered in oil.

At the same Mass the peace is not given, because we do not communicate with the dead. We are in the sixth age; they, however, are in the seventh [Col. 0426B]. Therefore, when the Mass of the day is celebrated, a body ought not to be within the enclosure of the church. If a body is present, it should be carried out into the church porch, even if it is that of a pope or emperor; and, when the Mass of the day has been sung, it should be brought back for the Mass for the dead. Or the peace is not given because we do not know whether they have peace with their Creator; or because in the exequies of the dead we follow the exequies of the Lord’s Passion, in which the kiss of peace is omitted.

How beneficial it is to celebrate Masses solemnly for the departed is apparent from what is found in the history of the English: namely, a certain priest believed that his brother had died in battle, though he was not dead but in chains. Therefore he daily celebrated Masses for him as though dead. At the times of the Masses, the bonds of the wounded man were daily loosened [Col. 0426C].

Observe that, when the full office of the dead is celebrated, it must begin at vespers: “I shall please the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0425] Ps. 114.], and it must not end at vespers, because this office will end when the souls of those to be saved, freed from every punishment, enjoy eternal joy. To the saints, of whom we are certain that they enjoy blessedness, we assign two vespers: the first for the robe of the soul already received; the second for the robe of the body yet to be received, which will never end.

After the vesperal and matutinal offices for the dead, we sing the psalm “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger” [Note: [Col. 0425] Ps. 6.]. Though it is sixth in order, it is entitled for the octave, as though in the six ages we were asking the Lord through this psalm that we might escape the torments of seven ages and attain the eighth age of glory [Col. 0426D].

Again, it should be known that some, at all times except feasts, pray generally for the departed in the vesperal and matutinal office; some celebrate Mass daily for them; some, at the beginning of the month, sing nine psalms, nine readings, and nine responsories. It is indeed a holy and saving religious practice to pray for the dead, that they may be freed from sins. If prayers for them were lacking, their lifeless bodies would be placed in places however holy to no purpose.

It pleases me to add something concerning the dead and dying, the buried and those to be buried, which may nourish the ears and comfort souls [Col. 0427A]. Therefore, while a dying person struggles in extremity, he should be laid upon ashes and straw, after the example of blessed Martin, who ended his life lying in ashes. By this it is indicated that he is ashes and shall return to ashes [Note: [Col. 0427] Gen. 3.]. Before Christ’s Passion, or part of it, is read, so that he may be moved to greater compunction, a cross should also be placed before his feet, so that the dying person may see it and be more deeply contrite. He should lie face upward, so that he looks toward heaven; and before he expires, his soul should be commended to the Lord.

After he has expired, bells should be rung, so that the people, hearing them, may pray for him: twice for a woman, because she introduced otherness. For she was the first to make humanity estranged from God [Note: [Col. 0427] ibid.]; three times for a man, because the Trinity was first found in man. For first Adam was formed from earth; second, Eve from his rib [Note: [Col. 0427] Gen. 2.]; third, humanity from both; and thus there is a Trinity there [Col. 0427B]. For a cleric, the bell should finally be rung as many times as he has orders, so that the people may know for whom prayer is to be made. It is rung likewise when the body is carried to church and when it is carried from the church to the tomb.

But observe that before it is carried to church, it should be washed, to signify that, if the soul has been cleansed from guilt through confession, then on the day of judgment both body and soul will obtain eternal glorification and purity. When the body has been washed, it should be clothed according to its rank and order. A layman should be clothed in haircloth [Col. 0427C], so that by this garment he may display the emblems of penitence; for ashes and haircloth are the weapons of penitents. In some places, however, especially the rich are clothed in shrouds and fitted with stockings and shoes. This is derived from what is read in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0427] John 20.] concerning Christ’s face-cloth and burial-sheet.

Clerics, however, should be tonsured and shaved, and buried clothed in the vestments of their order. Though this is more often omitted in other orders because of poverty, we do not permit it to be omitted for priests and bishops. For priestly vestments signify virtues, with which they, more than others, are to be presented to the Lord.

Here the question is raised whether people will be naked after the Day of Judgment. It seems that they will be clothed: first, from this universal custom of churches, which regularly clothes the dead; second, because the Lord appeared clothed at the Transfiguration [Note: [Col. 0427] Matt. 17.], whence his garments appeared white as snow; third, because after the Resurrection he also appeared clothed; and because angels customarily appear clothed [Note: [Col. 0427] John 20.]. I answer: all these things happen to us figuratively. We presume nothing concerning clothing or bodily condition, since it is sufficient to believe that among those who are saved there will be no weakness or any deformity [Col. 0427D].

Thereupon the re-clothed body should be carried in a bier to church. When Mass has been celebrated, the priest should chant over it; and if there are several priests, all should wear stoles and say the prayers with him who chanted over it [Col. 0428A]. After it has been chanted over, it should be carried to the burial-place by persons of like rank: a deacon by deacons, a priest by priests, if they are present; otherwise necessity knows no law; then a cleric by clerics, a layperson by laypeople, and especially by those of the same fellowship or fraternity. Women ought not to carry the bodies of the dead, lest they be compelled to uncover their limbs that incite lust.

Blessed water is placed in the burial-place because of the deceptions of demons. For they customarily rage against the bodies of the dead, so that, if they could not do so during life, they may at least do so at burial. Incense is added either to avoid stench or to show that the assistance of prayers benefits the dead. Coals are added as evidence of burial, for charcoal lasts longer underground than anything else. Therefore, when charcoal is found beneath a pit, it is recognized that there was a burial there. Hence the place is not afterwards returned to common use [Col. 0428B]. Ivy or laurel is also added, to signify the soul’s everlasting life. Although the body perishes, the soul nevertheless does not cease to live. In some places cypress is added, along with other foliage able to restrain the stench. Some say that cypress is added because, once cut, it does not sprout again but dies entirely; so a dead human being does not come to life again. These things are done not because corpses possess sensation, but for symbolic meaning, or in hope of the resurrection, or to invoke God’s favour, to whom such offices of devotion are pleasing.

[Col. 0428C] Observe that graves are called by various names. Of places, one is *sacred*, one dedicated to God by the hands of a bishop, as a church; another is *holy*, as one assigned to servants of the Church, concerning which it has been decreed under threat of eternal punishment that no one should presume to violate it—for example, according to the canons, the precincts of churches; according to the laws, the walls and fortifications of cities. Another is *religious*: where, according to Roman statutes, an intact body or a human head is buried. I say “head” because a trunk without a head does not make a place religious. No one can have two burials; where the head is, there his burial is said to be, whether he is a Jew or a pagan.

But according to Christian statutes, a place is not religious unless a Christian has been buried there [Col. 0428D]. Such a place is called a *cemetery*, as we said above—that is, a place of those who bury, or a sleeping-place of the dead—and measures thirty or forty paces, perhaps for the same reasons for which we said the thirtieth and fortieth day should be observed. It is also called a *polyandron* or an *andropolis*, as it were “city of men,” from *polis*, “city,” and *andros*, “man.” It is also called a *sepulcrum* [tomb], because those buried there are without pulse. It is also called a *mausoleum*. Mausolus was a certain man; when he died, his wife made him a glorious tomb, which she called a mausoleum after her husband. Hence the custom arose that every noble burial should be called a mausoleum [Col. 0429A].

It is also called a dormitory, from sleeping, because there the bodies of those who die in the Lord rest [Note: [Col. 0429] Rev. 14.]. It is also called a monument, as though reminding the mind of every passer-by that he is ashes and shall return to ashes [Note: [Col. 0429] Gen. 3.]. It is also called a mound, as though the earth were swelling. It is also called an *ergasterium*, from *erga*, meaning “labour,” and *staron*, meaning “station,” because there lie the bodies of spirits who rest from their labours [Note: [Col. 0429] Rev. 14.]. It is also called a sarcophagus, from *sarcos*, meaning “flesh,” and *phagum*, “to eat,” because flesh is eaten there, that is, consumed. It is also called a pyramid, from *pyr*, meaning “fire,” either because bodies burned and reduced to ashes by fire are laid there, or because this [Col. 0429B] kind of tomb, in the likeness of fire, begins broad and rises to a point and height, like that pyramid called the Needle of Saint Peter, where the ashes of Julius Caesar are deposited—concerning which it is doubtful whether it is one or several. Hence, if it is one stone, say by what art it was raised; if many stones, say where they are joined. And observe that in antiquity people were buried in their houses; but because of the stench of corpses, it was decreed that they should be buried outside the city, in every place assigned for that purpose: nobles upon hills, common people at their bases.

This concerns the Gentiles. But concerning those who worshipped one God, it must be known that in the first age only two sacraments were found: namely, offering and repentance [Note: [Col. 0429] Gen. 4.]. In the second [Col. 0429C] the observance of one day grew, on which Noah made the ark and enclosed the animals for sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0429] Gen. 7.]. In the third, worship was enlarged when Abraham bought a field in order to make a tomb [Note: [Col. 0429] Gen. 23.]. In the fourth, the worship of God was extended, because the law was given through Moses [Note: [Col. 0429] Exod. 34.], and sacrifices were instituted [Note: [Col. 0429] Lev. 1.]. In the fifth, it was again enlarged further through Solomon [Note: [Col. 0429] III Kings 7 and following], who built the Temple and appointed its servants. In the sixth came Christ, who offered himself as a sacrifice pleasing to God and sufficient for all [Note: [Col. 0429] Phil. 4.]. Therefore the cemetery took its beginning from Abraham.

Accordingly, in a Christian cemetery it is fitting to bury none but a Christian—not a Jew, not a pagan, and not every Christian either. For no one slain while committing a crime [Col. 0429D] is to be buried in a cemetery: for example, a thief in theft, an adulterer in adultery, a mounted soldier in a joust, a foot-soldier in a cudgel-fight, a combatant in an unjust war, a heretic, an excommunicate, or a self-murderer. All these are to be buried with the burial of an ass [Note: [Col. 0429] Jer. 22.], unless it has been proved that they departed in repentance or asked for a priest or for penance. Similarly, one who is known to have left a brothel or a similar place, if he dies in the very act of leaving, is to be buried with the same burial of an ass, unless, as stated above, it has been proved that he had repentance or sought it.

Therefore, a thief is to be buried beneath the gallows from which he hangs; the other persons written above may be buried anywhere, provided that they are buried outside cemeteries [Col. 0430A], unless they have made satisfaction. But if they have made satisfaction, cemeteries are not to be denied them. If, however, anyone suddenly dies at a game of ball or hoop, at dancing or bathing, or at similar activities, he may be buried in a cemetery; for although he was doing what he ought not to do, he nevertheless intended harm to no one. Yet, because he was occupied with worldly things, some say that he should be buried without psalms and the other funeral rites for the dead.

But if anyone suddenly dies while engaged in a necessary or useful work, unless it is publicly known either that he is guilty of some crime or that, by the nature of his offence, he ought to be marked with an anathema, he is to be buried in a cemetery and funeral rites are to be celebrated for him. Thus a woman who dies in childbirth, although she ought not to be carried into the church, as some say—perhaps lest the pavement be stained with blood [Col. 0430B]—but should have the service performed for her outside the church, is nevertheless to be buried in a cemetery. Others say that she may lawfully be brought into the church. But if she dies with a child in her womb, the child is to be drawn from her womb and, being dead, is to be buried outside the cemetery.

For a defender of justice, if he dies in a just battle, a cemetery and the office are freely granted. Those slain, however, are not to be brought into church, lest the pavement be stained with blood; and if they cannot have a cemetery, they are to be buried wherever they find a suitable place.

This, moreover, is noteworthy: wherever a Christian is buried outside a cemetery, a cross is to be placed at his head, either to indicate that he was a Christian or because the devil fears to approach where he sees a place [Col. 0430C] marked with the sign of the cross. If anyone dies at sea, if land is nearby, they should sail there to bury him; otherwise, he is to be enclosed in a small chest with money, if he has any, and thrown into the sea, so that whoever finds him may know that he is to receive payment with which he ought to commit him to the earth.

Let everyone, moreover, be buried in such a way that, his head being placed toward the west, his feet point toward the east. By this it is signified, and, as it were, prayed by the very position, that he may hasten from his fall to his rising, from the world to heaven. And observe that the prayers which precede death, such as the commendation of the soul, and those which follow it, such as vigils and the other funeral rites for the dead, are acts of thanksgiving for the very good; for the very wicked, they are whatever consolations they may be for the living; for those in the middle condition—that is, not very [Col. 0430D] good—they are purgations of punishments.

For there are souls which, as soon as they leave their bodies, fly like a sparrow to the Lord; there are others which descend into hell; and there are intermediate souls, which go to purgatory. For their sake alms, prayers, fasts, and sacrifices are made; but because of uncertainty they are also made for all. For it is better that these things should be superfluous for those to whom they neither benefit nor harm, than lacking for those to whom they can be of benefit.

## CHAPTER LI. ON THE FOUR CROWNED MARTYRS

Concerning the Four Crowned Martyrs, this noteworthy fact is found: [Col. 0431A] there were five who had come to construct Diocletian’s temple. When it became known that they were Christians, they were crowned with martyrdom; and because their names were known, they are placed in the collect. Two years later, another four received martyrdom. Their bodies were buried beside the bodies of the aforesaid five; and because their names were unknown, they claimed for themselves the name of the Four Crowned Martyrs. Melchiades decreed that their day should be celebrated under the names of the aforesaid five. Later, however, their names were revealed to a certain religious man, namely: Severus, Severianus, Carpophorus, and Victorinus; nevertheless, the names of the feast and of the place are not changed on that account.

## CHAPTER LII. ON SAINT MARTIN

[Col. 0431B]

Blessed Martin was born in Pannonia, which is near Austria; blessed Jerome also came from there. This Martin enjoys a twofold privilege: namely, he is called equal to the apostles in the office, and he alone among confessors has an octave. He is called equal to the apostles, some say, because great and numerous miracles shone forth through him; or, rather, because of the following special miracle.

When he was bishop at Tours, a certain poor and naked man asked him for a tunic. Martin therefore instructed his steward to buy the man a tunic; the steward bought a *penula*, that is, almost none at all, which scarcely reached to the knees and whose sleeves scarcely extended to the arms. When blessed Martin saw it, he put it on and [Col. 0431C] gave his own garment to the poor man. Thereafter, as he stood at the altar celebrating the solemnities of Mass, the loose sleeves of his sacred vestment fell back, leaving his arms bare to the elbow. Immediately golden torques encircled his arms, and a globe of fire appeared above his head, by which it was shown that the Holy Spirit had descended upon him, as upon the apostles [Note: [Col. 0431] Acts 2.]. For this reason he is said to have been equal to the apostles.

He alone among confessors has octaves, just as Lawrence among martyrs has vigils. For the latter said: “You have tested me by fire, and no iniquity has been found in me” [Note: [Col. 0431] Ps. 16]; while the former said to the devil: “You will find nothing in me, bloody beast.” Behold how they agree in their argument, and therefore share a privilege.

Observe that the kings of the Franks used to carry his cloak in battle; hence its keepers were called chaplains from the cloak itself. The sung history is compiled from his Life and miracles.

## CHAPTER LIII. ON SAINT CECILIA

Blessed Cecilia converted her bridegroom Valerian and his brother Tiburtius to the faith. Again, at her preaching Pope Urban baptized four hundred (*quadragintos*, as printed). At last Almachius caused her to be burned by fire and afterward ordered her beheaded; but her head, though she was struck a third time, could not be severed. From this Passion or legend the sung history is compiled; [Col. 0432A] and so, in the case of blessed Clement and the rest of the saints, generally speaking, it is customary to compile antiphons and responsories from their deeds, miracles, and passions.

## CHAPTER LIV. GENERAL OBSERVATIONS ON FEASTS

Concerning feasts in general, it must be observed that if two feasts with a full office coincide on one day, either one is to be celebrated fully and the other commemorated only through an antiphon and prayer, or one is to be deferred to another day, as in the feast of Paul.

Likewise, after Mass the Church makes no commemoration of a saint for whom she sings only three responsories; but a feast of nine lessons is observed at all the Hours. At every feast of nine lessons, *Te Deum laudamus*, “We praise thee, O God,” *Gloria in excelsis*, “Glory in the highest,” and *Alleluia* are sung, except in a special case, as in Advent, Septuagesima, and the feast of the Innocents. We use the antiphons from Lauds at Prime, Terce, Sext, and None, and we do not bend the knee, because we believe that they have passed into eternal joy.

Hence it is also that in the third period, which pertains to the glory of the New Testament, we often repeat *alleluia* in antiphons, as: “The horns of the righteous shall be exalted,” alleluia [Note: [Col. 0431] Ps. 74]; “Light has risen for the righteous,” alleluia [Note: [Col. 0431] Ps. 96.].

Likewise, if a greater feast precedes a lesser, everything is to be done for the preceding feast, and only an antiphon, as above, and a prayer for the following feast. But if a lesser feast precedes a greater, from the chapter onward the following feast is to be celebrated, unless the preceding feast has only three lessons, and unless the following feast is a principal feast, such as that of the Blessed [Col. 0432C] Virgin, the apostles, or the proper feast of an oratory. For then the entire Vespers is to be sung for the following feast. But if the feasts are equal, from the chapter onward the following feast is to be sung.

Likewise, if it is the feast of a pope who is a martyr, the whole office is to be that of a martyr, except for the Mass, which is to be celebrated as that of a bishop. Again, if a feast of nine lessons falls on Saturday, Vespers of Saturday is celebrated, unless the feast is principal. We call principal that feast at which we customarily sing *Credo in unum Deum*, “I believe in one God.” In that case, from the chapter onward, Sunday is to be sung. But if it falls on a privileged Sunday, it is to be transferred to Monday. We call privileged that Sunday for which we find an appointed history. On other Sundays it is permissible to celebrate the feast.

Some, however, lest they omit the Gospel homily, transfer [the feast] to Monday. Some pronounce six lessons for the feast and the homily for Sunday. But if a feast of nine lessons falls on Monday, on Sunday Vespers of that Sunday are to be said, unless the feast is principal; then, from the chapter onward, they are sung for the feast. We customarily do the same at the feasts of Saint Michael, Saint Lawrence, Saint Martin, and Saint Nicholas. But if it is a feast of the Blessed Virgin or the proper feast of an oratory, the entire Vespers is sung for the feast.

Again, at the vigils of those saints at whose vigils a vigil Mass is celebrated, None is to be sung for the feast.

## CONCLUSION

[Col. 0433]

[Col. 0433A] These are the dishes and cups of pure wine, brothers and sons, which we have set before you, like a cupbearer at a meal and in a dining room. With these we close the doors, lest jaws grow weary from chewing, lest a full stomach belch forth; because:

> Everything superfluous flows out from a full breast. [Col. 0434A]

Eat, therefore, and drink what is sufficient, yet hungering for righteousness and thirsting at this present feast, so that in the future you may be satisfied when the glory of the Lord appears [Note: [Col. 0433A] Matt. 5.]. Amen.

[Col. 0433] Here ends the *Mitrale*.

# CHRONICLE OF SICARDUS, BISHOP OF CREMONA

## PREFACE

(Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. VII, p. 523.)

Sicardus, bishop of Cremona, illustrious in his own age, had also won fame among posterity through a Chronicle extending from the most ancient times down to his own; nevertheless, through the negligence of our predecessors it has hitherto remained hidden. Long ago I found mention of this History in more than one place, namely in the manuscript books of Gualvaneus de la Flamma and Andrea Dandolo, and in the printed works of other writers. Therefore I left nothing undone in order to discover somewhere this monument of Italian learning, so long taken from us; for I lamented that so few of Italy’s ancient histories had come down to us, and fewer still had been brought into public light. Indeed, Sicardus was a man who seemed deserving of great esteem from us, both because of his learning and because of the time in which he flourished.

At last I learned from a catalogue of certain as yet unpublished books in the Imperial Royal Library at Vienna that the Chronicle of Sicardus, long sought by me, was preserved there under this title: “Chronicle of Sighardus, bishop of Cremona, beginning from the creation of the world and continuing to A.D. 1221.” Lambecius had also mentioned it in his *Commentary on the Imperial Library*, book II. Accordingly, I made repeated approaches to the most distinguished nobleman Count Antonio de Collalto, that he might obtain for me, from the then most eminent and learned prefect of the Imperial Library—afterward auditor of the Roman Rota and now most exalted bishop and prince of the city of Trent, Giovanni Benedetto Gentilotti—a copy of such a work. Yet no result then answered either his efforts or my wishes. Meanwhile I was informed that the same work in manuscript was to be found in the library of the most serene elector, duke of Bavaria.

But there too my hope was frustrated. For while that high-minded prince was compelled by a severe war to yield and leave his land, a parchment manuscript codex, having been taken from the library at the request of a certain Imperial official, disappeared with the untimely death of that official. Meanwhile, as I examined the manuscript codices of the Este Library with a more attentive eye, I seemed unknowingly to possess what I had sought elsewhere with such anxiety. For in the same library there is preserved a parchment codex of great antiquity, which I judge to have been written in the time of William of Bobbio, bishop of Reggio, that is, about the year of Christ 1290; for the catalogue of the bishops of Reggio placed at the end of the book ends with this bishop.

There is found there a chronicle by an unnamed author with only this title: “Here begins the Chronicle of the Latin and Greek emperors, and of the kings of the Lombards and other nations.” Its first chapter is on Ptolemy Dionysius, the deeds that occurred in his time, other barons, and the deeds of Pompey. Chapters on Julius Caesar and his deeds follow; then on Emperor Octavian, and so forth. Amid these materials, drawn from approved authors, I was astonished from time to time to find scattered certain fabulous inventions—for example, the vision seen by Emperor Octavian concerning blessed Mary; the father and mother of Pilate; and other things of that sort—which represented to me an insipid patcher-together, indeed a laughable one, and therefore turned my mind entirely away from the History itself.

But as I continued reading, the further I advanced the more worthy of esteem I found the writer. Then, in the final portion, passages confronted me which no one would deny had proceeded from a certain Sicardus; especially the passage in which, under the year 1198, he relates concerning Homobonus of Cremona, a most devout man entered by his own care in the catalogue of saints, and declares that he had travelled to Armenia in 1203. That was in fact done by Bishop Sicardus, as Ughellus testifies in *Italia Sacra*, vol. IV; and before him the writer of the Life of Pope Innocent III had noted it, declaring that the bishop of Cremona, having taken up the cross, sailed to the East. Moreover, he narrates what he did both at Constantinople and in Armenia, so that at last you recognize that Sicardus has portrayed himself in these very words.

What induced me yet more strongly to this opinion was that Gualvaneus de la Flamma, in the *Manipulus Florum*, more than once cites the Chronicle of Sicardus. Under the year 390, he writes: “Here, that is, in this city of Milan, Virgil, a Mantuan by birth, assumed the toga, according to Sicardus.” Gualvaneus could have adduced as witness for this matter the Chronicle of Eusebius rendered into Latin by Saint Jerome, from whom Sicardus took it; but it was enough for him, setting aside the very ancient writer, to mention the recent Sicardus, from whom these things are in fact reported in chapter 1.

Again, the same Gualvaneus, in chapter 37, states that Maximian Augustus laid aside the imperial purple at Milan according to Sicardus. The Este Chronicle gives the same account. Moreover, in chapter 49 of the same *Manipulus*, Gualvaneus writes: “At this time there was the war of Rivolta; and at that same time, according to Sicardus, the whole people of Cremona at Crema was led to Milan into prisons.” These same facts are presented in our Chronicle under the year 1139. Finally, omitting other passages, Gualvaneus, in chapter 205, recounting the battle and victory of the Milanese in the war against Frederick Barbarossa, says: “Hence Sicardus cries: ‘O wheel of fortune, which once humbled the Milanese and now has exalted them; indeed, [it is] the Lord, who made the Milanese poor and has now enriched them, casting down the proud from the throne.’”

The historian Corio of Milan repeats the same words [Col. 0439] under the name of the writer Aicardus, intending to refer to Sicardus; if you wish to attribute that error to the printers, I do not prevent you. Other ancient writers too borrowed this exclamation from Sicardus and inserted it into their histories. Yet the Chronicle of Este contains it in precisely the same words under the year 1176. When I had perceived this agreement of facts, although the chronicler’s name did not appear, I nevertheless finally determined that he could be no other than Sicardus.

For this reason I again approached by letter the above-mentioned most learned prefect of the Imperial Library, Gentilotti, now the most eminent bishop of Trent, and at the same time sent him a copy of the Este Chronicle, that he might determine whether it contained the same material as the Vienna codex. He found the same writer in both places, although the codices differed from one another in certain respects. Therefore, being as ready as he is for every act of kindness, after permission had been granted by the most august emperor of the Romans, Charles VI, the most gracious patron of this collection of mine, he arranged for the Imperial Library’s codex to be copied from the time of Charlemagne to its end and sent it immediately to me, so that I might more safely inform readers regarding this matter.

Here, then, is what I observed. The Vienna codex presents the pure, unalloyed Chronicle of Sicardus, carried down from the creation of the world to the year 1221. The title of the prologue, formed in red letters, begins with these words: “Here begins the Prologue to the Chronicle, which was published by Lord Syghardus, bishop of Cremona.” “The Creator of all things and maker of those same things placed the human race in such a condition that they might live for one another in turn,” and so forth. The beginning of the Chronicle then runs as follows: “Adam gave names to things; from his rib Eve was formed, by whom he begot Cain,” and so forth.

Thereafter it presents an abridgment both of sacred and secular history down to the times of Gaius Julius Caesar; but I have very willingly allowed all these things, being of no use in our age, to lie in their darkness. Afterward both codices, namely the Imperial and the Este, with equal agreement contain brief Lives of the Roman emperors, in the same words, down to the year 1213, where the Este codex ends.

Yet this difference exists between them: the Chronicle of the Este codex was interpolated in the same century in which Sicardus died by a certain anonymous person, whom I believe to have been from Reggio. For he inserted some matters wholly fabulous and fit to be hissed at; and besides, he added certain things concerning the kings of the Lombards and, finally, matters relating to the city of Reggio, especially the names of that city’s consuls and podestàs. Readers, I think, will readily pardon me for cutting away most of these additions, for no one in his right mind loves stale fables. What concerns Reggio Lepidi the reader will receive below in its proper place, that is, in the other Chronicle.

But it must especially be observed that these codices differ in this: certain things are lacking in the Este codex which occur in the Imperial one, and conversely the Este contains far more things which you would seek in vain in the Imperial codex. You may see this especially in what Sicardus of the Este codex tells concerning deeds done in the East in his own time by the crusaders. These have the same Sicardus as their author, since he had joined those travelling into that region. But Sicardus of Vienna contains not even a γρύ (“a whisper”) about those matters.

If anyone asks whence this dissimilarity between copies of the same Chronicle arose, let this conjecture of mine serve as an answer. As I shall explain below, Sicardus left behind two Chronicles. The Imperial codex contains only one of them, as it was produced by this author, that is, without any addition whatsoever. By contrast, the writer of the Este codex, since, as I conjecture, he pursued not the glory of a copyist but that of an author, inserted for his own use, in addition to a few histories by others, a great part of that very Chronicle of Sicardus into his own History; and besides, he clipped some fragments from the other Chronicle by the same author and mixed them into his work. This, then, is why our historian sometimes appears fuller and richer in the Este codex than in the Imperial one.

I have said that two Chronicles seem to me to have been written by Sicardus. For this matter I can cite an adequate witness: the above-mentioned Gualvaneus de la Flamma, who flourished about the year of Christ 1325 and composed the *Manipulus Florum*, or *Compendium of Milanese History*. Thus, under the year 1214, he writes: “In this year Sicardus, bishop of Cremona, who composed the most beautiful *Mitrale* and Chronicle, dies in the Lord.” Gualvaneus would have done better to place Sicardus’s death in the following year, 1215. But as to the point now under examination, you see that Sicardus composed two distinct works: one distinguished by the title *Chronica* or *Chronicon*, the other called the *Mitrale*.

That the latter, no less than the former, embraced historical matter seems to me highly probable [Note: [Col. 0439] After the publication above of Sicardus’s *Mitrale*, everyone sees that Muratori is entirely mistaken here. EDITOR.]; both because elsewhere Gualvaneus calls the *Mitrale* not [a work] of popes but of emperors, and because the same Gualvaneus cites and uses the *Mitrale*, no less than the Chronicle, as a historical book. Perhaps in one of these books he pursued the Lives of the emperors, and in the other the Lives of the Roman pontiffs and especially ecclesiastical history.

Accordingly, in publishing this work I have followed this method. Omitting as superfluous what precedes the Nativity of the Lord, I present the text of the Este manuscript from its beginning down to the reign of Charlemagne. I have removed the fictions scattered through it and, as I think, added by the Reggio compiler; but I have spared the remaining additions, if any, either because they did not seem wholly alien to Sicard’s hand, or because I judged them not useless to know. In the same Este manuscript codex, on parchment, there is another Chronicle, hitherto unpublished, which I mentioned in the Preface to Godfrey of Viterbo. [Note: [Col. 0439] See Patrology, vol. CXCVIII.]

Here is its title: “Here begins the Book concerning Times and Ages. A brief compendium gathered from various chronicles and arranged in order, concerning the times in which certain Roman pontiffs held office, emperors ruled, kings reigned, Reggian pontiffs sat, consuls and podestàs held office, and governed the city of Reggio, etc.” I have decided, as I recently promised, to publish in its proper place the final portion bearing the title “Memorial of the Podestàs of Reggio.”

This History begins with Christ’s birth and is concerned almost wholly with the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs. I found these, however, to be the same as those commonly circulated under the name of Anastasius the Librarian, though for the most part abridged. In the margin of the manuscript certain historical additions are entered, chiefly to preserve the memory of martyrs and other saints; among them some appeared to me to have been taken from Sicard. I shall demonstrate the matter by one example.

To the Life of Pope Damasus I the following is added in the margin:

> In the time of Pope Damasus, under the emperors Valentinian and Valens, in the second year of Valentinian, Damasus, and shortly afterward the deacon Ursinus, were bishops at Rome; but Damasus prevailed. He condemned Liberius and annulled everything that he had done. In the fifth year of Valentinian, Hilary of Poitiers died. In the seventh year, Eusebius of Vercelli died. In the eleventh year, Ambrose, while still a catechumen, having been sought for the priesthood at Milan and repeatedly fleeing, is said to have heard from Valentinian: “Do not fear, because God, who has chosen you, will Himself help you; and I too shall always be your helper and defender.” After this he was consecrated bishop. From that time Italy was converted to the faith, and the clergy of Aquileia were regarded as a kind of choir of saints. [Col. 0441] In the time also of Valentinian, Athanaric, king of the Goths, persecuted Christians. Eunomius, a disciple of Arius, attacked the faith, as did Apollinaris of Laodicea, who, etc.

That Sicard of Cremona is the author of this passage is attested for me by the highly reliable Andrea Dandolo, in his Chronicle, book IV, chapter 13, under the year 368, where these words are read: “Moreover, Bishop Sicard says that at this time the clergy of Aquileia were regarded as a kind of choir of saints.” But, in that Chronicle, I think no one can safely distinguish what belongs to Sicard and what to other writers; and therefore I have refrained from publishing those materials.

When Sicard’s History reaches the reign of Charlemagne, I begin to use the manuscript of the Imperial Library at Vienna, together with the Este manuscript, so that what our manuscript contains in greater abundance I shall append afterward, always indicating from which of the two codices the narrative has been taken. Variants of slight importance I shall place beneath in the manner of notes. By this method, whatever I have been able to gather of Sicard’s remains will henceforth lie ready to the hand of learned readers.

It remains for me now, setting aside every partiality, to declare what I think—and judge ought to be thought—of this very work of Sicard. What he compiled down to the age of Charlemagne will be of limited use to those learned persons who care to draw historical truth from springs rather than rivulets. Yet even there I think I perceive some matters which one would seek elsewhere in vain, since the histories which he used in his own time and which dealt with those earlier ages have perished.

If, however, you are offended there by something fabulous or badly stitched together which I have not dared to cut away, either attribute it to the Reggio writer patching up Sicard, or pardon Sicard himself, who lived in an age little given to criticism. For even in that part of the History which unquestionably acknowledges him as author, he did not sufficiently guard himself against the fables and errors of popular chronologers. For an example, one need only look at the Life of Charlemagne itself: Sicard reports that Charlemagne journeyed to Palestine and waged wars through twelve chief champions—whom we call Paladins—among whom were Roland, Oliver, and so forth. These things are drawn from romances.

Thus he thrusts upon us four Berengars as kings of Italy, an error which very many subsequently propagated in their histories. But, more surprisingly, Sicard shows himself a stranger even in his own house. If we believe him, under Otto I Augustus there was a bishop of Cremona named Luyso, who translated the body of Saint Hymerius; but under Otto II, Liutprand was bishop of Cremona. Sicard should be forgiven: through carelessness he made two men out of one bishop. For Liutprand is none other than Liuzo, as Ughelli rightly observed long ago, and as I think I have sufficiently demonstrated in my Preface to the Chronicle of that same Liutprand, volume II of *Rerum Italicarum*. [Note: [Col. 0441] See Patrology, vol. CXXXVI, col. 785.]

You now understand how easily historians in those unlearned centuries stumbled whenever the subject concerned events remote from their own age and contemporary writers failed them. Yet what I have mentioned thus far does not prevent Sicard’s offspring, added to other ancient sources, from rendering its own assistance to scholarship, especially where it relates events of his own age or the immediately preceding time. Even if nothing else commended him to us—and much else does—this alone might establish his reputation, and not a slight one. For, in language more elegant than was customary in his age, he describes individual events; and he sets before our eyes Frederick I Augustus’s final expedition to the East, and the ensuing deeds of the crusaders, in such a way that, in matters concerning the East of those times, he perhaps leaves most other writers behind him.

Add that none of our writers has left us so many monuments as Sicard concerning the illustrious lineage of the marquises of Montferrat and their renowned exploits in the East. This is why I regret that several works of this most useful author have already been lost, and that I cannot bring them all before public view. Even in the materials now published, I wish better manuscripts had been available to me; for both the Vienna Imperial manuscript and the Este manuscript abound in corrupt readings. But since it is not permitted to offer either more or better, it will be the part of the honorable Reader to congratulate himself and other lovers of good letters upon what I can give, and to wish me more favorable fortune in what remains.

# SICARD’S CHRONICLE

## On Ptolemy Dionysius; the events of his time; other leaders; Pompey’s deeds; and the death of that Pompey

[Col. 0441A]

Ptolemy Dionysius reigned in Egypt for thirty years. Among the Jews, Alexandra, after the death of her husband, reigned for nine years; she declared her firstborn, Hyrcanus, high priest. In the time of Dionysius the heresy of the Pharisees arose. Among the Romans, the city of the Albanians was captured during a civil war, and there was a gladiatorial war in Campania.

After this new wars arose in Spain, Pamphylia, Macedonia, and Dalmatia; the Romans triumphed over them all. Nicomedes, king of Bithynia, made the Roman people his heir. Lucullus drove out and crushed Mithridates, a man raging madly, at Byzantium, now Constantinople. [Col. 0441B] Meanwhile a new war arose in Italy, no less serious than Hannibal’s war.

Lucullus, after conquering Armenia and Mesopotamia and taking Nisibis, was the first to be called *imperator*. [Col. 0442A] Another Lucullus, after taking Bile and the other cities, triumphed over the Haesi as far as the Danube, and over fugitives in the Rhodope Mountains and many others. When the Macedonian war had been finished, although the Mithridatic war still continued, the Cretan war was renewed. Metellus was sent to it and captured the whole province, whence he was called Creticus.

In these times Marcus Porcius Cato, the Stoic philosopher, became known. After Alexandra’s death, Hyrcanus, son of Alexander and Alexandra, occupied the high-priestly seat among the Jews for thirty-four years; his brother Aristobulus persecuted him severely. But Hyrcanus then had as adviser Antipater the Idumaean. By his counsel Hyrcanus fled to Aretas, king of the Arabs, who came into Judaea and besieged Jerusalem.

When Pompey, who was in Armenia, heard of the brothers’ dissension, he marched up to Jerusalem, captured it, profaned the Temple, and, as is said, stabled horses in its porticoes. For this reason [Col. 0442B] it is said that he who had previously been most fortunate in battles thereafter became unfortunate. Pompey therefore imposed tribute on Jerusalem, confirmed Hyrcanus as high priest, took Aristobulus captive, and, returning to Rome, entrusted the administration of Syria and Judaea to Scaurus.

This is the man who subdued Spain, Albania, Armenia, Asia, Syria, Lusitania, the pirates, Mithridates, and Judaea, and for that reason was called *imperator*. But Catiline also conspired against his country; finally, he and his followers were stabbed to death in the territory of Picenum. Subsequently Gabinius succeeded Scaurus and divided the Jewish nation into five districts—that is, five assemblies. Marcus Antonius served under Gabinius.

Crassus succeeded Gabinius, becoming governor of Syria; and, in order to subdue the Parthians, he despoiled the Temple of gold. Therefore he rightly perished when molten gold was poured into his mouth. Cassius succeeded him.

Julius Caesar triumphed over the Germans, Gauls, and Britons, and subdued all the lands between the Rhine, the Rhône, and the Alps, as far as the Ocean. King Appius left Libya to the Roman people by will. In the same age Virgil was born in the village called Andes, near Mantua; he later studied at Cremona, assumed the toga at Milan, and then came to Rome. Horace was born at Venusia. The Greek Apollodorus, the historian Titus Livy, and Curio, an eloquent orator, flourished.

Julius returned victoriously from Gaul to Rome. Having dismissed his army at Rimini, he sought a second consulship; but Pompey, Marcellus, and Cato opposed him. Therefore [Col. 0443C] Julius Caesar released Aristobulus, who had been held in chains at Rome, and sent him with an army, hoping to win victory; but Aristobulus and his son Alexander were killed by Pompey’s friends. Another son, Antigonus, fled to a certain Ptolemy, who took Antigonus’s sister as wife and begot Lysanias, later tetrarch of Abilene.

Julius then returned to his army and took up arms against his country. Pompey, the entire Senate, and the whole multitude of nobles fled from the City, crossed into Greece, and prepared war against Caesar. Caesar entered the deserted City and made himself dictator. Then, going into Spain, he defeated Pompey’s army. Crossing afterward into Greece, he fought Pompey in Emathia. Hence Lucan:

> “Wars more than civil over the Emathian plains.”

[Col. 0443D]

Pompey, defeated, fled to Alexandria to seek help from Ptolemy, king of Egypt. But Ptolemy killed him and sent his head and ring to Caesar. Caesar then went to Alexandria and fought Ptolemy in a naval battle; Ptolemy’s body was found in a golden breastplate. After his death Caesar gave the kingdom to Cleopatra, Ptolemy’s sister, with whom Ptolemy had had an incestuous sexual relationship. She reigned twenty-two years and was called Cleopatra, sister and wife of that Ptolemy. She died by a serpent, and so the kingdom of the Ptolemies, or Lagids, came to an end, having stood for 295 years.

Antipater had been with Pompey; but after Pompey’s death he attached himself to Caesar and, by his prudence, inclined the Egyptians to obey Caesar. Therefore, through Antipater’s favor, Caesar [Col. 0444A] confirmed Hyrcanus in the high priesthood. He made Hyrcanus king and Antipater judge and procurator. Afterwards he triumphed in Thessaly, Africa, and Spain over Pompey’s supporters in every quarter. Returning to Rome, he obtained sole power.

## On Julius Caesar, his deeds, and his death

Julius Caesar ruled among the Romans for four years and seven months. Before this Rome had been governed under seven kings for 243 years. Afterwards the state was administered under consuls for 464 years. Julius began to rule in Cleopatra’s first year and in the year after Hyrcanus’s high priesthood.

Since he bestowed offices according to his own pleasure and did not rise when the Senate came to him, a conspiracy was formed against him; and he was stabbed with twenty-three wounds through the treachery of Brutus and Cassius. No man [Col. 0444B] ever shone more brilliantly in war: he fought fifty times. No one wrote more swiftly, no one read more quickly; he dictated four letters at once. His goodness was so great that he conquered by clemency even those whom he had subdued by arms. From this Caesar the Roman rulers were called Caesars.

Julius Caesar was killed by senators in the senate-house on the Ides of March. He died in the fifty-sixth year of his life. His body was burned and buried at the column called the Julian Column. Before his death lightning struck in the forum and tore the capital letter C from the inscription of his statue; and the windows of his chamber were flung open with such a crash that they believed the house was breaking apart. On that same day, as he was going to the Capitol, letters foretelling his death were given him; after he was killed, they were found still unopened in his hand.

After his death three suns appeared in the east, joining into one solar body, signifying either that the powers of three would return into a monarchy, or that knowledge of the triune and one God was about to come upon the whole world.
