At Rome the Julian Basilica was dedicated. Antonius named the month Quintilis “July,” because Julius had been born in that month.

In these times oxen in the Roman suburbs spoke to the ploughman, saying that they were driven in vain, since human beings rather than grain would fail. Note that Pompey was killed in Egypt by Ptolemy, king of Egypt, when Pompey fled to him for refuge. Caesar therefore pursued and killed Ptolemy because he had dared to kill [Col. 0444D] the leader of the Romans. In these times Servius Sulpicius, the jurist, and Publius Servilius Isauricus flourished. Cassius despoiled the Temple in Judaea.

## On the emperor Octavian; and the deeds and actions that occurred in his time

Octavian Caesar Augustus ruled among the Romans for fifty-six years and five months: twelve years with Antonius, and forty-four alone. In the 710th year from the founding of the City—some say 692—Antonius was pursuing Caesar’s murderers, whom the Senate supported. Therefore two consuls were sent against Antonius, and with them a third, namely Octavian, a youth of sixteen, born to Octavian the senator and descended on his mother’s side through the Julian family as Julius’s grandson. [Col. 0445A] Caesar gave him his own name and left him his inheritance by will.

Accordingly, they set out against Antonius and defeated him near Mutina. And behold, civil wars arose again. But afterward the two consuls died, and their armies obeyed Caesar; he made peace with Antonius and returned to Rome with the army and Antonius.

Antipater likewise died by drinking poison. He had four sons—Phasael, procurator of the Jews; Herod, procurator of Galilee; Joseph; and Pheroras—and a daughter, Salome. Thus Antonius and Octavian returned. Avenging Caesar’s death, they killed Cicero the orator and many nobles, and afterward Brutus and Cassius. Having won their battles, they divided the Commonwealth between themselves: Octavian received Spain, Gaul, and Italy; Antonius [Col. 0445B] Asia, Pontus, Syria, and the East. Antonius made Phasael and Herod procurator-tetrarchs.

But the king of the Parthians besieged Jerusalem and restored the kingdom to Antigonus, handing over Hyrcanus and Phasael to him. Herod fled to Rome and was crowned king over Judaea. Returning with the Romans, Herod captured Jerusalem; Antonius killed Antigonus and confirmed Herod in the kingdom.

Moreover, Antonius, having repudiated Octavian Caesar’s sister—whose guardian he had remained after Caesar’s death—strove with great effort to take the empire from him. He married Cleopatra, queen of Egypt, most powerful in gold, silver, precious stones, and people. When Antonius and Cleopatra [Col. 0445C] began to come against Rome with a great array of ships and men, this was heard at Rome. Octavian, with a huge force, went out to meet them and engaged them near Epirus; thus battle arose. In that battle the queen’s ship, which was entirely gilded, began to turn aside. Antonius, seeing this, turned aside as well; Octavian pursued him as far as Alexandria. There Antonius fell upon the sword and killed himself.

Cleopatra, seeing that she had been preserved for a triumph, adorned with gold and precious stones, wished to deceive Octavian by her beauty and, as with others, to provoke him to desire by her appearance. But he was not moved; indeed, he ordered her to be guarded. Seeing herself despised, she entered, so adorned, the mausoleum of her husband and placed two “Persians,” a kind of serpent, upon her breasts.

Octavian [Col. 0445D] carried away from that victory boundless wealth, triumphed over Alexandria, Egypt, and the entire region of the East, and thus returned victoriously to Rome. The senators and the whole Roman people received him with a great triumph. Because this victory occurred on the Kalends of Sextilis, they gave the month the name Augustus, from the enlarging of the Commonwealth. They decreed that every year on the Kalends of August the entire city should celebrate the festival of that victory in honor of Octavian Caesar, and that the whole City should flourish and rejoice in so great a festival.

## Addition of a later but ancient writer to Sicard’s Chronicle in the Este manuscript

This rite lasted down to the time of Arcadius’s wife Eudoxia, [Col. 0446A] who, after her husband’s death, remained with her little son Theodosius and ruled the empire manfully as though her husband Arcadius were alive. Inspired by divine prompting and by concern for the commonwealth, she went to Jerusalem to visit the Lord’s sepulchre and the other holy places.

Amid the many affairs of the commonwealth, her fellow provincials brought her immense gifts, among them the chains of the blessed apostle Peter. She resolved that those chains should be placed nowhere but where the body of blessed Peter rests in the dust. Coming to Rome on the Kalends of August, she saw the Roman people celebrating with the utmost solemnity on the Kalends of Sextilis that most ancient pagan rite which none of the Roman pontiffs had been able to remove.

She approached Pope Pelagius, the senators, and the people, asking that the favor she wished to request [Col. 0446B] be granted her. They promised carefully to grant it. The queen said:

> “I see that you are so zealous for the festivities of Sextilis in honor of the dead emperor Octavian, because of the victory which he won against the Egyptians. I ask you to grant me the honor paid to the dead emperor Octavian for the honor of the heavenly Emperor and of the apostle Peter, whose chains I have brought from Jerusalem. And as he delivered us from Egyptian bondage, so may that heavenly Emperor deliver you from the bondage of demons. I wish to build a church in honor of God and blessed Peter and place the chains there; let the lord apostolic dedicate that church on the Kalends of August, and let it be called Saint Peter in Chains, where the lord apostolic shall every year celebrate the solemnities of Mass in this church. [Col. 0446C] And as blessed Peter was released from chains by the angel, so may the Roman people proceed, released from sins with a blessing.”

When the people heard this, they received it with great displeasure; at length they yielded to pope and queen. She built the church, which the lord pope dedicated on the Kalends of August, as the most Christian Empress Eudoxia had proposed. There she placed the aforementioned chains of blessed Peter, the Neronian chains of blessed Peter, and those of blessed Paul, so that on this day of the Kalends of Sextilis the Roman people might gather there and venerate the chains of the apostles Peter and Paul.

In the forty-first year of Octavian Augustus, John [Col. 0446D] the Baptist was born: he leapt in his mother’s womb and, once born, loosed his father’s tongue. For the angel had foretold to the aged priest Zechariah that he would beget a son by Elizabeth, barren and aged; because he did not believe it, he became mute. But in the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent to the city of Nazareth to the Virgin Mary, betrothed to Joseph, saying: “Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee,” etc., as is contained in the Gospel (Luke 1).

In Octavian’s time, a spring of oil is said to have flowed from Trastevere as far as the Tiber, and from the *taberna meritoria* throughout the whole day, signifying Christ’s grace from the Gentiles. A circle in the likeness of a heavenly rainbow also appeared around the sun, signifying that same grace. In the time of Caesar Octavian Augustus, Falcidius enacted the law called the Falcidian Law.

[Col. 0447A]

Virgil, Horace, Ovid Naso, Varro, and Nicea; Aemilius of Verona, Quinctilius of Cremona, poets; Cornelius and Sallust, historians; Artorius, Augustus’s physician; Varro, philosopher; Albucius of Novara; and Messala Corvinus, rhetoricians, lived in this period.

Egypt was therefore subdued to the Roman Empire by Octavian in the fifteenth year of his reign. After Alexander it had been ruled there by twelve kings for 295 years. In these times Herod had been sent by Antonius against the king of the Arabs; but, returning, he was admitted into Caesar’s favor. Enlarging his kingdom, Caesar gave him Trachonitis, Myrrhaea, and the entire seacoast as far as the Tower of Simeon; Caesar also gave him four hundred Galatian guards, who were afterward called Herodians.

At the same time, as Tertullian says—or rather, in the forty-second year of the reign of Caesar Augustus and the thirty-second of Herod’s reign—Mary bore her firstborn son. This is the end of the fifth age, which is compared with old age, because in it the Hebrew people were oppressed by many evils; it contains fourteen generations. From Adam to Christ there were 5,199 years; from the Flood, 3,257; from Abraham, 2,015; from David, 1,046; and from the Babylonian deportation, 589. Others say 586. From the foundation of the City, 752; some say 33. Note: in order to clarify this time, let us set forth separately and more plainly a few years pertinent to the matter.

Accordingly, in the tenth year of Octavian Augustus, [Col. 0447C] the Jewish high priesthood failed. In the eleventh year Herod, a foreigner, son of Antipater of Ascalon and an Arabian mother from Epirus, received from the Romans, as we have said, the Jewish kingdom. Its rule had hitherto been held by Jews, now through leaders, now through kings, now through high priests. But as Christ’s birth approached, it was transferred to a foreigner, that the prophetic saying might be fulfilled: “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor shall the sceptre be taken from Judah, nor a leader from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he is the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49).

But Herod burned the books of the Jewish people’s genealogy, so that, when the proofs had disappeared, the kingdom might be believed to belong to him. Here the sixty-nine weeks of Daniel are completed, making 483 years. The succession of the priestly line likewise failed [Col. 0447D] when the priesthood was purchased from the Romans.

In the forty-seventh year of Octavian Augustus and the thirty-seventh of Herod’s reign, Herod died miserably, worms swarming from his body. He was most fortunate in other matters, but most unhappy in domestic affairs. He built many cities: Caesarea, formerly called Straton’s Tower; and, having rebuilt Samaria, he named it Sebaste, that is, Augusta. In Jerusalem he built many houses and a tower which he called Antonia in honor of Antonius, but which is now called the Tower of David. He also constructed a golden eagle over the Beautiful Gate of the Temple and set it there in honor of the Romans; the Jews cast it down at his death. He also built a royal residence at Ascalon, whence he was called the Ascalonite. He built many [Col. 0448A] temples in honor of Caesar, but he also adorned the Temple of the Lord. In each city of Syria he constructed many works; but he committed many murders and parricides.

For he caused Hyrcanus, Hyrcanus’s son, his own sister, his wife with her two sons, his mother-in-law, and two husbands of his sister, one after another, to be killed. He also ordered the noblest Jews at Silea to be killed at his death, so that, once he had died, all Judaea would at least weep unwillingly. Though he had fathered a numerous progeny by nine wives, he ordered three to be killed: Antipater, Alexander, and Aristobulus. Three survived: Archelaus, Herod Antipas, and Philip. Aristobulus, however, left behind his son Herod Agrippa and his daughter Herodias.

After Herod’s death, a dispute about the kingdom arose among the brothers. When they had pleaded at Rome before Caesar, Caesar divided the kingdom: one half to Archelaus, and the other half between Herod Antipas and Philip. He gave Judaea and Idumaea to Archelaus; to Herod, the territory beyond the river and Galilee; to Philip, Ituraea and Trachonitis. Archelaus was made *dynarch*, but at times [Col. 0448B] *monarch*—understand this according to popular opinion, or Augustus’s promise, or his own boastfulness. Herod and Philip were made tetrarchs.

In the forty-eighth year of Augustus’s reign, the first of Archelaus, and the seventh after Christ’s flight, Joseph was warned by an angel to return to the land of Jerusalem. But, hearing that Archelaus ruled in Judaea, he did not wish to go there; instead, coming into Galilee with the mother and the child, he lived at Nazareth.

In the fifty-fourth year of Augustus, when the boy Jesus was twelve years old, he went up to Jerusalem with his parents for the festival day and sat in the Temple among the teachers, listening and questioning them (Luke 2). In these times, when a census was conducted at Rome, 9,360,000 people were found. Archelaus came to Rome and, having been accused, was condemned by Caesar and banished to Vienne. The sun suffered an eclipse, and Augustus died after reigning fourteen years after the Lord’s Nativity. Some say that he reigned fifty-six years, six months, and ten days.

## On Tiberius Caesar, Octavian’s adoptive son and son-in-law; Pontius Pilate, whom that Caesar made procurator of Judaea; and the deeds and actions he performed and that occurred in his time

[Col. 0448D]

Tiberius Augustus was the adoptive son of Octavian Caesar. He ruled among the Romans for twenty-three years. While Augustus was still alive, Tiberius triumphed under him over the Raetians, Vindelicians, Armenians, and Pannonians; therefore Augustus adopted him as son. For he was both his stepson and his son-in-law. He likewise adopted Agrippa, that is, Herod.

Tiberius, once adopted, brought the Dalmatians or Sarmatians under Roman power. Having become emperor, he summoned many kings to himself by enticements and did not release them. Among these, retaining Archelaus of Cappadocia, he turned his kingdom into a province and renamed Mazara, the capital city of the kingdom, Caesarea.

Tiberius indulged in wine. Accordingly, although his name was Claudius Tiberius Nero, jesters called him “Caldius Biberius Mero”—that is, “Warm Drinker of Unmixed Wine.” After Archelaus had been exiled among the Jews, procurators were sent in succession: Coponius; Marcus Annius Cuphus; and Valerius, who frequently sold the priesthood.

In the twelfth year of Tiberius Caesar, Philip the tetrarch called Paneas Caesarea Philippi, establishing very many buildings in it; and he called another city, Sepphoris, Julia. In the thirteenth year, after Valerius had returned to Rome, Tiberius made Pontius Pilate procurator of Judaea. Pilate came to Jerusalem and set up statues of Caesar. When the Jews petitioned that the statues be removed, he threatened them with death; but they preferred death to profaning their ancestral laws. Admiring, therefore, the Jews’ constancy in their legal observances, [Col. 0449B] he ordered the statues removed.

In the fourteenth year of Tiberius, Herod the tetrarch founded Tiberias and Libyias. In the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar’s reign, while Pontius Pilate governed Judaea, Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, and Annas and Caiaphas were high priests, the baptism of repentance for forgiveness of sins was preached. All Judaea came to the region of Betharam beyond the Jordan and was baptized by him. John was clothed in camel hair, with a leather girdle about his loins; he ate locusts and wild honey and lived in the desert (Matt. 3).

At that time there were three Jewish sects differing from the common way of life and opinion. [Col. 0449C] The Pharisees wore on their arms and foreheads phylacteries—that is, little slips of paper on which the Decalogue was written—and thorns on their fringes. They said that the souls of the dead pass into other bodies until the resurrection. The Sadducees denied the resurrection, thinking that souls perish with bodies. The Essenes, living like monks, said that all souls were created at the beginning and are embodied according to the times.

In the same time of Tiberius Caesar, the Scathoarii came forth from the island of Scanadabia, situated in the Ocean Sea. Coming to the region of the Rhine, they made *burgi* (“fortified towns”), and were therefore called Burgundians. Its first inhabitants were called Allobroges. When Tiberius had reigned five years after the Lord’s Passion, he died. At the same time Veronica’s sudarium [Col. 0449D] was carried from Jerusalem to Rome, Tiberius was cured of leprosy, vengeance for Christ’s death was wrought upon the Jews, the chief priests were killed and destroyed and sold by Titus and Vespasian, and Pilate was brought alive by ship to Rome.

## On Gaius Caligula; Herod the tetrarch who caused John the Baptist to be killed; and the deeds he performed and that occurred in his time

In the year 38 from the Lord’s Incarnation, Gaius Caligula ruled among the Romans for four years and ten months. He was utterly wicked. For he committed sexual crimes with his sisters; afterward he condemned them to exile. In the first year of his reign he released Agrippa, that is, Herod, [Col. 0450A] from chains, made him king of Judaea, and he ruled among the Jews for seven years.

Caligula condemned Herod the tetrarch to exile at Lyons, where he died in utmost poverty with Herodias, the adulteress, in the year 38 from the Incarnation. In the seventeenth—or according to some, the sixteenth—year of Tiberius Caesar’s reign, Herod the tetrarch ordered John the Baptist to be beheaded. His head was given to the girl on a dish, and his body was buried at Jerusalem; the disciples buried him at Sebaste. Herod heard the report about Jesus and wondered whether he might be John, risen from the dead, and he sought to see him.

In the time of Gaius Caligula, Pontius Pilate, falling into many misfortunes, finally killed himself by his own hand. Gaius Caligula ordered both his own images and images of Jupiter to be erected in the Temple and synagogues of the Jews, [Col. 0450B] and ordered himself to be called Lord.

## On Claudius; the death of blessed James, brother of John; and the deeds he performed and that occurred in his time

In the year 43 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, Claudius, uncle of Drusus, who was buried at Mainz, ruled among the Romans for fourteen years, seven months, and twenty-eight days. He triumphed over the Britons and added the Orkney Islands to the Roman Empire.

King Agrippa—also called Herod—killed James, brother of John, by the sword; but the man who had delivered him up for martyrdom was punished by beheading because he confessed himself a Christian. Agrippa also put Peter in prison, but an angel of the Lord delivered [Col. 0450C] him from Herod’s hands.

In the fourth year Herod, or Agrippa, went down to Caesarea, sat upon the tribunal, gloried, and after death was enrolled among the gods and called divine. In his time a census was made: at Rome, 6,844,000 people; elsewhere it is said that 60,941,000 people were found. In those times thirty thousand men were killed on the day of Passover in a crush of people at the Temple gates, so that the feast-day was turned into mourning.

In the sixth year of Claudius there was such a famine at Rome that the emperor barely escaped the fury of the people. Afterwards Claudius appointed Agrippa, Agrippa’s son, to the kingdom of the Jews, and he ruled among the Jews for thirty-six years. At the same time Felix put to flight [Col. 0450D] a certain Egyptian false prophet, who had gathered many thousands of men to rush upon Jerusalem; the Acts of the Apostles mentions him. When Paul was accused before Felix, Felix granted him free custody. In the ninth year Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome for rioting.

## On the emperor Nero, who did and caused many evils in his time because he killed his mother, aunt, wife, brother, and his teacher Seneca; and on the death of blessed James, Mark, Peter, Paul, and Lucan, and other events.

In the year 58 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Nero reigned among the Romans for fourteen years, seven months, and twenty-eight days. He resembled his grandfather Caligula, and was worse than he, [Col. 0451A] because he killed his mother, his aunt, his wife, his brother, and his teacher Seneca, who was from the city of Córdoba and was Lucan’s paternal uncle. He also set fire to the city, in order to see a likeness of burning Troy. He undertook nothing in military affairs; he almost lost Britain and Armenia. His luxury was so great that he fished with golden nets and purple cords. At Rome he built baths. In the seventh year of Nero’s reign, James, the brother of the Lord and bishop of Jerusalem, was thrown from the pinnacle of the Temple by a fuller’s club and died. In the second year of his reign he appointed Festus governor of Palestine in place of Felix; from him Paul appealed to Caesar. Festus said to him: “You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you shall go.” When King Agrippa came to Caesarea to greet Festus, Festus informed the king about Paul, [Col. 0451B] before whom Paul also appeared. Much has been written in various ways about the death of blessed Mark the Evangelist.

### Addition by a later but ancient writer to Sicard’s chronicle in the Este manuscript

In his Passion it is read that he died while Gaius and Junius were emperors (elsewhere, in Nero’s first year; some say in the eighth). He was Peter’s son in baptism and his disciple in preaching. At the request of the Romans he wrote the Gospel in Italy, so that those who were literate might preserve in memory what Peter had taught orally. Afterwards, having baptized people throughout the whole region of Egypt, he ordained a bishop. He also healed many people afflicted by various diseases, cleansed lepers, and freed the possessed. Finally, [Col. 0451C] in a church constructed by the brethren in the place called Buculus, plotters, in the month Pharmuthi—that is, April—during a sevenfold festival, dragged him by a rope, saying: “Let us drag the buffalo from Buculus.” But the saint of the Lord gave thanks to the Lord Jesus Christ, saying: “Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit.” Then, while the pagans were burning his remains, darkness, a storm, and rain arose. Therefore righteous persons placed his body at Alexandria, with glory, in a place of cut stone, venerating his memory. It is believed that much later it was translated to Venice, where it is honoured and venerated. And it was fittingly translated to Italy, where his Gospel had first been preached. His disciple was Hermagoras of Aquileia. Hermagoras the Syrian [Col. 0451D] and Inventius of Pavia also flourished. In Nero’s time, Paul’s disciples included Dionysius the Areopagite, who attained the priesthood at Athens; Crescens and Trophimus, who went to Gaul; and Luke, who wrote the Gospel in accordance with Paul’s teaching and the Acts of the Apostles in accordance with his following.

At last, when the Romans sought him for punishment because he had killed a large part of the Senate, he was driven out by the Senate and killed. It is said that he killed himself, and that in him the entire family of Augustus was extinguished. In Nero’s time Lucan flourished; having been discovered in a certain conspiracy, he offered his arm for the cutting of his veins. Horatius the rhetorician, who is also called the *Thebaid*, flourished. In that time there were earthquakes at Rome [Col. 0452A] and in Asia. Lightning struck before Nero’s table. In his time Cornutus the poet, Persius’s teacher, flourished. But Nero sent Cornutus into exile. Likewise, in Nero’s twelfth year and the thirty-sixth after the Lord’s Passion, and in the seventieth from the Incarnation (elsewhere it is said: Nero’s fourteenth year and the thirty-eighth after the Lord’s Passion), Nero killed Peter on the gibbet of the cross, head downward as he had chosen, and he was buried in the Vatican beside the Triumphal Way; on the same day Nero killed Paul with the sword. Paul was a Jew, a disciple of Gamaliel, who wrote fourteen Epistles; but because of its style the last is doubted, and is believed to be by Barnabas, Luke, or Clement. And when Seneca had written letters to Paul, Paul also wrote to him. He is buried on the Ostian Way, in the twenty-seventh year, [Col. 0452B] as some say, after the Lord’s Passion. These two, as Clement says, had wives. For Peter, when he saw his wife being led to her Passion, rejoiced and said: “O wife, remember the Lord.” Paul says that he did not take his wife about with him, so that he might be freer to devote himself to preaching.

### On Galba, Otho, Vitellius, Vespasian, and other events

In the year 72 from the Incarnation of the Lord, after Nero’s death, Galba in Hibernia, Otho at Rome, Vitellius in Germany, and Vespasian in Palestine were chosen for imperial power. Nero had sent Vespasian against the Jews. But Galba was beheaded in the seventh month. In his time Linus was pope. Otho, defeated in a slight battle, killed himself; Vitellius was killed by Vespasian’s commanders. Thus Vespasian, entrusting the army to his son Titus, came to Rome and, once confirmed, reigned for nine years, eleven months, and twenty-two days. [Col. 0452C] He governed the empire with great moderation, for he was just, generous, cheerful, patient, and forgetful of injuries. The Church which had gathered at Jerusalem, having received an answer, crossed the Jordan to the fortress called Pella. Once the righteous men had been removed, Titus, in the second year of his father’s reign, overthrew Judaea and Jerusalem during the days of Unleavened Bread—fittingly, on the days on which they killed the Lord. Some were killed by the sword, others by famine, to such an extent that mothers ate their children. Others were burned by fire, others sold, others taken captive, to the number of one million. [Col. 0452D] This, then, is the “boar from the forest” which, according to the Prophet, devastated it (Ps. 79). From the first building of the Temple under Solomon until this ruin there were 3,102 years; others say 3,089. From the second building, under Darius, 590 years; from the captivity under Antiochus, 238; from the Lord’s Passion, thirty-nine, or rather forty (above, on Isaiah, forty-two is read).

This ruin was preceded by portents: namely, a comet-star like a sword, and an immense sudden flash in the Temple; voices saying, “Let us depart from here”; a gate secured by iron bars opening of its own accord; chariots and four-horse teams, companies of armed men in the air; a heifer giving birth to a lamb during sacrifices; and the prophecy of a certain rustic, who cried out and had no other words in his mouth than these: “A voice [Col. 0453A] from the east, a voice from the west, a voice from the four winds, a voice over Jerusalem and the Temple, a voice over bride and bridegroom: woe to the Israelites!” There was also division among the citizens: one party held the Temple, another the citadel, and another the rest of the city. Hence Isaiah (ch. 66): “The voice of a people from the city; a voice from the Temple.” After the destruction of the Jews, the Apostles and the remaining disciples gathered together from various places, chose Simeon, son of Clophas, and appointed him in James’s place. In Vespasian’s time Achaia, Lycia, Rhodes, Byzantium, Samos, Thrace, and many other regions—some of which had been free and some governed by kings—were brought under Roman rule after their kings had been removed. The Capitol was burned and began to be rebuilt.

### On Vespasian; the vengeance he inflicted upon the Jews; the Jews’ plague, famine, and mortality; other events; and Josephus

[Col. 0453B]

Josephus reports that the destruction of Jerusalem and the dispersion of the Jews took place because of the sin of killing James the Just. Yet this destruction occurred not only because of James’s death, but chiefly because of the Lord’s death, as the Lord says: “Not one stone shall be left upon another, because you did not recognize the time of my visitation” (Matt. 24). But because the Lord does not will the death of the sinner (Ezek. 33), and so that they might have no excuse, he awaited their repentance for forty years; and through the Apostles—especially James, the brother of the Lord, preaching continually among them—he called them [Col. 0453C] back to repentance. But, since he could not bring them back by admonition, he wished at least to test them by portents. For in these forty years granted them for repentance, many wonders and portents occurred, as Josephus reports.

For a bright star, altogether like a sword, was seen hanging over the city from above, and throughout the entire year it burned with destructive flames. At one feast of Unleavened Bread, in the ninth hour of the night, such a brightness surrounded the altar of the Temple that everyone thought it was the clearest day. At the same feast, a heifer brought for sacrifice suddenly gave birth to a lamb in the hands of the ministers. A few days later, near sunset, chariots and four-horse teams were seen moving through the air across the whole region, and companies of armed men mingling with the clouds and surrounding the city in unexpected ranks. On another feast day called Pentecost, priests entering the Temple by night to perform their customary ministries perceived certain movements and noises, and heard sudden voices saying: “Let us depart from these seats.” Four years before the war, a certain man named Jesus, son of Ananias, began suddenly to cry out at the Feast of Tabernacles: “A voice from the east, a voice from the west, a voice from the four winds, a voice over Jerusalem [Col. 0453D] and over the Temple; a voice over bridegrooms and brides; a voice over all Jerusalem.” The aforesaid man was seized, beaten, and scourged; but, unable to say anything else, the more he was beaten, the more loudly he cried the same words. He was therefore brought before a judge and afflicted with terrible tortures, torn until his bones decayed. Yet he uttered neither prayers nor tears; rather, with a sort of howl at nearly every blow, he repeated the same words, adding this: “Woe, woe to Jerusalem!” Thus Josephus.

But when the Jews were neither converted by admonitions nor terrified by such great portents, after the fortieth year the Lord brought Vespasian and Titus against Jerusalem, and they destroyed the city utterly. For Vespasian went to Rome and obtained from Tiberius permission to destroy Judaea and Jerusalem. Therefore, for several years he gathered an army; and Vespasian came against Jerusalem with a large force. On the day of Passover he powerfully besieged Jerusalem round about, and shut up there an innumerable [Col. 0454B] multitude who had come for the feast day. But for some time before Vespasian arrived at Jerusalem, the faithful who were there were warned by the Holy Spirit to depart and withdraw to a certain town beyond the Jordan called Pella, so that, after the holy men had been removed from the city, room might be made for heavenly vengeance upon both the sacrilegious city and the wicked people.

He first attacked among all the cities a certain city of Judaea called Jotapata, in which Josephus was leader and commander. But Josephus and his men resisted bravely. At length, seeing the city’s destruction impending, Josephus entered an underground dwelling with eleven Jews, where they lay afflicted by a four-day famine. With Josephus’s consent, the Jews preferred to die there rather than submit themselves to Vespasian’s servitude. They wished to kill one another and offer their own blood as a sacrifice to God. Since Josephus was the worthiest among them, [Col. 0454C] they wished to kill him first, so that God might be appeased more quickly by the shedding of his blood; or, as the Chronicle says, they wished to kill one another lest they be delivered into the Romans’ hands. But Josephus, a prudent man unwilling to die, made himself judge of death and sacrifice; and he ordered them to cast lots in pairs as to which one should kill the other first. When the lots were cast, the lot delivered now one, now another to death, until they came to the last man, with whom Josephus was to cast lots. Then Josephus, a vigorous and nimble man, took the sword from him [Col. 0454D] and asked which he chose more, life or death, commanding him to choose without delay. Fearfully the man replied: “I do not refuse to live, but through your favour I can preserve my life.” Then Josephus secretly spoke to one of Vespasian’s household, who was also his own acquaintance, and asked that his life be granted; and he obtained what he asked.

When Josephus was brought before Vespasian, Vespasian said to him: “You would have deserved death, if you had not been freed by this man’s request.” Josephus said: “If anything has been wrongly done, it can be changed for the better.” Vespasian said: “What can one who has been conquered do?” Josephus said: “I shall be able to do something, if I soothe your ears with my words.” Vespasian said: “Let it be granted that you may speak; and whatever good you are going to say shall be heard peaceably.” [Col. 0455A] Josephus said: “The emperor has died, and the Senate has made you emperor.” Vespasian said: “If you are a prophet, why did you not prophesy to this city that it was to be subjected to my rule?” Josephus said: “For forty days I foretold this to them.” Meanwhile Roman envoys arrived. They declared that Vespasian had been elevated emperor and paid him homage. The aforesaid Chronicle testifies that Josephus foretold to Vespasian both the emperor’s death and his own elevation. Vespasian, however, left his son Titus in the siege of Jerusalem.

Titus, as is read in the apocryphal History, upon hearing that his father had been elevated to the empire, was so filled with joy and exultation that he was seized, through coldness, by a contraction of the sinews and was tormented by paralysis, one leg being weakened. Hearing that he was suffering from illness, Josephus carefully investigated the cause, illness, and time of the illness. The cause was unknown; the illness was not understood. But the time was revealed: it happened to him when he heard of his father’s election. Josephus, a wise and provident man, inferred much from little and from the timing discovered both illness and cause. Knowing that he had been weakened by excessive joy and gladness, and observing that opposites are cured by opposites; knowing also that what is acquired through love is often lost through pain, he began to ask whether anyone held guilty as an enemy of the prince was in custody. There was there a slave so hateful to Titus that Titus could not look upon him [Col. 0455C] without violent disturbance, nor even hear his name. Josephus therefore said to Titus: “If you desire to be cured, make safe every person who comes in my company.” Titus replied: “Whoever comes in your company shall be safe and unharmed.” Then Josephus quickly ordered a meal to be prepared, placed his own table opposite Titus’s table, and seated the slave at his right hand. When Titus looked at him, he growled in anger, troubled by annoyance; and he who had formerly grown cold through joy grew hot through a surge of fury, stretched his sinews, and was cured. Afterwards Titus received both the slave into his favour and Josephus into his friendship.

Jerusalem having thus been besieged by Titus for two years, among the other evils which severely oppressed the besieged, so great a famine seized everyone that parents snatched food from children, children from parents, men from wives, and wives from husbands—not only from their hands, but even from their very teeth. Young men, stronger in age, wandered openly through the streets like images and fell lifeless. Those who buried the dead often died upon the dead themselves. Unable to bear the stench of corpses, they buried them at public expense; but when the funds failed and the multitude of corpses prevailed, they threw the bodies down from the wall. But Titus, going about and seeing the valleys filled with corpses and the entire country corrupted by their stench, raised his hands with tears to heaven and said: “God, you see that I do not do these things.” [Col. 0456A] The famine there was so great that they ate their shoes and straps.

Also, as is read in the Ecclesiastical History, a woman of noble family and wealth, when robbers entered her house, stripped her of everything, and nothing remained for her to eat, held her little nursing son in her hands and said: “Most unhappy son of an unhappy mother! For whom shall I preserve you in war, famine, and plunder? Come now then, my child: be food for your mother, rage for the robbers, and a tale for the ages.” Having said this, she cut her son’s throat and cooked him; eating one half, she hid the other part. And behold, the robbers immediately smelled the odour of cooked flesh, burst into the house, and threatened her with death unless she revealed the meat. Then she uncovered the infant’s limbs and said: “Look: I have kept the best part for you.” [Col. 0456B] Such horror seized them that they could not speak. And she said: “He is my son; the sin is mine. Eat without concern, for I ate first what I bore. Do not prove either more devout than a mother or more tender than women. But if filial feeling has overcome you and you recoil, I shall eat it all, since I have already eaten half.” Trembling and terrified, they departed.

At last, in the second year of Vespasian’s reign, Titus captured Jerusalem, destroyed it after capturing it, and utterly destroyed the Temple. And just as the Jews had bought Christ for thirty denarii, so he sold thirty Jews for one denarius. As Josephus relates, ninety-seven thousand Jews were sold, and eleven hundred thousand perished by famine and the sword.

### Addition by an ancient interpolator to Sicard’s chronicle in the Este manuscript

[Col. 0456C]

It is also read that, when Titus entered Jerusalem, he saw a very thick wall and ordered it pierced. When an opening had been made, they found within an old man venerable in appearance and white hair. Asked who he was, he replied that he was Joseph of Arimathea, a city in Judaea, and that the Jews had shut him in and walled him up there because he had buried Christ. He added that from that time until the present he had been fed with heavenly food and strengthened by divine light. Yet in the Gospel of Nicodemus it is said that, when the Jews had enclosed him, Christ, risen from the dead, [Col. 0456D] rescued him from there and took him to Arimathea. It may be said that, since after being brought out he did not cease preaching Christ, he was shut in again by the Jews.

After the death of the Emperor Vespasian, his son Titus succeeded him in the empire. He was a man of exceptional clemency and great generosity, and was of such goodness, as Eusebius of Caesarea says in the *Chronicle* and Jerome attests, that once in the evening, remembering that he had done no good or given nothing that day, he said: “We have lost a day.”

### On Josephus’s origin and birth, whose son he was, and the composition of the books that he made

It is certainly worthwhile after these matters to know who this Josephus was, and from where or what lineage he derived his origin—he who supplied us with so much material and knowledge of deeds performed. He himself explains these matters about himself in this way, writing: “Josephus, son of Matthias, a priest at Jerusalem, who in the first war itself fought against the Romans, and was likewise involved in the later battles by compulsion.” It is evident, then, that at this time this man was regarded as most noble not only among the Jews, his own fellow citizens, but also among the Romans, so that because of his literary achievement he was even granted a statue in the city of Rome and his books were placed in libraries. He wrote the history of the *Antiquities* in twenty books. He comprised the history of the Jewish War with the Romans in seven volumes, which he affirms that he published for his fellow citizens not only in elegant Greek [Col. 0457B] but also in the native—that is, Hebrew—language. He is worthy of belief above all others.

There are also two volumes by the same man, *On the Antiquity of the Jews*, in which he appears to answer a certain grammarian Apion, who had written against the Jews in those times, and certain others who had attacked the customs and institutions of the Jewish people. In the first of these two books he teaches, according to the tradition of the ancestors, which books are held authoritative among the Hebrews, as follows.

### Prologue concerning the books Josephus composed against Apion

“Among us,” he says, “there are not innumerable volumes discordant with one another; there are only twenty-two books, containing the sequence of all time, and rightly believed to be divinely inspired. Five of these are Moses’s, containing the law of life and the genealogy of human descent, extending to Moses’s own end; they cover a period of a little less than three thousand years. From the death of Moses to Artaxerxes, who reigned among the Persians, the prophets wrote down the deeds of those times in thirteen volumes. The remaining four books deliver hymns to God and rules and admonitions for human life. From Artaxerxes to our own time, individual events have indeed been written down, but they have not been accorded faith equal to the earlier writings, because there was no uninterrupted [Col. 0457D] and certain succession of prophets. The facts themselves show that we use our Scriptures with reverence. For although so many centuries have intervened, no one has ever dared to add, take away, or alter anything. Rather, this faith is in some way implanted and inborn in all persons of our nation: to believe that these are the ordinances of God, to adhere to them continually, and, if circumstances require it, willingly to lay down even one’s life for them.”

This portion of the historian has, I think, not improperly been inserted by us here. There is also another rather elegant volume by him: *That the Mind Holds Sovereignty within Us*. Some have entitled this little book *Maccabees*, because it contains the struggles and contests undergone by the Maccabaean brothers for piety. At the end of the twentieth book of the *Antiquities*, he also indicates that he composed four volumes, according to ancestral faith and religion, concerning God, his substance, the laws, and why some things are permitted among them and others not permitted. He also says that he composed certain other little works. At the end of the aforesaid twentieth book of the *Antiquities*, he accuses a certain Justus of Tiberias, who had attempted to undertake the same work that he himself had set forth, of falsehood in these words:

“But I did not imitate you in what I wrote. I presented my books to the emperors themselves while the events that occurred were still almost before their eyes, because I knew that I was preserving truth in every respect, and my expectation was not disappointed by the testimony concerning what I had written. I also presented them to many others, many of whom had themselves taken part in the wars, such as King Agrippa and certain of his relatives. Indeed, the Emperor Titus so approved that knowledge of the deeds should reach all people from these books that he publicly subscribed in his own hand that they ought to be read by all. King Agrippa, moreover, attested the truth of our work in sixty-two letters, two of which I have included.”

But enough about these matters. Now let us return to the sequence of our narrative.

### On Titus, son of Vespasian, emperor

In the year 82 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Titus, son of Vespasian, reigned among the Romans for two years and two months. He was most eloquent in Greek and Latin, articulate, devout, and generous, saying that no one ought to leave an emperor sad. Thus, when [Col. 0458C] one day at dinner he remembered that he had granted nothing to anyone that day, he said: “Friends, I have lost this day.” In his time Cletus, whom Peter had made a presbyter, succeeded Peter as pope.

### On the Emperor Domitian, son of Vespasian

In the year 84 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Domitian, son of Vespasian and younger brother of Titus, reigned among the Romans for fifteen years. He was so exceedingly proud that he ordered himself to be called God and Lord, ordered golden and silver statues of himself erected on the Capitol, and ordered October to be called Domitian after his own name. Nevertheless, he carried out many works at Rome: the Capitol, the Forum, the Portico of the Divine Ones, the Iseum, the Serapeum, granaries, preparatory buildings, the Pantheon, the Stadium, [Col. 0458D] and many others. He triumphed over the Dacians and Germans. He forbade the making of eunuchs. He expelled philosophers and astrologers from the city. He persecuted Christians; he put the Apostle John into a vat of boiling oil and, when John emerged unharmed, exiled him to the island of Patmos, where he wrote the *Apocalypse*. In Domitian’s time Josephus, already captured by Vespasian, came to Rome and wrote many works—especially twenty-four books of *Antiquities*, from the beginning of the world to the fourteenth year of this Domitian—for which he was awarded a statue at Rome. In the same time Quintilian held a school at Rome and was the first to receive a salary from the treasury. Also at that time every family and royal line of the Hebrews, especially that of King David, was utterly destroyed by the Emperor Domitian, except for some who said that no earthly empire was owed them, but a heavenly one; he allowed them to go away free according to their wish. Finally, after killing many noble members of the Senate, he was killed by a conspiracy of his own people.

### On the Emperor Nerva

In the year 99 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Nerva reigned among the Romans for one year and four months. He was an energetic and moderate man, who released those whom Domitian had sent into exile. The same is believed concerning the Apostle John, who returned to Ephesus. This is the metropolis of Asia. Hear the story of John. He entrusted a certain young man to a certain bishop. In the bishop’s absence, the young man became leader of robbers. When John came to ask for him, the bishop said: “He is dead.” John replied: [Col. 0459B] “A fine guardian I left you for your brother’s soul!” At last he was called back to repentance through John.

### On the Emperor Trajan

In the year 100 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Trajan reigned among the Romans for nineteen years, six months, and fifteen days. His civility and courage were so great that he is deservedly preferred to all preceding emperors. For whereas others had defended the empire, he nobly enlarged it. Having conquered Asia and Babylonia, he advanced as far as the borders of India. He triumphed over the Dacians and Scythians. He received the Cimbri, Sarmatians, Arabs, and Boffotani [reading uncertain] into allegiance. He established a fleet on the Red Sea in order to subjugate the borders of India. He subdued Armenia, Assyria, and Mesopotamia and made them provinces. He chose nothing unjust in order to increase the treasury. But he persecuted Christians. For when Pliny, procurator of a certain province, consulted him whether he should kill Christians, since he found nothing evil in them except their obstinacy in not sacrificing and their predawn gatherings to sing to a certain Christ as to a god, Trajan answered that no Christian was to be sought out; but if anyone should come before him incidentally, he ought to be punished. At last Trajan died, as is said, at Seleucia in Isauria; his bones, placed in a golden urn, were carried into the Forum and set upon a column. Of all men he alone was buried within the city, in the Forum. In these days Anacletus was pope at Rome. After him Evaristus succeeded as pope at Rome.

### On the Emperor Hadrian

[Col. 0459D] In the year 120 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Hadrian reigned for twenty-one years among the Romans. He was surnamed Aelius. He was most eloquent and most diligent in regard to the treasury and military discipline; learned in both languages. He was called Father of the Fatherland. He remitted the city’s taxes. He restored at public expense Alexandria, destroyed by the Romans; and he supplied public funds to restore the city of Nicomedia, which had collapsed in an earthquake. At the Athenians’ request, he compiled laws for them from the books of Draco and Solon. He waged war against the Sarmatians. In the second year of his reign he captured the Jews, who were rebelling for a second time against Roman rule. Sixtus was pope at Rome; Telesphorus succeeded Sixtus.

### On the Emperor Titus Antoninus

[Col. 0460A]

In the year 142 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Titus Antoninus reigned among the Romans for twenty-two years and three months. He was called Pius because of his clemency; Father of the Fatherland because he remitted debts arising from accusations that had been brought; he kept the treasury rich and was no less venerable to allied kings. At the same time the physician Galen flourished, born at Pergamum. At the same time Hyginus was pope at Rome. Anicius succeeded him; Pius succeeded Anicius in the episcopate. In the time of Pope Hyginus, the heretics Valentinus, Cerdo, and Marcion came to Rome. Valentinus said that there were two principles, Depth and Silence, and from these thirty aeons. Cerdo and Marcion held two principles, good and evil. Both denied the resurrection of the flesh, though they promised salvation to the soul. At Alexandria Basilides spewed out his teaching, saying that there were 365 heavens according to the number of days in the year. He commended the name *Abrasas*, because it contains that number. His disciples called themselves Gnostics, in presumption of superior knowledge. Others called them Bothonites, that is, “muddy ones,” from the obscenity which they practised in their mysteries. Learned Agrippa wrote against him.

### On the Emperors Marcus Antoninus Verus and his brother Lucius Aurelius

In the year 165 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Marcus Antoninus Verus reigned [Col. 0460C] among the Romans with his brother Lucius Aurelius for nineteen years and one month. Up to this time the Augusti had been sole rulers; from this point there were first two at once. They captured Seleucia and triumphed over the Parthians. They fought against Germans and Sarmatians, Marcomanni, Quadi, Dacians, Vandals, Suebi, and Pannonians. When their army was suffering from heat, certain Christian soldiers serving under him prayed, and contrary to expectation a most abundant rain was poured upon the army, while lightning and fire fell upon the enemy. After his brother’s death, Marcus made his son Commodus his partner in the kingdom and gave many things to many people, so that he exhausted the treasury. He remitted money that was owed by burning the account books. And lest anything be lacking to his goodness, he moderated older laws with new enactments. He was so magnificent that he displayed a hundred lions at once. When Smyrna, a city of Asia, collapsed in an earthquake, he remitted its taxes for ten years for its restoration. In the eighth year of Marcus Antoninus, Soter became pope at Rome.

### On Commodus, son of Marcus, emperor

In the year 184 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Commodus, son of Marcus, reigned among the Romans for thirteen years. He had nothing of his father except that he fought against the Germans. He wished September to be called Commodus after his own name. He built baths at Rome. He was killed by his wife's cup. He was so wicked that, even after death, he was called the enemy of the human race, because he killed many nobles. Victor succeeded Eleutherius in the apostolic see. In these times there were the heretics called Cataphrygians, from Phrygia, [Col. 0461A] who condemned second marriages. Their author was Montanus, who called himself the Paraclete and had with him two women, Prisca and Maximilla, possessed by a mad spirit, who boasted that they were prophetesses.

### On the Emperor Helvius Pertinax

In the year 197 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Helvius Pertinax reigned among the Romans for six months. When he was more than seventy years old and held the prefecture of the city, he was ordered by decree of the Senate to rule; and because he resisted stubbornly, he was called Pertinax. When the Senate asked him to call his wife Augusta, he replied that it was enough that he ruled unwillingly. Pertinax was killed by Julian’s crime.

### On the Emperor Julian

In the year 197 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Julian reigned among [Col. 0461B] the Romans for seven months. Severus killed him at the Milvian Bridge. He came after the said Helvius Pertinax.

### On the Emperor Severus

In the year 198 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Severus reigned for seventeen years among the Romans. He was of African origin, a philosopher, distinguished in civic pursuits, but frugal. He waged many wars successfully: he defeated the Parthians, Arabs, and Britons; and at Lyon he killed a certain Claudius Albinus, who had been present at Pertinax’s death and had made himself Caesar in Gaul. He had the recovered provinces enclosed with a wall from sea to sea for 122,000 paces, and built stations. He persecuted Christians. At last he died at York [Col. 0461C] in Britain.

### On Antoninus, son of Severus, emperor

In the year 217 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Antoninus, son of Severus, whose proper name was Bassianus, reigned among the Romans for seven years and six months. He was surnamed Caracalla from the kind of garment which he wore and which was called by his name. He built baths at Rome called the Antonine Baths. He was so unable to control his lust that he married his stepmother. He did nothing memorable except what has been stated. In his time Zephyrinus was pope, and Pope Callixtus succeeded him. In the time of this Antoninus, son of Severus, the Fifth Edition was discovered at Jerusalem, its author unknown. Ammonius of Alexandria compiled the Gospel canons. At Jerusalem Alexander was ordained while Narcissus was still living, because of Narcissus’s age; he was 116 years old and governed the Church together with Alexander. But Tertullian attacked the holy Church, and there was a great persecution of Christians.

### On the Emperor Macrinus

In the year 223 from the Incarnation of the Lord, an emperor named Macrinus reigned among the Romans for one year and two months. He did nothing worthy of memory.

### On the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus

In the year 224 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Marcus Aurelius Antoninus reigned among the Romans for four years. He was immoral, so that he omitted no form of obscenity.

### On the Emperor Alexander Aurelius

[Col. 0462A]

In the year 228 of the Lord, Alexander Aurelius reigned among the Romans for thirteen years. He defeated Xerxes, king of the Persians, and was so severe a reformer of military discipline that he cashiered certain mutinous legions. He had the jurists Ulpian, Paul, and Papinian as assessors. He built baths and rejected eunuchs, saying that they were a third sex of human beings, neither to be seen nor employed. At last he was beheaded at Mainz. In the same time Urban was pope at Rome.

### On the Emperor Maximinus
In the year of the Lord 241, Maximinus reigned among the Romans for three years. He was the first emperor chosen from the ranks of the soldiery and by the army without the authority of the senate. [Col. 0462B] He persecuted the churches; under him Pontianus, bishop of Rome, was deported to Sardinia and crowned with martyrdom. He was killed by Pupienus, who, while usurping the empire, was himself killed. Pope Anterus succeeded Pontianus. In the time of Pope Pontianus and Maximinus, Beryllus the heretic attacked the Church. Sabellius fell into error; his disciples were called Sabellians and Patripassians, because, while teaching identity and Trinity, they ascribed suffering also to the Father.

### On the Emperor Gordian

In the year of the Lord 244, Gordian reigned among the Romans for seven years. On entering Rome, he killed Pupienus and Albinus, who had seized the empire. [Col. 0462C] He overcame the Parthians, Persians, and Medes. He was killed by Philip’s treachery. After Gordian, Philip ruled with his son for twelve years. This Philip was made a Christian through Origen. Decius killed them both. At the same time Pope Fabian sat at Rome; he was chosen by the dove of the Holy Spirit. He decreed that chrism should be renewed yearly and the old chrism burned. He was crowned with martyrdom. At the same time Novatus came from Africa and separated Novatian and certain confessors from the Church, after Moses had died in prison, where he had remained eleven months; and thus many fled.

In these times there were heretics who said that souls perish together with bodies and are to be raised again together with the bodies. There were also others called Elcesaites. Although they used whatever testimonies from the [Col. 0462D] New and Old Testament they pleased, they nevertheless rejected many things, such as the Apostle; and they said that they possessed a book which had fallen from heaven.

### On the Emperor Philip

In the year of the Lord 250, Philip reigned among the Romans for twelve years. He made his son, who bore the same name as himself, partner in his rule, and founded in Thrace a city bearing his own name. He was the first of all Roman emperors to believe in Christ and, as it is said, became a Christian. When he wished to communicate at the Paschal solemnity, the bishop required him, until he had confessed his sins, to stand among the penitents; and he did this patiently. He gave treasures to [Col. 0463A] blessed Sixtus. Philip was severe, and both he and his son were killed by Decius.

### On the Emperor Decius

In the year of the Lord 257, Decius reigned among the Romans for one year and three months. He was born in Pannonia. He suppressed civil war. He made his son Caesar; and, after killing Philip father and son, he persecuted the Christians out of hatred for them and put to death the blessed Lawrence and Hippolytus. Decius was killed by the devil and by enemies.

### On Gallus with his son Volusianus

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 258, Gallus reigned among the Romans with his son Volusianus for two years and four months. In their time there was a plague which almost wiped out the human race. He was killed by Ejula. In these [Col. 0463B] times Novatus, a Roman priest, was a heretic, from whom the Novatians took their name. But they called themselves not Novatians but Cathari—that is, “the Pure”—on account of purity. They did not admit second marriages and denied reconciliation to penitents. At this time Pope Lucius sat at Rome.

### On the Emperor Aemilianus

In the year of the Lord 258, Aemilianus, a Moor by nation, reigned for two months; for in the third month he paid the penalty for his usurped tyranny.

### On Valerian and Gallienus

In the year of the Lord 258, Valerian and Gallienus, Valerian’s son, reigned among the Romans for fifteen years. Valerian was chosen by the army in Raetia; Gallienus [Col. 0463C] by the senate at Rome. Valerian persecuted Christians, but not for long: while waging war in Mesopotamia, he was captured by Sapor, king of the Persians, and grew old among the Parthians in ignoble slavery. For when Sapor mounted his horse, he placed his foot upon Valerian’s neck.

Gallienus, however, at first administered the empire successfully, but in the end ruinously. For while he abandoned himself to every kind of licentiousness, the Germans came as far as Ravenna. The Alamanni, after devastating Gaul, crossed into Italy. Dacia was lost. Greece, Macedonia, Pontus, and Asia were ravaged by the Goths. The Parthians occupied the Pannonias, Mesopotamia, and Assyria. The Germans gained possession of Spain and captured the city of Ceteto. Thus their rule was ruinous to the Roman name. Through their cowardice or ill fortune, [Col. 0463D] Gaul was at length recovered by Posthumus, who assumed the purple in Gaul. Finally Gallienus died at Milan.

Pope Dionysius divided the parishes and appointed one priest in each for the penitents. Pope Felix succeeded him. Under this Gallienus seven tyrants ruled: first Geminus at Nursia; second Posthumus, who ruled in Gaul for ten years and was killed; third Aemilianus, killed at Mainz; fourth Marius, killed in the same place; fifth Victorinus, made ruler of Gaul and killed; sixth Tetricus, killed by soldiers; seventh Maurus, killed in Syria by his wife.

### On the Emperor Claudius

In the year of the Lord 274, Claudius reigned among the Romans for [Col. 0464A] one year and nine months. He was frugal, moderate, just, and fit to govern the commonwealth. He defeated in battle the Goths who were ravaging Illyricum and Macedonia, and overcame the Alamanni at Lake Benacus. For these deeds a golden shield and a golden statue were set up for him in the Capitol, and after his death he was called divine.

In the time of Pope Dionysius, Claudius, Valerian, and Gallienus his son, there arose Paul of Samosata, a heretic who confessed Christ to be merely a man; and Manes, from whom the Manichaeans derive their name, a Persian who now called himself Christ and now the Paraclete, and made twelve disciples in imitation of Christ. The aforesaid Claudius died of illness. Afterwards Quintilius, Claudius’s brother, was chosen emperor.

### On Quintilius, Claudius’s Brother

[Col. 0464B]

In the year of the Lord 276, Quintilius, Claudius’s brother, was chosen emperor by the senate; but on the sixteenth day of his reign he was killed at Aquileia.

### On the Emperor Aurelian

In the year of the Lord 276, Aurelian reigned among the Romans for five years and six months. A man powerful in war, not unlike Alexander, he won three battles in Italy, namely at Placentia and Ticinum. He overcame Tetricus, who still held Gaul; he founded the city of Aurelianum; and he defeated at Immae, not far from Antioch, Zenobia, formerly the wife of Odenathus, who after her husband’s death still held power in the East. Thus, after [Col. 0464C] freeing the Roman world from invaders in three years, he entered Rome in triumph as though the recoverer of the East, with Tetricus and Zenobia proceeding before him.

He was the first among the Romans to place a diadem on his head and to wear a gilded garment. He enclosed Rome with stronger walls. He built a temple to the Sun. He established the people’s use of pork. Finally, after entering Greece, lightning struck close beside him between Constantinople and Heraclea; not long afterward he was killed and numbered among the gods.

### On Florianus

In the year of the Lord 282, Florianus reigned for two months and twenty-three days. He did nothing worthy of remembrance. He was killed at Tarsus.

### On the Emperor Tacitus

[Col. 0464D]

In the year of the Lord 282, Tacitus reigned for six months. He was an outstanding man, but accomplished nothing, being overtaken by death.

### On Probus

In the year of the Lord 283, Probus reigned among the Romans for six years and three months. A man of military and civil ability, he recovered Gaul, which had been occupied by barbarians. Having completed innumerable wars, he restored peace to the world, saying that soldiers would soon no longer be needed. This Probus was killed by his soldiers. He himself killed the tyrants Saturninus, Proculus, and Bonosus. In his time Felix sat as bishop of Rome, and Eutychianus succeeded him as bishop of Rome. In these times the heresy of the Manichaeans gained strength, teaching [Col. 0465A] two principles, good and evil, and promising purification through its sacraments. It did not receive the Old Testament and corrupted the New; it has poured forth poison even to the present day.

### On Carus with his Sons Numerian and Carinus

In the year of the Lord 289, Carus reigned among the Romans for two years with his sons Numerian and Carinus, whom he appointed Caesars. Carus, after defeating the Parthians and Persians, perished when struck by lightning beyond the Tigris. Numerian was killed by treachery and Carinus in battle, within a short time. In their time Caius sat as bishop of Rome; he was of the family of the Emperor Diocletian.

### On Diocletian

In the year of the Lord 290, Diocletian reigned among the [Col. 0465B] Romans for twenty years. He made Herculius Maximian Caesar; Maximian restored peace to Gaul, and therefore Diocletian made him Augustus from being Caesar, taking him as a partner in the empire, and he reigned for sixteen years. Since Britain, Africa, Egypt, and the East were being occupied, he also made Constantius and Galerius Caesars. He gave Theodora, the stepdaughter of Herculius, in marriage to Constantius; he gave his own daughter, Valeria, to Galerius. With and through these men he recovered Britain, Gaul, Africa, and Egypt.

When Diocletian had thus reigned so gloriously after defeating his enemies, he was the first to command that he be worshipped as a god; and he had gems set in his garments and footwear. Previously emperors had been greeted [Col. 0465C] as judges and worn the purple alone as their distinguishing private dress. Diocletian and Maximian built baths at Rome. They celebrated a triumph at Rome, with conquered enemies and the spoils of men preceding them. At last Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan laid aside the purple and chose private life, saying that because of their age they were less fit to govern the commonwealth—something unheard of before that time.

In these times Marcellinus became bishop of Rome, and Marcellus succeeded him. When Marcellinus’s body had lain unburied for thirty days, the blessed apostle Peter appeared to Marcellus in a vision and said: “Marcellus, bury the body of my brother Marcellinus beside me, so that those whom martyrdom did not separate, and whom God’s grace justified, may not be separated by burial.” [Col. 0465D] This was done, for he was buried near the apostle’s feet.

### On Constantius and Galerius

In the year of the Lord 310, Constantius and Galerius, formerly Caesars, were made Augusti and divided the world: Constantius held Italy, Gaul, and Africa; Galerius, Illyricum, the East, and Asia. But Constantius, an excellent and public-spirited man, did not heap riches into the treasury, saying that public wealth was better held by private persons than kept within one enclosure. He wished to be content with Gaul alone. He was a friend of Christians and allowed them to live according to their religion. He died at York and was enrolled among the gods.

He left three notable sons: Constantine by Helena his concubine, and Constantius and Dalmatius by [Col. 0466A] Theodora his lawful wife. Dalmatius begot another Dalmatius; Constantius begot Gallus and Julian. Constantine, the concubine’s son, succeeded him, having been made king in Britain.

Galerius, a military man residing in Illyricum, made two Caesars: Maximinus, whom he set over the East, and Severus, to whom he gave Italy. Meanwhile Maxentius, son of Herculius Maximian, was called Augustus among the Romans at Rome. Severus, sent by Galerius, therefore came into Italy and besieged the city, but was deserted by his soldiers and, fleeing to Ravenna, was killed.

Herculius Maximian aspired to resume his former eminence, intending to depose his son. He went to Constantine, to whom he had given his daughter Fausta as wife; but when he wished to kill him, his plot was discovered through his daughter, who revealed it to her husband. Herculius fled to Marseilles, where he also died. At the same [Col. 0466B] time Galerius made Licinius emperor and partner in his empire. Thus, after Galerius’s death, the commonwealth was ruled by four emperors: Constantine, Maxentius, Licinius, and Maximinus.

Maximinus, having planned a persecution of Christians, died at Tarsus; and so Licinius alone held the East. Constantine, having already reigned five years, sought the empire of the whole world. Concerned because Rome was held as a city, in the sixth year of his reign, when a multitude of barbarians was assembled beyond the Danube against him, he saw in a dream the figure of a cross shining in the sky and heard it said to him in Greek, *en to auto nica*, which in Latin means: “In this, conquer.” He therefore commanded this sign to be made of gold and precious stones on his standard and arms.

Thus, with this sign and by the counsel of priests, who said that Christ by this sign had conquered death, the devil, and hell, and victoriously ascended into heaven, he boldly entered battle and prevailed. Coming to Rome, he made war against Maxentius, defeated and killed him at the Milvian Bridge; and Constantine was thus placed on the throne at Rome, as he had been. Diocletian was still alive and died on his estate; alone among private persons he was enrolled among the gods.

Licinius, emperor of the East, persecuted Christians; under him Basil, bishop of Pontus, was crowned with martyrdom. But at length Licinius was killed at Thessalonica by private individuals. Constantine [Col. 0466D] therefore became sole ruler. He had three sons—Constantine, Constantius, and Constans—and made them Caesars to preside over Gaul, the East, and Italy. He triumphed over Goths, Cimbri, and many others. He composed many laws, but killed his wife Fausta.

In Constantine’s time Eusebius sat as bishop of Rome. Under him, as some say, the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ was discovered; Judas, brother of blessed Stephen, was baptized and was called Quiriacus. Eusebius instructed Constantine as a catechumen. Melchiades succeeded Eusebius. Timothy suffered for Christ at Rome, and holy Pope Melchiades dedicated his martyrdom. Melchiades too was crowned with martyrdom. All pontiffs, except . . . [lacuna] up to this point, [Col. 0467A] were crowned with martyrdom.

After him Sylvester became bishop of Rome. Because of persecution he was hiding on Mount Soracte. While he lay hidden, Constantine, who, entangled in various concerns, had delayed baptism, was struck with leprosy. When he had been advised to bathe in the blood of children, he heard the mothers’ weeping and said: “The dignity of the Roman empire springs from the fountain of piety.” Thus the piety of the pious emperor ordered that the children be restored to their mothers. Because of this piety, on the following night the Lord Jesus sent his apostles Peter and Paul to him. They urged him to receive baptism through Sylvester and to restore churches throughout the world.

Summoned to him, Sylvester advised him to fast for a week, close the temples of idols, release prisoners, and give alms. [Col. 0467B] When these things had been done, he baptized him. Before Constantine, the philosopher Crato, the philosopher Zeno, and distinguished judges, he overcame eleven Jews disputing concerning the articles of our faith, proving that there are three persons and one God, that Christ is God, and that he is the one foretold by the prophets. He overcame the twelfth, who was obstinate, by bringing to life a bull which the Jew had killed by a word.

Accordingly Helena, the Augustus’s mother, who had begun to Judaize, was converted to the faith; and, in a greater demonstration of her devotion to our faith, she closed the jaws of a certain dragon. Christian religion therefore multiplied in a short time and was spread everywhere throughout the world. What had hitherto assembled in hiding now became a public institution under the authority of rulers, as did Christ [Col. 0467C] and the sacraments of the Church.

For by Constantine’s edict the temples of the pagans were overthrown and churches established. He himself built the church of Saint Peter—digging the ground himself—and other patriarchal churches and others at Rome. He granted immunity to those taking refuge in a church. He decreed that tithes be offered for the dedication of churches and exacted through judges. He commanded cessation from work on the Lord’s Day. He forbade crucifixion. He ordered the sign of the cross to be portrayed on coinage. He granted possessions to churches. He also gave imperial insignia to Sylvester, decreed that all bishops should be subject to the Roman pontiff, and, so that the Church might remain in tranquility, withdrew to Byzantium. By buildings and honors he strove to raise it to such eminence that it would rival Rome and be called a second Rome; from Constantine it was named Constantinople.

Sylvester, therefore, sitting at Rome, publicly exercised pontifical authority. He decreed that the Roman prelate should be judged by no one; that a priest should not be condemned except by eleven witnesses; that a greater should not be accused by a lesser; and that a cleric should not be judged before a layman. Moreover, he changed the names of the days into *feriae*, and prescribed fasting on the fourth and sixth feria and on the Sabbath, because of the Lord’s burial. He ordered celebration on the Lord’s Day because of the Resurrection, and on the fifth feria because of the Ascension. He also decreed that the priest should anoint the baptized person on the crown of the head with chrism. He commanded the use in the Church of the half-full dalmatic, [Col. 0468A] which ought rather to be called a *colobium*.

In these times Arius, a priest of Alexandria, associated many with his impiety, teaching that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not of one essence. Against him the Nicene synod of 318 bishops was assembled. When the faith was under discussion, the emperor said to the priests: “God has given you authority to judge concerning us. But you cannot be judged by men. Again, ‘You are gods’ (Psalm LXXXI). It is not fitting for a man to judge gods, but only he of whom it is said: ‘God has stood in the assembly of gods’ (ibid.).” There the creed of the apostles’ faith was drawn up, and many other matters were established by the bishops.

Donatus also taught impiously: he rebaptized those who had been baptized and taught that the Son is less than the Father and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0468B] less than the Son. Some say, as is read in the *Tripartite History*, that Constantine was baptized in the last year of his life by Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia. For he had delayed baptism so long because he wished to receive it in the River Jordan. Others say that, having been baptized by Sylvester, he was rebaptized by this Arian because he had declined into Arian doctrine. If this is true, he began well but ended badly. Yet this is far from the truth, as the Catholic Church unquestionably believes.

Finally, when Constantine was preparing war against the Persians, he died near Nicomedia in the fifty-sixth year of his age and the thirty-first of his reign. A long-haired star foretold his death. In his times Alexander became bishop of Alexandria, a most valiant preacher of the Gospel; Paphnutius, confessor and bishop of Egypt; Quirinus, bishop; and Sisinius, crowned with martyrdom. Methodius, bishop of Tyre, wrote many works and at last was crowned with martyrdom in Constantine’s time—or, as some say, in that of Decius and Valerian. Juventius, a Spanish priest, rendered the Gospels into heroic verse. Spiridion was bishop of Cyprus. When thieves approached his cabbages, they were suddenly bound, though no one bound them. His deceased daughter answered him when he asked concerning a deposit. When his granary faithfully supplied provisions in abundance, it appeared emptied to a certain deceiver. When other food failed, he offered pork [Col. 0468D] to a needy traveler to eat during Lent; and, lest the traveler fear to eat, he ate first himself.

Helena, Constantine’s mother, went to Jerusalem and cleared the place of the Lord’s Passion, where an image of Venus had been erected. There she found three crosses, one of which was the Lord’s. At the prayer of Bishop Macarius it was identified because, at its touch, a dead person was raised and a woman was freed from illness. She also found the nails: she placed part of them in her son’s helmet and part in his bridle. Thus was fulfilled the saying of Zechariah: “That which is on the horse’s bridle shall be holy to the Lord.” A portion of the wood is also in the priestly tiara; a portion is said to be in Constantine’s statue.

### On Constantine, Constantius, and Constans

In the year of the Lord 341, Constantine, Constantius, [Col. 0469A] and Constans, sons of Constantine, whom their aforesaid father had appointed Caesars, reigned among the Romans for twenty-four years. Constantine their father had ordered that his nephew Dalmatius, son of his brother Dalmatius, should rule with his sons. But he was killed through faction. Constantine was killed at Aquileia. Constans for a time ruled prudently and subdued the Franks, but became an Arian; being intolerable to the soldiers, he was killed through the faction of the tyrant Magnentius, not far from the regions of Spain.

Constantius had varying fortune. He suffered much from the Persians, while Sapor king of Persia ravaged Mesopotamia and besieged Nisibis. He defeated the tyrant Magnentius, who had held Gaul, Spain, Africa, and Italy. Magnentius killed himself with his own [Col. 0469B] hand at Lyons; and his brother Decentius, whom he had sent as Caesar to defend Gaul, on hearing of his brother’s death hanged himself with a noose at Sens. Constantius also stripped a certain Veternio, elected around Illyricum, of the royal insignia.

Moreover, he made Gallus, son of his uncle, Caesar and placed him over the East. Gallus oppressed the Jews and killed many nobles at Antioch. Finally, he was killed by Constantius through envy. Silvanus too, who was attempting revolution in Gaul, was destroyed. Thus Constantius alone was prince and Augustus in the Roman empire. He made Julian, Gallus’s brother, Caesar, gave him his sister Constantia as wife, and sent him to Gaul, where many excellent deeds were done through him. Finally, after the barbarians had been put to flight, Julian was called Augustus by the soldiers. When he took up arms against Constantius, Constantius died between Asia and Cappadocia from excessive anxiety.

In the same times Marcus succeeded Sylvester; Julius succeeded Marcus; after Julius Liberius sat as bishop of Rome. Pope Felix succeeded him.

### On Julian the Monk and Apostate

In the year of the Lord 264, Julian, monk and apostate, reigned among the Romans for two years and eight months. He was learned in liberal studies and skilled in both languages. He disliked cooks, barbers, and eunuchs: cooks because, like a philosopher, he ate simple food; barbers because one was enough for a multitude; eunuchs because his wife had died. [Col. 0469D] He restored writers of ancient prosperity and assigned them salaries. To gain the empire without opposition, he feigned religion and ordered all bishops to be released completely from Constantius’s prisons.

But although he had been a Christian from the beginning and, as is said, a monk, after becoming emperor he returned again to idols and became a betrayer and persecutor of Christians. He forbade the Galileans—that is, Christians, for this was their earlier name—to read the disciplines of poets and philosophers, saying: “We are wounded by our own weapons, because Christians, armed with our writings, wage war against us.” Out of hatred for Christ he granted the Jews permission to rebuild the Temple of Jerusalem. While they were clearing it, earth rose from the valley; and while they were rebuilding it, an earthquake suddenly occurred, rocks were shattered, and a fiery globe issued from the inner temple and struck down the builders with fire.
