But lest this be believed to have happened by chance, the sign of the cross appeared on everyone’s garments.

He also ordered the sign to be removed from public images and the forms of Jupiter, Mars, and the like to be impressed upon them. So that pagan rites and sacrifices might be observed more devotedly everywhere, he commanded pagan priests to imitate Christian rites and the holiness of priests. Finally, Julian, returning victorious from the Parthians, set out against the Persians and died, pierced in the belly by a spear; he was enrolled among the gods by the pagans. Whether he was killed by a man or an angel is entirely unknown. A certain devout man, present in spirit but absent in body, recognized his death. After the said [Col. 0470B] Julian, the Emperor Jovian succeeded.

In the time of Pope Liberius and Julian lived the monk Hilarion. Many martyrs suffered for Christ, including Gordian and Epimachus; at Rome, John, Paul, and Donatus; and Theodulus in Phrygia, who, while being burned, said to the executioner: “Place my other side upon the fire, lest, when you begin to roast me, you find me half-cooked.” Basil, a priest, ended his life in martyrdom. The bones of blessed John the Baptist were burned and scattered into dust.

Athanasius, Eusebius of Vercelli, and Hosius of Corduba held the council of Alexandria, where they called Father, Son, and Holy Spirit the Trinity and permitted the use of the terms “substance” and “subsistence” for them, against those who said that these terms should not be used [Col. 0470C] because substance is defined, whereas God cannot be defined. Evagrius said: “That which is ineffable should be adored in the reverence of silence.”

Note that in the time of the aforesaid Pope Liberius and Constantius, son of the late Constantine, Maximian was bishop of Trier and received Athanasius with honor. But afterward Athanasius returned to Alexandria on Constantius’s letters. Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, martyr and a Sardinian by nation; Dionysius, bishop of Milan; and a Roman priest named Pancratius were condemned to exile because they opposed Arius. Serapion wrote many works. John surnamed Sappes, bishop of the Persians; Eusebius, a Roman priest, confessor and martyr; Martin, priest; and Archelaus, deacon, flourished. Bishop Lando carried Archelaus’s body to Cremona.

Hilary of Poitiers wrote many works on Christian religion. He was the light of the Romans, the lamp of the churches, a precious stone; in whatever he addressed with elegant speech, he spoke with a golden mouth. But synods were held at Seleucia, Rimini, and Milan, in which our faith was condemned, because throughout the whole world all churches were polluted by Arian impiety.

A certain Audæus, from whom came the Audæans, also called Anthropomorphites, taught that God conforms to the human image because he said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Genesis 1). Macedonius too, author of an error, taught that the Holy Spirit [Col. 0471A] is a creature; hence his disciples were called Macedonians, Pneumatics, or Semi-Arians, because they agreed with them in part. Photinus moreover denied that Christ was born before the ages. Acacius was the inventor—or rather imitator—of a new error. Aetius was expelled from the Church because of his lectures on categories and syllogisms. For the Apostles taught us faith, not dialectic. His disciples were not called Aetians but Eunomians, after Eunomius, his disciple. Eudoxius also called the Father *asebēs* and the Son *eusebēs*. Since these words may be used actively or passively, they were rejected by the Church together with their author. For *asebēs* means either “not worshipping” or “not worshipped”; *eusebēs*, either “worshipping well” or “well worshipped.”

In these times Sapor, king of the Persians, raging against Christians, came to Antioch. But through the prayers of Bishop Jacob he could not prevail: by Jacob’s prayers gnats and mosquitoes threw the army into confusion, injuring its animals and compelling them to flee. Macarius, Antony’s disciple, led the eremitical life. There were, however, several Macarii commendable for holiness. Donatus, Jerome’s teacher, taught grammar. Victorinus the rhetorician earned a statue in the forum. The relics of Timothy, the Apostle’s disciple, were found at Constantinople. The bones of blessed Andrew the Apostle and Luke the Evangelist, who had died in Bethany, were received by the people of Constantinople with marvelous enthusiasm after being brought from Achaia.

### On the Emperor Jovian

[Col. 0471C]

In the year of the Lord 367, Jovian reigned for eight months. When chosen by the army, he said that, being a Christian, he could not rule pagans. The army replied: “Through Julian we too cast off Christ’s name; we wish to be Christians with you.” On hearing this, he accepted the imperial scepter. Compelled by necessity, he made peace with Sapor, king of Persia, but a dishonorable peace: he surrendered Nisibis and a great part of Mesopotamia to him within fixed boundaries. Since the founding of the city, this had never happened: although Roman legions had been made to pass under the yoke, as occurred in Numidia, Numantia, and Spain, nevertheless they had surrendered no territory. Finally he died suddenly and was enrolled among the gods.

In his time the synod of Antioch was held, by which Macedonius was condemned. Indeed, church affairs would have been well ordered under him had death not taken such a ruler from humankind. In the same time as the aforesaid Jovian lived blessed Geminianus, bishop of Modena; likewise Pope Liberius and blessed Severus, archbishop of Ravenna, who was chosen by the dove of the Holy Spirit.

### On the Emperors Valentinian and Valens

In the year of the Lord 368, Valentinian and his brother Valens reigned among the Romans for fourteen years and five months. Their father was a certain Gratian, a Pannonian by birth and a rope-maker by occupation. When his son Valentinian was carrying a rope for sale, five soldiers could not wrest it from him; for this merit he was admitted to military service and afterwards to the command of a thousand men. While serving under Julian and professing the Christian faith, he was ordered by the emperor either to sacrifice to idols or leave the army; he left. But after Julian and Jovian had died, he who had lost a tribunate of a thousand men for Christ received the empire in place of persecution.

He took his brother Valens as partner in the kingdom and also made Augustus his own son, born of his wife Severa, though not yet of age. Valentinian subdued the Saxons and more than eighty thousand Burgundians, who not long afterward became Christians. Finally, while preparing war against the Sarmatians, he died of apoplexy at Burguion. In Valentinian’s second year Damasus and, a little later, Ursinus the deacon were bishops at Rome, but [Col. 0472B] Damasus prevailed.

The Emperor Valens, a supporter of the Arians, took a church from the Catholics and gave it to the Arians. Basil approached him and said: “Emperor, it is written, ‘The king’s honor loves judgment’ (Psalm XCV), and again, ‘The king’s judgment is justice.’ Why has your heart commanded that Catholics be driven from the church and it given to Arians?” The emperor said to him: “Again you return to insults, Basil. This does not become you.” Basil replied: “It becomes me even to die for justice.”

Then Demosthenes, prefect of the emperor’s banquets, a supporter of the Arians, speaking on their behalf, committed a barbarism. Basil said to him: “Your concern is to think about the king’s dishes, not to stew divine doctrines.” Immediately, put to shame, he was silent. The emperor said to Basil: “Go and judge between them, but not according to the excessive favor of the people.”

Basil therefore went and said in the presence of Catholics and Arians that the church doors should be shut and secured with the seal of each party, and that the church should belong to whichever party’s prayers opened them. All agreed. The Arians prayed for three days and nights and came to the church doors, but they were not opened. Then Basil, having arranged a procession, came to the church and, after prayer, touched the doors lightly with his pastoral staff, saying: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O everlasting doors, and the King of glory shall enter” (Psalm XXIII). Immediately they were opened. Entering, they gave thanks to God, and the church was restored to the Catholics.

The emperor had many promises made to Basil if he would agree with him. [Col. 0472D] Basil replied: “Such things are suitable for children; for those who are nourished by the divine sayings do not endure even one syllable of divine doctrines being corrupted.” Then, when the emperor angrily wished to write an order for Basil’s exile, his first, second, and third pen broke; enraged, he tore up the paper. At that time Pope Felix sat at Rome. Liberius succeeded him a second time.

### On the Emperor Gratian
In the year of the Lord 382, Gratian, after the death of Valens, reigned among the Romans for six years. He was moderately instructed in letters, restrained in sexual desire, food, sleep, and the exercise of his imperial power; he dedicated churches to the Lord and worked to ensure that orthodox pastors who had been exiled might return to their flocks. He associated with himself in the empire his young brother Valentinian [Col. 0473A], whom his father had begotten by Justina. For Valentinian, having repudiated his lawful wife Severa, the mother of Gratian, and captivated by the beauty of a certain maiden Justina, took her as wife; by her he begot Valentinian, and also Justa and Galla. Gratian moreover admitted Theodosius, son of Theodosius, to a share in the empire; retaining Spain for himself, he entrusted to Theodosius the rule of the East. He saw in a dream that Meletius, bishop of Antioch, clothed him in an episcopal cloak and adorned his head with a crown. When he came to Constantinople and ordered the bishops to assemble, he recognized Meletius from the earlier vision. When Gratian saw enemies threatening him in Gaul, trusting in Christ’s protection, he committed himself, though with inferior numbers, against the enemy [Col. 0473B], and defeated them with incredible success. But one Maximus was made emperor in Britain. When Gratian came into Gaul against him, Gratian was captured while fleeing at Lyons and killed. Advancing farther, Maximus expelled the Emperor Valentinian from Italy and made his own son Victor partner in the kingdom. Valentinian therefore fled eastward to Theodosius.

Meanwhile Theodosius, placing all his confidence in Christ’s aid, attacked and defeated without delay the Alans, Huns, and Goths; and he concluded a treaty with Athalaric, king of the Goths. Athalaric accordingly came to Constantinople; seeing the emperor’s and the city’s magnificence, he said: “Emperor, you are an earthly god.” When he died at Constantinople [Col. 0473C], Theodosius gave him a burial worthy of his rank. Therefore, considering Theodosius’s kindness, the Goths submitted themselves to the Roman Empire. The Parthians also, and the other barbarian peoples formerly hostile to the Romans, voluntarily sent envoys to Theodosius and concluded treaties with him. In these times Damasus was pope, and after Damasus, Pope Siricius.

### On Theodosius and Valentinian

In the year of the Lord 388, Theodosius and Valentinian reigned among the Romans for seven years, and afterward Theodosius alone for three years. When Theodosius had freed Thrace from the enemy, leaving at Constantinople his son Arcadius, whom he had made Augustus, he armed himself against Maximus. At Aquileia he captured and killed him, with greater faith but far [Col. 0473D] smaller military resources. He also killed Maximus’s son Victor. Coming to Rome, Theodosius restored Valentinian and returned to Constantinople. Valentinian, thus restored, held the empire of Italy. But when he crossed into Gaul, he was strangled at Vienne through the treachery of Count Arbogast and Eugenius, a most eloquent grammarian. Arbogast accordingly chose Eugenius as emperor in name, while he himself was emperor in fact.

Hearing this, Theodosius, supported by the prophecy of a certain monk John—indeed, by God’s help—made war upon Arbogast and Eugenius. When they set out from Milan, they had said that, if they returned victorious, they would turn the Church into a stable and place the clergy under arms. But though seemingly abandoned by his own men, Theodosius prevailed by the sign of the cross and prayer. [Col. 0474A] For a wind blew from Theodosius’s side, driving back the enemy’s missiles and fixing his own more firmly in their targets. Eugenius was therefore captured and killed. Arbogast killed himself; hence:

> O you too greatly beloved of God! For you the heavens make war;  
> And the winds, allied together, come at the trumpet-call.

When Theodosius thereafter ruled alone in peace, he utterly destroyed the temples of the pagans, enacted laws, prohibited wantonness at banquets, and forbade marriages to female cousins. How great his devotion was before the Lord and humankind is shown by the following example. When he wished to enter a church at Milan, Ambrose forbade him unless he made public penance, because he had caused many thousands of people to be killed at Thessalonica. He humbly endured the prohibition [Col. 0474B] and was not ashamed to make satisfaction. Again, when after the offering he remained within the sanctuary rail, Ambrose said: “Leave, for the purple makes emperors, not priests.” The emperor patiently obeyed.

His wife was Placidia, who cared for the poor: she visited hospices, wiped their pots with her own hands, tasted and served their broth, and did similar things that servants customarily perform. She used to say to her husband: “Consider what you were and what you are, and you will not be ungrateful to your Creator.” By her prayers she obtained that the emperor should not converse with Eunomius, for she feared that, through his cunning, he might fall into Eunomius’s error. By her Theodosius begot Arcadius and Honorius. After her death he married Galla, daughter of the elder Valentinian [Col. 0474C] and Justina; by her he begot Placidia, to whom her mother’s name was later added. Theodosius died at Milan, and his body was transported to Constantinople. He left both commonwealths peaceful to his sons Arcadius and Honorius. Theodosius reigned, partly with Valentinian and partly alone with his sons, for seventeen years.

### On Arcadius and Honorius

In the year of the Lord 398, Arcadius, who had already reigned twelve years with his father, reigned after his father’s death together with his brother Honorius for thirteen years: Arcadius in the East and Honorius in the West. Meanwhile Gildo, count of Africa, seized Africa. His brother Maselzer, horrified by his treachery, came to Italy. Gildo killed two sons. Maselzer, knowing through Theodosius [Col. 0474D] how powerful prayer is for Christ’s faith, continued for several days in fasting with holy persons. He saw by night the blessed Ambrose, who had died shortly before, indicating to him victory, its manner, its day, and its place. He therefore set out with five thousand men and, without battle, received eighty thousand enemies into surrender. Gildo, returning to Africa, perished by strangulation. Swollen with pride, Maselzer dared to violate God’s church: he dragged certain persons out of it, and was punished for that sacrilege.

Radagaisus, king of the Goths, suddenly flooded Italy with an army of two hundred thousand Goths. He at once attacked Rome. All cried out that they suffered these things because they had neglected the rites of the gods. Christ was blasphemed. But God did not permit his power to appear weaker than the strength of unbelievers. Radagaisus was captured [Col. 0475A], and such was the multitude of Goths on Mount Fiesole that they were sold, one by one, for single gold coins. Arcadius, however, died while returning from Rome, leaving his son Theodosius at Constantinople. In his time Anastasius was pope; after Anastasius, Pope Innocent. Anastasius wished secretly to restore the heretic Acacius and, struck by an angel, died.

### On Honorius with Theodosius, son of his brother Arcadius

In the year of the Lord 410, Honorius reigned among the Romans with Theodosius, son of his brother Arcadius, for fifteen years. Near the beginning of his reign Honorius prohibited gladiatorial combat among the Romans. The Goths armed themselves against him; under their leader Alaric, in the 1164th year from the founding of the city, they attacked Rome, burned part of it, and, on the sixth day [Col. 0475B] after their entry, departed after plundering the city. Behold, then, a second Babylon. For just as Babylon, 1,164 years after its foundation, was devastated by the Medes and by their king Arbaces, so Rome, after the same number of years from its foundation, was devastated by the Goths and their king Alaric. Alaric had first ordered that they should, as far as possible, refrain from bloodshed, and that anyone entering holy places, especially the basilicas of Saints Peter and Paul, should remain safe.

After Alaric’s death, the Goths appointed Athaulf king and returned to Rome, in order to gnaw away, like locusts, whatever remained. They took away Placidia from there, and Athaulf made her his wife. Meanwhile Stilicho, who had been Honorius’s guardian, stirred the Suebi, Alans, Vandals, and Burgundians to arms in order to install his own son [Col. 0475C] in the empire. When this became known, father and son were killed. Constantine also, a tyrant elected emperor in Britain, sent his son, named Constans, into Spain. Honorius sent the vigorous and warlike Count Constantius into Gaul against him; he killed Constantine at Arles. Constans his son was also put to death at Vienne. Moreover Athaulf, having become emperor of the Goths, was captured by Constantius. Through Constantius’s skill Honorius overcame these and many other tyrants.

Then Wallia became king of the Goths. He restored Placidia, honorably preserved, to her brother and made peace with him. Honorius gave her as wife to Constantius, and by him she bore Valentinian. Furthermore, he received Constantius [Col. 0475D] as partner in the empire; but after six months he died. After this Honorius sent an army into Britain to defend it against the Scots and Picts, and likewise into Spain to defend it against the Vandals and Alans. Placidia, a widow driven away by her brother Honorius, went eastward with her sons Honorius and Valentinian, and was honorably received by Theodosius, son of Arcadius. Honorius, having reigned two years with his father, thirteen with his brother, and fifteen with his nephew, died at Rome, leaving the city peaceful, and was buried near the martyrdom-place of the apostle Peter. No offspring survived him. Although he had successively married two daughters of Stilicho, by God’s judgment they died virgins.

After his death, one John seized the empire [Col. 0476A], supported by the aid of Casticus, master of the soldiers, and Aetius. In his time Zosimus sat as pope at Rome; Boniface succeeded him, and Pope Celestine succeeded Boniface.

### On Emperor Theodosius II

In the year of the Lord 426, Theodosius reigned among the Romans for twenty-five years. He was so wise that, in conversation, he seemed experienced in the causes of all things; so patient and merciful that he subjected none of those who injured him to death, saying: “Would that I could restore the dead to life!” Out of zeal for Christianity he fasted on the fourth and sixth days of the week. Trained in sacred letters, he practised philosophy through his deeds. His palace was like a monastery; he overcame anger, sadness, and lust as enemies. His wife Eudoxia was a most Christian and highly educated woman [Col. 0476B].

Theodosius made Valentinian, son of his aunt—that is, the Augusta Placidia—Caesar, and sent him with soldiers and his mother against John to recover the empire. On arriving, they overwhelmed John with remarkable success and received the kingdom as victors. Because the people of Ravenna had supported John, they plundered them. For them, as the Red Sea opened to Moses, so marshy and trackless ground became accessible and passable. They condemned Castinus to exile; Aetius was pardoned, because through his exertions the Huns returned to their own country. Thereupon Valentinian was made Augustus from Caesar.

Afterward Boniface became a rebel in Africa and admitted the Vandals and Alans to aid him; these ravaged Africa by plunder, sword, and flame [Col. 0476C]. But when peace was made, Boniface came to Italy, where he died of illness. Under that peace a portion of Africa was granted to the Vandals for settlement. There Genseric, their king, wishing to overthrow the Catholic faith through Arian impiety, expelled certain bishops from his cities and installed adherents of his own heresy; those unwilling to comply he afflicted with various punishments and killed. Later, under the deceit of peace, he captured Carthage and converted places of divine worship into private dwellings. Carthage was captured by the Vandals in the year of the Lord 585, after it had begun to obey Roman rule. Likewise Genseric grievously afflicted Sicily.

The emperor Theodosius sent an army with a great fleet against the Vandals; but they were more a burden than a protection to Sicily. When Genseric returned to Carthage and the Huns were ravaging Illyricum and Thrace [Col. 0476D], Theodosius’s army returned to defend the eastern provinces. Later peace was established between Valentinian and Genseric, and Africa was divided between them by fixed boundaries. Meanwhile Aetius was made patrician. In war he crushed Gundicarius, king of the Burgundians. Meanwhile the Goths also harassed the people of Narbonne; war was waged against them with the Huns as allies, and peace was made with them on terms humbler than they had demanded before the battle.

While Vandals and Goths raged thus, Theodosius went from Constantinople to Valentinian and took his daughter, named Eudoxia, as his wife. Again Britain was oppressed by the incursions of Scots and Picts. Pirates seized part of the island; the Angles promised them alliance, but from helpers [Col. 0477A] they became assailants. Pirates also ravaged Sicily. At length Theodosius died and was buried at Constantinople. He is said to have had a courier named Palladius, who traversed the boundaries of the Roman Empire; therefore someone said of him: “This man, though the Roman commonwealth is broad, makes it seem small by his speed.” At the same time the aforesaid Celestine sat at Rome; Pope Sixtus succeeded him, and Pope Leo succeeded Sixtus.

### On Emperor Martian

In the year of the Lord 452, Martian reigned among the Romans for seven years, while Valentinian was still reigning in the West. Martian was a man of great seriousness, necessary not only to the commonwealth but also to the Church. A very severe war arose against him and Valentinian. For Attila, king of the Huns, who had killed his brother Blenda, his partner in the kingdom, compelled Thrace and Macedonia, the Pannonias and Dacia, the Turks and Rugians, and other nations dwelling on the northern frontiers, together with their petty kings, to obey him. He also aspired to overthrow the Western Empire. Supported by no less shrewdness than strength of arms, he sought the friendship of the Goths against the Romans and of the Romans against the Goths, so that, if he divided them, he might more easily subdue both.

Foreseeing Attila’s stratagems, Aetius made treaties with Theodoric, king of the Goths. Aetius therefore met Attila; Aetius was aided by Gundicarius, king of the Burgundians, Theodoric king of the Goths, Franks [Col. 0477C], Saxons, Alans, and many others. The two sides assembled in the Catalaunian fields; they fought, and 280,000 men were killed. There the king of the Goths fell. The battle was grievous to both sides. Neither army yielded, yet Attila was defeated. Thorismund, son of Theodoric, grieving at his father’s death, resolved to press Attila with a siege until his utter destruction. But Aetius, fearing that, if Attila were killed, the Romans might be overwhelmed by the Goths, persuaded Thorismund to return home and assume the kingdom. After he returned, Attila restored his strength, gathered a larger army, and furiously entered Italy through Pannonia. He attacked Aquileia and besieged it for three years. Finally, when storks flew from the city in a single flight and carried their young outside in their beaks [Col. 0477D], Attila, encouraged by this omen, stormed and took the city.

### On Emperor Leo

In the year of the Lord 459, Leo the Great reigned at Constantinople for fifteen years. At Rome, meanwhile, a certain Avitus was made emperor. On his death Majorian seized the empire at Ravenna; after Majorian was killed near Tarragona, a certain Severus was chosen at Ravenna. In his time Sogor, king of the Alans, came into Italy, but was defeated by Ricimer, governor of Liguria, and killed near Pergamum. Anthemius succeeded Severus; in his time Genseric, returning to Italy, was defeated in a naval battle. Servandus, prefect of Gaul, and the patrician Romanus, aspiring to the empire, were captured.

Ricimer, who was residing at Milan [Col. 0478A], plotted against Anthemius. Although Epiphanius, bishop of Pavia, eminent for holiness, had arranged peace, Ricimer broke the treaty and attacked the city. Rome was divided: one party followed him, the other this man. Bilimer, governor of Gaul, came to help Anthemius, but was defeated and killed by Ricimer. Ricimer himself died after the third month, tormented by illness. A certain Olybrius also attained royal dignity for seven months and died.

### On Emperor Zeno

In the year of the Lord 464, Zeno reigned at Constantinople for eighteen years. The mother of the boy Leo, fearing Zeno’s attack, secretly made the boy a cleric; he remained in clerical office until the time of Justinian. When Zeno demanded the boy, his mother presented another [Col. 0478B] who resembled him. At Rome, a certain Augustulus, coming into Italy, drove out the patrician Nepos, who had seized the kingdom, and seized and held the empire.

Soon Odoacer hastened into Italy with a multitude of Heruli and Thuringians from the furthest borders of Pannonia. Passing through the lands of Noricum, he heard the fame of Severinus, servant of God, and approached him to seek a blessing. When Severinus had blessed him, he said: “Go now to Italy, Odoacer, clothed in very poor skins; you will soon bestow much upon many.” When Odoacer entered Italy, the patrician Orestes met him but withdrew into Pavia. Odoacer, however, entered the city after storming it fiercely; the sword raged, fire consumed everything, Orestes was captured, and was beheaded at Piacenza. Thereupon Odoacer [Col. 0478C] levelled many cities to the ground, subjected all Italy, and seized royal dignity: Severinus’s prophecy was fulfilled.

Augustulus, seeing all Italy subjected to Odoacer’s strength, laid aside imperial majesty after scarcely holding the commonwealth for eleven months. Thus the venerable Roman Empire and that Augustan majesty which had begun at Rome with Augustus—that is, Octavian—perished with this Augustulus. In the year 475 from the Lord’s Incarnation, Odoacer entered Rome and peacefully possessed the kingdom of Italy for fourteen years. But afterward Theodoric, son of King Theodemir and himself king of the Ostrogoths, enjoyed such favor with Emperor Zeno that Zeno had raised him to the consular fasces at Constantinople and erected for him a bronze equestrian statue before the palace. When the Ostrogoths complained that imperial pay did not suffice for them, Theodoric approached the emperor, laid before him his people’s want, and requested Italy. The emperor agreed, granted him Italy, and commended the Roman people to him.

Setting out, Theodoric first overthrew the king of the Gepids and the king of the Bulgars. At length he made camp beside the Sontius River, near Aquileia; there Odoacer met him and was put to flight. Then, as Theodoric approached Verona, Odoacer met him at Verona. His army was routed, and a large part was drowned in the Adige. Theodoric seized Verona. Odoacer returned to Rome, but, finding himself excluded because its gates had been barred, returned to Ravenna and fortified it with defensive works [Col. 0479A]. Theodoric passed through and came to Milan, where a multitude of soldiers joined him. But Odoacer’s army grew, and so Theodoric fortified himself at Pavia.

Meanwhile Gundobad, king of the Burgundians, entered Liguria, plundered much, and carried off captives. Theodoric came to Ravenna and besieged it for nearly three years. At last he killed Odoacer, whom he had received under a pledge of faith. After the most blessed Epiphanius he sent an envoy to Gundobad for the ransom of captives; apart from those for whom he paid a price, six thousand captives were granted to him. Theodoric then went to Rome and was received by the Romans with great joy. Every year he granted them 120,000 modii of wheat for support. Thus, in the third year after his entrance into Italy, he obtained dominion over all Italy—except that, when the Goths entered Pavia, the Rugians immediately attacked the city and ravaged it for two years.

This Theodoric, though unlettered, was nevertheless very wise. He used to say: “He who has gold and a demon cannot conceal them.” To a certain bride who, from fear of her bridegroom, denied her own son, he said: “You shall have no husband except this man whom you deny is your son.” On hearing this, she immediately confessed that he was her son. And behold another Solomon. He built palaces at Verona, Ravenna, and Pavia. In his time there was the greatest prosperity, great peace, and abundance. To strengthen the power of his kingdom, he took as wife the daughter of Clovis, king of the Franks. He gave his sisters [Col. 0479C] and nieces in marriage: one to the king of the Vandals, another to the king of the Thuringians, another to the king of the Visigoths, and others to other men, so that no nation was left which was not joined to Theodoric either by a treaty-bond or by kinship.

While these things were happening in Italy, Saxons and Britons fought one another in Britain; now these, now those gained the victory. But at last the stronger Saxons obtained possession of the whole island in its length. In Africa Huneric, an Arian, succeeded Genseric. He captured more than three hundred Catholic bishops; from many he cut off hands and tongues, yet he did not take away their speech in confession of the Catholic faith. He closed churches; but at Emperor Zeno’s entreaty they were reopened, and the bishops were restored. In the East, Thrace was devastated by the Bulgars. Constantinople [Col. 0479D] was burned. In his time Pope Simplicius sat; Pope Felix succeeded him, and Pope Gelasius succeeded Felix.

### On Emperor Anastasius

In the year of the Lord 492, Anastasius reigned at Constantinople for twenty-six years. He favored the Eutychian heresy, saying that in Christ there were two natures, of divinity and humanity. In his time Pope Anastasius sat at Rome. Many clerics withdrew from communion with him because he had communicated with Photinus, who had communicated with Acacius. After him two popes were elected, Symmachus and Laurentius. Therefore, after many murders had occurred, Symmachus prevailed and established that on feast days “Glory to God in the highest,” etc., should be sung; he also instituted dwellings for the poor.

### On the Elder Emperor Justin

[Col. 0480A]

In the year of the Lord 519, Justin the Elder reigned at Constantinople for nine years. Pope Hormisdas also sent to him Germanus, bishop of Capua, a man eminent in holiness, for the restoration of the faith. He was received with due honor and strengthened the faith. At this time the Catholic Church was restored in Africa. For after the death of the Arian Thrasamund, Hilderic succeeded him, his son, born from a captive daughter of Prince Valentinian. When dying, his father wished to bind him by an oath not to favor the Catholic Church; but before he assumed the rights of kingship, he restored all the bishops who had been sent into exile and re-established the Catholic Church in Africa, which had been deprived for seventy-four years.

Justin likewise began to rage in the East, so that the name of heretics might be extinguished. When King Theodoric, still living in Italy and polluted by the Arian stain, heard this, he sent Pope John, successor to Hormisdas, to Justin, declaring that unless he restored their churches to the heretics, he would kill all the peoples of Italy. As John entered Constantinople, crowds met him; before the people he gave sight to a blind man who begged him. Concerned for his own safety and that of his people, he entreated Justin with great tears to accept the substance of his embassy, unjust though it was, so as to provide for Italy, which was about to perish. The emperor consented.

### On Emperor Justinian

In the year of the Lord 527, Justinian reigned at Constantinople [Col. 0480C] for thirty-eight years. Justinian was the fifty-first emperor to assume power after Augustus, while the sons of Clovis were still reigning in Francia. This most Christian ruler most prudently revived an empire that was as if already dead; he restored the commonwealth. Through the patrician Belisarius he triumphed magnificently over the Persians. He brought together and corrected the earlier laws, which had been too diffusely spread out. All the constitutions of emperors, contained in many volumes, he compressed into twelve books and ordered that volume to be called the Code of Justinian. He reduced to fifty books the laws governing the courses of the individual magistracies and judicial proceedings, which had extended to nearly two thousand books, and named that code the Digest, or Pandects [Col. 0480D]. He also newly set forth four books of Institutes, in which the substance of all laws is briefly contained. He further decreed that the new laws which he had himself enacted, reduced into one volume, should be called the Novellae.

For through Belisarius he destroyed the people of the Vandals utterly, after capturing their king Gelimer, and restored all Africa to the Roman Empire after ninety-six years. Again, by Belisarius’s strength he overcame the Gothic people in Italy, capturing their king Witiges. Thereafter, through John the former consul, he crushed with remarkable power the Moors who were ravaging Africa and their king Antalas. In like manner he subdued other peoples by the law of war. Consequently, for all these victories he deserved to bear the additional names Alamannic, Gothic, Frankish, Germanic, Alanian, Vandalic, and African [Col. 0481A].

The same emperor built within Constantinople the church of Holy Sophia—that is, of divine Wisdom, which is Christ, the Son of God. Besides this, he constructed countless other benefactions for churches, remarkable in workmanship and ornament. He converted and baptized the king of the Heruli, named Craten. Then also the king of the Huns, named Garda, together with a certain widowed woman of the Hunnic nobility and others of that people, one hundred thousand in all, received the grace of baptism. King Athalaric, together with his mother Eudoxia, was received into the protection of Emperor Justinian. Not long afterward Athalaric was killed by his own people; his mother accepted Theodatus into the kingdom, but he later, ungrateful and treacherous, strangled her in the bath.

Justinian, having expelled the Vandals from Africa, reconstituted Africa as a Roman province. Theodatus, betrayer and strangler of his wife, fearing Justinian’s punishments, sent Pope Agapetus to the emperor to seek pardon and peace. Having obtained these, he had himself recalled to the Catholic faith by that pontiff. There the pontiff himself died; while his bier was being carried through the gate of the imperial city, a certain blind man was given sight by touching the bier. After this the patrician Belisarius killed Theodatus for the crime committed against his wife; he captured Witiges, who had seized the kingdom after Theodatus, and sent him to the emperor. Thus he ended the whole Gothic kingdom, which Jordanes, their author, records as having endured for more than two thousand years. Through him, under Justinian, with the Vandals uprooted from Africa and the Goths from Italy, both provinces were restored to their former Roman subjection [Col. 0481C].

Up to this point Jordanes, a bishop of Gothic nation, as he himself attests in his Chronicle, carried forward the histories of the Goths. The patrician Belisarius made war upon Theudebert, son of Clovis and brother of Lothar, who had invaded Italy with two hundred thousand men, and granted peace at the Franks’ request. Meanwhile the Parthians invaded and plundered all Syria and the city of Antioch. Belisarius, patrician and conqueror of Vandals and Goths, met them, defeated them, and drove them back from the Roman frontiers [Col. 0481D].

In these days the Goths, in revolt under their king Totila, moved into Italy. In the same period the Lombard people, who dwelt in Pannonia under their king Alboin and came from the island of Scantia—called Scandinavia by others, from which the first Goths also had emerged—soon afterward occupied Italy. While remaining in Italy, the patrician Belisarius unwillingly sent Pope Silverius into exile at the command of the Empress Theodora. He did likewise to Vigilius, Silverius’s successor. In these times also Saint Agapetus was pope; after him Pope Silverius; after Silverius Pope Vigilius; Pelagius succeeded him, and after him Pope John.

### On the Kings of the Lombards and the Deeds They Performed, and Their Times

[Col. 0482A]

The first king of the Lombards was called Agelmund, son of Agio. He reigned and governed the Lombards for thirty-three years, and adopted as his son the man who afterward became the second king of the Lombards.

The second king of the Lombards after Agelmund was Lamissio, and he reigned forty years.

The third king, Gildeoth son of Letech, reigned twenty-four years.

The fourth king, Gildeothot, king of the Lombards, reigned and ruled for twenty-one years.

The fifth king was Gedeus. In his time they dwelt in Rugiland, the province of the Rugians, in the days of Odoacer, of whom we have spoken above [Col. 0482B]; they had come there wearied by many wars and hardships.

The sixth king, Claffo son of Gedeon, reigned twenty-eight years.

The seventh king, Walterus, reigned seven years.

The eighth king, Vacco, was duke over some of the Lombard nation; receiving a son by his daughter, he named him Walterius.

The ninth king was Andolin, who led the Lombards into Pannonia and was the father of Alboin. He had Rodelinda as wife; she bore him Alboin, a man fitted for warfare and valiant in every respect. Andolin died after reigning twenty-one years. Then Alboin, now the tenth, succeeded to the kingdom to govern the homeland, with the assent of all [Col. 0482C].

Alboin, the tenth king of the Lombards, entrusted their own seats—that is, Pannonia—to his Hunnic allies, on this condition: should it ever be necessary for the Lombards to return, they would again reclaim their own fields. Thus the Lombards, leaving Pannonia with wives, children, and all their household goods, hastened to take possession of Italy. They had lived in Pannonia for forty-two years. They left it in April, in the first indiction, on the day after holy Easter; that feast, according to the calculation of that year, fell on the Kalends of April. By then 568 years had elapsed from the Lord’s Incarnation.

Cleph, the eleventh king, a most noble man, whom they established and made king of the province of Liguria [Col. 0482D], reigned two years and six months. After that king’s death they were under judges for ten years. Then they chose another king.

### On the Younger Emperor Justin, Nephew of Justinian

In the year of the Lord 567, Justin the Younger reigned at Constantinople for twelve years. He was Justinian’s nephew, a man given over to every kind of avarice, a despiser of the poor and a despoiler of senators. Such was his greed and frenzy that he ordered iron chests made, in which to heap up the talents of gold that he seized. They also report that he fell into the Pelagian heresy. Since he turned the ear of his heart away from the divine commandments, by God’s just judgment he lost the understanding of reason and became insane. He appointed Tiberius Caesar [Col. 0483A] to govern his palace and the individual provinces.

### On Emperor Tiberius

In the year of the Lord 578, Tiberius Constantine reigned among the Romans for eight years. The Augusta Sophia laid snares for him, wishing to exalt her own son Justinian, but her hope was frustrated. He fought and defeated the Persians, and brought back much booty together with twenty elephants. Finally he chose the vigorous man Maurice, along with Sophia’s son, for the empire; he gave Maurice his daughter, saying: “Let the empire be granted to you with this girl. Use it happily, always remembering to delight in equity and justice.” This Tiberius was a just, useful, and vigorous man: generous in almsgiving, fair in judgments, renowned in victories, and, surpassing all these qualities, a most true Christian. At the same time Benedict the First was pope, and Pope Pelagius the Second succeeded him.

### On Emperor Maurice

In the year of the Lord 585, Maurice the Cappadocian, the first of Greek stock, was confirmed in the empire; he reigned twenty years. He sent fifty thousand solidi to King Oldebert of the Franks, that he might attack the Lombards and drive them from Italy.

The Lombards elected Authari, son of Delphon, as king. He was the twelfth king of the Lombards, reigned seven years, and destroyed the city of Brescello, situated on the bank of the Po, now called Bersellus.

Agilulf was the thirteenth king of the Lombards. As Authari had assumed royal dignity, so he likewise took Authari’s wife Theodelinda in marriage. At her entreaty the king adhered to the Catholic faith and enlarged the Church’s possessions. Pope Gregory the First wrote many letters to this queen [Col. 0483C].

### On Emperor Phocas

In the year of the Lord 606, Phocas seized the kingdom at Constantinople and reigned eight years. In his second year, blessed Gregory, having sat for thirteen years, six months, and ten days, departed to Christ. At the same time the Blues and Greens raised wars throughout the East and Egypt. Agilulf made an annual peace with Phocas. The Persians took Jerusalem and many provinces from the Romans [Col. 0483D], profaned holy things, and carried away even the standard of the Lord’s cross. Heraclian, then governing Africa, made war upon Phocas, deprived him of kingdom and life, and handed the kingdom to his son Heraclius.

At the same time blessed Gregory the First sat as pope at Rome; Pope Sabinian the First succeeded him; then Pope Boniface the Third; then Pope Boniface the Fourth. Boniface the Fourth obtained from Emperor Phocas the temple called the Pantheon, which the emperor gave and granted to him. There the said pope made a church in honor of Blessed Mary and All Saints on the Kalends of November. In the time of the aforesaid Pope Boniface was Muhammad.

### On Heraclius, Son of Heraclian

[Col. 0484A]

In the year of the Lord 614, Heraclius, son of Heraclianus, reigned at Constantinople for thirty-two years; others say forty-eight. He was a most Christian man, who brought back the Lord’s Cross to Jerusalem. He had two sons, Heracleonas and Constantine. Agilulf made peace with Heraclius and with the Franks. But the Avars captured Forum Julii through the treachery of Romilda, wife of Gisulf, duke of Forum Julii, whom the king of the Avars had promised to take in marriage. Yet, after the Lombards had been slain and captured, the king possessed her in marriage for one night; on the next night he handed her over to twelve Avars, who in succession satisfied their lust upon her. Finally he ordered her bound to a stake, saying: “Such a husband [Col. 0484B] is fitting for you to have as a husband, you who chose rather to provide for lust than for the safety of your citizens and kinsfolk.” The two daughters of this duchess, lest they should be violated by the Avars, bound pieces of raw chicken flesh to their breasts with bandages so that, when putrefied, they might stink. Therefore, when the Avars touched them, supposing them to stink naturally, they said that all Lombard women were foul-smelling. Afterwards one of them married the king of the Alamanni, the other the prince of the Bavarians. Moreover, when Agilulf had reigned twenty-five years, he closed his final day; his son was King Adaloald.

Adaloald, son of Agilulf, the fourteenth king of the Lombards, succeeded together with his mother Theodelinda, and then the churches were restored. When [Col. 0484C] Adaloald had reigned ten years and became mentally deranged, he was expelled by the Lombards.

Arioald was appointed the fifteenth king of the Lombards and reigned twelve years.

Rothari, the sixteenth king of the Lombards, was strong and just, but Arian. At that time nearly every Lombard city had two bishops, one Catholic and the other Arian. In the city of Ticinum, at the basilica of St Eusebius, Anastasius, an Arian bishop, held office; but later he was converted to the Catholic faith, and there was then another Catholic bishop. Rothari compiled the code of laws called the Lombard laws, in the sixty-seventh year from the Lombards’ entry into Italy. He subjugated much territory; and, having reigned sixteen years, he left the kingdom of the Lombards [Col. 0484D] to his son Rodoald.

Rodoald, the seventeenth king of the Lombards, reigned five years. His wife Godiperga built the church of St John at Ticinum. Meanwhile Simsebinus, prince of the Goths, subjected many cities in Spain to himself and converted the Jews of his kingdom to the faith. Heraclius was succeeded by his son Heracleonas, who reigned two years, then by his brother Constantine, who reigned six months. He was succeeded by his son of the same name, also called Constans. In these times Deusdedit was pope at Rome; Boniface V succeeded him. After him came Honorius I; after him Severinus; after him John IV; and after him Theodore I.

## Concerning Constantine, also called Constans

[Col. 0485A]

In the year of the Lord 649, Constantine, also called Constans, reigned at Constantinople for twenty-eight years; he was a heretic. In his time Pope Martin I was pope. While he was celebrating the solemnities of Mass, a certain spatharius attempted to kill him; but, struck with blindness, he could not see him. At last Constantine sent him into exile, where he departed to the Lord and shone with miracles. He was succeeded by Pope Eugenius I, highly learned in knowledge of the canons. After him came Vitalian, who composed the chant which the Romans use today. In the time of this Constantine, the queen of the Persians, named Caesara, came to Constantinople in private dress and received the baptism she desired; the Augusta raised her [Col. 0485B] from the font. Hearing this, the king of the Persians sent envoys to the Augustus for his wife. The envoys asked for the queen. The emperor declared that he did not know the queen, but showed them a woman newly baptized. Recognizing her, the envoys venerated her and begged her to return. She replied: “Tell your king that unless he believes in Christ, he will no longer be able to have me as his consort.” Why say more? The king came to Constantinople with sixty thousand men and was baptized with them all, being raised from the font by the Augustus. He was sent back with his wife, honored.

Aripert, the eighteenth king of the Lombards, succeeded Rodoald and founded the chapel of the Holy Savior at Ticinum. Having reigned [Col. 0485C] nine years, he left the kingdom to his two sons, Bertarith and Gondipert. Gondipert held Ticinum; Bertarith resided at Milan. But Grimoald, duke of Benevento, treacherously killed Gondipert. When he heard this, Bertarith of Milan fled and remained in exile.

Grimoald, the nineteenth king of the Lombards, reigned; he inflicted a great slaughter on the Franks as they entered Italy near the city of Asti. Therefore Constantine, seeking to wrest Italy from Lombard hands, came to Athens, crossed the sea, and landed at Tarentum. He consulted a certain hermit whether he could courageously overcome the Lombard people. The hermit answered that the Lombard people could not then be overcome, because St John the Baptist continually interceded for them, since the queen had built [Col. 0485D] his basilica in Monza. Advancing from there, he destroyed the city of Nuceria. He was indeed unable to capture the city of Ageruntia. He besieged Benevento, where Romoald, son of King Grimoald, held the duchy. Romoald therefore sent word to his father Grimoald and requested help. The king hastened there. The emperor withdrew to Naples and, after waging war there to his own loss, went to Rome. Pope Vitalian met him devoutly with clergy and people. The emperor offered St Peter a pallium woven with gold; and, after he had stayed at Rome for twelve days, he stripped away the ornaments of the city and churches, including those of St Mary, where the Pantheon had been, and its bronze roofs, and despoiled the city of gold. He returned to Sicily and remained there for five years; and he imposed upon Calabria, Sicily, [Col. 0486A] Africa, and Sardinia such afflictions that no one’s hope of life remained. But he was killed in a bath at Syracuse.

## Concerning Constantine, son of the Augustus Constantine or Constans

In the year of the Lord 677, Constantine, son of the Augustus Constantine or Constans, reigned at Constantinople for seventeen years. In his time Archbishop Theodore and Abbot Adrian were sent by Pope Vitalian for the instruction of the churches. This Theodore, as some say, compiled a penitential book. Vitalian was succeeded by Pope Adeodatus; after him came Pope Donus, who wonderfully laid out the *paradisus*—the forecourt—before the basilica of Blessed Peter in white marble. Pope Agatho succeeded Donus, and [Col. 0486B] went to Constantinople to establish peace between the emperor and the Lombards. When, at the gate of the city, he gave the kiss to a certain leper, the latter was immediately healed. Among the Lombards likewise, Grimoald, having reigned nine years, died and was buried in the basilica of St Ambrose which he built at Ticinum.

Bertarith, the twentieth king of the Lombards, then an exile, was divinely admonished to return to Italy. On his return he was raised to the kingship. His wife Rodelinda built the basilica of St Mary ad Perticas. He himself built the church of St Agatha and the Palatine Gate at Ticinum, and deposited the bodies of the martyrs Primus and Felicianus. Having reigned fifteen years, he left the kingdom to his son Cunipert, [Col. 0486C] whom Alahis, duke of Trent, faithlessly deprived of the kingdom and palace at Ticinum, aided by Aldo and Agraso, citizens of Brescia. This Alahis hated clerics. When a certain Deacon Thomas came to him, he said: “Let him come, if he has clean breeches.” The deacon replied to him: “Tell him that God can find fault in my affairs; he cannot.” But by God’s grace he sent help to the king. The king won victory over Alahis and his army. Hearing his wife praise the beauty of a girl named Theodote, Cunipert had relations with her and placed her in the monastery at Ticinum which bears her name. Pretending to spend the night before the venerable body of St Benedict [Col. 0486D] in the fortress of Cassino, the Franks stole the bones of St Benedict and St Scholastica and carried them to their own country. Agatho was succeeded by Pope Leo II; after him came Pope Benedict II; after him Pope John V, who composed the book *On the Dignity of the Pallium* in the time of the below-mentioned Justinian the Younger, son of Constantine.

## Concerning Justinian the Younger, son of Constantine

In the year of the Lord 697, Justinian, son of Constantine, reigned at Constantinople for ten years. He recovered Africa from the Saracens and made peace with them by land and sea. Likewise, the province of Africa was restored under Roman rule. In his time the aforesaid Pope John was pope; Pope Sergius [Col. 0487A] succeeded him. Emperor Constantine ordered Sergius carried away by sending his spatharius Zacharias, because he refused to subscribe to the synod which he had held at Constantinople. But the troops of Ravenna and the neighboring regions disgracefully drove Zacharias away. Leo deprived this Justinian of his kingdom and placed him in exile in Pontus. Leo reigned with Tiberius for seven years. In these days a synod was held at Aquileia. After recovering the empire, Justinian killed Leo and Tiberius; and whenever he wiped mucus from his nose, he ordered one of Leo’s supporters to be beheaded. He sent to Rome the patriarch of Constantinople, Gallicinus, who had opposed him, after plucking out his eyes; and he made Cyrus, the abbot who had supported him in Pontus, patriarch.

Cunipert, the twenty-first king of the Lombards, [Col. 0487B] after reigning twelve years, left the kingdom to his son Liutpert and appointed Asprand as his guardian. But Aripert killed the boy, drove out the guardian, seized the kingdom, and captured Lodi and Bergamo. This Aripert, going about here and there, investigated in private dress what was said of him and what sort of justice the judges administered. This Aripert gave, or restored, the Cottian Alps to the Roman Church. But Gisulf, duke of Benevento, invaded Campania. In these times Benedict, archbishop of Milan, pleaded at Rome on behalf of the church of Ticinum, but was defeated. Pope Sisinnius succeeded John, and Constantine succeeded Sisinnius. Emperor Justinian had this Pope Constantine come to him at Constantinople and, prostrate at his feet in the city square, obtained pardon; [Col. 0487C] he received and dismissed him honorably, and renewed the privileges. In Constantine’s time two kings of the Saxons came to Rome for prayer, and both died. At last Justinian’s army, sent into Pontus against Philippicus, made him emperor. Coming to Constantinople, he killed Justinian. In his time there was a great famine in the city of Rome for three years; after these there was such abundance that the unwanted plenty was consigned to oblivion.

## Concerning Emperor Philippicus

In the year of the Lord 717, Philippicus reigned at Constantinople for one year and six months. He returned Cyrus to his monastery and sent Pope Constantine letters containing a corrupt doctrine. [Col. 0487D] The pope rejected them and, for this reason, had the acts of the six synods painted in the portico of St Peter. The Roman people also decreed that no document, image, or name of the heretical emperor should be received, and that no special prayer for him should be offered during the solemnities of Mass. Anastasius, called Anthemius, deprived this Philippicus of his eyes and kingdom.

## Concerning Emperor Anastasius

In the year of the Lord 718, Anastasius reigned at Constantinople for three years. He sent Pope Constantine letters in which he declared himself a supporter of the Catholic faith. He sent a fleet against the Saracens to Alexandria; but, on its return, the army chose Theodosius [Col. 0488A] emperor and confirmed him in the position by compulsion.

Aripert, the twenty-second king of the Lombards, after reigning twelve years, fled before his enemies and drowned in the river Ticino. Asprand, the twenty-third king of the Lombards, reigned three months; his son Liutprand succeeded him. In these times St Leonard the monk flourished.

## Concerning Emperor Theodosius

In the year of the Lord 721, Theodosius reigned at Constantinople for five years. He made Anastasius an ordinary priest. In these times the Germans were converted to Christ through Bishop Boniface.

## Concerning Emperor Leo

[Col. 0488B]

In the year of the Lord 722, Leo reigned at Constantinople for twenty-five years. At Constantinople he burned images of the saints and ordered Gregory III to do the same at Rome. But the pontiff disregarded this and excommunicated the emperor. The armies of Ravenna and Venice would unanimously have chosen another emperor, had the pontiff not opposed it. The Augustus advanced to worse deeds, for he caused images of the Savior and his Mother to be burned; and because many people at Constantinople resisted, some were beheaded and others mutilated in other ways. Then St Theodosia suffered martyrdom. The patriarch, not consenting to the crime, was expelled from his own see. In these times also the Saracens besieged Constantinople continuously for three years, but were overwhelmed [Col. 0488C] by famine and pestilence; on their return, their ships were shattered by a sudden storm and they perished. Within Constantinople three hundred thousand died of pestilence.

Liutprand, the twenty-third king of the Lombards, was of such courage that, when some had sworn to kill him, he entered a wood with them and, drawing his sword, said: “Do what you are plotting.” And he was of such mercy that, once they had confessed everything, he at once forgave them. When Liutprand held the kingdom of the Lombards and rode through the district of Milan, men of those regions came before him and complained that they had no standard measure and that one deceived another in measuring. He placed his foot upon a great, broad stone [Col. 0488D] and wished a mark to be made in it according to the size of his foot, by which they were to buy and sell. But by God’s power the imprint of his foot was carved and marked in that very stone, and remains visible there to the present day; it is called Liutprand’s Foot, and to its measure they buy and sell even to this day. He was of such power that he subjugated Bologna, Osimo, Sutri, Spoleto, and many other places. He besieged Ravenna and destroyed its fleet. He also fought many battles against the Romans. When he was besieging Rome, Gregory III sent Charles Martel the keys of the confession of St Peter, asking him to free the city and defend the Church from the Lombards. Yet he was of such devotion that he confirmed the Cottian Alps to the Roman Church. [Col. 0489A] After the Saracens had ravaged Sardinia, he transferred the bones of St Augustine to Ticinum and placed them in the church of St Peter in Golden Heaven, which he himself built. He also built the church of Berceto on Mount Bardone; the church of St Anastasius at Olonna; and, in his palace, the church of the Holy Savior, where he established clerics—and similarly in every place in which he wished to reside. He was of such wisdom that he trusted more in prayers than in arms. He was a lover of peace, preserving peace with the Franks and Avars; chaste and generous, though ignorant of letters. Having reigned thirty-one years and six months, he died.

Hildeprand, the twenty-fourth king of the Lombards, succeeded King Liutprand. Hildeprand reigned [Col. 0489B] six months.

Ratchis, the twenty-fifth king of the Lombards, reigned four years and nine months. In these times Zacharias succeeded Gregory in the apostolic see, skilled in Greek and Latin. He made peace with the Lombards and forbade the marriage of the children of godfathers and godmothers. Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, who made the church of Werden; the Venerable Bede, priest, who wrote much; and Peter, bishop of Ticinum, flourished. In the first year of Leo, Charles Martel died, who among the Franks had been mayor in the royal household. Let us review the kingdom of the Franks from times long past.

After the destruction of Troy, many thousands of Trojans under Priam and Antenor came to Ravenna and built Padua, where Antenor was buried. Later they founded the city of Sicambria in the Scythian region. Then they occupied Germany and were called Germans. But because, in the time of Emperor Valentinian, they defeated the Alans at his command, he called them Franks—that is, “the fierce.” Afterwards they crossed into Thuringia under the princes Marcomer and Sunno. When Sunno died, they made Faramund, son of Marcomer, king, and began to have laws through a certain wise man named Salagustus, from whom the Salic Law, used by the Franks, received its name. From this point Rome declined and Francia increased. For, having crossed the Rhine, they began to drive out the Romans [Col. 0489D] who lived there; and they captured Agrippina, now called Cologne from their new settlement, and Tournai, Cambrai, Reims, Trier, Soissons, Orléans; and they claimed almost all Gaul and Germany from Aquitaine as far as Bagucia. Among the kings of the Franks were Merovech, after whom the later kings were called Mirovei (Merovingians); and Clovis, who took as wife the Christian Clotilda, daughter of the king of the Burgundians. At her prayers and exhortations, he was baptized by St Remigius, while an angel from heaven ministered the oil with which the kings of the Franks are still anointed. This Clovis vowed that he would give his horse to Blessed Martin if he triumphed over the Goths. He triumphed and fulfilled his vow; but, wishing to redeem it, he sent one hundred solidi. Yet [Col. 0490A] the horse stood immovable. He therefore sent another hundred solidi, and then the horse followed; whence Clovis said: “St Martin is a good helper, but an expensive dealer.” The sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons of this Clovis afterwards reigned: namely, Lothair his son, and Lothair’s sons, who divided the kingdom. Aribert held Paris, Guntram Orléans, Hilperic Sens, and Sigebert Metz. But the kings of the Franks came to such weakness that, although they remained kings only in name, the mayor of the royal household governed the kingdom: such as the venerable Arnulf, bishop of Metz, distinguished for holiness of life; then his son Anchises, named after Anchises the Trojan; after whom came Pippin the Fat; and after him Charles Martel, son of Pippin the Fat by his concubine, Duchess Alpaida. He conquered Bavaria, Swabia, Gascony, Saxony, and Frisia; killed 385,000 Saracens in Spain; and, fighting at Narbonne, struck them down in a vast slaughter. After the Saracens captured Arles, he sent envoys with gifts to King Liutprand of the Lombards and requested help against the Saracens. As Liutprand hastened to his aid, the Saracens fled. He also subdued the province in which Paris is situated, which was then called Gaudiana. He named it Francia in Latin, Karlingia in German. The land called Franconia was named, as some assert, after a certain Duke Francon. With the consent of Pope Zacharias, he was the first to grant tithes in fief to soldiers [Col. 0490C] for the needs of the churches. Therefore, having administered the kingdom of the Franks so successfully for twenty-seven years, as we have said, he died in Leo’s first year, leaving three sons: Carloman, Pippin the Short, and Grifo, who divided the administration of the kingdom. But the wicked Grifo was expelled by his brothers and remained in a certain castle in Auvergne. Carloman had Germany; Pippin, Francia. But after four years Carloman, through Pope Zacharias, became a monk on Mount Soracte; later he went to Monte Cassino, where he sometimes even tended pigs. Thus Pippin the Short alone became administrator of the kingdom, while Childeric remained king only in name. But since [Col. 0490D] the king was sluggish and useless, by the authority of Pope Zacharias Pippin was chosen as king by Boniface of Mainz and the other princes. Childeric was made a monk at Monte Cassino; by the authority of Pope Stephen, Zacharias’s successor, Pippin, together with all the princes, was released from allegiance to Childeric and anointed king. There the kingdom of the Merovingians ended and the kingdom of the Carolingians began.

## Concerning Constantine, son of Leo

In the year of the Lord 742, Constantine, son of Leo, reigned at Constantinople for thirty-five years. He was worse than his father, because he offered sacrifices to demons.

Astulf, the twenty-sixth king of the Lombards, reigned eight years. He harassed God’s Church [Col. 0491A] and invaded the cities belonging by right to Blessed Peter. Therefore, at the request of Pope Stephen, Pippin the Short, king of the Franks, came into Italy and compelled Astulf to swear that he would no longer harass the Roman Church. Then Pippin came to Rome and was honorably received. When he had returned to Francia, Astulf kept none of his promises. Pippin therefore returned, captured Ravenna and twenty other cities, and gave them to the Roman Church; and he bound Astulf more strictly. He died in the fourteenth year of his reign, leaving two sons, namely Charlemagne and Carloman, who divided the kingdom. Pope Paul succeeded Pope Stephen and often urged Constantine to restore the images. Afterwards Constantine, still a layman, seized the apostolic see; then another Stephen, and afterwards Adrian. Desiderius, king of the Lombards, succeeded King Astulf.

This Desiderius, attacking the Roman Church, first captured Faenza and Ferrara, and took Comacchio from the exarchate of Ravenna.

In the year of the Lord 755, in the time of King Astulf and in the eighth year of Lord and Pope Sylvester I, the body of Blessed Sylvester was transferred to Nonantola.

In the year of the Lord 774, the kingdom of the Lombards was subdued by King Charles, after those who had reigned since they entered Italy had ruled for 206 years. Charles then returned to Francia and subdued [Col. 0491C] Saxony.

## Addition to Sicard’s Chronicle according to the Este manuscript

It is found in the *Legend of Blessed Julia, Virgin and Martyr*, concerning Desiderius, king of the Lombards:

“Afterwards, in the preceding time, there was a certain noble man of the city of Brescia, faithful and devout, named Desiderius. Once, when the barons and leading men of the Lombards were about to create a king at Ticinum, Desiderius spoke to his wife Ansa, saying: ‘I shall go to Ticinum, where the princes of the Lombards have assembled to make themselves a king.’ His wife, smiling, said: ‘Go; perhaps they will choose you as their king.’ Setting out, he came on the first [Col. 0491D] day to a place which to the present day is called Leno. There, lying down to rest beneath a certain tree, he fell asleep. Behold, a serpent suddenly rose up and came to his head; fastening its tail to its head, it made a crown in the form of a garland upon his head. His servant saw this but did not wish to awaken him, fearing that the serpent might harm him. While these things were occurring, Desiderius dreamed that the diadem of the king of the Lombards was being placed on his head. When he awoke and the serpent withdrew without doing him any harm, he said to his servant: ‘Rise; let us go, for I have seen a dream through which I think that I shall become king.’ While they were on the road, his servant confessed to him what had happened to him with the serpent.

“Upon entering the hall where the multitude was assembled, waiting and wishing to know whom the electors would choose as king, and after they had labored over the election for many days without being able by any means to agree upon one person, those waiting in the hall said to Desiderius: ‘Go, Desiderius; enter among them and tell them that we are all wearied by waiting so long for their election.’ He went in to them confidently and reported the grumbling of all those waiting for the king’s election. When they saw Desiderius—of whom no mention had been made among them—one of them said before them all: ‘Behold, Desiderius is a noble man, though not very rich in property, and valiant in arms. Let us choose him as king.’ In short, by God’s will they all agreed upon him. Thus was fulfilled [Col. 0492B] in him what is said: ‘The unexpected man shall bear the diadem.’ Having summoned him into the inner chamber, they placed the royal insignia upon him. When this was announced in the hall, all began to rejoice.

“Not forgetting the place where the serpent had encircled his head and had also set its sign, he built there, in honor of our Lord Jesus and St Benedict the Confessor, a great and noble monastery, where a large multitude of monks most devoutly served the Lord in holy religion. He also endowed it with privileges and with many estates and lands. His wife Ansa, a most devout queen, following in her husband’s footsteps, caused an equally noble and wealthy monastery to be built from her own resources within the city. She richly endowed it with estates, lands, meadows, mills, springs, slaves, and servants, both in the dioceses of Brescia, Cremona, Piacenza, and Reggio, and in many other places. She also bestowed very generous gifts upon the church of the said monastery: gold, silver, precious stones, censers, bowls, crosses, Gospel books, and other cloths of samite and silken garments, as befitted a Lombard queen—indeed, all the more so because she acted from great affection and pious devotion. She ordained that from the things she had given to the monastery there should be a large community of nuns and virgins, who might offer devoted service to the Lord day and night.

“After this, the devout queen of the Lombard people sent distinguished, trustworthy, and devout messengers to the island of Corsica, [Col. 0492D] and ordered that the body of the most blessed martyr Julia be brought with every care to the monastery which she had built. Faithfully and devoutly carrying out her commands, they brought the body of the said virgin to the city of Brescia and honorably placed it in the church of the aforesaid monastery. There, through her merits and prayers, many benefits are bestowed upon many, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.”

This King Desiderius was the last king of the Lombards.

## Concerning Emperor Leo

In the year of the Lord 777, Leo reigned at Constantinople [Col. 0493A] for six years. Afterwards the empire came into the hands of Leo’s wife, Irene.

## Concerning Irene, wife of Leo

In the year of the Lord 783, Irene reigned at Constantinople with her son Constantine for ten years. In her time, namely in the year of the Lord 786, the sign of the Cross suddenly appeared on garments, and blood flowed from heaven. Because Irene wished to marry Charles, [Col. 0494A] the Greeks forced her into a monastery and chose Nicephorus.

## Concerning Emperor Nicephorus and his son Stauracius

In the year of the Lord 794, Nicephorus reigned at Constantinople for eight years; after him his son Stauracius reigned four months. At Rome, in these times, Pope Adrian I was pope, and Pope Leo III succeeded him. This Pope Leo held a synod in which he condemned heretics who said that Christ, the Son of God, was adoptive.

[Col. 0493] What follows is taken from a manuscript codex of the Imperial Royal Library at Vienna, and likewise from a manuscript codex of the Este Library. Variants between them will be indicated either in the text itself or in the notes appended below.

## Concerning Emperor Charlemagne

[Col. 0493B]

In the year of the Lord 700, in the 1552nd year from the founding of the City, Charles, having already reigned in Francia for thirty-three years, was anointed Roman emperor by Pope Leo III and ruled for fourteen years, one month, and thirteen days. He confirmed for the Roman Church what his father Pippin had given it, added to it the duchy of Spoleto and Benevento, and enlarged other churches also with possessions. With Michael, who after Stauracius reigned at Constantinople for two years, and afterwards with his successor Leo, he established a perpetual peace on these terms: each should call the other brother, and each should always help the other. The Greek emperor was to possess the East and Constantinople, while Charles and his successors [Col. 0493C] were to possess Rome and the West. Therefore, leaving the deeds of the East to Greek chroniclers, let us proceed with the events which occurred among us, in the West.

When these terms of peace had been settled, Charles went through Constantinople to Jerusalem for prayer; he returned to Rome by way of Sicily, Calabria, and Apulia, and went back to Aachen, where he established the seat of his kingdom. There he met the end of his life in the year of the Lord 814: the forty-sixth year of his kingship and empire, the forty-fourth since the subjugation of Italy, and the seventy-second of his age. He had twelve principal warriors: Roland.

> [Note: From the Este Codex: Roland, Oliver, and Archbishop Turpin with their companions.]

And Volmar with his companions. He left two sons: Louis, king of Aquitaine, and Pippin,

> [Note: From the Este Codex: and Pippin, king of Italy.]

his second son, king of Italy. In his time flourished Alcuin, Charles’s chaplain; and Stephen, bishop of Cremona, of venerable life, [Col. 0493D] who together with Pippin, king of Italy, transferred the body of St Zeno to the church which they built and endowed with many possessions.

## Concerning Louis, son of Charles

In the year of the Lord 814, Louis, son of Charles, reigned among the Romans with his son Lothair for twenty-five years. Having heard

> [Note: From the Este Codex: “having indeed heard the death [Col. 0494D] of his father.”]

of his father’s death, he came from Aquitaine and, at Aachen, obtained the chief authority of the empire by consent of the princes. [Col. 0494B] Before him Pope Leo cleared himself through envoys of the charges brought against him. At Constantinople, after Leo had reigned eight years and six months, another Michael succeeded and reigned eight years and nine months. His son Theophilus succeeded him and, after his father’s death, reigned fourteen years and three months. Pope Stephen succeeded Leo and, as some say, anointed Louis. When Louis entered Italy, St John the Baptist appeared to him in a vision in Sabine territory and commanded him to build him a church; he built it at the place called Argentilla. He held the kingdom powerfully as far as the Pharos. He had three sons: Lothair, whom he made his partner in the empire; Charles, whom he made duke of Aquitaine; [Col. 0494C] and Louis, whom he appointed duke of Bavaria. This Emperor Louis, in order to attract nobles into the clergy, allowed clerics to wear precious clothing and to have separate households. In his time King Harald of the Danes and his people came to the faith. In his time also, namely in the year of the Lord 823, the body of St Mark was transferred from Alexandria to Venice. Pope Paschal succeeded Pope Stephen; he

> [Note: “The words from ‘granted authority’ as far as ‘granted’ are lacking in the Este codex.”]

granted Lothair, when he had come to Italy, authority over the Roman people while his father was alive. After Paschal came Eugenius, who compiled a *Book of Penances* and sent it to Francia. After Eugenius came Valentine; after him Gregory, who, during his pontificate, rebuilt from the foundations the church of St Mark which he had governed during his priesthood. [Col. 0494D] In the time of this Louis, Atto was bishop of Cremona.

## Concerning Empress Helena, and Nicetas, Lothair, and Michael Curopalates

In these times Helena alone ruled at Constantinople for five years. Nicetas ruled for nine years. At Rome Lothair ruled for ten years. At Constantinople Michael Curopalates ruled for two years.

## Concerning Lothair, son of Louis

[Col. 0495A]

In the year of the Lord 840, Lothair, son of Louis, reigned among the Romans for fifteen years. Emperor Theophilus of Constantinople sent envoys to him, promising to give his daughter to Louis, his son; but while these matters were being arranged, Theophilus yielded to nature. Lothair, returning from Rome after the imperial blessing, was attacked by his brothers, namely Charles, duke of Aquitaine, and Louis, duke of Bavaria, who wished to reign. Therefore he divided the empire with them: Francia and Brittany fell to Charles; Bavaria and Alamannia to Louis; while Italy, Provence, and Lotharingia fell to Lothair, after whom the latter was so named. Behold the great diminution of the empire. For whereas Charles had divided the empire almost in half with the Greek [Col. 0495B] emperor, this Lothair, Charles’s grandson, had only a third part of half the empire. He had three sons, Louis, Lothair, and Charles, to whom he had granted the kingdom:

> [Note: From the Este Codex: “what had fallen to his share, he divided among them, namely …”]

he divided it among them, giving Italy with the imperial title to Louis, Lotharingia to Lothair, and Provence to Charles. And behold a still greater diminution of the empire, since it came to only a third part of a third part

> [Note: From the Este Codex: “of half.”]

of the empire. Finally Lothair became a monk. In these times Sergius succeeded Gregory in the apostolic office; in his time the Saracens devastated Italy. At Cremona, Quemcroardus, successor of the aforesaid Atto, sat as bishop.

## Concerning Louis, son of Lothair
In the year of the Lord 855, Louis, son of Lothair, reigned among the Romans for eighteen years. Pope Sergius crowned him. Leo succeeded Sergius; he built the city called the Leonine after his own name, the ciborium of Saint Peter, and the church called Santa Maria Nuova. Benedict succeeded him.

> [Note: From the Estense codex: Benedict, whom Pope Paul II succeeded. Stephen V succeeded Paul. Nicholas I succeeded him. Adrian followed Nicholas.]

Thereafter came Nicholas, who excommunicated two kings: Michael, because of the deposition of the patriarch, and Lothair, because of his union with a concubine. For this Pope Nicholas wrote to Lothair the Younger, namely king of Lotharingia, concerning his marriage with Waldrada and Theutberga. In these times the Saracens invaded Benevento; therefore Louis summoned his brother Lothair to his aid. But Lothair died at Piacenza, and so Charles, his uncle, king of the Gauls, seized his kingdom of Lotharingia. But Emperor Louis arrived and divided the kingdom of Lotharingia with Charles, his uncle and king of the Gauls, along with the kingdoms of France and Brittany, in such a way that he retained for himself his seat at Aachen. Moreover, Adalgisus, duke of Benevento, rebelled against Emperor Louis; therefore the emperor, returning into Italy, captured Campania, Lucania, and all the cities of Samnium. In these times Adrian succeeded Nicholas, and John succeeded Adrian. At Cremona, Benedict was bishop.

### On Charles, son of Louis the Elder, uncle of the Younger, surnamed the Bald

[Col. 0496A]

In the year of the Lord 874, Charles, son of Louis the Elder and uncle of the Younger, reigned for one year and nine months. While he was king of France, he came to Rome and, anointed by Pope John, obtained the Empire. In those days his brother Louis, king of Bavaria and Alamannia, died at Frankfurt, leaving three sons—Carloman, Louis, and Charles—who divided the German kingdom among themselves. Carloman had a son named Arnulf by a noblewoman, but he was not legitimate.

### On Charles the Younger

In the year of the Lord 875, Charles the Younger, son of Lothair, reigned among the Romans for seven years.

> [Note: From the Estense codex: Charles the Younger, son of Louis.]
