While he was king of Provence, he came to Rome and was crowned by Pope John. Having been crowned, he issued a privilege for clerics and churches.

> [Note: From the Estense codex: He issued it concerning the liberty of clerics.]

In these times the Normans invaded France and devastated as far as Aachen and Cologne. Emperor Charles took up arms against them. Then Godfrey, king of the Normans, became a Christian, the emperor lifting him from the sacred font. Shortly afterwards, when all the descendants of the Carolingian line had failed, Charles alone became monarch. But because he was considered weakened by illness, Arnulf was elected to the Empire. In these times there were three glorious bishops in Lombardy: Paul, who restored the church of Piacenza after its destruction by Suffredus; Guibodus of Parma, who established the canonical community at Parma; and Lando of Cremona, who brought the body of the martyr Archelaus from Rome to Cremona and appointed Archarius, who assigned a benefice for lights. In these times Martin succeeded Pope John; Adrian succeeded Martin.

### On Arnulf

In the year of the Lord 882, Arnulf, illegitimate son of Carloman, while king of a third part of Germany, reigned among the Romans for twelve years. In these times Stephen succeeded Adrian, and afterwards Formosus. Arnulf was crowned by Formosus and became emperor; he captured Bergamo and subdued all Italy. In these times the Franks lost the Empire, which had been among them for about one hundred and twelve years. For the Empire had for many years been usurped in various ways by many persons; let us proceed with the order of their succession. The following popes succeeded Formosus in the order given: Boniface, Stephen, Romanus, Theodore, John, Benedict, Leo, Christopher, who was made a monk after having been pope.

### On Louis, son of Arnulf

In the year of the Lord 902, Louis reigned among the Germans for four years. After Louis, Henry the Saxon reigned, but did not place the diadem upon his head. In these times the Hungarians ravaged Italy, namely in the year of the Lord 906, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October [24 September]; thereafter they often returned year after year and plundered.

Louis was succeeded by Conrad, most wicked despoiler of the fortunate and of churches. Therefore God removed him. Henry, duke of Saxony, succeeded him, being called to the kingship.

### On Berengar the First

In the year of the Lord 907, Berengar the First reigned for six years. In his time Anastasius sat as pope; Lando succeeded him. John succeeded Lando, he being the son of Pope Sergius.

> [Note: From the Estense codex: In his time Pope Sergius III sat, who had been substituted for Christopher and elected pope. Pope Anastasius III succeeded him; Lando I succeeded Anastasius in the papacy. After him succeeded Pope John, who was the son of Pope Sergius.]

Among the Germans Conrad was the first to reign. This Berengar’s chancellor, named John, was bishop of Cremona; he obtained a county outside the city for five miles. In his time Pope Sergius sat, who had been substituted for Christopher.

### On Berengar the Second

In the year of the Lord 913, Berengar the Second reigned for six years.

### On Hugh

In the year of the Lord 923, Hugh reigned for six years. Henry reigned among the Germans. In these times Dalbert was bishop of Cremona.

### On Berengar the Third

In the year of the Lord 931, Berengar the Third reigned for eight years. In these times the following succeeded John in this order: Leo, Stephen, John; then Leo; then Stephen; afterwards Marinus and Agapetus.

### On Lothair

In the year of the Lord 944, Lothair reigned for two years.

### On Berengar the Fourth

In the year of the Lord 947, Berengar reigned for eleven years. He acquired the kingdom of Italy together with the Empire, and reigned with his son Adalbert. Among the Germans Otto, son of Henry, was the first to reign. In these times the Saracens invaded Capua, namely in the year of the Lord 949. The Roman patricians also usurped tyrannical power for themselves. John, Benedict, and Leo succeeded Agapetus. While the Church suffered these persecutions, and beyond them the greatest persecution from the tyranny of Berengar, legates were sent from the Apostolic See to Otto, king of the Germans, complaining of Berengar’s tyranny. Then this first Otto sent into Italy his son, likewise named Otto, who triumphed over Berengar and subdued all Italy. Adalbert fled to Corsica. Accordingly King Otto, crowned by John, acquired the title of emperor. Thus the Empire passed to the Germans for the glorious and victorious defense of the Church.

### On Otto the First, emperor

[Col. 0498A]

In the year of the Lord 961, Otto the First reigned among the Romans for six years. He substituted Leo for Pope John because John had come to an agreement with Adalbert. Leo having been expelled, John was restored by the Romans; upon John’s death, Benedict was substituted. But the emperor deposed Benedict, restored Leo, and obtained from him the coronation of his son, who bore the same name as himself. This Pope Leo remitted to Emperor Otto the donations made to the Roman Church by Emperor Justinian, King Aribert, Pippin, and Charles; and, with the consent of the cardinals, bishops, priests, deacons, and all the clergy and people of Rome, he granted and bestowed them upon Otto and his successors, so that they might free the Italian kingdom from invasions and defend it forever.

[Col. 0498B] In the time of this elder Otto, Luyso was bishop of Cremona; he transferred the body of Blessed Hymerius from the town of Saint Flavian, situated in the diocese of Imola, to Cremona.

### On Otto the Second, emperor

In the year of the Lord 961, Otto the Second reigned among the Romans for twenty-eight years. In his time John succeeded Pope Leo. John was seized by the prefect of the city and sent into exile in Campania. But the emperor took vengeance upon his persecutors by punishment and restored the apostolic bishop. Benedict succeeded John; he too was seized by Thuicius, son of Theodore, imprisoned in the Castle of Saint Angelo, and strangled. Donus, Benedict, and John succeeded Benedict; John died from hunger in the Castle of Saint Angelo. Then John again, likewise John, Silvester, John, and another John. In these times Liutprand was bishop of Cremona.

### On Otto the Third, emperor

In the year of the Lord 994, Otto the Third reigned among the Romans for six years. In his time an earthquake shook all Italy for ten days. In his time the venerable Odericus was bishop of Cremona; he made a shrine for Blessed Hymerius, brought the body of Saint Gregory the martyr from Spoleto to Cremona, and, building the church of Saint Lawrence—which had formerly been a chapel outside the city walls—also endowed it as a monastery.

### On Henry the Lame, duke of the Noricans

[Col. 0498D]

In the year of the Lord 1001, after the Ottos had died without heirs, Henry the Lame, duke of the Noricans, that is, of the Bavarians, was elected by the princes. He reigned for twenty-four years, and ruled as emperor for eleven. He won many battles.

> [Note: Estense codex: He became emperor in the year 1014; he won many battles; at Bamberg he was numbered in the catalogue of saints.]

In his time the following succeeded Pope John in this order: Sergius, Benedict, John, and Benedict, who was expelled from the papacy and replaced by Silvester. But when this man too had been deposed, Benedict was restored; when Benedict was again expelled, Gregory was substituted. Emperor Henry deposed Gregory, carried him beyond the mountains, and substituted Clement. In Henry’s time his chaplain, named Landulf, was bishop of Cremona and a most bitter persecutor of the monastery of Saint Lawrence and of the people of Cremona. Therefore the people expelled him from the city and destroyed his palace, fortified with towers and a double wall. Accordingly, although he acquired much for the bishopric, he lost much through pride and much through indolence. In this Henry’s time the moon became blood-red for three days. The sun was eclipsed, and there was a severe famine. In his time, namely in the year of the Lord 1005, the hermit Simeon departed to the Lord; his body lies at Saint Benedict’s between the Po and the Lirone.

### On Conrad

[Col. 0499B]

In the year of the Lord 1026, Conrad reigned among the Romans for sixteen years. In his time Damasus succeeded Clement in the papacy. Aribert was archbishop of Milan, and Baldus was bishop of Cremona; he too persecuted the monastery of Saint Lawrence and was attacked at Lake Obscuro. When Conrad died, the Empire was vacant.

> [Note: Estense codex: A certain Conrad, duke of the Franks, succeeded Henry the Second; he married a niece of Saint Henry and reigned among the Romans for thirteen years, entering Italy in that same year. In his time Damasus II succeeded Clement II. In the year of the Lord 1033, Michael succeeded to the Empire at Constantinople and reigned for four years; for Theodora the empress had his eyes torn out and expelled him from the kingdom. Constantine succeeded, who became Monomachus and reigned for three years. In the year of the Lord 1139, Conrad died and his son Henry was substituted.]

### On Henry the Second

In the year of the Lord 1040, Henry, son of Conrad, reigned among the Romans for seventeen years. In his time the following sat in the papacy: Leo, who fought the Normans in Apulia; Victor; Stephen, in whose time the Pataria arose at Milan; then Benedict and Nicholas. In Nicholas’s time, namely in the year of the Lord 1052, Marquis Boniface was killed by an arrow at Spinetta. Indeed, where the archer had planted his feet and knees, every root withered, and grass with its shoot thereafter did not spring up anywhere around it, so that the traces of the hidden murderer might appear as if by divine action.

> [Note: Estense codex: In his time, in the year of the Lord 1045, the church of the Holy Resurrection was built at Jerusalem; and in the year of the Lord 1054, Liutprand, legate of the Apostolic See, excommunicated Michael, patriarch of Constantinople, because he condemned the Latins as “Azymites,” that is, users of unleavened bread. In the year of the Lord 1056, after Constantine Monomachus died, the Empress Theodora ruled the Constantinopolitan Empire for two years. Michael Onricas succeeded her; he reigned for two years and, expelled by Isaac, became a monk. Isaac succeeded, and reigned for two years. In the year of the Lord 1056 Henry died; his body was carried beyond the mountains. The kingdom remained vacant for twenty-six years.]

### On Henry the Third

[Col. 0500A]

In the year of the Lord 1063, Henry reigned among the Romans for sixteen years. His son persecuted him so severely that Henry surrendered the royal insignia to him. In these times Robert Guiscard invaded Apulia and even presumed to attack Rome. Jerusalem was captured by pagans. Alexander succeeded Nicholas; he had been elected amid a dispute with Cadalus, bishop of Parma, but prevailed. Gregory succeeded Alexander; he was seized by certain Romans at the holy altar on the night of the Nativity of the Lord, but was released that same day and restored to his position. Arnulf was bishop of Cremona. In these times also, namely in the year of the Lord 1070, the city of Asti was captured by Adalasia. Finally, in the subsequent times, the following events occurred.

In the year of the Lord 1083, Countess Matilda besieged Nonantola. In the year 1084, a severe famine afflicted Italy. In the year of the Lord 1096, a multitude of pilgrims passing through Cremona crossed the sea; after three years had passed, by God’s grace they recovered Jerusalem. In the year of the Lord 1098, the first war over Cremona began, the vexation of the Cremonese. In the year of the Lord 1100, Pope Paschal was created. Certain members of the Roman clergy persecuted him so severely that, putting on three sets of papal insignia, they presumed to elect three men as supreme pontiffs. But in the end they were confounded and overthrown by Paschal himself. In the year 1102, Countess Matilda besieged Ferrara. In the year 1107, the Cremonese, the people of Lodi, and the Pavians burned the borough of Tortona in August.

> [Note: Estense codex: But fleeing the emperor’s plots—whom he accused concerning episcopal elections—he reached Apulia, where Robert Guiscard received him honorably; he was buried at Salerno. In the year of the Lord 1088, while Henry was emperor, Robert Guiscard invaded Apulia and even presumed to attack Rome. Jerusalem was captured by pagans and Turks. Certain Turkomans also seized the eastern kingdoms; they were so called after Turk, their leader. They are uncultivated people, having no permanent city, migrating from place to place and carrying all their possessions with them. In the year of the Lord 1070, the city of Asti was captured by Adelaide. At Constantinople, Constantine Ducas, his contemporary, reigned for eight years; after his death, his wife Eudocia ruled the Empire for six months and married Romanus Diogenes, who reigned for four years and three months and was captured by the Turks in a battle in the East. Afterwards, with his eyes torn out by the Greeks through the agreement of Emperor Michael and the aforesaid Ducas, son of Constantine, Michael reigned for six years. A Greek named Nicephorus deprived Michael of the Empire; after making him a monk, he married his fiancée and reigned for three years. But Alexius also deprived this man of the kingdom and made him put on the monastic habit. In the year of the Lord 1083, in the same time as Pope Gregory VII, the aforesaid Henry reigned among the Romans. At Constantinople Alexius reigned, first alone and then with his son Kalojannes, for thirty-seven years and five months. In that same year Nonantola was besieged by Countess Matilda.]

What follows is contained in the Estense codex as far as the chapter “On Henry the Fourth.” A few items from it are, however, repeated from time to time in the codex of the Imperial Library, as you will see below.

In the year of the Lord 1084, while the holy city of Jerusalem had long been possessed by the Gentiles, Christian merchants came to it and paid gold as tribute at the gate. Yet they had nowhere to lay their heads except among the Gentiles. Therefore the merchants of Amalfi obtained from the ruler of the city an empty plot before the gate of the church called the Sepulchre, and built at their common expense a refuge beside the monastery of their fellows, which is to this day called Saint Mary of the Latins. There Christians could stay whenever they happened to arrive; and they appointed guardians who were to receive Christians. Many pilgrims then came for devotion’s sake. A certain priest from Francia named Peter came, a hermit by office; seeing the Holy Places profaned, he hastened back and urged Christians to make haste to free the Holy City from the unbelievers. Pilgrims therefore gathered together; but more than one hundred thousand Christians passing through Constantinople, because they had sinned against the Lord, were miserably killed by the Turkomans. Peter nevertheless returned and, acting courageously, approached Pope Urban II.

### On the siege of the city of Antioch

In the year of the Lord 1098, the Franks besieged Antioch in October and happily gained it in June. The Franks were brought in over the summit of the wall by rope ladders, through the agency of a certain Turk, to whom Christ commanded in a dream, saying: “Why are you sleeping? Restore Antioch to the Christians.” Saint George the soldier appeared to them, seated on a white horse and clothed in white garments; all night he cried: “Come after me; let us enter the city.” They besieged it, while the Saracens were reduced by so great a scarcity of hunger that they ate horses, asses, camels, dogs, mice, and grains found in dung.

Of this victory it was said:

> When the city of noble Antioch was captured,  
> If from eleven hundred you subtract twice one,  
> Then so many will be the years of the Lord born of the Virgin.

Then the Sultan of Persia besieged the city with a huge army and pressed the Franks so severely that many fled. But the Lord said to a fleeing cleric: “Return, and tell the people to repent, and they will be saved.” For they had mingled with Turkish women. When they had repented, they went out from the city in July; and, fear of the Lord having been sent upon their enemies, they courageously put them to flight. The Sultan himself fled with thirty princes; Corogath also fled, exceedingly savage and exceedingly troublesome. Bohemond, by whose contrivance the city had been acquired, obtained Antioch as prince. In the same year there was the first war of Crema, which continues to the present day, a vexation not only to the Cremonese but also to other Lombards.

### On the capture, through Phoenicia, of Sidon, Tyre, Acre, Capha, Caesarea, and Jerusalem

In the year of the Lord 1099, the Franks advanced through Phoenicia, Sidon, Tyre, Acre, Capha, Caesarea, and came to Jerusalem. Each day they made a procession around it barefoot, and captured it by great force.

> In the year one thousand, less by one than one hundred  
> From the Virgin’s childbirth, when the Lord’s birth shone forth,  
> The Franks capture Jerusalem by mighty force,  
> When Phoebus’ light had touched the fifteenth day of July.  
> For Godfrey the father, having soon been made prince,

For, after about four hundred and twenty years, it was recovered, from the time when under Heraclius it had been captured a second time by the Saracens and then possessed by them. When the city had been captured, they found in a secret place a certain portion of the Cross, which they carried to the Lord’s Sepulchre. Hearing this, the king of Babylon hastened to capture the Franks in Jerusalem. But the Franks courageously went to meet him as far as Ascalon and vigorously attacked him; enriched by their wealth, they returned gloriously to Jerusalem. But Robert, count of Normandy, and Robert, count of Flanders, returned through Constantinople to their own lands. Count Raymond went to Laodicea. Duke Godfrey, retaining Tancred with him, held the principality of Jerusalem. Bohemond, prince of Antioch, and Baldwin, brother of the aforesaid Godfrey and prince of Edessa, hearing of their companions’ victory, came to Jerusalem with great labor. After Daibert, archbishop of Pisa, had been appointed patriarch, they happily returned to their principalities, their pilgrimage journey having been completed. This was in the time of Pope Urban II.

### On Bohemond

[Col. 0502C] In the year of the Lord 1100, Bohemond was captured by the Turks, and Godfrey’s brother Baldwin was elected. Entrusting Edessa to his kinsman Count Baldwin, he reached Jerusalem after many labors and, within a short time, ranged through the land beyond Ascalon and the regions of Arabia in order to subject them to his rule. In the same year Pope Paschal was created. Certain members of the Roman clergy persecuted him so severely that, putting on three sets of papal insignia, they presumed to elevate three men as supreme pontiffs. But in the end they were confounded and overthrown by Paschal himself.

### On Baldwin

In the year of the Lord 1101, Baldwin was crowned king at Bethlehem, a thing his brother had refused, saying that no one ought to be crowned in the kingdom, or from the kingdom, of Christ the King. But the wiser judgment was that what they did to Christ in dishonor, Christians should do in honor and glory. It is like Peter’s shaving and ours. The Christians did not yet have more than three hundred knights, and as many infantrymen, to guard Jerusalem, Joppa, Ramla, and the fortress of Capha; nor did they hold any port except Joppa—all the rest belonged to the Saracens. At that time a Genoese fleet arrived, and it was agreed between the king and them that whoever captured a city of the Saracens should have one third of it. Thus they first captured the town of Assur, then the city of Caesarea in Palestine, where they established an archbishop. As time went on, the king, with few men, fought near Ascalon against the commander of the Babylonian army and overcame him and his immense army.

### On the capture of Tortosa and the siege of Ferrara

In the year of the Lord 1102, another army of Franks arrived and suffered many hardships and losses; but afterwards they captured Tortosa. Among them were the count of Poitou, the count of Burgundy, and the count of Blois. With them, and scarcely two hundred knights, the king defeated twenty thousand Saracens within Ramla; on another occasion, by the Savior’s grace, he retained Joppa, which they had seized. In that same year in Italy Countess Matilda besieged the city of Ferrara.

### On Bohemond, who was freed from prison

In the year of the Lord 1103, Bohemond was freed from a Turkish prison and received as prince of Antioch. He also recovered Laodicea from Tancred, who had taken it from the men of the emperor of Constantinople.

### On the siege of Acre

In the year of the Lord 1104, the king besieged Acre, attacked it with Genoese assistance, and received it by surrender. In the same year Bohemond fought the Turks near Harran, which is close to the Euphrates, with great slaughter of his own men. Then, hurrying to France, he married Constance, daughter of King Philip, leaving the principality to Tancred.

### On Tancred, prince of Antioch; on the battle he fought against the Saracens

[Col. 0503C] In the year of the Lord 1105, Tancred, prince of Antioch, fought the Saracens and courageously defeated them. King Baldwin also, between Joppa and Ramla, with five hundred knights and two thousand infantrymen, overcame fifteen thousand Turks, Ethiopians, and Arabs. In the same year, on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, a great earthquake occurred at Jerusalem.

### On the comet, two suns, and stars

In the year of the Lord 1106, a great comet, red and snow-white, appeared in the world for fifty days, beginning in February. Two suns also appeared, and stars were several times seen from heaven. Hugh the Great, who governed Tiberias, defeated the Damascenes; but he perished on another expedition.

### On the knights of Joppa and Bohemond

[Col. 0503D]

In the year of the Lord 1107, the knights of Joppa overcame five hundred knights and one thousand infantrymen lying in ambushes between Joppa and Jerusalem. In the same year Bohemond, who had come from France into Apulia with five thousand knights and forty thousand infantrymen, besieged Dyrrhachium, because Alexius of Constantinople was hostile to pilgrims.

### On Bohemond’s peace with Alexius

In the year of the Lord 1108, Bohemond made peace with Alexius and returned to Apulia.

### On the king who captured Tripoli

In the year of the Lord 1109, the king captured Tripoli with Genoese assistance and with Count Bertrand, and invested that same Count Bertrand with it.

### On the capture of the city of Beirut and Baldwin’s siege

In the year of the Lord 1110, King Baldwin besieged and captured the city of Beirut. Going there with Tancred, prince of Antioch, to the people of Edessa, who were besieged by Saracens, he supplied them with provisions. Then, returning to Jerusalem, he besieged and captured the city of Sidon with the aid of Gernan, king of the Norwegians, who had come with sixty ships of pilgrims. In the same year the city of Novara was destroyed.

### On the siege of Tyre and the destruction of the city of Lodi

In the year of the Lord 1111, King Baldwin went to the principality of Antioch and brought assistance to Tancred against the Persians. Then he returned and besieged Tyre, but did not capture it. In the same year the city of Lodi in Italy was captured and destroyed by the Milanese.

### On Tancred’s death

In the year of the Lord 1112, Tancred died, and his kinsman Roger succeeded him.

### On the eclipse of the sun, the earthquake, the countess of Sicily, and the council

In the year of the Lord 1113, the sun suffered an eclipse, and an earthquake occurred twice that year in the kingdom of Jerusalem. In that year the Saracens gathered on an island which is in the Jordan, intending utterly to destroy the Christians. King Baldwin fought against them, to his loss; meanwhile the people of Ascalon destroyed the crops around Jerusalem. In the same year Adelaide, countess of Sicily, wife of the count who was brother of Robert Guiscard, arrived at Acre on pilgrimage. In the same year the apostolic bishop held a council in the Lateran Basilica, in which that privilege—better called a *pravilegium*, a wrongful privilege—extorted from the Fathers by violence, was annulled. In the same year the city of Cremona was burned by fire.

### On the multitude of locusts

In the year of the Lord 1114, a multitude of locusts flying from the regions of Arabia devastated the crops of Jerusalem. There was a most severe earthquake in the regions of Antioch; it overthrew many houses and fortifications, and before it flies did not enter buildings.

### On the Turkish encampment between Antioch and Damascus; the city overthrown by an earthquake; and the death of Countess Matilda

In the year of the Lord 1115, the Turks encamped between Antioch and Damascus. Doldequinus, king of the Damascenes, therefore made peace with King Baldwin and Prince Roger, and they joined together against the Turks. Meanwhile the people of Ascalon besieged Joppa. When the kings had returned to their own places, the Antiochenes alone defeated the Turks with strong courage. In the same year Mamistra was overthrown by an earthquake. In the same year King Baldwin built a fortress on a certain mountain in Arabia, situated between Mount Abarim, where the Lord buried Moses, Jor, and Sinai; he ordered it to be called “the Mount.” In the same year Countess Matilda died.

### On King Baldwin and Countess Adelaide

In the year of the Lord 1116, King Baldwin dismissed Adelaide, formerly countess of Sicily, whom he had unjustly taken as wife at Edessa while his own wife was still alive.

### On the multitude of locusts

In the year of the Lord 1117, in the Jerusalem region, a multitude of locusts devoured crops and trees. The moon was first suffused with redness and afterwards entirely with blackness. In the same year King Baldwin built a fortress near Tyre, which he ordered to be named Scandileon, that is, “lion’s head.”

### On the death of King Baldwin and Alexius

[Col. 0505B] In the year of the Lord 1118, King Baldwin paid the debt of all flesh, having reigned for eighteen years. Caeder, Egypt, Dan, and Damascus paid tribute to him. He was buried at Golgotha beside his brother Duke Godfrey. Since he left no offspring, another Baldwin, count of Edessa and his kinsman, succeeded him. He courageously resisted a multitude of Turks near Ascalon, but neither side attacked the other. In the same year Alexius of Constantinople entered upon the way of all flesh. His son Kalojannes reigned in his place.

### On Pope Gelasius II, the destruction of the prince’s army, and the knighthood and origin of the Knights Templar

In the year of the Lord 1119, Pope Gelasius II, successor of Pope Paschal, was unanimously elected and installed in the city. Fleeing the swift arrival of Emperor Henry, he received the blessing of consecration at Capua. The emperor, however, put forward Maurice, archbishop of Braga, whom the Roman people called Burdinus. Gelasius passed through Pisa and Genoa, arrived at Saint-Gilles, and came as far as Cluny. There he entered upon the way of all flesh and was buried. In the same year, seven thousand Antiochenes fighting the Turks near the town of Artah, which is near Antioch, were killed because of the lustfulness of their prince and great men. But afterwards, when King Baldwin came near the place, battle was fought by the town of Sardonis, or Sardarium. Although it was a bloody battle, the Christians gained victory. In the same year the knighthood of the Temple took its beginning.

### On Pope Calixtus II and other deeds that occurred in his time, especially in Lombardy, overseas, and at Antioch

In the year of the Lord 1120, Pope Calixtus II was created, having been elected at Cluny. Since he was born from a father who was count of Burgundy, he was as eminent among churchmen as he was illustrious among secular men. As he hurried toward the city and the Apostolic See, he consecrated the church of Pisa. Arriving at Sutri, he seized the intruder Burdinus, who, riding sideways on a camel in place of a palfrey, holding its tail in his hands in place of reins, and clad in a hairy skin instead of a red cloak, went before the pontiff’s retinue as it returned to the city. Thus mocked in many ways, the intruder ended his life in the monastery of Cava. In the same year the king of Jerusalem visited Antioch and courageously resisted the Turks near Caliptum. He remitted every exaction for all Saracens entering Jerusalem in order to sell wheat, barley, and legumes. In the same year there was a military clash in Italy between the Cremonese and the Parmenese, in which the Cremonese fought the Parmenese on the gravel-bank of Parma.

### On King Baldwin, who destroyed the fortress of Jaret

In the year of the Lord 1121, King Baldwin besieged and captured a fortress which Doldequinus, king of Damascus, had built sixteen miles from the Jordan; he destroyed it to the ground. The inhabitants called it Jarta. It was formerly the city of Gerasa, situated in Arabia.

### On the king of Jerusalem

In the year of the Lord 1122, the king of Jerusalem went to Antioch and restrained the Parthian people from their attacks.

### On King Henry

In the year of the Lord 1122, Emperor Henry, seeing that there is neither knowledge nor power against the Lord, returned to peace with the Church. He relinquished every investiture and everything he had extorted by a violent privilege concerning spiritual matters, and granted that election and consecration should be conducted canonically. Thus he said: “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, HENRY, etc.”

### On Baldwin’s capture by the Turks

In the same year the Turks captured Baldwin. Eustace, who possessed Caesarea, was appointed guardian of the land in his place. Moreover, they besieged Joppa; but at length, near Azotus, that faithless people was put to flight, slaughtered, conquered, and overcome by God’s power. Moreover, the most powerful Venetian fleet, which had undertaken a journey to aid the Holy Land, hastened there through the Lord’s favor and captured the immense Turkish fleet which had come for the siege. Moreover, Count Joscelin of Edessa, who had long been imprisoned there, was freed from prison. Although this may have been accomplished cunningly, we neither describe the cunning nor attribute it to cunning, but to the mercy and power of God.

### On the Venetian servants of Christ, who besieged Tyre

In the year of the Lord 1124, the Christians of Jerusalem besieged Tyre with the Venetians. But again the people of Ascalon harassed Jerusalem, at their own cost; and Balak invaded the Antiochenes with an innumerable army. Joscelin, count of Edessa, courageously defeated him and cut off his head. Thus was fulfilled his dream, in which he had seen that Joscelin would tear out his eyes. Therefore Tyre was captured by the Christians in June and possessed in God’s name. There, as formerly there had been a chief priest, so now an archbishop was established, who is in fact subject to the patriarch of Jerusalem, although the patriarch of Antioch murmurs against it, supported by the protection of the ancient law of the Greeks. Moreover, one third of Tyre was granted to the Venetians by hereditary right, while two parts remained under royal authority. In the same year Honorius III was pope, and sat for six years, one month, and twenty-eight days.

### On Baldwin’s release from prison
In the year of the Lord 1125, King Baldwin, having been held in chains for nearly two years, was released from prison, came to Jerusalem, and hastened back to Antioch. On their return, the Venetians attacked the islands of Tenedos, Methone, Samos, and Chios belonging to the Greek emperor; at will they demolished their walls, carried persons into captivity, and seized goods of every kind. King Baldwin, with one thousand knights and two thousand infantry, routed, near the castle of Hasar, the fifteen thousand soldiers of Bursuq and of the king of Damascus; he killed, captured, and wounded them. After this he built a castle near Beirut on Mount Gravianus, so called, as it were, from sword-fighting, because there matters were fought out—that is, men to be condemned were judged. Then he led an army toward Damascus, where he obtained very great booty. Afterwards he marched against Ascalon, where he drove back and shut in the enemy.

The Vienna manuscript follows.—Concerning Henry IV.

In the year of the Lord 1110, Henry, son of Henry, ruled among the Romans for fifteen years. In this year—that is, 1090—he came to Rome for his coronation, seized Pope Paschal [Col. 0507C], and kept him in chains for more than two months, because he had forbidden his father’s burial, so that he lay in his coffin for five years. And because Paschal would not consecrate him unless Henry confirmed by oath that he would thereafter not interfere in the investitures of churches, bishops, and abbots, Henry was at last crowned after a reconciliation had been effected.

The manner of the reconciliation was this: the Apostolic See, unwillingly and under compulsion, granted the emperor a privilege concerning the investiture of churches, bishops, and abbots; and ordained that an elected man should not be consecrated unless first approved and invested by the king. But afterwards the same pope held a synod in the Lateran basilica, in which that privilege—better called a *pravilegium*, a wrongful privilege—was annulled, because it had been extorted by the king’s violence.

In the time of this Henry, Walter was bishop of Cremona, and Hugh succeeded him as bishop-elect. In his time, namely in the year of the Lord 1090, there was a battle between the Milanese and Cremonese near Brixianorum, disastrous for the Cremonese. In the same year the city of Lodi was captured and destroyed by the Milanese. In 1113 the aforesaid synod was held, and Cremona was consumed by fire. In 1115 Countess Matilda died and was buried at the church of Saint Benedict between the Po and the Lirone, which she had enriched; her grandfather Tedald had built it, and her father Boniface had enlarged its possessions. In 1116 there was a great earthquake in January, on account of which the greater church of Cremona collapsed, and the body of the confessor Himerius long lay hidden beneath the ruins.

In 1119 Gelasius succeeded Paschal. Though he had been elected in harmony in the City and installed in the see, he fled the imminent arrival of Emperor Henry and received consecration at Capua. The emperor, however, intruded Maurice, archbishop of Braga, whom the Roman people called Burdinus. Gelasius, passing through Pisa and Genoa, came to Saint-Gilles; proceeding as far as Cluny, he there entered upon the way of all flesh and was buried. In 1120 Pope Calixtus was created, elected at Cluny. Born of a father who was count of Burgundy, he was as illustrious among secular men as he was eminent among churchmen. Hurrying toward the City and the Apostolic See [Col. 0508B], he consecrated the church of Pisa. Arriving at Sutri, he captured the intruder Burdinus, who, riding sideways upon a camel instead of a palfrey, holding its tail in his hands instead of a bridle, and clothed in a red cloak of hairy skin, preceded the returning pontiff’s company into Rome; after being mocked in many ways, he ended his life as an intruder in the monastery of Cava.

Seeing, therefore, that there is no wisdom and no power against the Lord, the emperor returned to peace with the Church, renouncing every investiture and whatever he had violently extorted from spiritual privilege, and granting that election and consecration should be performed canonically. Thus he says: “In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, I, HENRY,” etc.

Also in the year of the Lord 1120 [Col. 0508C], there was the first war of Parma, in which the Cremonese fought with the Parmesans on the gravel-bank of Parma.

Concerning Lothair.

In the year of the Lord 1126, Lothair ruled among the Romans for twelve years. He persecuted the line of the Henries with excessive severity. Conrad was elected against him; but Conrad withdrew by agreement, and Lothair was confirmed.

These things are added in the Este manuscript.

In this year, 1126, King Baldwin led an expedition toward Damascus and reached Tiberias. Then, having crossed the Jordan, they arrived at the Cave of Roob; and beyond Medda they threw down a certain tower. Then they proceeded to the castle of Solome, and from there, with bold courage, to the meadows of Sophar [Col. 0508D], where Paul the Apostle received a blow from the Lord and was deprived of sight for three days. Afterwards, fighting with the son of King Doldequin, they gained victory and returned to Jerusalem in triumph, having destroyed two towers on their return.

Later, invited by the count of Tripoli, he besieged the city of Rafanea, where the Sabbatical river displays a dry bed for six days and flows abundantly on the seventh. Having captured it, he entrusted it to the count’s governance. Moreover, when he had hastened to Antioch against the Turks, the Babylonians tested our ports in a naval battle; but, gaining nothing, they suffered losses. And behold, after many labours and dangers, the young Bohemond, son of the former Bohemond the elder, came from Apulia to Antioch [Col. 0509A]. There the king received him honourably, gave him one of his daughters in marriage, and assigned to him, together with the daughter, the kingdom to be inherited by hereditary right. In the same year there appeared in the eastern regions, between east and north, a comet which, rising before dawn, cast its ray toward the ninth hour.

In the same year, 1126, the city of Como was taken by the Milanese in August; and in that year the Po froze so completely that carts and horses travelled over the ice. During Lothair’s time Honorius sat in the papacy. Having been elected amid the opposition of Theobald, cardinal priest, he humbly laid aside the mantle. Seeing his humility, the brethren unanimously offered him obedience. When he descended into Apulia to fight Roger, investigating the treachery of the barons, he invested Roger with the duchy of Apulia by the sounder counsel.

He deposed Peter, cardinal priest, patriarch of Aquileia, and a Venetian. Innocent succeeded him as pope, himself elected in contention with Peter, cardinal priest, son of Peter Leo, who was named Anacletus. The clergy adhered to Innocent; the Roman populace, apart from the Frangipani, adhered to Anacletus. Taking a golden crucifix, golden crowns, and the treasures of churches, Anacletus withdrew into Apulia and granted that Roger should be king. Innocent, however, came by ship to Pisa [Col. 0509C], imposed a truce between the Pisans and Genoese, and then, proceeding onward, held a council at Saint-Gilles. Passing into France, he was honourably received by Louis, king of the Franks, and Henry, king of the English. Proceeding into Lorraine, he received from King Lothair a promise that he would restore him to the see of Saint Peter.

Returning, he held a second council at Reims and a third at Piacenza. Returning to Pisa, he settled peace between the Pisans and Genoese. Remembering the benefits conferred upon him by the Pisans and Genoese, he granted the church of Pisa the primacy of Sardinia and three bishoprics in the province of Corsica. He exempted the church of Genoa from subjection to the church of Milan, made it a metropolitan see, and subjected to it the see of Bobbio and certain Corsican bishops.

While these things were being done, behold, King Lothair came promptly, fulfilling his promise. The king and pontiff entered the City together: there the pontiff obtained the see of the Lateran church, and the king the imperial diadem. Afterwards the emperor returned to Germany and the pontiff to Pisa, where he held a fourth council. Since Roger continued to support Peter the heresiarch, surnamed Anacletus, in his error, the most Christian emperor, advocate of the Catholic Church, returning from Germany, invaded Apulia with the supreme pontiff and subjected the whole land by the arm of his mighty strength. Roger fled to Sicily. The pontiff and emperor then made Rainulf duke of Apulia. Thus the pontiff returned to the City and the emperor to Germany [Col. 0510A] in glory.

Peter the heresiarch rotted in his error and died. His followers elected another, whom the Romans called Carnicorvus. At last they sought pardon at the feet of the supreme pontiff and were mercifully received. By this supreme pontiff’s authority the church of Compostela was made a metropolitan see. This pope besieged Tivoli with the Romans; many were captured and killed, but eventually the Romans returned from Tivoli in victory and triumph.

During Lothair’s time Obert was bishop of Cremona. He found the long-hidden body of Saint Himerius and, in the year of the Lord 1129, placed it in an iron shrine. In 1132 Lothair besieged Crema with the Cremonese for a month. In the following year, namely 1133 [Col. 0510B], the castle of the viscounts, or *visconti*, was built. At last the Cremonese defended the imperial majesty. In 1135 the same victorious emperor invaded and laid waste Bassiano and the surrounding lands, and issued an edictal law concerning fiefs.

These things are added from the Este manuscript.—Concerning a multitude of mice.

In the year of the Lord 1127, in the land of the Palestinians, a multitude of mice swarmed forth. They devoured oxen and other animals and utterly devastated the crops. When they were swept away into the valleys of Tyre by a deluge, that region was corrupted by their stench.

Concerning Bohemond and the events of his time.

[Col. 0510C]

In the same year Bohemond of Antioch besieged the town of Capharda, near Apamea or Euphemia, and killed its inhabitants although they wished to ransom themselves at great cost. But immense discord arose between him and Count Joscelin of Edessa, so that Bohemond plundered everything as far as the walls of Antioch.

Concerning the destruction of Syracuse.

In the same year barbarians attacked the city of Syracuse, burned it, and plundered everything.

Concerning King Baldwin, the holding of a council, the confirmation of the knighthood, order, and Rule of the Temple, and the events of the same time.

In the year of the Lord 1128, King Baldwin besieged and captured the town of Blahasam [Col. 0510D], built in a difficult position four miles from Sidon. In the same year a council was held at Troyes of archbishops, bishops, and abbots, among whom was Saint Bernard of Clairvaux. There the knighthood of the Temple was strengthened and the Rule of the holy military order was established.

During Lothair’s time Honorius sat in the papacy. Having been elected amid the opposition of Theobald, cardinal and priest, he humbly laid aside the mantle. Seeing his humility, the brethren unanimously offered him obedience. When he descended into Apulia to fight Roger, investigating the treachery of the barons, he invested Roger with the duchy of Apulia by the sounder counsel. Through Peter, etc., as above, as far as the words [Col. 0511A], “The church of Compostela was made a metropolitan see.”

The continuation is: During Lothair’s time, Fulk, count of Anjou, succeeded King Baldwin. This Fulk had married a daughter of the king of England; when she had died, leaving sons born of her, he was summoned to marry Melisende, Baldwin’s eldest daughter. For Baldwin had left no son but four daughters. Fulk therefore came, received the queen and the kingdom, and by her begot Baldwin and Amalric, who were brothers of the king of England. Another of the sisters married the prince of Antioch; the third, the count of Tripoli; the fourth served God at Bethany in the office of abbess.

Concerning King Conrad.

[Col. 0511B] In the year of the Lord 1139, Conrad ruled among the Romans for twelve years. This is Conrad, who was elected after Lothair.

> **[Note: Col. 0511D, Este manuscript:]** His sister, named Julitta, was joined in marriage to Marquis William of Montferrat. By her he begot five sons of outstanding merit, to be recorded in this order: William, Conrad, Boniface, Frederick, and Raynerius. Fortune granted them differing gifts, as the pen will declare below.

In his time Celestine II and Lucius II sat in the papacy. Lucius ascended the Capitol by force of arms, but the Romans drove him out. Eugenius then succeeded. While abbot of Saint Anastasius, he was unexpectedly and unanimously elected. Fearing the citizens, Pope Eugenius fled to the fortress of Monticelli and thence to the monastery of Farfa, where he received the grace of consecration. Although the citizens were hostile to him at first, nevertheless, through God’s agency—who breathes where He wills—because he was powerful in deed and word, they were converted to the shepherd and bishop of their souls and received him into the City [Col. 0511C] with great joy and a solemn procession.

In King Conrad’s time, namely in the year of the Lord 1139, a great part of the Cremonese were captured by the Milanese near Crema and committed to prison chains.

> **[Note: Col. 0511D, Este manuscript:]** In the year of the Lord 1142 Innocent besieged Tivoli with the Romans; many of them were captured and killed. But at last the Romans returned in triumphant victory.

In 1142 Innocent, whom we mentioned above, besieged Tivoli. In 1146 a plague of caterpillars prevailed over the land and consumed its produce; consequently, in the following year famine wasted certain needy persons. Yet in the same year, 1147, King Conrad, fired with zeal for God and marked with the protection of the cross, crossed over; and with him likewise went Louis, king of the French.

> **[Note: Col. 0511D, Este manuscript:]** And the count of Provence, who passed through Constantinople. Manuel, who had succeeded his father, nevertheless betrayed them, although Conrad had married his niece: he caused them to be led through desert and waterless places, where the greater part were killed by hunger and the sword. Hardly the survivors reached Satalia. Having come by ship to Ptolemais, and having greeted the shield-bearers, together with King Baldwin, Fulk’s firstborn, who had succeeded his father in the kingdom [Col. 0512D], and likewise the Templars and Hospitallers, the battle-lines were encouraged, directed, and advanced against Damascus. While King Baldwin, with the Templars and Hospitallers, was encamped on the Jordan of Damascus, there came a very great and strong [lacuna], the springs having been blocked. Seeing the shortage of water, he charged against the multitude of Saracens that had come out of the city. Having personally killed two very fierce men in single combat on foot, while the rest turned their backs, he encamped on the bank before the gate of Damascus by the river. At that time the city could very easily have been captured, had iniquity not entangled the hunters in their own snares. For King Baldwin and his aforesaid associates—whether spurred by envy or corrupted by money—defrauded their fellow allies in bad faith and returned, themselves deservedly defrauded by counterfeit money. In this army Frederick, son of Frederick, duke of Swabia and brother of the king, was more valiant and glorious than all others; this later became the occasion for his obtaining the kingdom.

In this army Frederick, son of Frederick, duke of Swabia, was more valiant and glorious than all others; this was the occasion [Col. 0512A] for his later being summoned to the kingdom by the princes. In the year of the Lord 1149, the Piacentines were captured near Tabiano.

Concerning Emperor Frederick.

In the year of the Lord 1142, Frederick ruled among the Romans for thirty-seven years. He was a vigorous and high-minded knight, gentle, gracious, unlettered, but taught by practical moral experience:

> “He saw the customs and cities of many men.”

In his time many varied events followed. For in the same year, namely 1152, Medexena was captured and utterly destroyed by the Cremonese and Piacentines.

The Este manuscript adds this.

[Col. 0512B] In the year of the Lord 1153, Ascalon was captured by the Christians, King Baldwin—who was as it were a second Maccabee—fighting bravely against it. In due course, alas, he entered upon the way of all flesh and left no offspring. His brother Amalric ought to have succeeded him, but this was delayed because, being excommunicated for an incestuous marriage, he was not fit to be anointed. Therefore, having dismissed his related wife—by whom he had nevertheless begotten a son and daughter, namely Baldwin and Sibylla—he was crowned king; and taking another wife, he begot by her a daughter named Isabella.

This Amalric subdued the Egyptians and frequently crushed the Damascenes. At last Baldwin received the kingdom. Although afflicted with leprosy from childhood, he nevertheless manfully preserved the frontiers [Col. 0512C] of the kingdom of Jerusalem and marvellously crushed Saladin, enemy of Christ’s faith, at Mount Gisard; while he lived, he triumphed magnificently. But while these happy events occurred in the kingdom of Jerusalem through the course of many succeeding years, many unhappy deeds, hateful to God and deserving human condemnation, were committed in the Italian empire.

In the year of the Lord 1154, King Frederick first came into Italy. He captured the city of Asti, destroying its towers and city walls. In 1153 Pope Anastasius IV was created. Arnold the heretic was burned by the authority of King Frederick. The same king captured and utterly destroyed Tortona [Col. 0513A] and Spoleto. Then, hastening toward Rome, he subdued many enemies. In 1154 Pope Adrian IV was created; he anointed King Frederick and crowned him with the imperial diadem. The emperor attacked the Romans, who refused to render him due loyalty and right; in wrath against them and as an imperial punishment, he ordered the municipality of Tivoli restored. Afterwards he returned in imperial triumph to Germany and lodged beside the river Rhine.

In 1157 the Milanese destroyed the Pavians’ castle called Vegevalum and rebuilt the city of Tortona. In 1158 the emperor, returning to Italy, attacked the Brescian people, founded the city of Lodi, and besieged Milan; but after making a treaty he departed, made peace with the Lombards upon the surrender of the royal rights, and enacted a law at Roncaglia. In 1159 he destroyed the towers of the Piacentines and the fortifications of their city. In the same year he besieged Crema with the Cremonese and destroyed it on the sixth day before the Kalends of February [27 January]. In that same year Obert, bishop of Cremona, transferred the body of Saint Gregory the martyr into the church of Saint Michael.

In this period Pope Alexander was created, elected amid contention with Octavian, surnamed Victor. When the latter died in the error of schism, Guy of Crema, named Paschal, succeeded him. When he likewise died in error, John of Struma, surnamed Calixtus, was similarly substituted in the schism. The emperor supported these three heresiarchs and fostered schism in the Church for seventeen years. And because it is fitting that one who is filthy should become filthier still, during this time he inflicted many evils and also suffered many.

In 1159 he fought the Milanese near Carcano, and fortune was adverse to both sides. But in 1162 he captured and destroyed Milan, dividing its inhabitants’ residence among four boroughs. At last he installed rulers according to his own will in all the cities of Lombardy. Having victoriously accomplished these things, the emperor returned to Germany, glorious in victories.

As time passed, when the Romans attacked Tusculum and the imperial chancellery’s men defended it with strength of arm, and many thousands of Romans had fallen:

> **[Note: Col. 0513D, Este manuscript:]** During this period the Germans, who were staying near Tusculum for the emperor, attacked the Romans at Monte Porzio and killed so many from the ninth hour until Vespers that never had so many thousands of Romans been slain, though in Hannibal’s time so many were killed that Hannibal had three baskets of rings, taken from the fingers of the slain nobles, sent to Carthage. Many of them are buried at Saint Stephen’s and have this epitaph:
>
> “A thousand, ten tens, and sixteen times six.”

[Col. 0513D] In the year of the Lord 1167 the emperor came swiftly to the City and enthroned Paschal the heresiarch in the Apostolic See at Saint Peter’s. When the Romans had fortified the church of Saint Peter as a castle, he could not endure it patiently and burned the Atrium, profaning it. Therefore, by God’s nod—for He leaves no evil unpunished—he lost nearly all his men to a deadly plague.

But in that same year, 1167, the cities of Italy conspired against him and rebuilt Milan. [Col. 0514A] Alas! Even that city was not free from the conspiracy which it had placed at the summit over the others. It turned its hand against itself, reforging for itself with its own hammer the pestilential hammer.

> **[Note: Col. 0514D, Este manuscript:]** “But by divine vengeance the fashioned hammer strikes its fashioner, now an unforeseen enemy.”

And an increase of vengeance: that son against father, freedman against patron, servant against lord, or any person against whom he had sinned, should now presumptuously strike as an unforeseen enemy his venerable friend. Therefore, as Frederick returned to his homeland, his route through the plain was blocked and he had to pass through rugged and pathless mountain places, until he reached the German kingdoms.

In this time a priest of Cremona was elected, who, although worthy in other merits and learning, was nevertheless deposed because of the schism. And so may be fulfilled the popular proverb: “To whom one thing happens, that will not be the only thing.”

These are added in the Este manuscript. Concerning Emperor Manuel.

In the same year Emperor Manuel of Constantinople captured, in the space of one day, a vast multitude of Venetians scattered throughout Greece, as birds are caught by a hidden hunter’s snare. This was because, from envious jealousy, they had attacked other Latins who had entered the emperor’s favour, leaving them half-dead after wounds. Therefore the Venetians, with a great multitude of men and one hundred galleys, entered Romania and captured certain islands. But while wintering at Chios, nearly all died of plague. Those who returned alive killed their own doge [Col. 0514C].

These matters follow in both manuscripts.

In the following year, namely 1168, the Lombards founded a colony, or new settlement of colonists, and named it Alexandria after Pope Alexander. Others call it the New City; the Pavians call it Palea to this day. In the same year the Romans, recovering their strength, captured Albano and, after stripping it of every good, burned it.

This is contained in one Este manuscript only. Concerning the siege of Ancona.

In the year of the Lord 1172, Christian, archchancellor and archbishop of Mainz, besieged Ancona [Col. 0514D] with the Venetians. He pressed the besieged so severely that they ate unclean meat, preserved hides, and other forbidden or unclean things, and sold an ass’s head for one hundred and forty denarii. Yet, even defeated, they resisted bravely; and when they had been strengthened by Manuel of Constantinople’s treasures of money, the Lord delivered them from the hands of their persecutor.

This is in both manuscripts.

[Col. 0515A]

In the following year, 1169, the city of Cremona began to be encircled with the protection of walls. Later, returning to Italy in 1174, the emperor destroyed Susa and besieged Palea, but did not reap and carried nothing into his barns. In the same year almighty God performed many miracles at the invocation of Saint Himerius the confessor. In 1175, when the Lombards had assembled against the emperor at Castesio, he subdued them after their swords had been surrendered and received them into a submission worthy of the empire.

The Este manuscript adds:

Around this time, Baldwin, king of Jerusalem—magnificent in glorious victories, though leprous—gave his sister in marriage to William, eldest son of Marquis William of Montferrat [Col. 0515B]. He was handsome in appearance, a military man, a vigorous knight, armed with virtues, proven in strength. When the sick and elephantine king wished to place the crown upon him, William refused, holding the county of Jaffa by hereditary right. Yet he held the entire kingdom in guardianship and begot a handsome son named Baldwin. After his uncle the king and his father had died, Baldwin was later crowned king although under age; he was under the guardianship of the Templars. Raymond, count of Tripoli, was summoned by the barons to the guardianship of the kingdom.

[Col. 0515C] In the same year lightning struck the church of Cremona. In the year of the Lord 1176, fighting at Legnano, the emperor’s army was defeated by the Lombards. O wheel of fortune, which now humbles and now exalts! Or rather, not fortune, but the Lord, who kills and gives life, brings down to hell and brings back. “The Lord makes poor and makes rich; He humbles and exalts” (1 Samuel 2). Therefore, seeing that “a man shall not prevail by his own strength” (ibid.), seeing that God “exalts the humble and casts down the mighty” (Luke 1), and considering that He founded His Church upon the firm rock, so that the gates of hell should not prevail against it (Matthew 16), in the year of the Lord 1177 Frederick humbled himself beneath God’s mighty hand. At Venice he made peace with Alexander, the supreme pontiff; having been separated [Col. 0515D] from the bosom of Mother Church, he was reconciled to the universal Church. There also he concluded a truce for six years with the Lombards and for fifteen years with the Sicilian king.

> **[Note: Col. 0515D, Este manuscript adds:]** And then there was famine in Italy.

In that year Christians fought Saracens overseas and prevailed, because seven thousand Christians made a dish of thirty-two thousand Saracens. The emperor therefore returned to Germany, and the Apostolic See went to Rome, where in 1179 it held a general council, established canons, and promulgated them. At that time my ordainer Offredus, a simple, gentle man devoted to God, was bishop of Cremona. In 1181 [Col. 0516A] Pope Lucius was created; he attacked the Romans vigorously on behalf of Tusculum.

These things are from the Este manuscript.

Around this time the emperor of Constantinople commanded Marquis William of Montferrat to send one of his sons to Constantinople, to whom he would marry his daughter. Conrad and Boniface were then married; Frederick served in clerical orders and later became bishop of Alba.

> **[Note: Col. 0516D, Este manuscript:]** It reads “bishop of Galba.”

But family lineage made him more high-minded than episcopal order required. William therefore sent to Constantinople the younger son, Raynerius, a youth handsome in age and beautiful in appearance. Manuel gave him his daughter Kyramaria in marriage [Col. 0516B] and crowned him king of Thessalonica.

Concerning Manuel and Alexius.

Manuel of Constantinople was succeeded by his son, the boy Alexius, whom he had begotten by Almaton, daughter of the prince of Antioch. After Alexius had reigned two years, Andronicus killed him and reigned three years. Having begun his iniquity, he also killed the boy’s empress-mother, and Raynerius, the emperor’s son-in-law, together with Raynerius’s wife. Finally, he killed many Greek nobles and blinded very many others.

Concerning the rebuilding of Crema and the earthquake.

In the year of the Lord 1185, the emperor came into Italy and rebuilt Crema out of hatred for the Cremonese. In the same year Pope Urban III was created [Col. 0516C]. In the same year there was a considerable earthquake in Italy; and the army of William, king of Sicily, armed itself against Andronicus’s wickedness and captured Dyrrhachium and Thessalonica. But after those places had been retaken, they were captured or returned in confusion. In the same year the marriage of King Henry and Constance, daughter of the former Sicilian king Roger, was celebrated at Milan.

These things are from the Caesarean Vienna manuscript.

In the year of the Lord 1183, the emperor made peace with the Lombards at Constance. In 1184 Pope Lucius came to Verona. In the preceding year he had ordained me subdeacon, and because of this he had sent me to the emperor. In 1185 [Col. 0516D], the emperor, returning to Italy, rebuilt Crema out of hatred for the Cremonese. In that year I, Sicard, compiler and writer of the present work, was elected, although unworthy, at Cremona to episcopal office. Also in that year Urban, cardinal and archbishop of Milan, was created pope. Also in that year there was a moderate earthquake in Italy. In 1186 the emperor utterly destroyed a certain castle of the Cremonese called Manfredi. But by the Lord’s agency, through my ministry, a reconciliation was made between the emperor and my fellow citizens. In 1187 [Col. 0517A], Jerusalem was captured by Saladin and the Lord’s land was occupied by unbelievers.

These things are added in the Este manuscript.

The cause of this invasion was the wickedness of the Christians. For although peace between Saladin and the king of Jerusalem had been confirmed, Christians, by the command of Raynald, prince of Montreal and lord of the Vale of Hebron, wickedly violated it by seizing Saracen caravans. Another cause was the discord between King Guy and Bohemond, count of Tripoli. The cause of the discord was envy or indignation because Queen Sibylla, after her husband had died, married Guy of Poitou and, after her son’s death, gave the crown to a foreigner without the assent [Col. 0517B] of the count himself and the other barons.

The manner of the conquest was this. Entering the land, Saladin first besieged Tiberias. King Guy encamped at Mascalia. Hear an omen indicating the impending disaster. When, during that night, a reading was being read at Matins to Patriarch Heraclius under his tent, the passage encountered concerned the Ark of the Covenant, once captured by the Philistines. At daybreak he fought. The count of Tripoli fled. The king, the Holy Cross, the often-mentioned elder Marquis William of Montferrat—who had come to the Holy Land on pilgrimage and to guard his grandson—the other barons all together, and the people were captured. The Christians’ strongholds were overcome, and then Tiberias was taken. The aforesaid Raynald, author of the crime [Col. 0517C], was beheaded by Saladin’s order, and many others likewise had their heads cut off.

Moreover Acre, Sidon, Beirut, and Byblos were captured. Meanwhile, by God’s will, Conrad, marquis of Montferrat, came from Constantinople intending to visit the Lord’s sepulchre. Learning that Acre had been occupied by unbelievers, he came with a favourable second wind to Tyre. Its citizens, like men without a head, gladly received him, submitting themselves and their city to his direction. Saladin therefore came from Beirut to Tyre, bringing with him Marquis William, Conrad’s father, whom he had captured in war, so that he might obtain the son’s surrender and that of the city as the price of the father’s ransom. Through the father he informed the son that, for his own liberation and that of several others, he should surrender the city. Conrad replied that he would not give even one stone [Col. 0517D] of the city.

Saladin approached, threatening that the father would be pierced with spears; Conrad threatened that he himself would shoot the first arrow at his father. O happy impiety, which, for the salvation of Christians, boasts that he would pierce a father exposed to barbarian weapons, setting aside filial reverence! But O memorable, pious impiety, which judges the love of God to be preferred to love for one’s father! Yet at his father’s own urging, Conrad judged his father contemptible, as an old man to be redeemed for no price.

Tyre having been besieged for seven days, Saladin returned to Acre. Then, after subduing Neapolis, Nazareth, Capha, Caesarea of Palestine, Jaffa, Azotus, Gaza, Ascalon, and other places adjoining Jerusalem, he subjected Jerusalem by a surrender involving tribute. He sanctified according to his own custom, and kept sanctified, the Temple of the Lord, which Christians had earlier profaned irreverently [Col. 0518A]; but he entrusted the Lord’s Sepulchre and Bethlehem to Syrian guardians. Moreover, he allowed more than one hundred thousand conquered Christians to depart and be conducted as far as Tripoli. But stripped by the Tripolitans and Antiochenes, on foot and destitute, they entered Armenia; scattered as far as Iconium, they were reduced to nothing by hunger, cold, and nakedness through God’s just judgment, paying the penalty after they had defiled God’s inheritance.

Observe that through Emperor Heraclius the Cross was recovered; but under the same Heraclius Jerusalem was afterwards attacked by the followers of Muhammad. And now, recovered under Pope Urban, it has now been subdued under Urban by those same barbarians.

[Col. 0518B] Meanwhile Conrad of Montferrat, the high-minded lord of Tyre, had twice gained victory in naval battle; with the help of the Pisans he had bravely brought out and still more bravely secured galleys and several ships, even from the port of Acre; and he had procured sufficient provisions for the citizens. He had also strongly constructed a barbican, awaiting the enemy’s victorious assault. Accordingly, in the month of November Saladin came for a second siege of Tyre; and when night arrived, forty cubits of the barbican’s wall collapsed. The Tyrians, remembering Jericho, were greatly afraid. But the marquis did not sleep: on the following day he restored it through masons, with men and women alike carrying sand and stones even in their laps.

[Col. 0518C] Saladin sent forward archers. The marquis dispatched the Pisans to Acre, making women, dressed as men, climb the walls so that the city might appear full of people. The Pisans returned victorious, bringing back two laden ships. Saladin therefore attacked the city by land and sea, especially because, believing that the marquis and the Pisans intended to flee together, he had assigned galleys to keep watch. Five of these were captured, laden with noblemen and pirates, arms and provisions. Moved by grief, Saladin attacked the barbican in a land battle, assailing it with stone-throwers and mangonels, siege-engines, darts, arrows, and missiles. When the marquis was being too severely pressed, he recalled his men from their naval victory and fought a land battle, inflicting manifold losses upon the Saracens without loss to his own men.

[Col. 0518D] Saladin therefore, seeing that he was making no progress at all by naval warfare, ordered nine galleys to be taken to Beirut. The Christians bravely pursued them and pressed them so hard that Saladin had eight of them burned with his own Greek fire; the ninth was wrecked on the Sidonian shore. Thus Saladin’s fleet having been destroyed, and seeing that he could not succeed in the siege, he burned all his engines and withdrew from the siege on the day before the Kalends of January [31 December]. As a sign of mourning, he had the tail cut off his own horse, which he rode, in order thereby to incite his men to avenge the injury.

The two manuscripts continue.

In the same year the gates of the city of Cremona were built. In the same year Gregory was made pope at Ferrara. [Col. 0519A] He was a most devout man, whose presence the world, lying in wickedness, was not worthy to enjoy; and therefore, when he had sat scarcely two months, God took him away. He strongly exhorted Christians to take up the sign of the cross and hasten to recover the holy city of Jerusalem, the cross, and the Lord’s sepulchre.

The victorious emperor, therefore, leaving Italy peaceful both for himself and internally, returned to Germany. Having received the sign of the cross, he sent noble and high-minded envoys to Saladin, warning and inviting him to leave the land of Christ which he had invaded. At that time Clement succeeded Gregory in the papacy. At the request of our fellow citizens, however, we went to Germany to obtain from the emperor permission to rebuild Manfred’s castle. [Col. 0519B] But, disappointed in our hope, we returned and, in the year of the Lord 1188, began the Castle of the Lion more fortunately. In the year 1189, moreover, we sent overseas the Cremonese Bursa, which we had caused to be built, laden with persons and goods to aid the land.

The Este manuscript inserts the following. On the siege of Azotus.

In the year of the Lord 1188, when the Tyrians, hard pressed by severe famine, did not dare to go out for timber or fodder because the Saracens met them, they attacked Azotus by command of the marquis with a naval fleet commanded by Hugh of Tiberias. There they captured the admiral—the man who had captured King Guy—and freed forty Christians [Col. 0519C] from prison; they also took five hundred captive knights, and, proceeding to Tyre with immense money, carried off an abundance of provisions. In exchange for this admiral, the marquis recovered his father. Moreover, ships of pilgrims began to arrive; and Margaritus, admiral of the king of Sicily, came to Tyre with his fleet. Since his pirates mistreated the Tyrians, they were forced to leave Tyre and put in at Tripoli, where, dying of hunger, they received their deserved punishment.

In the same year Saladin came to Tripoli; seeing that he could make no progress there, he turned his course toward the principality of Antioch, subduing Gabulum, Laodicea, Saone, Guard, Trapessac, Guasconum, and many other places. Afterwards, [Col. 0519D] returning to Galilee, he compelled by starvation the exceedingly well-fortified castle of Belvoir, which guarded the Jordan frontier and controlled the roads of Tiberias, Neapolis, and Nazareth, to surrender. Moreover, two counts of King William of Sicily arrived at Tyre with five hundred knights and fifty galleys. Many other pilgrims also arrived, with the venerable G., archbishop of Ravenna and legate of the Roman See. With these men the marquis overthrew by strong hand a multitude of Saracens from Sidon.

In the same year the magnanimous emperor, in accordance with imperial custom, sent Count Henry of Deti to Saladin, warning and admonishing him to leave the land of Jesus Christ which he had invaded. For it is the custom of the Empire to declare war on its enemies, [Col. 0520A] since it is accustomed to attack no one secretly in war.

## On the pilgrimage of Archbishop Ubaldo with other pilgrims overseas

In the year of the Lord 1189, Ubaldo, archbishop of Pisa and likewise legate of the Apostolic See, and pilgrims from every western province, arrived at Tyre. Since Tyre could not contain them, divisions arose among different parties, to such a degree that the question of King Guy’s entrance into the city—he being come from Tripoli—and the marquis’s prohibition produced sedition, scandal, and civil war. Among the pilgrims’ many plans, Acre was chosen for siege. They therefore attacked and besieged it in the month of August. But they themselves were likewise besieged by Saladin, [Col. 0520B] and were so fiercely attacked that they had no hope of escape. Yet unexpectedly forty ships arrived, followed by innumerable knights and barons.

Saladin afflicted the Christians day and night without interruption. Therefore the marquis and the archbishop of Ravenna, who had neither come to the siege nor approved of coming, were humbly invited by the besieged, through the bishop of Nenorensis and the landgrave of Thuringia, to come to their aid. They came, but against the marquis’s will, for he knew the Turks’ cunning. The French, confident in themselves, approved going out to battle. Battle was fought; the Templars and about seven thousand pilgrims were struck down. On the following day Saladin had the bodies disembowelled and thrown into the river, in order to [lacuna] increase it and corrupt the air and water. [Col. 0520C]

After this the Lombard marquises and counts, and more than five hundred knights, arrived; among them was the Cremonese Bursa, which had been built at Cremona and sent overseas, laden with persons and goods for the assistance of the Holy Land. The pilgrims then devised a plan to prevent the Saracens alike from entering and leaving the city, since the way lay open freely from Mount Muscard. When no one could be found willing to encamp there, the marquis—ready and bold for every undertaking—encamped there; and for that reason Saladin attacked him more fiercely. He ordered sea-rocks cut away so that a harbour might be made there to receive the Tyrian vessels; and to this day it is called the Marquis’s Harbour.

[Col. 0520D] The pilgrims fortified themselves by ditches dug inside, around, and outside, so that, standing in the middle, they might more easily defend themselves from attacks from either side. They also appointed leaders or governors, so that all dispute might be removed: the French were to obey their own leaders, and those from the Empire the imperial leaders. And behold, forty-five galleys, coming from Egypt on the feast of Saint Stephen, put in at the harbour of Acre. The pilgrims, therefore, astonished and hemmed in by land and sea, chose rather to die fighting than be subdued without a contest. The marquis, skilled in warfare, encouraged them when they had become dispirited, assuring them all that he would utterly crush the Saracens’ galleys.

Accordingly he went to Tyre in a small galley, though in that night he was a hundred times tormented to death by the violence of the winds. [Col. 0521A] Having explained to the Tyrians the army’s necessities and encouraged them to man the galleys, they said: “We are ready to live with you and to go with you to death.” And behold, at the end of February the marquis appeared bravely with a fleet in the harbour of Acre, peacefully unloading the Saracens’ vessels, laden with provisions, in their very presence. Moreover, although the city would doubtless have been overcome and captured by siege-towers, the Saracens on the other side burned the siege-towers with Greek fire. Two Saracen galleys were also captured in naval combat.

Both manuscripts continue, though with not a few variations and additions from the Este manuscript.

In the same year the most fortunate emperor, having five sons—Henry, his firstborn among the others, whom he had made Caesar; Frederick, duke of Swabia; Otto, count; Conrad; and Philip, duke—and Adelaide, wedded to Christ, entrusted himself and the rest, together with the kingdom and royal prerogatives, to Caesar Henry. Leaving the western Empire in the most peaceful and orderly state, he went to the regions of the East with these companions, and in the order here written.

> [Note: Col. 0521C] Este manuscript: “And on the feast of Saint George [Col. 0521D] he set out. Departing from Germany, he travelled by ship from Regensburg down toward Austria, while the army followed overland with horses and wagons. Then, after establishing a hospital in Pannonia for poor sick persons and assigning it hospital staff and necessities, he entered Hungary, where he is said to have had ninety thousand fighting men, including twelve thousand knights. Received honourably by Béla of Hungary at Esztergom, he passed through Hungary and sent ahead to Emperor Isaac, etc.”

Departing from Germany, he entered Hungary, where he is said to have had ninety thousand fighting men. Received honourably by the king of Hungary, he passed through Hungary and sent the bishop of Münster and Count Robert of Nassau to the emperor of Constantinople. The latter detained them and sent three armies to the entrance of Bulgaria [Col. 0521C] to prevent the passage. There was there a forest four days’ journey in extent; the governor of Bulgaria devastated its very narrow road, and, constructing a fortification at the forest’s exit, prepared with his armies to attack the emperor. But after the great forest had been crossed with much toil and difficulty, the duke of Swabia, who led the army, destroyed the fortification and killed a great multitude of its defenders.

> [Note: Col. 0521D] Este manuscript: “When he approached the city of Niš, the counts of Serbia eagerly sought to submit themselves gratefully; but the most serene emperor, desiring peace, refused to receive them. Then, on the ninth day before the Kalends of September [24 August], they attacked and captured the city called Philippi. It is a metropolitan city of Macedonia. Elsewhere we have learned that they went not to Philippi but to Philippopolis. There the emperor was assured of the capture of his envoys; and there Emperor Isaac sent a letter to the emperor, [Col. 0522C] full of haughtiness and arrogance, saying: ‘Isaac, [Col. 0522D] most holy, most excellent, most powerful, sublime emperor established by God, ruler of the Romans, Augustus, heir to the crown of the great Constantine, to the beloved brother of his empire, the most eminent prince of Germany: his favour and brotherly and pure affection.’ The content of the letter was indignation at the emperor’s presumptuous arrival in Greece. Then the Greek emperor [text unfinished], etc.”

At length the Greek emperor sent a very great army of Greeks and Turks against the Roman emperor. Against them his son, the duke of Swabia, fighting fiercely, overcame and routed them; and after they had withdrawn within certain [Col. 0522A] walls, he took the place by great force and killed them all. He burned alive twelve Turks who had taken refuge in a certain fortification and were resisting bravely. Then the Greek emperor sent sixteen honourable envoys to the Roman emperor, promising safe and unharmed passage. Although the magnanimous emperor wished, in revenge for the aforesaid wrongs which the Greek emperor had wickedly committed, to attack Constantinople, he was nevertheless persuaded by the counsel of princes urging him to hasten to the Holy Land for the Christians’ aid. He demanded and obtained hostages, who conducted him to Gallipoli and secured his sea-passage. The army crossed during five days of August, the duke first and the father afterwards.

After they had crossed, [Col. 0522B]

> [Note: Col. 0522D] Este manuscript: “After many labours and many hardships, they reached the city of Tyachitum and the Lycian city, namely Aegeae, where Cosmas and Damian were crowned by martyrdom; then Sardis and Philadelphia.”

they came to Philadelphia. The duke of Philadelphia, refusing a market, armed himself for battle; but at last, seeing that he could not resist, he promised a market and allowed the emperor, with a few men, to enter the city. Later, because of high prices, conflict arose between Greeks and Germans. War began, and for two days and nights they fought continuously without the emperor’s consent. At last the defeated Greeks withdrew into the city fortification, made an agreement, and granted a tolerable market, passing goods in baskets by ropes and receiving the price in the same manner.
