Moreover, as the emperor was leaving Philadelphia, the duke gave him a guide in return for the duchy; the guide led the army through trackless and impassable, mountainous and wooded places, [Col. 0522C] where for two days they found no provisions whatever.

> [Note: Col. 0522D] Este manuscript: “They also passed through the city of Hierapolis, where the blessed Philip suffered.”

At the exit from the forest, certain Greeks and Armenians peacefully supplied them with such a market as they could.

Moreover, the Turcomans of Betia—

> [Note: Col. 0522D] Este manuscript: “Of Becia, who are also called Oebeduini.”

—rustic people subject to no ruler, who dwell not in walled towns or cities but in the countryside, assembled an infinite and innumerable army—

> [Note: Col. 0522D] Este manuscript: “An army of more than one hundred thousand.”

—and attacked the Christian army night and day for four weeks, so that the Christian army always marched armed. Nevertheless, it killed a multitude of them, together with a certain admiral, commander of their forces. Restanus, however, their lord, [Col. 0523A] blocked the passage in a mountain defile with a great army, saying that they would not pass unless they gave a hundred pack animals laden with gold and silver. The emperor answered that he would gladly give them, but only one *menolatum* [a term of uncertain meaning].

Meanwhile the sultan’s envoys, who were deceitfully leading him, said that they would soon enter the sultan’s land, where that people could no longer harm him. Then, because God does not abandon those who hope in him, a certain admiral, inspired by heavenly grace—

> [Note: Col. 0523C] Este manuscript: “Inspired—or perhaps because he had fallen into our men’s hands, he approached the emperor [Col. 0523D] through fear of death, etc.”

—revealed the deception to the emperor and foretold a battle for the following morning. Making him avoid the plain into which he had begun to enter, he led him through the mountains. They met in the mountains; battle was fought on both sides. But after leaving the baggage and provisions behind, the duke descended bravely from the mountain, [Col. 0523B] and the emperor descended also; attacking the enemy victoriously, they overcame their foes. In this battle the duke, struck by a stone, lost two teeth. Thereupon the guides appointed by the sultan fled, fearing that the emperor would punish their exposed treachery.

The Christian army, trusting in the Lord who led Israel through the wilderness, advanced for fifteen days across a certain plain and ate horseflesh. The rustic Turks mentioned above, believing that they had entirely perished from hunger, again rose to war near the city of Pholomena with a great force of cavalry and infantry, but the unconquered emperor defeated them. When a great multitude had crowded into a certain enclosure, the Germans burned them all; and from that time [Col. 0523C] those rustic Turcomans pursued the army no further.

> [Note: Col. 0523D] Este manuscript: “But they vanished before the emperor like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth. In the year of the Lord 1190, Melechinus, the sultan’s son, came to meet [him] with an army of five hundred thousand horsemen, and …”

But on the next day Melectinus, the sultan’s son, came to meet them with an army and sent envoys to the emperor, saying: “Turn back. What do you think you can do, when I have more banners than you have soldiers?” When the emperor reached a certain bridge, the Turks fled both in front and behind. But the duke defeated those in front, and the emperor killed most of those behind; thus the entire army crossed the bridge.

At length an immense and innumerable multitude of Turks surrounded the Christian army on every side, so that for four [Col. 0524A] weeks, as it marched, they attacked fiercely day and night; and the Christians lacked provisions other than horseflesh. Having found no water for a day and night, they captured a Turk who showed them where, thirsty and hungry, they found brackish water. On the following day they encamped in the garden of Leonium, a city of Isauria. From there the sultan had sent word to the emperor that he had entered his land wrongly. The emperor sent back asking whether he would grant a market or not. The sultan answered that he would grant one; but because he offered goods at an excessive price, the Christians armed themselves for battle.

When the Friday of the Ember Days was at hand, Godfrey, bishop of Würzburg, declared that he had seen blessed George fighting powerfully against the enemies on the Christians’ behalf. Battle having been proclaimed, [Col. 0524B] and permission given to eat meat, they advanced to war. The duke stormed the city and bravely took it, killing nearly all the rebels. The emperor likewise—

> [Note: Col. 0523D] Este manuscript: “Directing the victorious eagles against the sultan’s son, who was fighting in the rear, he exterminated the aforesaid thousands of Turks and Turcomans, and from among them, etc.”

—defeated the sultan’s son fighting in the rear and killed an innumerable multitude of his men.

The city having been taken by force, the sultan withdrew into an extremely strong fortification within the city and sent to the emperor, saying that he wished to grant a market and would give whatever he might wish to receive. The emperor demanded hostages; and because of the stench of corpses—for the houses and streets were full of corpses—he went down from the city and encamped in the suburbs. The sultan therefore gave hostages, and also granted a market and fodder for the horses. But because he tried to sell the horses at an excessive price, [Col. 0524C] offering a horse for a hundred marks, the Germans countered deceit with deceit and accepted Ferron [perhaps a coin or unit] for one mark. Hearing this, the sultan sent to the emperor, complaining that his men were being cheated in price. The emperor replied: “If they gave a good market, they would receive a good mark.” Assessors of justice were therefore appointed on both sides.

Moreover, as the Christian army proceeded, it suffered many troubles from certain rustic Turcomans who were not under the sultan’s authority, until—

> [Note: Col. 0523D] Este manuscript: “Until it reached the city of Laurenda, which separates Armenia from Lycaonia, and came to the mountains of Armenia. There, in the silence of night, the unexpected clatter and tumult of arms was heard; since there was no one [present], it was conjectured that this was an omen of approaching misfortune. In the mountains of Armenia it found Greeks and Armenians eagerly providing a market. When news of these victories reached Saladin, he was alarmed; and on the holy day of Pentecost [Col. 0524C] Saladin, with so great a multitude of his men covering mountains, hills, and plain as is believed never to have appeared together anywhere, [Col. 0524D] attacked the Christians powerfully, hoping to seize all the tents and capture the wretched Christians. But his plan came to nothing, for the Christians resisted bravely and inflicted considerable injury upon him with crossbows. Saladin therefore withdrew and sent a great part of his army to resist the emperor. But alas! A few days later the emperor’s death became known, and a report arriving of the Sicilian king’s death greatly disturbed the Christian army. Descending from the mountains, the emperor found the river Saleph; he travelled along its bank for two days and on the third day rested in pleasant places.

> **On the death of Emperor Frederick I**
>
> Since the heat was very great, the emperor went down into the river with two knights, wishing to bathe. When he began to swim, he struck against a rock and lost his life while swimming. Seized by the knights, he was brought half alive to the bank; having received penance and the body of the Lord, he died that day. Alas for grief! The watery element suffocates him whom fiery wars could not conquer. Unvanquished by the hardness of iron, he is conquered by the softness of the fluid element. That day was fulfilled the prophecy inscribed in Chaldean letters on a tower built near the river: “The better than men and mightier than all shall be drowned in the waters of Saleph.” For this reason Emperor Manuel of Constantinople, intending to cross there, had a bridge built at that place. Carrying him to the city of Selaphim, they embalmed him with spices. Having appointed the duke lord over the army, [Col. 0525C] they reached Tarsus, a city of Cilicia, where they embalmed the emperor’s flesh. Then, meeting Leo of the Mountains, they were magnificently received by him and led with great triumph to the city of Mamistra, where flows a river called Geon by the inhabitants. Its spring—or rather source—is each year filled only during Lent with such a multitude of fish that on that day religious Armenians are adequately fed, though they will eat no more fish during the rest of Lent. When the duke fell ill there, the Armenian Catholicos visited him. Thereafter, when the duke had reached Antioch by ship, the Christian army proceeded through Portella, where Darius is said to be buried and Alexander’s treasure hidden. Then, through a certain gateway structure, they reached a castle called Guasconum by the inhabitants. Since Saladin held it, the Christian army was hindered by archers.”

—came to the mountains of Armenia. In the mountains of Armenia it found Greeks and Armenians eagerly providing a market. Descending from the mountains, it found the river Caleph; travelling along its bank for two days, it rested on the third day in pleasant places.

Since the heat was very great, the emperor went down into the river with two knights, wishing to bathe; and when he began to swim, he was drowned. Alas for grief! Behold, the watery element suffocates him whom fiery wars could not conquer: unconquered by the hardness of iron, he is conquered by the softness of the fluid element. Carrying him to the city of Salaphim, they embalmed him with spices. Having appointed the duke lord over the army, they reached Tarsus. Then, meeting Leo of the Mountains, they were magnificently received by him and led with great triumph to the city of Mamistra. [Col. 0525B] When the duke fell ill there, the Armenian Catholicos visited him. Then they travelled to Thegium; then through a narrow pass called the Gate they came to a castle called Gastorium. Since Saladin held it, the Christian army was hindered by archers. Then the patriarch and prince of Antioch came to meet them and led the duke and army with triumph to Antioch.

> [Note: Col. 0526C] Este manuscript: “They honourably buried the emperor’s flesh. There, by counsel of the prince and patriarch, he stayed until he summoned to himself the marquis of Montferrat, who was then at the siege of Acre. On receiving this summons, and after consulting the barons, he hastened to Antioch. During his absence, because the foot soldiers of the army at Acre were restrained by no one, on the feast of Saint James more than eight [the reading is materially uncertain] of the roaming men were killed in a Saracen attack. Passing through Tyre, the marquis received with the highest honour Count Henry of Champagne, then arriving; when he came to the army, the count was approved as duke by all. Passing through Tripoli, the marquis supported needy widows, orphans, and nobles with gold and silver. Then he put in at the harbour of Saint Symeon, also called Soldinus by the inhabitants. Near it is the Black Mountain, inhabited by a multitude of hermits praising God in diverse languages and customs. There, received by the patriarch, prince, and duke with great triumph, he was led into the city, to whom the duke wholly entrusted himself and the army, declaring that he wished to obey him as a father’s commands. Hearing this, Saladin sent an army under his brother Rachahadin and his son Marahalin to occupy the district of Beirut. When the duke and marquis learned this, having come from Antioch as far as Tripoli and having been harassed in many ways by Saracens, Audocras, and others, they went by ship from Tripoli to Tyre, where they entrusted the emperor’s bones to a coffin-tomb.”

There, by counsel of the prince and patriarch, he stayed until he summoned Conrad, marquis of Montferrat, to himself; Conrad was then at the siege of Acre. Having heard the summons and consulted the barons, he hastened to Antioch, passing through Tyre, where he received with the highest honour Count Henry of Champagne, who was then arriving. [Col. 0525C] Passing through Tripoli, he supported needy widows, orphans, and nobles with gold and silver. Arriving at the Gate of Saint Symeon, he was received with great triumph by the patriarch, prince, and duke, and entered the city. [Col. 0526A] The duke wholly entrusted himself and the army to him, declaring that he wished to obey paternal commands. Hearing this, Saladin sent an army under his brother Rachahadin and his son Mirrhalin to occupy the district of Beirut. When the duke and marquis learned this, they travelled by ship to the siege of Acre.

Who and how great Conrad, marquis of Montferrat, was, let us review the preceding sequence. William, marquis of Montferrat, married the lady, sister of Lord Conrad king of the Romans and of Lord Frederick duke of Swabia. By her he begot five sons: William Longsword, Conrad, Boniface, Frederick, and Rayner. This was the order of their birth; their fortunes bestowed different gifts upon them. For the patriarch, the king of Jerusalem, and the princes of that kingdom arranged that William the Generous, [Col. 0526B] a military man, strong in physical power and proved in virtues, should marry the king’s sister. When the sick king, named Baldwin, wished to place the crown upon him, William refused the crown; but he held the whole kingdom in guardianship. He begot a son of elegant appearance who, after the death of his royal uncle and father, was crowned king despite being under age; the queen mother diligently maintained his guardianship.

Moreover, Emperor Manuel of Constantinople instructed the elder William, namely the marquis, to send one of his sons to Constantinople to receive his daughter and the kingdom of Salonica. Since Conrad and Boniface had wives and Frederick bore the clerical girdle, he sent Rayner, a handsome youth, to Constantinople; there he received the promised imperial daughter together with the crown of Salonica. But after enjoying the royal diadem for a short time, both departed this world. Frederick, the son of the aforesaid marquis, was bishop of Alba—

> [Note: Col. 0527D] Manuscript Caesar reads “bishop of Galba.”

—and his lineage made him more high-spirited than episcopal order required. Now let us continue the history of Conrad.

The following occur in the Este manuscript.

In the month of September the Germans encamped in the plain of Acre, and then the archbishop of Canterbury arrived. Afterwards the Christians went out from camp and determined to fight; they pursued Saladin, who after the Lombard manner carried his banner on a *carroccio*, as far as Saffuriya and Recortana, where the river of Acre rises. Having moved their camp from that place to pursue them, they afterwards returned unharmed to the plain. In the month of November severe famine seized the Christians, so that they were forced to eat horseflesh purchased at extremely high prices; and thus throughout the whole winter they were worn down by hunger, cold, and the sword.

Then Isabella, daughter of the former King Aymeric, claiming the inheritance of the kingdom by hereditary right after her sister’s death, was separated by sentence of the bishops from Sighifred of Tours, whom she had married. The barons joined her in marriage to the marquis and chose him king and lord. Being generous and high-minded, he maintained galleys at sea and refreshed the army with grain and barley when forty merchant ships arrived. [Col. 0527C] In a single day the price of a modius fell from one hundred bezants to eight, and continued falling until the year’s end.

## On Philip, count of Flanders; the king of the Franks; the duke of Burgundy; the count of Nevers; the count of Bar; and other events

In the year of the Lord 1191 Philip, count of Flanders, and afterwards the king of the Franks, the duke of Burgundy, the count of Nevers, and the count of Bar arrived. The king set up the royal camp before the Accursed Tower and built a stone palace, reasonably called Malvicinum (“Evil Neighbourhood”), so that the Accursed Tower, through the evil neighbourhood of the palace, might receive the true effect of its name from blows of stones. He ordered mangonels to be erected, siege-engines and mantelets prepared, and covered with sheets of lead because of Greek fire.

[Col. 0527D] When the count of Flanders died shortly afterwards, the king received fealty from the Flemings, cursed the Accursed Tower more frequently with mangonels, and attacked the city of Acre more fiercely. For after all his engines had been burned, at the command of the violently enraged king the pilgrims set ladders and climbed the walls, but were finally driven back by the oppressive heat and smoke. Alberic, the royal marshal, descended within the city walls and raged like a roaring lion; killing many men alone with a battle-axe, also called an axe, he was killed. The Saracens hurled his head to his fellow soldiers by a mangonel in place of a stone.

After the wall had been pierced, two Saracens left the city and asked to be baptized in Christ’s name; reborn, they proved faithful in their deeds. Under the marquis’s direction the mangonels were repaired. He surrendered Tyre to the king, keeping his promise that he would in every respect yield the city to the first king to arrive crowned. The king, however, fortified it with his own men.

[Col. 0528A] Meanwhile Richard, king of England, subdued the island of Cyprus to himself, capturing Isaac, who called himself emperor, and carrying off immense riches, provisions, and animals. Sailing from Cyprus across the sea, he encountered a Saracen ship sailing from Beirut and hastening to Acre. On it were seven hundred men very strong in war, with ample pay, every kind of weapon, Greek fire, serpents, crocodiles, and agents wickedly assigned for killing without distinction. [Col. 0528B] He attacked it three and four times with the twenty-four galleys with which he was approaching in the rearguard of his ships, at great loss to his own men. Afterwards, by the king’s reproaches and entreaties, threats and promised rewards, his men armed themselves, pierced the ship in attacking it, and sank it, preserving only two survivors from the shipwreck. One of these, when he reached the camp, he sent to Saladin; the other he sent into the city.

Moreover, the king of the Franks proclaimed battle, though the king of England disagreed. Battle was fought and the walls were cut with axes, while the Saracens sent to Saladin, asking him to hasten eagerly to their aid. When night came, a guard was refused to the marquis; but he received from Mostubus, with the consent of the king of France, [Col. 0528C] a guarantee of safety for a conference. When day came, the conference was held before the kings and other barons. In it Mostubus promised to surrender the city with all its possessions, provided that its inhabitants were allowed to depart unharmed. The Christians, however, demanded the Holy Cross, all captives, and the entire kingdom. Mostubus declared that Saladin must be consulted. Hostages were therefore given and Saladin was consulted; he promised to restore the Cross together with Acre, fifteen hundred Christians, one hundred knights, and two hundred thousand bezants.

While these things were being done, the king of England attacked the wall. The city was obtained by surrender on 12 July, in the year of the Lord 1191. Guards having been placed by the kings at the gates, entrance was open only to Frenchmen and Englishmen; all others, whether from the Roman Empire or elsewhere, although they had laboured for two years, were shamefully excluded. [Col. 0528D] For those wishing to enter were beaten with blows and cudgels. Thirteen, moreover, of the *polins had their feet cut off. Since, therefore, the kings had in their hands nearly fifty thousand people, apart from women, little children, and the multitude of others, which could scarcely be counted; vessels of Greek fire; galleys with *Salandri; seventy great ships; and other riches without number, they divided everything between themselves.

Let the Church and posterity to come judge whether it was fitting that the summit of royal honour should appropriate entirely to its own hands things acquired by the blood of others and by winter labours—when those men were not ashamed to have toiled scarcely three months. [Col. 0529A] They ought to have ascribed the victory not to themselves but to the Lord. Yet, since they presumed to ascribe it to themselves, they should have remembered the others whose bones the holy field reduced to ashes, or whom the present life endured as free men. For the archbishop of Ravenna, the Landgrave of Thuringia, Frederick duke of Swabia, and many counts and barons of the Empire died in the Lord; and the total number of the dead who perished by plague, famine, and sword is uncertain. Yet there is scarcely any doubt that, apart from princes, nearly two hundred thousand passed from this world during the siege.

Moreover, the king of France endeavoured to raise the marquis to kingship; the king of England, to restore Guy. At last, under an intervening agreement, Tyre, Sidon, and Beirut, together with half of Ascalon and Joppa, came to the marquis by hereditary right. In addition, the other half of Acre and of the whole kingdom acquired and to be acquired fell to Guy; but only during the other’s lifetime, and on the condition that neither should use the diadem. [Col. 0529B] After this, the king of France, having hired five hundred knights for himself and distributed the arms which had fallen to his share among the Temple, the Hospital, and the marquis, returned home—though everywhere the immense reproach was shouted in his face: “Shame on you, who flee and abandon the Lord’s land!”

But the king of England, because the promised money was not paid, killed all the captives, contrary to justice and law; they ought rather to have been preserved and reduced to servitude, except Monostobius [al-Mashtūb?], Carcosa, and certain other knights whom he released for money. [Col. 0529C] Saladin, however, did not repay evil for evil to the Christian captives. Thereafter the king of England recovered by land and sea Caph[a] and Caesarea; and when he came to Azotus, James of Avesnes was killed. Then, while advancing toward Joppa, wintering at Ramla, Lydda, the Tower of the Knights, and Berthenubile, they came to Ascalon; and, seeing its walls broken down, they wept over it, rebuilding the walls and towers in a short time.

Meanwhile, a violent quarrel arose between the king of England and the duke of Burgundy, together with the other French barons, because he held them in contempt. They therefore returned to Tyre and proceeded to the marquis, with five hundred picked knights; with these they made great gains by raiding the villages of the Saracens. [Col. 0529D]

Both manuscripts proceed here. Concerning Emperor Henry VI.

In the year of the Lord 1190, Henry VI, son of Frederick I, reigned among the Romans for seven years after his father.

> [Note: Col. 0529D. Estense manuscript: “For eight years.”]

Celestine, the pope who had succeeded Clement, anointed him in 1191 and crowned him with the imperial diadem. In the same year the emperor gave Tusculum to the Apostolic See, and the Apostolic See gave it to the Romans. The Romans, however, destroyed the city [Col. 0530A] and its citadel, blinding some Tusculans and shamefully mutilating others.

In the same year the emperor descended into Apulia with the empress named Constance, daughter of the late Roger, king of Sicily—

> [Note: Col. 0529D. Estense manuscript: “of Sicily, and sister of King William.”]

—in order to obtain for himself the kingdom which was due to him by hereditary right—

> [Note: Col. 0529D. Estense manuscript: “by hereditary right, after the death of her brother.”]

But Tancred, who had already been set up in his place, had been crowned at Palermo. When the empress had therefore come to Salerno, the citizens of Salerno wickedly seized her [Col. 0530D] and sent her to King Tancred at Messina; he kept her in the palace at Palermo, with honour, etc.] … was due, and which a certain petty king had seized, in order to obtain it. But a certain pirate named Margaritus, having captured the empress at Salerno, led her, as befitted a queen, all the way to the city—namely Palermo—and preserved her with the honour most worthy of an empress.

The emperor, while besieging Naples, had almost all his men carried off by the death of plague—

> [Note: Col. 0530D. Estense manuscript: “carried off, was frustrated in his hope or purpose, and scarcely, etc.”]

—and scarcely returned to Germany.

In the same year occurred the disaster which the Cremonese call *Malamort* (“Evil Death”), because, near the city of Bergamo, while they were defending a castle against the Brescian force gathered with the Bergamese, by divine judgement they turned upon one another: some fell into boiling oil, others were captured and mutilated, others died. But the emperor, returning from Apulia, freed the captives from prison. In the same year the emperor granted Crema to the Cremonese and confirmed it by a privilege.

In the same year the king of France and the king of England, having crossed the sea, courageously attacked and captured Acre, which had been occupied by the unbelievers and besieged for a long time by Christians. Afterwards the king of England fought with Saladin and destroyed Ascalon. He too, when he crossed the sea, had received certain cities in Sicily by surrender, triumphantly taken possession of the island of Cyprus, and sunk Saladin’s ships, filled with serpents wickedly intended for the destruction [Col. 0530C] of Christians.

In that same year Conrad the marquis was killed by the Assassins: a military man, skilled in warfare, prudent and vigorous, brave and bold, proud, high-minded, devout, and most humble.

In 1192 the emperor held in custody the king of England, who was returning in a pilgrim’s garb and had been captured by the duke of Austria, because he appeared to have *praesconsisse* (sic; perhaps “presumed”) certain things against him in the kingdom of Sicily, and was believed wickedly to have plotted the death of Conrad the marquis.

The following is added in the Estense manuscript. Concerning the king of England and other events which occurred in his time.

In the year of the Lord 1192, the king of England, at Ascalon, [Col. 0530D] anxious about his departure and the governance of the land, asked the whole army to whom he might most safely entrust the land already conquered and yet to be conquered. After diverse votes—for some preferred Guy, who had been anointed, others the unconquered marquis, others the count of Champagne—the marquis was chosen and approved in the presence of the army. The king therefore summoned him to hasten, to receive royal mitres and sceptres. On the eighth day before the Kalends of May [24 April], letters were presented. On the same day he was murdered by the Assassins, who cried: “You shall not be marquis! You shall not [Col. 0531A] be king!” One of them was burned; another, while being flayed, confessed that he had done this, sent by command of his old master, at the order of the king of England.

On the third day, his pregnant wife was joined in marriage, against her will, to Count Henry when he came there. He quickly returned to Acre, took possession of the city, and prohibited Guy from entering. The king therefore gave Guy the kingdom of Cyprus, purchased for twenty thousand Byzantines.

After this Saladin besieged Joppa. There the patriarch-elect Ralph obtained a truce from Saladin: unless he had relief within two days, he was to surrender the town. Since he had no other means, he gave himself as a hostage for his sheep. Two days having passed, the king arrived by ship with the Pisans and bravely destroyed the Saracens who were storming the castle; a horse was provided for him by the castellan. [Col. 0531B] Infantrymen accompanied this one knight alone, and he pitched camp outside the city in the face of the Turks. The Turks were astonished, put to flight by the charge of one knight. They feared greatly that the king, so fierce, might wish to invade Egypt.

Therefore, with both armies withdrawing, a truce for three years was arranged, on the terms that Ascalon should be destroyed and possessed by neither side. Yet the king sinned even in this, because he did not free the patriarch, a chained hostage. The Christians therefore visited the Sepulchre and found there a naked Ethiopian collecting the libations of offerings, to the disgrace of Christians. But the king refused to approach in adoration the Sepulchre held under the hand of an unbeliever, and hastened to depart.

Since he was suspected in the death of the marquis, he reached Austria safely in the dress of a servant of the Templars and Hospitallers, having sent his own followers elsewhere. [Col. 0531C] There, while roasting chickens, he was recognized, captured, and presented to the duke of Austria. When the emperor heard that the king of England, returning in a servant’s garb, had been captured by the duke of Austria, he detained him in custody, because he appeared to have undertaken certain measures against him in the kingdom of Sicily and was believed wickedly to have plotted the death of Conrad the marquis. At last he released him under terms satisfactory to himself.

Both manuscripts continue.

In the year of the Lord 1194, the emperor returned to Italy and descended to the southern regions. He subdued Apulia, Calabria, [Col. 0531D] and Sicily; having powerfully obtained everything, he carried the wealth of the land and the treasures of the kingdom into Germany, and blinded Margaritus—

> [Note: Col. 0531D. The Estense manuscript adds: “He captured the queen and her son, who had succeeded his father, and whomsoever he wished. O how worthy is God’s recompense, who lets no evil go unpunished! The great men who sat in ambush with the rich in secret places are measured by the measure with which they had measured, and are judged by the judgement with which they had judged. Philip, however, the emperor’s brother, found in the palace at Palermo the daughter of Isaac, emperor of Constantinople, who had married Roger, Tancred’s eldest son, now a widow after her husband’s death; and, having found her, joined her to himself in lawful marriage. But Alexius, Isaac’s brother, blinded that same Emperor Isaac [Col. 0532D] and imprisoned his son Alexius, and usurped the Empire.”]

—himself, and captured whomsoever he wished.

In the year of the Lord 1196, we placed the bodies of the holy martyr Archelaus and the confessor Himerius in a stone shrine, consecrating the altar on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July [15 June], and solemnly holding a procession with one hundred and thirty ecclesiastical banners. [Col. 0532A]

In the year of the Lord 1197, the emperor returned to Italy and died and was buried in Sicily. At this time there was a certain Joachim, an abbot of Apulia, who possessed a spirit of prophecy. He prophesied the death of Emperor Henry, the future desolation of the Sicilian kingdom, and the failure of the Roman Empire; this was most clearly fulfilled. For the kingdom of Sicily has long been disturbed, and the Empire divided by schism.

(In the margin of the Caesarean manuscript a later hand added this note: “This author would have said more [Col. 0532B] had he lived and seen the deposition of Frederick and the vigorous successes of King Charles in the kingdom of Sicily.”)

In the same year we happily completed the castle of Jovis-alta, which we had begun from its first stone for the honour and benefit of the palace of Cremona.

In the year of the Lord 1198—

> [Note: Col. 0532D. Estense manuscript: “Emperor Henry, son of the late Emperor Frederick, died on the feast of Saint Michael in the kingdom of Sicily; and there was, etc.”]

—there was rebellion in the kingdom over the election of an emperor. For Emperor Henry, leaving a boy under guardianship by the empress, had obtained from the princes their election of the boy, and they had already sworn fealty to him. A struggle then arose in the German [Col. 0532C] lands between Philip, son of Frederick, brother of Henry, and paternal uncle of the boy, and Otto, son of the late Duke Henry of Saxony, both aspiring to the Empire; for each was elected by princes.

At this time Pope Innocent was created. In order that he might aid the boy and defend the rights of the Church, he fought with both swords against a certain Markward, who, by I know not what spirit, also professed himself to be the defender of the boy’s rights; and he weakened him by force. Yet Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily still wavered amid shifting loyalties. There was likewise diversity of allegiance in Germany; but among the contenders there was neither equal justice nor equal strength of support.

At this same time there was at Cremona a simple man, exceedingly faithful and devout, named Homobonus. At his death, and through his intercession, the Lord made many miracles manifest to this world. Therefore—

> [Note: Col. 0532D. Estense manuscript: “Therefore, setting out as a pilgrim for Rome in that same year, namely 1199, I came before the supreme pontiff and, by divine mercy, happily obtained that they should be enrolled in the Catalogue of Saints by ecclesiastical authority. In the year, etc.”]

—setting out as a pilgrim, I came before the supreme pontiff [Col. 0532D] and obtained the canonization for which I was asking.

In the year of the Lord 1199, the Milanese and Plaisantines came to Borgo San Donnino, and afterwards to Castrum Novum in the passes; grieving over their adverse loss, they returned. But the Veronese [Col. 0533A] defeated the Mantuan force, taking an innumerable multitude of them captive.

In the year of the Lord 1200, the Milanese and Brescian forces besieged the castle of Soncino, but vanished in their pride. For the Pavians defeated the Milanese army at Rosate, and the Cremonese and Plaisantines at Saint Andrew near Busseto. In the same year peace and concord were made between the Cremonese and the Mantuans, between whom there had long been discord, with a reciprocal exchange of services in the kiss of peace.

But civil discord arose between the Brescian knights and the people whom they call the Bruzella, exceedingly harmful to both sides. For, as the Lord testifies, every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and house will fall upon house. The Bruzella, indeed, dispersed the party of the knights. The knights, however, [Col. 0533B] allied themselves with the Cremonese and pressed hard upon the common people, whom Count Narisius commanded. The Romans, moreover, subdued the people of Viterbo with a strong arm.

In the year of the Lord 1201, the Cremonese, having gathered with Brescian knights, took captive the Bruzella of Brescia and brought their cart to the forum, or square, of the Cremonese. Then peace was made between the Cremonese, Bergamese, Comaschi, and Brescian forces, among whom there had been such discord that they spared neither sword nor fire. For just as many evils arise from good tidings, so God draws some good from evil. In the same year the Milanese captured a Pavian castle called Regenale. [Col. 0533C]

In the year of the Lord 1202, treaties of peace were arranged between the Cremonese and Plaisantines. In that year, as though in a Jubilee, truces were bound throughout almost all Lombardy for a five-year period. During this five-year period—

> [Note: Col. 0533C. The Estense manuscript expresses this as follows: “I should rightly call it a Jubilee, in which an immense multitude of pilgrims bound for Jerusalem equipped themselves in hope of the remission of sins. Chief among them were Baldwin, count of Flanders; Louis, count of Blois; and Boniface, marquis of Montferrat. In the same year there was a great earthquake in Syria, by which cities and towns shook; Tyre itself almost entirely collapsed. In that same region there was seen a very great battle of stars, the northern stars gaining victory over the eastern. This was undoubtedly a presage of the future overthrow. For the aforesaid pilgrims assembled at Venice and, setting out with the Venetians, first attacked Zara, a most strongly fortified town of Dalmatia, situated in the Adriatic gulf and exceedingly hostile to Venice, at the urging of the venerable man Enrico Dandolo, duke, and of the Venetian fleet. After a short siege the Venetians destroyed it. Meanwhile the young Alexius, son of the aforesaid Emperor Isaac, having been released from prison, came to Philip, his kinsman and king of Germany, begging him to furnish aid.”]

—there was a very great movement of pilgrims going overseas. Chief among them were Baldwin, count of Flanders; Louis, count of Blois; and Boniface, marquis of Montferrat. All of them assembled at Venice [Col. 0534A] and destroyed Zara, a town exceedingly hostile to Venice. Meanwhile the son of Emperor Isaac, released from prison, came to Philip, his kinsman, king of Germany, begging him to provide him with aid.

> [Note: Col. 0533D. The Estense manuscript adds: “In the year of the Lord 1203, there was such a multitude of locusts that they destroyed all growing things.”]

In the year of the Lord 1203, the duke of the Venetians and the other barons, unanimously taking the young Alexius with them, reached Illyricum. First they subjected Durazzo to the boy; and, after subduing the other coastal places, they reached Constantinople. Meanwhile the savagery of the Greeks and Varangians raged against the Venetians and the other Latins dwelling at Constantinople, attacking, capturing, and killing them. When the citizens, though admonished, refused to receive their lawful lord, the Latins bravely rushed into the city itself, took it, besieged the palace, [Col. 0534B] and seized—

> [Note: Col. 0533D. In the Estense manuscript these events are described thus: “And when they besieged the palace of Blachernae, the *oclighita*, that is, the icon of the Blessed Virgin, made in the Virgin’s likeness by the evangelist Luke, was set upon the walls to confound the enemies; but it was more reverently adored by the Latins. Then the *basilographia*, that is, the royal writing of a certain Greek prophet Daniel, who wrote enigmas concerning the successions of the emperors of Constantinople, was brought forth publicly. When it was read [Col. 0534D] that a nation with yellow hair would come for the city’s destruction and would take the city in hard battle, but would at last perish—which may fall upon the Greeks themselves—the Greeks, trusting in this event, suddenly rushed upon the Latins. At last, after the city had been bravely attacked by land and sea and largely burned, the tyrant fled. Isaac was restored, and the young Alexius was magnificently crowned in July in the church of Saint Sophia. Afterwards, since the Greeks publicly inflicted many injuries upon the Latins and privately killed them, the Latins took up arms, burned the city again, and carried away immense plunder. Then, when the tyrant had withdrawn to Adrianople, the young emperor, having gathered an army with the barons, drove him out and subjected the land to himself. But when, etc.”]

—Then, after the city had been taken, largely laid waste, and burned, the tyrant fled. Isaac was restored, and the young Alexius was magnificently crowned in July in the church of Saint Sophia. Afterwards, when the Greeks publicly inflicted many injuries upon the Latins and privately killed them, the Latins burned the city and carried away immense plunder. Then, when the tyrant had withdrawn to Adrianople, the young emperor, having gathered an army with the barons, drove him out and subjected Thrace to himself.

But when the pilgrims pressed for the great rewards promised them, Alexius, ungrateful for their benefits, opposed his benefactors secretly and openly. Thus, discord having been sown between him and the Latins, the Greeks, who hated [Col. 0534C] him, made a certain Constantius emperor.

> [Note: Col. 0534D. Estense manuscript: “Constantine.”]

The people, however, crowned Alexius Murtzuphlus. In this conflict that Alexius Murtzuphlus prevailed. The young Alexius, having scarcely reigned seven months—

> [Note: Col. 0534D. Estense manuscript: “six months.”]

—was suffocated; his father Isaac died. The tyrant Murtzuphlus, pressed by the pilgrims for payment of money, refused to pay. Therefore the Venetians [Col. 0535A] and pilgrims together unanimously attacked the city, devastated the entire surrounding country, and one day drove Murtzuphlus out while he lay hidden in a wooded ambush, capturing his brother, his standard, and the imperial icon.

The following additional material is included in the Estense manuscript.

On the contrary, the Greeks, trusting in their own strength, armed more with insults of the tongue than with courage of heart, rebelled. In the same year the king of Armenia besieged Antioch; although he encircled it with an army, he did not take it. In the same year Master Peter, cardinal and legate of the Apostolic See, at the town of . . . . in Cilicia, bestowed pastoral mitres and a staff, in my presence and in the presence of the king of Armenia, upon the Armenian Catholicos and fourteen bishops, receiving from him the due [Col. 0535B] fealty to the Holy Roman Church.

In the year of the Lord 1204, as Greek insolence and arrogance increased, the Venetians prepared for war with the barons. Having attacked the city, they fought man by man, by sea and land. The Greeks resisted with engines, missiles, and darts; but when their strength failed, the knights rushed forcefully into the city. Murtzuphlus took flight. Another, namely Ascari, was chosen for the Empire by the deluded citizens. But when daylight came, the palaces of Blachernae and Boukoleon were occupied by the Latins.

What more need be said? After a slaughter of Greeks, that people—once the daughter of wisdom, now deprived of the spirit of counsel and without wisdom—perished like scattered dust, vanished like smoke, and withered like hay. The Latin people victoriously took possession of Constantinople in the month [Col. 0535C] of April.

Then the barons crowned Baldwin, count of Flanders, emperor with the diadem, apportioning the Empire while the Venetians and Genoese concurred in their votes. For one fourth was allotted to the imperial majesty; half of the four parts went to the Venetians, and the rest to the pilgrims. But Boniface the marquis, who married the Empress Margaret, formerly [the wife] of Isaac and sister of Emeric, king of Hungary, claimed Thessalonica.

Murtzuphlus, moreover, having gone to the tyrant Alexius and, while bent on war, sought by blandishments and words of some hope to seduce him, was deprived of sight. Returning to the city, he obtained mercy from the Latins. But when he again plotted treason, he was cast down from the Column of Taurus by sentence, so that, as he had presumed [Col. 0535D] to rise high, so he might fall from on high into destruction. Ascari too having fled beyond the Hellespont, the victorious Latins held almost the whole monarchy of the Greeks.

These same events are described as follows in the Caesarean-Viennese manuscript.

In the year of the Lord 1254, the Venetians with the barons took the city of Constantinople. Murtzuphlus, who considered himself emperor, fled from the city. Another, [Col. 0536A] namely Astari, was more readily chosen for the Empire by the citizens. But when daylight came, the palaces of Blachernae and Boukoleon were occupied by the Latins. Therefore, after an immense slaughter of many Greeks, the Latin people victoriously took possession of the city of Constantine in the month of April.

Then the barons crowned Baldwin, count of Flanders, emperor with the diadem, and, in concordant votes, received shares of the Empire. For one fourth went to the imperial majesty; half of the remaining three fourths went to the Venetians, and the rest to the pilgrims. Boniface the marquis obtained Thessalonica. Murtzuphlus, having gone to the tyrant Alexius and sought to seduce certain persons, was deprived of sight; returning to the city, he obtained pardon from the Latins. But when he again plotted treason, he was cast down from the Column of Taurus. Astari too having fled across the Hellespont, the victorious Latins held almost the entire monarchy of the Greeks. In the same year the Greeks also rose up and, after the Latins had been expelled, withdrew to Adrianople.

The following material occurs in the Estense manuscript.

The prophecy was fulfilled which a certain Greek mathematician had foretold: “Rejoice, Seven Hills, but not for a thousand years.” For the thousandth year had not yet come from Constantine when the Seven-Seated City, that is Constantinople, fell from the height of greatest joy to the depths of sorrow. In the same year a great comet illuminated the sky.

In the same year the venerable men Lord Soffredus and Master Peter, cardinal priests and legates of the Apostolic See, came from Syria to Constantinople, [Col. 0536C] where they were honourably received at Saint Sophia by the emperor, the Latin citizens, and the Greeks. There they settled spiritual affairs among Greeks and Latins alike. The divine offices were solemnly celebrated with me assisting. For at the command of the aforesaid cardinal, Master Peter, I solemnly celebrated ordinations in the church of Saint Sophia on the Ember Saturday before the Nativity of the Lord. For, travelling in Syria out of love for the crucified Lord, I had accompanied him first to Armenia in order to assist him, and afterwards also to Greece. In the same year the Greeks rose up, as it were, and, after the Latins had been expelled, withdrew to Adrianople.

Both manuscripts continue.

[Col. 0536D]

In the year of the Lord 1205, Baldwin, emperor of Constantinople, besieged the Greeks assembled at Adrianople. But the emperor himself, with certain of his barons, was captured and killed by the Blachi and Cumans gathered from outside.

> [Note: Col. 0535D. The Estense manuscript adds: “Therefore the Latin army, departing in confusion from the siege, nevertheless returned unharmed to the city of Constantine. The emperor’s brother, named Henry—a bold man, practised in warfare—commanded it after the death of the Venetian duke. [Col. 0536D] Boniface the marquis also, reigning at Thessalonica and having subdued the surrounding provinces, suffered at the hands of the Greeks and Blachi, etc.”]

The army, however, returned unharmed to Constantinople, under the command of Henry, the emperor’s brother, since the duke of Venice had now died. Boniface the marquis, who reigned at Thessalonica, also suffered much from Greeks and Blachi. This year fortune smiled favourably and kindly upon the Greeks but was adverse to the Latins. [Col. 0537A]

The Estense manuscript continues.

As the Greek mathematicians had foretold. Nevertheless, the unconquered marquis sent the captive Alexius, whom he had taken—the former emperor—with his wife to Lombardy, that he might be kept in custody and restrained from the tyranny which he had repeatedly exercised.

The following stands thus in both manuscripts.

In 1206, in both the eastern and western Empire, at Antioch the aforesaid eminent persons contended for the aforesaid reasons. In 1207 Boniface, marquis of Montferrat, was killed in battle, leaving as successors [Col. 0537B] his son William in Italy and Demetrius at Thessalonica.

In 1208 the disturbance among those contending for the Empire of the West was quieted. For after Philip had been wickedly murdered in his bedchamber, Otto prosperously succeeded him. Concerning Otto, a man who uttered future things had foreseen in a dream by night, and it was prophesied in these verses:

> I breathe forth: yield to the earth, King Otto; King Adolf errs.  
> Alas! Otto, look to yourself: there it ends.

> [Note: Col. 0537C. The Estense manuscript adds: “The meaning of this riddle was made clear in this year. *Insufflo*, that is, ‘I breathe.’ *Da terrae*: ‘tell earthly men that King Otto, king at Rome, grieves.’ And ‘Adolf errs,’ the chosen one of Cologne. ‘Alas, Otto, look to yourself’ is the exposition of the preceding clause. ‘There it ends’: for the vision showed the seer that this year, fixed in time, was painted upon a wall and marked with letters.”]

In 1209 Pope Innocent crowned King Otto. Once crowned, he immediately armed himself against the father who had crowned him, against mother Church, and against the boy king of Sicily, who had no helper except the Church. Therefore, in the following year, namely 1210, Pope Innocent excommunicated the aforesaid [Col. 0537C] emperor. Otto nonetheless sent the marquis with an army into Apulia. Afterwards, marching through Tuscany, he acquired some places by force and some by surrender. Then, hastening onward, he wintered at Capua.

[Col. 0538A] In 1211, advancing through Apulia, he received cities and places by surrender as far as Policorno. While these things were occurring, the princes of Germany elected Frederick, king of Sicily, son of the late Emperor Henry, of whom we have spoken, as emperor, summoning him to hurry to Germany. When he heard this, the emperor hastened back; he also held an empty court at Lodi. For the marquis of Este had already agreed with the Pavians, Cremonese, and Veronese to enter into the supreme pontiff’s alliance. He therefore entered Germany ingloriously.

In 1212, the aforesaid king of Sicily came to Rome and was magnificently received by the supreme pontiff and the Romans. Then, reaching Genoa by ship, he was conducted through their hands and those of William, marquis of Montferrat, [Col. 0538B] as far as Pavia; the Cremonese eagerly came to meet him at the Lambro and led him to Cremona with rejoicing and a tournament.

> [Note: Col. 0537C. Estense manuscript: “and, gloriously received, is conducted by them as far as the Lambro.”]

> [Note: Col. 0537C. In the Estense manuscript the material is described as follows:
>
> [Col. 0537D] “But, while the Pavian knights were returning, many were captured by the Milanese. The king, however, passed most successfully through Mantua, Verona, and Trent, and was received with honour in each city. From there he entered Germany through Chur; receiving fealty from the princes day by day, he was crowned at Mainz. Afterwards, holding a solemn court at Regensburg, he received acts of fealty from the king of Bohemia and many other princes.
>
> “In the same year the Almohad king of Mauretania came into Spain with an innumerable multitude of Saracens, threatening to take not only Spain but also Rome, indeed all Europe. But Pope Innocent III caused a multitude of Christians marked with the sign of the Cross to be assembled against them. At the first encounter they took the castle of Malagón, then occupied Calatrava, Alarcos, Benavente, and Petrabona. They pitched their tents at the pass of Muradal. The pass was so narrow that two hundred men might almost have prevented the whole world from passing.
>
> “While our men hesitated, behold, two worshippers of Christ appeared in the guise of hunters. With these men leading the way, the entire Christian army crossed the mountain by another side, contrary to the Saracens’ expectation, and on Saturday pitched tents not far from the camp of the enemies of Christ. On Monday, at dawn, the Christians and the enemies of Christ met in battle, their ranks drawn up in the field, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August [16 July]. By the grace of the Saviour, as the most Christian kings of Aragon, Navarre, and Castile slaughtered the enemy, they turned their backs; the sword devoured [Col. 0538D] countless thousands of Christ-worshippers. For, put to flight for five leagues, they fell without number. Then our men, advancing after the victory, courageously occupied the city of Úbeda, where sixty thousand heathens of both sexes fell. At last the Christian army returned home, giving thanks to the Saviour, to whom be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.
>
> “In the same year it is said that the king of France, together with the count of Montfort and other men signed with the Cross, [the text is corrupt] from the battle and army which was in Spain when the emperor of the Saracens, who had fifty kings, was defeated at Muradal by the three kings of Spain—namely those of Castile, Navarre, and Aragon—with the help of the Portuguese, of whom eleven thousand died in the first battle-line, and with the help of the Portuguese. In that same time, year, and month of November, Pope Innocent celebrated a council at the Lateran in the year 1215.”]

From there he passed happily through Mantua, Verona, and Trent, and was received with honour in those cities. From there he entered Germany through Chur; and, holding solemn court with the princes day by day, he received acts of fealty from the king of Bohemia and many other princes.

In that same year, namely 1212, Almeramomeley, king of Mauretania, came into Spain with an innumerable multitude of Saracens, threatening to take not only Spain but Rome, indeed all Europe. But, with the aiding grace and power of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the holy lord [Col. 0538C] Pope Innocent, the kings of Aragon, Navarre, and Castile confronted the pagans and drove them in part from their territories on the seventh day before the Kalends of August [26 July].

In the same year a child under ten years of age came from Germany with an innumerable multitude of poor people, [Col. 0539A] asserting that he would cross the sea without a ship and recover Jerusalem.

The Estense manuscript narrates this as follows.

In the same year, 1212, under the leadership of boys about twelve years old who said that they had seen a vision, an innumerable multitude of poor people of both sexes and children, taking the sign of the Cross, spread through the region of Cologne, travelled through Germany as pilgrims, and came into Italy. With one heart and one voice they declared that they would cross the seas on dry land and, by God’s power, recover the holy land of Jerusalem. But at last the whole movement, as it were, vanished away.

In the same year there was a famine so severe, especially in Apulia and Sicily, that mothers [Col. 0539B] even devoured their children.

Both manuscripts continue.

In 1213, on the holy day of Pentecost, which in that year fell on the feast of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, namely the second day after the beginning of June—

> [Note: Col. 0539D. In the Estense manuscript the same events are narrated as follows:

At the beginning of June, the people of Cremona, coming to aid the people of Pavia—many of whom, as we said above, had been captured by the Milanese while the king was passing from Pavia to Cremona—assembled unanimously with their carroccio at the castle of Leon. They had no allies except three hundred Brescian knights. And behold, there suddenly arose the sound of the Milanese advancing with their carroccio, like flying arrows and like hurrying lightning. To aid them had gathered Piacenzan knights and archers, Lodi men, and Cremonese knights and foot-soldiers, [Col. 0540D] Novarese and Como knights, and as many or more Brescians as we said had arrived to assist the Cremonese. All these, unanimously, with one shout and fury—or rather, with one spirit and onset—attacked and assailed the Cremonese and the other foreign knights, putting them to flight, capturing, and overcoming them. But the Cremonese won the victory over the said Milanese and their army, and forcibly led the carroccio of the aforesaid Milanese, with great victory and rejoicing, into the city of Cremona. Thus far the Este manuscript.]

… the Cremonese, coming to aid the Pavians—many of whom had been captured during the king’s passage from Pavia to Cremona—assembled with their carroccio at the castle of Leon, having no allies except three hundred Brescian knights. And behold, there suddenly arose the sound of the Milanese hastening against the Cremonese with their carroccio, more swiftly and vigorously than the Cremonese were able. To aid them had gathered Piacenzan knights, archers from Lodi, [Col. 0539C] Cremonese knights, Novarese foot-soldiers, knights of Como, and an equal or greater number of Brescians. About the third hour the battle began. Both sides fought stoutly and manfully until the ninth hour. About the ninth hour, however, the Cremonese charged them, struck down a great multitude of them, captured their carroccio, and brought many thousands of combatants into the castle of Leon.

Additions of the continuator in the Caesarean manuscript.

In the year 1215, Bishop Sicard, compiler of this present work, died in the month of June. In the same year, in November, Lord Pope Innocent celebrated a council at the Lateran.

[Col. 0539D] In the year 1217, the Cremonese and Parmesans entered the territory of the Piacenzans and burned many of their villages. On the same return journey, the Cremonese alone captured Pontenure; having driven the Piacenzans as far as Montale, they returned to the castle with much booty and many [Col. 0540A] captives. On the second day they fought the Milanese and Piacenzans between Fontana and Caurcium. Although a large part of the Cremonese and Parmesans had already returned home, those remaining in the rear fought bravely, completely resisted them, struck down many enemies, and at last returned with joy and exultation. In the same year Lord Pope Innocent died at Perugia in the month of June, and Pope Honorius succeeded him.

In the year of the Lord 1218, the Milanese, having recovered their strength, with an innumerable multitude—namely Piacenzans and Pavians, men of Vercelli, Novara, Tortona, Como, and Alessandria, men of Lodi and Crema, and many [Col. 0540B] others—at the request of the Piacenzans presumed to march against the borough of San Damiano, declaring that they wished and were able to deliver it into Piacenzan hands. The Cremonese and Parmesans, with the men of Reggio and Modena, encamped bravely near the aforesaid castle and opposed them with a strong hand. Thus the Milanese, in accordance with their wrongful purpose, moved their camp and pitched it between a certain castle, Zubellum, and the place called Altisvillis. The Cremonese, together with those aforesaid, rapidly met them at the same place. On Thursday, the sixth day of June, battle was joined between them. It lasted from the ninth hour until sunset. In this battle the Milanese and their allies were decisively defeated and put to flight; many of them were killed, and the two carrocci of the Milanese and Piacenzans were carried off. Barely rescued from danger, they returned to their homes in great confusion and disgrace. In the same year Emperor Otto died, and Lord Frederick succeeded him, having been unanimously elected by all the princes of Germany.

In the year 1221, Lord Frederick was first crowned Emperor of the Romans at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

In the twelve hundred and twenty-second year, O Christ,  
after you had taken flesh, as the years ran on,  
you performed such miracles, blessed King.

At the end of August a comet-star shone with varied tails.  
September’s rain submerged vines and grapes.  
God destroyed the ravaging river from the mountain.  
And the moon suffered an eclipse in November.

[Col. 0540D] On Christ’s Nativity, likewise, in the middle of daylight,  
the earth gave a roaring groan and trembled repeatedly;  
roofs fell, cities were shaken, churches collapsed:  
walls rendered many masters lifeless.  
Above all, ruinous Brescia crushed its inhabitants.  
Rivers changed their course, returning toward their sources.

[Col. 0539] Praise be to you, Christ, for this book has ended.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1218: PETER OF VAUX-DE-CERNAY

[Col. 0541]

## NOTICE

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. V, p. 280)

Peter of Sarnay, or Vaux-Sarnay or Vaux-de-Cernay (*des Vaux de Cernay*), a Cistercian monk, in the region of the dioceses of Chartres and Paris [Note: [Col. 0541] The Sammarthani, vol. IV, p. 901.], was the author of a *History of the Albigensians and of the Holy War undertaken against them in 1209*, under the leadership and command of Simon de Montfort, which the author dedicated to Innocent III. It was first published by Nicolas Camusat, canon of Troyes, at Troyes in 1615, in octavo [Note: [Col. 0541] Under this title: *History of the Albigensians and of the Holy War Undertaken against Them in the Year 1209, under the Leadership and Command of Simon de Montfort, later Count of Toulouse, with deeds bravely accomplished; by the distinguished Peter, monk of the Cistercian monastery of Vaux-de-Sarnay, an eyewitness of this crusading campaign.*]; then, collated with the manuscript of Martin Marier, monk of Saint-Martin in Paris, by François du Chesne in vol. V of the *Scriptors of France*, pp. 554–665; and also by Bertrand Tissier at the beginning of vol. VII of the *Cistercian Library*, published in 1669. Compare Bzovius under the year 1199, no. 34; and Charles Visch, p. 276 of the *Cistercian Library*, who mentions a French translation published at Paris in 1569, translated by Arnaud Sorbin, later bishop of Nevers [Note: [Col. 0541]

Concerning the French versions of Peter of Vaux-de-Cernay’s book, D. Petit-Radel makes the following observations in the *Literary History of France* (vol. XVII, p. 251):

“Three French translations of this history were known, only one of which was published, and this was by Arnaud Sorbin. It appeared at Paris in 1569, more than forty years before the first publication of the Latin original. The other two, which remained in manuscript, are attributed to Guillaume Pellicier, bishop of Montpellier, by Father Lelong (*Historical Library of France*, vol. I, p. 376, no. 5743); but this is an error that we must here correct.

“One of the two manuscripts that truly contains Guillaume Pellicier’s version exists in the library of Sainte-Geneviève and forms a folio volume of 249 leaves. It bears this title: *History of the exploits and valiant deeds of the noble lord Sir Simon, Count of Montfort, performed by him for the Catholic faith in God’s Church against the Albigensian heretics, from the year of grace 1206 until 1218; first composed in Latin by Brother Peter . . . . . ; then translated into French in the year of the Saviour 1565 by Sir Guillaume Pellicier, bishop of Montpellier.* This manuscript begins with the translation of three letters of Innocent III, preserved for us by Peter of Vaux-de-Cernay, which he placed as documentary evidence after his history.

“The manuscript containing the other translation belongs to the king’s library. It is easy to establish, by comparing it with the preceding one, that these two translations bear not the slightest relation of identity. Indeed, the latter manuscript contains neither the translation of Innocent III’s three letters, which form the beginning of the other, nor that of the letter ending Peter of Vaux-de-Cernay’s work, in which Simon de Montfort, a few days before his death, ordered his seneschals to protect all the property and houses of Saint Dominic as their own. Since the author of manuscript version no. 9644 in the king’s library did not translate Peter of Vaux-de-Cernay’s first chapters, his version begins with the sixth. Finally, this translator’s style bears no relation to that of Guillaume Pellicier, which is generally easier and clearer, and whose translation appears more faithful.

“Father Lelong (*ibid.*) indicates a fourth translation of the same work, made, he says, by an unknown person living around 1456. It formed part of the d’Urfé library, no. LXIII; but we have been unable to recover the manuscript, any more than the one entitled: *Francisci Roaldi, Two Books of Commentaries on Peter of Vaux-de-Sarnay’s History of the Albigensian War*, folio. We must regret all the more not having seen these commentaries, since they undoubtedly contained critical observations upon the events reported by Peter of Vaux-de-Cernay. Finally, Dom Martène says (*Literary Journey*, part II, p. 108) that at Quincy Abbey, of the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Langres, there was to be seen a history of the Albigensians whose beginning resembled that of Peter of Vaux-de-Cernay, but whose end was different.”]

.

[Col. 0543]

# HISTORY OF THE ALBIGENSIANS AND OF THE HOLY WAR UNDERTAKEN AGAINST THEM IN THE YEAR 1209, UNDER THE LEADERSHIP AND COMMAND OF SIMON DE MONTFORT, BY PETER, MONK OF THE MONASTERY OF VAUX-DE-CERNAY.

(Du Chesne, *Writers of French Affairs*, vol. V, p. 544, from the edition of Nicolas Camusat, canon of Troyes, collated with the manuscript codex of Dom Martin Marier, monk of Saint-Martin in Paris.)

## AUTHOR’S DEDICATORY LETTER TO INNOCENT III, ROMAN PONTIFF

To the most holy Father and most blessed lord INNOCENT, by God’s grace supreme pontiff of the universal Church: his humble, though unworthy, servant, Brother PETER, a monk of Vaux-de-Cernay of whatever poor quality, offers not merely kisses to his feet, but humbly kisses the very traces of his footsteps.

Blessed is the Lord God of Sabaoth, who in these latter days, most holy Father, through your untiring care, mercifully rescued his Church in the regions of Provence—already almost completely shipwrecked amid the storms of persecuting heretics—from the mouths of lions through the hands of his ministers, and delivered her from the claws of beasts. But lest so glorious and wonderful a deed, through the successive passage of time, fall into oblivion, and so that the mighty deeds of our God may become known among the nations, I offer to your majesty, most blessed Father, an account of the event put into writing in whatever fashion I can. I humbly beg that it not be imputed to presumption that an elementary schoolboy has put his hand to difficult matters and presumed to undertake a burden beyond his strength. For my purpose in this work has been solely to write these things, so that the nations may know God’s wonderful works; especially since, as may be judged from my very manner of speaking, I have not sought to adorn the book with superfluous words, but simply to express the simple truth.

Therefore, good Father, may your holy dignity firmly hold this: although I may not have been able to reach, in order, everything that occurred in this affair, what I have written is true. For I have never added anything except what I saw with my own eyes or heard from persons of great authority and entirely worthy of belief. At the beginning of this work, I briefly touch upon the sects of the heretics and how the people of Provence had, in past times, been infected with the leprosy of unbelief. Afterwards I set forth how the aforesaid heretics of Provence were admonished by preachers of God’s word and ministers of your holiness to return, as transgressors, to their heart; how they were repeatedly summoned; then the arrival of the crusaders, the capture of cities and castles, and, as I am able, the other matters pertaining to the progress of the cause of the faith, in due order. Let those who will read know that in many places in this work the heretics and defenders of Toulouse and of other cities and castles are generally called “Albigensians,” because other peoples have customarily called the heretics of Provence Albigensians. And so that the reader may more readily find in this little book what he seeks, let him know that this work has been arranged into various divisions according to the manifold and successive developments of the cause of the faith.

# THE HISTORY OF THE ALBIGENSIANS BEGINS

## CHAPTER I. On the mission of Brother Peter of Castelnau and Brother Ralph of the Cistercian Order to the province of Narbonne

[Col. 0543A]

In the province of Narbonne, where faith had once flourished, [Col. 0544A] the enemy of the faith began to sow tares among the wheat. The people became foolish, profaning Christ’s sacraments—he who is the savour and wisdom of God—and, made foolish, turning away from true reverence for God (*theosebia*), wandering and straying through errors down into the depths, becoming people without a path and not upon the way (Ps. [Col. 0545A] 106). Two Cistercian monks, inflamed with zeal for the faith—Brother Peter of Castelnau and Brother Ralph—were appointed legates by the authority of the supreme pontiff against the plague of unbelief. Casting aside all negligence and diligently discharging the mission imposed upon them, they entered and undertook the city of Toulouse, from which the poison chiefly flowed forth, infecting the people and causing them to fall away from knowledge of Christ, from the true splendour, and from divine love.

The root of bitterness, springing upward, had grown stronger deep in human hearts and could not be uprooted without great difficulty. The Toulousains were often and earnestly urged to abjure heresy and banish heretics. They were urged by apostolic men, but by no means persuaded; for they clung so closely to death, having departed from life, affected and infected by wicked wisdom—animal, earthly, devilish—without that wisdom which is from above, open to persuasion, and in agreement with good things (Jas. 3). At last, these two olive trees, these two lampstands shining before the Lord (Rev. 4), striking servile fear into servants and threatening them with confiscation of possessions and the indignation of kings and princes, persuaded them to abjure heresies and expel heretics. Thus they acted, not from love of virtue, but, according to the poet:

> The wicked hate to sin because they fear punishment.

This they demonstrated by clear evidence. For they immediately became perjurers and suffered a relapse of their misery: in their conventicles, in the middle of the night, they preached and concealed heretics. Alas, how difficult it is [Col. 0545C] to be torn away from habit! This Toulouse, wholly deceitful, from its first foundation—as is asserted—was rarely, if ever, free from this plague or detestable pestilence, this heretical depravity, the poison of superstitious unbelief being passed down successively from fathers to sons. Therefore, in vengeance for so great a crime, it is said that it long ago endured such destruction by the hand of righteous retribution that, in the very middle of the city, a plain of fields lay open, furrowed by ploughshares. One of its illustrious kings who then ruled there, believed to have been named Alaric, was hanged in utmost disgrace on a gallows before the gates of that city.

That offspring, infected with the dregs of this ancient stickiness—the offspring of the aforesaid city, a brood of vipers—could not even in our own times be torn away from the root of its perversity. Indeed, though heretical nature and a springing heresy had been expelled by the fork of deserved punishment, it nevertheless allowed them to return into itself again and again:

> It yearns to take after its fathers, refusing to degenerate;

by the example of whose neighbouring influence, just as

> A clustered grape takes its dark hue from a grape,  
> and the whole flock in the fields  
> falls through the mange of one sheep and the swine through the scab.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* II.81)

Neighbouring cities and towns, in which heresiarchs had taken root, were miserably and astonishingly infected by this pest, sprouting through shoots of the same unbelief. Nearly all the barons of Provence became defenders and receivers of heretics; they loved them most ardently and defended them against God and the Church.

## CHAPTER II. On the various sects of heretics

Since an opportunity of some sort presents itself here, I have thought it worthwhile to give a more explicit, though concise, account of the heresies and sects of the heretics. First, one must know that the heretics posited two creators: one of invisible things, whom they called the good God, and another of visible things, whom they called the evil God. They attributed the New Testament to the good God and the Old to the evil one, and utterly rejected the latter, apart from certain authorities from the Old Testament that are inserted in the New, which they judged worthy of acceptance out of reverence for the New Testament.

They asserted that the author of the Old Testament was a liar because he said to the first-formed humans: “On whatever day you eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall die” (Gen. 3), and, as they said, they did not die after eating. In truth, however, after tasting the forbidden fruit they became subject to the misery of death. They also called him a murderer, both because he reduced the Sodomites and Gomorrites to ashes and destroyed the world with the waters of the Flood, and because he overwhelmed Pharaoh and the Egyptians in the sea. They affirmed that all the patriarchs of the Old Testament were damned, and asserted that John the Baptist was one of the greater demons.

They also said secretly that the Christ who was born in earthly and visible Bethlehem and [Col. 0546C] crucified in Jerusalem was evil; that Mary Magdalene was his concubine; and that she was the woman taken in adultery of whom the Gospel speaks (John 8). The good Christ, they said, never ate or drank, did not assume real flesh, and was never in this world except spiritually in the body of Paul. We have said “earthly and visible Bethlehem,” because the heretics invented another new and invisible land; according to some of them, the good Christ was born and crucified in that other land. Likewise, the heretics said that the good God had two wives, Collant and Colibant, and begot sons and daughters by them. There were other heretics who said that there is one Creator, but that he had sons, Christ and the devil. [Col. 0546D] These also said that all creatures were good, but that everything was corrupted through the daughters mentioned in the Apocalypse (Rev. 19).

All these—members of Antichrist, firstborn of Satan; evil seed; criminal sons; speaking in hypocrisy and deceiving the hearts of the simple by falsehood—had infected the province of Narbonne with the poison of their perfidy. They said that almost the entire Roman Church was a den of thieves (Matt. 21), and that it was the harlot of whom the Apocalypse speaks (Rev. 17). They so completely nullified the Church’s sacraments that they publicly taught that the water of holy baptism differed in no respect from river water, and that the host of Christ’s most holy body did not differ from ordinary bread. They instilled into the ears of the simple [Col. 0547A] this blasphemy: that, even if Christ’s body contained within itself the bulk of the Alps, it would long since have been consumed and annihilated by those eating it.

They considered confirmation and confession wholly frivolous and empty. They preached that holy matrimony was prostitution, and that no one could be saved within it while begetting sons and daughters. Denying also the resurrection of the flesh, they invented certain unheard-of fictions, saying that our souls are those angelic spirits who, cast down from heaven by the apostasy of pride, left their glorified bodies in the air; and that these souls, after successive inhabitation of seven earthly bodies of whatever kind, would then, as though their penance had at last been completed, return to those bodies left behind.

[Col. 0547B] One should know, moreover, that some among the heretics were called “the perfect,” or “the good men”; others were believers of the heretics. Those called perfect wore black clothing, falsely claimed to observe chastity, utterly abhorred eating meat, eggs, and cheese, and wished to appear not to lie, although they themselves most continually lied, as it were, about God. They also said that one must never swear for any reason. The believers of the heretics were those who, living secular lives, did not attain to imitation of the life of the perfect, yet hoped to be saved in their faith. They were divided in their manner of life, but united in faith and unbelief.

[Col. 0547C] Those called believers of the heretics were given over to usury, robbery, murder, the enticements of the flesh, perjury, and every kind of perversity. They sinned more securely and without restraint because they believed that, without restoring what had been taken, without confession or penance, they would be saved, provided that at the final moment of death they could say the *Our Father* and receive the laying-on of hands from their masters. Among the perfect heretics there were officials whom they called deacons and bishops; without the laying-on of their hands, no believer facing death believed that he could be saved. But if they laid hands upon any dying person, however criminal, provided he could say the *Our Father*, they judged him so saved, according to what in their vernacular they called being “consoled” (*consolatum*), that without any satisfaction or other remedy he would immediately fly to heaven.

Accordingly, we have thought it fitting to insert an amusing thing which we heard about this. A certain believer of the heretics, at the last moment of death, received consolation through the laying-on of hands from his master, but could not say the *Our Father*, and so expired. His consoler did not know what to say of him. He seemed saved because he had received the laying-on of hands; damned, because he had not said the Lord’s Prayer. What more? The heretics consulted a certain knight, named Bertrand of Saxiac, who was a heretic, as to what they ought to judge about him. The knight gave this counsel and response: “In this case, we shall maintain and say that he is saved; but we judge all others damned unless they say the *Our Father* at the end.”

[Col. 0548A] Another amusing case: a certain believer of the heretics, at death, bequeathed three hundred solidi to the heretics and ordered his son to give them that money. When, after the father’s death, the heretics demanded it from the son, he said to them: “First I want you to tell me how my father fares.” They replied: “Know with absolute certainty that he is saved and already placed in heaven.” Smiling at them, he said: “Thanks to God and to you. Yet since my father is now in glory, his soul has no need of alms; and I know you to be so kind that you will not henceforth recall my father from glory. Know, therefore, that you will obtain no money from me.”

We do not think it should be passed over that certain heretics also said that no one could sin from the navel downward. They called the images in churches idolatry and declared their bells to be crowds of demons. They further said that a person sinned no more grievously by sleeping with his mother or sister than with any other woman. Among their greatest absurdities, they also said that if one of the perfect committed a mortal sin—namely, by eating even the smallest quantity of meat, cheese, egg, or something else forbidden to him—all whom he had consoled lost the Holy Spirit and had to be consoled again; and even those already saved fell from heaven because of their consoler’s sin.
