There were besides other heretics called Waldensians, from a certain man of Lyons named Waldo. These were indeed evil, [Col. 0548C] but compared with the other heretics they were far less perverse. They agreed with us in many things and differed in some. To omit most of their unbeliefs, their error rested chiefly upon four points: wearing sandals in the manner of the apostles; maintaining that one must never swear or kill for any reason; and further asserting that any one of them, in a case of necessity, provided he had sandals, could consecrate Christ’s body without having received orders from a bishop. Let this brief extract concerning the sects of the heretics suffice.

When someone gives himself over to the heretics, the person receiving him says: “Friend, if you wish to be one of us, you must renounce the whole faith held by the Roman Church.” He replies: “I renounce it.” “Then [Col. 0548D] receive the Holy Spirit from the good men”; and then he breathes into his mouth seven times. He likewise says to him: “Do you renounce that cross which the priest made for you at baptism, on your breast, shoulders, and head, with oil and chrism?” He replies: “I renounce it.” “Do you believe that that water works salvation for you?” He replies: “I do not believe it.” “Do you renounce that veil which the priest placed upon your head when you were baptized?” He replies: “I renounce it.” Thus he receives the baptism of the heretics and denies the baptism of the Church. Then they all lay hands upon his head, kiss him, and clothe him in a black garment; from that hour he is, as it were, one of them.

## CHAPTER III. How and when preachers first came to the province of Narbonne against the heretics

[Col. 0549A]

In the year of the Incarnate Word 1206, the bishop of Osma, named Diego, a great man and one greatly to be exalted, came to the Roman court, ardently desiring to resign his bishopric so that he might more freely go among the pagans to preach Christ’s Gospel. But Lord Pope Innocent would not consent to the holy man’s desire; rather, he ordered him to return to his own see. It happened, therefore, as he was returning from the curia and was at Montpellier, that he found there the venerable man Arnaud, abbot of Cîteaux, and Brother Peter of Castelnau and Brother Ralph, Cistercian monks and legates of the Apostolic See. Wearied, they wished to resign the mission entrusted to them, because they had been unable to gain anything, or almost anything, by preaching to the heretics. Whenever they wished to preach to the heretics, the heretics objected to them the extremely bad conduct of the clergy, saying that unless they wished to correct clerical life, they ought to desist from preaching.

[Col. 0549B] The aforesaid bishop offered a salutary counsel against this dilemma. He urged and advised them, putting other things aside, to labour more ardently at preaching; and, so that they might shut the mouths of the malicious, he urged them to lead by example in humility: as pious masters, they should do and teach; they should go on foot, without gold or silver, imitating in all things the apostolic model. But the said legates did not wish of themselves to undertake all this as something new. They said that if a man of favourable authority would lead them in this manner, they would most willingly follow him.

What more need be said? The man full of God offered himself. Immediately sending his household to Osma and content with one companion, he entered Montpellier with the two aforementioned monks, Peter and Ralph. The abbot of Cîteaux went to Cîteaux, both because the Cistercian chapter was shortly to be held and because, after its celebration, he wished to bring with him certain abbots of his order who would assist him in carrying out the preaching office entrusted to him. Departing from Montpellier, the bishop of Osma and the aforesaid monks came to [Col. 0549D] a certain castle, Caraman, where they found a heresiarch named Baldwin and a certain Theodoric, a son of perdition and kindling for fire. The latter, French by origin, was noble by birth and had been a canon of Nevers. Later, however, when a certain knight—his uncle and a most wicked heretic—was condemned for heresy at the Council of Paris before Cardinal Octavian, legate of the Apostolic See, this man, seeing that he could not remain hidden any longer, removed himself to the regions of Narbonne. There he was held by the heretics in the greatest affection and reverence, both because he appeared somewhat keener than the others and because they gloried that they had obtained from France, where the wellspring of learning and Christian religion was located, a companion in their iniquity and a defender of their wickedness.

[Col. 0550A] It must not be passed over that he had himself called Theodoric, though previously he had been called William. After an eight-day disputation with these two, Baldwin and Theodoric, our preachers, by salutary admonitions, turned the whole people of the said castle to hatred of the aforesaid heretics. They would most gladly have expelled the heretics from among them, but the lord of the castle, infected with the poison of perfidy, had made them his familiar associates and friends. It would take too long to recount every word of that disputation. But I have thought it worthy to add only this: when the venerable bishop, disputing, had driven the said Theodoric to the lowest point of his argument’s conclusion, [Col. 0550B] Theodoric said: “I know, I know what spirit you are of; for you have come in the spirit of Elijah.” To this the holy man replied: “And if I have come in the spirit of Elijah, you have come in the spirit of Antichrist.”

After spending eight days there, they left the castle, and the people accompanied the venerable men for almost one league. Proceeding straight on, they approached the city of Béziers, where for fifteen days, disputing and preaching, they confirmed the few Catholics who were there in the faith and confounded the heretics. The venerable bishop of Osma and Brother Ralph advised Brother Peter of Castelnau to withdraw from them for a time, for they feared that Brother Peter might be killed, since the heretics hated him above all others. Brother Peter accordingly separated from the bishop and Brother Ralph for some time.

They departed from Béziers and made their way successfully to Carcassonne. Staying there for eight days, they devoted themselves to preaching and disputations. At that time a miracle occurred near [Col. 0550C] Carcassonne which must not be omitted. Heretics were harvesting their grain on the feast of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; for they said that he was not a prophet but utterly evil. While they were harvesting, one of them looked at his hand and saw that his sheaf was bloody. Seeing this, he thought he had cut his hand; but finding it unharmed, he cried out to his companions: “What more?” Each of them looked at the sheaves he held and found them bloody, while their hands remained uninjured. The venerable Guy, abbot of Vaux-de-Cernay, was then in that land; he saw the bloody sheaf and himself told me this.

But since it would be lengthy to recount in order how the apostolic men, namely our preachers, went around through the castles, evangelizing and disputing everywhere, let us omit these matters and come to the chief events. One day all the heresiarchs gathered at a certain castle in the diocese of Carcassonne called Montréal, intending unanimously to dispute against the often-mentioned men. Brother Peter of Castelnau returned for this disputation, having, as we said a little earlier, departed at Béziers. As they debated, judges were appointed from among the believers of the heretics. [Col. 0551A] The disputation was prolonged for fifteen days, and the propositions put forward on both sides were committed to writing and handed to the judges so that they might pronounce a definitive judgment. But when these judges saw that their heretics had been most plainly defeated, they would not issue a judgment. Nor would they return the writings they had received from our side, lest they become public; instead, they gave them to the heretics.

Once this had been done, Brother Peter of Castelnau left his companions and went to Provence, where he worked to reconcile the nobles of Provence, intending that with the help of those who had sworn peace he might uproot the heretics from the province of Narbonne. But the count of Toulouse, named Raymond, an enemy of peace, would not assent to the proposed peace until he was compelled to swear it, both through the wars waged against him by the nobles of Provence through the agency of the man of God, [Col. 0551B] and through the excommunication pronounced against that count by the same man. But he who had denied the faith and was worse than an unbeliever (1 Tim. 5), never observing his oath, swore repeatedly and repeatedly committed perjury. The most holy man, Brother Peter, rebuked him with great courage: fearlessly confronting the tyrant and resisting him to his face because he was blameworthy—indeed, altogether condemnable. A man of great steadfastness and unstained conscience put him to shame, so that he reproached him for being in every respect perjured; and indeed he was.

## CHAPTER IV. Description of the corrupt life and morals of the Count of Toulouse toward God and his Church

[Col. 0551C]

Since an opportunity has presented itself, let us here briefly set forth something concerning the unbelief of this count. First it must be said that, almost from his earliest cradle, he always loved and fostered heretics; having them in his land, he honored them by every means he could. Even to this day, as is asserted, wherever he goes he takes heretics with him in ordinary dress, so that, should he happen to die, he may die in their hands. For he believed that, without any repentance whatsoever, however great a sinner he might have been, he would be saved if, at the very point of death, he could obtain the laying-on of their hands. He also had the New Testament carried about, so that, if necessary, he might receive the laying-on of hands with the book from the heretics.

[Col. 0551D] For heretics detest the Old Testament. They say that the God who instituted the old law is evil, calling him a betrayer because of the despoiling of Egypt; a murderer because of the Flood and the destruction of the Egyptians. They say also that Moses, Joshua, and David were robbers and servants of that evil God. The aforesaid count also said one day to the heretics, as we know for certain, that he wished to have his son brought up at Toulouse among heretics, so that he might learn their faith—or rather, their unbelief. On another occasion he said that he would give a hundred marks of silver if a certain knight of his could embrace the faith of the heretics, to which he had often invited him and which he frequently caused to be preached to him.

Moreover, whenever heretics sent him any gifts or food,

[Col. 0552A] he received them most gratefully and had them carefully kept; nor did he allow anyone to eat of them except himself and some of his household. Very often also, as we have learned with the greatest certainty, he worshipped heretics with his knees bent to the ground, asked their blessing, and kissed them. One day the said count was awaiting certain men who were to come to him; but when they did not come, he said: “It is plainly evident that the devil made this world, because nothing succeeds for us as we wish.”

The same count further said to the venerable bishop of Toulouse, as I heard from that bishop himself, that Cistercian monks could not be saved because they kept sheep that practised lust. O unheard-of heresy! The count also told the bishop of Toulouse

[Col. 0552B] to come by night to his palace and hear the preaching of the heretics; from this it may be inferred that he often heard them by night.

Once the aforementioned count was in a church where Mass was being celebrated. He had with him a certain mime, who, as is the custom of such jesters, mockingly ridiculed people by his facial gestures. When the priest celebrating Mass turned toward the people and said, “The Lord be with you,” the most wicked count told his performer to do the opposite and mock the priest.

The aforesaid count also once said that he would rather be like a certain heretic who, at Castres in the diocese of Albi, had had his limbs cut off and was miserably clothed, than be king or emperor. We have a most convincing proof that he always fostered heretics from the fact that no legate of the Apostolic See could ever induce him to expel the aforesaid heretics from his land, although, compelled by those legates, he repeatedly abjured them.

[Col. 0552C] Moreover, he held the sacrament of marriage in such contempt that whenever his own wife displeased him, he left her and took another; thus he had four wives, three of whom are still alive. First he had Beatrice, sister of the viscount of Béziers. Having left her, he married the daughter of the duke of Cyprus. Having left her, he married the sister of Richard, king of England, who was related to him in the third degree of consanguinity. When she died, he took the sister of the king of Aragon, who likewise was related to him

[Col. 0552D] in the fourth degree.

Nor should it be passed over that, while he still had his first wife, he repeatedly urged her to assume religious dress. Understanding what he intended, she deliberately asked him whether he wished her to become a nun in the Cistercian order. He said no. She asked again whether he wished her to become a nun in the order of Fontevraud. The count answered that he did not. Then she asked him what he did wish; and he replied that if she wished to become a hermitess, he would provide for her in every respect. And so it came to pass.

There was at Toulouse a most wicked heretic named Hugh the Smith (*Hugofaber*), who once fell into such madness that beside the altar of a certain church he relieved his bowels,

[Col. 0553A] and, in contempt of God, wiped his backside with the altar-cloth. O unheard-of crime! The aforesaid heretic also said one day that, when the priest at Mass received the sacrament of the Lord’s body, he transferred a demon into his own body. When the venerable abbot of Cîteaux—who was then abbot of Grandselve in the territory of Toulouse—reported all these things to the count and urged him to punish the man who had committed such an outrage, the count answered that he would by no means punish one of his citizens on that account.

The lord abbot of Cîteaux, who was then archbishop of Narbonne, recounted the aforementioned abominations to nearly twenty bishops, I being present, at the council held at Lavaur. The said count was always so lustful and debauched that, as we learned

[Col. 0553B] for certain, he abused his own sister, in contempt of the Christian religion. From his childhood he sought out his father’s concubines with the greatest diligence and lay with them with equal diligence; scarcely could any woman please him unless he knew that his father had first slept with her. Therefore his father often foretold that he would disinherit him, both because of heresy and because of this enormity.

Moreover, the count embraced brigands (*ruptarii*) with remarkable affection; through them he plundered churches, destroyed monasteries, and disinherited all his neighbors whom he could. Thus this limb of the devil, son of treachery, firstborn of Satan, enemy of the Cross and persecutor of the Church, defender of heretics, oppressor of Catholics, minister

[Col. 0553C] of perdition, abjurer of the faith, storehouse of every crime and sin, always conducted himself.

One day the count was playing chess with a certain chaplain, and during the game he said to the chaplain: “The God of Moses, in whom you believe, will not be able to help you in this game”; and he added: “May that God never help me.” On another occasion, when the count was about to depart from the region of Toulouse against certain enemies of his in Provence, he rose at midnight, came to the house in which the heretics of Toulouse were assembled, and said to them: “Lords and brothers, the outcomes of wars are various. Whatever happens to me, I commend my body and soul into your hands.” Having done this, he additionally brought with him two heretics in ordinary dress, so that if it should happen that he died,

[Col. 0553D] he might die in their hands.

At one time the accursed count fell ill in the land of Aragon. As his illness grew very severe, he had a litter made and had himself carried in it to Toulouse. When one day he was asked why he was having himself transported with such haste while suffering from so grave an illness, the wretch answered: “Because there are no good men in this land in whose hands I can die.” For heretics were called “good men” by their supporters. He confessed himself to be a heretic also by more explicit signs and statements, for he said: “I know that I shall be disinherited for the sake of these good men; but I am prepared to endure not merely disinheritance,

[Col. 0554A] but even beheading for them.” Let it suffice to have said this concerning the unbelief and wickedness of this wretch; let us now return to our subject.

## CHAPTER V. On the arrival of twelve abbots of the Cistercian Order, the purpose of their preaching, and the return and death of Lord Diego, bishop of Osma, and the disputations

After the aforementioned disputation had been held at Montréal, while our preachers still remained there, sowing the word of God and counsels of salvation throughout the surrounding region and begging their bread from door to door, the venerable abbot of Cîteaux, named Arnaud, arrived from France. He had with him twelve abbots—men wholly religious,

[Col. 0554B] of perfect and holy learning, and of incomparable holiness—who, according to the most sacred number of the apostles, arrived as twelve with their thirteenth, the abbot, ready to give an answer to every questioner concerning the faith and hope that was in them (I Peter 3).

All of these, with the many monks whom they had brought with them, following utter humility according to the pattern shown them on the mountain (Exodus 25)—that is, according to what they had heard concerning the bishop of Osma—went on foot. They were immediately dispersed far and wide, each separately, by the abbot of Cîteaux; and to each were assigned his own districts, through which he was to travel, devoting himself to preaching and laboring in disputations.

## CHAPTER VI. On the conference at Pamiers and the death of the bishop of Osma

[Col. 0554C]

The bishop of Osma wished to return to his bishopric, both to arrange his own household and to provide from his revenues for the necessities of the preachers of God’s word in the province of Narbonne. As he departed toward Spain, he came to Pamiers in the territory of Toulouse. There the bishops Fulk of Toulouse and Navarre of Couserans, together with many abbots, assembled before him. A disputation was held there with the Waldensians. The Waldensians were plainly convicted and confounded, and the people of the town—especially the poor, for the most part—favored our side.

Indeed, the man appointed judge in the disputation, who favored the Waldensians and was a person of importance in that town, renounced heretical depravity and placed himself and his possessions in the hand of the lord bishop of Osma.

[Col. 0554D] From that day onward he vigorously attacked the followers of heretical superstition.

That most wicked traitor, the count of Foix—the most cruel persecutor of the Church and enemy of Christ—attended this disputation. He had a wife who was openly a heretic of the Waldensian sect, and two sisters, one of whom professed the sect of the Waldensians and the other the heresies of other unbelievers. After the aforesaid disputation had been held in the palace of the count himself, the same count entertained the Waldensians on one day and our preachers on the next. O feigned humility!

After this the bishop of Osma went to his bishopric, firmly intending to return as soon as possible to carry on the work

[Col. 0555A] of the faith in the province of Narbonne. But after spending only a few days in his bishopric, as he was preparing to return, death overtook him, and in his old age he happily fell asleep.

Before his death, the aforementioned Brother Ralph, a man of good memory, had departed this life in a Cistercian abbey near Saint-Gilles called Vallis Franca. Thus, these two lights—the bishop of Osma and Brother Ralph—having been removed, the venerable Guy, abbot of Vaux-de-Cernay in the diocese of Paris, who had come with the other abbots into the province of Narbonne for the purpose of preaching, a man noble by birth but far nobler in learning and virtue, and later bishop of Carcassonne, was made chief and master among the preachers.

[Col. 0555B] The abbot of Cîteaux, meanwhile, departed for other regions, being at that time occupied by certain important affairs.

The holy preachers therefore traveled about and most plainly convicted the heretics by disputation. But because the latter were obstinate in wickedness and could not be converted, after a long time, having made little or no progress by preaching or disputation, they returned to Gaul.

Nor should it be omitted that when the said abbot of Vaux-de-Cernay had disputed several times with the aforementioned Theodoric and with another great heresiarch, Bernard of Cimorra, who was considered preeminent in the diocese of Carcassonne, and had often convicted them, one day, when the aforesaid Theodoric

[Col. 0555C] could give no other answer, said to the abbot: “A harlot held me long, but henceforth she shall not hold me.” By this he meant that the Roman Church was a harlot.

Nor should it be concealed that, on another day, when the aforesaid abbot of Vaux-de-Cernay entered a certain castle near Carcassonne named Laurac for the purpose of preaching, he made the sign of the cross upon himself at the very entrance of the castle. Seeing this, a certain heretical knight who was in the castle said to the abbot: “May that sign never help me!”

## CHAPTER VII. The miracle of the written slip, penned by the hand of Blessed Dominic, which, thrown three times into flames, sprang out unharmed

At that time a miracle occurred which we have judged worthy to insert here.

[Col. 0555D] One day certain of our preachers, religious men, had disputed against the heretics. One of our side, named Dominic, a man of complete holiness and companion of the bishop of Osma, put in writing the authorities he had brought forward and handed the written slip to a certain heretic, that he might consider the objections made above.

That night the heretics were gathered in one house, sitting by the fire. The man to whom the servant of God had handed the slip produced it before them. Then his companions said that he should throw it into the fire: if the slip were burned, the faith—indeed, the perfidy—of the heretics would be true; but if it remained unburned, they would confess that the faith preached by our side was true. What more need be said? They all agreed to this.

[Col. 0556A] The slip was thrown into the fire; but after remaining for a short time in the midst of the fire, it sprang entirely unburned from the flames. While those present were astonished, one man, harder than the rest, said: “Let it be thrown into the fire again, and then you will test the truth more fully.” It was thrown in again and again sprang out unburned. Seeing this, the hard-hearted man, slow to believe, said once more: “Let it be thrown in three times, and then without doubt we shall know the outcome of the matter.” It was thrown in a third time; nor then was it burned, but it sprang whole and unharmed from the fire.

Yet the heretics, having seen so many signs, were unwilling even then to turn to the faith. Remaining in their wickedness, they most strictly forbade one another to allow this miracle to come to the knowledge of our people through anyone’s report.

[Col. 0556B] But a certain knight who was with them, who somewhat favored our faith, would not conceal what he had seen, but told it to many. This happened at Montréal, as I heard from the mouth of the most religious man who handed the inscribed slip to the heretic.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the martyrdom of Brother Peter of Castelnau, who fell beneath the swords of the ungodly

Having briefly set forth these matters concerning the preachers of God’s word, let us now, with God’s help, turn to the martyrdom of the venerable man and most valiant champion, Brother Peter of Castelnau. We believe that we can do this in no better or more authoritative way than by inserting into our narrative the letter of the lord pope

[Col. 0556C] sent to Christ’s faithful, which contains a fuller account of that martyrdom. The form of the letter is as follows:

**INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, noble men, counts, barons, and all knights established throughout the provinces of Narbonne, Arles, Embrun, Aix, and Vienne: greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We have heard a credible report, fit to be brought before the whole Church in common mourning: that when Brother Peter of Castelnau, of holy memory, monk and priest, a man truly virtuous among men, distinguished in life, learning, and reputation, had been sent with others into the province of Auch to preach peace and confirm the faith, he had made praiseworthy progress in the ministry entrusted to him

[Col. 0556D] and did not cease to make progress. For he had fully learned in the school of Christ what he was to teach: he was one who, by holding fast to the faithful word according to doctrine, could exhort in sound teaching and refute gainsayers (Titus 1), always ready to give an answer to every questioner (I Peter 3)—a man Catholic in faith, learned in the law, eloquent in speech.

The devil stirred up against him his servant Raymond, count of Toulouse. Because of many great offenses that he had committed against the Church and against God, he had often incurred ecclesiastical censure, and had often, like a shifty and cunning man, slippery and inconstant, obtained absolution through feigned repentance. At last, unable to restrain the hatred he had conceived against him because the word of truth was not in his mouth (Psalm 118 [119]) to execute vengeance among the nations and punishments among the peoples (Psalm 149), and all the more against the same count insofar as he was to be reproved for greater crimes, as though they were his colleagues, he summoned the legates of the Apostolic See to the town of Saint-Gilles,

[Col. 0557A] promising to offer complete satisfaction for every charge brought against him.

But when they had assembled at the said town, the aforementioned count sometimes, like one truthful and compliant, promised to carry out the salutary counsels given him; and sometimes, like one deceitful and stubborn, utterly refused to do them. At length, when they wished to depart from that town, he publicly threatened them with death, saying that whether they turned aside by land or by water, he would carefully watch their departure. Immediately matching deeds to words, he sent his accomplices to lay elaborate ambushes.

Since the madness of his rage could not be softened either by the prayers of the beloved son, the abbot of Saint-Gilles, or by the urgent appeals of the consuls and burgesses, they themselves, despite the count’s unwillingness and extreme displeasure, escorted the legates under armed guard to a place near the bank of the Rhône,

[Col. 0557B] where, as night approached, they rested. Certain retainers of the same count, entirely unknown to the legates, lodged with them there; as the event proved, they sought their blood.

Accordingly, when morning came and Mass had been celebrated as usual, the innocent soldiers of Christ prepared to cross the river. One of the aforesaid servants of Satan, brandishing his spear, wounded the aforesaid Peter below the ribs. Peter, founded with unshakable firmness upon Christ the rock (I Corinthians 10), was unaware of so great a treachery. First looking upon the man who struck him, and following the example of Christ his master together with blessed Stephen, he said to him: “May God forgive you, for I forgive you,” repeatedly uttering this word of mercy and patience.

[Col. 0557C] Then, pierced in this way, he forgot the bitterness of the wound inflicted upon him in hope of heavenly things. At the imminent moment of his precious death, he did not cease to instruct the companions of his ministry, who were advancing faith and peace; and, after many prayers to the Lord, he happily fell asleep in Christ.

Since he shed his blood for faith and peace—than which there is no cause at all more praiseworthy for martyrdom—he would, we believe, already have shone with clear miracles, had their unbelief not hindered this. Of people like them it is written in the Gospel that Jesus did not perform many mighty works there because of their unbelief (Matthew 13). For although tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers (I Corinthians 14), yet when the Savior was brought before Herod—who, Luke testifies, greatly rejoiced at seeing him because he hoped to see some sign performed by him—he disdained to perform a sign or answer the questions put to him (Luke 23), knowing that unbelief did not lead to faith through signs, but that vain curiosity delighted that man.

[Col. 0557D] Although that wicked and perverse generation of the provincials [Col. 0558A] is not worthy that a sign should so soon be given them through their martyr, as perhaps they themselves seek, we nevertheless believe that it was expedient for this one man to die for them, lest the whole should perish (ibid.). Let the contagion infected with heretical depravity be more effectively recalled from its error through the interceding blood of the slain man. This is the ancient sacrifice of Jesus Christ; this is the miraculous design of the Savior: when he is thought to be defeated in his own servants, then he conquers more powerfully in those same servants, and by the power through which he destroyed death by dying, he sometimes causes those who overcame his servants to be overcome by the servants whom they conquered.

Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12). Therefore, hoping that from the death of this most fruitful

[Col. 0558B] grain fruit will arise in Christ’s Church—since he is grievously culpable and culpably hard whose soul no sword pierces (Luke 2)—and never utterly despairing, since such great benefit ought to lie in his blood, that God may grant growth through the messengers of his preaching in the aforesaid province, for which he descended into corruption, we have judged that our venerable brother archbishops and their suffragans ought to be admonished and earnestly exhorted through the Holy Spirit, strictly commanding them by virtue of obedience that, by the streams of their preaching, they cause the word of peace and faith sown by him to grow strong; and that they labor unweariedly, with diligent zeal, to fight heretical depravity, confirm the Catholic faith,

[Col. 0558C] root out vices, and plant virtues.

Let them declare publicly throughout their dioceses that the murderer of the said servant of God, and all those through whose help, deed, counsel, or favor he perpetrated so great a crime, as well as his harborers and defenders, are excommunicated and anathematized by the authority of almighty God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of ourselves. Let them cause every place to which he or any of them comes in their presence to be subject to ecclesiastical interdict. Every Sunday and feast day, with bells rung and candles lit, let them solemnly renew this sentence until, approaching the Apostolic See, they deserve absolution through worthy satisfaction.

But let those who, inflamed with zeal for the orthodox faith, have manfully armed themselves to avenge the righteous blood which does not cease to cry from the earth to heaven (Genesis 4), until the God of vengeance descends from heaven to earth to confound the overthrown and their overthrowers, be securely promised remission from God and his vicar of their sins,

[Col. 0558D] so that such labor may suffice as satisfaction for the deed, likewise for those offenses for which they have offered to the true God contrition of heart and true oral confession.

For these pestilential provincials now plot not merely to despoil us but to destroy us; they sharpen their tongues not only to destroy souls, but stretch out their hands also to destroy bodies, becoming destroyers of souls and murderers of bodies. Although the aforesaid count has long been struck by the sword-point of anathema for many great crimes, which would take too long to recount in every detail, nevertheless, because by certain indications he is presumed guilty of the holy man’s death—not only because he publicly threatened him with death and laid snares for him, but also because he admitted Peter’s murderer into great familiarity and rewarded him with great gifts, to say nothing of the other presumptions, more fully known to many—for this reason too let the same archbishops and bishops publicly declare him anathematized.

[Col. 0559A] And since, according to the canonical decrees of the holy Fathers, faith need not be kept with one who does not keep faith with God, let all those bound by an oath of fealty, association, or such covenant to the said count be declared, by apostolic authority, released from it for the present, he having been separated from the communion of the faithful as one to be avoided rather than supported. Let it be declared lawful for every Catholic man, preserving the right of the chief lord, not only to pursue the count’s person but also to occupy and hold his land—especially so that, through their diligence, it may be vigorously cleansed from heresy, which until now has been shamefully wounded and stained by his wickedness.

For it is fitting that the hands of all should rise against him whose hand has been against all.

[Col. 0559C] But if not even thus affliction gives him understanding, we shall see to it that our hand is made heavier upon him. If, however, he should promise in any way to render satisfaction, he must first give these signs of repentance: he must expel, with all his power, the followers of heretical depravity and strive to be reconciled to fraternal peace, since ecclesiastical censure has been pronounced against him principally because he is known to have sinned in both respects. Yet if God chose to take account of his iniquities, he could scarcely make suitable satisfaction not only for himself but for the great multitude whom he has led into the snare of damnation.

But since, according to the saying of Truth, those who kill the body are not to be feared, but he who can cast body and soul into Gehenna (Luke 12), we trust and hope in him who, in order to remove fear of death from his faithful, died and rose on the third day (Luke 24), that the death of the aforesaid man of God will not only not instill fear in our venerable brother the bishop of Couserans, in our beloved son A., abbot of Cîteaux, legates of the Apostolic See, and in the other followers of the orthodox faith, but will kindle love in them;

[Col. 0559D] so that, following the example of him who happily purchased eternal life with temporal death, they may not fear, if necessary, to lay down their lives for Christ in so glorious a contest.

Therefore we have judged it right to counsel the archbishops and bishops, impressing exhortations with commands and commands with exhortations, that, heeding effectively the salutary admonitions and commands of those legates,

[Col. 0560A] they may stand by them in all things which they judge ought to be enjoined upon them for these purposes, as most valiant fellow-soldiers. Let them know that we command the sentence which the legates pronounce not only upon the rebellious but also upon the negligent to be held valid and observed inviolably.

Come then, soldiers of Christ; come, valiant recruits of Christian warfare: let the groaning of the universal Church move you; let pious zeal inflame you to avenge so great an injury done to our God. Remember that our Creator did not need us when he made us. Although he does not need our service, as though he would become more wearied in acting if we were less willing to labor, or as though his omnipotence were diminished for want of our service, nevertheless in this crisis he grants us an occasion for acceptable service.

[Col. 0560B] Therefore, after the murder of the aforesaid righteous man, since the Church in those regions is said to sit in sadness and grief without a comforter, faith to have vanished, peace to have perished, and the pestilence of heresy and hostile fury to have grown stronger; and since, unless help is powerfully brought to it in this new storm, the ship of the Church appears on the point of total shipwreck, we earnestly admonish and more urgently exhort your whole body. In this hour of such necessity we confidently command you in Christ’s power, and grant remission of sins, that you do not delay to meet such great evils; that you endeavor to bring those peoples to peace in him who is the God of peace and love; and that, by whatever means God reveals to you, you labor to abolish heretical perfidy there, attacking its followers with a strong hand and outstretched arm even more securely than Saracens, because they are worse than Saracens.

[Col. 0560C] Do not cease to press, by the weight of oppression imposed upon him, the aforesaid count—who, as though he had made a covenant with death, gives no thought to his own end (Isaiah 28)—and his supporters, if perhaps affliction gives him understanding and, his face filled with disgrace, he begins to seek the name of God by making satisfaction to us and to the Church—indeed, to God. Drive them from the camps of the Lord and take away their lands, in which, once heretics have been banished, Catholic inhabitants may be installed, that they may serve before God in holiness and righteousness according to the discipline of our orthodox faith (Luke 1).

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of March, in the second year of our pontificate.

Having set forth these matters concerning the death of the most holy man, let us return to the course of our narrative.

## CHAPTER IX. The bishops of Toulouse and Couserans are sent to Rome to explain to the supreme pontiff the condition of the Church in the province of Narbonne

The prelates of the province of Narbonne, and others concerned in the business of peace and faith, saw that the good men—the bishop of Osma, Brother Peter of Castelnau, and Brother Ralph—had died, men who had been

[Col. 0561A] leaders and masters of preaching in the land mentioned above. Observing that this preaching had now for the most part run its course and had made little progress—indeed, had been wholly deprived of the hoped-for fruit—they judged that the matter should be referred to the feet of the supreme pontiff.

Therefore the venerable men Fulk, bishop of Toulouse, and Navarre, bishop of Couserans, set forth and hastened to Rome, to beseech the lord pope to extend a helping hand to the province of Narbonne, and also to the provinces of Bourges and Bordeaux, which were in danger for the peace of the Church and were as it were utterly shipwrecked.

Pope Innocent, who labored with all his strength for the needs of the defense of the Catholic faith, applied a healing hand to so great a disease, sending into France general and effective letters concerning this matter, as we shall set out more fully below.

[Col. 0561B] When the count of Toulouse heard—indeed, let us call him rather “count of Dolosa,” that is, Deceit—that the aforementioned bishops had gone to the Roman court, he feared that he would be punished as he deserved and saw that his deeds could not go unpunished. Feigning repentance and taking precautions for himself, if he could, for the future, he sent to Rome, in addition to the many others whom he had already sent, certain execrable and malicious men: the archbishop of Auch and Raymond of Rabastens, who had formerly been bishop of Toulouse but had been deposed for offenses meriting it.

Through these messengers he complained to the lord pope of the abbot of Cîteaux, who was acting as legate in the affair of the faith, asserting

[Col. 0561C] that the abbot harassed him too harshly and beyond what was just. The count also promised that if the lord pope sent someone from his own side to him, he would conform himself in every respect to that man’s will.

But he said this not because he wished to reform himself in any degree. Rather, he thought that if the lord pope sent one of his cardinals to him, he might, as a shifty and cunning man, deceive him. But the Almighty, who searches hearts and knows secrets (Wisdom 1), did not wish apostolic purity to be deceived, nor the wickedness of the said count to remain any longer concealed. The righteous Judge therefore provided justly and mercifully that the lord pope should satisfy the count in what he appeared justly to request, while the count’s malice should no longer remain hidden.

For the lord pope sent one of his household clerics

[Col. 0561D] into Provence, a man named Milo, of honorable life, distinguished learning, and eloquent speech, who, to state his integrity briefly, could neither be frightened by terror nor in the least broken.

When the count heard that Master Milo was coming, he rejoiced greatly, for he thought that the aforesaid master would accommodate himself entirely to the count’s own will. Traveling through his land, the count began to boast and say: “Now all is well with me, because I have a legate after my own heart—or rather, I myself shall be the legate.” But all things turned out contrary to his wish, as will be related below.

## CHAPTER X. Master Theodisius is sent with Master Milo

[Col. 0562A]

[Note: [Col. 0561D] In Ciaconius, *Hugo* is corruptly read in place of *Milo*.] There was sent with the said Master Milo a cleric named Master Theodisius, a canon of Genoa, to assist the aforesaid Master Milo and aid him in carrying out the business of the faith. This Theodisius was a man of great learning, of remarkable steadfastness, and of exceptional goodness. He conducted himself well in the cause of Jesus Christ; the outcome of events made clear how many dangers and labours he endured for that cause, and we have subsequently taken care to relate these more fully. The lord pope had, moreover, instructed Master Milo that in all matters pertaining to the business of the faith, and especially in the affair of the count of Toulouse, he should proceed according to the counsel of the abbot of Cîteaux, since the abbot fully knew both the state of the matter and the count’s cunning devices. Thus the lord pope had expressly said to Master Milo: “The abbot of Cîteaux will do everything, and you will be his instrument; for the count of Toulouse suspects him, whereas he will not suspect you.”

Master Milo and Master Theodisius therefore came down into France [Note: [Col. 0562D] Thus the manuscript exemplar: *Theodisius*, not *Theodosius*, as Ciaconius has it in his work on Innocent III.] and found the abbot of Cîteaux at Auxerre. Master Milo accordingly consulted the Cistercian abbot concerning several definite articles relating to the business of the faith. Having instructed him most carefully on every point, the abbot gave him his counsel in writing and under seal. He also warned and advised him that, before proceeding against the count of Toulouse, he should summon such archbishops, bishops, and other prelates as seemed expedient [Col. 0562B], and seek and obtain their counsel. He expressly and particularly named certain prelates whose counsel Master Milo ought to follow.

After this, the abbot of Cîteaux and Master Milo went to Philip, king of France, who was holding a solemn assembly at Neuville in the territory of Sens with many of his barons. Present were Odo, duke of Burgundy; the counts of Nevers and Saint-Pol; and many other nobles and powerful men. The lord pope was sending the king special letters, admonishing and entreating him either to provide in person, or at least through his son Louis, timely aid to the Church endangered in the province of Narbonne. The king gave the pope’s messenger this reply: that he had two great and grievous lions at his side [Col. 0562D], Otto, who was called emperor, and John, king of England, who on either side were exerting all their strength to disturb the kingdom of France. Therefore, he said, he himself would by no means leave France, nor would he send his son. Indeed, for the present it seemed enough to him if he permitted his barons to go and disturb, in the province of Narbonne, the disturbers of peace and faith.

The supreme pontiff, however, in order to make the faithful peoples more ready to extirpate the heretical pest, had sent general letters to all prelates, counts, barons, and the whole people established in the kingdom of France, vigorously admonishing and exhorting them to hasten to avenge the injury done to the Crucified One in the province of Narbonne [Col. 0563A], knowing that remission of all sins had been granted by God and His vicar to all who, inflamed with zeal for the orthodox faith, should undertake this work of piety, provided that they were likewise contrite and confessed. Why say more? This indulgence was proclaimed in France, and a great multitude of the faithful armed itself with the sign of the cross.

## CHAPTER XI. A council is held at Montélimar, and a day is fixed at Valence for the count to appear before Milo.

After the above-mentioned assembly at Neuville had been held, Master Milo, with his colleague Master Theodisius, proceeded into the province. Coming to a certain castle called Montélimar [Col. 0563B], he summoned very many archbishops and bishops. When they had come to him, he carefully asked them how they ought to proceed in the business of peace and faith, especially in the affair of the count of Toulouse. He also wished each prelate to give him, in writing and under seal, his counsel on certain articles concerning which the abbot of Cîteaux had instructed him. It was done as he commanded; and, marvelous to hear, the counsels of the abbot of Cîteaux and of the prelates all agreed without any disagreement. “This is the Lord’s doing” (Psalm 117 [118]).

After this Master Milo sent to the count of Toulouse, commanding him to come to him at Valence on a day fixed by him [Col. 0563C]. The count came on that day; and, false, cruel, slippery, and perjured as he was, he promised the legate, Master Milo—that is, deceitfully—that he would in all things do his will. But the legate, being a cautious and prudent man and acting upon the counsel of the prelates, wished and ordered the count of Toulouse to hand over to him, as security for the land which he held in the province, seven castles. He also wished the consuls of the cities of Avignon and Nîmes, and of the town of Saint-Gilles, to swear to him that, if the count of Toulouse should presume to oppose the command of the legate, they would not be bound to him by loyalty of homage or alliance. Furthermore, the county of Ingrue (*Comitatus Ingruensis*) should fall into forfeiture to the Holy Roman Church. The count of Toulouse, although grieved and unwilling, compelled by necessity, promised to fulfil everything the legate commanded [Col. 0563D]. Thus it came about that he who had called the abbot of Cîteaux severe called the legate far more severe. By God’s ordering, this is believed to have been most justly done: where the tyrant expected a remedy, he found vengeance and a scourge.

Immediately Master Theodisius, a man of complete goodness, came into the province by the legate’s command, in order to receive and occupy on behalf of the Holy Roman Church the seven castles mentioned above, and to fortify them.

## CHAPTER XII. By certain ceremonies long in use, the count of Toulouse is reconciled to the Church.

When all these things had been duly performed, the legate went down to the town of Saint-Gilles to reconcile the count of Toulouse there. The manner of reconciliation and absolution was as follows [Col. 0564A]. The count was brought naked before the doors of the church of Blessed Giles, and there, before the legate and more than twenty archbishops and bishops assembled for this purpose, he swore upon the body of Christ and upon the relics of the saints—displayed before the church doors with great veneration and held there in great abundance by the prelates—that he would obey the commands of the Holy Roman Church in all things. At once the legate caused a stole to be placed around the count’s neck; then, taking the count by the stole, he brought him, absolved and with scourging, into the church.

Nor should it be left unmentioned that, when the count of Toulouse was brought into the church of Saint-Gilles with scourging, as we have said, he was, by God’s ordering, utterly unable to leave the church because of the crowd by the way through which he had entered [Col. 0564B]. Rather, he had to descend into the lower part of the church and pass naked before the tomb of the blessed martyr Peter of Castelnau, whom he had caused to be killed. O just judgment of God! He whom the count had despised while alive, he was compelled to honour after his death.

I think it should also be noted that, when the body of the aforesaid martyr, which had first been buried in the cloister of the monks of Saint-Gilles, was transferred into the church after a long time, it was found so sound and unharmed as if it had been buried that very day. Moreover, a fragrance of marvelous sweetness issued from the saint’s body and garments.

## CHAPTER XIII. The count of Toulouse deceitfully takes the cross, the sign of holy warfare, which the soldiers of the Catholic army wore sewn upon their breasts.

After all these things, the most cunning count of Toulouse, fearing the approach of the cross-bearers, who were soon to come from France into the regions of Narbonne to expel the heretics and their supporters, asked the legate to give him a cross, so that he might thereby protect his land from attack by the cross-bearers [Col. 0564C]. The legate consented and gave crosses to the count and to only two of his knights. O false and utterly faithless cross-bearer—the count of Toulouse, I mean—who took the cross, not to avenge the injury done to the Crucified One, but so that for a time he might conceal and cover his wickedness!

When all this had been done, the legate and Master Theodisius returned toward Lyons, in order to meet the cross-bearers who were soon to come against the provincial heretics. For throughout the entire province the indulgence which the lord pope had granted to those setting out against the aforesaid heretics had been proclaimed; and thus very many nobles and common people had armed themselves against the enemies of the cross with the sign of the cross upon their breasts [Col. 0564D]. Therefore, when so many thousands of faithful people in France had taken, and were taking, the cross in order to avenge the injury done to our God, nothing remained except that the Lord of Hosts—who, in His accustomed goodness and unheard-of kindness, had repeatedly shown compassion to His enemies, namely the heretics and their supporters, and had sent many men to them time and again—should, having sent forth His armies, and destroy those most cruel murderers. For they persisted in their perversity and were obstinate in their wickedness; they had subjected some men to insults and killed others [Col. 0565A].

## CHAPTER XIV. The arrival of the crusading army in the province.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1209, in the pontificate of Pope Innocent III, while Philip was reigning as king of the Franks, around the feast of Saint John the Baptist, all the cross-bearers set out from different parts of France and, by common counsel and provident arrangement, assembled at Lyons, a city of Gaul. Among those present there, the following were especially prominent: the archbishop of Sens; the bishop of Autun; the bishop of Clermont; the bishop of Nevers; Odo, duke of Burgundy; the count of Nevers; the count of Saint-Pol; the count of Montfort; the count of Bar-sur-Seine; Guichard of Beaujeu; William des Roches, seneschal of Anjou; Gaucher of Joigny; Guy of Lévis; Lambert of Thury; besides many nobles and powerful men whom it would take too long to name individually [Col. 0565B].

## CHAPTER XV. The count of Toulouse goes to meet the cross-bearers.

When Raymond, count of Toulouse, saw the multitude of cross-bearers approaching, and feared that they would invade his land—as the sting of conscience accused him concerning the wicked deeds he had committed—he went out to meet them and came as far as the vicinity of the city of Valence. But they had set out with a high hand. Finding them near that city, the said count pretended peace and promised a false obedience, most firmly undertaking to conform himself, at the command of the Holy Roman Church, even to their judgment. To secure observance of these terms, he gave certain castles. He also wished to give his son as a hostage, or himself. Why say more? This enemy of Christ was even joined to them; they proceeded together and, going straight onward, reached the city of Béziers [Col. 0565C].

## CHAPTER XVI. On the wickedness of the citizens of Béziers, and the siege, capture, and destruction of that city.

Béziers was a most noble city, but wholly infected with the poison of heretical depravity. Nor were its citizens merely heretics: they were plunderers, unjust men, adulterers, most wicked robbers, full of every kind of sin [Col. 0565D]. Let it not weary the reader if we discuss something in particular concerning the wickedness of these citizens.

One night, at the very break of day, a priest of that city was going to church to celebrate the divine mysteries, carrying a chalice in his hands. Certain men of Béziers, who had laid an ambush, seized the priest, beat him severely, broke his arm, and wounded him most grievously. Taking the chalice he held and uncovering it, they urinated into it in contempt of the body and blood of Jesus Christ.

At another time, in the church of Blessed Mary Magdalene situated in the said city, the citizens, most wicked traitors, killed their lord, Trencavel, viscount of Béziers. They also broke the teeth of their bishop, who was attempting to defend the viscount from their hands [Col. 0566A].

On a certain day a canon of Béziers, after celebrating Mass, came out of the principal church. Hearing the tumult of men working at the city ditches, he asked what it was. Those present answered: “It is the uproar of men working on the ditches, because we are fortifying the city against the Frenchmen who are coming.” For the arrival of the pilgrims was already imminent. While they were speaking thus, an old man of venerable age appeared and said to them: “You are fortifying this city against the pilgrims; but who will be able to fortify you from above?” By this he indicated that the Lord would fight against them from heaven. On hearing it, they were greatly stirred and troubled; and when they wished to attack the old man, he suddenly disappeared and could nowhere be found.

Let us now continue our narrative. Before the cross-bearers reached Béziers, the viscount of Béziers, named Raymond Roger, noble indeed by birth and nephew of the count of Toulouse, followed his uncle’s wickedness and in no respect restrained the heretics. He had most firmly promised the citizens of Béziers that he would by no means abandon them, but would remain with them in the aforesaid city even to death and await the arrival of Christ’s soldiers. But when he heard that our forces were approaching, forgetful of his compact and faithlessly violating the alliance, he fled to Carcassonne, another of his noble cities, taking with him many heretics from Béziers [Col. 0566B].

When our men reached Béziers, they sent into the city its bishop, who had come out to meet them: namely Master Reginald of Montpellier, a man venerable in age, life, and learning. Our men said that they had come for the destruction of heretics, and commanded the Catholic citizens, if there were any, to hand over to them the heretics whom that venerable bishop—who knew them fully and had also recorded them in writing—would name. Or, if they could not do this, they were to leave the city and abandon the heretics, lest they perish together with them. When the aforesaid bishop conveyed this message from our men to the citizens, they refused to consent. Raising themselves against God and the Church, having made a covenant with death, they chose rather to die as heretics than to live as Christians [Col. 0566D].

Before our men had attacked them in any way, certain inhabitants came out of the city and began fiercely to assail our men with arrows. Seeing this, the army’s servants, commonly called *ribalds*, approached the city walls in the greatest indignation. Without the nobles of the army knowing or being consulted at all, they launched an assault that very hour and, marvelous to relate, took the city. Why say more? Entering immediately, they killed almost all, from the least to the greatest, and gave the city to the flames. The oft-mentioned city was taken on the feast of Saint Mary Magdalene.

O most just measure of divine dispensation! As we said at the beginning of this book, the heretics said that Blessed Mary Magdalene had been Christ’s concubine. Moreover, in her church in the city, as we have mentioned above, the citizens of Béziers had killed their lord and broken their bishop’s teeth. They were therefore deservedly captured and destroyed on her feast day: she of whom they had uttered so many insults, and whose church those shameless dogs had defiled with the blood of their lord—their viscount—and of their bishop [Col. 0567A]. In that same church, in which, as has often been said, the citizens of Béziers had killed their lord, as many as seven thousand of the Béziers people were killed on the day the city was taken.

It should especially be noted that, just as the city of Jerusalem was destroyed by Titus and Vespasian in the forty-second year after the Passion of our Lord, so the city of Béziers was laid waste by the French in the forty-second year after the killing of its lord [Col. 0567B]. Nor should this be omitted: the aforesaid city had many times been devastated on account of the reason mentioned above, always on the feast day of Saint Mary Magdalene. In the church of that saint so great a crime had been committed, and it received the fitting vengeance for that crime.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the siege of the city of Carcassonne and its surrender.

After Béziers had been taken and destroyed, our men resolved to proceed directly to Carcassonne. For the citizens of Carcassonne were most wicked heretics and exceedingly great sinners before the Lord. Those dwelling in the castles situated between Béziers and Carcassonne had fled in fear of the army, leaving their castles empty; some, however, who were not implicated in heretical depravity surrendered to our men [Col. 0567C].

When the viscount heard that our forces were advancing to besiege Carcassonne, he gathered whatever knights he could and, withdrawing with them into Carcassonne, prepared to defend the city against our men. Nor should it be passed over that the wicked and faithless citizens of Carcassonne destroyed the refectory and cellar of the canons of Carcassonne, who were regular canons, and even, more abominably, the stalls of the church, in order to fortify the city walls with them. O profane counsel! O fortification without protection, built by the destruction of the inviolate house of God, protected by sacred immunity, and therefore deservedly destined for destruction! The houses of peasants are preserved untouched, while the houses of God’s servants are cast down and overthrown [Col. 0567D].

When our men reached the city, they pitched their tents around it, establishing the siege. After the troops of warriors had been posted all around, they abstained from battle that day and the following one. The city of Carcassonne, situated on the brow of a mountain, was surrounded by two suburbs, each fortified with walls and ditches. On the third day our men hoped to take by assault, without siege engines, the first suburb, which was somewhat less strong than the second. They attacked it unanimously, while the bishops and abbots, gathered together with all the clergy, sang with the greatest devotion, “Come, Holy Spirit,” and prayed for divine aid to be present at once. The first suburb was immediately abandoned by the enemy and was taken by force [Col. 0568A].

Nor should it be omitted that the noble count of Montfort was the first of all—indeed the only one among the knights—to throw himself boldly into the ditch while the others were attacking the said suburb. When it had been taken, our men filled in the ditches and completely levelled it to the ground.

Seeing how easily they had taken the aforesaid suburb, our men thought that the second, far stronger and better fortified, could likewise be taken by assault. The next day they approached the wall of this second suburb. But when they pressed hard in the assault, the viscount and his men defended themselves so valiantly that the frequent and repeated throwing of stones compelled our men to withdraw from the ditch they had entered [Col. 0568B]. In this conflict, one of our knights was left in the ditch with a broken leg. As no one dared approach to draw him out because of the unceasing rain of stones, the count of Montfort, a man of complete virtue, threw himself into the ditch and, assisted by a single squire, rescued him at no small risk to his own life.

After this our men quickly erected engines called *petrariae* for breaking down the wall of the suburb. When the upper part of the wall had been somewhat weakened by the blows of the stones, our men with great difficulty brought up against it a four-wheeled cart covered with oxhides, and sent workmen beneath it to dig through the wall [Col. 0568C]. The enemy, throwing fire, wood, and stones with the greatest persistence, immediately smashed the cart. But the diggers withdrew into the hollow already made in the wall, and the enemy could in no way delay them from piercing it. Why say more? At daybreak on the following morning, the undermined wall collapsed. Our men immediately entered with a shout, and the enemy retreated to the upper city. Later, however, seeing that our knights had left the suburb and returned to their tents, they came out of the city, drove out whatever of our men remained in the suburb, killed many of our men because of the difficulty of escape, set fire throughout the suburb, and again withdrew to the upper city.

During that siege something happened which should not be passed over, but must be regarded as a very great miracle [Col. 0568D]. It was said that there were as many as fifty thousand men in the army. Our enemies had destroyed all the mills around the city, so that our men could obtain bread only from a few neighboring castles. Nevertheless, bread was so abundant there that it was sold at a very low price. Accordingly the heretics said that the abbot of Cîteaux was a magician and had brought demons in the form of men, because it seemed to them that our men did not eat.

After these events, our men deliberated how they might take the city. They observed that, if they did here what had been done at Béziers, the city would be destroyed [Col. 0569A], and all the goods in it would be consumed. Then the man who was to be set over that land would have nothing from which to live, nor could he keep knights and servants to guard the land. Therefore, on the barons’ advice, a peace settlement was negotiated as follows. It was ordered that all should leave naked and thus escape; the viscount, however, was to be held in custody; and all property was to remain for the man who would become lord of that land, for the necessity named above. And so it was done. Thus all left the city naked, carrying nothing with them except their sins.

Then was fulfilled what had been said by the venerable Berengar, formerly bishop of Carcassonne. One day, while preaching in his city and reproaching the citizens, as was his custom, for heresy, they would not listen to him. He said to them: “You do not wish to listen to me. Believe me: I shall utter such a bellow against you that men will come from remote parts of the world and destroy this town. Know most certainly that even if the walls of this city were iron and of the greatest height, you could not defend yourselves from receiving, for your unbelief and wickedness, the fitting vengeance of the most just Judge” [Col. 0569B].

On account of these and similar things which that most holy man thundered against them, the said citizens at one time expelled him from the city, strictly proclaiming by the public crier, under penalty of most severe punishment, that no one should dare to deal with him or his people in any matter of buying or selling. Let us now continue what we began. After the city had been surrendered and everyone had departed, knights were selected from the army to guard the city’s goods faithfully [Col. 0569C].

## CHAPTER XVII bis. The count of Montfort is chosen prince of the territory and dominion of Count Raymond.

When all these things had been done, the barons deliberated among themselves whom they ought to set over the aforesaid land. First, lordship over the land was offered to the count of Nevers, and afterward to the duke of Burgundy; but they refused to accept it. Therefore two bishops and four knights from the whole army, together with the abbot of Cîteaux, legate of the Apostolic See, were selected to choose the lord of the land. They firmly promised that they would choose the man whom they knew to be more useful according to God and the world [Col. 0569D].

These seven men, with the grace of the sevenfold Holy Spirit working with them and looking mercifully upon the whole land, chose a faithful Catholic man, of honourable character and valiant in arms: Simon, count of Montfort. Immediately the abbot of Cîteaux, legate of the Apostolic See and father and master of this holy enterprise, together with the duke of Burgundy and the count of Nevers, came to him and admonished, entreated, and advised him to accept both the burden and the honour. When this most prudent man most insistently refused, confessing himself inadequate and unworthy, the abbot of Cîteaux and the duke immediately cast themselves at his feet, pressing entreaty upon entreaty. As the count still refused, the abbot, exercising the authority of his legation, most strictly commanded him, by virtue of obedience, to do what they requested [Col. 0570A]. Thus the aforesaid man accepted the governance of the land, to the praise of God and honour of the Church, and for the suppression of heretical depravity.

Here should be added a matter most worthy of narration, which had happened a little earlier in France concerning the noble count of Montfort. One day the venerable abbot of Vaux-de-Cernay, named Guy, mentioned above, who did all he could to promote the cause of the faith against heretics, was returning from the duke of Burgundy. He carried the duke’s letters, in which the duke asked the count of Montfort to join him in the knighthood of Jesus Christ against the heretics, offering great gifts if he would consent. It happened that the abbot, coming from the duke, found the count occupied with certain business in the church of one of the count’s castles, called Rochefort. When the abbot had called him aside to show him the duke’s letters, the count passed through the chancel screen of the church, took up a book of the Psalter which he found upon the lectern, opened it deliberately by divine prompting, placed his finger upon the first line, and said to the abbot: “Explain this Scripture to me: ‘God has given His angels charge over you, to keep you in all your ways; they shall bear you in their hands, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone’” (Psalm 90 [91]) [Col. 0570B]. The outcome of events most clearly proved that this had been provided by divine ordering.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the splendid qualities of mind and body of Simon, count of Montfort.

Since the opportunity of the place presents itself, as the order of reason requires, let us set down here what we know of the noble count of Montfort. First it should be said that he was illustrious in birth, strong in courage, and highly practiced in arms. Furthermore, to come to his appearance, he was tall in stature, distinguished in hair, handsome of face, pleasing in aspect, broad-shouldered, strong-armed, graceful in body, agile and firm in every limb, keen and alert, and in no part of himself—not even the smallest—open to reproach from enemy or envier [Col. 0570C].

Finally, to ascend to greater matters: he was eloquent in speech, gracious in manner, agreeable in companionship, most pure in chastity, outstanding in humility, endowed with wisdom, firm in purpose, provident in counsel, just in judgment, diligent in military exercises, measured in his actions, vigorous in undertakings, unwearied in completing them, and wholly devoted to divine service. O provident choice of leaders! O wise acclamation of the pilgrims, which by its choice provided a faithful man to defend the orthodox faith; which desired that a man so fitted for the whole commonwealth should rule in the most sacred cause of Jesus Christ against the pestilent heretics! Such a man, indeed, was worthy to command the army of the Lord of Hosts: a man adorned, as has been said, by nobility of birth, purity of character, and martial excellence. Such a man, I say, such a man, it was worthwhile to raise up for the defence of the endangered Church [Col. 0570D], under whose protection Christian innocence might stand secure, while the presumptuous rashness of heretical depravity would not hope for impunity in its detestable error. And it was fitting enough that one originating from Montfort should defend the shipwrecked Church from persecuting heretics through Christ—if it is not carried over the mountain.

It should be noted that, although some might be found equal to him in one grace or another, I say boldly that scarcely, or never, will one be found in whom such a fullness of gifts, both natural and gratuitous, flowed together at once. Lest the greatness of so many and such gifts bestowed by the divine majesty should exalt him, the Lord gave him the spur of unceasing anxiety and most pressing poverty. For while God worked so marvelously and magnificently with him in the capture of castles and destruction of enemies, He also afflicted him with so many cares and pressed him down by such want of poverty that he was scarcely permitted rest, lest he should be allowed to grow proud [Col. 0571A].

That the virtue of this most illustrious man may become more clearly known, let it not weary the reader if we briefly recount some things which we saw that he did in former days.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Simon the count’s goodwill toward the people of Zadar, and his singular reverence for the Roman Church.

At one time this same noble count and Guy, abbot of Vaux-de-Cernay—who afterward became bishop of Carcassonne, and of whom we have often made mention—were setting out with the barons of France overseas [Note: [Col. 0571D] The author means the Byzantine expedition undertaken in 1203, whose history Geoffrey of Villehardouin wrote in French truthfully. But here the author treats the Venetians with little prudence, indeed with complete thoughtlessness. The said Geoffrey, who was present at the events and almost directed them, or at least played a great part in them, warmly praises the Venetians’ good faith, extraordinary industry, and courage in this expedition, and condemns the troubled counsels of certain monks. For this reason I would have the reader consult him.].

When the nobles of France saw the most wealthy city of Venice, where they were to embark upon ships hired jointly for crossing the sea, they hired these ships at a very high price. There were present the noblest men in all France: Baldwin, count of Flanders; Henry, his brother; Louis, count of Blois; the noble count of Montfort; and many others whom it would not be easy to number. The citizens of Venice, however, crafty and wicked men, saw that our pilgrims had been exhausted of money and almost entirely drained because of the excessive price of the ships, and could not pay a large part of the fare then demanded. Seizing this opportunity—namely, that our pilgrims were indebted and subject to them—they led them to destroy a certain Christian city belonging to the king of Hungary, named Zadar [Col. 0571D].

When our pilgrims reached it, they pitched their tents near the city walls, as besiegers customarily do. But the count of Montfort and the abbot of Vaux, not following the crowd to do evil, refused to besiege it with the others and stationed themselves farther away from the city. Meanwhile the lord pope sent his letters to all the pilgrims, strictly forbidding them, under peril of the remission of sins which he had granted them and under pain of the gravest excommunication, to harm the city of Zadar in any way. One day, when the abbot of Vaux read these letters to the nobles of the army assembled together, and the Venetians wished to kill him, the noble count of Montfort rose among them and, opposing and resisting the Venetians, prevented them from killing the aforesaid abbot [Col. 0572A].

The citizens of Zadar, who had come there to seek peace, were addressed by the noble count in the presence of all the barons as follows: “I did not come here to destroy Christians. I shall inflict no harm upon you; whatever others may do, I make you secure against myself and my men.” Thus spoke this most valiant man, and immediately he and his followers left the place of conference.

Why linger longer? The barons of the army, disregarding the apostolic command, took and destroyed the city. Again they were miserably and most severely excommunicated by the lord pope; and I, who was there, bear witness to the truth, because I saw and read the letters containing the apostolic excommunication [Col. 0572B].

The most noble count, however, did not consent to the opinion of the many and so depart from the right path. Rather, leaving the fellowship of sinners, he came, with great hardship and loss, through desert and pathless country, after many distresses and labours, to a most noble town of Apulia. There he again hired ships and set out. Crossing overseas with a favourable voyage, he remained there for a year and more, performed many valiant military deeds against the pagans, and then returned alive and well with honour to his own lands. The French barons whom he had left at Zadar [Note: [Col. 0572D] Jadera, today Zara [Zadar], a city of Dalmatia or Slavonia.] had almost all perished or died. From that time, therefore, he foreshadowed the triumphs which he afterward happily accomplished, and he then earned the honour which he later attained in suppressing heretical depravity [Col. 0572C].

Nor do we think it should be left unsaid that, great and distinguished as this count was, the Lord provided him with a helper like himself: namely, a wife who, to state it briefly, was devout, wise, and diligent. In her, devotion adorned diligence and wisdom; wisdom shaped devotion and diligence; diligence exercised devotion and wisdom. Moreover, the Lord had blessed the said countess in the bearing of children. For the count had by her many children, exceedingly handsome.

Having thus briefly treated these matters in praise of the oft-mentioned count, let us prepare to continue the course of our narrative [Col. 0572D].

## CHAPTER XX. On account of certain dissensions, the count of Nevers leaves the camp of the cross-bearers.

After the oft-mentioned count had been elected, [Col. 0573A] in the manner and order noted above, the abbot of Cîteaux and he himself immediately approached the duke of Burgundy and the count of Nevers, begging and entreating them to deign to remain yet a little while in the service of Jesus Christ. For there were still many and very strong castles of the heretics to be taken. To omit countless others, there were three exceedingly well-fortified strongholds around Carcassonne, inhabited at that time by the chief enemies of our faith: on one side Minerve, on another the castle of Fines, and on the other Cabaret.

The duke of Burgundy, being most gracious, graciously yielded to their entreaties and promised to remain with them for some time in this undertaking. But the count of Nevers would by no means listen to their pleas, [Col. 0573B] and immediately returned home. For the duke and that count did not get on well; rather, the devil, enemy of peace, so sharpened their mutual hostility that our men daily feared that they would kill one another. Our people also suspected that the count of Nevers bore no sufficiently good will toward our count, because our count was an intimate of the duke of Burgundy and had come with him from the regions of France.

O how great is the malice of the ancient enemy! Seeing and begrudging the advancement of the cause of Jesus Christ, he wished to hinder what he grieved to see advancing. Indeed, the army of crusaders which had been at the siege of Carcassonne was so large and strong that, had it wished to advance further and unanimously [Col. 0573C] pursue the enemies of orthodox faith, it could in a short time have acquired that whole land, since it would have found none able to resist it. But, insofar as human reason can understand, heavenly mercy ordered matters otherwise, because, providing for the salvation of humankind, it wished to reserve the acquisition of the land for sinners. The merciful Lord did not wish this most holy war to end all at once and quickly; providing thereby for sinners an opportunity for pardon and for the righteous a fuller grace, he willed that his enemies should be subdued gradually and successively, so that, while nobles gradually and successively took up arms to avenge the injury done to Jesus Christ, they might, by prolonging the war, prolong the time of pardon for sinners.

## CHAPTER XXI. The Capture of the Castle of Fanum Jovis

[Col. 0573D]

After a few days had been spent at Carcassonne, the noble count left the city with the duke and a large part of the army, intending, with the Lord’s help, to advance farther; for the greater part of the army had departed with the count of Nevers. Setting out from Carcassonne, they pitched their tents that same day near a village called Alzonne. On the following day the duke advised the count to go to a castle called Fanum Jovis.

That castle, abandoned in fear of our men by its knights and inhabitants, had been entered and fortified by certain Aragonese knights who were with our count; for many of the more noble and stronger castles of the enemy had been left empty through fear of the crusaders.
