Therefore the count took a few knights with him, while the duke remained with the army, and went to the aforesaid castle. Having taken it, he fortified it with his own people.

Nor should it be passed over that the count of Toulouse, who had been at the siege of Carcassonne and envied our successes, advised our count to have certain castles destroyed which lay near the land of the count of Toulouse. He himself, as though acting for our count’s benefit, utterly overthrew and burned several castles, under the pretext that they might no longer attack our men. That faithless and wicked man did this because he wished the land to be devastated, so that no one might be able to resist him.

## CHAPTER XXII. The Count Enters the Diocese of Albi

[Col. 0574B] While these things were taking place, the burgesses of a most noble castle called Castres, in the territory of Albi, came to our count, prepared to receive him as lord and to do his will. The duke therefore advised the count to go and take that castle, since it was, as it were, the head of the whole territory of Albi. The count accordingly went with a few men, leaving the duke with the army.

While the count was in the aforesaid castle, and its inhabitants had done him homage and surrendered the castle, knights from a very noble castle near Albi called Lombers came to him, prepared to do for the count what those of Castres had done. But the noble count, wishing to return to the army, did not then go with them; [Col. 0574C] he merely received the castle into his protection until he could go there at a suitable time.

We do not wish to omit a miracle which occurred at the castle of Castres in the count’s presence. Two heretics were presented to the count. One was a *perfectus*—a “Perfect”—in the heretical sect; the other was, as it were, a novice and the other’s disciple. After taking counsel, the count wished both to be burned. But one of the heretics, namely the disciple of the other, inwardly touched by compunction of heart, began to convert and promised that he would willingly abjure heresy and in all respects obey the Holy Roman Church.

When this was heard, a great dispute arose among our men. Some said that, since he was prepared to fulfil what we have stated, he ought not to be condemned to death. [Col. 0574D] Others, on the contrary, maintained that he was deserving of death: first, because it was evident that he had been a heretic; and second, because it was thought that he promised what he said more from fear of impending death than from love of observing the Christian religion.

What more need be said? The count agreed that he should be burned, with this intention: if he were now truly converted, the fire would serve him as an expiation for sins; but if he spoke falsely, he would receive punishment in kind for his treachery. Both were therefore tightly bound with very hard and strong bonds around their legs, bellies, and necks, their hands also being tied behind their backs. This done, the man was asked in what faith he wished to die. He said: “I abjure heretical depravity. I wish to die in the faith of the Holy Roman Church, praying that this fire may be for me as purgatory.”

A great fire was then kindled around the stake. [Col. 0575A] He who was perfect in heresy was burned in an instant; but the other, immediately breaking his very strong bonds, came out of the fire so unharmed that no mark of burning appeared upon him, except that the tips of his fingers were somewhat scorched.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The Count Attempts in Vain to Take the Castle of Cabaret by Siege

Returning from the castle of Castres, the count went back to the army which he had left in the region of Carcassonne. Thereafter the duke of Burgundy, the knights, and the army resolved to march upon Cabaret, if perhaps they might harass the men of Cabaret and compel them by assault to surrender the castle. Our men therefore set out and came within half [Col. 0575B] a league of Cabaret, where they pitched their tents. On the next day the knights and a great part of the army armed themselves and approached Cabaret in order to storm it; but after making the assault and achieving little, they returned to the tents.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The Departure of the Duke of Burgundy, and the Surrender of Pamiers, Saverdun, and Mirepoix

On the following day the duke and the whole strength of the army prepared to depart, and on the third day they left our count and returned home. Thus the count remained almost alone and desolate, with only about thirty knights, who had come from France with other pilgrims and who, beyond the rest, loved the service of Christ and the count.

After the army had departed, [Col. 0575C] the noble count came to Fanum Jovis. When he had arrived there, the venerable abbot of Saint-Antonin at Pamiers, in the territory of Toulouse, immediately came to him, begging him to come to him, and offering at once to surrender to him the most noble castle of Pamiers. As the count was going toward Pamiers, he came to the castle called Mirepoix and immediately took it. That castle was a refuge for heretics and brigands, and belonged to the lordship of the count of Foix.

Having taken that castle, the count went directly to Pamiers. The abbot received him with honour and surrendered to him the castle of Pamiers, which the count received from him; and the count did homage to the abbot, as he ought to have done. For the castle properly belonged to the lordship of the abbot and the canons of Saint [Col. 0575D] Antonin, who were regular canons, and no one ought to have held anything in it except from the abbot. But the most wicked count of Foix, who ought to have held that castle from the abbot, maliciously wished to claim the whole of it for himself, as we shall show below.

From there our count came to Saverdun, and the burgesses surrendered themselves without any condition. That castle, namely Saverdun, was in the power and lordship of the count of Foix.

## CHAPTER XXV. Albi and Lombers Come into the Power of Count Simon

Returning to Fanum Jovis, our count resolved to go to the castle of Lombers, mentioned above, in order to receive it. There were more than fifty knights in [Col. 0576A] that castle. When the count arrived, he was honourably received. The knights said that on the next day they would do his will.

But when morning came, those knights attempted treachery against the count. After they had prolonged their deliberation until the ninth hour, the matter became known to the count, who immediately feigned a pretext and without delay left the castle. When the knights saw this, they followed him; and, overcome by fear, they did his will, surrendered the castle, rendered him homage, and swore fealty.

The same count came to Albi. Albi was a city which the viscount of Béziers had held; but William, bishop of Albi, who was chief lord of the city, gladly received him as lord and surrendered [Col. 0576B] the city to him. What more need be said? The count then received the whole diocese of Albi, except for certain castles held by the count of Toulouse, which the count of Toulouse had taken from the viscount of Béziers.

When these matters had been duly completed, our count returned to Carcassonne. A few days later he went to a castle called Limoux, in the territory of Razès, in order to establish a fortification there. That castle had surrendered to the count immediately after Carcassonne was taken. As he proceeded there, he took certain castles which resisted the Holy Church, and deservedly hanged on gallows many men from those castles for their deeds.

Returning from the castle of Limoux, the count came to a small castle near Carcassonne, belonging to the count of Foix and called [Col. 0576C] Preixan, and besieged it. While he was besieging that castle, the count of Foix came to him and swore that in all things he would abide by the command of the Church; moreover, he gave his son to the count as a hostage, and relinquished the castle which the count had besieged. These things done, the count returned to Carcassonne.

## CHAPTER XXVI. The King of Aragon Refuses to Receive the Count’s Homage Owed Him for the City of Carcassonne, Though the Count Urges It in Vain

Peter, king of Aragon, to whose lordship the city of Carcassonne belonged, would by no means receive the count’s homage, but wished to possess Carcassonne. [Col. 0576D] When on one occasion he wished to go to Montpellier and did not dare, he sent to the count and ordered him to meet him at Narbonne. This having been done, the king and our count arrived together at Montpellier. After they had spent fifteen days there, the king could not be persuaded to receive the oft-mentioned count as his vassal.

Moreover, as was said secretly, he ordered the nobles throughout the whole viscounty of Béziers and Carcassonne who still resisted the Holy Church and our count not to make terms with the count, promising them that he himself would attack the count with them.

As the count was returning from Montpellier, men came and told him that very many knights of the dioceses of Béziers, Carcassonne, and Albi [Col. 0577A] had withdrawn, together with their castles, from the fealty they had promised the count; and this was indeed true. Furthermore, certain traitors had besieged some of the count’s knights, namely Almaric and William of Pissy, in a tower of a castle near Carcassonne.

On hearing this, the count hastened in the hope of reaching the castle before his knights were captured. But he could not cross the river called the Aude, for the waters had overflowed, and he had to go by way of Carcassonne, since there was otherwise no way to cross that river. As he was proceeding there, he learned that his knights had been captured.

It happened, while the count was at Montpellier, that Bouchard of Marly, Gobert of Essigny, and certain other knights were at Saissac, [Col. 0577B] a very strong castle in the diocese of Carcassonne which the count had given to Bouchard. One day they pursued enemies as far as Cabaret. There was a very strong and almost impregnable castle near Carcassonne, well supplied with many knights. This castle resisted Christendom and the count more than all others; it was indeed a fountainhead of heresy. Its lord, Peter Roger, inveterate in evil days, was a heretic and an open enemy of the Church.

When Bouchard and his companions approached Cabaret, the knights of Cabaret, who had laid an ambush, rose up, surrounded them, and captured Bouchard. They killed Gobert because he would not surrender in any way. Taking Bouchard captive to Cabaret, [Col. 0577C] they put him in an underground prison, where they kept him in chains for sixteen months.

At the same time, before the count had returned from Montpellier, Raymond Roger, viscount of Béziers, who was held in the palace at Carcassonne, died while suffering from illness. Now let us return to the sequence of our narrative.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The Treachery and Cruelty of Guirald of Pepieux against Count Simon and His Knights

When the count had returned to Carcassonne from Montpellier, Guirald of Pepieux, a knight of Minerve, whom the count held in the greatest affection and intimacy, and to whom he had entrusted the guarding of his castles [Col. 0577D] near Minerve, proved a most wicked traitor and a most cruel enemy of the faith. Denying God, abjuring the faith, forgetful of benefits and affection, he withdrew from the count’s friendship and from the fealty he had rendered him. Even if he had not held God and His faith before his eyes, at least the count’s kindness, which he had received, ought to have recalled him from such cruelty.

This Guirald, together with certain other enemies of the faith, came to a castle of the count in the territory of Béziers, named Puy-Sorgues, and captured two of the count’s knights who guarded the castle, along with many sergeants. They promised under oath that they would not kill them, but would bring them unharmed to Narbonne with all their equipment.

When the count heard this, he came as quickly as he could to [Col. 0578A] that castle. Guirald and his companions were still within it. When the count arrived, he did not wish to besiege it; but Aimeric, lord of Narbonne, who was there with the count, and the men of Narbonne did not wish to undertake the siege with him, but immediately returned to Narbonne. Seeing that he was left almost alone, the count withdrew that night to a neighbouring castle called Capestang, intending to return at first light on the following day.

A miracle occurred in the aforesaid castle which we must not pass over. When Guirald had come to the castle of Puy-Sorgues and captured it, he made light of the agreement he had made, namely to bring those whom he had captured without harm to Narbonne. He put as many as fifty of the count’s sergeants, whom he had captured in the castle, into its tower. [Col. 0578B] On the very night that the count left that place, Guirald, fearing that the count would return the next day to besiege the castle, fled from it at midnight. Since in his haste he could not take with him the men whom he had placed in the tower, he put them in the ditch of that tower and ordered straw, fire, stones, and whatever else he could find to be thrown upon them, until he believed them dead. He then immediately abandoned the castle and reached Minerve, taking with him the two knights of the count whom he had captured.

O most cruel treachery! At first light the count returned to the aforesaid castle and, finding it empty, utterly destroyed it. He ordered those whom [Col. 0578C] Guirald had placed in the ditch, who had fasted for three days, to be drawn out unharmed and unburned. O great miracle! O unprecedented event!

Proceeding from there, the count destroyed to the ground very many castles belonging to the said Guirald, and after a few days returned to Carcassonne. But after bringing the count’s knights to Minerve, the aforesaid traitor Guirald, making light of his promise and disregarding his oath, did not kill them; rather—what is more cruel than death—he tore out the knights’ eyes and, cutting off their ears, noses, and upper lips, ordered them to return naked to the count.

When he had driven them out naked that night, amid wind and freezing cold—for the winter was exceedingly harsh—one of them, a thing which cannot be heard without tears, died in a dungheap. The other, as I heard from his own mouth, was brought to Carcassonne by a poor man. O wicked crime! O unheard-of cruelty! These are the beginnings of sorrows.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The Abbot of Vaux-de-Cernay Comes Again into the Territory of Albi to Strengthen the Nearly Broken Spirits of the Crusaders

At that time the venerable Guy, abbot of Vaux-de-Cernay, a prudent and good man, who embraced the cause of Jesus Christ with wondrous devotion and, after the abbot of Cîteaux, promoted it above all others, came from France to Carcassonne in order to encourage our men, who were then deeply [Col. 0579A] dejected. For he loved the cause of Christ so ardently, as we have said, that from the beginning of the enterprise he travelled throughout France preaching.

Those who were in the city of Carcassonne were so overcome by distress and fear that, almost entirely despairing, they thought only of flight. They were indeed surrounded on every side by countless and very powerful enemies. But that strong man, trusting in Him who with temptations provides a way out, daily softened their fears and discouragement by salutary exhortations.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Robert of Mauvoisin Returns from the Roman Curia

At the same time there also arrived Robert of Mauvoisin, whom the count had sent to Rome: a most noble knight of Christ, a man of remarkable valour, perfect learning, and incomparable goodness. For many years he had devoted himself and his possessions to Christ’s service, and he promoted this undertaking especially ardently and effectively. [Col. 0579B] This is the man through whom, after God, the army of Christ was revived above all others, as we shall show in what follows.

## CHAPTER XXX. The Bitter Death of a Cistercian Abbot, Slain near Carcassonne

At that time the count of Foix had sent a certain abbot of the Cistercian order, from a house between Toulouse and Foix called Elne, on his business to the legates at the town of Saint-Gilles. As he was returning, he came to Carcassonne with two monks and one [Col. 0579C] lay brother.

When the abbot and his companions had gone out from Carcassonne and had travelled nearly a mile, that most savage enemy of Christ, that most ferocious persecutor of the Church—namely William of Rochefort, brother of the bishop of Carcassonne then in office—suddenly rose against them: armed against the unarmed, cruel against the gentle, savage against the innocent. For no other reason than that they were Cistercians, that most cruel of men killed them on the spot, inflicting thirty-six wounds on the abbot and twenty-four on his lay brother. One of the two monks, after receiving sixteen wounds, he left half-dead. The other, who was known and somewhat familiar to those who were with the aforesaid [Col. 0579D] tyrant, escaped alive.

O ignoble war! O shameful victory! When our count, who was at Carcassonne, heard what had happened, he ordered the bodies of the slain to be taken up and honourably buried at Carcassonne. O Catholic man! O faithful prince! He had the monk who had been left half-dead carefully treated by physicians and, once healed, sent back to his own house.

But the count of Foix, who had sent the abbot and his companions on his business, received their murderer into great familiarity and friendship: he kept the executioner with him. Moreover, the abbot’s mounts, which the aforesaid traitor had seized, were found shortly afterward in the company of the count of Foix. O most wicked man—I mean the count of Foix! O most vile [Col. 0580A] traitor!

Nor should it be omitted that the oft-mentioned murderer, struck by the divine vengeance of God, the lawful judge, while the blood of those slain cried against him to God from the ground (Gen. IV), received the reward of his cruelty. For he who had inflicted many wounds upon religious men, soon afterward received countless wounds and was deservedly killed by Christ’s soldiers at the very gate of Toulouse, in fitting recompense for his deeds. O just judgment! O equitable measure of divine dispensation!

[lacuna]

> For there is no law more just  
> Than that those who devise death should perish by their own art.  
> —Ovid, *The Art of Love*, Book I

## CHAPTER XXXI. The Castle Called Castres Is Lost

At the same time the burgesses of Castres withdrew from friendship [Col. 0580B] and allegiance to the count. They captured one of his knights whom he had placed to guard that castle, together with several sergeants, though they did not dare to harm them, because some of the more powerful men of Castres were being held as hostages at Carcassonne.

About the same day the knights of the castle of Lombers, withdrawing from God and our count, captured the count’s sergeants who were in the castle and sent them to the castle called Castres, to be consigned to prison and chains. The burgesses of Castres placed them, together with the aforesaid knight of our count and the sergeants whom they had captured, as we said above, in a certain tower. But one night, making a kind of rope from their clothes, they lowered themselves through a window [Col. 0580C] and, by God’s providential help, escaped.

## CHAPTER XXXII. The Count of Foix Withdraws from Friendship with the Count of Montfort

At that time the count of Foix, who, as we said above, had sworn friendship, treacherously seized the castle of Preixan which he had surrendered, withdrew from intimacy with our count, and began to attack him more fiercely.

For not long afterward, on the feast of Saint Michael, the traitor came by night to the castle called Fanum Jovis. Ladders having been raised against the wall, the enemy entered, climbed the walls, and began to run through the castle. When our men in the castle—who were very few—learned this, they attacked them, [Col. 0580D] drove them out in confusion, forced them to throw themselves into the ditch, and killed some of them.

There was also near Carcassonne a noble castle called Montréal. Its lord had been a knight named Aimeric; after the counts, no one in all that land was more powerful or more noble than he. During the siege of Carcassonne, he had abandoned the castle of Montréal empty, through fear of our men. But afterward he came to our count and was his intimate for some time; then, a few days later, the most wicked traitor withdrew from God and the count.

When our count intended to occupy Montréal, he entrusted its custody to a French cleric. But the cleric, corrupted by a diabolical suggestion and worse than any unbeliever (1 [Col. 0581A] Tim. V), shortly afterward committed a most cruel treachery by surrendering the aforesaid castle to the said Aimeric, and remained for some time with our enemies. But by the ordinance of the most just judgment of God, the noble count soon afterward captured the aforesaid cleric together with enemies of the faith in a castle near Montréal which he was storming, called Bram. After first having him degraded by the bishop of Carcassonne and dragged through the whole city of Carcassonne at a horse’s tail, he ordered him hanged, repaying him with fitting retaliation for his deeds.

Why delay further? With an equal spirit of malice, almost all the local inhabitants likewise withdrew from our count, so that, having lost more than forty castles in a very short space of time, nothing remained to him [Col. 0581B] but Carcassonne, Fanum Jovis, Saissac, the castle of Limoux—which itself was considered hopeless—Pamiers, Saverdun, the city of Albi, and the neighbouring castle called Ambialet.

Nor should it be omitted that many of those whom the noble count had placed to guard castles were either killed by the traitors of the land or mutilated. What could the count of Christ do? Who would not fail amid such adversity, or despair in such peril? But the noble man, casting his whole self upon God, who did not know how to be exalted in prosperity, could not be cast down in adversity. All this took place around the feast of the Lord’s Nativity.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Count Raymond Sets Out for Rome

[Col. 0581C]

While these things were happening, the count of Toulouse approached the king of France, to see whether he could obtain from the king assistance and confirmation in retaining the new tolls which he had abjured at the command of the legates. For the count had increased tolls in his land beyond measure, on account of which he had often been excommunicated. But since he could achieve nothing with the king concerning the retention of those tolls, he left the king of France and approached the lord pope, trying somehow to be restored to his land, which the legates of the pope had occupied for security, as stated above, and to obtain the supreme pontiff’s favour.

That most deceitful man displayed every appearance of humility and submission, [Col. 0581D] promising diligently to fulfil whatever the lord pope should command. The lord pope assailed him with so many charges and overwhelmed him with so many reproaches that, reduced almost to despair, he did not know what to do. The pope called him an unbeliever, a persecutor of the cross, and an enemy of the faith; and this was indeed true.

Nevertheless, the lord pope, considering that, if driven to despair, the said count might attack still more fiercely and openly the Church, which was like an orphan in the province of Narbonne, imposed upon him a purgation regarding the two crimes of which he was chiefly accused: namely, the murder of the legate Brother Peter of Castelnau and the crime of heresy. Concerning these purgations, the lord pope sent his letters to the bishop of Riez in Provence and to Master Theodisius, [Col. 0582A] ordering that, if the count of Toulouse could sufficiently clear himself of the two aforesaid crimes, they should receive his purgation.

Meanwhile Master Milo, who, as stated above, was exercising the office of legate in Provence for the business of peace and faith, convened a council of prelates in the province of Avignon. At that council the citizens of Toulouse were excommunicated and publicly denounced because they had scorned to fulfil what they had promised the legate and the crusaders concerning the expulsion of heretics. The count of Toulouse was also excommunicated at the aforesaid council, on the condition, however, that he should attempt again to impose tolls after having abjured them.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Count Raymond Loses His Hope Placed in the King of France

[Col. 0582B]

Returning to Toulouse from the Roman curia, the count came to Otto, who was called emperor, in order to gain his favour and seek his aid against the count of Montfort. From there he came to the king of France, hoping through false words to corrupt him and incline the king’s mind toward himself. But the king, being a discerning and prudent man, despised him because he was very contemptible.

When the count of Montfort heard that the count of Toulouse was travelling through France, he instructed his chief men in France to place his land and all that he possessed at the count of Toulouse’s disposal; for they were not yet openly enemies to one another. The count of Toulouse had also promised under oath that his son would take the daughter of the count of Montfort as his wife; but afterward, scorning his oath, he deceitfully and inconstantly refused to do so.

When the count of Toulouse saw that he could achieve nothing with the king, he returned home in confusion. Now let us return to what we left aside. Thus the noble count of Montfort, surrounded by enemies on every side, kept to himself during that winter, guarding the small portion of land that remained to him and frequently harassing his enemies. Nor should it be omitted that, though he had countless enemies and very few helpers, they never dared attack him in open battle.

Toward the beginning of Lent, news reached the count that his wife, the countess—whom he had summoned [Col. 0582D] from France—was arriving with many knights. On hearing this, the count went to meet her as far as a castle in the territory of Agde called Pézenas. Finding her there, he returned carefully to Carcassonne.

When he came to a castle called Canet-le-Pendu [literally, “the Hanged Dog”], he was told that the men of a castle called Montlaur, near the monastery of Lagrasse, had committed treachery and begun to attack his sergeants who were in the tower of the castle. The count and his knights immediately went there, leaving the countess in a castle. Finding matters as they had heard, they captured many of those traitors and hanged them on gallows; for many had fled at the sight of our men.

After this the count and those with him came to Carcassonne. From there they marched to the village called Alzonne and found it empty. Proceeding thence, they came to a castle called Bram. Finding it fortified against them, they besieged it and took it by assault within three days, without siege engines. They tore out the eyes of more than one hundred men of that castle and cut off their noses, leaving one of them with one eye so that he might lead all the others to Cabaret as a taunt to our enemies. [Col. 0583A]

The count caused this to be done not because he took pleasure in such mutilation of human limbs, but because his adversaries had begun it; and whenever those most cruel executioners could find any of our men, they butchered them by mutilating their limbs. For it was just that, falling into the pit which they had dug (Ps. VII), they should at last drink the cup which they had so often offered to others. The noble count never took delight in any cruelty or anyone’s suffering, for he was most gentle toward all. The following poetic saying applied to him most plainly:

> This prince is slow to punish, swift to reward,  
> And grieves whenever he is compelled to be fierce.  
> —Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, Book I, Epistle 2

From that time the Lord, who had seemed to be somewhat asleep, rose to the aid of his servants and began more openly to show himself on our side. For in a short space of time we acquired the whole territory of Minerve, except Minerve itself and a castle called Ventajou.

A miracle occurred one day [Col. 0583C] near Cabaret which we do not think should be omitted. Our pilgrims had come from France and, at the count’s command, were uprooting the vineyards of Cabaret. One of the adversaries, shooting a crossbow bolt at one of our men, struck him hard in the breast, at the spot where the sign of the cross was fastened. Everyone thought that he was dead, for he was entirely unarmed. Yet he was found so unharmed that the bolt could scarcely penetrate even a little of his clothing; rather, it rebounded as if it had struck a very hard stone. O wondrous power of God! O boundless might!

## CHAPTER XXXV. The Siege of Alaric

[Col. 0583D]

Around Easter the count and his men came to besiege a castle between Carcassonne and Narbonne called Alaric. That castle stood in mountainous country and was surrounded everywhere by rocks. Our men besieged it with very great difficulty and in harsh weather; within eleven days, while those inside fled by night, they took it. Very many of those from the castle who could not escape our men’s hands were killed.

Returning from there to Carcassonne, our men soon afterward went to the castle of Pamiers. The king of Aragon, the count of Toulouse, and the count of Foix had assembled near that castle in order to make peace between [Col. 0584A] our count and the count of Foix. Since they could not do so, the king of Aragon and the count of Toulouse went to Toulouse.

The count of Montfort then led his battle-line toward Foix, where he showed remarkable valour. Coming near the castle, he attacked, with a single knight, all the adversaries standing before the gates and—what is astonishing—drove them all inside. He would even have entered after them, had they not shut the castle bridge in his face. But as the count was returning from the castle, those in the castle, who were everywhere upon the walls, overwhelmed with stones the knight who had followed him; for the road was narrow and enclosed on all sides by walls. Having devastated the lands, vineyards, and trees near Foix, our count returned to Carcassonne.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. The Heretics Wish to Set the King of Aragon over Themselves, but He Refuses

[Col. 0584B]

At that time Peter Roger, lord of Cabaret, Raymond of Termes, Aymeric lord of Montréal, and other knights who were resisting the Church and the count sent word to the king of Aragon, who was in those parts, asking him to come to them; they would make him their lord and hand over to him the whole land. When our count heard this, he took counsel with his knights as to what he ought to do. Then, while different persons gave different advice, the count and his men agreed to besiege a certain stronghold near Montréal. [Col. 0584C] For the aforesaid knights had gathered at Montréal, awaiting the king’s arrival there; and the count wished to do this so that his adversaries might know that he did not fear them. At that time, however, our count had very few knights.

What more need be said? Our men went to besiege the aforesaid stronghold, called Bellagarde. On the following day the king of Aragon came near Montréal. The knights who had summoned him, having for many days made the most abundant preparations of provisions, came out from Montréal and went to the king, begging him to enter Montréal and receive their homage, as they had promised. They wished to do this in order that they might expel Count Montfort from that land. But as soon as they approached him in this manner, [Col. 0584D] the king required them to hand over to him the fortress of Cabaret. Moreover, he said that he would receive them as his men on condition that, whenever he wished, they should surrender their fortresses to him. Having taken counsel among themselves, the aforesaid knights again asked the king to enter Montréal, and said that they would do for him as they had promised; but the king would by no means enter until they had first done what he wanted. Since they refused to do this, each of them withdrew in confusion from the place of conference.

The king then sent to Count Montfort and ordered him, while the count was besieging the aforesaid stronghold, to grant Count of Foix a truce until Easter. This was done; the strongholds were taken by the enemy and demolished.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. The siege of Minerve

[Col. 0585A]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1210, about the feast of the blessed John the Baptist, the citizens of Narbonne sent word to our count that he should besiege Minerve, and that they would assist him to the best of their ability. They did this because the people of Minerve greatly harassed them; yet their own love of advantage moved them more to this than zeal for the Christian religion.

The count sent word to Aymeric, lord of Narbonne, and to all the citizens that, if they wished to assist him better than they had previously done, and to persevere with him until its capture, he would besiege Minerve. When they had promised this, the count immediately hastened with his knights to besiege Minerve. When they had arrived, [Col. 0585B] Count Montfort pitched his tents on the east; a certain knight of the count named Guy of Lucé, with the Gascons who were present, pitched tents on the west; Aymeric of Narbonne with his citizens was on the north; and certain other pilgrims on the south. For in the entire army there was no one especially powerful except the count and Aymeric of Narbonne.

That castle was of incredible strength, being enclosed by very deep natural valleys. Thus, should necessity arise, one section of the army could not assist another without the greatest danger. Thereafter, on the side of the Gascons, a certain engine called a mangonel was set up, upon which they laboured most diligently by day and night. Likewise, on the south and north [Col. 0585C] two engines were set up, one on this side and another on that. On the count’s side—that is, on the east—there was a large and excellent stone-thrower (*petraria*), which cost twenty-one pounds each day merely to hire the men who drew it.

After our men had laboured for some time in attacking the aforesaid castle, on a Sunday night the people of the castle came out and went to the place where the stone-thrower stood. They fastened to its rear baskets filled with tow, small dry pieces of wood, and implements smeared with fat; fire having immediately been set beneath them, the flame rose high. It was summer and exceedingly hot weather, about the feast of St John, as was said. But it happened, by God’s will, that one of those drawing the stone-thrower [Col. 0585D] went aside at that hour to relieve himself. Seeing the fire, he cried out loudly. At once, one of those who had set the fire threw a spear and gravely wounded him. An uproar arose in the army; many ran up and so miraculously and suddenly defended the stone-thrower that it did not cease firing except for two shots.

After several days, when the said engines had greatly weakened the castle and provisions were also failing, those inside lost heart for resistance. What more need be said? The adversaries asked for peace. The lord of the castle, named William of Minerve, came out to speak with the count; while they were speaking, the abbot of Cîteaux and Master Theodisius, whom we mentioned above, unexpectedly arrived. [Col. 0586A] Our count, being a prudent man who conducted everything with counsel, said that he would do nothing concerning the surrender and reception of the castle except what the abbot of Cîteaux, master of Christ’s whole undertaking, should decide ought to be done.

When he heard this, the abbot was greatly troubled. He desired the enemies of Christ to die, yet did not dare to pronounce a sentence of death, since he was a monk and priest. Considering therefore how he might withdraw the count or the said William—who had likewise submitted himself to the abbot’s judgment concerning the surrender of the castle—from the arbitration which they had entered into with one another, he ordered each of them, namely the count and William, to put in writing the terms of the castle’s surrender. He did this so that, if one man’s written terms displeased the other, he might withdraw from the arbitration they had made.

[Col. 0586B] When William’s document was read before the count, the count did not agree to it, but told the lord of the castle to return to his castle and defend himself as best he could. William refused, however, and submitted himself in every respect to the count’s will. Nevertheless, the count wished everything to be done as the abbot of Cîteaux should direct.

The abbot therefore decreed that the lord of the castle and all who were in the castle, including believers in the heretics’ doctrines, should escape alive if they were willing to be reconciled and to obey the Church’s command, the castle remaining to the count. The “perfect” heretics also, of whom there was a very great multitude there, should likewise escape if they wished to be converted to the Catholic faith.

When the noble Robert Malvoisin, [Col. 0586C] who was present and wholly Catholic in faith, heard that the heretics were to be spared—the pilgrims having come in order to destroy them—he feared that, once captured, they might under fear promise to do whatever our people wished. Opposing the abbot openly, he said that our men would never tolerate this. The abbot replied: “Do not be afraid, for I believe that very few will convert.”

In these days, with the cross going before and the count’s banner following, our men entered the town. Singing *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise thee, O God”), they went to the church; having reconciled it, they placed the Lord’s cross upon the summit of the tower and set the count’s banner in another place. For Christ had taken the town, and it was fitting that His banner should precede and, set in the more eminent position, bear witness to the Christian [Col. 0586D] victory. The count himself, however, did not then enter.

After these events, the venerable abbot of Vaux-de-Cernay, who was with the count in the siege and embraced Christ’s cause with single-minded devotion, heard that a multitude of heretics had gathered in a certain house. He went to them, bringing words of peace and exhortations to salvation, desiring to turn them to a better course. Interrupting his words, they all said with one voice: “Why do you preach words to us? We do not want your faith; we reject the Roman Church; you labour in vain. Neither death nor life can recall us from the sect which we hold” (Rom. VIII).

On hearing this, the venerable abbot at once left that house and went to the women, who were assembled in another dwelling, [Col. 0587A] intending to offer them the word of preaching. But if he had found the heretics hard and obstinate, he found the heretical women still more obstinate and utterly harder. Immediately our count entered the castle and, coming into the house where all the heretics had assembled together (Acts IV), being a Catholic man and wishing all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, began to exhort them to convert to Christ’s faith. But since he made no progress whatever, he had them led out of the castle. There were one hundred and forty or more “perfect” heretics.

A great fire having been prepared, they were all cast into it. Yet our men did not need to cast them in, for, obstinate in their wickedness, they all voluntarily hurled themselves into the fire. Three women nevertheless escaped; the noble lady, mother of Bouchard of Marly, rescued them [Col. 0587B] from the fire and had them reconciled to holy Church. When the heretics had been burned, all the others who were there abjured heresy and were reconciled to holy Church.

The noble count also gave William, formerly lord of Minerve, other revenues near Béziers. But not long afterwards William despised the fidelity which he had promised to God and the count; departing from God and the count, he joined himself to the enemies of the faith.

We do not think that two miracles which occurred during the siege of Minerve should be omitted. For when the army came to besiege the castle, a certain stream flowed near the castle and was very small. But by divine mercy [Col. 0587C] that water increased so suddenly upon the arrival of our men that throughout the whole siege it supplied the army’s men and horses in the greatest abundance. The siege itself lasted almost seven weeks. When the army withdrew, the frequently mentioned water receded and became as scanty as before. O mighty works of God! O goodness of the Redeemer!

Likewise, another miracle: when the count withdrew from the castle of Minerve, the infantry of the army set fire to the little huts which the pilgrims had made from branches and leaves. The huts, being exceedingly dry, immediately caught fire, and such a flame burst upward throughout the entire valley as though some very great city were being burned. There was likewise a hut of leaves in which a certain priest had celebrated during the siege. It was surrounded by other [Col. 0587D] little huts, yet was so miraculously preserved untouched by the fire that not even a trace of burning appeared in it, as I heard from venerable persons who were present. Our men immediately ran to the marvellous sight and found that the huts which had burned stood on every side within half a foot of the hut that remained unburned. O immeasurable power!

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Crosses, shining like lightning, appear visibly on the walls of the church of the Virgin Mother of God at Toulouse

We have thought fit to insert here another miracle which occurred at Toulouse while our count was besieging Minerve. In that city, near the palace of the count of Toulouse, there is a church founded [Col. 0588A] in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary; the exterior walls of that church had recently been whitewashed.

One evening countless crosses began to be seen everywhere upon the walls of that church. They appeared silvery, whiter than the walls themselves. The crosses were continually in motion, and, as soon as they appeared, were immediately no longer seen. Many saw them, but they would not show themselves to others: before anyone could lift a finger, the cross which he wished to point out had disappeared. For they appeared like flashes of lightning, now larger, now medium-sized, now smaller. This vision lasted for almost fifteen days, each day at evening, so that nearly all the people of the city of Toulouse saw these things.

That faith may be given to these statements, [Col. 0588B] let the reader know that Fulk of Toulouse, Raymond bishop of Béziers, the abbot of Cîteaux, legate of the Apostolic See, and Master Theodisius, who were then at Toulouse, saw them and related the matter to me in order.

It happened, by God’s ordering, that the chaplain of the aforesaid church was unable to see the crosses described above. Therefore, one night, entering the church, he gave himself to prayer, asking the Lord to deign to show him what nearly everyone else had seen. Suddenly he saw innumerable crosses, not on the walls but in the surrounding air. One among them was greater and more prominent than all the rest. As soon as the greater cross went out from the church, all went out after it and began to proceed straight toward [Col. 0588C] the city gate. The priest, utterly astonished, followed those crosses.

When they were leaving the city, the priest thought he saw a certain man, reverend and handsome in appearance, going toward the city, holding a drawn sword. With the crosses providing him assistance, he killed at the very entrance a great man who was coming out of the city. The aforesaid priest, as though lifeless from fear, ran to the bishop of Uzès and, falling at his feet, recounted all this to him in order.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Count Raymond is separated from the communion of the faithful by the legate of the Apostolic See

About the same time the count of Toulouse, who, as [Col. 0588D] stated above, had gone to the lord pope, returned from the Roman curia. The pope, as we touched on above, instructed the bishop of Riez and Master Theodisius to require the aforesaid count to undergo purgation concerning two especially grave crimes: namely, the murder of Brother Peter of Castelnau, legate of the Apostolic See, and the crime of heresy.

Master Theodisius entered Toulouse while our men were at the siege of Minerve, as is contained in the aforementioned miracle, in order to consult the abbot of Cîteaux, who was in the Toulouse region, concerning the imposition of the said purgation upon the count. He was also to absolve the citizens of Toulouse, by command of the supreme pontiff and according to the Church’s form, upon receiving their oath that they would obey the Church’s command. But the bishop of Toulouse [Col. 0589A] had already absolved them according to the aforesaid form, taking in addition ten of the leading citizens as hostages and security.

When the said Master Theodisius entered Toulouse, he held a private conference with the abbot of Cîteaux concerning the admission of the count of Toulouse to purgation. Master Theodisius, being cautious and provident and deeply concerned with God’s cause, strove in every way to find legal grounds to exclude the said count from being required to undergo purgation. For he saw that, if he admitted him to purgation and the count could clear himself by certain falsehoods and deceits, the Church in those regions would be destroyed, and Christian faith and devotion would perish.

While he was therefore troubled about all this and considered it within himself, [Col. 0589B] the Lord opened a way, suggesting a means by which he could deny purgation to the aforesaid count. He turned to the pope’s letters, in which the supreme pontiff said among other things: “We desire that the count of Toulouse fulfil our many commands.” Commands had indeed been given to the count of Toulouse, such as expelling heretics from his land, abolishing newly imposed tolls, and many other things, all of which he had disdainfully failed to fulfil.

Therefore Master Theodisius, with his colleague, namely the bishop of Riez, in order not to appear to burden or wrong the count of Toulouse, set him a day for the admission of his purgation at the town of Saint-Gilles. Accordingly, when archbishops, bishops, and many other [Col. 0589C] prelates of churches had been summoned to Saint-Gilles by the bishop of Riez and Master Theodisius, the count of Toulouse was also present, intending, if he could, somehow to clear himself of the legate’s death and the crime of heresy.

But Master Theodisius, on the counsel of the prelates, told the count that his purgation would not be admitted, because, in accordance with the supreme pontiff’s command, he had fulfilled none of the things enjoined upon him, though he had repeatedly sworn that he would fulfil them. The master said that it was likely—indeed, wholly manifest—that the count, who had not kept certain oaths concerning the fulfilment of lighter commands, would most easily, indeed most willingly, commit perjury himself and through his accomplices in clearing himself of such enormous crimes as the death of the legate and heresy. He therefore declared [Col. 0589D] that the count should by no means be admitted to purgation for such great crimes unless he had first fulfilled the lighter commands.

On hearing this, the count of Toulouse, from the wickedness innate in him, began to weep. The master, knowing that these tears were not tears of devotion and repentance but of malice and grief, said to the count: “In a flood of many waters, they shall not come near unto him” (Psalm XXXI).

Immediately, by the common counsel and assent of the prelates, for many and very reasonable causes, the utterly wicked count of Toulouse was again excommunicated in that place, together with all his supporters and helpers. Nor should it be left unmentioned that, before all this happened, in the previous winter Master Milo, legate of the Apostolic See, had died at Montpellier.

Let us now return to the sequence [Col. 0590A] of our narrative. After the castle of Minerve had been taken, about the feast of St Mary Magdalene, a certain knight, lord of a castle called Ventillon, came to our count and surrendered himself and his castle to him. Since many evils had befallen Christians through that castle, the count marched to it and razed its tower to the ground.

When Aymeric, lord of Montréal, and the men of his castle heard that Minerve had been captured, they feared for themselves and sent to the count seeking peace on these terms: Aymeric promised to surrender the castle of Montréal to the count, provided that the count gave him another suitable, open, and exempt landholding. The count agreed and did for him as he requested; but afterwards Aymeric, [Col. 0590B] being a most wicked traitor, broke the agreement, abandoned the said count, and joined the enemies of the cross.

## CHAPTER XL. The siege of Termes

At that time a certain nobleman named William of Decaix, marked with the cross, came from France, together with certain other pilgrims, announcing also to the count that a great multitude of Bretons was coming. The count therefore took counsel with his men and, trusting in God’s help, led his army to besiege the castle of Termes.

As the count was proceeding to that castle, the knights who were at Carcassonne brought out the engines constructed in the city and had them carried beyond it, to be conveyed after the count, who was hastening [Col. 0590C] to besiege Termes. When our enemies at Cabaret heard that our engines had been left outside Carcassonne, they came at midnight with a great armed multitude, in the hope that they might damage them with axes. When they arrived, our men—who were very few—came out from the city, attacked them, and bravely drove them away, pursuing the fugitives far and wide.

The fury of the adversaries did not cease. At dawn they returned, if perhaps they might damage the said engines in some way. Our men, perceiving this, came out against them and drove them off farther and more vigorously than before. They would even have captured Peter Roger, lord of Cabaret, two or three times; but in fear, as though he were one of ours, [Col. 0590D] he began to cry out with our men: “Montfort! Montfort!” Thus escaping, he fled through the mountains and did not return to Cabaret until two days later.

The Bretons mentioned above, travelling toward the count, came to a castle called Ari, which was still held by the count of Toulouse in the Toulouse territory. But the burgesses of the new town of Ari refused to admit them within the castle, making them remain that night in the fields and gardens; for the count of Toulouse secretly hindered Christ’s cause as far as he could. On reaching Carcassonne, the Bretons carried after the count, who was moving to the siege of Termes, the engines mentioned above.

The castle of Termes was in the [Col. 0591A] territory of Narbonne, five leagues from Carcassonne. It was of marvellous and incredible strength and, by human estimation, seemed wholly impregnable. It stood on the brow of a very high mountain, upon a great solid rock, itself surrounded on every side by very deep and inaccessible chasms, from which water flowed around the aforesaid castle. Moreover, these valleys were encircled by cliffs so great and, so to speak, impossible to descend, that anyone wishing to approach the castle would have to plunge into an abyss and then, so to speak, crawl upward toward heaven.

Near the castle, at a stone’s throw, was a certain rock, upon whose summit stood a small but very strong towered fortification, popularly called Tumet. [Col. 0591B] Thus the castle of Termes could be approached from only one side, because on that side the cliffs were lower and less inaccessible. The lord of this castle was a certain knight named Raymond, an old man given over to a reprobate mind and an open heretic. To express his wickedness briefly, he neither feared God nor respected men. So greatly did he presume upon the strength of his fortified stronghold that at one time he attacked the king of Aragon, at another the count of Toulouse, and at another his own lord, the count of Béziers.

When this tyrant heard that our count intended to besiege the castle of Termes, he gathered whatever knights he could [Col. 0591C] and fortified the aforesaid castle with the greatest abundance of provisions and all other things necessary for defence, preparing himself to resist. When our count came to the castle, he besieged it, occupying with few men only a small part of it. Those inside, however, being numerous and equipped, did not fear our small army; before the eyes of our men, who could not resist them, they freely went out and came in to draw water and obtain all they needed.

While these and similar things were happening, French pilgrims came to the army day by day, few at a time and by driblets. As soon as our adversaries saw these pilgrims arrive, they climbed the walls and, mocking our men because those coming were very few and unarmed, cried derisively: “Flee before the army! Flee before the army!” Not long afterwards pilgrims began to come in crowds and great numbers from France and Germany. Seeing this, our adversaries became afraid; they ceased their mockery and grew less presumptuous and bold.

Meanwhile the people of Cabaret, at that time the chief and cruellest enemies of the Christian religion, came near Termes and ranged the public roads night and day. Whomever of our men they could find, they either condemned to the most shameful death or, in contempt of God and of us, cruelly mutilated their eyes, noses, and other limbs, then sent them back to the army.

## CHAPTER XLI. The bishops of Chartres and Beauvais, with the counts of Dreux and Ponthieu, arrive in the camp of the Catholics

[Col. 0592A]

While matters stood thus, noble and powerful men came from France: namely the bishop of Chartres, Philip bishop of Beauvais, Count Robert of Dreux, and the count of Ponthieu, bringing with them a great multitude of pilgrims. The count and the whole army rejoiced and were glad at their arrival. It was hoped that, being powerful, they would act powerfully “with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm” (Psalm CXXXV), and crush the enemies of the Christian faith. But He who casts down the mighty and gives grace to the humble (Luke I), by [Col. 0592B] His secret judgment known to Himself, did not wish to accomplish anything great or honourable through those powerful men.

Nevertheless, so far as human reason can judge, it is believed that the righteous Judge did this either because they were unworthy persons through whom the great and praiseworthy God might do great and praiseworthy things (Psalm XCV), or because, if anything were accomplished by great men or magnificently, all would be attributed to human power rather than divine power. The heavenly disposer ordained better: He reserved this victory for the poor, and, triumphing gloriously through them, the glorious One gave glory to His name.

Meanwhile our count had caused engines called stone-throwers to be set up. Throwing against the first wall of the castle, these kept our men labouring daily in the attack. There was in the army a venerable man, William, archdeacon of Paris, who, inflamed with zeal for the Christian faith, devoted himself wholly to laborious cares in Christ’s service. [Col. 0592C] He preached daily, organized collections for the expenses of the engines, and prudently discharged the other offices of this necessary diligence. Very often he went to the wood, taking a multitude of pilgrims with him, and had timber brought in great abundance for use in the stone-throwers.

One day, when our men wished to erect an engine near the castle but were impeded by a deep valley, this man of great constancy and incomparable zeal devised, in a spirit of counsel and fortitude (Isaiah XI), [Col. 0592D] a necessary remedy against this hindrance. Taking pilgrims to the wood, he ordered a great abundance of timber brought, and had the valley filled with logs, earth, and stones. This done, our men placed the said engine on the resulting level ground.

Since we cannot fully describe all the prudent and energetic deeds of the said archdeacon, or the labours he endured in that siege, we state briefly that to him above all others—indeed, to him alone after God—must be attributed the sleepless and most diligent care of this siege and the victory of its capture. He was distinguished in holiness, prudent in counsel, and strong in spirit. In conducting this undertaking divine power had granted him such grace that he was regarded as most skilled in all things that seemed [Col. 0593A] necessary to the siege. He taught the smiths, instructed the carpenters, and surpassed every craftsman in teaching what pertained to the business of the siege. He had valleys filled, as has already been said, and likewise, when necessary, high hills levelled with deep valleys.

When the engines had thus been placed near the castle and were daily throwing at the castle wall, our men saw that the first wall had been weakened by the continuous barrage of stones. They armed themselves to take the first borough by assault. Seeing this, as our men approached the wall, the adversaries set fire within that borough and withdrew into the upper borough. But when our men had entered [Col. 0593B] the first borough, the adversaries came out against them and quickly drove them out, expelling them from it.

While matters stood thus, our men saw that the tower near the castle, mentioned above and called Tumet, was manned by knights and greatly impeded the taking of the castle. They considered how to take it. At the foot of that tower, which, as we said above, stood upon the summit of a certain rock, they posted guards, lest those from the tower should go to the camp, or those from the castle should assist the men in the tower if necessity arose. After a few days, with the greatest difficulty and danger, our men set up a mangonel between the castle of Termes and the aforesaid tower, in an inaccessible place. [Col. 0593C]

The people of the castle set up a mangonel and threw great stones at our engine, but could not destroy it. As our mangonel kept firing upon the aforesaid tower, those inside saw that they were besieged and that the people in the castle could in no way help them. One night, fearing daylight, they sought the protection of flight and left the tower empty. When the servants of the bishop of Chartres, who were keeping watch at the foot of the tower, learned this, they immediately entered and placed their bishop’s banner upon the summit of the aforesaid tower.

While this was happening, our stone-throwers on the other side kept firing at the castle walls. But our adversaries, being very strong and clever, whenever they saw that [Col. 0593D] our engines had weakened any part of their walls, immediately built, on the inner side near that wall, another barrier of wood and stones. Thus it happened that whenever our men entered any part of the walls, they could not advance further because of the barrier the adversaries had made. Since we cannot recount every event of this siege, we say briefly that the people of the castle never lost any portion of their walls without, as we said above, building another wall within.

While this was taking place, our men set up a mangonel beneath a certain rock, near the castle wall, in an inaccessible place. When it fired, it caused our enemies no little damage. Our count assigned [Col. 0594A] three hundred sergeants and five knights to guard that mangonel. It was much feared: both because our men knew that the enemies were doing everything possible to destroy it, since it harassed them greatly; and because those in the army could not assist its guards if danger threatened, owing to the inaccessibility of the place where the mangonel stood.

One day our adversaries came out of the castle, as many as eighty with shields, prepared to destroy the mangonel. Countless others followed them, carrying wood, fire, and other things necessary to kindle a blaze. When our three hundred sergeants guarding the mangonel saw the adversaries coming, they all fled in fear, so that [Col. 0594B] only the five knights remained to guard it.

What more need be said? As the adversaries drew near, all our knights fled except one, named William Scuret. When he saw them coming, he began with the greatest difficulty to climb up the rock above them, against them. They all rushed upon him together, but he defended himself most bravely. Seeing that they could not capture him, the enemies threw him with spears upon our mangonel, then threw dry wood and fire after him. This most excellent man immediately rose and scattered the fire, so that the mangonel remained unharmed. Our knight again began to climb toward the enemies; [Col. 0594C] they threw him down as they had before and cast fire upon him.

What more need be said? Again he rose and attacked the enemies; they threw him back onto the mangonel as many as four times. Seeing that our knight could not escape, since none of our men could assist him, our men approached the castle wall on the other side, as though to attack it. Learning this, the adversaries who were harassing our aforesaid knight withdrew into the castle. Our knight, though greatly weakened, escaped alive; and through his incomparable bravery our mangonel remained unharmed.

Meanwhile the noble Count Montfort suffered such great and pressing poverty that, very often, when even bread itself was lacking, he had nothing to eat. As we learned most certainly, when the hour of the meal approached, the count would often deliberately absent himself and, from shame, would not dare return to his own tent at mealtime because he had not even bread alone. The venerable Archdeacon William, establishing confraternities and making collections, as we have said, spent with diligence whatever he could extort—as an outstanding collector and pious despoiler—upon engines and the other things pertaining to the siege.

While matters were thus, our adversaries ran out of water. Our men had long since blocked the approaches, and they could not go out to draw water. When their water failed, their strength and courage for resistance failed. What more need be said? They spoke with our men [Col. 0595A] and negotiated for peace on these terms: Raymond, lord of the castle, promised that he would hand over that castle to the noble count, provided the count left him all his other land; moreover, he was to restore the castle of Termes to him immediately after Easter.

While this agreement was being discussed, the bishops of Chartres and Beauvais, Count Robert, and the count of Ponthieu intended to depart from the army. The count begged them, and all entreated them, to remain a little longer at that siege. But since they could not be moved in any way, the noble countess of Montfort threw herself at their feet, earnestly begging that, at so critical a moment of necessity, they would not turn a withdrawing shoulder to the Lord’s cause, and that they would assist the count of Jesus Christ, who daily exposed himself to death for the universal [Col. 0595B] Church, in so grave a danger.

But the bishop of Beauvais, Count Robert, and the count of Ponthieu, despite the countess’s entreaties, would not consent. They said that they would leave on the following day and would not wait even a single day. The bishop of Chartres, however, promised that he would remain with the count for a little while longer.

## CHAPTER XLII. The heretics refuse to surrender the castle of Termes; but God sends them an immense abundance of water for their destruction.

Seeing that, with the departure of the men mentioned above, he would be left almost alone, our count, compelled by so manifest a necessity, reluctantly consented to accept the terms of settlement offered by his adversaries. What more need be said? Our side again conferred with the adversaries, and the settlement described above was confirmed. At once the count ordered Raymond, lord of the castle, to come out and surrender his castle. But he refused to leave that day, firmly promising that he would surrender the castle early the following morning.

This delay was willed and provided by divine providence, as the event itself proved by the clearest evidence. For God, the most just judge, did not wish the man who had inflicted so many and such great evils upon His holy Church—and who, if he could, would yet commit greater ones—to depart unscathed and go away unpunished after so many deeds of cruelty. For, to pass over his other wickednesses, more than thirty years had already elapsed, as we heard from trustworthy persons, during which the divine sacraments had not been celebrated in the church of the castle of Termes. The ensuing night, as though heaven had been torn open and its floodgates unlocked, such an abundance of rainwater suddenly poured forth that our enemies, who had long suffered from a shortage of water and had therefore intended to surrender, were most abundantly refreshed by it. “Our harp is turned into mourning” (Lam. V); the enemies’ mourning is changed into joy (Jer. XXXI). At once, swelling with pride, they recovered strength and courage to resist, made all the more cruel and more dangerous in persecuting us because they presumed that divine help had more visibly come to their aid in their need.

O foolish and wicked presumption: to boast of the help of Him whose worship they abhorred and whose faith they had rejected! They said, indeed, that God did not wish them to surrender, claiming for themselves what divine justice had done against them. While matters stood thus, the bishop of Beauvais, Count Robert, and the Count of Ponthieu, abandoning Christ’s cause unfinished—indeed, leaving it in the most pressing and perilous extremity—withdrew from the army and returned home. And, if we may say of them what they themselves were unwilling to do, they departed before completing their forty days. For the legates of the Apostolic See had decreed, since very many of the pilgrims were lukewarm and ever longing for home, that no one should obtain the indulgence granted by the lord pope to those who had taken the cross unless he completed at least one forty-day period in the service of Jesus Christ.

At earliest dawn our count sent to Raymond, lord of the castle, ordering him to surrender his castle as he had promised the preceding day. But Raymond, refreshed by the abundance of water for want of which he had wished to surrender, and seeing as well that nearly the whole strength of the army was departing, faithlessly and fickly withdrew from the agreement he had made. Yet two knights who were in the castle, because on the preceding day they had firmly promised our count’s marshal that they would surrender, came out from the castle and surrendered themselves to the count.

When the marshal had returned to the count—for the count had sent him to speak with Raymond and report Raymond’s words to him—the bishop of Chartres, who intended to depart on the following day, urged and advised that the marshal be sent again to Raymond and offer him any terms of settlement whatsoever, provided only that he surrender his castle to the count. And so that, in replying, he might more easily persuade him to do what was sought, the bishop of Chartres advised that the marshal take with him the bishop of Carcassonne, who was in the army, since he was a native of the region and known to the butcher. Moreover, Raymond’s mother, a most wicked heretic, was in the castle, as was the bishop’s own brother, William of Roquefort, whom we mentioned above. This William was exceedingly cruel and, so far as he could, one of the Church’s worst enemies.

The said bishop and marshal therefore came again to Raymond. They added entreaties to their words and threats to their entreaties, striving most urgently that the tyrant, yielding to their counsel, might according to the arrangement described above surrender himself to our count—indeed, to God. But since the marshal had found him hard and obstinate in his wickedness, the bishop of Carcassonne and the marshal now found him harder still. The aforesaid Raymond would not even allow the bishop to speak privately with his brother William. Thus accomplishing nothing, the bishop and marshal returned to the count. Yet our men did not fully understand that, as we have already said, divine mercy was ordering these matters, making better provision for its Church.

At earliest dawn on the following day the bishop of Chartres departed. The count went out with him from the army to escort him some distance. When he was a little way from the army, many armed enemies came out and wished to break apart one of our mangonels. Hearing the army’s cry, the count swiftly returned and came upon those who were destroying the engine. Alone, whether they wished it or not, he compelled them to enter their castle; pursuing them manfully, not without risk to his own life, he drove them off for a long time. O the prince’s boldness! O manly courage!

After the departure of the aforesaid nobles—namely, the bishops and counts—our count saw that he was left almost alone and nearly wholly deserted. Greatly anxious and troubled, he did not know what to do. He was in no way willing to withdraw from the siege, yet he could no longer remain there: he had many armed adversaries and few helpers, most of whom were enemies. For, as we said above, the entire strength of the army had left with the bishops and counts mentioned above.

Moreover, the castle of Termes was still extremely strong, and it was thought impossible to take it except by many very strong men. Winter was also approaching, and in those regions it is usually exceedingly harsh. The castle of Termes lay in mountainous country, as we have said; because of the flooding rains, the turbulence of the winds, and the extraordinary abundance of snow, the place was very cold and virtually uninhabitable.

While the count was in this distress and difficulty, uncertain what course to choose, one day foot-pilgrims from Lorraine arrived. Rejoicing in their arrival, the count strengthened the siege of Termes. Through the efforts of the venerable archdeacon William, our men recovered their strength and began vigorously to work at everything required for the siege. At once they moved the engines, which previously had achieved little, nearer to the castle walls. They worked constantly upon them and greatly weakened the walls of the castle. And, by a wonderful event through the incomprehensible judgment of God, it happened that the engines had done little or nothing while the nobles so often mentioned were in the army; after their departure they cast so accurately as though each stone were directed by the Lord—and indeed it was so. “This was done by the Lord, and it is wonderful in the eyes of our people” (Ps. CXVII).

After our men had worked for some time with the engines and had greatly weakened the walls and tower of the castle, on the feast of St Cecilia the count made a covered approach by which miners could reach the wall and undermine it. After he had spent the whole day preparing this approach and fasting, as night drew on—on the vigil of St Clement, that is—he returned to his tent. But those within the castle, through divine mercy’s ordering and the help of blessed Clement, were seized by terror and fell utterly into despair. They immediately came out of the castle and attempted to flee. When those in the army learned this, they immediately raised a shout and began to run about to seize the fugitives.

Why delay further? Some were captured alive, and more were killed. A poor and low-born pilgrim from Chartres, running with the others and pursuing the fleeing enemies, seized Raymond, lord of the castle, who had hidden himself in a certain place, through the ordering of divine judgment. He presented him, once captured, to our count. Receiving him as a great gift, the count did not kill him; rather, he had him shut up at the bottom of the tower of Carcassonne, where for many years he endured punishments and miseries deserved for his deeds.

Something happened during the siege of Termes which we ought not to omit. One day our count had a small engine, called in the vernacular a *Catus* (“Cat”), brought forward to dig beneath the castle wall. While the count was near that engine, speaking with a knight, and holding his arm about the knight’s neck in familiarity, behold: a huge stone, thrown from the enemies’ mangonel and descending with tremendous force from above, struck the aforesaid knight on the head. By God’s wondrous power the count, who was as it were embracing that knight, remained unharmed; but the knight received a mortal blow and died.

On another Sunday the count was in his pavilion, hearing Mass. While he stood upright and heard Mass, it happened, by God’s merciful providence, that a servant, through God’s ordering, stood behind him close to his back. Behold: an arrow shot from an enemy’s crossbow struck and killed that servant. No one ought to doubt that this was arranged by divine mercy: the servant standing behind the count received the arrow’s stroke, so that the merciful God might preserve for His holy Church His most valiant champion.

After the castle of Termes had been taken and fortified by our men on the vigil of St Clement, our count led his army against a castle called Constance. Finding it empty, he proceeded to another castle called Greenfield (*Viridepodium*), which he received when it surrendered to him within three days. Having done these things, the count proposed to go into the diocese of Albi in order to recover the castles which had revolted from their lord. He therefore came to the castle called Castres; its burgesses surrendered the castle to him and submitted in all things to his will.

From there the count came to the castle of Lombers, previously mentioned. He found it empty of inhabitants but full of provisions. For the knights and burgesses of the castle had all fled in fear of the count, because they had betrayed him. The count immediately fortified that castle, and retains it in his power to this day. Why say more? In the same period the noble count of Christ recovered almost all the castles of the territory of Albi on this side of the river Tarn.

At the same time the count of Toulouse came to a certain castle near Albi to hold a conference with our count. Our count went to the conference, while enemies stood ready to seize him. For the count of Toulouse had brought with him certain most wicked traitors who openly attacked our count. Our count said to the count of Toulouse: “What have you done? You summoned me to a conference, and you have brought my traitors with you.” The count of Toulouse replied: “I did not bring them.” When our count heard this, he wished to seize them; but the count of Toulouse begged him and would not permit their capture. From that day, then, the count of Toulouse began to exercise to some extent the hostility which he had conceived against the Church and our count.

## CHAPTER XLIII. A solemn conference is arranged at Narbonne concerning the affairs of the counts of Toulouse and Foix; the king of Aragon, the legates of the Apostolic See, and Simon of Montfort attend, but the meeting is dissolved without result.

Not many days later, the king of Aragon, the count of Montfort, and the count of Toulouse met at Narbonne to hold a conference. Present at this conference were the bishop of Uzès and the venerable abbot of Cîteaux, who above all, after God, advanced the cause of Jesus Christ. This bishop of Uzès, named Raymond, had for many days ardently loved the cause of the faith and promoted it to the extent of his ability; at that time he and the abbot of Cîteaux were serving as legates in the same cause. Also present at the conference were Master Theodisius, mentioned above, and many other wise and good men.

At the conference the case of the count of Toulouse was discussed. Great favor and abundant mercy would have been shown to him if he had been willing to accept sound counsel. For the abbot of Cîteaux, legate of the Apostolic See, wished the count of Toulouse, provided that he expelled the heretics from his land, to retain intact and unharmed all his lordships and properties. As for the rights which he possessed in the castles of other heretics, castles held of his fief, which the count himself said numbered at least fifty, the said legate wished that a fourth, or even a third, part should pass into the ownership of the aforesaid count.

The count despised this great favor—God thereby making provision in the future for His Church—and so made himself unworthy of every benefit and favor. The conference also discussed restoring peace between the Church and its most savage persecutor, namely the count of Foix. At the request of the king of Aragon it was further arranged that, if that count swore that he would obey the Church’s command, he should also swear never thereafter to attack those who had taken the cross, especially the count of Montfort. Our count was to restore to him what he already held of his land, except for a certain castle called Pamiers. He was in no way to recover that castle, for many reasons to be stated below.

But the eternal God, knower of hidden things, who knows all things before they happen (Dan. XIII), did not wish the many and great cruelties of His most savage enemy to remain unpunished. Knowing also how many evils would arise from this settlement in the future, by His high and incomprehensible judgment He hardened the count of Foix’s heart, so that he refused to accept this peace. Thus God mercifully visited His Church: by refusing peace, the enemy himself already pronounced upon himself a confirming sentence of his future tribulation.

It must not be passed over that the king of Aragon, from whom the count of Foix held the greater part of his land, placed his own knights as guards in the castle of Foix, and promised before the bishop of Uzès and the abbot of Cîteaux that no harm to Christendom should be done through that land. The same king also swore before the said legates that, if the count of Foix should ever withdraw from communion with Holy Church and from the familiarity, friendship, and service of the count of Montfort, the king himself would, at the first request of the legates just mentioned or of our count, deliver the castle of Foix into our count’s hands. On this matter the king gave our count his letters patent, fully setting out this agreement. I, who saw, held, and carefully examined the letters, bear witness to the truth. But how badly the king afterwards kept his promise, and how greatly he thereby rendered himself infamous among us, will become clearer than daylight.

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the malice and tyranny of the count of Foix toward the Church.

Since the occasion calls for it and opportunity has presented itself, let us briefly touch here upon the cruel malice and malicious cruelty of the count of Foix, though we could not express even a hundredth part of it.
