First, it should be known that he retained, cherished as far as he could, and promoted heretics and supporters of heretics in his land. At the castle of Pamiers, which belonged to the abbot and canons of St Antoninus, he maintained his wife and two heretical sisters, together with a great multitude of other heretics. In that castle, against the will of the canons mentioned above and despite all their resistance, they sowed openly and secretly the poison of their wickedness and deceived the hearts of simple people. The count had even caused a house to be built for those sisters and his wife on the canons’ own freehold estate.

The castle of Pamiers belonged to the canons, as we have said; but that count held it from the abbot during his lifetime and had sworn upon the Holy Eucharist that he would inflict no injury upon either the abbot or the castle. The monastery of the canons lay outside the castle, half a mile away.

At one time, two knights, kinsmen and intimates of the said count, most wicked and openly avowed heretics, at whose counsel that count did everything, brought their mother, a foremost heresiarch, who was a friend [perhaps aunt] of the aforesaid count, into the castle of Pamiers so that, living there, she might spread the poison of heretical superstition. When the abbot and canons saw this and could not endure so great an outrage against Christ and the Church, they expelled the heresiarch from the castle. Hearing this, the traitor—the count of Foix—was turned to anger and fury.

One of the two heretical knights, sons of the said heresiarch, came to Pamiers. In hatred of the canons he most cruelly butchered and dismembered one of the canons, a priest who was celebrating the divine offices at the altar of a church near Pamiers. To this day that altar remains reddened with the blood of the slain man. Nor did the butcher’s fury rest there. Seizing one of the brothers of the monastery of Pamiers, he tore out his eyes in hatred of the Christian religion and contempt for the canons.

Not long afterwards the count of Foix himself came to the monastery just mentioned, bringing with him brigands, minstrels, and prostitutes. Calling for the abbot of the monastery—to whom, as stated above, he had sworn upon the body of the Lord that he would cause no injury—he ordered him to hand over all the keys of the monastery without delay. The abbot refused. Nevertheless, fearing that the tyrant would take the keys by force, the abbot went inside and placed them upon the body of St Antoninus the martyr, which lay upon the altar with many other relics of saints. The church itself had been founded in honor of that saint.

The said count followed the abbot. Showing no reverence for the church and taking no heed of the relics of the saints, this most shameless violator of sacred things snatched the keys from upon the body of the most holy martyr. What more? He shut up the abbot and all the canons in that same church; he barred the doors and kept them there for three days, so that during those three days they neither ate nor drank, nor could they even go out to relieve the necessities of nature. Meanwhile the tyrant plundered all the property of the monastery and, in contempt of religion, slept with his prostitutes in the canons’ own infirmary.

After three days he expelled the abbot and canons, almost naked, from the church and monastery. Moreover, throughout the entire castle of Pamiers, which belonged to the canons as stated, he had it proclaimed by the crier’s voice that no one should dare receive the abbot or any of the canons as guests, under penalty of the gravest punishment. O new kind of inhumanity! For whereas a church is usually a refuge for prisoners and the condemned, this author of perversity imprisoned innocent persons in the church itself. The tyrant immediately demolished the church of St Antoninus in large part; as we ourselves established by sight, he destroyed the canons’ dormitory and refectory, and used their materials to construct fortifications in the castle of Pamiers.

To increase the account of this traitor’s evils, we have judged it fitting to insert into this work a matter worthy of report.

## CHAPTER XLV. The count of Foix behaves irreverently toward the relics of the holy martyr Antoninus, which were borne in solemn procession.

There is a church on the brow of a mountain near the monastery mentioned above. Once a year, as was their custom, the canons visited it, carrying in honorable and reverent procession the body of their venerable patron Antoninus. By chance the aforesaid count happened to ride past. He showed reverence neither to God, nor to the holy martyr, nor to the religious procession. He could not even humble himself by outward signs; he did not think fit to descend from the horse on which he rode, but, with neck stretched out in pride and stiff-necked arrogance—an attitude all too familiar to him—passed by in pomp.

A venerable man who saw this, namely the abbot of Mont-Sainte-Marie of the Cistercian Order, one of the twelve preachers mentioned much earlier who had come to preach and who was then present at the procession, cried after him: “Count, you do not show reverence to your lord, the holy martyr. Know that in the town in which you now possess a share of the saint’s lordship, you will be deprived of that lordship, so that, by the saint’s action, you will experience dispossession during your own lifetime.”

The event confirmed the words of this good man, as the outcome plainly showed. I heard these cruelties of the count of Foix, and those which follow, from the mouth of the abbot of the monastery of Pamiers itself, a trustworthy man, a man of deep religious devotion and manifest goodness.

## CHAPTER XLVI. Sacrileges and other crimes violently committed by the count of Foix.

At one time the aforesaid count went with a multitude of brigands to a monastery called St Mary’s, in the land of the count of Urgell, where there was an episcopal see. Fearing the count, the canons of that church withdrew into the church itself. They were so long besieged there by him that, in the extremity of thirst, they were compelled to drink their own urine. When at last they surrendered, this most cruel enemy of the Church entered the church. He removed all its furnishings, broke its crosses and sacred vessels, and even smashed its bells; he left nothing in it except its walls. Moreover, he compelled that church to ransom itself for fifty thousand solidi.

After this, one of his most wicked knights said to him: “Behold, we have destroyed St Antoninus and St Mary; nothing remains for us except to destroy God.” At another time, when the same count and his brigands plundered the church mentioned above, they went so madly far in cruelty as to cut off the legs and arms of images of the crucified Christ and grind pepper and herbs upon them for seasoning food, in contempt of the Lord’s Passion.

O most cruel butchers! O most wicked mockers! O men more cruel than Christ’s very crucifiers, fiercer than those who spat upon Him! When Herod’s servants saw Jesus dead, the Evangelist says, “they did not break His legs” (John XIX). O new device of savagery! O proof of unheard-of cruelty! O most wretched of wretches—by whom I mean the count of Foix! O beast more cruel than every wild animal! The brigands even stabled their horses in the church itself and made them walk over the most holy altars and feed there.

One day the said tyrant was in a church with a great multitude of armed men. Immediately one of the count’s squires placed a helmet upon the head of an image of the crucified Christ and armed the image with shield and spurs. Then the same squire took a lance, repeatedly attacked the image with blows, and told it to ransom itself. O unprecedented perversity!

At another time the count summoned the bishops of Toulouse and Couserans to a conference, fixing a day and place for them. But on the very day when those bishops went to the conference, the aforesaid count spent the entire day attacking a castle belonging to the abbot and canons of St Antoninus of Pamiers. O wicked and perverse treachery!

The tyrant in question did another thing which we do not think should be omitted. He had entered into an agreement with the count of Montfort, as we said much earlier, and had handed over his son as a hostage for the settlement. The venerable abbot of Pamiers had already handed his castle over to the count of Montfort. One day, therefore, the count of Foix came with his brigands near Pamiers. Leaving his brigands in ambush, he approached the castle and told the burgesses to come out to confer with him. He most firmly promised them under oath that they could come out safely, because he would do them no harm. But as soon as the burgesses came out to him, he secretly summoned his brigands who lay hidden in ambush. Before the burgesses could re-enter the castle, the brigands came and captured many of them, carrying their captives away. O wicked treachery!

The often-mentioned count also said that, if he had killed with his own hand every person who had taken the cross against the heretics, every person about to take it, all who labored for the cause of the faith, and indeed everyone pleased by that cause, he would think that he had rendered service to God.

It should also be known that the often-mentioned count swore before the legates of the lord pope that he would expel heretics from his land; yet he was unwilling to do so for any reason. This most cruel dog committed many other evils against the Church and against God. If we wished to recount them in order, neither could we suffice for the task nor would anyone easily give credence to our words; his wickedness exceeds all measure. He plundered monasteries, devastated churches, and, more cruel than every cruel man, ever thirsted for the slaughter of Christians and remained always thirsty for blood. He renounced humanity and imitated bestial savagery, becoming a most wicked beast and not a man. Having briefly touched upon his malice, let us return to the matter we left.

## CHAPTER XLVII. The count of Montfort renders to the king of Aragon the homage due for the city of Carcassonne.

At the aforesaid conference at Narbonne, the bishop of Uzès and the abbot of Cîteaux begged the king of Aragon to receive the count of Montfort as his man, for the city of Carcassonne was held of the king of Aragon. When the king refused, on the following day the men just named again approached him, fell at his feet, and humbly and most urgently begged him to deign to receive the count’s homage. The count himself, kneeling before the king, humbly offered his homage.

At last the king, overcome by entreaties, consented and received the count as his man for the city of Carcassonne, to hold that city from the king. This done, the king, our count, the count of Toulouse, and the bishop of Uzès left Narbonne and proceeded as far as Montpellier.

While these nobles and prelates were still at Montpellier, a marriage was proposed between the king’s eldest son and the daughter of the count of Montfort. What more? The proposed marriage was confirmed by both parties—the king and our count—each side having sworn an oath. Moreover, the king entrusted the said eldest son to the count’s custody. Yet the king who had entrusted his son to the count soon afterwards gave his sister in marriage to the son of the count of Toulouse. By this he rendered himself considerably, and not undeservedly, infamous and suspect among us, for when that marriage took place the count of Toulouse was openly persecuting God’s holy Church.

It must not be omitted that, while the aforesaid men, together with many bishops and prelates of churches, were at Montpellier, the affairs of the count of Toulouse were again discussed. The legates—the bishop of Uzès and the abbot of Cîteaux—wished to show that count the greatest favor and mercy, as has been described above. But although he promised that on the following day he would carry out whatever the legates ordered, he departed from Montpellier at earliest dawn the next day without greeting the legates. For he had seen a certain bird, which the natives call St Martin’s bird, flying on his left, and he was greatly frightened. Like the Saracens, he placed his hope in the flight and song of birds and in other omens.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. The bishop of Paris and other nobles come to the army of Count Montfort.

In the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1210, about the middle of Lent, noble and powerful crusaders arrived from France: namely, the bishop of Paris, Enguerrand of Coucy, Robert of Thorigny, Ives of Meulan, and many others. These noble men conducted themselves nobly in Christ’s cause.

When they came to Carcassonne, after taking counsel together, all the said pilgrims agreed to march to besiege Cabaret. The knights of the diocese of Carcassonne had long before, in fear of our men, abandoned their castles and fled to Cabaret. Among them were two brothers by blood: one was called Peter Miro, the other Peter of St Michael. These men had captured Bouchard of Marly, as we touched on above.

But the two knights had left Cabaret, with several others, come to our count, and surrendered themselves to him; accordingly the count had given them lands. Seeing that the count and pilgrims intended to besiege Cabaret, Peter Roger, lord of Cabaret, considered how much weakened he was by the departure of the knights mentioned above. Moved by fear, he made this arrangement with our count and the barons: he surrendered the castle of Cabaret and also restored the aforesaid Bouchard. The count gave him another suitable estate in exchange for Cabaret. Immediately the count and barons led their forces to besiege the castle called Lavaur.

## CHAPTER XLIX. The siege of Lavaur.

That castle was very noble and extensive, situated on the river Agout, five leagues from Toulouse. In it were that traitor Aimery, formerly lord of Montréal, and many other knights—enemies of the cross, numbering as many as eighty—who had entered and fortified the castle against our men. The lady of the castle was a widow named Girauda, a most wicked heretic and sister of the said Aimery.

When our men came to the castle, they besieged it on one side only, for our army was not sufficient to surround the aforesaid castle on every side. After engines had been erected some days later, our men began, as was customary, to attack the castle, while the adversaries defended it as far as they could. For there was an immense multitude of people in the castle, very well equipped with arms, so that there were almost more defenders than attackers.

It must not be omitted that, when our men first came before the castle, the adversaries came out of it, captured one of our knights, brought him inside, and immediately killed him. Although our men had besieged the place from one side, they were divided into two armies and so arranged that, if necessity arose, one army could not assist the other without danger.

But not long afterwards many nobles came from France: namely, the bishop of Lisieux, the bishop of Bayeux, the count of Auxerre, and many other pilgrims. They besieged the castle from the other side. Moreover, after making a wooden bridge across the river Agout, our men crossed the water and surrounded the castle on every side.

The count of Toulouse persecuted God’s Church and the count as far as he could, though not openly; for provisions still came to our army from Toulouse. While matters stood thus, the count of Toulouse came to the army. The count of Auxerre and Robert of Thorigny, who were his blood relatives, began to urge the count of Toulouse to return to his right mind and obey the commands of the Church. But when they achieved nothing, the count departed from the count of Montfort in resentment and indignation. The men of Toulouse who were at the siege of Lavaur also withdrew from the army. The count of Toulouse further forbade the citizens of Toulouse to bring provisions any longer to Lavaur.

Here must be told a most wicked crime of the counts of Toulouse and Foix: an unheard-of treachery.

## CHAPTER L. Many pilgrims are treacherously killed by the count of Foix at the instigation of the count of Toulouse.

While, as we have said, negotiations were being held near Lavaur for restoring peace between the Count of Toulouse and holy Church, a multitude of pilgrims was coming from Carcassonne to the army. But those agents of treachery, craftsmen of betrayal—namely the Count of Foix, his son Roger Bernard, Gerald of [Col. 0606B] Pépieux, and many of the Count of Toulouse’s men—lay in ambush with innumerable routiers in a certain castle called Montgey, near Puylaurens. When the pilgrims reached it, they rose against them; and, since they were unarmed and unaware of the betrayal, they killed countless numbers of them. Carrying all the money of the slain to Toulouse, they divided it there among themselves. O blessed companies of the slain! O precious in God’s sight is the death of his saints! (Ps. CXV [116].) Nor should it be left unsaid that, while the aforesaid executioners were killing the pilgrims just mentioned, a certain pilgrim priest fled to a church nearby, so that, dying for the Church, he might die in a church. But that most wicked traitor Roger Bernard, son of the Count of Foix, [Col. 0606C] not falling short of his father’s depravity, followed the said priest. Boldly entering the church and attacking him, he asked what manner of man he was.

“I am,” he said, “a pilgrim priest.”

To him the executioner replied: “Show me that you are a priest.”

Then the priest, removing the hood from his head—for he was clothed in a cape—showed him the clerical tonsure. But that most cruel man, showing reverence neither for the holy place nor for the person, raised the exceedingly sharp axe which he held and, striking the priest with great force through the middle of the tonsure, killed the minister of the Church within the church. Let us now return to what we left aside.

We do not think it should be omitted that the Count of Toulouse, the savage enemy of Christ and most cruel [Col. 0606D] persecutor, had secretly sent one of his seneschals into the castle of Lavaur, where lay the source and origin of all heresy. Although it did not belong to the Count of Toulouse—indeed, for many years it had attacked the people of Toulouse solely out of hatred for the Christian religion—he had sent several knights to defend the castle against our men. After the castle was taken, our count found them there and kept them in chains for a long time. O new kind of treachery! Within, he had stationed his knights for the castle’s defence; without, while pretending to provide assistance, he permitted provisions to be brought from Toulouse. For, as we said above, at the beginning of the siege of Lavaur, provisions, though scanty, were brought from Toulouse to our army; yet, although provisions came from Toulouse, the Count of Toulouse strictly forbade siege-engines to be brought. [Col. 0607A] About five thousand citizens of Toulouse also came, at the exhortation of their venerable bishop Fulk, to assist our men at the aforesaid siege. The bishop himself, exiled for the Catholic faith, arrived there as well. We do not think it superfluous to recount the manner of his departure from Toulouse.

## CHAPTER LI. Fulk, Bishop of Toulouse, driven from his bishopric, goes into exile with great constancy of spirit, even prepared to offer his neck to the sword for Christ’s name.

One day the bishop was at Toulouse—on the Saturday after Mid-Lent—and, as is customary in episcopal churches, he wished on that day to confer orders. Yet the Count of Toulouse was then in the city; because of his many offences he had been specifically excommunicated by the legates of the Apostolic See. [Col. 0607B] Therefore no one could celebrate the divine mysteries in any town in which he was present. The bishop accordingly sent humbly to the count, asking and urging him to leave the city for recreation and go out for a walk, only until the bishop had celebrated the ordinations.

But the tyrant, enraged, sent a knight to the bishop, commanding and strictly ordering him, under pain of death, to depart at once from the city of Toulouse and from the count’s entire territory. On hearing this, the venerable man, fervent in spirit, undaunted in mind, and with a most serene countenance, is said to have given the knight this reply:

“The Count of Toulouse did not make me bishop, nor was I ordained here through him or for his sake. Ecclesiastical humility elected me; [Col. 0607C] princely violence did not thrust me in. I shall not depart on his account. Let him come, if he dares: I am ready to receive the sword, that through the cup of suffering I may attain to majesty. Let the tyrant come, attended by knights and armed: he will find me alone and unarmed. I await his arm; I will not fear what man may do to me” (Ps. CXVII [118]).

O constancy of spirit! O wondrous strength of mind! Thus that fearless servant of God remained, from day to day awaiting the tyrant’s sword. But since the latter did not dare to kill him—being one who had long inflicted such great and numerous evils upon God’s Church, and fearing, as the saying goes, for his own skin—the bishop, after spending forty days in this expectation of death, resolved to leave the city of Toulouse. Therefore, on a day in the octave of the Lord’s Resurrection, [Col. 0607D] the bishop departed from the city and came to our count, who was besieging Lavaur.

Our men were labouring continuously to take the castle; their opponents, being exceedingly proud, defended themselves most obstinately. Nor should it be left unsaid that, sitting on iron-clad horses, they rode along the walls in mockery of our men, thereby displaying, as it were, the vastness and strength of their walls.

## CHAPTER LII. Lavaur is taken by the Catholics; many noblemen are there put to death by hanging, and others are consigned to the flames.

Moreover, on a certain day our men erected near the castle walls certain wooden towers, on the summit of which Christ’s soldiers placed a cross. The opponents, [Col. 0608A] shooting more fiercely with engines at the banner of the cross, broke one arm of that cross. Immediately those shameless dogs raised such a howl and laugh together, as though they had won a great victory through breaking the cross. But the Consecrator of the cross miraculously and most visibly avenged this injury. Not long afterward an event occurred, marvellous and greatly to be extolled: the enemies of the cross, who had rejoiced at its breaking, were captured on the feast of the Cross, the cross avenging its injuries, as we shall show below.

While this was happening, our men had a machine made, commonly called a *catus* [covered siege-engine]. When it was ready, they drew it to the castle ditch. After this, our men brought up wood and branches with great exertion and, making bundles from them, cast them into the ditch to fill it. But the opponents, being very cunning, made an underground passage extending nearly to our engine. Emerging by that passage at night, they drew out the wood and branches which our men had thrown into the ditch and carried them into the castle. Some of the opponents also, coming near the aforesaid engine, tried secretly and deceitfully to drag toward themselves with iron hooks those who, under the engine’s protection, did not cease filling the ditch. On another night the opponents left the castle by the underground passage, entered the ditch, and, hurling burning darts most vigorously, fire, [Col. 0608C] tow, fat, and other fuel for fire, sought to burn the aforesaid engine.

Two German counts were keeping watch around the engine that night. Immediately an alarm was raised in the army; men ran to arms, and help was brought to the engine. The said German counts and the Teutons with them, seeing that they could not reach the enemies in the ditch, threw themselves into it with great courage and at great risk. Manfully attacking their enemies, they drove them back into the castle, after killing some and wounding many more.

Meanwhile our men began to be greatly troubled and in some measure to despair of taking the castle, since whatever they could throw into the ditch by day [Col. 0608D] the opponents drew out by night and carried into the castle. But while our men were thus troubled, some of them, devising a more subtle plan, found an effective remedy against the enemies’ ambushes. Before the outlet of the underground passage through which the enemy habitually emerged, they had green wood and branches thrown down. Then they placed small dry pieces of wood, fire, fat, tow, and other kindling materials at the very exit of the underground passage; again, above these they threw green wood, crops, and much grass. Immediately the smoke rising from the fire so filled the entire underground passage that the opponents could no longer emerge by it because of the smoke. For the smoke, unable to burst upward because of the green wood and crops laid [Col. 0609A] over it, filled the entire aforesaid passage, as we have said. Seeing this, our men filled the ditch more freely than before.

When it had been filled, our knights and armed sergeants, dragging the said engine toward the wall through many struggles, set miners against the wall. Those in the castle did not cease to cast down upon the engine wood, fire, fat, and also very sharp and very large stakes. But, since our men defended the aforesaid engine bravely and miraculously, they could neither burn the engine nor drive the miners from the wall. While our men were labouring most earnestly at this assault, the bishops who were present, a certain venerable abbot of the Cistercian Order, of the curia of God, who was then acting in the army on the authority of the legates, and all the clergy gathered [Col. 0609B] together and sang *Veni, Creator Spiritus* (“Come, Creator Spirit”) with the utmost devotion. At the sight and sound of this, the opponents were, by God’s ordinance, so stunned that they almost entirely lost their power of resistance; for, as they afterward confessed, they feared them more when singing than fighting, chanting psalms than rushing upon them, praying than attacking them.

When the wall had been breached, our men were entering, and the opponents, being no longer able to resist, surrendered. By God’s will and through his merciful visitation of our men, the castle of Lavaur was taken on the feast of the Finding of the Holy Cross. Immediately Aymeric, mentioned above, who had been lord of Montréal, was led out of the castle, together with as many as eighty other knights. The noble count resolved that all should be hanged from the gallows. [Col. 0609C] But after Aymeric, who was the greatest among them, had been hanged, the gallows collapsed, since in excessive haste they had not been firmly fixed in the ground. Seeing that this caused great delay, the count ordered the others killed; the pilgrims eagerly undertook this task and quickly killed them in the same place. The lady of the castle, Aymeric’s sister and a most wicked heretic, was thrown into a well, which the count ordered to be filled over with stones. Our pilgrims also burned innumerable heretics with great rejoicing.

## CHAPTER LIII. Roger of Comminges joins himself to the Count of Montfort, but afterward breaks the faith which he had given.

[Col. 0609D] It should be known that, while our count was at the siege of Lavaur, a certain Gascon nobleman named Roger of Comminges, a kinsman of the Count of Foix, came to surrender himself to him. While he stood before the count on Good Friday to do him homage, the count happened at that moment to sneeze. When the said Roger heard that the count had sneezed only once, he called aside those who were with him to consult them, and did not wish at that time to do what he had intended toward the count. For the foolish people of that land observe omens and most firmly believe that, if they themselves, or anyone who has some business to undertake, sneeze once, nothing favourable can happen to them that day. Nevertheless, seeing that our men [Col. 0610A] mocked him for this and fearing that the count might mark him as guilty of perverse superstition, though unwillingly he did homage to him, received his land from him, and remained in his service for many days. But afterward, wretched and pitiable man, he withdrew from the loyalty which he had sworn to him.

We do not think we should omit a certain miracle which we learned, on trustworthy report, to have occurred at Lavaur. The cloak of a crusading knight was being burned by some mischance. But by God’s miraculous judgment, although the whole cloak was burned, that part alone to which the cross had been sewn remained whole and entirely unburned.

When Sicard, lord of Puylaurens, who had once been with our count [Col. 0610B] but had departed from him when Lavaur was taken, heard this, he was seized by fear. Abandoning the castle of Puylaurens, he hurried to Toulouse with his knights. Puylaurens was a noble castle, three leagues from Lavaur in the diocese of Toulouse. When our count recovered it, he gave it to Guy of Lucé, a noble and faithful man, who immediately entered it and fortified it.

Meanwhile, after Lavaur had been taken, the Bishop of Paris, Enguerrand of Coucy, Robert of Tournai, and Ivo of Meulan departed and returned home. After the capture of Lavaur, when our men entered the castle, they considered that the Count of Toulouse himself had left our count in anger; moreover, he had forbidden engines and [Col. 0610C] provisions to be brought from Toulouse to the army; and, besides and above all, he had been excommunicated and denounced by the legates of the lord pope for his many offences. Having carefully considered all these matters, they resolved to attack that count, now seemingly openly condemned, more openly.

Accordingly our count struck camp and began moving toward a castle called Montgey, where pilgrims had been killed by the Count of Foix. As the army advanced toward that castle, while it was still some distance away, a pillar of fire appeared at the place where the pilgrims had been killed by the Count of Foix, shining and descending upon the bodies of the slain before our men’s eyes. When our men came to the place, they saw [Col. 0610D] all the slain lying on their backs, their arms stretched out in the form of a cross. O wondrous thing! I heard this miracle from the lips of the venerable Bishop Fulk of Toulouse, who was present.

Our count then approached the aforesaid castle and razed it to its foundations, for its inhabitants had fled in fear. From there our count went to another castle called Cassès, belonging to the Count of Toulouse. In the meantime the Count of Toulouse came to Castelnau. This was a noble castle, which the aforesaid count set on fire, fearing that our men might capture it; he left it empty. Coming to the castle of Cassès, our count besieged it. The knights of the Count of Toulouse who were in that very strong castle, seeing that they could not hold it long, surrendered [Col. 0611A] to the count on this condition: they promised to hand over to our men all the heretics in the castle, while they themselves should escape. And so it was done; for there were many “perfect” heretics in that castle. The bishops who were in the army entered the castle and began preaching to the heretics, desiring to recall them from error. But when they could not convert even one, they departed from the castle. Our pilgrims then seized nearly sixty heretics and burned them with great rejoicing. Here it appeared most clearly how much the Count of Toulouse loved heretics, since in one of that count’s very insignificant castles more than fifty perfect heretics were found.

## CHAPTER LIV. The clergy of Toulouse, reverently carrying Christ’s body, depart from the city itself, the nurse of heretics and under interdict.

[Col. 0611B]

After these events, the Bishop of Toulouse, who was in the army, ordered the provost of the church and the other clerics to leave the city of Toulouse. They immediately obeyed the command and left Toulouse barefoot, carrying the body of Christ.

After the castle of Cassès was taken, our count proceeded to another castle of the count called Montferrand. There was there the brother of the Count of Toulouse, named Baldwin, whom his brother had sent to defend that castle. When the count came to the castle, he besieged it.

A few days later, when our men were making an assault, Count Baldwin, as he was called, seeing [Col. 0611C] that he could not resist long, surrendered the castle on these terms: he and his men were to leave free; and, once released, he also swore that henceforth he would in no way attack the Church or our count, but rather, if our count wished, would assist him against all men and in all things. Count Baldwin therefore left the castle and came to his brother, the Count of Toulouse. But a few days later he returned to the Count of Montfort; coming to him, he asked that the count might deign to receive him as his man, and that he himself might serve him faithfully in all things and against all men.

What more need be said? The count consented. Count Baldwin was reconciled to the Church; from a minister of the devil he became a minister of Christ, and henceforth, conducting himself faithfully, [Col. 0611D] he attacked the enemies of the faith with all his strength. O divine regard! O mercy of the Redeemer! Behold two brothers of one and the same father, yet utterly unlike one another. He who said through the prophet, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. I; Rom. IX), leaving one of them fixed in the mire of unbelief, marvellously and mercifully rescued the other by his secret counsel, known to himself.

Nor should it be passed over in silence that, when Count Baldwin had left Montferrand but before he came to our count, certain routiers despoiled pilgrims returning from the pilgrimage of St James out of hatred for crusaders. When Count Baldwin heard this, he carefully investigated who had done it and had everything taken from the pilgrims [Col. 0612A] restored in full. In this the noble Count Baldwin gave a token of his future valour and fidelity.

After Montferrand and certain other castles round about had been captured, and after our men had fortified the new castle which, as stated above, the Count of Toulouse had burned, our count crossed the river Tarn and came to a castle called Rabastens, in the Albigensian territory. When the townsmen had surrendered it to him, he advanced, gained strength, and likewise acquired six other noble castles without any condition: Montaigut, Gaillac, Causac, Saint-Marcel, Guespia, and Saint-Antonin. These castles, situated close together, had been taken by the Count of Toulouse from the Viscount of Béziers.

## CHAPTER LV. The first siege of Toulouse by the Counts of Bar and Montfort.

[Col. 0612B]

After these events, our count was told that the Count of Bar, hastening to Christ’s knighthood, was at Carcassonne. At this news the count rejoiced exceedingly, for great things were said of that count, and our men placed much confidence in his arrival. But events proved very different from what we had hoped, so that the Lord might show, giving glory to his own name, that trust should be placed in himself and not in man.

Our count sent knights to the said count to lead him toward Toulouse, to a certain riverbank where our count and his army [Col. 0612C] were to meet him. And so it happened. But the Count of Toulouse, the Count of Foix, and a host of enemies, hearing that the army was coming toward Toulouse, went to the said riverbank, which was no more than half a league from Toulouse. There our men gathered on one side and the enemies on the other. The opponents, fearing that our men might cross the bridge over the riverbank, quickly had it destroyed. But our men, going round about to find a ford, found another bridge, which the opponents were then also demolishing. Yet our men, with the greatest courage, some over the bridge and some swimming through the water, crossed the river and bravely drove their enemies all the way to the very gates of Toulouse.

Returning thence to the riverbank, they remained there that night. There it was decided that they should besiege Toulouse the next day. Thus our men moved against Toulouse and pitched their tents before the gates. The Count of Bar and many noblemen from Germany were at that siege. The city was besieged from one side, for our forces were insufficient to besiege it from the other. The Count of Toulouse was in the city, as was the Count of Comminges, his kinsman, who aided him as much as he could. There were also the Count of Foix and countless other knights, as well as the citizens of Toulouse, whose multitude was innumerable.

What more? Compared with the multitude of those besieged, our men appeared very few. Since it would take too long to recount every attack of that siege, this may briefly be said: whenever the opponents came out to harass our men, our men resisted bravely and compelled them to re-enter the city in confusion. On one day, when the enemies had come out and our men were more boldly forcing them back into the city, they killed in the assault a kinsman of the Count of Comminges and William of Rochefort, brother of Bernard, Bishop of Carcassonne, whom we mentioned above.

On another day, when our men had eaten and, as is customary, were resting at midday after their meal—for it was summer—the opponents, knowing that our men were at rest, came out by a hidden route and rushed into the army. Our men rose and resisted the enemies bravely, forcing them back into the city. While this was happening, Eustace of Quen and Simon, castellan of Malpha, noblemen who had left [Col. 0613B] the army to escort those bringing provisions to it, entered the army at that very hour, conducting provisions. As they were at the entrance to the camp, they encountered the enemies who, as we have said, had come out of the city and attempted to capture them. But while they defended themselves bravely, one of the opponents, throwing a sword as was their custom, struck the said Eustace in the side and killed him. The castellan of Malpha escaped alive and unharmed through many hardships and displays of remarkable courage.

There was great scarcity in the army, since provisions were failing. Moreover, good reports were being spread about the Count of Bar, while all who were in the army held an unfavourable opinion of him. O just judgment [Col. 0613C] of God! Men had hoped that the count would accomplish marvels, and they presumed too much upon a man. But God, who had said through the prophet, “I will not give my glory to another” (Isa. XLVIII), knew that if our men should greatly prosper in that siege, it would be attributed to man rather than to God; therefore he did not choose to act there magnificently.

Seeing, then, that he was making no progress, that great loss was being suffered, and that the advancement of Christ’s cause was being harmed, our count withdrew from the siege of Toulouse and came to a castle toward the territory of the Count of Foix, called Hauterive. After fortifying this castle with sergeants, he came to the castle of Pamiers. And suddenly routiers came to Hauterive. The inhabitants of the castle immediately wished [Col. 0613D] to seize the sergeants whom our count had left there and hand them over to the routiers. But the sergeants withdrew into the castle’s fortification, which was of little strength, and began to defend themselves. O frenzied betrayal! O wicked crime! Seeing that they could not resist, the aforesaid sergeants told the routiers that they would surrender the fortification if they were allowed to depart alive and unharmed. And so it was done. But not long afterward our count passed through the aforesaid castle and set the whole of it on fire.

Setting out from Pamiers, our count came to a castle called Varilhes, near Foix. Finding it burned and empty, he fortified it with his own people. Penetrating into [Col. 0614A] the territory of the Count of Foix, he devastated many of his castles and burned the entire borough of Foix itself.

After spending eight days about Foix, destroying trees and uprooting vines, our count returned to Pamiers. The Bishop of Cahors had come to him, sent by the nobles of the territory of Cahors, begging the count to come to them; they would establish him as their lord and receive their lands from him. The Count of Toulouse had exercised lordship in the territory of Cahors. The noble count then asked the Count of Bar and the German nobles to go with him. All consented and promised that they would go.

They began their journey; but when they came near Castelnau, [Col. 0614B] the Count of Bar withdrew from the promise he had given the count. Without regard for his reputation or honour, he told him that he would by no means go with him. All were astonished. Our count was deeply troubled; he himself begged, all entreated, but they could achieve nothing. The noble count immediately asked the Germans whether they would go with him; they most gladly promised that they would.

Our count therefore set out toward Cahors, while the Count of Bar, taking another road, began to make for Carcassonne. At that departure, the Count of Bar endured such reproach that it could not easily be described. Those in the army publicly pursued him with insults to such an extent that, from shame, [Col. 0614C] we do not dare say or write what they said. Thus, by God’s just judgment, he who, on arriving in the Albigensian country, had been honoured by men in cities and castles and feared by all, returned disgraced by all and made contemptible in everyone’s eyes.

Making for Cahors, our count passed through a castle of the Count of Toulouse in the territory of Cahors, called Catus, and, launching an attack, burned the entire outer borough of the castle. Thence he came to Cahors, where he was honourably received. After spending a few days there, he went with the aforesaid Germans, escorting them as far as the town called Rocamadour. From there the Germans returned to their own land, while the count returned to Cahors with very few men.

While the count was at [Col. 0614D] Cahors, word came to him that two of his knights—Lambert of Thury and Walter of Langton, brother of the Bishop of Canterbury—had been captured by the knights of the Count of Foix.

> [Note: [Col. 0613] Namely Stephen, whom Innocent III made a cardinal and whose death Matthew Paris records under the year 1228.]

Let us briefly relate something concerning the manner of their capture, as we heard it from the lips of both men themselves.

On a certain day the said knights were riding near the territory of the Count of Foix with many local inhabitants. When the Count of Foix heard of this, he pursued them with a great multitude. But the local people who were with our men, and who, as is said, had committed this betrayal, fled immediately when they saw the approaching multitude. Thus only six of our men remained. [Col. 0615A] The many opponents surrounded the six on every side—for the Count of Foix was pursuing the fleeing locals—and killed all their horses.

Having lost their horses and being surrounded by a multitude of enemies, our men defended themselves bravely. Then one of the opponents, more noble than the others and a kinsman of the Count of Foix, who knew Lambert, told him to surrender. Hearing this, the man of great courage said: “The hour has not yet come.” Then, when he saw that he could not escape, he said: “We surrender on this condition: that you promise us five things—namely, that you will neither kill us nor cut off our limbs; further, that we shall be kept in honourable custody, that you will not separate us from one another, that you will bring us to a suitable ransom, [Col. 0615B] and that you will not put us into another’s power. If you firmly promise all this, we shall surrender to you. But if you refuse, we are ready to die; yet we trust in the Lord that we shall not die alone. Rather, selling our lives dearly, with Christ’s help we shall first kill many of you. Our hands are not yet bound, and you will not take us freely or with impunity.”

Hearing Lambert’s words, the said knight promised most willingly to do everything he asked.

“Come then,” said Lambert, “and pledge your faith to me upon this in my hand.”

But the man did not dare approach him until our men had first assured his safety. Lambert and the other five gave him assurance. He came to them and took them captive with him on these terms. But, immediately breaking the promise he had made, [Col. 0615C] he handed them over to the Count of Foix.

That count bound them with enormous chains and put them in a prison so dreadful and so narrow that they could neither stand nor lie stretched out. They had neither light nor candle. Only when they ate was there one very small opening in that dungeon, through which food was passed to them. The Count of Foix kept them there for a very long time, until they were ransomed for much money. Let us now return to what we left aside.

After the noble count had completed at Cahors the business for which he had come there, he resolved to go to the Albigensian country. Returning from Cahors, passing through his castles, and visiting his borderlands, [Col. 0615D] he made his way back toward Pamiers. He came to a certain fortification near Pamiers and found it fortified against him. There were six knights in it and many men. The count could not take that fortification on that day, but the next morning, making an assault, burning the gate, and undermining the wall, he captured it by force and destroyed it. He killed the three knights who were in it and its other inhabitants, reserving only three knights at the counsel of his men, because they had promised to procure the surrender of Lambert of Thury and Walter of Langton, the Englishman, whom, as stated, the Count of Foix held.

Our count then came to Pamiers. While he was there, he was told that the people of Puylaurens had committed treachery and handed over the town to Sicard, who [Col. 0616A] had been lord of the castle. Sicard and his knights, as well as those people, were already attacking the knights of Guy of Lucé, who were stationed in the castle fortification as its guardians. For, as we said above, our count had given that castle to Guy.

On hearing this, the count was disturbed and began hastening to aid the knights. When he came to Castelnau, someone came to tell him that Guy’s knights had surrendered the tower of Puylaurens to the opponents—and it was indeed so: with it went all the castle’s walls. A certain knight, to whom the aforesaid Guy had especially entrusted the custody of his castle, had, as has been said, surrendered that tower to the opponents for money. But a few days later, when that knight was accused of treachery in the count’s court and refused to defend himself [Col. 0616B] by judicial combat, the said Guy had him hanged from the gallows.

Leaving some of his knights at Castelnau for the castle’s defence, the count himself went to Carcassonne. Yet before leaving Castelnau he had sent certain knights and crossbowmen to Montferrand to guard that castle. For the Count of Toulouse and the other enemies of the faith had now recovered their strength to resist, seeing that our count was almost alone; they were ranging through the land in order to recover by treachery the castles they had lost.

While our count was at Carcassonne, he was told that his opponents were coming in great numbers to besiege Castelnau. On hearing this, the count [Col. 0616C] was greatly troubled. He immediately sent to his knights at Castelnau and ordered them not to fear the enemy, for he himself would come and help them.

## CHAPTER LVI. The Count of Toulouse besieges Castelnau and Count Simon defending it.

One Sunday, when the count was at Carcassonne and had heard Mass and received the divine sacraments, he was about to set out immediately for Castelnau. A certain Cistercian who was present turned to him and began to comfort and encourage him as much as he could. To him the noble man, placing all his confidence in God, said: “Do you think that I am afraid? It is Christ’s cause that is being conducted; the whole Church prays for me. I know that [Col. 0616D] we cannot be overcome.”

Having said this, the most noble man hurried to Castelnau. But certain castles near Castelnau had already withdrawn from his lordship, and many of the men whom he had stationed in those castles had already been killed by the opponents through treachery. While our count was at Castelnau, behold: the Count of Toulouse, the Count of Foix, Gaston of Béarn, and a certain Gascon nobleman, having left Toulouse with an innumerable multitude, hurried to besiege Castelnau.

There also came with the opponents that most wicked apostate, that transgressor, that iniquitous son of the devil, minister of Antichrist—namely Savaric of Mauléon—surpassing every heretic and worse than every unbeliever (I Tim. V), an assailant of the Church and enemy of Christ. O man—rather, most deadly poison—Savaric, I say: wicked and lost, in shame and shamelessness, running against God with neck outstretched, he dared even to attack the holy Church of God! O man, prince of apostasy, artificer of cruelty, agent of perversity! O participant in evil men, companion of the perverse, reproach of mankind, stranger to virtue, diabolical man—rather, wholly devil!

Hearing that so great a multitude was approaching, some of our men advised the count to leave some of his people for the castle’s defence and withdraw to Fanjeaux, or even to Carcassonne. But, after taking sounder counsel, with God making better provision, the count chose to await the opponents’ arrival at Castelnau.

[Col. 0617B] Nor should it be left unmentioned that, while the count was at Castelnau and was already, as it were, in the enemy’s hand, behold, Guy of Lucé arrived, sent by God, with nearly fifty knights. For the noble count had sent all his men to the king of Aragon as aid against the Turks; the count rejoiced at their arrival, and the spirits of all our men were strengthened. But that utterly wicked king, who had never loved either the cause of the faith or our count, behaved very discourteously toward the knights whom the count had sent to his assistance. Indeed, when those knights were returning to our count, at the count’s command conveyed to them by letter, that most faithless king, as has been said, had prepared ambushes on the road to capture our knights. The treachery became known to the aforesaid knights, and they turned aside from the public highway. O cruel recompense for a pious deed! O harsh wages for so great a service!

We now carry out our purpose. While the count at Castelnau was secretly awaiting the arrival of his enemies, one day the hostile forces suddenly came with an innumerable multitude. Like locusts covering the earth, they began to range about on every side. But when they had approached the castle, the inhabitants of the outer borough immediately threw themselves down over the wall, went over to the enemy, and surrendered the borough to them at their first approach. Entering the borough, the adversaries began to run about here and there, rejoicing and exulting. Our count was then at table.

[Col. 0617D] After eating, our men armed themselves, came forth from the castle, quickly put to flight whatever enemies they found in the borough, and bravely drove the fleeing and trembling adversaries out of it. When this had been done, the count of Toulouse and those with him pitched their tents on the hill on the castle side. Thereafter they enclosed themselves with ditches, timber, and barricades so thoroughly that they seemed not so much besiegers as besieged; indeed, the place where the besieging army stood appeared stronger and more difficult of access than the besieged castle.

When evening came, the adversaries entered the borough. It was empty of inhabitants, because our men, owing to their small numbers, could not garrison it. There were no more than five hundred men in the castle altogether, knights and serjeants included,

[Col. 0618A] whereas the enemy were believed to number nearly a hundred thousand. Yet, fearing that our men might expel them as before, the enemies who had entered the borough fortified it from the wall-side with timber and whatever else they could procure, so that our men might not come out against them. They also pierced the outer wall, which lay between the borough and the army, in many places, in order that they might escape more freely if need arose.

On the following day our men came out of the castle, destroyed all that the adversaries had made, drove them from the borough as they had done before, and pursued them as they fled as far as their tents. Nor do we think it should be omitted into what peril the noble count had then fallen. The countess was at Lavaur; his firstborn, Amaury, was ill at Fanjeaux;

[Col. 0618B] his daughter, born to them in that land, was being brought up at Montréal; and none could see or assist another.

Nor should this be suppressed: although our men were very few, every day they went forth and attacked the enemy most frequently and vigorously. As we have already said, our men seemed not to be besieged but rather to be besieging. Yet the adversaries had enclosed themselves with such a multitude of barricades that our men could not enter among them, though they desired it most ardently. It should also be added that, before the enemy’s eyes, our serjeants daily led our horses to water as far as half a league from the castle. Our foot soldiers also harvested the vineyards near the enemy army daily, while the adversaries looked on with envy;

[Col. 0618C] for it was the season of the vintage.

One day that most wicked traitor, the count of Foix, with his son Roger Bernard, no less wicked than himself, and a great part of their army, came near the castle. They wished to attack our men, who stood armed before the castle gates. But our men, seeing them approach, charged them with great force, unhorsed the son of the count of Foix and several others, and compelled them to return in confusion to their tents. Since we cannot fully recount all the assaults and events of that siege, we state this briefly: whenever the adversaries dared approach our men

[Col. 0618D] in order to make an attack, our men remained outside the castle throughout the day before its gates, seeking battle, and sent them back to their tents in utter humiliation.

While these things were happening, the neighboring castles round about withdrew from the dominion of our count and surrendered themselves to the count of Toulouse. On one day the people of Cabaret sent to the count of Toulouse, bidding him come or send someone to them; and they immediately surrendered Cabaret to him. The castle of Cabaret was five leagues from Castelnau. Accordingly, one night many adversaries, sent from their camp by the count of Toulouse, set out to take Cabaret. But while our enemies were on the road, by the merciful disposition of God,

[Col. 0619A] they lost the road that led to Cabaret; wandering for a long time through trackless places, they could not reach the aforesaid castle of Cabaret. Thus, after long wanderings, they returned to the camp from which they had set out.

Meanwhile the count of Toulouse had a machine called a mangonel erected, and the mangonel began to hurl missiles into the castle, but it harmed our men little or not at all. After some days, however, the count of Toulouse caused a certain engine of remarkable size to be prepared for destroying the castle wall. Very great stones were hurled from that engine, and whatever they struck they destroyed. After the enemies had fired this aforesaid engine for many days, one of the count of Toulouse’s crossbowmen came to him and said: “Why do you spend so much and such great expense on that engine?

[Col. 0619B] Why do you labor to destroy the walls of this castle? Do you not see daily that our enemies come as far as our tents, while you do not dare come out? Surely you ought to wish the wall were of iron, so that they could not get at us.”

For during that siege an extraordinary thing occurred, contrary to the usual order: whereas besiegers ordinarily attack the besieged, our besieged men, by a reversal of right, attacked their besiegers more often. Our men also mocked the adversaries in these words: “Why do you expend so much and so great an outlay on your engine, laboring so long to destroy the wall? Trust us: we will spare you the expense; we will free you from the labor. Give us only twenty marks,

[Col. 0619C] and we shall utterly demolish one hundred cubits of this very wall in length, levelling it with the ground, so that, if you dare, you may pass freely to us despite the wall.” O courage of spirit! O most steadfast strength of mind!

One day our count went out from the castle, intending to destroy the aforesaid engine. But the adversaries had made so many barricades and ditches around it that our men could not reach it. The most courageous man, namely our count, seated on horseback, wished to cross a very broad and deep ditch and rush boldly upon his enemies. Some of our men, seeing this and recognizing the inevitable danger if the count did it, seized his bridle

[Col. 0619D] and held him back, lest he expose himself to imminent death. This done, all our men returned to the castle, without losing any of their own, after killing many of the adversaries.

In this situation, our count sent his marshal Guy of Lévis, a faithful man and valiant in arms, to have provisions brought to the count from Fanjeaux and Carcassonne, and to order the people of Carcassonne and Béziers to hasten to the count’s aid. But since he could accomplish nothing—for all the land had corrupted its way (Gen. 6)—he returned to the count. The count sent him out again, together with the noble Matthew of Marly, brother of Bouchard. They came to the count’s subjects and repeatedly urged them to come to the count,

[Col. 0620A] adding threats to entreaties. But the perverse men, already wavering and unwilling to listen to them, did not respond. They then went to Aimery, lord of Narbonne, and the citizens of Narbonne, urging and admonishing them to hasten to aid the count. The citizens of Narbonne replied to the marshal that, if Aimery their lord went with them, they would follow him. But he, being a very shrewd man, could by no means be persuaded to do so.

When those knights of ours left Narbonne, they could scarcely draw three hundred men from so populous a city. When they reached Carcassonne, they could obtain no more than five hundred men from that entire region. When they wished to lead them to the count, they absolutely refused, and all at once fled back

[Col. 0620B] to their homes.

Meanwhile the utterly faithless count of Foix had occupied and fortified against our men a certain castle of Bouchard of Marly, near Castelnau on the eastern side toward Carcassonne, called Saint-Martin, along with several other fortifications in the surrounding area. The count had ordered Bouchard of Marly and Martin Algais, who were with the countess at Lavaur, to come to Castelnau. This Martin was a Spanish knight, formerly one of our party; but how wickedly he afterward behaved will be shown in what follows.

## Chapter LVII. By a most fierce engagement and a distinguished victory, the Crusaders rout the count of Foix at the fortress of Saint-Martin.

[Col. 0620C]

There was with our count a certain knight of Carcassonne, from Montréal, William surnamed Catus. The lord count had given him land and made him a knight. He held him in such intimacy that this William had lifted the count’s daughter from the sacred font in baptism. The count, the countess, and all our party trusted him above all the native inhabitants, so much so that the lord count had at one time entrusted his own firstborn son to his care.

The count had sent him from Castelnau to Fanjeaux to bring men from the neighboring castles to the count’s aid at Castelnau. But this man, worse than every enemy and the most wicked of all traitors,

[Col. 0620D] ungrateful for benefits and forgetful of affection, joined with certain natives who shared the same cruel disposition. Together they agreed upon such wickedness as to capture the aforesaid marshal and his companions as they returned from Carcassonne, and hand them over to the count of Foix. O unjust kind of treachery! O grievous pest! O contrivance of cruelty! O devilish invention! But it became known to the aforesaid marshal, and he turned aside from the ambush.

Nor should it be passed over that many people of that land, including certain abbots who possessed many castles, then abandoned our count and swore fealty to the count of Toulouse. O execrable oath! O faithless infidelity!

Meanwhile Bouchard of Marly, Martin Algais, and certain

[Col. 0621A] other knights of our count came from the castle of Lavaur, hastening to assist the count, and reached Saissac, Bouchard’s castle, because they did not dare travel by the direct road from Lavaur to Castelnau. On the day before their entry into Castelnau, the count of Foix, who knew beforehand of their arrival, had gone out to the aforesaid castle called Saint-Martin, through which our knights had to pass, in order to attack them.

When our noble count learned this, he sent Guy of Lucé, the castellan of Malfa, the viscount of Donges, and up to forty other knights to aid his men, ordering them to be ready without doubt on the following day to fight against the aforesaid count of Foix.

After these knights had been sent, there remained with the count no more than sixty mounted men, including knights and squires.

[Col. 0621B] Seeing that our count had sent aid to his own men, the count of Foix withdrew from the castle of Saint-Martin and returned to the army, intending to take armed men from there and return with them to attack the marshal and those remaining with him.

Meanwhile our count addressed William Catus and the native knights who were with him at Castelnau in this manner: “Behold, dearest brothers, the count of Toulouse and the count of Foix, powerful men with an innumerable multitude, seek my blood. I stand, as it were, alone in the midst of my enemies. Therefore I beg you, for God’s sake: if, led by fear or affection, you wish to go over to them and leave me,

[Col. 0621C] do not conceal it; I shall have you safely conducted to them, sound and unharmed.” O nobility of the man! O excellence of the prince!

But the other Judas, namely William Catus, answered: “Far be it, my lord, far be it that we should leave you. For even if all abandon you, I shall remain with you unto death” (Matt. 26). All likewise said the same. Yet not long afterward that traitor departed from the count with certain companions, changing from the most intimate associate into a most cruel persecutor.

After these events, early in the morning the marshal, Bouchard of Marly, and those with him heard Mass, made confession, received communion of the Lord’s body, mounted their horses, and set out toward the count. The count of Foix, learning that they were coming,

[Col. 0621D] took with him an innumerable multitude of armed horsemen, chosen from the best of his entire army, together with many thousands of selected foot soldiers, and hurried to meet our men in battle. That count had formed three squadrons.

Our count, who was outside the gates of Castelnau that day, anxiously awaiting the arrival of his men, saw that the count of Foix was hurrying to fight them. He consulted those with him about what they should do. Opinions differed: some said that he should remain to guard the castle; others, on the contrary, said that he should hasten to aid his knights. That man of tireless valor, that man of unconquered courage, is reported to have said: “Very few of us remain in this castle, and the whole cause of Christ

[Col. 0622A] depends upon this battle. Far be it that our knights should die gloriously in battle while I escape alive in disgrace. I wish either to conquer with my men or to die with them. Let us go also; and, if need be, let us die with them.” Who could refrain from tears at this? Speaking thus in tears, he immediately hastened to aid his own men. As the count of Foix approached them, he reduced his three squadrons to one.

It must here be added that the bishop of Cahors and a certain Cistercian monk, who, by order of the abbot of Cîteaux, were directing the affairs of Jesus Christ, came with the marshal. When they saw the enemies coming and battle imminent, they began to exhort our men to conduct themselves manfully, firmly promising that, if they fell in so glorious a struggle

[Col. 0622B] for the Christian faith, they would obtain remission of sins and immediately, crowned with every glory and honor, receive the reward of their struggle and labor.

Our most valiant knights, certain indeed of the reward and also hoping confidently for victory, advanced cheerfully and fearlessly against the enemy, who came massed together. The adversaries formed their battle line: those on horseback rode in the middle, with their horses covered in iron; the other horsemen were on one side, and the foot soldiers, very well armed, on the other. Our men therefore took counsel together to attack first those with armored horses.

While this was taking place, our men looked into the distance and saw our count coming out

[Col. 0622C] from Castelnau and hurrying to their aid. Their courage was immediately doubled; made bolder, they invoked Christ, threw themselves into the midst of the enemy, and at once broke through them. The enemy, defeated and confused in a moment, took to flight. Seeing this, our men immediately turned toward the foot soldiers standing on the other side and killed innumerable numbers of them.

Nor should it be omitted that, as the marshal affirmed in a truthful account, there were more than thirty enemies against each one of our men. Let the divine power therefore be acknowledged at work. For our count could not take part in the battle, although he arrived with the greatest haste: victorious Christ had already granted victory to his knights. As our men pursued the fleeing adversaries

[Col. 0622D] and cut down all those at the rear, there was a great slaughter of the enemy. No more than thirty of our men fell, while innumerable enemies were killed.

Nor should it be passed over that Martin Algais, whom we mentioned above, recoiled from the battle at the first onset and began to flee. The venerable bishop of Cahors, who was nearby, saw him fleeing and asked what had happened. “We are all dead,” he replied. But the Catholic man did not believe him, rebuked him harshly, and compelled him to return to the fight.

It must also not be omitted that the fleeing enemies, from fear of death, cried aloud: “Montfort! Montfort!” so that they might pretend to be of our party and escape the hands of their pursuers by that device.

[Col. 0623A] But our men defeated this trick by another. When one of our men heard an enemy cry “Montfort!” in fear, he said to him: “If you are one of us, kill that fugitive,” pointing to one of the fleeing men. Then he, driven by fear, killed his companion; but the man who had killed his companion was himself killed, receiving from our men the reward of his fraud and crime. O wonderful and unheard-of thing! Those who had entered battle to kill our men, by God’s just judgment served us, though unwillingly, by killing their own people.

After our men had pursued the enemies for a long time and killed countless numbers, the count stood in the middle of the field in order to gather again his men, who, pursuing the enemies, had scattered in all directions.

[Col. 0623B] Meanwhile the chief of all apostates, namely Savaric of Mauléon, and a great multitude of armed men, came out from the place of their camp and approached the gates of Castelnau. There, standing with great arrogance and with their banners raised, they awaited the outcome of the battle. Many of them also entered the lower borough and began fiercely attacking those who had remained in the castle—only five knights and very few serjeants. Yet, though they were very few, they defended themselves most bravely, repelling from the borough innumerable enemies very well armed with weapons and crossbows.

Seeing, therefore, that our men had won victory on the field of battle, and perceiving that those with him could not take the castle, the said traitor Savaric gathered

[Col. 0623C] his men and returned in confusion to the tents. Our count and those with him, returning victorious from the field, did not wish to break into the enemy’s very tents. O unconquered knights! O soldiers of Christ! As has already been said, the enemy had shut themselves in with so many barricades and ditches that our men could not reach them unless they dismounted. When the count was hastening to do this, some advised him to postpone it until the following day, because the enemy were fresh while our men were fatigued by battle. The count consented, for, acting always with counsel in all things, he wished to comply with them.

The noble man therefore returned to the castle. Knowing that the power and the victory were God’s, he dismounted

[Col. 0623D] from his horse at the very entrance of Castelnau and went barefoot to the church, in order to give thanks to almighty God for the benefits bestowed. In that church our men, singing *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise you, O God”) with great devotion and rejoicing, blessed the Lord in hymns and thanksgivings, who had done great things among his people and granted them victory over their enemies (2 Macc. 10).

We do not think a certain miracle should be omitted, which happened at that time in a Cistercian abbey in the territory of Toulouse, called Grandselve. The monks of that house were in great distress, because, if the noble count of Montfort were captured at Castelnau or fell in battle, death

[Col. 0624A] and the sword threatened them. For the count of Toulouse and his accomplices hated the monks of the Cistercian order above all others, and especially that house, because the abbot of Cîteaux, Arnaud, legate of the Apostolic See—to whom they attributed their disinheritance above all else—had formerly been abbot of that house.

One day, therefore, while a monk of that house, a religious and holy man, was celebrating the divine offices, at the consecration of the Eucharist he prayed from the deepest devotion of his heart for the said count of Montfort, then besieged at Castelnau. A divine voice said to him: “Why do you pray for him? So many are praying for him that your prayer is not needed.”

## Chapter LVIII. Castelnau is freed from siege.

[Col. 0624B]

Meanwhile the count of Foix devised a new artifice of treachery, imitating his father the devil, who, when defeated in one matter, turns to other schemes for doing harm. He therefore sent messengers far and wide through the castles, asserting that the count of Montfort had been defeated in battle. Some even said that he had been flayed and hanged. On this account, at that time, they surrendered themselves to our adversaries.

On the day after the glorious victory, the count’s knights advised him to leave Castelnau, leave some of his men there, and travel through his territory to gather whatever men he could. The count therefore left Castelnau and went to Narbonne. At that time pilgrims were coming from France, namely Alan of Roquecézière, a man of great worth,

[Col. 0624C] and certain others, though few. The count of Toulouse and those with him, seeing that they had accomplished nothing in the siege of Castelnau, burned their engine and returned in great confusion to their own lands after a few days. Nor should it be left unsaid that they did not dare leave their camp until they knew that our count had left the castle.

While our count was at Narbonne, having with him the aforesaid pilgrims and having gathered many native inhabitants, so that on his return he might fight the count of Toulouse and those with him, word came that the said count and his men had withdrawn from the siege of Castelnau. Our count then dismissed

[Col. 0624D] the natives whom he had assembled, took only the pilgrims with him, returned to Castelnau, and resolved to raze utterly all the surrounding fortifications that had withdrawn from his dominion.

While this was being done, word came that a certain castle named Constance, toward Termes, had fallen away from his jurisdiction and surrendered itself to the enemies of the faith. On hearing this, the count immediately hurried to besiege it. After attacking it for some days, those inside, seeing that they could not resist, surrendered themselves and the castle to the count, to do with them entirely as he wished. This done, the count returned to Castelnau.

Immediately our count was informed that the people of the castle called Montaigut, in the diocese of Albi,

[Col. 0625A] had surrendered themselves to the count of Toulouse and were attacking the castle’s defenses and those whom our count had stationed there as guards. Our count hurried there; but before he could arrive, those in the aforesaid fortification had already surrendered it to the adversaries.

Why say more? All the most noble and strongest castles round about, except for only two, surrendered themselves to the count of Toulouse at almost a single moment. The names of the noble castles then lost in the diocese of Albi were: Rabastens, Montaigut, Gaillac, the castle of Gravi, Cahuzac, Saint-Marcel, Guespia, and Saint-Antonin. In the diocese of Toulouse, before the siege of Castelnau, during that very time of siege, the following had already surrendered: Puylaurens, Casser, Saint-Félix, Montferrand, Avignonet, Saint-Michel, Cuc, and Saverdun.

[Col. 0625B] Besides these, other lesser castles were lost which we could not enumerate one by one; they are said to have numbered more than fifty.

We do not think that a certain most wicked and unheard-of betrayal, committed at that time in the castle of Gravi in the diocese of Albi, should be passed over. Our noble count had entrusted that castle to a French knight. But the knight trusted the castle’s inhabitants more than he ought, while they plotted his death. One day the aforesaid knight had his casks repaired by a carpenter of that castle. When this carpenter had repaired one cask, he told the knight to inspect it

[Col. 0625C] and see whether it had been properly repaired. As the knight put his head into the cask, the carpenter raised his axe and cut off his head. O unheard-of cruelty! The inhabitants of the castle immediately rose up and killed the few Frenchmen who were in the castle.

When the noble count Baldwin, mentioned above, brother of the count of Toulouse, heard of this, he came before the castle very early one day. The inhabitants came out to meet him, thinking he was the count of Toulouse because he bore similar arms. They brought him into the castle and, rejoicing and exulting, told him of the cruelty they had committed. But he sprang upon them with an armed multitude and killed nearly all of them, from the least to the greatest.

[Col. 0625D] Seeing that he had lost so many and such great castles, our count came to Pamiers to fortify that castle. While he remained there, the count of Foix sent him word that, if he would wait only four days, he himself would come and fight him. Our count sent word back that he would wait not merely four days but more than ten at Pamiers. But the count of Foix did not dare come. Moreover, our knights, even without our count, entered the land of Foix and destroyed a certain castle of that count.

After this our count returned toward Fanjeaux and sent the castellan of Malfa and his brother Geoffrey, valiant knights, with a very few others to a certain castle, in order that they might have grain brought from that castle

[Col. 0626A] to Fanjeaux, to provision the castle itself. As they were returning from the aforesaid castle, the son of the count of Foix, not falling short of his father’s wickedness, laid an ambush beside the road by which those knights had to come. That traitor had with him a large multitude of armed men.

As our men passed by, the enemies rose from the ambush and attacked them. Surrounding the said Geoffrey, they assailed him on every side. But he, being an excellent knight, defended himself bravely; yet he had very few helpers. When he had already lost his horse and was in the utmost peril, the enemies told him to surrender. But that man of remarkable worth is reported to have replied: “I have surrendered myself to Christ; far be it that I should surrender myself to his enemies.”

[Col. 0626B] Thus, amid the enemies’ blows, he gave up his spirit gloriously, as we believe. With him also fell a most valiant young man, a kinsman of Geoffrey, and a few others. A certain knight named Droco surrendered alive; the count of Foix kept him imprisoned. The castellan of Malfa escaped alive, and, mourning the loss of his brother and kinsman, returned to the castle from which they had departed.

Afterward our men returned to the place, recovered the bodies of the slain, and buried them in a Cistercian abbey called Boulbonne. At that time William, the venerable archdeacon of Paris, and another master, James of Vitry, at the command and request of the bishop of Uzès, whom the lord pope had appointed legate for the cause of the faith against the heretics—and who himself loved and vigorously promoted that cause—undertook the office of preaching.

[Col. 0626C] Inflamed with zeal for the faith, they traveled through France—indeed, through Germany—and throughout that winter marked an incredible multitude of believers with the sign of the cross upon their breasts for Christ’s soldiery. These two, especially after God, promoted the cause of the faith in the French and German lands.

## Chapter LIX. Robert of Mauvoisin, attended by one hundred knights, comes from France to assist the count of Montfort.

In these circumstances, that most noble of knights, servant of Christ, foremost lover and promoter of the cause of Jesus—namely Robert of Mauvoisin—who in the preceding season had gone to France, returned with more than one hundred chosen knights of France, all of whom had made him their leader and master.

[Col. 0626D] Admonished by venerable men, namely the bishop of Toulouse and the abbot of Les Vaux, they had taken the cross and girded themselves for the warfare of Jesus Christ. Persevering throughout that winter in the service of Jesus Christ, they nobly raised up the aforesaid cause, which was then in deep decline.

Hearing that these knights were arriving, the count went to meet them as far as Carcassonne. When he arrived there, there was incredible exultation among our men and very great joy. From there the count came with those knights as far as Fanjeaux.

At that time the count of Foix was besieging a certain castle belonging to a native knight named William Daura, who adhered to our count and assisted him as far as he could.

[Col. 0627A] This castle lay near the land of the count of Foix and was called Carun. The count of Foix had already been attacking it for fifteen days. Our men therefore set out from Fanjeaux, hastening to compel the count of Foix to withdraw from the siege of that castle.
