When that count heard that our men were coming, he left his engines there, fled in great confusion, and withdrew from the siege. Our men then devastated his land for several days and destroyed four of his castles.

Returning thence to Fanjeaux, they hastened to besiege a certain castle in the diocese of Toulouse called Pomaireda. After attacking it for several days, they made an assault one day and forcefully filled the castle ditch. But when night came on, they did not take the castle that day. Seeing that they were nearly captured, those inside pierced the wall at midnight and secretly fled.

[Col. 0627B] After this, word immediately came to the count that a certain castle named Albedunum, in the diocese of Narbonne, had withdrawn from his dominion. As the count went there, the lord of the castle came to meet him and surrendered both himself and his castle to his will.

## Chapter LX. Guy of Montfort comes to his brother, the count of Montfort, from overseas; the count exults wonderfully at his arrival.

[Col. 0627C] After these events, the count came to that noble castle in the diocese of Albi called Castres. While he was staying there and the feast of the Lord’s Nativity was being celebrated, his full brother Guy arrived, returning from overseas. This Guy, the count’s brother, had gone overseas with him; but when the count returned, Guy remained overseas because he had married there a most noble wife of royal lineage, lady of Sidon. She too was coming with him, together with the sons she had borne him.

Nor should it be omitted that, while the said Guy was coming to the count, certain castles in the territory of Albi which had fallen away from the dominion of the aforesaid count surrendered themselves to Guy. No one could explain how great was the exultation of the count and our men

[Col. 0627D] at the arrival of his brother.

After a few days our men hurried to besiege a certain castle in the diocese of Albi called Tudelle. It belonged to the father of that most wicked traitor Gerald of Pépieux. After attacking the castle, our men took it within a few days and put almost all to the sword. Only Gerald’s father escaped. The count gave him in exchange for a certain knight whom the count of Foix held in chains, named Droco of Compans, a kinsman of Robert of Mauvoisin.

After this the noble count hurried to besiege a certain castle called Cahuzac in the territory of Albi. There, although it was midwinter, he was unusually engaged in a siege and had very few men with him; yet through many hardships and difficulties

[Col. 0628A] he took the castle.

The count of Toulouse, the count of Comminges, and the count of Foix had gathered with an innumerable multitude at a nearby castle named Gaillac. They sent messengers to our count, ordering him to come out to be attacked by them. They said this in hopes that, if they could frighten our count, he might perhaps abandon his siege. They sent once; they sent again; and still they did not dare come.

Seeing that they would not come, the count said to his men: “Since they certainly do not come, I shall go and visit them.” Taking armed men of his own with him, he began to hasten toward Gaillac. With few men he went, breathing and panting for battle. When the count of Toulouse and those with him heard this, they left Gaillac and fled

[Col. 0628B] toward a nearby castle called Montaigut. Our count pursued them to that castle; seeing this, they fled from there, and, after leaving that castle, fled toward Toulouse. Seeing that they did not dare await him, our count returned to the castle from which he had come.

With these matters thus duly accomplished, the count sent to the abbot of Cîteaux, who was at Albi, asking what should be done. The abbot’s counsel was that the count should besiege the castle of Saint-Marcel, situated about three leagues from Albi. The count of Toulouse had entrusted that castle to a most wicked traitor, Gerald of Pépieux. When our men came to the castle, they besieged it only from one side [Col. 0628C], for they were exceedingly few, whereas the castle was large and very strong. At once our men began vigorously to attack it with a certain siege-engine.

After a few days the count of Toulouse, the count of Comminges, and the count of Foix came with an incredible multitude and entered the castle to defend it against our men. Since the castle, though spacious, could not contain so great a number, many of the enemy pitched their tents on the other side of it. This having been done, our men did not cease from assaulting the castle, while their opponents defended themselves as best they could. O wonderful and astonishing thing! Although besiegers ordinarily surpass the besieged in number and strength, the besieged were nearly ten times more numerous than the besiegers [Col. 0628D]; for our men numbered no more than five hundred. Moreover, the aforesaid counts had an innumerable multitude of infantry; our men, on the other hand, had none or very few foot-soldiers. O great deed! O unprecedented novelty! Nor should it be passed over in silence that, whenever the opponents dared to come out against our men, they were immediately repulsed by them with the greatest force.

At last, one day the count of Foix came out of the castle with many men, intending to disable our stone-throwing engine. When our sergeants saw this, they courageously repelled them by showers of stones and shut them back inside the castle before our knights could arm themselves. A great scarcity arose in the army, for our men could obtain provisions only from Albi. Moreover, our opponents [Col. 0629A], coming out in a very great multitude, guarded the public roads so closely that those from Albi did not dare come to the army unless the count sent half his force as an escort. Therefore, after a month had passed in that siege, the count knew that, if he divided the few knights whom he had—keeping one half with himself and sending the other half for provisions—the enemies, who were countless, would attack either one group or the other. Compelled by such manifest necessity, and after bread had failed in the army for several days, he withdrew from the siege.

Nor should it be omitted that, on Good Friday itself, when the count—being wholly Catholic and devoted to divine worship—had the office of the Lord’s Passion solemnly celebrated in his tent, the opponents, hearing [Col. 0629B] our clerics singing, climbed the walls and, in mockery and derision, uttered a most hideous howl (Ps. 43). O perverse unbelief! O faithless perversity! Yet if anyone considers carefully, our count gained greater honor and glory in this siege than he had ever gained in the capture of any castle, however strong. From that time onward his valor shone forth greatly and his constancy shone more brightly. Nor should it be passed over that, when our count withdrew from the aforesaid castle, the opponents, though countless, did not dare come out even to attack our men a little as they departed.

We do not wish to pass over a miracle which occurred at the same time in the diocese of Rodez [Ruthenium]. One Sunday, a certain abbot of Bonnevaux, of the Cistercian order, was preaching in a castle. The church was small and could not contain the people who were present; therefore all had gone outside and were hearing the abbot’s sermon before the church doors. Toward the end of the sermon, when the venerable abbot wished to exhort those present to take up crosses against the Albigensians, suddenly, in the sight of all, a cross appeared in the air, seeming to move toward the region of Toulouse [Col. 0629C]. I heard this miracle from the mouth of the said abbot, a religious man of great authority.

Withdrawing from the siege of Saint-Marcel, on the day before Easter, the count came to Albi and there celebrated the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection. [Col. 0629D] The venerable abbot of Les Vaux, whom we have mentioned above, had come there from France; for he had been elected bishop of Carcassonne. When the count and our knights found him in that city, they rejoiced greatly, for all loved him with special affection. For many years he had also been most intimate with the count; indeed, the count had, as it were from childhood, submitted himself to his counsels and conformed himself to his will. At the same time Arnold, abbot of Cîteaux, whom we have often mentioned, had been elected archbishop of Narbonne.

On Easter Day itself, the count of Toulouse and those with him left the castle of Saint-Marcel and came to Gaillac, three leagues from Albi. Our count, thinking that the opponents might perhaps boast [Col. 0630A] that they had defeated our men, and wishing openly to show that he did not fear them, left Albi with his men on the day after Easter and went to Gaillac, challenging his enemies to battle. Since they did not dare come out against him, he returned to Albi. The bishop-elect of Carcassonne, of whom we have spoken above, was in that city, and I was with him. For he had brought me with him from France, as companionship for himself while a stranger and pilgrim in a foreign land, since I was a monk and his nephew.

## CHAPTER LXI. The siege of Hautpoul, its most vigorous assault, and its glorious capture.

After spending several days at Albi, the count went with his men to the castle called Castres. [Col. 0630B] After we had remained there for a few days, the count, having taken counsel, resolved to besiege a certain castle between Castres and Cabaret, called Hautpoul. That castle had surrendered itself to the count of Toulouse around the time of the siege of Castelnau.

Thus, leaving Castres on a Sunday—the fifteenth day after Easter—we came before the aforesaid castle. The enemies who had entered it to defend it, a castle with a large suburb, came out against our men and began fiercely to harass them. But our men immediately forced them back into the castle and pitched their tents on one side of it, for they were few. The castle of Hautpoul stood on the precipitous height of a very lofty and exceedingly steep mountain, upon enormous [Col. 0630C] and almost inaccessible rocks. It was so strong—as I myself saw with my eyes and learned by experience—that, even if the gates of the castle stood open and absolutely no one resisted, a person could not without great difficulty traverse the castle itself and reach its tower.

Our men therefore prepared a single stone-throwing engine; on the third day after their arrival they erected it and made it cast stones at the castle tower. On that same day our knights armed themselves and, descending into the valley at the foot of the castle, tried to climb into it, in case they might capture it by assault. But when they had entered the first borough, those in the castle climbed upon the walls and houses and began to hurl huge and very frequent stones down upon our men. [Col. 0630D] Others kindled a great fire at the place by which our men had entered. Seeing that they were accomplishing nothing, since the place was virtually inaccessible to human beings and they could not endure the barrage of stones, our men came out through the midst of the fire, not without serious loss.

One day, moreover, we must not pass over the most wicked and cruel treachery committed by those in the castle. There was with our count a native knight, kinsman of a certain traitor who was in the castle and who had also been, in part, lord of Cabaret. Those in the castle therefore sent word to our count that he should send them the said knight, so that they might discuss terms with him and send back to the count through him whatever they wished. When the aforesaid knight, with the count’s permission, had approached them [Col. 0631A] and was speaking with them at the castle gate, one of those in the castle shot him with a crossbow bolt and wounded him most grievously. O most cruel treachery!

But not long afterward—on that very day or the next—it happened, by God’s just judgment, that the traitor who had summoned his own kinsman, our knight, to the conference, received a very severe wound from one of our men in the same place in which the knight had been wounded: namely, in the leg. O just measure of divine retribution! Meanwhile our stone-throwing engine continuously cast stones at the castle tower. On the fourth day from the beginning of the siege, after sunset, a very thick mist arose. Those in the castle, seized by divine fear and finding an opportunity in the favorable moment, began to flee from the castle. [Col. 0631B] When our men perceived this, they immediately raised a shout, rushed into the castle, and killed every enemy they found. Others, pursuing the fugitives through the darkness of the night, captured some of them. The next day the count had the castle destroyed and burned. After these events, the knights who had come from France with Robert of Mauvoisin, as stated above, and who had remained with the count throughout the preceding winter, nearly all departed from him and returned home.

## CHAPTER LXII. The people of Narbonne maliciously rise against Almaric, son of Count Simon.

We do not think we should omit a crime committed at that time by the citizens of Narbonne. The citizens of Narbonne were very wicked men and had never loved the cause of Jesus Christ, although through that cause innumerable benefits had accrued to them. One day Guy, brother of our count, and Almaric, the count’s eldest son, went to Narbonne. While the said Almaric was in that city, being a boy, he entered the palace of Aimeric, lord of Narbonne, for recreation. That palace was old and had been reduced almost to an abandoned wilderness. When Almaric touched a certain window of the palace with his hand and attempted to open it, the window, decayed through excessive age, fell by accident. Having done so, Almaric returned to the house of the Templars, where he was then lodging. [Col. 0631C]

At that hour Guy, the count’s brother, was in the house of the archbishop of Narbonne. Immediately the citizens of Narbonne, seeking an occasion to do evil, accused the count’s aforesaid little son of having wished forcibly to enter Aimeric’s palace. O slight occasion for accomplishing a crime—or rather, none at all! The aforesaid citizens immediately armed themselves and ran to the place where the boy was. They tried to break into the very house of the Templars. Seeing that they sought his life, the boy armed himself and took refuge in a tower of the Templars’ house, hiding himself from the enemy. But they attacked the aforesaid house with the utmost persistence. Seizing Frenchmen whom they found in the city, some killed many of them. O frenzy of the wicked! [Col. 0632A] They also killed two of the count’s own squires. At that hour Guy, the count’s brother, was in the archbishop’s house and did not dare go out. After the said citizens had attacked the house in which Almaric was for a long time, at last, on the advice of a certain citizen of Narbonne, they ceased their attack. Thus the boy was delivered from grave danger and escaped alive and unharmed by God’s grace. Now let us return to what we left aside.

The noble count withdrew from Hautpoul with very few knights and entered the territory of the count of Toulouse. After a few days, many pilgrims from Germany came to him. Moreover, day by day there began to arrive pilgrims who, as we have said above, had taken the cross at the preaching of the venerable William, [Col. 0632B] archdeacon of Paris, and Master James of Vitry. Since we could not relate every event in detail—namely, how from those days merciful God began wonderfully to advance His cause—we say briefly that our count in a very short time captured many castles by force and found many others deserted.

The names of the castles which the count recovered in less than three weeks are these: the castle called Cuc, Montmaur, Saint-Félix, Casser, Montferrand, Avignon, Saint-Michel, and many others. While the army was at the castle called Saint-Michel, one league from Castelnau, Guy, bishop of Carcassonne, formerly abbot [Col. 0632C] of Les Vaux, arrived, and I was with him. After the capture of Hautpoul, he had left the army while still bishop-elect and gone to Narbonne in order to receive consecration, together with the lord abbot of Cîteaux, who had likewise been elected archbishop of Narbonne.

After the complete destruction of the castle called Saint-Michel, the count resolved to besiege the noble castle called Puylaurens, which, as we have said above, had withdrawn from his lordship in the preceding year. Setting out and heading for that castle, we pitched our tents at a place near Puylaurens, about two leagues away. On that same day pilgrims arrived: namely, the powerful and noble provost of the church of Cologne, and with him many noble Germans. The count of Toulouse was at [Col. 0632D] Puylaurens with his innumerable *ruptarii* [mercenary raiders]. Yet, hearing that our men were approaching, he did not dare wait, but hurried out of the castle, took all the inhabitants of the castle with him, and fled toward Toulouse, leaving the castle empty. O man’s senselessness! O contemptible dullness of mind!

The next day, at first light, we came to the castle and found it empty. We advanced farther and pitched our tents in a certain valley. Guy of Lucé, to whom the count had long before granted the castle of Puylaurens, entered it and fortified it with his own men. The army remained two days in a valley near the castle. There word was brought to our count that many and important pilgrims were coming from France to Carcassonne: Robert, archbishop [Col. 0633A] of Rouen; Robert, bishop-elect of Laon; the venerable William, archdeacon of Paris; and many other nobles and commoners.

Seeing that he had a large army with him, the count took counsel and sent his brother Guy and Guy the marshal to meet the said pilgrims at Carcassonne, so that they might form a separate army and turn toward other regions, advancing the cause of Christ. The count himself set out and began to march toward the castle of Rabastens. But, leaving aside superfluities in order to reach matters more useful, let us say briefly that the three noble castles of Rabastens, Montaigut, and Gaillac—of which we have often spoken—surrendered themselves to our count virtually in one day, without siege or any difficulty [Col. 0633B].

When the burgesses of the castle called Saint-Marcel heard that our count, having recovered many castles, was hastening to besiege them, they were moved by fear and sent to him, begging that he would deign to receive them in peace; they would surrender the castle to his will. But the count, recalling their crimes and unheard-of perversities, would by no means make terms with them. Sending their messengers back to them, he declared that by no payment or price could they ever obtain his peace or agreement. Hearing this, the said people fled their castle and left it empty. When we came there, the count had it burned and had its tower and all [Col. 0633C] its walls utterly leveled to the ground. Proceeding from there, we came to the nearby castle called Guespia. Finding it deserted, the count ordered it destroyed and burned. From there the count advanced farther, in order to besiege Saint-Antonin. The count of Toulouse had granted that castle to a certain knight, a thoroughly wicked and perverse man.

As we were proceeding to that castle, the bishop of Albi had gone ahead of us and come to the aforesaid castle, intending to offer peace and to warn the said knight to surrender it to our count. But he, being exceedingly arrogant, replied with great indignation: “Let the count of Montfort know that *burdonarii* will never [Col. 0633D] be able to take my castle.” He called the pilgrims *burdonarii* because they customarily carried staffs, which in the common language we call *burdones*. Hearing this, the count hastened to besiege the aforesaid castle.

One Sunday, in the octave of Pentecost, we came to the castle of Saint-Antonin to besiege it and pitched our tents on one side of the castle before its gates. This most noble castle lay in a certain valley, at the foot of a mountain, in a most pleasant place. Between the mountain and the castle, close to the castle walls, clear water flowed. On the other side of the castle was an agreeable plain, and we besiegers occupied that side. The opponents came out of the castle and throughout the day began to harass our men with arrows from afar. As evening [Col. 0634A] drew on, the enemies came out of the castle, advanced somewhat, and attacked our men from a distance, shooting their arrows as far as the tents.

When the army’s sergeants saw this and could no longer endure it because of the disgrace, they attacked the opponents and began to drive them back into their castle. What more need be said? A shout arose in the army. Poor and unarmed pilgrims ran forward and, without the knowledge or counsel of our count himself or the army’s knights, began to assault the castle. They attacked the opponents with such great, incredible, and wholly unheard-of valor that, by their uninterrupted throwing of stones, instilling both fear and astonishment in them, within the space of one hour they took from them three very strong barbicans. O battle, as it were, without iron! O glorious [Col. 0634B] victory! For I call God as witness that, after the castle’s surrender, I entered the castle itself and saw the walls of its houses, as though gnawed away by the blows of the stones cast by our pilgrims.

When those in the castle saw that they had lost the barbicans, they left the castle by another side and began to flee through the water. Seeing this, our pilgrims crossed that water and put to the sword all whom they could seize. Having captured the barbicans, our pilgrims withdrew from the assault, for day was already declining and night was approaching. About midnight the lord of the castle, seeing that, with the barbicans lost, the castle was virtually taken, sent to our count, as though ready to surrender the castle provided that he himself might escape. [Col. 0634C] When the count rejected this condition of surrender, the lord of the castle again sent to him, placing himself wholly at his will.

At first light the count ordered everyone brought out of the castle. Having taken counsel with his men, he judged that, if he had the inhabitants—being simple people and peasants—killed, the castle would be reduced to desolation once its inhabitants had been destroyed. The count therefore adopted the sounder counsel and dismissed the people. But he ordered the lord of the castle, who had been the cause of all this evil, confined in the depths of the prison at Carcassonne, where he was held under guard and in chains for many days. The count also had the few knights who were with him committed to prison.

## CHAPTER LXIII. Summoned by the bishop of Agen, the count goes and receives the city.

[Col. 0634D]

At that time the bishops of Uzès and Toulouse, and the bishop of Carcassonne, who never left the army, were in the army. Having taken counsel with them, the count and his knights agreed that the count should direct his army toward the territory of Agen. For the bishop of Agen had long before sent word to our count that, if he transferred himself to the region of Agen, he and his kinsmen, who were powerful in that land, would assist him to the best of their ability.

Agen was a noble city, situated in a most pleasant place between Toulouse and Bordeaux. From ancient times that city with its territory had belonged to the king of England. [Col. 0635A] But King Richard, when he gave his sister Joan in marriage to Raymond, count of Toulouse, gave the aforesaid city with its territory to the count of Toulouse as his sister’s marriage portion. The lord pope had also commanded our count to attack, with the help of the crusaders, all heretics as well as the supporters of heretics.

Thus, setting out from the castle of Saint-Antonin, we marched directly to a castle of the count of Toulouse called Montcuq. Nor should it be omitted that the count had the fortifications through which we passed—fortifications abandoned by their inhabitants out of fear of our men, and from which some harm might arise to Christendom—utterly demolished or burned. Moreover, at that time a certain noble castle near Saint-Antonin, called Caslution [Caslutium], [Col. 0635B] which the count of Toulouse held, was surrendered to our count through the agency of a noble and faithful man, Count Baldwin. Our count had previously possessed that castle, but in the preceding year the inhabitants had withdrawn from him and surrendered it to the count of Toulouse. When the inhabitants of the hill-castle heard that our men were then coming, all fled in fear, leaving the castle empty. It was a noble castle, situated in an excellent and very strong position. Our count gave it to the aforesaid Count Baldwin, brother of the count of Toulouse.

Proceeding from there, we came within about two leagues of a certain castle in the territory of Agen called Penne. [Col. 0635C] The count of Toulouse had entrusted it to a certain knight, his seneschal, called Hugh d’Alfar, a Navarrese. Moreover, he had given him in marriage his own daughter, born outside lawful wedlock. Hearing that the count of Montfort was coming, the knight assembled about four hundred of his well-armed and very strongly equipped *ruptarii* [mercenary raiders]. He drove all the inhabitants of the castle, from the least to the greatest, out of it. He himself withdrew with his *ruptarii* into the fortress, amply supplied it with provisions and everything apparently necessary for defense, and made ready to resist.

When our count heard this, he resolved to besiege it. But, having taken counsel with his men, he first wished to go to Agen, so as to receive [Col. 0635D] the city into his power. Taking with him such knights from the army as he chose, he went to Agen, while the army remained where it was and awaited his return. When he reached Agen, he was honorably received. The citizens moreover, establishing him as their lord and having sworn an oath of fidelity, surrendered the city to him. Once all this had been duly done, the count returned to the army to besiege the castle of Penne.

In the year of the Lord 1212, on the third day before the Nones of June [3 June], a Sunday, we came to destroy the castle of Penne, intending, with the Lord’s help, to besiege it. Hugh d’Alfar, the guardian of the castle, of whom we have spoken above, saw the army of the crusaders approaching, withdrew himself and his *ruptarii* into the castle fortress, and set fire throughout the entire lower borough. The castle of Penne was a most noble one in the territory of Agen. [Col. 0636A] Situated pleasantly upon a certain hill, it was surrounded on every side by very broad and fertile valleys. The castle was adorned on one side by the richness of its lands, on another by the lovely expanse of its meadows; on one side by the delightful beauty of its woods, on another by the cheering fertility of its vineyards. The wished-for healthfulness of the air smiled upon it, as did the rich pleasantness of its surrounding streams. The fortress itself, founded upon a great natural rock and defended by very strong walls, appeared almost impregnable.

King Richard of England, to whom, as we have said, the castle of Penne had belonged, had fortified this stronghold very strongly and had had a well dug within it, because this castle was, as it were, the head and [Col. 0636B] key of the whole territory of Agen. The aforesaid count—that is, Hugh, to whom the count of Toulouse had given that castle—had so stocked the fortress with chosen warriors and small provisions, and moreover with siege-engines called stone-throwers, timber, iron, and all things needed for its defense, that no one could believe that the said fortress could be taken in the course of many years. Finally, he had established inside the aforesaid fortress two workshops of smiths, an oven, and a mill. Thus protected by manifold defenses, he awaited the siege almost without fear.

When our men came before the castle, they pitched their tents all around it. During the pitching of the tents, some came out of the castle [Col. 0636C] and began fiercely to harass our men with arrows. After several days our men set up stone-throwing engines inside the borough which had been burned, to cast against the fortress. Seeing this, those in the castle set up stone-throwers of their own to disturb and impede ours. Throwing large and very frequent stones, they harassed our men considerably. After this, our men erected more stone-throwers. Yet, though our machines continuously cast stones and broke the houses within the fortress, they weakened the fortress walls little or not at all. It was summer and extremely hot weather, around the feast of Saint John the Baptist.

We also think it should not be passed over that our count had few knights, though he had many pilgrim foot-soldiers. [Col. 0636D] Thus, whenever our men approached the fortress for purposes of assault, the opponents, because they were fortified and trained for battle, defended themselves bravely, and our men could make little or no progress. One day, when our men were attacking the aforesaid fortress, they captured by force a wooden barricade near the wall. But the opponents, throwing a very frequent shower of stones down from above the wall, immediately drove our men back from the barricade they had taken. When our men withdrew farther inward, the opponents came out and, in the heat of day, attempted to burn our engines, bringing with them fire, straw, and other materials needed to kindle a blaze. But our men resisted bravely, so that they could not only not burn our stone-throwers but could not even approach [Col. 0637A] them.

The opponents did not come out against our men on that day alone; they came out many times and harassed our men as far as they could. In that siege was the venerable bishop of Carcassonne, whom we have often mentioned, and I was with him. In the army of the Lord, by the command of the archbishop of Narbonne—formerly abbot of Cîteaux and, as stated above, legate—he acted in the legate’s stead. With unwearied fervor of spirit and incredible bodily labor, he diligently exercised the office of preaching and performed the other duties belonging to the siege. To put it briefly, we were so oppressed by the great and unbearable weight of cares continually succeeding one another that we scarcely had time to eat or even briefly rest.

Nor should it be omitted [Col. 0637B] that, while the count was at the siege of Penne, all the nobles of that land came to him and, doing him homage, received their lands from him.

While matters stood thus, Guy of Montfort, brother of our count; Robert, archbishop of Rouen; Robert, bishop-elect of Laon; William, archdeacon of Paris; Enguerrand of Boves, to whom our count had long before granted a portion of the count of Foix’s land; and many other pilgrims had left Carcassonne, crossed into the land of Foix, and come to a certain castle called Anclanet. They immediately captured it by assault and force and killed the enemies within it. When those in neighboring castles heard this, [Col. 0637C] they set fire to their castles and fled from our men. Our men, moving through those castles, utterly demolished them.

Then, proceeding toward Toulouse, they destroyed completely many very strong castles that had been left deserted. After they captured Anclanet, they found no one who dared await them in any castle, however strong. Great fear had indeed fallen upon all the inhabitants of that land. While our aforesaid men were acting so bravely, our count sent them word to come to him at Penne. For nearly all the pilgrims with him, having completed their forty days in the army, wished to return home. The aforesaid men therefore hurried to the count.

One day they came [Col. 0637D] to a very strong castle called Penne in the Albigeois. That castle still resisted Christendom and the count, and was always full of *ruptarii*. When the aforesaid pilgrims came before it, the *ruptarii* in the castle came out against our men and killed one of our knights. But our men did not wish to delay long over capturing the castle, because our count was urgently summoning them. They destroyed the crops and vineyards around the castle and hurried away to the count. After our men, who had been there for several days, departed, those in the castle came to the place where our men had buried the knight who had been killed. They pulled his body from the grave, dragged it through the streets, and exposed it to beasts and birds. O [Col. 0638A] wicked frenzy! O unheard-of cruelty!

When the aforesaid pilgrims reached the count, who was besieging Penne, he received them with immense joy. They immediately divided their forces around the place and pitched their tents near the castle. The count with his knights besieged the castle on the western side, for our engines had been set up there. Guy, the count’s brother, pitched his tents on the other side, namely the eastern side, set up an engine there, and likewise began vigorously to assault the castle. What more need be said? More engines were set up; our men pressed the attack on the castle. There were nine engines erected around the circuit of the castle. Since we cannot recount individually everything done in that siege, let us come to [Col. 0638B] the principal events.

Our count, seeing that our engines could not bring down the wall of the castle, had another engine made, far larger than all the rest. While that engine was being prepared, the archbishop of Rouen, the bishop-elect of Laon, and the others who were with them wished to depart, their forty days’ service having been completed. Indeed, every day pilgrims whose forty days were complete departed, while none, or very few, arrived. Our count therefore, knowing that he was being left almost alone and placed in great distress, approached the leading men of the army and begged them not to abandon Christ’s cause in so great a necessity, but to remain yet for a little while. It was said that a great multitude of pilgrims coming from France was at Carcassonne, and this was indeed so. Nor should it be omitted that the provost of Cologne and all the Germans—many and noble men, who had come with and after him—had already left the army.

When the bishop-elect of Laon heard the count’s entreaties, he did not heed them; rather, alleging some illness, he could by no means be detained. Nearly all the others acted likewise. Only the archbishop of Rouen, who had conducted himself praiseworthily in God’s service, keeping at his own expense very many knights and an exceedingly large household, graciously agreed with the count; and he remained with him until, when new pilgrims had arrived, he returned with honour to his own country, by the count’s leave and wish. When therefore the bishop of Laon and a great part of the army had departed, the venerable archdeacon William, a man of great steadfastness and remarkable worth, began to labour most earnestly in matters concerning the siege. The bishop of Carcassonne, however, had gone to Carcassonne on certain business.

Meanwhile, that great engine mentioned above was being prepared. When it was ready, the said archdeacon had it erected on one side near the castle. This engine, being great and hurling great stones, began gradually to weaken the castle wall. After several days the pilgrims mentioned above arrived: namely, the abbot of Saint-Remi at Rheims, a certain abbot of Soissons, the dean of Auxerre, who later died there, and the archdeacon of Châlons—great and learned men—together with many pilgrim knights and foot-soldiers. When they had come, the venerable bishop of Rouen, departing from the army with the count’s goodwill and favour, returned home. Those who had newly arrived, however, began vigorously to labour in attacking the castle.

One day our adversaries drove from the castle the poor people and women whom they had with them, exposing them to death lest they consume their provisions. Our count did not wish those expelled to be killed, but drove them back into the castle. O nobility of a prince! He disdained to kill those whom he had not captured, nor did he believe that he would gain glory from the death of persons whose capture had brought him no victory.

Accordingly, after our engines had long hurled missiles within the fortification and shattered all the houses and shelters in it, and after the great newly erected engine had begun further to weaken the very wall of the fortification, those in the castle saw that they could not hold out long. They also saw that, if the castle were taken by force, all would be given to the sword; and, moreover, that they would receive no aid from the count of Toulouse. They therefore attempted to make terms with our men, as follows: they were to surrender the castle to our count, provided that they themselves might escape with their arms. Hearing this, the count took counsel with his men whether he should accept the terms offered by the adversaries.

Our men considered that nearly all the pilgrims were about to depart, their forty days’ service having been completed, and that the count would remain there almost alone. They also considered that those in the castle could still resist for many days, that the count had many other great and necessary matters to undertake, and that winter was approaching, during which he could not maintain a siege.

Having weighed all these considerations, they advised the count to accept the terms offered by the adversaries. Thus, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1212, in July, on the feast of Saint James, the adversaries having been expelled, the count received the noble castle of Penne. On the following day there arrived the venerable Alberic, archbishop of Rheims, a man of great goodness, who embraced the cause of Jesus Christ with most devoted affection. With him came the cantor of Rheims and certain other pilgrims.

We do not think it should be suppressed that, while our count was besieging Penne, he asked Robert Mauvoisin to go to a very noble town called Marmande, which had belonged to the count of Toulouse, to take it on behalf of our count and hold it. This most noble man, though suffering from a most severe illness, did not complain of the labour or plead debilitating sickness, but readily and generously consented. He was the man upon whose especially prudent foresight and most salutary counsel the count—and indeed the whole cause of Jesus Christ—depended.

When Robert came to the aforesaid town, he was honourably received by the burgesses. But certain servants of the count of Toulouse, who were guarding the castle’s fortification, refused to surrender and began to resist and defend the fortification. Seeing this, Robert, that valiant man, immediately had a mangonel erected before it. When it had hurled several stones, the said servants surrendered the fortification. Robert remained in that town for several days and then returned to the count at Penne.

After the castle of Penne had been taken and fortified, our count proposed to besiege a nearby castle called Biron. The count of Toulouse had given that castle to a traitor named Martin Algais. For, as we said above, he had once been with our count, but later departed from him after committing treachery. Remaining in the aforesaid castle, he chose to await the arrival of our men there—a course whose outcome showed the just judgment of God.

Our men therefore came before the castle and besieged it. Then, after an assault, through many labours and feats of remarkable courage, they climbed the walls and took the town by force. The adversaries immediately withdrew into the fortification. Seeing that they could not resist, they sought peace, prepared to surrender the fortification provided they themselves might escape alive. The count was wholly unwilling to grant this. Yet, fearing that the said traitor, Martin Algais, for whose capture he had chiefly besieged the castle, might secretly escape, the count offered the adversaries this: if they delivered that traitor into his hands, he would free them from the peril of imminent death.

On hearing this, they ran most eagerly, seized Martin, and handed him over to the count. Seizing him, the count offered him confession, as that Catholic man was accustomed to do for others condemned to death. Then he had him tied to a horse’s tail and dragged through the army; after he had been dragged, he was, as his merits deserved, hanged from the gallows.

There came to him there a certain noble prince of Gascony, Gaston of Béarn, a most wicked man who had always adhered to the count of Toulouse, intending to negotiate terms. But because they could not reach an agreement that day, our count appointed him another day at Agen. Yet he, an enemy of peace, withdrawing from the proposed agreement, refused to come on that day.

While this was taking place, the noble countess of Montfort, the venerable bishop of Carcassonne, and I with him were hastening from the region of Carcassonne to the count, having with us a few poor people and pilgrims.

Nor should it be omitted that, as we travelled, many of our pilgrims collapsed on the way because of the intense heat and the difficulty of the road. The venerable bishop of Carcassonne and the noble countess, pitying their suffering, carried them behind themselves on their horses throughout the day. Sometimes each of them—the bishop and the countess—had two pilgrims mounted on his or her horse, while they themselves travelled on foot. O pious compassion of the bishop! O noble humility of the countess!

When we came to Cahors while hastening to the count, we were told that nearby there were castles in which routiers and enemies of the faith were staying. As we approached the castles, though we were very few, by the marvellous working of divine mercy the terrified enemies fled before us and left several very strong castles empty. After we had destroyed them, we came to the count at Penne.

After all this had been duly accomplished, the noble count, having taken counsel with his men, proposed to besiege a castle called Moissac, which was under the power of the count of Toulouse. Thus, arriving at the castle on the vigil of the Assumption of Blessed Mary, we besieged it.

The castle of Moissac was situated at the foot of a mountain on a plain near the river Tarn, in a place very fertile and pleasant. It is called Moissac from *moys*, meaning “water,” because it abounds within in very sweet springs. When the inhabitants of the castle heard that our men were approaching, they summoned very many routiers and men of Toulouse, so that with their aid they might resist us. These routiers were perverse and utterly wicked men. For, although that castle had long before been placed under interdict by the legates of the lord pope because it favoured heretics and attacked the Church alongside the count of Toulouse, the said routiers, in contempt of God and of us, had the bells of the church—which was noble and exceedingly large—rung festively every day, at every hour. King Pippin of France had founded in that castle a monastery of a thousand monks.

After a few days the count had engines prepared and erected near the castle; hurling missiles, they began somewhat to weaken the wall. The adversaries also erected their own engines and had them hurl against ours. The venerable men who were leaders and masters of this undertaking—namely, the bishop of Carcassonne and William, archdeacon of Paris—laboured most earnestly in matters necessary to the siege. The archbishop of Rheims, who was there, was also very necessary to the cause of Jesus Christ: he most often and willingly ministered preaching and exhortation to the pilgrims, humbly devoted himself to whatever the siege required, and spent his own resources generously.

One day the adversaries came out from the castle and began advancing to damage our engines. But our count and some of our armed men ran forward and drove the enemy back into their fortification. In that clash, one of the adversaries, aiming an arrow, wounded our count in the foot. They also captured a young man of ours, a nephew of the archbishop of Rheims, and dragged him away; after killing and shamefully mutilating him, they threw him back to us. The venerable archbishop, uncle of the slain youth, though he loved him with special affection, nevertheless endured his nephew’s death with equanimity for the service of Jesus Christ, and, concealing his grief with great strength of spirit, displayed to all in the army an example of extraordinary patience and magnanimity.

Nor should it be omitted that, at the beginning of this siege, because the fewness of the pilgrims prevented us from besieging the castle on every side, the adversaries daily came out of the castle and, passing over the mountain that overlooked it, insolently harassed the army. Our pilgrims climbed up to them and fought against them there throughout the day. Whenever the adversaries killed one of our pilgrims, they surrounded the body in contempt of our men and each thrust his sword into it. Such was their cruelty that it was not enough for them to see one of ours slain: adding fresh wounds, every one of the enemies pierced the dead man’s body with his sword. O contemptible combat! O rage of the wicked!

While this was happening, pilgrims began to arrive from France day by day. Bishop Reginald of Toul also arrived one day with other pilgrims. As the multitude of pilgrims grew, they occupied the said mountain, and, as pilgrims continued gradually to arrive, they besieged the castle almost on every side, as they had formerly been accustomed to do.

Nor should it pass without notice that, before the castle was surrounded on every side, the adversaries came out of the castle and climbed the mountain. Whenever they saw the bishop of Carcassonne delivering an exhortatory sermon to the people, they shot arrows from crossbows into the crowd listening to the sermon; but by God’s grace they could harm no one. Since we cannot describe at length everything done there, let us proceed to the principal matters.

After our engines had long hurled missiles and weakened the castle walls, the count had a certain machine made which the vernacular calls a *Cat*. When it had been made, the count ordered it drawn to the castle ditch, which was extremely broad, deep, and full of water. The adversaries had made certain wooden barricades outside the ditch, and beyond those barricades another ditch. They stayed continually between the two ditches, frequently coming out from there to harass our men.

Meanwhile, our said machine was drawn to the ditch. It was covered with fresh oxhides so that the enemy could not burn it. The adversaries, however, kept firing a stone-throwing engine at it in order to destroy it. While the aforesaid machine was over the first ditch, and nothing remained except for our men to fill the ditch itself under its protection, one day after sunset the adversaries came out of the castle. Bringing fire, dry wood, straw, tow, salted meat, fat, oil, and other inflammable materials, they began most vigorously to throw them down in order to burn our machine. They had crossbowmen besides, who severely wounded our men defending the machine.

What more need be said? The flame rose higher, and we were all thrown into confusion. The count and his brother Guy were within the machine.

As the adversaries tirelessly threw materials needed for the fire, our men, with the utmost constancy and much labour, threw wine, water, and earth upon the blaze. Others used iron implements to draw from the fire the pieces of meat and vessels full of oil which the adversaries threw down. Thus, amid unbelievable suffering from heat and exertion—something that could scarcely be witnessed without tears—our men rescued the aforesaid machine from the fire.

On the following day our pilgrims armed themselves and advanced upon the castle on every side. Boldly entering the first ditch, through much labour and most steadfast courage they broke down the wooden barricades. The adversaries who were between the barricades and in the barbicans defended the barbicans as best they could. During this assault, the bishop of Carcassonne and I ran about through the army exhorting our men.

The archbishops of Rheims and Toul, the bishop of Albi, William archdeacon of Paris, the abbot of Moissac with certain monks, and the rest of the army’s clergy stood on the slope of the mountain before the castle, clothed in white garments and barefoot, holding the cross before them with relics of saints. In voices most loud and devout they sang, “Come, Creator Spirit,” imploring divine aid. Nor did the Paraclete fail those who prayed. As soon as they began for the third time to repeat the verse of the hymn, namely, “Drive the enemy far away,” the adversaries, divinely terrified and repulsed, abandoned the barbicans, fled into the castle, and shut themselves within the circuit of the walls.

Meanwhile, the burgesses of a nearby castle of the count of Toulouse called Château-Sarrasin came to our count and surrendered that castle to him. The count also sent his brother Guy, Count Baldwin, brother of the count of Toulouse, and other knights to another noble castle belonging to the count of Toulouse, called Verdun, situated on the river Garonne five leagues from Toulouse. The inhabitants of that castle surrendered themselves to our count without any condition. Likewise, all the surrounding castles surrendered, except one called Montauban.

When the burgesses of Moissac heard that the surrounding castles had surrendered to our count, and saw also that they could not resist, they sent to the count seeking peace. The count considered that the place was still sufficiently strong and could not be taken by force without great slaughter among our men. He also considered that, if it were taken by force, the town—which was excellent and belonged to the monks—would be destroyed, and that everyone in the castle would perish together. He said that he would receive them on this condition: that they hand over to him those routiers and all who had come from Toulouse for the defence of the castle’s fortification, and that they further swear upon the most holy Gospels never again to attack Christians.

When these matters had been duly carried out and the routiers and men of Toulouse delivered up, the count received the castle and restored it to the abbot, preserving whatever rights the counts of Toulouse had lawfully held in it. Our pilgrims, taking the routiers, killed them with great eagerness.

Nor do we think it should be omitted that the castle of Moissac, besieged on the vigil of the Assumption of Blessed Mary, was taken on the feast of the Nativity of that same Virgin. Thus the working of the Blessed Virgin is acknowledged.

Departing from Moissac, the count proposed to besiege a castle near Foix named Saverdun, in the diocese of Toulouse. That castle had withdrawn from the lordship of our count, and the count of Foix, who held it, used it as a base from which greatly to harass the castle of Pamiers.

Meanwhile certain noble German pilgrims had arrived at Carcassonne. Our count had granted Enguerrand de Boves, mentioned above, a great part of the land of the count of Foix. Other knights of ours guarding the territory of Carcassonne led the said Germans to Pamiers. The count of Toulouse and the count of Foix were at Saverdun. When our knights set out with the Germans and hastened toward Saverdun, the count of Toulouse and the count of Foix fled from it. Thus Enguerrand recovered Saverdun without terms or battle.

While this was happening, our count was coming from Moissac with his army. When he was near Saverdun, he went to Pamiers, where the Germans were, while the army proceeded to Saverdun. Taking the Germans, the count rode before the castle of Foix, then returned to the army, which had left Saverdun and gone to Auterive. The people of Auterive had fled before them and left the castle empty. The count fortified Auterive, since by means of it he could restrain his enemies; for it lay between Toulouse and Foix.

After these events, the count proposed to invade the land of the count of Comminges. He came to a castle near Toulouse called Muret, a most pleasant castle situated on the river Garonne. As we approached the castle of Muret, its inhabitants, fearing us, fled and entered Toulouse. Some of them also set fire to the bridge of the castle, a very long wooden bridge over the Garonne by which we had to cross.

When we came before the castle and could not enter it because the bridge had been burned, the count and many of our men threw themselves into the water, which was deep and swift, and crossed at no small risk. The army pitched its tents on this side of the river. The count at once ran with some of his men to the bridge and, with much labour, extinguished the fire. Immediately such an abundance of rainwater burst forth, and the aforesaid river rose so greatly, that no one could cross it without grave peril to life.

When evening came, the noble count saw that nearly all the knights and stronger members of the army had crossed the water and entered the castle, while the foot-soldiers and weaker men, unable to cross, remained on this side of the river. He called his marshal and said: “I wish to return to the army.”

The marshal replied: “What are you saying? The whole strength of the army is in this castle; beyond the river there are only pilgrim foot-soldiers. Moreover, the river is so great and swift that no one could cross it now. Besides, the men of Toulouse may come and kill both you and all the pilgrims.”

The count answered the marshal: “Far be it from me to do what you advise! Christ’s poor are exposed to the sword, while I remain in a fortification! Let the Lord’s will be done with me. Certainly I shall go and remain with them.”

At once he left the castle, crossed the water, returned to the army of foot-soldiers, and remained there with very few men—namely four or five knights—for several days, until a bridge was made and the whole army crossed. O great valour of a prince! O unconquered courage! He would not remain with the knights in the castle while the poor pilgrims were exposed in the field.

## Chapter LXIV. The Count of Montfort occupies Saint-Gaudens and harasses Toulouse in every way. Count Raymond takes refuge with the king of Aragon in order to obtain his assistance.

While our count remained in the castle of Muret, the bishops of Comminges and Couserans came to him, venerable men full of God, who loved the cause of Jesus Christ with undivided devotion and advanced it by active service. By their counsel and efforts the count had also entered those regions. They urged him, therefore, to advance farther and receive, without battle or bloodshed, the greater part of Gascony.

The count hastened to a castle called Saint-Gaudens, which had belonged to the count of Comminges. The inhabitants of the castle surrendered it to him and received him joyfully. The nobles of that district also came to him; doing him homage, they received their lands from him. Furthermore, penetrating the mountain country near Foix, he devastated for the most part the land of Roger of Comminges, nephew of the count of Foix.

Meanwhile the bishop of Carcassonne, who had remained with some pilgrims at the castle of Muret, laboured continually over the fortification of that castle. When our count had completed in Gascony the business for which he had gone, he returned to Muret. He had no pilgrim knights except the count of Toul and a very few other knights; yet, though he was with few men, he frequently rode as far as the gates of Toulouse. Those in Toulouse, countless and very strongly fortified though they were, did not dare to come out against him. He devastated everything around them and destroyed fortifications before their eyes.

Toulouse was extraordinarily full of people, for the heretics and supporters of heresy and routiers of Béziers, Carcassonne, and Toulouse, having lost their lands by divine judgment, had entered Toulouse and filled it so completely that, after expelling the canons, they made the cloisters of the city’s monks into sheepfolds and stables for horses. O Toulouse, nest of heretics! O dwellings of robbers!

Nor should it be passed over how Toulouse was at that time afflicted and besieged. Our count was on one side at Muret; some of our knights were on another side at Verdun; Count Baldwin on another; and Guy, the count’s brother, on yet another. All of these surrounded Toulouse from every side, often riding up almost to its gates and grievously harassing it.

The count of Toulouse, who, compelled by his sins, had been disinherited and had lost his land except for Toulouse and Montauban, had fled to the king of Aragon to seek counsel and assistance from him in recovering his land. O just judgment of God, the most just Judge! O true pronouncement of the most merciful brother P. of Castelnau! For that good man used to say—as I heard from those who had often heard it from his own mouth—“The cause of Jesus Christ in these regions will never attain a prosperous outcome until one of us preachers dies in defence of the faith; and would that I might be the first to receive the persecutor’s sword!”

Behold, that wretched count of Toulouse, after he had inflicted death on this most holy man because the good man publicly rebuked him to his face for the wicked deeds he had committed, believed afterwards that he had escaped and that he would recover his land. But as the Lord exacted vengeance and avenged the blood of His martyr, from the very thing in which he expected profit, he received not merely the gravest loss but irreparable ruin.

It should also be carefully noted that this wretched count received the murderer of the man of God with the greatest affection and familiarity, to such an extent that, leading him through cities and castles as though displaying him to all, he said: “This man alone loves me; this man alone most agrees with my wishes; he delivered me from my enemy.” Yet although the aforesaid count thus exalted that most cruel murderer, even dumb animals abhorred him.

For, according to the truthful report of many worthy men, canons of the Church of Toulouse, from the day on which the aforesaid murderer killed the remembered man of God, no dog ever deigned, in detestation of so great a crime, to take anything from his hand. O marvellous thing! O unheard-of thing! We have inserted this in order to show how justly the count of Toulouse was disinherited.

While matters stood as described above, Roger, son of Bernard, count of Foix, was passing near Carcassonne with routiers. One day he rode toward Narbonne, intending, if he found any pilgrims, to lead them bound to Foix or condemn them to a most cruel death. As he went, he encountered a few pilgrims travelling from the French regions toward our count. Seeing the enemies coming and thinking that they were our men, those pilgrims fearlessly went to meet the adversaries.

> **[Note: Col. 0647D]** It is also reported as certain that some of them wore the habit of Cistercian monks over their armour and went ahead of the others. — This is found in the margin of the manuscript.

The aforesaid traitors took this precaution in their wickedness: they walked at a slow pace and along the public road, so that it would not be easy to notice that they were not our men. But when they drew near one another, those most cruel executioners immediately rose against our men, who were few and unarmed, being unaware of the treachery. They killed many of ours, tore them limb from limb, and led the rest with them as far as Foix. There, holding them in chains, they mangled them with most severe tortures, zealously devising every day new and unheard-of punishments by which to torment their captives.

For, as I heard from the mouth of one of our knights who was held there in chains, who was present and saw it, they tortured their prisoners with so many and such great torments that their wickedness might be compared with, or even preferred to, that of Diocletian and Maximian. To pass over the lesser things, they often hanged priests themselves and ministers of the divine mystery; sometimes also—horrible to tell!—they tied ropes to their genitals and savagely pulled them apart. O monstrous cruelty! O unheard-of fury!

## Chapter LXV. A gathering of bishops and barons is held at Pamiers by Count Simon, where many decrees and laws are established which the count promises to observe.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1212, in November, the noble count of Montfort summoned the bishops and nobles of his land to hold a general assembly at the castle of Pamiers. The purpose of this assembly was that, in the land which our count had acquired and subjected to the Holy Roman Church, good customs might be instituted; that the filth of heresy, which had corrupted that entire land, might be driven far away; and that good practices might be planted, both in the worship of the Christian religion and in temporal peace and tranquillity.

For that land had from ancient times lain open to plundering and robbery: the powerful oppressed the powerless, the stronger the weaker. Therefore the noble count wished to establish for all the lords of the land customs and fixed limits which they might not transgress, so that knights might live rightly from their fixed and lawful revenues and the lesser people might live under the protection of their lords, not burdened by excessive exactions.

Twelve men were chosen to establish these customs. They swore on the most holy Gospels that, to the best of their ability, they would establish such customs as would allow the Church to enjoy her freedom and would confirm the whole land in a better condition. Of these twelve electors, four were ecclesiastics: two bishops, of Toulouse and Couserans; one Templar; and one Hospitaller. There were further four French knights and four natives—two knights and two burgesses—by whom the said customs were established and confirmed in a sufficiently fitting manner.

In order that these customs might be observed inviolate, before they were publicly promulgated the noble count and all his knights swore upon the four Gospels that they would never presume to violate the aforesaid customs. So that they might obtain still greater force, they were put into writing and confirmed and secured by the seals of the count and of all the bishops, who were numerous there.

While this was being done at Pamiers, enemies of the faith came out from Toulouse, began ranging through Gascony, and committed every evil they could. The venerable bishop of Comminges, taking with him some of our knights, went into Gascony and courageously defended that land from the enemies of the faith.

Our noble count went to Carcassonne and thence to Béziers to confer with the archbishop of Narbonne concerning matters pertaining to the cause of Jesus Christ. While we were at Béziers and the episcopal see was vacant, the canons of that Church, by common assent, elected the venerable William, archdeacon of Paris, as their bishop and shepherd; but by no reasoning could he be induced to give his assent to their election.

## Chapter LXVI. The king of Aragon comes to Toulouse and holds a conference with Count Simon and the legate of the Apostolic See.

Around the feast of the Lord’s Epiphany, Peter, king of Aragon, who was greatly hostile to the cause of the faith, came to Toulouse. There he made knights while associating with excommunicated persons and heretics. The king sent word to the archbishop of Narbonne, legate of the Apostolic See, and to our count, that he wished to hold a conference with them and seek peace and an agreement between our count and the enemies of the faith.

Accordingly, by common agreement, a day and place were appointed between Toulouse and Lavaur for the conference. When we came to the place of counsel, the king began asking the archbishop of Narbonne and the bishops that the lands be restored to the counts of Toulouse, Comminges, and Foix, and to Gaston of Béarn. The archbishop of Narbonne replied to the king that he should put all his requests in writing and send them, written and sealed, to the bishops at Lavaur.

After giving our count, his brother, and his sons great marks of favour, King Peter of Aragon asked the count to refrain for eight days from doing harm to his enemies. That most noble and courteous man replied: “I shall not refrain from doing harm; but out of reverence for you, during these eight days I shall refrain from doing good.”

Likewise the king promised on behalf of our enemies that, during the time of the conference, they would not harm our men. But those utterly faithless persons, though they knew that our men had assembled for the conference and though the king had assured us of safety, began ranging through our land toward Carcassonne. Committing many evils, they also killed very many people. O wicked deceit!

On the third day after the king left the place of conference and entered Toulouse, he wrote his petitions to our archbishops and bishops, in these words:

**Petitions of the king of Aragon to the prelates gathered in council at Lavaur.**
Because the holy mother Church is taught to possess not only words but also lashes, P., by God’s mercy king of Aragon, a devoted son of the Church, desiring on behalf of the count of Toulouse that he return to the bosom of that same mother Church, humbly asks and earnestly begs Your Holiness that, after making personal satisfaction for whatever offences [Col. 0649B] he has committed, as may seem expedient to the Church herself, and after making satisfaction to the various churches and prelates for the damages and injuries inflicted—doing whatever the mercy of mother Church may judge fit to impose upon that count—he may mercifully and compassionately be restored to his possessions and to the other things which he has lost. But if perhaps the Church should be unwilling to hear his petition in the person of the count, he asks and begs the same thing for his son; provided nevertheless that the boy personally make satisfaction for the offences, either by going with knights to the Saracen frontier in aid of Christians, or to overseas regions, according as the Church shall judge most expedient; and that the child be kept in his own land, in such careful custody and faithful care, for the honour of God and of the Holy Roman Church, until manifest signs of his goodness [Col. 0649C] appear.

And since the count of Comminges neither was ever a heretic nor a receiver of heretics, but rather their opponent, and is said to have lost his land because he stood by his cousin and lord, the count of Toulouse, the same king asks and begs on his behalf, as for his vassal, that he be restored to his land, likewise making satisfaction at the Church’s discretion, should he be found to have offended in anything.

Likewise, since the count of Foix neither is nor has been a heretic, the aforesaid king asks and begs on his behalf, as for his dearest kinsman, whom he cannot without dishonour so fail in justice, that, out of respect and favour for himself, he be restored to what is his, nevertheless making satisfaction [Col. 0649D] to the Church in and for those matters in which he may be found to have offended against the mercy of mother Church.

Likewise, on behalf of Gaston of Béarn, his vassal, the aforesaid king earnestly asks and begs that he be restored to his land and to the fealties of his vassals, especially since he is prepared to obey and to make satisfaction at the Church’s discretion before judges not open to suspicion, if it is not permitted for us to hear and determine his case.

In all the foregoing matters, however, the aforesaid king has judged that mercy rather than judgment should be invoked, sending his clerics and barons to Your Clemency concerning the foregoing, and undertaking to ratify whatever you may arrange with them. He beseeches you [Col. 0650A] to deign to exercise such circumspection and diligence in this matter that, in the cause of Christendom in the regions of Spain, the aid of the aforesaid barons and of the count of Montfort may be available for the honour of God and the enlargement of holy mother Church.

Given at Toulouse, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February [16 January].

### Reply of the council

To the illustrious and beloved in Christ P., by God’s grace king of Aragon and count of Barcelona: the council assembled at Lavaur, greeting and sincere love in the Lord.

We have seen the petitions and prayers which your royal serenity [Col. 0650B] has sent on behalf of the counts of Toulouse, Foix, and Comminges, and of the nobleman Gaston of Béarn, and on behalf of the son of the count of Toulouse. In those letters you also call yourself, among other things, a devoted son of the Church. For this we give thanks to the Lord Jesus Christ and to your royal highness; and in all matters in which, according to God, we could do so, because of that mutual affection by which, as we understand, the holy Roman mother Church embraces you and you embrace her, and also out of reverence for your royal excellence, we would the more willingly admit your petitions.

Concerning what you ask and request for the count of Toulouse, we have judged this answer should be made to your royal serenity: both the case of the count and that of his son, which depends upon the deed of his father, have been removed from our jurisdiction by the authority of a superior, since the same count of Toulouse caused his case [Col. 0650C] to be committed by the lord pope, under a definite form, to the bishop of Riez and Master Theodisius. Therefore, as we believe, you remember well how many and how great favours the lord pope granted the said count after his many offences; and likewise what favour, at your intercession and prayer, the venerable archbishop of Narbonne, legate of the Apostolic See—then abbot of Cîteaux—granted that same count at Narbonne and Montpellier, two years ago, if we remember correctly. For the same legate wished all lordships and properties to remain whole and unimpaired to that count; and that the rights which he held in the castles of other heretics that were held from his fief should remain entire to him, without *alberga*, *quista*, or *cavalcata* [feudal hospitality, levy, or riding-service]. [Col. 0650D] Moreover, of those castles belonging to other heretics which were not held from his fief, and which the same count said numbered fifty, the aforesaid legate wished a quarter and a third part to fall into the ownership of the aforesaid count.

But the count despised that great favour of the lord pope, of the aforesaid legate, and of the Church of God. Acting directly contrary to all the oaths which he had formerly sworn into the hands of the legates, and adding iniquity to iniquity, crimes to crimes, evils to evils, he attacked and injured the Church of God and Christendom, faith and peace, together with heretics and *ruptarii* [brigands]. Thus he rendered himself unworthy of every grace and benefit.

As to what you request for the count of Comminges, we have judged that the following answer should be made. We have learned for certain [Col. 0651A] that, after his many offences and violation of his oath, he made an alliance with heretics and their supporters; and that, although he had never been harmed by the Church in any respect, he attacked that Church together with those same pestilent persons. Although he was afterwards carefully admonished to desist from what he had undertaken and, returning to his senses, at last to be reconciled to ecclesiastical unity, nevertheless that same count persisted in his wickedness, bound by the bond of excommunication and anathema. Indeed, as is said, the count of Toulouse was accustomed to assert that the count of Comminges himself urged and induced him to make war. Thus that count became the author of that war and of the evils which came in many ways upon the Church. Yet if he conducts himself in such a manner as to deserve [Col. 0651B] the benefit of absolution, then, after he has been absolved and is able to stand judgment, if he has a complaint concerning anything, the Church will not deny him justice.

Your royal highness further petitions for the count of Foix. To this we answer that it is established concerning him that for a long time he has been a harbourer of heretics—especially since there is no doubt that believers in heretics must be called heretics. After his many offences, after oaths sworn, after pledges of both persons and goods, after laying hands on clerics and casting them into prison—causes for which, and for many others, he was struck by the sword of anathema [Col. 0651C]—and after that favour which the same legate formerly showed the count at your intercession, he perpetrated a bloody slaughter of the Cross-bearers, both laymen and clerics, who in their poverty and simplicity were advancing in God’s service against the heretics of Lavaur. Your royal highness, we believe, remembers well what that favour was and how great it was, since at your request the said legate made an agreement with that count. But that agreement was not concluded solely because of the count himself. For letters addressed to the lord count of Montfort, bearing the royal seal, survive containing this clause:

> “We also tell you that, if the count of Foix should be unwilling to abide by that settlement, and if thereafter you do not heed our prayers on his behalf, we shall not on that account be displeased [Col. 0651D] with you.”

Yet if he takes pains to obtain the benefit of absolution, and thereafter, once he has obtained the grace of absolution, complains of anything, the Church will not deny him justice.

You further ask and request, on behalf of Gaston of Béarn, that he be restored to his land and to the fealties of his vassals. To this we answer as follows. To pass over in silence for the present the many—indeed, innumerable—things said against Gaston himself: allied with heretics and with their harbourers or defenders against the Church and the Cross-bearers, he is a most manifest [Col. 0652A] persecutor of churches and ecclesiastical persons. He came to assist the Toulousans at the siege of Castrinovi. He keeps with him the murderer of Brother Peter of Castelnau, legate of the Apostolic See; he long kept, and still keeps, brigands.

In the preceding year he brought brigands into the cathedral church of Oloron. There the rope from which hung the pyx containing the body of our Lord Jesus Christ was cut, so that it fell to the ground; and, dreadful to say, the Lord’s body itself was scattered upon the ground. He violated his oaths and laid violent hands upon clerics. For these and many other reasons, which we now pass over, the same Gaston is bound in the chains of excommunication and anathema. Yet if he makes satisfaction to the Church as he ought, obtains [Col. 0652B] the benefit of absolution, and has a complaint concerning something, he shall be heard regarding his right. Otherwise, most illustrious prince, it would not be fitting for your royal majesty to intercede for persons thus excommunicated; nor do we dare answer otherwise on behalf of, or in such matters concerning, such persons.

Moreover, we admonish and exhort your royal serenity in the Lord to deign to recall to mind the honour [Note: [Col. 0651D] For in 1204 Peter was invested at Rome with royal insignia by Innocent III; Ciaconius records a literary memorial of the ceremony, performed [Col. 0652D] with great pomp, in his account of that same Innocent.] which the Apostolic See has conferred upon you, and that which it now confers upon the illustrious king of Sicily, your brother-in-law; also what you promised the lord pope at your anointing, and what the Apostolic See commanded you. We pray that God may preserve you for many years to His honour and that of the Holy Roman Church. If, however, [Col. 0652C] your royal majesty has not been satisfied by our answer, then, out of regard and favour for you, we shall arrange for it to be communicated to the lord pope.

Given at Lavaur, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February [18 January].

When the king of Aragon heard the replies of our prelates, saw that the petitions he had made were wholly rejected, and that his purpose could not be brought to effect, he found another method of deception. Accordingly, he sent envoys to the prelates, commanding and requesting that they induce the count of Montfort to grant a truce to the count of Toulouse and the other enemies of the Christian faith until the next coming Pentecost, or at least until Easter. When our prelates heard this and observed that the king sought it for no other reason than that [Col. 0652D] it might be heard in France and thereby the devotion of the Cross-bearers might grow lukewarm, they rejected this petition, just as they had rejected the earlier ones.

Since it would take long to recount in sequence everything that that king demanded and that our men judged should be answered to him, let this be said briefly: the whole purpose of the said king was to labour for the restoration of the count of Toulouse and his other enemies of the Christian religion to their lands; or at least to obtain for them a truce from our side, for the reason mentioned above. Our men, however—prudent and steadfast men—would neither restore the lands nor grant a truce. Seeing that he could achieve nothing, to the serious injury alike of his reputation [Col. 0653A] and honour, the king undertook to receive under his protection the excommunicated persons and the lands which they still held. To cloak his wickedness somewhat, he appealed to the Apostolic See. Our prelates, however, did not yield to this appeal, because for many reasons it was frivolous and invalid. But the archbishop of Narbonne, legate of the Apostolic See, sent a letter in this form:

To the most illustrious lord PETER, by God’s grace king of Aragon: Brother A., by divine mercy archbishop of Narbonne and legate of the Apostolic See, greeting in the love of the heart and the bowels of Jesus Christ.

Not without great disturbance and bitterness of spirit have we learned that you propose to receive into your protection and custody, and to defend against Christ’s army, the city of Toulouse, the castle of Montauban, and the lands which, because of the crime of heresy [Col. 0653B] and many other wicked and abominable deeds, have been delivered to Satan, separated from every communion of mother Church, and exposed by God’s authority to the Cross-bearers—whose name is gravely blasphemed in these places. If, then, these reports are true—may God avert it!—they may bring harm not only to your salvation, but also to royal honour and to your reputation and fame. We, who with all the inward affection of charity are zealous for your salvation, glory, and honour, ask, counsel, admonish, and exhort your royal highness in the Lord; and, in the power of this strength and on behalf of God our Redeemer Jesus Christ and of His most holy [Col. 0653C] vicar, our lord the supreme pontiff, by the authority of the legation which we exercise, we forbid and beseech you by every means available to us not to receive or defend the aforesaid lands, whether by yourself or through others.
