We desire you to make such provision both for yourselves and for them that, by associating with excommunicated and accursed heretics and their supporters, you do not incur the stain of excommunication. We do not wish your royal serenity to be unaware of one thing: if you leave any of your men in defence of the aforesaid land, since they are all excommunicated by the law itself, we shall publicly declare you excommunicated as defenders of heretics.

The king of Aragon, repenting in no respect but carrying out [Col. 0653D] more wickedly what he had wickedly planned, received into his protection all heretics and excommunicated counts—namely, those of Toulouse, Comminges, and Foix—Gaston of Béarn, all the knights of Toulouse and Carcassonne who, disinherited for heresy, had fled to Toulouse, and also the citizens of Toulouse. He received an oath from them; and he presumed to receive into his custody the city of Toulouse itself, which properly belongs to the dominion of the king of France, and all the territory which they still held.

We do not think it should be omitted that, when our men were near the said conference at Lavaur and the count of Montfort, out of reverence for the king, had granted the enemy a truce during the days of the conference, while the king likewise had confirmed a truce on behalf of the opposing party, the truces still being in force during the conference [Col. 0654A] and our men taking no precautions, the enemy repeatedly rode through our land. Seizing much booty, killing many persons besides, carrying many off captive, they inflicted the gravest evils everywhere. Although our men repeatedly demanded redress from the king for these evils, he did nothing whatever to repair them.

Our men therefore saw that the king was delaying them with envoys, letters, and even superfluous appeals, while nevertheless allowing our people to be openly and repeatedly attacked during the time of the conference and truce by excommunicated men whose cause he supported. They departed from Lavaur. Before departing, however, they wrote to the lord pope concerning the common cause of the Church and the aforesaid conference in this form:

### Letter of the Synod of Lavaur to Lord Pope Innocent

[Col. 0654B]

To the most holy father in Christ and most blessed lord, INNOCENT, by God’s grace supreme pontiff: his devoted and humble servants, the archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of churches assembled at Lavaur for the cause of the holy faith, with every affection, wish a long span of life and salvation.

Since neither tongue nor pen suffices us to render thanks worthy of the care of your fatherhood, we beseech the rewarder of all good things to supply our deficiency in this respect and abundantly to repay you every good which you have bestowed upon us, our people, and the other churches of our regions. For in these regions the heretical plague, sown long ago, had grown among us to such a degree [Col. 0654C] that divine worship there was held wholly in reproach and derision; heretics and brigands ravaged the clergy and ecclesiastical goods; and prince and people alike, given over to a reprobate mind, departed from the right path of faith. But through your armies of Cross-bearers, whom you most wisely dispatched to cleanse away the filth of this plague, and through their most Christian leader, the count of Montfort, an altogether fearless champion and unconquered fighter in the Lord’s battle, the Church which had fallen there so miserably has begun to raise its head. In the greater part, all adversities and errors having been destroyed, the land formerly trampled by the adherents of these doctrines has at last become accustomed to divine worship.

There remain, however, remnants of the said plague: the city of Toulouse, namely, with certain castles, where, like filth running into a cesspool, the residue of heretical depravity has gathered. Their leader is the count of Toulouse, who from ancient times, as you have already heard many times, has been a supporter and defender of heretics. With the strength remaining to him he attacks the Church and, as far as he can, opposes its worshippers on behalf of the enemies of faith. Since he returned from the presence of Your Holiness with instructions in which you had dealt mercifully with him beyond all the measure of his deserts, the angel of Satan has plainly entered his heart. Ungrateful for the benefits of your favour, he has fulfilled none of the things he promised before you. Rather, he has greatly increased the tolls which he had repeatedly abjured, and has turned to everyone he knew to be an enemy of us and of the Church. [Col. 0655A]

Indeed, believing that through Otto, enemy of God and the Church, he would acquire strength against the Church itself, he openly threatened, as is asserted, under Otto’s protection, that he would extirpate the Church and clergy utterly from his territories. He began thereafter to protect and maintain more fervently than usual the heretics and brigands whom he had often abjured.

When the Catholic army besieged Lavaur, where was the seat of Satan and, as it were, the province of this heretical error, he sent knights and retainers to aid the perverse party. In his castle called Casser, more than fifty heretics were found and burned by the Cross-bearers, besides a very numerous multitude of their believers. [Col. 0655B] He also summoned against God’s army Savaric, an enemy of the Church and seneschal of the king of England. With him he presumed to besiege the aforesaid champion of Christ, the count of Montfort, at Castelnaudary; but through the working of Christ’s right hand his presumption was swiftly turned to confusion, so that a few Catholics put to flight an innumerable multitude of Arians at Castrumnovum Arii.

Frustrated in his reliance upon the aforesaid Otto and the king of England, like one leaning upon a reed-staff, he conceived an abominable iniquity and sent envoys to the king of Morocco, imploring his assistance for the destruction not only of our land but of all Christendom. But divine mercy prevented his attempt. [Col. 0655C] By expelling the bishop of Agen from his own see, he stripped him of all his goods; he captured the abbot of Moissac and held the abbot of Montauban captive for nearly a year. His brigands and accomplices also subjected innumerable clerical and lay pilgrims to various tortures; they still hold some captive and held others for a long time. In all these things his wrath has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out, so that each day he becomes worse than himself and perpetrates every evil he can against God’s Church through himself, his son, and his accomplices—the counts of Foix and Comminges and Gaston of Béarn, most criminal and perverse men.

When, however, by divine vengeance and ecclesiastical censure, the aforesaid champion of faith, the most Christian count, occupied in holy and just warfare almost all their lands as enemies of God and the Church, they nevertheless persisted in their malice, scorning to be humbled beneath the mighty hand of God (1 Peter 5). [Col. 0655D] They recently had recourse to the king of Aragon, through whom they perhaps intend to deceive Your Clemency and insult the Church. They brought him with us to Toulouse, while we had assembled at Lavaur by command of the legate and our delegates to hold a conference. From the rescripts which we send to you under seal, you will learn more fully what he proposed, of what sort it was, and what answers we judged should be made to him.

Therefore, unanimously and in agreement, we make known all the foregoing to Your Holiness, freeing our souls, lest anything that occurs in the cause of faith be omitted through failure to report it. For know with certainty that if the land taken from the said tyrants with such justice and with much shedding of Christian blood is restored to them or their heirs, not only would the last error become worse than the first (Matthew 27), but an inestimable destruction would thereby threaten the clergy and the Church. Since we do not think the abominable enormities and other crimes of the aforesaid persons should be set down individually in this present document, lest we appear to be composing a book, we have placed certain matters in the mouths of our envoys, which can be reported orally to your holy ears. [Col. 0656A]

The envoys who carried these letters to the lord pope were the following: the venerable bishop of Comminges; the abbot [Col. 0656B] of Clairac; William, archdeacon of Paris; Master Theodisius; and a certain cleric, who for a long time had been corrector of letters in the court of the lord pope and was called Peter Marci. Before these prudent and discreet men came to the papal court, the king of Aragon intended through his envoys to deceive apostolic simplicity. By a false representation and suppression of the truth, he had obtained letters in which the lord pope ordered the count of Montfort to restore their lands to the counts of Comminges and Foix and to Gaston of Béarn. He also wrote other letters to the archbishop of Narbonne in which the lord pope appeared to revoke the indulgence which he had granted to those proceeding against the Albigensian heretics.

When our envoys came to the Roman court, they found the lord pope somewhat stern, because he had been too credulous of the false representations made by the envoys of the king of Aragon. But afterwards, once the truth had been learned through our envoys, he annulled everything he had done in response to the king’s envoys’ representation, and sent the king himself a letter in these words:

### Letter of the lord pope to the king of Aragon, that he should not oppose the cause of the Church

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to PETER, illustrious king of Aragon.

May He in whose hand are the hearts of all kings (Ecclesiasticus 10), humbly invoked, inspire you so that, prudently considering that in accordance with the apostolic command [Col. 0656D] we must “rebuke, entreat, reprove” (2 Timothy 4), you may receive with filial devotion our rebukes, which we utter toward you with paternal affection. Thus obey our wholesome admonitions and counsels, and, by accepting apostolic correction, demonstrate both that you have had a sincere disposition in those matters in which you are known beyond doubt to have sinned in deed.

Certainly it has now come to the knowledge of almost the whole world—and we do not believe that your serenity either ignores or denies it—that among other Christian princes we have taken special care to honour you. By this both your power and your fame have increased; and would that prudence and devotion had increased together with them! Though this would have been pleasing to us, it would have been more advantageous to you. But in this you are known neither to have provided for yourself [Col. 0657A] nor to have shown us the deference that was fitting. For, since the citizens of Toulouse have been cut off like rotten limbs by the sword of excommunication and the city itself has been placed under interdict—because some of them are manifest heretics, while many more are their believers, supporters, harbourers, and defenders, so that others too, whom Christ’s army, or rather Christ Himself, has made to depart from their dwellings because they provoked Him by their contrivances, have fled to the city of Toulouse as to a kind of cesspool of error—you, forgetting the fear of God, as though you could prevail against the Lord or turn aside His hand, stretched out against them because of their sins, received them into your defence. Under the appearance of piety, you exercised impiety, to [Col. 0657B] the scandal of the Christian people and the harm of your own reputation.

Recently, after hearing what our venerable brother the bishop of Segovia, our beloved son Columbus, the envoys of your own side, and the envoys of our legates and of the count of Montfort wished to set forth in our presence, and after a more moderate understanding of the letters sent from both sides, and after careful discussion and counsel with our brethren, we wish with paternal care to provide for your honour as regards reputation, your salvation as regards soul, and your security as regards land. Therefore, in the power of the Holy Spirit and under protection of divine and apostolic grace, we enjoin upon your serenity that you abandon the aforesaid Toulousans, notwithstanding any promise or obligation made in evasion of ecclesiastical discipline, and that, so long as they remain such, you grant them no counsel, aid, or favour. [Col. 0657C]

But if they desire to return to the unity of the Church, as was proposed before us by your said envoys, we give instructions by our letters to our venerable brother F., bishop of Toulouse, a man of unimpaired reputation and life, who has testimony not only from those within but also from those outside: he is to associate with himself two others and reconcile to ecclesiastical unity those who wish to return with a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith (1 Timothy 1), after receiving from them sufficient security. Those, however, whom the same bishop identifies as persisting in the darkness of their error and stained by heretical depravity, he is to have expelled [Col. 0657D] from the said city and all their goods confiscated. They are never to be readmitted to it, unless perhaps, divinely inspired, they demonstrate themselves true Christians of the orthodox faith by the performance of good works. Thus, once the city itself has been reconciled and cleansed, it shall stand under the protection of the Apostolic See, not thereafter to be troubled by the aforesaid count or other Catholics, but rather defended and supported.

Furthermore, we are astonished and troubled that, concerning the lands of your nobles—the count of Foix, the count of Comminges, and Gaston of Béarn—to be restored to them, you caused an apostolic mandate to be fraudulently obtained through your envoys, who concealed the truth and presented falsehood. For, because of their many and grave crimes in support of heretics, whom they openly defend, [Col. 0658A] they are bound by the bond of excommunication. Since therefore a mandate so obtained for such persons has no force, we entirely revoke it as fraudulently procured.

But if, as they say, they desire reconciliation to ecclesiastical unity, we give instructions by our letters to our venerable brother, the archbishop of Narbonne, legate of the Apostolic See, that, after receiving from them not merely sworn security, since they have already violated their oaths, but also such other security as he considers expedient, he grant them the benefit of absolution. When these things have been duly accomplished as signs of true devotion, we shall take care to send into those regions a legate from our side, an honourable, prudent, and steadfast man, who, turning neither right nor left but proceeding on the royal road, shall always approve and confirm what he finds rightly done, correct and amend errors, and cause the full administration of justice to be given both to the aforesaid nobles and to other complainants. [Col. 0658B]

Meanwhile, we will and command that firm truces be made and kept between you and your land on the one hand and the aforesaid count of Montfort on the other. We nevertheless command the aforesaid count to render reverently, concerning the land which he holds from you, what he is bound to render. We do not wish your excellence to be ignorant that, if the Toulousans and the aforesaid nobles still choose to persist in their error, then by renewed indulgences we shall stir up the Cross-bearers and other faithful persons, trusting in divine aid, to extirpate this plague. They shall proceed in the name of the Lord of Hosts against those persons and against any other harbourers and defenders of them, who are more harmful than the heretics themselves. [Col. 0658C]

Therefore we admonish your serenity, ask and beseech you in the Lord to carry out with ready mind, so far as concerns you, what we have promised. Know certainly that if you should choose to act otherwise—which we do not believe—you could incur, besides the divine indignation which you would undoubtedly thereby call forth against yourself, grave and irreparable loss. However much we may love your person, we could neither spare nor defer to you against the cause of the Christian faith. For both ancient and recent examples can move you to consider how great the danger threatening you would be if you opposed yourself to God and [Col. 0658D] the Church, especially in a cause of faith, so as to impede the completion of the holy work.

Given at the Lateran, the twelfth day before the Kalends of June [21 May], in the sixteenth year of our pontificate.

After the council of prelates at Lavaur had concluded, the king of Aragon left Toulouse, having left in that city several of his knights for the city’s protection and the assistance of Christ’s enemies. A few days later he informed our count that he wished to hold a conference with him near Narbonne. Our count, wishing as far as he could according to God to show deference and obedience to the king as his lord, replied that he would gladly attend the [Col. 0659A] aforesaid conference. But the king did not come to the place of conference, nor had he ever intended to come. Instead, many men came, both Aragonese and Toulousan heretics and brigands, and it was feared that they would treacherously seize the count when he came to the conference with few men. The count learned what was being done and withdrew from the place of conference.

## Chapter LXVII. The king of Aragon declares war upon the count of Montfort through heralds.

After a few days, the aforesaid king sent messengers to the count bearing his letters, in which it was stated that the king renounced his allegiance to the count and threatened him as much as he could. Nevertheless, although the king had thus repudiated him with such pride, our count was unwilling to inflict any injury upon the king’s land, though day after day he endured many grave evils from him; for Catalan men entered our land and ravaged it as far as they could. After some days our count sent to the king Lambert of Turreio, a worthy and prudent knight, and through that knight asked the king whether he stood by the repudiation previously conveyed through the king’s messengers. He also informed him that the count had never committed any offence against him, but was ready to render him what was due.

Moreover, he offered that, if the king had a complaint against him concerning the lands of the heretics which he had acquired by command of the supreme pontiff and with the aid of the crusaders, he was prepared to submit to judgment in the court of the lord pope or in that of the lord archbishop of Narbonne, legate of the Apostolic See. He also gave the aforesaid knight certain letters, which he commanded him to present to the king if he found him resolved to persist in his obstinacy. The contents of the letters were as follows: the count wrote to the king without greeting, informing him that, since the king, after so many offers of justice and peace made to him, persisted in his repudiation and obstinacy, the count likewise renounced allegiance to him, declaring that henceforth he owed him no obligation of service, but would, with God’s help, defend himself against him and against the other enemies of the Church.

When the aforesaid knight came before the king, in the presence of him and many barons of his land, he carefully and prudently set forth in order all that the count had put into his mouth. [Col. 0659D] But the obstinate king rejected every means of peace and would not turn his mind away from his repudiation of the count. Immediately the aforesaid messenger presented to the king the count’s letters concerning the repudiation; they were read aloud in the common hearing of the king himself and his barons. When they had been read and more fully understood, the king and his men were turned to anger and fury.

After this, the messenger having been sent out from the royal court and carefully kept under guard, the king asked his men’s counsel concerning what he ought to do with him. Certain of his barons advised him to send to our count, commanding and ordering him to come to the king’s court and render to him, as his lord, what was due; if the count refused to come, they judged the messenger guilty of death. On the following day [Col. 0660A] the messenger came before the court and repeated more carefully what he had said the preceding day on the count’s behalf. He also boldly offered that, if any of the king’s knights wished to say that our count had wrongfully offended the king or had ever proved faithless to him, he was prepared in the king’s own court to defend his lord’s fidelity by judicial combat. Yet although no one dared challenge him, all cried out more harshly against him. At last, at the prayers of certain Aragonese knights, to whom he was somewhat known, he was released by the king after many dangers of death and returned to the count.

From that time the aforesaid king, who in earlier days had persecuted the count of Jesus Christ, though only secretly, began openly to harass and persecute him in every way.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. Louis, son of the king of France, takes the badge of the military cross and induces many to take it.

[Col. 0660B]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1212, in the month of February, Louis, son of the king of France, a most gentle young man and a youth of good disposition, marked himself with the sign of the cross against the heretics. When this was heard, countless knights, stirred by love and emulation of him, took up the sign of the life-giving cross. But when the king of France heard that his son had been signed with the cross, he was greatly distressed; yet it is not for us to explain the cause of his distress.

On the first day of Lent the king held a general assembly in the city of Paris, to make arrangements concerning his son’s expedition and learn who would go with him, how many, and of what sort. At that time the bishops of Toulouse and Carcassonne, men of every holiness, were at Paris; they had then come to France in order to advance the cause of the faith against the pestilent heretics.

But the king of Aragon, who hindered the undertaking as much as he could, sent his messengers to the king of France: namely, the bishop of Barcelona and certain knights with him. The king of Aragon sent those messengers for two reasons. Through them he solicited the king of France to give him his daughter in marriage. For the aforesaid king of Aragon wished to put away his lawful wife, the daughter of William of Montpellier—indeed, so far as lay in his power, he had already put her away. But she had approached the lord [Col. 0660D] pope, complaining that her husband had unjustly dismissed her. The supreme pontiff, having more fully learned the truth, gave judgment against the king and confirmed the marriage between him and the aforesaid queen.

That king wished to marry the daughter of the king of France so that, by such an alliance, he might draw the latter to himself and turn his heart away from love for the cause of the faith and from aiding the noble count of Montfort. But when the aforesaid messengers of the king of Aragon saw that it was already manifest and public in the court of the king of France that the lord pope had confirmed the marriage of the king and queen of Aragon, they did not dare mention the marriage which they had come to arrange.

The second reason for their coming [Col. 0661A] to France was this. The often-mentioned king had received into his custody and protection the city of Toulouse—which from ancient times had been, and was, a refuge and sewer of heretics—as well as the heretics themselves and their supporters, maintaining open and complete communion with excommunicated heretics. As far as he could, while seemingly acting out of piety, he laboured in impiety to make the devotion of the pilgrims cease and the zeal of those signed with the cross grow cold. He wished Toulouse and certain neighbouring castles, which still assailed Christianity, to remain unharmed, so that he might later destroy and utterly dissipate the whole cause of the most holy faith.

For this reason he also sent letters to the king of France, the countess of Champagne, and many others, sealed with the seals of many bishops of his land, asserting that the lord pope intended to revoke the indulgence which he had granted against the often-mentioned heretics. He had these letters published throughout France in order to turn all men’s minds away from pilgrimage against the heretics.

Having briefly touched upon these matters, let us continue our account of his malice. The bishop of Barcelona and the other messengers of the king of Aragon had come in order to work against the departure of pilgrims for the campaign against the heretics. But when they saw that Louis, son of the king of France, and many nobles with him had taken the cross against the heretics, they did not dare even mutter about withdrawing our people from devotion to the aforesaid pilgrimage. Thus, accomplishing none of the things for which they had come, they returned to the king [Col. 0661C] of Aragon.

The king of France, who, as we have said, had summoned his barons to Paris, arranged the pilgrimage of his son and of the others signed with the cross, and fixed the day of departure: namely, the octave of the Sunday of the Resurrection. What more need be said? There was immense joy and exultation among Christians, but grief and great fear among the heretics. Yet alas! shortly afterward our harp was turned to mourning (Job 30), and the mourning of the enemies was changed into joy (Esther 13). For the ancient enemy of the human race, the devil, seeing that Christ’s cause was almost brought to completion through the labour and industry of the crusaders, devised a new artifice of harm and sought to hinder what grieved him to see completed. He stirred up for the king of France wars [Col. 0661D] and occupations so many and so great that the king had to delay his son and the crusaders from carrying out the proposed pilgrimage.

## CHAPTER LXIX. Manasses, bishop of Orléans, and William, bishop of Auxerre, brothers, take up the cross against the Albigensians.

At that time Manasses, bishop of Orléans, and William, bishop of Auxerre—men in every respect praiseworthy and steadfast, two great, indeed the chief lights at that time of the Gallican Church, and brothers by blood—had taken up the cross against the heretics mentioned above. Seeing that the multitude of those signed with the cross had remained behind, and knowing that the cause of the faith stood in grave peril because the enemies of the faith had, owing to the pilgrims’ failure to arrive, raised their horns more cruelly than usual, they gathered with them as many knights as they could. With wondrous fervour of spirit and courage, they set out against the heretics, prepared not only to spend their possessions but also, if necessary, to expose themselves to danger and death in the service of Jesus Christ.

Hastening, therefore, these men filled with God came by a direct route to Carcassonne. The noble count of Montfort and the few with him rejoiced exceedingly at their arrival (Matthew 2). The said bishops found our men in a certain castle near Carcassonne called the Temple of Jupiter (*Fanum Jovis*). They spent a few days in that castle, after which the count went with the bishops to the castle of Muret [Col. 0662B] near Toulouse, of which we have spoken above. From there our men rode before Toulouse in order more frequently to restrain the enemies of Christ and their own enemies.

But a knight named Alard of Estrepiq, and some few others who had not behaved well enough in Christ’s cause, refused to go with him. Since the count did not have an army large enough to establish a siege around Toulouse or any other strong castle, he resolved to ride frequently before Toulouse with the force he possessed, to overthrow the many strong fortifications around Toulouse, strip the bark from the trees, and uproot the crops and vines; for harvest-time was at hand. And as he had resolved, so he did.

The aforesaid bishops [Col. 0662C] were always with the count and daily exposed themselves to dangers in Christ’s service. Moreover, they gave generous gifts from their own resources to the knights who were with them in God’s service; they ransomed captives and diligently performed the other offices of lavish and holy virtue, being most holy men. Since we cannot recount everything separately, we say briefly that within a few days our men overthrew seventeen fortifications and destroyed for the most part the crops, vineyards, and trees of Toulouse.

Nor should it be passed over in silence that, when our men rode before Toulouse, the Toulousans and the *ruptarii* who were in Toulouse, twice as numerous as our men, frequently came out and harassed our men from a distance. But whenever our men wished to attack them, they took flight.

[Col. 0662D] Among the fortifications which our men destroyed was one near Toulouse, rather weak and undefended. Certain knights of distinguished valour—Peter of Sissi, Simon of Sesnes, and Robert of Sartis—who had borne the burden of the war from the beginning, asked the count to leave them that fortification, so that by staying there they might ride before Toulouse and more often harass the Toulousans. The count, though unwilling, yielded to their prayers and granted their request.

Around the feast of the Nativity of Blessed John the Baptist, the count wished his eldest son Amaury to be made a new knight. On the counsel of his men, he arranged that this ceremony of new knighthood should be celebrated at Castelnaud, between Toulouse and Carcassonne, on the feast of John’s Nativity.

[Col. 0663A] While these things were being done by the count and those with him, Guy of Montfort, the count’s full brother, was besieging a certain castle called Puycelsi, in the diocese of Albi. Departing from it, he hastened to his brother the count, who himself was hastening to Castelnaud-d’Ari because of the new knighthood of his son Amaury, mentioned above, since the Nativity of John was approaching. The barons and knights of the count’s land also came to the festival of the new knighthood. We wish to describe the very manner in which the aforesaid son of the count was made a knight of Christ, as something new and unheard of through the ages.

## CHAPTER LXX. Amaury, son of Count Simon, is made a knight.

[Col. 0663B] In the year of the Incarnate Word 1213, the noble count of Montfort and many of his barons and knights assembled at Castelnaud-d’Ari on the feast of the Nativity of Blessed John. The two venerable bishops already mentioned and certain pilgrim knights were with the count. The most Christian count wished and asked the bishop of Orléans to make his son a knight of Christ and himself gird him with the knightly belt. The venerable bishop long resisted strongly, but at last, overcome by the entreaties of the count and our men, he consented to their request.

Because it was summer, and because Castelnaud could not suitably contain so great a multitude, having already once or twice been destroyed, the count had many tents pitched [Col. 0663C] on a pleasant plain beside the castle. On the very day of the Nativity of Saint John, the venerable bishop of Orléans dressed in pontifical vestments in order to celebrate the solemnity of Mass in one of the tents. Clerics and knights assembled to hear Mass. As the bishop stood before the altar and celebrated Mass, the count, taking his eldest son Amaury by the right hand and the countess by the left, approached the altar and offered him to the Lord, asking the bishop to make him a knight for the service of Jesus Christ.

What more need be said? Immediately the bishops of Orléans and Auxerre, kneeling before the altar, girded the boy with the knightly belt, beginning with the greatest devotion: “Come, Creator Spirit.” O new [Col. 0663D] and untried manner of knighthood! Who could have restrained himself from tears there? In this manner and order the aforesaid boy was made a new knight with great solemnity.

When the solemnity was completed, the count, leaving Castelnaud a few days later with the bishops and his son, rode before Toulouse. Having captured some Toulousans, our men went to Muret. Many nobles of Gascony came there to the count, for he had summoned them and wished them to do homage to his young son; and so it was done. A few days later the count departed from Muret toward Gascony, taking his son in order to give him the part of Gascony already acquired and, with God’s aid, to acquire what remained to be acquired.

The bishops remained at Muret, intending to return home on the third day. They had praiseworthily completed their pilgrimage of forty days, as men praiseworthy in every respect, with great labour and expense. On the third day, the bishops departed from Muret and made for Carcassonne.

[Col. 0664A] Seeing that our count was going with his son into Gascony, while the bishops and the pilgrims who accompanied them were returning home, the Toulousans and the other enemies of the faith, seizing this occasion of security, marched out from Toulouse with a great army and besieged certain of our knights: namely, Peter of Sissi, Simon of Sesnes, Roger of Sartis, and a few others, who, as we said above, held a rather weak and undefended fortification near Toulouse.

When the adversaries came to that fortification, they began fiercely to assail our men, while the besieged defended themselves as well as they could. But after a few days, our besieged men, seeing that they could not hold out long and considering also that they could not receive timely assistance—because the count had gone into Gascony and the bishops and pilgrims were returning home—after harsh distress surrendered to their adversaries, upon the condition and assurance that the adversaries should preserve their lives and limbs.

[Col. 0664B] It should not be suppressed that the aforesaid bishops, already at Carcassonne, when they heard that our knights were besieged near Toulouse, advised, urged, and entreated the pilgrims who were with them to return with them to relieve the besieged. O men commendable in every respect! O men of courage! All consented, and, leaving Carcassonne, hastened to aid the besieged. But when they came near Castelnaud-d’Ari, they were told that our besieged men had already been captured by the Toulousans; and indeed so it was. Hearing this with great sorrow, they returned to Carcassonne, while the adversaries took the captured knights to Toulouse.

Immediately, worse than all unbelievers, disregarding promise and oath, they had our knights—whom, as has been said, they had assured of life and limbs—dragged through the streets of the city at horses’ tails, and then hanged on gibbets after they had been dragged. O grievous manner of treachery and cruelty!

The noble count of Montfort, [Col. 0664D] who, as we have said, had taken his son into Gascony and had already, with God’s aid, acquired many castles and strongholds, heard that the Toulousans had besieged his knights near Toulouse. Leaving his son in Gascony, he returned in haste to relieve the besieged; but before he could reach them, they had already been captured and taken to Toulouse.

In the previous winter, Peter, king of Aragon, had sent messengers to Rome, falsely representing to the lord pope that the count of Montfort had unjustly taken the lands of the counts of Comminges and Foix and of Gaston of Béarn. The king also said that those three nobles had never been heretics, although it was perfectly clear that they had sheltered heretics and assailed the holy Church with all their might. He persuaded the lord pope that the cause of the faith had been completed against the heretics, the heretics themselves having been driven far away and utterly exterminated from the land of Albi; and therefore it was necessary for the lord pope entirely to revoke the indulgence which he had granted to those going against the heretics and transfer it either against the pagan Spaniards or to the aid of the Holy Land.

[Col. 0665A] O unheard-of impiety under the guise of piety! For this most wicked king said, not because the distresses and necessities of Holy Church concerned him, but in order that he might in a moment smother and destroy Christ’s cause against the heretics—a cause which for many years had been miraculously advanced with the greatest labour and much shedding of blood—as he demonstrated by the clearest indications.

The supreme pontiff, too readily believing the king’s false representations, easily consented to his requests. He sent letters to the count of Montfort, ordering and commanding him without delay to restore to the aforesaid counts of Comminges and Foix and to Gaston of Béarn—men most wicked and depraved—their lands, which he had acquired by God’s just judgment and with the help of the crusaders. Moreover, he revoked his indulgence granted to those going against the heretics.

Afterward the lord pope also sent his legate into France, Master Robert of Courçon, [Note: [Col. 0665D] He is commemorated in the necrology of the Church of Troyes on 6 February, where he is called Robert de Torcon; Ciaconius, in his account of Innocent III, calls him [Col. 0666D] R. Corson; and Matthew Paris, in his account of Henry III, calls him R. de Sumercote, asserting that he was killed by poison in the year 1241.] an Englishman by nation, with many sets of letters and indulgences, to preach diligently and cause preaching to be done for the aid of the land of Jerusalem.

[Col. 0665C] Coming into France, the legate, with unwearied diligence carrying out the office entrusted to him, began to travel throughout France, hold councils of archbishops and bishops, appoint preachers, and promote in every way the cause of the Holy Land. He also withdrew for that same cause the preachers who had been labouring for the cause of the faith against the aforesaid heretics, and made them preach for the cause of the Holy Land. Thus, in human judgment, the cause of the faith against the pestilent heretics came almost to be abolished.

Indeed, throughout all France there was only one man, the venerable bishop of Carcassonne, a man of outstanding holiness, who laboured for the aforesaid cause of the faith. With great persistence he travelled through France and promoted that cause by every means in his power, lest it fall [Col. 0665D] into oblivion. Having said these things concerning the condition of France, let us return to the thread of our narrative.

When apostolic letters had issued from the curia, in which the lord pope commanded the count of Montfort to restore their lands to the three nobles mentioned above, our most Christian count and the bishops of the land of Albi sent their messengers to the lord pope: namely, the bishop of Comminges, William the archdeacon of Paris, and a certain abbot of Clairac, prudent and steadfast men; they also sent two clerics whom the lord pope himself had already dispatched from his side [Col. 0666A] to the count of Montfort, namely Master Theodisius of Pisa, who embraced the cause of the faith with wondrous affection, and Peter Marci, formerly the lord pope’s notary and a native of the diocese of Nîmes.

All these men, on coming to the curia, found it harsh and exceedingly difficult to deal with, because messengers of the king of Aragon, some of whom remained at the curia, had by false representations bent the minds of nearly all who were there in their own favour. At last, after much labour, the lord pope, having examined the truth more fully, sent letters through the count’s messengers to the king of Aragon, in which he rebuked him most severely for having received the Toulousans and other heretics into his protection and custody. In the power of the Holy Spirit, he most strictly enjoined him to depart from them without delay and thereafter to give them neither aid nor favour.

The lord pope also complained in his letters about the king of Aragon because, by wholly false representations, he had obtained apostolic letters ordering the restoration of lands to the counts of Comminges and Foix and to Gaston of Béarn. Therefore the lord pope revoked those letters as fraudulently obtained. Furthermore, in the same letters he commanded the aforesaid nobles and the citizens of Toulouse to make satisfaction to God and return to the unity of the Church, according to the counsel and will of the archbishop of Narbonne, legate of the Apostolic See, and of the bishop of Toulouse. If they refused, the lord pope ordered that, by means of the aforesaid indulgences, the peoples should be stirred up against the Toulousans and their supporters [Col. 0666C]. This was the substance of the letters. Having obtained them, our messengers returned from the curia.

But the noble count of Montfort and those with him were then pressed by a grave crisis. They were almost alone and nearly utterly forsaken, because few or no pilgrims came from France to assist them. As we have already said, the cause of the faith had almost fallen into oblivion through the new preaching of the legate whom the lord pope had sent into France for the cause of the Holy Land; therefore almost no one took the cross against the pestilent heretics. Moreover, because of the civil wars which the king of France had, he did not allow knights who had long before taken the cross against the heretics to proceed to fulfil their vows.

Besides all this, throughout the land of the Albigensians it was said, and it had become widely current report, that the king of Aragon was gathering his armies in order to enter our land arrogantly and utterly exterminate Christ’s knights from it. Our count, faced once more with danger, sent to his son, who was in Gascony besieging a castle called Rochefort, commanding him to abandon the siege and come to him in haste. For he feared that, if the king entered Gascony with his army, he might capture the son, since he had very few Frenchmen with him.

But the pious Lord Jesus, who is ever a helper in times of need and tribulation (Psalm 9), so arranged matters that the son obeyed his father’s command and need not be ashamed of abandoning the siege. For on the very night when the count’s letters arrived, the adversaries besieged in the castle asked for terms of peace, ready to surrender the castle and the nearly sixty captives whom they held, provided that they themselves might be allowed to depart unharmed. Because necessity pressed, this was granted. Amaury, the count’s son, having fortified that castle with a few knights, hastened to his father.

[Col. 0667A] The entire land of the Albigensians was in great disturbance and uncertainty. For the enemies of the faith and the knights of the king of Aragon, because they had now remained a long time at Toulouse, went about before our castles, inviting the inhabitants to apostasy and our surrender. Many of them, relying on the security afforded by the king of Aragon, whose arrival they awaited with the greatest desire, went over to the adversaries; and so we lost many great and strong castles.

At that time the noble count of Montfort and the bishops of the land of Albi sent two abbots to the king of Aragon to deliver to him the letters and command of the lord pope, beseeching him, according to the apostolic command, to desist from aiding the heretics and not to assail Christianity. But the king, deceitful and crafty as he was, replied deceitfully that he would gladly fulfil everything that the supreme pontiff commanded him. Yet although he always promised [Col. 0667C] that he would most willingly carry out the apostolic command, he would not recall his knights whom he had left at Toulouse during the previous winter, through whom he assailed Christianity together with the Toulousans and other heretics; indeed, he sent many more knights to Toulouse.

Moreover, he gathered from his own land all whom he could, and, as we heard, mortgaged no small part of his land in order to have the means to hire mercenaries to assist the heretics and attack Christianity. O cunning cruelty! O most cruel treachery! Though he assembled armies against us with all his power, he nevertheless promised that he would gladly fulfil the lord pope’s command to abandon the heretics and the excommunicated, so as to leave us unharmed and secure. But because “there is no wisdom or counsel against the Lord” (Proverbs 21), the outcome of the matter demonstrated otherwise.

At that time the often-mentioned king of Aragon, in order to bring forth the iniquity he had conceived against Christ and His people, departed from his land with an innumerable multitude of horsemen and entered Gascony. He wished, if he could, to restore to the heretics and subject to his own dominion the whole land which had been acquired by God’s grace and the aid of the crusaders. Having entered the borders of Gascony, he began to march toward Toulouse. Many castles of Gascony through which he passed surrendered to him out of fear.

What more? Throughout the whole land report of the king’s arrival became widespread. Many inhabitants rejoiced; many apostatized; the rest prepared themselves to apostatize. The impious king, having gone round many castles, came before Muret, a noble castle but rather weak in strength, three leagues from Toulouse. Though weak in walls and ditches, it was nevertheless defended by thirty knights and a few foot-soldiers, whom the noble count of Montfort had left there to guard the castle, and who attacked the Toulousans more fiercely than others. When the king of Aragon reached Toulouse, he assembled the Toulousans and other heretics in order to establish the siege around Muret.

## CHAPTER LXXI. The siege of Muret.

In the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1213, on 10 September, the third weekday after the Nativity of Blessed Mary, Peter, king of Aragon, having assembled the counts of Toulouse, [Col. 0668B] Comminges, and Foix, together with a large army of Aragonese and Toulousans, besieged Muret. The castle of Muret stood on the River Garonne near Toulouse, three leagues away in the direction of Gascony.

When the adversaries approached the castle of Muret, at their first assault they immediately entered the first borough of the castle, because our besieged men could not defend it. They were few and had withdrawn to another, somewhat stronger borough. Yet the enemies quickly abandoned that first borough of the castle.

Immediately our knights in the castle sent to the noble count of Montfort, informing him that they were besieged and asking him to help them, since they had scanty, indeed almost no, provisions and did not dare leave the castle. The count was at the castle called the Temple of Jupiter, eight leagues distant from Muret. He had intended to go to Muret in order to furnish it both with men and provisions, because he suspected something concerning the approach of the king of Aragon and the siege of Muret.

On the very night when the count intended to depart from the Temple of Jupiter, our countess, who was there, saw a dream which greatly terrified her. It seemed to her that blood flowed in great abundance from both her arms. When in the morning she reported the dream to the count and declared herself exceedingly troubled by it, the count answered: “You have spoken like one of the women. Do you think that we follow dreams or omens in the manner of Spaniards? Certainly, even if I had dreamed [Col. 0668D] this night that I was to be killed in the battle toward which I hasten, I would go more securely and gladly, in order more completely to oppose the folly of the Spaniards and of the people of this land, who attend to dreams and omens.”

Having said this, the count left the Temple of Jupiter and hurried with his men toward Saverdun. While he was on the way, a messenger sent by the knights besieged in the castle of Muret came to him, bringing their letters stating that the king of Aragon had established a siege before Muret. On hearing this, all our men, already hoping for the coming victory, rejoiced greatly.

Immediately the count sent word to the countess, who herself had left the Temple of Jupiter and was making for Carcassonne, to gather as many knights as she could. He also asked a certain nobleman of France, namely the viscount of Corbeil, who after completing his pilgrimage was returning home, to turn back and hasten to the aid of our count. He willingly consented and promised that he would gladly present himself.

Accordingly, the aforesaid viscount with his men and the few knights whom, as we have said, the countess was sending to assist the count, set out and came to the Temple of Jupiter. Our count and those with him, hastening toward Saverdun, came near a certain Cistercian abbey called Boulbonne. Turning aside to it, our count entered the church to pray and to commend himself and his men to the prayers of the monks. After he had prayed at length and for a long time, he took the sword with which he was girded and placed it upon the altar, saying:

“O good Lord! O gracious Jesus! You have chosen me, though unworthy, for Your battles. From above Your altar I receive arms today, so that, fighting Your battles, I may receive from You the justice of fighting.”

Having said this, the count went out with his men and came to Saverdun. There were with the count seven bishops and three abbots, whom the archbishop of Narbonne, legate of the Apostolic See, had caused to assemble in order to speak with the king of Aragon about peace and concord. Certain knights too—about thirty—had very recently come from France to fulfil the vow of their pilgrimage. Among them was a young knight, a maternal half-brother of our count, named William of Barres. These things were done by the Lord.

[Col. 0669C] When the count arrived at Saverdun, he summoned the knights who had come with him and asked their counsel about what ought to be done. He himself was wholly inclined, as we afterward heard from his own lips, to go and enter Muret that very night, for, being a most faithful prince, he was deeply concerned for his besieged men. The others, however, wished to remain at Saverdun that night because they were fasting and weary, and said that perhaps they might have to fight the enemy on the very road. The count consented, though unwillingly, since he always did everything with counsel.

At earliest dawn on the following day he called his chaplain, made confession, and arranged his testament. He sent the written and sealed testament to the lord abbot of Boulbonne, commanding and directing [Col. 0669D] that, should he fall in battle, the aforesaid testament be sent to Rome and confirmed by the lord pope.

Once day had broken, the bishops who were at Saverdun, the count, and all his men assembled in the church. At once one of them put on the sacred vestments to celebrate Mass in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary. During this Mass all the bishops excommunicated the count of Toulouse and his son, the count of Foix and his son, the count of Comminges, and all their supporters, helpers, and defenders. King of Aragon was doubtless included in this sentence, although the bishops deliberately suppressed his name; for the excommunication was pronounced against him, since he was not only the helper and defender of the said counts, but also the head and instigator of the entire force conducting the siege of Muret [Col. 0670A].

When Mass had been celebrated, the count and his men armed themselves and, leaving Saverdun, drew up their battle-lines on a plain near the castle, in the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Advancing, they came to a castle called Auterive, midway between Saverdun and Muret. Proceeding from there, they reached a place difficult to cross, between Auterive and Muret. Our men thought that they would encounter the enemy there, because the place was muddy and the road narrow and waterlogged. Near that place was a church, which the count entered, according to his custom, in order to pray. At that hour rain was pouring down [Col. 0670B] and greatly harassing our knights; but as the knight of Jesus Christ—namely, our count—prayed, the rain ceased, and clouds gave way to clear sky. O immeasurable goodness of the Creator! When the count rose from prayer, they remounted, crossed the aforesaid place, and found no hostile obstacle.

Advancing from there, they came near Muret, on this side of the Garonne. King of Aragon and those with him had besieged the castle from the other side, beyond the Garonne, as numerous as the sand of the sea. Our knights, being exceedingly eager, advised the count to enter the castle at once and engage the enemy that very day. But the count would by no means consent to battle that day, because it was evening, and our men, both knights and horses, were weary, whereas the enemy were fresh [the printed text has *recedentes*, perhaps for *recentes*].

Moreover, the count wished to show every humility, to offer King of Aragon words of peace, and to entreat him not, by coming against the Church, to join himself to Christ’s enemies. For these reasons, then, the count would not allow an engagement that day. Having crossed the bridge, they entered Muret. At once our bishops sent messengers to the king, again and again, begging and beseeching him to deign to have mercy upon the holy Church of God. But the king, most obstinate as he was, would agree to none of their requests, nor give any peaceful answer, as is set out below. That night the viscount of Corbeil [Corboliensis] and a few French knights coming from Carcassonne, of whom we spoke above, entered Muret; the count and those with him rejoiced greatly at their arrival. Nor should it be omitted that there were provisions in Muret insufficient for our men even for one day. Such was the situation that night.

## Chapter LXXII. On the most valiant battle and the most glorious victory of the count of Montfort and his men, won on the field of Muret over the king of Aragon and the enemies of the faith

Very early the next morning the count entered his church, which stood within the castle’s stronghold, to hear Mass. Our bishops and knights, however, went to the church in the town, that they too might hear Mass [Col. 0671A]. When the count had heard Mass, he went out from the stronghold into the town with his men, to take counsel with them; and our men conferred together. They were unarmed, because negotiations for peace with the king were in some fashion being conducted through the bishops.

At once the bishops, with the common assent of our men, wished to go barefoot to the king, to beseech him not to attack the Church. When they had sent a messenger to announce this approach of the bishops, behold: several armed enemies on horseback entered the town where our men were. The gates stood open, because the noble count would not permit them to be shut. Immediately our count addressed the bishops:

> “You see that you accomplish nothing; indeed, the disturbance grows worse. We have endured enough—more than enough [Col. 0671B]. It is time for you to give us leave to fight.”

Since necessity pressed them so, the bishops granted permission. Then our men left the place of conference and each went to his own lodging to arm himself. As the count entered the castle’s stronghold to arm himself and passed in front of his church, he suddenly looked in and saw the bishop of Uzès celebrating Mass and saying, after the Gospel, at the offertory, “The Lord be with you.” At once the most Christian count ran forward; kneeling on the ground and joining his hands before the bishop, he said:

> “I give and offer to you also my soul and my body.”

O devotion of a prince! After this he entered the stronghold and equipped himself with arms. [Col. 0671C] Returning again to the bishop in the aforesaid church, he once more offered himself and his arms to him. But as he bent his knees before the altar, the strap from which his iron leggings hung broke in the middle. Yet the Catholic man conceived neither fear nor disturbance from what had occurred, but ordered another strap to be brought. This done, the count left the church.

As he went out, his horse was brought to him. When he wished to mount, standing in an elevated place where the men of Toulouse outside the castle could see him, the horse raised its head, struck the count, and made him recoil somewhat. Seeing this, the Toulouse men uttered a great howl in mockery of the count. To them the Catholic count said:

> “You now mock me with your shouting; but I trust [Col. 0671D] in the Lord that I shall shout victoriously after you, even to the gates of Toulouse.”

Having said this, the count mounted his horse. Coming to the knights who were in the town, he found them armed and ready for battle. A knight advised the count to have his knights counted, so that he might know how many there were. The noble count answered him:

> “There is no need. By God’s help, we are enough to overcome our enemies.”

All our men, knights and mounted sergeants together, numbered no more than eighty, while the enemy were believed to number one hundred thousand. Our men had very few foot-soldiers, indeed almost none. Moreover, the noble count had forbidden anyone on foot to go out to the battle.

While the count and our knights were speaking together [Col. 0672A] and deliberating about the battle, behold, the bishop of Toulouse arrived, wearing a mitre on his head and carrying in his hands the life-giving wood of the Cross. At once our men began to dismount from their horses, each to adore the Cross. But the bishop of Comminges, a man of remarkable holiness, saw that in this adoration of the Cross each person was delaying too long. Taking the wood of the Cross from the bishop of Toulouse’s hand, he went up to a higher place and signed them with it, saying:

> “Go in the name of Jesus Christ; and I am your witness and shall stand surety for you on the Day of Judgment: whoever falls in this glorious battle shall obtain eternal rewards and the glory of martyrs, without any punishment of purgatory—provided that he has confessed and is contrite, or at least firmly resolves that, immediately after the battle is over, he will present himself to a priest concerning the sins which he has not yet confessed.”

[Col. 0672B] At the urging of our knights this promise was repeated, and was frequently and repeatedly confirmed by the bishops. Immediately our men, cleansed from sins by contrition of heart and confession of mouth, forgiving one another if anyone had a grievance against another, went out from the castle. They arranged themselves in three battle-lines and, in the name of the Trinity, advanced fearlessly against the enemy.

The bishops and clergy entered the church to entreat the Lord for His servants, who were exposing themselves to imminent death for His name. Praying and crying to heaven, they sent up such a roar to heaven in their impending distress that they ought rather to have been called howlers than worshippers [Col. 0672C]. Thus Christ’s knights went joyfully to the place of combat, ready to suffer for His name not merely insult but death as well. When they had left the castle, they saw on the plain beside it the enemy prepared for battle, as though they were the whole world.

At once our first battle-line boldly sprang upon the enemy and threw itself into their midst. The second immediately followed, penetrating the enemy as the first had done. In that clash the king of Aragon fell, and many Aragonese with him; for, being exceedingly proud, he had placed himself in the second line, whereas kings ordinarily remain in the rear. Moreover, he had changed his arms and put on another man’s armour. Seeing his two battle-lines swallowed up in the midst of the enemy and seemingly no longer visible, our count attacked from the left the countless enemies who stood opposite [Col. 0672D].

Their battle-array stood beside a ditch lying between them and our count. Immediately the count rushed upon the aforesaid enemies. Although he could see no route by which he could reach them, he at last found in the ditch a very small path, prepared at that moment, as we believe, by divine ordering. Crossing by it, he gave himself into the enemy and, as a most valiant knight of Christ, penetrated them most vigorously. Nor should it be left unsaid that, when the count wished to charge them, they struck him on the right with their swords so violently that, from the force of the blows, his left stirrup broke. The noble count wished to plant the spur of his left foot in the horse’s covering, but [Col. 0673A] the broken spur sprang away from his foot. Yet the most powerful knight did not fall, but struck the enemy hard.

One of the adversaries struck our count forcefully on the head. The noble man, however, struck that knight under the chin with his fist and caused him to fall from his horse. Seeing this, the companions of that knight, who were innumerable, and indeed all our other opponents, quickly defeated and confused, sought the refuge of flight. Seeing this, our men—namely, those who had been in the first and second lines—pursued the fugitives with the utmost determination and pressed them hard. Cutting down the rearmost, they killed many thousands of them.

Our count and those with him deliberately followed at a slow pace behind our men pursuing the enemy, so that if the enemy should perhaps gather together and recover courage to resist, our men, who were pursuing the fugitives separately from one another, might be able to fall back upon the count [Col. 0673B]. Nor should it be omitted that, once he saw the enemy fleeing and turning their backs, the most noble count did not deign to strike anyone in battle.

While this was taking place, countless citizens of Toulouse who had remained in the army, ready for battle, were exerting all their strength to storm the castle. Seeing this, the bishop of Toulouse, who was in the castle, a good and gentle man and compassionate toward their misery, sent a religious man to them, warning and advising them at last to turn to the Lord their God, lay down their arms, and let Him rescue them from imminent death. As a token assuring them of this, he sent them his hooded cloak, for he was a monk. But they, obstinate and divinely blinded as they were, replied that the king of Aragon had defeated all our men, and that the bishop wished to hand them over to death, not save them. For this reason, taking the cloak from the messenger, they beat him severely with lances [Col. 0673C]. Meanwhile our knights returned from the slaughter with glorious victory, and coming upon those Toulouse men, killed several thousand of them.

After this, the count ordered some of his men to lead him to the place where the king of Aragon had been killed; for he was wholly unaware of the place and hour of his death. Coming to the place, the count found [Col. 0673D] the king of Aragon’s body lying naked in the middle of the field. Our foot-soldiers had already stripped him, because, on seeing the victory, they had left the castle and killed any men whom they could find still lying alive. The most devout count, seeing the king lying prostrate, dismounted from his horse, portraying another David over another Saul.

When all this had duly been done, and about twenty thousand enemies of the faith had been killed, both by drowning and by the sword, the most Christian count understood that so great a miracle had been accomplished by God’s power, not by human strength. From the place where he had dismounted, he went barefoot to the church, to give thanks to almighty God [Col. 0674A] for the victory granted. He also gave his horse and armour to the poor as alms. So that the truth of this wonderful battle and most glorious victory might be more fully impressed upon the hearts of hearers, we have thought it proper to insert in our work the letters which the bishops and abbots present sent to all Christ’s faithful.

## Chapter LXXIII. Letters of the prelates who were in Count Simon’s army when he triumphed over the enemies of the faith

[Note: [Col. 0673] Matthew Paris inserted this letter in his *History of England*, under King John, for the year 1213.]

“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men” (Luke 2) who love the holy Church with good will. God, strong and mighty, mighty in battle (Psalm 23), on Thursday within the octave of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, granted the holy Church [Col. 0674B] a glorious victory and a glorious triumph, by the miraculous defeat of the enemies of the Christian faith, in the following manner.

After the supreme pontiff had most diligently admonished the king of Aragon with deepest affection and the zeal of fatherly kindness, and had most strictly forbidden him to give aid, counsel, or favour to the enemies of the faith, commanding him to withdraw from them without delay and maintain most firm truces with the count of Montfort; after certain letters, which messengers of that king had procured by a most false allegation against the count of Montfort, ordering lands to be restored to the counts of Foix and Comminges and to Gaston of Béarn, had, once the truth was known, been annulled by the lord pope and entirely revoked as having no force whatever [Col. 0674C]—after all this, the same king did not receive the correction of the most holy Father with filial devotion. Instead, proudly resisting, he transgressed the apostolic command, as though his heart were hardened beyond measure. Although the venerable fathers, the archbishop of Narbonne, legate of the Apostolic See, and the bishop of Toulouse, had conveyed to him the letters and command of the supreme pontiff, he afterward wished to bring forth the evils that he had long conceived. He entered, with an army, the land acquired by God’s power through the aid of those marked with the cross against heretics and their defenders; he attempted, contrary to the apostolic command, to subjugate it and restore it to the aforesaid enemies. One part of it had already been somewhat subdued by him, while a great part of the remainder, relying on his protection, was planning apostasy and already preparing to apostatize [Col. 0674D].

Having gathered together the counts of Toulouse, Foix, and Comminges, and a very great army of Toulouse men, on Tuesday after the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, he besieged the castle of Muret. When this was heard, Simon, count of Montfort—at one with and devoted in Christ to the venerable fathers, archbishops, bishops, and abbots whom the venerable father the archbishop of Narbonne, legate of the Apostolic See, had caused to assemble for the holy cause, and who had come to negotiate diligently concerning that cause and peace—set out bravely to relieve the besieged castle. He had with him certain noble and powerful crusaders who had recently arrived from France to assist him and Christ’s cause [Col. 0675A], and also his own household, which had long laboured with him in Christ’s cause.

When, on Tuesday within the said octave, that army of Christ had come to a castle called Saverdun, the venerable bishop of Toulouse, to whom the supreme pontiff had entrusted the reconciliation of the Toulouse people, sent his letters to the king and the Toulouse men assisting at the siege of Muret. Although he had admonished them three or four times concerning reconciliation, they had deferred to obey his salutary warnings, replying that they would make no answer at all on this matter. He informed them that the aforesaid bishops were coming to negotiate diligently concerning peace and concord, and requested that a safe-conduct be given him.

On the following day, Wednesday, because the situation was urgent, the aforesaid army left Saverdun, hastening to reach the relief of Muret quickly. The aforementioned bishops had proposed that they should wait at a castle called Auterive, midway between Saverdun and Muret and two leagues from each, for the messenger whom they had sent. The messenger returned with the king’s response: because the bishops were coming with an army, he would not give them a safe-conduct. They could not go any other way without manifest danger because of the war [Col. 0675B].

As the bishops and the army of Christ approached Muret, the prior of the Hospital at Toulouse came, sent by the citizens of Toulouse to the bishop of Toulouse, bearing their letters. [Col. 0675C] These stated that they were ready in every way to do the will of the lord pope and of the bishop himself—something that would indeed have been good for them, if their deeds had more truthfully matched their words. The bishop immediately sent the prior back. The king replied that he would not provide the bishop with a safe-conduct; but if he wished to go to Toulouse to speak with the Toulouse men, he would allow him to go there. This was said mockingly. To this the bishop replied:

> “It is not fitting for a servant to enter a city from which his lord has been driven into exile. Nor, since the body of Christ has been expelled from that city, will I return there until my God and my Lord return.”

Nevertheless, the said bishops entered Muret with the army on the Wednesday mentioned above. With untiring concern, they sent two religious men to the king [Col. 0675D] and the citizens of Toulouse. From the king they received this answer: that he sought a conference with him because of the four rascals whom the bishops had brought with them. He said this in mockery and contempt of those marked with the cross. The Toulouse men replied to the aforesaid messengers that they would answer about this on the next day; and for this reason they detained them until the next day.

On the following day, Thursday, they answered that they were allied with the king of Aragon and would do nothing except the king’s will in all things. When the messengers returned on Thursday morning and reported this, the bishops and abbots proposed to go barefoot to the king. As they were sending a religious man to announce their coming to the king, the gates having been opened and the count of Montfort and the crusaders being unarmed because the bishops and abbots were jointly discussing peace, the enemies of God arrogantly and treacherously attempted to rush with force into the town. But by God’s grace they were frustrated in their desire [Col. 0676A].

When the count and the crusaders saw their arrogance, and could no longer delay without danger and very great loss, they were salutarily cleansed from sins through contrition of heart and confession of mouth, as men devoted to the Christian faith. They girded themselves manfully with their arms, came to the aforesaid bishop of Toulouse, who, by authority of the lord archbishop of Narbonne, legate of the Apostolic See, was performing the office of legate, and humbly sought permission to go out against the enemies of the faith. Since the affair was in a desperate condition, and necessity compelled, this permission was granted. The enemies were already hastening to attack directly the house in which the bishops stayed, having erected siege-engines and other instruments of war, and shooting crossbow-bolts, missiles, and lances about it on every side. Therefore the venerable knights of Christ, marked with the sign of the Lord’s wood together with the episcopal insignia, went out in three battle-lines in the name of the Holy Trinity [Col. 0676B].

The enemy, on the other hand, having many and very large battle-lines and now equipped with their arms, came out of their tents. Though they had very many knights and a vast multitude of people, the servants of Christ, trusting in His help and though extremely few by comparison with them, did not fear the great multitude [Col. 0676C], but armed, courageously attacked from higher ground. At once the power of the Most High, by the hands of His servants, broke and crushed His enemies in a moment. Turning their backs, they were put to flight like dust before the wind, and the angel of the Lord pursued them. Some fled shamefully and by shameful flight escaped the danger of death; others, avoiding the sword, perished in the peril of the waters; very many were devoured by the sword.

The death of the illustrious king of Aragon, who fell among the slain, must be deeply lamented. So powerful and noble a prince could and ought, if he wished, to have been of great service to the holy Church; but now, joined to Christ’s enemies, he wickedly disturbed Christ’s friends and the holy Church [Col. 0676C].

[Col. 0676D] Moreover, when the victors returned from slaughter and pursuit of the enemy with glorious victory, the aforesaid bishop of Toulouse, charitably and compassionately pitying in his merciful heart the destruction and misery of the Toulouse men, wished to save from destruction those who remained from the slaughter and still stayed within their tents. He hoped that, at least chastened by the blows of such great scourges and escaping imminent danger, they might turn to the Lord and live, persevering in the Catholic faith. He sent to them through a religious man the hooded cloak he was wearing, telling them that now at last they should lay down their arms and their ferocity and come unarmed to him, so that he might save them from death. But still persisting in their malice, and maintaining that they, though defeated, had defeated Christ’s people [Col. 0677A], they not only scorned to obey their bishop’s warnings, but also took away the cloak and beat the messenger more harshly. Christ’s army then returned against them and killed them as they fled about their tents.

The certain number of enemies killed, both nobles and others, cannot be known at all because of their multitude. But only one knight of Christ’s army was killed in the encounter, and very few sergeants. Therefore let all Christian people, with devout mind and whole-hearted affection, give thanks to Christ for the Christians’ victory: He overcame an innumerable multitude of unbelievers through a few faithful men, and granted His holy Church faithfully to triumph over its enemies. To Him be honour and glory for ever and ever [Col. 0677B]. Amen.

We, the bishops of Toulouse, Nîmes, Uzès, Lodève, Béziers, Agde, and Comminges, and the abbots of Clairac, Villemagne, and Saint-Thibéry, who had come at the command of the venerable father the archbishop of Narbonne, legate of the Apostolic See, and who endeavoured with the utmost diligence and earnestness to negotiate concerning peace and concord, attest upon the word of God that all the foregoing is wholly true, as things which we saw and heard. We authenticate it with the protection of our seals, as worthy to be preserved in everlasting memory.

Given at Muret, on the day after the glorious victory, namely Friday within the octave of the Nativity of the Blessed Mary [Col. 0677C], in the year of the Lord 1213.

## Chapter LXXIV. After victory had been won at Muret, the Toulouse men offer to give hostages to the prelates for their reconciliation

After the glorious and unprecedented victory, the seven aforesaid bishops and the three abbots still at the castle of Muret believed that the citizens of Toulouse, frightened alike by so great a miracle of God and by this punishment, might more quickly and readily be recalled from their errors to the bosom of mother Church. In accordance with the command, authority, and terms of the apostolic mandate, they again negotiated, begging, warning, and frightening them in order to induce them to unity with the Church.

When the Toulouse men promised to fulfil the apostolic command, the bishops orally requested from them sufficient security that they would abide by the apostolic command: namely, two hundred hostages from among the citizens. They could in no way be content with the guarantee of an oath [Col. 0677D], since the Toulouse men had repeatedly violated their oaths concerning this same matter. After much verbal disputation, they promised to give only sixty hostages from among their citizens. The bishops, however, for greater security, because of the size of the city and the deceitful, ungovernable multitude of its people—and because on another occasion they had allowed hostages given on the same matter, from among the wealthier citizens, to lapse into forfeiture—demanded as many as two hundred. The others, seeking an evasion, promised to give sixty and no more [Col. 0678A].

At once, lest the Toulouse men should have any ground for excuse or any occasion to evade and cloak their errors, the bishops replied that they would gladly accept the sixty hostages which they promised, reconcile them accordingly, and preserve them in the Church’s peace and in the unity of the Catholic faith. But they, now unable any longer to conceal their malice, replied that they would by no means give hostages. Thus they plainly revealed that their earlier promise of sixty hostages had been made only in deceit and with fraudulent intent.

Here it should be added that the inhabitants of a certain noble castle in the diocese of Albi, called Rabastens, who shortly before had departed from God and our party and surrendered themselves to the Toulouse men, fled in terror when they heard of the aforesaid victory, leaving the castle empty of inhabitants [Col. 0678B]. Guy of Montfort, brother of the count of Montfort, to whom the castle belonged, sent men, occupied it, and fortified it with his own people.

A few days later pilgrims arrived from France, but few: namely, Ralph, bishop of Arras, and a few knights with him, together with not many pilgrim-knights. Our count and all those with him rode into the land of the count of Foix and burned the lower town of Foix itself. Then, riding farther through the said count’s lands, they burned everything that they could find outside fortified places.

## Chapter LXXV. Montfort invades the lands of the count of Foix; Narbonne and Montpellier rebel

[Col. 0678C] After this, our count was informed that certain nobles of Provence, having broken the bond of peace, were disturbing the holy Church of God; moreover, lying in wait on the public roads, they inflicted whatever evils they could upon crusaders coming from France. Having taken counsel with his men, the count proposed to go down into those regions, to crush the disturbers of peace and make the public roads clear of the assaults of evildoers.

Setting out with the pilgrims who were with him, the count came to Narbonne. But the citizens of Narbonne, because they had always hated Christ’s cause and had very often, though secretly, opposed it, could never be induced on any account to permit our count with his pilgrims—or even the pilgrims without the count—to enter their city [Col. 0678D]. Therefore all our men had to remain outside that night in the city’s gardens and thickets. The following day they came to Béziers; two days later, going on from there, they reached Montpellier.

The people of Montpellier, equal to the Narbonnese in malice, would by no means permit our count or those with him to enter their town for lodging that night; in every respect they treated them as the citizens of Narbonne had done. Leaving Montpellier, they came to Nîmes. At first the citizens of Nîmes would not allow the count to enter their city; but, seeing his anger and indignation, they received him and all those with him into the city and bestowed upon them many services of due hospitality [Col. 0679A].
