Proceeding thence, our count came to the castle of Boucoiran [*Boucolio*], where the lords of the castle honourably received him. From there the count went to the town called Argentat, because in those regions there was a nobleman named Pons of Montlaur, who, as far as he could, disturbed the bishops of the land, peace, and the Church. By then all the crusaders had departed from the count; he had with him only a few hired soldiers and the archbishop of Narbonne. Hearing of our count’s arrival, the aforesaid Pons, moved by fear, came to him and submitted himself and his possessions to the count’s will.

There was also in those regions a certain powerful but evil nobleman, Aimar of Poitiers, who had always hated Christ’s cause and [Col. 0679B] was devoted in heart to the count of Toulouse. Hearing of our count’s arrival, he fortified his castles and assembled as many knights as he could in one castle, intending that, if the count passed near that castle, he would come out with his men and attack him. But when the noble count passed before the castle, although he had very few men, the said Aimar, though he had many men with him, did not dare to come out against our men.

While our count was in those regions, Odo, duke of Burgundy, a powerful and good man who greatly cherished both the cause of faith against heretics and our count, came to him. The archbishops of Lyon and Vienne also came with the duke. While the duke and our count were near Valence [Col. 0679C], at Rome, they summoned Aimar of Poitiers, the Church’s enemy, to a conference. He came when summoned, but would not agree with either the count or the duke on matters concerning peace. Again the duke and our count summoned him to a conference, but then too they could accomplish nothing.

Seeing that he could accomplish nothing, the duke, moved by anger and indignation against Aimar, promised our count that, unless the aforesaid Aimar obeyed in all things the Church’s command, submitted himself to our count’s will, and furnished good security in these matters, the duke would attack him together with our count. The duke also immediately summoned many of his knights, intending to go with our count against the oft-mentioned Aimar. Hearing this, Aimar was finally compelled by necessity to come to the duke and our count, offer himself in all things to their will, and hand over certain of his castles as security. The count entrusted these castles to the duke for safekeeping [Col. 0679D].

Meanwhile the venerable father, the archbishop of Narbonne, a man prudent in counsel and altogether virtuous, at whose summons the aforesaid duke of Burgundy had also come into the region of Vienne, began to negotiate with the duke concerning the matter for which he had summoned him: namely, contracting a marriage between the first-born son of our count, named Amaury, and the daughter of the Dauphin, a powerful prince and the duke’s own full brother. The duke agreed to the archbishop’s counsel and wish.

Meanwhile, while these things were occurring, Aragonese brigands and other enemies of the faith began to range through our count’s land. Coming as far as Béziers, they inflicted whatever evils they could. Moreover, many knights of our count’s land, having become perjurers and relapsing into their inborn malice, departed from God, the Church, and the lordship of our count [Col. 0680A]. But the noble count, having completed the affairs in Provence for which he had gone there, returned to his own land. Immediately attacking the territory of his enemies, he rode before Toulouse and, remaining there for fifteen days, utterly demolished and destroyed many fortifications.

While matters stood thus, Master Robert of Courçon, cardinal and legate of the Apostolic See, who, as we said above, was labouring in France as far as he could for the business of the Holy Land, had taken from us our preachers—who were accustomed to preach for the cause of the faith against heretics—and was making them preach more urgently for the relief of the Holy Land. At the counsel of worthy and prudent men, he restored to us some of the aforesaid preachers, that they might preach for the cause of the faith. He himself also took upon his breast the life-giving sign of the cross for the overthrow of the Toulouse heretics. What more need be said? Preaching for the cause of the faith revived in France; many marked themselves with the cross; and there was exceedingly great joy for the count and for our people.

Nor do we wish, nor ought we, to pass over the most cruel treachery perpetrated at that time against Count Baldwin. This Count Baldwin, brother of the count of Toulouse and cousin of the king of France, far removed from his brother’s wickedness and exerting himself with all his strength in Christ’s warfare, assisted Count Montfort and Christendom against his brother and the other enemies of the faith, as far as he was able. One day, namely the Monday after the first Sunday of Lent, the aforesaid count came to a certain castle in the diocese of Cahors, called Olima. Immediately the knights of that castle, who were men of the count himself, sent to the raiders and to certain native knights, most wicked traitors, who were in a neighbouring castle called Mont-Léonard; and they informed them that Count Baldwin was at Olima, directing them to come and that they would hand over Count Baldwin to them without any difficulty. They reported the same thing to a most wicked but secret traitor, namely Raterius of Castelnau. This Raterius had long before entered into an alliance with Count Montfort and had sworn him fealty. Count Baldwin too trusted him as though he were a friend. What more? He came at once; and Count Baldwin, secure as being among his own people, gave himself to sleep and rest.

There was with Count Baldwin a French knight named William of Contris, to whom Count Montfort had given a castle called Sarracenum. A French serjeant also held the castle called Moissac. While the count and those with him rested, separated from one another in different houses, the lord of the castle seized the key of the chamber in which Count Baldwin slept, locked the door, and hastened out of the castle to the aforesaid Raterius and the raiders. Showing them the key, he said: “Why do you delay? Behold, your enemy is in your hands. Make haste, and I shall hand him over to you asleep and unarmed; and not him alone, but I shall hand over to you several more of your enemies.” Hearing this, the raiders rejoiced and hurried together with the greatest speed to the gates of Olima.

Immediately the lord of the castle—who was the leader of those intending to seize the count, another Judas indeed—summoned the inhabitants of the castle in utmost secrecy and carefully asked each one how many of Count Baldwin’s companions lodged with him. Having made this careful inquiry, he stationed at the doors of the houses twice as many armed raiders as there were of our men sleeping unarmed. At once innumerable candles were lit, a cry was raised, and the enemies rushed upon our unprepared men. Raterius of Castelnau and the aforesaid lord of the castle came to the chamber where the noble Count Baldwin slept; opening the door, they seized him asleep and unarmed—indeed naked. Some of our men throughout the castle were killed, others captured, while a number escaped with the aid of flight.

Nor should it be passed over that they killed in that same church one of our men whom they had taken alive and had made secure in life and limb by an oath, while he was afterward hiding there. Having seized Count Baldwin, the enemies led him to one of the count’s own castles, called Mont-Ève, in the territory of Cahors. The men of the castle, being utterly wicked, gladly received the raiders who were leading their lord captive. The raiders immediately told Count Baldwin to cause the tower of the castle, which certain Frenchmen held by his command, to be surrendered to them. But the count most strictly forbade those Frenchmen to surrender the tower on any account, even if they should see the count himself hanging from the gallows; rather, they were to defend themselves most resolutely until they received aid from the noble Count Montfort. O courage of a prince! O wondrous strength of mind!

On hearing this, the raiders were greatly enraged and made the count fast for two days. When these had passed, the count summoned a most diligent chaplain and made a full confession to him. This done, he requested communion of the body of Jesus Christ. But while the chaplain was bringing the sacraments of the divine mystery, a most wicked raider came in, swearing and solemnly declaring that Count Baldwin should neither eat nor drink until he surrendered a certain raider whom he had captured and caused to be kept in chains. To this the count replied: “O most cruel man, did I ask for an abundance of bread or wine, or for a morsel of meat? I sought communion in the divine mystery not for the sustenance of my body, but for the salvation of my soul.” Again the executioner began, with vehement assertions, to swear that he should neither eat nor drink unless he did what he demanded. To this the noble man replied again: “Since I am not permitted to receive communion in the divine sacraments, let the Eucharist at least be shown to me—my salvation—so that in this life I may behold my Saviour.” When the chaplain lifted it up and displayed it, the count adored it with the greatest devotion.

While this was taking place, those who were in the tower of the castle, through fear of death, surrendered the tower to the raiders, having first received their oath that they would allow them to depart safe and unharmed. But those most wicked traitors, scorning the sanctity of their oath, immediately condemned them to the most shameful death on the gallows. This done, they seized Count Baldwin and led him to a castle of the count of Toulouse called Mont-Alban, where they kept him in chains while awaiting the arrival of the count of Toulouse.

After a few days the count of Toulouse came, bringing with him those most wicked traitors: namely, the count of Foix and his son Roger Bernard, and a knight from the land of the king of Aragon, called Bernard of Portellis. At once, by command of the count of Toulouse, the most noble Count Baldwin was brought out from the castle of Mont-Alban. Who could ever read or hear without tears what follows? Immediately the count of Foix, his son—who had not fallen short of his father’s wickedness—and Bernard of Portellis tied a rope around the neck of that most noble man, intending to hang him by the will—indeed by the command—of the count of Toulouse. Seeing this, that most Christian man urgently and humbly requested confession and the viaticum; but those most cruel dogs utterly refused him both. Then the soldier of Christ said: “Since I am not permitted to present myself to a priest, God is my witness that with ready and ardent will I have always defended Christendom and my lord Count Montfort, and that for this defence and in this defence I wish to die.” He had scarcely finished speaking when the three aforesaid traitors lifted him from the ground and hanged him from a walnut tree.

O unheard-of cruelty! O another Cain—indeed, a Cain far worse: I mean the count of Toulouse, for whom it was not enough to kill his brother, and such a brother, unless he condemned him to the unheard-of cruelty of this death!

## CHAPTER LXXVI. Aymericus and the citizens of Narbonne admit the enemies of Count Montfort into the city; on that account the count devastates the territory of Narbonne.

[Col. 0682D]

At about the same time Aymericus, lord of Narbonne, and the citizens of Narbonne, who had never loved the cause of Jesus Christ, in order to bring forth the iniquity which they had conceived long before, openly withdrew from God. They received into their city raiders, together with Aragonese and Catalans, so that through them they might, if possible, expel the noble Count Montfort. For the Aragonese and Catalans pursued the said count in vengeance for their king. The people of Narbonne committed this wickedness not because the count injured them or had injured them in any respect, but because they thought that crusaders would no longer come. Yet He who catches the wise in their own craftiness ordained otherwise.

For while all the enemies of ours whom we have mentioned were gathered at Narbonne in order to make a united attack upon our count and the few who were with him, behold, pilgrims suddenly came from France: namely William des Barres, a man of proven knighthood, and many knights with him. Joined and aided by them, our count came near Narbonne; ranging through and devastating the land of Aymericus, lord of Narbonne, he captured almost all his castles. One day our count determined to ride before Narbonne. When all his men had armed and three battle-lines had been arrayed, the count himself approached the gate of the city in the first line. Our enemies had come out of the city and stood in the gateway.

Then the unconquered knight, our count, sought suddenly to leap upon them by a steep and inaccessible place. But the enemies, standing on high ground, struck him with so many lances that the saddle of the horse upon which he sat broke, and he fell from his horse. Immediately enemies rushed from every side to capture or kill the count, while our men came to protect him. Yet by the grace of God, after much exertion, our men bravely raised up the count. After this William, who was in the rearmost line, and all our men made an attack upon the enemies and compelled them swiftly to enter the city. This done, the count and our men returned to the place from which they had come that day.

## CHAPTER LXXVII. Peter of Benevento, cardinal and legate of the Apostolic See, reconciles the counts of Foix and Comminges to the Church.

[Col. 0683C]

While these things were being done, Master Peter of Benevento, cardinal and legate of the Apostolic See, was coming to the region of Narbonne, sent by the lord pope to arrange matters of peace and faith. When the legate heard the conduct of the people of Narbonne, he sent them word and strictly commanded them to maintain a firm truce with Count Montfort until he himself arrived. He similarly commanded our count not to harm the people of Narbonne in any way. A few days later the legate came and entered Narbonne, having first seen our count and held a careful conference with him.

Immediately the enemies of the faith came to him: namely the counts of Comminges and Foix, and many others who, owing to their deserts, had been disinherited, intending to petition the legate for restoration. The wise and discerning legate reconciled them all, receiving from them not only sworn security that they would obey the command of the Church, but also certain very strong castles which still remained in the possession of the aforesaid enemies.

While matters stood thus, the men of Moissac treacherously handed over the town of Moissac to the count of Toulouse. But those who were in the town on the side of our count withdrew into a rather weak and unfortified stronghold of the town. The count of Toulouse, with a great multitude of raiders, began to attack that stronghold for three uninterrupted weeks; but our besieged men, though very few, defended themselves bravely. Hearing this, the noble count immediately hurried to aid the besieged. But the count of Toulouse and those with him—and also many of the inhabitants of the said town, who had been the principal perpetrators and instigators of the treachery—having learned beforehand of our count’s approach, fled with the utmost haste, abandoning the siege which they had maintained for so long.

Our count and those with him, hearing that the aforesaid enemies had fled, went down into the Agenais, in order, if possible, to take by assault a castle called Mansum, on the extreme border of the diocese of Agen, which had apostatized that same year. For John, king of England, who had always opposed the cause of Jesus Christ and Count Montfort, had gone that year towards the Agenais. Many of the nobler men of that land, hoping for his assistance, withdrew from God and from the lordship of Count Montfort; but afterwards, through God’s grace, they were disappointed of their hope.

Our count therefore hurried with his men toward the aforesaid castle and came to a place where he had to cross the Garonne. He had only a few unprotected little boats. But the men of La Réole, a castle of the king of England, had embarked with many ships and arms in order to prevent our men’s crossing. Nevertheless, our men entered the water and crossed freely despite them. Coming to the aforesaid castle, namely Mansum, they attacked it for three days. But because they had no engines, and the count could not establish a siege there, since by command of the legate he had to return to the region of Narbonne, he withdrew from the aforesaid castle towards Narbonne.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. The bishop of Carcassonne returns from France with a huge multitude of pilgrims.

In the year of the Incarnate Word 1214, the venerable bishop of Carcassonne, who throughout the preceding year had laboured in the regions of Gaul, travelling about and preaching for the cause of the faith against heretics, set out for the Albigensian country around the octave of Easter Sunday. For he had fixed a day of departure for all the crusaders—both those whom he had signed and those who had received the cross from the hand of Master James of Vitry, a man praiseworthy in every respect, and from certain others—so that they might gather together during the fortnight after Easter and set out with him through the region of Lyons against the pestilential heretics.

But Master Robert of Courçon, legate of the Apostolic See, and the venerable Archdeacon William had appointed a day for their crusaders to be at Béziers during the fortnight after Easter, intending to set out against the aforesaid heretics by another route. Thus the bishop of Carcassonne and the aforesaid pilgrims set out from Nevers and, with a favourable journey, arrived at Montpellier. I myself was with the bishop of Carcassonne. There we found the archdeacon of Paris and the pilgrims who had come with him from the regions of Gaul. The cardinal, namely Master Robert of Courçon, was occupied with certain business in the region of Le Puy.

Setting out from Montpellier, we came near Béziers to the castle of Saint-Thibéry; and there the noble Count Montfort met us. We pilgrims, horsemen and footmen alike, numbered about one hundred thousand, among whom was the viscount of the castle of Dun, one of the knights, together with many other knights whom there is no need to enumerate individually. Proceeding from the region of Béziers, we came to Carcassonne and remained there for a few days.

It is especially to be observed, and the whole course of that year should be regarded as a miracle, as we said above. When the aforementioned Peter of Benevento came into the Albigensian land, Aragonese and Catalans were gathered at Narbonne against Christendom and Count Montfort; and for this reason our count was near Narbonne and could not often go far away, since the enemies would immediately devastate all the surrounding country. Moreover, the people of Toulouse, the Aragonese, and the people of Cahors were waging very grievous wars against him from distant places.

While the athlete of Christ was in this tribulation, there did not fail him “a helper in due time, in tribulation” (Psalm IX). For in one and the same period of time the legate came from the Roman curia and pilgrims came from France. O great abundance of God’s mercy! For the pilgrims, as many thought, could have accomplished nothing great without the legate; nor could the legate have advanced so far without the pilgrims. If the enemies of the faith had not feared the pilgrims, they would not have obeyed the legate; conversely, had the legate not come, the pilgrims who then arrived could have made little headway against so many and such great enemies. Thus divine providence acted mercifully: while the legate drew in and restrained, by a pious stratagem, the enemies of the faith gathered at Narbonne, Count Montfort and the pilgrims who had come from France were able to pass into the regions of Cahors and Agen and attack their own enemies—or rather, Christ’s enemies. O pious stratagem of the legate! O stratagem of mercy!

## CHAPTER LXXIX. Guy of Montfort and the pilgrims invade and devastate the lands of Raterius of Castelnau.

[Col. 0685D]

After the aforesaid pilgrims had spent a few days at Carcassonne, the noble Count Montfort requested that, with the bishop of Carcassonne and Guy of Montfort, the count’s own brother, they should proceed into the regions of Rodez and Cahors, in order utterly to devastate the lands both of Raterius of Castelnau—who had most cruelly betrayed the most noble and most Christian Count Baldwin—and of the other enemies of Christ.

The count himself, with his eldest son Amaury, went down as far as Valence, and there found the duke of Burgundy and the Dauphin. After consultation and agreement concerning the aforesaid marriage, our count—because the time was not suitable for contracting it, and because, owing to the many necessities of war, he could not remain there many days—took the said girl with him to Carcassonne, where the wedding was celebrated.

The pilgrims, who had long since left Carcassonne and had already entered the diocese of Cahors, devastated the lands of the enemies of the faith, which had been abandoned empty through fear of them. Nor should it be passed over that, when we were passing through the diocese of Rodez, we came to a castle called Mauriliac. Its inhabitants wished to resist us, because the castle was of remarkable strength and wholly inaccessible. In our army was Master Robert of Courçon, legate of the Apostolic See, of whom we have spoken above, who had very recently come from the regions of Gaul. Immediately upon his arrival our men approached the castle and began to attack their enemies fiercely. Seeing that they could resist no longer, the inhabitants surrendered themselves that same day to the legate, entirely at his will; and, by the legate’s will, our men utterly destroyed the castle.

Nor should it be left unsaid that there we found seven heretics of the sect called that of the Waldensians. Brought before the legate, they more fully confessed their unbelief; our pilgrims seized them and burned them with great rejoicing.

After this, our count was informed that certain knights of Agen, who had withdrawn from his lordship in the preceding year, had fortified a castle called Monspisatus. What more? We came to besiege it. But the aforesaid knights of Monspisatus, hearing of the crusaders’ arrival, fled in fear, leaving the castle empty; and our men, coming to the castle, utterly destroyed it. Setting out from Monspisatus, our count proceeded further through the diocese of Agen in order to occupy the castles which had withdrawn from his lordship in the preceding year. But all his adversaries, moved by fear, surrendered to him before the count came to them, except for a certain noble place called Marmande.

For greater security, lest they should apostatize again as was their custom, the count had almost all their towers and walls demolished, except for a few of the stronger castles, which he wished to fortify and retain both for himself and for the French. Coming to besiege the castle of Marmande, the count found it fortified against him. For a knight of the king of England had brought certain serjeants into the castle and placed his banner upon its summit in order to defend it against our men. But when our men drew near and, at their very arrival, reached the walls, after a slight defence they began to flee from the castle. Taking to boats, they swiftly went down the river Garonne to a nearby castle of the king of England called La Réole. The serjeants of the king of England who had come to defend the castle escaped to safety. Our men entered the castle and plundered all its goods; but the count allowed the serjeants of the king of England who were in the tower to depart alive and unharmed.

After this, his men advised the count not to destroy the castle utterly, because it was rather noble and stood at the edge of his land. They advised him to fortify the greater tower, but to demolish the other towers and part of the walls. This done, the count returned to Agen.

There was a noble and very strong castle called Casseneuil in the territory of Agen. It stood at the foot of a certain mountain in a most pleasant plain, surrounded by flowing waters and natural rocks. In that castle was one of the principal seats of the heretics, and it had been so from ancient times. The inhabitants of that castle were for the most part robbers and perjurers, filled with every iniquity and kind of sin. They had already once and twice surrendered themselves to Christendom, and now for a third time they attempted to resist Christendom and our count.

The lord of that castle was Hugh of Rominiac the elder, brother of the bishop of Agen. He had been an intimate and friend of the count; but that year, breaking their friendship and his oath, he had treacherously withdrawn from God and from the aforesaid count. Very many other traitors had also assembled in that castle. Therefore the noble Count Montfort came with his army before the castle on the vigil of the Apostles Peter and Paul, and established a siege on one side of it, upon the mountain; for his army was not sufficient to besiege the castle all around.

A few days later the count had engines erected to destroy the castle walls. Firing continuously both at the walls and within the castle, those engines soon destroyed many houses of the castle. After several days, when pilgrims arrived, the count descended from the mountain and pitched tents on the plain near the castle, taking part of the army with him. Many, however, remained on the mountain with Amaury, the count’s most noble and valiant young son, and with Guy, the venerable bishop of Carcassonne, who there performed the office of legate and laboured most urgently and effectively for the conquest and capture of the castle.

The count also had engines called stone-throwers erected in the plain where he was stationed; firing day and night, they greatly weakened the castle walls. One night toward dawn, many of the adversaries came out of the castle and ascended the mountain, intending to make a united attack upon the army. Coming to the tent in which Amaury, the count’s son, slept, they rushed upon it with great force, intending if possible to capture or kill him. But our men ran up, attacked the enemies bravely, and compelled them to return to their castle.

While these things were being done in that siege, John, king of England, grieving over the disinheritance of his nephew, namely the son of the count of Toulouse, and envying our successes, came near those parts, namely to the city of Périgueux, with a very great army. Many enemies had fled to him, who, owing to their sins, had been disinherited by God’s just judgement; the king received them and maintained them for a long time, not without scandal to many and grave loss to his own reputation. Those besieged in the castle frequently sent messengers to the aforesaid king, asking for aid; and he greatly encouraged them through messengers and promises.

What more? A widespread report arose in our army that the aforesaid king intended to attack us—and perhaps he would have done so, had he dared. But the most valiant Count Montfort was in no way terrified by what he heard. He firmly resolved that, if the king wished to attack the army, he would not therefore withdraw from the siege; rather, defending himself and his men, he would fight against him. But the aforesaid king, adopting a wiser plan, attempted nothing of what was said, and perhaps what he had intended, to do.

Nor should it be omitted that Master Robert of Courçon, cardinal and legate of the Apostolic See, of whom we have spoken above, came to the army at the siege of Casseneuil. Staying there a few days, he laboured, as far as he could, being a man of good will, for the capture of the castle; but recalled by the affairs of the legation entrusted to him, he did not wait until the castle was taken.

While our men laboured in that siege and the castle walls had been greatly weakened by the shots of the engines, one night the count summoned the leading men of the army and a certain skilled carpenter. He asked the craftsman how our men might approach the walls and take the castle by assault. For there was deep water between the army and the castle, which our men had to cross if they wished to approach the walls; and there was no bridge, because the adversaries had destroyed it on the outer side before our arrival.

After many had said many things, they finally agreed, on the advice of the said craftsman, that a bridge of timbers and hurdles should be made, which, propelled over large casks by a remarkable device, would carry our men across the water. Immediately the venerable bishop of Carcassonne, who laboured day and night so that an advance might be made in all the things needed for the siege, summoned a multitude of pilgrims and had an abundance of timber brought for making the bridge.

When the bridge had been completed, our men armed themselves and prepared for an assault; pushing the bridge forward, they brought it as far as the water. But as soon as the bridge touched the water, because of its weight and because the bank on the other side was high, it slid down to the bottom with such force that it could by no means be drawn back or raised. Thus all our labour on that bridge was dashed to pieces in a moment.

A few days later our men made a bridge of another kind, in hopes that they might cross the water by means of it. They also prepared a few little boats, through which, though at great risk, part of our men might cross. When everything was ready, our men armed themselves, drew the bridge toward the water, and others embarked on the boats. But those in the castle had many stone-throwers and fired most persistently and vigorously upon our men.

What more? Our men cast the bridge over the water; but they gained nothing, because that little bridge was far too short and wholly inadequate. There was mourning and lamentation among our men, joy and exultation among the enemies.

Yet the most steadfast count conceived no despair from what had happened. He summoned his craftsmen, comforted them, and ordered them to attempt to devise engines for crossing the water. The master craftsman conceived a remarkable and unprecedented type of engine. He had much large timber brought, and first constructed upon the largest timbers something like a spacious wooden house, roofed with hurdles—not a peaked roof, but a flat one. Then, in the middle of the roof, he raised something like a very high tower of timbers and hurdles, having five storeys in height, in which crossbowmen could stand.

After this, around that tower, he made upon the aforesaid roof something like a wall of hurdles, where many of our men could stand to defend the tower. They had much water in large casks, so that they might extinguish any fire cast by the enemies. Moreover, lest the enemies be able to burn that engine, the craftsman had its entire front covered with ox-hides.

When all was ready, our men began to draw and push the engine toward the water. The enemies, on the other hand, hurled large and very frequent stones with their stone-throwers, but by God’s grace caused little or no harm. When our men had pushed the engine as far as the water, they brought earth, timber, and such materials in baskets to cast into the water. Those beneath the lower roof, safe and unarmed, filled up the ditch, while the crossbowmen and others stationed in the upper fortifications checked the attacks of the enemy.

One night certain adversaries filled a little boat with dry wood, salted meat, fat, and other inflammable materials, intending to drive it against our engine and burn it. But they could not do so, because our serjeants burned that little boat. What more? While our men laboured to fill the ditch, our engine passed over dry and unharmed. For as much as they filled of the ditch, so much farther did they push the engine.

One Sunday, seeing the engine crossing and perceiving the danger of capture threatening them, the adversaries cast fire against the engine. But since our men extinguished the fire with water, they could accomplish nothing. Our men and the adversaries were now close together and attacked one another with lances. Our count, therefore, fearing that perhaps the adversaries might burn the engine during the night, had his men arm that same Sunday toward evening and summoned all to the assault with trumpets sounding.

The bishop of Carcassonne and the clerics who were in the army with him gathered at a higher place near the castle, to cry aloud to heaven and pray for our fighting men. Then our men entered the engine and, breaking through its front hurdles, crossed the ditch with great bravery. Meanwhile our clerics sang *Veni, Creator Spiritus* (“Come, Creator Spirit”) with the greatest devotion. Seeing our men rushing in, the adversaries withdrew within the walls and began fiercely to assail our men from above the walls with a constant shower of stones. But since night was approaching and they had no ladders, our men could not climb the walls. Standing in a small level space between the walls and the ditch, they destroyed that night the barbicans which the enemies had made outside the walls.

The next day our craftsmen laboured the whole day in making ladders and other engines, so that on the third day they might scale the castle by assault. Learning and fearing this, the raider-knights who were in the castle came out on the following night with arms as though to attack the army, and all fled. Many of our men pursued them for a long time but could not catch them. The rest came to the castle at midnight, entered it by force, set it on fire, and put to the sword all whom they could find. Blessed in all things be God, who delivered up the wicked, even if not all of them.

After this, our count had the walls of the castle almost levelled to the ground all around. Thus Casseneuil was taken and destroyed on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September [17 August], to the praise of our Lord, to whom be honour and glory for ever and ever.

## CHAPTER LXXX. On the destruction of the castle of Doma in the diocese of Périgueux, belonging to the most wicked tyrant G. de Cahusac.

[Col. 0690C]

With these things having been done, it was reported to our count that in the bishopric of Périgueux there were castles inhabited by enemies of peace and faith; and indeed it was so. The count therefore resolved to advance and attack the castles, so that, by God’s grace and the assistance of the pilgrims, having expelled the brigands and banished the robbers, he might leave peace to the churches—indeed, to the whole land of Périgord. But all the adversaries of Christ and of our noble count, hearing that Casseneuil had been taken, were struck with such fear that they dared await neither the count’s nor the army’s arrival in any fortress, however strong.

Accordingly, the army moved from Casseneuil [Col. 0690D] and came to one of the castles, called Domme, which it found empty and without a defender. It was a noble and exceedingly strong castle, situated above the River Dordogne in a most pleasant place. At once our count caused the castle’s tower, which was very lofty and beautiful and fortified almost to its summit, to be undermined and pulled down. Half a league away was another castle of remarkable strength, called Montfort. Its lord, Bernard de Casuac, a most cruel man and the worst of all men, had fled from the face of our count in fear, leaving his castle empty. So numerous and great were the cruelties, robberies, and enormities of that utterly wicked and criminal man that they could scarcely be believed or even imagined.

[Col. 0691A] Since he was such a man, the devil had procured for him a helper like himself: namely, his wife, who was the sister of the viscount of Turenne. This second Jezebel—indeed far worse and more cruel than Jezebel—was the worst of all wicked women, no less than her husband in cruelty and wickedness. Thus, since both were utterly depraved, they despoiled—rather, destroyed—churches; attacked pilgrims; and mutilated innocent persons’ limbs. So it was that in one monastery of Black Monks, called Sarlat, our men found one hundred and fifty men and women who had been mutilated by the aforesaid tyrant and his wife: their hands or feet had been cut off, their eyes gouged out, or their other limbs severed. This tyrant’s wife herself, forgetting all compassion, had poor [Col. 0691B] women’s breasts torn out or their thumbs cut off, so that they might thereby be rendered incapable of work. O unheard-of cruelty! But, passing these matters over, since we could not express even a thousandth part of the wicked deeds of the said tyrant and his wife, let us return to our subject.

Domme having therefore been destroyed and overthrown, our count wished to demolish Montfort, which, as we have said, belonged to the aforesaid tyrant. Immediately the bishop of Carcassonne, who devoted all his efforts to the cause of Christ, took with him a part of the pilgrims, went there, and had that castle pulled down. Its walls were so very strong that they could scarcely be demolished, because the mortar had hardened into stone [Col. 0691C]; hence our men had to spend many days demolishing the castle. The pilgrims went out to work in the morning and returned in the evening to the place where the army was encamped. The army had not left Domme, since the site was more suitable and convenient for it.

Moreover, near Montfort was another castle, called Castrumnovum, no less wicked than the others; it too had been abandoned through fear of the army. Our count resolved to hold and occupy that castle, in order that by these means he might better restrain the disturbers of the peace; and as he conceived it, so he did. There was besides a fourth rather strong castle, called Baenatium. Its lord was a most wicked man and a most grievous oppressor of churches. Our count gave him the choice [Col. 0691D] of one of two alternatives: either within a term fixed by the count and those present there he should restore what he had wrongfully taken, or the walls of his castle should be lowered. A truce of several days was granted for carrying this out. But since within those days he had made no restitution of his plunder, our count would not spare the fortifications of Baenatium; and, against the tyrant’s will and to his great grief, our count had the tower and walls of Baenatium lowered. For the oft-mentioned criminal alleged that his castle ought not to be lowered, because he alone in that land was one who would aid the king of France against the king of England. But the count, knowing those allegations to be empty and frivolous, did not desist from his purpose. Indeed, the aforesaid allegations [Col. 0692A] had already been presented by the said tyrant to the king of France, but he was unable to accomplish anything.

In this way those four castles—Domme, Montfort, Castrumnovum, and Baenatium—were subdued. In these four castles, for a hundred years and more, Satan had had his seat; from them wickedness had gone forth over the face of the land. Thus, after they had been subdued through the labor of the pilgrims and the thoroughly proven excellence of Count Montfort, peace and tranquillity were restored not only to the people of Périgord, but also in great measure to those of Cahors, Agen, and Limoges.

After these things had been done to the glory of Christ’s name, our count and the army returned to the region of Agen; and, having the opportunity, he caused the strongholds throughout the diocese [Col. 0692B] of Agen to be demolished. Afterwards the count came to Figeac, to hear, in the king of France’s place, the causes and disputes of the inhabitants, for the king had entrusted him with his authority in many matters in those regions. He heard much and corrected much, and would have corrected more, but did not wish to exceed the limits of the royal commission.

Proceeding thence toward the diocese of Rodez, he occupied a very strong castle near Figeac, called Capdenac, where from ancient times the nest and refuge of brigands had been. From there the count came with the army to the city of Rodez. The count made many claims against the count of Rodez. For the latter was the liege man of our count; but seeking some evasion, he said that he held the greater [Col. 0692C] part of his land from the king of England. What more need be said? After many disputes, he acknowledged that he held all his land from our count and did homage to him for all of it; and so they became friends and were reconciled.

Near Rodez was a strong castle called Sévérac, inhabited by brigands and disturbers. So many and such great evils proceeded from that castle that they could not easily be described. Those in it harassed not only the diocese of Rodez, but the whole surrounding country as far as Le Puy of Blessed Mary. While our count was at Rodez, he ordered the lord of the castle to surrender the castle to him. But the latter, relying on the strength of the fortification and also thinking that at that season the count could not [Col. 0692D] maintain a siege around the castle—because it was winter and the castle stood in mountainous, cold country—refused to surrender it.

One night Guy de Montfort, our count’s full brother, took knights and sergeants with him, departed from the city of Rodez, and rode by night to near the aforesaid castle. At earliest dawn, as daylight broke, he suddenly rushed into the lower borough, immediately began to occupy it, and took it. The inhabitants of the borough withdrew into the lower fortification. The fortress stood on the summit of the mountain, while the outer borough stretched down the slope from that fortification. Guy occupied [Col. 0693A] the borough so that the enemy, when the army arrived, could not burn it.

When the count came with the army to the castle of Sévérac, he found the said borough unharmed and many houses suitable for the army’s lodging. Our men occupied these and established the siege. This was the Lord’s doing: He is a true helper in time of need and a merciful provider in necessity. After a few days they set up an engine called a stone-thrower and began hurling stones against the castle. The enemy likewise set up an engine and with it harassed our men as much as they could.

Nor should it be left unmentioned that the Lord had reduced those besieged to such scarcity of provisions that extreme want constrained them. Moreover, the cold and harshness of winter afflicted them so greatly—for they had only scant and very poor clothing—that they did not know what to do. [Col. 0693B] If anyone wonders at their poverty and misery, let him know that they had been caught so suddenly that they had not been allowed to provision themselves either with arms or food. For, as we have said, they did not think that our men could maintain a siege in midwinter and in such cold places.

After a few days, afflicted by hunger, thirst, cold, and nakedness, they asked for peace. What more need be said? After long and varied discussion about the terms of settlement, at last, on the counsel of prudent men, our side and the lord of the castle agreed that he should surrender the castle to the count, and that the count should entrust the castle to the bishop of Rodez and to a certain noble knight called Peter Brimund [Col. 0693C] for safekeeping. And so it was done.

Immediately the noble count, out of pure generosity, restored to the aforesaid lord of Sévérac all the rest of his land which Guy de Montfort had occupied. Yet before restoring his land, he induced him not to harm his own men because they had surrendered to the said Guy. Afterwards the noble count, most generous as he was, also restored Sévérac to him, having received from him an oath and pledge of homage; and so he was received into the count’s favor and intimacy. Nor should it be omitted that, through the surrender of Sévérac, peace and quiet were restored to all that country. In all things God is to be praised, and His most faithful champion embraced—namely, the most Christian Count [Col. 0693D] of Montfort.

When all these things had duly been accomplished, Master Peter of Benevento, legate of the Apostolic See, of whom we have spoken above, returned from the regions of Aragon, where he had made a long stay on serious business. He summoned a most celebrated and very general council at Montpellier during the fortnight following the Lord’s Nativity.

## CHAPTER LXXXI. The legate holds a council at Montpellier, attended by five archbishops and twenty-eight bishops, concerning lordship over the conquered land; with the unanimous voice and consent of the whole council, the Count of Montfort is made prince of the entire land.

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1214, during the fortnight following the Lord’s Nativity, the archbishops and bishops summoned by Master Peter of Benevento, legate of the Apostolic See, assembled at Montpellier [Col. 0694A] for a council, so that the same legate, according to the counsel of the prelates, might make arrangements concerning matters of peace and faith.

Five archbishops assembled at that council: Narbonne, first; Auch, second; Embrun, third; Arles, fourth; Aix, fifth. There were twenty-eight bishops, and many of the barons of the land were also present. But the noble Count of Montfort did not enter Montpellier with the others. During the days of the council he remained in a nearby castle belonging to the bishop of Maguelonne. The men of Montpellier, being most wicked and arrogant, had always hated the count and all Frenchmen, so that they did not permit the count himself [Col. 0694B] to enter Montpellier. For this reason he remained, as we have said, in the aforesaid castle, and daily came as far as Montpellier, to the house of the brethren of the Order of the Temple outside the walls. There [lacuna] archbishops and bishops went out to him whenever necessary.

Accordingly, when the legate, archbishops, bishops, abbots, and other prelates of churches had assembled at Montpellier as stated above, the legate delivered a sermon in the church of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Afterwards, in the house where he was staying, he summoned the five archbishops, the twenty-eight bishops, innumerable abbots and other prelates of churches. When they had gathered together, he first addressed them in these words:

> “I repeat and require of you, under the attestation of divine judgment and by the obligation of obedience by which you are bound to the Roman Church [Col. 0694C], that, putting aside all favor, hatred, and envy, you give us faithful counsel, according to your knowledge, as to whom Toulouse, which the count of Toulouse held, and the other lands occupied by the armies of Christian crusaders, ought most advantageously and usefully to be granted and assigned, for the honor of God and holy mother Church, for the peace of the land, and for the overthrow or cleansing away of the filth of heretics.”

All the archbishops and bishops deliberated long and carefully, each with the abbots of his diocese and his household clerics. Since it seemed good and right, they reduced their decision to writing; and at last the votes and counsels of every one of them concurred in choosing the noble Count [Col. 0694D] of Montfort as prince and monarch of that whole land.

O marvelous event! If a bishop or abbot is to be created, the assent of even a very few people scarcely agrees on one person. But behold: in the election of a prince for the land, so many and such great persons unanimously bestowed their votes upon the aforesaid champion of Christ without any dissent. This was undoubtedly done by God, and is marvelous in our eyes.

Therefore, after the archbishops and bishops had chosen the most noble count in the manner described, they most urgently requested the legate immediately to deliver the whole land to that count. But on consulting the letters which the lord pope had sent to the legate, it was found that the legate could not do this without consulting the lord pope. For this reason, [Col. 0695A] with the common assent both of the legates and of the prelates, Gérard, archbishop of Embrun, a man of much learning and every virtue, was sent to Rome together with certain clerics. They carried letters from both the legate and the prelates, in which all the prelates urgently begged the lord pope to grant to them as lord and monarch of the land the noble Count of Montfort, whom they had unanimously chosen.

We do not think it should be passed over that, while the said council was being held at Montpellier, one day the legate had our count, who was outside the walls in the house of the Order of the Temple, summoned to enter and come to himself and the prelates. The count at once entered with a few men. [Col. 0695B] While his knights, who had entered with him in small number, were wandering about the town, the count was with the legate and prelates, together with his two sons. Immediately the townsmen, being most wicked, armed themselves secretly in great numbers. Entering the church of Blessed Mary, after the count had come in, they watched the whole route by which they thought he would return and waited for his return, intending to kill him if they could. But the merciful Lord ordered matters otherwise, and far better. Our count learned what was happening and, departing by a route other than that by which he had entered, avoided the ambush.

When all this had duly been done and the council had been held for many days, the prelates present returned to their own homes. The legate and our count came to Carcassonne. Meanwhile [Col. 0695C] the legate sent the bishop of Toulouse to Toulouse, so that on his behalf he might occupy and fortify the Château Narbonnais—for this was the name of the stronghold and palace of the count of Toulouse. At the command of the lord legate—or rather, out of fear of him—the citizens of Toulouse caused the count of Toulouse’s son to leave the aforesaid fortification, which they had hitherto held, and handed it over on the legate’s behalf to their bishop. Entering the stronghold, he held it and garrisoned it with knights and sergeants, though at the citizens’ expense and cost.

## CHAPTER LXXXII. The first arrival of Louis, son of the king of France, in the Albigensian regions.

In the year of the Incarnate Word 1215, Louis, firstborn son of the king [Col. 0695D] of France, who three years previously had taken the cross against the heretics but had been hindered by many serious wars, set out for the Albigensian regions to fulfill the vow of his pilgrimage. The many and very serious wars which his father had waged against his enemies had for the most part been quieted. Many noble and powerful men came with Louis, all of whom assembled at Lyons on the day appointed by him, Easter Sunday.

There were with Louis Philip, bishop of Beauvais; the count of Saint-Pol; Walter, count of Ponthieu; Robert, count of Sées (Seez) and Alençon; Guichard of Beaujeu; Matthew of Montmorency; the viscount of Melun; and many other worthy, noble, and powerful knights. Also present [Col. 0696A] was the venerable Guy, bishop of Carcassonne, who shortly before, at the request of the noble Count of Montfort, had gone down into the French regions for the cause of the faith and was coming with Louis. Louis and those with him loved him most tenderly and in everything deferred to his will and counsel.

On the day after Easter, the bishop and his party set out from Lyons and came to Vienne. The Count of Montfort came joyfully and gladly to meet his lord Louis, and had descended as far as Vienne. How great was the rejoicing at that mutual meeting and sight cannot easily be expressed. Louis proceeded with his companions from Vienne and came to Valence. The legate mentioned above, Master Peter of Benevento, came to meet Louis and had reached Valence. [Col. 0696B]

As we have explained above, the said legate had absolved the citizens of Toulouse and Narbonne and others who had opposed Christendom and Count Montfort, by his own secret and prudent counsel, as he knew how. Moreover, he held in his own hand and protection the cities of Toulouse and Narbonne and the other castles of Christ’s enemies in the Albigensian regions. He feared that Louis, as firstborn of the king of France and principal lord of all the land held by the legate, might wish to do something by authority contrary to the legate’s counsel and ordinance—either by occupying the cities and castles held by the legate or even by destroying them. Therefore, as was said and was plausible, the arrival and [Col. 0696C] presence of Louis did not please the legate; nor is this surprising. For since the whole oft-mentioned land had been infected with the poison of heretical depravity, the king of France, as principal lord, had been warned and repeatedly asked to apply a remedial hand to so great a disease and to undertake to purge his realm of heretical filth. But he had not offered the counsel or help that he should have done. Therefore, when that land had been acquired by the lord pope through the aid of those who had taken the cross, it did not seem to the legate that Louis either ought or could attempt anything contrary to his arrangements. It also seemed to the legate that Louis had taken the cross and came as a pilgrim; therefore he ought not in any matter to oppose the legate’s direction.

Louis, however, being gentle and most gracious, [Col. 0696D] replied to the legate that he would conform himself to the legate’s will and counsel. Leaving Valence, Louis came to the town of Saint-Gilles. While Louis was in Saint-Gilles, with the noble Count of Montfort also there, messengers came from the Roman curia. As mentioned above, the legate and the archbishops and bishops of Provence had sent them to the lord pope, asking that the most noble and Christian Count of Montfort be made lord and monarch there.

The lord pope sent letters in the same form to the legate, the prelates, and also the Count of Montfort. They stated that the lord pope entrusted to Count Montfort’s care the whole land held by the count of Toulouse, as well as those lands which the crusaders had acquired and which the legate held [Col. 0697A] through hostages and guardians, until the general council which he had summoned at Rome for the Kalends of November of that year, when fuller arrangements would be made concerning the aforesaid lands. On hearing this, Louis and our count informed the legate of the arrival of the messengers. At that time the legate was near Saint-Gilles with several bishops in the city of Arles.

The form of the lord pope’s letter to the Count of Montfort is as follows:

> INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the nobleman S., Count of Montfort: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> We commend your nobility with worthy praises in the Lord, because with pure love, sincere mind, and unwearying strength, as a true and valiant soldier of Christ and invincible defender of the Catholic faith, you fight the Lord’s battles praiseworthily. Therefore, throughout almost all the earth the report of your faith and fidelity has gone forth. For this reason many blessings are poured upon your head, to acquire for you yet greater grace; the prayers of the whole Church are heaped up for you; and, through multiplied intercessors, a crown of glory is reserved for you, to be given you in the future by the just Judge—a crown which, because of your merits, we hope is now laid up for you in heaven.
>
> Come then, soldier of Christ: fulfill your ministry, running the course set before you until you gain the prize. Never fail in tribulations, knowing that God of Sabaoth—that is, the Lord [Col. 0697C] of Hosts and prince of the Christian soldiery—stands by your side. Do not wish to wipe away the sweat of warfare before you obtain the palm of victory. Rather, since you have well begun a good beginning and have thereafter taken care praiseworthily to pursue the intervening stages, strive through the long-suffering and perseverance which crowns to complete them more praiseworthily with the desired end. Know, according to the Apostle’s word (2 Tim. 2), that no one is crowned unless he contends lawfully.
>
> Therefore, the entire land held by the count of Toulouse, together with the other lands obtained by the crusaders, which are held through hostages or guardians by our beloved son Peter, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Aquiro [Ciaconio has “Aequiro”], legate of the Apostolic See, we have deemed fit to entrust to your prudence until the time [Col. 0697D] of the general council, at which, with the counsel of the prelates, we may make fuller and salutary arrangements concerning them. You are to preserve, guard, and defend them. We grant you their revenues and proceeds, together with judicial rights and the other things belonging to jurisdiction, since you neither can nor ought to serve at your own expense. Excepted are the expenses for the fortification and keeping of castles held by our command.
>
> We admonish your nobility with all diligence, ask you with our whole affection in the Lord for the sake of the divine majesty, and, enjoining it upon you for the remission of sins, beseech you under the attestation of the divine majesty not to refuse to undertake this mission for Christ. For He, having accepted a mission from the Father for your sake, ran as a giant [Col. 0698A] as far as the gibbet of the cross and death. Since you have wholly devoted yourself to Christ’s service, do not fail through weariness, nor refuse to perform good military service for Christ until the end. Let it never enter your heart to resist such sweet fatherly counsels and commands; rather, with all desire and affection strive to embrace what we command, that you may forever be cherished in Christ’s embraces—He who, inviting you to His embraces, stretched out for you His tireless arms.
>
> Also, with prudent deliberation diligently take care lest you have run or labored in vain, if through your negligence the multitude of locusts which came out of the pit of the abyss, but have through your ministry been driven from the land they occupied, should—God forbid!—occupy it again for the destruction [Col. 0698B] of God’s people.
>
> Since we confidently hope that, being solicitous for your salvation, you will never oppose apostolic commands, we have ordered the barons, consuls, and other faithful of Christ established in the aforesaid lands—strictly commanding them in the power of the Holy Spirit—to devote themselves fully to your commands concerning the business of peace and faith and the other matters expressed above, and to ensure their inviolable observance. Against the assailants of the Catholic faith and disturbers of the peace, they are to furnish you generously and powerfully with counsel and aid, so that through their supporting assistance you may beneficially carry out the business of peace and faith.
>
> We also command the legate, directing him to establish and arrange in these matters whatever he sees to be expedient for the said business, to give you suitable counsel and aid and to ensure that what you establish is firmly observed; if there are any opponents or rebels, he is to compel them by coercive measures to do what he sees expedient, removing the obstacle of any condition or appeal.
>
> Given at the Lateran, 2 April, in the eighteenth year of our pontificate.

Proceeding from Saint-Gilles, Louis came to Montpellier and from there to Béziers. The city of Béziers is only four leagues from Narbonne. The citizens of Narbonne, moved by fear, sent to Louis, declaring that they were ready to do his will in all things. [Col. 0698D] Nor should it be omitted that Arnald, archbishop of Narbonne, worked as hard as he could to prevent Narbonne’s walls from being demolished; for this reason he had come down as far as Vienne to meet Louis. He said indeed that Narbonne was his, and this was partly true. Moreover, the archbishop had appropriated to himself and held the duchy of Narbonne, which from ancient times the count of Toulouse had held.

Although the men of Narbonne were in part under the archbishop’s lordship, they had opposed God and Christendom and Count Montfort; indeed, with all their force they had attacked Christ. For this reason they had admitted Christ’s enemies into their town and had kept them there for a long time. The preceding year they had also inflicted grave fears of death upon the archbishop, who was working so ardently [Col. 0699A] to preserve the walls. It therefore seemed to our men that the archbishop was pressing for Narbonne’s walls not to fall contrary both to the Church’s interest and to his own. On this account, and for certain other reasons which need not be repeated, some discord had arisen between the archbishop and Count Montfort. Almost everyone thought that the archbishop, regarding the matters mentioned, was not sufficiently providing for the future welfare of the cause of the Christian faith.

While the legate, Louis, Count Montfort, and the pilgrims were at Béziers, it was arranged, by the will of the legate and the counsel of the prelates—many of whom had assembled there—that Louis, by the legate’s will and authority, should cause the walls of Narbonne, Toulouse, and certain castles to be demolished, because those fortifications had brought many evils upon Christendom. But he forbade Louis to trouble the inhabitants of the said cities in any respect except the demolition of the walls. [Col. 0699B]

To ensure better observance of this, Louis ordered the citizens of Narbonne to destroy their walls within three weeks, at the discretion of two knights whom he sent to Narbonne for this purpose; otherwise they were to know that they would be severely punished. Thus the people of Narbonne began to demolish the walls of Jericho—that is, of the city of Narbonne. Louis then departed from Béziers and came with his party to Carcassonne. After he had stayed there some days, the legate arrived.

One day [Col. 0699C] the legate summoned to himself, in the house of the bishop of Carcassonne, the bishops who were present, Louis, Count Montfort, and the nobles who were with Louis. When all had assembled, the legate, in accordance with the form of the apostolic command, entrusted the land to the count until the general council. Afterwards Louis left Carcassonne and went to a nearby castle called Fanum Jovis, where he spent a few days. Meanwhile the legate and Count Montfort went to the castle of Pamiers. There the thoroughly wicked count of Foix came to the legate. Our count did not wish to see him. There the legate entrusted to our count the castle of Foix, which he had long held in his own hand; our count immediately sent knights and garrisoned the castle of Foix.

Nor should it be omitted that, before [Col. 0699D] the legate and Louis left Carcassonne, Count Montfort sent his brother Guy and knights with him to receive and occupy Toulouse on his behalf. Afterwards they received oaths of fidelity from the citizens on behalf of our count and ordered them to demolish the city walls. The citizens complied, although most unwilling and deeply grieved; impelled more by fear than led by love, they began to demolish their own walls. From that time the pride of the city of Toulouse was humbled.

After the legate had entrusted the castle of Foix to our count, the legate himself, Louis, Count Montfort, and all the pilgrims proceeded and entered Toulouse. From there Louis and the pilgrims, having completed the term of their pilgrimage—namely forty [Col. 0700A] days—returned to France. The legate likewise left Toulouse and came to Carcassonne, where he awaited Count Montfort for some days. The noble count, after spending a few days at Toulouse, came to Carcassonne to the legate.

After the legate had spent many days in the Albigensian land and, as a circumspect and prudent man, had praiseworthily carried out the office of legation entrusted to him; and after the whole oft-mentioned land, by command of the supreme pontiff, had been entrusted to the noble Count of Montfort, the same legate went down into Provence and returned to the supreme pontiff. The noble Count of Montfort escorted the legate from Carcassonne as far as Saint-Antoine near Vienne. The legate went thence to Rome. The noble count, after spending a few days in Provence, returned to the region of Carcassonne and, after a few days there, went to the lands of Toulouse and Agen, in order to visit those lands and correct what required correction.

Nor should it be omitted [Col. 0700B] that the walls of Toulouse had for the most part already been overthrown. After some days, Bernard de Casuac, the most wicked and cruel man mentioned above, treacherously recovered a castle in the diocese of Périgueux which had been his and was called Castrumnovum. A French knight to whom the count had entrusted the castle’s custody had fortified it inadequately and left it almost empty. On hearing this, Bernard came to the castle and besieged it; he immediately took it [Col. 0700C] and condemned the knights who were there to death by the gallows.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. The Lateran Council is held: the county of Toulouse, entrusted to Count Simon, is granted to him by decree of the council.

In the year of the Incarnate Word 1215, in November, Pope Innocent III summoned patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, abbots, and other prelates of churches, and held a solemn general council in the Lateran church in the city of Rome. Among the other arrangements and decrees made at the council, the matter of the faith against the Albigensians was considered.

For Raymond, the former count of Toulouse, and his son had come to the council; so also had the count of Foix—most manifest disturbers of peace and faith—to petition the council for the recovery of the land which they had lost through divine judgment, aided by the support of those who had taken the cross. But the noble Count of Montfort sent there his full brother Guy de Montfort and other faithful and prudent messengers.

It is true that there were some present—even, more grievously, among the prelates—who were hostile to the cause of the faith and worked for the restoration of the said counts. But Ahithophel’s counsel did not prevail; the desire of the wicked was frustrated. For the lord pope, with the approval of the greater and sounder part of the most holy council, made the following arrangement [Col. 0701A] concerning the matter in question. He decreed and provided that the city of Toulouse and the other lands acquired by the crusaders should be granted to Count Montfort, who had labored in the said cause more bravely and faithfully than all others. But the supreme pontiff wished the land which the count of Toulouse had held in Provence to be kept in custody, so that provision might be made concerning it, in whole or in part, for the son of the said count of Toulouse, provided that through clear proofs of fidelity and good conduct he showed himself worthy of mercy. But how badly these matters turned out, and how he turned mercy into harsh judgment against himself, we shall show in what follows.

After the return of his envoys from the council, the Count of Montfort, on the counsel of the prelates of the Albigensian land [Col. 0701B] and of his barons, went to France to his lord the king, in order to receive from him the land which was held from him in fief. Yet the honour shown him in France could neither be written by us nor readily believed by anyone hearing of it. For in whatever city, castle, or town he entered, clergy and people came out to meet him in procession, crying and saying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 21). So great and such was the pious and religious devotion of the people that he called himself blessed who could touch the fringe of his garment.

When the count came to the king, he was received by him most kindly and honourably. After pleasant conversations of welcome intimacy, the king invested the count with, and confirmed to him [Col. 0701C] and his heirs, the duchy of Narbonne and Toulouse, as well as all the land which the crusaders had acquired within the king’s fief from the heretics and their defenders.

While the noble count was in France, Raymond, son of Raymond P., formerly Count of Toulouse, a boy but not boyish—indeed, rather foolish—acting in every respect contrary to the apostolic commands, and moreover scorning the great favour and abundant mercy which the Apostolic See had shown him, though unworthy, entered Provence. Having formed a conspiracy against God and against civil and canon law with the people of Avignon, Tarascon, and Marseilles, and with the counsel and aid of certain nobles of Provence, he occupied that land which the noble Count of Montfort was holding in custody by commission of the lord pope [Col. 0701D].

Having occupied the land beyond the Rhône, he came to a very noble castle in the kingdom of France, in the diocese of Arles, situated on the bank of the great river Rhône. That castle had belonged to the Count of Toulouse; but the Roman Church had granted it, and the king had confirmed it, to the Count of Montfort. Moreover, the Archbishop of Arles, whose is the lesser lordship of that same castle, had granted it in fief to the same count as his vassal and had received homage from him for it.

When the said Raymond came to Beaucaire, summoned by the men of that castle, who had rendered homage to our count, he was admitted into the borough. Immediately certain nobles of Provence, citizens of Avignon and Marseilles, and also townsmen [Col. 0702A] of Tarascon—treacherous and malicious men—gathered around him. He besieged in the very stronghold the seneschal of the Count of Montfort, together with the knights and serjeants who were holding the fortification with that seneschal, and began fiercely to attack it.

On hearing this, Guy, brother of the Count of Montfort, and Amaury, the count’s eldest son, together with the other barons and knights of the count who were in the region of Toulouse, hastened towards Beaucaire in order, if possible, to assist their besieged men. With them was the venerable Guy, Bishop of Carcassonne, who, as has often been said, was wholly ardent in the cause of the faith. Meanwhile the most noble Count of Montfort was coming in haste from France, bringing with him many knights whom he had hired in France at great expense.

Guy, the count’s brother, and Amaury, his son, hurrying towards Beaucaire, came to the city of Nîmes, four leagues distant from Beaucaire Castle, and remained there for one night. In the morning, after hearing Mass, making confession, and receiving Communion in the Lord’s sacrament, they mounted their horses and left Nîmes, hastening to Beaucaire. They went ready for battle; for this was their highest and sole desire: that they might engage in a decisive encounter with their enemies.

While we were on the way, we were told that near the public road was a castle named Bellegarde, which had surrendered itself to our enemies and could greatly [Col. 0702C] harass that same public road. Therefore, on the counsel of our nobles, we turned aside to that castle. Having captured it at once, we rested there that night. On the following day, at first light, after hearing Mass, we left that castle and hastened to Beaucaire. Our men advanced ready for battle, drawn up in three divisions, in the name of the Trinity.

When our men came before Beaucaire Castle, we found an innumerable multitude of men besieging our knights and serjeants in the castle’s stronghold. Although the enemies were countless and our men few by comparison, the former nevertheless did not dare to come outside the lower walls of the castle, though our men stood before the walls for a very long time inviting them to battle. Seeing that the enemies would not come out to fight them [Col. 0702D], after waiting for them and inviting them to emerge, our men returned to Bellegarde Castle, whence they had come, intending to return on the next day.

While we were at Bellegarde, the noble Count of Montfort, returning from France and hastening to Beaucaire, came to Nîmes. Early the next morning the count set out from Nîmes and we from Bellegarde; arriving before Beaucaire, the count on one side and we on the other, we besieged the besiegers.

Seeing that the Count of Montfort had besieged Beaucaire, Raymond, son of the former Count of Toulouse, summoned all whom he could: men of Avignon, Tarascon, and Voloberc [probably Vauvert], many others from neighbouring castles, and a faithless, apostate people. Gathered together, these men [Col. 0703A] attacked as much as they could, against God and Christ’s athlete—that is, the Count of Montfort—our men besieged in the stronghold. For we were not merely besieging Beaucaire, but the aforesaid cities and castles—indeed, almost the whole of Provence.

On the outer side around the fortification the enemies had made a wall and ditch, so that our men could not approach it. They also fiercely attacked the stronghold with engines called stone-throwers (*petrariae*), and made frequent and violent assaults upon our men inside it. But our men defended themselves manfully and wonderfully, killing very many of them.

The enemies made a battering ram of astonishing size and, applying it to the wall of the stronghold, struck that wall violently. But our men, by contrivances of remarkable courage and ingenuity, impeded the blows of the ram so that they weakened the wall not at all, or only slightly [Col. 0703B]. The opponents also made many other engines of various kinds, but all these were burned by our besieged men.

The noble Count of Montfort maintained the siege outside at great danger and expense, for all the country round about had turned from its course. We could obtain provisions for the army only from Saint-Gilles and Nîmes. Whenever we wished to get provisions from these two towns, armed knights had to be sent to escort those carrying them. Moreover, without interruption, by day as well as by night, one third of the knights in the army had to remain under arms: both because it was feared that the enemies might unexpectedly rush upon the army—though they never dared attempt this—and because the engines had to be guarded.

The noble count also caused a stone-thrower to be prepared, which hurled stones at the first wall of the borough. He could not have more engines, because he had no knights to draw them. He had very few native knights, and they were lukewarm and fearful, rendering little or no service to Christ’s army [Col. 0703C]. Those on the opposing side, however, were spirited and bold.

Nor should it be passed over that whenever the enemies could capture any of our men, whether clerics or laymen, they condemned them to a most shameful death. After hanging them, they killed some and mutilated others. O ignoble war! O confused victory! One day they captured one of our knights; they killed the captive, hanged the dead man, and cut off the hands and feet of the hanged man. O unheard-of cruelty! Moreover, they hurled the knight’s severed feet into the stronghold with a mangonel, in order thus to terrify and provoke our besieged men.

Meanwhile Raymond, the former Count of Toulouse, was travelling through Catalonia and Aragon, gathering whatever knights he could, so that with their aid he might enter our land and seize Toulouse. The wicked and faithless citizens of Toulouse were ready to receive him if he came.

Furthermore, provisions failed our men besieged in Beaucaire. The enemies could never have captured them had they merely possessed food enough for their maintenance [Col. 0704A]. The shortage suffered by his besieged men was reported to our count. Placed in great anxiety, he did not know what to do: he could neither free his besieged men nor in any way consent to leave them exposed to death. Moreover, the city of Toulouse and the other lands which he held were in the gravest danger of destruction.

Having carefully considered all these things, the noble and faithful count began to devise how he could release and recover his besieged men. Why say more? Our men negotiated with the enemies through intermediaries, and such an arrangement was made—let us not call it a surrender. It was agreed that our besieged men would relinquish Beaucaire’s stronghold to the enemies, on condition that the opponents allowed them to depart with all their possessions. And so it was done.

If anyone considers the circumstances of this siege, although the noble count gained no victory from the capture of Beaucaire [Col. 0704B], he nevertheless bore away the marks of faithful nobility and most noble fidelity.

The noble count withdrew with his men from the siege of Beaucaire and came to Nîmes. Leaving knights there to guard the city and range through the countryside, he himself hastened to Toulouse. On hearing this, Raymond, the former Count of Toulouse, who was likewise coming to seize Toulouse, fled in confusion.

When the count approached Toulouse, he sent some of his knights ahead into the city. But the treacherous citizens, prepared for betrayal, seized them and kept them confined in one house. Hearing this, the count was greatly angered and astonished. Seeing that the people of Toulouse wished to resist [Col. 0704C], he ordered fire set to part of the city. The citizens fled into the borough, still wishing to resist; but seeing that the count meant to attack them by assault, they were overcome by fear and surrendered themselves and their city wholly to his will. The count caused the city’s walls and towers to be utterly demolished; moreover, he took hostages from among the citizens and placed them under guard in his castles.

Meanwhile the apostate and faithless men of Saint-Gilles received into their town the son of the former Count of Toulouse, against the will of the abbot and monks. When the abbot and monks saw this, they took the Body of Christ out of the church and went barefoot out of the town, placing the town itself under interdict and anathema.

After the noble count had spent some days at Toulouse [Col. 0704D], he went into Gascony. There a marriage was contracted between Guy, the count’s second-born brother, and the Countess of Bigorre. A few days later the count returned to Toulouse.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV. The Siege of Montgrenier

At that time the ancient enemy and tireless persecutor of the cause of Jesus Christ, the Count of Foix, acting contrary to the commands of the supreme pontiff and the Second General Council concerning peace, or at least a truce, to be observed for a fortnight, had built a fortification near Foix called Montgrenier. This fortification was founded on the summit of an exceedingly high mountain and, in human estimation, appeared not merely impregnable but almost inaccessible [Col. 0705A]. There dwelt disturbers of peace and overthrowers of the faith; there the enemies of the Church had refuge and recourse.
