Hearing that this often-mentioned fortress was causing many grave injuries, and that, unless he promptly met the imminent danger, the cause of Jesus Christ might suffer irreparable loss, the noble Count of Montfort resolved to besiege it.

Therefore, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1216, on the eighth day before the Ides of February [6 February], the most valiant Count of Montfort besieged Montgrenier. In that fortress was Roger Bernard, son of the Count of Foix, not departing from his father’s wickedness; many knights and serjeants were with him. For he did not believe that any mortal could not only capture Montgrenier [Col. 0705B], but even dare to besiege it at such a season. As we have said, it was situated amid very high and bitterly cold mountains; winter still prevailed, and in those places it is accustomed to rule more harshly.

But the most valiant count, trusting in Him who commands waters and winds and who provides an outcome with temptations, fearing neither the whirlwinds of the winds, nor trembling at the severity of snow or the abundance of rain, established his siege amid mud and cold and began vigorously to attack the besieged castle. Those in the castle defended themselves with all their strength.

Since we could scarcely recount in order all the difficulties and stratagems of this siege, we say briefly that its whole course ought to be called not so much labour as martyrdom. After many days the besieged ran out of water, and, as provisions also failed, they lost the will to resist [Col. 0705C]. Yet our besiegers, though with the greatest difficulty, blocked all access night and day, so that the besieged could neither bring provisions into the castle nor dare descend to draw water.

Pressed by these hardships, they spoke of surrendering the castle. But our men did not fully know their condition, and therefore more readily assented to their request. The manner of surrender offered by the opponents was as follows: they offered to give the castle up to the count provided they were allowed to depart with their arms. Roger Bernard went out from the castle with his men, and Roger swore to the count that for one year he would not make war upon him—a vow which, as we shall show below [Col. 0705D], he kept very badly.

The castle was surrendered on the vigil of the Lord’s Resurrection. At once the noble count garrisoned it with serjeants, and afterwards went to Carcassonne. There were certain castles in the diocese of Narbonne and near Termes, inhabited by *ruptarii*—outlaw raiders—who, through sins demanding it, had been expelled from their own lands. The count went into those parts; he took certain of those castles by force, while others surrendered without any condition.

When these matters had been properly accomplished, the noble count came towards Provence, namely to the diocese of Nîmes. For the town of Saint-Gilles, having entered into a pact of death with the people of Avignon and Beaucaire, and several castles of that diocese, had in that same year departed from God [Col. 0706A] and the Church and surrendered themselves to Raymond, son of Raymond, the former Count of Toulouse.

When the noble count, on pilgrimage and with the consent of the abbot—who possessed full lordship in that town—arrived at Saint-Gilles, he was not admitted by its inhabitants. Instead, appealing to Lord B., the cardinal, they closed the gates of the town. But our count, as a humble and devout man, respecting the appeal, withdrew.

For at that time Master Bertrand, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, legate of the Apostolic See, a man of great learning and immense worth, had come into Provence. He had been sent by the supreme pontiff to establish what concerned peace and faith in the provinces of Vienne, Arles, Aix, Embrun, and Narbonne [Col. 0706B]. He was beyond the Rhône, in the city of Orange. But the citizens of Avignon and Marseilles, the inhabitants of Saint-Gilles, Beaucaire, and Tarascon, given over to a reprobate mind and turned to apostasy, refused obedience.

Meanwhile the noble Count of Montfort vigorously attacked the castles in the diocese of Nîmes which, as we have said, had apostatized that year. Gerard, Archbishop of Bourges, and Robert, Bishop of Clermont, powerful men who in the preceding year had taken the cross against the disturbers of peace and overthrowers of the faith, came to his aid. Very many knights and serjeants came with them. Supported by their assistance, the count besieged a castle near Saint-Gilles called Posquières [Col. 0706C]. Having captured it shortly, he besieged another castle called Brémes. Attacking it manfully, he took it by force and, as their deserts required, hanged many of the men of the castle on gallows.

This so terrified all the apostates of that land that, struck with amazement, they fled before the count and left every castle in which they lived empty. Indeed, in all that land on this side of the Rhône scarcely anyone remained to resist the count, except the town of Saint-Gilles, Beaucaire, and a very few other fortifications.

After these events, the count went down towards a settlement on the Rhône called the port of Saint-Saturnin. The cardinal crossed the Rhône towards Viviers, wishing to see the count and confer with him [Col. 0706D] about the cause of Jesus Christ. There was no free crossing of the Rhône at any nearer place, because the people of Avignon and the other enemies of the faith obstructed his purpose and attempt. As the cardinal himself complained, they were in a sense holding him besieged in the city of Orange.

He came to Saint-Saturnin. Among the other injuries which the enemies of faith and peace inflicted upon that legate, this was no small one: while the legate sat with many clerics in sight of the Rhône, suddenly the enemies of God, who had fortified the port, shot seven or eight bolts at the legate himself. God preserved him unharmed, but the pope’s messenger who was present was wounded.

The count came there to the legate with the greatest rejoicing and haste. The honour which this most Christian count showed the cardinal would not be easy to describe [Col. 0707A].

At about the same time, the Archbishop of Bourges and the Bishop of Clermont, having completed the term of their pilgrimage—namely, forty days—returned home. Our count, however, vigorously besieged, captured, and utterly demolished the very strong tower of Draconet, situated on the bank of the Rhône, taking captive and putting in chains all who were within. The tower had been built to serve as a den of robbers who plundered pilgrims and others travelling both by land and along the Rhône.

After all this, it was the cardinal’s counsel and wish that the noble count should cross the Rhône and restrain the disturbers of peace in Provence. For Raymond, son of the former Count of Toulouse, Adhemar of Poitiers, and their accomplices were with all their efforts troubling the cause of peace and faith in those regions [Col. 0707B].

The noble count obeyed the cardinal and had boats prepared at Viviers for crossing the Rhône. When his opponents heard this, they assembled on land to prevent his crossing. The people of Avignon also came by the Rhône in heavily armed boats, intending to bar the count’s passage. But when they saw that only very few of the count’s knights were crossing, they were, by a divine miracle, overcome by fear and sought safety in flight. So great a terror likewise seized all those in that land who supported the count’s opponents that they abandoned many strong castles.

The noble count therefore crossed with his men and came to a castle called Montélimar [Col. 0707C]. The cardinal crossed with him, and the count did everything by his wish and command. Guitaldus Adhemar, who was lord of Montélimar for the greater part, was with the count’s opponents. Although he was the liege man of the lord pope, and although he was asked, he refused to surrender the castle to the cardinal, though he had made it a refuge for heretics. But the men of the castle received the count, for a certain knight, a kinsman of the said Guitaldus and the other lord of Montélimar, adhered to the count and had always adhered to him.

After the count had spent a few days at Montélimar, he proceeded to besiege a castle in the diocese of Valence called Crest, belonging to Adhemar of Poitiers [Col. 0707D]. Adhemar, as we have already said, opposed the Count of Montfort and had greatly persecuted the Bishop of Valence. For the city of Valence adhered, and had always adhered, to the aforesaid count.

When the count came to Crest Castle, he besieged it. It was a very noble and strong castle, well supplied with knights and serjeants. Once the siege had been established, the count began vigorously to attack the castle, while the besieged defended themselves as best they could. With the count were several bishops of that land and nearly one hundred French knights, whom King Philip had sent to serve him for six months.

While the count was at that siege, an attempt was made to arrange an agreement and peace between the count and Adhemar of Poitiers. After many words and lengthy negotiation [Col. 0708A], an agreement was confirmed between the count and the said Adhemar. Each firmly promised that Adhemar’s son should have the count’s daughter as his wife. Adhemar also surrendered certain castles as security that thereafter he would in no way attack the count. Moreover, a certain nobleman of that land, named Draconet, who had departed from the count in the preceding year, returned himself to him. An agreement and peace were also made between the Bishop of Valence and the aforesaid Adhemar.

Thus, while the Lord Jesus was so miraculously advancing His cause in those regions, the ancient enemy, seeing this, wished to hinder what he grieved to see prosper. In those same days the citizens of Toulouse—indeed, let us more properly call them Deceitful-men (*Dolosani*)—stirred by diabolical prompting, apostatizing [Col. 0708B] from God and the Church and withdrawing from the Count of Montfort, received into their city Raymond, their former count and lord. By his deserts he had been disinherited by authority of the supreme pontiff—indeed, of the Second General Lateran Council.

The noble countess, wife of the Count of Montfort, together with the wives of Guy, his brother, and of Amaury and Guy, his sons, and many sons and daughters both of the count and of his brother, were in the stronghold of Toulouse called the Narbonnais Castle. Immediately the said Raymond, Roger Bernard, son of the Count of Foix, and certain others who had come with him, together with the citizens of Toulouse, began day and night to fortify Toulouse with many barriers and ditches.

When news of Toulouse’s treachery was heard, Guy of Montfort, the count’s brother, Guy, the count’s son, and many knights with them, whom the count had left in the region of Carcassonne to guard the land, hastened to Toulouse. They entered the aforesaid stronghold, where the countess was, in the outer buildings, so that the opponents might not besiege the stronghold from outside [Col. 0708C].

## CHAPTER LXXXV. The Second Siege of Toulouse

Hearing that Toulouse had apostatized, the noble count crossed the Rhône and returned in haste; the cardinal crossed with him. The cardinal and count therefore came to Toulouse and besieged it in the year 1217. It was a very large and populous city. *Ruptarii*, *faydici* [men involved in private feuds], and many others who had formerly been secret enemies of the Count of Montfort withdrew into it, in order to defend it against God, the count, and holy Church, for which the noble count laboured with all his strength.

In that betrayal many castles and nobles around Toulouse had concurred, promising assistance in place and time. When the noble count came with his men to the ditches of Toulouse, intending to take the city by assault, he was violently driven back by the citizens, and he pitched his tents near the Narbonnais Castle. But since Toulouse could not effectively be besieged unless there were an army beyond the river Garonne—which enclosed Toulouse on the Gascon side—to prevent the exit available to the people of Toulouse over two bridges across that river [Col. 0709A], the count crossed with many men, leaving many on this side with his son Amaury.

The noble count remained there for some days. At last, understanding that Amaury’s army was insufficient to withstand the enemies, he crossed the river, so that from two weak forces one strong and secure army might be made.

But we shall not omit the miracle that God performed in that crossing, so that God may always and in all things be magnified. As the Count of Montfort, fully armed and on an armoured horse, was about to enter a boat, he fell into the river, where the water appeared exceedingly deep. When he did not reappear, fear, trembling, and excessive lamentation seized us all. Rachel weeps for her son; deceitful hell exults and howls, calling us orphans while our father lives. But He who, at Elijah’s prayer, willed the axe-head to float upon water raised our prince from the abyss of water, devoutly stretching joined hands to heaven. Our men received him joyfully from the boat and preserved him unharmed for holy mother Church, for which that count had set himself as a barrier [Col. 0709B]. O ineffable mercy of the Saviour!

Meanwhile the people of Toulouse erected many engines—stone-throwers and mangonels—in order both to bring down the Narbonnais Castle and to overwhelm Bertrand, cardinal and legate of the Apostolic See, with stones, together with his companions, and thereby stone the Roman Church in him. O how often that cardinal feared death—yet, as a prudent man, he by no means refused to live for the cause of Jesus Christ!

At the same time the noble count took hostages from the people of Montauban, because they were suspected of plotting deceit with the people of Toulouse against the peace. They bore honey in their mouths, I say, but carried conceived gall in their hearts. This appeared afterward. For when the seneschal of Agen, on behalf of the Count of Montfort, and the Bishop of Lectoure came to Montauban and slept securely that night, behold, the people of Montauban had sent to Toulouse for Raymond, the former count, to come with the people of Toulouse to the castle, deliver the seneschal to them, and kill all his companions [Col. 0709C].

Raymond sent ahead five hundred armed men. Entering the castle that same night—for it was near Toulouse—with the counsel of the castle’s inhabitants, who numbered three thousand or more, they fortified the streets with obstacles. At the doors of the houses where the seneschal and his companions lay they stationed armed guards, lest those men escape; they also piled much wood against the doors, so that, if the men could not otherwise be captured, they might be entirely consumed by fire.

When this had been done, the people of Toulouse raised a cry, trumpets sounded, and great fear and tumult arose. The Frenchmen woke, sleepy and astonished, trusting not in their own strength but relying upon God’s aid alone. They armed themselves immediately. Though scattered throughout the castle, they were all touched by one will, one faith in the Lord, and one hope of triumph. They came out of the houses against the enemies’ will and rushed upon them like an impatient lion. The enemies fled; some fell into the traps [Col. 0710A] which they had made, while others threw themselves from the walls, though no one pursued them. Our men seized almost all their movable goods; the rest were consumed by fire.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI. The Besieged People of Toulouse Attack Their Besiegers. The Noble Count of Montfort Is Killed on the Day after the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist

When the noble count had already spent about nine months in the siege of Toulouse, one day—namely, on the morrow of Blessed John the Baptist—the men in Toulouse fortified themselves at the first light of dawn, so that, while some of our men still slept and others were engaged in hearing the divine offices, they might make their customary treacherous and ingrainedly malicious sudden assault upon us. To attack the unprepared more fiercely and harass their enemies more cruelly, they arranged that some of those assigned to guard the engines should rush upon our men, while others should charge the army from another side. Thus, as we have said, our men, unfortified and attacked from two sides, would be less able to meet the enemies and less strong to endure the assault [Col. 0710B].

It was reported to the count that his enemies had armed themselves and were lying concealed within their fortification near the ditch. The count was hearing Matins. On hearing the report, he ordered his arms prepared. Having put them on, this most Christian man hastened to church to hear Mass.

While he was in church and Mass had already begun, the devout man was praying most attentively. Behold: a very great multitude of Toulouse men emerged from their ditches by secret passages, with banners raised and amid the greatest clamour and trumpet-blast, and rushed upon our men guarding the engines near the ditch. Others came out on the other side and directed their battle-lines against the army. A cry arose in the army, and our men fortified themselves as swiftly as they could. But before our men were armed, the few men among ours assigned, as we have said, to guard the engines and army, fighting against the enemies, endured so many and such perils of assaults and wounds that they could not readily be reckoned [Col. 0710C].

At the enemies’ very emergence, a messenger came to the count, who, as we have said, was hearing Mass, urgently asking him to aid his men without delay. To him the devout man said: “Allow me first to hear the divine mysteries and behold the sacrament of our redemption.” While he was still speaking, another messenger came, saying: “Hasten! The battle has grown severe, and our men cannot endure longer.” To this the most Christian man replied: “I shall not go out until I have first seen my Redeemer.”

When the priest, according to custom, raised the victim of sacred consecration, the most devout man, with knees bent to the earth but hands raised to heaven, said: “Now dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2). And he added: “Let us go, and, if it is necessary, let us die for Him who deigned to die for us.”

Having said this, the most invincible man hastened to battle [Col. 0711A]. The fighting intensified on both sides, and many had been wounded and killed here and there. But when Christ’s knight arrived, the courage and strength of our men were doubled; all the opponents were driven back, and our men forcefully thrust them as far as the ditches.

The count and those with him withdrew a little because of the hail of stones and the unbearable shower of arrows. They stood before the engines with hurdles placed before them, by which they might protect themselves from stones and arrows. For the enemies hurled extremely frequent stones upon our men with two trebuchets, a mangonel, and several *matafundi* [stone-throwing engines].

Who can write or hear what follows? Who, I ask, can recite it without sorrow? Who can hear it without sobbing? Who, I ask, is not dissolved and wholly melted on hearing that the life of the poor has been shattered? For with him fallen, all things were shattered; with him dying, all things died. He was the consolation of the sorrowful, the strength of the weak, refreshment in affliction, and refuge of the wretched [Col. 0711B]. We relate a purpose mournful before God.

While the most valiant count stood, as has been said, with his men before his engines, so that the enemies might not again emerge to destroy those engines, behold, a stone hurled from an enemy mangonel struck Christ’s knight on the head. Having received the mortal blow, he struck his breast twice, commended himself to God and the Blessed Virgin, and, imitating the death of Blessed Stephen—himself stoned in the city—fell asleep in the Lord with him.

> [Note: [Col. 0711] The principal church of Toulouse is dedicated to Saint Stephen.]

Nor should it be passed over that this most valiant soldier of the Lord—indeed, lest we be mistaken, this most glorious martyr of Christ—after receiving the mortal wound from the stone’s blow, received five wounds from archers in likeness of the Saviour, for whom he patiently endured death, and with whom, as we believe, after death he happily glories and lives [Col. 0712A].

His eldest son Amaury succeeded him, a good and vigorous young man, in every respect an imitator of his father’s goodness and valour. All the French knights to whom the father had given lands rendered to him their oath of fealty and homage.

A few days later, seeing that he could not maintain the siege at Toulouse any longer—both because, on hearing of the count’s death, many of the worst apostates among the native inhabitants withdrew from him and the Church, indeed joining themselves to Christ’s enemies; and because he was exhausted by expenses, provisions failed the army, and the pilgrims wished to return to their own land—the new count withdrew from the siege. He surrendered the Narbonnais Castle, which he could not hold, and carried away the body, first prepared at Carcassonne according to French custom [Col. 0712B].

[Col. 0711] Here ends the history of the memorable deeds and triumphs of the noble man, Lord Simon, Count of Montfort.

# MISCELLANEA OF AN ANONYMOUS TWELFTH-CENTURY AUTHOR

[Col. 0713]

## LETTER OF AN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR TO HUGH, HIS FRIEND, ON THE METHOD AND ORDER OF READING HOLY SCRIPTURE

(Marten, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 486, from the manuscript of St Mary of Josaphat.)

[Col. 0713A] **On the Method and Order of Reading the Books of Holy Scripture**

Hugh, my beloved brother in the Lord, I am compelled by the law of my promise to write you something, in a concise and modest style. What I delayed because of my occupations, and what I have at last written out, must be credited to your charity, which roused me from sluggishness. For I preferred to discharge my promise, even late, rather than seem for longer inexorable and unhelpful to a friend who asked.

My present purpose, however, is not to explain the method and order by which the sacred page is taught in the schools. Rather, from what follows one must observe in what manner or order the divine utterances ought to be read and examined, especially by those who, having taken up the bond of religious profession, are bound to another’s obedience. Yet here too a distinction must be made. Some, before conversion, [Col. 0713B] have been thoroughly instructed by reading both pages [i.e. the Old and New Testaments]; others have commendably advanced in one page or the other before renouncing the world; others, having scarcely learned the first rudiments of grammar, shut themselves within cloisters in order to serve God.

The task at hand, then, will be to teach by what path and by what steps those who are almost unlearned, and almost ignorant of all literature, may ascend to a full understanding of the sacred page. Such persons should attend, along with others, to what is said: “Search the Scriptures” (John 5); and: “Blessed are those who search his testimonies; they seek him with their whole heart” (Psalm 118); and: “Blessed is the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night” (Psalm 1); and: “You err, not knowing the Scriptures” [Col. 0713C] (Matthew 22), nor his power. And, confident in him who says, “I confess to thee, Father, because thou hast hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones” (Matthew 11), let them chew over divine teaching with burning throats until they become “the silvered wings of a dove, and the rear parts of her back in the pallor of gold” (Psalm 67): that is, until they themselves become teachers of the Church, with brilliance of expression and with their charity founded in true wisdom.

First, therefore, let the number of the books of both the Old and New Testament [Col. 0714A] be distinguished, their names set forth, and thereafter it should be shown which books ought to be read, in what order, and how.

The books of the Old Testament are, according to one reckoning, twenty-two; according to another, twenty-four. These books are divided three ways: some are books of the Law, some prophetic, and some Hagiographa—that is, writings simply called “holy Scripture.”

There are five books of the Law: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.

There are eight prophetic books: Joshua the son of Nun; Judges; Samuel, which is the first part of Kings; Kings, called in Hebrew by some *Malachim*, by others *Malachor*; Isaiah; Jeremiah; Ezekiel; and the Book of the Twelve Prophets, which in Hebrew is called *Tharaasra*.

The Hagiographa [Col. 0714B] are nine: Job, the Psalter, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, Daniel, Chronicles, Ezra, and Esther. Add together these five, eight, and nine, and there will be twenty-two. To the nine Hagiographa some add the book of Ruth and the Lamentations of Jeremiah.

There are only eight books of the New Testament: the four Gospels—Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John—and four other books called apostolic Scripture: the book of Paul’s Epistles, the Catholic Epistles, the Acts of the Apostles, and the Apocalypse. These books possess first and principal authority in the Church.

Besides the specified books, there are five which [Col. 0714C] the Hebrews call apocryphal, that is, hidden and doubtful; nevertheless, the Church honors and receives them. The first is the Book of Wisdom; the second, Ecclesiasticus; the third, Tobit; the fourth, Judith; the fifth, Maccabees.

Besides all the books previously distinguished, there are the writings of the blessed Fathers—Jerome, Augustine, and others—whose multitude it would be superfluous to enumerate. Nevertheless, in what follows mention will be made of those which seem more necessary than the rest for understanding the aforesaid books.

Let this suffice concerning the number and names of the books. Let us now say in what order and manner they should be read. For understanding this, it must be recognized that the reading of both Testaments is threefold. The first is according to history; the second according to allegory; the third according to moral instruction, or rather, tropology.

The whole sequence of the sacred page should first be investigated and gone through three or four times according to history. In each passage one should carefully note what can in no way be understood literally; what is false according to the literal sense; what is absurd if literally understood; what is useless; what is indifferent; and what obstructs eternal life—so that by examples of this kind anyone, even unwillingly, may be compelled to accept an allegorical understanding.

[Col. 0715B] The books of the Old Testament should be read literally in this manner and order: first the books of the Law; second, Joshua and Judges; third, Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles; alongside these, Josephus and Hegesippus.

But if, in such books, a word of unknown meaning occurs, then, lest we be hindered from proceeding with the reading, there should be at hand, as certain instruments for an easier understanding of the aforesaid books, Isidore’s *Etymologies*, Jerome’s book *Expositions of Hebrew Names*, the book of Derivations, which is found in well-stocked libraries, and the book called the *Partionary* or *Glossary*. The older the latter is found to be, the more explanations of unknown words it will contain. When the origin and meaning of an unknown word have been found in these works, progress in reading will become easier and more intelligible.

[Col. 0715C] From all the foregoing, a summary must be gathered and retained in memory: concerning the works of the six days; the construction of the ark and its compartments; the promise made to Abraham; the names and number of the patriarchs, their wives, concubines, and children; the number of years of the people Israel’s servitude in Egypt; the number of signs and plagues; the introduction of the people; the Law given and received on Mount Sinai; the construction and placement of the tabernacle; the twelve tribes; how they arranged their camps in a circle around the tabernacle; the priestly ornaments; the number and order [Col. 0715D] of priests and Levites; the kinds of sacrifices; the number of encampments; the wars carried out by the people Israel before they entered the land of promise; the cities destroyed, retained, and restored before they entered the land of promise; the kings found there—who and how many they were; the names and number of the leaders, and their deeds up to the time of the kings; the names, number, and order of the kings, and their deeds, whether outstanding or remarkably shameful; the construction of the Temple and its vessels; and the number and order of priests, Levites, and singers.

In all these matters Augustine’s book *Questions on the Old Testament* will be necessary and highly useful.

When these matters have been carefully noted, anyone may approach with full confidence the books of the prophets—Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, the Twelve Prophets, and Daniel. In them one should note what prophecy has been fulfilled literally, what is reserved for literal fulfillment, and under which king each prophet prophesied; this information is sometimes found through the diligence of certain persons at the end of a Bible.

[Col. 0716A] After these books one should read Esther, Ezra, Maccabees, Judith, and Tobit. After those: Solomon’s Proverbs, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, and Ecclesiastes. Finally: the Psalter, Job, and the Song of Songs; in these, because no literal sense concerning Christ and the Church is useful, let them be read immediately at the outset.

The books of the New Testament should be read in this manner and order: first Matthew; second, Mark, his follower; third, Luke; fourth, John. In these, one should carefully note the number of discourses and miracles, and what was done or said by the Lord, where, when, and before whom. For this you will need Jerome’s book *On the Description of the Places of Palestine* and the book *On the Harmony of the Gospels*. Next, Acts of the Apostles should be read; then the Catholic Epistles and Paul’s Epistles; lastly, the Apocalypse.

When the whole sequence of both Testaments has thus been surveyed and understood, the next step is to be instructed in the sacraments of the Church, which are fully set forth in the books of Master Hugh. Then the nature of the cardinal virtues and [Col. 0716C] the vices opposed to the virtues must be sought out and investigated wherever it can be found.

Whoever wishes to know the reasons for the individual observances performed in the Church throughout the course of the year should consult the book called Gerland’s *Candle* [Note: [Col. 0715] Above I have reproduced the preface of this book from a Clairvaux manuscript.], and the book of Master Simon called *Why*. After these, Augustine’s *On Christian Doctrine* and his *City of God* should be read with all diligence and study.

And when a diligent mind has exercised itself attentively and earnestly in the ark of the sacred page in the manner described, let it turn fearlessly to allegorical and moral reading; and let it reread, at will and in whatever order it pleases, the books of both the Old and New Testament according to this twofold reading. Whatever it encounters that has been, or is to be, signified allegorically, or noted, or to be noted, morally, it will absorb promptly and without effort.

Thus at last, joyfully exhilarated by a happy and delightful result, the mind will devote itself to studying new allegories and reflecting upon new moral instructions. Yet at times it should approach Origen’s works and similar writings as a horned viper (*cerastes*) on the path, as though a scout; and there it should learn to seek pearls in a bed, grapes among wild vines, and roses among thickets, so that what was said may be fulfilled: “And if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them” (Mark 16).

[Col. 0717A] But if anyone is troubled either by the variety of readings distinguished here or by the multitude of books, let him consider what Jerome says concerning the manner and order of reading the sacred page in his Letter to Laeta, *On the Education of a Daughter*. He says:

> “Let her first learn the Psalter; let her summon herself to holiness by these songs, and let her be instructed for life in Solomon’s Proverbs. In Ecclesiastes let her become accustomed to trampling underfoot the things of the world; in Job let her follow examples of virtue and patience. Let her proceed to the Gospels, never laying them down from her hands; let her drink in the Acts and Epistles of the Apostles with her whole heart. And when she has enriched the storehouse of her breast with these treasures, let her commit to memory the Prophets, the Heptateuch, and the books of Kings and Chronicles. Let her read also the volumes of Ezra and Esther; lastly, [Col. 0717B] let her learn the Song of Songs without danger. If she reads it at the outset, she will be wounded because, under its carnal words, she does not understand the epithalamium of spiritual marriage.
>
> “Let her beware of all apocryphal books; and if she should ever wish to read them, not for the truth of doctrines but out of reverence for individual authors, let her know that they are not by those whose names are prefixed to their titles, that much faulty material has been mixed into them, and that it requires great prudence to seek gold in mud.
>
> “Let her always keep Cyprian’s shorter works in her hand; let her run with uninjured foot through Athanasius’s letters and Hilary’s books. Let her delight in the treatises and talents of those in whose books the piety of faith does not waver. Let her read the rest in such a way that she judges rather than follows. Farewell.”

They nourish [the reading is perhaps corrupt: *Nutriunt*] a lot often pleasing to Christ;  
May this merit be for them an unceasing heavenly *Dindima* [uncertain word/reading].

[Col. 0717]

## Letter of a Certain Regular Canon to the Prior of Charity, concerning a Regular Canon Who Had Become a Monk and Whom the Prior Sought to Reclaim

(D. Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictines*, VI, 677, from an Ottobonian Library manuscript.)

[Col. 0717C] To the venerable and deservedly beloved lord N., prior of Charity: may S. H. always fare well.

You have heard Scripture saying: “Charity does not seek its own” (1 Corinthians 13). You know what I mean: where charity is, there is light and no darkness at all; charity does nothing false, and truth is not obscured. Therefore I speak to a friend, concealing nothing, but with the confidence which you know, because what I say comes from charity. And if you too think the same, since you have the same charity toward me, do not believe that I say anything to you except from charity and for truth. Therefore I shall speak confidently, fearing no offense against charity.

I have been informed that you secretly removed from his own church a certain brother of the church of St. John at Sens, received him, and clothed him with the cowl in [Col. 0717D] your monastery. Moreover, I have been told that you gave certain harsh and improper answers to the abbot and to the church already mentioned when they sought their sheep. These things do not befit servants of Christ. The Apostle did not wish to build upon another’s foundation, and the divine Law forbids one to put a sickle into another’s harvest.

But if you say—which I do not think you say, though perhaps some who are with you do—that because your life is better, every person may choose, however and wherever he wishes, a better life and a preferable manner of living, remember what the Master teaches us. The apostles contend about primacy: “A dispute arose among the disciples as to which of them seemed to be greater” (Luke 22). Perhaps the dispute arose because a dispute was to come. We still contend: one says, “I am better”; another says, “Not you, but I.” What does Christ say? Listen: “Whoever,” he says, “wishes to be greater among you shall be your servant” (ibid.). He shall be a servant; he shall be Canaan; he shall be the servant of servants who says to a member of Christ: “You are bad; be good.” He mocks his father’s shame, and he shall be a servant of servants.

[Col. 0718C] O Canaan, why do you laugh? Why do you mock? You shall be a servant of servants; you are the seed of Canaan, not of Judah. Appearance has deceived you, because truth is not in you. You glory in your outward appearance and think it sufficient although you lack truth. For if you possessed truth, you would never glory in appearance.

O shameless tongue, after Christ do you dare to say: “You are bad; I am good”? He has already said: “Whoever wishes to be greater shall be a servant”; and do you still shamelessly cry: “I am better”? You attend to your appearance and glory in it. You look at your blackness and do not consider my whiteness. Why? Because blackness is the appearance of humility; and I say that whiteness is the appearance of purity. Blackness is the appearance of lowliness; whiteness, of glory and exaltation.

Now we commend ourselves on the basis of appearance: you glory in blackness; I in whiteness; you glory in humility—and would that you gloried well! For if you gloried properly in humility, you would never be proud of humility, mixing opposites with opposites. Humility and pride are opposites; these two cannot exist together. You can be proud of humility, but you cannot possess pride along with humility. Therefore, because you are proud of humility, you show that you do not possess humility.

You wish to be greater: what will you be? It is too little for me to say “lesser,” because you will be a servant. Monks say, “We are better”; canons say, “No, we are better.” [Col. 0719A] I say: neither you nor we, because we are all bad; but where all are bad, no one is better.

The monks say: “Let the canons come to us, that they may become good, because we are better.” If you are better, then they too are good. How, then, will they become good among you, when even without you they are already good? But you say: “They are good, but let them come to become better.” No one may be prevented from becoming better, if he wishes.

Listen: you say that a canon, abandoning and despising his own profession, may pass over to your way of life because, as you say, it is better. Therefore a married woman may, despite the law of marriage, transfer herself to continence, because—what you cannot deny—continence is better than marriage.

You have forgotten the Law (Numbers 30), which says: neither worse for good nor better for bad; render that very thing, not another thing, which you vowed; for this you owe. If you wish to give something better, give it with that thing, not in place of it. For you cannot give except through him to whom you owe this, and through that by which you owe it; so far as lies in you, [Col. 0719B] you owe no other thing than that which you vowed. If he to whom you owe this wishes to accept something else, that lies in his will, not in your power.

Furthermore, because the Apostle says, “Outdo one another in showing honor” (Romans 12), those who commend themselves perhaps suppose it should be understood in this way: that each person should hasten to seize honor before another, boasting and preferring himself. I understand it thus: if anyone asks me whether I am a canon, I say that monks are better; if I am a monk, I say that canons are superior. This is Christ’s command and the Christian rule. Therefore, if you believe my lowliness, you will neither think nor do otherwise.

But if perhaps you neglect to correct what has been done with insufficient discretion by your people, I fear that it may displease God; and the censure of ecclesiastical law, if the brothers whom you have injured appeal to the hearing of the Roman pontiff, [Col. 0720B] will not permit it to go unavenged. Therefore do not forget your moderation, which by God’s grace you have maintained until now. Farewell.

[Col. 0719]

## Explanation of the Lord’s Prayer

(Edited from a manuscript of approximately the eleventh century by Cardinal Angelo Mai in the book entitled *A New Collection of Ancient Writers Drawn from Vatican Manuscripts*; Rome, Vatican Press, 1825–31, quarto, vol. IX, p. 377.)

[Col. 0719C] Our Lord and Savior, the most merciful instructor of his own, when he was about to teach his disciples what they ought to pray for, first taught them how they ought to pray, saying: “But when you pray, enter into your rooms” (Matthew 6).

What are these rooms, if not the hearts themselves? They are also signified in the Psalm where it is said: “What you say in your hearts, be contrite upon your beds” (Psalm 4). “And, shutting [thus this manuscript] the doors, pray to your Father in secret.” It is a small thing to enter the rooms if the door stands open to intruders, through which the things outside improperly force themselves in and seek possession of our inward parts.

By “outside” we mean all temporal and visible things which enter our thoughts through the door—that is, through the bodily sense—and [Col. 0719D] disturb those who pray with a crowd of empty images. Therefore the door must be shut, that is, bodily sense must be resisted, so that spiritual prayer may be directed to the Father. This prayer is made in the innermost heart, where the Father is prayed to in secret. “And your Father,” he says, “who sees in secret, will repay you.”

And it was fitting that this should conclude with such a clause. For he is not here instructing us what to pray, but how to pray. Therefore he commanded that the heart be cleansed; and nothing cleanses it except a single and simple intention toward wisdom, with sole and pure love.

“But when you pray,” he says, “do not speak much, as the Gentiles do; for they think that they will be heard because of their much speaking.” [Col. 0720C] And indeed all verbosity comes from the Gentiles, who devote themselves to exercising the tongue rather than cleansing the mind, supposing that, just as a human judge is led to judgment by words, so God too must be bent by much speaking.

“Therefore do not be like them; for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.” By these words we are taught that we should not deal with God through words in order to obtain what we wish, but through the things which we carry in the mind and the intention of thought, with pure love and a suppliant disposition. Yet our Lord taught us the very things themselves in words, so that, having committed them to memory, we might recall them at the time of prayer.

But again it may be asked: whether prayer is made through things or words, what need is there for prayer itself if God already knows what we need? Unless it is because the very intention of prayer makes our heart serene, purifies it, and renders it more capable of receiving divine gifts poured spiritually into us. For God does not hear us because of the eagerness of our prayers; he is always ready to give us his light—not visible light, but intelligible and spiritual light. But we are not always ready to receive it, when we bend toward other things and are darkened by desire for temporal goods.

Therefore prayer brings about the turning of the heart toward him who is always ready to give, provided that we are capable of receiving what he gives. But now we must consider what he commands us to pray for, through whom we both learn and obtain what we pray for. “Thus,” he says, “pray: Our Father, who art in heaven,” and the rest.

[Col. 0721A] Since in every petition the goodwill of the person petitioned must first be won, and then what we seek must be stated, goodwill is customarily won by praise of the person to whom prayer is directed; and this is customarily placed at the beginning of prayer. In this beginning our Lord commanded us to say nothing other than: “Our Father, who art in heaven.”

And because our call to inheritance, to be co-heirs with Christ and to come into the adoption of sons, is not due to our merits but to God’s grace, we place that very grace at the beginning of prayer when we say, “Our Father.” By this name charity is stirred up: for what ought to be dearer to children than a father? A suppliant disposition is also stirred, when human beings say to God, “Our Father”; and there is a certain confidence of obtaining what we are about to ask, since before we ask anything we receive so great a gift that we are permitted to say to God, “Our Father.” For what will he not now give to sons who ask, when he has already given them this—that they may be sons?

Finally, how great a care touches the mind, lest one who says “Our Father” should be unworthy of so great a Father. And thanks are due to his mercy, who requires this from us, that our Father should be [the manuscript reads *nullo*, “by no one”]—a thing which can be acquired at this cost, from good will alone.

[Col. 0721C] Here also the rich, or those noble by worldly birth, are warned, once they have become Christians, not to be proud toward the poor and lowborn, since together they say to God, “Our Father.” They cannot say this truly and devoutly unless they recognize that they are brothers.

Therefore let the new people, called to an eternal inheritance, use the voice of the New Testament and say: “Our Father, who art in heaven”—that is, in the holy and righteous. For God is not contained by spatial places. But just as a sinner was called earth when it was said to him, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis 3), so conversely a righteous person may be called heaven. For it is said to the righteous: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Corinthians 3).

Therefore, if God dwells in his temple, and the saints are his temple, it is correctly said, “Who art in heaven,” that is, “who art in the saints.” This comparison is most fitting, so that the difference between righteous persons and sinners may seem as great spiritually as that between heaven and earth bodily.

To signify this, when we stand for prayer we turn toward the east, whence heaven rises and light comes forth. This is not because God is there as though he had abandoned the other parts of the world—he who is present everywhere, not through extension in space but through the power of his majesty—but in order that the mind may be reminded to turn toward the higher nature, that is, toward God, while its body, which is earthly, turns toward a higher body, that is, the heavenly body.

[Col. 0722A] Thus it is rightly understood that the words “Our Father, who art in heaven” mean that he is in the hearts of the righteous, as in his holy temple. At the same time, the one who prays is to desire that he whom he invokes should dwell within himself also; and he should hold fast to righteousness with affection, by whose gift God is invited to dwell in the mind.

Now let us see what is to be requested. For it has been stated who is prayed to and where he dwells. The first of all the requests is this: “Hallowed be thy name.” This is not requested as though God’s name were not holy, but that it may be held holy by human beings; that is, that God may become known to them in such a way that they think nothing holier, and therefore fear to offend nothing more.

For when it is said, “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Psalm 75), it must not be understood as though God were lesser elsewhere and greater there. Rather, his name is great there where he is named in accordance with the greatness of his majesty. Thus his name is called holy where it is named with reverence and fear of offense. This is relevant to what we say of him in the Psalm: “With the holy you will be holy” (Psalm 17), and the rest; and to the statement in the Gospel that the Father is glorified by the good works of the saints.

Then follows: “Thy kingdom come”; that is, let it be manifested to human beings—not as though God does not now reign on earth and has not always reigned, but just as present light is absent to the blind and to those who close their eyes, so the kingdom of God, although it never departs from earth, is nevertheless absent to those who do not know it.

[Col. 0722C] But no one will be allowed to remain ignorant of God’s kingdom when his Only-Begotten has come from heaven, not only intelligibly but also visibly, in the Lord’s human nature, to judge the living and the dead themselves. After that judgment—that is, once the righteous have been distinguished and separated from the unrighteous—God will so dwell in the righteous that no one will need to be taught by another human being, but all will be, as it is written, “taught by God” (John 6). Then blessed life will be made perfect in every respect in the saints for ever, just as the most holy and blessed heavenly angels are now wise and blessed through God alone enlightening them. For the Lord promised this also to his own: “In the resurrection,” he says, “they shall be like the angels in heaven” (Matthew 22).

And therefore, after that petition, we say: “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth.” That is: as your will is done in the angels, who are heaven, so that they wholly cleave to you and enjoy you, with no error clouding their wisdom and no misery hindering their blessedness, so may it be done in your saints who are on earth and, as regards the body, made from earth; and although they are to be assumed into heavenly dwelling and transformation, they are nevertheless to be taken up from earth.

Again, “Thy will be done” is rightly understood as “Let your commandments be obeyed, as in heaven and on earth”—that is, as by angels, so by human beings. For the Lord himself says that God’s will is done when his commands are obeyed: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4); and often: “I came not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me” (John 6).

[Col. 0723A] There is also this interpretation: “Thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth”—as in the holy and righteous, so also in sinners. This may be understood in two ways. Either we pray also for our enemies—for what else are those to be considered whose will opposes the increase of the Christian and Catholic name? Thus it is as though one said: “May they do your will as the righteous do, even sinners also, so that they may turn to you.” Or it may mean: “Thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth,” so that each may receive what is due; this takes place at the last judgment, when reward is rendered to the righteous and condemnation to sinners, when the sheep are separated from the goats.

There is also an interpretation neither absurd nor unfitting, but indeed most suited to our faith and hope: that we take heaven and earth as spirit and flesh. The Apostle says: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Romans 7). Let us see God’s will done in the mind, that is, in the spirit: “To will,” says the Apostle, “is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish the good” (ibid.). We pray, therefore, that God’s will may be done as in heaven and on earth: that, just as the spirit does not resist God but follows and does his will, so the body may not resist the spirit.

Nor is it alien from truth to understand “Thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth” as meaning: as in our Lord Jesus Christ himself, so also in the Church—as in the man who fulfilled the Father’s will, so in the woman who is betrothed to him. For heaven and earth are fittingly understood as man and woman, because the earth becomes fruitful when heaven makes it fertile.

[Col. 0723C] The fourth petition is: “Give us this day our daily bread.” Let us understand daily bread as spiritual bread, namely, the divine commandments which we ought daily to meditate upon and perform. For the Lord says of them: “Work for the food which does not perish.” Food is called daily as long as this temporal life is passed through succeeding and declining days.

And indeed, as long as the mind’s affection turns now upward and now downward—that is, now toward spiritual things, now toward carnal things—it needs daily bread, like one who is sometimes fed with food and sometimes suffers hunger, so that the hungry may be refreshed and the one who falls back may be raised up.

“Give us this day” is said as long as “today” is said—that is, during this temporal life. For after this life we shall be filled eternally with spiritual food, and then it will not be called daily bread, because there will be no temporal change there, in which one day succeeds another and from which the term “daily” derives.

But if anyone wishes also to understand this saying as referring to things necessary for bodily sustenance or to the sacrament of the Lord’s body, all three meanings must be understood together: namely, that we ask at once for daily bread necessary for the body, for the visible sacrament, and for the invisible sacrament of the Word of God.

“And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” It is evident that debts mean sins, whether from what the same Lord says: “You shall not come out until you have paid the last farthing” (Matthew 5); or from his calling debtors those reported to him as killed by the collapse of a tower, or those whose blood Herod mingled with sacrifice. For he said that people thought those persons were debtors beyond measure—that is, sinners—and added: “Truly I say to you, unless you repent, you shall all perish in the same way” (Luke 13).

[Col. 0724A] Therefore no one is here compelled to remit money to debtors, but whatever another has sinned against him. We are commanded rather to remit money by the precept mentioned above: “If anyone wishes to take your tunic in court” (Matthew 5), and the rest. Nor is it necessary there to remit a debt to every monetary debtor, but to one who refuses to repay, so far as even to be willing to litigate; but, as the Apostle says, “the servant of the Lord must not quarrel” (2 Timothy 2).

It is also understood that in this fifth petition, in which we say “forgive,” and the rest, the reference is not indeed to money but to all things in which anyone sins against us. For, it says [the manuscript reads *in te*, “in you”], someone has money owed to you and the means to repay it, but refuses to repay. If you do not forgive that sin, you cannot say: “Forgive us, as we also forgive.”

This point may certainly be considered: when we say “forgive us,” and the rest, we are then proved to have acted against this rule if we do not forgive those who ask pardon, because we too wish to be forgiven by the most gracious Father when we ask him for pardon. It must be acknowledged that all sins committed against us must be forgiven, if we wish the Father to forgive the sins we commit.

The sixth petition is: “And do not lead us into temptation.” Some manuscripts have “bring us,” which I think has the same force; for both have been translated from the one Greek expression, εἰσενέγκῃς, found in the text [Col. 0724C]. But many people pray thus: “Do not allow us to be led into temptation,” thereby explaining the meaning of “bring us”; for God does not Himself lead anyone in, but allows to be led in the person whom He has abandoned to his own resources. By a most hidden ordering—and often for causes evident from their merits—He judges worthy of abandonment the one whom He abandons and allows to be led into temptation.

But it is one thing to be led into temptation, another to be tempted. For no one can be proved without temptation, whether to himself, as it is written: “He who has not been tempted, what does he know?” (Ecclus. XXXIV); or to another, as the Apostle says: “You did not despise my trial in my flesh” (Gal. IV). For by this he himself knew that they were steadfast: they had not turned aside from charity because of his tribulations, which had befallen the Apostle according to the flesh [Col. 0724D]. Yet they were most fully known to God, who knows all things before they occur, even before every trial.

Therefore what is written, “The Lord your God tests you, that He may know whether you love Him” (Deut. XIII), is phrased as “that He may know” in the sense of “that He may make you know”; just as we call a day cheerful because it makes people cheerful, and cold sluggish because it makes people sluggish, and innumerable things of that kind.

Thus we do not pray here that we may not be tempted, but that we may not be brought into temptation. It is as though one who must be tested should pray, not that he may not be touched by fire, but that he may not be burned up. “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests men” (Ecclus. XXXII). Joseph, therefore, was tempted by the enticement of fornication [Col. 0725A], but was not brought into temptation. Susanna was tempted, but neither was she led or brought into temptation; and so were many others of both sexes, but especially Job, whose steadfastness in the Lord his God was admirable.

Temptations therefore occur through Satan, not by his power but by the Lord’s permission: either to punish men for their sins, or by God’s mercy to test and train them. And it makes a very great difference into what sort of temptation each person falls. Judas, who sold the Lord, did not fall into the same kind as Peter, when frightened, denied the Lord.

There are also, I think, human temptations: when someone of good intention nevertheless, through human frailty, errs in some deliberation, or is provoked against a brother through zeal for correction, yet somewhat beyond what Christian tranquillity requires [Col. 0725B]. Of these the Apostle says: “No temptation has overtaken you except what is human” (I Cor. X). The same Apostle says: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation will also make a way out, that you may be able to endure it” (ibid.). In this statement he sufficiently shows that we should pray, not not to be tempted, but not to be led into temptation. For we are led in if such temptations befall us as we cannot endure.

But when dangerous temptations, into which it is ruinous to be brought and to fall, arise either from temporal prosperity or adversity, no one is broken by the trouble of adversity who is not captured by the delight of prosperity.

The last and seventh petition is: “But deliver us from evil” [Col. 0725C]. For we must pray not only that we may not be led into the evil from which we are free, which is requested in the sixth place [Col. 0726A], but also that we may be delivered from that evil into which we have already been led. When that has happened, nothing fearful will remain, and no temptation at all will be feared. Yet while we bear this mortality in the present life, into which we were led by the serpent’s persuasion, we must not hope that this can happen now; nevertheless, we must hope that it will one day happen. And this is the hope that is not seen.

Three things will remain for eternity. For God’s sanctification will be everlasting; His kingdom has no end (Luke I); and eternal life is promised to our perfect blessedness. These three, then, will remain perfected and fulfilled in that life which is promised to us. But the other four things for which we pray seem to me to belong to this temporal life. The first is: “Give us this day our daily bread” [Col. 0726B]. For by the very fact that it is called daily bread—whether spiritual bread is meant, or sacramental bread, or this visible food in our diet—it belongs to the time called “this day.” Sins are now forgiven us, and we now forgive them; this is the second petition among the remaining four. But then there will be no forgiveness of sins, because there will be no sins. Temptations harass this temporal life, but they will not exist when that is perfected which was said: “You will hide them in the secrecy of Your countenance” (Ps. XXX). And the evil from which we desire to be delivered, as well as deliverance itself from evil, certainly belongs to this life: the life which, through God’s justice, we deserved to be mortal, and from which His mercy delivers us [Col. 0726C]. Amen.

[Col. 0725]

## EXPLANATION OF THE APOSTLES’ CREED

*(Mai, ibid., from the same manuscript.)*

[Col. 0725C] When we read that the blessed Apostle Paul said to the faithful: “But you are children of light and children of the day; you are not of the night or of darkness” (I Thess. V); and again: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. V), no one may be ignorant that through unbelief [Col. 0725D] we were children of darkness and night, and through faith were made children of light and children of the day; or rather, through faith we ourselves began to be light in the Lord, who had formerly been darkness in ourselves through unbelief.

Therefore, since through faith we have gained so great a benefit, that by it we were rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of the Son of God’s brightness, we ought most earnestly to advance day by day in the strength of that same faith, and with the apostles ask the Lord that He may deign to increase our faith. For by faith each person is rescued from the dominion of the devil and joined to Christ’s kingdom; by it the devil is resisted and God approached; by it those who were children of the devil and children of death are made children of God and children of the resurrection.

Since these things are thus beyond all doubt, who could be so foolish and opposed to his own salvation as not, with every striving of devotion and affection for purity, seek now to know in faith what he will afterwards see in sight? What can be more blameworthy [Col. 0726D] than for anyone to be ignorant of his own profession? For the Apostle commands all the faithful: “Be ready,” he says, “to give an answer to everyone who asks you for an account of your faith” (I Pet. III). If it is unbecoming that we should be unable to answer orally someone asking us for an account of the faith, how much more improper will it be to be ignorant of what each one of us ought to believe in his heart?

But because the profession of the faithful is set forth throughout the whole series of divine books, partly veiled in enigmas, partly figured in mystical matters, and partly expressed in open words; and because not all people can learn Holy Scripture, divinely inspired as it is—Scripture which, according to the Apostle, serves for teaching, correction, and training in righteousness [Col. 0727A]—so completely that what follows may be fulfilled in all: namely, that the man of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work; at least let each person strive, with the diligent study of his whole mind, humbly to meditate upon, truly to know, and to understand the words of the Apostolic Creed, so that he may not be found wholly ignorant of his profession. Especially since the words of this Creed are so few that no one at all can be excused for being unable to retain them by memory—unless perhaps someone is so brutish as deservedly to be judged devoid of reason.

Concerning this Creed, called Apostolic, ecclesiastical authority hands down the following. When the holy apostles were still assembled at Jerusalem and were about to disperse in order to preach Christ’s Gospel everywhere [Col. 0727B], they issued this Creed by the authority of the Holy Spirit, mutually contributing a confession of faith in marvellous brevity. It was therefore called the *Symbolum*, that is, a contribution or compact, because they contributed it to one another. It was also to be a token for preachers separated [manuscript: *divis*] into the various regions of the world: the person was to be believed to preach the true Gospel who handed down this Creed to his hearers without adding or subtracting anything. In this Creed the mysteries of the whole faith were marked in so brief a form of speech in order that it might be difficult for no sex, age, or capacity to retain.

It is also believed that Isaiah spoke of this Creed, or of the Lord’s Prayer, when he said: “I have heard consummation and abridgment from the Lord God of hosts over the whole earth” (Isa. XXVIII) [Col. 0727C]. This consummation—that is, perfection—and abridgment of such lofty things could by no means have been effected by human intelligence, but was effected by the Creator’s power, so that, as has been said, the holy preachers might deliver to the ears of the Church throughout the whole world a uniform rule of faith, easy for everyone coming to faith to commit to memory.

But now let us consider what the text of the Creed itself says, insofar as the Lord has deigned to grant. When we say “I believe God” (*credo Deum*), “I believe God” (*credo Deo*), and “I believe in God” (*credo in Deum*), these three expressions must first be distinguished, and we must see what is common, what is special, and what we fittingly owe to God alone.

For when we say, “I believe God,” what is understood except “I believe that God exists”? And certainly we believe not only that God exists; we also believe that the things He made exist, whether spiritual and invisible or bodily and visible. Unless, perhaps, the discussion concerns God’s ineffable immutability. For in comparison with that immutable essence, mutable created things are said to be as though they were not; and He alone is called “is,” as He Himself says of Himself to Moses: “I am who I am.” And you shall say to the children of Israel: “He Who Is has sent me to you” (Exod. III). And the Psalmist says: “But You are the same; the heavens shall perish” (Ps. CXLV). And blessed Job: “For You alone are” (Job XXIII).

But if the creature is not compared with the Creator, we believe each thing to exist in its own kind. Thus we believe not only that God exists, but also that the heavenly powers exist, because they were created by Him. We also believe that the lower regions exist. For heaven and earth are not believed by us, but known; because “faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. XI). Thus this first mode cannot be spoken of God alone, but also of things made by Him; consequently it will not be special or appropriate to God alone.

In the second mode, when we say, “I believe God,” what else does it mean except: “I believe the things which Truth says”? We also believe things said by truthful persons—that is, by persons truly wise—who speak of Truth. Thus this mode too will not be special, as though it belonged to God alone.

In the third mode, however, when we say, “I believe in God,” we cannot say this likewise of anyone else [Col. 0728B], nor can it ever fittingly be said of any thing. This, then, is the special mode, spoken of the supreme and true God alone. And what is it to believe in God, or who believes in God, except one whose faith is so certain as knowledge? Faith opens understanding for such a person: he understands not merely that God is, but that He must be loved and worshipped; and he does what he understands must be done—that is, he loves God—so that he cannot, that is, does not at all wish to sin, lest perhaps he offend Him whom he loves.

To believe God with such faith is to be born of God. The Apostle John speaks of such faithful persons when he says: “He who is born of God does not sin, because God’s generation keeps him” (I John V). By “God’s generation” he meant birth from God; and to be born from God is to be reborn through God by this faith—that is [Col. 0728C], by believing to know, by knowing to love, and by loving to cleave without offence. In other words, you show your faith and understanding by love, and make your love evident through obedience.

But those who sin voluntarily, even if they confess God in faith, nevertheless deny Him by their deeds, according to the Apostle; he also calls them unbelieving. We do not say this in order that we may believe truly faithful persons to be without sin, but to be without a will to sin. For even if not by will, they nevertheless certainly sin through some sudden slipping, weakness, or forgetfulness; and therefore they daily cry to God in sure faith: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. VI). And every day they confidently say: “I believe in God,” that is, Father, Son [Col. 0728D], and Holy Spirit. We owe this faith to no other, because nothing else is God.

“I believe, therefore, in God the Father almighty.” When I say “God,” I confess the name of essence, because “God” is the name of the essence of the whole nature of the Trinity, not of one person only. But when I add “Father almighty,” I declare the distinctive person of the Father. For when we speak of God, the names pertaining to His substance are equal and common to Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; but those which designate a person are called relative and indicate only the properties of the persons.

Therefore when we say, “I believe in God,” since “God” is the name of substance, a designation of the whole Trinity—because the whole Trinity is of one substance—we should understand it as said of the whole Trinity. But because, together with the Godhead of undivided majesty, the distinctions of the persons must also be shown, we add “Father almighty.” “Father” is a relative name indicating distinction, or a property of the person, because the one who begot is not a son but a father; just as the one who was begotten is not a father but a son. This is the relation of the name: from the name “father” a son is understood, because no one is a father unless he has a son; just as from the name “son” a father is understood, because no one can be a son unless he was begotten by a father.

Although the whole Trinity is almighty God, the whole Trinity is not Father—unless the term is referred to creation, of which the Trinity is God the Father. Yet in that supreme Trinity, He alone who begot the Son is Father. Of Him it is said that He is creator of heaven and earth [Col. 0729B]. Although this can be said of the whole Trinity, because as the Trinity is one God, so it is one Creator, one Governor, and one Ruler, nevertheless in this place the creation of heaven and earth is properly assigned to the Father because Scripture is accustomed to say that God the Father made all things, but that He made all things through the Son. Thus at the beginning of Genesis Scripture testifies of the Father: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” And the Gospel says of the Son: “All things were made through Him” (John I).

Accordingly, in this Creed every word must be weighed with the greatest care: whatever is said substantially of the Father is to be understood likewise of the Son and Holy Spirit; but whatever is said personally is to be assigned to the Father alone [Col. 0729C]. Likewise, whatever is said of the Son, if it is said of substance or essence, is also to be understood of the Father; if of person, it is to be attributed to the Son alone. The same must be understood in the case of the Holy Spirit.

It follows: “and in Jesus Christ, His only Son, our Lord.” “I believe” is understood. Here the frenzy of heretical slander finds no place, because it says of the Son, “He is Lord,” not “He is God”; for according to the above scriptural reasoning [manuscript: *scripturationem*; perhaps *scripturae rationem*, “the reasoning of Scripture”], we ought to believe in no one except God. Therefore the Son is without ambiguity God, because we believe in Him as in the Father. For when at the beginning of this Creed we profess, “I believe in God the Father almighty,” and then add: “and in Jesus Christ, His only Son, our Lord,” we confess that we render one faith to Father and Son; and because we believe them with one faith, we proclaim beyond doubt one God.

And just as theirs is one substance, so our confession is one faith. We believe in Father and Son, not with one faith in the Father and another in the Son, because God the Father is not one God and the Son another. They are different in person, certainly, but not different in substance. That conjunction which we insert when we say, “and in Jesus Christ, His Son,” belongs to the distinction of persons, not to division of nature; as though we said: “I believe in the Father; I also believe in the Son.” For the person of the Father is one thing and that of the Son another; nevertheless [Col. 0730A] our faith is one and undifferentiated, because the Godhead of Father and Son is undivided and inseparable.

It should also be known that the name Jesus is Hebrew; in Latin speech it is translated “saving” or “saviour.” Yet the Son does not have the character of Saviour merely by title but essentially, in common with the Father: for the Son alone does not save; the Father saves, and the Holy Spirit saves. Nor is the salvation of the Father one thing, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another; rather, the salvation of the Father is the same as that of the Son, and the same as that of the Holy Spirit. Nor does the Father save some, the Son others, and the Holy Spirit still others; rather, those whom the Father saves, the Son saves, and the Holy Spirit saves.

But in this place the Son alone is called Jesus because He alone was sent by the Father and the Holy Spirit for the salvation of the world. Yet He did not alone accomplish the salvation of the world. Although He alone was sent, He does not act alone. His mission is personal, but His operation substantial; and, as has already been said, what is personal is not shared with another person, whereas what is substantial is undifferentiated and common to the whole Trinity [Col. 0730B].

“Christ” is a Greek title, expressed in Latin as *unctus*, “anointed.” That He was anointed with the oil of gladness—that is, with the Holy Spirit—is acknowledged to apply to the assumed flesh, not to the divinity of the Word who assumed it. Therefore this title is not common to the Father and Holy Spirit, but is distinctive to the Son alone, and this, as has been said, on account of the flesh. Yet because flesh and Word are one person, Christ is Christ also according to the flesh, Christ according to the soul, Christ according to divinity; just as we say that Christ descended into the lower regions and Christ lay in the tomb.

And the Apostle says: “Let us not test Christ, as some of them tested Him” (I Cor. X): that is, some of those who were led out of Egypt through Moses, at a time when Christ did not yet exist except according to His eternal divinity [Col. 0730C].

“His only Son.” In calling Him “only,” it undoubtedly makes us understand His eternal birth from the Father’s substance, a birth which He does not share with the other sons of God. For holy angels are called sons of God, and holy human beings are also called such; but they are adopted through His grace, not brought forth from His substance. The Only Son, however, is not freely adopted but is Son by genuine birth from His substance. Therefore He cannot be less than the Father, because, being the figure and image of His substance and the Father’s wisdom, the Father cannot be greater than the figure, image, and wisdom which are His own [Col. 0730D].

“Our Lord.” The Son alone is not our Lord; the Father and Holy Spirit are also our Lord, just as the Father alone is not God, but the Son and Holy Spirit are God also. Nor is the Son’s lordship one thing and the Father’s another, just as the Father’s deity is not one thing and the Son’s another; rather, the deity and lordship of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one. Yet in the divine writings the Father is often understood under the title “God,” and the Son under the title “Lord.”

“Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary.” To be conceived by the Holy Spirit [Col. 0731A] is to be conceived through the grace or power of the Holy Spirit. For we do not believe, as certain most wicked and impious persons have dared to say, that the Holy Spirit was in the Virgin’s womb in place of semen, as though the Holy Spirit did in the conception of the Lord’s flesh what paternal seed does in the conception of other human beings. Rather, Christ’s flesh was created by the power of the Holy Spirit.

It is reasonably asked why, since the works of the whole Trinity are inseparable, the Holy Spirit alone is said to have effected the conception of the Lord’s flesh. But because sanctification is through the Spirit, and that same Spirit is God in such a way as also to be God’s gift, the Holy Spirit is said to have created the flesh in the Virgin’s womb so that we may understand that Christ’s flesh was created through the sanctification of divine grace by the gift of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0731B]. Thus it was both a divine work and, in the unity of the person of the only Son of God, was assumed without any stain of original sin. Sanctified from its very conception and substantially united to God’s Word, it could thereafter receive no sin.

And it was sanctified, and made divine flesh, to such an extent that He not only could not have sin Himself, but could also most effectively cleanse sins in others. For other human beings are sanctified in order to be free from sins; but the Lord’s human being was sanctified so that, receiving sin in no way, He might justify sinners through the power of His divinity.

For He was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. Yet He was not born of the Holy Spirit in such a way as to have the Holy Spirit as Father; but He was born of the Virgin Mary in such a way as to have her as mother. Born of the Holy Spirit, He was born from the Holy Spirit according to His humanity, so that He did not have His substance from the Holy Spirit; but born of His mother, He received the substance of flesh from her substance—that is, He drew His own body from the Virgin’s body. Thus, as He was consubstantial with the Father in divinity, so through becoming human [manuscript: *humanarationem*] He became consubstantial with His mother, so that the incomprehensible and invisible One might have that in which He could be seen and comprehended [Col. 0731C].

“He suffered under Pontius Pilate.” Just as it belongs to the truth of faith to believe that He secured for us a remedy from weakness—that is, by His passion delivered us not only from the sufferings of sins [Col. 0731D], but also from the sufferings of punishments—so it belongs to the truth of history that He suffered under Pontius Pilate. As it is necessary for us to believe that He suffered for our salvation, so it is fitting that we know when He suffered. For, as the Gospel indicates, the Lord was born in the time of Caesar Augustus, that is, Octavian, when Herod ruled the Jews; He suffered in the time of Tiberius Caesar, when Pilate governed Judaea.

It is established that this Pilate was a Roman man, sent by the Roman emperor, namely Tiberius, to govern Judaea shortly before the Lord suffered. He was called Pontius from a certain island near the city of Rome, where he is said to have been born. Under this governor [Col. 0732A], therefore, the Lord endured many and diverse injuries of bitter death, so that He might enrich us with the ineffable honours of a most sweet life.

“Crucified, dead, and buried.” The mysteries of His cross, death, and burial are so inexplicable that they cannot worthily be expounded by the praises of any tongue, nor even by anyone’s understanding.
