Yet in contemplating the cross, it is fitting that we consider that among other forms of death the Lord chose suspension upon wood in order through it to restore the first transgression involving wood: so that, as the fall of humankind came about in Adam through love for wood, so in Christ its raising might come about through the harshness of wood.

Many useful things are said for edification about the structure of this cross, and it would take long to attempt even a portion of them [Col. 0732B]. Yet, for the necessary meditation upon the most sacred Creed, it is appropriate to say something briefly. The holy teachers perceived that the Apostle’s words, where he says, “Rooted and founded in charity, that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the length, breadth, height, and depth” (Eph. III), are marvellously and truly fitted to the structure of the cross.

The breadth of the cross is the transverse piece of wood on which the hands are fixed; the length is the upright piece on which the whole body is extended; its height is the part rising above the transverse wood, to which the head is joined; and its depth is the part fixed in the earth.

Since the Apostle says that we are dead with Christ (Gal. II) [Col. 0732C], and that our old man was crucified with Him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed and we might no longer serve sin, we should give full attention to how these four—breadth, length, height, and depth—correspond to our crucifixion.

Joy and gladness of mind are customarily signified by breadth; our works too are signified by hands. Since the hands of the Crucified are fixed upon the breadth of the cross, that is, on the transverse beam, this signifies that our good works are made acceptable to God when they are done with gladness. And what are those works except those concerning which it is said to a person: “Take up your cross and follow Me” (Matt. XVI)? And again: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh” (Gal. V).

The flesh is crucified when our members upon earth are put to death: fornication, uncleanness, lust, greed, and other such things (Col. III) [Col. 0732D]. Therefore let us do with gladness and charity all the good things that we now perform, as though fixed in the fear of God by the nails of His commandments, so that we may be able to say with the Apostle: “Not only so, but we also glory in tribulations” (Rom. V). Let us not murmur at difficulties, lest we lose upon the cross the breadth of gladness; rather, let us rejoice in hope.

By length, upon which the whole body is extended, power and endurance are signified; hence those who endure are called long-suffering. It pertains to perseverance. By the height, to which the head is joined, is signified the expectation of recompense [Col. 0733A], according to the lofty justice of God, who will render to each according to his works (Rom. II): eternal life to those who, through patience in good work, seek glory, honour, and incorruption [variant: *merentibus*, “those deserving,” for *parentibus*, “those preparing/seeking”].

The depth, fixed in the earth, prefigures the hiddenness of the mystery and pertains to hidden grace, by which things work invisibly. Just as the portion fixed in the earth, the depth itself, is not seen, yet the higher visible parts are held up by it. Therefore, when anyone takes up Christ’s cross in order to follow Him, let him hold fast the breadth of charity and the length of perseverance. Let him also possess the height, so that he may refer to the heavenly end the things which he does gladly and perseveringly in charity, placing no other intention among his actions [Col. 0733B]. Rather, let it be as it is written: “I have inclined my heart to perform Your ordinances because of the eternal recompense” (Ps. CXVIII).

Let him also hold fast the depth, that he may know that all the good he does, his perseverance, and his acting for a heavenly end, are wrought through him and in him by God through hidden grace.

These things concern the structure of the cross; its position, however, has another signification. The standing position of the cross signifies the universality of Christ’s power, of which He Himself said: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to Me” (Matt. XXVIII). And the Apostle says: “At the name of Jesus every knee bends, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II). In this universality our head is raised on high [Col. 0733C], where angels minister to Him; the lower regions are subject to Him; and the intermediate things—namely those below heaven and on earth—He governs, rules, and directs, as it were, with the outstretched arms of His power.

There is also a characteristic of the cross such that, if you hold it not upright but flat and balanced on an even plane, it appears to indicate the four regions of the world: as though those to whom the world has been crucified, and they to the world (Gal. VI), were chosen and called by God from east and west, north and sea.

All the faithful know this concerning the mystery of His death: the Immortal died in order to restore mortals to immortality, and in order to take from the devil the spoils which he had deceitfully carried off from paradise—not by power, but by justice [Col. 0733D]. That is, by justice, so that the devil might justly lose those whom he had subjected to himself through sin, and over whom he rightly ruled while they sinned, because he had unjustly killed One who was sinless and innocent.

The mystery of His burial, which was enacted in the Head, is also enacted figuratively in His body, which is the Church. For as the Lord laboured in His Passion on the sixth day, so the Church, from the sixth day—that is, the sixth age—of the world, labours amid the miseries and dangers of this present life. And as He rested in the tomb on the seventh day, that is, the Sabbath, so the souls of the saints, after the troubles of this present life, are received into that rest which lies between the labours of this life and the final resurrection of bodies. As though keeping Sabbath after the sixth day of the age—that is, resting [Col. 0734A] in souls alone—they also await the eighth day of resurrection, when, having received their bodies and when the mutability of times has ended, souls with their bodies will be raised, without any further fear, in immutable light to the vision of Divinity; just as Christ, risen from the dead, dies no more (Rom. VI).

Therefore in this most sacred threefold sequence—crucified, buried, raised—we enact in the present life the one part signified by the cross. But the two parts signified by burial and resurrection we enact by faith and hope, because we do not yet see or possess them. For as the Lord was crucified in order to be buried and to rise, so the things we do in this present life are reckoned among necessary means, in order that through them we may come to the things to be sought and desired for their own sake: namely, that rest of souls for which Paul sighed when he said, “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. I) [Col. 0734B]; and thereafter that most perfect renewal, when death is swallowed up in victory, the last enemy—death—has been destroyed, we are changed, and are made equal to angels. Hence the Lord says: “They will be angels of God” (Matt. XXII). This is what the glorification of the Lord’s resurrection signifies.

“He descended into the lower regions, that He might free the saints who were held there by the first debts of death” [manuscript: *liberabit in se*, uncertain]. “On the third day He rose from the dead,” so that He Himself might show us the life which will exist after the general resurrection of humankind. Christ’s resurrection, however, occurred where His death had occurred: that is, in the flesh alone [Col. 0734C].

“He ascended into heaven”: that is, He raised the assumed flesh to the kingdom of the heavenly dwelling, so that He who bore our evils on earth might possess His good things in heaven. “He sits at the right hand of the Father”: that is, He reigns in the blessedness of the Father. For to sit is to reign, as the Apostle explains when he says: “He must reign until He has placed all His enemies as a footstool beneath His feet” (Heb. X). The Father’s right hand is eternal blessedness, just as His left hand is eternal misery.

“From there He will come to judge the living and the dead.” By the living He means those whom He will find alive in the world at His coming; by the dead, those who will have departed this life before His final coming.

“I believe in the Holy Spirit,” in the same way as in the Father and the Son. Therefore the Holy Spirit is God, because we must believe in no one other than God; and the faith is one, because we believe in one God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This Holy Spirit is consubstantial with those from whom He proceeds, namely the Father and Son [Col. 0734D]. For just as the begetter cannot be one thing and the begotten another, but the One begotten is the same God as the begetting One, so the proceeding Spirit cannot be one thing and God Himself, from whom He proceeds, another. Rather, what He Himself is, that also is He from whom He proceeds. That is: God is born from God; God proceeds from God. There is not one God who begets, another God who is begotten, and another who proceeds; but the begetting, begotten, and proceeding One is one God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

“The holy catholic Church.” “I believe” is understood [Col. 0735A]. For we do not say, “I believe in the holy Church,” but “I believe [the] holy Church.” That is, I do not believe in her as in God, but I believe that God is in her and that she is in God. I believe, namely, that she is God’s house and God’s dwelling-place—not a dwelling-place that contains God, but one contained by God. And this is what I meant when I said that she is in God.

For *ecclesia*, a Greek word, is rendered in Latin as “calling forth” or “assembly,” with “of the faithful” understood. But *catholica* is interpreted “universal,” because from east and west, from north and sea, she praises the Lord’s name and cries to the Lord from the ends of the earth, being indeed spread throughout the whole world.

Remission of all sins: that is, “I believe” that the remission of all sins, namely both original and actual sins, is effected through baptism [Col. 0735B], yet only in the Church of Christ, which is also the house of God. Outside it one may rightly believe there to be no remission, no righteousness. For in whatever way anyone departs from the Church of Christ, thereafter he will obtain no remission of sins and perform no righteousness, since ecclesiastical sacraments not only do not avail for salvation for those placed outside the Church, but rather contribute to their destruction.

The resurrection of the flesh: “I believe” is understood; of the flesh, certainly, not of the soul. For although the soul dies on account of its sins—that is, is deserted by its life, which is God—it nevertheless lives substantially and does not die. And because it does not die in its substance, it has no need of resurrection for its substance. Rather, as has been said, man will rise only in the flesh [Col. 0735C], because he dies in the flesh; and the same flesh which dies will also rise, but made so immortal and spiritual that thereafter it cannot die or experience any corruption [Col. 0736A]. After the resurrection man will be of the same nature but of another quality, according to the Apostle’s argument where he says: “A natural body is sown; a spiritual body will rise,” etc. (1 Cor. 15).

And life eternal: “I believe” is understood. One must ask: since eternal life is to be the lot of the righteous and eternal death that of the ungodly, why do we not confess in the profession of the Creed that we believe in eternal death as we do in eternal life? But it should be known that it is easy to understand contraries from their contraries. For in the profession of this faith the cause of the faithful is included; those alien from the faith, however, will be excluded also from the cause of the faithful—that is, eternal life. For when we confess the holy Church, remission of sins, and eternal life [Col. 0736B], what is to be thought concerning the ungodly from their opposites, except that those who do not share in the holiness of the Church remain in their impurities? Those who do not partake with it in the remission of sins remain held in their sins; and then, because they will not be possessors of eternal life, they will be sufferers of eternal death. From that death this faith will rescue the truly faithful, not those who, though with words they say that they know God, deny him by their deeds.

There remains indeed the conclusion of this Creed, namely *amen*, which is a Hebrew word and is translated into Latin as “truly” or “faithfully.” Since throughout the text of the Creed we either expressly say, or silently imply, “I believe,” and finally conclude with *amen*, what else is conveyed except: “I truly believe what I have recited in the Creed; I faithfully believe the things contained in the Creed”? Amen.

[Col. 0735]

## EXPLANATION OF THE ATHANASIAN CREED

(Ibid., p. 396, from the same codex.)

[Col. 0735C] You have enjoined upon me that I should expand, as it were by exposition with sayings of the holy Fathers, that little work on the faith which is recited everywhere in churches and which our priests study more regularly than other short works. You have done so out of concern for the priests of our parish, who can by no means acquire an adequate supply of books, but scarcely and with labour obtain for themselves a psalter, lectionary, or missal, by means of which they may perform the divine sacraments or offices. And because, amid a lack of books, many have no assistance either for the study of reading or of learning, you wish that they should at least be required to study this exposition of the faith, so that they may be able to know and understand God somewhat more fully.

For this is the greatest of all disasters: priests who ought to teach the people of God are themselves found to be ignorant of God. For just as blasphemy is reckoned to a layman, so voluntary ignorance of God is reckoned as sacrilege to a priest [Col. 0736C]. This little work is not obscure through lofty language, nor difficult through elaborate propositions, since it was written in an almost popular style [Col. 0736D]. Yet, if the words of commentators on the faith are added where necessary (*tractatorum*; the manuscript reads *tractorum*), it greatly assists in knowledge of the faith.

It is handed down that it was composed by the most blessed Athanasius, bishop of the Church of Alexandria [as the codex reads]. For I have always seen it so entitled, even in ancient codices. And I think that it was then set forth in so plain and brief a style in order to provide all Catholics, even the less educated, with a safeguard of defence against that storm which the adverse wind—that is, the devil—raised through Arius. In that storm the little ship, that is, Christ’s Church, was long tossed by such great waves in the midst of the sea, namely the world [Col. 0737A], but was neither broken apart nor submerged, because he who commanded the wind and the sea promised that he would be present with that Church until the end of the age. Therefore whoever desires to be saved from the waves of this sea, and fears being plunged into the depth of the abyss, namely eternal perdition, must hold the truth of the faith whole and inviolate.

For the little work itself begins thus: “Whoever wishes to be saved must, above all things, hold the catholic faith; unless each person preserves it whole and inviolate, without doubt he will perish eternally.” What is said at the beginning of these verses is repeated at the end. For to perish eternally is not to be saved, and to be saved is not to perish. But what does the admonition to preserve the faith whole and inviolate mean, except that nothing may be removed from it and nothing changed? This is fearfully attested at the end of the book of Revelation. For heretics and schismatics remove from and violate—that is, diminish and corrupt—the mysteries of the faith; and therefore the Church casts them outside and excludes them from herself, so that she herself may be found without spot or wrinkle [Col. 0737B].

For as God is truth, so the things which the apostolic Church has taught concerning God are true. If you lessen or alter any of them, decay from the serpent’s poison enters in, the worm of falsehoods is born, and nothing whole remains; for where there is the corruption of falsehood, there cannot be the integrity of truth.

It seems fitting to me briefly to indicate what that faith is which does not permit one to perish eternally [Col. 0737C]. Certainly it is not the faith by which demons believe and tremble, yet neither love nor hope for what they believe; rather, it is the faith which works through love—namely, that love of which the Lord says: “He who loves me keeps my words” (John 14). Whoever has attained that love unquestionably perceives how great and what kind of good God is. This is also plainly shown by the fact that no one who departs from him fares well. For from him a human being has both being and well-being; and this is the human good: to cleave to the highest and unchangeably good nature. If one refuses this, one deprives oneself of that good, by participation in which one could oneself be good; and it is a great evil for one not to be good [Col. 0737D]. On this account one also undergoes torment through God’s justice. For what could be more unjust than that one should fare well who voluntarily abandons the highest good?

Yet many do not perceive this evil which results from abandoning the highest good, because they love a lower, temporal good. But it is divine justice that one who voluntarily abandons God should lose with pain what one loves apart from him; and faith does not free such a person from this pain. Faith is also called *credulitas*, “belief”; for among the Greeks faith and belief are called by one name. *Catholic* is a Greek name, but in Latin speech it is interpreted as “universal,” because the Church, spread throughout the whole world and throughout all time, holds and has held this faith; nor has it ever been changed by time [Col. 0738A] or varied by places. For the faith of heretics cannot be called catholic, because it is not public but private, is not held everywhere, and is not shown to have existed always.

It continues: “But the catholic faith is this: that we worship one God in Trinity, and Trinity in Unity.” Unity is in the Godhead; Trinity in the persons. Therefore let us worship the unity of the Godhead in the Trinity of persons. In that Trinity there is so great a unity of substance that it maintains equality and does not admit plurality; and so great a distinction of persons that they are not mingled by their union. The three persons are of one essence or nature, one power, one operation, one blessedness, and one authority, so that the Unity is threefold and the Trinity one: each of them is true and perfect God, namely from the fullness of the Godhead [Col. 0738B]. Nothing less is to be understood in each, nothing more in the three. One is not a third part of this Trinity, nor are two a greater part than one.

Thus the whole Godhead is equal in its perfection, so that, apart from the terms which indicate the properties of the persons, whatever you say concerning one person can most fittingly be understood of all three. There is not more in the three than in each individually, nor less in each individually than in the three. For example, if you say of three human beings that they are immortal, I do not understand that the three together can live more than each individually, nor that each can live less than the whole three, because the immortality of the three is one. Or if they are equally wise, they are not wiser together than each individually; rather, there is as much wisdom in each as in the three. If these things are found in creatures [Col. 0738C], where there is neither one soul nor one body except perhaps through love and faith, how much more are they found in the Creator—namely, in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—who is eternal and immutable Unity, undifferentiated Trinity, one, one light, and one principle.

It continues: “Neither confounding the persons nor dividing the substance.” For just as, in refuting Arius, we say that the substance of the Trinity is one and the same, and confess one God in three persons, so, avoiding the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish three persons by their respective properties. Because Sabellius understood that the Trinity has one substance, he therefore confused the persons, saying that the Father himself was his own Son and his own Holy Spirit. We, however [Col. 0738D], confess not merely names but also the properties of the names, that is, the persons. The Father never excludes the person of the Son or of the Holy Spirit; nor, conversely, does the Son or the Holy Spirit assume the name and person of the Father. Rather, the Father is always Father, the Son always Son, and the Holy Spirit always Holy Spirit.

Arius, on the other hand, because he recognized three persons, asserted also three divided substances. But we confess that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one in substance and distinguished in persons and names.

It continues: “For the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another; but the Godhead of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, the glory equal, and the majesty coeternal.” The glory is equal because the Father is not greater in glory than the Son or the Holy Spirit, nor is the glory of the Holy Spirit less than that of the Father or Son. The majesty is coeternal because the Father is not earlier than the Son or the Holy Spirit; nor is the Holy Spirit later than the Father or the Son [Col. 0739A].

It should nevertheless be understood that necessity of controversy against heretics led to the use of the word “persons,” for it is not found as such in the divine Scriptures. Teachers, however, adopted it permissibly, not because Scripture says it, but because Scripture does not contradict it. For when you say, “There are three,” and are immediately asked, “What are the three?” absolutely nothing remains to be answered except “persons.” You have nothing else to answer, since you cannot say three gods, three substances, or anything of that sort—far be it!

The term *persona* is so called as though “one through itself,” because it exists through itself. It is also called *subsistentia*, “subsistence,” because it subsists through itself. What we call persons the Greeks call ὑποστάσεις, *hypostases*, which is translated into Latin as “subsistences”; and what among us is called *substantia*, “substance,” among them is called οὐσία, *ousia* [Col. 0739B]. In the Latin language, *substantia* and *subsistentia* indeed appear to be virtually one thing. Yet at the Alexandrian council, where this matter was first treated, it was defined thus: *substantia* denotes the very nature and constitutive principle of a thing; *subsistentia*, however, indicates that which exists and subsists in each individual person.

The person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another, because the Father is one person, the Son another person, and the Holy Spirit another person [Col. 0739C]. They are not different in Godhead or in glory. The Father is other than the Son, because the Father is not the Son; yet the Father is not one thing and the Son another thing, because the Father is what the Son is.

It must also be carefully noted that it is said, “The Father is not the Son.” The Father is begetter, not begotten; the Son is begotten, not begetter; the Holy Spirit is not begetter, because he is not Father; nor begotten, because he is not Son; but he proceeds, because he is Spirit [perhaps *spiratus*, “breathed forth”]. Nevertheless, the Son is what the Father is: God, Creator, Almighty; and the other names which are substantial, not personal, are equal for the whole Trinity. It should also be understood most fully that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are inseparable even in their persons [Col. 0739D]. For as the Father is everywhere, so too are the Son and the Holy Spirit everywhere. The Father does not occupy one place, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. They have not divided the world among themselves into three parts, each filling one part, as though the Son and Holy Spirit would have nowhere to be in the world if the Father occupied the whole. Such is not the character of the true, incorporeal, immutable Godhead.

They are not bodies, whose magnitude is greater in the three than in each individually; nor do they occupy places by bodily bulk so that they cannot be together when spaces are separate. For if the soul situated in a body not only experiences no confinement but even finds a certain spaciousness of incorporeal places, but [perhaps *seu*, “or”] of spiritual joys [Col. 0740A], although the Apostle says: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God?” (1 Cor. 6), and we do not say—even if such a thing could most foolishly be said—that the Holy Spirit has no place in our body because our soul has filled it all, how much more foolishly is it said that the Trinity can somewhere be hindered by any narrowness, so that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit cannot all be everywhere together?

The work of the Trinity is likewise inseparable, because each person, just as it cannot exist without the other persons, so does not act without them; and inseparable love does nothing separately.

It continues: “Such as the Father is, such is the Son, and such is the Holy Spirit.” It must be understood without qualification that “quality” is not properly said of God. For among the ten kinds of categories, these are the kinds which God lacks: quality, quantity, position, habit, place, time, and passion [Col. 0740B]. Yet he does not lack substance or relation, because Father and Son are relative names of one substance.

Therefore, as far as we can, let us understand God apart from those categories: good without quality; great without quantity; Creator without need; present without position; containing all things without habit; wholly everywhere without place; eternal without time; making mutable things without any change; and suffering nothing. I have omitted one of these categories, namely action, because the action of the Creator is very unlike the action of a creature. A creature can do nothing without movement and labour; but the action of the Creator is accomplished without movement and labour by his will alone [Col. 0740C].

Yet this statement—“Such as the Father is, such is the Son, and such is the Holy Spirit”—was adopted out of necessity against heretics who asserted that the Son was unlike God the Father, and likewise that the Holy Spirit was unlike him. We must, however, recognize what the quality of a substance is in a creature, and what substance without quality is in the Creator. Accordingly, if we say of God that he is eternal, immortal, incorruptible, immutable, living, wise, beautiful, just, good, blessed, and spirit: the last of these, “spirit,” seems alone to signify substance, while the rest appear to be qualities of his substance. But this is not so in that ineffable and simple nature. Whatever there appears to be said there according to quality must be understood according to substance or essence [Col. 0740D]. Far be it that God should be called Spirit according to substance and good according to quality; both are according to substance, just as God is called wisdom according to substance.

It continues: “The Father uncreated, the Son uncreated, and the Holy Spirit uncreated.” Nothing in the Trinity is created, because the whole Trinity is one Creator. Therefore every substance which is not God is a creature, and whatever is not a creature is God. There is consequently no difference in the Godhead of the Trinity, since whatever is less than God is not God.

It continues: “The Father immeasurable, the Son immeasurable, and the Holy Spirit immeasurable.” God the Trinity is immeasurable because he cannot be measured by any reasoning or estimation [Col. 0741A]. He is not contained by the world; rather, he so fills the world that he contains it and is not contained by it. For he is above, beneath, outside, and within the world: above by governing, beneath by sustaining, outside by encompassing, and within by filling. Thus he is diffused through all things, not as a quality of the world but as the creative substance of the world. He reigns without labour and sustains the world without burden.

Yet he is not diffused by spatial extension as though by bodily mass: not so that he is half-present in one half of the world and half-present in the other half, and then whole throughout the whole. Not so; rather, he is whole in heaven alone, whole on earth alone, whole in each part, whole through all things, and contained by no place, but everywhere whole in himself. So is the Father, so the Son, so the Holy Spirit: one God, Trinity.

But in a wonderful and ineffable manner, although he is whole everywhere through the presence of his Godhead, he is not everywhere through the grace of indwelling [Col. 0741B]. And although he abandons some who sin, he is nevertheless present to those same people in judgment, from whom the help of his aid is seen to be absent. Hence we do not say, “Our Father who art everywhere,” though it is certainly true, but “Our Father who art in heaven.” He is said to be in the holy angels and holy human beings not only through the presence of his immensity, but also through the grace of his indwelling.

For this reason, when I said above that God is everywhere, I thought it necessary to add “in himself.” He is everywhere because he is absent nowhere; but he is in himself because he is not contained by those to whom he is present, as though he could not exist without them. For remove spatial extension from bodies, and they will be nowhere; and because they will be nowhere, they will not exist. Again, remove bodies themselves from bodily qualities, and there will be nowhere for them to be, and therefore they must not exist [Col. 0741C]. But God, who is not contained in a bodily place, is in himself, diffused everywhere through all things; yet not diffused as water, air, or even light itself, which is less in a smaller space and greater in a larger. But God—whose immensity and greatness are not of bulk but of power—is whole in any one human being just as he is whole throughout the entire structure of things.

It continues: “The Father eternal, the Son eternal, and the Holy Spirit eternal.” In the Godhead of the Trinity, being is perpetual, because its nature lacks a beginning and needs no increase; as it does not begin, so neither is it bounded by an end [Col. 0741D]. For there is that state in which one does not await what is to come, nor pass through what must be recalled, but there is one thing which is always being. And if we and the angelic [being?] begin to see that God is, we nevertheless see him without beginning, in whom being is always without end, so that the mind never directs itself [the codex: “but”] toward what follows. In him no part of his duration passes away for another part to succeed; in him the mind sees all that is, and sees it to be not slow and to be long.

We know these things by faith; but what this eternity itself is—without past before the ages, without future after the ages, without prolonged delay, without perpetual waiting—we do not yet see. It continues: “And yet they are not three eternals, but one eternal; just as they are not three uncreated nor three immeasurable, but one uncreated [Col. 0742A] and one immeasurable.” They are not three eternals but one, because just as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one nature, so their uncreatedness, immensity, and eternity are one.

It continues: “Likewise the Father almighty, the Son almighty, and the Holy Spirit almighty; and yet they are not three almighties, but one almighty.” He is called almighty because he can do all things, as it is written: “With God all things are possible” (Matt. 19); or because all things that exist are upheld in existence by his power, lest they collapse. Yet many people either speak superfluously about God’s omnipotence, as though flattering him, or teach unnecessary truths when they say that the multitude of bugs, flies, or gnats belongs to God’s care and knowledge. Because the Gospel says that not one of two or five sparrows falls to the ground without God, or that he clothes the grass of the field (Matt. 6), they dare proclaim that God knows not merely the kinds but also the number of worms—however many are brought to life from the corruption of bodies, whether living or dead, of wood, or of waters [Col. 0742B]. Another reading: “Yet nothing escapes God’s knowledge.”

Some say that God cannot do everything, since he cannot grant death to himself or be changed from goodness. But those who take pleasure in saying or hearing such things should understand with the greatest care that God is of a simple nature: in God, being is not one thing and having another; nor is his willing one thing and his being able another. Rather, his willing is his being able. Therefore he can do all that he wills, and wills all that he can do, because he is powerful in such a way as to preserve his own ordering and in no way overturn his own ordinances. His will is neither greater nor less than his power; both are as great as he himself is, because God is what he has. He has eternity, but he himself is his eternity; he has light, but he himself is his light.

For no creature possesses a truly simple substance in which being is the same as knowing; a thing can exist without knowing. But the divine nature cannot, because it is itself what it has. Accordingly, it does not possess knowledge as though the knowledge by which it knows were one thing and the essence by which it is another; rather, both are one—although one ought not to speak of “both,” because what is most truly simple is one [Col. 0742C].

It continues: “Thus the Father is God, the Son God, and the Holy Spirit God; the Father Lord, the Son Lord, and the Holy Spirit Lord; and yet they are not three gods or three lords, but one God and one Lord.” Enough has already been said on the unity of the Godhead and lordship of the holy Trinity. It should nevertheless be known that “God” is said with reference to himself, and “Lord” with reference to the creatures over whom he rules: God because he alone is to be worshipped, Lord because he alone is to be feared; God of the devout, Lord of servants.

It continues: “For as we are compelled by Christian truth to confess each person individually God and Lord, so we are forbidden by catholic religion to say three gods or three lords.” “Individually” means man by man, or singly: the Father individually is God and Lord; the Son individually is God and Lord; the Holy Spirit individually is God and Lord [Col. 0743A]. Christian faith compels us to speak thus, because unless we say this, we cannot be Christians. Yet catholic religion forbids us to call the Father one God or Lord, the Son another God or Lord, and the Holy Spirit another God or Lord; for if we spoke thus, we could be neither catholic nor religious. But in order that we may be Christians and Catholics, let us say—or rather believe—that the Father is God, the Son God, and the Holy Spirit God, and at the same time not three gods but one God, who is truly one in substance and nature.

It continues: “The Father was made by none, neither created nor begotten. The Son is from the Father alone, not made or created but begotten. The Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, neither made nor created nor begotten, but proceeding.” That neither Father, Son, nor Holy Spirit is made or created has already been said above. It has also already been stated concerning the Father that he is not begotten, because he is not Son, but only begetter because he is Father.

Now, however, it must be particularly observed that the Son is said to be begotten from the Father alone, while the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, that is, from the Father and the Son. The Spirit belongs to both, namely Father and Son; but the Son belongs to the Father alone. This is the reason which distinguishes the Son’s birth from the Holy Spirit’s procession. The Son is from the Father as begotten, not as given; but the Holy Spirit is from Father and Son together as given, not as born [Col. 0743C]: that is, he is the gift of both. Thus the Son proceeds by being born, while the Holy Spirit, by proceeding, is not born, lest there be two Sons.

It continues: “Therefore there is one Father, not three fathers; one Son, not three sons; one Holy Spirit, not three holy spirits.” These are the relative names or appellations in which the Trinity is found. For “one Father” or “one Son” is not said in the way that “one immeasurable,” “one eternal,” or “one God” is said; because the latter are names of substance, that is, of unity, while Father, Son/Word, and Holy Spirit are names of persons, that is, of Trinity. They are therefore relative names because the Father is referred to another, namely to the Son. He is not Father to himself but to another, namely the Son. Similarly, the Son is referred to the Father; and when the Holy Spirit, or Gift, is named, he is referred to the Father and Son from whom he proceeds or is given [Col. 0743D].

But those substantial names—God, Lord, eternal, and the others already sufficiently discussed—when said of any person, are referred not to another but to that person itself. Although the Apostle says that Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1), “power” and “wisdom” are not relative in him as “Word” or “Son” is. For power and wisdom are substance in God, but Word, image, and Son are relative terms. If the Father who begot Wisdom were wise because of it, and being were not the same in him as being wise, then the Son would be a quality of him rather than his offspring, and supreme simplicity would no longer be there. But far be it that this should be so!

The Father himself, then, is Wisdom; and the Son is called the Father’s Wisdom in the way that he is called the Father’s light [Col. 0744A]: namely, so that, as light is from light and both are one light, so Wisdom is understood to be from Wisdom and both one Wisdom. The Father and Son together are therefore one essence, one greatness, one power, and one wisdom. Yet the Father and Son together are not both one Word, because together they are not one Son. “Word” is understood relatively, “Wisdom” essentially. Thus the Son is Wisdom from the Father who is Wisdom, as light from light and God from God; so that the Father individually is light and the Son individually light; the Father individually God and the Son individually God; therefore the Father individually Wisdom and the Son individually Wisdom. As the two together are one light and one God, so they are one Wisdom. Yet the Son “was made wisdom for us by God”; whenever something is said in the Scriptures concerning that Wisdom, the Son is made known to us. The Holy Spirit also is Wisdom; and yet Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three wise beings but one Wisdom [Col. 0744B].

It continues: “But in this Trinity none is before or after, none greater or less.” This Trinity is one God; and because he is one, he cannot be diverse, since one nature cannot itself be earlier or later, greater or less. The Father is not before or greater than the Son; the Holy Spirit is not later than or less than the Father or the Son.

It continues: “But the whole three persons are coeternal with one another and coequal; so that in all things, as has already been said, both Trinity in Unity and Unity in Trinity must be worshipped. Whoever therefore wishes to be saved must think thus concerning the Trinity.” These matters have already been stated.

It continues: “But it is necessary for eternal salvation that one also faithfully believe the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ.” As the Godhead of the reigning one must be faithfully believed, so the humanity of the saving one must be faithfully believed. For it is equally perilous to think wrongly concerning the mystery of the incarnation as to understand wrongly the mystery of the Godhead. Nothing is more just than that one should not be saved who has not feared to detract from the mystery of salvation [Col. 0744D].

It should certainly be known that *Jesus* has one meaning and *Christ* another, though there is one Saviour. Jesus is his proper name, just as Elias or Abraham are proper names; Christ is a sacramental title, as when one says “prophet” or “patriarch.” The name *Jesus*, moreover, is Hebrew and is interpreted in Latin as “saving” or “Saviour.” *Christ* is Greek, translated into Latin as “anointed,” from anointing, that is, chrism; in Hebrew he is called Messiah.

It continues: “Therefore the right faith is that we believe and confess that our Lord Jesus Christ is both God and man.” This is that mystery ordained from the beginning from the womb: that the Creator of the world should take hold of Abraham’s seed, so that in himself he might demonstrate the first-fruits of our nature; that God might become man; that, joining both natures in the singularity of his person, he might appear to human beings as the mediator between God and men (1 Tim. 2) [Col. 0745A], and might himself be for those whom he had come to redeem one God and lawgiver, king and teacher, redeemer and redemption, priest and offering, truth and way, wisdom and teacher. Thus he might show examples of life to those who followed, and, himself made man by grace, might provide help to his own race—that is, to humankind—for whom righteousness could provide assistance in no way. So that when he conquered death in man, the nature of the human race might triumph in him. For in him is our portion, because our flesh and blood are his; and where our portion reigns, we too may be glorified.

Therefore, even though one is a sinner, one should not despair of this communion of grace. For though sins hinder us, our substance claims us; though our own offences exclude us, communion of nature does not reject us. For God could bestow no greater gift upon human beings than to make his Word, through whom he created all things, their head, and to join them to him as members, so that he might be Son of God and son of man: one God with the Father, one man with humankind [Col. 0745B].

It continues: “He is God, begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages; he is man, born from the substance of his mother in the age; perfect God, perfect man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh.” Therefore the Son of God entered the virgin’s womb in order to be born again—he who had already been begotten before. He took on the whole human being [Col. 0745C], because he already possessed from the Father the fullest Godhead: not unlike the Father when born from eternity as everlasting; not unlike a human being when born from a mother as one who would die; consubstantial with the Father according to Godhead, consubstantial with his mother according to the weakness akin to us. For he was essentially born from the Father and essentially conceived and born from his mother, in order to be of one nature with the Father and one nature with the Virgin. Thus he is perfect God, because he is not unlike God the Father; and perfect man, because he is like the human being, his mother, who conceived him while her virginity remained unharmed. For true God became true man because he took on all that is ours which he himself created in us, namely flesh and a rational soul. Therefore we confess him to be God and perfect man.

[Col. 0745D] It continues: “He is equal to the Father according to his Godhead, less than the Father according to his humanity.” He is therefore equal and less, because he is God and man, everlasting and temporal: so that the incomprehensible might be comprehended, and the immortal might have that in which he could die.

It continues: “Although he is God and man, he is not two but one Christ.” There is not one Christ in Godhead and another in humanity, because there are not two persons but one. For God the Word did not take on the person of a human being, but human nature; and the person of the Godhead took on the substance of flesh, so that, because the whole humanity was assumed in the singularity of person, there is one Christ and one Son of God and of man. For as we believe three persons of the holy Trinity in unity of nature [Col. 0746A], so we believe two natures of Christ in unity of person.

In the one Christ, as we believe two natures, so we believe two natural wills and two natural operations, indivisibly, unchangeably, inseparably, and without confusion. These two wills are not contrary: his human will follows and does not resist or oppose, but is rather subject to his divine and almighty will. For just as his flesh is called and truly is the flesh of God the Word, so the natural will of his flesh is called and truly is proper to God the Word. For as his most holy, immaculate, animate flesh was made divine—not destroyed, but remaining in its own proper condition and principle—so too his human will was made God’s. For the Saviour took on human nature in order to save it [Col. 0746B]; and therefore, by taking on human will and operation, he also saved them.

It follows: “One, not by the conversion of the divinity into flesh, but by the assumption of humanity into God.” Conversion is called change; for the divinity was not converted, that is, changed into flesh, but, remaining what it was, assumed flesh. Humanity likewise was assumed into God, not consumed; for as God is not changed by mercy, so man is not consumed by dignity. Man drew near to God; God did not depart from himself. He consented to be what he was not; he did not cease to be what he was.

It follows: “One altogether, not by confusion of substance, but by unity of person.” Confusion means mixture, as two liquids are commonly so mingled that [Col. 0746C] neither preserves its own integrity. Therefore, in Christ the substances are not mingled, because each, in communion with the other, preserves its own property in the singularity of the person.

It follows: “For as the rational soul and flesh are one man, so God and man are one Christ.” As in any human being there is not one person of the soul and another of the flesh, but one human being is made from soul and flesh, so in Christ there are not two persons but one divine person that was incarnate. For as the soul bears the person of the human being—for a dead body is not called a person, any more than a stone or a piece of wood—so the divinity which assumes humanity bears the person of Christ. Therefore, in each substance he is called and believed to be the only and only-begotten Son of God; whence the Word, because of the flesh, [Col. 0746D] is man, and the flesh, because of the Word, is God.

It follows: “Who suffered for our salvation,” but in the assumed substance alone. Although according to his own nature he was free from suffering, nevertheless he suffered in the flesh for us, because the Word of God was in the crucified body, impassibly making the sufferings his own. Yet, by the grace of God, he tasted death for all, giving over to it his own body, although he himself is by nature life and the resurrection of the dead.

It follows: “He descended into hell,” in order that, by his death, having trampled down death through ineffable power, he might despoil hell. “On the third day he rose from the dead,” so that he might become the firstborn from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep, and might make a way for human nature to return to incorruption.

It follows: “He ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father.” [Col. 0747A] For this reason God was humbled in man, that man might be exalted in God; and that the one Christ, who is bowed down in the things assumed, might glorify the things assumed in those things which are his own, since he did not disdain to be afflicted by insults and returns to equality with his begetter. He sits at the right hand of the Father, that is, he reigns in heavenly blessedness; for to sit is to reign, and the Father’s right hand is everlasting blessedness.

It follows: “From thence he shall come to judge the living and the dead.” From thence—that is, from the Father’s right hand—he will come, because he will present to all the sight of his humanity, so that in judgment he may be visible in that form in which he was judged. Yet one must inquire how this is to be understood when the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “I will not judge, but the Word which I have spoken to you will judge you” (John 12), whereas elsewhere he says: [Col. 0747B] “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5). It is to be understood thus: I will not judge by human power, but I will judge by the power of the Word. Therefore the Son of Man will judge, yet not by human power, but by that power through which he is the Son of God. Again, the Son will judge, yet he will not appear in that form in which he is God, but in that in which he is the Son of Man. Thus too it is said, “The Father judges no one,” as though it were said: No one will see the Father in judgment, but all will see the Son, because he is the Son of Man, so that he may be visible in judgment to the good and the evil. For the whole Trinity will invisibly judge the living and the dead: that is, those whom the day of judgment finds alive, and those who had already died before it.

[Col. 0747C] It follows: “At whose coming all people shall rise again with their bodies, and shall render an account of their own deeds.” At the Lord’s coming [Col. 0748A] the dead are raised with their bodies, so that each person may render an account of his deeds in that body in which he performed good or evil, and may receive in that body, through which he acted, the recompense for his deeds.

It follows: “And those who have done good shall go into eternal life.” Then human substance will be raised to the likeness of its Creator, and all the good things which, though naturally received, it had ruined through sins will be restored in a better state: understanding without error, memory without forgetfulness, thought without wandering, charity without pretence, sensation without injury, soundness without weakness, health without pain, life without death, capability without hindrance, fullness without disgust, and complete health without sickness.

It follows: “But those who have done evil shall go [Col. 0748B] into eternal fire.” Many have done evil who nevertheless will not go into eternal fire, because before their death they exercised true repentance for their sins. But this is said of those who did evil, persevered in evil, and did not amend their lives. The fire is eternal because it brings eternal torments: it will never end, nor cease to torment them (*thus the manuscript*).

It follows: “This is the catholic faith, which unless everyone believes faithfully and firmly, he cannot be saved.” Let us believe faithfully, so that we may not err in faith; let us believe firmly, so that we may not doubt what we believe, if we wish to attain eternal salvation. There, praising God with the angels, may we live by his [Col. 0748C] praise and likewise glory in his praise—he who lives and reigns through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0747]

# ANONYMOUS TREATISE AGAINST A JEW

(D. Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. V, p. 1507, from a manuscript codex of Saint Peter of Conques.)

## NOTICE

If heresies and schisms must exist, so that those who are approved may be made manifest, it was not without the singular providence of God that the faithless nation of the Jews—because of the dreadful crime committed against Christ, abhorrent to all—was not utterly destroyed, but was scattered everywhere throughout the world, so that even while bearing witness to the pagans themselves concerning the truth of the sacred books, it might hold forth to others the light of faith which it itself is unwilling to behold.

Hence Peter of Blois aptly says, in chapter 1 of his book *Against the Faithlessness of the Jews*, following Saint Augustine and Bede: “For this reason life is still granted to the Jews today: they are our book-carriers, since they carry about the prophets and the Mosaic law in support of our faith; and we read Christ’s passion not only in their books but also in their faces.”

Since, however, they pursue the Christian religion with implacable hatred and have never ceased to attack it in deed and word, ecclesiastical teachers could not avoid frequent controversies with them. Especially when Jews were hostile to Christians in the twelfth century, it became necessary for very many writers of that time, and indeed distinguished ones, to sharpen their pens against them. Hence the elegant works on this subject of Gilbert of Westminster, Rupert of Deutz, Peter the Venerable of Cluny, the abbots Guibert of Nogent, and Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath; among these must be counted the author of the following treatise, plainly weighty and learned and much occupied in the study of Scripture.

Since he had dealings with [Col. 0749] Jews more than once, as is evident from sections 10 and 70, he refutes all their evasions and their vain and empty interpretations of Scripture as soundly as he knew them well. This may readily be perceived from reading the following treatise, in which he endeavors to establish, from certain and unquestionable Old Testament testimonies and arguments, the mystery of the Holy Trinity, the abolition of legal rites, the Virgin’s conception and childbirth, Christ’s divinity, the rejection of the Jews, and the calling of the Gentiles. The author himself indicates his own age in section 34, where he says: “The year one thousand one hundred and sixty, I mean in my own times, is now passing since the virgin-born Son shone forth in the world.” He also hints at this in section 48.

Moreover, besides this treatise, which we copied from an old manuscript of the monastery of Saint Peter of Conques, in the diocese of Évreux, about five hundred years old, he composed another work on the serpent’s cunning and envy, of which he makes mention in section 12.

# HERE BEGINS THE TREATISE AGAINST A JEW

## How one should dispute against Jews

[Col. 0749A]

1. As I am about to write against a Jew, I ask the reader first not to seek in what is to be said any display of secular learning, but rather the earnest intention of our lowliness. Let him attend rather to our effort to set forth the rationale of faith than to our desire to win praise for Ciceronian eloquence. For this simple purpose of ours, under the gaze of him who searches hearts and reins (Ps. 7), does not proceed from a desire for empty glory, but so that we may be equipped to answer something from the Scriptures against the faithlessness of the Jews who disparage the Christian faith.

I write for myself and for those like me, not for great and wise men, who, according to the blessed Apostle, are always prepared to give an answer concerning the hope that is in us, but for those for whom faith alone and holy simplicity suffice with me. For we know that the kingdom of God does not consist in speech or dialectical disputation, but in the simplicity of faith.

Therefore, as we seek a kindly corrector, so we detest a malicious detractor. We expect to have both; yet we prefer to endure the hatred of certain persons who circle about us with snares, rather than patiently hear opponents of the Christian faith uttering disparagements and pass over Christ’s victory in silence. We write, therefore, not that our own words may be praised, but lest we provide Jews with laughter at our ignorance, since they so often insult us and, as it were, say with Goliath: “Choose from among yourselves one man who may enter into single combat with us” [Col. 0749C] (1 Sam. 17).

We must by no means enter into conflict with them concerning the New Testament; rather, whatever we set against them must be taken from the Old Testament, so that, once convicted on points which they cannot deny, they may be held more tightly and, as though bound with the strongest cords, be compelled either to confess the truth or to prove that they do not know the Law. Therefore we maintain in writing the manner in which we know they wish to contend, lest they be able to complain that they have been defeated more by sophistical disputations than by truth or reason. Hence we always oppose them and answer them according to the letter, and introduce questions and solutions very differently from the regular order of disputation, because they run about in every direction; and when they perceive that they are being caught, they leap, like a fox in a den, from place to place. Where they seem to be held most firmly, unless their snares are anticipated, they escape more quickly.

We endeavor to meet these tactics [Col. 0750A] with the assertions of the prophets, which they cannot contradict; and we prove, by prophetic authority, the truth of what they most hate—namely, that God became man—as will be shown in what follows.

## The mystery of the Trinity proved from the beginning of Genesis

2. “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). Here I first wish to ask the Jew whether he says that God was the beginning of heaven and earth, or that heaven and earth had some beginning other than God. Perhaps he will say that their beginning was that at which they began to exist. If so, God will no longer be the beginning of heaven and earth, since he never began to exist; but every being that is a creature began to exist from him. Therefore he himself is the beginning of the whole creation.

If God is the beginning of the whole creation, there is no other beginning in which he created all things besides himself; for in him is that in which he created all things, as the Prophet testifies when he says: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103). But whatever is in God is God. Therefore that beginning itself, in which he created all things, is God. Who created heaven and earth? God. In what? In the beginning. What is that beginning? God. Therefore God is in God.

“You wish,” you say, “there to be two gods, when Scripture says: ‘The Lord your God is one God’” (Deut. 6). We answer: Light and its radiance are one substance. The radiance is from the light, yet they are not two but one. They may be called two, but cannot be proved to be anything but one. Thus, when Scripture says, “The Lord, your God, God,” does it not designate three in its names? And when it adds, “is one,” does it not affirm that the three are one substance? It distinguishes the properties of the persons; it does not divide the unity of substance.

Therefore carefully recognize one God in substance: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, from whom, through whom, and in whom all things have been created. Otherwise, if you wish the beginning of heaven and earth to be that at which they began to exist, we wish to hear from you whether God created all things in that beginning. If God created all things in that beginning, all things were created while they already existed. Therefore all things began to exist before they were created. Since this is false, we ask you: what is that beginning in which God created all things?

You will answer again: that beginning is when God created all things. We still ask whether it was eternal [Col. 0751A] or temporal. If temporal, it belonged to some time; but time could not exist before it had been created. Therefore it was not temporal. If it is eternal, nothing is eternal except God, and that beginning is eternal. Therefore that beginning is God.

If God created all things in the beginning, and the beginning itself is God, you must confess a beginning from a beginning in which all things were created—yet not two beginnings, but one beginning. If not, answer how God, creating all things in the beginning, had another beginning in which he created all things besides that which is in himself.

But you will say: “Did not all created things begin to exist? They were not eternal; therefore they began to exist in time.” What must be distinguished? They began to be in time; nevertheless, they did not have being from time. They had a beginning of existence—that is true. But I should like to know from whom: from their own original substance, or from him who created every created substance? If from their own substance, they had their beginning from themselves; if from him who created all things, he is the beginning. In what beginning, therefore, were all things created? You cannot answer: in any other than that which is God himself. Confess, therefore, a beginning from a beginning, God from God—yet not two beginnings, but one beginning.

And lest you object that what this work proclaims concerning the Trinity is empty Christian faith, explain yourself what follows shortly afterward: “And the Spirit of God was moving over the waters” (Gen. 1). You have God creating all things, the beginning in which he created all things, and his Spirit cherishing [Col. 0751C] and governing all things. Can you deny this? Either Scripture lies—which it is impious to say—or you are deceived by error, which is certainly true. For God was never without the beginning which is always in him, nor without the Spirit, who is his Spirit. Therefore recognize the Trinity in Unity: one God in substance, three in persons, reigning in one majesty and containing all things. Let Scripture prove this and explain the mystery of the Trinity more plainly to us.

## Another argument drawn from the beginning of Genesis

3. “And God said: ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness’” (ibid.). Certainly one spoke, though his operation is designated in the plural number as something to be performed when it is said, “Let us make.” How is there one, and how “Let us make”? Does he need anyone’s help?

If you answer that by this word, “Let us make,” God disclosed his will to the angelic spirits, then the angels too are makers and co-workers with God in making man. Thus the Creator will no longer be one but many—which is altogether false, as Isaiah says: “Who has helped the Spirit of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Isa. 40). No one speaks to another in this way, saying, “Let us make,” unless he wishes to make something with him.

If this is referred to angels, how can what immediately follows stand: “God created man in his image and likeness” (Gen. 1)? It does not say, “God and angels created,” but “God created”; nor “in their likeness,” but “in his likeness.” Nor can the image or likeness of God and angels be one, when it is written of God: “There is none like you” (Ps. 39). Therefore “Let us make” was said in the plural number because of God, his image, and his Spirit, so that the Trinity in persons might be shown. Likewise, because of unity of substance and indivisible operation, “created” and “made” were said in the singular number.

Either allow to be true what the Lord testifies concerning himself, or prove it false—which you cannot do, because truth does not lie. Since God says that he himself has an image and a spirit, who are you to oppose this with rash presumption and say, “God is not Trinity”?

4. Yet I know that your whole effort labors in vain to say that this word “image” cannot be referred to any person or substance. First, I ask you: is there anything in God that is not substance? Certainly you cannot prove that this image, of which we are speaking, belongs to anyone other than God alone. For Scripture says: “He created him in the image of God; male and female he created them” (Gen. 1). Therefore this image too belongs to the unity of substance which is God, because God is not two substances but one substance.

If this image is of one substance with God, it is of one power, one nature, one majesty, and one might. Therefore it is equal, since I see nothing greater or lesser, nothing unequal or different. Since, then, it is referred to the substance which is God, I judge that henceforth you cannot prevail against reason. But consider with me how it is referred [Col. 0752C] to a person, and grant your assent to truth, even unwillingly.

5. What is that according to which man was created? The image of God. Is it something that has life in itself? Certainly it is, because it is of one substance with God. It is life; for the substance which is God is life living in itself. I ask you: can that which is life living in itself be a person? It is something from someone, because it is the image of God and is from God himself. Therefore, since it is of the same substance and the same nature, just as God himself is a person in himself, so his image is a person in itself. You cannot deny that this is the second person.

Or, if you are contentious, you must consequently explain of whom God speaks, whom he calls his image, with whom he shares his power [Col. 0752D] and operation in the creation of man, and who that person is who speaks in Proverbs: “I dwell in the highest places, and my throne is in a pillar of cloud” (Ecclus. 24). And shortly afterward, where she speaks of God: “When he prepared the heavens, I was present with him, ordering all things” (Prov. 8). Likewise: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, firstborn before every creature” (Ecclus. 24), begotten by none other than the Lord. “Firstborn,” she says. Who begot? The Lord. What? Wisdom. Was she then begotten? Certainly.

Up to this point you might have had an escape, but now I do not see where you can turn. This one speaks who dwells in the highest places, whose throne is in a pillar of cloud, who testifies that she was with God when he made the heavens, and says: “I am firstborn before every creature” [Col. 0753A]—for nothing is begotten without a begetter. You are compelled to confess both begetter and begotten. What is that which is begotten? That which foresaw all things, disposed all things, and created all things with the Lord. This is what was previously called the beginning in which all things were created; afterward, the image according to which man was made; here it is called Wisdom, which teaches and instructs us, so far as is permitted, concerning that wonderful and ineffable divine generation.

Elsewhere it is called the arm of the Lord; elsewhere, mouth; elsewhere, word; elsewhere, hand; elsewhere, right hand. Although it is called by so many names, there is one name which, for some reason I do not know, you hate, in which its divinity is manifestly declared, when the Lord himself says to the same Prophet: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” [Col. 0753B] (Ps. 2).

## The generation of the Son asserted

6. Why do you grind your teeth and look at me with a grim eye? These testimonies which I bring against you are divine and spoken by the Lord himself. If you can refute them, you will prove that the true God has spoken falsehoods—which is impossible. The true God speaks truth concerning himself; he testifies truth concerning his Son. “You are my Son,” he says; “today I have begotten you.” What will you say here? Perhaps that the Lord spoke this concerning David.

Explain, then, as true of David what follows: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession” (ibid.). David did not possess the ends of the earth; indeed, he foretold that another would possess them, when he said: “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the world” [Col. 0753C] (Ps. 72). Nor did his son Solomon ever possess Egypt, Ethiopia, or the other nations, as Scripture more plainly shows: “King Solomon,” it says, “joined himself by marriage alliance to the king of Egypt and took his daughter as wife” (1 Kings 3). Again: Solomon possessed this and that—not the whole world.

Tell me, I ask, who is this Son whom the Lord testifies that he has begotten, who obtained dominion over the entire world? Pretend that you are ill and therefore unable to answer. He is he, he is he of whom it is again said: “In the splendors of the holy ones, from the womb, before the morning star, I have begotten you” (Ps. 109). What is there said, “Today I have begotten you,” means “eternally”; here “before the morning star” means before all temporal things. These and other similar passages concerning the Son of God you yourself can draw from many places in Scripture against your own faithlessness, conscious that you wickedly deny what, whether you wish it or not, you understand.

## The divinity of the Holy Spirit proved

7. That the Holy Spirit himself is, with the Father and the Son, one creator and maker is taught in the second verse when it is said: “And the Spirit of the Lord was moving over the waters” (Gen. 1). What does “was moving over the waters” mean except that he was cherishing and giving life to the still tender beginnings of the world? If he gives life, he is consequently also maker and God. This is testified by the prophet when he says: “His Spirit adorned the heavens” (Job 26). To have adorned the heavens is the same as to have made them. For who made the ornaments of the heavens except God? “God made,” it says, “the two great lights”; and immediately it adds, “and the stars, and placed them in the firmament of heaven to shine upon the earth” [Col. 0754A] (Gen. 1). Therefore the Spirit of God is God.

Ask Isaiah whether their operation is indivisible: “And now,” he says, “the Lord has sent me and his Spirit” (Isa. 48). Not Isaiah alone, but all the prophets were filled by this Spirit, creator and maker, the third person in the Trinity, true God with the Father and the Son in unity of substance. Thus it is said by the elect in Ecclesiasticus: “O how good and sweet is your Spirit in us, Lord!” (Wis. 12). What is better or sweeter than God? What is sweeter than that sweetness which illumines the hearts of the saints?

Yet they subtly called by the name “Spirit” that which is so sweet and so pleasant; and in its being called good and God’s, unity of nature and the property of person are indicated. For although there are other spirits called good, none of them has such goodness or such power as to dwell in the hearts of the saints as God and mingle them with such sweetness—which is nothing other than God—so that they say to him: “You are in us, Lord, and your holy name is invoked upon us” (Jer. 14).

For the office of servitude is one thing; the goodness and sweetness of the Creator another. If another did this in their hearts and cherished them with the same great sweetness as God himself, they would by no means say with equal longing to the Lord alone: “O how good and sweet is your Spirit in us, Lord!” (Wis. 12). Certainly good: he inspires the one and only good, apart from whom there is no other; whoever has obtained him cannot possess anything better. He is good: at his presence every evil departs and every good is given, because he himself is present who is the fountain and origin of every good.

“How sweet!” they say. Truly sweet is that delight of the Holy Spirit’s presence which bathes the hearts of believers in a certain ineffable sweetness. It can be felt but cannot at all be comprehended. For as he enters by sweetness and delight together, the one inspired does not know which of the two is greater, though both are given by the one who inspires; yet no one who has experienced it is ignorant that both are present together. Therefore, because this cannot be comprehended by the elect, ascribing glory for the greatness of grace to the Lord alone, they say: “O how sweet is your Spirit in us, Lord!” [Col. 0754D]

Much might be said on this chapter, but it is not for us to discuss with you a sweetness which you do not know, a grace which you deny, a delight which you make bitter to yourself, or a mercy which you make an offense to yourself. Nevertheless, whether you wish it or not, here he is called God’s Spirit and is proved to be the worker of goodness and sweetness in the saints.

## The procession of the Holy Spirit from Father and Son

8. That the Spirit is the Son’s as well as the Father’s, hear what the same Son, who is the Father’s Wisdom, says in Proverbs: “Behold,” he says, “I will bring forth for you my Spirit” (Prov. 1). Since he promises that he will give what is his own, and he himself is the Wisdom of God, the Spirit is certainly the Spirit of both. Thus the Father is fully God in himself; the Son fully God in himself; the Holy Spirit fully God in himself; yet not three, but one [Col. 0755A] God.

Isaiah too testifies that, in his vision of the Lord sitting upon a high throne, he heard the Seraphim cry, “Holy, holy, holy” (Isa. 6). And lest we understand three—although they named “holy” three times—and not one, it is added: “Lord God of Sabaoth.” By proclaiming “Lord God” to be one God, they declared that he whom they had called holy in threefold repetition was one God. These very hosts of Seraphim testified to this, not a human being, so that if you refuse to believe your own books, you may at least believe heavenly mysteries and angelic spirits.

## The mystery of the Trinity proved from Abraham’s vision

9. The same is more plainly indicated in Abraham, who saw three descending to him and worshipped one in the three. Do you wish to say that Abraham worshipped a creature? For angels are creatures. He worshipped either Creator or creature. If a creature, he was an idolater, since everyone who worships a creature departs from the worship of the true God. Therefore he worshipped the Creator in the three; and what is the Creator in three except God in the Trinity?

He speaks to the three as though to one and says: “Lord, if I have found favor in your eyes” [Col. 0755B] (Gen. 13). And shortly afterward he adds: “Therefore you have turned aside to your servant” (ibid.). Explain to us why he now speaks in the singular number, as though with one, and now in the plural, with three.

The appearance of the Lord itself is described thus: “The Lord appeared to Abraham in the vale of Mamre, and when he had lifted up his eyes, three men appeared. When he saw them, he ran, worshipped, and said: ‘Lord, if I have found favor in your eyes,’” etc. (ibid.). Tell me which of these three was called Lord. Perhaps you will say that one of them was the Lord and the other two were his angels. What then follows: “They said: ‘Do as you have spoken’” (ibid.)? Are the Lord and angels equal in speaking, equal in commanding? Or, when Abraham believed that he was offering service to the Lord, did he, deceived by error, offer the same service to angels?

Is it credible that Creator and creature were honored by a holy man with equal service? Nor is one person less honored than another, nor worshipped, nor treated with lesser service, nor less obeyed in speech. I ask: what is this great equality of three persons, that they are worshipped as one, served as [Col. 0755D] one, speak alike as one, command with an equal voice, and reply with equal speech? Either these three are one God, or angels are equal to the Lord in commands—which it is absurd to believe.

For who are those who said, “Do as you have spoken”? Did a creature presume to utter a command while the Creator was present? If so, how is it true what he himself spoke through Isaiah: “I am the Lord; I will not give my glory to another” (Isa. 42)? Certainly to command is the glory of a king. Angels do not command but carry out commands; they do not presume to usurp the Creator’s authority, but fulfill the office of the one who commands.

Who, then, are those who said this? The three who appeared. And who are those three? The Lord, as Scripture testifies when it says: “The Lord appeared to Abraham.” Abraham himself, seeing three, worshipped one in the three, as we read: “And he said to them: ‘Lord, if I have found favor,’” etc. [Col. 0756A] He called them “Lord,” not “lords”; he worshipped them as one God, not as three. He understood and believed the Trinity in persons, and nevertheless worshipped Unity in Trinity, as the authority of divine Scripture itself proves.

How can you refute that Abraham believed these things? First prove that he neither saw these things then, nor heard or said them; and then you will easily be able to dispute about denying the faith. Let this suffice for the present concerning our faith in God against your faithlessness.

## On Sabbath observance: the Jews’ Sabbath rejected by God

[Col. 0756B]

10. Let us come to the Sabbath and set forth our objections in the order in which the questions occur in the sacred writings, so that we may hear what you will answer to each. Concerning the Sabbath, in whose rest you especially glory and which you say must be observed before all else, hear that it was annulled from the beginning by the Lord himself. For it is written: “And on the seventh day he completed his work which he had made, and rested from all the work which he had accomplished” (Gen. 2).

Answer: how did the Lord not work on the Sabbath, when on that day he is said to have completed all his works? If he completed all his works on the Sabbath, they were not yet finished on the sixth day. If anything remained to be completed and finished on the sixth day, it was completed and finished on the Sabbath day. Therefore God’s rest on the Sabbath day was not complete, since he is read to have completed his works in part [Col. 0756C] and rested in part. What was completed yesterday ought not, surely, to be called completed today. For if I said of a work completed on the preceding day, “It was completed today,” would I not plainly be lying?

Therefore the Lord, Creator and Maker, was not, as you claim, idle throughout the Sabbath day. Rather, on that day he completed all his works as it pleased him. Nor were all things completed before the Sabbath, but on the Sabbath day itself, as Scripture testifies. Now I should like to know from you: at what hour on the Sabbath day did God cease from work? If at the ninth hour, you celebrate the Sabbath in vain before that hour in remembrance of his rest. If in the morning or at the first light of dawn, the whole Sabbath day should not be observed, since the Lord began it not with rest but with work.

“At midnight,” someone once told me, “he ceased from work.” But, unable to restrain my laughter, I said: “Did the Lord not have time to work during the day?” These are trifles, like children’s games.

But you say: “Is it not written, at the Lord’s command through Moses: ‘Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day’?” (Exod. 20). We answer: it is true that in the Law the Lord commanded the Sabbath to be observed and sacrifices to be offered—namely, the red heifer, cattle from the herd, goats and lambs, sheep, and so forth. But through the prophet he set an end to these things and commanded that they end. Do you wish to hear through whom? Isaiah says at the beginning of his book: “What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? says the Lord. I am full. I have not desired the burnt offerings of rams, the fat [Col. 0757A] of fattened animals, and the blood of calves, lambs, and goats” (Isa. 1).
