And shortly afterward: “Bring no more sacrifice; your incense is an abomination to me. I will not endure new moon, Sabbath, and other festivals. Your new moons and your solemnities my soul has hated. They have become burdensome to me; I have grown weary of enduring them” (ibid.).

The Sabbath is counted among the other festivals. Therefore it too, among the others, has been rejected by the Lord. Ezekiel likewise says in the person of the Lord: “I gave them statutes that were not good and judgments by which they would not live” (Ezek. 13). What statutes or judgments, except those of the Law? You glory in vain in Sabbath, circumcision, or the other legal observances, since they are now shown to have been rejected by the Lord through the prophets.

Hosea, first of the twelve prophets, testifies that they have been rejected, with the Lord saying through him: “I will cause all her joy to cease—her solemnity, her new moon, her Sabbath, and all her festivals, the seasons and people of the Jews” [Col. 0757B] (Hos. 2). Micah likewise says: “Can the Lord be appeased by thousands of rams, or by many thousands of fat goats?” (Mic. 6). And David in the Psalm: “Hear, my people, and I will speak” (Ps. 49). And shortly afterward: “I will not take calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks” (ibid.). Again: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (ibid.).

These and other assertions of the prophets plainly show that the Law and circumcision were given for a time, until they might lead you onward to better things. What, then, is this presumption: that, after the Law has ended and the Lord has forbidden sacrifice to be offered any further or the Sabbath to be celebrated, you still languish in the idle vanity of Sabbath observance? To have rejected it is sufficiently to have forbidden it.

## Jews: transgressors of their superstitious Sabbath observance. The Jews walked two thousand feet on the Sabbath.

11. Moreover, with what face do you claim to observe the Sabbath when you do not at all keep the law of the Sabbath? For the command of the Law is that on the Sabbath day every person should sit in his own house and neither go out nor walk away from the place where he lives. Therefore the law of the Sabbath is that on it you neither walk nor stand nor lie down, but only sit. If you move even one foot beyond the threshold [Col. 0757D], you have violated the Sabbath. Either you will observe the command—and the Sabbath—or you will lie under a curse, because it is written: “Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all the things written in the Law” (Gal. 3). Therefore you are cursed, because I see you, who do not keep this law, wandering through the streets throughout the Sabbath, running here and there. And although it is written, “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day” (Exod. 20), in this respect you break both the Law and the Sabbath, because you scorn to observe either one.

But you say that Barachibas [Note: [Col. 0757D] Barachibas, or Achibas, was one of the leading teachers of the sect of the Scribes, from whom they also received, for the most part, their traditions, as we learn from St Epiphanius, *On Heresies*, book I, heresy 15.], Simeon, and Helles [Note: [Col. 0757D] It seems that Sammai and Hillel should be read, from whom arose the Scribes and Pharisees, whose school Achibas adopted. St Jerome says, in book III on Isaiah, chapter VIII, that they consider him the teacher of Aquila the proselyte; and, as Jerome adds shortly afterward, they were born in Judaea not long before the Lord as well.], our masters, handed down to us that we should walk two thousand paces on the Sabbath. I ask you: who are these persons who are preferred to the divine pronouncement? Or what is their authority, that their decision should be believed rather than the law of God’s commandments? This is not worshipping divinity, but openly offending God. For who, to speak of those who rule among a people, would not resent having even an inferior person set above him? God commanded you to sit; Barachibas urges you to walk—not as much as you please, but to a prescribed number, namely two thousand paces. What absurdity! Unless you have with you a master carefully counting the paces, you can easily exceed the prescribed number and reach [Col. 0758B] three thousand.

Or, if you have gone two thousand paces from your house, must you not at the very place where you complete the measured number be compelled to stand, sit, or lie down, lest you transgress your master’s written ruling? For if you wish to return home, the distance will not be two thousand but four thousand paces. Nor may you proceed farther. What then? Perhaps Barachibas, Simeon, and Helles will be present and, having seized you by a lock of hair, will restore you home—as the Angel of the Lord once carried Habakkuk—lest they seem to have issued a false and ignorant ruling. But believe me: nowhere is it written in the Law that a Jew ought to fly through the air on the Sabbath day, but rather that he should sit in his house and not leave the place in which he dwells. So much concerning the empty observance of Sabbath and circumcision after the Gospel. [Col. 0758C] Let us pass on to the rest.

### The Virgin’s childbirth foretold in Genesis

12. And the Lord said to the woman, “Why have you done this?” And she said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.” And the Lord God said to the serpent, “You shall be cursed,” etc. (Gen. 3). And shortly afterward: “I shall place enmities between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. She shall crush your head” (ibid.).

You know very well who this serpent is: namely, the one of whom it was previously said, “And the serpent was more cunning than all the animals which the Lord God had made” (ibid.). It is true that among God’s creatures nothing is more cunning or more crafty than he; for although he lost blessedness, he nevertheless did not lose the subtlety of his nature. We have spoken in the preceding treatise of his deceits and envy. After he committed the wickedness by which he deceived the human race [Col. 0758D], God pronounced upon him a sentence of curse and threatened him with a greater punishment through the woman’s victory, since He foretold that his head would be crushed by the woman’s seed.

And one must carefully note the more hidden meaning which this pronouncement suggests. He promises that from the seed of a woman, and not of a man, will come that by which the human race triumphs over the serpent. Therefore this was foretold of a woman without a man. Blessed and glorious is that woman to whom the Lord promised that He would give so great a power [Col. 0759A]: namely, to exact vengeance in the hostility directed against him, and at the same time to bear the blessed and benedict seed which would bring an end to the war between the human race and its adversary by not merely humbling or wounding his head, but crushing it utterly.

Who, do you suppose, is this woman? Or what is this seed, which is nothing other than the woman’s son? For it is said, “She shall crush your head.” We Latins read *ipsa*, “she,” but the Hebrew is better rendered, “He shall crush your head.” For these words indicate that the woman would bear a son who, by His own power, would break and crush the head of the devil and ancient serpent—that is, what was chief in him, namely the pride by which he ruled the human race. Thus, through the woman who had enmity against him, and through the son avenging the injury done to His mother, victory would come to fallen humanity and everlasting destruction to the deceiver.

13. And observe that He did not say, “I place enmities” in the present, but, promising this in the future, says: “I shall place enmities between you and the woman.” Therefore it was not Eve, whom he had already deceitfully deceived and who then existed, but a woman to be born long afterward. “How,” you ask, “do you prove this?” I ask you to attend carefully and listen to the truth of Scripture. Authority will not depart from truth for my sake, nor will the most steadfast truth wish to lie for yours.

Of Eve we read: “She conceived and bore Cain, saying, ‘I have acquired a man through God.’ [Col. 0759C] And again she bore Abel” (Gen. 4). Scripture makes still clearer what these two did: Cain killed his brother. I do not know whether you would wish to say here that Abel, who is first in the order of the righteous, was the devil and serpent, and that because his brother killed him the Lord’s pronouncement was fulfilled: “The woman’s seed shall crush your head.” But this is false, because it is written: “The Lord looked upon Abel, but upon Cain and his offerings He did not look” (ibid.).

### Which serpent deceived Eve

14. If you object that this was said of the crawling serpent which moves upon the ground every day, that too is certainly false. For how could a serpent speak when it was never given the use of speech? “No,” you say, “the serpent did not speak, but the devil spoke in the serpent.” Here you must explain how, before human sin, the devil received power to enter any creature, when Scripture testifies: “God saw all the things that He had made, and they were very good” (Gen. 1). Was this reptile alone evil among all the things God made? But they “were very good.” Therefore it too was good among the other good things.

Tell me: how could evil clothe itself in what was good, or through what was good accomplish an act of iniquity? Far be it from the supremely good God to permit an innocent creature, still having done no harm, to be taken over by a malignant spirit, or to allow what was good to be possessed by evil in order to deceive the human being whom He Himself had made good! “Why then,” you ask, “was he called a serpent?” Because of death’s sting, [Col. 0760A] the poison of malice, and the desire to injure. Therefore God’s threat does not concern crushing this reptile, which scarcely knows how to avoid snares, though venomous by nature; but concerns him who is “more cunning than all the animals which the Lord God made.”

And, to conclude the remaining points briefly: every possible evil is in him. God’s word concerns crushing or condemning this being. And although he is himself a spirit of subtle nature and has nothing in common with fleshly bodily limbs, nevertheless the Lord foretells that he will be crushed by a human being living in the flesh, when He says: “He”—that is, the woman’s seed—“shall crush your head” (Gen. 3). What is the woman’s seed, designated in the masculine gender when it says *ipse*, “he,” except a human being? And how can a human being clothed in flesh exact the vengeance which God promised upon an incorporeal spirit?

It is now your task to show the woman and her son, since you can no longer argue that this very person was Eve. Examine the volumes of Moses’ five books, as well as Ruth, Judges, Esther, Isaiah, the Twelve Prophets, Ezekiel, Daniel, Jeremiah, Baruch, and so forth. In all these you will not find any woman who bore a son who achieved a complete victory over an incorporeal spirit, unless you return to her who is ours—once yours in the tribe of Judah, now ours through God’s mercy. If you deny that she is this woman, know that you must be bound by the prophets’ assertions as by very strong ropes. You will not be able to turn this way and that, for your enemies will surround [Col. 0760C] you with a rampart of pronouncements; the truth of prophecy will surround and hem you in on every side, overcoming you.

Therefore, with the aid of the Lord God Almighty, let us bring forward against you things which you cannot deny and cannot meet with crafty arguments. Here God declares that victory will come through the woman’s seed, and at this point you cannot resist. In the same seed He promised a blessing beneficial to all nations when He spoke to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 18).

### Christ, Abraham’s seed in whom all nations shall be blessed

15. It is not a different seed, but the same one. For if victory over the devil came through one, and blessing came to all nations through another, they would certainly be two; whereas in this passage for nations to be blessed is nothing other than to be freed from the devil’s power. The Lord Himself overturns this view by saying, “He shall crush your head” (Gen. 3), and not “she.” Therefore the seed through which victory was first promised is the same seed through which blessing is said to be bestowed upon all nations through Abraham: “In your seed,” He says—not in the multitude of Jews, as you maintain, but in one who would come from his seed, not in many.

For if you wish to attribute this word to the multitude of Jews, tell me where all nations ever received blessing through the Jews. Since you cannot find this, you ought to worship and believe with us in what we worship. Abraham understood that something divine, beyond what human nature could know, would be in this seed when he spoke to his servant: “Place your hand under my thigh, and swear by the God of heaven” (Gen. 24). What has Abraham’s thigh to do with the God of heaven? Or what comparison is there between his thigh and God, unless heavenly divinity would give blessing through his seed—that is, through his flesh—and not merely through flesh, but in flesh, as the Lord Himself says: “In your seed”?

“In Isaac,” He says, “your seed shall be called” (Heb. 2); yet Isaac himself is not that seed. Therefore one other than Isaac must be sought, through whom and in whom blessing is to be sent to the nations. Who is this great and such a one, to be born from Abraham’s seed, through whom and in whom the blessing of divinity shines forth upon the whole [Col. 0761B] world? You can give no other answer than the one whom David testifies to be, saying: “The Lord will give goodness” (Ps. 84).

If blessing is to be given to all nations in flesh from Abraham’s stock, and if no one other than the Lord is to give it, then neither can Abraham’s flesh give it without the Lord present in it, nor can the Lord, if what He promised is true, give it unless He is present in flesh. For a human being, though from Abraham’s seed, could not of himself give divine blessing to all nations unless God, who is blessing itself, remained present in the flesh. But how would God and flesh—that is, God and man—give one blessing unless they were in some manner one? No one can bless the whole world except God, and according to God’s promise no one but a human being should do so. Therefore God-man will give it.

16. He proves this more clearly in the preceding psalm, saying: “The lawgiver will give blessing” (Ps. 83); that is, He who gave the Law will give blessing. Those to whom He gives it will go from strength to strength—that is, from the good received through the Law’s commandments to something better, which will be the blessing God Himself gives. Hence, “from strength to strength” (ibid.): they will pass from a good Law to a better grace, because “the God of gods will be seen” (ibid.) by the eyes of flesh and bodily sight in Zion—that is, in the city of Jerusalem itself.

We say this in the sense in which your unbelief must be refuted, not in order to establish the Church’s authority. And the order of the words must be considered carefully. He affirms that after the Law is given, blessing is to be given, by which those who are to see God Himself in Jerusalem advance from good to better. Of virtues, one is higher and another lower. Does God’s promise to make Himself visible on earth mean that those who are to see Him will go from the higher to the lower? By no means; rather, from good to better—that is, from Law to grace—if He who gave the Law, or the Lawgiver, gives blessing. And for this reason the elect will go from strength to strength. From where, or to where, except from the Law first given to the blessing to be given after the Law?

He also adds consecutively the reason why this change of the right hand of the Most High is made: “The God of gods,” he says, “will be seen in Zion.” See what that blessing is, better than sacrifice and more fruitful than the Law: the very vision of God, by which He may be seen by a human being in Zion—that is, Jerusalem. Whether you wish it or not, you who reject the Church’s teaching and want to interpret everything literally according to your own interpretation, this proposition will stand.

### God to be seen in the flesh, eye to eye; how angels appeared to humans

17. Isaiah testifies to this more plainly when he says: “Therefore my people shall know my name in that day, because I myself who spoke—behold, I am present” (Isa. 52). That is: He who spoke in the Law through Moses and the prophets, I myself am now present. And shortly afterward: “They shall see eye to eye when the Lord restores Zion” (ibid.). What is it to see the Lord restoring Zion eye to eye? Can God be seen by a human being in His divinity as He is? Certainly He Himself said to Moses: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 30); and yet He is proclaimed as to be seen eye to eye in Jerusalem when He restores it.

Nothing can be seen eye to eye except a body; and what has a body can be seen, sensed, and touched. If it is true, according to the prophet, that the Lord will be seen eye to eye in Zion, and if the Lord Himself cannot be seen by a mortal human being in His divinity, then He will be seen either in this manner or some other, but not in divinity. Therefore He will be seen in a body—not just any airy or phantom-like body, but a human one.

“But,” you say, “the Fathers often saw angels, yet the angels themselves did not become human beings.” We by no means deny this. But it is one thing for an angel, for a time, by God’s nod and will, to appear to human beings in a body formed from air; it is another for the Lord Himself, promising through the prophets His own presence, to bring His promise to effect and fulfill His word by an actual deed of truth. If angels appeared to Abraham, Lot, Moses, Joshua, Balaam, and Manoah, they nevertheless did not appear in flesh, but in bodies taken from air. The Lord, however, is not so. For if one creature is assumed by another, it is by the Creator’s command or promise. What is assumed once does not remain so forever, but only for a time, because neither can an angel be air nor air an angel; but what is assumed by God is God, because there is nothing in God that is not God.

### The visible God could not appear except in human flesh

18. Since God therefore promises that He will come visibly among human beings, I ask whether He is to be seen through a rational or an irrational creature. You are not so mad as to say that He who is supreme reason assumes something irrational into Himself. Among all creatures, only human beings and angels are rational; and since an angel is an invisible spirit, it is wholly contrary to reason to declare that the invisible God becomes visible through another invisible being. What then? Either He will appear visibly in a human being, or He will not be able to be seen eye to eye, according to what the prophet, divinely inspired, has asserted concerning Him.

If it is necessary that God be seen through a human being for the prophetic word to be fulfilled, then God and man will surely be not two persons but one. “But,” you will say, “will Zion say, ‘A human being’? Can it believe that God is human?” And why should it not believe? “A human being was born in her.” Who? “He Himself who founded her” (Ps. 86). A human being only? No, rather the Most High, who founded her as God before He was born in her. Therefore God and man are one person. For by being said to have been born in Zion, He is proved to be human; and by being proclaimed as Himself born there, its founder and the Most High, He is plainly shown by decisive reasoning to be God.

For who is Most High except God alone? Or who can found or make anything before becoming human except Him who is before all things? Here you cannot equivocate or seek evasions, because nothing is clearer than this truth proclaimed through the prophet. For He who is human and was born in Zion is Himself God, since He was born human and is Most High. Most High before being human, God before being born: He founded Zion—and not merely the things around Jerusalem, but He created and made all things whatsoever that were created or made before He was born human in Zion: “A human being,” he says, “was born in her, and the Most High Himself founded her.”

What an outstanding miracle, and one deeply astonishing to the Jew! The Most High is declared to have been born human, and to have founded Zion before the time of His birth arrived. God before He is human; and, after the mysteries of His birth are fulfilled, God and human.

19. You will answer that this is not found in Hebrew. Would you have us discuss the Hebrew wording with you? It contains this: “Of Zion it shall be said: a man—and he was born in her; and the Most High Himself founded her. The Lord counted the peoples as He wrote: he was born in her” (ibid.).

Listen carefully now. “Of Zion it shall be said: a man.” By whom? By the prophet Zechariah, who says: “Behold, the man—his name is Rising” (Zech. 6). What will happen concerning this man? “He,” he says, “was born in her”; and lest you understand merely a man in a simple sense, it follows: “The Most High Himself founded her.” In Hebrew and Latin the same most steadfast truth resounds.

The Lord Himself declared these things because He foretold them in the writings of the nations, from which comes that poetic passage:

> Now a new offspring is sent down from high heaven.  
> (Virgil, *Eclogue* IV)

And the Sibyl prophesies thus:

> A king shall come from heaven, destined to endure through the ages,  
> namely, present in the flesh, to judge the world.

### The passage of Jeremiah concerning the Virgin’s childbirth examined

20. This was taken from the writings of the nations. Now let one of the chief figures who were among them, Jeremiah, speak thus: “The Lord will make some new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man.” Truly it is new and unheard of for a woman, without the work of a man, to carry a man in her womb. For at that time it could not be something new for a woman to conceive by a man, since human life has proceeded in that fashion from the beginning of the age until now. But for the Lord to do some new thing can mean nothing other than doing something He had never done before. Otherwise it could not be new if He had done the same thing before.

I do not know what “a woman shall encompass a man” can mean except that the man is wholly enclosed by the woman—not, as usual, in an embrace and kiss, for that is not new, but encompassed in such a way that the entire man is in the woman; that is, a male conceived in the womb. Yet even that would not be new, because it has been customary throughout all preceding ages. Therefore, if it is new that a man is conceived by a woman, the usual order and customary course of nature must be changed: the man must proceed from a woman without a man, and, after a new conception, a singular and unprecedented birth must appear.

“Some new thing,” he says—not only that a virgin conceive a man without a man, but also that a virgin give birth. “You want her to be a virgin because he called her a woman.” Listen: every virgin of the female sex is a woman, but not every woman is a virgin. Therefore, if he said “woman,” he did not thereby exclude virginity. Further, just as it is new for a virgin to conceive without a man, so it is new for a virgin to give birth without sin. This new thing, because the Lord Himself performed it, was beyond nature. If a woman gave birth who was not a virgin at the time of birth, this is neither new nor wonderful, for every day we see similar things occur. Clearly, what the Lord is to do upon earth—namely, that a woman should encompass a man—cannot be new or wonderful unless a virgin conceives and a virgin gives birth. For a non-virgin woman’s conceiving or giving birth cannot be new.

### Micah’s prophecy concerning the place of Christ’s birth

21. Among the other things which the Holy Spirit uttered through his mouth, the prophet Micah said of this man and His birth: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, are small among the thousands of Judah. From you shall come forth one who is ruler [Col. 0764C] in Israel; and His goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity. Therefore He shall give them up until the time when she who is in labour shall give birth” (Mic. 5).

The prophet plainly announces that this man will be born, and the place of His birth: namely, the one who is ruler in Israel. And lest you think He did not exist before becoming human, he immediately adds: “His goings forth are from the beginning.” Is this a temporal beginning? No, but “from the days of eternity,” that is, from everlasting. And as if someone wished to inquire more subtly of him what would happen to the people of Israel, he says: “He shall give them up until the time when she who is in labour shall give birth.” This is more plainly stated thus: He shall give them—that is, the Jews—over to celebrate the Law’s ceremonies and sacrifices, not forever, but until the time when she who is in labour gives birth to Him who is ruler not only in Israel but in the whole world. And His goings forth are from the beginning and from the days of eternity, because He is eternal from eternity.

Therefore, because this is to happen, the Lord will sustain the Jewish people until the time when she bears the son whose childbirth is the singular sign of the calling of the nations and the rejection of the Jewish people. For she will bear a son who is from the beginning and from the days of eternity. At that time not all will be converted, but “the remnant of His brothers”—that is, of the woman or of her son, who according to the flesh is brother to the Jews. For this follows: “The remnant of His brothers shall be converted to the children of Israel.”

That is: those who at that time believe the things I now proclaim—namely, that the eternal one, from the beginning, was born in Bethlehem, and is Lord and ruler in Israel—will not be the entire people, but only a remnant of the people. They will turn in faith and deed to the children of Israel, who will be from the remnant of their father Jacob and will understand that what Moses said was fulfilled in Him: “May the blessing of Him who appeared in the bush come upon Joseph’s head, and upon the crown of the Nazirite among his brothers” (Deut. 33). Therefore they will turn to Him as ruler and teacher in Israel. He will be God because He is from eternity, and human because He will be born from a Virgin.

When He comes, what is to be done? Let Hosea, first among the Twelve Prophets, come forward and say what we ought to do at the time when she who is in labour gives birth.

### The time at which the Lord must be sought

22. “It is the time,” he says, “to seek the Lord, when He comes who will teach you righteousness” (Hos. 10). The order of the words is this: then it will be time to seek the Lord when He comes; when He is present among you, you will have an opportune time to seek Him concerning the things pertaining to salvation. And what will He do? “He will teach you righteousness”—not only that righteousness which is in the Law, which we have learned thus far, but that which will suffice for salvation.

Then truly will be the time in which the teaching of righteousness shines forth, because that ruler and Lord, so great and such as He is—He Himself, I say, not another—will teach righteousness, which, if observed, is useful for life, and if despised, plunges one into punishment. Therefore it is the time to seek the Lord when the Lord Himself comes after the prophets.

### Christ’s divinity established from His various names

23. Joel follows and confirms the meaning of the preceding prophet in these words. He says: “Daughters of Zion, exult and rejoice in the Lord, because He has given you a teacher of righteousness” (Joel 2). Him whom Isaiah calls Lord, David Man and Most High, Jeremiah the new man, Micah ruler, Hosea Lord, Joel calls a teacher of righteousness. He urges the daughters of Zion to gladness and exultation because the Lord has given them one who teaches righteousness by word and deed, and such a teacher has disciples rejoicing in gladness and exultation.

In all these things what else is proclaimed except God-man? At one time they call Him Lord, as Isaiah does; at another, man and human being, as Jeremiah does; speaking and teaching, as Joel does; born and conceived, as David does. The meaning of all is one and their statement one, because in all there was one Spirit and one faith.

### Amos’s prophecy concerning Christ’s coming

24. After the prophet Amos had subtly described the Lord’s threats against the fat cows that were on the mountain of Samaria, he added this concerning the coming of the Lord and Saviour: “After I have done these things to you, prepare to meet your God, O Israel; for behold, He who forms the mountains, creates the wind, declares His word to humankind, and walks upon the heights of the earth—the Lord God of hosts is His name” (Amos 4).

The meaning of these words, therefore, is: O Israel, after you have endured all these things which the Lord threatens, know certainly that He Himself is soon to come; and therefore prepare yourself, so that you may be such as can meet so great a Lord. Prepare not for the coming of a prophet or an angel, but to meet your God, who created and made you.

God will therefore meet you, for behold, He forms the mountains and creates the wind, declaring His word to humankind, so that He Himself may speak to a human being as a person ordinarily speaks to a friend. Not at all from heaven or in a cloud, as He spoke to Moses and Solomon, but Himself walking upon the heights of the earth, according to David, who says: “Righteousness shall walk before Him and shall set His footsteps in the way” (Ps. 84). He will go as a human being, speak as a human being, live among human beings, and be seen on earth.

### On the book of Baruch

25. “This is your own interpretation,” you say, “since you expound the prophets as you please.” I answer: let it be neither mine nor yours, but let it be divided into parts. What I said—that He will go as a human being—is not mine, but David’s, who says, “He shall set His footsteps in the way.” That He will speak as a human being is Isaiah’s, who, speaking of the Lord, says: “I myself who spoke, behold, I am present” (Isa. 52).

Baruch, secretary of the prophet Jeremiah, although that book is not included by you in the canon, says thus concerning the Lord: “He found the whole way of instruction and gave it to Jacob His servant; after this He was seen on earth and lived among human beings” (Bar. 3). Do you see that I do not, deceived by my own will, wrench passages to a contrary meaning, [Col. 0766C] but set them forth in the light as the prophets foretold them? Prove, if you can, that the prophets did not say these things, and I shall beg forgiveness for my error.

### Christ, envoy to the nations

26. Let the prophet Obadiah come forward, and let us bring out what he heard concerning these matters together with the chorus of prophets. “We have heard a report from the Lord,” he says, “and He sent an envoy to the nations” (Obad. 1). He says that not he alone but all the prophets heard from the Lord that He would send an envoy to the nations.

An envoy ordinarily acts in the place of the one by whom he is sent: whatever he commands or decrees remains fixed and firm as though the sender himself had spoken it. Who is this envoy, sent by the Lord, who sets the Jew aside and enters among the nations? What is His purpose, or the fulfillment of His commission? Certainly that all the ends of the earth may remember and turn to the Lord. This is His purpose, and this is God’s express command, which one person after the prophets announced to all nations.

“Who,” you ask, “is this person of whom you speak?” Let the whole world—or rather, the nations themselves—answer who He is whom they received long ago, sent by the Lord, as Lord. They themselves are witnesses that prophecy has been fulfilled in the reality of the event. But Jonah (chapter 1), the prophet who left Judaea to preach repentance to Nineveh, plainly shows that this embassy, Judaea having been rejected, would pass over to the nations. Thus the difficulties of his journey, the dark confinement in the belly of the whale, and the ivy which covered his head and withered when the sun rose [Col. 0767A] occurred to him as figures of the one whom he foreshadowed by these actions.

### Micah’s prophecy concerning the Lord’s passion and Jerusalem’s overthrow

27. Micah, of whom we have spoken above, often makes Christ’s ministries [perhaps: mysteries] known. Now he recalls His birth, as was foretold, and His passion, as here: “Now you shall be ravaged, daughter of a robber. They have laid siege against us; with a rod they shall strike the cheek of the judge of Israel” (Mic. 5).

He speaks to Judaea and Jerusalem and assigns one name to both: “Daughter of a robber,” he says—not of God, but of the devil—“now you shall be ravaged.” The time will soon come when, upon the arrival of the Roman army, you will be despoiled and almost reduced to nothing. “They have laid siege against us,” which means nothing other than being besieged by the Romans. And he adds why the cause of so great a ravaging will come: “With a rod they shall strike the cheek of the judge of Israel.” No one who has read of the Lord’s passion is ignorant how this was fulfilled. He says that Jerusalem will be besieged and, after the siege, utterly ravaged because it struck the cheek of the judge of Israel, who is Christ.

### On the preaching of the Gospel

28. After describing its overthrow, the prophet Nahum plainly foretells that Christ’s Gospel will be preached throughout the entire world, saying: “Behold, upon the mountains are the feet of one bringing good news and announcing peace” (Nah. 1). He indicates one person who brings the good news—that is, who first preaches the Gospel—and announces the peace which is to come, not between Babylon and Judaea, but between God and humankind.

He says that His feet stand upon the mountains, which cannot at all be understood of a mere human being. A human being can stand upon one mountain; but I do not see how, with legs spread apart, one can stand upon two, nor did the writer intend this meaning. Who then can this be of whom he speaks, except God, who established mountains and hills by His nod and will? His feet are said to stand upon the mountains because all prophets and teachers under the Law, who were called mountains because of their knowledge of this divine Law and their eminent virtues, are inferior to Him. His Gospel stands out as much more excellent as it more perfectly declares the peace given to humankind.

If you do not accept that this is said of Christ, make plain to us who that person is who literally stands upon mountains and announces peace through the Gospel. For I would rather be pierced by your sword than wounded, as though by a prick, by my own arrow.

### Habakkuk’s prophecy concerning Christ’s coming
29. Habakkuk follows, and shows that Christ will come at the end of the age, saying thus: “I will stand upon my watch, and set my foot upon the fortress, and I will look out to see what may be said to me” (Hab. 2). At the beginning of his book he had made a complaint in the person of the people crying to the Lord; and, according to the manner of human impatience, he had wished to argue with the Lord, [Col. 0768A] alleging why He allowed Nebuchadnezzar to make the yoke of captivity heavier upon His people, rather than render to the wicked according to his wickedness and to the righteous according to his righteousness, saying: “How long, O Lord, shall I cry out and You will not hear? I shall cry aloud while suffering violence, and You will not save?” (Hab. 1). To this the Lord responded, as though to his questions: “For behold, I will raise up the Chaldeans, a bitter nation, over the breadth of the earth,” etc. (ibid.).

The Lord answered that first complaint and set out more fully, point by point, what the cause was. “Therefore,” He says, “I do not spare Judah and Jerusalem, because for this purpose I have raised up Nebuchadnezzar: that, on account of the people’s sins, he may burn the city and the Temple, and that those who despised Me may experience My vengeance.” When the prophet understood this, repenting, as it were, of his rash inquiry, he moderates his question and withdraws from his intention. He no longer provokes the Lord by asking why He does this or that, but leaves divine secrets to divine judgment alone; and, in prophetic speech, he adds what, having returned to himself, he will do thereafter: “I will stand upon my watch” (Hab. 2).

The sense is: Set by the Lord upon the height of my prophecy, I shall carefully attend to what the divine revelation announces to me and commands me to bring forth. “I will set my foot upon the fortress” (ibid.): I shall persevere with the whole intention of my mind in Him who is firm and unchangeable; and I shall contemplate in Him as from a watchtower, in order to see what things are to happen after long periods of time, and what may be said to me [Col. 0768C] concerning those things which will be fulfilled in their own time.

“And the Lord answered me and said: Write the vision, and make it plain upon tablets, that he who reads it may run through it; for the vision is yet afar off, and it shall appear at the end and shall not lie. If it delays, wait for it; for, coming, it shall come and shall not tarry” (ibid.). While the prophet deliberated within himself, and at length pronounced a judgment after prolonged deliberation about what he should do, he fixed the whole gaze of his contemplation upon this: that he might persevere in holiness and, by the merit of holiness, hear what happy things the Lord would promise after sorrowful things, and what He would foretell as future.

“And He answered me,” he says—not just anyone, but the Lord. He answered, not in response to my argument which I had earlier proposed in the person of the people, [Col. 0768D] but to me, as I thought in my heart what I should do and what future things I should foretell. And He said—because He ordained the reward of future things—“Write the vision”: not what you saw bodily, but what you saw in your mind.

And what is this vision? He stood upon his watch, that he might preserve his heart with all diligence. He set his foot upon the fortress, that he might persevere in his resolve and be considered worthy, through divine favor, to know the heavenly secret and to speak of the future mysteries of Christ. “And make it plain upon tablets.” You shall not merely write, in the prophetic manner, through figures and riddles, those things which you saw by My permission; rather, make the vision plain—that is, announce it openly—so that the reader need not seek teachers because of the difficulty of the reading. Indeed, let the one who reads run through it with swift understanding and immediately become a believer, because whoever reads and remains unbelieving, his soul will not be upright within him.

Here, Jew, you are plainly condemned, because you read and do not believe. “If it delays, wait for it.” If it delays for four hundred and ninety years—for so many years, according to the reckoning of lunar years, are counted from the time when the Temple was rebuilt under Ezra and Nehemiah until Christ—O prophet, do not despair that the promise cannot be fulfilled. Rather, wait for Him whom you see in the Spirit as one who will come in the flesh; for He who comes will come, not in appearance, but truly. And although He may seem to delay His presence within the span of the prescribed time, He will not fail to arrive at the appointed time as promised.

And this indeed is the sign: whoever is unbelieving [Col. 0769B] at the time when these things occur, his soul will not be upright with him, because he will be found a transgressor of the Law, since I say through Moses: “You shall hear Him as Myself; and if anyone does not hear Him, that soul shall be cut off from his people” (Gen. 17).

30. So much concerning Habakkuk according to the letter. But you ask where this vision was made plain by the prophet. We answer: in the subsequent writing entitled *The Prayer of Habakkuk*, he not only made plain the vision—that is, what he saw—but openly expounded it, like a good hearer: “O Lord,” he says, “I heard Your report in the spirit of prophecy” (Hab. 3), like the whisper of a gentle breeze. What is heard from the Lord is altogether sweet and mild; and I feared, recognizing and foreseeing what You would do. I was amazed at so great a miracle, and I feared to write it in speech too unworthy.

But because Your purpose must be fulfilled, O Lord, let Your work be; and this I pray: that it may be according to the good pleasure of Your will, at the appointed time—that is, “in the midst of the years.” Let Your word, O Lord, be fulfilled at that time when, the Old Testament having ended with the years spent under the Law, or before the Law, there succeed the years of which You have spoken: “I considered the days of old, and I held the eternal years in mind” (Ps. 76). And elsewhere: “I will make with you an everlasting covenant, the faithful mercies of David” (Jer. 32). And again: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will establish a covenant with the house of Judah” (Amos 8), not according to the covenant which I gave their fathers.

Therefore, in the midst [Col. 0769D] of the two Testaments—that is, at the end of the preceding one and the beginning of the one which follows, when this middle of the years shall come between the two periods—“make alive, O Lord, that work of Yours” which You earlier commanded to be made plain on tablets and written more openly.

Thus, made certain concerning future things, he continues, not by praying but by prophesying: “In the midst of the years You will make it known” (Hab. 3). Then, without any ambiguity, You will make known what You now promise, when that middle comes which divides the two: namely, the covenant which You gave our fathers and the covenant which You promise to give, very different from the first. And then, when You have been angry, because propitiation will be made for all through One, “You will remember mercy” (ibid.). It will no longer be necessary to exact eye for eye or tooth for tooth, [Col. 0770A] because You will have mercy upon the people who are Yours—that is, those who will believe—and will temper the severity of the Law with the mercy of grace.

“You will remember mercy”: namely, that mercy which the first human being lost by sinning, and which You seem to have forgotten so greatly while, in anger, You render what we justly deserve and rightly withhold the affection of one who shows mercy, until the time for mercy comes and that work of Yours is accomplished, which I heard. Because it is terrible and holy, I feared when I saw in the Spirit the manner in which You intend to fulfill it. But because You commanded it to be written more openly and made plain upon tablets, I shall gladly fulfill the office commanded by You and carefully expound that work of Yours through clear indications.

31. Hear, tribes and languages, nations and peoples, what I announce at the Lord’s command: “God will come from the south, [Col. 0770B] and the Holy One from Mount Paran” (ibid.). This is the vision which the Lord showed me and commanded me to make plain: this work of His which I heard and feared, which must be made alive and known in the midst of the years—that is, in that time when the Law receives its end and grace takes its beginning.

And lest the time when the vision is fulfilled and the work of the Lord comes should be doubtful to you, I now proclaim to you, as I foretold, what will happen in the middle: gratuitous mercy succeeding the years of the old covenant, and the sacrificial rite ceasing. The reality itself will prove that God’s work has already come; and it will be nothing other than God Himself coming.

“He will come from the south”: that the vision may be made plain according to the letter, He will arise from Bethlehem, which lies to the south, because there He will be born, according to Micah, who says: “From you will go forth one as ruler in Israel” (Mic. 5). He is also, and no other, “the Holy One from Mount Paran,” a mountain near Mount Sinai. He is therefore said to come from it because He will arise from Bethlehem not only as temporal and born, but also as eternal—the One who gave the Law on Mount Sinai and spoke with Moses face to face.

Or: God will come from the south, or midday, when the daylight is brightest—from Him, that is, “who dwells in inaccessible light”; and the Holy One will come from the mountain, from the height of heaven, according to David, who says: “His going forth is from the highest heaven” (Ps. 18). He is the Mouth and Word of the Father, who sees and governs all things. For *Pharan* is interpreted “the mouth of one who sees.” He is rightly said to come from Paran because the Word proceeds from the mouth of the Most High. Therefore He is said to come from the south inasmuch as He was born in time, and from Mount Paran because, eternally, He proceeds from the mouth of the all-seeing Most High Father.

32. Perhaps I have been excessive in explaining a single chapter and have caused the reader weariness. Let us therefore repeat what has been said and briefly restate what the Jew is asked to hear. He had said above that he stood upon his watch and set his foot upon the fortress, so that he might contemplate and see what would be said to him; and the Lord answered him and commanded him to write and make it plain upon tablets. But he, carrying out the command of the One commanding, gave this explanation: that the Lord would make His work known in the midst of the years.

What do you contend, friend? Either this prophet, in obeying the Lord’s command, made the vision plain by indicating its time and place; or he left everything obscure and, as though disobedient, scorned to fulfill the Lord’s will. But in this verse he himself testifies that he performed what was commanded. For he openly teaches that Christ, who is also God, will come in the midst of the years.

“On what grounds,” you ask, “do you refer the vision to Christ and the midst of the years to His advent?” We answer, first concerning Christ, that apart from Isaiah no prophet proclaimed Christ’s name more openly than this prophet. For he says: “I shall rejoice in God, my Jesus” (Hab. 3). He also clearly foretold in a loud voice those things that were to happen to this Jesus of ours: namely, His passion and death.

For, after declaring that He would come from the south, he immediately adds His omnipotence, saying: “His glory covered the heavens” (ibid.). It belongs to God alone to cover the heavens with glory, and “the earth is full of His praise” (ibid.). You can see that this is now fulfilled according to the letter. The whole world acknowledges Jesus the Savior. You alone are blinded, together with those like you: seeing little on earth, destined to see nothing in heaven, wholly going below into outer darkness unless you look upon the light which is the splendor of Him whose praise fills the earth.

“His splendor,” he says, “will be as light” (ibid.)—the splendor of Him who comes from the south, God, who rules the heavens with glory and fills the earth with praise. And what is said of Him who is to come so great and such as this? According to Isaiah, He will come in strength; yet “horns are in His hands, and there His strength is hidden” (ibid.). And what is the strength of God except God Himself? He will be manifest inasmuch as He is human, hidden inasmuch as He is God, as Isaiah likewise says: “I will wait for the Lord, who hides His face from the house of Jacob” (Isa. 8).

33. Let him who seems to explain the vision itself explain how horns are in His hands. “The height,” he says, “lifted up its hands” (Hab. 3). What? His feet penetrate the depth of the abyss, and His hands are lifted on high: that He may pray, or that He may work? I judge: that He may pray, work, and die—pray in heaven, work in the lower regions, and die on earth. For what great thing would it be if the Height lifted up its hands without cause? But the Height, who is God, lifted up His hands in order to fulfill according to the letter what He had foretold through the prophet: “Horns are in His hands” (ibid.).

“How,” you ask, [Col. 0771D] “was this fulfilled in Christ?” Do you ask what you are unwilling to be compelled to hear? Look upon Christ dying on the cross, with His hands nailed upon each horn of the cross, and, as He dies with bowed head, raised aloft. You will see horns in His hands, where His strength is hidden, because, set upon the cross, He “reaches mightily from one end to the other,” governing all things at the higher end and dying strongly at the lower, “disposing all things sweetly” with both hands (Wis. 8). He conquers in hell and reigns in heaven; between the two, as between right and left, He Himself dies in the one sweet sleep of death. For willingly He gives glory to heaven, life to earth, and death to hell—that is, to the princes of hell—so that all things may return to their proper order: that human nature, for whose sake all temporal things were made, may ascend from [Col. 0772A] the depths to the heights. This is the hidden strength of the One dying on the cross and holding horns in His hands.

### How “the midst of the years” is to be understood. The author’s age

34. We have spoken of the vision and how it refers to Christ. It remains to say how the midst of the years signifies His advent. You assert that Christ is to come at the end of the age. First, I ask you to teach how the end of the age can be called the midst of the years. If the end of the age is the midst of the years, there will be as many years of the age after its end as preceded it; therefore that which is the middle cannot be called the end. If, according to the prophet, God’s promise will not be made known in the midst of the years, distinguish at what time it will occur: at the end, according to your opinion, or in the midst of the years, according to the prophet. Which of you is to be believed more?

Just as the end of a period cannot be called its middle, so neither can the middle be called its end. But according to the prophet it will be made known in the midst of the years; therefore it will not occur in the finished state of times. Your assertion that Christ is to come at the end of the age is therefore false.

Let us then consider the midst of the years and prove that the prophet spoke true in every respect. The year 1166, I mean in my own times, is now passing since the virginal Son shone forth into the world at the appointed time, according to the prescribed number of Daniel’s weeks, concerning which, God willing, we shall speak more fully in its proper place. [Col. 0772C] But how much time yet remains is known to God alone and unknown to all mortals.

Yet we do not doubt that this was the midst of the years: the time when the sweetness of Christians distilled from heaven upon the earth, and one blessing was compounded, according to Isaac, from the dew of heaven above and the richness of the earth—namely, one Christ arising from divine and human nature. In Him the Lord, making His salvation known, revealed His righteousness before the nations.

We call this the midst of the years because one Law preceded and another, that is, the new Law, followed. For when the priesthood was transferred, a transfer of the Law necessarily took place, He succeeding to whom it was said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109). If you do not grant that this is the midst of the years of the first and second Law, show us the Temple, priesthood, and kingdom in Judaea, so that the first advent of the Savior must still be awaited. “If you look at the heifer, there is nothing to praise in the cups.” So much is enough to have said concerning Habakkuk.

Here I again and again ask the reader to receive these things in the sense in which the preceding matters were stated: namely, the sense in which the Jew ought to be pressed and convicted by the authority of the prophets. We do not deny that subtler interpretations are held among the older writers; but our purpose is to contend with the Jew, not to discuss the exposition of Scripture with the Christian.

### Concerning the prophet Zephaniah

35. Let us come to Zephaniah, who, because of the depth of the mysteries he foreknew concerning Christ, was called “the Secret [*Arcanum*] [Col. 0773A] of the Lord.” Filled with the Holy Spirit, by whom he became foreknowing of future things, he declares with the inexpressible exultation of mind the joy which he had conceived in his heart concerning Christ’s advent: “Praise and exult, daughter Zion; shout for joy, Israel; exult and rejoice with all your heart, daughter Jerusalem” (Zeph. 3). A little later he adds the reason: “The Lord your God is mighty in your midst; He Himself will save you” (ibid.).

“Praise,” he says, “the Lord for the multitude of His mercy; and above all exult, according to Joel, who says: ‘Daughters of Zion, exult in the Lord your God, because He has given you a teacher of righteousness’” (Joel 2). Let praise of God first proceed from the mouth because His mercy so abundantly overflows through Christ; and let exultation of mind be joined to praise of the mouth, so that everything within you may rejoice and praise with heart and mouth, mind and deed, because the Lord your God will be in your midst.

And not only “praise and exult, daughter Zion”—that is, the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin—but you also, O Israel, shout for joy, and fill your heart with such great gladness that you express more by mind and countenance than by the voice of song or the practice of speech how eagerly you await the Lord Savior, with how many prayers you receive Him when He comes, and with what praiseworthy faith you preserve love for Him in your heart.

“Exult and praise, daughter Jerusalem,” to whom I earlier foretold that you should praise in faith and exult in hope. Again I say, “Exult and rejoice with all your heart,” so that double joy may produce double love, and one perfection may consist in the threefold praise—namely, faith, hope, and charity. I enjoined praise and exultation upon you when you were first called daughter Zion, that is, “the watchtower which is with Me,” because this too is My name: through your prophets you foresee future things. But now I truly call you daughter Jerusalem because you see face to face Him who, according to Micah, will be peace in your midst when He comes.

### Christ compared to a rhinoceros

36. Do you ask who this is? “The Lord your God, mighty in your midst,” of whom Balaam spoke in Numbers, saying: “His strength is like that of a rhinoceros” (Num. 23). No hunter can capture the rhinoceros. If a virgin spreads her bosom before one coming toward her, it immediately leaps into her, and it approaches through love rather than force.

Therefore Balaam compared His strength to the rhinoceros because, after leaving behind all His pursuers, the Lord, in likeness to it, inclined His head in the bosom of the daughter Jerusalem—that is, the Church—and she received in her bosom Him whom the Synagogue could not grasp in its arms. He inclined toward her more willingly because He found in her the modesty of chastity, the gentleness of humility, tranquillity of character, and the keeping of discipline.

Therefore the humble Lord God became mighty in the midst of the daughter Jerusalem. Hence she is summoned to gladness and exultation: to temporal gladness over His advent, and to exultation over the perpetual attainment of salvation, because it follows: “He Himself will save you.” Therefore I urge you to rejoice and be glad, daughter Jerusalem, because not, as hitherto, will a prophet [Col. 0774A] or angel act toward you in the bridegroom’s place or render service; but He Himself, who is Lord and God, will save you.

This “Himself,” which must not be passed over carelessly, means that by His own presence, which He will show in your midst, He will save you. For He will be present with a presence that saves, because He who is present everywhere by the power of divinity will be seen bodily in flesh. He will display in the body this presence of which the prophets speak. Those who so often foretold His advent did not mean only the presence of His divinity; rather, by their frequent variation of expression, they testified that something unprecedented in earlier ages would occur.

For what truth would the prophetic statements contain when they say, “He will come, He will come; He will appear, He will appear; He will be seen; He will not delay,” unless Truth Himself, so to speak, were at some time to come in truth? Zephaniah, then, indicating the Lord’s bodily presence, says: “The Lord your God is mighty in your midst; He Himself will save you.” Lord, to govern all nations; God, to form them; mighty, to defeat the aerial powers; in your midst by bodily presence—He Himself, not another, will save you, that is, free you from the power of eternal death.

“You say that I do not accept your explanation because it appears more contrary than consonant to the sequence of truth.” Take this brief answer from me: neither do I assent to your contention, because it rests neither upon truth nor upon anything that appears plausible. Therefore, just as we do not accept your falsehood, so by the authority [Col. 0774C] of the prophets we easily refute your assertions.

### Concerning the prophecy of Haggai. The patriarchs’ longings for Christ

37. Let Haggai—whose name is interpreted “festive”—be brought forward, and let us hear to which of us he agrees more. He introduces the Lord God Almighty as speaking thus to the Jewish people: “Yet one little while, and I will shake heaven and earth, sea and dry land; and I will shake all nations, and the Desired One of all nations will come” (Hag. 2).

Who is this Desired One, or by whom is He desired, whom the Lord promises will come? Burning with desire for Him, the patriarch Abraham says to the Lord: “Lord God, I shall go childless, and this Damascus Eliezer is my heir” (Gen. 15). He had heard that blessing was to be given to all nations in the seed; yet, grieving that it was delayed, he asks that it be fulfilled with the intense affection of one who desires it greatly.

Isaac, with equal longing, prays that the blessing of his son may come, saying: “Be lord of your brothers, and let the sons of your mother bow before you” (Gen. 17). You cannot prove that this was fulfilled literally in Jacob or in any of his descendants. If you say it was fulfilled in Joseph or in any of the kings, how will what follows be true: “And let the tribes worship him” (ibid.), when none of them was worshipped by all nations? It belongs to God alone to be worshipped by all; therefore it is fulfilled in Christ, as is seen today—Christ, who is God and man, born from his seed.

Jacob, in the blessings of his sons, directs his expectation toward [Col. 0775A] Christ, saying: “I will await Your salvation, O Lord” (Gen. 49), as though he said: “I shall await the Savior, who will restore to me true and eternal salvation.” Answer: where did this man await the Lord’s salvation? For as soon as the blessing was completed, he drew himself together upon his bed, departed from the light, and, being gathered to his fathers, went down to the places of souls. Yet he believed that there he would be saved through the Savior.

Job too was not without this longing, but desired Him to come in the flesh, whom he had foreseen in the Spirit, saying: “Who will grant that my petition may come, and that God may give me what I await?” (Job 6). “Who,” he says, “will grant”—that is, may it truly happen—that my petition, so long desired, may come and not be delayed? This petition is nothing other than Christ. And may God, who will send Him, grant me what I await: namely, His presence.

Moses likewise, with the same longing, says: “I beseech You, Lord, send Him whom You are going to send” (Exod. 4). This plainly means: “You intend, Lord, to give the Law to Your people and, with me as their guide, lead them into the land of promise. Yet I beseech You, Lord, that what is now done in figure may, when the time has come, appear in truth; and, to fulfill this mystery of Your will, send, Lord, Him whom You are going to send—Christ, who may truly turn waters into blood and come both in water and blood, so that, after giving baptism, He may redeem by His own blood and thus lead His people through the Red Sea into the land of promise: that is, into the peace of eternal rest.”

David prayed for this same thing in the psalm, saying: “Show [Col. 0775C] us Your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79). Isaiah, asking the Lord for the Savior’s advent, says: “Send forth, O Lord, the Lamb, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the wilderness to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. 16). “Send forth,” he says, “O Lord, that which is still in Your secret counsel: namely, the Lamb, gentle, innocent, and just, who is called Lamb because, before the one who slays Him, He will not open His mouth. Send Him, O Lord, from the rock of the wilderness: Ruth comes from the Gentiles into Judaea and bears Obed; Obed, Jesse; Jesse, David. From David’s fruit give us the Ruler of the earth, and let Him come as far as the mountain of the daughter Zion—that is, that He may be seen in Jerusalem.”

This is the Desired One of whom the prophet Haggai now speaks, whom the Lord promises will come. “Yet one little while,” He says: a small space of time remains, because “a thousand years before Your eyes are as yesterday which has passed” (Ps. 89). “And I will shake heaven and earth, sea and dry land.” The meaning is this: Once I shook heaven, when I gave the Law upon Mount Sinai and came down upon it in fire. I shook earth, when the fountains of the abyss were broken open and I brought the flood upon the earth. I shook the sea, when it was divided into two parts and the people crossed on dry foot. I also shook dry land, when it opened its mouth and swallowed the sinners.

After these things there is yet one little while, because not even a thousand years will pass; and I will shake heaven because I shall send the Lord of heaven. I will shake earth because it will open and bring forth the Savior (Isa. 45). [Col. 0776A] I will shake the sea because I shall kill the whale which is in it. The dry land also will be shaken, of which Isaiah speaks: “Waters have broken out in the wilderness and torrents in the solitude; what was dry land shall become a pool, and thirsty ground springs of water” (Isa. 35).

When I have completed all these things, the Desired One will come: for salvation in this world and eternal life in the world to come, to be bestowed not merely upon Judah and Israel but upon all nations. He will come, desired indeed by the patriarchs, foretold by the prophets, desired by all nations, because He is drawn by a certain ineffable love of that fervent [lacuna] which has been gathered from all nations, so that it almost dies from longing for Him, [lacuna] which says in the Song of Songs: “Let Him kiss me with the kiss of His mouth” (Song 1). Thus far Haggai concerning Christ’s advent.

38. If you wish to expound these signs according to the letter, we say that heaven was shaken when the sun was darkened as Christ died. The earth was shaken in the sense which we have explained above, because “the heavens distilled before the God of Sinai”; and further, literally, because the rocks were split. He shook the sea upon which He walked with His feet; and when He stood in the boat, at His command the fluid element now swelled with storms, now, its tempest calmed, stood peaceful. He shook the dry land, which is nothing other than the multitude of the Gentiles, watered by His preaching so that it might flourish and bear the fruit of good work, according to Isaiah, who says: “It will blossom like a lily; budding it will bud, and it will exult, rejoicing and praising” (Isa. 35).

It will blossom with the fragrance of good works like a lily, with the whiteness of purity, [Col. 0776C] in the midst of which the golden color will be God reconciling the world to Himself in Christ. “Budding, it will bud”: the beginning of good work will put forth the fruit of perfection. “And it will exult,” rejoicing in the promised saying, “Where I am, there also will My minister be” (ibid.), and praising the Lord for the benefit of salvation received.

A little later he adds: “They themselves will see the glory of the Lord and the beauty of our God” (ibid.). This cannot literally be understood of dry or desert land. For when he had first said, “The desert and impassable land will rejoice, and the wilderness will exult” (ibid.), he urged that the nations be understood when he added: “They themselves will see the glory of the Lord” (ibid.). For they saw Christ working miracles, heard Him preaching, received Him teaching, followed Him commanding, loved Him dying, embraced by faith Him rising again, and now hold by faith Him reigning. Therefore they saw the glory of the Lord in the world; they will see the beauty of God in heaven. Thus He was desired by them, came as desired to them, gave them faith, and promised eternal life as the reward of faith.

### Concerning the prophecy of Zechariah. The Jews’ vain hope concerning the Messiah

39. Let us now hear what Zechariah the prophet said concerning His advent. After many diverse things which he said in the text of his prophecy, he introduces a poor king seated upon an ass and upon a colt, the foal of an ass; and he urges the daughter of Zion to come forth to meet this poor king and his poverty, saying: “Exult, daughter Zion; shout for joy, daughter Jerusalem: behold, your King will come to you, just and Savior” (Zech. 9).

This same poor one, ascending upon an ass and upon a colt, the foal of an ass, according to the prophet, will be poor, not rich, and yet is called King of Zion. Where, then, is all that vain hope of yours, by which you promise yourself that some king—I know not who—will reign for a thousand years in Jerusalem, abounding in such a wealth of gold that all the streets will be paved with the purest gold? How can he who, according to your assertion, will be so abundant in gold and silver, be foretold as poor? Either the prophet is mistaken, or your prophecy deceitfully tells a lie.

But leaving aside the fable of vanity, let us come to the poverty of the true King. “Exult,” he says, “daughter Zion; shout for joy, daughter Jerusalem.” What was fully said above need not be repeated. “Behold your King,” he says, “will come to you”—He who is now your King, God living through the ages. “Behold,” which denotes certainty in pointing out: behold, the Just One will come to you to judge, and the Savior to heal, showing bodily presence, as He says elsewhere: “I will come and heal the brokenness of My people” (1 Macc. 2).

And lest you think that His coming is not a coming but merely an indication of His will through angels, or help supplied through powers—for in these ways He has hitherto appeared both to the fathers and to us—hear what He will do, so that from these things you may more swiftly perceive the reality of the matter. He Himself will be poor according to human judgment: poor in clothing, poor in food, poor in outward appearance; poor and mighty, poor and humble, [Col. 0777C] poor and meek, poor and just; and, to conclude all else briefly, at once rich and poor.

To show the reality of His body, the lover of poverty will not ride in royal power upon a chariot or horses, but, as a poor man ascending upon an ass—a beast of burden—your King will come to you, losing nothing thereby of His power. This was literally fulfilled in the Savior, who, six days before His passion, came seated upon an ass to Jerusalem to suffer.

In the mystical sense—which I do not think the Jew is willing to hear—He ascended upon the ass because He disposed, according to His will, the kingdom of the Jewish people, upon which He placed the Law as a bridle and the priesthood as ornamental trappings. He ascended upon the ass because it was always subject to His power; otherwise, how was He its king before He came to it? “Your King,” he says, “will come to you”—He who was already your King and God in the past ages of the world, indeed is still and will be. He will come to you not as severe and punishing, but as just and Savior, teaching righteousness in the present, according to the prophet Hosea. For he says: “It is time to seek the Lord, when He comes who will teach you righteousness,” by which He will save those who seek Him, whose hearts will live for ever (Hos. 10).

Therefore the Just One and Savior will come; and lest you excuse yourself as through ignorance because you did not know the certain preceding signs, know that this is the mark of His royal power: He Himself is poor. And, “that every word may stand in the mouth of two” (Deut. 19), behold another sign: He Himself will ascend upon an ass and upon a colt, the foal of an ass. Seated upon an ass, He will enter the city, so that what I foretell may be literally fulfilled; and upon the colt, the foal of an ass, because He will command that both be brought to Him.

And what else do these words indicate than that justice and salvation would come to humankind through royal poverty? I am indeed not greatly surprised that you do not accept a poor King, just and Savior, though the prophetic description teaches that He is to come such as this. “I expect,” you say, “a rich and powerful one who will gather us from every place of captivity into one, and restore to us the city and the Temple.” Certainly you ought to prove this by the authority of the prophets, not so readily assert a false lie at your own pleasure. But enough of these matters.

### Malachi’s prophecy concerning the rejection of the Jews and Christ’s advent

[Col. 0778B]

40. Let us now see what Malachi, who is twelfth in the order of the prophets, foretold concerning the rejection of the Jewish people and the coming of Christ. He introduces God speaking as follows: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord, and I will not accept an offering from your hand; for from the rising of the sun even to its setting my name is great among the nations, and in every place a pure offering is offered to my name, because my name is great among the nations” (Mal. 1).

“I have no pleasure in you,” he says: that henceforth you shall not be my people, nor shall I receive from your hand gift, sacrifice, or libation. “I have no pleasure in you” [Col. 0778C], because I have now foreseen and chosen a better people—namely, the nations spread throughout the whole world—which please me not by observance of Sabbath or circumcision, but by a disposition of good will and the fruit of perfect religion. Since my pleasure is not in you, why do you vainly offer sacrifice or immolate victims? Something else is more acceptable and welcome to me: namely, that my name is great among the nations. What I did not have among you, I have found among the nations: namely, love of divine worship—indeed, the fulfilment of the divine will—because they possess circumcision of the heart, not of the flesh; they observe Sabbaths because they cease from the servile work of sin; they offer as victims a humbled heart and bodily continence, by which [Col. 0778D] I especially desire to be appeased.

“My name is great among the nations,” not only from India to Ethiopia, but from the rising of the sun to its setting; and this is not among the Jews but among the nations. Here the whole assertion of the Jews is frustrated, who say that sacrifice must not be offered, nor an altar constructed, except in Judaea, whereas Isaiah says: “In that day there shall be an altar of the Lord in the midst of Egypt, and the Egyptians shall worship the Lord with victims and gifts, and shall make vows to the Lord and fulfil them” (Isa. 19). And in the present passage he says: “In every place sacrifice is offered, and a pure offering is offered to my name.” Lest they should wish to claim for themselves the words “in every place,” on the ground that they are dispersed and thus celebrate the ceremonies of the Law everywhere, let them hear what was stated beforehand: “I have no pleasure in you,” but in the nations, by whom [Col. 0779A] a pure offering is offered to my name.

By these words it is plainly proved that the Lord’s favour and his acceptance of offerings have passed from the Jews to the nations. Where then will be the kingdom and priesthood which you, Jew, promise yourself to be yet future? If they exist at all, they will be contrary to God: for neither is his will among you, that you should reign, nor will he receive a gift from your hand, that you should exercise the priesthood. How much your solemn observances count with him he makes clearer in the following verse: “I will scatter upon your faces the dung of your solemnities, and it shall take you away with itself” (Mal. 2). What else does “it shall take you away with itself” mean? Dung—the Jew—so that he who denies Christ to be the Saviour may rightly perish with dung.

41. This much concerning the rejection of the Jewish people. Concerning the coming [Col. 0779B] of the Saviour, he proceeds as follows: “Behold, I will send my angel, who shall prepare the way before my face; and immediately the Ruler whom you seek shall come to his holy temple, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire” (Mal. 3).

Explain this parable to us, that we may hear what these things mean according to your opinion. “The angel,” you say, “whom the Lord promises that he will send, is Elijah, who will go before, announcing the things to come, and will prepare the way before Haymenon—that is, our Christ—who is to come immediately after him. He will come to his temple as Ruler, and he will be to us the angel of the covenant, because he will renew the Law of Moses and establish the celebration of sacrifices.” We have heard [Col. 0779C] your opinion. Now, with God’s help, let us answer each point.

42. You say that this angel is Elijah, who will precede Haymenon. First, we wish to know from you whether this Haymenon who is to come will be God. Second, what laws or sacrifices he will establish, when the Lord’s will is in these, as he testified a little above. Third, what temple will be the one to which he comes, when the temple has been destroyed down to its foundations; and, since he himself is to restore the temple, how he comes to it before he restores it.

The outcome proves the deeds, and the very truth of the matter teaches that what is prophesied is not future but already fulfilled. “I send,” he says, “my angel, and he shall prepare the way before my face.” He did not say, “before Haymenon,” [Col. 0779D] or before anyone else, but “before my face,” that is, before myself. And, as is the practice of the prophets, suddenly changing person and speaking of himself as though of another, he adds: “And immediately the Ruler shall come to his temple.” This was fulfilled in Christ, who was presented in the temple on the fortieth day after his birth.

He sent his angel before his face—not such an one as you maintain, but such as Isaiah foretold: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord” (Isa. 40). We say that this is John the Baptist, who was called an angel because of the purity of his life and his proclamation of the Lord who was coming. He prepared the way before his face by announcing that he was present, saying: “One has stood in your midst, whom you do not know” (John 1). As if he said: In your midst [Col. 0780A] and among you is he whom the prophets foretold, whom you do not know, because you will not receive him.

“I send,” he says, “my angel before my face.” By these words he indicates that he himself will come in person: in saying “I send,” he suggests the proper attribute and action of his own person; and in adding “before my face,” he shows more plainly the presence of God coming to humankind. Since the speaker and sender are one and the same, it is recognized that God himself, and not another, is the one who is to come, when he says, “before my face”; and immediately “the Ruler shall come to his temple.” Either Haymenon is lord and ruler, and you will appear to assert two gods, in opposition to Scripture, which says: “The Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6); or, in place of the Ruler who is God, you await another, [Col. 0780B] who is proved already to have come, because there is not, nor will there be, a temple to which he might come.

That this is true we prove from Daniel, who says: “The people with the prince who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary, and its end shall be desolation” (Dan. 9). And shortly afterward: “Desolation shall continue until consummation and the end” (ibid.). If the desolation of the temple is to continue until consummation and the end, and if it is impossible for God, who spoke through the prophets, to be mistaken in his pronouncement, who will this Haymenon be who, against God’s purpose and against the decrees of the prophets, can build a temple or city whose desolation will continue until consummation and the end? Since it is ridiculous to expect or believe this, [Col. 0780C] when you have no authority on which you can establish your opinion, acknowledge that the Ruler—that is, God—has already come to his temple, and that, as is evident today, those things which you contend are future have already taken place.

43. But you say: “Elijah, of whom this prophet says, ‘Behold, I will send you Elijah’ (Mal. 4), has not yet come; and therefore we delay in assenting to Christians, because we await his coming.”

A brief answer suffices for this argument. Different things are promised in different passages, and by frequent changes of person prophetic speech describes what is to come in differing states of time. For when he had said above: “Behold, I send my angel, and he shall prepare the way before my face,” he added, to show when this was to be fulfilled, [Col. 0780D] “Immediately the Ruler shall come to his temple.” Show me the temple that was destroyed by Vespasian and Titus, and I shall confess that Christ has not come. If there is no temple in Judaea, neither will the Ruler come to that which does not exist. Therefore, he has already come, while the temple was in Judaea.

What is woven into this prophecy, then, is not future but past. Nor is any mention there made of the coming of Elijah where the first coming of the Lord is prophesied, but only of him of whom Isaiah says: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness” (Isa. 40). The time and place, the event and its outcome, prove that this is so; and what is more certain than these, hearing and sight.

But the final verse states when Elijah will come: “I will send you Elijah before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes” [Col. 0781A] (Mal. 4). The terrible and great day is the day of judgment: great for the righteous because they gain the everlasting kingdom, and terrible for sinners because endless destruction with torments is inflicted upon them.
