Elijah will precede that day, so that, as the end of the world approaches, he may turn the hearts of the fathers toward the children, and that at least at the very end of time the remnant of the people of Israel may be saved.

And note that he says “that he may turn,” not those already converted, who will not need to be turned, but those opposed—that is, the Jews—to whom it is said: “I will send you Elijah, that he may turn,” he says, “the hearts of the fathers toward the children” (ibid.): namely, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. To the first it was said: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22), and he immediately believed and was justified by faith. The second, having perceived the fragrance of the future flower, [Col. 0781B] said: “Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 27). The third, enriched by this faith, said: “I shall await your salvation, O Lord” (Gen. 49).

But all the elect, whom it would be lengthy to enumerate now, felt this in their hearts; all loved it; some loved and foretold it, as the prophets did; some loved, foretold, and saw it, as did the apostles and apostolic men. Elijah turns their hearts toward the children, so that those whom he finds living in the flesh may be of the same faith as the aforementioned fathers were, and may receive a worthy reward because they deserve to be instructed by the fathers’ example.

44. Thus far, relying on the testimonies of the twelve prophets, we have endeavoured, by the mercy of the Lord God, to reach this conclusion: by examining the pronouncements of each, to prove that the seed of the woman, through whom triumph over the serpent would come to the human race, is Christ himself, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary.

Do you still wish, Jew, to oppose the veil of your falsehood to so many champions fighting for Christ? If you think that you can easily contradict these, I have still reserved two men for myself, as most powerful leaders: Daniel and Isaiah. In the name of the Lord they will vindicate the wrong done to their fellow prophets and inflict vengeance upon their enemies. Daniel treats the sequence of times; Isaiah, prophecy together with gospel. It remains, therefore, that we set Daniel against you, so that with his first blow and strongest onset he may cast Judaea down to the depths and, with its own sword-point, cut from its body, as though a head, the hope of its expectation. Let him declare the time when Christ, who is everlasting righteousness, will come, and fix a limit beyond which, if the Jew wishes to wait, deceived by error, he will receive falsehood as truth. To Daniel the angel Gabriel—whom one ought to trust more than a Jew—by God’s command and word, “Gabriel, make this man understand the vision” (Dan. 8), revealed not only the things that would come to pass, but also the time at which they would be fulfilled.

45. “Seventy,” he says, “weeks have been shortened concerning your people” (Dan. 9). Since much has been said by the elders on this chapter, I greatly fear offending the reader: if I say anything, he may judge me superfluous; if I remain altogether silent, he may accuse me of having given my right hand to the Jew, as one defeated. But lest I be found either superfluous or defeated, I shall proceed between the two with a certain moderation: neither turning to the right nor to the left, but travelling the royal road of truth from Daniel all the way to Christ. Therefore, with the help of the Lord our God, let us say what he himself grants.

### Daniel’s prophecy concerning the seventy weeks explained

46. In seventy weeks there are found four hundred and ninety years. He calls them “shortened” because they must be reckoned according to lunar months, each of which has twenty-nine days and twelve hours; and the lunar year has eleven days fewer than the solar year, which consists of three hundred and sixty-five days and six hours. Thus they must be reckoned by the months and years of the lesser number, so that the weeks may be shortened; and the years must be counted in groups of seven, so that each week contains seven years. If these are counted by lunar years, as I have said, they will be four hundred and ninety years; but if by solar years, there will be an excess of three hundred and sixty-five days and six hours, and in the twelve months of each year there will be found eleven days and six hours more.

For the solar year is that in which the sun traverses the whole zodiacal circle, that is, the twelve signs of the Zodiac, and remains in each sign for thirty days, ten hours, and a half. Therefore, since, according to the statement of Gabriel the archangel, the weeks are shortened, their reckoning must be understood according to lunar months [Col. 0782C].

### When they ought to begin

47. We have stated how they are to be reckoned. Let us now see from what time their number ought to begin. It is clear to all readers that in the third year of the reign of Joachim, king of Judah, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem, besieged it, and the Lord delivered Joachim king of Judah into his hands. In the third year of his reign, therefore, on the tenth day, he was captured by Nebuchadnezzar’s commanders and taken to Babylon. In his place Zedekiah, son of Josiah, his uncle, was appointed. In the eleventh year of Zedekiah Jerusalem was captured and overthrown. In this captivity Daniel too was taken with the others; because of his interpretation of dreams and foreknowledge of future events, he became great and remained in Babylon until the time when Belshazzar, fourth after Nebuchadnezzar, ruled the Babylonian empire.

Cyrus, joined by Darius his uncle, killed him and overthrew the empire of the Chaldeans. After obtaining the kingdom, this same Cyrus sent back to Judaea about fifty thousand captive persons. He also restored the vessels which Nebuchadnezzar had taken away and ordered the temple to be built in Jerusalem. He appointed as leaders of the people who returned Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak. Under them, only the foundations of the temple having been laid, an altar was constructed. The work therefore remained unfinished, the surrounding nations hindering it, until Nehemiah and the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes.

At that time one hundred and [Col. 0783A] fifteen years of the Persian kingdom had elapsed, while it was the one hundred and eighty-fifth year of the captivity of Jerusalem. Then, for the first time, Artaxerxes ordered the walls of Jerusalem to be built. Nehemiah supervised this work; the broad place was built and enclosed with walls. Therefore, from the one hundred and fifteenth year of the Persian kingdom, when Artaxerxes, king of the same empire, was in the twentieth year of his reign, and when it was the fourth year of the eighty-third Olympiad, until the two hundred and second Olympiad and its second year, and the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, seventy weeks are made according to lunar calculation—that is, four hundred and ninety years.

Moreover, on the Evangelist’s testimony we know that in the fifteenth year of the reign of Caesar the word of the Lord came upon John, son of Zachariah, in the wilderness, that he might preach and show the presence of the Lord who was coming.

48. This reasoning having been set out, let us proceed to the remainder, carefully noting at what time the mystery of the seventy weeks was revealed to Daniel. “In the first year,” he says, “of Darius son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, who first ruled over the kingdom of the Chaldeans” (ibid.). This is the Darius who, with Cyrus, conquered the Chaldeans and Babylonians. He was sixty-two years old; after Babylon had been overthrown, he returned to his own kingdom in Media, taking Daniel with him in the same honour to which Belshazzar had promoted him. He left the administration of the kingdom to Cyrus, his kinsman.

In the first year of this reign, whether of Darius or of Cyrus, the mystery of the seventy weeks was revealed to Daniel. If the seventy weeks are counted from the time when, by the first favour of Cyrus, the captivity of the Jews was relaxed, more than a hundred additional years will be found beyond the number fixed for the seventy weeks. Still more will result if the day on which the angel spoke to Daniel is taken as the starting point; and a larger number still if we wish the beginning of the captivity to be the beginning of the weeks. For the Persian kingdom lasted until the beginning of the Macedonian kingdom for two hundred and thirty years; the Macedonians reigned for three hundred years; and from then until the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, when Christ suffered, sixty years are counted. Together these make five hundred and ninety years, leaving an excess of one hundred years. From whichever of these times they are counted, the periods do not coincide; indeed, many contradictions are found.

Let us therefore hold to what is most certain and in no way contrary to reason, and prove this from the wording of the chapter itself.

“Consider,” says the angel, “the word, and understand the vision: seventy weeks have been shortened concerning your people and your holy city, that transgression may be completed and sin brought to an end, that iniquity may be removed, and everlasting righteousness brought in, and vision and prophecy fulfilled, and the Holy of holies anointed [Col. 0784A]. Know therefore and consider from the issuing of the word that Jerusalem is to be rebuilt” (ibid.).

“Consider,” he says, “the word,” lest, deceived by error, you receive falsehood as truth. Rather, as you will be taught in what follows, consider the word carefully in heart and mind, and understand not only the word but also the vision. For great understanding and subtle reflection are required when something from the secrets of God is revealed to a mortal human being. The vision is great and is to occur after a long time; but in order that you may understand it in word and sense, hear its beginning and end, defined not uncertainly but by a fixed number and appointed limit.

Your people have now been held in captivity nearly seventy years. Yet seventy shortened weeks are to come concerning your people [Col. 0784B] and your holy city, for which you now pray. For that length of time your people will be a people and your city a city, and no longer: until the transgression of the first human being, by which he transgressed against God, is completed, and his sin comes to an end, with the coming of everlasting righteousness, which is Christ—not of one human being only, but of the whole world.

Where, Jew, is all your mockery with which you used to mock us? “How,” you ask, “has sin come to an end? Where is that everlasting righteousness?” If you say that the period of seventy weeks has not yet passed, although after the four hundred and ninety years there have been added, since the Lord was incarnate, one thousand one hundred and sixty-six years—[Note: [Col. 0783D] Note the author’s date.]—then, according to Daniel’s statement, there will no longer be a set period of seventy weeks for the expectation of human salvation, the end of sin, or the coming of everlasting righteousness, but a hundred or more [Col. 0784C], according to your foolish and ignorant assertion.

But let the angel who spoke to Daniel explain more openly to us what will be the sign of the coming of so great a mystery: “And vision and prophecy shall be fulfilled, and the Holy of holies shall be anointed.” Since it is established that Law, vision, and prophecy have long since ceased, it is plain that the Holy of holies has come, though you resist for some reason unknown to me and maintain that he will come at the end of the world. If the things which the angel here spoke to Daniel are to occur at the end of the world, the angel lied in fixing a limit for the vision—a suspicion which it is utter madness to dare entertain. “Within seventy weeks,” he says, [Col. 0784D] “the things which I state will happen. Christ will come; Christ will be killed; and it shall not be his”—that is, the Jewish people who will deny him will no longer reign through him as hitherto. For when Pilate said, “Behold your king,” they cried, “Crucify him; we have no king but Caesar” (John 19).

And after Christ has been killed, the Roman people with the coming leader Vespasian will destroy the city, “and its end shall be desolation” (Dan. 9), because there will not be left in it one stone upon another that shall not be destroyed (Luke 21). After the end of the war—that is, after the city’s overthrow and the dispersion of the Jews throughout the whole world—there is decreed desolation, because it will be permanent and cannot be resisted. For desolation will continue until the consummation and end of the world [Col. 0785A] (Dan. 9).

49. Thus speaks the angel Gabriel. The Jew, on the contrary, says: “The seventy weeks have by no means been fulfilled.” O mad head! Has not that been fulfilled which the angel foretold would happen at the end of the weeks? “In the middle of the week,” he says, “victim and sacrifice shall fail” (ibid.). Has not the temple been destroyed to its foundations? Have not the immolations of victims failed, together with sacrifice both morning and evening?

Suppose, if you will, that the time of the weeks still remains. Count from the day on which the angel spoke to Daniel, and there will be one thousand seven hundred and twenty-six years and more. Let the discerning reader review what was said above: the years of the Persian [Col. 0785B] and Macedonian kingdoms, likewise those of the Roman emperors down to the coming of Christ, and the years which have elapsed after his coming. He will easily observe by what great falsehood you are blinded, you who try to reckon two hundred and fifty-six weeks and more as seventy.

Nor does the angelic utterance agree that you ought to set the times by such a limit. For it says: “Know and consider from the issuing of the word that Jerusalem is to be rebuilt” (ibid.). You whom I had previously urged to understand the vision, I now again summon to a deeper understanding, so that you may know from what time the number of the weeks ought to begin. “Know,” therefore—that is, hold as certain—“and consider”—that is, retain in your mind—that the beginning of the weeks must be taken from the issuing of the word by which Jerusalem is rebuilt, not from the time when, by the first favour of Cyrus, Jewish captivity was relaxed and permission was given by Cyrus himself to build the temple and walls of the city. Rather, it is from that issuing of the word by which Jerusalem was rebuilt again—that is, at another time—that he plainly indicates the twentieth year of the reign of King Artaxerxes.

For Nehemiah, his cupbearer, as we read in the book of Ezra, asked the king and received the answer that Jerusalem should be built. This is the issuing of the word for building the city and the permission given to surround it with walls. Since an earlier, first permission was granted by Cyrus, the divine word urges us to take the beginning of the weeks from the time when Jerusalem was rebuilt again—that is, the second [Col. 0785D] occasion on which permission to build the city was granted.

### How the Jews explain Daniel’s seventy weeks.—Daniel’s seventy weeks already completed.—A day in Scripture taken as one year

50. But there is no dispute about this, since it is established that the seventy weeks have passed and that the vain expectation of the Jews is proved wholly false. Yet because they cannot answer on these matters—for truth cannot be changed into falsehood by their stubbornness—they turn to what they cannot prove at all. They say that a certain very learned Jew reckoned Daniel’s weeks in the following manner: “We must count each day in the week [Col. 0786A] as seven years, so that seven times seven years make one week, that is, forty-nine years. When this number is carefully considered, seventy weeks contain three thousand four hundred and thirty years. We cannot be constrained by the interpretation or number calculated by Christians, since there still remain one thousand nine hundred years and more before the seventy weeks are completed.”

We answer them, first, that they should prove this by the authority of Scripture, and demonstrate that a day ought to be reckoned as seven years, since the Lord himself, speaking to Ezekiel, described the span of time for which a day was to stand: “Son of man, I have given you a day for a year” (Ezek. 4). If, according to the Lord’s declaration and the customary usage of holy Scripture, we must take a day for a year [Col. 0786B], let the ignorance of the Jews cease to maintain what is wholly contrary to reason and impossible to prove true.

Or, if they wish to dispute about the number, let them show how at the end of the world those things which, according to the prophetic text, have already happened will occur a second time. “The people with the coming leader,” he says, “shall destroy the city” (Dan. 9). No one who has read history is ignorant that Jerusalem was overthrown by the coming of the Roman people with their leader Vespasian. Hence it is easily proved that the seventy weeks are ended, since what the prophet foretold would happen at their end has demonstrably taken place. If the devastation of the city and overthrow of the temple have not yet occurred, and the people with their leader have not removed the Jewish people from the city, then all that occurred under the Romans is false. But the whole world testifies to what Vespasian and Titus did. Therefore it is true that the saying has been fulfilled: “The people with the coming leader shall destroy the city and sanctuary.”

Do not then be deceived about the number of the weeks, nor extend the time to infinity, when the number by which you seek to calculate is found in no book of holy Scripture—that a day should be understood as seven years. Read what the Lord said to Moses when he exercised vengeance upon the spies of the land of Canaan, and prove, if you can, that the Lord himself and lawgiver taught that a day must be counted as seven years. “Your children,” he says, “shall wander in the wilderness forty years and bear your fornication, until the bodies of your fathers are consumed [Col. 0786D] in the wilderness, according to the number of the days in which you surveyed the land. A year shall be reckoned for a day, and for forty years you shall receive your iniquities and know my vengeance” (Num. 14).

He compared forty days with forty years, in Moses as in Ezekiel, intending that a day should be understood as reckoned for a year. And I wonder whence you have received the cause of this madness, since in the entire sequence of the Old Testament there is nowhere any rationale by which you can prove that a space of seven years is contained by the meaning or numerical unit of one day.

If what must happen—that the people with the coming leader should destroy the city and sanctuary—is still future, then the temple, long ago overthrown to the ground, must first be built so that it can be destroyed again. But according to your view it must be restored once, so that golden ages may come and the city of Jerusalem may abound in stores of gold and silver. Therefore it must be destroyed again, for the prophecy to stand literally. Tell me whether, after it has once been rebuilt, it must be overthrown further, and after its overthrow renewed again. If this too is true, the many and great things which, through deceptive hope, you promise will occur through I know not whom are hoped for in vain, since they must again be destroyed and utterly reduced to nothing. If you can answer here that the seventy weeks have not yet passed, that Christ has not come, that the people with their leader have not destroyed the city and sanctuary, and that victim and sacrifice have not failed, then keep Phillida to yourself alone.

### In what sense sin is said to have come to an end

[Col. 0787B] 51. But you say: “If Jesus, as you maintain, is everlasting righteousness, and if at his coming, according to the prophet, sin and transgression ought to end, how has sin come to an end when every human being still sins today?”

To this we answer: In those for whom Christ has become everlasting righteousness, every sin or transgression comes to an end, because all are one in him. Scripture testifies to this when it says: “You will have mercy on the people who are in you” (Hos. 14). If the people are in God, and God himself is everlasting righteousness, then certainly all are one in him through grace and mercy, not by nature—those on whom he has mercy. Therefore every transgression and sin ends in them, because, since they are in God, insofar as they are one with him they cannot sin. Thus in them is an end of sin and transgression, because everlasting righteousness, which is Christ, reigns in them.

If you do not accept the prophet, hear the disciple of Gamaliel—I mean the apostle Paul: “Slave and free, we are all one in Christ” (1 Cor. 12). And again: “All of you who have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3). Likewise: “There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8).

Let this brief discussion of Daniel’s weeks suffice. Let us therefore set a limit to this reading, so that in what follows we may take our beginning from Isaiah.

### Isaiah’s prophecies concerning the rejection of the Jews and the coming of Christ

52. Having completed the testimonies of the twelve prophets, [Col. 0787D] and, as far as we could, unravelled the question concerning Daniel’s weeks, let us come to Isaiah the prophet. Since he sees the mysteries of Christ more plainly than all the rest, he holds primacy in the choir of prophets, David excepted, from whose seed the King of kings himself was born. Isaiah embraces matters so extensive, investigates things so profound, and speaks so plainly concerning Christ, that no one—unless deceived by madness, Jew or Gentile—can oppose his words.

From the beginning of the book as far as the passage where he says, “The word which Isaiah son of Amos saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem” (Isa. 2), he prophesies the rejection of the Jewish people. After describing this, he passes to the birth and infancy of the Saviour; and, what I do not believe the Jew willingly hears, he asserts that a virgin will bear a son who will be called not merely by the one name Emmanuel, but also by six other names: Wonderful, Counsellor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace (Isa. 9). Of these, by the bounty of the Lord God, we shall speak in their place. Let us therefore begin from the head and call upon the Jew to answer each point.

### Isaiah’s prophecy is to be understood not of the city of Jerusalem, but of its inhabitants

53. “The vision of Isaiah son of Amos which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem” (Isa. 1) begins with the casting down of the Jewish people, showing that what he is about to say is spoken not *of* Judah and Jerusalem but *concerning* Judah and Jerusalem: that all the things added by prophetic speech are foretold as coming against them. He does not speak of all Israel, but specifically against the tribe of Judah—that is, the Jews who then ruled in Jerusalem. Against them the Lord inveighs through the prophet and calls all creation, both heavenly and earthly, to witness, that they may hear what he did for the Jews and how they, in return, rendered evil for good.

54. “Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth” (ibid.). Once, through Moses, when I entered into covenant with the children of Israel, I appointed you witnesses between them and me: if they obeyed my commandments, I would advance them to higher things; if not, I would punish them for contempt. I said, “This day I call heaven and earth to witness.” Now again I summon you, as witnesses between myself and the Jews, to hear the catalogue of benefits and the ingratitude shown for favours. Hear therefore, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, that I may justly exact vengeance from my enemies.

### Why the Jews were called firstborn sons.—The firstborn are often rejected

[Col. 0788C]

55. “I have nourished and exalted sons, but they have despised me” (ibid.). It is known to you who dwell in heaven, and likewise to those who dwell on earth, what great and numerous things I have done for the Jewish people: whom I adopted as sons and called “Israel my firstborn”; whom I nourished for forty years in the wilderness and exalted in the land of Canaan, giving them their possession. Yet for all that I did for them, they rendered contempt in return for service to him whom they ought to have adored as Lord, because they despised me.

The Lord spoke these words, making his complaint concerning the Jews to the inhabitants of heaven and earth. If the Jews take pride in the fact that the Lord called them his sons and firstborn, [Col. 0788D] let them hear that they are called firstborn because after them he would choose a people better and stronger, as he himself said to Moses: “Let me alone, that my anger may burn against this people, and I will make you into a nation stronger than this one” (Exod. 32). Let the Jew answer who that people is, who will be far stronger and better after him; and let him know that in the Old Testament the firstborn is frequently rejected.

Cain was firstborn, but Abel pleased God. Ishmael was firstborn, but in Isaac the blessing promised to be given to all nations is found. Esau was firstborn, but Jacob the supplanter received his blessing. Reuben was firstborn, but the blessing concerning the future incarnation of Christ [Col. 0789A] was transferred to Judah. In all these cases it is demonstrated that a better people would succeed the former people.

It follows:

56. “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger; but Israel has not known me, my people have not understood” (Isa. 1). He shows wherein their contempt consists: namely, that although brute animals recognize the Lord and Creator, the Jewish people did not recognize or understand him. I should like the Jew to tell me, if he wishes this to be understood of the Father and not of the Son, how Israel failed to know the Lord who himself brought it out of Egypt, made it pass dry-shod through the midst of the Red Sea, fed it with manna in the wilderness, and finally led it into the land of promise. Since he cannot prove that this is said of the Father, he will be compelled to confess it of the Son: that he was neither recognized nor understood by them, though born of the Virgin Mother and laid in a manger, where shepherds saw and understood him, and glorified him as God.

57. “Woe to the sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, an evil seed, criminal children!” (Ibid.) “Woe,” he says, “to the Jewish nation, sinful in this respect: that it neither recognized nor received the Savior, but killed him. A people laden with iniquity”—that is, burdened with the sins of murder and contempt for God. “An evil seed,” because they are from their father the devil. “Criminal children,” into whom every kind of wickedness has flowed. And he adds the reason why the Jewish people are marked by so great an infamy.

[Col. 0789C] 58. “They have forsaken the Lord, blasphemed the Holy One of Israel, and turned themselves away backward” (Ibid.). They forsook the Lord when they cried, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19). They blasphemed the Holy One of Israel, saying, “You have a demon and are a Samaritan” (John 8). They turned themselves away backward: those who had once been at the head are now turned into the tail. And for what reason they are thus estranged, the Lord himself explained through Jeremiah, saying: “I have forsaken my house, I have abandoned my inheritance; my inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest; it has raised its voice against me” (Jer. 12). Therefore he hates her who was once his inheritance, because she raised her voice against him, crying: “Away, away, crucify him!” (John 18).

[Col. 0789D] 59. “You have become a weariness to me; I will by no means forgive your sins.” In these words he sets out in detail the reason why he rejected the Jews. “I will not forgive your sins,” he says (Isa. 1). Why? “Because your hands are full of blood” (ibid.). And what he means by this, he adds shortly afterwards while speaking of the city: “How has the faithful city, full of judgments, become a harlot? Justice dwelt in her, but now murderers” (ibid.).

The Jew says: “He threatened all these things because of our sins, in order that thereafter he might restrain us from evil.” But this conflicts with Scripture. For it expressly declares, “You have become a weariness to me,” which means the same as if he had said, “a disgust.” Against the defense you advance—that the Lord’s threat is a punishment for your sins—he states his own judgment: “I will not forgive your sins”; and he adds the reason: “For your hands are full of blood.” Whose blood, or what blood? Not that of an ox, a ram, or any brute animal, but of a man. The blood of the one righteous man whom you shed has stained your hands; and because of the guilt of this crime committed, your hands are full of blood. That this sin is homicide, as was said above, the prophet himself testifies when he speaks of the city: “Justice dwelt in her, but now murderers.” Therefore, because of the Savior’s death, whom they killed, they are called men of blood and murderers.

Although he had said above, “I will not forgive your sins,” he nevertheless shows that nothing is impossible with him if they are willing to be saved by the one remedy alone, namely the saving washing of baptism. Hence he adds:

### The sins of the Jews are to be washed away by the water of baptism

60. “Wash yourselves; be clean; remove the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes” (ibid.). What is washing except baptism? Water is of no benefit unless he who grants forgiveness of sins is present. Therefore they are not commanded to wash in every kind of water, but only in that water in which sins are cleansed—and this is none other than the water of baptism.

This can readily be proved. For when he had said above, “Your hands are full of blood,” and, “Justice dwelt in her, but now murderers,” he declares that they had contracted sin through the shedding of blood and murder; and immediately [Col. 0790C] adds that he will not forgive them this sin unless they are washed and cleansed. It is as though he said: “I do not forgive you the sin of murder which you committed unless you are washed with the water of baptism, by which sins are cleansed.” Let the Jew answer where he has found it written in the Law that homicide ought to be removed by water of expiation. Since he cannot find this, let him know that the water of baptism is better than the rivers Abana and Pharpar of Damascus, and indeed than all the waters of Israel: in it alone, through the working of the Holy Spirit, forgiveness of all sins is granted.

“Remove,” he says, “the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes.” By these words the religion of the New Testament is plainly commended, which commands that not only deeds but also thoughts be separated from evil. At the same time it teaches that, instead of victims and holocausts, the fat of fatlings, the blood of bulls and goats, incense, new moons, Sabbath, feast-day, fasts, calends, and other solemn observances, the religion of Christian faith is more acceptable.

And in what follows he proves that, if the Jews are willing to be washed in the water of baptism—the only means by which they can be cleansed from sin—the blackness of their sins can be changed into the whiteness of purity. “If your sins are as scarlet,” he says, “they shall be made white as snow” (ibid.). That is: although you have shed the Savior’s blood, at whose Passion Rahab’s scarlet sign once hung in the window, prefiguring that she and her house forever—the Church gathered from the Gentiles—would be saved from death through his death, yet know that where transgression abounded in deed, merit abounded in grace (Rom. 5). If you are washed in the water which flowed with Christ’s blood from his side [lacuna], you shall be made white as snow: for redness shall be blotted out by redness—that is, the blood of sin by saving blood—and blackness by whiteness.

“And if they be red as the worm”—dyed, in the likeness of gore, with the poison of malice—yet know that that most tender worm of the wood, who will hang on the cross in order by one onset of his death to kill him who increased the yoke of sin upon the Lord’s people, he, I say, in place of your twofold shame and disgrace, will clothe you in the purest wool from his own fleece. You shall be sheep, and he the shepherd, as it is written: “I myself will seek my sheep and visit them, as a shepherd visits his flock on the day when he is among his scattered sheep” (Ezek. 34).

Hear, Jew, Isaiah’s counsel, and hasten to be washed. For whatever waters you may be washed in, unless baptism comes to your aid, you will always remain unclean with the filth of sin. Job bears witness, saying: “Though I should wash myself as with living waters, and my hands should shine as the purest, yet you will plunge me into filth, and my garments will abhor me” (Job 9). These words show that no one can be saved from sin except through the grace of baptism, which is described in the preceding verse in subtle language.

Let what has been said concerning the rejection of the Jewish people suffice. Let us consider what follows, and bring forward those things which we know to be more displeasing to the Jew. For it is not our purpose to expound Isaiah in order, but to explain more openly, against Jewish unbelief, those things that have been manifestly said concerning Christ.

### Isaiah’s prophecy concerning the calling of the Gentiles examined

61. “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains, and shall be raised above the hills; and all nations shall flow to it, and many peoples shall go and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord” (Isa. 2).

After describing the rejection of the Jewish people, he passes to the calling of the Gentiles; and, when one people has been cast aside, he firmly declares that a multitude of peoples will come to the mountain of the Lord. He first speaks of the Word, whom he afterwards calls the Mountain, and says that he saw the Word concerning Judah and Jerusalem; then he immediately adds that this Word will become a mountain on the summit of the mountains in the last days.

62. “In the last days,” he says, “the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains.” This plainly means: In the final age, the Word of the Most High will become a mountain upon the summit of mountains—that is, exalted above the exaltation of the exalted. “It shall be prepared,” because it was predestined that he should become man. “On the summit of mountains,” because he will be man above men and Holy of holies. Nothing is higher than him, beneath whom is every creature.

Yet he will be prepared in order to be raised above the hills, because for this reason God will become humble: that man may be exalted, ascend above all heavens, and sit at the right hand of Majesty on high. [Col. 0792A] This indeed is what he says: “The word which Isaiah saw” (ibid.). In the first vision he sees the rejection of the Jewish people; in the second, the Word of God appearing under the form of the highest mountain; in the third, after the mystery of his Incarnation, he sees that same one who was called the mountain—the Lord himself—sitting upon a lofty throne, so that he may explain more plainly what the mountain of the house of the Lord upon the summit of the mountains is.

“It shall be raised above the hills; and all nations shall flow to it”: not only one nation from Judaea, but all nations, so that one people having been forsaken, many peoples may come and say: “Let us ascend the mountain”—not Sinai or Olivet, but the mountain of the Lord. Let the Jew now say who this mountain is, so lofty that it is raised above all hills, yet so accessible that all nations flow to it. Would that he would cast his eyes over all Judaea, because this mountain was supposed to arise from there, and keep looking upon the mountain-tops until he proves that a piled-up mass of earth ought to be called this mountain of which Isaiah spoke.

“The Temple,” he says, “which is situated on the mountain will be built so loftily when the Messiah comes that it can be seen above all mountains and hills. And therefore he says that the law must go forth from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.” But if this is true, how is it that the prophet, after foretelling that all nations would come to this mountain and be taught there concerning the ways of the Lord, exhorts his own people to come with him to this mountain and walk in the name of the Lord? For he says: “House of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the Lord” (ibid.).

If the Jews will possess the Temple and the city, how are they invited to come to that which they possess? The prophet overturns this interpretation when he adds: “For you have cast off your people, the house of Jacob” (ibid.). Because they would not listen to the prophet exhorting them to come and walk in the light of the Lord, it is plainly implied that the Lord himself is this mountain. For he says that he cast off his people for that reason. And lest there be uncertainty about which people this is, he adds, “the house of Jacob.” If the Jewish people was cast off because it would not approach this mountain, then this mountain is not the Temple which is to be, if indeed there will be one, as the Jew maintains.

Let the prophet himself convict the Jew of having spoken falsely concerning this mountain. First let it be asked of him, since he cannot prove that these words are spoken of the Temple, what he says the house of the Lord is. If heaven, in which God dwells, is the house of the Lord, and God is higher than heaven, then this mountain is certainly God. Therefore this entire passage concerns the Lord: namely, that he is prepared on the summit of the mountains—that is, the Holy One incarnate in the midst of the holy ones. He is raised above the hills because God-made-man became higher than every human being.

To him the Church, gathered from every nation, has now flowed; and with it many peoples say: “Let us ascend to the Lord, and he will teach us the way of salvation, that we may walk in it.” Both the Jerusalem and Roman Church prove this true today; and what was said in the same prophet is fulfilled: “Your sons shall come from afar, and your daughters shall rise from the side” (Isa. 60).

And because the prophet could not obtain what he had asked—for he had exhorted the people to come with him and walk in the name of the Lord—he shortly thereafter warns the Jews, as if by counsel: “Cease from the man whose breath is in his nostrils, for he is reckoned as exalted” (Isa. 2). As though saying more plainly: Since you have been cast off because you were unwilling to believe in the mountain of the house of the Lord, that is, in Christ the Savior, beware henceforth lest you lay hands on him who has become God-and-man among human beings. He has spirit and soul; he breathes and lives like others. Cease from him; do not persecute him, do not oppose him, because it will not turn out prosperously for you. For he will be your ruin and snare, “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” [Col. 0793B] (1 Pet. 2), unless you cease from the hatred by which you strive to injure him.

But because he sees that their unbelief has by no means ceased thereby, leaving them aside after recounting many varied matters concerning this man’s glorification, he adds:

### Prophecy concerning Christ’s glorification — The Jews’ absurd explanation of the Branch

63. “In that day the Branch of the Lord shall be in magnificence and glory, and the fruit of the earth shall be lofty and an exultation for those who have been saved from Israel; and everyone who remains in Zion and is left in Jerusalem shall be called holy—everyone found written in life in Jerusalem” (Isa. 4).

He who above was called a mountain because of the height of his divinity, and afterwards the light of the Lord because the Son is light from light from the Father, was finally openly called man, where he says: “Cease from the man whose breath is in his nostrils” (Isa. 2). Now, as if anew, he is called the Branch of the Lord, that the loftiness of his divinity may be understood more clearly. And he is rightly called the Branch of the Lord because he is the power and image of the Father.

He says that this Branch of the Lord will be in magnificence and glory in those days—namely, when the Branch of the Lord becomes man: first in magnificence, because of the glorious deeds he was to perform among human beings; afterwards in glory, because of the glorification of his assumed humanity at the throne of Majesty. What the Branch in glory is, he immediately explains: “And the fruit of the earth shall be lofty.” Of this fruit David said that the Lord would give goodness, would send his Son from heaven, and that our earth would give its fruit: that is, the virgin body would bring forth the Son of God. That fruit was made lofty because the nature of his assumed humanity was exalted above every creature.

The Jew maintains that this fruit must be a fig, a pomegranate, or something of that sort. But if a fig, contrary to its usual nature, grew into the height of a loftier stature, what exultation would arise from that for the people to be saved? Rather, the lofty fruit is the Son of the Virgin, raised to the Father’s right hand, through whom joy and exultation in salvation come to those who are saved. And he did not say that all the people would be saved, but only the remnant: that is, the apostles and those who believed through the apostles and their successors. For he says: “Everyone who remains in Zion and is left in Jerusalem shall be called holy—everyone found written in life in Jerusalem.”

What remains and is left is not normally said of a whole thing, but of a part of the whole, and indeed its smallest part. Therefore only the remnant of the people was saved, not the entire multitude of the people. And, good God! On what grounds do you promise yourself, Jew, Saturnian kingdoms, a golden Jerusalem, and the scattered from every quarter of the world flowing together into Judaea? Isaiah declares that, once the Jewish people has been cast off, all nations will come to the mountain that is Christ; yet the Jew still awaits new times of Solomon. For Solomon caused there to be such abundance of gold and silver in Jerusalem as of stones. He contends that these things, or similar things, will occur, while this same prophet opposes him and says: “The daughter of Zion shall be left like a shelter in a vineyard, like a hut in a cucumber-field, like a city being devastated” (Isa. 1). Something more has been said above concerning this devastation in the chapter on Daniel.

It follows: “Everyone found written in life in Jerusalem shall be called holy.” He for whom the Branch of the Lord, the lofty fruit of the earth—which is Christ—shall be glory and exultation, shall truly be called holy and shall be holy, because he will be found written in life, in that heavenly Jerusalem, for which another prophet yearned, saying: “My soul longs for and fails for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. 83). He will truly be holy who has embraced the religion described above: namely, one who has been washed in baptism and thereafter remains clean in the sacrament of baptism. He will be found [Col. 0794C] written in life—that is, chosen in Christ.

### In what form the prophets and patriarchs saw God

64. After these predictions concerning Christ, the prophet, following certain intervening matters which it would take too long to enumerate now, passes to another vision, in which he sees the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne (Isa. 6). But before discussing the vision, I wish to ask the Jew in what form the prophets or patriarchs saw the Lord.

Abraham saw the Lord not in divinity but in human form; the Jew cannot deny this, because it is written: “The Lord appeared to Abraham in the valley of Mamre, as he sat at the door of his tent” (Gen. 18). “And when he lifted up his eyes, three men appeared to him.” Therefore what he saw of the Lord was in human form. But lest any of my friends object to me that this is not true, I say in your ear, reader, so that the Jew may not hear it: Jerome, commenting on the same chapter of Isaiah, said:

> “We read that the Lord was seen by Abraham in the figure of a man, and that he wrestled with Jacob as a man, though he was God. Hence the place itself was called Phanuel, that is, ‘the face of God’: ‘For,’ he says, ‘I have seen God face to face, and my soul has been saved’ (Gen. 32 [printed: 37]). Ezekiel also saw the Lord in the form of a man sitting above the Cherubim; from his loins downward he was like fire, and the upper parts had the appearance of electrum.”

These are Jerome’s words, to whom none is comparable in the exposition of Scripture. If God was seen by patriarchs and prophets in the figure of a man, let the Jew permit us to say that in these last days God appeared to us through a man.

It remains for him to explain to us what Moses saw of the Lord, or in what figure he saw God. Thus he said to the Lord: “If I have found grace in your eyes, show me your face” (Exod. 33). To him the Lord said: “You cannot see my face. Behold, there is a place with me; you shall stand upon the rock, and when my glory passes by, I will put you in the cleft of the rock and protect you with my right hand until I pass by; then I will remove my hand, and you shall see my back” (ibid.).

If Moses could not see the Lord’s face, what does it mean that he says: “The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak to his friend” (Exod. 33)? Moreover, if he could see only the Lord’s back, I ask what he saw: heels, shoulders, back, or the rest? Yet the Lord says: “I will remove my hand, and you shall see my back.” The prudent reader sufficiently understands to what absurdity one may be led if the course of argument proceeds on this subject. It is not my present task to expound Jewish trifles, but to investigate the mysteries of truth. Let us return, therefore, to the prophet’s vision and hear what he saw.

### Another vision of Isaiah examined — Who the Son of Man seen by Daniel is — The mystery of the Trinity

65. “In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne” (Isa. 6). Certainly he whom above he called the lofty fruit of the earth, he now explains more plainly in that same loftiness, and calls the Lord reigning in divine majesty. His throne is the height of the heavens; he presides over it as pleased his will, because every height which is not God is beneath him. Therefore his throne is high and exalted, because every height which is not God is beneath him. Therefore his throne is high and exalted, because whatever is more sublime among creatures is submitted and subject to the divinity itself.

The prophet thus saw the Lord, who is above all things, sitting upon a high and exalted throne. “Seraphim stood above it”—that is, those companies of blessed spirits which, after God, are highest and ever dwell in the heights. “Six wings to one and six wings to the other” (ibid.). Those who are around the Lord are said to have six wings because they provide mortals, according to God’s command, knowledge only of the creation of the world, which was made in six days. For all who are God’s ministers, whether higher or lower, serve to fulfill his will, as the Prophet testifies: “Bless the Lord, all his angels, mighty in strength, who perform his word, hearkening to the voice of his utterance.”

“With two they covered his head, with two they covered his feet, and with two they flew” (Ps. 102). With their upper wings they cover God’s head and with their lower wings his feet, because, while the things before the world and those after the world are known to God alone, only the intervening things that have been done in this world can be seen.

It should be noted that the Seraphim are said to cover the Lord’s head and feet with their wings. That divine substance of the Trinity, which is the total perfection of Deity, cannot properly be said to have either head or feet; in its own nature it is invisible to human beings, incomprehensible to angels, marvelous to both, and to be adored and venerated above all things. Although, therefore, the prophet sees the Lord sitting upon a high throne and understands the whole Trinity, he nevertheless does not see in its entirety that perfect and ineffable substance of Deity. He sees only what made itself visible, to signify the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation which would occur many ages later.

Nor is it surprising if he sees God in bodily form before he became man, since the Lord himself says: “I have multiplied visions, and I have been likened in the hands of the prophets” (Hos. 12). Many things went before in figure which were afterwards fulfilled in the reality of the event. Let us prove this by an example. Daniel testifies that, as if in a night vision, he saw the mystery of the Incarnation of the Son of God, saying: “I looked in the vision of the night, and behold, with the clouds of heaven one like a son of man came, and he came even to the Ancient of Days; and he gave him power, honor, and kingdom, and every people, tribe, and language shall serve him” (Dan. 7). These things went beforehand in figure and were later fulfilled in the reality of the event.

Manoah too testifies that he saw the Lord in the form of a man, saying to his wife: “We shall surely die, because we have seen the Lord” (Judg. 13). He did not say, “Because we have seen an angel,” but “Because we have seen the Lord.” Yet let the Jew answer who this Son of Man is, who comes with the clouds of heaven and ascends to the Ancient of Days and everlasting God; to whom God himself gives power, honor, and kingdom, so that every people, tribe, and language may serve him. Let him also show how his power is eternal power and his kingdom cannot be corrupted.

Since every man is a son of men, why should “Son of Man,” in the singular number, be understood of one generated from the procreation of two persons? Moreover, which of the sons of men can ascend to the clouds, penetrate heaven, and come to the throne of Majesty on high, so that there he may receive from the Most High power and honor, the service of all peoples, and an eternal kingdom without end? Let him seek until he finds, and seek until he fails in seeking. No other can be found but that flower of Mary, the Virgin’s Son, who came from heaven as God in order to assume flesh from her; he was born without any male agency and became Son of Man. He raised his own humanity to the heights, as the Prophet singing in the Psalm foretold concerning him: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (Eph. 4); and: “Sing to the Lord, who ascends above the heavens of heavens” (Ps. 67).

Hence the supreme Father gave him, insofar as he is man, power and royal honor, that he might sit at his right hand until he places all his enemies beneath his footstool (Ps. 109; Heb. 11). His kingdom is eternal because, although it began insofar as he is man, insofar as he is God he neither began to be nor ceases to be. Therefore power is given to him only insofar as he is man, because insofar as he is one God with the Father and Holy Spirit, he has the same power as they do—a power which cannot be taken from him, because God and man are one person.

Isaiah therefore saw not the whole substance of Deity, but only the Lord’s middle parts: namely, what he became in this world, which is rightly called a kind of middle placed between the things before the world and those after the age. The Lord’s other parts are veiled by the Seraphim’s wings because they are hidden from us. We cannot comprehend in our understanding either the things that were before the world was made or those that will be after its end. We can know only what has been done in the present age. This is what is meant by their flying with the two middle wings, while the middle parts of the Lord are shown to be visible: thereby making it understood that God would appear visibly to the world in a man.

“And they cried one to another” (Isa. 6). Not merely two—that is, one to one—but each one to another, resounding the mystery of the Trinity. Blessed and glorious is that multitude of happy spirits, to whom it is granted to see the beauty of that supreme divinity, perceive its sweetness, contemplate its face, and adore its majesty; they do nothing but resound the Lord’s praises. What they cry he indicates when he adds: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory” (ibid.). To signify the distinct properties of the persons and the mystery of the Trinity, they cry “Holy” three times; and, that they may proclaim the unity in substance of that same Trinity, they add: “Lord of hosts,” that is, of all heavenly powers. “The whole earth is full of his glory”: not only the Temple or Judaea alone, but the whole earth.

The hosts of the heavenly powers marvel that the Lord of Majesty should wish to descend to the lowest parts and humble himself in becoming man, and show his glory not to the Jewish people alone but to the whole world. In worthy amazement they praise him, saying: “The whole earth is full of his glory.” When Moses was pleading with the Lord on behalf of the people because of the calf they had worshipped, saying, “I beseech you, Lord, forgive the sins of your people,” the Lord answered him: “I will be gracious to them; nevertheless, as I live, and as my name lives, my glory shall fill the whole earth” (Num. 14). It is as though he said: Since I see that this people is stiff-necked and, while I was still present, worshipped a calf, as I live and as my name lives, since they despised me, I too will despise them; and, with one nation abandoned, my glory shall fill the whole earth. Everyone who calls upon my name shall be saved, and it shall not be confined within the boundaries of one land, so that they may boast and say, “He has not done thus for every nation”; but it shall abound by grace throughout the whole world, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “The whole earth shall be filled with his majesty.”

Why, then, should the Jew expect a new mercy-seat, in which the glory of the Lord may dwell, when it already shines forth through the whole earth? It is frivolous to maintain henceforth that God’s glory will leave the entire earth and, according to the Jews’ pleasure, sit as though hidden between the wings of the cherubim. Let them think what they wish; leaving idle tales aside, let us see what the prophet heard after the vision.

### The mystery of the Trinity again explained

66. “And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: Whom shall I send? And who will go for us?” (Isa. 6). Answer, Rabbi: we ask you what it means that the Lord, speaking of himself, first uses the singular number, saying, “Whom shall I send?” and then adds in the plural, “Who will go for us?” Do you still see that in substance the Lord wishes himself to be understood as one, and as three in persons? What is this variation in the Lord’s words—or rather, this affirmation of Trinity and unity in the Lord himself? “Whom shall I send?” belongs to unity. “Who will go for us?” Of whom is this said? Not of the companies of Seraphim, because the prophet heard no voice except that of the Lord alone, saying: “Whom shall I send? And who will go for us?”

Remember what the Seraphim cried above, how they showed unity in Trinity and Trinity in unity, saying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts” (ibid.), and you will find the answer to this question. “I grant,” you say, “that he spoke of himself and of his Spirit, but I do not accept that he has a Son.” Let the powers of heaven answer here and indicate more plainly whether your view is right or wrong. “Holy,” they say, “holy, holy.” If the Trinity is not God, who is he who is called Holy a third time in the Godhead? Either you will be compelled to confess three persons and one God—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—or, according to your custom, you will discover something new and unheard of, which will be false and abominable and which you will be wholly unable to prove. Therefore, since you realize that you can easily be refuted on this point, henceforth restrain your lip with your finger.

### The blinding of the Jews

67. It follows: “And I said: Behold, I am here; send me” (ibid.). He did not say this from presumptuous rashness, but from the great affection of one who desired to obey the command of the Almighty and announce his will to his people. At the same time, it should be noted that, when the Lord commands, the Trinity gives command; and the prophet declares himself in every respect the servant of the Trinity.

“And he said: Go and say to this people: Hear with hearing and do not understand; see with sight and do not know” (ibid.). What does it mean that the Jews are commanded to hear and not understand? Certainly it is the mystery of the Savior which the prophet above knew and understood, heard and believed. For he had seen the Lord sitting upon a high throne (ibid.); and, because the exalted God deigned to become humble man, he had heard the Seraphim proclaiming that, by his descent from heaven, because of the presence of him coming in the flesh, the whole earth would be full of his glory. Turning this understanding completely away from the Jews, he commands the prophet to preach to them what is to happen: “Hear,” he says, “the words of the Savior when he comes, and do not understand, because the Lord has permitted your hearts to be hardened and they will by no means be softened to repentance. See him visibly, present in the flesh, and do not recognize him, lest God’s purpose be frustrated: that one nation should become blind so that the whole world may see.”

After the prophet had heard the command, understanding also the Lord’s will, he prays and entreats that his will may be done in every respect: “Blind the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and be converted, and I heal them” (ibid.). Here I should like, through you, Jew, to know whose prayer this is: that of the Lord who commands, the prophet who entreats, or of him who, by righteous judgment, ordains and is neither to be heard nor understood by the Jewish people?

If it is the Lord’s command, it is not the people’s fault that it becomes blind, but the power of him who commands. If it is the prophet’s entreaty—although it may indeed be understood in that way—how can what follows, “and be converted, and I heal them,” be referred to him, when it belongs to God alone to grant salvation after conversion? But it may fittingly be said, consistently with the rule of faith and with greater authority, to belong to him for whom it is possible first to convert and then, after conversion, to grant salvation.

But whoever it may be, he prays this against the Jewish people: that they may hear and not understand, see and not recognize, become blind and deaf, lest they be converted and healed. Here it is plainly shown by what great misery they are held: they can neither hear, nor understand, nor see, nor recognize the Lord Savior; nor are they even worthy of repentance, so that they may be converted and obtain salvation. It follows:

68. And I said: “How long, O Lord?” And he said: “Until the cities are laid waste without inhabitant, and the houses without a human being, and the land is left desolate” (ibid.). And as though he had said above: “O Lord, you command me now to speak to the Jewish people so that they may hear and not understand the Savior, see him and not recognize him; yet how long, O Lord, will this sentence remain—that one who hears may not hear, and one who sees may not see?” To this the Lord replied: “They shall neither hear nor see, and their heart shall remain blinded, until the cities of Judaea, while Vespasian and Titus wage war, are utterly overthrown—so completely that not even their name remains; and until such houses as remain are without inhabitants, the land is reduced to a wilderness, and the Jewish people are scattered throughout the whole world either by flight or by captivity.”

He therefore gives the Jews a definite sign of captivity and devastation, and describes its cause: namely, that they did not receive or understand the Savior coming to them, but instead killed the son of the householder, saying: “This is the heir; let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance” (Luke 10). After the prophet had learned from the Lord’s revelation these things concerning the blindness of the Jewish people and the overthrow of Jerusalem, he turns to the siege which took place in the days of Ahaz, when Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah fought against Jerusalem. Under the occasion of the mercy by which the Lord delivered the besieged people, he may announce that his Son is to be born of a Virgin. Since it would take too long to examine this word by word, it is better to leave the Jew to chew over the historical account and come to the matter itself, so that with the prophet we may understand the prophecy of Emmanuel: both that he is to be born of a Virgin [Col. 0800A], that he will deliver souls in the lower world, and afterwards ascend above all the heavens. For these are the two signs which the Lord offered King Ahaz to seek, giving him the choice of which he wished first to receive: from the height of heaven or from the depth of hell.

69. “He spoke,” he says, “to Ahaz, saying: ‘Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, in the depth of hell or in the height above’” (Isa. 7). Above, at the Lord’s command, the prophet had told him: “Do not fear these two tails of smoking firebrands” (ibid.). That is to say in other words: “Take care not to be frightened by the face of these two who have risen against you—Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah—because [Col. 0800B] the dominion of each will end within sixty-five years.” I call them tails of firebrands because all their strength is near its end; and whatever remains thereafter will vanish like smoke. Therefore do not fear, because I have decreed to free you and your people from their hands.

“But if, because of excessive despair, you do not believe this, ask for yourself a sign from the Lord, for he is ready to reveal what he will do after many ages, whether among those below or above the heavens. Ask, then, for this sign: that he is powerful in both realms, namely in heaven and in hell. Even though you do not ask for it, nevertheless he will give it to the house of David, in order to fulfil what he promised when he said: ‘Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne.’” And Ahaz said: “I will not ask, and I will not tempt the Lord” [Col. 0800C] (ibid.).

He would have spoken rightly if he had said this in order not to become a transgressor of the Law, in which it is said: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Deut. 6). But he was an idolater, and therefore did not wish to ask the Lord for a sign, lest the Lord should be glorified in him if he granted the sign for which he had asked. When the prophet realized this, abandoning the impious king, he turned the sign and the Lord’s speech toward the house of David—that is, toward Judah and Jerusalem—saying: “Hear, therefore, house of David”; and after inserting a few words, he adds: “Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign” (Isa. 7), that on this occasion you are to be delivered from the hands of those besieging you.

Not the prophet, not an angel, but the Lord himself will give you what Ahaz refused to receive: namely, a sign [Col. 0800D] which will not happen now, but in the future, since to give this sign belongs to God alone. Remember that whatever God has said will be future must necessarily come to pass. Therefore place faith in God’s promise, so that, strengthened by the certainty of the future sign, you may by faith in it be delivered from the immediate danger. What he speaks of will not occur at once or immediately, but at a distance; and therefore the merit will be greater if you are saved in the present by hoping for what does not yet exist and believing what you do not see. And now hear, house of David.

### The prophecy concerning the Virgin’s childbirth examined.—The Jews’ threefold explanation of it.

70. “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (ibid.). Behold the sign which the Lord gives you in the present: truly new and wonderful. For a virgin shall give birth—that is, not now, [Col. 0801A] but in the future. Her childbirth is foretold now, and the Son is given as a sign, so that you may recognize that the God who will then be born from the Virgin is now with you, and, by the proclamation and grace of what follows, will anticipate you and deliver you from the immediate danger through the preceding gift of mercy.

“For he shall be called Emmanuel” (ibid.), which means “God with us”: so that he who was God before the ages, born of the Virgin, may dwell in the world with us as Man. God has foretold to you that a Son will be born who will be called “God with us,” and has in a manner allowed you to know beforehand his secret. Believe what is to come, and through the merit of faith rejoice also in the present benefit, because the effect of the future sacrament already precedes it: when his name is invoked, the enemies will be driven away, and you will be secure both in peace and in triumph [Col. 0801B].

Do not wish to say that this sign—the birth of Emmanuel—must precede the victory promised in the present; for the benefit which comes first does not take away the effect of the sign which follows. Thus the present deliverance is a signification of the sign, but not itself the sign of the future sacrament; for the sign itself will be that the Virgin shall conceive and bear a son.

Here the Jew advances armed with all his strength for battle, fortified by diverse questions, so that, if he cannot strike with the first, he may strike with the second or third, until by falsehood he prevails in proving the Christians’ hope vain. And because this question has often been debated between us, it has made the Jews more skilful in devising an answer. They offer us a threefold solution, striving to prove that these words were spoken not about Christ but either about Hezekiah, or Isaiah’s son, or some other person unknown to me, begotten of a married woman who had known a husband and not of a virgin. Their objections we shall easily reduce to nothing, and, with his help, prove that the virgin-born Son is God and our Lord Jesus Christ.

### It is shown that this prophecy is not to be understood of Hezekiah’s son.

71. Let us therefore begin to answer the adversaries of our faith and oppose truth to falsehood, so that those who hope to convict us may understand themselves convicted in every respect. They say that the person of whom the prophet speaks is Hezekiah, son of Ahaz, under whom Samaria was captured and overthrown. Pekah son of Remaliah then reigned there, and after him Hoshea son of Elah. They assert that these are the two tails of firebrands, whose dominion ended and was destroyed before Hezekiah knew to reject evil and choose good.

The history proves all this false. For it reads as follows: “Ahaz, son of Jotham, reigned over Judah and Jerusalem for sixteen years. His son Hezekiah succeeded him in the kingdom at the age of twenty-five, and reigned in Jerusalem for twenty-nine years” (4 Kings 16). If Hezekiah was twenty-five years old when he succeeded his father in the kingdom, and his father reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem, Hezekiah is found to have been nine years old in the first year of his father’s reign. How, then, was a boy of nine years already at that time [Col. 0802A] to be conceived, or how was some woman to bear him again? For these things which Scripture records were prophesied in the first year of Ahaz’s rule.

Again, how can what follows stand: “Before the child knows to reject evil and choose good, the land which you detest shall be abandoned from before the face of these two kings”? For in the sixth year of Hezekiah’s rule, Shalmaneser king of Assyria came and besieged Samaria for three years; in the ninth year of King Hoshea he captured it, sent Hoshea bound to prison, and transferred Israel to Assyria. If the one to be born was so small that he could not distinguish evil from good, and if before he passes out of infancy the land of Samaria is to be devastated by the Assyrians, let them answer how Hezekiah is described as an infant at thirty-one years of age, and of such immature age that, eating butter and honey, he does not know what good or evil is. Since they cannot prove this, let them acknowledge that what they attempt to interpret concerning Hezekiah is false.

72. Furthermore, let them notice that he who is to be born from the Virgin is called by the prophet not Hezekiah but Emmanuel. “This,” they say, “may be referred to Hezekiah, because throughout all the days of his life God was with us,” which is what Emmanuel means. We answer that this would be true if Hezekiah were to be born at the time when these things were foretold; but he was already nine years old. Therefore neither the name nor the birth can be applied to him.

But the one who is to be born from [Col. 0802C] a maiden, as they wish, or from a Virgin, as we prove, must bear this name. Let them prove that Hezekiah, nine years old, was born a second time—not from his own mother but from a maiden—and that one man according to the flesh can have two mothers and two births; then we shall grant him, with the second birth, this name, Emmanuel. But if he has been born twice, he will also have been conceived twice, since the prophet says concerning the one to be born: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son.”

Yet that a youth nine years old can be begotten again by his father, or conceived again by his mother, and that a body already mature in age can again be dissolved into fluid fit for conception—just as it is wicked to believe this, so it is utterly foolish to assert it. Let them therefore cease to transfer the prophecy from Christ to Hezekiah, because it is clear from what has preceded that what they say is altogether impossible. And this, indeed, we hope we have shown sufficiently plainly.

### It is shown that the prophecy concerning Christ is not to be understood of Isaiah’s son.

73. They move to another argument and say that Isaiah had two sons, one called Jashub, the other Emmanuel; and because the following passage reads, “I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son” (Isa. 8), they contend that the prophecy was spoken about his son Emmanuel.

We answer them: If these words were spoken about Isaiah’s son, how did his father presume to give his son the name Emmanuel, against the command of the Lord who ordered otherwise? For it follows: “And the Lord said to me: Call [Col. 0803A] his name, ‘Swiftly take away the spoils; quickly plunder’; for before the child knows to call his father and mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of the Assyrians” (ibid.). How were these things spoken about Emmanuel, Isaiah’s son, when he himself had been born before the prophet foretold them? For it is written: “And the Lord said to Isaiah: Go out to meet Ahaz, you and your son Jashub, who has been left behind” (Isa. 7).

They say that Jashub is called “left behind” because his brother, of whom the discussion is now concerned, had fled to the Assyrians, according to the Jews’ opinion, and had betrayed to them part of the city. They further say that this was Rabshakeh, who spoke Hebrew to those sitting upon the wall when Sennacherib’s army besieged Jerusalem. But leaving to those who made them the credibility of these statements, let us prove that he is not the same son of Isaiah whom the prophet here affirms to be born of a Virgin.

It is clear to all who know the history that, under King Ahaz, Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria went up against Damascus, devastated it, transferred its inhabitants to Cyrene, and killed Rezin. From this the Jews derive an argument. They pass from Emmanuel to some unknown third son of Isaiah, whom, as they assert, the prophetess conceived and bore according to the prophet’s word; she gave him the name “Quickly plunder.” They say that before the one born under King Ahaz knew to call father and mother, the king of Assyria devastated Damascus.

But I ask them to answer how the same king of Assyria took away the spoils of Samaria [Col. 0803C] before that foretold child had passed beyond infancy, when it is evident that Samaria was overthrown in the sixth year of Hezekiah’s reign by Shalmaneser king of Assyria. The one who said, “Before the child knows these and those things, the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of the Assyrians” (Isa. 8), asserted that both must be fulfilled before the child knew to call father and mother. Or how will they prove that what was done under two kings was fulfilled under one?

In whatever year of Ahaz’s reign Damascus was overthrown by Tiglath-pileser, it is nevertheless known that Samaria was devastated by Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, in the sixth year of Hezekiah’s reign. And if, in the first year of Ahaz’s reign, when these things were said, the child was conceived and born—for this is what [Col. 0803D] the Jews wish, namely that Isaiah immediately approached the prophetess, she conceived and bore a son, and called his name “Swiftly take away the spoils; quickly plunder”—or even, at the very latest, in the third or fourth year, how did he not know to call father and mother when, at the time Samaria was overthrown, if we reckon the years carefully, he was eighteen years old?

For Ahaz reigned sixteen years; and if the child was born within the first four years of his reign, he spent the remaining twelve years under Ahaz and six under Hezekiah, making eighteen in all. Was he mute for so long that he could not call father and mother, or did not know how? Let them choose whichever they wish, and tell us whether this child was born before Damascus was overthrown or before Samaria was overthrown. Since they cannot prove that both occurred at one time, let them first prove how the infant whom they wish to have been born at that time remained speechless from the overthrow of Damascus for twenty years and more, until the overthrow of Samaria, and did not know how to distinguish good from evil.

At the same time let them show of whom the following words are spoken, where the prophet soon afterwards describes the Assyrian army coming against Jerusalem, saying: “The spreading of its wings shall fill the breadth of your land, O Emmanuel” (ibid.). Did Emmanuel, whom they say was Isaiah’s son, possess all Judaea? No king was called Emmanuel. Who, then, is the one to whom the prophet speaks, saying that the spreading of the Assyrian king’s wings—that is, the multitude of his army—shall cover the whole land of Emmanuel? “It is called his land,” they say, “because he was born in it.”

If they say this of Emmanuel, Isaiah’s son, already born, it is completely false; if of the Virgin’s Son yet to be born, it is entirely true and certain. For the whole world belonged to him before he was born; but Judaea is properly called his land because he was to be born in it. For the prophet said: “She shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. 7), and this cannot at all be understood of the past. It should also be observed that he calls it his land before he becomes man, thereby indicating the power of his divinity, by which he governs all things as God, although he is to be born from a Virgin as man.

But if they insist by every means that Isaiah begot this Emmanuel from the prophetess [Col. 0804C], let them hear that the one who was born—if indeed there was such a person—was called by the Lord “Swiftly take away the spoils; quickly plunder” (Isa. 7). Let them also answer how the prophet was not ashamed, in the presence of two witnesses, to approach the prophetess in order to conceive. For he says: “I took to myself faithful witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah son of Barachiah; and I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son” (ibid.).

Let us compel them, willing or unwilling, to admit that the prophet acted contrary to the Law, when Moses says: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your wife” (Lev. 18), since he compelled two persons to be present where he lay with his wife. They could not be witnesses unless they had seen or heard what the prophet had done. But far be this from the holy man: that he should have done anything dishonourable or contrary to the holy Law.

Let them therefore cease, no less foolishly than ignorantly, to refer the prophecy concerning Christ to Hezekiah or Isaiah’s son, since neither interpretation is plausible. For it is abundantly clear from the foregoing that they rely more on open falsehood than on the testimony of truth. Leaving these arguments aside, then, let us look upon the truth of the matter and prove to be ours what they refuse to acknowledge as their own.

### The true meaning of the prophecy explained.

74. “Hear, therefore, house of David” (Isa. 7). To those of whom above I said, “Hear, and do not understand,” lest I seem contrary to my former statement, hear what the Lord will do—he who grants hearing but withholds understanding. Hear the mystery of a new birth, but let the mystery of the divine sacrament remain hidden from you [Col. 0805A]. For the Lord said to me: “Blind the heart of this people, so that, although you hear, you may nevertheless not understand. You may see God made man, and not recognize him.”

It is vain, therefore, for the Jews to assert that they understand this prophecy, since their heart has been blinded and hardened by the Lord himself—that is, permitted to be blinded and hardened—and understanding of this prophecy has been taken from them, lest they be converted and healed. “Hear,” he says, “house of David. Is it too little for you that you are troublesome to men, not believing what the prophets, who are men, foretell, unless you are also troublesome to my God, not believing that he himself will give you this sign which he promises?”

“Therefore”—not through another shall what he is to give be accomplished—“but he himself will give you a sign,” namely himself. Although you hear it, you shall not understand, because you are blinded and hardened, lest this sign come to you for salvation; rather, he himself will become for you “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence” (1 Pet. 2), a snare and a ruin. It will not be what has happened before, or anything similar that will happen after it, but something which the course of nature does not know and human reason does not comprehend.

### Many signs in Scripture contrary to the order of nature.—The fourfold formation of humankind.

75. “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. 7). Behold something new; behold something wonderful, unprecedented through the ages and unheard of by human ears.
