Behold: for the one rib which the Lord took from Adam to form it into woman, a man shall be returned in exchange for bone, an entire body in exchange for a rib. And she whom man deceived will deceive man’s deceiver, restoring man for man, the Savior for the lost one, the Lord for the servant, the Creator for the creature [Col. 0805C].

And how is this? A virgin shall conceive, not from a man; for if she has known a man, a virgin cannot conceive. But the Lord himself will give this sign: that a virgin shall conceive. Therefore what is impossible to nature will be fulfilled by the power of divinity. Do not marvel if a virgin conceives, for many signs contrary to every customary practice and to nature’s order have hitherto occurred. The bush in the fire was not dried up; Aaron’s rod produced flower and fruit; the fleece on the threshing-floor became wet—and do you marvel that a virgin conceived? Nature cannot act against nature’s gift, nor custom against God, who is almighty and to whose will nothing is difficult. Therefore what he himself has ordained can be true: namely, that a virgin shall conceive.

But since Creator and creature are so far apart, and a virgin cannot conceive from a man while remaining a virgin in conception, and a human being cannot be conceived by another creature except a human being, it remains that, if a virgin conceived, she conceived not from a creature but from the Creator. And since every conception proceeds from the pleasure of the flesh, as the Prophet testifies when he says: “My mother conceived me in sins” (Ps. 50), no one is conceived without sin. But the Lord himself will give this sign, that the Virgin shall conceive. Therefore this conception will be without sin.

Virginity shall therefore conceive in the wholeness of its virginity, not from flesh but from the Spirit; not the heat of flesh, but a divine flower, upon which that same sevenfold Spirit will rest. Virginity shall conceive from power [Col. 0806A] and shall put forth a lily; yet it will conceive and bear neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit, but the Son alone. It shall conceive him begotten from eternity; it shall bear in time the Only-begotten Son of the Most High, conceived in time.

Why do you marvel at nature? It is God’s power that the Virgin shall conceive. Set aside ordinary course and do not inquire into customary practice. Let custom cease and familiar knowledge be changed. Let divine reason alone prevail, to whom all things are possible, whose willing is power and whose being able is all things. A virgin shall conceive, not from fleshly heat but from divine love; from power, not from vice; from the Creator, not from a creature—that is, from the Holy Spirit. The power of the Most High will cause her to conceive, and she will bear the power of the Most High—that is, God’s Son.

And since there will be no vice in the conception, there will be no difficulty in the birth; for the Virgin shall conceive and the Virgin shall give birth. Far be corruption from divinity, which penetrates all things by its power and surveys all things by its might. He who enters, without any bodily injury, into the desire of the human mind—will he not be able to be born from a Virgin while her bodily integrity remains intact? He who does not divide the mass of the earth and yet beholds the depths—will he not be able to come forth while his mother’s integrity remains unimpaired?

It is easy for the Almighty, who created all things from nothing, to form a body from a body, and in a new manner to form the new human being for the fourth time. For first he formed man from the clay of the earth; second, he formed woman from the side of man; third, from the union of male and female; the fourth kind is that a Virgin shall conceive and bear a son. Formerly a woman was formed without a woman, from man; now a man shall be formed without a man, from woman, because a Virgin shall conceive [Col. 0806C] and bear a son.

Truly he will be conceived from the Holy Spirit in the womb by an ineffable transformation of nature, and will have the beginnings of growth until the new man is perfectly formed in the womb. Thus he who is God’s Son from eternity will become the Virgin’s son in time; she herself will conceive him and, without any violation of her integrity, bear her son. For it is fitting that the incarnate Divinity should preserve the mother unviolated, and that the new birth of incarnate divinity should magnify the honour of that virginity: what God’s power began without any sin, it should complete without any corruption.

### The name Emmanuel indicates two natures.

76. She shall therefore conceive and bear a son, and he shall be called by one [Col. 0806D] name which indicates in him two natures, divine and human. “For he shall be called Emmanuel,” which means “God with us” (Isa. 7). For this name means that God among human beings was conceived and born from a virgin. He is called “God with us” because, invisible in his own nature from eternity, in time he came visibly into ours: one person, God and man, composed from two natures; man among human beings, so that what he will be called may truly be fulfilled: Emmanuel.

He will indeed be called by other names which follow: “Swiftly take away the spoils; quickly plunder”; and, though born and still small, by six other names: “Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. 9). By these his everlasting power and divinity will be proclaimed. But this name Emmanuel will express both his natures, divine and human: that is, that God has become man among human beings.

The Virgin shall conceive him and bear him as a son, so that he may exact vengeance for the enmity and, by avenging his mother’s injury, triumph over the serpent. Thus will be fulfilled in truth the Lord’s sentence which said: “She herself shall crush your head” (Gen. 3). He will go forth against the strong one with stronger power; the left hand will fight as the right; the Son for his mother, God for humankind. There will be true redemption for the offence of the first parent and glorious victory over the deceit of the deceiver. The Virgin shall conceive him and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel.

### The Jews’ objection to the virginity of her who is to bear Christ.—What the Hebrew word *alma* means.

[Col. 0807B] 77. Here the Jews resist, asserting that the Hebrew does not at all say “a virgin shall conceive,” but “a maiden.” We answer them: let them tell us who that maiden was who conceived the son of whom the prophet is now speaking. Unless they turn to the opinions explained above, they will by no means find anyone who fulfilled this prophecy; and I think it has been sufficiently proved that those opinions are altogether false.

Furthermore, concerning their objection that the Hebrew does not contain *bethula*, which in Latin is *virgo*, “virgin,” but instead has the word *alma*, which means “maiden,” let them hear that among them *alma* is an ambiguous word and is interpreted not only as “maiden,” but as “young woman” or “hidden one.” It signifies not just any maiden, but one below the age of womanhood, most carefully guarded by her parents’ watchfulness, and one who has never been exposed to the sight of men [Col. 0808A].

Let them also answer where they have ever read *alma* used of a married woman who had known a man. Rebekah was indeed called *alma*, but before she came to Isaac’s marriage-bed. Therefore whether she is called a maiden or a young woman, it supports our case. For we accept both: that she was a maiden of lesser age and a young woman below the age of womanhood. Since they cannot prove, whether from history or authority, that she conceived by a man, let them tell us who this woman or maiden is, or who her son is, and we shall be ready to assent to truth in every respect.

But let them beware of saying anything on this subject which they cannot prove. For, as it seems to me, the sentence still remains upon them which says: “Blind the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy, lest they see and understand and be converted, and I heal them” (Isa. 6). God’s mercy will release this sentence when the veil is removed from Moses’ face and the mantle from Elijah’s countenance, so that the remnant of the Jewish people may at least see the Lord’s back parts and recognize that through passion and death he has come to the glory of majesty. Let this brief statement against the Jews concerning the present chapter suffice.

[Col. 0807]

# BOOK ON THE VARIOUS ORDERS AND PROFESSIONS IN THE CHURCH

(D. Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. IX, col. 1027, from an old manuscript codex of St. James at Liège.—This not unworthy little work was written around the beginning of the Premonstratensian Order, which the anonymous author extols with remarkable, but deserved, praises. He seems to us to have been a regular canon, since he treats at much greater length of canons than of monks, and speaks of them as a member of that household; for example, no. 34: “For if you observe us,” he says, “watching and praying, how people marvel and say that what we do is beyond them,” etc.)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0807C]

Brother R., united to his most beloved brother R. in a singular affection, wishes him to hold firmly and confidently, as he has begun, to the way of God, in which one person walks in one manner and another in another.

Since from the beginning of the rising Church there have existed different ways of advancement among God’s servants and different states of profession, and since especially in our own times diverse institutions of monks and canons arise in habit and observance, it must be shown, with God’s help, what difference there is among such servants of God and what intention belongs to the various forms of profession. I therefore undertake to show that these diverse professions please God [Col. 0808C].

First I shall speak of the various orders and professions of monks, canons, and others; second, of different clothing; third, of meals; fourth, of manual labour. Let no one truly be disturbed that he finds the order of professions somewhat altered. For I know with certainty that canons and monks hold the greater place in the Church, and yet he will find neither of these set first. For lest it be said of me that in this work I seek what is my own and wish to honour myself, I shall not put canons in first place.

Yet neither did I think monks should be put first, lest any canon complain that those who deserved to be first in the work of God and in the testimony of Jesus at the beginning of the primitive Church have not been placed first, before monks, who began to exist later. I have therefore arranged to treat the orders and professions in such a way that hermits, who are fewer and sometimes live alone, are placed first. This is like our usual practice in counting: the number rises from one to many, and after the number has been multiplied, the reckoner returns to one. For example, when he has reached one hundred, if he finds something further to count, he begins counting again from one.

So too we shall do here: first placing hermits, who are fewer and often live alone; then monks, whose number is more numerous; and thus we shall come to canons, whose very great and frequent habitation in various places, living in diverse ways, is established [Col. 0809B]. Then, beginning again with recluses and with those who live continently, and who are neither canons nor monks nor hermits nor recluses, but may be called worshippers of God, or *licoisi*—that is, as it were, guardians of the law—we shall return in the same place to women who lead the eremitic life, ascending to the holiness of nuns, and likewise to those women who accept Christ’s sweet yoke with holy men or under holy men.

Finally, we shall bring the order of professions to an end almost with female recluses and women who worship God, whom in common speech we call *licoisae*, that is, guardians of the law, or *nicoisae*, as though imitating Saint Nicholas. Afterwards we may discuss more freely clothing, meals, and manual labour. I shall then add something on the diverse customs of churches, wishing to show that nothing is done by custom in the Church of God which does not please the Creator himself and Head of the Church.

Therefore we ask and beseech the Lord our God, Creator of all things—and we ask you to pray—that he may aid us as we are about to speak of the institution of God’s servants, so that by imitating their life we may one day attain the fellowship of the saints. May your affection prosper in Christ, dearest brother.

## I. On hermits, who often live alone or with a few others

1. Since we are about to speak of the various orders or professions which religious men, fleeing the pomp of the world, vow to maintain for God in the Church, we must first show that the earliest age willingly cultivated the service and worship of God [Col. 0809D]. There Abel offered an acceptable sacrifice; Seth with his offspring invoked the name of God; Noah also, found righteous in his generation and prompt to obey God, built the ark at God’s command.

Since we have determined to begin with hermits, let us consider whether perhaps we may find in the first human beings some likeness of these servants of God. For we are taught by this reasoning that those first people at times lived alone: Cain, after killing his brother Abel, is recorded as the first to build a city, and to name it after his son Enos. Josephus also testifies that he did this in order to practise brigandage and to compel his relatives and household members to assemble within the walls to carry it on with him.

It is therefore clear that the first age lived very innocently, though for only a short time. They had not yet the concern of building houses, nor the diligence regarding food and drink which exists now, nor vanity in clothing, nor such eagerness to acquire gold and silver. For they used grasses, simple water, and the fruits of trees, as God had said. Therefore one of our most eloquent philosophers, celebrating in a wonderful poem the praise of the first human beings, says:

> Happy beyond measure was the former age,  
> Content with faithful fields,  
> Not ruined by idle luxury.  
> It was accustomed to break its easy fasts  
> With the readily available acorn,  
> And did not know how to mingle Bacchus’ gifts  
> With clear honey,  
> Or to blend the shining fleeces of the Seres  
> With Tyrian dye.  
> The wholesome grass gave sleep,  
> The flowing stream gave drink,  
> And the lofty pine gave shade.  
> No one yet cut through the deep sea,  
> Nor had the traveller, gathering wares from every quarter,  
> Seen new shores.

At the very end of this poem, the same author adds:

> Alas! Who was the first  
> To dig up the hidden masses of gold  
> And gems that wished to lie concealed—  
> Costly perils?  
> (*Boethius, On the Consolation of Philosophy*, book II, metre 5.)

2. If, then, I am allowed to say that the earliest human beings more often lived alone, since before Cain no one is read in Genesis to have built either a city or a house [Col. 0810C], and since Josephus likewise testifies that these things were devised because of that fratricide’s plundering, and the poem of that philosopher celebrates them as dwelling in the shade of trees, living without luxury, without that greed and ostentation which now exist among us, and since grasses for the use of life were given by God both to animals and to human beings: it is evident that those earliest people bore some resemblance to hermits. For though perhaps they occupied some fixed place, or visited one another from time to time as human beings do, they did not greatly concern themselves with buildings or clothing, food or drink, or money. I infer that they did not occupy a fixed place in that sense because no house or city was built before Cain [Col. 0810D]. And Josephus maintains that he was the first to impose boundaries and limits upon lands.

Therefore concern for building houses does not at all suit hermits, lest it be said of them that they do not inhabit the wilderness, but are eager to bring the houses of cities into the wilderness. Cheap clothing, coarser food, and moderate quantities suit such persons. Bodily discipline, fasts, and vigils make them glorious. Let hermits, therefore, not bear their name in vain, but adorn it by their deeds.

Thus in the earliest age we have a clear likeness of hermits, where we find righteous Abel dwelling in the shade of trees and occupied with the pasturing of sheep. Without doubt he sought solitude, in which he might live free from disturbance, nurture sheep as tokens of his own innocence, and then draw profit from those same sheep in order to offer it to the Lord. For it was fitting [Col. 0811A] that, since humankind was still few in number, he whom the Lord deigned to call righteous should serve the Lord alone and should, in a certain manner, establish a solitary life by singing psalms among sheep—an animal unquestionably friendly to quiet.

But why is he called righteous by the Lord? Because he fed sheep? No; but because, while feeding sheep, he strove to please God. For those shepherds of Israel also seemed, according to Ezekiel’s prophecy, to feed sheep; yet the Lord says that he will require his sheep from their hands, because they did not pasture them, but pasture themselves—a threat the Lord uttered terribly. Thus this was not what pleased God.

3. I say, certainly, that the work of feeding sheep is fitting and suitable to the solitary life, where both the greatest quiet is possible and the usefulness of its produce is greatest [Col. 0811B]. For, if you look carefully, what is there in a sheep that lacks usefulness? If you consider its fleece, it clothes us; if its skin, it is useful in many ways; if its flesh, it feeds us; if its milk, it nourishes little children and likewise delights adults. Even that which is thought more vile—see how very useful it is for agriculture, so that dry ground is enriched by the nourishment of its dung.

The one who tended such livestock, therefore, embraced contemplation (*theoria*). For, seeing his flock increase daily, he related the enlargement of the sheepfold to the expansiveness of his heart; and as those flocks increased in number, so in him the multitude of virtues grew. What praises, do you suppose, he rendered to the Lord in his heart, when no disturbance was present to him and when the growth both of virtues and of flocks never failed him? I believe that he did not even despise the bleating of the animals, but bewailed it in accordance with the misery of this mortality, certainly as a companion of him who said: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. VII).

I also perceive, in a manner, that he loved the solitary life: he sought an occupation different from the occupation of his most wicked brother, and he did not seek the bond of marriage. For, as I believe, no one in the catalogue of human generations is named, down to Noah, as having lived without a wife except this man. Thus it might surely become known that a solitary person ought, without a wife, to consider the things of the Lord and how he may please the Lord [Col. 0811C].

4. Come then, whoever you are who love the solitary life: receive from him who was first called righteous an example and an increase of good work [Col. 0811D]. See also whether our Jesus anywhere performed something similar to this life. It is written of him in the Gospel of John: “But Jesus, when he knew that they were about to come and seize him in order to make him king, fled alone to the mountain” (John VI).

Behold: my Jesus withdraws alone to a mountain, lest a hermit should doubt that he may dwell alone in mountainous country or in the wilderness. Therefore, if the Lord Jesus—as has often been said before us—was a reader in the synagogue by reading from the book of Isaiah; a doorkeeper by driving the money-changers from the Temple; an exorcist by casting out demons; a candle-bearer by giving sight to the blind; a subdeacon by ministering; a Levite by preaching the Gospel of the kingdom; and a priest by offering himself [Col. 0812A], it will not be absurd if, by withdrawing to a mountain or into the desert, which is proper to hermits, he himself consecrated their life in his own person.

So too ought they to act, even if the world smiles upon them because of their good works, if by measuring themselves they recognize that they cannot perform good works among people without the sin of ostentation. You have also written in Mark that, after he had cleansed a leper and said to him, “See that you tell no one” (Mark I), the man went out and began to proclaim and spread the report, so that Jesus could no longer enter a city openly, but remained outside in certain places. Did Jesus, then, fear the ostentation accompanying a good work? No; rather, he showed us that human praise must be avoided.

I see also that the Lord Jesus displayed in himself almost all ecclesiastical offices; this too we shall demonstrate in its proper place, when we have woven our discourse concerning the other orders. Thus, in the first age you have Abel, a shepherd of sheep, pleasing God in solitude, and for this reason his offerings were accepted. In the second age you have the patriarchs, intent upon sheep-pastures and, with their flocks—that is, with their simplicity—fleeing worldly people hither and thither. You have Moses, alone and feeding a flock, beholding the glory of the Lord in the deserts of Sinai. See also Elijah after the giving of the Law, and many others who pleased God in solitude. Receive gladly also that my Lord Jesus fled to mountain or desert, and you will have before you those whom you may imitate. In the time of revealed grace, moreover, you know how crowded the habitation of solitudes became. But if perhaps [Col. 0812C] you do not know, read the histories of Antony and Paul, that you may recognize it.

5. But someone will say: “What do you dare to say which no one before you has dared to assert? Who has ever compared Abel and the patriarchs, Moses and again the Lord, to hermits?” To this I answer that I do not presume to judge beforehand against anyone wiser and more understanding, but I am ready to hear better things said. But because, perhaps owing to the weakness of my intellect, I do not know how to say the best things, must I therefore always be silent? Since I do not possess gold, I do what I can: in the house of God I offer even goats’ hair. For these too cover the adornment of the divine tabernacle and are useful in the house of the Lord.

For I confidently say, with Christian faith and peace preserved, that I am not far from the truth if I compare to hermits one who perhaps did not possess the name “hermit,” because perhaps it had not yet been invented, but who kept the hermit life excellently. I do not contend greatly about the name where I see the result of the work; for the fruit of the same life can be obtained without this name, whereas without the life the name alone is empty.

Therefore make yourself a participant not merely in the name but also in the hermit life; and, whoever you are who have undertaken it, pursue it as a perfect follower. Having become humble, make the ground of your heart moist and fertile by repentance, with the basket of manure of the evangelical husbandman, lest it be like the unfruitful fig tree. Then, like a little child in Christ, receive his milk of humanity for your nourishment; and so put on the righteousness which is from faith, like sheep’s fleece [Col. 0813A]. Also draw from his skin—that is, the mortality which Jesus assumed for you—every benefit for yourself, so that at last, worthily receiving his flesh and blood, which truly are food and drink, what is mortal in you may be swallowed up by life, so that, when Christ who is our life appears, you too may appear with him in glory.

6. While observing all these things, take care not to reproach a person of another order because of his resolve or profession, even if he lives a less rigorous life; lest, by enlarging your phylacteries and magnifying your fringes with the Pharisees, God should come to you and assign your portion with the hypocrites. Love, therefore, in another what you yourself do not have, so that another may love in you what he himself does not have; thus what each has done may be the good of both, and those divided in work may be joined [Col. 0813B] in love. Let each become, with the Apostle, all things to all people, so that you may attain with us to him who is all in all.

Moreover, let no one be disturbed if a certain diversity appears in this order and each one orders his life differently: for example, some of them dwell alone, while others have two, three, or more companions joined to them; or one lives more easily and another more harshly. For we find this diversity also among the ancient hermits, and each uses the power of his own judgment, undertaking as much as he measures his strength able to bear, and is not therefore condemned by the Lord.

7. But if it should at any time happen that one who has undertaken this discipline sees that it is not very useful to him, he should not be judged if he takes up another, though this sometimes occurs through excessive fickleness—unless perhaps he vowed that he would observe the former discipline. For we see a tree’s planting remain barren and useless in one place, but, when moved from that place, grow, put forth leaves, and raise its fruit aloft [Col. 0813C].

But if you still dislike the fact that not all people of this profession live in one manner, look at the fabric of the world, variously ordered by its good Creator, who made a harmonious concord from things diverse: heaven above, earth below, water heavier, air lighter, humankind wiser than beasts—one thing set above, another below. Then you will not wonder if, even among the servants of God, one is preferred to another; and, according to the Gospel, “In my Father’s house are many dwelling-places” (John XIV). According to blessed Augustine, each will receive there a dwelling-place according to his merit.

This diversity of life among his servants therefore pleases God. Nor ought the clay to say to the potter, “Why have you made me, or him, thus?” For the potter has power to make from the same lump one vessel for honour, another for dishonour; and in a great house there are vessels not only of gold and silver but also of wood and clay, both kinds useful for the service of the house. Be, therefore, a useful and chosen vessel in the house of your God, lest through unbelief and slandering a brother you be broken and, like a shard from an earthen vessel, have something with which to bite the one who touches you, but have nothing with which [Col. 0813D] to preserve what is put into you. Praise the craftsman from his work, the Creator from the creature, so that, even if you cannot attain what another possesses, by loving it in another you may nevertheless attain with him the rewards of heavenly life.

## II. On monks who live near people, such as the Cluniacs and those like them

8. Let our discourse now be directed to those who properly bear the name of monk. Some of them, wholly separated from crowds, lead a life pleasing to God by fasts, prayers, and bodily discipline. Others, situated near people in cities, towns, and villages, are sustained by the alms of the faithful, the revenues of churches, and tithes; they devote themselves solely to contemplation and seek first the kingdom of God, hoping [Col. 0814A] that the necessities of this life will be added to them even though they do not seek them.

9. Let us say a few words about the name “monk” itself. This name signifies “one” or “alone.” “What then,” someone will ask, “is this great difference between the name and the practice? If a monk means one or alone, why do all, or almost all, monks live in communities?” I answer that he is rightly called one and alone because he has one and single purpose of living with his brothers, wholly separated from the pleasure of worldly people.

But perhaps this may be granted concerning those who have placed themselves far from crowds. If, however, anyone wonders how those who live in cities can possess this name, when Father Jerome says, “Solitude makes a monk, not public life,” I answer that no monk ought to be joined to worldly people, either in disposition or fellowship. Although it may sometimes happen that they build structures among people, they do not lose the prerogative of the name, if a brother with brothers—whose fellowship is good and delightful when they dwell together in unity—puts worldly things behind him and, stationed in the sea of this life, passes the enticing Sirens with a deaf ear and shrinks from them.

For then a monk is truly one and alone when he is of one mind with his brothers, worships one and only God, and, according to Solomon, a brother helped by a brother establishes in his heart one strong city: namely, love of God and neighbour [Col. 0814B]. These things have been said concerning the name “monk.”

10. Let us now see whether we can find examples of these observances among the ancients, and show that this practice of diversity, flourishing among monks in our own times, was celebrated not recently, nor only after Christ’s death and resurrection, but also long ago. Let us speak, then, of those who live in cities and towns, to see whether we may find anyone like them among the ancients.

It is written in the book of Malachim (Kings) that Samuel said to Saul after anointing him king: “After this you will come to the hill of the Lord, where there is a garrison of the Philistines; and when you enter the city there, you will meet a band of prophets coming down from the high place, with psaltery, drum, pipe, and lyre before them, and they themselves prophesying. And the Spirit of the Lord will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them, and you will be changed into another man” (1 Kings X).

See how ancient history lends support to modern monastic ways of life. For to the one raised to kingship in order to govern the people of God—that is, to uproot vices and nurture and protect the people in virtues—it is given as a sign that he should come to the hill of God. This hill, as Jerome testifies, was the dwelling-place of prophets, because it befits the anointed one of the Lord to imitate such men, who, though in body upon earth, showed by their way of life that they were in heaven above the earth. This is fittingly indicated here by the dwelling-place on a hill.

That a garrison of Philistines is shown to be there where the prophets dwell supports our interpretation [Col. 0814C]. For it befits those who are separated from crowds to have their habitation near the malicious and those who are “fallen” or “the ruin of the people,” which is said to be the meaning of *Philistines*: so that, being to some “an aroma of life leading to life,” according to the Apostle (2 Cor. II), the malicious themselves may fall and collapse from their malice—those who kill and bring about the fall of the sinful people within themselves—in order that, humbled, they may be healed; while, remaining to others “an aroma of death leading to death,” they may endure persecution from the children of death, so that, refined to purity by the fire of tribulation, they may say with the Psalmist: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment” (Ps. LXV).

11. The reading continues: “And when you enter the city there, you will meet a band of prophets coming down from the high place” [Col. 0815A]. Observe that the prophets themselves both dwelt on high and sometimes came down from the high place and passed through the city. See whether this too occurs in the present age, when monks who dwell in cities receive visitors as well, in order that they may expend, according to their ability, upon others the gift of God which they themselves possess. Thus they are said to come down from on high because they sympathize with the weak, becoming weak to the weak in order to win the weak.

They come also in a group, so that, where you find several companions in one manner of life—whom you know to be weak human beings like yourself—you should not hesitate to share one spirit with them. It is also said there: “Before them were psaltery and drum and pipe and lyre, and they themselves prophesying” (1 Kings X). Such people ought always to have the word of God, which sounds from above like a psaltery, which comes from heaven, from the royal seats, and is above all. They ought also to have the drum, which is made from dead animals, after their skin has been stripped and dried, so that, strengthened and hardened by good works, they may resound the immortality which they desire to attain.

The pipe also suits them: it rises from one and extends into two, namely that they should love God and neighbour. They have before them also the lyre, which sounds from below, because it is fitting for all such people to carry the mortification of Christ in their body [Col. 0815B]. Otherwise they cannot attain the Holy Spirit unless they observe these things, nor can they make anyone who desires to destroy the kingdom of death within himself and establish within himself the kingdom of life and righteousness an imitator of themselves.

12. It is also said in that Scripture: “And the Spirit of the Lord will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them, and you will be changed into another man” (1 Kings X). For anyone who shares in the kingdom of heaven and is worthy of the divine calling, seeing the servants of God living in this manner, receives divine love; joining himself with them in their way of life, he proclaims the future glory of the elect and is changed into another man, so that he who was formerly a blasphemer and an insolent man may now be a constant preacher of divine mercy [Col. 0815C].

13. But someone will say: “Why do you assign to monks alone who dwell in cities what may also suit clerics and many others, or indeed all the faithful?” I answer that virtues of the soul, the kingdom of virtues against vices, the fervour of the Holy Spirit, and the reception of so great a gift suit all Christians. But in the matters I have mentioned I see a certain particular description of such monks. For there I see the hill of the Lord near the garrison of the Philistines; I find also a city, and in it servants of God gathered together and praising God. Therefore, with faith preserved, I infer that servants of God who live in cities and are monks—who concern themselves not with worldly affairs, as clerics and priests do, but only with themselves—are prefigured here.

Accordingly, I maintain that such monks also ought to take the precaution which I see in many places: their workshops should not look toward the dwellings of nearby people, but should direct their gaze beyond worldly habitations. Thus, led with Jesus by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil, if perhaps the devil should show them that worldly dwelling and say, “I shall give you all these things for pleasure, if, falling from the standing of your profession, you worship me,” then, set with Moses against the god of Pharaoh—that is, against the destroyer—they may answer themselves, not the tempter: “O soul, you shall worship the Lord your God, not Satan.”

Look further at the Lord Jesus, to see whether perhaps he did something similar. The evangelist John relates: “Jesus no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went away into the region near the wilderness, to a city called Ephraim, and there remained with his disciples” (John XI). Here you have Jesus, near to death among the Jews, his killers, no longer walking openly, but seeking a region near the wilderness and remaining there with his disciples, in a city called Ephraim [Col. 0815D]. Ephraim means “fruitful” or “increased,” from increasing.

You see what Jesus sought in his temptations, in which his disciples too remained with him. For he sought, hungered, and thirsted for the salvation and increase of his servants, and this near the wilderness, according to the prophetic utterance: “Waters have burst forth in the wilderness and torrents in the solitude, so that the desert and trackless place may rejoice, and, budding, may bud and bear fruit: one thirtyfold, one sixtyfold, and one a hundredfold” (Isa. XXXV).

But you who have become a monk and dwell, as it were, with Jesus under an abbot’s rule: flee, lest you walk in the dark paths of the earth. Instead, turn your face away from the ways of the world and from the dwellings of people, whose thoughts God knows to be vain. Be in Ephraim, seeking to increase and be enlarged in a multitude of virtues and in the number of brothers, so that by your good example and conduct very many worldly people may be converted and the number of your brothers increased. Thus you will overcome the devil; and if anyone disparages your order and purpose on account of its stricter discipline, dwelling with Jesus in Ephraim you will despise him [Col. 0816A].

14. Now, if I am asked—as I am often asked by many—why they themselves live from revenues and tithes, since priests and Levites are commanded by the Lord through Moses to be maintained by these, I answer simply, preserving peace with those who may perhaps contradict what I am about to say: those who serve the altar ought to share in the altar; and those who reproduce in themselves, insofar as their predecessors have permitted them, the works of priests and Levites ought not to be wholly deprived of the reward of priest and Levite.

For I see their churches, whether they wish it or not, frequented by the faithful; I see them regularly sing Masses, frequently preach the Gospel, be compelled to address the church in sermons, touch the sins of the people with the coal of the divine altar, and declare to the people their crimes. I also read that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel, and that “the labourer is worthy of his wage” (Luke X); and I fear to judge them for receiving what they themselves deserve [Col. 0816B]. But I fear more for myself, if I judge them for this, lest I myself be judged.

For in receiving these things their intention can be simple and pure: it may seek not superfluities but await necessities. If it is said that it is not theirs to receive these things, let it also be said that they ought not to perform those holier things. It is also most improper that we should wish to condemn for one matter—namely, the literal observance of the monastic Rule—so great a multitude of monks who have gone before us in God’s service and who still remain with us in this life, especially since, when asked about their vow to observe what the Rule prescribes, they answer and confidently affirm that they observe it well.

I favour those who understand rightly; I believe those who answer that they observe the Rule; I praise those living according to the rule of their own monastery; I proclaim and call them lords and fathers; I admire and venerate even those who observe the Rule wholly according to the letter. For I wish to disparage no one whom I know not to hold anything contrary to the Christian faith, even if he thinks differently from another’s understanding [Col. 0816C].

15. But if monks themselves dispute among one another about the Rule, and one says to another that he ought to labour in the field, wear such garments as are prescribed in the Rule, and use this or that food according to the Rule, let the speaker understand and believe that, if wiser people have considered anything differently from himself, this was done not without reason but wisely: either so that the weakness of many might be relieved, or so that the frailty of those wishing to be saved by the example of such monks might not be frightened.

This is how I understand their institutions to have been made, judging neither group to be a transgressor of its Rule; and I ask the prayers of both, whom I know to agree in the unity of faith. For I do not seek to reproach anyone because of his order, but desire to show that, though they live differently, both yearn from one beginning toward one end—Christ.

For the servants of God who live among people also have Christ walking among people; they also have him withdrawing himself for a time from unbelievers at the feast, and, when he later went up, doing so not openly but as it were in secret. This shows that servants of God living [Col. 0816D] among people must sometimes descend from the height of their mind in order to save people; and sometimes, lest the envy of the wicked disparage them, they must ascend secretly with their Saviour to the feast where there are “remnants of thought”—that is, remembrance of sins forgiven and remitted—a feast-day on which God alone sees.

Let tax collectors and sinners now feed Christ in his servants; let Pharisees, who shut the door of true knowledge, disparage them; let Zacchaeus receive him; let Levi make a banquet, so that, healed by the heavenly physician, he may write the Gospel. A monk who lives among people as Jesus did cannot fear another monk who, like a Pharisee, repels the sinful woman from himself.

He too who rightly observes his Rule even according to the letter will have his reward, if he does not reproach Jesus for his disciples plucking ears of grain on the Sabbath while passing through the fields of this life—that is, seeking sustenance from people. For on the Sabbath the disciples pluck ears of grain because, resting from worldly work, they receive sustenance from worldly people as though ears of grain [Col. 0817A].

16. Indeed, as I noticed while reading it, the Rule of monks requires sober interpreters and calls for moderate readers. For there are many things which that holy founder of the Rule did not set down because he knew without doubt that they ought to be done. Such is the provision that he says the reader and the ministers of the table should receive a mixed drink (*mixtum*) before undertaking their office; he excepts no day. Therefore some monks say that, according to the Rule, even during Lent the reader ought to receive a *mixtum* before reading, because the Rule says this and excepts no day; and thus they compel one who is well enough to fast to eat.

Others, on the contrary, say that the *mixtum* should not be received, because the fast is common and solemn. These speak rightly. Yet I hear that certain abstinent monks argue, from the life of blessed Benedict which he led while dwelling in a cave, that they ought, or are permitted, to fast even on the Lord’s Day, because, fasting every day, he did not omit even Sunday. I see both parties; concerning both I give my judgment.

To the person who says that able-bodied people may eat twice even in Lent, I answer: for the peace of the universal Church, which observes that fast, every person who is able ought to fast; nor is this contrary to the Rule, which, although it did not except Lent or solemn fasts, nevertheless wished to preserve the peace of the Church. For it is not fitting that drinkers at table should take occasion, from the monks’ *mixtum*, to break the fast; nor is it fitting that gluttons, when reproved for loosening the fast, should say, “This can rightly be done, because monks do it too.” Thus, perhaps, for the monks’ small meal, the religious discipline of Christians will be disturbed [Col. 0817B].

But to the person who asserts that monks may fast daily, even on Sunday, according to the life of blessed Benedict which he observed while dwelling in a cave, I answer—not from myself, but from the judgment of blessed Gregory. He says that Benedict, living far from people, did not know that the day on which a priest came to him by the Lord’s command was the Paschal feast. Therefore I confidently say that if that saint, who did not know it was Sunday and fasted on that day, is to be praised, then that priest also must be commended, who said to him: “It is the Paschal day of the Lord’s Resurrection; it is by no means fitting for you to abstain, for I have been sent for this purpose also, that we may together partake of the gifts of almighty God.”

See now whether, after this statement of the priest, that saint fasted and abstained; see whether he despised the Lord’s word. And if you can, contend that it is permissible to fast on Sunday.

17. As for what is written in their Rule and established without any exception—that from the Ides of September they should extend the fast until the ninth hour—I believe that it passed over Sunday for this reason: it knew that one must not fast on that day, and that no one should doubt this, either because of reverence for the Lord’s Resurrection or because Christian custom has so prevailed that it is not permitted to fast on that day, lest scandal arise in the Church [Col. 0817C].

There are besides certain principal days, such as the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, and similar days, and also the feast of the saint in whose honour the monastery has been dedicated. On these, some, fearing to offend the Rule, think that the fast must be continued. Now I wish monks and canons or clerics to fast and abstain more than lay Christians, for this is fitting; but I also wish the aforesaid men sometimes to share, especially on solemn days, in the common Christian rejoicing in food and drink, as far as each one’s Rule permits. Nor do I believe it contrary to the monks’ Rule—which did not except those days—if the rule of ecclesiastical joy is observed even by those who flee worldly joys.

For I often hear, when such fasts are kept on days so solemn, that many murmur about it. They do not take an example of abstinence from it, but attach the stigma of harshness to religious men. I do not say this as a reprover of those who pursue perfect abstinence, but I wish provision to be made for the peace and joy of the universal Church [Col. 0817D].

18. Nor, indeed, will I omit the fact that in both orders, monks as well as canons, there are some afflicted by differing faults. Some defend their own customs as though righteousness consisted in them, unwilling that anything in the Church be changed for time, place, or person. Others are so fastidious that nothing done in their own church pleases them; instead, they continually seek new practices from the customs of another monastery, in order to impose burdens on their companions. Both groups must be answered for the peace of their church.

Concerning those who observe their customs beyond measure, Augustine says in the letter *On the Diverse Customs of the Church*, addressed to the notary Januarius (Epistle 54, new edition, no. 5): “Perhaps a traveller is in a place where those who persevere in observing Lent do not lift or relax the fast even on the fifth day of the Sabbath [Thursday]. ‘I shall not fast today,’ he says. Let the reason be asked. ‘Because this is not done in my own country,’ he says. What else is this man trying to do except to prefer his own custom to the custom of another? For he will not recite this to me from the book of God, nor contend with the full voice of the Church spread throughout the world, nor prove that the other acts against faith while he himself acts according to faith, or that the other violates the best morals while he himself preserves them. Certainly they violate quiet and peace by quarrelling over a superfluous question. Yet in matters of this sort I would prefer that the former, in the latter’s country, and the latter, in the former’s country, should not depart from what the rest do” [Col. 0818A].

These are Augustine’s words concerning those who wish to preserve their own customs beyond measure. Concerning those who quickly change custom, he says in the same letter: “Let each do what he finds in the church to which he comes; for none of these things is contrary to faith, nor do morals become better on one side or the other because of them. For it is on these grounds—that is, either for faith or for morals—that what was wrongly done must be corrected, or what was not done must be instituted. For a change of custom, even when assisted by usefulness, nevertheless disturbs by its novelty. Therefore a change which is not useful, being a fruitless disturbance, is consequently harmful” (Num. VI).

He says these things also concerning those who follow new and foreign customs. Let the reader’s prudence, however, see that schism and disturbance may arise both from holding one’s own customs beyond measure and from following alien ones. Therefore each Church ought to preserve old practices in such a way that they may be relaxed according to place and time, and establish new practices in such a way that the ancient authority of the Fathers is not violated by novelty.

19. I would wish, moreover, that among the monks of each province [Col. 0820D], and likewise among the canons, there should be such uniformity that they would follow one another: those living in one province would fast in one manner and observe silence according to one custom. I speak of those who live in cities and towns. Perhaps both practices would thus be kept better and more willingly; for if anyone broke what all observed, he would more readily acknowledge that he himself had erred, and perhaps be corrected sooner. For just as a fast observed by the Fathers and kept by all in a common rite is better and more willingly observed even among laypeople than one newly invented and not kept by all—and the person who breaks it is more easily rebuked—so, I believe, it would be among monks and canons if all followed one observance. Concord would be praiseworthy above every fast [Col. 0821A], where all of one order maintained one rule of life.

But because we see, even in one place, some wishing to eat a meal according to the customary practice, while others wish, contrary to the ancient practice, to fast, an intolerable quarrel indeed arises. One believes that he does what he does on the basis of authority; another believes himself inflamed with zeal for righteousness. Hence pride and envy sometimes arise among such people: those who wish to fast grow proud over those who do not fast, while those who do not fast envy the fasters. Thereupon a more serious illness is added: those who are proud because of fasting, not content with despising those who live with them, do not shrink from despising even those outside their own way of life and church, because they do not fast in the same manner as they themselves desire. For I have heard one man—and, unless it were shameful to say so, several puffed up with empty swelling—denigrating the order of another church and saying: “What sort of order is this, where people eat thus, fast so little, keep silence so little, and so often take so many dishes?” They think they say this in praise of their own church and order; but see what they incur thereby.

First, they are led to the summit, so to speak, and accumulation of pride; and pride itself becomes so lofty that it cannot be seen, and while it is not recognized as pride, it is believed to be humility. Then, while one’s neighbor is despised, Christ is held in contempt. Therefore let whoever is such a person return to himself. Let him not raise himself above himself, lest, by despising one of these little ones who believe in Jesus, he fall from the height of pride and be judged worthy of Christ’s saying—that a millstone be hung around his neck and he be cast into the sea.

Let him learn from the Apostle both to abound and to suffer need. Let him also invite his brother, if his church permits it, to that very practice which is good: not to eat flesh or drink wine—that is, to abstain completely from bodily foods, insofar as each person’s capacity permits—while knowing also that nothing is to be rejected by those who are not yet willing to undertake this, if it is received with thanksgiving. Let him know also that it is not food but the appetite for food that is at fault. Thus Esau, burning with desire for a worthless lentil dish—though he often disdained hunting—lost his birthright through that desire. Conversely David, restraining his desires, longing not for cups of wine but for water, and offering that water itself in sacrifice to the Lord, justified himself.

Therefore he acts badly [Col. 0821D] who stuffs his belly with cheap foods. He acts well who keeps measure even with cheap foods. He also acts well who receives in moderation and with thanksgiving the good things sold in the market. Worse than all is the person who either disdains whatever is brought to him, or desires that it be prepared expensively or luxuriously. Let him who can ascend and follow the more abstinent; let the abstinent person condescend and offer charity to the weaker, so that, waiting for his infirm brother, he may rejoice with him when the course is completed, and that both, sensing no obstacle on the way of God, may receive the prize of eternal recompense. Let the faint-hearted learn to be strengthened. Let the strong learn to be humbled.

20. Finally, lest I omit it: those very monks who dwell in cities and villages often seem to deal in secular affairs [Col. 0822A]. They determine cases in civil courts; they have male and female *capitales* (chief) servants; they judge, govern, and protect; they bring up the children of servants, who are to become servants; they possess estates for hospitality; they lease them at a rent, draw income from them and exact it; like secular judges, they hear the cases of individuals; they impose laws upon their lands and people. All these things appear secular and less religious.

Yet of such persons I shall say what I think. I do not believe they devised this from greed, but for the benefit of servants and guests. For we see many people fleeing cruel masters and taking refuge under the lordship of churches. In protecting and defending them there is no greed at all, but the greatest mercy. For in a certain sense, when they receive fugitives, they establish cities of refuge [*urbes fugitivorum*] on the possessions of saints, like that ancient people.

But if anyone says that monks therefore ought not to involve themselves in secular affairs, I admonish the person who says this to be a sober critic and not to judge anything before its time. For I read that Jacob, after embracing the Rachel he desired, returned to intercourse with fertile Leah: that is, those who have tasted the sweetness of the contemplative life return to perform the works of the active life, not for themselves but for others. For I see an equal mercy in defending, as far as possible, the poor against wrongdoers, and in nourishing or receiving people. If anyone reproves them for receiving what belongs to the poor or to their guests [Col. 0822C], let him read that the Lord said: “Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. XII). Nor should he be further surprised if they render to monks the things that are Caesar’s, since the fugitives themselves have made them Caesars for the protection of themselves, their wives, their children, and their possessions. For monks do not always do this for their own sakes, but for those people themselves, who, although secular, seek the aid of protection from holy men.

21. But someone may still say: “If it is good, then, for them to sustain, protect, and feed such people, why do they sometimes put them in prison, beat them, impose laws upon them, and take away their property?” To this I reply that moderation ought to be observed in these matters: those sent to prison must not be brought to ruin; those beaten by such persons must not die [Col. 0822D]; those imposing laws must not make the poor excessively poor. Nor should they do these things for revenge, but for the correction of their other servants and guests, so that the others, seeing these things, may fear and dread doing evil.

For it is better, both in religious orders and among secular people, that one person be beaten and saved together with many, than that unrestrained humanity—which can scarcely restrain itself even when punishments and blows are inflicted for crimes—should perish after receiving, through mercy, permission to sin. In exercising such measures, the monks themselves must maintain fitting moderation, lest they exceed the measure in doing them, so that it may be clear that they are led to these things not by their own will but by concern for the need and welfare of the poor.

Nor should persons of immature age be allowed into these affairs, nor should recent converts quickly be assigned to them. For if a lofty cedar is often shaken from its standing, how much more quickly will a young plant be uprooted if it begins to be touched by the wind of worldliness? Perhaps in saying this I offend some men of holier purpose; but I say it insofar as I can, seeking the peace of the Church, believing and hoping that all things observed in the churches of Christ that remain in the one faith please the supreme pontiff, and that the devout priest rejects no one’s offering, however small, when it is offered from a contrite heart and a humbled spirit.

This is what we have said concerning monks who dwell in cities, towns, and similar places: embracing the interpretation of another who may have thought better, and asking the reader that, if we have said anything wrong [Col. 0823B], he not ascribe it to ill will; but if anything good has been written, that he love it; and if anything bad, that he confidently correct it and pardon us, who do not know how to speak better.

## III. On monks who withdraw far from people, such as the Cistercians, and any who are similar

22. Let my pen now turn to those who bear the name of monk while wholly separating themselves from crowds. One may not rightly suspect anything unfavorable concerning their life and institution; nor need one who speaks of them fear that he will sin even in their praise, however great the praise he offers. For they live in their places in such a way that, though remaining in the flesh, because they abandon and transcend fleshly things, they may rightly be said to be above the flesh. Whoever sees them marvels at so great a transformation of human frailty [Col. 0823C]: they are said no longer to be of the earth, but to be upon the earth.

Let us nevertheless consider whether we may find anything of this kind among the ancients. It is written in the Third Book of Kings that Obadiah, the servant of King Ahab, during a time of persecution and famine, fed a hundred prophets in caves, divided into groups of fifty, with bread and water. The Hebrews also say—and blessed Jerome agrees—that this Obadiah was the one numbered among the twelve Minor Prophets, and that the Spirit of the Lord was given to him because he had fed prophets who possessed the Spirit of God. Obadiah is interpreted “servant of the Lord.” Since, then, we have a servant of the Lord feeding prophets; a time of famine and persecution; a hundred prophets signifying perfection, because such a number is received in the divine Scriptures as signifying perfection; and groups of fifty signifying remission, because in the Law the fiftieth year was called the year of remission, inasmuch as in it people were released from servitude, recovered their possessions, and were set free in jubilation—

23. Let us consider how greatly that ancient history favors our own time, in which, if perhaps not the very same thing, at least something similar is done. For in our time also, people occupied with earthly affairs place such servants of God in hidden and remote parts of their lands, so that by the outpouring of their prayers they may redeem those people’s sins and so that they themselves, like Obadiah, may receive the Spirit of God.

This also occurs in a time of persecution, when the most wicked queen Jezebel—that is, the pride and luxury of the world—has God’s servants as vehement enemies and kills, by seducing them, whomever she can [Col. 0824A]. These things also occur in a time of famine, when one seeks a person who maintains justice, keeps truth, does not seize another’s goods, and preaches the word of God with a pure heart, and scarcely finds one, so that Isaiah’s saying may be fulfilled among you: “I shall send famine into the land,” etc. (Ezek. V). And this: “A man shall be more precious than gold, and a human being than pure gold” (Isa. XIII).

It is further added that he fed a hundred, so that perfect charity, casting out servile fear, may receive chaste fear which remains for ever and ever. Thus he becomes Obadiah, which is interpreted “servant of the Lord”; and, as that Obadiah shared in the prophetic gift, so this nourisher and trainer of servants, loving their life and wishing to imitate it, may someday be brought to do what they do, and thus burn fervently, inflamed by their spirit.

We often see such people who, while they were secular, abounded in wealth and in an abundance of pleasures, and in whom no virtue of mind was perceived by others except this alone—that they founded and nourished servants of God—come to the point that, made poor, they follow the poor Christ, take up their cross, undertake the narrow and arduous life of monks, and leave merely worldly-minded people astonished and dumbfounded at the suddenness of an unexpected salvation. Thus it might be said of them: “This is the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. LXXVI).

For the Lord knows those who are his. Obadiah himself was believed to be a persecutor of Saint Elijah because he was servant to a persecuting king; yet it was entirely hidden that he was a lover of God’s servants, even of those lesser than Elijah [Col. 0824C]. They too were divided by him into groups of fifty in caves, because such servants of God, perfectly retaining in their hearts love of God and neighbor, signified by the caves, afterwards attain full remission while serving God himself together with God’s servants, as indicated by the fifty.

But how do they attain it? Do not those attain full remission who, freed from worldly tumult, serve God alone, and, if they had made use of anything soft or lax in the houses of the kings or princes of this world, now eat Christ, the Paschal Lamb, with loins girded—that is, with the allurements of this corruption restrained—and are made drunk from the abundance of the house of God? Thus they are divided into groups of fifty: because, possessing charity toward God, they first receive remission from him; and, maintaining the offices of charity toward their brethren, if any persons had suffered anything from them, or if they had done or said any wrong, then, seeing the great beauty of their profession, those persons most willingly forgive them the past sins committed against themselves.

24. We have spoken of Obadiah and those like him, who hid the prophets: how much he advanced, what he attained. What shall we say of those who were hidden? Let us therefore consider what their life was like at that time, when a very strong man supplied their necessities through the charity of their prince, and separation from worldly intercourse restrained every disturbance.

If I wished to speak of their abstinence, I would be judged superfluous, since they used bread and water—which is ordinary, and perhaps fasting, fare—so that, living abstinently, they might grow lean to the praise of God; not weighed down by more substantial foods, they would not be hindered by the weight of flesh, but, becoming thin, slender in body, subtle in mind, and light in spirit—which in the Book of Wisdom is called subtle and mobile—they might be filled.

And how soberly did those prophets live who remained before the prophet Elisha, into whose pot an ignorant boy put something deadly! They drove away bodily hunger with wild herbs. I do not say this as though I believed righteousness to be established in taking or not taking such things, since rewards do not follow one who does these things unless peace, justice, and mercy have preceded them; but because, after those virtues, more abundant gifts of God accompany one who also does these things [Col. 0825B].

25. Look, then, at those people—monks of our own time—living in like manner. See with what concord one spirit has united them, so that, possessing one spirit, they live together, think one thing, desire to differ from one another in nothing, eat alike, and are clothed in one dress and manner, so that harmony of soul may be displayed through the outward agreement of their habit.

For I do not believe that those ancient prophets used the common dress of ordinary people, in which each changes his clothing according to his own preference. Rather, I think that there was among them what may be observed among monks of different orders, who are often recognized merely by being seen, without being questioned, from the indication of their dress—where they are from, or of what profession or monastery. Hence I find that the king of Israel asked his servants for the identifying marks of the man of God Elijah; and, when he was described as a hairy man girded about the loins with a leather belt, the king declared him to be Elijah the Tishbite [Col. 0825C].

Therefore I believe that there was also some difference of dress between those who lived in cities and those who inhabited the wilderness like Elijah, who was hairy: those living near people wore clothing somewhat more accommodating and moderate, while those inhabiting the wilderness wore rough and harsh garments as a witness to their stricter institution. For I do not believe Isaiah and Elijah prophesied in the same attire, since the former was noble and urban and, as is read, father-in-law of King Hezekiah, whereas the latter, frequently fleeing crowds of people, lived more rigorously. But, as we promised in the preface, we shall speak elsewhere, God granting it, of the dress of these or of others.

26. But since we speak of the abstinence of prophets and monks, or of their dress, what shall we say about charity, mercy, almsgiving, hospitality, and the other virtues? I think it superfluous to say much on this subject, except insofar as others may thereby be kindled; for those who come to such persons are more likely to experience these things in God’s servants than we are to say anything true about them.

Saul was graciously received by the prophets even while he was persecuting holy David; and, made a prophet himself by the Spirit of God, he unwillingly proclaimed what the Apostle says: that God is truly among you. Likewise, monks living like the prophets receive even those who attempt to take their possessions away [Col. 0826A]. Thus we have heard from certain people that those who came to plunder, or had proved rapacious, on seeing the humility of their way of life either remained and became monks, or, accusing themselves that they had deserved to obtain such gifts, departed peacefully to their own homes. These monks also perform whatever is enjoined upon them by their superiors with such goodwill that it may rightly be said of them that no trace of virtue passes them by.

27. Consider with me also my Lord Jesus: perhaps somewhere he did something like this, or performed some action comparable to the deeds of such men. The Gospel says that, when day came, he went out into a desert place, and the crowds sought him. Elsewhere it says: “And it came to pass in those days that he went out into the mountain to pray, and he spent the night in the prayer of God” (Luke VI).

First consider the setting: “the crowds sought him and came as far as him,” and whether we may apply this act of the Lord Jesus to the life of monks separated from crowds. For before this the Evangelist describes the healings of illnesses and fevers in Peter’s mother-in-law and others, and also the casting out of demons saying, “You are the Son of God” (Matt. XVI); this happened when the sun had set, and then, after morning came, his journey into the desert is described.

How many fevers, then, did my Jesus command? What illnesses did he heal? What demons did he cast out, except the incitements of vices? By his regard and command he extinguishes them; by healing he remedies them, lest wounds not well healed should rot again and malignant spirits nest through negligence in the sinner’s heart. This especially befits the monk: that, purified from these things when day has come for him with Jesus—that is, when his heart has been enlightened—he should go out into the desert, entirely leave the crowd of vices and both the fellowship and dominion of that world which lies in wickedness. Then, advancing and becoming able to care not only for himself but also for others, he may be sought by crowds troubled on account of their wickedness and asking, “What shall we do?”; and, being detained, he may say: “I must preach the kingdom of God to other cities also” (Luke IV). That is, he ought to speak to other crowds or other sheep which are not yet of the monks’ fold but will be, so that they may imitate him and his followers.

For just as, with Antony, he penetrates into the inner part of the desert [Col. 0826D], there he will deserve both the assistance of angels against demons and the fellowship of people who follow him for God’s sake.

28. Consider further whether he will not also fulfill what we cited above as done by Jesus in the Gospel: “And it came to pass in those days that he went out into the mountain to pray, and he spent the night in the prayer of God” (Luke VI). Here too one must consider in what order he did it. For before this event, on the Sabbath Jesus healed the man who had a withered hand, and first released the hand useless for good works, so that he might surely show that one must rest from evil works as on a Sabbath, and in turn extend all hands—that is, all actions—to doing good. Hence the man who was healed is told: “Stretch out your hand” [Col. 0827A] (Matt. XII), that is, exercise yourself in good works from which you had been observing Sabbath-rest.

But when you have done good, then you must go out with Jesus onto the mountain for prayer and there spend the night in the prayer of God: placed on the height of the mind, as upon a mountain, you must follow the high God; departing from bodily things, you must be carried away to the highest and heavenly things; and, spending the night there—that is, remaining throughout your whole life, which in comparison with the heavenly light is not day but night, however full of good things it may be—you must always wait and pray to be released from the body. Thus, with his father Benedict, he will behold the whole world set before him as though a small sphere, and will be enlarged with him in the vision of the Creator.

29. But among servants of Christ of this kind, as we trust there is, let the foundation of true humility be firm and solid, so that the nearer they are believed to be to Christ, who is the foundation of the whole Church, the more they may humble themselves. Otherwise, placed upon sand, they may fall under the easy assault of flooding temptations. But, clinging to Christ and becoming with Christ strong stones of the heavenly building, they may be able to bear others who are weaker and more infirm.

They will also observe, as we believe, that they are servants of God, so that they may not despise men of another ecclesiastical order, even though they are less strong, nor think highly of themselves, but agree with the humble [Col. 0827B].

## IV. On monks called secular, whose profession is nonexistent

30. What I should say about monks called secular I do not know, for they neither follow the profession of a monk nor is their manner of life described anywhere. This mode of life has gained strength through the negligence of teachers, through abundance of goods, and sometimes even more through lack of goods. For it happens sometimes that abundance of possessions produces laxity; and while no temporal thing is lacking, concern and strength of soul are immediately absent.

It also often happens that, when necessities to give monks are lacking in an abbot’s hand, he does not dare rebuke them for some laxity or fault. Thus, when earthly things are sought by monks without order, the strictness of the order and concern for eternal rewards are abandoned. Both parties, therefore, will do well if they correct themselves and honor the name of monk which they bear.

## V. On canons who set themselves apart from people, such as the Premonstratensians and the Canons of Saint-Josse

31. Having set forth these few observations on monks, according to our ability, we must proceed to canons. Their order had once grown lukewarm as the charity of many cooled; but in our age, by God’s grace, it has now begun to flourish again somewhat. With God’s help, we shall endeavor, as far as we are able, to show the authority of their order and profession.

First, then, one must observe that this order is now threefold: some separate themselves altogether from crowds as much as possible by their manner of life, dress, and dwelling; others are situated near people; others live among people, and are therefore called secular. We must also see what the name “canon” signifies. A *canon* is understood as a rule, and a canon is called regular.

From where did this order take its beginning? Perhaps from the Apostles? This is partly true, because they ought to live in common and possess nothing of their own. But there is something that may be investigated more deeply. It belongs to them to teach the people, receive tithes, accept offerings in the house of the Lord, rebuke offenders, reconcile those corrected and penitent to the Church, and observe now in the Church of our time other things that were formerly observed in the ancient Law.

Let us read the Book of Numbers, to see whether we may perhaps find in it a foreshadowed form of canons. For in that book are described the offices of the Levites, whom God says he took from among the children of Israel in place of their firstborn, to minister in his tabernacle; and among them was the high priest. It is also described what the Gershonites should do, what the Kohathites, what the sons of Merari; and some of them are said to enter the tent of the covenant before the high priest and carry the wrapped objects, while others carry the curtains, covering, tent, and all that belongs to the altar—cords and vessels of ministry; and others, the boards of the tabernacle and its coverings, its pillars and their bases, the pillars of the court with bases, pegs, and cords, and all the vessels and furnishings.

If we wished to give an explanation of all these things, or of other matters written there, the poverty of our little intellect would fail. Therefore we refer the reader to holy teachers. One thing alone is to be understood: just as under the old Law it was the office of Levites to guard, carry, and cleanse sanctified things, so I believe it belongs to canons in this time to do similar things. No one should be admitted to the ministry of the Church unless he has lived regularly and honorably, as the very name “canon” indicates.

For just as a rule of life was prescribed for Levites under the old Law—what each should do, and that he was not allowed to attend to anything other than that for which he had been appointed, nor were others allowed to perform their offices—so, I believe, it should be done in our own time. Let us therefore see whether we may perhaps find the threefold order of canons in the three families of the Levitical order, setting aside the family of the high priest, which undoubtedly prefigured the supreme pontiff and bishops of this time [Col. 0828D], and foreshadowed their power and dignity.

32. First, then, let us speak, according to the significance of the reading in Numbers, of those canons who withdraw farther from people and, in action, life, and manner of living, remove themselves as far as possible from them in order to minister to God more freely. Let us consider the offices of the Kohathites. By the high priest and his sons they are commanded to carry, wrapped up, the ark of the covenant, the golden altar, the lampstand, the table, and the more dignified vessels. They serve closer to the inner sanctuary, after the family of the high priest, than do the Gershonites and Merarites, so that they enter the inner sanctuary and receive for carrying the items wrapped by the high priest or his sons.

Therefore, the sons of Kohath, the nearer they were to the inner sanctuary, the farther they were from the people. Hence those canons are not undeservedly compared with them: like those Levites, they receive ecclesiastical offices and, withdrawing far from people, carry with themselves the vessels closer to the inner sanctuary—that is, the joys of contemplative life. The name Kohath also suits them. For Kohath is interpreted “penitent” or “sorrowing.” Such people are first pierced by fear, afterward by love; first repenting of their evil deeds and weeping truly, they then, from thirty years upward—that is, from the perfection of virtue and faith in the holy Trinity—receive holy orders in the Church, so that the fiftieth year may receive those who have served well, and, freed from fleshly pleasures, they may not carry the Lord’s vessels with burdened shoulders but preserve them as justified and tested persons [Col. 0829B].

33. In them too, according to the tenor of the reading in Numbers, there is a divided ordering, so that the high priest assigns to each the burden that he ought to carry. From this we may infer that some of them received holier things to carry because of holiness of life, while others, considered less strong in virtues, were assigned lesser offices. For the same family which carried the golden altar, lampstand, table, and even the ark itself is later said to carry blue skins, poles, lamps, tongs, snuffers, as well as forks, tridents, hooks, and firepans.

See, then, that a similar pattern is now preserved in the orders of canons who withdraw far from people. Though taken from the people of God as Levites, they do not all receive holy orders equally. Some are raised to priestly ministry; some are promoted to the office of deacon; some are admitted to the grade of subdeacon; some are assigned to the order of acolytes, exorcists, doorkeepers, or readers; and finally others, less fit for performing these duties, are received in the Church only into the clerical state, and are therefore also called *conversi* among their own people. But one who has advanced in his order, by the judgment of the elders, though formerly placed in a lower order, receives a higher order from the bishop as from Eleazar.

34. Besides these offices required by the universal Church—as it is said in the ordination rites, not that this or that church requires it, but that holy mother Church asks it—there are other offices distributed to each person according to the merit of his life. In them they serve not the universal Church but their own brethren, guests, and pilgrims. Thus one is chosen as abbot, another appointed prior, another almoner, cook, or cellarer; and, to descend to humbler offices, another is assigned to tend livestock.

Thus is fulfilled in them too what is written concerning the Kohathites: “But to the sons of Kohath he gave neither wagons nor oxen, because they serve in the sanctuary and carry the sacred things upon their own shoulders” (Num. VII). So also the canons who withdraw far from people carry burdens on their own shoulders. They minister spiritual things to the servants of God, and in bodily matters, serving themselves, they earn their sustenance by their hands.
