They carry burdens on their own shoulders because they serve God in his sanctuary—that is, in the holy Church—and, strong as it were in both respects, bear Christ’s yoke. They do not extort from believers tithes or revenues belonging to priests, canons, or clerics, though they sometimes receive gifts freely given, surely imitating those who, though they had received authority to live by the Gospel they preached, nevertheless worked with their hands so as to burden no one [Col. 0830A].

35. Consider also whether the Lord Jesus did anything similar, or performed some act comparable with the deeds of such canons. Since we compared such canons with the sons of Kohath, who nevertheless belonged to the order of lesser priests, apart from the family of the high priest, it should not seem unworthy that our Jesus be compared to both. He “was made a little lower than the angels” and “learned obedience from the things which he suffered,” so that he might be as a Kohathite—not in himself, but in his members—under Eleazar, son of the high priest, whose name is interpreted “God is my helper.”

Going, then, to his passion, Jesus was seized and led out by the Jews; carrying his cross for himself, he went out to the place called Calvary, in Hebrew Golgotha, where they crucified him. First see the order which Jesus observed here as well. For, as was said above, the family of Kohath was divided into greater and lesser priests, and the supreme pontiff was from the same family. So Jesus also acted, being obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. II). First he carried the cross, as though it were the golden altar of the sons of Kohath, so that, having proved worthy of the high priesthood, he might afterward ascend that altar of the cross, which is more precious than all gold and the entire world. Thus, sorrowing for us and wounded for our crimes, he might rightly attain the rank of high priesthood and receive the name which is above every name (ibid.).

36. Therefore you who are a canon, withdrawing far from people because of the dignity of your life and profession, and perhaps for that reason ministering nearer the sanctuary: if you wish to receive, step by step, either the virtues of Jesus or the ecclesiastical sacraments, as the order of the canonical family requires, imitate and contemplate my Jesus, who did not seek the highest things suddenly but advanced gradually to them.

Carry your cross with him and follow him. If you belong to Christ, crucify your flesh with its vices and desires; go out with him beyond the camp; fasten your whole self to the cross in the place of Calvary. Like one made bald, with your entire head—that is, that governing faculty of your mind—stripped of earthly things, rejoice to bear his reproach [Col. 0830D].

Then the name Kohath will also suit you; in another interpretation it means “molar teeth,” or “patience.” For by the teeth of your inner person you chew over the word of God and break it down finely, so that you may be able to swallow it and commit it to memory; having patience toward detractors and persecutors; dividing the hoof, kindly disposed toward God and kindly disposed toward your neighbor; and chewing the Word of God rather than swallowing it whole—you will become a clean animal. Eating the flesh and drinking the blood of Jesus Christ, you will be changed into him and become a member of his body.

37. But if anyone should object that the Kohathites may also be compared with other canons, priests, or ministers, and again that the Lord Jesus, bearing his cross, may be applied to all his faithful who bear his cross within themselves, I too agree and approve one who says these things. Yet no one ought to find it burdensome if I judge him nearer to the inner sanctuary who has undertaken the greater labor for Christ, or if I say that he is somewhat more like Christ than I in bearing his cross, who has taken up a greater portion than I of that most gracious burden. For when I behold those who keep vigil, fast, labor, endure cold more than I do, and, to come to matters of greater worth, are humbler and poorer for Christ’s sake, I see them, as though taller and stronger, bent beneath that most gracious burden in the midst of it; while I see myself, together with them beneath that same burden, lowering my shoulders as one humbler, setting my hands to it and stretching out my arms, doing what I can as the weaker person. For they are such as preserve humility wholly and purely, so that they perform the lowliest tasks for the brethren, cleansing stables, as we have heard, and carrying out the other duties of despised servants. They do not disdain to clean stables or the stalls of oxen and asses, when they read in the Gospel that their Lord, for our sake, deigned to lie in a manger.

[Col. 0831C] They likewise pursue such hospitality and kindness toward those who arrive that they may rightly be called like Abraham and Lot, who once received angels because they loved strangers. They also practice such austerity in food and clothing that they seem to imitate John the Baptist, who, though born of a priestly stock, fled the company of worldly people, clothed himself in camel’s hair and a leather belt, and ate wild honey. Lest through much speaking they incur sin, they are said to keep continual silence or to speak little, so that they may follow the practice of righteousness altogether. I praise the greatness of spirit in this profession; I commend their severity toward the body; [Col. 0831D] I love so great a humility in them; but I declare that moderation must be maintained in all things. For when I hear that priests, and even the abbot himself, in this order of canons—who separate themselves far from secular people in life and conduct—and likewise in that order of monks who similarly withdraw, of which we treated above, milk their sheep and clean stables, I can scarcely believe it. Yet when at last I do believe it, I venerate and admire their humility. For I see that they do these things in order that pride may be utterly confounded in them and humility raised up.

38. Nevertheless, I should wish that those who minister daily at the altar, and especially those who daily handle Christ’s body by virtue of the priestly office, should not do these things, out of reverence for that body, since nothing can be cleaner; [Col. 0832A] but should leave such tasks to others who are not yet fit in the Church to undertake those offices. For in the book of Numbers, of which we recalled some matters above, when the Levitical tribe was numbered according to God’s command, and the count began from one month old and upward and rose to twenty-two thousand, nevertheless only eight thousand five hundred and eighty were found from thirty years old and upward to fifty who could be appointed to the ministry of the tabernacle or altar. What, then, shall we say of those younger in age? Are we to say that those of fifteen or twenty years did nothing? I believe that they too—and it must be believed—had exercises in virtue, so that, tested and trained in lesser things, they might not eat the tithes in vain, but, obedient and humbly submissive to their fathers, each might succeed his father according to the merit of his life when those fathers were released from office.

[Col. 0832B] So it may also be done here: if there are brethren in the Church not yet sufficiently fit to handle those holy things, let them be trained in those tasks which exercise humility and break pride, so that afterward, when the elders who have earned their rest are at leisure and guard the vessels—that is, the ministers themselves or any of the faithful—they may rightly succeed them. But let the latter honor in every respect their own offices, which especially require cleanliness.

39. But if someone says to me: “All things are clean to the clean,” I too approve; but I ask whether the vestments in which they approach the altar ought also to be outwardly clean, and with what care the corporals, linens, or hand-towels [Col. 0832C] ought to be handled. If indeed these ought to be clean, as subdeacons are also commanded when receiving orders to make them clean, how much more must the hands which consecrate, touch, raise, carry, embrace, and distribute Christ’s body be kept outwardly clean! If they wish to clean houses, they have within this their own office: they ought to clean the floor of the church, not horse-stables. Read in the book of Maccabees, where Judas chose priests without blemish, devoted to the law, and they cleansed the holy places. Saint Jerome also, in his Commentary on Matthew, reproaches the priests because, when they ought to have been smoothing walls, sweeping floors, and cleaning vessels, they were then taking counsel how to kill [Col. 0832D] the Lord. Behold: in cleaning the walls or floors of a church you have the example of the ancients, whom it will not be contrary to humility to imitate, nor contrary to the cleanliness and reverence owed, even outwardly, to Christ’s body.

40. But if someone says that the aforesaid filth is quickly washed away with water, what if things adhere which do not quickly come off? And what of everyday garments, in which one must necessarily approach the altar, if they are stained with such filth? For they cannot themselves be changed every day. But if someone should still say that cleanliness ought to be inward, not outward, and that Jesus in our region did not refuse, for our sake, to suffer outward filth, as he did hunger and thirst, [Col. 0833A] for our sake: I indeed embrace humility; but I say that the spittle of the Jews is no longer upon the face of Jesus who hung upon the wood, nor do I receive such a body of Christ as it was when passible, but such as it now is when seated at the Father’s right hand. Such is the body of Christ that I believe, hold, embrace, receive, and carry into the depths of my inner self; and I declare that body, inwardly and outwardly, like his soul, to be clean beyond every cleanliness; and I love the reverence shown toward his body, whose flesh did not see corruption. But if such great humility and self-abasement please them, let my worship and devotion toward Christ’s body please them also. Yet if they allege against us the manual labor enjoined upon them by their Rule, there are many things that can be done consistently with that reverence for the Lord’s [Col. 0833B] body: digging, felling trees and harvesting crops, planting, sowing, and similar work.

41. I do not say this as though I reproved their humility, which is the guardian of the other virtues and is made manifest by such signs; rather, I set forth my own devotion toward Christ’s body. If they think otherwise on another point, God has revealed this also to them. Certainly, concerning that Rule which very many canons, because it bears such a title, affirm to be Saint Augustine’s, I dare to determine something definite. If I say that it is not his, the title itself, which everywhere bears Augustine’s name, will contradict me. Again, if I wish to affirm that it is his, two objections can be made—and are made by many: it is not included in the book of the *Retractations*, where many of his books are listed; [Col. 0833C] nor do the manner of expression and the gravity of style prove it to have been the work of that Aurelius, qualities which are very much lacking in that Rule. More certain is what he himself records about his life in the book of the *Confessions*: that, having become a priest, he promptly founded a monastery of clerics and began to live according to the Rule established under the holy apostles; and also what Possidius, his disciple, wrote concerning his life. Therefore let no one think a companion on God’s way to be a transgressor on account of that Rule, which many doubt to have been the work of its purported author. But let all canons have one intention: to observe whatever each has vowed, or whatever each finds in his own church that is not opposed to religion.

## VI. Concerning canons who have their dwelling alongside human society, such as those of Saint-Quentin, Prato, and Saint-Victor

[Col. 0833D]

42. Since above, after treating of monks of differing habit and order, we have said, according to our ability, a few things concerning canons who keep themselves far from people, we must now come to the customs and order of those canons whom we may view as placed, as it were, in the middle: they neither wholly flee the company of worldly people like those who withdraw farther away, nor share their dwelling with people like those called secular canons. For these too are set forth for the correction of human conduct, so that the wicked, seeing their life, may turn from wickedness; and, having turned, may either undertake such a life [Col. 0834A] or, if they cannot undertake it, may by loving it and imitating it as far as they are able, and by giving alms, receive the reward of both the one who receives a righteous person and the one who gives even a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple. And since above we mentioned that what is written in the book of Numbers concerning the tribe of Levi’s son may, in a figurative sense, serve for the life of canons, and since we compared secluded canons to the sons of Kohath, let us now consider whether we may, by analogy, compare Gershon or his sons, who seem to be placed in the middle, to such an order of canons.

43. First, then, let us consider what the name Gershon signifies. Gershon is interpreted “a sojourner there.” Attend more carefully; and when you have considered such a name, note diligently whatever suitable or serviceable point you find.

[Col. 0834B] Consider him who says: “I am a resident alien with you and a sojourner, as all my fathers were” (Ps. 38); and you will be able to understand that God’s servants, wherever they may be, while they are in the body are away from the Lord, and may truly be called sojourners with God: they follow in order to attain, and walk in God’s way with God and before God, so that they may be able to reach him. They imitate their fathers in this: by observing how far those fathers kept themselves from the pleasures of the world, and by doing like things, they show by their deeds that they are their sons. Thus they are “sojourners there,” since they both make God their dwelling-place and recognize that they are still far from their heavenly homeland. But if you prefer that the interpretation of Gershon as “a sojourner there” be referred to the fact that holy men often dwell alongside worldly people and remain there as strangers rather than natives, [Col. 0834C] because their citizenship is not here but in heaven, you have a harmonious prophetic verse for this also, where he prays and says: “I am a sojourner upon the earth; do not hide your commandments from me” (Ps. 118). But whether “a sojourner there” is referred to God’s servant in relation to God himself, or to God’s servant in relation to the world, both apply to that servant of God: for in this life he follows God, yet does not attain him fully as his capacity permits, and therefore is a sojourner with God; and, dwelling among people as a stranger, he cries and groans: “Alas, my exile has been prolonged, and my dwelling among Kedar!” If, moreover, we may apply this interpretation of “sojourner” to every believer, how much more to those who hold this not only in life and conduct, but also in their very habit, way of life, and place, so that they seem in no way to differ from what Gershon is said to mean, namely “a sojourner there”!

[Col. 0834D] Therefore this interpretation has some correspondence with canons who dwell in cities, castles, or villages yet do not mingle themselves with the inhabitants: it is properly said of them, though not excluded from other believers. And because we have mentioned the place and manner of dwelling, just as above we said of monks living in cities or castles that their workshops should not look upon people’s dwellings, so I decree that canons must likewise act here, and I declare that these canons too must observe the principle laid down concerning monks’ dwellings.

44. Having therefore considered the name Gershon and examined its interpretation, it can now, I think, be understood that the name of the Gershonites does not seem very different from such canons, who profess by deed and place that they are sojourners in the world. Let us now consider the duties by which the Gershonites ministered in the tabernacle, in case we may perhaps fit their burdens or works to such canons. First, then, let us observe that they are commanded to minister from thirty years old and upward until the fiftieth year—that is, from perfection in virtue to the mortification of the flesh and of the members which are upon the earth—and let us attend to what follows thereafter.

[Col. 0835B] It must also be considered that, just as the Gershonites received burdens from the high priest or from his son Ithamar according to the worthiness of their lives, so these men too are advanced by the bishop, according to each one’s progress, either to the lot of acolytes, the rank of subdeacons, the dignity of deacons, or the watchfulness of priests. And lest what we say trouble you, examine the reading of Numbers carefully: you will find one person, as though more worthy, carrying the things pertaining to the altar and the vessels of ministry, the blue veil; another carrying the curtains of the tabernacle, the covering of the covenant, and similar things; and, to descend to lesser matters, others carrying the curtains of the court, the veil at the entrance of the tabernacle, and the cords. And lest you think that they carried these or other things indiscriminately, it is added: “Each shall know to what burden he ought to be assigned” (Num. 4). [Col. 0835C] Hence it may fittingly be inferred that the burdens were distributed according to the merit of one’s life. A similar arrangement is also kept now, when such canons receive holy orders from the bishop, each according as he seems worthy, and are gradually advanced to the Church’s sacraments.

But if it troubles you that we compare these canons with the Gershonites, attend watchfully to their rite in the Law and to these men’s corresponding purpose, and you will understand that there is great agreement in both; I do not begrudge explaining it somewhat. Since those men are recorded to have been carriers of the sacred vessels and of everything pertaining to the altar, consider how fitting it is for canons who dwell in cities, castles, and villages, while remaining among people, to devote themselves inwardly to the realities signified by the things pertaining to the altar and by the vessels of ministry, for their own sakes; and conversely, for the sake of others, to look outward. Consider also carefully the burdens of the Gershonites. Although they are, I think, set down without distinction in that book, some of them, as I said, care for the inner things, such as those pertaining to the altar; [Col. 0835D] while others, carrying the curtains of the tabernacle and the covering of the covenant, and another covering, do not remain as much in the inner place as the former do—namely, those who carry the vessels of ministry and the things pertaining to the altar. Nor, therefore, should those Gershonites be left unconsidered who, almost exposed and almost leaving the inner things behind, are recorded to carry the tent hanging at the entrance of the tabernacle of the covenant, the curtains of the court, and the veil at its entrance before the tabernacle.

45. Divided into this threefold arrangement, the Gershonites can signify canons who profess to serve God in churches situated alongside people. Some of them, ordained by bishops to the common orders of the Church, live under the hand of their abbot, as though under the hand of Ithamar, son of the high priest. By prudent administration, according as the abbot knows each person’s ability, he commands one to remain within, as it were, near the altar and the vessels of ministry; another—neither wholly inward nor wholly outward—to be assigned, according to the merit of his life, as it were to the curtains and the covering of the covenant, which, I think, were in the place of the inner things but could be seen from afar; [Col. 0836B] and another, whom he sees to be capable in outward matters, he confidently sends forth, as it were, to the tent hanging at the entrance of the tabernacle of the covenant and to the curtains of the court. To make what we say clearer: one is kept in the cloister to serve God in inward things; another, in that same place, takes care of the brethren and of guests or pilgrims; another is indeed sent far away in obedience and to a parish.

46. Since we have mentioned the parishes which they undertake and govern once undertaken, it is fitting to say a few things on this subject. For I have heard many priests and clerics praise the order of such canons, yet murmur because those who have left the world are sent back to care for worldly people, as though it were not fitting for them to deal with secular matters either for themselves or for others. Therefore the first point to consider is that this same family of Gershonites received the curtains of the court for ministry.

[Col. 0836C] The court was outside the tabernacle and near the tabernacle. For the courts of a house too are outside the house and beside it, attached to the house, so that no one can leave or enter the house except through the court joined to it. Observe that those who carried the curtains of the court may signify the lives of those who carefully examine people coming to the church. Consider also that this family is recorded to have carried, together with the vessels of the altar, cords, and vessels of ministry, only curtains and coverings—veils or tents—and the curtains of the court; and if you read Exodus, you will find that all these were fine things. Since we have wished to draw an analogy from this family to canons who live among people, let us first consider how clean and how fine the office of that family was. What could be found cleaner than the curtains of the tabernacle when they were made, or finer? Perhaps they prefigured the purity of all God’s servants, and indicate fineness either in understanding the Scriptures or in regulating their own conduct and that of others, so that the inner things of the tabernacle may not be harmed, as it were, by a storm of advancing wickedness.

[Col. 0836D] If, therefore, all these things indicate the purity and fineness of God’s servants, how much more do they indicate those of persons who both practice this in deed and bear witness to it by habit or dwelling! For if you inspect such canons prudently and consider their profession, you will find that those among them who remain inside the cloister carefully examine their own actions and those of their companions, lest anything offend the eyes of the divine majesty; and that those sent outward, whether in obedience or to a parish, carefully weigh either their own actions or those entrusted to them, and above all preserve purity in the ministry of the altar. If, then, as was stated above, those Levites who carried the curtains of the court can prefigure the canons who carefully weigh the deeds of outward people, it will no longer be absurd for the canons themselves to govern the people, since they know how to scrutinize their deeds and make them clean in view of their office.

47. But if it is asked why they too have male and female servants, and why, like secular judges, they govern and protect them, the reason given above concerning monks who do the same must apply. As for the tithes which they receive, there should be no question, because, like Levites and priests, they claim what is theirs.

[Col. 0837B] We add to the foregoing argument that, by the Lord’s command, cities to inhabit were given to the Levites, and six towns as refuges for fugitives, and forty-eight other towns with their suburbs. From all this it is clear that some Levites were occupied in the tabernacle and around the tabernacle, while others, stationed far away, taught distant peoples the things of God, obedient to the high priest and his sons. Canons situated among people likewise preserve this arrangement: keeping some in the mother church, as though in the tabernacle, while sending others far away to teach and govern the people, so that they themselves may live from the revenues and tithes of the faithful, and may bring what remains over to their brethren in the church, as it were to the priests and ministers in the tabernacle.

[Col. 0837C] But if you ask why the Gershonites themselves—that is, “sojourners there”—are placed under the hand of Ithamar, son of the high priest, whose name means “bitterness,” the answer is readily apparent. Those who know themselves to be strangers in this world, while they are in the body away from the Lord, always seek their homeland through a saving, God-given bitterness; and thus, under Ithamar, the son of the high priest—that is, under a deferred desire for the heavenly homeland to be attained—they live in a certain bitterness and minister to God.

48. Behold, while we seek to discover that canons or Levites, and the priests of this time, were foreshadowed in the shadow of good things to come—that is, in the Old Law—and while after that shadow we follow the truth, our Jesus is recalled to mind: he was born not figuratively but truly from human weakness, lived justly and according to rule among people, and therefore was rightly, as it were, taken up as a Levite and made priest or high priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. Let us then inquire concerning him, in case he did anything by which he represented such canons. Read attentively in the Gospel according to Luke of him going, near his passion, according to [Col. 0838A] custom to the Mount of Olives: “And his disciples also followed him. And when he came to the place, he said to them: Pray, lest you enter into temptation. But he was withdrawn from them about a stone’s throw, and kneeling down he prayed, saying: Father, if you will, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will but yours be done. And an angel appeared to him from heaven, strengthening him. And being in agony, he prayed more earnestly. And his sweat became like drops of blood running down to the ground. And when he rose from prayer and came to his disciples, he found them sleeping because of sorrow; and he said to them: Rise, pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Luke 22).

Let us consider our high priest, the Lord Jesus, who penetrated the heavens, going out according to custom to the Mount of Olives in order to impress his mercy upon all who followed him. Let the canon also go out from the tumult of this life with the Lord, that he may have mercy on all and become all things to all, that he may gain all. Note that he is said to go out according to custom to the Mount of Olives. For who could more rightly be said to go according to custom to the Mount of Olives than that Father of mercies, who is also the mountain of mountains, in which God is pleased to dwell forever? [Col. 0838B] So too ought the canon to act, imitating him who bore everyone’s wounds, that he may have mercy on all.

49. His disciples followed him, wishing to go where he went, yet unable to do so, as he had foretold Peter. For they were still weak. This often happens to us when we do good things before people: they become our imitators, as we are imitators of Christ. Yet they follow us as those still-weak disciples followed the Lord, and they cannot follow us in all things. For when they arrive with us at the place of prayer, as those disciples did with the Lord, and are invited by us to pray lest they enter temptation, they cannot pray long or remain long with us. What then must we do? We must withdraw from them with the Lord by a stone’s throw—that is, we must be borne toward perfection as far as a human being can imitate Christ the stone—leaving for a time the weakness of the people and praying for them, lest they be able to share Christ’s sufferings with us.

And, kneeling down, he prayed, saying: “Father, if you will, [Col. 0838D] remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will but yours be done.” It is clear to all that the Lord said these things not for himself, who had power to lay down his life and take it up again, but for those who, groaning in this tabernacle, did not wish to be unclothed but clothed over, so that what is mortal might be swallowed up by life. What then? Can none of the faithful now, and especially no canon or any servant of God, say the prayer which the Son offered to the Father? He can, I believe. For it is permitted to one more practiced in God’s service to take upon himself the person of one who is weaker, just as the Lord cries out, the head for the members; nor is it absurd if a greater member cries out for a lesser, just as it is not absurd for a larger finger to cover and defend a smaller.

[Col. 0839A] Therefore let any perfect person say it; let the canon say it too, who becomes weak with the weak and burns with the scandalized, and let him pray, taking another’s person upon himself: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” For I see my brethren, my own inward parts, greatly afraid to leave their former practice; and I pray that the cup of inveterate habit may pass from my inward parts, that they may leave the world which passes away with its desires, and that the cup mixed with wine in the cup of God’s wrath may leave and pass away from them; that the cup of Babylon—that is, secular covetousness—may depart and die within them, so that they too may receive the saving cup and perfectly call upon the Lord’s name. But if what we wish—that all people might be like ourselves—cannot be, “not our will, but yours, be done,” you who have mercy on whom you will and harden whom you will, who make the perfect to think the same thing, and whose eyes saw our imperfection. For those who are not yet perfect will not altogether perish, but believing they shall be saved.

[Col. 0839B] A canon who perhaps by his abbot’s command governs God’s people, or who remains within and pours out prayer for God’s people, can, I believe, quite properly utter that word of the Lord, reckoning his brother’s weakness as his own. If he says it generally, moreover, he will seem to pray both for himself and for others: that the sinful passions working in our members to bear fruit for death may pass from us, so that, freed from sin as from a cup of death, we may pay our vows in the courts of the Lord’s house in the midst of Jerusalem.

But what shall we say of such a canon or Levite? Does he whom he invokes and obeys—the Father of spirits—leave him unconsoled? No. See, then, what effect follows that prayer of the Lord: “An angel appeared to him from heaven, strengthening him” (ibid.). The Angel of Great Counsel, that Bread who came down from heaven (John 6), now also appears to us, that he may strengthen the human heart when we make supplication for ourselves and for his people, by granting effect to our prayers, strengthening us that we may pray without ceasing, and ensuring that nothing be lacking in prayer which did not proceed in Christ Jesus the head.

50. See him laboring in prayer; whence it follows: [Col. 0839D] “And being in agony, he prayed more earnestly.” What then does it mean that my Lord Jesus, praying to the Father, enters agony, except that when we pray, and when he appears, granting effect to our prayer and strengthening us, the breath of worldly thought, bodily weakness, or the favor of human praise seeks to disturb us and tear us away from prayer? Therefore that struggle which Jesus undertook must also be undertaken, though in another manner, so that we may flee worldly and carnal things and, praying more earnestly, overcome the whirlwinds of fluctuating thoughts.

51. It follows: “And his sweat became like drops of blood running down to the ground.” First consider the Lord Jesus praying more earnestly in agony, commending the labor of prayer by his sweat. [Col. 0840A] Then consider that sweat flowing to the ground in the likeness of blood, so that the labor of his prayer might be the beginning of our labor, and that his sweat might become an encouragement for our testimony—by which we bear witness for Jesus—to run down, as it were, by some step to the earth, that is, to earthly people. For if you observe us keeping vigil and praying, and see how people marvel and say that what we do is beyond them, you will understand that our labor for the testimony of Jesus has flowed and reached the earth like blood—that is, like suffering—when people judge our prayers and vigils to be a great suffering.

52. And see what follows that bloody sweat: “And when he rose from prayer and came to his disciples, he found them sleeping because of sorrow.” What does it mean that, while Jesus prays, the sorrowful disciples sleep, except that, while we pray and labor in prayer, those people still weak and not yet able to rise to imitation of us are nevertheless already put to sleep with respect to carnal desire? [Col. 0840B] And what else is the sorrow that follows them and makes them sleep than repentance for sins, which frightens the mind and puts it to sleep with respect to sin? When this comes about through heavenly regard, then we must come with Jesus to the disciples—that is, to people still weak. Then they must be rebuked, admonished, awakened; then we must say to them what Jesus says next: “Why do you sleep?” (ibid.). You must do more than leave behind the evils and desires of the world. This saying is indeed salutary—to cease, according to Isaiah, from acting perversely—but see what has been said: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36); and what follows in the same prophet: “Learn to do good” (Isa. 1). Rise, then, and pray, lest you enter into temptation. For if you are lukewarm, the Lord Jesus, vomiting you out of his mouth, will allow you to be led into a temptation which you cannot bear, and thus you will stray from God’s way.

[Col. 0840C] Behold, the things which Jesus, the true Levite and true priest, did near his passion while praying at length can, I believe, suitably be applied to canons who dwell among people. A canon who observes them may rightly be called regular; and if he has authority over secular people and urges them toward good, he cannot therefore be condemned by anyone. But while I infer that my Jesus, the fountain and source of every good, also undertook the works of these canons, my mind recalls those who dwelt at Jerusalem in the primitive Church. The holy apostles, leaving them bodily for the preaching of the Gospel, nevertheless dwelt with them in mind; and during the famine that occurred under Claudius, as is read in Acts, they strove to support them from the alms of believers. If you consider this rightly, you will see that canons dwelling among people do similar things: those who dwell inwardly, as though at Jerusalem, accompany with their prayers those who are outwardly engaged, whether in preaching and governing or in obedience. Those who are outwardly engaged, like apostles throughout the world, [Col. 0841A] magnify God while serving him inwardly; and, lest they have a reason for going out and praying less, they do not cease to sustain them from the alms of the faithful.

53. Consider also that carts and oxen were given to the Gershonites, of whom I spoke a little earlier, so that their weakness might be relieved and they might not fail under their burden. For what are vehicles but remedies for our weakness? We therefore have carts; we also have oxen by which the burdens undertaken in the house of the Lord are borne, when, devoting ourselves to perfect prayer, we carry around our cart—that is, our changeableness and mortality—by oxen, that is, by preachers or outward workers, together with our burdens, that is, with our labors in serving God. For through those who minister to us in outward [Col. 0841B] matters, our prayer is greatly helped, since it can scarcely happen that someone devotes himself perfectly to prayer while his mind is occupied with outward matters or bodily concerns. But if anyone is able to do even this—for the Church does not lack such perfect men—let him praise God with the Apostle, who worked with his hands so as not to burden anyone and always remembered the brethren in his prayers, as he himself declares that he did for the Romans. These men, moreover, use the authority granted them, having permission that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel, knowing that it is no great thing, since they sow spiritual things, if they reap the carnal things of the people.

55. But if anyone objects that many among them do not know how to proclaim the Gospel, such as certain simple men or converts: [Col. 0841C] to this I answer that one who lives well, has the purpose of living well, and follows his profession as far as he can is rightly said to evangelize—that is, to announce good things. For he who lives well seems to me to proclaim more effectively than he who speaks well. The former will receive a reward for a good work or a good fragrance; but the latter, who knew his master’s will and did things deserving blows, will receive condemnation under many stripes.

56. But if anyone is troubled because most canons—I mean those who live near laypeople—do not work with their hands, we may first answer briefly with the Apostle’s words: “Bodily [Col. 0841D] exercise is useful for a little, but godliness for all things” (1 Tim. 4). For in saying that bodily exercise is useful for a little, he shows indeed that it has some value, but not so great that he should impose a precept concerning it upon anyone, or judge a man worse because he does not labour bodily. Yet godliness, which he declares useful for all things, is then most fully displayed in canons who live near people when they are kept in cloisters, lest, by going out, they see the worldly things placed around them and, having seen them, cling to them, soften their weak minds, and perish through such a sight. For it is ordinarily the praise of cloistered persons if they have remained long in the cloister and have despised seeing worldly things.

But if those too who sit in the cloister wish to do something with their hands, I pronounce this good [Col. 0842A], and judge idleness to be cut off from them as from others, saying with the Apostle: “If anyone will not work, neither let him eat” (2 Thess. 3). I understand this to mean not only manual labour, but every work suitable to ecclesiastical persons: whoever does not do this should not eat. Blessed, therefore, is the life which, while sitting in the cloister, in some manner imprisons itself away from worldly things and expands itself in heavenly things. Nor should he who works with his hands boast over him who labours while seated, since it is plain that labour exists in both. They are idle judges who grow weary while labouring with their hands and become torpid while sitting in the cloister. Our own weakness is also a witness: while working, it becomes tired, and while contemplating divine things [Col. 0842B], it is all too quickly brought back to human concerns. But if such persons, residing in the cloister and near people, should wish to work at something, brethren of this kind ought not to go farther afield, but should work around their own dwellings. Let these remarks, to the extent of our ability, suffice concerning canons who live near people.

## VII. On canons who live among secular people and are called secular

57. The explanation given above concerning canons who live farther away, and those who live near people, invites us to speak of those who live among people, whose profession and actions we both wish and fear to describe. For if we wish to praise them, we fear offending men of a holier purpose [Col. 0842C], who very often rebuke them; but if we blame them, we must fear grieving our brethren who live in the same faith and Christian devotion, and who govern God’s people. Yet we neither wish, nor are permitted, to judge anything before its time.

For we have seen, and still see, many canons of this kind, living among people and therefore called secular, faithfully administer the goods entrusted to them by the Church; content with simple food and clothing, they distribute the remainder to the poor and do many good things either for churches or for the needy. Therefore, setting aside those things which they do and which seem less pleasing to God—such as costly garments, used by many of them, houses painted with excessive ornament [Col. 0842D], and the worldly business affairs which many of them conduct more than is right—let us attempt, with God’s help, to show what their profession contains, what office they have in the Church, how they please God, and what place they hold in his tabernacle, provided that they fulfil what belongs to them. For the purpose of this work is not to tear at the deeds of others with a biting pen, but to demonstrate what good each profession possesses and what resemblance it has to the ancient saints, or to the Lord himself.

58. And first, let us, if we can, turn to their benefit the very name by which they are called secular, a name which seems to many not to turn out favourably for them. Let us therefore consider the Apostle Paul in the Epistle to the Hebrews, where he speaks of the former covenant: “It [Col. 0843A] had,” he says, “ordinances of worship and a worldly sanctuary” [*sanctum saeculare*] (Heb. 9). For, as I have found in a certain book, he calls the court a “worldly sanctuary,” where Gentiles converting to Judaism stood to worship after the Jews; and priests and Levites undoubtedly guarded it.

Consider, then, whether these whom we call secular canons do not guard the outer courts of the Church; whether they do not keep unclean persons, and those opposing true Judaism—that is, the confession of the true faith—away from consecrated places, and expel them by excommunication under the authority entrusted to them. Having carefully considered these matters, you will be able to understand that the name “secular” does not belong to them because many of them live in a worldly way; rather, they are fittingly called secular because they ought to rule and instruct the people of the world among whom they live [Col. 0843B]. They will therefore do well if they live from common resources, cut away superfluities from themselves, and are thus rightly called canons, that is, regulars. They will do best if they diligently govern the sheep committed to them—that is, secular people. Thus the secular name will do them little harm.

59. I also say that they ought in no respect to differ from those who live near people, unless perhaps someone says that they ought to be allowed greater latitude and to frequent more places, in order that they may benefit more persons, since they receive primacy over more persons. But in other matters—that is, clothing, bearing, and manners—I determine that they ought to be alike. Yet we must speak of them with such moderation that what needs correction in them, but cannot immediately be corrected because the custom has become so deeply rooted [Col. 0843C], may be tolerated, while what is good in them and acceptable to God may be praised.

Therefore, leaving aside a biting rebuke, which might perhaps generate scandal among listeners and possibly benefit those canons not at all, let us consider their office in the Church; let us also consider their place, and, as we proposed, draw their likeness from the book of Numbers. Since we have likened the sons of Kohath, who served God more remotely and secretly in his tabernacle, to the more remote canons; and have compared the Gershonites, who had something more inward in their office, to canons who live near people and have more inward and less outward activity: let us now draw a likeness from the sons of Merari, who themselves ministered both inwardly and outwardly in God’s tabernacle, to the canons [Col. 0843D] whom, according to the reasoning stated above, we wish to call secular.

60. First, however, let us see what the name Merari signifies, and afterward recognize how it suits canons of this kind. For *Merari* is interpreted “making bitter,” or “bitterness”; and these canons likewise, who rule peoples, expel the unclean from the Church, impose penance on those returning to the Church, preach that all transitory things are to be despised, and set before the wicked the punishments of hell unless they repent—what else can they be called but makers of bitterness?

For they make themselves bitter when they lament their own evils and sins, or those of the people committed against them or inflicted upon others. They also make bitter those entrusted to them when they expel them from the assembly of believers for their offences [Col. 0844A], or burden penitents with the labours of penance. Since we recognize offices from their works, let us see from what age they begin to bear burdens, so that afterward we may weigh what their burdens are. For they too, like the others, are commanded to minister from thirty years of age and upward until their fiftieth year, so that both perfection of virtue and mortification of the flesh may be shown to be required in them.

61. They carry the boards of the tabernacle and its bars, the pillars and their bases, likewise the pillars of the court with their bases, pegs, and cords. By the Lord’s command, they receive all the vessels and furnishings according to number, and so carry them. If we carefully consider the burdens of the Merarites, we shall find that they were heavy. Therefore those in the old Law to whom burdens so heavy and so worthy were entrusted must also have been strong [Col. 0844B] in keeping the commandments of the Lord. But if those who served God in the shadow of things to come are to be called strong in the Lord’s commandments, how much more those who have undertaken the office of supporting his Church in truth?

And if anyone is troubled that we liken the sons of Merari to canons living among people, and compare their burdens to these canons’ offices, let him carefully attend to whether we find anything fitting in what we say. Since we said above that the Merarites ministered inwardly and outwardly, see whether canons among people do not do the same. For they minister inwardly when they receive ecclesiastical offices in due rank in the Church, so that they may serve daily in God’s house; and they minister outwardly [Col. 0844C] when they summon God’s peoples to the Church, instruct them, lay commandments upon them, and tell them what each should do in church, at home, and in the field each day—whether they may rest or work, fast or eat. Moreover, they expel from the Church those who despise the Lord’s commandments or their own; they recall those who have been corrected and condemn the uncorrected, so that they may not receive communion even at death or have burial in consecrated places.

These offices which we have enumerated, inward and outward, are plainly exercised by the canons called secular. Thus persons of this kind, if they fulfil their office well, may deservedly be equated with the bearers of the boards and bars of the tabernacle, of the pillars and bases, and likewise of the pillars of the court [Col. 0844D], its bases, pegs, and cords. For they carry the boarding of the tabernacle when they set before and teach the peoples committed to them, as an example, the works and writings of the holy Fathers, by which they bore and adorned God’s Church; for, just as the tabernacle rested fixed upon its boards, so the Church stands, resting upon the words and works of apostles and prophets.

They carry the bars by which the boards were made firm, so that the structure built upon them should not move, when they set before the people testimonies and commandments given to us to keep, so that we may cling firmly to them. They also bear the pillars when they teach the people that the teachers who followed the prophets and apostles, and who themselves bore God’s Church, are to be imitated. They carry the bases of the pillars [Col. 0845A] when they show the peoples the governance which the Church has always possessed. For a king is called a “base.”

And attend carefully to what follows concerning the Merarites: they carry around the court its pillars with their bases, pegs, and cords. When they were said above to carry the boards of the tabernacle, its bars, pillars, and bases, they were shown to have an office within the tabernacle. But when they are mentioned as carrying the pillars of the court with their bases, pegs, and cords, they are shown to have held authority over the peoples who gathered at the tabernacle and were outside the tabernacle. For they could not carry the structure of the courts and fail to restrain those behaving disorderly in the courts.

62. Therefore, since we have likened these sons of Merari to canons called secular, we must see that, just as they served in God’s tabernacle and again guarded the courts outside the tabernacle, so these too ought to serve God inwardly and devote themselves to contemplation, while outwardly they must wage service for the sake of others entrusted to them and bear others’ burdens [Col. 0845B]. They must also cling to the peoples subject to them and not abandon those committed to them. This is signified by the pegs fixed to the tabernacle. They are also commanded to carry the tabernacle’s cords, so that they may bind themselves and those entrusted to them by mutual love.

Having considered all these things, you can see that the canons whom we call secular, if they carefully keep the office they have in the Church and observe the profession which they make to God’s Church, ought not to be called secular because they live in a worldly manner, but because they ought to rule worldly people. For if we first consider the devotion of their parents, who offer their sons to the Church to be educated, and if we observe what sort of men holy Church, after their instruction, requires for promotion to the grades of orders [Col. 0845C], we shall be able to understand that those who are trained in order to be set afterward as watchmen over the house of Israel ought not to live worldly lives.

Nor should this be omitted: the sons of Merari, as is read in Numbers, received all the vessels and furnishings by number along with the other burdens, and so carried them. Here we may understand as well what we said above concerning the other families of the Levitical order, although it is not explicitly stated here: each person received his allotted office in God’s tabernacle according to the merit of his life. For I do not think those who carried the boards of the tabernacle, the bases, pillars, and vessels should be considered equal to those who received furnishings for service. But we must also observe that this family received furnishings together with more worthy offices, so that those to whom we compare this Levitical family may understand that it belongs to their office to despise nothing in the Church, however small, that pertains to themselves or to the peoples entrusted to them [Col. 0845D]; rather, they must exert the utmost care that everything may be done in an orderly manner and according to God. For the more persons over whom they receive authority, the more they ought to care for matters many, great, and small, remembering that from him to whom much has been entrusted much will be required.

[Col. 0846A] 63. Nor ought we to leave aside those priests who are ordained by pontiffs, as if by Aaron and his sons, and are sent by bishops or their ministers to govern parishes, and remain obedient to them. Their life ought not to differ from the manner of life of canons—that is, regulars—but they ought to live among secular people in an orderly and regular fashion, as befits rulers of peoples. It is also fitting that wherever they live among people, both they and their households should conduct themselves more religiously than other common people, so that in all their actions they may honour their office and order [Col. 0846B], and may not consume the alms of the faithful in vain, but in all things make God worthy of praise.

64. But if an ancient likeness for these men is required of me, you have above that they are signified by those Levites who carried the pillars and bases of the court. For the court in which worldly people gathered beside the tabernacle to pray can signify the breadth of the universal Church, which, spread everywhere through the world, presents itself like a spacious court and has its bearers—that is, its rulers—as it were carrying pillars and bases.

You also have the example mentioned above, where it was said that, together with six cities of refuge, forty-eight towns were distributed to the Levites. We showed above that this can signify those who are sent far from the chief priests to govern peoples and protect them [Col. 0846C] from the ungodly. What else can now be fittingly understood concerning them? From the mother Church, as if from the tabernacle, and from the pontiffs, as if from Aaron’s sons, they receive authority to govern peoples.

65. But if you ask me how those who are called merely clerics and are not canons ought to live, you may read Jerome’s book to Nepotian and another of his to Oceanus. Read also Isidore’s little book *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, and you will be able to see how they ought to conduct themselves.

But, to return to the canons of whom we are speaking, this too should not be omitted: only two carts and four oxen were given to the sons of Gershon for carrying burdens [Col. 0846D]; but to these—that is, the sons of Merari—four carts and eight oxen were allotted. Perhaps this shows that, just as the Gershonites cared less for earthly matters and received less from earthly people, so the canons who live near people, whom we said could be signified by the Gershonites, receive less from earthly people because they care less for earthly matters. But the sons of Merari, who signify those canons more concerned with secular people, receive more aids from secular persons; and by this they indicate those who, bearing a more extensive care for secular persons, receive from them greater temporal goods.

66. But if someone silently says to himself: “Why, then, do canons called secular, placed in mother churches, have authority even over men of a holier purpose—that is, over canons and monks—and stand, as it were, first in God’s tabernacle, when they lay commands even upon more religious persons, as deans and archdeacons do?” To this I can briefly reply that the canonical order had grown somewhat lukewarm in ancient times, and it was necessary that those found from this order should undertake the governance of churches and peoples [Col. 0847A].

But if they now preside also over other canons of holier purpose and over monks, they ought not to exalt themselves as though they were worthier, but should behave modestly and believe those worthier whom God has chosen, setting worldly concern aside, to serve himself and the few committed to them more fully and to care little for temporal matters. See also that the Merarites were placed under the hand of Ithamar, son of Aaron the high priest, whose name is interpreted “bitterness,” so that canons likened to the Merarites may understand that the authority they possess over God’s peoples ought not to become sweet to them. Rather, when the necessity of exercising authority comes upon them because of their subjects’ obstinacy, they ought then to grieve and become bitter, and with fear and trembling work out their own salvation [Col. 0847B].

67. Thus we have spoken, as we could, of the canons called secular according to the shadow of truth—that is, the old Law. What shall we say of them according to Truth itself, which is Christ? [Col. 0847C] Let us consider that Levite or priest whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, to see whether he did anything that might suit the profession and order of such canons.

When he was about to celebrate the Passover—indeed, when he himself was about to become the true Passover, since “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5)—he had preparations made in the city, saying to his disciples: “Behold, when you enter the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him into the house into which he enters, and say to the master of the house: ‘The Teacher says to you: Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ And he will show you a large furnished upper room; prepare it there.” And they went and found it as he had told them, and prepared the Passover (Luke 22).

Let us return to the beginning of the passage which we have set forth [Col. 0847D], and compare the disciples of the Lord Jesus, entering the city at the Lord’s command, with canons living among people, in order that they may celebrate the Passover—that is, set before secular people the passage from death to life which is to be made. For his own entry into the city shows the Son of Peace seeking a dwelling among people through the ministers of his Church; this happens when canons or any servants of God are received by people.

The man who meets the disciples as they enter the city with a jar or measure of water can signify those who, when God’s servants come to a place, show them the manner of cleansing and sanctification which they need, and show themselves already made fit through God’s grace for Christ to deign to enter as a guest where they dwell, and to celebrate the true Passover with his servants [Col. 0848A]. And it should be noted that he who carried the jar was the master of the household, though, as it were, one of the household already carrying water for the Paschal services. Hence I think that this master of the household, whoever he was, was hospitable and had sent such a servant for water, one who would kindly receive those arriving and confidently lead them into his master’s house.

He led them into the house, not merely by bringing them into a house, but also by indicating that they ought to be hospitable. For this reason the Lord Jesus commands his disciples to follow him into the house into which he enters: that is, those who seem religious ought to imitate a secular man already devoted to hospitality. For if secular persons possess some good work in which they excel, in this too they are worthy of imitation by holy men.

For there are many holy men of this kind in the world who have God in their hearts and do God’s works, as was Cornelius the centurion, who, before he was baptized, gave many alms to the people and prayed to God continually. Thus it happened that, after the angelic vision, he received as a guest Peter, chief of the Lord’s disciples, and received baptism from him [Col. 0848B]. So too many other servants of God in the world do good works; but when religious men come to them, they are perfected in good work and are thus saved.

It often also happens to God’s servants that, on coming to some place suited to God’s service, they immediately find people there who receive them and from whom they receive a place to dwell, where Jesus may eat the Passover with his disciples and institute how the sacrament of his body and [Col. 0848C] blood ought to be celebrated. Hence it is added: “And he will show you a large furnished upper room; prepare it there.”

68. Here the “large furnished upper room” may be understood as the mind of those who receive the poor Christ with his servants and offer a place in their dwellings for the building of monasteries. They have a mind already raised above earthly things; hence it is said that the man himself shows the upper room, which is plainly always in the higher parts. It is large because they offer it with their heart enlarged. It is furnished because it is ready for every purpose connected with preaching and spreading the Lord’s name.

69. The Gospel continues: “And the disciples went [Col. 0848D] and found it as he had told them, and prepared the Passover.” When God’s servants come to cities and places where Christians live, if they are truly God’s servants, they find faithful people to receive them and provide them places for serving God, in order that they may prepare the Passover there—that is, teach the people among whom they live to pass from death to life. Jesus desires to eat such a Passover with his disciples, so as to do in people the will of him who sent him and to accomplish his work.

70. But someone says to me: “What correspondence do you show between this Gospel passage and canons living among people? Could not all these things have other meanings and suit other servants of God?” I reply: I know indeed that holy expositors have treated these matters otherwise [Col. 0849A], but they contain something suitable to these canons. For Jesus entered the city with his disciples, remained in a certain house in the city—indeed, in its upper room—celebrated the Passover there with his disciples, and delivered the sacraments of his body and blood.

Consider, therefore, whether canons living among people do not similarly act, or ought not to act. They enter the city in order to celebrate the Passover—that is, to show the way to be followed from death to life. They remain in someone’s house when the devotion of one person, above the others, provides them with a house to inhabit or grants, in fulfilment of his religious commitment, that both a church and a dwelling may be made. He also shows a large furnished upper room when he indicates such a place as is suitable for heavenly offices [Col. 0849B].

This certain man of the Gospel may also signify several persons, or may be several; but they are called one because of their united will toward God and his servants. In such a place too the Passover is prepared by the disciples and desirably eaten by Jesus when dwellings are made suitable for brethren serving God, so that, as the brethren sing psalms and pray in assembly and are gathered in the name of the Lord Jesus, he walks in their midst and is refreshed by their progress.

71. If you ask me what I should answer concerning common houses, which many of them do not have, I do not know—unless someone wishes to say that they can dwell separately and live from common resources. For we find this also among the ancient hermits, most of whom lived in their individual cells and yet lived from the common store [Col. 0849C]. If the same were done here, separate cells or houses would do no harm, or little harm. But when each person gathers a household and, moreover, allows women to live with him, you yourself see what follows from this.

But let us say something fitting also about their dwellings, whose good qualities we wish to praise and love. In many places, the very site of their dwelling adjoins the fabric of the churches and is called a cloister. We have also heard that in many places it is observed that nothing secular be done throughout that whole space, and that nothing jesting or less religious be done by anyone. Women too are excluded from those places; and thanks be to God that even in this order many are found who honour their order to some extent [Col. 0850A].

Many of them also have ancient common buildings, such as a cloister and refectory, and frequently, indeed very frequently, eat together. I have also heard that some rest together. Let those who do well invite other men of their order to the same practices; and let those who are still weak imitate the stronger.

72. But if it is asked whom such canons ought to call, after Christ and his apostles, the father of this institution and order, we find none better—although many who were fathers of clerics preceded him—than blessed Augustine. Since near the city of Hippo he established a church of brethren according to the Rule instituted under the holy apostles, he is rightly called the father of those who live near people [Col. 0850B]. And since, while established in the bishop’s residence, he lived also in common with brethren, he will rightly be called the father of those who live among peoples with bishops or under bishops.

His sermons concerning the life of clerics are also extant. From them it is evident that both those who lived with him before his episcopate and those who remained with him during his episcopate lived alike in common and according to rule. Whatever is done in this order of which we speak, if it is good, let it be retained; if wrong, let it be corrected, so that Christ may be praised in them and, when the Judge of all comes, each person, rising in his own order, may attain eternal rewards.

And I pray your charity, whoever reads this: if you are such a person, may God grant you understanding. If you find anything good, bless the Lord; but if you find anything discordant or unsuitable, correct at once whatever you find noteworthy.

73. Thus, having described the two threefold orders of monks and canons, whose first division is called that of hermits, who were frequently called monks even by the ancients; having set aside and abandoned one [order], which is not in the number of the ecclesiastical Rule—namely, secular monks alone—and, would that it were removed from the midst of the Church; and having, to the extent possible, commended and praised the other orders: here let this first book on the professions, or diverse orders, which exist in the Church come to an end.  
*[The syntax of this concluding sentence is evidently corrupt or compressed in the printed text.]*

[Col. 0849]  
(In the manuscript codex the other books are missing.)

[Col. 0851]

# DIALOGUE ON THE CONFLICT BETWEEN THE LOVE OF GOD AND THE DECEITFUL TONGUE

By an anonymous author who appears to have flourished in the twelfth century.

(Dom Bernard Pez, *Bibliotheca ascetica antiquo-nova*, Regensburg, 1723, duodecimo, vol. I, p. 1; from a manuscript codex of the monastery of Wiblingen, Order of St Benedict.)

## NOTICE

This is an elegant and ingenious little work, full of the spirit of piety, in which are briefly set forth and refuted all the objections which the spirit of the world and the flesh is accustomed to make to persons wishing to embark upon the way of salvation, and especially upon the religious life. So far I have been unable by any means to discover the author’s name.

One might reasonably conjecture from certain things shortly before the end of the second day that he belonged to the Cistercian Order. For when the Deceitful Tongue accused cenobites of having grown up in the world like tares, so that they ought altogether to be avoided because of their vices, and of having changed their garment but not their mind, the author replies under the person of the Love of God as follows:

> Although these things which you have mentioned are in part true—and concerning many I agree with you—I do not dare to say and assert this of all. For although some are darkened by the blackness both of their garments and of their vices, who boast that they possess the Rule of Benedict, yet have now for the most part fallen away and turned aside to the sect of the Accursed One [*Maledictus*]; nevertheless, they have not been so utterly cast down into the pit of vices that they do not have some among them who groan and grieve at what they see being done contrary to the most holy Rule.

Then he adds:

> You may also see some among them who have distinguished themselves from these by their habit and bind themselves somewhat more strictly to the order.

These last words, unless I am greatly mistaken, refer to the Cistercian Order, in which, after black garments were exchanged for white ones about the year of the Lord 1103, the vigour of monastic discipline praised by the author flourished anew. Finally, since it cannot be doubted that the author of the *Dialogue* was a monk, I can scarcely believe that he would have conceded so much to the Deceitful Tongue concerning the Benedictines if he himself had been a Benedictine.

The very reverend Father Coelestinus Mayr, an ascetic and librarian of the same place, our exceedingly diligent friend, communicated this little work to me from a manuscript codex of the celebrated monastery of Wiblingen near Ulm.

# HERE BEGINS THE CONFLICT OF THE LOVE OF GOD AND THE DECEITFUL TONGUE

## FIRST DAY

[Col. 0851A]

Let him who can unfold how many and how great are the ways in which the tumult of the Deceitful Tongue now hinders old men, now young men, now men, now women, and, to speak briefly, every sex and every age; and how it infects every profession. For our smallness, it is enough for the present to say at least a few things about beginners in the religious purpose.

Why we use personification, let us leave for our betters to judge. They themselves know by experience that variety of speech removes the weariness occasioned by truth. But who is sufficient to estimate, who able to explain, how many and what great snares it sets before one who tramples the world underfoot and burns with heavenly desire; by how many methods and stratagems it tries to deceive him, entangle him, and turn him away from the purpose of religion?

[Col. 0851B] Yet Solomon’s words can be a consolation to those converting: “The net is spread in vain before the eyes of winged creatures.” For those who already bear the purpose [Col. 0852A] of religion, if they suspend themselves on high by the wing of heavenly love, who will be able to harm them? For if God is for them, who is against them?

Nevertheless, the subtle Tongue does not cease from making a din, and speaks in this way to the delicate:

> What are you doing? What you are attempting is an intolerable labour. Stop, I beg you, stop. There is great folly in your attempts.

But if heavenly love has prevailed in their hearts, do they not break the Deceitful Tongue by devout replies? How then do they answer this first stratagem?

> You say that what I strive to undertake is an intolerable labour. But you must consider this: my God’s kindness is greater than my weakness, and the physician’s wisdom greater than the sick person’s illness. I know indeed that there is some difficulty in this matter [Col. 0852B]; I know also that narrow is the way which leads to life, and that few enter by it. But though it is difficult for those who hate it, for those who embrace the Lord’s light yoke it is wonderfully sweet. I know likewise that the way by which one goes to heavenly things is broad to the hope of believers, though narrow to the vanity of unbelievers.

[Col. 0853A]

To this the Deceitful Tongue replies:

> I wonder that you say your God’s yoke is light, when we see good people harassed, pursued, shaken, and troubled by such great labours that they seem called not from labour to rest, but from rest to labour; so much so that your books proclaim that one who is devoted to the worship of your God declares himself destined to be afflicted in many strange ways.

To this the Love of God replies:

> Above I told you enough for you to know how my God’s yoke is light. But as for your speaking particularly of some worshipper of my God, I do not know whom you strike at—unless perhaps you call to mind the one whom we know truly [Col. 0853B] said of himself that he had suffered dangers in prisons, in blows beyond measure, and frequently in deaths.

The Deceitful Tongue replies:

> He is the one of whom I spoke.

The Love of God replies:

> If you spoke of him who endured so many and such great labours that it is even wearisome to recount what he was willing to suffer for my God, it is nevertheless not fitting to say that his labours were too heavy for him, since he received them with his whole heart. For he gloried in tribulations; when he had fallen into diverse tribulations, in accordance with the words of his fellow apostle he counted it all joy; and he was not sad, but “as sorrowful,” while always rejoicing from the depths of his being. For he considered that the sufferings of this present time were not worthy to be compared with the future glory which would afterward be revealed to him and to all who love my God [Col. 0853C] (Rom. 8). In this glory he often rejoiced, although he was still burdened by a corruptible body.

The Deceitful Tongue replies:

> I see many who, even at the very beginning of conversion, are so harassed, shaken, and distressed by so many and such great temptations that they would rather never have begun any good work than pass the time of this life in such great labour.

The Love of God replies:

> No athlete is crowned without sweat. I have a faithful God, who is my strongest anchor amid the waves of temptations and will not allow me to be tempted beyond what I can bear, but will make with the temptation a way out, so that I may endure it (1 Cor. 10). Solomon too is a consolation to me, through which my God has been released [wording uncertain].

[Col. 0853D]

The Deceitful Tongue replies:

> Tell me what he said to you, and whence you are suffused with such great joy.

The Love of God replies:

> “It is bad,” says every buyer; “and when he has gone away, he will boast.” These are the words of the aforesaid Wise Man.

The Deceitful Tongue replies:

> Who is the buyer of whom you speak?

Love of God: Nor may I give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine (Matt. 7).

To this Deceitful Tongue: If not for my sake, at least for others, disclose what you said.

To this Love of God: Since my God did not deprive Peter and the other apostles of salutary exhortation on account of faithless Judas, I agree with you in this.

Deceitful Tongue: Then speak.

[Col. 0854A] Love of God: The buyer is the one who, having turned from the vanity of the world, leaves temporal things in order to possess eternal ones. At the beginning of conversion, what he suffers seems exceedingly burdensome to him. For a new conversion still has an admixture of the former life. But when he has withdrawn—that is, when he has more fully separated his mind from love of the world—then he glories, because he rejoices more in spiritual gifts than he formerly took pleasure in carnal delight.

Deceitful Tongue: Now do as I advise. If conversion pleases you, wait until old age, when you know that your God rewarded even with a denarius those who entered his vineyard at the eleventh hour, just as he did those who began to labour at the first hour.

[Col. 0854B] Love of God: I now see more clearly that you indeed wear the appearance of offering counsel, but conceal the poison of deceit, presenting and administering the bitterness of gall beneath the sweetness of honey. For by your deadly persuasion you urge me to await the time of old age, whereas my God has told me through Solomon to remember him in the time of youth. Those who lend an ear to your flattering words, when they say in their hearts, “Peace and security,” will then be overtaken by sudden destruction (1 Thess. 5). Such persons plainly either do not know or pretend not to know the words and provident comparisons of my God. For, wishing his beloved ones to be ready, he said: “If the householder knew at what hour the thief would come, he would not permit his house to be broken into” (Matt. 24). What, moreover, does it mean that the bridegroom is said [Col. 0854C] to come at midnight, and that some virgins meet him prepared and others unprepared, except that the day of judgment will arrive so suddenly that it cannot be foreseen? Why do I not attend to what this same God of mine says: “Watch, because you know neither the day nor the hour” (ibid.)? Since therefore nothing is more certain than death and nothing more uncertain than the hour of death, I must always be prepared for the coming of my God, so that, when he comes and knocks through the affliction of illness, I may immediately open to him—that is, receive it ardently and willingly. If I knew when death threatened, perhaps I would yield to your persuasion, reserving one time for pleasure and another for repentance. But I do not wish to offend the patience and mercy of my God, so as to store up wrath for myself on the day of the revelation of the just judgment of my God. [Col. 0854D] For I know that those who are waited for longer are judged more severely. He himself wished us to be ready at every hour and at every time—he who tears the soul from the dwelling-place of flesh in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow, and in the morning, as one who carefully considers what happens to humankind at different ages recognizes. What you say, however, that those entering the vineyard at the eleventh hour are not denied the denarius, would indeed be great comfort to me. Yet this strikes me with fear: I do not know whether so much time will be granted me that I may reach that hour. He who promised pardon to the penitent did not promise tomorrow’s day to the procrastinator. Why do you not consider that those called in the morning did not wait until the third hour; those called at the third did not wait [Col. 0855A] until the sixth; and those called at the sixth and ninth did not wait until the eleventh hour? They refused, certainly, to await an uncertain time. They wished to take precaution for themselves, lest their flight should occur in winter or on the Sabbath: lest they should begin to flee when it was no longer permitted them to walk with the foot of good work; when it was no longer the time for earning, but for receiving.

Deceitful Tongue: How do you wish to be saved alone, when you suggest that many people—not only those endowed with little rank, but also those exalted by royal power—have gone down to hell?

Love of God: You have just spoken like one of the foolish women. I shall burn no less if I burn with many. What you say is not sound counsel but empty consolation. Tell me, I pray, what advantage is it to me if I am gathered [Col. 0855B] into one bundle of condemnation with Alexander the Great, Herod, Nero, and the other kings who did not know my God?

Deceitful Tongue: If nothing else held you back from conversion, you might at least fear human mockery, and so wait a little.

Love of God: We often read that very young girls overcame both the world and their sex, surpassed their age in character, and endured most grievous sufferings. Why then should I refuse to endure mockery? I know that God’s martyrs were often deprived of their possessions, overwhelmed by false reproaches, burned in flames, submerged in water, stoned, cut to pieces, exposed to beasts, and subjected to every sort of torment. Examples of tears are insignificant if I do not recall the deeds of the Sun of righteousness.

Deceitful Tongue: Say something about that Sun.

[Col. 0855C] Love of God: This Sun was frequently mocked by the Jews. They mocked him when he said that the girl who was to be raised was not dead but asleep. Some even presumed to say to him, “Hail, King of the Jews” (John 19). Though he was king not only of the Jews but of all human beings—indeed, also of angels—they did not fear to call him king ironically. And what is written concerning the Pharisees themselves, when he disputed against their avarice? Hear the Evangelist saying: “But the Pharisees, who were avaricious, hearing these things, mocked him” (Luke 16). In all these things their fury was not turned away; rather, when he was still hanging upon the cross, they insulted him and said: “If he is the king of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him. He saved others; himself he cannot save” (Matt. 27). [Col. 0855D] I shall therefore confess him before human beings, that he may confess me before his Father.
