Deceitful Tongue: Why do you look so carefully at what your author did or suffered?

Love of God: Because I endeavour to imitate the wise man.

Deceitful Tongue: What is written about the wise man?

Love of God: “The eyes of the wise man are in his head” (Eccl. 3).

Deceitful Tongue: Who uttered this saying?

Love of God: The most wise Idida.

Deceitful Tongue: I do not know who he was.

Love of God: He was the one of whom someone said:

> The Almighty granted to Idida, asking for Sophia’s gifts,  
> Such favour that he might overcome the course of nature.

[Col. 0856A] Deceitful Tongue: I do not care who he was. This I see and consider: the saying is empty. For I have seen many foolish and wise people, none of whom had eyes in the belly or any other member, but all had them in the head.

Love of God: You criticize in vain what you do not understand. In Holy Scripture, which my God handed down to us through the mouths of those who love him, many things appear vain and false to the ignorant which appear useful to those who understand rightly. Hence a certain prophet of my God, speaking of the wheels—that is, the two Testaments—said: “The wheels had stature and height, and a terrible appearance” (Ezek. 1).

Deceitful Tongue: You tire me uselessly with many circumlocutions. When you ought to unfold, you entangle; [Col. 0856B] and you explain the unknown by the unknown.

Love of God: The fruit produced by more prolonged hope is more pleasing. What is freely offered has a cheaper price. I have not yet explained how the wise man’s eyes are in his head; rather, by prophetic testimony I refuted your foolishness when I said that the wheels had stature—that is, that uprightness inheres in the Scriptures.

Deceitful Tongue: What then did you also say: that height inhered in the wheels, and that their appearance was terrible?

Love of God: In breadth is understood the promise of heavenly sweetness, as in the words, “They shall obtain joy and gladness; sorrow and groaning shall flee away” (Isa. 35). In the terrible appearance understand the threat of everlasting punishment, as is said of the reprobate: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. 66). [Col. 0856C] But, to speak briefly, the wise man’s eyes are in his head because he unceasingly considers how his head—that is, Christ—walked. For whoever says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked (1 John 2).

Deceitful Tongue: One thing greatly delights me: in the speech of certain women I find room and complete repose.

Love of God: Allow me to rest today, and tomorrow I shall answer you more fully, when by silence during this night I have restored my strength for speaking.

SECOND DAY.

[Col. 0856D] Love of God: Yesterday you were lifted up by a certain most evil joy when you said that you rejoiced because in the speech of certain women you had found room and complete repose. Speak more fully about this, then.

Deceitful Tongue: Remember how I captured Adam through Eve. I also captured that most wise king, so that through women’s persuasion he fell into idolatry.

Love of God: Who is that king?

Deceitful Tongue: He is the one whose sayings you praise but whose deeds you partly condemn.

Love of God: Perhaps both of them did penance?

Deceitful Tongue: If, as you suppose, these men did penance, my wiles have nevertheless not yet failed. Through feminine blandishments I bend the stony hearts of many, [Col. 0857A] so that some are at times drawn back from conversion by their mothers’ tears.

Love of God: What you say is true. But just as effeminate persons yield to women’s weeping, so men—that is, those endowed with a manly mind—despise it manfully and, with dry eyes, fly to the banner of the cross. They leave the world, unclean in worldly works, and, scorning parents and all kinds of friends, wealth, home, homeland, rich foods, and all such things, transfer themselves to the service of the highest King.

Deceitful Tongue: If men and women sometimes overcome me in this matter, I greatly rejoice that through my beloved heretics I often disturb the Church, the bride of your God.

[Col. 0857B] Love of God: I do not wish to answer you fully about this matter now; but I say briefly that all heresies exist by my God’s permission, so that those who are approved may be made manifest. For those lights of heaven—Ambrose, Augustine, and Jerome—scattered the rays of their teaching all the more widely the more they were assailed by heretics with deceitful questions; they exposed your aforesaid beloved ones, confounded them once exposed, and caused them, once confounded, to be despised.

Deceitful Tongue: Earlier you were speaking about certain people’s conversion. Why have you suddenly digressed to other things?

Love of God: I answered your folly when you said that you rejoiced in most evil things.

[Col. 0857C] Deceitful Tongue: Since you are pleased to speak again about conversion, tell me, I pray, why you do not consider certain people who put their hand to the plough and looked back, and are therefore not fit for the kingdom of your God.

Love of God: I answer you briefly: I see that Judas fell and remained in the mire of vices. I know that Peter denied three times and washed away his fault with tears; for the Lord looked at him, and he wept bitterly (Matt. 26).

> The tiller of the soil now holds the stars of heaven.

Deceitful Tongue: Consider more carefully, and see that there are now many kinds of converts, of whom I disdain to speak more fully. But I divide them into three kinds: hermits, cenobites, and recluses, so that I may briefly show that all deserve disgrace.

[Col. 0857D] Love of God: Be silent, I pray; be silent.

> Cease your lofty speech: God breaks every proud person.

This disgrace will recoil upon your own head.

Deceitful Tongue: The society of hermits, as you know, is altogether to be avoided, and their life should be held in contempt. For they are in solitude, which Solomon taught you to despise when he said: “It is better for two to be together than for one. For they have the advantage of their companionship. If one falls, he will be supported by the other. Woe to one alone, because if he falls, he has no one to raise him up” (Ecclus. 4).

Love of God: I call him alone who seeks only what is his own, not what belongs to Jesus Christ (Phil. 2). Even if he is surrounded by a thousand, he is rightly called alone because he is alienated from brotherly love. Woe, therefore, to this one who is alone—[Col. 0858A] that is, who does not have charity. Why do you not consider that my God, who came into the world for the salvation of humankind, at times avoided human society, entered the wilderness, and dwelt with beasts? If you despise the examples of most holy men who hid themselves in desert places, you also despise the example just mentioned. Does solitude seem contemptible to you because of Solomon’s words cited above? Attend carefully to what the same Solomon said where he gave me timely and most salutary counsel concerning solitude.

Deceitful Tongue: What did he say?

Love of God: “It is better to sit in a corner of the roof than with a quarrelsome woman in a full house” (Prov. 25).

Deceitful Tongue: Tell me what the corner of the roof is.

[Col. 0858B] Love of God: The corner of the roof is the religious life, removed from every secular activity.

Deceitful Tongue: What is the quarrelsome woman?

Love of God: The quarrelsome woman is the turbulent activity of this world, which incessantly stirs quarrels among its lovers, sows scandals, brings in strife, divides unity, violates peace, destroys friendship, and allows them neither to rest in themselves nor to remain joined in brotherly love.

Deceitful Tongue: Since you have answered me concerning hermits, tell me what you think concerning recluses. I maintain that their life is utterly vain: they are not bound by love of your God but confined by walls.

[Col. 0858C] Love of God: When I attend carefully, I see that you impose no limit upon your folly. You say that walls confine recluses but the love of my God does not bind them. Why have they withdrawn from whatever common liberty belongs to this life, except to obtain heavenly sweetness? They would not restrain themselves from ordinary human conversation unless they might devote themselves more freely to my God. Yet if some of them conceal hypocrisy within themselves, we must not judge all by what is known and discovered to be blameworthy in some and among some, whose Sabbaths enemies see and mock. For although they rest from wrongful work, they do not rest from wrongful thought. But others keep a holy Sabbath: they are still and see that God is, and [Col. 0858D] they rest not only from perverse work but also, as far as they can, from vain meditation. For them, according to Isaiah’s prophecy, “month shall be from month, and Sabbath from Sabbath” (Isa. 66).

Deceitful Tongue: What is this that you have just said?

Love of God: In a month there is the completion of days; and here it signifies the completion of works. But Sabbath here denotes holy rest. Those, therefore, who in this world have perfection of work will afterwards have the perfection of holy recompense; and those who now rest from perverse work with purity of heart will afterwards rest eternally from every labour of mind and body. After the Sabbath of hope they will have the Sabbath of rest.

Deceitful Tongue: Concerning hermits and recluses, because of [Col. 0859A] their small number, I do not now wish to prolong the discussion. But I shall come to cenobites, who have now grown up in the world like tares and must altogether be avoided because of their vices. They have changed their garment but not their mind.

Love of God: Although what you have mentioned is in part true, and I agree with you concerning many, I do not dare to say and maintain it of all. For although some are darkened by the blackness of garments and of vices, who boast that they possess Benedict’s Rule but have nevertheless largely fallen away and turned toward the sect of the Accursed One (*Maledictus*, a wordplay on Benedict); they have not fallen so completely into the pit of vices that they do not have some among them who groan and grieve at what they see being done against the most holy Rule. You may also see some [Col. 0859B] among them who distinguish themselves from these by their habit and bind themselves somewhat more strictly to the Order.

Deceitful Tongue: I judge that none of the cloistered will be saved, nor do I distinguish any from another. I see, to be sure, that they are subject to so many vices that I assign them all to one bundle of condemnation.

Love of God: Earlier I maintained that you spoke as a fool; now, however, I see that you have broken out into manifest madness. Hence I am greatly moved, so that because of the agitation of my mind I cannot answer you now. But tomorrow, with my God’s favour, I shall confound your folly.

THIRD DAY.

Deceitful Tongue: When I left you yesterday evening, [Col. 0859C] I had stopped up your mouth so thoroughly that you had nothing you could say; you saw yourself overwhelmed by great confusion and therefore fell pitiably silent.

Love of God: You were not, as you suppose, driven away from me yesterday as superior, but as worse. For when I saw you roused to manifest madness, I did not wish to pour holy words out, but to pour them into a tranquil mind. Whatever is said to a mind drunk with frenzy, however right it may be, nevertheless appears perverse. I am not hindered from answering you by lack, but by abundance. So many examples support me that I am uncertain what I should choose from them or what I should omit. For if I had earlier brought forward Martin, Anthony, Benedict, Columbanus, Gregory, and Paphnutius, what do you say concerning the most holy apostles, in whose time [Col. 0859D] “the multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul” (Acts 4), and none of them said that anything he possessed was his own?

Deceitful Tongue: Perhaps I said jokingly and playfully that no cloistered person would be saved. But now I shall speak with greater seriousness, so that my words may carry great weight and cannot be rejected by anyone. Hear, then, my faithful counsel by which I fortify you: strengthen your heart and body with richer foods in the world, which you cannot do in a cenobium.

Love of God: I hear my God saying: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness” (Luke 21). Nor do I despise the words of his Apostle, where he says: “It is best for the heart to be strengthened by grace, not by foods, which have not profited those who walked in them” (Heb. 13).

[Col. 0860A] Deceitful Tongue: Why, then, does the same Apostle of your God say to a certain disciple: “Use a little wine because of your stomach and your frequent infirmities” (1 Tim. 5)?

Love of God: I do not refuse to use wine; but I carefully consider the wholesome moderation which he prefixed when he did not say that his disciple ought to use much wine, but a little. More perfect, however, if it can be done without the pressure of infirmity and if I am master of myself, is to use none at all and to restore myself not even with a little for pleasure, but for necessity.

Deceitful Tongue: Solomon overturns all these statements of yours when he says that it seemed good to him for a person to eat and drink and enjoy gladness from his labour.

Love of God: But do you understand in this place the sacrament of my God, namely bread and wine, by which God’s priests are daily refreshed at the altar? Nothing is better than that each should test himself and thus eat of that bread and drink of the cup, receiving the sacrament in such a way that it may not become a more severe torment for him; that he may receive it not unto destruction but unto salvation.

[Col. 0860B] Deceitful Tongue: I understand him to have said this concerning the simple refreshment of the body, not of the soul.

Love of God: In this I do not differ greatly from you. But I want you to consider that, in the same book in which he says these things, he introduces many statements in the person of the infirm, but makes determinations concerning the house of mourning and the banquet on rational grounds. Something is lacking here in the manuscript codex.

Love of God: Nobility of birth is of little account [Col. 0860C] without nobility of mind. Nobility of character adorns more than one’s father.

Deceitful Tongue: How can you subject your will to another’s will?

Love of God: Because I desire to imitate him whose will is one with the Father’s, and who, to give us an example of breaking our own will, said: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6), namely the Father; and who did not disdain to be subject to his parents.

Deceitful Tongue: To whom do you leave your riches?

Love of God: To him who will give, in exchange for fleeting riches, enduring riches; in exchange for perishable and temporal things, eternal things. “Treasures are of no profit on the day of vengeance, but righteousness will deliver from death” (Prov. 11).

[Col. 0860D] Deceitful Tongue: I observe great folly in certain religious persons, who afflict themselves with such fasts, vigils, humiliations, and sometimes manual labours that they can scarcely endure, although they know, in considering the Scripture of your God, that those predestined to life will be saved and those foreknown for punishment will be damned.

Love of God: “He who searches out majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. 25). But if I find honey, I should eat what is enough for me. For I do not consider what a certain pagan said: “We seek the secrets of God and inquire what heaven is.” You ought therefore to be wise unto sobriety, and I ought to venerate the judgments of my God which I cannot search out. For I know that they are just in secret and secretly just. But if I ought for that reason to dissolve into sloth because I do not know the judgments of my God, [Col. 0861A] then likewise I may expose myself to every danger of temporal death. However much I take care not to die, I cannot pass beyond the appointed limits of death. Yet I ought to consider this: predestination is fulfilled through prayers. For those things which are not predestined cannot be obtained by prayers. But the predestination itself of the everlasting kingdom has been ordered by almighty God in such a manner that the elect attain it by meriting through prayer to receive what almighty God ordained before the ages to give them.

Deceitful Tongue: What profit is there in singing psalms in a cloister and being subject to innumerable vices? For when life does not disagree with the voice, when the voice does not reproach life, the harmony is sweet.

Love of God: Look, I pray, at the example of many—indeed, of almost every region of the world—that have turned to these pursuits. With what brow, what heart, what shamelessness, what folly do you criticize what all who are devoted to contemplation either do or extol with praises? As for your saying that harmony is sweet when the voice does not reproach life, I assent; yet I do not concede the consequence that psalmody should for this reason be omitted. If you say that the office of the psalms ought to be omitted even because of some persons’ perverse intention, a great absurdity follows you: namely, that prayers, fasts, almsgiving, preaching, and other good works are to be abandoned because all these things are sometimes done with a perverse intention. There is no work so holy that it is not sometimes infected by the aforesaid blemish. [Col. 0861B] Therefore I say—indeed, my God said through a certain luminary of the Romans and of the whole world: “When the voice of psalmody is performed with the intention of the heart, by it a way is then prepared to the heart of almighty God, so that he may pour into the attentive mind either the mysteries of prophecy or the grace of compunction.”

Deceitful Tongue: I do not care about this luminary. But I say that the Apostle of your God told certain persons to sing to the Lord in their hearts.

Love of God: If one is to sing only in the heart, why did he himself exhort us concerning psalms and hymns, and why did the Psalmist so often urge us to sing? Words should certainly sound outwardly in such a way that hearts are beneficially stirred inwardly to compunction, and our attention is held suspended upon the heavenly Jerusalem.

[Col. 0861D] Deceitful Tongue: What profit is there in pronouncing certain words distinctly and slowly in chant and reading?

Love of God: When words are pronounced distinctly, they are understood better and impressed more keenly upon the heart. Look, I pray, at what is read in the Old Testament: the book of the law was read distinctly and intelligibly to the Jewish people. What was therefore done there in the assembly of the Jews ought now to be done in the congregation of monks, so that a sorrowful heart may be soothed by sweet melody, the world’s sorrow that works death may be driven away by the sweetness of psalmody, and the mind may be suffused with spiritual joy, so that the joy of possession may follow the joy of hope.

Deceitful Tongue: This ought to deter everyone who wishes to enter [Col. 0862A] the monastic order: they know that all cenobites are corrupted by grumbling, infected by detractions, and divided by quarrels.

Love of God: Not all, but some among them. Others devote themselves to reading, that they may be instructed; to prayer, that they may be purified; to work, that they may be made blessed. While others infect themselves with grumbling or detraction, these refresh themselves by mutual conversation, stir one another by the Lord’s precepts, inflame one another by the examples of the holy Fathers, and thus, according to Solomon, “iron sharpens iron” (Prov. 27): one person sharpens the countenance of his friend, because by living words they spur one another so that they return more eagerly to reading.

Deceitful Tongue: If anyone considered how great an evil quarrelling is, he would never join himself to the oft-mentioned hypocrites.

[Col. 0862B] Love of God: Tell me how great this evil is.

Deceitful Tongue: I very gladly agree with you in this. Weigh my words. Strife is the beginning of murder, the stirring up of scandals, the disturbance of ecclesiastical custom, and contempt for imitation of the Lord.

Love of God: I now see more carefully that your speech creeps like a cancer and pours deadly poison into the unwary. Tell me, I pray, tell me: how is strife the beginning of murder?

Deceitful Tongue: Because hatreds are stirred up through quarrels. But whoever hates his brother is a murderer (1 John 2), as the Apostle of your God says.

Love of God: How is it the stirring up of scandals?

[Col. 0862C] Deceitful Tongue: Because scandals are often stirred up through strife. Many are scandalized when they seek the fruits of love in those of whom I have often spoken and find the thorns of dissension.

Love of God: The diligent and pure worshippers of my God avoid scandal as far as they can and preserve peace with all people, if possible. Yet they take this rule from my God: among the hard-hearted they sometimes permit scandals to arise. For if scandal is taken from the truth, it is more useful to permit it to arise than to abandon the truth. Now explain to me how strife is a disturbance of ecclesiastical custom.

Deceitful Tongue: Read the Apostle of your God, who says: “If anyone seems to be contentious, we have no such [Col. 0862D] custom, nor does the Church of God” (1 Cor. 11).

Love of God: Tell me finally how it is contempt for imitation of the Lord.

Deceitful Tongue: See whether it is not written in the prophet of your God concerning your God that “he will not contend nor cry out” (Matt. 12). Those, therefore, who tear themselves apart in quarrels are not imitators of your God, but despisers.

Love of God: Not all are infected with this vice; rather, certain cloistered persons are inflamed with the ardour of charity, which my God frequently commends both through himself and through others, and in whose commandments he says that the Law and the Prophets hang. The Apostle of my God says that the distribution of possessions and the burning of the body profit nothing without it. Now, however, I most wish to speak to you about perfect charity. It is also the despiser of temporal life, the bond of a multitude, the covering of guilt, and the mark of heavenly discipleship.

[Col. 0863A] Deceitful Tongue: Tell me how it is the despiser of temporal life.

Love of God: Consider how the Apostle of my God, endowed with charity, says: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1). And my God himself says: “No one has greater charity than that someone should lay down his life for his friends” (John 15).

Deceitful Tongue: Explain how it is the bond of a multitude.

Love of God: Turn the eyes of your mind back to the beginnings of the holy Church, where “the multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul” (Acts 4), and see how [Col. 0863B] the multitude was bound into one, joining itself in a certain sweet and praiseworthy concord.

Deceitful Tongue: How is it a covering of guilt?

Love of God: Because, as it is said, “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (James 5). And elsewhere it is said that charity covers all offences (Prov. 10). I know [Col. 0864A] it to be the wedding garment which most fully wards off from us the cold of unbelief. The man who deserved to be cast into outer darkness lacked that garment.

Deceitful Tongue: How is charity the mark of heavenly discipleship?

Love of God: My God did not tell his disciples that they would be recognized as his disciples by enlightening the blind, cleansing lepers, or raising the dead. Rather, he said: “By this all shall know that you are my disciples: if you have love for one another” (John 13). Charity itself is the bond of perfection, because every work is quickly dissolved by temptation if it is not bound by charity.

Deceitful Tongue: I am weary of your speech.

Love of God: I give thanks to my God that your wiles have been somewhat [Col. 0864B] lulled to sleep. Now you are silent; now you lie defeated, because you are not merely weary of speaking but also ashamed. And:

> [lacuna] Now you will lie defeated,  
> Nor will you dare any longer to scatter deadly flames.  
> Deceitful Tongue falls, overcome by holy Love.  
> Let him praise Christ who rejoices after these battles.

[Col. 0863]

## THE NOTABLE BOOK ON REPENTANCE AND THE TEMPTATIONS OF RELIGIOUS PERSONS, BY AN ANONYMOUS BENEDICTINE WHO WROTE UNDER THE EMPEROR FREDERICK BARBAROSSA

(D. Bern. Pez, *Bibliotheca Ascetica*, vol. II, p. 1, from a manuscript codex of the library of Melk.)

## EDITORIAL NOTICE

I begin this second volume also of the *Ancient-and-Modern Ascetical Library* with an Anonymous author, of whom, apart from his period and his order—which I judge to have been Benedictine, as chapter 25 makes sufficiently clear—almost everything else is obscure and uncertain. Indeed, chapter 32 seems to show that the author deliberately concealed his name, where, against his detractors, he considers it a consolation that they do not know the author’s identity. Perhaps, however, this might be discovered if another little work by the same author survived, which he entitled *Sorrows That Are According to God* and which he himself praises below in chapter 10—unless he also wished his name to be absent from that work, as I strongly suspect from a notable little work, *On Conscience*, which reproduces in every respect the style, method, talent, and period of this Anonymous author, and therefore has scarcely any author other than the same man.

Moreover, it concludes in these words: “Nevertheless, hide the letter—or the book, if you prefer it to be called so; or, if you decide to publish it, keep silent about the author’s name. The Author of salvation knows, to whom alone belong all honour and glory,” etc. Thus it seems that the author generally intended, in the little works he published, to withhold his name either from modesty or in order to avoid envy. This latter-mentioned little work, *On Conscience* [Note: [Col. 0863] It appears below.], which is to be published next, is preserved in the parchment manuscript of the library of Melk designated by me K, no. 32.

That the author of the work here published flourished under Frederick Barbarossa is entirely clear from chapter 59, where there appears his rhythmical poem against monks who, in the holy expedition undertaken by Emperor Frederick to the Holy Land in the year 1189, forgot their vow and duty and, deceived by the spirit of the seducer, prepared, on joining that journey, to fight with weapons like laymen. This little book is found in two paper codices of the library of Melk: the first, designated G, [Col. 0865] no. 171, from which the Reverend Father Gerard Eineder, our most beloved confrere, transcribed it; the other is marked R, no. 30. I saw a third copy in the monastery of Mondsee, but it was written no earlier than the fifteenth century, as were both Melk codices.

This treatise can conveniently be divided into three parts. The first, from the beginning through chapter 25, discusses various questions concerning repentance, according to the opinions and practice of the ancients. The second, from there through chapter 33, confronts diverse temptations of cloistered persons. The last, from the following chapter to the end of the little book, teaches how a person may always be at one with himself and with the Spirit of God. The author, seventy-three years old according to chapter 32, treats all these matters in a concise, pointed, and elegant style.

# TREATISE ON REPENTANCE

[Col. 0865]

[Col. 0865A] The elder sends greetings to his beloved son.

Stesichorus, wavering between praise and blame of Helen, deserved first to lose the eyes with which he blamed her and then to recover them by praising her. But I remain equally blind in your eyes, both by praising and by blaming you. My fortune, therefore, is worse than Stesichorus’s. For you calumniate the praise with which I praised you: you say that it is feigned, not true, because I do not speak from a true heart when I speak those things about you. But if the praise is not true and I do not speak from a true heart, it is either mockery or flattery. He who mocks is mocked. Of the flatterer someone says:

> A flatterer praises, but is not a true lover.

By your judgment I stand under the charge of both faults. If this were true, I would rightly bear the designation of both. But [Col. 0865B] I am conscious of neither; therefore your judgment errs in this respect. Why should I mock, when I have no material for mockery? Why should I flatter you, when I seek from you no other advantage than that I may enjoy you in the Lord?

You say: “I do not wish to be praised too much or blamed.” In neither respect was I excessive. I criticized certain expressions in you which you had used less grammatically—for example, where in the penultimate verse of your poem you put *cubitu* in place of *cubito*. I did this as a friend, not in blame. Quintilian did not wish to be an enemy when he said, “Here correct the blemishes.” Nor did I exceed moderation in praise when I said:

> However grave your voice may be, it is always sweet to me.

[Col. 0865C]

> Your golden tongue makes all things so dear to me.

I said little, nothing hyperbolic; these statements do not exceed credibility. Therefore do not call my praise of you feigned or hyperbolic. Thus I answered your verse. I shall now turn to the prose you appended. And because what I am about to write will be a longer text, you shall regard it not as a letter but as a little book.

## CHAPTER I. Various questions are proposed concerning the fruitful performance of repentance, and the temptations of a wavering religious person.

The Prophet speaks in the person of the Lord: “I attended and listened: no one speaks what is good, nor is there anyone who says, ‘What have I done?’” (Jer. 8). When a person, anticipated by God’s grace, returns to his heart and begins to consider what and how greatly he has sinned, and begins to contend with himself because he has offended God in so many and such great matters, God seeks such contention. For here the salvation of a person begins. He recalls his faults to memory; he considers repentance, conversion, confession, and satisfaction; and he wavers over which of these is especially important or ought to be done. I understand you to be such a person from your letters.

For you say that you are troubled by the thought that God has never allowed you to be put to shame before people for your sins, perhaps having deferred this until the future, when He comes to judge the hidden things of human beings, so that then your sin may be made manifest to angels and people. You ask whether confession is free; whether it is enough to confess only to one priest, provided the sin is not repeated and the assigned penance is completed. [Col. 0866B] You inquire whether, when a sin is repeated, a second repentance is admitted. You also ask how great and what kind repentance ought to be. You complain that your mind is pulled in many directions: now into the abyss of despair, now toward return of heart and a perfect repentance of satisfaction; how you now wish to change your place for the sake of stricter discipline, how you now wish to be enclosed, now to become a hermit. These and some other questions of this sort you raise, concerning which you suffer a great tumult in your heart.

## CHAPTER II. Uncertainty about the future should produce not despair but concern in a person.

I confess that my own mind has also often been disturbed by these matters. And not only by these questions with which we are occupied concerning sins and on account of sins, but even when a person does every good thing that he can do, he does not know whether he is worthy of hatred or love, because all things are reserved as uncertain for the future (Eccl. 9). Job likewise says: “I was afraid of all my works” (Job 9). “These,” you say, “are words—words of despair; but I asked you for words of consolation, so that my mind, instructed concerning each point I proposed, might find some rest.”

Hear, then, briefly the consolation that corrects every despair. “We know,” he says, “that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those saints who are called according to His purpose” (Rom. 8). “And this too,” you say, “is uncertain: who are those saints called according to His purpose?” And I say: Why do you seek to know what belongs to God alone? “The Lord knows those who are His” (Prov. 4). If you wish to be certain, pray, labor, [Col. 0867A] and persevere, that you may be one of those who are His. This foreknowledge of God ought not to make a person secure; for the kingdom of God comes not to the idle, not to the lukewarm, not to the negligent, but to the watchful, the laboring, and the persevering. Therefore all these uncertainties, rightly received, do not produce despair but send a person into fear; fear produces concern; concern, fulfilment of God’s commandments; fulfilment of God’s commandments, hope; and hope breaks despair. Whoever, led by the Holy Spirit, ascends by these steps cannot despair. For “all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. 8). Again: “The Spirit bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER III. That God permits some to be put to shame before people but not others is partly mercy and partly judgment. What shame is useful and necessary for the sinner?

[Col. 0867B]

Having set out these headings, as it were, let us recapitulate everything and say, point by point, what the Lord has given.

You commend God’s great mercy toward you, namely in this: although you have sinned shamefully and greatly, apart from patiently bearing with you while you sinned, He has never allowed you to be put to shame before people for your sins. And shortly afterward you say: “Should I call His patience toward me great, or His wrath? Perhaps it differs from my being put to shame—what I say tremblingly—before angels and people when He comes in His majesty” (Luke 9). And you seek counsel concerning what you should do about this.

Nor do I know better counsel than what you yourself added. You said: “I am greatly afraid; but I shall go before—and have gone before—His face in confession.” Yet why He permits some to be put to shame before people for their sins but not others is partly clear, partly hidden; it is partly mercy and partly judgment. It is mercy when God patiently bears with a sinner for a long time in sins, that he may be converted; and that person, considering this patience, is ashamed within himself and, blushing to be found ungrateful for God’s mercy, returns to God and laments, beyond the sins he committed, this very fact—that he has so long abused God’s patience.

Can there be shame for the sinner unless he is put to shame before people? Thus He willed who said: “What fruit had you then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6). This shame is voluntary and sufficient for God, and it does not need the shame that is before people. Lord Jesus, what do You decide concerning this saying? Is there some teaching concerning it in Your Gospel? That sinner who prayed with the Pharisee in the Temple, standing afar off, would not lift his eyes to heaven but beat his breast. By his position, bodily bearing, and the guilty awareness of his heart he indicated shame: by his position, because he stood afar off; by his bearing, because he would not lift his eyes to heaven; by his conscience, because he beat his breast. He stood afar off because, [Col. 0868A] like another Adam, he feared the Lord’s patience; he would not lift his eyes to heaven because he knew that the God whom he had offended by sinning dwelt in heaven; he beat his breast because the guilty conscience that gnawed at him lay hidden beneath it. Is such shame sufficient before God? Say, Lord Jesus, You who said it then—say now too, I pray: “Amen, I say to you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other” (Luke 18). Therefore such shame is sufficient for God and does not need the shame that is before people.

But if God spares you, do not spare yourself. Tell your confessor; rehearse each of your sins daily to God in your heart; “wash your bed every night” (Ps. 6), that is, lament each of your sins. Put yourself to shame in God’s sight, and you will have taken away from the Lord the reason to put you to shame before people. “The Lord our God is merciful” (Ps. 85). This is the reason why He does not put a sinner to shame before people: through voluntary shame, by which a person is ashamed before God within himself, the person is humbled; being humbled, he is delivered; being delivered, he is saved. This shame is from mercy, and it is plain. This shame makes a person hope, not despair. I want you to be in it, because this shame brings glory.

## CHAPTER IV. God wills some to be put to shame before people so that, with the neck of their hard mind broken, they may return to the way of salvation.

It must also be said why some are put to shame before people for their sins. There are some of such hard mind that they will never cease from sinning unless they are put to shame before [Col. 0868C] people. They are carried along by a certain impulse, until, by God’s merciful permission, they are caught in their perverse courses in something for which they cannot bear reproach and shame from worldly people; and thus they are compelled to turn to God. Hence the prophet says: “Come to Babylon; there you shall be delivered.” For when, on account of their sins, something happens to them by which they cannot retain worldly honor—as with that Corinthian whom Paul handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh after he had been publicly rebuked and put to shame by all, that his spirit might be saved; or if someone has been caught in adultery and castrated, or something else of that kind happens to him or them—such persons, unable to bear worldly shame and reproach, turn to God [Col. 0868D] and are thereby delivered.

There are other shames too, which do not belong to this question: when someone is despised and rejected by the world, whether because he was born with crooked feet or hunchbacked, or has become poor from being rich, or obscure from being noble. Such things indeed sometimes change persons of this kind for the better. But happy is the shame, however it comes about, which is the cause of salvation for a person. Those who use this shame rightly are not to despair. These are the shames of those to be saved, because whether they are ashamed secretly before God or before people, they are ashamed for the salvation of the soul.

## CHAPTER V. The shame of those to be condemned begins here in some and will be completed in the future.

[Col. 0869A]

There is also the shame of those to be condemned, which begins here in some and will remain consummated in the future. “And where,” you ask, “is the saying: ‘God will not judge twice for the same thing’ (1 Cor. 11), if some are punished both here and there?” This was said concerning those who voluntarily punish their sins within themselves, in whom there is no place for God’s second vengeance, according to the Apostle’s saying: “If we judged ourselves, we certainly would not be judged by the Lord.” But some who remain obstinate in sins are punished both here and there, like Antiochus and Herod, who, consumed by worms, ended their present life in great torment, going to that place where “their worm does not die and the fire is not [Col. 0869B] quenched” (Isa. 66). Nor is it a double vengeance but one: begun here, continued there, and eternal; thus in them it is a single vengeance.

Perhaps you ask why a similar punishment, both here and there, is not evident in some others equally destined for condemnation. Clearly, if He deferred punishment in all, He might be thought either not to know sins or to despise them. But why manifest vengeance comes sooner upon one person than another, I exclaim with the Apostle: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, how incomprehensible,” and so forth (Rom. 11).

Of these shames, then, the first humbles, the second purges, the third condemns; the first is sweet, the second grievous, the third terrible. The first is more devout, [Col. 0869C] the second safer, the third more damnable. The first is to be embraced, the second endured, the third fled. Therefore you, man of God, wisely discern what you ought to hold to and what to avoid in these matters. But if you fear to rely on your own prudence, commit yourself to the most merciful and almighty Lord. “He will give you understanding” (2 Tim. 2), and “He will nourish you, and will not allow the righteous to be shaken for ever” (Ps. 54).

## CHAPTER VI. The custom of the ancient monks, who were permitted to confess their sins only to their own abbot, except in a case of extreme necessity.

You ask whether confession is free—that is, whether it is lawful for you or for anyone to confess to whomever he wishes. That it is not lawful, we have in the customs of our order by command: no one, not even the prior of the same cloister, may dare to confess grave sins except when the abbot or superior is absent, and then only at the extremity of his need. “But,” you say, “the privileges of individuals do not make a common law.” To this I answer: you are bound by right to the rule which you have accepted and know. Moreover, what I said was not lawful by custom seems also to be prohibited by the canons. Urban II: “It has been decided that henceforth no priest may receive for penance a person committed to another priest without the consent of the one to whom he first committed himself.”

The following statement of Augustine seems contrary to this: “Whoever wishes to confess sins in order to find grace, let him seek a priest who knows how to bind and loose.” But note that this was said in the question where it is asked [Col. 0870A] whether one may confess even to one’s companion or neighbor, though a layperson, if a priest is absent and cannot be had. Whoever cannot obtain a priest whom he has sought in a case of necessity may confess to his companion or neighbor, even if that person does not possess the power of binding and loosing. Augustine: “So great is the power of confession that, if a priest is lacking, one should confess to one’s neighbor. For it often happens that a penitent cannot make confession before a priest, whom neither time nor place offers him the opportunity to seek; and although the person to whom he confesses has no power of absolution, still the one who confesses his crime to his companion is worthy of pardon because of his desire for a priest. For the lepers were cleansed while going to show their faces, or themselves, to the priests, before they came to them.” Hence it is clear that God looks to the heart when people are prevented by necessity [Col. 0870B] from reaching priests.

“Then,” you say, “is some dispensation to be admitted from the fact that I am forbidden to confess to anyone except the master-priest to whom obedience has bound me, just as in the case where a sought priest cannot be found, yet one may confess to a companion or neighbor? For my master is unlearned and undiscerning; he does not know how to weigh any fault according to its due measure. He is too lenient in greater matters, too severe in lesser ones; he does not know how to impose an appropriate penance; therefore he cannot heal. Perhaps I am constrained by this necessity.”

To this I first answer: attribute it to your sins that you have deserved to have such a master. Nevertheless, what he does too little in your case, fulfil yourself by contrition of heart and a more fervent devotion of satisfaction. [Col. 0870C] Finally, if you wish to free yourself from all these questions, do what I say. First confess to your superior, to whom obedience has bound you, even though he is unlearned and undiscerning. Then it will be free to you to confess the same sins to other priests also; for, as Augustine says, “The more priests to whom one confesses the shamefulness of one’s crime in hope of pardon, the more easily one obtains the grace of remission. For those priests are now more able to help, more able to spare those who confess.”

But take the greatest care not to seek other confessors because of contempt or hatred of your master, except because of his ignorance. For Urban II decrees: “Let no priest [Col. 0870D] receive for penance a person committed to another priest without the consent of the one to whom he first committed himself, except on account of the ignorance of the one to whom he first confessed.” Otherwise, how will you be able to know whether the physician is inadequate? You will also have fulfilled your obedience.

There is another circumstance that makes your confession free: namely, if the priest is full of cracks—that is, if he cannot contain himself and keep silent, but reveals the sins of those confessing to others. Flee him as a kind of plague. Gregory gives this decree concerning him: “Before all things, let a priest beware of recounting to anyone the sins of those who confess to him, neither to relatives nor to strangers. For if he does this, let him be deposed, and let him go dishonorably in pilgrimage all the days of his life.”

I have discharged what I thought concerning the dispensation in this question, without prejudicing a better opinion. [Col. 0871A] But if my judgment errs, follow what is better. In this matter, however, one must take every care that no one invent any of the above allegations concerning his master merely in order to obtain a mobile or wandering confession.

## CHAPTER VII. What confession is and how many kinds there are.

Since we have mentioned confession, it does not seem irrelevant to say what confession is and how it should be made, although you omitted this point in the sequence of your questions.

First note that the word *confessio* has a double meaning. There is confession of praise and confession of sin. Confession of praise occurs here: “His confession is over heaven and earth” (Ps. 148), that is: the praise of God is in heaven and on earth, or above heaven and earth—that is, God’s praise is higher than angels or human beings know or can praise. Confession of sin occurs here: “I said: ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and You forgave the impiety of my sin” (Ps. 31). “I said,” that is, I resolved within myself: I shall confess with the tongue of the heart; and to the priest, a human being, with the tongue of heart and mouth. “Against myself”: I do not excuse myself through the devil, fate, or this or that, but lay the blame upon myself. “My injustice”: because I did not do what I ought to have done, and did what I ought not to have done—which is injustice. For as justice is to render to each what is his, so injustice is to withhold from each what is his. “And You forgave the impiety of my sin,” [Col. 0871C] that is, the guilt of my sin, which God alone first remits without human agency, when He makes the sinner live inwardly in the soul. If such confession is made with a contrite and humbled heart, is persevering, and is voluntary, it has hope of pardon.

There is also another confession, that of despair, as in Judas; and that which the Judge of the world extracts from the accused after they have been condemned by sentence. Of this there is nothing to say for the present matter. True confession of sin, therefore, is when the sinner, in the fear of God and with a repentant heart, confesses the sins he has committed, in heart and mouth, to God and to a human priest for the remission of sins, as the Catholic Church believes.

## CHAPTER VIII. How sins ought to be confessed to a priest according to the opinion of the ancients.

[Col. 0871D]

As to how confession should be made, do not expect me to be your teacher, but blessed Augustine, who, as in all things, so in this matter is our doctor and master. Augustine, in the book *On Repentance*: “Let one who repents repent in every way, and show his grief with tears. Let him present his life to God through the priest; let him forestall God’s judgment by confession. For the Lord commanded those who were to be cleansed to show their faces to the priests, teaching that sins must be confessed by bodily repentance, or made known in writing.”

Again, Augustine, in the book *On Faith to Peter*: [Note: This passage does not occur in the cited book under Augustine’s name; elsewhere it is attributed to St Fulgentius.] “Let him consider the quality of the crime in place, in time, [Col. 0872A] in persistence, in the variety of persons, in the temptation under which he did it, and in the actual execution of the vice. For one who has committed fornication must repent in accordance with the excellence of his rank or office, with the condition of the prostitute, with the manner of his act, and with the way in which he committed the shameful deed: whether in a sacred place, whether at a time set apart for prayer, such as feast days and times of fasting. Let him consider how long he persisted, and bewail that he sinned persistently, how persistently he did so, and how great an assault overcame him. For there are some who not only are not overcome, but freely offer themselves to sin; they do not wait for temptation but anticipate their own desire. And let him examine with himself how manifoldly he sinned pleasurably in committing the vice. All this variety must be confessed and bewailed, so that, when he has recognized what the sin was, [Col. 0872B] he may quickly find God gracious. In recognizing the increase of the sin, let him observe at what age he was, of what wisdom and rank. Let him dwell on every one of these points and perceive the measure of the crime, cleansing every quality of the vice. Let him bewail the virtue of which he was meanwhile deprived. For one must grieve not only because he sinned, but because he deprived himself of virtue. Thus confession must be made.”

You are troubled and anxious; perhaps you say that making such confession is impossible and improper: first because “who understands his offences?” (Ps. 18); then because it is shameful to state certain sins as nakedly as they were committed. Your confessor himself is scandalized by hearing such things. Do, then, what I say. Confess the sins you understand; for those you do not understand, let your will stand in place of ability. What is so shameful—what is altogether shameful—you can make known by circumlocution. You did not blush before God to do it in that way, and yet you blush to confess before a human being that you did it? If you keep silent now, the time will come when you will be laid bare before all. “It is fearful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10).

“Why,” you ask, “must I confess in this way?” Listen. No sin will be unpunished. If no sin will be unpunished, every sin is known. But it is known either by the person or by God. What a person knows in himself, let the person punish in himself. What God knows in a person and the person does not know in himself, let him have the will to confess it if he knew it; and let him patiently bear the wrath of the Lord, saying with Job: “I will bear the wrath of the Lord” (Mic. 7), because I deserved it, even if [Col. 0872D] the person himself does not understand his sin; for God will not judge twice for the same thing. Job testifies that none of our sins escapes God’s knowledge: “You have observed all my paths,” he says, “and considered the tracks of my feet” (Job 13). And the Lord Himself says through the prophet: “I will search Jerusalem with lamps” (Zeph. 1).

Therefore confess what you did, as you did it, when you did it, how much you did, where you did it, who you were when you did it, and what and what kind of person was the one with whom you did it; or, if what you did is impersonal, confess that. Confess all these things—how often and how pleasurably, and at what age you were—if you wish to be secure. For, as I said above, [Col. 0873A] “it is fearful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10).

## CHAPTER IX. A sin confessed to one priest may be confessed to several, though this is not necessary unless it is repeated.

You ask whether it is enough to confess once and to one priest only, provided the sin is not repeated and the assigned penance is completed. If the sin is not repeated and the assigned penance is completed, in my judgment it is enough to confess once and to one priest only. Hence John Chrysostom: “It is not necessary that what we have confessed once to a priest should be confessed again, but we ought continually to confess it before the true Judge with the tongue of the heart, not of the flesh.” But if your fault troubles you and you wish to become more certain of pardon, confess to whomever you wish, so that you may blush before each; because as many blushings as you undergo, so many remissions you receive. John Chrysostom: “For this reason we are commanded to confess sins: that we may suffer shame as punishment. For this itself is part of the divine judgment.” Augustine: “He has offered much satisfaction who, overcoming shame, has denied none of the things he committed to God’s messenger. For the mind labors in suffering shame; and because shame is a great punishment, one who is ashamed for Christ becomes worthy of mercy.” Hence it is clear that the more persons to whom someone confesses the shamefulness of his crime in hope of pardon, the more easily he obtains the grace of remission.

Although, therefore, in your first confession your sin has been erased and you are not compelled to confess the same [Col. 0873C] sin a second time to anyone unless it is repeated, nevertheless, if you wish, you may confess through several persons, because shame is a kind of punishment for sin, just as satisfaction by works is; and thereby you will be humbler and more cautious. It is enough, then, to confess a sin once and to one priest only if it is not repeated; to confess through several is indeed permitted, but judge for yourself whether it is expedient. “All things are lawful for Paul, but not all things are expedient.”

## CHAPTER X. As often as we fall into sins, hope of pardon is always available to those who rise again.

Finally, you ask: when a sin is repeated, is a second repentance admitted? In the little book *On Sorrows* [Note: [Col. 0873] The author’s little work *On Sorrows Which Are According to God*.], I said concerning the sorrows that are according to God what could have sufficed you, if you had committed it to memory. [Col. 0873D] But, as I see, I wrote upon ice in you, or sent it into a perforated sack (Hag. 1). A clean animal ought not only to divide the hoof but also to chew the cud. Observe and compare God’s words in your heart, so that you may have an answer concerning the faith and hope that are in us for everyone who asks you. Receive and believe, then, once for all, and confess that where there is repentance, there is also pardon. Repentance comes to the sinful person from God; pardon too comes from Him. Therefore, as often as God gives repentance to a person, so often He also gives pardon. Thus there is a second, third, and subsequent repentance.

If repentance is true, we are plainly taught, by the authority of the prophets, the Law and the Gospel, and the clear testimonies of the holy Fathers, that it may be performed not only once but often, and that through repentance after a fall [Col. 0874A] we may rise again a second, a third, and thereafter.

## CHAPTER XI. The same point is confirmed by examples from the Israelite people.

How often the children of Israel sinned in the wilderness, and, after entering the promised land, how often and in how many ways they sinned, and how often God received their repentance—no one who has read the history of the Old Testament is ignorant of this. David bears witness to the matter: “In all these things,” he says, “they still sinned. And when He slew them, they sought Him and returned. And they loved Him with their mouth, and lied to Him with their tongue. But He is merciful and will be propitious to their sins” (Ps. 77).

“What,” you ask, “does their false repentance have to do with the matter? The question concerns true repentance.” I answer: just as some among them repented falsely, so too there were some among them who repented truly. You say: “I read the former; I do not read the latter.” Listen: neither do I read of Moses’ or Aaron’s repentance—Moses’ because he despaired of bringing water from the rock; Aaron’s because he made the golden calf. Yet that both truly repented is established from this, that they were saved. Thus there were some among them who, seeing God’s wrath, truly repented; and as often as they repented, they obtained pardon, although this is not written. Hence Moses lifted up the bronze serpent in the wilderness, so that those who had been struck might be healed by looking upon it. Therefore, if God spared some so often because of false repentance and delivered those who repented of evil, much more did He receive and save, again and again—that is, many times—those truly repenting of their sins.

Lest an example be lacking: what does David say, who, after the sin involving Uriah, sinned a second time when he ordered the people to be numbered, repented, and God received his second repentance? For when he saw the angel striking the people, he said: “I am the one who sinned; I am the one who acted wickedly. What have these sheep done?” (2 Sam. 24). Because this repentance was from the heart, the angel immediately ceased from slaughtering the people. What I say about David, David himself shows in the psalm that is one of the seven called penitential: that there is a second, [Col. 0874D] third, and subsequent repentance. “My scars,” he says, “have become rotten and corrupt” (Ps. 37).

The hardened skin left from a healed wound is called a scar. A healed wound is a sin corrected through repentance. Corrupted scars are sins committed anew. And what must be done about them? In the same psalm he teaches this: “For I will declare my iniquity, and I will think upon my sin” (ibid.). In what hope? “Attend to help me, O Lord God of my salvation” (ibid.). The God whom he calls the God of his salvation is the one from whom he expects pardon of sins.

Therefore, as often as anyone sins and truly repents, [Col. 0875A] so often he will have pardon of sins. “Until when?” you ask. “In whatever place a tree falls, whether toward the south or toward the north, there it shall be.” After this, no repentance will be fruitful.

You say further: “The matter under discussion is, according to some, doubtful. But a doubtful matter can be confirmed neither by a forced interpretation of Scripture nor proved by one witness.” To this I answer: in interpreting Holy Scripture, if anyone, as blessed Gregory says, seeks the power in the Lord’s words and understands them differently from the person through whom they were uttered, yet under that other understanding seeks the edification of charity, the words he relates are the Lord’s words. For God speaks to us throughout all Holy Scripture only in order to draw us to love of Himself and of our neighbor. My interpretation, therefore, is not forced, because I interpret for the consolation of sinners, lest they despair; nor do I depart either from the words or from the meanings of the truth set forth.

## CHAPTER XII. The teaching of the prophets likewise concerning the sinner’s relapse and repeated repentance.

What do you mean, that nothing can lawfully be proved by one witness? It is true, because, as someone says, “the testimony of one is as if of none.” Let another witness, therefore, proceed together with David in the same matter. Jeremiah says (ch. 2): “How base you have become, repeating your ways! Nevertheless, return to me, says the Lord.” A person’s ways are that person’s good or evil works. By good works a person walks toward life; by evil works, toward death. But a person [Col. 0875C] repeats his ways when a sinner sins again and again. He therefore becomes base, because what comes later is always worse than what came before; because he continually becomes worse than himself. Join what follows—“Nevertheless, return to me, says the Lord”—to each repetition; for as often as a person sins, if he returns to God, so often is his repentance received by God.

All the prophets unanimously thought this, wrote it, and left it written for us, “that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope.” Thus all the prophets up to John the Baptist, whether they wrote or preached, intended this: that human beings might turn to God and be healed through repentance. From the days of John the Baptist also, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent—that is, those who repent perfectly—seize it, when through mercy they are given what is not owed through justice. Are these things from the Old Testament sufficient for you? Or do you still wish to hear something from the New—namely, whether second, third, and subsequent repentance is granted to sinners who truly repent? Let us first ask Him whose words admit no doubt.

## CHAPTER XIII. The assertions are confirmed by the teaching of Christ Himself and of the holy Fathers.

Publicly, Lord Jesus Christ—You who did not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance (Mark 2)—most mighty, most wise, most gracious Lord, give a plain and decisive judgment that may remove every question, exclude error, and produce consolation. “I do not say to you,” He says, “Peter, seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (Matt. 18). A faithful saying and worthy of all acceptance: a saying of clemency, a saying of pardon, a saying consecrated by the number of the Holy Spirit; a stream from the eternal fountain, whose vein is mercy, which is above all the Lord’s works, always flowing and never failing. Say, Lord Jesus, say again, I pray, the same saying, by uttering which You will give joy and gladness to my hearing. For if David, naked and with all his strength, danced before the ark of the Lord because he foresaw Him who was to come, who both preached repentance and gave pardon; if likewise, after [Col. 0876B] the sin against Uriah, he prayed that through repentance the joy of the Lord’s salvation might be restored to him; if, I say, he acted thus and thus in hope, how much more should I in the reality? Therefore say again, Lord, the saying: “I do not say to you, Peter, up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven.” O good saying beyond the best gift! This saying is the joy of God, the joy of angels, and also the joy of human beings. It is God’s joy because God the Father rejoices and keeps feast for His Son whom He has received back. It is the joy of angels, because “there is joy among the angels of God over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15). It is the joy of human beings because of the certain pardon of sins.

Where are those now who separate themselves from this joy? Where are those now who deny that there will be a second, third, and subsequent repentance? Where are those now who wish the fountain of mercy to be stopped up for themselves, but not for me? For there are some who presume upon their innocence and righteousness, and therefore think that they have no need either of a physician or of repentance, led by these authorities: “Those who are healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are ill” (Matt. 9). Again: “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Mark 8). Others, however, weighed down and terrified by the number, measure, and weight of their sins, lose confidence concerning second, third, and subsequent repentance. This saying corrects both groups. This judgment of the Lord, spoken to Peter, corrects the righteous, lest they think repentance unnecessary to themselves when they cannot avoid sin; [Col. 0876D] and sinners, lest they doubt, despair, and perish concerning a second, third, and subsequent repentance.

But those who do not admit a second, third, and subsequent repentance say that this saying to Peter must be understood not of grave sins but of light ones. They say that because light sins are unavoidable, there can be a second, third, and subsequent repentance for them; but grave sins, because they ought and can altogether be avoided, have no place for a second repentance. Yet, as it seems to me [Note: [Col. 0875D] The manuscript reads: *ut inde vid.* (“as it seems from this”).], because the Lord stated this without limitation, it must be understood of grave as well as light sins. For He first set forth a certain judicial order, which pertains more to the handling of grave sins than of light ones. For He said: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone. If he does not listen to you, take with you one or three. If he does not listen to them, tell the Church. If he does not listen to the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a publican” (Matt. 18). And lest He should think this to be disregarded, excommunication follows: “Amen,” He says, “I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven” (ibid.). Behold rebuke; behold admonition; behold witnesses; behold the Church as judge; behold excommunication! And if all the rest were to be observed even in light sins, is anyone excommunicated for light sins? Therefore, by this authority, second, third, and subsequent repentance for both grave and light sins is fruitful, provided only that it is true.

[Col. 0877B] The holy Fathers agree on this point as well. Augustine, to Macedonius: “Although it has been cautiously and beneficially provided that the place of that most humble penitence be granted only once in the Church, lest a remedy made cheap become less useful to the sick—though it is the more health-giving the less contemptible it is—who nevertheless would dare say to God: Why do you still, once more, spare this man, who after his first penitence again binds himself in the snares of iniquity?” Again, to Macedonius: “Human wickedness sometimes advances so far that, even after penitence has been performed and reconciliation to the altar obtained, people commit like or more serious sins. Yet God makes his sun rise even upon such persons, and grants them no fewer than the abundant [Col. 0877C] gifts of life and health that he granted before. And although that place of penitence is not granted them in the Church, God nevertheless does not forget his patience toward them.”

Likewise John Chrysostom, *On the Restoration of the Fallen*: “Such, believe me, such is God’s mercy toward human beings: he never despises a person’s penitence if it is offered to him sincerely and simply. Even if someone has reached the height of evils, and from there wishes only to return to the path of virtue, he gladly receives and embraces him, doing everything possible to restore him to his former state.”

Likewise John Chrysostom on the Apostle’s passage: “For if we sin willingly, there remains no sacrifice for sin” (Heb. 10). “It should be known,” he says, “that some seize upon these words as an occasion for taking away penitence, as though by penitence [Col. 0877D] a sinner could not rise again after a fall, a second, third, and further time. But even here he does not exclude penitence, nor propitiation, which often occurs through penitence, but a second baptism and sacrifice.”

## CHAPTER XIV. Statements of the Fathers which appear opposed to the doctrine given are explained.

I have collected certain statements which seem contrary to this assertion, as many as I could have at hand. And lest they generate error among the simpler people, I have added their explanation.

The Apostle to the Hebrews says: “If we sin willingly, there remains no sacrifice for sin” (Heb. 10)—that is, no sacrifice by which Christ might suffer again, since Christ had to suffer once in order to exhaust the sins of many. Nor does a second baptism remain, since no one is rebaptized after the first [Col. 0878A] baptism; yet there are other means which may be repeated.

John Chrysostom likewise says on the same passage: “It should be known that some seize upon these words as an occasion for taking away penitence, as though by penitence a sinner could not rise again after a fall, a second, third, and further time. Thus even here he does not exclude penitence, nor propitiation, which often occurs through penitence, but a second baptism and sacrifice.”

Ambrose: “There are those who think that penitence ought to be performed repeatedly, who indulge themselves in Christ. For if they truly performed penitence in Christ, they would not think it should afterwards be repeated; because, as there is one baptism, so there is one penitence.” He says this not according to the [Col. 0878B] general practice, but according to the special custom of the Church concerning solemn penitence, which, having been celebrated once among some communities, is not repeated.

Likewise Ambrose’s statement: “Penitence undertaken once, but not truly carried out, both takes away the fruit of the former and loses the use of the subsequent,” is to be understood of solemn penitence. Solemn penitence, as Ambrose himself says, is that which is performed publicly outside the church, in ashes and haircloth, and which is imposed only for the more serious, dreadful, and public offences. And it is not to be repeated, out of reverence for the sacrament, lest it become cheap and contemptible to people.

Origen on Leviticus: “In more serious crimes, opportunity for penitence is granted only once.” He too says this concerning solemn penitence, which in earlier [Col. 0878C] times was imposed only once for more serious crimes. But in the present time, in all the churches known to us, if those more serious offences are repeated, penitence itself is also repeated, as may be seen in murderers, adulterers, and perjurers.

Likewise, the statement found written elsewhere, “There is no place for a second penitence,” is either to be understood of the aforesaid solemn penitence, or understood thus: that a person has an opportunity for repentance only in this present life. When this life is ended, a second penitence will have no place, because it will not be fruitful. For then too the wicked will have penitence, but an unfruitful penitence; for it will have punishment only, and no forgiveness.

[Col. 0878D] I think it is now sufficiently clear from these considerations that there is a second, third, and subsequent penitence. But if there are any who do not concede this and argue contentious objections, let them consider what absurdity follows. For if penitence is granted only once and a person cannot obtain the fruit of any subsequent penitence when he has fallen again, then that first and only penitence must be deferred until the end of his life, while meanwhile he may sin as much and in whatever way he pleases. This is a great absurdity; and Scripture commands the contrary: “Do not delay from day to day to turn to the Lord” (Ecclus. 5).

There is another absurdity. If there is no hope of subsequent penitence when, after that first and only penitence, a person has again fallen into grave sins, then he will perish in despair. Yet this too is a great absurdity, since Scripture offers the contrary consolation: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (Rom. 10). It does not say “at one hour,” but “at whatever hour”; otherwise the power of the Holy Spirit would be found less, if he could forgive sins only once and not always. Let those who deny this therefore beware lest they fall into that unforgivable blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XV. Those who deny that repeated penitence benefits the fallen themselves shut off the way of salvation.

Holy Lord Spirit, look upon me and hear me graciously. I do not wish to belong to the company of those who detract from your power, who shut against themselves the entrance to forgiveness if they should fall again after their first penitence. I know, Lord, that it is within your power to have mercy when, how often, and upon whom you will. “I will exult, Lord, and rejoice in your mercy” (Ps. 30). My iniquity is great, but I rely upon your great mercy. As often as you give me a contrite and humbled heart (Ps. 50), so often you will give penitence also; for this itself is penitence. Therefore there is not only one penitence: as often as you visit the hearts of sinners, so often there will be penitence in them. It is necessary for me, Lord, to confess your mercy and power, because I have often fallen into grave sin. I neither wished nor was able to stand, because human life is prone to evil from youth onward; for that reason it needs repeated penitence.

Before the throne John saw a sea of glass, [Col. 0879C] which is the life of the baptized: fragile and slippery toward falling.

> Lord, you know well  
> human falling;  
> frail is our substance;  
> we live amid misery.

Whoever sang this invoked your mercy upon himself, because he believed that you could have mercy whenever you wished. “I believed, therefore I spoke”; and I truly believe that the Church indeed believes this also. Therefore, you who contend so as to bar the entrance of salvation against yourselves, believe with us that the gift of the Holy Spirit is not bound by law. But those who refuse to believe this are either despairing, or seek an opportunity to sin freely [Col. 0879D].

## CHAPTER XVI. What sort of penitence, and how great, ought it to be?

Your sadness would have been briefer if you were not another Thomas. As he was, so are you: unless you have seen and touched—that is, unless you have examined everything—you do not rest. For among other questions, you have asked this also: what sort of penitence, and how great, ought it to be?

On this matter we all have John the Baptist as teacher: “Produce fruits worthy of penitence” (Luke 3). Observe what he said: not every worthy fruit is a fruit worthy of penitence. Augustine says: “Let the soul seek worthy fruits, even if they are not worthy of penitence.” For there are worthy fruits of virtues which do not suffice for penitents. Penitence demands weightier things, so that one dead through grief and groaning may obtain life. Do not deceive yourself, then; do not flatter yourself; [Col. 0880A] do not indulge yourself. For not all worthy fruits are fruits worthy of penitence. Yet this is to be understood of penitence for the greater crimes. What suffices for those who sin less seriously or only slightly does not suffice for serious offenders.

There is also a saying of the blessed Pope Gregory, whose teaching is golden. “In order,” he says, “to speak in terms of fruits worthy of penitence, it is right that one who has committed unlawful acts should abstain even from lawful ones; and one who has committed no unlawful act should make use also of lawful things.” What does he say? Namely, that one who has committed unlawful acts—such as murder, adultery, theft, sacrilege, perjury, and other grave crimes of that kind—should not eat flesh, drink wine, wear soft clothing, or consume richer foods; finally, he should leave the world, if neither wife nor something similar prevents it; he should set another person over his own head, bear tribulations on his back, relinquish ownership of possessions, and not do his own will. Let him do all these things with counsel, lest he presume anything more or less, according to that saying of the Wise Man: “Nothing in excess.”

## CHAPTER XVII. What is the form of penitence for lighter sins?

This is the rule for penitents who wish to be secure concerning their penitence. But one who has committed no unlawful act may use lawful things, yet use this world as though not using it; have a wife as though not having one; rejoice as though not rejoicing; buy as though not possessing (1 Cor. 7), and other things [Col. 0880C] in this manner. Why? Because there are certain light sins which, though small, nevertheless creep frequently upon human frailty. If they are neglected and accumulated against us, they will burden and overwhelm us just as one great sin would do. What difference does it make for shipwreck whether a ship is covered and overwhelmed by one great wave, or whether water gradually entering the bilge fills and sinks the ship through the fault of the negligent?

Therefore, even for such deeds, though lighter, some penitence ought to be performed: namely, the Lord’s Prayer, fasting, almsgiving to the poor, and especially the saving sacrificial offering of the altar.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The penitent must grieve not only over sins committed, but also over good deeds omitted.

[Col. 0880D] There is another manner of penitence, which the Apostle teaches: “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. As you presented your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification” (Rom. 6). This manner is one of recompense; the former was one of satisfaction. It is recompense because the sinner must grieve and weep not only for what he has sinned, but also because he did not do the good that he ought to have done.

Augustine, in *On Faith to Peter*: “Let the sinner consider what age, what wisdom, and what rank he had when he sinned. Let him dwell upon each of these things and perceive the measure of the crime, purifying every quality of the crime with tears; let him lament the virtue of which he was meanwhile deprived.” For one must grieve not [Col. 0881A] only because one sinned, but also because one deprived oneself of virtue. This too therefore belongs to a fruit worthy of penitence: that one should match the number of virtues to the number of vices.

## CHAPTER XIX. David as an example of a true penitent. Various ways of lamenting sins, etc.

If this teaching does not suffice for you concerning what sort of penitence and how great it should be, and if you still inquire, take, read, and understand the Psalter. See what rule of penitence that great sinner, that great penitent, David, dictated and taught in the Spirit, and what example he gave in his deeds. For he set before sinners a complete, full, and perfect rule of penitence not so much in writing as by example. What he taught in writing in the Psalter, he fulfilled in deeds in the history [Col. 0881B] of the Book of Kings, as is written.

What then did he teach in the Psalter? Namely, how a sinner ought to turn: “I was turned in my affliction, while the thorn is driven in” (Ps. 31). How one ought to confess: “I said, I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord” (ibid.). How one ought to lament individual sins: “Every night I will wash my bed” (Ps. 6), that is, for each of my sins. For sin is night, because it blinds the soul so that it cannot see God.

Concerning fasting he says: “I will humble my soul with fasting” (Ps. 34). And how do I fast? “I ate ashes as bread, and mingled my drink with weeping” (Ps. 101). Concerning harsh clothing [Col. 0881C] he says: “When they troubled me, I clothed myself in haircloth” (Ps. 34). Concerning leaving the world: “Behold, I fled far away and remained in solitude” (Ps. 54). Concerning bearing discipline: “You placed tribulations upon our back” (Ps. 65).
