Concerning rendering obedience: “You set men over our heads” (ibid.). Concerning patience in persecutions: “I became like one who does not hear and has no rebukes in his mouth” (Ps. 37).

When all these things have been done, that they may have a saving effect and be precious before God, the Prophet adds what is still especially necessary, and, turning to God, says: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite [Col. 0881D] and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 50). For just as, according to Paul, neither faith, almsgiving, nor martyrdom benefits anyone without charity, so neither can those bodily exercises suffice without a contrite and humbled heart. He addresses this saying to God because God alone sees the heart, and God alone knows human thoughts. “There is one who wickedly humbles himself, while his inward parts are full of deceit” (Ecclus. 19). God alone, therefore, can discern this.

And when someone has fulfilled all these things, even with contrition and humility of heart, he ought not to rely on merits but to hope in God’s mercy. Thus the Psalmist says: “But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord, have hoped in the mercy of God for ever [Col. 0882A] and unto the age of ages” (Ps. 51). But why do I gather these ears of grain with such effort, when the whole harvest of the Psalter itself, insofar as it concerns penitents, has this very purpose?

You say: “These things are great, these things are difficult, these things are impossible.” Brother, a great illness requires strong medicine. One who has spread himself abroad in wickedness must be abundant in satisfaction. The Lord Jesus also signified this in raising Lazarus (John 11). See how much Jesus did. Lazarus’s sisters sent for and called Jesus. Jesus came; he saw Lazarus’s sisters weeping and the Jews mourning; and Jesus wept. Jesus came to the tomb; Jesus ordered the stone removed; Lazarus, already four days dead, stank; Jesus weeps, Jesus groans, and Jesus groans again; he looks up to heaven [Col. 0882B] and prays that Lazarus may come out; Jesus cries out, commands him to be untied and go away, and at last Jesus made him his guest. Jesus did these and other things in that raising, not because of any inability in himself, but to signify the greater labor required of penitents.

Now you say: “Since you have proclaimed magnificently what sort of penitence and how great it ought to be, and nowhere allowed moderate penitence, I should like to know to what manner of penitence you have conformed yourself, so that I may hope for pardon through your example. For by your writing, revealing, and accusing yourself, I have learned that you are one of the great sinners.” Listen: I did not wish to say less, though I do less. It is easier to speak than to act. It is better to act than to speak; best of all is to speak and act. But because you wish to have me as an example [Col. 0882C] in penitence, do what I say.

“Son of man, enter the house and dig through the wall, and see the abominations which they have done here; dig through the wall, and dig again, and dig a third time,” as was commanded to the prophet (Jer. 8). Dig through the wall of thoughts, the wall of words, and the wall of actions; and see whatever you have sinned in each of these. When you recognize that you have sinned grievously in each of them, receive upon yourself the T, which is the sign of those who groan and mourn. T is the figure of the cross; the cross is suffering. Therefore imitate Christ’s suffering, and fulfill in your flesh what is lacking of Christ’s suffering. Then, when the man clothed in linen, with an inkhorn upon his back, sees the T upon you, he will pass by and will not strike [Col. 0882D] you.

Take the tenor of the proposed chapter in this concise sense: if you see your iniquities, abandon them, and receive the sign upon yourself—that is, if you possess the bitterness of true penitence after the likeness of Christ’s suffering—the striking angel will not harm you; that is, God’s vengeance will not come upon you.

Enter also the forest of your sins to cut it down, dig it up, and root it out. This forest consists of thorns and thistles, which the first man received in the curse of his ground because of transgressing the commandment. “When you cultivate the ground, it shall not give its fruits, but shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3). A person’s ground is his flesh. He cultivates the ground who nourishes and cherishes his flesh in pleasures and [Col. 0883A] desires. A thorn is coarser and wounds openly. A thistle has a subtle point, pricks more secretly, and is removed with greater difficulty.

Thorns, therefore, are manifest sins which, according to the Apostle, are committed outside the body: murder, theft, perjury, and similar acts. A thistle is a sin concealed within the flesh, when, according to the Apostle, someone sins against his own body, as one who commits fornication of any kind. This thistle is difficult to uproot because, according to the Lord’s saying, “This kind of demon can come out only through prayer and fasting” (Mark 9). Therefore, whether your sins are thorns or thistles, cut them down by abandoning them, dig them up by confessing them, and root them out by concealing nothing.

You say: “My sins are so many, so great, so shameful [Col. 0883B] that I am ashamed to confess them.” That shame, brother, is a great part of penitence. If you master it by confessing everything, you will also merit the Lord’s mercy more quickly. And when you have done these things, you will not immediately be secure. Let your sins always be before you. Reflect upon your sins. Weep for each of your sins, as the Prophet says: “Streams of waters flowed from my eyes because they did not keep your law” (Ps. 118).

You say: “I cannot have tears.” Seek them from God, because they are God’s gift. “You will give us drink in tears by measure” (Ps. 79). If you cannot have tears, offer a contrite and humbled heart, which God does not despise. Choose for yourself patrons among God’s saints, who are fit and sufficient for this, and appoint individual saints for your individual sins, so that what you cannot obtain by your own merit, you may obtain through their intercession.

Pray always. Be like a solitary sparrow on the roof (Ps. 101) by day; be a cicada singing by night. Imitate the Prophet who says: “O Lord God of my salvation, I cried out before you by day and by night” (Ps. 87). Love vigils; multiply acts of prostration; strike your breast with your fists; seek solitude at suitable hours; send forth roaring with groaning: “I roared from the groaning of my heart” (Ps. 37). Lie in a sack; let a coarser tunic serve you as haircloth; do not allow yourself prolonged rest in bed, nor let warmth relax your limbs. Long rest in bed and limbs relaxed by warmth nourish the worms of vices.

[Col. 0883D] May the devil never find you idle. Let prayer be continually in your mouth, holy meditation in your heart, or divine reading in your hands. These and other things belong to more perfect penitence, through which “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence” (Matt. 11). Let these things suffice for you, brother. Why should I tell you of my corners and of the soliloquies of my thoughts accusing or even defending one another? Why should I tell you this or that secret of mine? “My secret is mine; my secret is mine” (John 24).

You now say, then: “Alas, alas, brother! What shall I do? For I am too small and insufficient for all these things. I thought that both aspects of your manner of penitence had been easier. But, as I see, you do nothing less than the more perfect practices, if you carry out what you say.” Hear what the Prophet [Col. 0884A] says, and say it yourself: “Your eyes saw my imperfection” (Ps. 138). And what shall I do? Hear the Lord: “What king, going to engage another king in battle, does not first sit down and calculate whether he can meet, with ten thousand, the one who comes against him with twenty thousand? Otherwise, while he is still far away, he sends an embassy and asks for terms of peace” (Luke 14).

Merciful Lord Jesus, whom shall we send, or who will be our envoy against this king, who comes with his double against our single? Are you that king, and yet our envoy? Surely, Lord: according to your divinity you are that king; according to your humanity you are our envoy, by which you intercede for us not only with the Father, but also with yourself, who are one with the Father. You come with your double against our single, because you come to judge not only our works but also our words and thoughts. Who, then, can be saved without you? You came in three ways to save us: by teaching, example, and prayer. By teaching, that you might instruct the ignorant; by example, that you might stir the hardened; by prayer, that you might strengthen the failing.

That you taught is clear, because you taught either in the temple, or in the synagogues of the Jews, or on a mountain, or in open country—now your disciples, now the Jews, now the crowds. To what end? “I have spoken these things,” you say, “that you may be saved” (John 5). Your example is equally evident. For you said: “I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, so you also may do” [Col. 0884C] (John 13). Again: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble” (Matt. 11). Why? “And you shall find rest for your souls” (ibid.). Concerning prayer too you said: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22). Again: “I pray not for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word” (John 17).

But we despise your teaching and turn aside from your examples. What remains, then, except your prayer alone, by which we may be saved? Therefore, merciful Jesus, save by your prayer those whom you can help less by teaching and less by example.

I have answered your questions as I could, not as I wished. It was, and is, more than enough for you, since you know everything. Yet I believe that, among so great a multitude of the human race, there will be some who, if they come upon [Col. 0884D] this sheet, will draw some instruction from it. For not all are great; there are also middling people and humble people. Of the remaining parts of your letter, because they are private to you, I shall make another beginning of my discourse.

## CHAPTER XX. What it is to come into the depth of evils, and what despair is and how many kinds there are.

You are angry because I answer you slowly. I have no delays except whatever I can steal from my appointed sleep. I have no delays except whatever time remains to me after common and private prayers—and that is very little. Add to this that my intellect is now slow and my hands tremble, because I am decrepit. I have never been able to have scribes; I could not have them without payment, and I had no money. Another reason was [Col. 0885A] that my writings are judged superfluous—indeed, worthless. Leaving these things aside, I shall turn to discussing yours.

But so that mine may be better understood, I have set before them your own words, by which you depicted yourself, using the very wording of your letter. They are as follows:

“You said: ‘When I was in sins and had come into the depth of evils, despising and even despairing, I often thought of apostatizing and following wherever pleasure might draw me. But now that, by God’s grace, the passions of my flesh have been lulled, having somewhat returned to myself, I intend to undertake perfect penitence, namely, to move from the place in which I sinned to another way of life, stricter or even more disciplined. For nearly all our discipline has perished. I desire, for Christ’s sake, either to go on pilgrimage, be enclosed, or even become a hermit. I would do one of these things were I not held back by my vow and obedience, and because I seem necessary to the Church that nourished me, whether for life or death I do not know; God knows. Amid these uncertainties, I do not know what I ought chiefly to choose. I often think of freeing myself from all the affairs of cloister and world, but make no progress.’ Thus far your words.”

First, I can say to you what the poet says:

> “With what knot shall I hold Proteus as he changes his forms?”  
> (Horace, *Epistles* 1.1.90)

For since you change yourself into so many forms of will, should I not rightly call you, in a way, Proteus, who was changed now into a man, now a woman, now tall, now short, now an old man, now a boy?

You say, “When I had come into the depth of evils.” I shall explain what the depth of evils is and how one comes into it—not to teach you, but the simple. I do not teach in order to teach, but teach in order to be taught. I do not teach that evil should be done, but teach so that it may not be done. The depth of evils is a multitude of greater crimes, into which no one comes suddenly. For just as no one suddenly becomes best, so no one suddenly becomes worst.

When someone has gone into the counsel of the ungodly and has first committed some sin, he is distressed by some penitence, still considering the fear of God. But when that fear has been consumed, and he sees that he has sinned with impunity because God did not choose to punish that sin at once, delight in repeating it or committing another follows—like Herodias’s daughter, who danced in the midst and, by her mother’s counsel, took away John’s head. Herodias’s daughter is the sweet delight of sin, which dances in the midst when delight repeatedly tickles the human heart toward sinning. By her mother’s counsel—that is, by the counsel of sin—she seeks John’s head, when the sin committed takes Christ, who is our head, away from a person; through this the person is joined to the devil, just as Herodias was unlawfully joined to Herod.

Therefore, when one sin is added to another—because one cannot cease or remain in a single vice, according to the saying, “Let the one who is filthy become filthier still” (Rev. 22)—when, I say, he falls from sin into sin and God instantly punishes none of them, he begins to run without turning back [Col. 0886A] through the gates of death (for as many sins as there are, so many are the gates of death) and hastens into the depth of evils. And when he has gradually put away the fear of God, he begins to despise; because, rendered falsely secure by impunity, no sorrow, not even the final sorrow, now touches his heart. Thus he is held fast, blinded by habit.

From this despair arises. But what despair? Consider.

There are three kinds of despair. One is that by which a person is deterred by the difficulty of penitence, because he despairs of being sufficient to complete penitence and delays conversion. This is remissible, provided he does not remain in it. There is another, by which a person despairs not that sins will be forgiven if he repents, but that God takes any care over his penitence. This is remissible, because humility excuses it: it fears lest it presume. Indeed, a great many of us suffer from this. For when someone has done the good he can, he does not know whether he is worthy of hatred or love; “all things are reserved as uncertain for the future” (Ecclus. 9). Despairing in this way, we do not despair: we fear justice, but rely upon mercy.

There is a third, dreadful despair: namely, the unforgivable blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. This occurs when a sinner does not believe that the Holy Spirit can grant him forgiveness because of the magnitude of his crimes and, obstinate in this, despises God because he does not care what he does. Then Behemoth tightens his tail in that person’s heart like a blacksmith’s anvil; this knot will remain eternally insoluble. This sinner is the fourth dead person, reported indeed to the Lord but not raised by the Lord. He is, I say, the person of whom the prophet says: “For three crimes and for four I will not turn him back” (Amos 1).

Now I shall repeat the same kinds of despair with some further definition. The first is despair of faintheartedness; the second, of doubt; the third, of perdition. The first needs strengthening of spirit; the second, the consolation of the Holy Spirit; the third remains without every remedy, without end.

Against the timidity of the first despair, which a person feels because of the difficulty of penitence, Solomon promises strength, saying: “I will show you the way of wisdom; I will lead you through the paths of equity. When you have entered them, your steps will not be confined, and when you run [Col. 0886D] you will not stumble” (Prov. 4).

To remove the doubt of the second despair, by which a person is uncertain of pardon, hear what the Lord Jesus says: “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Mark 2). It is always true: where penitence is true, there true forgiveness is also present.

Concerning the third despair, this alone is taught: it is unforgivable. “Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit,” he says, “will be forgiven neither here nor in the future” (Matt. 12). If you doubt that anyone obstinately refusing to believe that the Holy Spirit can grant forgiveness of sins commits blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, be made certain by this. When the Lord Jesus said to the paralytic, “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you,” the Jews said, “This man blasphemes” (Matt. 9). They believed Christ to be a mere human being, and therefore said that he blasphemed, because forgiving sins belongs to God alone. Although Christ himself has authority to forgive sins through the co-operation of the Holy Trinity, forgiveness of sins belongs in a special sense to the person of the Holy Spirit, because he is the forgiveness of all sins. As Christ casts out demons in the Holy Spirit, so in the Holy Spirit he forgives sins. Thus whatever he does, he does wholly in the Holy Spirit. If, therefore, the Jews said that Christ had blasphemed because he seemed to have taken from God and claimed for himself the authority to forgive sins, much more do those blaspheme who deny that the Holy Spirit can forgive sins. This is unforgivable because it is obstinate and incorrigible.

[Col. 0887B] I am not unaware that there are other opinions concerning this blasphemy, whose question it is not the time to discuss. Therefore, when you say, “When I was in sins and had come into the depth of evils, despising and despairing,” distinguish for yourself which kind of despair you meant. Let only that third kind be far from you. And you showed that it is far from you when you immediately added concerning your penitence: “Having returned to myself, I often intend to undertake perfect penitence.” That this despair and this blasphemy may be far from all of us, let us believe in our hearts and confess with our mouths that the Holy Spirit is the forgiveness of all sins.

## CHAPTER XXI. Prayer to the Holy Spirit for obtaining hope of forgiveness of sins.

Lord, Holy Spirit, who are justice in the heights, [Col. 0887C] mercy in the depths; who are spiritual anointing for the healthy, wine and oil for the wounded; who are the finger of God’s right hand, divided in gifts, yet one and the same in each; who are called the Paraclete, who console those grieving over their sins; gift of God, inexhaustible living fountain of waters, mercy, consuming fire removing the rust of sin, charity joining God and us together! Most omnipotent and merciful Lord, we ask you to guard us from this blasphemy, because we truly believe and confess that you are the forgiveness of all sins. There is no multitude or quantity of sins that exceeds your power and mercy. Examples are at hand by which we may prove what has been said.

[Col. 0887D] There was a multitude of sins in Mary Magdalene, to whom many sins were forgiven; there was magnitude in Paul the persecutor, and in David, in the matter of Uriah. The former obtained mercy because he acted in ignorance; the latter, because he said that he had sinned, deserved to hear: “The Lord also has taken away your sin; you shall not die” (2 Kings 12). Likewise, in that Corinthian fornicator, whose like in fornication was not even heard among the Gentiles, whom the Corinthians and Paul forgave. All this was especially your work, Lord Holy Spirit, although God the Father and the Son acted as well. Therefore perform the same mercy in all who worship and invoke you and confess your omnipotence.

## CHAPTER XXII. Must a person change the place in which he sinned for the sake of penitence?

[Col. 0888A]

Now let us return to discussing your concerns. You say that you wish to move from the place in which you sinned to another place. And you give, as it seems to you, a necessary reason: a stricter and more disciplined way of life, because almost all our discipline has perished. Remain in the place in which you sinned, so that the little places [Note: [Col. 0887D] F. “locelli.”] in which you sinned here and there may be before your eyes, so that, if you act negligently, they may warn you. If you wish to conceal it, let the stones cry out that you are guilty and make you remember, lest through forgetfulness you leave anything unpunished and uncorrected. For perfect penitence requires that you punish yourself individually in each place in which you sinned individually. For just as, in each [Col. 0888B] member in which a person sins more, he is punished more—as the rich man, who had sinned more with his tongue—so also in every place in which a person sins especially, he ought to be punished especially.

This is no fable that I offer: it is true. In our times a certain knight burned nearly twenty villages of his enemies in one day. On the following night he was killed by those enemies, and, because of the sin of arson, was kept from burial for three days. Meanwhile a certain priest, the vicar of the parish priest, saw in a dream how that knight was pierced through with a thick, long pole, like a goose, and was roasted over each individual hearth of each of the houses that had been burned. And when he had become incandescent like iron, very cold water stood beside him; he was plunged into it, drawn out again, and roasted anew. [Col. 0888C] Thus it was done at each of the hearths of those houses. Finally, when those roastings were completed, he was carried to a great and lofty mountain. It opened, and a vast flame rose from it; when he had been put inside, the mountain closed itself.

Behold, you have testimony that in each particular place in which a person sins, he must also be punished. Thus, for each sacred season, for each holy order, for each profession, for each degree of kinship, and for every comparable circumstance in which people sin, they should punish themselves individually. Remain therefore in the place where you sinned, so that you may live and repent there, lest after death you be tormented there. [Note: [Col. 0888D] Codex: “be required” (*exigaris*).]

## CHAPTER XXIII. Some penitents fortify themselves by the example of the adulteress whom Christ absolved with few words, but they are deceived.

[Col. 0888D]

Perhaps you now say: “I am weary of your discussion, because scarcely anywhere, when the opportunity presents itself, do you cease speaking of penance. You multiply and magnify it so much, and portray it as so difficult, that I am frightened even by hearing of it and become fearful. And it is very strange where you have obtained this form and manner of penance, when the Lord prescribed for the woman caught in adultery a simple, easy, and brief penance.”

Brother, I rejoice at this objection of yours, because there are some who fortify themselves with this example, but are deceived. [Col. 0889A] First, we may say that this privilege does not establish a general law. For sometimes God has done certain things, and commanded others to do certain things, which are not to be drawn into an example for us. Moreover, if you examine it rightly, you will find the most perfect form of penance in this penitential act of the Lord.

Come then, brother: be here with yourself; be here with me. Let us examine the fullness of this penance, leaving aside certain circumstances: namely, that before this work which he was about to perform in that sinful woman, he went up to the Mount of Olives—that is, to the height of mercy: “For the Lord’s mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 144). Likewise, by causing the woman’s accusers to know themselves, he gave an example that teachers might learn in themselves [Col. 0889B] how they ought to have mercy on others who confess their sins. Setting aside these matters, I say, and others, let us consider only the words of penance now imposed on the woman by the Lord, to see whether the kind of penance you abhor may be found here.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The adulterous woman, rescued by Christ from the hands of the Jews, displayed a model of perfect penance.

Penance is thus defined: Penance is to bewail sins that have been committed, and not to commit thereafter those which must be bewailed. Three things are considered in it: contrition of heart, confession of mouth, and satisfaction by works. In contrition of heart there is humility; in confession of mouth, shame; in satisfaction by works, labor. Consider now whether these were present in that sinful woman, and how they were present.

[Col. 0889C] She had a contrite heart because Christ changed her stony heart into a soft one. He signified this by that writing which, bending down, he wrote upon the ground: for with his finger, that is, with the Holy Spirit, he formed her heart unto penance. There was humility there, because she acknowledged that she had sinned. There was confession of the mouth, because, owing to her guilty conscience, she had nothing to say in contradiction. How great, do you suppose, was her shame, when her guilt was known to her accusers, and she had God—whom nothing can escape—as inspector and judge? Shame is a very great part of penance, because the penitent voluntarily suffers for his or her own guilt. How great, too, do you suppose, was her fear, when she awaited only the sentence of stoning?

[Col. 0889D] The principal question now is how satisfaction by works was present in her, since neither do the Lord’s words to her contain anything of the kind, nor do we read that she did anything for her guilt. “Go,” he says: do not be idle, but go—that is, make progress in virtues. But no one can attain virtues without labor. “Sin no more henceforth” (John 8). He did not say, “Do not sin,” because while a person lives, no one can be entirely without sin; nevertheless, every mortal sin must be avoided. “Do not sin” means: do not have a will to commit any mortal sin. Let no one suppose that he can perform severe penance while at the same time retaining a will to sin. Those who abandon sins in deed and will are immediately assailed by temptations which cannot be overcome without labor.

Take one example in place of many. The vice of fornication is not overcome except by fasting and prayer. [Col. 0890A] Thus, in the victory over fornication, the virtue of chastity is acquired. By one labor both the vice is conquered and the virtue gained. Therefore, if she was obliged to advance in virtues and not to will sin, and neither could occur without the labor of struggle, the Lord gave this woman a model of perfect penance in these words. Do not therefore grow weary concerning matters necessary to know and to do.

## CHAPTER XXV. Because of human wickedness, a religious should not readily move from place to place.

You admit that the reason why you contemplate moving from one place to another is that all our discipline has perished.

[Col. 0890B] There are indeed three reasons for which a change of place may occur: persecution, lack of necessities, and the destruction of a place or an order. But at this time, where will you go, and where will you flee? There is a common proverb: “Bite one finger, then another, and then another: all hurt equally.” We read in Josephus that a certain man, as a portent of the future destruction which took place under Vespasian and Titus, cried out daily for a long time: “Woe from the east, woe from the west, woe from the south, woe from the north, woe from every direction, and woe to me as well!”

I can similarly cry: Woe from the scapular of the Cistercians! Woe from the cowl of the Cluniacs! Woe from the tunic of the Premonstratensians! Woe from the shirt of the Regulars! Woe from every corner of the world! Where is law? Where is righteousness? Where is order? Where is silence? Where is reading? Where is manual labor? Where is the common [Col. 0890C] life? All seek what is their own, whether publicly or privately.

You say to me: “Of whom do you say these things—of subjects or of masters?” “Begin at my sanctuary.” For there are masters with itching ears. Indeed, these are now the times which the apostle Paul foretold would come, in which all alike, teachers and disciples, have an appearance of godliness but deny its power. In the world, moreover, there is deceit everywhere, fraud everywhere, treachery everywhere: no faith—and so completely none that the Lord himself said: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke 18). And the prophet says: “There is no truth, no mercy, no knowledge of God in the land. Cursing [Col. 0890D] and lying and homicide and theft and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood” (Hos. 4).

Yet in some of these matters cenobites have so outdone secular people in this age that it may deservedly be said to them: “Be ashamed, O Sidon, says the sea” (Isa. 23). Likewise the prophet: “You have justified your sister Oholibah in your wicked ways” (Ezek. 23).

Remain therefore in your place, and say what that man said: “Woe to me as well!” But in what sense? Lest it seem harsh to you, hear: Woe to you, woe to me as well, woe to all who have zeal for God, because we have lived long enough to see these times! “Because iniquity has abounded, the love of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24). Remain therefore in your place. Scorpions are everywhere, dragons everywhere, among and with whom Ezekiel dwells. Lot likewise [Col. 0891A] dwelt with the worst of men, who afflicted the soul of the righteous man day by day with their wicked deeds.

And because you find no place where your foot may rest, remain in your place, as the dove returned and remained in the ark. Yet observe and beware lest, while you strain out a gnat with others, you swallow a camel yourself. Do not take what I say badly, for I say it so that you may be saved. For I desire, if I cannot gain several for the Lord by my counsels, at least to gain you alone. When I was young, I used to fish with a hook. I often tried and labored much; throughout all my fishing I caught one grayling, in which I greatly delighted, and I offered it as a gift to the lord with whom I lived. I interpret that grayling as you, if only I may be able to catch you with the hook of God’s word, so that I may have you alone to offer to the Lord [Col. 0891B] my God, and may rejoice with you and be permitted to delight in you in the Lord. Amen.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How one may visit holy places spiritually while remaining physically at home.

Nor shall I pass over what you said: that your mind often suggests to you that you should make a pilgrimage. Where? To Jerusalem. For what purpose? “That I may visit there,” you say, “the places sanctified by the Lord’s bodily presence: namely Bethlehem, Bethphage, Bethany, Jehoshaphat, the Mount of Olives, and finally the Jordan itself.”

You have no need to go, because:

> Those who run across the sea change their sky, not their mind.

You have no need to go, because you can find all these things at home—not the places themselves, indeed, but what they signify. Bethlehem means “house of bread.” Christ, who was once born according to the flesh in Bethlehem and found in a manger, is now found everywhere on all altars of the holy Church, although he is not here as he was there. “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh,” he says, “yet now we know him no longer” (2 Cor. 5). Therefore you need not seek in one place beyond the sea what is found everywhere. Your distant altar is your Bethlehem.

[Col. 0891C] Bethphage means “house of the mouth.” Your house at home is a house of the mouth, because you have with you the writings of the holy Fathers, whose mouths the Holy Spirit breathed upon so that they might speak such things. By them we are taught that we are pilgrims in this land and do not have here an abiding city, but ought to seek the city to come: not that Jerusalem which is in bondage with her children, but that Jerusalem which is above, which is free, which is the mother of us all. This Bethphage is available to you daily—something that the one beyond the sea cannot be. Therefore let your book-chest be your Bethphage.

Bethany means “house of obedience.” Your cell, in which you bound yourself to a known abbot and a place, is your Bethany. That one beyond the sea is enough to visit once; in this one you must remain continually. You must, I say, strive so that, just as Christ from Bethany—that is, from the house of obedience, for he became obedient to the Father unto death [Phil. 2]—went up to heaven, so you too, found in obedience, may deserve to be where he is. Therefore let your cell be your Bethany.

Jehoshaphat is the valley of the future judgment. Jehoshaphat beyond [Col. 0892A] the sea is enough for one who has seen it once. But Solomon urges us always to keep before our eyes the fear of the future judgment: “Always remember your last things,” he says, “and you will never sin” (Ecclus. 7). You can do this at home even if you never see Jehoshaphat.

The Mount of Olives is a mountain of richness, sweetness, and mercy. Nothing is as sweet as having mercy upon a sinful person. Nothing is as great as being able to justify a person from sin: for to justify a person from sin is greater than to have created a person. But you can find this mercy with God through a contrite and humbled heart, even if you never see the Mount of Olives beyond the sea.

The Jordan is a river flowing together from two springs, namely Jor and Dan, which rise at the foot of Mount Lebanon [Col. 0892B] and flow separately in fairly large streams; then they are gathered into one river and thereafter are called Jordan, which is interpreted as “their descent.” Without the water of that Jordan you can be washed and cleansed through baptism and penance, these two remedies working together like two springs flowing into one, if you descend—that is, if you humble yourself.

Therefore, if your altar is your Bethlehem, if your book-chest is your Bethphage, if your cell is your Bethany, if fear of future judgment is your Jehoshaphat, if mercy is your Mount of Olives, if baptism and penance are your Jordan—if, I say, these things, that is, what they signify, are and can be available to you at home—then you have no need to go to Jerusalem and visit [Col. 0892C] those places beyond the sea.

Stripped of all these grounds, you still say: “At least grant me this, that I may go to that Jerusalem, if only to pray there.” Hear: the Samaritan woman said to Jesus, “Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, and you say that Jerusalem is the place where one must worship” (John 4). And the Lord Jesus says: “Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem”—understand: according to the rite and opinion that then prevailed among them—“but the hour is coming when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth” (ibid.). Understand: everywhere, according to what Paul likewise says: “I desire you to pray in every place and lift pure hands to God” (1 Tim. 2). Jerusalem, therefore, is everywhere. You have no need, then, to go to Jerusalem in order to pray there.

[Col. 0892D] “Why then,” you ask, “does such a great multitude of people run to Jerusalem?” I answer: Why does Jesus say to his disciples, “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables” (Luke 8)? For the uneducated populace, always occupied with secular affairs, must meditate in some fashion, so that those who are almost without God at home may be instructed by the devotion of this pilgrimage, and may merit by such labor the God whom they are less able to grasp in spirit. For a similar reason painting is made in churches: not for the literate, but for the unlearned, because what Scripture is to the literate, painting is to the unlearned.

The Apostle’s saying can likewise be applied to this: “The law is not laid down for the righteous, but for the unrighteous” (1 Tim. 1)—for kidnappers, murderers, [Col. 0893A] parricides, perjurers, and the like. Therefore you do not need to go to Jerusalem in order to pray there. Permit those to go who are marked by the foregoing description; but fulfill your vows at home.

## CHAPTER XXVII. A religious may not pursue military service for the sake of martyrdom.

Beyond these thoughts—or rather, temptations—of yours, a temptation not unlike them has seized you, as I learned from other letters of yours sent to me before these, or rather, as I heard from your own mouth. For you said that a very great desire had come upon your mind that you might become a martyr. Therefore, in the expedition [Note: [Col. 0893D] The author’s age.] undertaken in the present year against the pagans under the Roman Emperor Frederick, with the emperor himself as leader, you wished to go and fight with the pagans so that, by this occasion of battle, you might become a martyr. [Col. 0893B]

Since then I answered this less fully, I answer more fully now. You have sworn another military service; such a battle is not permitted to you. You have before you the example of blessed Martin, who, while still a layman, said: “I am a soldier of Christ; I am not permitted to fight.” And to Peter fighting in this way the Lord said: “Put your sword into its place” (John 18). Read all the lives and passions of the holy martyrs, and you will not find any martyr who wished to kill his persecutor so that the persecutor might kill him. It is a new kind of martyrdom: to wish to kill another so that he may kill you.

If fighting delights you, fight as Moses did. Moses alone on the mountain fought more by praying than Joshua with his whole army fought with material weapons. [Col. 0893C] For when Moses prayed, Joshua prevailed; but when Moses, exhausted, ceased, Amalek prevailed. Therefore, if Martin did not wish to fight with the sword because he contemplated, desired, and at last exercised at a fitting time another, spiritual military service; if Peter was not permitted, the Lord forbidding it, to fight with another’s sword; if none of the martyrs attacked his persecutor with such a sword in order to make himself a martyr—then you too, moved by their admonition, put this thought—or rather, temptation—far from you.

In this expedition already begun, many who have forgotten their monastic vow, and some even their office, deceived by the spirit of the deceiver, were preparing to undertake that journey and fight with weapons as laymen. What I thought, rebuked, and advised concerning their madness, [Col. 0893D] I set forth in rhythmical verse. Some monks took its reading badly; others, to whom it pleased, eagerly seized it for exposition. I have taken care to inscribe it here, lest what may be useful perish:

> Frederick the emperor, comforter of the afflicted,  
> Let it be known to every age: he wishes to expose himself to danger.  
> Let Christians go with him; they shall return safe and sound!  
> But if anyone should fall, he shall be saved forever.  
>
> The wood of the cross, the leader’s banner;  
> The way of peace, the hope of salvation.  
> Let the army, marked by its sign, follow it.  
> The cross went before; it did not withdraw: let it atone for what the pagan has done.  
>
> Pope Clement sent his letters to all and promised this:  
>
> [Col. 0894A] Whoever devoutly and faithfully undertakes this journey  
> Shall be freed from sin, God being reconciled to him.  
>
> Let armed soldiers go—not monks, not bearded men [Note: [Col. 0894D] That is, lay brothers.]:  
> Let such men remain at home and fulfill their vows.  
> They certainly help more by prayer than by fighting with hand and slaughter.  
> A sword girded with a tassel adds to, rather than removes, sins.  
>
> The seducing spirit drives these men toward worse things.  
> Emperor Frederick, be their examiner.  
> Cleanse your camp; cut such men off from it.  
> Their apostasy; through you, your victory.  
>
> Achan, guilty among the people, was a danger to all.  
> Go, blessed by God, you who are rightly enrolled for this war.  
> May he grant you victory for everlasting remembrance.  
> May Jerusalem be liberated and restored as before.  
> May the victory of the holy cross be our joy! Amen.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Not earthly Jerusalem, but the heavenly Jerusalem, is the vision of true peace.

Human thoughts are manifold, and even after truth is known a person does not easily [Col. 0894B] rest. You still say, therefore, that temptations of this kind do not easily or quickly depart but cling persistently, after the likeness of that saying:

> The leech will not release the skin until it is full of blood.  
> (Horace, *Art of Poetry*, v. 477)

You still say: “If you do not permit me to fight with the sword for Jerusalem, at least allow me to be at peace near Jerusalem, since Jerusalem is the vision of peace.”

You are mistaken. Indeed, the Jerusalem of which you speak has never, or only rarely, had peace; it has always been in wars, and still is, as can be seen today. You will therefore be unable to have peace there, neither peace of body nor peace of heart. Thus the interpretation of the name that you give—that Jerusalem is “vision of peace”—cannot apply to this earthly Jerusalem, but to that heavenly Jerusalem which this one signifies, whose borders the Lord has established in peace.

What then is this Jerusalem which is warlike and has peace only in its name? It is the people of God—that is, it signifies the people of God—which, as long as it here wanders in the flesh away from the Lord, must endure wars of temptation from enemies: from the devil, from its neighbor, and from its own flesh. It now possesses peace only in its name. But it will be Jerusalem in reality when it reaches the place where there will be perpetual peace and no war. Therefore you need not go to that Jerusalem, because you yourself are Jerusalem. Strive only to reach, after the labor of this warfare, that heavenly Jerusalem which truly is the vision of peace.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Neither solitude nor the eremitic life, but obedience rendered to a superior, frees the mind from its passions.

[Col. 0894D]

You are like a hydra with many heads: when others have been cut off, one still remains for you, namely that you contemplate becoming a hermit. But why? I gladly hear this; but I ask why. I think I know. For I infer that you desire the solitude of the desert for this reason: because, owing to the weakness and passions of your mind, you cannot endure the importunity and ill conduct of the brothers living with you, and you think it lighter for you if you are alone and remain in solitude the same person you were in the monastery.

[Col. 0895A] You are not alone in solitude because of the continual attacks of demons and temptations, to which solitude is more familiar for this purpose, but more dangerous for you because, if you fall, you have no one to lift you up. Reading the *Lives of the Fathers* proves what I say to be true. Moreover, in solitude you are the kind of person you were when you came there, because there too you suffer the passions of mind which you suffer in the monastery. And it is more shameful to be conquered by the same passion in solitude by a lesser cause than perhaps to be conquered in a monastery by a greater one.

For example: you were often stirred to anger in the monastery; but because in solitude you have no one with whom to quarrel, you think that that passion of anger has become quiet within you.

Something like this is read in the sayings of the Fathers. A certain brother left the monastery for solitude. While living there alone, one day he filled a vessel with water and set it beside himself. It fell and was overturned; [Col. 0895B] this happened three times. The third time, seizing that vessel, he angrily broke it. When he came to himself, he reflected that he had been overcome by anger and said: “Behold, I am alone, and yet I have been conquered by irascibility. I will therefore return to the monastery, because everywhere there is need of struggle and patience, and especially of God’s help.” Thus he returned to his place.

Note that this man said: “Everywhere there is need of struggle.” But where the struggle is harder, there the victory is more glorious. Therefore, if it happens to you to endure more in the monastery, think of the greater reward.

After the pattern of this, other passions of the soul—such as fornication, pride, and similar vices—have driven and still drive hermits, once conquered, from solitude into public life (*sic*). Remain therefore [Col. 0895C] in your cell; be subject to your abbot; and remain in the calling in which you were called. Be of one countenance, because “a double-minded man is unstable in all his ways.” Do not be a Proteus of changing forms, but Anna, whose countenance was no longer changed in different directions.

## CHAPTER XXX. The common life is to be preferred to the life of recluses.

What shall I say of the matter I had almost forgotten? Among the other things by which you were troubled, you said that you also had it in mind to wish to be enclosed as a recluse. I have no teaching on this matter, because neither from experience nor from reading have I learned anything concerning it. Yet it seems to me more praiseworthy and more perfect to remain in a community of brothers, where, whether willing or unwilling, you must always be ready at the appointed times and hours for the observances [Col. 0895D] of choir, chapter [Note: [Col. 0895D] Thus the codex.], dormitory, and refectory, and where, at the command of your superior and elders, you break your own will.

It is more praiseworthy, I say, to live thus in a congregation than to be enclosed, one who prays when he wishes and ceases when he wishes; who, when he sins, has no one to rebuke him; who sleeps when he wishes and rises when he wishes; who fasts when and how he wishes; who eats when and how he wishes; who freely does all his own wills whenever and however he wishes, and in none of all these matters admits any arbiter. He himself is both law and judge to himself.

## CHAPTER XXXI. In every order a person can attain salvation if he lives rightly.

[Col. 0896A]

There are many sects which people choose and follow, but one must carefully consider where their ends lead: whether to heaven or to hell. For he did not speak in vain who said: “There are ways which seem right, but their ends lead to hell” (Prov. 16). I do not accuse sects which are according to God; for “the law is good, if anyone uses it lawfully.” But there are some who migrate from sect to sect like a sparrow, whether because of weariness, curiosity, pride, vainglory, or inconstancy. This is what he wished to forbid who said: “I trust in the Lord; how do you say to my soul, ‘Migrate to the mountain like a sparrow’?” (Ps. 10).

[Col. 0896B] For there are people who urge certain others, saying: “Come over to us; our life and order are higher.” Such people should know that in every order one serves the one Lord, and that each person can attain in it a perfection suited to himself. Therefore do not be a sparrow: remain in your order and place. It is not safe to change often, because every sudden change does not occur without a certain alteration of minds. It is not safe to wander, because you will not quickly find a manger as secure as your own. You asked for counsel; this is my counsel.

## CHAPTER XXXII. The author promises his disciple his intercessions with God and excuses his own errors.

After all that you set forth in your letter, you said that I was a great prophet in your eyes. I know who I am: I am a sinner, not a prophet—[Col. 0896C] unless you wish to call me a prophet in this respect, that I do not depart from the meaning of the prophets. Whatever they spoke or wrote about the past, present, or future, taught by the Holy Spirit, I believe; and in accordance with these things I speak what I speak and write what I write, to the praise of God and the edification of my neighbor. Thus, where I err, do not adhere to my writings as though they were authoritative; rather, consult the *filios excussorum*—that is, the interpreters of the prophets. You may safely listen to them.

[Col. 0896D] At last you conclude your letter by asking me to invoke the grace of the Holy Spirit upon you and more earnestly to bestow on your behalf the help of prayer. The one whom you are preparing as an intercessor has need of a patron. Yet that Canaanite woman, compared by the Lord to a dog because of idolatry, was heard for her daughter’s sake. For she heard from the Lord: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done to you as you asked.” And her daughter was healed from that hour (Matt. 15). Therefore let it be done to you according to your faith.

Behold, I have complied with your request. I have written to you as you asked—or rather, as you demanded—like a faithful interpreter who renders word for word. I answered each point you proposed as I could, not as I wished. I have wrapped thoughts in unskilled language; great matters crawl upon the ground. This alone consoles me: what I have written is plain and brief. You read and praise it because you love me; another reads, is disgusted, criticizes, and says: “After the pleasing tables and so many sweet dishes of the holy Fathers, who write rightly, well, and magnificently, [Col. 0897A] this man thrusts in his own worthless offerings, like poppy seed added to tripe, to provoke a vomit of disgust. The meal could have proceeded without these things.” Every

> Superfluity, therefore, flows from a full breast.

Against such people this consoles me: they do not know the author’s person. Enough has been said about this.

The end has come, the end has come, the end has come: the end of writing, the end of living, the end of meriting. Why the end of writing? Because I have neither eye nor hand, nor can I have a scribe. Why the end of living? Because I am seventy-three years old, and therefore nature itself now presses me toward death. Why the end of meriting? Because I am useless and can do no good. After this, judgment awaits me, where, when I rise again, what I have merited will be repaid to me. Therefore, my brother, have mercy on me and remember me in [Col. 0897B] your prayers. Since I do not believe that I shall write to you further, I wish to put the finishing hand upon you. I do not wish to leave you half-finished—that is, imperfect. But you will be perfect if you do what I say.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. How may a person always be one with himself?

Do not be a many-sided man—that is, a man of many thoughts. Be a man of one will and one intention, and direct that will and intention of yours toward one thing. And what is that one thing? Namely, the one thing that is necessary. What is that one thing? Free and full contemplation of God. Therefore be one, seek one, cleave to one, so that you may be one with the One.

[Col. 0897C] You say: “How can it happen that we are one, when, according to Paul, there are two persons in each of us, namely the inner and the outer person; and these oppose one another, and this struggle remains between them as long as we live in this mortal flesh?” Paul himself teaches much concerning what you say: “Although,” he says, “our outer person is decaying, yet the inner person is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4). Behold, two persons in one person! And he makes clear what he calls the two persons, explaining their struggle: “The flesh,” he says, “desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5). Thus the flesh and spirit of one person are the two persons of one person.

[Col. 0897D] But in what matters do flesh and spirit disagree? “The works of the flesh,” he says, “are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, lust, sorceries, enmities, quarrels, jealousies, angers, disputes, dissensions, heresies, envies, murders, and things like these. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity” (ibid.). These—those things and these—are the matters in which flesh and spirit oppose each other, but only in those who do not walk according to the flesh and resist the flesh, as Paul does, according to his own clear testimony concerning himself: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind” (Rom. 7). Hence, exhausted by this struggle, he cried out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death [Col. 0898A]?” (ibid.).

But in those who are according to the flesh and savor the things of the flesh, this struggle is at rest, because in them the flesh, which ought to be subject to the spirit, through a perverse order rules over the spirit, so that the spirit no longer resists the desires of the flesh.

You say: “If, then, there is struggle in those who walk according to the spirit, and I wish to be one of those who follow the spirit, how can I be one, as you advise?” To this I say: As long as we remain for a long time in the mortality and mutability of this present age, no one can become entirely one, because the flesh that desires against the spirit does not permit it. Yet no one ought to desist or despair; rather, he should strive to tame the flesh as much as he can and [Col. 0898B] subject it to the spirit, after the example of those of whom it is said: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. 5).

And even if this cannot be accomplished fully in the present, as it will be in the future, one must nevertheless labor so that what is now partial may someday be made perfect. The Apostle promises this: “We know in part,” he says, “and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect comes, that which is partial will be done away” (1 Cor. 13). And the Lord says to Martha: “Mary has chosen the better part” (Luke 10). He said “part,” not “whole,” because whatever a person knows, loves, or tastes of God in this life is a part, not the whole, of the future fullness. “For now we see through a mirror and in an enigma; but then we shall see [Col. 0898C] him face to face as he is” (1 Cor. 13).

There are also other hindrances that prevent a person from being one unto One: namely, worldly possessions and affairs, in which one person becomes entangled unwillingly, another willingly. Meditation upon, pursuit of, and desire for these things are hovering flies that confuse the eyes of the heart by which God ought to be seen. Whoever wishes to be one unto One must drive them away with the hand of solicitude. The Psalmist commands this, saying: “Be still and see that I am God” (Ps. 45). Therefore God is that One.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. By what means a person may become one with God.

How a person may become one unto One—that is, [Col. 0898D] a human being unto God—is rightly asked, since human nature is one thing and God’s another, and a human is one in one way while God is one in another. A human being is composed of soul and body, but the nature of the soul differs from that of the body; therefore a human being is composed of different things. How, then, can he be one?

Not indeed because flesh may ever become soul, or conversely; but because the desire of the soul and that of the body become one desire, always and unchangeably tending toward the one thing, namely God. Hence the Psalmist says: “My heart and my flesh have exulted in the living God” (Ps. 83). This cannot happen in this life, but will be fully so in the future. Thus a human being will become one when he has one desire: not corrupted but renewed, directed not toward himself but above himself, not momentary but everlasting.

[Col. 0899A] But that One to which a human being ought to become one is the one God. God, moreover, is one because his essence is simple. It is simple because there is not one thing and another thing in it from which that essence is composed. Nothing is added to him from outside; nothing diverse is in him within. Therefore whatever he is, he is essentially one, for whom to be wholly one and to be simple are identical with what he is. Therefore it is true being for him to be what he is, because what he is is wholly one and simple being.

There are several things that are called one, but in different ways. There is a one that is called one by aggregation, as when we speak of one flock, in which there are many animals. There is a one that is called one by composition, as a body, in which there are many members. There is a one that is called one by likeness, as [Col. 0899B] when we call a voice one voice, though it has been uttered by many. None of all these is truly one; yet they are called one according to some effect, because in some manner they approach unity. Some things are found that are truly called one, such as our souls, which truly are one insofar as they exist essentially; but they are not supremely one, because they are not unchangeably so. Therefore that which is one essentially and unchangeably is truly and supremely one: this is God alone.

Since, therefore, human nature and divine nature are so different, as has been said—for man consists of body and soul, whose natures are different, and is therefore multiple, nor can he be truly one, because in a body size is one thing, colour another, shape another, and these can change reciprocally; [Col. 0899C] for with size changed the same colour and shape can remain, with colour changed the same shape and size can remain, and, though the shape does not remain the same, it can be just as large and coloured in the same way; and whatever other attributes are predicated of the body can be changed both together and, in greater number, apart from the rest—thereby the nature of body is proved to be multiple, and in no way simple.

The soul, considered in itself, although simpler in comparison with the body, is nevertheless itself multiple, not altogether simple. For in the soul it is one thing to be skilful, another to be unskilled; one thing memory, another desire, another fear, another joy, another sorrow, and other such things that may be found in the soul’s [Col. 0899D] nature. It is evident that its nature is not simple but multiple. The nature of God, however, is altogether simple, altogether immutable, altogether unchangeable: truly and supremely one. Since, I say, the nature of man and the nature of God differ from one another so greatly, it is rightly asked how a man can be one spirit with God, since Scripture says: “He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6).

## Chapter XXXV. How the several names in human nature signify multiplicity, but not likewise in the divine nature

Before I solve this question, I shall set forth another question, lesser than this one, so that, once it is solved, it may not obstruct the meaning of the former. What then is this question? Namely: how do many terms signify multiplicity and mutability in human nature, while many different terms are likewise predicated of God, who is neither non-simple nor mutable? This arises because the things said of man signify differently from the things said of God. The things said of man are said to be in man, not to be man—as memory, understanding, love, wisdom, and whatever similar things you may gather. But whatever such things are said of God, and are said relatively to himself—such as living, eternal, immutable, wise, powerful, just, good, blessed, and the whole catalogue of these, which seem to be said according to a quality of substance—must be understood to be said not according to quality, but according to substance. [Col. 0900B] Far be it that God should be said to be according to substance but good according to quality: rather, both are according to substance! For in that simple and unchangeable nature of God, being is not one thing and being good another; nor being great, wise, true, or indeed simply being itself. Rather, all these things, and whatever is said relatively to himself, are one simple and immutable essence; that is, they are one and the same.

God’s substance therefore surpasses all created substances, so that it may be called a supersubstantial substance. I said “substances” in the plural, because “substance” is understood in more than one sense.

For sometimes substance is so called from “standing under” (*substare*), which is properly said of prime matter, which, [Col. 0900C] as Plato says, underlies all forms, both substantial and accidental. Although it is never found in the actual order of things without forms and accidents, nevertheless it does not need them in order to be its own substance. For bodies and spirits could exist in the nature of substance even if all forms departed from them. Although this can never occur in actuality, the intellect can nevertheless consider them in this way.

Substance is also called from “subsisting,” as it were *subsistence* (*subsistentia*), which is said with reference to the substantial form that subsists in matter, because it causes the flux of matter to stand beneath it. This may be seen both in artificial and natural things. In artificial things thus: let there be gold, and let it be unworked. There is a certain flux in [Col. 0900D] it, because it can receive any form, whether of Achilles or of a lion. If the form of Achilles is engraved upon it, that matter is arrested in its flux, because for as long as it has that form it receives no other into itself. Likewise in natural things that primordial flux is arrested when such a form is impressed upon it by nature—namely, humanity—so that, in the same part, it cannot receive the form of an ass or of any other thing whatsoever.

Substance is also called from both “standing under” and “subsisting”: namely, that which consists of matter and form, as any individual man. Thus Aristotle’s substance is substance from standing under, because it underlies substantial and accidental forms; and it is substance from subsisting, because it in some manner subsists—that is, it arrests the flux [Col. 0901A] of its matter—when, by the collection of accidents that concur in it, it becomes in some manner distinct and determinate from another thing. This it has from the property of form.

Because of the poverty of the Latin language, we signify these modes by one word. The Greeks, however, whose language abounds in terms, have three words here: *hypostasis*, which means substance from “standing under,” because it underlies forms; and *ousiosis*, interpreted “subsistence,” which is substantial form; and *ousia*, interpreted “essence,” which is a name composed from both, namely matter and form, and resembling something composed of matter and form, such as the soul. Therefore *essence* is used for the composite of both, because neither form nor matter exists by itself, but what is composed of both is properly said to be.

## Chapter XXXVI. Return to the solution of the principal question concerning the unity of the human spirit with the divine

According to this consideration, God’s substance surpasses, as has been said, all created substances, because it is uncreated; it is neither matter from matter, nor does it underlie forms, nor is it a subsistence that arrests the flux of matter. For it is form without form; it is not collected from any accidents, nor is it an essence composed from both. Therefore, because God’s substance—or, better said, essence—is so solid and so immutable that it neither changes nor can change at all, it is rightly called a supersubstantial substance [Col. 0901C] and a superessential essence.

Since, therefore, God’s nature and human nature are so different, it is rightly asked how what is said can come to pass: “He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6). It was for the sake of this question that the foregoing points were so elaborately set out. First know this: no one in this life, in which “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wisdom 9), however holy or spiritual, can become one spirit with God fully and perfectly. This is reserved for the future.

Therefore I think it is said, “He who is joined,” not, “He who adheres inwardly.” He who is joined is outside; he who adheres inwardly is within. He who is joined can be separated; he who adheres inwardly is firmly cemented fast. In this manner, according to the state that now is and that which is to come, that saying of the Lord may also be understood: “On these two commandments,” namely those of love, “hang all the law and the prophets” (Matt. 22). He said “hang,” not “remain.” What hangs can fall; what remains does not fear falling. In this life love hangs, because it can be lost—namely, love that is beginning and progressing. But the love that is perfect and perseveres to the end will never fail.

You will say: “Whence comes this presumption in you, that you thus correct the words of divine authority?” I do not correct them as though they were superfluous or wrongly spoken; rather, one statement gives birth to another statement.

Come then, let us consider how God and man, who are different in nature, can become one [Col. 0902A] spirit. Things unlike cannot be united. But God and man are unlike; therefore they cannot be united as long as they are unlike. Sin and the punishment of sin produce this unlikeness. As long as this unlikeness remains, they cannot be united. But man will be like God when he is restored to the ancient dignity in which he was created in the likeness and image of God—indeed, when he becomes greater than he was created, and greater than he received in creation. In creation he received the power not to die; in the future he will receive the inability to die. In creation he received the power not to sin; in the future he will receive the inability to sin. Yet he lost both the power not to die and the power not to sin when he sinned, by which he departed from God into the region of unlikeness. But he will return to God’s likeness when he has become wholly immortal and confirmed so that he can sin no more.

When will this happen? Let the Apostle say: “For the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (1 Cor. 15), both in body and in soul. How? From death to immortality, from corruption to incorruption, from mutability to immutability. By whom? By our Lord Jesus Christ our Saviour, “who will refashion the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3). And the soul will be where he himself is, according to the saying: “Father, I will that where I am, there also my servant may be” (John 12). And where is Christ? In the full vision of divinity: for whatever God is, [Col. 0902C] Christ’s soul sees it, understands it wholly, and has it wholly united to itself. If Christ has the whole, what remains for us? What shall we see there? As much as he himself gives. For “no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matt. 11). It is a great honour that where the Only-begotten is, there also the adopted child may be—not made equal to divinity, indeed, but associated with eternity.

How, then, shall we be one spirit with the Lord? Namely, when the flux of our nature is arrested in him. How is the flux of nature arrested in him? When it is inseparably cemented to the likeness of the divine form, which does not change. We shall be such as that which we shall see is. And we shall see God face to face (1 Cor. 13). But God’s face is one; therefore our face shall be one, because it will accord with the one face of God; and it shall always be one, because God’s face shall immutably be one. God’s face is the whole of what he is. I say “the whole,” because whether God is called holy, eternal, good, just, or blessed, these are not said of him as accidents; rather, all these are his one truly and supremely simple essence, because there is not one thing and another in him, but all are one and the same. Therefore God’s face is one.

Our face, however, is our knowledge by which we know God as he is. We are joined to God in three ways: by sight, understanding, and love. By sight, when we see what he is; by understanding, when we understand what he is; by love, when we love what we see and understand.

## Chapter XXXVII. Exhortation to seek steadfast union with God, and conclusion of the work

[Col. 0903A]

In this manner we adhere inwardly to God, and by thus adhering inwardly we become one spirit with the Lord; yet not equal to God. But we shall be brought to equality with God, because we shall be changed; and what is now impossible will then be possible. For what else is our change but that our nature will then be above what it now is? And from that which we now see, understand, and love, we shall never turn aside throughout eternity, because beyond it we shall seek nothing else. For it contains every delight in itself, as manna of old possessed the desired flavour according to each person’s wish. And if this could occur in a material thing so far unequal to God, why do you doubt that something beyond this, and far better, may come to pass for us in [Col. 0903B] the Creator?

But meanwhile, while we live in this corruption, the eye of the heart must be cleansed, so that God may then be seen clearly and [Col. 0904A] fully. The understanding must be trained, so that God may then be perfectly comprehended. Love must be nourished and made chaste, so that God may then be loved with all one’s powers and chastely. If you, brother, do all these things, you shall be perfect and one spirit with the Lord. Let us all agree in this, that we may all be one, just as the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one. Let us all be one, that we may all have one will, one intention, and one love; that we may see, understand, and love the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, one God in Trinity and Trinity in unity—and that is the end. Let this also be the end of this book. Live and prosper, brother; may eternal peace be upon you. Amen.

[Col. 0904B] Here ends the good little treatise on repentance and the various temptations of a certain religious, in which another aged religious instructs him by the same little book.

[Col. 0903]

# The Little Book on Conscience of an Anonymous Benedictine, who appears to have flourished in the twelfth century

(D. Bern. Pezius, *Bibliotheca ascetica antiquo-nova*, Regensburg, 1724, vol. VI, p. XXIX, from a manuscript codex in the library of Melk.)

## Notice

Concerning this little work of the present anonymous author, by no means lacking in elegance, I have nothing further to say now beyond what I have already mentioned concerning the little book *On Repentance* (above, col. 863). The parchment Melk manuscript from which I brought it forth was written three hundred years ago, and indeed very badly; without a second exemplar, it was not possible to cure all its errors. The little book is divided into two parts. The former, from chapters 1 through 6, treats briefly and acutely of the various state and disposition of human conscience, interspersing several maxims full of prudence and piety. The latter part concerns the principles and modes of our thoughts, a matter that is most perplexing of all in ascetic practice.

# Little Book on Conscience

[Col. 0903]

## Prologue

[Col. 0903C]

You ask of me, my beloved, what is above me—indeed, contrary to me—namely, the light of knowledge and purity of conscience. In both you are mistaken, but you do not believe yourself mistaken; you are moved either by affection for me or by opinion of me. I know what I am and what I can do. For I am a sinner, a sinner sinning beyond measure, and no liveliness of intellect has any place in me. Added to this is a multiplicity of affairs, which, even in an intelligent person, either overwhelms or drives away the seeds of all learning. For according to the Wise Man, wisdom is to be written in a time of leisure, [Col. 0904C] and “he who is lessened in activity will receive it” (Ecclus. 38). Yet, though not because you are a friend, nevertheless because you are importunate, according to the Lord’s precept, I shall rise and give you what is necessary for you, if anything comes to hand for me. May the Lord grant you according to your heart. For he is the one who gives to his voice a voice of power, who in his sweetness prepares for the poor, who fills your desire with good things.

## Chapter I. Conscience is called an abyss

The conscience of man is a vast abyss. For just as [Col. 0905A] the depth of an abyss cannot be drained by its own thoughts. It is “a great and spacious sea, wherein are creeping things without number” (Ps. 103). How aptly he says “creeping things”! For just as a creeping creature creeps secretly and wanders here and there through winding turns, so poisonous thoughts gently enter and leave the conscience of man, so that the person does not know whence they come or whither they go. He knew this who said: “The heart of man is perverse and inscrutable; and who,” he says, “shall know it?” (Jer. 17). Nor is “who” said for what is difficult, but for what is impossible; because what admits no searching admits no knowing either.

Look at that great apostle—I speak of Paul—the unique investigator of his conscience: “But to me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by a human day” (1 Cor. 4). See how he had escaped human judgment, doubting nothing from those who are outside! “But,” he says, “neither do I judge myself” (ibid.). And where, holy Apostle, is your own saying: “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged”? (ibid.) Why do you either refuse or neglect to judge yourself? Hear why: “I am conscious,” he says, “of nothing against myself” (ibid.). Happy the conscience that is conscious to itself of nothing, and does not fear its own judgment! Do you see by how exalted a manner of life he feared neither the judgment of others nor his own? Yet the snare and great pit still lie hidden from the vessel of election, though they could not escape that most watchful eye of yours. For he added: “But I am not thereby justified” (ibid.). [Col. 0905C] And he added: “He who judges me is the Lord” (ibid.).

This, then, is the third judgment, God’s judgment, which even that most purified conscience does not comprehend, not knowing, according to Scripture, whether it is worthy of hatred or love, since all things are reserved for it in the future (Eccles. 9). Shaken and struck by fear of this judgment, he groaned and said: “For what I do, I do not understand” (Rom. 7). Even if I have escaped the judgment of the world and judgment of myself, God’s judgment still remains. It does not allow me to understand what I do, because I do not know whether it accepts what I do. For he knows me better than I know myself, searching reins and hearts (Ps. 7), knower of hidden things (Dan. 13), reaching even to the division of soul and spirit. He alone knows all things [Col. 0905D] and the grounds of all things.

O unique instrument of the Holy Spirit, if you do not understand what you do, why do you say elsewhere: “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1), calling your conscience your glory? But he understands in part and does not understand in part. He plainly understands, because he has surpassed both his own judgment and that of others. But he is held fast concerning God’s judgment, where without doubt he does not know what he does. For he is not justified by those two judgments, but shall be justified by the third, which, just as it is unknowable, is also incomprehensible. Yet exclusion from the two judgments and justification in the present are in some manner a sure sign of eternal predestination, in which God foresaw us to be made conformable to the image of his Son (Rom. 8), and of future glorification, when we shall be in him and he in us, when he shall be all in all (1 Cor. 15).

For this reason he spoke elsewhere as securely as sincerely: “I am certain,” he says, “that neither death nor life, nor many other things—indeed, almost everything that he there enumerated—will be able to separate me from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8). And when he had said so many and such great things, he retained one thing, namely his own will, which is the cause of salvation and damnation. Observe how this man filled with God called his conscience his glory, as though fully understanding it and himself in it; and yet said that he did not understand what he did, thus holding his conscience captive not now in glory but in ignorance. Therefore the Apostle failed while searching his conscience with searching (Ps. [Col. 0906B] 63); and when he thought he had reached its depth, having set aside the judgment of others and his own, he encountered the abyss—namely, God’s judgment—which he cannot penetrate. Thus he now declares, whether summoned or convicted: “Your judgments are not merely an abyss, but a vast abyss” (Ps. 35).

What shall we miserable and pitiable people do, if he who laboured more than all others, to whom even the keeper of the keys of the kingdom, together with John and James, appears to have contributed nothing, who was caught up to the third heaven (2 Cor. 12), thinks and speaks so of himself? But now, to disclose to your purity in plain and unadorned words all that I think concerning conscience, I have decided to set out four modes of distinction, so that what has been distinguished part by part may be read more pleasantly and retained better.

## Chapter II. On the fourfold conscience. First, on the good and tranquil conscience

[Col. 0906C]

One conscience is good and tranquil; another good and troubled; another evil and tranquil; another evil and troubled. Let us first consider the first.

A good conscience is one that both punishes past sins and shrinks from committing sins that ought to be punished; and which, although it feels sin, does not consent to sin. “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Ps. 31), says the saint. He did not say, “Who has committed no sin.” For there is no such person here except one, and he is the Son of God, “who committed no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2). Therefore everything that he has decreed not to impute to me is as though it had never been. Blessed, then, are not those in whom no iniquities have been found, but those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered (Ps. 31), so that by some covering they are in some manner hidden from God’s eyes.

Happy is the soul which, though feeling sin, does not consent to sin; though thought defiles it, reason washes it, struggling and resisting the law of sin. The struggle is troublesome but fruitful. For if it has punishment, it brings a crown. In this conflict, where there is perception but not consent, “there is no condemnation,” according to the Apostle, “for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8).
