Moreover, the person who has the will not to sin and guards his feet against falling; who both laments and punishes the sins committed in former time; who repels malicious thoughts by dashing them against Christ—such a one, as though bound and constricted by [Col. 0907A] a threefold cord, has a conscience cleansed and pure. I would call it tranquil when the Spirit himself now bears witness to that person’s spirit that he is a child of God; when he is gentle toward all and burdensome to none, making use of a friend for grace, an enemy for patience, all persons for goodwill, and, so far as he can, for beneficence. Such a conscience is rare on earth; but the rarer it is, the dearer it is to God.

## Chapter III. On the good but troubled conscience

A conscience is good but troubled when it admits nothing soft, nothing lax, but cleanses itself as strictly as it can from the stain of the world; yet not in sweetness, but in much bitterness. That is, the more upright way and more austere life seem hard to it. Yet however hard it may be, it chooses both to endure and to persevere. Everywhere it sees what displeases the flesh; but it restrains itself with the bridle of the fear of God, and in every storm of its heart it raises itself to this anchor, according to the Prophet: “He was troubled and did not speak” (Ps. 76).

But hear what the Lord says of this person: “I am with him in tribulation” (Ps. 90). For what purpose? “I will deliver him and glorify him” (ibid.). I will deliver him from bitterness and glorify him in delight [Note: [Col. 0907D] The manuscript reads “will” (*voluntate*).], when what he formerly did from fear he will do from love. This conscience speaks to God in the Psalm: “You have moved the earth, O Lord, and troubled it; heal its breaches, for it has been shaken” (Ps. 59). The earth is moved when the sinner confesses and repents; it is troubled when, in conversion, he endures bitterness. [Col. 0907C] But to heal these fractures belongs to him alone who heals all our infirmities. Yet hear what follows: “You have shown your people hard things” (ibid.). Why say more? “You have made us drink the wine of compunction” (ibid.), not the milk of anointing.

Milk is set before some who live in religion, wine before others; yet both are divine. Those drink milk to whom vigils seem brief, foods sweet, bread pleasant, and labours desirable; to whom what is great in the exercises of holy living seems little. Milk is drunk pleasantly, flows down sweetly, and is taken without injury or bitterness. Thus the righteous proceed pleasantly in their holy purpose, run sweetly, without injury to their own conscience or bitterness toward another’s. The person who drinks this kind of milk has this particular quality: his own sin displeases him, he does not consent to another’s sin; for this reason he does not abandon the sinner; he does not, as far as lies in him, overlook that person’s faults; and, when he has rebuked him, he does not exult over him. This is enough concerning the drinking of milk.

Hear concerning the drinking of wine. Wine is harsh and unpleasant. Those drink wine who, having undertaken and entered upon the ways of life, are tormented by tribulations both of flesh and soul, yet neither yield nor withdraw in tribulation. These are they to whom God himself, with his own mouth, proclaims and foretells: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations” (Luke 22). We have discussed them fully and abundantly above. Which of these seems worthier to you: the one who runs the way of God’s commandments in sweetness, or the one who runs it in harshness? The first seems happier, the second stronger; both are righteous, both devout, each having his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that.

Do you wish to know that in each there is what is pleasing before God? “I have drunk,” he says, “my wine with my milk” (Song 5). The first he delivers from temptation; the second he strengthens in temptation. And whereas one experiences how sweet the Lord is (Ps. 33), the other experiences how strong the Lord is. Strong indeed, mighty in battle (Ps. 23), in which he allows his servant to be pressed, but not crushed, in the multitude of his mercies. “Come,” says the prophet, “buy wine and milk without money” (Isa. 55). For every conscience that fears God and comes to him buys from him either milk or wine, according to what has been stated and treated above. And note that in both places he put wine first, perhaps because one who steadfastly bears greater tribulation for God receives greater reward. Let this be said concerning the distinction between the good and tranquil conscience, and the good but troubled conscience.

## Chapter IV. On the evil and tranquil conscience

There follows the evil and tranquil conscience, than which nothing is worse and nothing more unhappy. You ask what it is. It is that which neither fears God nor reveres men; which, when it has reached the depth of evils, despises. See the slipping—indeed, the fall—of the evil conscience: how little by little and step by step it declines from God and descends into the depths, until [Col. 0908C] the pit presses its mouth upon it.

First, when a person accustomed to good deeds sins grievously, it seems to him so unbearable that he seems to descend alive into hell. In the course of time it seems not unbearable, yet still serious; and between unbearable and serious there is no small descent. Shortly afterwards he judges it light; forgetting both its unbearableness and seriousness, he later does not feel it. Though beaten with repeated blows, he does not feel the wounds or heed the blows. Concerning such persons Scripture says expressly: “They beat me and I did not suffer; they dragged me, and I did not feel it” (Prov. 23). Within a short space of time, not only does he fail to feel it, but it even pleases him: what was bitter becomes sweet, and what was harsh is changed into pleasantness. [Col. 0908D] He is then led into habit, so that it not only pleases him, but pleases him continually, and he cannot restrain himself. At last he cannot be torn away, because habit turns into nature; and what was formerly impossible to do has now become impossible to refrain from doing. Thus one descends—indeed, falls—from Jerusalem to Jericho; thus one enters into turning away and hardness of heart. Here the sinner stinks; here he has been dead four days; here the stone placed over the cave does not admit the merciful rays of divine light. Here, according to Scripture, “from the dead man, as from one who is not, confession perishes” (Ecclus. 17), unless perhaps God in his mercy should at some time change the heart of stone into a heart of flesh.

[Col. 0909A] This is the evil conscience that rushes, falls, and collapses through such perils—indeed, precipices—making itself in some fashion tranquil when the prosperity of this world plays with and deceives it; when the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul and the wicked person is blessed; when the favour of preachers and the fear of those unwilling to sin, though unwilling and grieving, smile upon it; when there is no one among all who surround it to rebuke it, or even to dare to rebuke it. Thus is fulfilled what is written: “The prosperity of fools destroys them” (Prov. 32).

Nothing so provokes the majesty of that dread Judge as to sin and sin securely, and to glory in vices as though in virtues. “Do not have mercy,” says the righteous man, “on all who work iniquity” (Ps. 58). This is the iniquity of which God has no mercy: when a person defends what God hates and asserts that sin is righteousness, so as to resist the Almighty and have the Almighty resist him. This is that pride concerning which it is written: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Pet. 5). Understand what he says: “resists.” For to resist is to stand against as an equal. But the person who sets out to resist God as an equal is one who, so far as lies in him, destroys what God establishes and establishes what God destroys, calling evil good and good evil, bitter sweet and sweet bitter, light darkness and darkness light (Isa. 5). This tranquillity is nourished by impunity, mother of security and negligence, stepmother of virtues, destruction of religious life, moth of holiness.

## Chapter V. On the evil and troubled conscience

[Col. 0909C] An evil conscience is also troubled when it is both detected and caught in the act of its sins. While it believes itself to feed on pleasures, it yields to human anxieties, struck by shame and confusion, as it is written: “The sinner is caught in the works of his hands” (Ps. 9). For example, someone seeks adultery for pleasure. There he is caught for anxiety, and anxiety is far greater than pleasure, to the complete shame and distress of a person who both lives and thinks as a human being. Although some are converted to God in the very act of being caught, yet the number of those who remain in sin in that very conversion is greater than that of those who leave sin because of shame over sin. Of both it is written: “Fill their faces [Col. 0909D] with shame, and they shall seek your name, O Lord” (Ps. 82). And of others: “I struck them, and they did not grieve; I crushed them, and they refused to receive correction” (Jer. 5).

These are the four streams of consciences, flowing from the fountain of the will. In them the righteous are purified and the unrighteous defiled, so that what is read may come to pass: “Let the one who is filthy become still more filthy, and let the one who is righteous become still more righteous” (Rev. 22). And because the thoughts of human beings, whether good or evil, are rolled about in continual motion, I have resolved, according to my measure, to enumerate for you all the modes of thoughts, whichever way they turn, so that you may know how far we are from him who remains in the same state: our Lord Jesus Christ.

## Chapter VI. On the seven modes of thoughts

[Col. 0910A]

Some thoughts are burdensome, some affectionate, some obscene, some idle, some curious, some suspicious, some distracting.

Understand burdensome thoughts in the soul of the righteous to be those which he wishes to resist but cannot. Whether he wishes it or not, the plague of Egyptian flies rushes into the eyes of his mind, and frogs croak noisily in the inner chambers of his heart. A person often thinks terrible things about faith and horrible things about the Godhead; carried around through phantasms of bodily images, he experiences things which the sinner, burdened by them, shudders to vomit forth even in confession. And the more strictly he does not present his members as weapons of iniquity to sin, the more tightly he is shaken and assailed by such a spirit. For when that insatiable [Col. 0910B] murderer sees himself excluded from outward sensuality, he attacks and enters the inner regions with gathered strength. But the spiritual person, who judges all things, is not ignorant of his wiles: he represses what he can; what he cannot repress, he endures. For if he bears a dog’s barking, he does not fear its bite. It bites when it draws a person into consent; it barks when it suggests, yet does not impose, what it has suggested. Then it does not wound but crowns. Thus, though it torments one who feels it, it does not bind one who does not consent.

Nevertheless, thoughts are burdensome also when, having undertaken Martha’s office, a person is anxious and troubled about many things for many people, so that they may have the means to be sustained in the divine office.

[Col. 0910C] Thoughts are affectionate when a person is concerned with the care of his flesh, as in food and clothing. He is also touched by affection for relatives according to the flesh.

They are obscene when fleshly delight tickles and pricks. But these, like most unclean dregs, must be driven away at the very beginning and from a greater distance.

They are idle when he neither takes delight in them nor is affected by them: for example, when he thinks of a horse running or a bird flying. Here he sits, as it were, between vice and virtue, neither descending to the former nor ascending to the latter.

They are curious when he sets himself to investigate the secrets of his neighbours and, forgetting himself, attends to what belongs to others instead of the things that he himself ought diligently to have examined; now inside, now [Col. 0910D] outside, wandering, talkative, and unable to bear quiet.

They are suspicious when, having no evidence, he suspects evil of his neighbour and interprets in the worse sense things that can incline either way.

They are distracting when he makes plans and deliberates about distant kingdoms and regions, when he is stretched out in questions and reasonings of this kind. “What a most wretched occupation,” according to Solomon (Eccles. 1), “God has given to the children of men, that they should be occupied with it.”

## Chapter VII. On the four spirits that speak continually to a human being

By all these thoughts of human hearts four spirits speak continually: the spirit [Col. 0911A] of the world, the spirit of the flesh, the spirit of the devil, and the Spirit of God.

The spirit of the world suggests vanities; and it then speaks to our heart’s mouth when we love vanity, rejoice in vanity, and take delight in vanity. The spirit of the flesh speaks when we seek what is soft for the flesh and its senses, when we provide for its care in desires and pleasure. The spirit of the devil speaks when we think bitter thoughts and utter harsh ones: sorrowful within ourselves, angry with others, ungrateful and envious, without affection, without faithfulness. The Spirit of God speaks when we both meditate and speak sweet things, cheerful toward ourselves and our neighbours in every sweetness and goodness, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

## Epilogue of the Little Book

[Col. 0911B] These are the states of conscience, these the thoughts of consciences, these the spirits speaking in our thoughts; and your conscience sees and distinguishes them better than my page does. I have become foolish; you compelled me. Yet I preferred to pour out my ignorance [Col. 0912A] rather than put your face to shame. If anything has been well said, attribute it to yourself, for the sake of whose faith the Son of God gave both understanding and word. If anything has been said otherwise, attribute it nonetheless to yourself, who commanded it.

Spare also my haste; for nothing is so contrary, nothing so discordant in writing, as thoroughness and speed. For finding worthily what you seek, and clothing more worthily in suitable words what you find, requires an apt place, leisure time, a lively intellect, and a practised pen.

Yet hide the letter—or the book, if you prefer to call it so; or, if you decide to publish it, keep silent about the author’s name. The Author of salvation knows—He alone to whom belong all honour and glory—how much I love and honour [Col. 0912B] your person and the salvation of your soul. He is the Lord Jesus, who both gives Himself to you and crowns you with mercy and compassions. Farewell, servant of God, and remember me in your prayers.

[Col. 0911]

# A Very Ancient Anonymous Book of the Order of Saint Benedict, On the Stability of the Soul

D. Bern. Pez, *Ascetic Library*, vol. IV, p. 1, from a Melk manuscript codex.

## Notice

This most elegant little book—so elegant, that is, as the Middle Ages could produce—was brought to my attention by two Melk manuscripts. The first, a quarto paper manuscript marked with the letter N, no. 14, was written by our Conrad of Geisenfeld in 1444 at the renowned monastery of Tegernsee, where today, however, no copy of this little work is to be found, so far as I recall. The other, an octavo marked B, no. 90, was likewise copied at Melk not much later by an unknown monk.

From neither manuscript, moreover, can anything certain be determined concerning the author. For although, in the table prefixed to the latter codex, this little work is attributed to Hugh of Saint Victor, the illustrious ornament of the Regular Canons of Saint Augustine, scarcely anyone who reads even a few lines will fail to think it entirely different. Without doubt, the compiler of that table received the occasion for error from another work of not greatly dissimilar subject, entitled *The Cloister of the Soul*. In more recent manuscript codices this is assigned to Hugh of Saint Victor; in older ones, to Hugh of Fouilloy, a Benedictine, to whom it truly belongs.

But whoever may ultimately have been the genuine author of *The Cloister of the Soul*, that work, being exceedingly diffuse and divided into four books, is altogether unlike this little book *On the Stability of the Soul*, both in style and title. Besides, it is sufficiently clear from the prologue that our anonymous author wrote at least around the beginning of the twelfth century. There he confesses that he had read the other virtues treated sufficiently and abundantly by the Fathers, but that concerning this virtue—stability, the bond holding the other virtues together—he could find nothing written specifically. This an author could scarcely have said after the publication of the four books *On the Cloister of the Soul* by Hugh of Saint Victor or Hugh of Fouilloy, both of whom flourished around the year 1130.

Finally, one may reasonably judge from the beginning of the cited prologue, from the familiar use of the Benedictine Rule’s term “stability,” and so forth, that the writer of this little work was a monk, perhaps an abbot, and moreover attached to the Benedictine order. I say nothing of the name Benedict, which he appears to have bestowed upon the person of his spiritual son, for whose benefit he wrote, solely out of love for his own order and for Benedict, its founder.

# Book on the Stability of the Soul

[Col. 0911]

## Prologue

[Col. 0911C]

After, through prevenient divine grace, I had withdrawn to the camp of spiritual warfare, despising the vanity of the world, and when I was repeatedly asking the Lord in prayer for stability in this blessed undertaking, I began often and long to consider with myself the ways in which this stability, which I desired, might consist; how it might be acquired; and how, once acquired, it might be retained. For I had read that the Fathers had treated the other virtues sufficiently and abundantly. [Col. 0912C] But concerning this virtue, the binding agent, so to speak, of the others, I could find nothing written specifically.

Therefore, what occurred to my mind while I was contemplating the good of this most necessary virtue and investigating what it is and of what sort, I have taken care to set down in writing and send to you, most beloved son Benedict. For if I exhort you in writing of whatever kind, as I had been accustomed to exhort you by living voice—you whom the Lord, with my ministry cooperating, has deigned to call to His service, and whose stability gives me joy no less than my own—[Col. 0913A] I do not think that I should therefore be accused of rashness. For why should it not be permitted to instruct with childish writings one whom it was permitted to form from childhood by spoken words? Thus I think that I may justly be charged by no one with presumption for daring to write though unskilled, since I have sent what I think to be read by no one except you, who are not unaware of my ignorance.

## Chapter I. That the virtue of stability consists of three parts

We judge the virtue of stability to consist of three parts and, as it were, to have three members. For there is stability of body, of the senses, and of mind. Stability of body properly concerns place: namely, that each person, content with a place suited to his vow and purpose, should move from it only when necessity compels or special usefulness strongly recommends it.

By stability of the bodily senses, however, we mean that a person should set all the senses of his body, as it were, in a prison-house of discipline and not allow them to wander off in search of anything useless or unbecoming.

Stability of mind is that, establishing all one’s impulses, desires, and thoughts, as it were, in a most narrow place of divine fear and love, one should desire, seek, or think of nothing except God and those things that help and assist in seeking, finding, and meriting Him.

If you wish to sever and separate from one another these three members of the one true stability—so as to desire to attain and hold the first without the second and third, or the second without the first or third, or the third [Col. 0913C] without the second or first—you will not only be deprived of the fullness of this threefold virtue, but will not perfectly or usefully obtain any portion of it. For who has attained the first member of this virtue, namely stability of place, without the second and third—that is, without senses steadied under spiritual discipline, or without stability of mind? How can one be stable in bodily senses while wandering and wanton, unstable in mind?

To give an example from each bodily sense: if you are eager to see novel things, to hear diverse and pleasant kinds of music or new reports, and desire varied and exquisite flavours of food, sweet [Col. 0913D] and pleasant scents, and soft, voluptuous touches, how can you remain stable in a place suitable to a spiritual purpose, where you cannot have these things? Moreover, the matter of stability of mind is clear: one who lacks it can be stable in no place.

It is futile effort and vain labour to wish to steady the bodily senses without stability of place and mind. For one who wanders about everywhere in body and is led in mind toward various desires and different lusts—how will such a person restrain the senses of the body under spiritual discipline, so that they do not run about wherever the wandering body has brought them, or wherever the wanton mind has ordered them to run as servants of its desires?

However much anyone may strive, he will by no means attain stability of mind without stability of place [Col. 0914A] and of the bodily senses. For the mind readily changes with its place; and you cannot in any way establish mind and thought in the fear and love of God unless you first endeavour to restrain the bodily senses with the reins of reason and the bridle of spiritual discipline.

Therefore you will either lack the good of this threefold virtue entirely, or certainly possess it all together. For to desire to seize and retain some portion of true stability apart from its whole is like wishing, when building a house, to set a foundation without wall and roof, or a roof without wall and foundation, or a wall without foundation and roof.

## Chapter II. On the foundation of the house of stability

[Col. 0914B] We may, then, without impropriety identify in this house of stability, as stated above, three parts of a house: foundation, walls, and roof. Its foundation may fittingly be understood as stability of mind. For just as the foundation gives the whole structure of a house resting upon it, as it were, its principle of subsistence, bearing and holding the entire fabric, so stability of mind in some way produces, governs, and contains the other parts of this virtue. And just as a structure raised without a foundation will undoubtedly fall when wind drives against it or a storm shakes it, so the rest of this virtue’s building cannot stand without stability of mind when driven by the wind or storm of temptations.

The disciplined stability of the senses may likewise appropriately be called the walls of this [Col. 0914C] spiritual house. For the walls of a house are made to guard and preserve the possessions of the future inhabitant; they create within for the householder a certain private space, and contain doors and windows which are opened and closed at the appropriate time: opened indeed for necessities, closed to exclude what is harmful or useless. Thus, for guarding and protecting the spiritual wealth of our guest—that is, the inward human being—there must be erected, as it were, a wall of the spiritual house: the moderation or discipline of the senses. This wall should make a certain private space for the inward householder, lest the external senses, wandering everywhere and roaming as though outside without discipline, take in something unbecoming or useless [Col. 0914D] by which the peace or privacy of the inward guest is disturbed.

## Chapter III. On the windows of the same house

This house of ours also has its windows and its door, which, at the householder’s discretion, should be opened or closed at a time appropriate to them, to admit necessities or exclude harms. What, then, are these windows, and what is this door? I would most rightly call these windows the five bodily senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. Through these windows the inward human being looks out upon external things, knows what has been seen, and desires what has been known.

These windows were placed in the structure of our body by God Himself, the maker of the bodily house, in order to confer a most necessary light: knowledge both of visible things and, from the consideration of those things, of Himself. [Col. 0915A] Yet although these windows have been granted for the use of necessity, the guest himself can abuse them, so that they admit darkness rather than light, and introduce death rather than what is necessary for life. Hence the prophet says: “Death has climbed through our window; it has entered our houses” (Jer. 9). What else is it for death to climb through our windows and enter our houses than for the lust of sin to enter the dwelling-place of the mind through bodily senses, by which, while the soul delights in it, it dies by the death of sin?

Therefore close the windows of your body at a fixed and fitting time: “Turn away your eyes, lest they see vanity” (Ps. 118 [119]). Do not look carelessly outside upon harmful things, lest death creep in through the very place from which you should have drawn necessary light. Necessary light is knowledge of the Creator, which can be conceived from consideration of visible creation. For, as the Apostle says, “the invisible things of God are perceived through understanding from the things that have been made” (Rom. 1).

Look upon the beauty of the universe—heaven, earth, sea, and all things in them. Consider what a fabric it is, how great and how beautiful. Reason with yourself and say: “Oh, who, what kind, and how great is He by whom all these things were created, arranged, and ordered? By whom are they ruled, governed, and sustained?” Such a one, so great, is most justly to be feared, honoured, and loved. O unhappy human being, if he does not serve Him whom all these things serve; does not obey Him whom all these things obey; [Col. 0915C] and does not love Him who, from no necessity but solely from His goodness, created both humanity and all things!

If you consider these and similar things within yourself by reasoning, so as from examining creatures to know, honour, and love their Creator, the windows of your body draw in the necessary light for which they were surely granted to you by the Creator Himself. But if, while looking at these visible creatures, you wish to love them more than their Creator, and take more pleasure in their sight and use than in knowledge and love of their Maker, death has entered through your windows. Those things that ought to have enlightened you have taken away your true light; and those which ought to have been necessary servants have become wicked robbers [Col. 0915D] to you, because they have stolen from you the soul’s life, which is knowledge and love of God. The bodily senses, therefore, are the windows of the inward human being; yet according to the choice of the person whom they serve, they may be either beneficial or harmful.

## Chapter IV. On the door of the house

What can more fittingly be called the door of this wall than a human being’s mouth? For just as, when a door is shut, those outside do not know what is in the house, whereas when it is opened they learn what is held within, so, when the door of the mouth is shut, what is in the heart remains hidden. But if it is opened for forming the words of speech, what the speaker holds within is readily seen. Hence it is written: “Even a fool, if silent, will be thought wise” (Prov. 17).

For when a fool is silent, because the mouth’s door is shut, the folly hidden within [Col. 0916A] is concealed; without doubt it would betray itself if the speech of the speaker opened the mouth’s gate. “For the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart” (Matt. 12), because what lies hidden in the heart’s secret place flows out through words to be made public. Thus the body’s mouth is not inappropriately called the door of the house about which we are speaking, for it is opened and shut at a person’s discretion.

## Chapter V. On the roof of the spiritual house

We have therefore laid the foundation of this spiritual building, raised its walls, and set windows and a door within them. It remains for us also to place a roof above it.

The roof of the building so often mentioned may fittingly be called stability of place, provided that the location is not contrary or hostile to the purpose of spiritual life. For a house’s roof holds back storms, wards off rain, receives the force of winds, and provides its inhabitant with peace and security. So also stability of place—or a place suited to the school of virtues and God’s service—restrains the storms, rains, winds, and tempests of temptations, and safeguards for you peace and serenity in living well.

Is it not a grievous storm to be placed in a location where the very appearance of the place, wickedly alluring, draws you toward doing things that you ought not do at all? Where it is unavoidable to see what it is not lawful to desire? Where, even unwillingly, you see and hear things which you would not dare not only to perform but even to think? Are not the world’s riches, blandishments, and luxuries violent rains, pouring down, oppressing, and softening the whole substance of the soul? Unless they are kept off by stability in a place suited to a spiritual purpose, they draw, oppress, and soften even one who resists and is unwilling. [Col. 0916C] Are not the companionships of lovers of the world violent winds? Often by word, but always in some measure by example, they compel one to love what they love, assault the very substance of virtue with all their strength, and very often make it fall.

It is therefore necessary that, once you have laid stability of mind as the foundation of this spiritual structure and established the bodily senses in the fear and love of God, you add stability of place as a necessary roof, so that you may be wholly steadfast, continually protected, always peaceful, and secure. Thus you have the complete house of the spiritual structure: foundation, walls, and roof.

Now that we have portrayed the spiritual building of stability, it remains to describe its stewards and inhabitants: the male guest and female guest, the offspring of both, and the entire household of the house. Finally, let us see what can keep this house stable, quiet, and peaceful, and what can disturb its stability, peace, and quiet.

## Chapter VI. On the inhabitants of the house

Who, then, can more truly be called the inhabitant, guest, and ruler of this house than the human spirit within it? For, relying on divine grace, it builds this house for itself, inhabits the house once built, and rules and governs it. But is it alone? No, [Col. 0917A] not alone. It has a diligent fellow-worker and tireless helper. It has a sober and modest, chaste and honourable wife. It has, I say, reason, naturally innate and joined to it as a wife. If the spirit does all things by her counsel and presumes to do nothing except what she exhorts, suggests, and advises, it will provide wisely and fittingly, and order all things justly. For reason naturally desires and loves everything just and honourable, while it recoils from and hates everything disgraceful and unjust with all its strength.

O happy spirit, therefore, if it delights in the chaste embraces of so wise a wife, resplendent with such sober beauty, so lovely and gracious! Taught by her counsel and supported by her help, it will avoid everything harmful [Col. 0917B] and seek and do whatever is beneficial.

God has placed two natures in the soul: one higher, namely reason; the other lower, namely sensuality. Reason is the higher power or virtue of the soul, by which it inclines toward spiritual things and preserves within itself the image of God. Sensuality administers and orders these lower, visible things, which can be perceived and desired by the bodily senses.

## Chapter VII. On the threefold offspring of spirit and reason

This happy union will abound not only in so many and such great goods, but will also be blessed with beloved, elegant, noble offspring. For the first fruit of this spiritual marriage is faith; the second, hope; the third, charity. For nothing can be hoped for or loved as hoped for unless it is first believed to exist. Yet something may be believed even if it is neither hoped for nor loved.

We therefore call faith the firstborn. As soon as reason and spirit join in mutual embraces, faith shines forth. Reason gives birth to faith. For, concerning things whose knowledge we receive from the spirit that inhabits and gives life to the body, we investigate their causes and origins under the guidance of reason. When a human being looks upon the beauty of the universe, the structure of heaven and earth, a wonderful and delightful work, reason seeks the craftsman and author of the work. For by reasoning it concludes that none of these things received the beginning of its existence through itself or from itself. For if these things had been made through themselves or from themselves, why would not other similar things afterward have been made by themselves, or be made at present? [Col. 0917D] It is therefore clear that they had a creator, who made them when He wished and later made no similar things because He did not wish to.

Further: if these things had their existence from themselves, they would surely be subject to no change, variation, or defect; for just as they would have conferred existence upon themselves, so they would have conferred upon themselves immutability and the eternity of an unbounded state, and just as they would have claimed being for themselves, so surely they would have claimed true and perfect being. Since, therefore, they are subject to change and defect, they show by that very fact that they are not from themselves. There must consequently be something from which all things have their existence. Whoever that is, He alone is the true Creator, Ruler, God, and Lord.

[Col. 0918A] When reason thus instructs a person, it gives birth to faith in the one true God. Reason therefore asserts that God exists and proves it by the irrefutable truth of its arguments. Faith, then, is the firstborn offspring begotten from the union of spirit and reason. After its emergence, hope is born second in order and age.

## Chapter VIII. On hope

Once someone has begun to believe that God exists and to believe in God, it follows that he cannot doubt that God is good and just. Reason utterly refuses to believe that He is not good, or unjust, or can be so; nor does a sound and uncorrupted human understanding dare even to entertain such a thought.

For since justice is giving to each thing what belongs to it, nothing is so just as God, who alone truly and fully observes this, and who implanted in a creature capable of perceiving justice an inseparable and natural principle of justice—the teacher of justice—which continually demands this of that creature and does not permit it to depart from justice insofar as it wishes to follow that principle.

Since every heart and tongue therefore unanimously confess God to be just and good, it is evident that He cannot fail to love what He Himself is, nor be contrary or hostile to His own essence. Thus the good person is God’s friend; the evil and unjust person is God’s enemy. Reason, moreover, maintains that God’s and justice’s benefit is necessarily owed to a friend, but God’s and justice’s punishment to an enemy. For a creature is good, or called good, only by willing what its Creator wills; and it is evil by refusing to will what its Creator wills. Who, using reason, would not judge that one who obeys the Creator—to whom every creature most justly ought to be subject—is worthy of glory, and that one who rebels is worthy of punishment? Reason therefore establishes by necessary arguments that good things are owed to the good, and evil things to the evil.

From this, then, hope is born. For after a person has believed that God exists and is good and just, reason does not permit doubt that, justice requiring it, He ought to repay good things to the good and evil things to the evil. Thus you have faith and hope issuing from the marriage of spirit and reason.

## Chapter IX. On charity

Charity is generated last in age, but first in dignity. For nothing is loved unless it is first both hoped for and believed. Therefore, one who believes that God exists and made all things, who sees the works of the world’s structure so delightful and useful to himself, and knows that through the Creator’s gratuitous mercy they serve his need and advantage—how can he fail to love with all his inmost being Him whose work he sees to be so lovable and so useful to himself? How can he fail to love Him whose works he cannot fail to love?

When people see a human work that is useful, sound, beautiful, and artfully composed, they usually admire the skill and praise and love the artisan—although a human being can do nothing except join things which the Creator makes separately or separate things which He has joined. If, then, a human being is loved by another human being for that tiny thing which he somehow appears able to make, God will most justly be loved: He made the universe, a work of the utmost elegance and infinite wonder, and made humanity itself, and gave human beings the ability to do whatever they can do.

[Col. 0919A] Look upon the sun, moon, stars, birds of heaven, animals of the earth, flowers, and fruits; and if you are human, if you are rational, you surely cannot fail to love the Creator of all these things. For who would not love with all the marrow of the heart Him who gives life to everything breathing, light to everything seeing, and food to everything eating? Count, if you can, the benefits granted to you by your Creator, the indications of His love by which He cherishes you. Since you cannot repay Him anything else for all these things, at least return love to Him who loves you—not as much as you ought, but as much as you can.

Behold, to say nothing of the countless benefits to body and soul, let us bring forward only two: life and sustenance. If you had these from any human being, [Col. 0919B] you would undoubtedly love that person with your inmost and whole affection. We see people who have received from others not life and sustenance itself, but some assistance toward life and sustenance, love them with such ardour that they do not hesitate to lose their very lives for them. How much love, then, ought you, O human being, to render to God, from whom you have whatever you have, whatever you are, and whatever you can do?

When reason speaks these things to the spirit and thus instructs a person without any clatter of words, it gives birth to charity, offspring most like itself. It is therefore clear from what we have briefly and concisely said, and from similar considerations, that charity is reason’s daughter. Thus faith, hope, and charity are begotten from the lawful union of spirit and reason.

## Chapter X. On sensuality, reason’s maidservant

[Col. 0919C] But it sometimes happens that the spirit, forgetting lawful, chaste, and honourable love, delights and lingers in adulterous and incestuous embraces. For reason has a maidservant naturally wanton and impudent, uncontrolled and shameless—namely sensuality. If she wished to observe the law appointed for her by God, her duty would be to obey her mistress, reason, in all things and through all things. For she proceeds rightly only when she does not depart from reason’s teaching and command.

And it very often happens that the insolent maid begins to hold her mistress in contempt and follow her own desires, and entices her mistress’s very husband to her shameless embraces. Ensnared by her blandishments, the spirit forgets its lawful wife and gives itself wholly to the maidservant’s loves. By the flesh’s allurements she makes it so foolish, mad, and senseless that it savours only visible and earthly things, and utterly sets aside faith, hope, and love of heavenly and invisible things.

## Chapter XI. On the threefold offspring of spirit and flesh

It follows that from this adulterous union there are begotten most foul offspring, wholly contrary to and unlike the offspring of the lawful marriage: namely unbelief, despair, and contempt of God.

For when the spirit, captivated by sensuality’s blandishments, begins to love only what is taken in through bodily senses, it often happens that, because it loves only things that are seen, it utterly loses faith in invisible things. And because it loves visible things and things perceptible to bodily senses, it thinks that only the things it loves exist. From this unbelief or faithlessness is born: because, while earthly and visible things are loved excessively, faith in heavenly and invisible things is lost.

Thus a person is often so overwhelmed and blinded by the habit of sinning that, though once enlightened by nature’s endowment, and both seeing and desiring true and eternal goods, later, made mad by disgraceful desires, he neither sees nor desires them. Hence it is written that, after the king of Babylon captured the king of Jerusalem, he gouged out his eyes. For after the king of confusion—the devil, or the habit of sinning—has conquered and taken captive by wicked desires the king of Jerusalem, that is, the human spirit ruling the kingdom of its charge in peace, [Col. 0920B] he extinguishes every light of faith within it. Thus from the incestuous union of spirit and sensuality arises the wicked fruit of unbelief.

Despair follows it in the order of generation, because no one can hope for what he does not believe exists.

Then contempt of God follows, because one who has lost the eyes of faith and also the anchor of hope has nothing left but to despise God Himself. Neither faith binds nor hope attracts the faithless and despairing person to God’s honour or love. Therefore, just as faith, hope, and charity are begotten from the lawful and honourable marriage of reason and spirit, so from the adultery of sensuality and spirit there spring shameful shoots contrary to these. And just as the whole choir of virtues is propagated from those three, so all the monsters of vices are propagated from these three.

[Col. 0920C] For what virtue is lacking, or can be lacking, where faith, hope, and charity exist? Indeed, it cannot even truly be imagined that any virtue is absent where these are present. Hence the Apostle, after stating, “Now,” that is, in this world, “I know in part; but then,” that is, in the future life, “I shall know as I also am known,” adds: “But now faith, hope, charity, these three remain” (1 Cor. 13). It is as though he said: “Then I shall know; but now, in order that I may arrive there, faith, hope, and charity—these three—remain.” These three are few indeed, but very useful; from them the entire household of virtues is begotten.

For has humility, obedience, patience, prudence, justice, courage, or temperance ever been, or could it be, praiseworthy and acceptable to God unless faith nourished it at the breast, hope fed it, and charity strengthened it?

From these three, then, the other virtues proceed, are nourished, and subsist. Conversely, from the three vices just mentioned, which are contrary to those three virtues, the foul ranks of all vices rush forth; and whatever corrupts and defiles character springs from this corrupted threefold root: unbelief, despair, and contempt of God.

## Chapter XII. On the conflict of virtues and vices

There consequently arise grave dissensions and an implacable war between the lawful camp of virtues and the turbulent ranks of vices, because the two armies naturally disagree, necessarily opposing and continually fighting one another.

[Col. 0921A] From this discord and continual war, the inward peace of the householder is disturbed, and the whole structure of the house is weakened, shaken, and overthrown. But if the faithful husband does not abandon the lawful marriage chamber of his mistress, reason, this entire building of his house will be made stable forever, and he himself will enjoy in it unceasing quiet and endless peace.

## Chapter XIII. How reason humbles the wanton maidservant, and how reason admonishes her husband

For the continual preservation of her own salvation and peace, and that of her household, reason’s necessary duty will be to tame, restrain, and chastise the wanton maidservant, so that she may know herself to be a servant and not shamelessly seek her mistress’s marriage chamber. If reason perceives that she is even slightly attempting this crime, she must humble her by such great and numerous [Col. 0921B] labours and torment her with such sufferings that, while miserable life is scarcely permitted her, no wantonness whatever may delight her.

Reason must also admonish her husband without ceasing not to be softened by the seductive enticements of the wickedly flattering maidservant; he should remember that all her blandishments are snares for his salvation, and regard with suspicion everything that she presents as outwardly and temporarily pleasant and delightful.

If, therefore, by such counsels and continual exhortations reason steadfastly strengthens and instructs the spirit, and firmly restrains the unlawful and unbridled impulses of sensuality the maidservant, then reason and her spouse will rest in the delight of mutual and chaste love. They will be enriched with noble and blessed offspring, adorned with every beauty of virtue, and with a well-ordered and disciplined household. The entire, most narrow structure of their house will remain stable and inviolable, and no storm driving from without will shake it, provided that chaste love and proper order are preserved inwardly in all things and through all things.

Yet this shameless and unbridled maidservant very often disturbs this chaste love and proper order, when the ignoble maid presumptuously seeks the place, marriage chamber, and dignity of her mistress. For, in order to draw her master, her mistress’s husband, into her degraded love, she is accustomed to offer him the world’s riches, honours, and pleasures as cups of honeyed poison. These taste sweet for a time, but at last pierce the throat of the soul with the sting of eternal death. Yet the deceitful maidservant exerts all the powers of her ingenuity to make what delights be loved and what kills be concealed.

## Chapter XIV. The maidservant’s suggestion to her master

She proposes and, with unceasing whispering, instils into the ears of the house’s master how pleasant and useful it is to abound in money, gold, silver, translucent gems, precious stones, varied and elaborate clothing, broad and spacious fields and estates; how honourable it is to glory in human power and rank, and in the splendour of a celebrated name gained from transitory power and honour; how sweet it is to delight in diverse flavours of food, sweet fragrances of spices and flowers, the ringing songs of every kind of music, the charms of meadows, groves, and streams, hunts with dogs, the leaps of stags and roe deer, the sport and flight of hawks, beautiful sights of women, and voluptuous touches.

[Col. 0922A] While sensuality thus suggests to the spirit these and other pleasures of the same kind, it raises and stirs up, so to speak, certain quarrels in this peaceful and quiet house of stability. For it strives with all its powers to bring about a divorce in the lawful marriage between reason and spirit, so that it may itself succeed into the place of the repudiated wife. For transitory pleasures belong to its jurisdiction. Therefore they cannot be loved at all unless reason, naturally the enemy of all temporal pleasures, is repudiated, and sensuality, the harlot, is substituted for the lawful wife, loved, [Col. 0922B] and made mistress.

When, therefore, sensuality has impelled the spirit toward love of pleasures, it has already seized the mistress’s place; the foul handmaid has already persuaded him to love her in place of noble Reason. It follows that the structure formerly governed with the counsel and assistance of Reason, once she has been repudiated and the concubine loved, totters, falls, and is destroyed. Such are the ways of this concubine; such is her inborn emptiness: whoever clings to her love, she plunges into love of temporal and unstable things. Whoever loves what is unstable must himself become unstable. For, according to the Prophet, “the wicked walk in a circle” (Ps. 11); they do not stand—that is, they cannot be stable—but walk in a circle, that is, amid the shifting and instability of temporal things, in the desire for shifting and [Col. 0922C] unstable things. Therefore those who love unstable things cannot be stable, but are rolled and whirled about with the very things whose temporal enjoyment they congratulate themselves upon.

It is therefore clear that, when the spirit, given over to love of sensible and unstable things, becomes unstable, the edifice of stability—which, while itself remaining stable, it ought to govern with the aid of Reason—slips, is overthrown, and is scattered. Hence it is evident that the unlawful union of spirit and sensuality is the source of inward rebellion and of total destruction; and that this most orderly house and all its goods are reduced to nothing unless this public evil is prevented.

## CHAPTER XV. How vigilant Reason should warn her husband and address the spirit.

[Col. 0922D]

Let Reason, then, keep watch in order to avert this danger; let her keep watch. Let her look about on every side, and not neglect continually to warn and fortify her own companion against this wickedness. At convenient and inconvenient times let her preach to him and instruct him that the pleasures of the world, which the cunning and deceitful handmaid promises in order to commend herself to him, bear only the empty name of good or blessedness, and that in them there is no reality or essence of blessedness. Thus let her speak to him continually, lest he be drawn by the seductive flatteries of evil-persuading sensuality into love of fleeting and false goods:

What good is, or can be, that which must pass away and perish? Indeed, how is that [Col. 0923A] good which assuredly is nothing? For things that can pass away do not truly exist. Transitory things do indeed possess some image of being, but no truth of being. If, therefore, they do not truly exist, how can they be true goods? Those who embrace and love them as though they were goods are truly foolish. Is it not folly to love things that you cannot love for long? To call, or wish to be, your own things that neither are yours nor can become yours? Do you wish to hear what is yours? Hear briefly: you yourself, and what is in you or beneath you, are yours. For whatever you are not, or is not situated beneath you, is not yours. If, therefore, you possess yourself, you will have all that is yours within yourself. Do not then seek anything of yours outside yourself, since you can find it only within yourself. For all transitory things have been granted to human beings not as property, but for relieving the needs of the body.

[Col. 0923B]

For if they were truly a human being’s own possessions, they could neither be abandoned by the human being nor abandon the human being. But now, because they both are abandoned and abandon us, they themselves show that they are not a human being’s own possessions. Do not, therefore, desire as your own what nature has made foreign to you.

Whoever among mortals says that any earthly thing situated outside himself is his own property has assuredly not yet understood well or fully either his own condition, the order of created things, or the Creator’s intention concerning them. For God created man in such a way that He gave the rest of visible creation to humanity not as property, but as a provision for relieving need; and He intended that those things demanded by human need should be supplied equally to all, so that all might use them equally and in common, not for pleasure but for necessity.

[Col. 0923C]

The Creator’s intention may be inferred most clearly from the fact that the most welcome benefit of this visible light, and one most necessary to humanity, is supplied equally to all, and not more to one person than another. The brightness of sun, moon, or stars, rain or dew, and the changing seasons never serve one person more than another; nor do they show greater regard in their service for a rich person than for a poor one, a nobleman than for a commoner, a king than for a soldier. It is clear, therefore, that, just as the benefits of heaven are common to all, so also the fruits and riches of the earth ought to be common to all—

[Col. 0923D]

—if human beings’ insatiable greed allowed it.

Why, then, O man, do you seize for yourself a larger share of the earth or of its fruits, when the very elements from whose combination and productive power the fruits of the earth arise do not favor you more than your neighbor, but bestow upon all alike the benefit of their natural efficacy? Whatever things your need does not require, if you draw them to yourself as though they were or could be your own, this is not gathering your own possessions but plundering another’s. Hence it was rightly said by a certain wise man:

> Every rich man is either unjust or the heir of an unjust man.

[Note: [Col. 0923D] Augustine.]

For, according to these deceptive riches, the rich man is he who surpasses others in abundance of earthly goods. Certainly, therefore, either he himself gathered these riches—

[Col. 0924A]

—or he inherited them after they had been gathered by others. But whichever of these is the case, he is undoubtedly unjust, because the things God created to be common to all and distributed equally among all according to each person’s need, he either himself—unsatisfied with necessities—seized away from the use due to others, or received and possesses as heir the plunder unjustly acquired by others. Such a man has deservedly inherited both the name and the injustice of a plunderer, if he refuses to distribute to the needy and make common what exceeds his own need. He therefore strays far from God’s justice who reckons as his own anything in this world that lies outside himself. Thus human beings ought not to love things that are not their own and that must either be abandoned or abandon them.

[Col. 0924B]

But come now, I ask: even if these earthly goods were not momentary and fleeting, and could belong to man, what is there in them which a rational person ought rightly to love—indeed, which, when examined and considered carefully, does not become contemptible? Are these, then, the things people admire and love: riches, honors, pleasures? Let us now investigate each of them more attentively and see whether they are worthy of human love.

## CHAPTER XVI. Reason urges the contempt of riches.

Earthly riches, for whose desire human ambition burns, consist in gold, silver, precious stones, broad fields and estates, and varied and elaborate garments. First, concerning gold, silver, and precious stones—which mortals rank first—it may be said that their high value among human beings has not been produced by any inborn dignity or usefulness in them, but, so to speak, by the deluded vanity of mankind.

[Col. 0924C]

For what is so foolish, so empty, as to assign first place in dignity or usefulness to a thing that scarcely possesses the last, and to love as necessary—or more than necessary—things which human need appears not to require at all? Although this is evident and almost unknown to no one, it is clearer than light from the fact that many nations neither possess nor care to possess riches of this kind, since they are useless. As most people can do without them, so certainly all people everywhere on earth could do without them if they wished. And O, if they could only wish to do without them as well! Undoubtedly the human race would thereby fare more happily and more evenly.

[Col. 0924D]

For to what does the accursed hunger for gold not compel mortal hearts? No fire, no flood has ever brought about slaughters as great as those wrought by this dog-like hunger; nothing has so perverted and overthrown the human race from the welfare of body and soul.

Why, then, is that loved with so great affection and desired with so great a clamor, in which there is nothing, or at least very little, of usefulness or good, but which is the material and cause of very many and immeasurable evils? Yet the vain and insane foolishness of human beings prefers this snare of the human race to things most useful and most necessary, and by its own false estimation attaches the name of dignity and usefulness to a thing of almost no worth.

[Col. 0925A]

O mind of rational man, greatly degenerate from reason! Men are accustomed to exchange a very great weight of silver or gold for a small weight of precious and most necessary things—namely, grain, wine, or oil. For these sustain and nourish human life; but gold and silver have contributed nothing to human welfare or advantage, and very much to human harm and ruin. It is therefore an error to judge things otherwise than they really are, and to esteem things of the lowest worth better than better things.

But people who do not yet walk in every respect along the path of purified truth are deceived by a certain superficial and wholly useless beauty of such things, so that the unskilled value them as highly as they are beautiful.

[Col. 0925B]

But grant that such things have as much worth as beauty: what, nevertheless, does another’s beauty matter to you, O man—a beauty which you can admire but certainly cannot make your own? Why, then, do you admire or love things that are not yours and are wholly unworthy of your love and admiration? For if you weigh your own dignity, you will admire the splendor of no inanimate thing. All inanimate things, being beneath your excellence, appear unworthy of admiration.

Whoever, therefore, admires, loves, or highly values such things, or believes that in obtaining or possessing them there is a greater share of blessedness than in other metals, does not yet in every respect follow Reason, the guide of truth and light of the soul.

[Col. 0925C]

For if he obeyed her counsels, he would seek or love gold and silver no more than iron, nor value gems more highly than pebbles. Iron is more useful than gold or silver, and pebbles are more necessary than gems.

## CHAPTER XVII. It urges the abandonment of ambition for possessions.

Ambition for fields and estates, while it pleads the needs of human frailty—which cannot subsist without their revenues—endeavors to cloak the vice of greed under the pretext of necessity. Because bodily weakness requires the use of such things, man supposes that he may lawfully gather them beyond necessity and claim them as his property.

[Col. 0925D]

We know, indeed, that the fruits of the earth are owed for the nourishment of living creatures; but, with all due respect to human beings, beasts of burden seem to use them more moderately and soberly than men. For all brute animals desire only what they are drawn to by natural appetite and do not exceed the bounds of necessity in using it. Man, however, not content with necessity, gives free rein to greed and thinks he needs as many things as, under greed’s urging, he desires to possess. Hence comes what would that it did not come to pass: one little man claims as his private property what could suffice for many; and because one person has a superfluity of many things, even necessities are taken away from many persons.

[Col. 0926A]

Thus wretched poverty and grievous want first arose in the human race, because things which, divided equally among all, could have been sufficient for all, were seized by some who were not content with this equality and who drew to themselves, however acquired, superfluities; thereby they robbed what was owed to the need of many. For if human beings were content with necessities, everything could suffice for everyone; and if they wished only to fill the need that is enough for nature, they would not seek the revenues of many fields and broad estates. One ought to seek only what is sufficient for nature, not what pleasure desires. Therefore, if you seek merely to satisfy nature, you will be content with very few and very small things; and you will endeavor to live in such a way that you desire in life nothing without which you can live.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On despising the beauty and costliness of clothing.

[Col. 0926B]

To glory in the beauty or costliness of garments appears wholly unworthy of a person whose mind is like God. For how can something far more unworthy and lowly than a human being adorn or embellish a human being? Things better and more worthy can add dignity or ornament to things of lower dignity and worth; but lower things cannot bestow upon superior things a fitting beauty which they themselves do not possess. Since man surpasses visible creation in dignity, whatever is beneath him cannot add fitting adornment to him. Therefore a person thrusts himself far beneath himself when he, the adornment of other things, seeks ornaments from the lowest things.

[Col. 0926C]

Hear of a vanity unworthy of man, laughable to every wise person. Men are accustomed to dye the foul skins of little beasts—indeed, of certain mice—and adorn themselves with this ridiculous covering, esteeming themselves thereby much more worthy and honorable. O splendid adornment, bestowed by a ridiculous mouse! They also strive to glitter with silk, gold, silver, and gems, arrogating to themselves a splendor alien to them; and they are not ashamed to glory in it, as though whatever is outstanding in such splendor had not been sewn onto one human being by another, but bestowed upon man by nature.

Yet however much of this non-your-own adornment you fasten upon yourself, O man, you are certainly surpassed by the beauty of lilies and roses; for not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.

[Col. 0926D]

And if you reckon that there is any blessedness in such adornment, you must confess that the grass of the field is more blessed than you.

## CHAPTER XIX. That worldly honor is nothing.

Consider with me from this how slight, how trivial—indeed, how nothing—is the honor of the world, to acquire which almost the entire human race goes mad. Riches and pleasures can provide some aid to human need. But honor can bring nothing of health or usefulness either to soul or body. For what can praise or renown, dignity or illustrious reputation spread far and wide—all of which are referred to honor as limbs to their own head—what, I say, can these add to human welfare or virtue? I know absolutely nothing.

[Col. 0927A]

They can show or proclaim health or virtue already possessed by someone; they cannot give it. What can honor or glory bestowed from outside add to the wise person, who seeks only the glory that is within? For, as the Prophet says: “All the glory of the king’s daughter,” that is, of the wise soul, “is within” (Ps. 44). The wise person performs works of virtue not in order to win transient favor, but solely in order to enrich his own conscience.

Indeed, he would lose both the name and the merit of a wise person if he labored for human favor or honor, which is useful for nothing. For what use is that which can benefit neither body nor soul? It cannot benefit at all, but it can do no small harm. It can take away the virtue or welfare that it cannot bestow, and often destroys the good that it cannot confer.

[Col. 0927B]

For many who have not yet attained the manly and perfect strength of virtue, when received with human honors and favors, begin to delight and glory in them; and those who seemed to flourish with the fruit of virtue, when they abandon humility—the nurse and mother of all virtues—are struck by the rust of arrogance and wither. Unless it remains in humility, virtue itself kills itself: for while it inflates the mind, it destroys itself; and while it lifts the heart into pride, it pierces itself with the sword of self-exaltation. When the mind is inflated by consciousness of virtue, whatever virtue it seemed to possess is slain.

Why, then, do you desire what commonly brings no usefulness but a great deal of vanity? Do not, therefore, be eager for honor or praise; rather, with all eagerness strive by upright conduct to be worthy of praise and honors.

[Col. 0927C]

The one belongs to vanity, the other to uprightness; and as the one is accustomed to weaken and kill virtue, so the other is accustomed to give and preserve it. Whoever, therefore, walking the path of virtue thinks about spreading his reputation, making his name known, or gaining honor, thereby assuredly deprives himself of the virtue which he sought to attain; and unless he resists this vanity with all his strength, he loses whatever virtue he rejoiced to have.

What, then, is to be said of those most wretched persons who do not know how to do good except for human eyes and popular applause, and who, abandoning the treasure of conscience, desire rewards from the talk of others?

[Col. 0927D]

This is to offer for sale at a cheap price a thing of the greatest worth; this is to labor vainly and without fruit; this is to exchange works of virtue, by which true and eternal goods might have been purchased, for the worthless trifles of transient favor.

## CHAPTER XX. It urges that bodily pleasures should not be loved.

Moreover, it should be very easy to persuade a person in whom reason is vigorous, and who is even slightly wise, not to love bodily pleasures. For who would love the most troublesome and most hostile pest of mankind? Pleasure is plainly opposed to body and soul, and hostile both to flesh and spirit. How many diseases, pains, and plagues, like certain fruits of wickedness, are accustomed to arise in the bodies of the pleasure-loving?

[Col. 0928A]

And as for the mind, than which God has given nothing more excellent to man—this divine gift shining forth from the image of God—nothing is known to be so hostile to it as pleasure. For pleasure, strengthened by long habit, extinguishes every light of the heart, hinders counsel, pours darkness upon the understanding, dims the eyes of the mind, and, finally, is accustomed to make foolish even those who seemed wise. When lust rules, intelligence itself must wither and grow dull; nor can wisdom or virtue have any place in the kingdom of pleasure.

Anyone who has experienced the goads of this fury knows that, while afflicted by such madness, he could do or think nothing worthy of a human being, nothing in keeping with wisdom or virtue.

[Col. 0928B]

Therefore nothing is so detestable as pleasure, which, so to speak, strips man of his humanity and changes him into the mind and appetite of a beast; which perverts, overthrows, and extinguishes wisdom, intelligence, and understanding, wherein human dignity chiefly consists. What person, then, would not strive with all his might to banish far from himself this corruption of human dignity? He will certainly be able very easily to do without it forever, if only he lays aside the desire for it. Those eager for this muddy plague think it burdensome to be without it; but for those not eager for it, to be without it is plainly more pleasant than to enjoy it.

If this insane plague of the human race possesses any mad delight or foul pleasure, it does so in order that, like bait placed on a hook, it may taste sweet for a little while, but pierce the jaws with the barb of a tormenting conscience, fouling itself in this mire.

[Col. 0928C]

For pleasure indeed delights briefly and seems sweet for a moment, but immediately leaves behind it the long-lasting torment of sorrowful repentance and cruel conscience.

It is foolish, however, to attend to a delight that will soon pass and not perceive the enduring bitterness that follows; to seek a good—if indeed that is a good—which passes away, and not beware the evil that knows no end. Therefore man, to whom it has been granted and commanded by the Creator not only to look upon present things but also to foresee future ones, should flee those things that feign themselves to be false goods in order to bring true evils; should flee those things which are gentle in appearance but in reality utterly execrable; should flee those things which delight briefly, yet drag those whom they entice into everlasting destruction.

[Col. 0928D]

## CHAPTER XXI. The author’s exhortation.

If, then, by these and similar counsels and continual exhortations Reason does not cease to teach and admonish her husband, the spirit, she will make him perfect in love for herself; and she will prove that the foolish and alluring counsels of her rival and concubine—namely, sensuality—are exceedingly harmful and useless. She will also establish in perpetual firmness the edifice which she herself joined together with her own hands, because she will provide everything conducive to its stability and remove everything harmful to it.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the firmness of the spiritual house.

This, therefore, is the house and edifice: the stability of body, senses, and mind, which, according to Truth’s own assertion, neither descending rains, nor rivers, nor rushing winds can make fall, because it is founded upon firm rock.

[Col. 0929A]

For what is meant by rain except desire, by which each person is tempted, which gradually softens the firmness of faith and makes it dissolve in pleasures? What are rivers except the torrent of all vices, gathered together to shake or destroy this house of virtuous stability? What are winds except the perverse counsels of evil spirits, which they incessantly whisper through sensuality, their familiar attendant, into the human spirit they seek to pervert?

Rains, rivers, and winds rushing upon this house of virtues can indeed strike it, because every kind of temptation and every monstrous vice can assault or tempt the mind of the elect, which clings to its Creator with true and perfect stability; but they cannot move or harm it, because it is founded upon the rock—that is, upon true faith, hope, and love of its Creator.

[Col. 0930A]

This faith, hope, and love are produced, nourished, and kept within us by the divine gift, implanted in us by God, of Reason most like to God.

Here ends the book on the stability of body, senses, and mind, at the monastery of Tegernsee, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December [18 November], in the year 1444.

[Col. 0929]

# DIALOGUE ON THE EATING OF FOWL BY AN ANONYMOUS BENEDICTINE, WHO WROTE ABOUT THE TWELFTH CENTURY

Whether it is permitted in the Rule of St Benedict for robust and healthy cenobites.

(D. Bern. Pezius, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. II, part II, col. 546.)

## NOTICE.

When our most holy lawgiver, in chapter 39 of his Rule, wished to prescribe a definite measure, to be observed perpetually by his monks in food and drink, and the kinds of foods, he used, after some preliminary words, these:

> But all are altogether to abstain from eating the flesh of quadrupeds, except those who are altogether weak and sick.

It is incredible how much diversity of opinion this statement of blessed Benedict has generated from almost the first centuries of his Order down to our own age. Some suppose that by this regular decree monks are forbidden only the flesh of quadrupeds, but not likewise that of bipeds and birds; others, on the contrary, affirm that this rule forbids monks the eating of every kind of flesh without exception.

Those wishing to know the arguments of the two sides should consult the extensive commentary of Fr Edmund Martene on the Rule of St Benedict, where, on chapter 39, he discusses this matter fully and recounts every argument of the defenders of eating fowl. All their arguments come down to this: that St Benedict did not without cause and reason expressly name the flesh of quadrupeds at the cited place, rather than the flesh of whatever animals; and that therefore one who eats birds does not in any way act contrary to St Benedict. They add that this was granted to monks at the Council of Aachen under Emperor Louis the Pious; that the general custom of cenobites and dispensations granted by prelates made such fowling lawful; and, finally, that it is clear that fishes and birds, being produced from waters, have bodies of the same nature, and that the flesh of birds does not provide human bodies with such great inducement to lust as the flesh of land animals—animals which are of the same nature as our bodies—as Peter Abelard argues in his *Exposition on the Hexaemeron*, quoted by Martene in the *Thesaurus novus Anecdotorum*, vol. V, col. 1388.

The author of this dialogue vigorously refutes all these and many other little arguments, and demonstrates that no healthy and vigorous cenobite can eat birds or use fattening food without being deemed a transgressor of St Benedict’s Rule. If this displeases any cenobite of our own day, and he consequently judges that we have acted with insufficient prudence in publishing little works of this kind, in which the most accepted practices and most widespread customs of our age are criticized, let him consider that we have wished to prescribe no rule of life to anyone, but only to show what holy men of God have thought concerning matters of this kind. It will belong to superiors to weigh the words and arguments of the ancients, and to strive ever more each day that the Rule to which both they and the monks are subject may be observed not according to the lax interpretations of the moderns, but according to the judgment, teaching, holiness, practice, and custom of men most celebrated for these things.

Moreover, shall we always sit beside pots of meat, good sirs? Shall we always pass over, as though with deaf ears, the most clear and salutary decrees of our most holy Father concerning the rejection of meat? Is no hope left, amid so great an abundance of necessary and convenient things, of recovering the ancient and most grievous custom of abstaining from meat? Let us here employ the words of Venerable Peter—what a great man!—in book VI, letter 15: “By what reasoning will the transgression of this chapter (chapter 39 of the Rule of St Benedict) be excused? By what cause will a monk, healthy and in full strength, who eats meat, be shown not to be guilty? Tell me, I beg, if you have anything to say; and if there is any true or plausible reason, vindicate meat for yourself, if you can. You have nothing—you have nothing, I say, as I judge—to say; you have plainly nothing by which to cleanse away the stain, not to say the guilt, of perjury. The Rule confronts you; justice contradicts you.” Thus spoke that most holy abbot of Cluny.

We shall present more on this matter elsewhere. Meanwhile, even this Dialogue alone, which we now make public, will provide sufficient encouragement for men devoted to a stricter observance of the Rule, to imitate the illustrious examples of the ancients. We publish it from three-hundred-year-old manuscript codices in the libraries of Gemnic and Melk. Another notable parchment codex, about two hundred years older, exists in the library of Göttweig; but because of the grievous fire by which the whole monastery was burned down and the resulting general disorder, we were unable to compare our edition with it.

Furthermore, we have not yet been able to conjecture who was the author of this elegant little work. For some time we suspected Honorius of Autun, since it was customary for him to present the subject of a composition in dialogue, in which the Disciple asks and the Master answers. The man’s date would also agree. For since near the end of the work the author mentions Gregory VII, but nowhere Innocent III, Honorius III, or Gregory IX—whose enactments concerning the eating of meat would have been extremely useful to our author—one can scarcely doubt that he flourished about the twelfth century.

[Col. 0931]

But because Honorius himself, in book IV of *On the Lights of the Church*, does not list this Dialogue among his own works, and no codex bears Honorius’s name, it seemed preferable, after rejecting that opinion, to leave the matter uncertain.

**Here begins the Dialogue of a certain master concerning the eating of fowl, not permitted to healthy monks.**

[Note: [Col. 0931D] Melk codex: “A Dialogue, composed in didactic fashion by a certain professor, concerning the eating of meat and abstinence from it by robust and healthy professed adherents of the Rule of St Benedict.”]

[Col. 0931]

[Col. 0931A] **Disciple.** I should like to know whether, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, the eating of fowl is permitted to healthy monks. For it seems to me—and to many others who share this view—

[Note: [Col. 0931D] Melk codex: “agreeing.”]

—that the aforesaid founder allowed us to eat birds, since he took care expressly to suspend us only from the eating of quadrupeds.

[Note: [Col. 0931D] Melk codex: “the flesh of quadrupeds.”]

**Master.** Many have understood and taught it thus. But, to use the words of the Apostle writing to the Philippians (ch. 3): “If in anything we think otherwise, God will reveal this also to us.”

**Disciple.** I beg you, do not conceal from me what, God revealing it, you judge should be thought and maintained concerning this matter as a definitive—

[Note: [Col. 0932D] Gemnic codex: “defined.”]

—opinion, so that you may fulfil the saying: “He who hears, let him say, ‘Come’” (Rev. 22). For perhaps, on hearing from you things better and nearer to salvation, I may begin to wipe from the eyes of my heart the darkness of carnal understanding and, enlightened, recognize the light of spiritual knowledge.

[Col. 0931B] **Master.** I shall do so, insofar as God gives me strength; nor will your request burden me, provided only that you are willing to give a hearing and assent to sound teaching, and, once you have grasped the argument, take care not to attack truth against your own conscience.

**Disciple.** Do not fear. I do not think there is any shame in being defeated by you in such a way that I myself overcome my false opinion. You too, forewarned and forearmed by me, should take care not, through the subtlety of your intellect and the fluency of your tongue, to twist the words of the aforesaid Father into a contrary and harmful sense.

[Note: [Col. 0932D] Melk codex: “twist back.”]

[Col. 0931C] **Master.** May it not please God.
