**Disciple.** First, then, you ought to interpret by a plausible exposition the verse in the Rule of that same teacher which is for many, and perhaps for most, a great cause of doubt. For it appears to support my opinion considerably and to oppose yours greatly. It is as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0932D] Rule of St Benedict, chapter 34.]

> But all are to abstain from eating the flesh of quadrupeds, except those who are altogether weak and sick.

For a prudent reader, who is accustomed to infer greater things from the least and more things from a few, can understand with equal force here that blessed Benedict permits healthy monks the flesh of birds for food, since he so expressly denies them the flesh of—

[Col. 0931D]

—quadrupeds. Otherwise there seems to be no reason why this same Father should in this place have singled out the flesh of quadrupeds—

[Col. 0932A]

—and allowed it to the sick, if he did not without distinction permit birds as food both to the healthy and to the sick.

**Master.** By the cleverness of your quibbles you strike at the weak conscience of simple brothers, so as to set a trap for them under the appearance of truth and deceive them by saying what seems true. Moreover, I see that you are struggling because you do not wish to speak truth; and because you are a natural man, you cannot perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God.

**Disciple.** Since, then, I am a natural man, as you put it, and cannot understand spiritually the foregoing verse of the Rule, you should say whether you can draw from it a sounder understanding by which you may overthrow my interpretation.

[Note: [Col. 0932D] Melk codex: “correct.”]

**Master.** I shall do so, if you first answer me briefly while I ask questions.

[Col. 0932B]

[Note: [Col. 0932D] Melk codex: “answer the questions.”]

**Disciple.** Ask as you please.

**Master.** What do you think Benedict meant when elsewhere he says:

[Note: [Col. 0932D] Rule, chapter 36.]

> Let all abstain from meat according to the customary practice.

**Disciple.** You act in a manner fitting the habits of a pious teacher, in striving to bring before me, or to my memory, a statement that is against you. For what else does “Let all abstain from meat” mean than what I said above: namely, that the healthy eat only birds, while the sick eat both birds and quadrupeds?

**Master.** As I see, you are carnal; and therefore you explain this passage also, like the former one, carnally and childishly. But the law given through Benedict is holy and good for those who lawfully live by it and understand it spiritually; yet, through the carnal observance of certain monks who do not understand it, it has, so to speak, become so tasteless and watered down from its ancient purity that, unless the water of the law is turned into wine—that is, into a spiritual understanding—it fades away into nothingness.

[Col. 0932C] **Disciple.** Since, therefore, as you say, I understand carnally those passages of the Rule under discussion, it will be your duty to expound them spiritually.

**Master.** Do you wish to listen attentively?

**Disciple.** I do.

[Col. 0932D] Master. Observe, then, that Benedict does not merely say, “Let all abstain from meat,” but adds, “[Col. 0933A] according to the customary practice.” For it was indeed the custom of the most ancient and most approved monks to abstain from meat—not only that of four-footed animals, but also that of birds—except where illness made this necessary. Moreover, as ecclesiastical history teaches, this abstinence was generally customary among those who, in the primitive Church, were eminent as founders of the monastic profession by name, example, and word. Therefore Benedict, the remarkable follower of their footsteps, did not wish his sons to degenerate from this paternal nobility, and commanded all to abstain from meat according to the customary practice. Hence he did not say specifically, “from this kind or that”; but, using the general term, “Let all abstain from meat,” he established beyond doubt for every monk that, not only the eating of birds, but also that of four-footed animals, was equally forbidden to him both in this ruling [Col. 0933B] and in the customary practice.

For, preserving the rule concerning illness, need, and necessity, our ancient Fathers are not readily found in authoritative Scriptures to have permitted themselves any kind of meat; and it is exceedingly well known, both from practice and authority, that they refrained alike from birds and from four-footed animals. For since Cassiodorus says that the meat of birds is sweeter than that of four-footed animals, what reason could there be for monks to abstain from the meat of four-footed animals, yet to presume to eat the meat of birds, which is sweeter, unless they were ill? Moreover, Jerome, writing to Savina [Note: [Col. 0933D] C. Mel.: Salvinam, “Salvina.”], supports the interpretation we have stated, as follows: “Let the birds of Phasis, fattened turtle-doves, and every bird by which vast [Col. 0933C] estates fly away, be far from your banquets. And do not suppose that you do not eat meat merely because you reject the fare of swine, hares, deer, and four-footed animals.” [Note: [Col. 0933D] C. Mel.: animantium, “living creatures,” for animalium.] “For here the judgment is made not by the number of feet but by the pleasantness of the taste.”

This being so, he is greatly mistaken who believes that Benedict, distinguished for wisdom, forbade healthy monks the less savoury meat of four-footed animals, while permitting them the meat of birds—unless they were utterly weak. For holy doctors state, and experience confirms, that bird-meat is sweeter than the meat of four-footed animals: more refined and wealthier people of this age, when they wish to dine with more than usual magnificence, first sampling the meat of four-footed animals and then, because of its greater sweetness and pleasant taste, have bird-meat [Col. 0933D] finally served to them. Furthermore, the Church’s more familiar custom is this: those who abstain, in accordance with the canons’ rulings, generally refrain from every kind of meat because of the pleasures of taste, not because of the number of feet. Since monks, therefore, ought to chastise the body more than the other members of the Church and not to love delicacies, they are rightly commanded—apart from the ill—to abstain, according to the customary practice of abstainers, from all meat, so that they may more easily restrain the incentives of the flesh. These are especially apt to prick them when they refuse to curb their bodies from the greater sweetness of foods.

Hence the prudent care and instructive experience of the holy Fathers decreed that monks’ food should be that which supplies the sustenance of life, not that which furnishes fodder for lusts and vices. I am mistaken if Jerome does not support this view [Note: [Col. 0934D] C. Mel.: concurrit, “agrees.”], when he says that bellies carrying flesh are to be filled with meat; but he declares vegetables and legumes with little fish more suitable for Christ’s recruits and consecrated virgins, as being less burdensome and more desirable for ready service to God. To this is added the authority of Prudentius, a religious man though a layman, who says in the hymn which he composed, as it were, for the blessing of a meal: “Far be that hunger which imitates beasts, thirsting for another’s blood!” And shortly afterward: “In such abundance of things, what thirst is there for blood?”

[Col. 0934B] Disciple. I would not presume further to oppose your arguments, if it could be proved by some stronger argument that Benedict understood the matter in this way.

Master. As I see, you will not give up eating meat without pain, since you have served it out of love.

Disciple. Do not take it ill if I still hesitate over your interpretation—both because of the weakness of my faith and the slowness of my understanding, and because of the weakness of the flesh, which resists the law of the mind. Moreover, the number of religious monks in these days, and their united authority in defending this very position—an authority not lightly to be spurned—commends my opinion to me.

Master. Wisdom did not say, “I dwell among many,” but “I dwell in counsels” (Prov. 8), lest any of us, in defending truth, should plead the smaller number as a reason. Truth [Col. 0934C] consoles us, saying: “Do not fear, little flock” (Luke 12). But let us now put aside these evasions and, as it were, lay hands on the matter itself; let us proceed to settle this controversy.

Disciple. To return again to the same point: since what must be carried out with great difficulty cannot be persuaded with such ease, I do not find it credible that Benedict prohibited birds to healthy monks. I understand him to have forbidden them only four-footed animals when he says: “But let the eating of the flesh of four-footed animals be abstained from by all, except the utterly weak and the sick.”

Master. At least believe true what I have said; for unless you believe, you will not understand. But I believe and [Col. 0934D] understand that Benedict said healthy monks must abstain from the meat of four-footed animals so that none of them could say: “I wish to eat the meat of four-footed animals, which is less sweet than that of birds, because Benedict forbade me to eat only the sweeter kinds, such as birds; since the divine Scriptures prohibit things pertaining to bodily pleasure, not things pertaining to the support of human weakness and infirmity.”

Disciple. If this is so, as you say, why did he nowhere expressly forbid the meat of birds as he did that of four-footed animals?

[Col. 0935A] Master. He followed the practice of holy teachers, who commonly address specifically that point which, if left untouched, may generate doubt. Thus the Psalmist mentions Aaron, the Lord’s holy one, not Moses, because no one is ignorant that Moses was holy. Benedict did the same in this place, where he particularly prescribed that healthy monks must abstain from the meat of four-footed animals. Otherwise this doubt might have arisen: whether, because their sweetness is not excessive, healthy brethren ought or ought not to be refreshed by them. But he did not need to say specifically that birds were not to be eaten, because he was certain that, being sweeter, they were not to be eaten except by the ill.

Moreover, that birds are sweeter than four-footed animals—to say nothing of an experience [Col. 0935B] known to many—we establish by Cassiodorus’s testimony. He says that the Lord surpassed the wishes of those desiring meat in the wilderness, not by supplying them with the meat of four-footed animals, but by raining down winged birds like the sand of the sea. Thus we may affirm, on the basis not only of blameworthy experience but also of credible knowledge, that meat is sweeter in birds than in four-footed animals.

Disciple. This cannot be denied.

Master. If, then, Benedict forbade you the meat of four-footed animals, in which the sweetness is less, how much more did he forbid the meat of birds, in which it is greater?

Disciple. How do you know that by cutting off the lesser sweetness he cut off the greater?

Master. Reason and examples consonant with reason [Col. 0935C] compel us to say so.

Disciple. What you say appears plausible, but it is difficult to concede.

Master. One who thinks it hard to accept the conclusion must fairly either show that some falsehood has preceded it, or show that the inference from the propositions is not effective for a necessary conclusion.

Disciple. I grant that what has been said is true, if what remains to be said does not oppose it.

Master. Once the preceding matters have been granted, there will be hope of granting the subsequent ones.

Disciple. Though I now see to some extent what has been said, I nevertheless wish to hear it more plainly from you; and although reason shines clearly by itself, simple people are greatly [Col. 0935D] edified when authority is added to reason. You must therefore prove that Benedict followed the practice of sacred speech when, in prohibiting four-footed animals, he prohibited birds, so that I may be prepared to give an answer to everyone who asks me a reason concerning this controversy.

Master. You demand this of me in abundance, since to the wise a word is enough. Yet I shall do what you ask, if not for friendship’s sake, at least because of your importunity.

Disciple. I shall not be an ungrateful hearer; for, according to the saying of the Wise Man, “The satisfied soul tramples on the honeycomb” [Note: [Col. 0935D] C. Mel.: anima saturata calcat fav., “the satisfied soul tramples on the honeycomb.”]; “but to a hungry soul even bitter things seem sweet” (Prov. 27).

[Col. 0936A] Master. I like what you say.

Disciple. Continue [Note: [Col. 0935D] C. Mel: quod, “what.”] as you promised.

Master. It is the practice of holy teachers to comprehend the greater matter within the lesser [Note: [Col. 0935D] Ib.: in minori comp. majus, “in the lesser [they] comprehend the greater.”]. Thus the Lord is read to have said concerning Jerusalem: “This was the iniquity of your sister Sodom, that she ate her bread in fullness” (Ezek. 16). Behold, varieties of feasting are understood by “bread.” And that this is so is made clear in the place where it is said: “Lot saw Sodom as though it were paradise” (Gen. 13). If Sodom was like paradise, it does not follow that we should understand them to have eaten bread alone, without other delicacies. You have the same with Laban, where it says: “And bread was set before them.” Was bread alone set before them, without any dish? But now, to return to what we began: behold, I have proved that Benedict followed the practice of sacred speech by comprehending the greater matter in the lesser. Yet you cannot prove that he did not follow it. Therefore hold fast to what is certain and abandon what is uncertain.

Further, tell me, please: if Benedict had permitted me, while healthy, to eat bird-meat, and I did not wish to eat it for God’s love, would that be sin or not?

Disciple. Not at all.

Master. Do you know why?

Disciple. Because he himself said [Note: [Col. 0936D] Rule, ch. 40.]: “Let him to whom God has given greater endurance in abstaining know that he will have his own reward.”

[Col. 0936C] Master. You have answered shrewdly. Again, if he had not permitted bird-meat and I ate it, would I sin or not?

Disciple. There is no doubt that you would sin.

Master. Therefore it is better and safer that we abandon uncertainty and hold to certainty. For if we eat while healthy, we know that we sin; but if we do not eat at all, we know that we do not sin.

Disciple. These things are certainly contrary to what was conceded a little earlier.

Master. You judge rightly.

Disciple. Since, then, no one can deny that the Father himself forbids both bird-meat and the meat of four-footed animals to those professing [Col. 0936D] Benedict’s Rule, unless they are ill: are modern monks, transgressors of the same Rule, truly to be said—as some maintain—to be so if, while healthy, they use rendered animal fat (*sagina*) from four-footed animals, which seems not to be meat but the juice of meat?

Master. They certainly are.

Disciple. In God’s name, what are you saying? Have you forgotten yourself for a while? Are you suffering from lethargy? “Do not be too righteous,” lest Solomon’s saying be directed at you: “He who squeezes milk too much brings forth blood” [Note: [Col. 0936D] C. Mel.: emungit, el. san., “squeezes out, brings forth blood.”]. Set a guard upon your mouth, for this is a hard saying [Col. 0937A] (John 6); this opinion is strange, and therefore we can neither hear it with equanimity nor yet put it into practice.

Master. You have heard the truth that you sought; why then are you angry with me?

Disciple. Is rendered fat meat?

Master. It certainly is.

Disciple. What then? Is the use of rendered fat likewise unlawful, just as that of meat is, so that you judge us too to be transgressors of the Rule because we eat it?

Master. You cannot be ignorant of this unless you wish to err or to dissemble.

Disciple. Is it not a flower?

Master. From what does that flower come?

[Col. 0937B] Disciple. From four-footed animals.

Master. Therefore no one but the utterly weak and the sick ought to eat it.

Disciple. If fat is meat, then cheese and milk too, since they come from flesh, are likewise meat.

Master. Milk and cheese, although they come from flesh, are not properly called meat, because flesh is not transformed into milk; rather, by God’s ordering, the foods themselves are converted into milk.

Disciple. Are wine and oil not likewise wood, because they come from trees?

Master. It does not follow.

Disciple. What then are they?

Master. The juice of the earth, which is transformed into wine and [Col. 0937C] oil.

Disciple. Prove it.

Master. Augustine says: “Every day the Lord turns water into wine when he transforms into wine the very juice which grows from the earth.” An evident sign of this is that in spring water flows from a cut vine. Hence it is said:

> Let the wave yield pure wine; the vine now gives water.

But fat is different, because by human contrivance flesh is fattened with grain, crushed, cooked, strained, and made into fat, so that almost nothing but dross remains from it. Thus it is shown, not without reason, to be meat.

Disciple. I fear that on hearing this statement many will be scandalized and will speak against it [Col. 0937D] and snarl even to bloodshed.

Master. You tremble with fear where there is no fear. “He who observes the wind will not sow, and he who considers the clouds will never reap” (Eccl. 11). For if scandal is taken because of truth, it is better that scandal arise than that truth be abandoned. Although another Nebuzaradan, in a manner reviving, has long since destroyed Jerusalem’s walls, and although another Epicurus has spread his sect far and wide, yet the divine response consoles us, saying: “I have reserved for myself seven thousand men who have not bent their knees before Baal” (Rom. 11).

Disciple. Unless you restrain tongue and pen, in displaying at the crossroads of Ashkelon the shameful things of modern Fathers which ought not to be published in Gath, you will rather expose yourself to mockery than gain a paternal blessing by veiling them behind your back.

[Col. 0938A] Master. To blush for evil is wisdom; to blush for good is folly. And since it is human to sin—for there is no human being who cannot be deceived as a human being—but devilish persistently to defend errors, we accuse that excess of our elders sympathetically, not insultingly; and with filial charity, mindful of our own frailty, we excuse it—provided that they deliberately avoid assailing the law of our most ancient Fathers; provided that they strive to renew it after long neglect; provided that they refuse to defend their own lukewarmness; and provided that, once truth has been revealed and an honourable opportunity offered to them, they zealously embrace better models of abstinence, observe them, and commend their observance to others. For one who has failed through some deceptive lapse or compelling necessity ought to be rebuked only in a spirit of gentleness—unless, after admonition, refusing correction and grieving not for his fault, he is not ashamed merely to defend his deeds, but even presumptuously undertakes and strives to overturn the law.

[Col. 0938B] Disciple. As we have learned from the report of many, the use of rendered fat was granted to monks at a certain assembly, at which the Emperor Louis the Pious sat with many religious abbots; and they decreed that rendered fat should be substituted for birds. Do you accuse their decree [Note: [Col. 0937D] C. Mel.: statuta, “decrees”]?

Master. Do you remember that you conceded above that birds belong only to ill brethren?

Disciple. I remember it very well, because I hold it fixed in my memory.

Master. Judge, then, for yourself by what reasoning rendered fat could be relaxed in place of birds, when it would thereafter be served to both healthy persons and sick. Is their exchange, then, praiseworthy—those who styled so timid an exchange an equivalent exchange? By a thing they falsely thought lawful, they acquired an unlawful thing, not sufficiently considering how [Col. 0938D] many would abuse this liberty as an occasion for the flesh and, under a cloak of religion, become corrupted by this newly introduced custom. For, degenerating from paternal nobility, enticed by novelty, they neglected to stand firm and hold the traditions they had learned; consequently they enacted their new law for monks. And since, writing a bill of divorce from holy obedience, they relaxed the strictness of regular abstinence, they crossed the ancient boundaries which their Fathers had set. Alas, how many yielded from so praiseworthy a custom, held by the more ancient [Note: [Col. 0938D] C. Mel.: seniores, “elders.”] Fathers, at the suggestion of one secular person! They did not consider that Esau lost his birthright [Col. 0939A] through gluttony, nor that he could later recover at will the right from which he had once withdrawn.

Disciple. The moderation of dispensation has never displeased any wise person. Beware, then, lest you be considered foolish because you so vehemently detest the adjustment of that dispensation.

Master. A dispensation by prelates ought not to be censured when they admit or tolerate nothing contrary to any ordinances of their predecessors, and nothing which generates such great scandal for the Church, so that they may preserve the lives of their subjects in the purpose of their holiness. Certainly no small diligence must be exercised by rulers in dispensation, lest they permit what harms or forbid what benefits. But at the little assembly of the aforesaid emperor a dispensation was admitted contrary to the general vow of monks, and from it no useful or honourable compensation followed, either in moral integrity or in benefit to souls. For what the holy Fathers of monks and Benedict, their follower—whose Rule was canonized in a general synod—instituted regarding monastic abstinence under the Holy Spirit’s inspiration, as we must believe, the mediators of this modern little assembly altered by their new tradition, without consulting the Roman pontiff, whose office it is to judge concerning the whole Church and the state of all persons, prompted by the praise of a false mercy.

[Col. 0939C] Blessed Pope Gelasius, a most diligent investigator of the Scriptures, showed this in his Decrees. There, together with seventy most learned bishops, he examined books by various Greek and Latin authors and carefully determined which were to be received or rejected. He showed that Louis’s chapter, promulgated to permit monks the use of rendered fat, must for this very reason be rejected: while reverently receiving Benedict’s Rule, wholly contrary to that chapter, he numbered it among the canonical Scriptures. Therefore the abbots said to have sat with the aforementioned emperor in that little assembly and believed to have assented to his decree granting monks the use of rendered fat, however venerable they may have been, ought never to make us receive out of reverence for them anything which we plainly find opposed to Benedict’s holy Rule, to the ordinances of the remaining Fathers who wrote concerning monastic life, indeed to the Holy Spirit, author of them all.

Nor is this surprising: for we cannot possibly observe Benedict’s Rule and the general ordinance of the holy Fathers, promulgated to monks concerning abstinence from meat, if out of reverence for those persons we fulfil what they decreed—namely, the widespread relaxed use of rendered fat or birds on the three days of the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and Pentecost.

[Col. 0940A] Disciple. Since the ordinances of modern and ancient monks differ from and oppose one another in this matter, and since one of two contrary positions must necessarily be weakened, I should like to hear from you more plainly whose authority ought to be considered weightier.

Master. Since modern Fathers diminished or changed, as they wished, what antiquity decreed, the custom of venerable Fathers preserved in times past, and sacred authority confirmed, your prudence can very easily judge who contributed more to our salvation—those who ought in every respect to have benefited us—and whose ordinance should rather be maintained, or to whom obedience should more fully be given: to those holy Fathers who still speak to us in their writings, or to those whose only purpose was to follow and honour [Col. 0940B] the footsteps of their predecessors. Pope Zosimus, writing to the people of Narbonne, can instruct us on this matter: “Not even the authority of this see may permit or alter anything contrary to the ordinances of the Fathers.”

Moreover, the practice of a few modern men ought not to be preferred to, or prejudice, the general practice of the most ancient Fathers. For whatever a few modern persons presumptuously undertake which was not held throughout the whole body of ancient [Note: [Col. 0939D] C. Mel.: antiquissimorum, “most ancient.”] Fathers must be judged superfluous, arrogant, and harmful; it displays a specimen of vanity rather than an exhibition of virtue. Therefore we must give unquestioning faith and wholly unexamined obedience not to what the will of a few modern persons introduced, but to what the antiquity [Col. 0940C] of so many ages and the number of holy Fathers promulgated for posterity by a concordant decision.

Certainly Benedict, filled with the spirit of all the righteous, maintained and taught in life and doctrine both strictness of discipline and moderation of indulgence, and sufficiently instructed his sons by his writings, so that, without that indulgence of rendered fat which modern Fathers admitted, neither can indulgence soften the strong nor excessive strictness break the weak. But, to come to the conclusion: because that gathering of a few modern persons of which we spoke above could impose nothing upon, and ought not to prejudice, the general and solemn custom of ancient monks concerning abstinence, monks of the present age should be advised finally to return to their senses and strive to direct their course according to the models of the preceding Fathers, so that they may escape the peril of those who make their vows void. Do you think otherwise?

[Col. 0940D] Disciple. Not at all, if we are governed by truth as our guide. But since I see that you are most ready in answering, I shall heap upon you the frequent questions which can still be raised on this matter, so that truth may be freed on every side from every scruple of falsehood and no place may remain for excuse.

Master. If you preserve unshaken what has been conceded above, however many questions you multiply for me on this matter, you will not find me fail in answering; nor will you laugh, as a victor, before those on the opposing side.

Disciple. A great road still remains for you.

[Col. 0941A] Master. On this road, with God as my guide, I do not fear striking my foot against a stone—that is, against the antiquity and hardness of the letter. Rather, I shall show you the way that will bring you back to spiritual understanding.

Disciple. The canons come to the aid of monks who eat rendered fat against you, where they say: “If anyone declares the use of meat profane, let him be anathema” (Gal. 1).

Master. The canons say this because of those who abominate meats as unclean. Such persons, as this argument maintains [Note: [Col. 0941D] C. Mel.: astruant, “may maintain.”], ought to eat vegetables cooked with meat, lest they abominate meat. But those who do not abominate meat and yet strive not to eat it for the sake of abstinence are not bound by the anathema. Therefore, if those who cite these things wish to understand them so that abstainers who do not abominate meat should eat the vegetable [Note: [Col. 0941D] C. Mel.: jus, “broth,” for olus, “vegetable.”] in which meat is cooked, let them likewise say that such persons must contract marriages, because the same council says concerning marriage: “If anyone profanes marriage, let him be anathema.”

[Col. 0941B] Disciple. I recognize that these things are excessively contrary [Note: [Col. 0941D] C. Mel.: convenire, “to accord”; the printed text has contraire, “to be contrary.”] to what was previously conceded. Since meat, therefore, is not to be rejected as unclean, what reason is there for denying monks the eating of it [Note: [Col. 0942D] C. G.: usus, “use,” for esus, “eating”], especially since Augustine says in the book of the *Confessions*: “We know that after the flood every kind of animal was given to Noah and his sons for food as green herbs, whether birds, creatures that move upon the earth, or fish of the sea; and therefore I do not condemn a choice dish, but the desire for a choice dish. For Esau lost his birthright through lentils, not through meat. Hence I determine nothing—neither never to touch it nor always to eat it—but according to circumstances, now to tighten the reins of the belly, now to loosen them.” The Apostle also says: “All things are clean to the clean” (Titus 1); and elsewhere: “Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (1 Tim. 4).

[Col. 0941C] Master. We most willingly receive and fully approve these statements, not rejecting meat as unclean. But, accepting the counsel of the same doctor of the Gentiles, who says, “It is good not to eat meat and not to drink wine” (Acts 14), we nevertheless also follow the aforesaid Augustine, determining neither never to touch it nor always to eat it; but, in consideration of strength, we now loosen the reins of the belly because of illness and now tighten them. Thus it is also read in his life that his table had meat, not for the healthy brethren living with him, but for guests and the sick.

We likewise follow Father Benedict. If we compare his ordinances with Augustine’s ordinances promulgated concerning abstinence [Note: [Col. 0942D] C. G.: abundantia, “abundance,” for abstinentia, “abstinence.”] from meat, they will agree in every respect, as having one and the same face and intention. For our lawgiver says [Col. 0942A] [Note: [Col. 0942D] Rule, ch. 36.]: “The use of meat should be granted to the sick and weak for the restoration of their strength. But when they have improved, let all abstain from meat according to the customary practice.” Behold the agreement of Augustine’s and Benedict’s Rules!

Disciple. I cannot deny it. But since the Apostle says, “All things are lawful” (1 Cor. 6), and every creature of God is good, and likewise places abstinence from meat within human choice, tell me, please, what reason is there why this should be required of a monk by a coercive command as though necessary and owed?

Master. I thought that you had long ago understood the reason which your mind has scarcely yet dreamed of. But your inquiry, so childish, reveals that you have not yet arrived at knowledge of it.

Disciple. I seem indeed to glimpse it through a kind of little crack, [Col. 0942B] but I would prefer to learn it from you more clearly.

Master. The reason is very ready. But you, because you distinguish so keenly between the voluntary and necessary state, cannot lift the eyes of your heart, accustomed to darkness, toward the light of clear truth; nor can I satisfy you because of your slowness of understanding.

Disciple. I beg you, through charity, bear with and instruct my importunity and blindness in a spirit of gentleness.

Master. I shall, since charity bears all things (1 Cor. 13); and you, as it seems to me, seek to be edified, not puffed up.

Disciple. You judge rightly.

[Col. 0942C] Master. Listen carefully, then, to the arguments by which I shall approach the resolution of the proposed question.

Disciple. Gladly.

Master. Observe, then, that although the Apostle says, “All things are clean to the clean” (Titus 1), he nevertheless adds immediately: “But it is evil for the person who eats through an offense” (Rom. 14). The saying in the Gospel is similar: “Not what enters into the mouth defiles a person, but evil desire proceeding from the heart” (Matt. 15). Therefore the consumption of meat, good and clean in itself, does not defile one who partakes of it with good use; it defiles only one who eats it through an offense. Consider carefully, then, that the eating of meat is not reckoned a fault, but the offense is. To eat any food “through an offense” [Col. 0942D] is to fail through intemperance to restrain oneself while eating within the bounds of sobriety and a frugal table; or to scandalize a weak neighbour by one’s example; or to dishonour God by breaking one’s vow.

Disciple. If this is so, how shall we excuse Spyridon, the Cypriot man of remarkable holiness, from the blemish of offense? Ecclesiastical history testifies that, on fasting days, he offered his guests meat which he had kept and himself tasted it with them.

[Col. 0943A] Master. If you had understanding, you would not interrupt the argument.

Disciple. Let love of knowledge excuse the vehemence of my reply.

Master. I do not blame Spyridon in this act for two reasons. First, because he had nothing else; second, because the simplicity of the holy man can be excused by the charity of worthy hospitality. What he is read to have done once, others should not imitate as a customary practice. Finally, if you wish to imitate Spyridon in eating meat, imitate him also in addressing corpses. If you wish to eat when, or whatever, he ate; if you take delight in eating meat with him, command the dead, as he did, to speak from their tombs.

Disciple. I cannot, because not all of us can do everything.

[Col. 0943B] Master. Since you cannot do what you wish, wish what you can do.

Disciple. So be it. But what shall we say of John the Baptist? Though he ate pleasing foods—namely, the flesh of locusts and wild honey—he was praised for abstinence; whereas Esau, gorged upon a cheap and humble food, namely lentils, was condemned for the lust of gluttony. Would it not likewise be more praiseworthy abstinence for monks to use richer foods without the foul flame of desire and not be filled, than to gorge themselves on cheap foods with the foul flame of gluttony?

Master. You who introduce these things in support of the point you undertook to persuade are not using a good thing well, because [Col. 0943C] by John’s example you appear to wish to suggest something that harms the undiscerning more than it benefits the discerning. For although your objection, understood soundly, is praiseworthy and to be embraced, and although John’s refreshment is likewise worthy of reverence and imitation, you nevertheless seem on the one hand to have prepared arguments in defense of some persons’ gluttony and, on the other, to have loosened the restraints of stricter [Note: [Col. 0943D] C. Mel.: districtioribus, “for stricter persons.”] abstinence for certain emulators of frugality who have zeal for God but not according to knowledge.

Disciple. It is therefore your task to explain the example of John, brought forward here, so holily and intelligibly that its permission may not perhaps generate an offense for weak minds.

Master. Bede says concerning John: “Although the principal statement stands, ‘In many things we all offend,’ who among us would dare to say that blessed John sinned in deed, word, dress, or food?” Thus Bede. Since John, therefore, was free from every vice and worldly allurement that is accustomed to disturb the state of the mind, he could lawfully and without danger of corruption [Note: [Col. 0943D] C. G.: puritatis, “purity,” for pravitatis, “corruption.”] eat flesh; for no law forbade it to him, nor had he bound himself by any vow not to eat it.

[Col. 0943D] Yet this example of blessed John, though he was a monk, did not establish for monks a common law of eating meat. For since, in a congregation of monks, the number of imperfect persons is greater than that of the perfect, a universal Rule must be proposed to them not on the basis of the smallest part—that is, consideration of a few—but on the basis of what lies within the capacity of many, indeed of all. Things which can be fulfilled only by very few, as most rare gifts granted above the condition and nature of human frailty and thus exceeding common possibility, must be separated from the general law and adduced not so much as examples as miracles.

[Col. 0944A] Therefore, except in illness, perpetual abstinence from meat was beneficially decreed for monks by the Fathers—not because eating it is evil, especially for those who know when, why, and how much refreshment ought or is expedient to be taken, but because of the imperfect, who cannot yet set a limit to their bellies and have not yet learned with the Apostle both to abound and to endure want. This common law of abstinence was imposed so that permission to eat, granted to some and denied to others, might not become a cause of murmuring and revelry.

Disciple. I agree very strongly, and I foresaw—though only by a faint suspicion—that you were about to say this. It remains, then, that you return to the subject from which you digressed a little earlier at my insistence.

Master. May God forgive you for imposing so much labour upon me.

Disciple. Virtue is perfected not in idleness, not in luxuries, not in security, but in weakness.

Master. Why do you not use that saying to rebuke those whose entire purpose hastens to fill the bodily void with meat or rendered fat [Note: [Col. 0944D] C. G.: lasciviam, “lust,” for lacunam, “void”]?

[Col. 0944C] Disciple. Who henceforth would not despise and put to shame the servant of a thing so worthless and fragile—the body? Who would make provision for the flesh in its desires, when its craving is full of anxiety and its satiation of repentance? Who would not listen to Paul saying: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink” (Rom. 14)? Again: “Food is for the belly and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Cor. 6).

Master. Blessed be God, because so true and salutary an understanding concerning abstinence from meat or rendered fat has dawned upon you.

Disciple. Since you rejoice that from the little spark of your arguments life-giving warmth has shone upon me, tell me what you remember still to be lacking.

[Col. 0944D] **Master.** Indeed, I shall be all the readier and more eloquent in speaking, the more teachable and receptive I see you to be in listening, and the more devoted I hope you will be in carrying out what you have heard. Attend carefully, then, to the arguments by which I shall distinguish the voluntary from the necessary state—a point which you interrupted a little earlier. Any matter whatsoever that is lawful to individual persons before a vow becomes unlawful after the vow. For example: if someone, before making a vow, urges another to abstain from meat, he urges upon one who consents and perseveres in it a course worthy of reward. Yet one who does not consent, although he remains inferior to the person who does so, does not thereby become worse than he was; but if he falls away from a vow, he becomes inferior and [Col. 0945A] worse than he was. Therefore, before the vow one must deliberate; after the vow, one must persevere.

For once anyone has bound himself by vow to this abstinence, it becomes obligatory, and entails punishment if it is not observed—whereas before this obligation he was not compelled to it, being, of course, free in the matter. Whoever professes that he wishes to order his life according to the Rule of blessed Benedict promises to abstain from meats; for the authority of so great a leader and teacher establishes this abstinence so unequivocally that those who wish to live devoutly are under an obligation to observe it. For it is not a counsel which may be passed over without fault before a vow, although passing it over does not merit praise; rather, it is the institution of a commandment, which after a vow no one violates without fault. Hence: “If you have vowed anything to the Lord, do not delay to pay it; for the Lord your God will require it of you” (Eccles. 5). Whatever is first voluntarily vowed is, after the vow, necessarily required and owed. Thus, either every professed adherent of the aforesaid abstinence carries it out by free choice, or, as one guilty of violating his vow, he is justly compelled by the force of regular discipline to return to its observance. For, as Augustine testifies, an evil will must not always be left to its own freedom; rather, where authority is given, it must both be restrained from evil and compelled toward good—as the children of Israel, resisting and murmuring, were afflicted by harsh scourges and compelled toward the promised land.

**Disciple.** I confess that I now see without doubt [Col. 0945C] what formerly seemed uncertain. One thing remains, which I ask you now to do: namely, to provide us with answers that will arm us, as with an invincible shield, against those who speak against us. Though lacking authority, they nevertheless strive to overcome us with a rhetoric armed with human arguments but barren of truth. Believing that in a multitude of sinners their own guilt may be diminished and concealed, and flattering themselves with harmful complacency, they confront us with these objections, as though battering our foreheads with a stone: “Excessive is the time during which this custom of ours has endured; under it many religious men have departed this life; and therefore practices and customs of long duration now imitate law.”

**Master.** What they say, since it rests upon no authority of sacred Scripture, is as easily despised as it is asserted. For the contrary answer is given them: however long a custom requiring correction may endure, if justice is satisfied, it ought not for that reason to remain fixed and unshaken. The Hebrew people, though sitting beside pots of meat, nevertheless toiled in the severe oppression of the Egyptian kings, serving for four hundred years in the hard labor of brick and clay; yet at last God visited them and freed them, when and how he willed, so that in the repose of the wilderness they might continually feed their minds upon heavenly delights. Likewise, held captive in the capital of the Chaldeans, they groaned [Col. 0946A] for seventy years beneath the harsh yoke of servitude; yet when the time had come for the Lord to have mercy upon them, he restored them to their native soil and their desired freedom. So we too, led away from our ancestral tradition through stealth and negligence, have at last, by God’s favor, been brought back to the model of the most ancient abstinence. In vain, then, do carnal persons flatter themselves, for the establishment of their carnal custom, with the length of time and the antiquity of their abandonment of the practice.

And although it has been demonstrated very fully above that this perverse custom of theirs conflicts with the worthy custom of the most ancient monasteries [Note: [Col. 0945D] C. G.: “monks.”] of the provinces of Egypt and Palestine—from which, as from a most pure fountain, whatever regular discipline we possess has flowed—yet we may establish it also from the fact that such abandonment of the practice is still maintained either nowhere, or scarcely anywhere, in any monastery of the aforesaid regions. But if this wretched custom is still found in some monastery of the provinces mentioned, though it is seen to have become so widespread among the monasteries of our regions, we say that the correctable abandonment of the practice by a few modern men ought neither to be preferred to nor prejudice the general and truly most ancient custom of the Fathers. For although that reprobate custom is held in esteem among nearly all modern persons, nevertheless, in Augustine’s words, we say that reason must be preferred to the custom of a few modern men, [Col. 0946C] a reason to which the examples of all the ancients agree.

And that we may show law to accord with reason and examples, let us bring forward the opinion of blessed Cyprian, that we may crush the objections of our adversaries with irresistible authority. “Every custom,” he says, “however ancient, however widespread, must altogether be set below truth; and a practice contrary to truth must be abolished.” Hence Isidore, in the second book of his *Synonyms*: “Let practice yield to authority; let law and reason overcome corrupt practice.” Augustine also, in book III of *On the One Baptism*: “Once truth has been made manifest, let custom yield to truth.” Clearly, who can doubt that truth yields to custom? Likewise: “Let no one prefer custom to reason and truth, because reason and truth always exclude custom.” Likewise, the same writer to Casulanus the priest: “All such things as are contained neither in the authorities of the holy Scriptures, nor found established by councils of bishops, nor strengthened by the custom of the universal Church, must be cut away.” Likewise Gregory VII, on the same matter, to Wimo, bishop of Avensa [Note: [Col. 0945D] C. Mel.: “Wimo, bishop of Ausana”; Codex Gem.: “Winifrid, bishop of Ausana.” See Gratian, *Decretum*, Distinction VIII, chapter 5.]: “If perhaps you oppose custom, you should have observed what the Lord says: ‘I am the truth’ (John 19).” He did not say, “I am custom,” but “truth.” In the book of the *Code*, title II: “Customs and long-established practices are not of slight authority. But remember that they are not to prevail so far as to overcome either reason [Col. 0947A] or law.” Hence Pope Nicholas to Hincmar, archbishop of Reims: “An evil custom is to be avoided no less than a pernicious corruption; unless it is more swiftly uprooted at the root, evildoers claim it as a right of privilege. Then transgressions and various presumptions, if not very quickly restrained by laws, begin to be revered and perpetually observed in the manner of privileges.”

Relying, therefore, upon these and other authorities, we firmly maintain that the custom of monks—by which, except for the restoration of strength after grave illness, they permit themselves the eating of any flesh or fat food, which are nearly one and the same thing—is contrary to law and reason, and likewise to the examples of the most ancient Fathers; and must therefore be cut away with the sickle of justice. But if those who recommend and practice the contrary can establish by truer and more powerful proofs—which we do not believe—that the things which we have shown to be unlawful are lawful, it would be right for us effectively to give both hearing and assent to those who teach what is more correct and do what is more salutary. But since they cannot [Col. 0948A] do this, they are wise if they accept our opinion; for whoever leaves truth in any respect finds nothing but falsehood.

**Disciple.** I most strongly agree; nor may there ever be a day that drives me away from the truth of this judgment.

**Master.** “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Psalm 113). We have written these things not as enemies but as friends; nor have we inveighed against those who have hitherto sinned ignorantly in eating fat food, but we warn them so that they may not sin. Nor have we been severe judges only against them, but also against ourselves; wishing to remove the speck from another’s eye, we first cast out our own beam. Our discourse has attacked no one by naming a person. The discussion [Col. 0948B] has been general concerning this vice. But those who may wish to be angry with me because I rebuke those who, while healthy, presume to eat fat food because they are carnal [Note: [Col. 0947B] Both C. texts: “before they are carnal.”] destroy themselves.

[Col. 0947] Here ends the good Dialogue, through the hands of George, etc.

[Col. 0947]

# EASTER PLAY ON THE COMING AND DESTRUCTION OF ANTICHRIST

Performed on stage in the twelfth century.

(Dom Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. II, part II, col. 185, from a Tegernsee manuscript.)

## NOTICE

In the notes to chapter 23 of the *Life of the Venerable Wilburgis, or Wilbirgis, the Recluse*, published by us at Augsburg in quarto in 1715, where it is said that, one night at the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection, while an Easter Play was being performed in the monastery [of St Florian] by clergy and people alike, the virgin of Christ—because she could not be physically present—began to desire that, through the joys of his Resurrection, the Lord might grant her some particular grace of consolation: we observed that this Play appeared to have been a kind of theatrical representation, by which the glory of the risen Christ was devoutly displayed in order to awaken the devotion of the faithful, just as even today Christ’s Nativity and Passion are presented again before the eyes of the faithful in various figures and scenes in many Catholic places. But what we then merely supposed and suspected, we later found to be entirely certain after seeing and discovering several examples of such Easter Plays.

Among these, distinguished is an Easter Play in a five-hundred-year-old manuscript of the canonry of Klosterneuburg, in which the history of the Lord’s Resurrection is presented in a most elegant and devout drama. It begins in this fashion: “First let Pilate be brought forth, with the responsory: ‘Pilate entered.’ And let him sit in the place assigned to him beforehand. After this . . . . the high priests sing: ‘O Lord, we rightly remember what we often heard from the crowd: that the deceiver was accustomed to say, “After three days I wish to rise again.”’ Pilate answers: ‘As prudence dictates to me,’” etc. At the end: “And now that all the people have been assured concerning the Lord, the cantor begins thus: ‘Christ is risen,’ etc.” Nor were only the mysteries of the Passion, Resurrection, and so forth, of Christ the Lord represented in these sacred scenes, but other sacred histories as well—whose conclusion, however, most often concerned the glory of Christ triumphant.

An illustrious example of this is the present Easter Play on the coming and destruction of Antichrist, which we publish from a twelfth-century Tegernsee manuscript. From it we further learn what the Germans’ and Frenchmen’s opinion was concerning the power and extent of the Roman emperor; not to mention many other things regarding both the stage of our forebears and their opinion about the manner of the coming, which may be drawn from this monument. I would most gladly have added the Klosterneuburg Easter Play, had the requests and letters in which we eagerly sought a copy of it not proved fruitless.

# EASTER PLAY ON THE COMING AND DESTRUCTION OF ANTICHRIST

[Col. 0949]

[Col. 0949A] Let the Temple of the Lord and the seven royal seats first be arranged as follows: to the east, the Temple of the Lord; beside it are placed the seat of the king of Jerusalem and the seat of the Synagogue. To the west, the seat of the emperor of the Romans; beside it are placed the seats of the king of the Germans and of the king of the Franks. To the south, the seat of the king of the Greeks. To the south, the seats of the king of Babylon and of the Gentile world. When these have been arranged, let Gentility first enter with the king of Babylon, singing:

> The immortality of the gods must be worshipped by all,  
> And their plurality everywhere feared.  
> Foolish, indeed truly mad, are those who call God one,  
> Because they contradict the everlasting rite of antiquity.
>
> For if we believe in one who rules all things,  
> We admit that he is subject, in contrary ways, to diverse things:  
> On this side he cherishes the good of peace in gentle mercy;  
> On that, he stirs up the tumult of war in fierce cruelty.
>
> Thus the offices of the gods are many and diverse,  
> And these are for us signs of their difference.  
> Whoever, therefore, says that one rules over things so manifold  
> Must necessarily attribute contrary qualities to him.
>
> Therefore, lest we say that one is subject to contraries  
> And concede that the divine nature is affected by them,  
> By this reasoning we determine that the gods are distinct,  
> Whose offices we see to differ from one another.

This too must be sung throughout the play at the appropriate times. Thus Gentility and the king of Babylon ascend [Col. 0949C] to their seat.

Then follows the Synagogue with the Jews, singing:

> Our salvation is in you, O Lord;  
> There is no hope of life in a human being.  
> It is error to place hope of salvation in the name of Christ.
>
> It is strange if he succumbed to death  
> Who bestowed life upon others.  
> He who could not save himself—by him who can be saved?
>
> He who is Emmanuel is not a man;  
> O Israel, you shall worship God.  
> I command you to detest Jesus as you do the gods of Ishmael.

She too will sing this at each appropriate time, and thus ascend her throne.

Then the Church enters, in women’s dress, wearing a breastplate and crowned, with Mercy standing at her right holding oil, [Col. 0949D] and Justice at her left holding scales and a sword—both dressed as women. The Pope follows her on the right with the clergy, and the Roman emperor on the left with his army. The Church sings *Alto consilio* (“By high counsel”), while those following her respond to each verse:

> This is the faith from which life comes,  
> In which the law of death is put to sleep.  
> Whoever believes otherwise,  
> Him we condemn eternally.

She herself then ascends the same throne with the Pope and clergy, the emperor, and his army. Afterwards the other kings enter with their armies, each singing whatever seems suitable. Thus each with his army ascends his own throne, while the Temple and one throne remain vacant.

Then the emperor sends his messengers to each king, and first to the king of the Franks, saying:

> As the writings of historians relate,  
> The whole world was once the treasury of the Romans.  
> The valor of the first Romans achieved this,  
> But the negligence of later generations dissipated it.
>
> Under them the power of the empire collapsed,  
> Which the majesty of our power now reclaims.  
> Therefore let every king pay the tribute formerly established  
> Now to the Roman Empire.
>
> But let the king of the Franks serve that empire in arms,  
> For the Frankish people are strong in warfare.  
> Command him to do this for us shortly  
> With the loyalty proper to subjects.

Then the envoys, coming before the king of the Franks, sing:

> The emperor of the Romans sends greeting  
> To his beloved and renowned king of the Franks.  
> We know that it is known to your discernment  
> That you ought to be subject to Roman right.
>
> Therefore the binding and ever-feared decree  
> Of the supreme empire lays claim to you;  
> We invite you to its service  
> And command you to come quickly under its order.

To them he replies:

> If any credence is given to historians,  
> We do not owe this to the empire; rather, it owes it to us.  
> For the elder Gauls possessed it,  
> And left it to us, their descendants.
>
> But now we are despoiled of it by invading force;  
> Far be it from us to obey invaders!

Then the envoys return to the emperor and sing before him:

> Behold, the Franks, excessively exalted against you,  
> Insolently oppose your majesty.  
> [Col. 0950D] Indeed, even the right of your empire is weakened,  
> While that of the invader is affirmed.
>
> Let them therefore be corrected by worthy punishment and come to their senses,  
> So that through them others may learn obedience.

Then the emperor sings:

> Hearts are wont to be exalted before ruin.  
> Do not wonder that fools speak proudly.  
> Certainly we shall restrain their arrogance,  
> [Col. 0951A] And crush them beneath our feet.
>
> Those who now refuse to obey as soldiers  
> Will afterwards be compelled to serve as slaves.

And immediately, with his battle-lines, he goes to attack the king of the Franks. The king meets him and fights with him; defeated, he is led captive to the emperor’s seat. As the emperor sits, he stands before him, singing:

> The glory of triumph is to spare the conquered.  
> Conquered, I now obey your decrees.  
> I confess that my life together with royal dignity  
> Is placed in your power.
>
> But if you restore me to my former honor,  
> The victor’s greatest praise will be the conquered man’s honor.

Then the emperor receives him as his man and grants him his kingdom, singing:

> Live by grace and receive honor,  
> Since you acknowledge me as the sole emperor.

Dismissed with honor, he returns to his kingdom singing:

> We revere the honor of the Roman name;  
> We glory in serving Augustus Caesar,  
> Whose imperial power must be feared;  
> May his honor and glory remain venerable.
>
> We acknowledge you alone as ruler of all;  
> With our whole mind we shall always obey you.

Then the emperor sends messengers to the king of the Greeks, singing:

> As the writings of historians relate,  
> [Col. 0951C] Whatever the world possesses is the treasury of the Romans.  
> The valor of the first Romans achieved this,  
> But the negligence of later generations dissipated it.
>
> Under them the power of the empire collapsed,  
> Which the majesty of our power now reclaims.  
> Therefore let every king pay the tribute formerly established  
> Now to the Roman Empire.
>
> Therefore announce this edict to the Greeks,  
> And bring back from them the tribute owed.

When they come before the king, they sing: “The emperor sends greeting,” changing there:

> We invite you to his service  
> And command you under his order to pay tribute.

He receives them courteously and sings:

> We revere the honor of the Roman name;  
> [Col. 0951D] We glory in rendering tribute to Caesar, etc.

And dismissing them with honor, he himself ascends [Note: [Col. 0951D] The manuscript reads: “ascending.”] to the emperor, singing: “Of the Roman name,” etc. The emperor receives him as his man and grants him his kingdom, singing: “Live by grace.” Then he returns, having received his kingdom, singing: “Of the Roman name,” etc.

Then the emperor again sends his messengers to the king of Jerusalem, saying: “As the writings relate,” etc. Coming before the king, they sing:

> The emperor of the Romans sends greeting  
> To his beloved king of Jerusalem, etc.

[Col. 0952A] Having received them courteously, he sings: “Of the Roman name,” etc. Ascending to the emperor, he sings the same, repeating: “Of the Roman name,” etc.

The emperor receives him and grants him his kingdom. When he has returned to his own seat, and the whole Church is now subject to the Roman Empire, the king of Babylon rises in the midst of his people, singing:

> Behold the superstition of vain novelty,  
> Which the error of the Christian sect devised!  
> It has nearly destroyed the rite of antiquity  
> And withdrawn from the gods the honor of divinity.
>
> Let us by no means allow their worship to be wholly erased;  
> Let us wipe the Christian name from the earth.  
> We must begin at that place  
> From which this sect first began to spring up.

And arranging his battle-lines, he goes to besiege Jerusalem. Then the king of Jerusalem sends messengers to the emperor, singing:

> Go and report these evils of the Church,  
> Asking her for help on our behalf.  
> When the Roman emperor learns this,  
> He himself will be our deliverer from the enemy.

Coming before the emperor, they sing:

> Defender of the Church, have pity upon us,  
> Whom the enemies of the Lord desire to destroy.  
> The nations have entered God’s inheritance;  
> They hold the holy city under siege.
>
> They seek to pollute by a most foul rite  
> The place where his holy feet stood.

He replies:

> [Col. 0952C] Go, quickly comforting your brothers,  
> That, joyfully asking for our aid,  
> They may know for certain that we are coming soon,  
> And that the enemies may not triumph over them.

Returning, they stand before the king, singing:

> Act manfully; be secure against the enemy;  
> For the one who will redeem you from him is drawing near.  
> You must steadfastly await him in battle;  
> Through him you shall rejoice to be freed shortly.

Meanwhile, while the emperor gathers his army, an angel of the Lord suddenly appears and sings:

> Judah and Jerusalem, do not fear,  
> Knowing that tomorrow you will see God’s help;  
> For your brothers are at hand, who will free you  
> [Col. 0952D] And mightily overcome your enemies.

Then the choir sings: “Judah and Jerusalem.” Meanwhile, the emperor and his forces proceed to battle; when the battle is ended, he engages with the king of Babylon to a responsory. When the latter has been defeated and begins to flee, the emperor enters the Temple with his men. After worshipping there, he takes the crown from his head and, holding it together with the sceptre and imperial authority, sings before the altar:

> Receive what I offer; for with a gracious heart  
> I resign the empire to you, King of kings,  
> Through whom kings reign; you alone may be called  
> And truly are emperor and governor of all.

Having laid these things upon the altar, he returns to [Col. 0953A] the seat of his ancient kingdom. The Church, which had gone down with him to Jerusalem, remains in the Temple. Then Church, Gentility, and Synagogue sing in turn, as above.

Let the hypocrites enter silently and in an appearance of humility, bowing everywhere and courting the favor of the laity. Finally, let them all assemble before the church and the seat of the king of Jerusalem. Receiving them courteously, he wholly submits himself to their counsel. Immediately Antichrist enters, wearing a cuirass beneath his wings, with Hypocrisy accompanying him on the right and Heresy on the left. He sings to them:

> The hour of my kingdom has come.  
> Therefore through you, without delay,  
> Let it happen that I ascend the royal throne:  
> [Col. 0953B] Let the world worship me and no other.
>
> I have recognized that you are suited to me;  
> I have fostered you for this until now.  
> Behold: your labor and industry  
> Are necessary to me for this.
>
> See, the nations honor Christ,  
> Reverence and worship him.  
> Therefore erase his memory,  
> Transferring his glory to me.

To Hypocrisy:

> In you I place the foundation.

To Heresy:

> Through you shall come the increase.

To Hypocrisy:

> [Col. 0953C] Build up the favor of the laity.

To Heresy:

> Destroy the teaching of the clergy.

Then they reply:

> Through us the world will believe in you;  
> The name of Christ will yield to you.

**Hypocrisy:**

> For through me the laity will give their favor.

**Heresy:**

> And through me the clergy will deny Christ.

Then they precede him, while he himself follows little by little. When they have come before the seat of the king of Jerusalem, Hypocrisy whispers to the hypocrites, announcing Antichrist’s coming. They immediately go to meet him, [Col. 0953D] singing:

> Sacred religion has long been wavering;  
> Vanity has seized Mother Church.  
> Why destruction through men decked with finery?  
> God does not love secular prelates.
>
> Ascend the heights of royal power;  
> Through you may the remnants of old things be changed.

Then Antichrist:

> How will this happen? I am an unknown man.

Then they:

> By our counsel the whole world will favor you.  
> We have occupied the favor of the laity;  
> Now through you let the teaching of the clergy fall.
>
> With our help you will occupy this throne;  
> By your own merits you will complete the rest.

[Col. 0954A] Then Antichrist, coming before the seat of the king of Jerusalem, sings to the hypocrites:

> Whom you conceived in the bosom of the Church  
> Through long efforts, you have at last brought me forth.  
> Therefore I shall ascend; I shall subjugate kingdoms;  
> I shall overthrow the old and prescribe new laws.

Then they remove their outer garments, draw their swords, depose the king of Jerusalem, and crown Antichrist, singing:

> May your hand be strengthened and your right hand exalted.

Then the king of Jerusalem goes alone to the king of the Germans, singing:

> I had been deceived by hope of good things.  
> Behold, I am cast down by the fraud of deceivers.  
> I thought the heights of kingship blessed  
> [Col. 0954B] If they were ordered by such men’s decrees.
>
> While you were defender of the Roman summit,  
> The Church’s condition flourished under honor.  
> Now the evil of your falling away is manifest;  
> The law of destructive superstition flourishes.

Meanwhile the hypocrites conduct Antichrist into the Temple of the Lord and place his throne there. But the Church, which had remained there, is subjected to many insults and beatings and returns to the seat of the Pope.

Then Antichrist sends his messengers to each of the Greek kings, saying:

> You know that I have been given to you by God  
> To hold dominion over every land.  
> For this I have chosen you as suitable ministers,  
> [Col. 0954C] Through whom the whole world may be subjected to our law.
>
> First seize the borders of the Greeks from here;  
> Subdue the Greeks by terror or by war.

Coming before the king of the Greeks, they sing:

> King, may salvation be yours from our Savior,  
> The ruler of kings and of the whole world,  
> Who, as Scripture promised to the world,  
> Came down from heaven, sent from the Father’s citadel.
>
> Ever remaining the same in divinity,  
> In his mercy he invites us into life.  
> He wishes himself to be venerated as God by all,  
> And commands that the whole world worship him.
>
> If you disregard the terms of this edict,  
> You and yours shall perish by the sword’s edge.

He replies:

> [Col. 0954D] Willingly I render service to the king  
> Whom you say is exalted with such great honor.  
> It is honor and glory to obey such a one;  
> With my whole mind I desire to serve him.

Repeating this, he comes before Antichrist, stands before him, and sings:

> I acknowledge your imperial majesty;  
> That I may serve you, I ask royal right.

And, bending his knee, he offers him the crown. Then Antichrist marks the first letter of his own name upon the king’s forehead and upon the foreheads of all his people, replaces the crown upon his head, and sings:

> Live by grace and receive honor,  
> Since you acknowledge me as creator of all.

[Col. 0955A] Then he returns to his own seat. Again Antichrist sends hypocrites to the king of the Franks with gifts, saying:

> You shall offer these gifts to the king of the Franks,  
> By which you shall convert him and his people to us.  
> They devised the pattern of our rite;  
> They prepared the way for our coming.
>
> Their subtlety labored for us  
> To ascend the throne which power has occupied.

Then the hypocrites, taking the gifts, go to the king of the Franks and, standing before him, sing: “King, may salvation be yours,” etc., changing this final stanza:

> But, assured of your kingdom’s devotion,  
> He repays the return due to your good will.

[Col. 0955B] Then the king, having received the gifts, sings: “Willingly I render service,” etc. Repeating it, he comes before Antichrist and, bending his knee, offers him the crown, singing: “I acknowledge,” etc. Antichrist receives him, marks him with a kiss on the mouth and marks his followers on their foreheads; placing the crown upon him, he sings: “Live by grace,” etc.

Then again he sends hypocrites to the king of the Germans, singing:

> Great is the German title in arms,  
> As those who have experienced their strength attest.  
> The king must be softened with gifts;  
> It is dangerous to fight the Germans.
>
> They are a most grievous scourge to those who fight with them.  
> Subject them to us by gifts, if you can.

Then the hypocrites, taking the gifts, go [Col. 0955C] to the king and sing before him: “King, may salvation be yours,” etc., again changing the last verse thus:

> And, honoring you with these gifts while you are absent,  
> He desires to see you present as his friend.

Then the king of the Germans sings:

> I am compelled to meet trickery with stratagems,  
> By which wickedness is accustomed to lie.  
> Beneath an appearance, truth is thought to be virtue;  
> Falsehood will show that the appearance lies.
>
> Through you the faith of Christians has been corrupted;  
> Through me the kingdom of deceivers will be crushed.  
> The deceiver’s gifts are full of fraud;  
> Upon them will fall the sword of the avenger.
>
> Let their money go with them into perdition;  
> A grave injury awaits grave vengeance.

Then the hypocrites return in confusion and, standing before Antichrist, sing:

> O glory of the kingdom, head of the whole world,  
> Behold the offense of an enraged people.  
> Surely it was foretold by the faith of the ancients  
> That you would subject the necks of the proud.
>
> If the whole world is sustained by your power,  
> By what force does the fury of the Germans resist you?  
> Therefore Germany blasphemes your dominion,  
> Raises its horns against religion.
>
> Look upon our humiliation;  
> Judge in it the offense against you.  
> Their injury testifies to your power,  
> Whose empire they threaten with ruin.

[Col. 0956A] Then Antichrist:

> I shall indeed bring to an end the people of perdition  
> For so great a scandal against religion.  
> Behold, the power of divine majesty  
> Terrifies the arrogance of human power!

Then he sends individual messengers to the kings, saying to them:

> Go, gathering the resources of the kingdoms;  
> Let them trample down in force the fury of the proud.

The messengers, coming before the kings, sing:

> Behold, our Lord and God of gods  
> Calls together his army through us,  
> That through them he may condemn the German fury.  
> In war he will mark the blood of martyrs.

Then the kings assemble before the throne of Antichrist. [Col. 0956B] He says to them:

> I shall indeed bring to an end, etc.  
> Go, invade the borders of Germany;  
> Crush the proud people with their king.

Then all sing:

> God is with us; he powerfully protects us;  
> Therefore let us fight confidently for the faith.

And arranging their battle-lines for an encounter with the Germans, they fight them, and Antichrist’s army is defeated. Then the king of the Germans returns, sits on his throne, and sings:

> The honor of the fatherland must be defended with blood;  
> The enemy must be expelled by the valor of the fatherland.  
> Right lost through deceit is purchasable with blood;  
> Thus shall we retain imperial splendor.

[Col. 0956C] Then the hypocrites bring a lame man before Antichrist. When he has been healed, the king of the Germans begins to waver in faith. Then they bring a leper; when he has been healed, the king doubts more greatly. Finally, they bring in a bier on which lay a certain man pretending to have been killed in battle. Antichrist orders him to rise, saying:

> The ignorant and unbelieving always seek signs.  
> Rise, rise quickly; reveal who I am.

Then the man sings from the bier:

> You are the wisdom of heavenly truth,  
> The unconquered power of divine majesty.

And the hypocrites sing with him: “You are wisdom,” etc. Then the king of the Germans, seeing the signs, is deceived, saying:

> [Col. 0956D] By our own attack we are always endangered;  
> Unwarily we fight against the Lord.  
> In his name the dead are raised,  
> The lame walk, and lepers are cleansed.
>
> Therefore let us revere his glory.

Then the king goes up to Antichrist and sings the same. When he has come before him, he bends his knee and offers him the crown, singing: “I acknowledge,” etc. Then Antichrist marks him and his followers on their foreheads and, placing the crown upon him, sings: “Live by grace,” etc. Then he entrusts to him an expedition against the Gentiles, saying:

> Since you have believed, we turn toward the Gentiles.

And giving him a sword, he sings:

> Through you we intend to make these people believers.

[Col. 0957A] Then the king comes before the throne of Gentility and, sending an envoy to the king of Babylon, sings before him:

> May the Lord’s power remain forever,  
> To be worshipped as an everlasting divine being.  
> It utterly condemns the worship of idols  
> And commands the rites of images to be cast away.

Then Gentility says to the envoy:

> Envy invented this singularity,  
> That a human being should worship one Divinity.  
> He is rightly judged a covetous god  
> Who especially wishes to be worshipped alone above the rest.
>
> Therefore we follow the rite of antiquity;  
> We render to the gods the distinctions of divinity.

Then the messenger:

> [Col. 0957B] One is the Lord whom we rightly revere.

And casting down an image, he sings:

> We detest the idol.

Immediately the Gentiles gather and fight with Antichrist’s army. The king of Babylon is defeated and led captive to Antichrist. Then the king, bending his knee, offers his crown to Antichrist, saying: “I acknowledge,” etc. Then Antichrist marks him and his followers on their foreheads, places the crown upon him, and sings: “Live by grace,” etc. Immediately they all return to their seats, singing:

> We acknowledge you alone as ruler of all;  
> With our whole mind we shall always obey you.

Then Antichrist sends hypocrites to the Synagogue, [Col. 0957C] singing:

> Tell the Jews that the Messiah has come  
> And that I have received tribute among the Gentiles.  
> Tell the Jews: Behold, I am the Messiah;  
> I am he promised to them through the prophecies.

Then the hypocrites address the Synagogue:

> A race of royal stock, you are a people set apart;  
> You are everywhere proclaimed a faithful people.  
> Long ago you were exiled to defend the Law;  
> Far from your homeland, you awaited the Messiah.
>
> This expectation will restore your inheritance;  
> Joyful novelty will transform old things.  
> Behold the mystery of your redemption:  
> For the king has been born, the author of religion.
>
> [Col. 0957D] This is Emmanuel, whom the Scriptures attest,  
> Through whose grace you shall reign securely.  
> He has raised up the humble and cast down the proud;  
> He has powerfully subjected all things beneath his feet.
>
> Rise, Jerusalem; rise, be enlightened;  
> Rejoice, Synagogue, long held captive.

Then the Synagogue:

> This consolation of divine goodness  
> Has looked upon the labor of our captivity.  
> Therefore let us go to meet the Savior;  
> It is fitting to render glory to the Redeemer.

Then the Synagogue rises and goes to Antichrist, etc.

> Be present, Emmanuel, whom we always revere,  
> In whose glory we too glory.

[Col. 0958A] Then he receives the approaching Synagogue, marks her, and says:

> Through me pass out beyond the bar of confusion;  
> I restore to you the land of promise.  
> Behold, in your light the nations walk,  
> And under the law of your peace kings reign.

Then, as the Synagogue returns, the prophets enter, saying:

> The Word of the Father, possessing divinity,  
> Took humanity in a virgin;  
> Remaining God, he became mortal;  
> Ever God, he became temporal.
>
> This occurred not by the course of nature,  
> As the witness says, but by God’s working.  
> He took our weakness  
> [Col. 0958B] That he might grant strength to the weak.
>
> The Jews recognized him as mortal,  
> Not knowing that he was immortal.  
> They believed neither his word nor his signs;  
> Under Pilate they crucified Christ.
>
> By dying, he put death to death;  
> He freed believers from Gehenna.  
> He truly rose, never again to die;  
> He reigns forever and is soon to come.
>
> He will judge the world by fire;  
> He will raise all persons in the flesh;  
> He will separate the saved from the rejected,  
> Damning the wicked and glorifying the good.
>
> You know what the true Scriptures say;  
> They attest Enoch alive and Elijah. [Col. 0958C] Then the Synagogue:

“Where are they?” They:

We are truly those  
Upon whom the ends of the ages have come.

This one is Enoch, and I am Elijah,  
Whom the Messiah has preserved until now—  
He who has already come and is yet to come,  
Who will first redeem Israel through us.

Behold, the man of perdition is coming,  
Completing the great walls of Babylon:  
“He is not Christ.”

Then they remove his veil. Immediately the Synagogue turns to the words of the prophets, saying:

[Col. 0958D] We have indeed been deceived by Antichrist,  
Who falsely claims to be the Christ of the Jews.  
Elijah and Enoch, prophets of truth,  
Are sure signs of our deliverance.  
We give thanks to you, Adonai, king of glory,  
Trinity of persons, of one and the same substance.  
Truly God is the Father, whose Only-Begotten is God;  
The Spirit of both is likewise God.

Meanwhile hypocrites come to Antichrist, singing:

O royal summit of divine majesty!  
The honour of divinity is being taken from you.  
The old men, teachers of falsehood, have entered,  
Who blaspheme the honour of your power.  
They preach to the Jews, according to the tenor of the Scriptures,

[Col. 0959A] That you, almighty king, are the chief of hypocrites.

Then Antichrist says to the hypocrites:

Since the whole world strives to worship me,  
Who would dare deny the right of my name?  
Bring the Synagogue and the elders before me.  
I shall arraign the guilty for this insolence.

Then the ministers come to the prophets and the Synagogue, singing:

Witnesses of falsehood, heralds of deceit,  
The tribunal of divine majesty summons you.

Then the prophets:

The man of iniquity shall not deceive  
The servants of Christ through ministers of falsehood.

Then the messengers bring the prophets and the Synagogue to Antichrist, to whom he says:

[Col. 0959B] You, whom the appearance of authority deceives,  
Are driven into madness by your own disposition.  
I am the redemption to come promised to the saints,  
Truly the Messiah, as Scripture testifies.  
Receive from me the form of religion.  
To unbelievers I am a stone of stumbling.

Then the prophets:

You are the blasphemous author of iniquity,  
Root of evil, disturber of truth,  
Antichrist, deceiver of godliness.

Then Antichrist, enraged, says to his ministers:

Behold: let the hand of divine majesty  
Avenge the blasphemies against my Divinity.  
Let those who blaspheme the divine goodness in me  
Taste the severity of the divine Godhead.  
Let the sheep destined for slaughter wholly perish

[Col. 0960A] For so great an offence against holy religion.

At last the Synagogue sings this confession:

We repent of our error; we are converted to the faith.  
Whatever the persecutor may inflict on us, we shall endure.

Then the ministers lead them out and kill them. Meanwhile, as they are being killed, the Church sings: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh” (Song of Songs 1). Then, when the ministers have returned, Antichrist sends his messengers to each of the kings, singing:

Let the kings and the companies of the saints assemble;  
I desire to be worshipped by the glory of kingdoms.  
The divine hand has established all things below;  
Divinity has exterminated its enemies.  
All the laws of kingdoms have been settled in peace;

[Col. 0960B] The God of gods calls his own to the crown.

Then all the kings gather from every quarter with their followers before Antichrist, singing: “The divine hand has established all things,” etc. Antichrist says to them:

These things my preachers foretold—  
Men devoted to my name and guardians of my law.
