This is my glory, which they foretold long ago,  
And which all who have deserved it will enjoy with me.  
After the fall of those whom falsehood deceived,  
Peace and universal security have been established.

Immediately there is a sound above Antichrist’s head; he falls, and all his followers flee. The Church sings: “Behold the man who did not make God his helper! But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God.” Then, as all return to the faith, the Church, receiving them, begins: “Speak praise to our God.”

[Col. 0959] End.

[Col. 0959]

## AN ANONYMOUS WRITER OF MELK, FLOURISHING IN THE TWELFTH CENTURY, ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS

First brought to light and illustrated with chronological-critical notes by the Reverend Father Bernard Pez, Benedictine and librarian of Melk, in the year 1716.

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca ecclesiastica*, Hamburg, 1718, folio, p. 141.)

## NOTICE

We call this anonymous work *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, or *On Illustrious Men*, which we now for the first time publish for the benefit of the republic of letters, “of Melk”—not at all because we possess definite evidence for enrolling its author among the monks of Melk, but because it has hitherto been preserved in the manuscript library of Melk, in its quarto paper codex, now marked R, no. 28, written about the fourteenth century, and was taken thence by us. Examples of designating anonymous authors in this manner occur everywhere among Freher, Acheri, Chesnius, and other learned collectors and editors of historical materials.

Moreover, we spared no effort in seeking to discover our author’s own name and circumstances, but in vain; for no one has anywhere given any indication of these matters, not even the author himself. From a certain special zeal with which he pursues and praises Benedictine writers, someone might perhaps infer that he was a monk, and indeed a Benedictine. Yet even this is not sufficiently certain. Something more definite can apparently be determined about the man’s date; and it is highly probable that he set his mind to writing in the twelfth century of Christ. For in chapter 91 he relates that Hermann the Cripple, who died in 1054, was more subtle in music than almost all modern writers; and in chapter 105 he celebrates Manegold, a contemporary of Pope Gregory VII, as the “master of masters” among modern men, while in chapter 71 he calls Rupert the late abbot of Deutz. Rupert died in the year of the Lord 1135. Indeed, this writer seems to have composed his work at about the same time as Honorius of Autun and Sigebert of Gembloux wrote on ecclesiastical writers: the former flourished about the year of the Lord 1130, while the latter died in 1093. Certainly our author had not learned even by report of either work, as is clear from his preface, in which he states that, besides Jerome, Gennadius, Cassiodorus, and Isidore—though he himself lacked the works of the latter two—he had so far known no other writer on illustrious men.

Furthermore, in listing his writers our anonymous author does not everywhere observe chronological order, frequently placing later those whom our chronological notes, written in the margin, show plainly to have been earlier in date. He mentions some authors almost still unknown to learned men, such as John the English musician; Paul the Jew, monk of Fulda; a certain Symphorosius; Albert, perhaps a monk of Sigeberg; Achelinus or Athelinus, bishop; Stephen the musician; Manegold; Aribo the Younger, musician; Fucraldus; Dietger, formerly a Benedictine monk and then bishop of Metz; Meginhard, bishop of Würzburg, commentator on the Song of Songs; Deusdedit, cardinal, against the Guibertines; Gottschalk, monk of Deking, Order of St Benedict; Gerald of St Blaise in the Hercynian Forest; Placidus of Nonantola; and so forth. To writers whose names have been entered in published bibliothecae he also ascribes quite a few new works, hitherto unknown to nearly everyone. Such are: a *Book of Flowers* and a *Book of Synods* by St Gregory the Great; Cassiodorus’s *Book on Illustrious Men*; Freculph, bishop of Lisieux’s, *Explanations of Genesis*; Remigius of Auxerre’s *Commentary on Genesis*; Paul Orosius’s *Work on the Book of the Twelve Prophets*; St Odo of Cluny’s *Dialogue on Music*; a commentary on the Song of Songs by Haymo, bishop of Halberstadt, whom our author makes a monk of St Germanus of Auxerre; Christian, bishop of Apulia’s *Book against Berengar*; Fulbert of Chartres’s *Treatise against Jews and Bad Christians*; Ivo of Chartres’s most orderly *Martyrology concerning the Saints*; several works by the priest of Constance; Guitmund of Aversa on Luke; Anselm of Lucca’s enormous work on the Psalter; writings by St Ulric of Cluny, including a *Life of Saint Herman, a margrave who became a monk*; and so forth.

Finally, most worthy of consideration and notice are the statements he makes concerning Ratramnus, monk of Corbie, and his work *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, because they admirably confirm John Mabillon’s opinion concerning the author, set out in the preface to Part II of the fourth Benedictine century. But it is preferable to preserve and leave all these matters intact for the learned reader. We also ask him to pardon the omission of fuller and more learned notes, which our author not infrequently requires: lack of time and leisure excluded the former; narrowness of ability, the latter.

+ We have recently found this work of Remigius in the library of Garsten, O.B., in Upper Austria, in a parchment folio codex, under this title: *Remigius on Bereshit [“In the beginning”].* It begins: “There was a bishop called Desiderius,” etc. Then follows the text: “In the beginning God created,” etc. (Genesis 1). “The author of this work, as the holy doctors hand down, is recognized to have been Moses,” etc.

## [ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS]

### PREFACE OF THE ANONYMOUS AUTHOR TO HIS BOOK ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS

[Col. 0961A] Following, as far as we are able, the example of those writers who compiled a catalogue of illustrious men, we shall transmit to posterity in writing both the works and the names of the holy Fathers whose genius thereafter laboured for the Church of God. In this undertaking, although in an inverted order, yet by a necessary alteration, we have somehow gathered together those who prescribed something to be said in the celebration of the Masses—namely [Note: [Col. 0961] perhaps “besides.”] because of Telesphorus, Gelasius, Sixtus, Clement of Alexandria, Alexander I, Leo the Great, Gregory I, Gregory III, and Sergius. Moreover, not allowing blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan—whom indeed blessed Jerome mentions among the illustrious men, though he sets down no appraisal at all of his books and entirely withholds his judgment of Ambrose himself, because Ambrose was still alive—to pass by unknown to us, we have decided that the very front of this work should be distinguished by the title of so great a name.

There are, however, other illustrious men, namely Cassiodorus and Isidore, who likewise wrote *On Illustrious Men*. Since their books have not yet reached our hands, we are wholly ignorant whom they included or whom they omitted.

Beginning, therefore, from the end of Gennadius, who himself began his work from the end of Jerome, we have taken care diligently to note down all whom we have found to have written anything worthy of remembrance from that time onward. Yet, lest anything be lacking to the curiosity of readers, we judged that Berengar, formerly a heretic, should be included; likewise Wibert, formerly bishop of Ravenna; and Urban II—not because any writings of theirs have reached us, or indeed because they themselves ever wrote anything, but because each left us fitting memorials of his own talent. Berengar, [Col. 0962B] having at some time been converted, did not delay to profess the Catholic faith in two apt little verses. Clement, however, who was also called [Note: [Col. 0961] read: Wibert or Guibert.] Ewibert, attacked the lawful successor of Peter, yet nevertheless sported rather elegantly in the same number of verses. Urban, in turn, answering his rival in verse, openly showed that he had obtained nothing of apostolic dignity except an empty title. But if anyone should at any time disapprove of what we have written, let them blame our lack of knowledge, not our zeal; and let them also consider that, where no fruit of a good work can exist, the disposition of good will alone is sufficient.

## THE BOOK BEGINS

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0963A] Pope Telesphorus [Note: [Col. 0963] A.D. 128.], the seventh pope, who succeeded blessed Sixtus—of whom we shall speak presently—in the pontificate, decreed that Masses be celebrated on the night of the most holy Nativity of the Lord, and that at the time of sacrifice “Glory [Col. 0963B] to God in the highest” be sung. Under Emperor Hadrian, as did his predecessors Alexander and Sixtus, he deserved to be crowned with martyrdom on the Nones of January.

## CHAPTER II

Pope Gelasius [Note: [Col. 0963] 492.], in the days of Leo, who succeeded Marcian in the empire, governed the Roman Church nobly. He established many decrees for the Church’s benefit and wrote much of use. He also instituted the manner of saying Masses and the number of prefaces. In the time of this pontiff the Missal-book was compiled which is also called the Gelasian.

## CHAPTER III

Pope Zosimus [Note: [Col. 0963] 417.] instituted the blessing of the candle, customarily blessed by the deacon on Holy Saturday. The beginning of that blessing is: “Let now the angelic host of heaven rejoice.”

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0963C] Bishop Sixtus [Note: [Col. 0963] 117.], who succeeded blessed Alexander I in the Roman pontificate, instituted the singing of “Holy, holy, holy” during the solemnities of Mass. Under Emperor Hadrian he too deserved to be crowned with martyrdom on the eighth day before the Ides of April.

## CHAPTER V

Clement [Note: [Col. 0963] 192.], presbyter of the Church of Alexandria and teacher of Origen, long maintained a school in Alexandria. He was eminent in both sacred and secular learning. He composed several short works in an elegant style. There survives by him one book *On Easter*, one dialogue *On Fasting*, one work *On the Salvation of the Rich Man*, one *On Slander*, one *On Canons*, one *Against the Nations*, and one *Against Those Who Investigate the Errors of the Jews*. He was a man of remarkable learning and eloquence. He composed the priest’s prayer which we call the Canon, and which the whole Church has held in such esteem that it has been ordered to be recited continually at the consecration of the Lord’s body. He was renowned in the times of Severus and his son Antoninus.

## CHAPTER VI

Alexander [Note: [Col. 0963] 108.] I, a Roman by nation, born of a father named Alexander, originating from the district of [Note: [Col. 0963] alternatively, Caput Tauri.] Capurtam, inserted the Passion of the Lord into the priest’s prayer when Masses are to be celebrated. Hence the Canon contains: “May you, O God, make this offering,” and what follows in order. On the fifth day before the Nones of May, under Emperor Hadrian, he suffered martyrdom with Eventius and Theodolus and passed to heaven.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0964A] Leo the Great [Note: [Col. 0963] A.D. 440.], pope, was an outstanding orator, who greatly benefited the Christian religion by word and example. The number of his sermons is uncertain; many, however, survive concerning the Advent [Col. 0964B] of the Lord, the Nativity, the Epiphany, fasting, the Passion, and holy Pentecost. Some are also found to have been delivered on the feasts of saints. He also added to the Canon: “Humbly we beseech you, almighty God,” and the rest which follows in order. On the fourth day before the Kalends of July, under Emperor Marcian, full of holiness, he rested in peace.

## CHAPTER VIII

Gregory the Great [Note: [Col. 0963] 590.], also called Gregory I, born of an illustrious senatorial family and trained from boyhood in the liberal disciplines, was then apocrisiarius of the Roman see at Constantinople. At the request of Leander, bishop of Seville, he wrote thirty-six books of *Morals*, which he divided into seven parts. When a plague arose at Rome, while still archdeacon he instituted the sevenfold Litany; afterwards, when Pelagius died, he unwillingly assumed the Roman pontificate. In the time of Agilulf he wrote a dialogue, which he promised as a gift to Queen Theodelinda. He also dictated forty homilies and composed twenty treatises on Ezekiel; he ceased this exposition upon hearing of the approach of King Agilulf. He also wrote the book of pastoral care to Bishop John, and another book which he chose to call *Flowers*. He wrote likewise a book of Responses to Augustine, bishop of the English. He composed also, with the bishops of Italy, a book of Synods concerning necessary affairs of the Church. Some other small works which he wrote are not extant, because they are said to have been removed from circulation when the envy of his rivals burned fiercely.

[Col. 0964D] He added the words spoken in the Canon, “And dispose our days in your peace,” and decreed that the Lord’s Prayer should be recited at Mass, judging it fitting that at the consecration of the Lord’s body there should be said, together with the prayer of the human priest, the prayer of the God-and-man, the Saviour. The people, hearing this as something new and unfamiliar, took it badly; but the holy pontiff at once satisfied them with a humble reply: “If,” he said, “at the consecration of Christ’s body, a prayer must be said which some learned man, a human being, composed by human understanding, how much more ought that prayer to be said which the mediator of God and men [Col. 0965A] instituted, who also taught his disciples to pray in this way?” He also wrote a little explanatory work on the Song of Songs, from the beginning of the book as far as the words: “To my cavalry in Pharaoh’s chariots” (Song of Songs 1). Therefore this most holy pontiff Gregory, apostle of the English, after converting the English to the Lord by the teachers he sent, passed to the Lord in the second year of Emperor Phocas, on the fourth day before the Ides of March.

## CHAPTER IX

Gregory III [Note: [Col. 0965] A.D. 731.] held the Roman pontificate for eight years and added to the Canon: “Into their fellowship.” He died in the time of Emperor Leo, on the fourth day before the Kalends of December.

## CHAPTER X

Pope Sergius [Note: [Col. 0965] 688.], a Syrian by nation, born at Antioch to a father named Tiberius, decreed that at the breaking of the Lord’s body the clergy and people should sing: “Lamb of God.”

## CHAPTER XI

Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0965] 374.], archbishop of Milan, wondrous doctor of the Church, renowned under Emperor Gratian—indeed, most famous throughout the whole world—the Church’s pillar and the ruin of heretics, always and everywhere acting and speaking freely for justice: for he did not spare even Emperor Theodosius when he sinned. He contributed greatly, by writing and teaching, not only to the Church of Milan, over which he presided, but to the universal mother Church.

He wrote one book *On the Holy Spirit* for Emperor Gratian. He also wrote a book *On Faith*, and a book *On the Incarnation of the Lord*. He wrote *On Paradise*, *On Virgins*, *On the Funeral of His Brother*, the *Hexaemeron*, *On Flight from the World*, *On the Patriarchs*, *On the Perpetual [Col. 0965C] Virginity of the Mother of the Lord*, *On Isaac and the Soul*, *On the Good of Death*, *On Joseph*, and an apology concerning David. He wrote on “Blessed are the undefiled” (Psalm 118); on “Lord, who shall dwell?” (Psalm 14); on the death of Gratian; on the death of Theodosius; on fasting; on duties; on Isaiah; on the Apostle; on Luke; against the heretic Auxentius; and to Fritigern, queen of the Marcomanni. Beyond these he wrote many diverse small works, which the Church counts and preserves among her greatest treasures. His memory shall not depart from her, and his name shall be sought for ever.

This most blessed pontiff, outstanding teacher, exceptional in devotion, unconquered in adversity and provident in prosperity, after delightful departures at morning and evening, himself delightful to all, rested in the Lord under the emperors Arcadius and Honorius.

## CHAPTER XII

John of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0965] 398.], surnamed Chrysostom, was twice deposed by the ungrateful Church, and, with the approval of Archbishop Theophilus, was moreover sent into exile. At first deceived by Origen’s error, but forestalled by God’s grace and corrected through its cooperation, he was reconciled to the Church. Learned in both Greek and Latin speech, besides sermons delivered on feasts and written in excellent style, he wrote on the Epistle to the Hebrews; he also wrote an outstanding work on Matthew; a book *On the Restoration of the Fallen*; seven homilies *In Praise of the Apostle Paul*; and a dialogue with Basil on the honour of the priesthood. Renowned under the aforesaid emperors, he left the Churches a renowned memory of himself.

## CHAPTER XIII

Epiphanius [Note: [Col. 0965] 368.], bishop of Salamis, Catholic in faith and excellent in talent, dictated to John Chrysostom a letter not to be despised, exhorting him to the Catholic faith and the preservation of peace, because John had offended him by ordaining two presbyters in Epiphanius’s own diocese. Blessed Jerome the priest translated this letter into Latin at the request of the brethren, for the edification of readers.

## CHAPTER XIV

Fulgentius [Note: [Col. 0965] 507.], bishop, who presided over the Church of Ruspe under Theodoric, king of the Goths, was eminent in his homilies for confession of faith and knowledge. He was an orator, and delivered many useful sermons to the people and transmitted them in writing to posterity. He also wrote a notable book *On Predestination and Faith*, and another to Thrasamund, king of the Vandals.

## CHAPTER XV

Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius [Note: [Col. 0965] 510.], eminent in both sacred and human learning, and also consul at Rome, composed an outstanding work on *Peri hermēneias* [Greek: “On Interpretation”]. He also wrote another work *On Music*, in which he subtly investigated the profundity of that art; and he left yet another written work *On the Faith of the Holy Trinity*. He also wrote to Pope John against the heretics Eutyches and Nestorius. But when Theodoric, king of the Goths, exercised tyranny over the Romans, Boethius the consul secretly sent letters to the Greeks, intending, that is, through their assistance, to withdraw [Note: [Col. 0965] perhaps “to rescue.”] the city and its citizens—and himself among them—from the king’s tyranny. When the impious king learned this, he ordered him, as if guilty of treason, to be sent into exile at Ravenna and shut up in prison. There the wise man, applying philosophical consolation to himself, produced five books in satirical form; and because he intended to console both himself and all who mourn, he entitled his work *The Book of Consolation*. This man left many memorials of his genius to posterity. Leaving two sons in the consulship, he fell, struck by the sword of the wicked king along with several others.

## CHAPTER XVI

Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus [Note: [Col. 0965] A.D. 514.], consul at Rome, then senator, and finally monk, built a monastery. He shone brilliantly in both sacred and secular letters. He expounded the Psalms, wrote the books of *Institutions* and a *Chronicle*, composed a book *On Illustrious Men*, dictated Theodoric’s letters, and in addition arranged a *Tripartite History*.

## CHAPTER XVII

Arator [Note: [Col. 0965] 544.], subdeacon of the Roman Church, who flourished under Pope Vigilius, wrote the book of the Acts [Col. 0967A] of the Apostles in verse, and afterwards read it publicly to the clergy, the people, and the pope.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Priscian of Caesarea [Note: [Col. 0967] A.D. 550.] was a most skilled grammarian and composed an excellent book on the art of grammar. Those who assert that he erred in the faith because he wrote and offered a book to Julian the Apostate are mistaken. They are mistaken, I say, and plainly mistaken: for he wrote not to Julian the emperor but to Julian the consul, brother of Symmachus, Boethius’s father-in-law. Nor did Priscian of Caesarea flourish at Constantinople under Julian the Apostate, who was so foolish in the faith, but under Justinian, a worshipper of Christ. From Julian Caesar to Emperor Justinian there are reckoned two hundred and twenty-seven years.

## CHAPTER XIX

Dionysius [Note: [Col. 0967] 533.], Roman abbot, wrote the Paschal Cycles in the sixth year of Emperor Justin, beginning them with the first year of Emperor Diocletian.

## CHAPTER XX

Benedict [Note: [Col. 0967] 540.], the venerable Father, after the eremitic life which he led in the place called Subiaco, became renowned on Monte Cassino for teaching and miracles. When he first made his way there after leaving his former dwelling, three ravens which he fed daily followed him at God’s command, as is read in the *History of the Lombards* [Note: [Col. 0967] Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book I, chapter 27.]. When he arrived at a crossroads, two angels appeared to him in the form of two young men, showing him the way by which he should go to the place. Now in that place there lived a servant of God, to whom a voice from heaven said:

> Spare these places; another friend is at hand.

The sense of this little verse is: “Leave this place, friend, because another friend ought to live here.” Saint Benedict therefore came to the summit of the mountain and bound himself to the greatest abstinence. There he also wrote the Rule of monks, as blessed Gregory testifies [Note: [Col. 0967] Book II of the *Dialogues*, chapter 26.], remarkable for its discretion and elegant in style. In it, besides other indications of his holiness, he shows sufficiently what a heavenly life he led on earth, because the holy man could not teach otherwise than he lived.

## CHAPTER XXI

Victor, bishop of Capua [Note: [Col. 0967] A.D. 545.], composed an outstanding book *On Easter*, in which he refuted the erroneous writings of Victorius. For Victorius too had written Paschal Cycles at the command of Pope Hilary [Note: [Col. 0967] Hilary.], but they were full of errors; Bishop Victor destroyed them in his writings, as we have said.

## CHAPTER XXII

Jordanes [Note: [Col. 0967] A.D. 552.], bishop, wrote an abridged Chronicle of Roman affairs, which he began with Adam and carried down to Justin the Younger Augustus.

## CHAPTER XXIII

Victor, bishop of Africa [Note: [Col. 0967] 484.], writes a history of the Vandal persecution; and that persecution eventually enveloped its own historian.

## CHAPTER XXIV

Paterius [Note: [Col. 0967] 601.], disciple of Gregory the Great, gathered together the testimonies of Scripture which the blessed Pope Gregory had set down here and there in his treatises, and, once set down, expounded appropriately. For among other commentators Gregory has this almost unique characteristic: he customarily expounds individually the scriptural testimonies he introduces. This writer applied his mind to gathering them anew, since he thought that they would be of no little benefit to posterity.

## CHAPTER XXV

Columba [Note: [Col. 0967] 589.], also called Columbanus, abbot, a native of Ireland, travelled through many lands with his disciples Gallus and others; by exhortation of the word he brought many to faith in Christ, and also founded many monasteries in various places. He wrote with his own hand a Rule for monks, and dictated to them one brief exhortatory letter which, though short, treats abundantly of contempt for the world.

## CHAPTER XXVI

Isidore, bishop of Seville [Note: [Col. 0967] 633.], who succeeded blessed Leander in the episcopate, published many and great works. Among other things he wrote *Synonyms* and an *Abridgment of Times*, which he brought down to Constantine, son of Heraclius. He also wrote the book of *Etymologies*, the *Book of Offices*, and the *Book of Illustrious Men*. Moreover, he transmitted to posterity many sermons delivered at different times and written in an excellent style.

## CHAPTER XXVII

[Col. 0968C] Theodore [Note: [Col. 0967] 668.], venerable archbishop of the English, ordained by Pope Vitalian and sent to England, after benefiting the people over whom he presided by word and example, finally wrote a book concerning the penance of the guilty, composed with outstanding discernment. Hearing also that the Church of Constantinople was severely troubled by the heresy of Eutyches [Note: [Col. 0967] Eutyches.], he convened a synod; and when he heard the agreement of all in the Catholic faith, he committed it to synodal letters for the instruction and remembrance of those who would follow [Note: [Col. 0967] corrected by a fifteenth-century hand: “he took care to commend.”]. The beginning of these letters is as follows: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ the Saviour, in the reign of our most pious lords and kings.” Their conclusion is: “We all subscribe, who with Archbishop Theodore have set forth the Catholic faith.” He was a native of Tarsus in Cilicia and, renowned for many virtues, rested in peace.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

Peter [Note: [Col. 0967] A.D. 433.], archbishop of Ravenna, wrote an excellent book of sermons on topaz and precious refined gold.

## CHAPTER XXIX

Adamnan [Note: [Col. 0967] 679.], presbyter and abbot of the monks who were on the island of Hy, a good and wise man, most nobly instructed in knowledge of the Scriptures, wrote a book *On Holy Places*, very useful to many readers [Note: [Col. 0967] below, chapter 75, “most useful.”]. Its author, who taught and dictated [Col. 0969A] it, was Artwolf [Note: [Col. 0969] others read “Arculf.”], bishop of Gaul. Coming to Jerusalem for prayer, he surveyed the whole land of promise; he also visited Damascus, Constantinople, Alexandria, and the islands of the sea. Returning to his homeland by ship, he was driven by a storm to the western coast of Britain. After many experiences he came to the same servant of God, the presbyter Adamnan, and this latter committed to writing [Note: [Col. 0969] the earlier hand: “took care to commit.”] everything which Arculf reported that he had seen in the holy places worthy of remembrance.

Adamnan presented his book to King Aldfrith [Note: [Col. 0969] read: Aldfrith, king of the Northumbrians.] of the Northumbrians, by whom he was rewarded with many gifts and sent home. But because there is no doubt that few among us have read or even known either the little book or its author, we have excerpted from it, by way of digression, something that may greatly benefit readers—those, at least, who know only what they have learned by reading about the holy places in which patriarchs, prophets, and apostles lived with the Lord himself.

Accordingly, he writes as follows concerning Bethlehem, which is the house of the bread of angels, in which the Virgin of virgins gave birth from herself to the Word made flesh:

Bethlehem, the city of David, is situated on a ridge. It is narrow [Note: [Col. 0969] others read “with a narrow [wall].”] on every side and surrounded by valleys, a thousand paces long from east to west, furnished with a low wall without towers along the edges of its level summit. At its eastern corner is, as it were, a natural half-cave. Its outer part is said to have been the place of the Lord’s birth; the inner part is called the Lord’s Manger. This cave is entirely lined within with precious marble, and above the place where the Lord is especially said to have been born it contains a great church of Saint Mary.

He also wrote as follows concerning the place of Christ’s Passion and Resurrection:

On entering the city of Jerusalem from the north, the first place among the holy sites to which one must turn, owing to the arrangement of the streets, is the Constantinian church called the Martyrium. Emperor Constantine built it with magnificent and royal adornment because the Lord’s cross was found there by his mother Helena. Then, to the west, appears the church of Golgotha, in which may also be seen the rock which once bore the cross when the Lord’s body was fastened to it. It now supports a very large silver cross, while above it hangs a great bronze wheel with lamps. Below the actual place of the Lord’s cross is a crypt cut in the rock, in which sacrifice is customarily offered upon an altar for honoured dead, while their bodies are meanwhile laid in the open court.

To the west of this church is the Anastasis—that is, the church of the Lord’s Resurrection—a round church surrounded by three walls and supported by twelve columns. Between each wall is a broad passageway, since it contains three altars at three points of the middle wall, namely the southern, northern, and western points. It has twice four gates—that is, entrances—through the three corresponding walls [Col. 0970A]; of these, four face the Vulturnus wind and four the Eurus wind. In its middle is the Lord’s round tomb, hewn from rock. A man standing within can touch its roof with his hand. It has an entrance on the east, against which that great stone was placed; to the present day, the marks of the tools are visible inside. Outside, however, it is wholly covered with marble up to the summit of the roof. Its highest roof, ornamented with gold, bears a large golden cross.

On the north side of this tomb is the Lord’s sepulchre, cut in the same rock. It is seven feet long and three palms in measure; it rises above the floor and has an entrance on the south side, where twelve lamps burn day and night—four within [Col. 0970B] the sepulchre and eight above it on the right-hand edge. The stone which had been placed at the door of the tomb is now fixed in place: its smaller part stands as a square altar before the door of the same tomb, while its larger part forms another four-cornered altar, covered with linen cloths, in the eastern part of the same church. The colour of this tomb and sepulchre appears to be a mixture of white and reddish hues.

Regarding the place of the Lord’s Ascension, the aforesaid author relates as follows:

The Mount of Olives equals Mount Sion in height, but exceeds it in breadth and length. Except for vines and olives, it is seldom productive of trees; it is also fertile in wheat and barley. For the nature of its soil is not scrubby but grassy and flowery. On its highest summit, where the Lord ascended into heaven, there is a round church having around it three large vaulted porticoes, roofed above. The inner structure, indeed, could not be vaulted and roofed because of the passage of the Lord’s body; it has an altar toward the east, covered by a narrow roof. In its middle, beneath the heaven left open above, where he ascended, the Lord’s final footprints are seen [Col. 0970C]. Although earth is daily removed from them by believers, it nevertheless remains [Note: [Col. 0969] supply: “and”] and still preserves the same appearance, as though marked by impressed footprints. Around this is a bronze wheel, lying at a height up to the neck; it has an entrance on the west, with a great lamp suspended above on chains, shining all day and night. In the western part of the same church are eight windows and, opposite them, the same number of lamps hanging on cords, whose light shines through the glass as far as Jerusalem [Col. 0970D]. It is said that their radiance makes the hearts of those who look upon it tremble with a certain joy and compunction. Every year, on the day of the Lord’s Ascension, after Mass has been completed, a storm of mighty thunder customarily comes down from above and throws to the ground all who are in the church. Concerning the site of Hebron and the monuments of the fathers, he likewise writes:

Hebron, once a city and the capital of David’s kingdom, now reveals what it formerly was only by its ruins. One stadium to the east it has a double cave in a valley, where the tombs of the patriarchs are enclosed by a square wall [Col. 0971A], their heads turned northward. Each is covered by a separate stone, fashioned like squared ashlar: those of the three patriarchs with white stones; Adam’s with work darker and less costly, he resting not far from them, toward the north and at the far end of that wall. The memorials of the three women are likewise seen, smaller and less splendid. The hill of Mamre lies a thousand paces north of those monuments, very grassy and flowery, with a level plain on its summit. On its northern side the oak of Abraham, with a trunk of the height of two men, is surrounded by a church.

These extracts from the small works of the aforesaid writer we here present for readers’ benefit: they convey the sense of his words, but are compressed in briefer and more concise language. Whoever delights to know more of that volume [Col. 0971B] may seek it either in the volume itself [Note: [Col. 0971] It is extant in Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, century III, part II.], or in the epitome which the venerable priest Bede [Note: [Col. 0971] *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, book V, chapter 16.] briefly made from it.

## CHAPTER XXX

Althelmus [Note: [Col. 0971] A.D. 680], while still a priest and abbot of the monastery which the English call the town of Maildub, wrote, at the command of the synod of his people, an excellent book against the error of the Britons. They either celebrate Easter at the wrong time or commit many other acts contrary to ecclesiastical chastity and peace. By means of this work he brought many Britons subject to the West Saxons to the celebration of Catholic Easter. He also wrote an outstanding book on virginity [Col. 0971C], which, after the example of Sedulius, he composed as a double work, both in hexameter verse and in prose. He wrote several other works as well, being in every respect an exceedingly learned man. For he was elegant in expression and remarkable for his learning in both liberal and ecclesiastical writings.

## CHAPTER XXXI

Bede [Note: [Col. 0971] 701], the Venerable priest and monk, English by nation, was entrusted to Christ’s service under Abbot Geolfrid [Note: [Col. 0971] elsewhere, Ceolfrid.] and served ecclesiastical needs through many small works. Yet concerning both himself and his works we shall present his own testimony. For in the book which he wrote concerning the history and deeds of his native land, he took care to record that he was born in England; that at the age of four he was given by the care of his kinsfolk to Benedict, and afterward to Abbot Geolfrid, in the monastery of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, to be educated in sacred letters; that, spending the whole remaining time of his life in residence at the same monastery [Col. 0971D], he devoted all his effort to meditation upon the Scriptures; that amid observance of regular discipline and the daily duty of singing in church, he always found it sweet either to write, learn, or teach; that at the nineteenth year of his life he received the diaconate, and at the thirtieth the priesthood, by the command of his abbot; and how much, after receiving priestly orders and until the fifty-ninth year of his life, he had briefly annotated from the works of the venerable Fathers or added in accordance with their meaning and interpretation [Col. 0972A].

“In the beginning of Genesis, as far as the birth of Isaac and the casting out of Ishmael, four books; on the Tabernacle and its vessels, and the garments of the priests, four books; on the building of the Temple, two books of allegorical exposition, as also in the case of the rest. Likewise, thirty Questions on the book of Kings; two books on the Proverbs of Solomon; seven books on the Song of Songs; on the prophet Isaiah, Daniel, the Twelve Prophets, and seven divisions of the chapters of Jeremiah, extracted from the treatise of blessed Jerome; three books on Ezra and Nehemiah; one book on the song of Habakkuk; one book of allegorical explanations on the book of the blessed Father Tobit, concerning Christ and the Church [Col. 0972B]; chapters for readings on the Pentateuch of Moses, Joshua, Judges, the books and words of Chronicles, the book of the blessed Father Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs; on the prophet Isaiah, and also on Ezra and Nehemiah; four books on the Gospel of Mark; six books on the Gospel of Luke; two books of Gospel homilies; on the Apostle, I took care to transcribe in order everything I found expounded in the small works of Saint Augustine; two books on the Acts of the Apostles; one book each on the seven Catholic Epistles; three books on the Apocalypse of Saint John; likewise, a chapter-list for readings throughout the whole New Testament except the Gospel; likewise a book of Letters to various persons [Col. 0972C], one of which is on the six ages, one on the stations of the children of Israel, and one on the saying of Isaiah: ‘And they shall be shut up there in prison, and after many days they shall be visited’ [Isa. 24]. One book on the calculation of leap-year; one on the equinox according to Anatolius.

“Likewise, from the metrical work of Paulinus I translated into prose the book of the life and passion of Saint Felix the confessor. I corrected, as far as I could, in accordance with the sense, the book of the life and passion of Saint Anastasius, badly translated from Greek and still more badly corrected by an unskilled person. I described the life of the holy Father Cudbrect [Note: [Col. 0971] elsewhere, Cudbert], monk and bishop alike, first in heroic verse and afterward in plain prose. I wrote in two little books the History of the Abbots of this monastery, in which I joyfully serve the heavenly mercy: Benedict, Geolfrid, Hey, and Berect [Col. 0972D]. I wrote the Ecclesiastical History of our island and people in ten books; a Martyrology concerning the feast-days of holy martyrs, in which I diligently sought to note all whom I could find—not only on what day, but also by what kind of contest or under what judge they overcame the world; a book of Hymns in various metres or rhythms; a book of Epigrams in heroic or elegiac metre; one book each on the nature of things and on times; likewise, a larger book on times; a book on Orthography, arranged in alphabetical order [Col. 0973A]; likewise a book on metrical art, and added to it another small book on Figures or Tropes—that is, the figures and modes by which sacred Scripture is composed.”

## CHAPTER XXXII

Zacharias [Note: [Col. 0973] A.D. 741], pope, skilled in both languages, translated the four books of the Dialogues of blessed Gregory from Latin into Greek.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

Peter [Note: [Col. 0973] 1057] Damiani, cardinal-bishop, wrote a book most pleasing alike in title and in worth, and another book entitled *The Lord Be with You*, against those who said that this form of greeting ought not to be used by solitaries in the celebration of Masses.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

Paschasius [Note: [Col. 0973] 844], also called Radbertus [Col. 0973B], distinguished for faith and learning, wrote a book on the Lord’s body which should be faithfully embraced by all throughout the world.

## CHAPTER XXXV

Sedulius [Note: [Col. 0973] about 450], a bishop, wrote to Macedonius, his teacher and priest, two books on the Old and New Testaments in heroic verse, to which he prefixed a lengthy prose prologue.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

Theodolus [Note: [Col. 0973] uncertain date] was born of parents who were neither low-born nor non-Christian. Educated as a boy in Italy, he studied in Greece. Thus, learned in both languages, while at Athens he heard pagans disputing with believers. Gathering their arguments, he transferred them into an allegorical *Eclogue*, which death prevented him from revising; hence we find a few blemishes in his work. When he wrote, “Tell also that you know the secret of Trojan praise,” he incorrectly shortened *scire* [Note: [Col. 0973] Theodolus, *Eclogue*, verse 319: “Tell also that you know the secret of Trojan praise.”]. At last, endowed with excellence both of character and learning, he died under the clerical rule. His book is entitled *Eclogue*, a term evidently derived from goats; as though it were called *aigōn logos* [Note: [Col. 0973] αἰγῶν λόγος.], that is, “goatish discourse”; or because it censures the foulness of vices, signified by that animal. Some also interpret it from the Greek *eklogē* [Note: [Col. 0973] ἐκλογή, or ἐκλογεῖον: collection, selection, etc.] as “exercise” in Latin [Note: [Col. 0973] perhaps “excerpt.”], because it is composed from a collection of many histories and fables.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0973] A.D. 573], archbishop of Tours, an outstanding teacher and historian, wrote many histories [Col. 0973D] and an excellent volume on the miracles of the saints.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

Martin [Note: [Col. 0973] A.D. 560], archbishop of Braga [Note: [Col. 0973] Braccarensis.], wrote for King Miro a small book on the four virtues.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

Caesarius [Note: [Col. 0973] A.D. 502], monk of the monastery of Lérins and afterward archbishop of Arles, wrote ten exhortatory homilies for monks [Col. 0974A], all of which discuss at length contempt for the world.

## CHAPTER XL

Ado [Note: [Col. 0973] 859], archbishop of Vienne, wrote among other things a Martyrology of saints. Letters addressed to Ado by Pope Nicholas are extant.

## CHAPTER XLI

Albinus [Note: [Col. 0973] 780], also called Alcuin, a priest by office, most excellent in intellect, and Catholic in faith, wrote on grammar, rhetoric, dialectic, and astronomy; he also wrote a book on the Trinity. He wrote to Count Gwido on the eight vices, and also wrote on John. He arranged corresponding offices for the seven weekdays, with an eighth—that is, Sunday—added: on Sunday, the Holy Trinity; on Monday, Wisdom; on Tuesday, the Holy Spirit; on Wednesday, the angels; on Thursday [Col. 0974B], charity; on Friday, the Holy Cross; and on Saturday, Saint Mary—so that an office proper to each is celebrated for each. I thought this worth mentioning because the order of that institution is still observed in many churches today. He also wrote *Questions on Genesis according to the Letter*.

## CHAPTER XLII

Justus [Note: [Col. 0973] others say bishop of Urgell, flourishing in 529], archbishop of Vienne, wrote for Pope Sergius a book of explanations of the Song of Songs.

## CHAPTER XLIII

Hetto [Note: [Col. 0973] A.D. 841], a venerable priest of the monastery of Reichenau in the time of Louis, described in prose the marvelous vision of a monk of Reichenau named Wertin: taken out of his body, he saw it; restored, he died after three days. The same man afterward [Col. 0974C] became bishop of Basel and, sent to Constantinople with Counts Hugh [Note: [Col. 0973] others read Hugo.] and Ajo, described his own *Hodoeporicon*, or account of a journey.

## CHAPTER XLIV

Waltfrid [Note: [Col. 0973] A.D. 842] Strabo [Note: [Col. 0973] elsewhere Walafrid.], a learned man who presided over the monastery of Reichenau for seven years, left posterity many memorials of his genius in verse and prose. He diligently described in verse the same vision of that monk.

## CHAPTER XLV

Magnentius Rabanus Maurus [Note: [Col. 0973] A.D. 850], first abbot of Fulda and then archbishop of Mainz, was exceedingly devoted to writing. He composed a book on the mystery of the Holy Cross in varied figures and verse, which he sent to Pope Sergius. Writing also on the whole Old Testament, he left nothing untouched. He wrote an excellent volume on Matthew [Col. 0974D]; he also wrote on computation, for Louis on the songs of the prophets, and on the Apostle.

## CHAPTER XLVI

Hincmaurus [Note: [Col. 0973] elsewhere Hincmarus; A.D. 741], most reverend archbishop of Rheims, wrote for Charles on collections and on canons; he also wrote a work of no slight value on the life and virtues of Saint Remigius.

## CHAPTER XLVII

[Col. 0975A]

Ratramnus [Note: [Col. 0975] A.D. 840], a learned man, wrote a small book for a certain prince on the body and blood of the Lord. For the present we refrain from praising this book, until, having read it—if it should happen to come into our hands—we may ascertain whether it agrees with sound and Catholic faith.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

Laurentius [Note: [Col. 0975] 705; of Novara], distinguished for learning and knowledge, wrote a book on the two times, in which penitents may find many remedies.

## CHAPTER XLIX

Rudolfus [Note: [Col. 0975] 850], priest and monk of Fulda monastery, a notable teacher, called also a poet and a sufficiently learned historian, departed this life on the eighth day before the Ides of March, after writing many useful works.

## CHAPTER L

Smaragdus [Note: [Col. 0975] A.D. 810], abbot, wrote a most useful work on the epistles and Gospels appointed for each Sunday [Col. 0975B]. He also wrote another small book, collected from diverse virtues, and gave it the title *The Diadem of Monks*, because, as a diadem shines with gems, so this book shines with ornaments.

## CHAPTER LI

Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0975] 760], also called Autpertus, abbot [Note: [Col. 0975] elsewhere, of San Vincenzo al Volturno.] of the monastery of Agaunum, wrote an exposition of the book of the Apocalypse of John the Apostle. In the manner of Prudentius’ *Psychomachia*, meaning “battle of the soul,” he also wrote *The Conflict of Virtues and Vices*, which he sent to Abbot and Priest Lantfrid, living in Bavaria.

## CHAPTER LII

Julian [Note: [Col. 0975] A.D. 680], bishop of Toledo, a man supremely learned in letters [Col. 0975C], wrote for Idalius, bishop of Barcelona, a book of *Prognostics* concerning the last days and the beginning of the age to come.

## CHAPTER LIII

Bachiarius [Note: [Col. 0975] 440], a man of excellent talent, wrote for Januarius a book *On the Restoration of One Who Has Fallen*.

## CHAPTER LIV

Regino [Note: [Col. 0975] 892], abbot of Prüm, wrote a Chronicle which he began from the first year of the Lord’s Incarnation and carried down to the year 1005.

## CHAPTER LV

Eucherius [Note: [Col. 0975] 434], very practiced in the divine Scriptures, wrote *Questions on the Book of Kings*. He likewise wrote on the form of spiritual understanding and on the interpretation of names. Another book written by him is also extant, entitled *On More Difficult Questions*.

## CHAPTER LVI

[Col. 0975D]

Marcellinus [Note: [Col. 0975] 380], a Roman by nation, wrote a Chronicle in which he gave a clear indication of his keen intelligence.

## CHAPTER LVII

Paul [Note: [Col. 0975] uncertain date], a monk, wrote a Rule for monks, in whose composition he had his colleague Stephen as collaborator. It was therefore thought fitting to entitle the same Rule under the names of both, for example: “Here begins the Rule of Paul and Stephen.”

## CHAPTER LVIII

[Col. 0976A]

Porcharius [Note: [Col. 0975] a fifteenth-century hand reads Burcharius elsewhere], a man of venerable life [Note: [Col. 0975] A.D. 500], abbot of the monastery of Lérins, who sent blessed Caesarius to be bishop of the church of Arles, wrote for monks certain writings which he chose to call *Admonitions*. In them he discussed contempt for the world both briefly and extensively: briefly in words, but extensively in the marrow of his thoughts. He is said to have been captured and killed by the Saracens with a great multitude of his flock.

## CHAPTER LIX

John [Note: [Col. 0975] uncertain date], a musician and an Englishman by nation, was a man of very subtle intellect; he composed an outstanding small book on musical art.

## CHAPTER LX

John [Note: [Col. 0975] A.D. 875], Roman by nation and archdeacon of the Roman Church, a man acute in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote, by the authority and assent of blessed Pope John [Col. 0976B], a rather famous work on the life of the most blessed Pope Gregory.

## CHAPTER LXI

Fricholphus [Note: [Col. 0975] elsewhere Freculphus; A.D. 824], a bishop outstanding in knowledge and learning, wrote explanations of Genesis and wove together a truthful history from the beginning of the world down to the time of the Northmen.

## CHAPTER LXII

Arnulf [Note: [Col. 0975] 1041], priest and monk of the monastery of Saint Emmeram, wrote the *Dialogue of Collectitius and Admonitius* on the virtues of the saints who are buried in peace in that same place and await the final trumpet.

## CHAPTER LXIII

Arbo [Note: [Col. 0975] elsewhere Atibo], also called Cyrias [Note: [Col. 0975] in the same hand, elsewhere Cyrinus; A.D. 760], bishop of Freising, wrote two substantial small works on the deeds of Saints Emmeram and Corbinian.

## CHAPTER LXIV

[Col. 0976C]

Paul [Note: [Col. 0975] uncertain date], a Jew and monk of Fulda, composed the life of Saint Erhard, bishop of Regensburg, and also a prose work on the conversion of Saint Paul the Apostle, commonly called a sequence, whose beginning is: “The Lord said, ‘From Bashan’” (*Dixit Dominus ex Basan*, Ps. 67), etc.

## CHAPTER LXV

Nocherus [Note: [Col. 0975] elsewhere Notgerus], abbot [Note: [Col. 0975] A.D. 912] of Reichenau, a man distinguished in faith and deeds, highly learned in letters, and very skilled in music, composed the small book which he was pleased to call, in the customary term, *Sequences*. Prefacing it with a prologue, he sent it to the venerable Luitward, bishop of Vercelli.

## CHAPTER LXVI

Remigius [Note: [Col. 0975] 880], a distinguished man adequately instructed in both sacred and secular letters [Col. 0976D], wrote, among other works, an exposition of Genesis. He also composed a notable commentary on the Psalter. Another commentary of his, written on Donatus, is likewise extant.

## CHAPTER LXVII

Paul [Note: [Col. 0975] 820], a learned man, wrote among other things a most useful book entitled *On the Meaning of Words*.

## CHAPTER LXVIII

Egebert of Hersfeld [Note: [Col. 0975] about A.D. 1100], a Swabian by nation and priest by office, wrote among other things the Life [Col. 0977A] of Saint Nemorad [Note: [Col. 0977] a later hand reads “Jeremedad,” but Heimerad appears to be the intended reading], confessor, who flourished in the time of Emperor Conrad.

## CHAPTER LXIX

Orosius [Note: [Col. 0977] A.D. 416], venerable and, as is supposed, a bishop, wrote among other things a commentary on the book of the Twelve Prophets.

## CHAPTER LXX

Erchard [Note: [Col. 0977] 1040], monk of the monastery of Saint Gall and a man of rather keen intellect, composed the *Deeds of Walter* in heroic verse, while Henry III was reigning.

## CHAPTER LXXI

Amularius [Note: [Col. 0977] 810], venerable archbishop of Trier, wrote among other things an outstanding work *On the Offices*. Rudwert, abbot of Deutz, of blessed memory, mentions this work—indeed, its author—in his own book which he wrote on the offices.

## CHAPTER LXXII

Achelinus [Note: [Col. 0977] Athelinus; uncertain date], a bishop, published certain writings called *Riddles*.

## CHAPTER LXXIII

Symphrosius [Note: [Col. 0977] Symposius; uncertain date], a most learned man in his style and learning, likewise wrote *Riddles*. Although these are still possessed by many today, we have not yet been able to obtain copies to read them.

## CHAPTER LXXIV

Zenophirus [Note: [Col. 0977] perhaps Theophanes of Byzantium, flourishing A.D. 580], bishop of Constantinople, wrote among other things a book entitled *Chronography*.

## CHAPTER LXXV

Otto [Note: [Col. 0977] A.D. 926; elsewhere Odo], venerable abbot of Cluny, a most ardent lover of monastic religion, the jewel of monks and the glory of his disciples, composed a very useful Dialogue on musical art. He also wrote an outstanding and most useful book for monks, namely the book of *Occupations* [Col. 0977B].

## CHAPTER LXXVI

Heymo [Note: [Col. 0977] 841], a wise man dwelling under monastic profession at Saint Germanus in Auxerre, wrote many and varied small works. He wrote a book of enormous size on the Apostle; an excellent exposition of the book of the Apocalypse; a work on the Song of Songs; and the text of the Twelve Prophets. He also wrote several treatises on the Gospels.

## CHAPTER LXXVII

Albert [Note: [Col. 0977] uncertain date], a monk, was an incomparable computist and wrote a notable small book on the rules of computation.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII

Willeraminus [Note: [Col. 0977] A.D. 107; elsewhere Willeramus], abbot of Ebersberg, irreproachable in life and learning, possessed a very keen talent for composing verse [Col. 0977C]. He also elegantly expounded the Song of Songs in heroic metre.

## CHAPTER LXXIX

Stephen [Note: [Col. 0977] A.D. 910], a musician and most expert man [Note: [Col. 0977] perhaps bishop of Liège], composed among other things an outstanding small book on musical art.

## CHAPTER LXXX

Gwido [Note: [Col. 0977] A.D. 1020], an abbot incomparable in faith and learning, flourished also in many virtues in this life. After his death he was buried at Sutri [Col. 0978A], but was afterward transferred to Speyer by Emperor Henry. In his lifetime he contributed greatly to the welfare of churches by writing and teaching; among several other things which he wrote, he produced an outstanding work on music, in which he gave manifest proof of his subtlety to students of that art.

## CHAPTER LXXXI

Bern [Note: [Col. 0977] 1020; elsewhere Berno], a musician, pious and learned, lived under monastic profession in the monastery of Prüm. Emperor Henry the Pious afterward made him abbot of Reichenau. Graciously received by the brethren, he gathered together the scattered brothers again, and, consecrated by Lampert, bishop of Constance, presided with great and distinguished piety and learning for forty years. He wrote a book *On the Institution of Masses* and an outstanding work on music, as well as the Life of Saint Ulric, bishop of Augsburg.

## CHAPTER LXXXII

Husardus [Note: [Col. 0977] A.D. 876], also called Charles, an illustrious man, wrote among other things a Martyrology of saints.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII

Bruno, bishop of Segni [Note: [Col. 0977] read Signiensis, A.D. 1087], a good and Catholic man, produced a highly useful treatise in which, after invoking grace and peace upon all believers throughout the world and beginning with praise of the most blessed Pope Leo, he wrote certain things concerning simoniacs and the sacraments of simoniacs. At the request of the venerable bishop of Maguelonne, he also wrote mystical material on the dedications of churches and other sacraments of the Church.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV

[Col. 0978B]

Another Bruno [Note: [Col. 0977] 1033, bishop of Würzburg], distinguished in learning and knowledge, likewise wrote against simoniacs. He wrote an outstanding work on the Psalter.

## CHAPTER LXXXV

Bruno [Note: [Col. 0977] A.D. 1040; the manuscript incorrectly has “Uruno”], bishop of Toul, also Pope Leo IX, wrote a letter to Leo of Constantinople and Michael of Acrida, bishops, teaching them to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. He was most subtle in music and, among many other chants which he produced, composed with considerable artistry a History of the most blessed Pope Gregory.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI

Frederick [Note: [Col. 0977] A.D. 1057], envoy of Pope Leo IX, later himself Pope Stephen—his own name having been changed [Note: [Col. 0977] perhaps “his own.”] to Stephen [Note: [Col. 0977] Stephen IX, Supreme Pontiff.]—wrote a notable treatise against the heresy of the “ferment-bread party” [Note: [Col. 0977] perhaps “fermentarians.”].

## CHAPTER LXXXVII

Humbert [Note: [Col. 0977] A.D. 1054], bishop of Santa Rufina [Col. 0978C], wrote extensively against the aforesaid heresy.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII

Berengar [Note: [Col. 0977] 1035], born at Tours and archdeacon of the church of Angers, was at first a heretic; for he maintained that the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood was only a sign of a sacred reality. Some followers of his error were also called Berengarians after the name of Berengar. This Berengar [Col. 0979A], indeed, finally overcome by heavenly power and the truth of arguments, renounced that heresy of his in writing, though not in heart. Pope Nicholas received from him, in a universal council gathered at Rome, the formula of his oath, which the holy Roman Church customarily requires from all converted heretics. Yet he is said to have confirmed the Catholic faith concerning the sacrament of the Savior’s body and blood by these verses:

> It is certain that flesh is created from bread upon the altar;  
> That very flesh is God: whoever denies this is guilty.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX

Lanfranc [Note: [Col. 0979] A.D. 1070], bishop of the English, was a man of remarkable holiness and learning, who left several memorable works against the heresy of the Berengarians.

## CHAPTER XC

[Col. 0979B]

Christian [Note: [Col. 0979] 1040], bishop of the Apulians, a man distinguished in learning and holiness, argued most invincibly against that same heresy.

## CHAPTER XCI

Hermann [Note: [Col. 0979] 1050] the Lame, a Swabian, was a philosopher most subtle in computation; he wrote a book on the chief rules of calculation. He also wrote in verse a book called *The Conflict of the Sheep and the Flax*; likewise another poem in the manner of Theodolus; and a third poem on contempt for the world. In music, indeed, he was subtler than almost all modern writers, and he produced many musical songs and highly authoritative chants concerning saints. He also composed a Chronicle and the deeds of Conrad and Henry; in all these works his ability shone forth clearly.

## CHAPTER XCII

[Col. 0979C]

Berthold [Note: [Col. 0979] 1066], who had been his hearer and disciple, wrote the Life of his Master and a Chronicle.

## CHAPTER XCIII

Folbert [Note: [Col. 0979] 1007], bishop of Chartres and also teacher of Berengar, whom we mentioned above, wrote among other things a treatise against Jews and bad Christians. He wrote the Life of Saint Giles and a sermon on the Nativity of Saint Mary, Mother of the Lord.

## CHAPTER XCIV

Burchard [Note: [Col. 0979] 996], bishop of Worms, wrote most useful collections on the canons.

## CHAPTER XCV

Ivo [Note: [Col. 0979] 1092], bishop of Chartres, wrote among other things several extracts from the canons. He wrote many letters to various persons, a Martyrology [Col. 0979D] of saints, and *Sentences on the Divine Offices*.

## CHAPTER XCVI

Anselm [Note: [Col. 0979] 1093], archbishop of Canterbury, fittingly adorned with learning and character, while still presiding over the monastery of Bec, wrote a Letter to Brother Maurice concerning a fugitive brother. In it he added and resolved another question: namely, how evil is said to be and is nothing, although it appears to be something. He also produced another work which, according to the subject of which it treats, he named *Why God Became Man*, and divided into two books. At different times he composed three treatises pertaining to the study of sacred Scripture, alike in this respect: they were written in question-and-answer form, the questioner being identified by the name “Disciple” and the respondent by the name “Master” [Col. 0980A].

One of these three is *On Truth*: what truth is, in what things it is customarily said to exist, and what justice is. Another is *On Freedom of Choice*: what it is; whether a human being always possesses it; and how many are its modes with respect to possessing or not possessing the rectitude of will, for preserving which it was given to rational creatures. The third concerns the question: What sin did the devil commit in not standing in truth, since God did not give him perseverance—which he could not have unless God gave it, and which he would have had had God given it, just as the good angels had it [Col. 0980B], because God gave it to them? Although in that treatise he spoke of the confirmation of the good angels, he titled it *On the Fall of the Devil*, since what he said of the good angels was incidental, while what he wrote of the evil ones was the intended subject of the question.

Finally, he produced in the same manner a fourth work, not useless for one beginning dialectic, whose opening is *On the Grammarian*. Since it pertained to a different study from those three, he did not give it the same title. He furthermore wrote two substantial works, namely the *Monologion* and *Proslogion*, chiefly in order that what we hold by faith concerning the divine nature and its persons, apart from the Incarnation, might be demonstrated by necessary arguments without the authority of Scripture [Col. 0980C]. He also wrote a book on virginal conception and original sin; for Pope Urban II, a book *On the Incarnation of the Word*; and against the Greeks, a book *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*. He wrote also to Williram, bishop of Neuburg, a letter concerning the Greeks’ disagreement in the sacrificial rite. Moreover, on the Gospel passage, “Jesus entered a certain village” (Luke 10), he wrote a new exposition, most fittingly suited to the feast and praises of Saint Mary, Mother of God. He also wrote a most orderly Martyrology of saints.

## CHAPTER XCVII

Gisilbert [Note: [Col. 0979] 1080; elsewhere Gillebert], abbot of Westminster, wrote a dialogue between a Jew and a Christian, which he sent to Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, for examination.

## CHAPTER XCVIII

[Col. 0980D]

Clement [Note: [Col. 0979] A.D. 1080], also called Gwibert, bishop of the see of Ravenna and afterward, through King Henry, intruded into the Roman Church over Gregory VII—unwillingly, though according to some forcibly—had no good fortune either at Ravenna, much less at Rome. Yet he was eloquent in speech and acute in intellect, and outlived three men who succeeded one another in the papacy. Reproaching blessed Pope Urban for his exile, he directed these verbal missiles against him in verse:

> You are called Urban, though you have been cast out from the city;  
> Either change your name, or return to the city.

## CHAPTER XCIX

[Col. 0981A]

Pope Urban II [Note: [Col. 0981] A.D. 1088], eminent in learning and holiness, having received this insult, replied thus in verse to his rival:

> You bear the name Clement, but cannot be clement;  
> No power to loose has been handed down to you.

By these words he plainly declares that his opponent had attained nothing of apostolic dignity except the name.

## CHAPTER C

Anselm [Note: [Col. 0981] 1071], bishop of Lucca, a man in every respect Catholic, endowed with every kind of learning to perfection, and renowned for miracles after death, loved blessed Gregory VII uniquely and wrote an outstanding work against Gwibert and his followers. He also wrote an immense work on the Psalter [Col. 0981B], in which, at suitable places, he argues in apostrophe against Gwibert and Henry.

## CHAPTER CI

Bernard [Note: [Col. 0981] 1070; Simler reads Bernold], a learned and Catholic priest, had a useful disputation with a colleague under the priest Albanus concerning the incontinence of priests. He then wrote an *Apologeticum* on the decrees which the venerable Pope Gregory VII, bearing the same name, promulgated in the Roman synod against simoniacs and incontinent ministers of the altar. He further wrote a book on the power of priests, a book on the concord of the offices, and a book on confession. He also wrote a quite useful Chronicle.

## CHAPTER CII

Guidmund [Note: [Col. 0981] A.D. 1066], also called Christian, was first a monk in the monastery of Stavelot. When he was to be made abbot there and sent to govern another place [Col. 0981C], he fled. Seeking an unknown province so that he could not be recognized, he changed his name for a better one, taking the name “Christian,” common to all believers. At length, when sought and found, he was made bishop of Aversa under Gregory VII. He wrote for the brethren of the aforementioned monastery an excellent exposition of the Gospel according to Matthew. In the prologue to this exposition he promises that he will also write on John; but whether he did not write it at all, or did write it but it has not reached us, remains unknown to us. He did, however, write an exposition on the Gospel according to Luke.

## CHAPTER CIII

[Col. 0981D]

### Chapter CIII

Rudolph [Note: [Col. 0981] perhaps Rudolph of Truaxdon, who flourished in A.D. 1120.], an abbot most acute both in other arts and in music, also wrote, among other works, a Chronicle.

### Chapter CIV

Ekehard [Note: [Col. 0981] perhaps the Younger, monk of St Gall, who flourished in A.D. 1013.], an abbot, was a man exceedingly learned and devout; he likewise wrote his own Chronicle.

### Chapter CV

Manegold [Note: [Col. 0981] 1070.], a priest, master of the masters of his age, was a vigorous defender of the truth, from which neither promises nor the threats of the schismatic king could turn him. Indeed, in the dispute which arose between Gregory VII and Henry IV, he laboured in defence of justice even to the point of imprisonment. There survives an exhortatory letter written to him by Ivo, bishop of Chartres. He divided the text of the prophet Isaiah by divisions of pages; on Matthew he wrote continuous glosses. He also wrote on the Psalter a most excellent work, more precious than topaz and refined gold.

### Chapter CVI

Aribo Cirinus [Note: [Col. 0981] 1090.], a musician, wrote a work on music which, because of the swiftness of its metre, he called *The Goat*: “For,” he says, “it ran more swiftly while I was hunting it, because it was God’s will that what I desired should quickly come to meet me.” In this treatise he discusses the practice of the same art more subtly than others. In it he also mentions Lord William the musician, saying:

> William, formerly a monk of St Emmeram at Regensburg, but now elsewhere a venerable abbot [Note: [Col. 0981] of Hirsau.], devised a new measure of the pipes [Note: [Col. 0981] the manuscript reads *vistularum*, perhaps *versiculorum*, “of little verses.”], changing the tension of the former into relaxation; and he shared it with me. For he loved my littleness beyond the worthiness of littleness, though he was first among musicians: namely, a modern Orpheus and Pythagoras.

He therefore presented this treatise to his bishop, to whom he also writes, as he says:

> Aribo the musician adorned this treatise,  
> And gave it as a gift to his own bishop.

### Chapter CVII

Fucrald [Note: [Col. 0981] date uncertain.], a musician, possessed extensive knowledge of the musical art and wrote a book on music.

### Chapter CVIII

William [Note: [Col. 0981] A.D. 1090.], a most reverend abbot, descended among the Bavarians from devout parents and educated in the monastery of St Emmeram at Regensburg, possessed—divine mercy accompanying him—such excellence of intellect that, together with the eminence of his honourable character, he stood out through his study of various arts. Of these he left us many memorials of his remarkable genius.

For he devised a natural clock in the likeness of the celestial hemisphere; he demonstrated by certain experiments how to discover the natural solstices or equinoxes and the condition of the world; and he took care to commit all this to writing. He also resolved many questions concerning calculation by the soundest arguments. He was exceedingly skilled in music and clarified many subtle matters unknown to ancient teachers. He also corrected, in accordance with art and with sufficient reason, many errors detected in chants. In the Quadrivium [Note: [Col. 0981] By the quadrivium are meant the four mathematical disciplines: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astrology; just as by the trivium are meant the three disciplines of grammar, logic, and rhetoric.] he seemed to surpass almost all the ancients.

He nevertheless wrote one treatise on music, which he did not complete after he had been called by God to govern the monastery of Hirsau. He urged Lord Ulrich, monk of the monastery of Cluny, to write the customs of the monks.

### Chapter CIX

Dietger [Note: [Col. 0983] A.D. 1070.], called Theogorus by the Latins and by certain Teutons [Note: [Col. 0983] perhaps “Teutons.”] Theokarius, was first a disciple of Lord Abbot William, then the third abbot of the monastery of St George, and finally bishop of Metz. After administering the bishopric for some time, he was buried at Cluny. He too wrote one treatise on music, in which he discusses, briefly indeed but quite subtly, its invention, numbers, and proportions according to the arithmeticians.

### Chapter CX

Ulrich [Note: [Col. 0983] A.D. 1070.], a canon of the church of Regensburg and afterwards a monk of the monastery of Cluny, was a man of great learning and great patience. For he patiently endured many bodily afflictions sent by the Lord and many injuries inflicted upon him by false brethren.

He wrote many letters to various persons, rebuking those who needed rebuke and praising those who needed exhortation. He also wrote a letter to the venerable Abbot William, in which he reproved him because of the irregular cloak which, though innocently, he wore as a result of the usurpation of German abbots. He taught him that he ought not to exceed the dress of those subject to him, since he knew what is written: “They have appointed you their leader; be among them as one of them” [Note: [Col. 0983] Ecclesiasticus 32.].

Then was fulfilled the Scripture which says: “Reprove a wise man and he will love you; teach a just man and he will hasten to receive it” [Note: [Col. 0983] Proverbs 9.]. For immediately, as he received the letter with one hand and perceived that the cloak had been reproved, with the other hand he removed it, never to put it on again; nor did he delay until he had read through the letter.

He also composed the Life and epitaph of St Herman, monk, son of Margrave Duke Berchtold and brother of Gerard, bishop of Constance. Moreover, he wrote a volume on the customs of the monks of Cluny, which is read almost everywhere in the world.

### Chapter CXI

Meginbard [Note: [Col. 0983] I. year II. A.D. 1033 or 1088.], bishop of Würzburg, wrote an exposition of the Song of Songs, an outstanding work.

### Chapter CXII

Ponizo [Note: [Col. 0983] otherwise Bonizo; A.D. 1070.], priest of Sutri, in the time of Gregory VII, wrote extracts from the canons [Note: [Col. 0983] “thus I supply the passage.”].

### Chapter CXIII

Deusdedit [Note: [Col. 0983] A.D. 1070.], cardinal, wrote against the Guibertines in the same period.

### Chapter CXIV

Gottschalk [Note: [Col. 0983] date uncertain.], monk of Deching, wrote, among other works, a little book of four sermons: the first on the conception of St John the Baptist; the second on St Mary; the third on the dispersion of the apostles; and the fourth on the beginning of the Gospel according to Matthew.

### Chapter CXV

Placidus [Note: [Col. 0983] A.D. 1070.], prior of the monastery of Nonantola, wrote against investitures and the unjust power of Henry IV.

### Chapter CXVI

Gerald [Note: [Col. 0983] date uncertain.], a learned man who became a monk at the monastery of St Blaise, led the religious life for some time. Among other works, he wrote a treatise on dialectic. He also wrote collections of quite useful sayings.

### Chapter CXVII

Rupert [Note: [Col. 0983] 1120.] the Great, having acquired a great and marvellous gift of learning, was educated from childhood in regular disciplines at Liège, in the monastery of St Lawrence; afterwards he became a monk of Siegburg [Col. 0984B], and at last was made abbot of Deutz in the year of the Lord 1111, under Henry IV. Being a learned writer, he began to write and continued for many years, until the reign of Lothair III [Note: [Col. 0983] alternatively, “the Second.”] and under him.

But where, when, or how he received the grace of writing, he himself reveals in Book XII of his work *On the Glory and Honour of the Son of Man*. Some of the books which he wrote he entitled in the name of the archbishop of Cologne, and others in that of Cuno [Note: [Col. 0983] “Chunonis.”], abbot of Siegburg and afterwards bishop of Regensburg, because each of them had urged him to write.

In the book *On the Glorification of the Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit* he writes one letter to Pope Honorius; and in the second book *On the Divine Offices* another to the venerable Cuno of Regensburg [Col. 0984C], containing a complete summary of all his books.

Thus he wrote:

- A commentary on Job, in ten books;
- A treatise on the Gospel of John, in fourteen books;
- A work *On the Works of the Holy and Undivided Trinity*, in forty-two books;
- A work on the Apocalypse, in twelve books;
- A work on the Twelve Minor Prophets, in thirty books;
- A work *On the Victory of the Word of God*, in thirteen books;
- A work *On the Glory and Honour of the Son of Man*, on the Gospel according to Matthew, in the same number of books;
- A work drawn from books on the glorious King David; and
- A work on the Song of Songs, completed in seven little books.

He also wrote a small work in three books, in the form of a dialogue between a Jew and a Christian, on the sacrament of faith; and a work *On the Glorification of the Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit*. He also wrote books *On the Meditation upon Death*, which he began shortly before he died but, overtaken by death, could not finish.

Thus far the Melk manuscript.

[Col. 0985]

# History of the Roman Pontiffs by the Anonymous Author of Zwettl, from St Peter to Celestine III, That Is, to the Year of the Lord 1191

(D. Bernhard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, III, 325.)

## Notice

It has not been possible to learn either from this History itself, from the manuscript from which we brought it to light, or from elsewhere, who the author of this History was or what his circumstances were. Of one thing we are entirely certain: he cannot be later than the twelfth century, in which the manuscript was most certainly written.

Moreover, that he spent his life in the diocese of Passau or Salzburg is indicated by the fact that he omits no place where he could discuss a settlement of the famous and long-standing dispute concerning metropolitan precedence between the archbishops of Salzburg and the bishops of Passau. This may be seen in the pontificates of Agapetus II and Benedict VII, and of many other Roman bishops.

We have entitled the author “the Anonymous Author of Zwettl,” not because he was, or could have been, a Cistercian monk of that place, but because the work was extracted from a manuscript in the library of Zwettl; nor is this without precedent among learned men.

As for the present History itself, it is noteworthy especially for those years which come nearer to the author’s own age, namely the eleventh and twelfth centuries. For the events said to have occurred in earlier centuries are already found elsewhere, being drawn from the ancient catalogues and deeds of the Roman pontiffs, from the forged decretal letters of the earliest popes, from Prosper, and so forth—although even in these one may find some matters not at all commonly known.

Nor is it unworthy of notice that in our author—who is otherwise by no means slow to censure the vices of pontiffs—there is found no trace of Pope Joan, that most absurd fable. Rather, Benedict III succeeds Leo IV in a consistent and uninterrupted order, although the fictitious Joan is commonly inserted between them.

There is a comparable silence concerning the magical arts by which Sylvester II, formerly Gerbert, is alleged by some to have forced his way to the Roman pontificate—an entirely foolish invention. Yet the author does not at all conceal that Sylvester was excessively devoted to secular learning and was therefore beloved by the inquisitive Emperor Otto III.

But James Gretser, S.J., refuted this calumny against Sylvester II—first brought forward by Benno, the most mendacious of men, a hundred years after Sylvester’s death, carelessly renewed by Martin of Poland, and frequently repeated by modern heretics, enemies of the papal name—with a negative argument that was nevertheless effective and decisive, in his examination of the *Mystery of Plessis*, chapter 43. So says the most learned Papebroch, S.J., in the *Chronological Essay on the Catalogue of Roman Pontiffs*, p. 177. Whoever wishes may consult it.

## Here Begins the Prologue to the History of the Roman Pontiffs

[Col. 0987B] Knowledge of the Roman pontiffs succeeding one another in order was held in such reverence by the holy Fathers that, with keen diligence and diligent keenness, they investigated most carefully the times of each, and the institutions worthy of remembrance through which the Church gradually received growth.

For if the merits of those saints who, established in lower ranks, devoted their efforts to Catholic instruction and canonical formation are not to be passed over in silence, much more must the holiness of those Fathers be extolled who established the condition of orthodox faith from the primitive Church, strengthened it under the tyranny of persecutors against enemies of the faith, both heretics and idolaters [Col. 0988B], and subdued every deformity of human life by definite laws and boundaries. It must be praised all the more because the Church grew and expanded through not only their teaching but also the glorious contests of some of them.

The deadly seeds of every heretical perversity, uprooted by synodal decrees, would have sprouted more widely unless the Lord of Hosts had left us, in these defenders of the faith themselves and successors of apostolic tradition, the seed of Catholic doctrine.

Yet this is especially to be noted: although thirty-two pontiffs are counted from the pontificate of Peter, prince of the apostles, to the episcopate of Pope Sylvester—leaving aside Linus and Cletus, who, while Peter was still alive, were his assistants and exercised episcopal office—none of them, Chrysogonus alone excepted, who is reckoned the twenty-eighth from Peter himself, failed to enact something in his decretals [Note: [Col. 0989A] That is, “to enact.”]. Some also omitted him from the catalogue of these pontiffs for that reason.

Again, although thirty-two bishops are reckoned from St Sylvester to Blessed Gregory, all alike, except Mercury alone, who was the fifty-seventh bishop to exercise the episcopal office after Peter the apostle, are recorded as having issued canons. Thus men apostolic in character and sharing the faith gave instruction through their writings, making known what people ought to seek, avoid, hold, and finally reject.

It is therefore fitting and proper for every Christian to know those through whom, as diligent shepherds keeping watch over the Lord’s flock, one recognizes the pattern of due religion and innocence. Thus he may also know through their succession who sat first and who later; and he may know those to whom our elders decreed greater reverence, both because of the veneration due to antiquity and because of the greater merit of their learning and holiness. And when an advocate wishes to cite some canon to support his case, he should rely rather upon that author whom antiquity has commended to us, since antiquity carries very great weight of judgment and authority in all cases.

## Here Begins the History of the Roman Pontiffs

[Col. 0989B]

### I. Blessed Peter

Blessed Peter, apostle and prince of the apostles, son of John, of the province of Galilee, from the village of Bethsaida, brother of Andrew, first occupied the episcopal chair at Antioch for seven years. Afterwards he sat at Rome for twenty-five years and nearly three months, until the fourteenth year of Nero.
