He ordained two bishops as assistants, Linus and Cletus, to provide priestly ministry to the Roman people and to visitors. He himself devoted himself to prayer and preaching. Pope John III of that name affirms this in writing to the bishops of Germany:

> Peter, prince of the apostles, took to himself Linus and Cletus as assistants. Yet he did not hand on to them pontifical authority or the rule of binding and loosing, but to his successor Clement. We never read that Linus and Cletus exercised anything through pontifical ministry by authority; they did only what Blessed Peter commanded them.

But when he was about to suffer, he entrusted the chair of the Church to Clement in these words:

> I hand over to Clement himself the power of binding and loosing, handed down to me by the Lord, so that whatever he decrees on earth may be decreed in heaven. For he shall bind what ought to be bound and loose what it is expedient to loose, as one who knows fully the rule of the Church. Therefore listen to him, etc.

Likewise:

> This chair does not seek the man who desires and boldly claims it, but one adorned with good character and learned in speech.

From the episcopate of Blessed Peter to the time of Emperor Constantine, either because bishops were few or because of the fury of the persecutors, it is believed that no councils of pontiffs—or scarcely any—were held.

He wrote two letters called canonical, and the Gospel of Mark. He was crucified by Nero in the thirty-eighth year after the Passion of the Lord, and was buried in the Vatican, in the temple of Apollo, near the place where he was crucified. He condemned Simon, the founder of the heresy from whom simony began to spread; Philip the deacon is said in the Acts of the Apostles to have baptized him.

### II. Linus

Linus, martyr, an Italian by nation, son of Herculanus, ordained bishop by Blessed Peter himself, sat for eleven years and nearly four months, until the consulship of Capito and Rufus—that is, the twelfth year of Nero. According to the Chronicle of Eusebius, he was crowned with martyrdom in the second year of Emperor Titus. He was buried in the Vatican on the sixth day before the Kalends of December. By command of Blessed Peter, he decreed that a woman should enter the church with her head veiled.

### III. Cletus

Cletus, martyr, a Roman by nation, son of Aemilianus, ordained bishop by Blessed Peter, served for twelve years and nearly two months, until the ninth consulship of Domitian and the consulship of Rufus—that is, the first year of Domitian; according to the Chronicle of Eusebius, until the twelfth year of Domitian.

As chorepiscopus of Blessed Peter, he ordained twenty-five priests in the city of Rome. Under Domitian he was crowned with martyrdom and was buried near Blessed Peter on the third day before the Ides of July.

### IV. Clement

Clement, martyr, likewise a Roman by nation, from the Caelian Hill, son of Faustinus, ordained by Blessed Peter, as they say, served for nine years and nearly three months, until the ninth consulship of Vespasian and that of Titus—that is, the eighth year of Vespasian; according to the Chronicle of Eusebius, until the third year of Trajan.

Under Trajan he was sent into exile beyond the Pontus and, by Trajan’s command, was drowned in the sea on the eighth day before the Kalends of December. Peter had handed over to him the power of binding and loosing.

He divided the seven regions among faithful notaries of the Church, who were to seek out and write down diligently the acts of the martyrs. He established canons in twenty-five chapters; because it would be long to set them down here, we refer the reader to the decrees of the pontiffs.

### V. Anacletus

Anacletus, a Greek by nation, of Athens, son of Antiochus, served for nine years and two months, until the seventeenth consulship of Domitian and the consulship of Clement—that is, the tenth year of Domitian. He too suffered under Domitian.

He arranged the memorial of Blessed Peter and the places where bishops were to be installed. He had also been ordained priest by Blessed Peter. When led away to sacrifice to idols, he sacrificed. Afterwards, moved by repentance, he was beheaded for confessing the true faith. He established canons in twenty-four chapters.

### VI. Evaristus

Evaristus, martyr, a Greek by nation, son of a Jew, from the city of Bethlehem, served for nine years and ten months, until the consulship of Gallus and Bradua—that is, the seventh year of Trajan. Under Trajan he suffered and was buried in the Vatican on the sixth day before the Kalends of November. According to the Chronicle of Eusebius, he served until the eleventh year of Domitian.

He appointed two priests in the City and ordained seven deacons to guard the bishop while he preached. He established six canons.

### VII. Alexander

Alexander, martyr, a Roman by nation, son of Alexander, from the district called the Head of Taurus, served for ten years and ten months, until the consulship of Aemilius and Vetus—that is, the fifteenth year of Trajan; according to the Chronicle of Eusebius, until the third year of Trajan.

Incomparable in holiness and most renowned in faith, he converted a great part of the senators of the City to the Lord. He established nine canons, one of which concerns the mingling of salt and water, to be blessed every Sunday for the dwellings of the faithful. Another provides that water ought to be mixed with wine in the chalice. We pass over the rest to avoid weariness.

By Trajan’s command, Aurelianus, commander of both branches of the army, committed him to prison. Afterwards, following innumerable tortures, he was pierced by very frequent punctures throughout all his limbs until he failed. He died on the fifth day before the Kalends of May. He incorporated the Passion of the Lord into the preaching of priests when Masses are celebrated.

### VIII. Sixtus

Sixtus, martyr, a Roman by nation, son of a shepherd, served for ten years and two months, until the consulship of Verus and Ambiguus—that is, the sixth year of Hadrian. In Hadrian’s time he suffered and died on the eighth day before the Ides of April; according to the Chronicle of Eusebius, he served until the twelfth year of Hadrian.

He was from the district of the Via Lata. He established canons in four chapters, one of which provides that sacred vessels must not be handled except by consecrated persons dedicated to God.

### IX. Telesphorus

Telesphorus, martyr, a Greek by nation and formerly an anchorite, served for eleven years and nearly four months in the time of Antoninus and Marcus; according to the Chronicle of Eusebius, until the first year of Antoninus.

He established six canons:

1. Concerning the fast of clerics, namely the seven weeks before Easter.
2. That clerics are not to be accused by laypersons.
3. Concerning the night Mass at the Nativity of the Lord and the singing of the angelic hymn.
4. Concerning the hour of daily Mass.
5. That the common people are not to be admitted in accusations against priests.
6. That an accuser who accuses an absent person is not to be believed.

He endured an illustrious martyrdom and, having suffered, was buried in the Vatican near Blessed Peter on the fourth day before the Nones of January.

### X. Hyginus

Hyginus, a Greek by nation, formerly a philosopher from Athens, served for four years and three months until the consulship of Orsitus and Priscus; according to the Chronicle of Eusebius, until the fifth year of Antoninus. He died on the fourth day before the Ides of January and was buried in the Attican district.

He established the clergy and distributed the ecclesiastical rank. He established three canons:

1. That the judgment of an archbishop is void without the consent of his fellow bishops.
2. That foreign courts are to be prohibited.
3. That one who abandons his purpose is not to be received.

### XI. Pius

Pius, an Italian by nation, son of Rufinus and brother of the Shepherd from the city of Aquileia, served for nineteen years and four months; according to the Chronicle of Eusebius, fifteen years, until the twentieth year of Antoninus. He died on the fourth day before the Ides of July.

He established five chapters of canons. The first concerns the confirmation of Easter, in this form:

> We wish you to know that Easter must be celebrated every year on Sunday. In these times Hermes, teacher of faith and Scripture, shone among us. Although we celebrate Easter on the aforementioned day, and some were doubtful, an angel appeared to that same Hermas in the guise of a shepherd, in order to strengthen their souls, and commanded him that Easter should be celebrated by all on Sunday at its proper time. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we decree that all must observe the same, because we ourselves observe the same, and you ought in no manner to differ from the head.

### XII. Anicius, or Anicetus

Anicius, or Anicetus, a Syrian by nation, son of John, served for eleven years and four months, until the consulship of Praesens and Rufinus; or, according to the Chronicle of Eusebius, until the eighth year of Verus. In the time of Severus and Marcus, he suffered and died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May.

In his time Hegesippus the historian came to Rome and remained until the time of Pope Eleutherius. Polycarp too then came to Rome and freed many people from error. He established six canons. The first was that clerics should not grow their hair long.

### XIII. Soter

Soter, a Campanian by nation, son of Concordius, from the city of Fundi, served for nine years and nearly seven months, until the consulship of Cethegus and Clarus—that is, the tenth year of Verus; according to the Chronicle of Eusebius, for eight years, until the sixteenth year of Verus. He died on the eighth day before the Kalends of June.

He established two canons:

1. That consecrated women should not touch sacred vessels or altar-cloths, nor carry incense about the altars.
2. That bridegroom and bride should be blessed by a priest before their marriage.

### XIV. Eleutherius

Eleutherius, a Greek by nation, son of Habundius, from the town of Nicopolis, served for fifteen years and three months until the consulship of Maternus and Bradua—that is, the sixth year of Commodus; according to the Chronicle of Eusebius, until the thirteenth year of Commodus. He had formerly been a deacon of Pope Anicetus.

He received letters from Lucius, king of the Britons, asking that the king might become Christian by Eleutherius’s command; and this was done. He died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May.

He established four canons:

1. Final judgments concerning clerics are to be referred only to the apostolic see.
2. No judgment is to be made until both sides have been heard.
3. Actions brought by one who has been wronged are to be pursued within the province.
4. No judgment is to be made when the person judged is absent—that is, the person whose case is being judged.

### XV. Victor

Victor, martyr, an African by nation, son of Felix, served for fifteen years and two months until the consulship of Lateranus and Rufinus—that is, the fourth year of Severus. Under Severus he suffered and died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May; according to the Chronicle of Eusebius, he served until the eighth year of Severus.

He established canons in four chapters. In one, writing to Theophilus and the brethren of Alexandria about the day and date of Easter, as Pius had done before, he discussed the matter as follows:

> Our predecessors decreed that the feast of holy Easter should be celebrated on Sunday, and we command that it too be solemnly celebrated on the same day, because it is unfitting that the members should differ from the head and act contrary to it. This feast is to be celebrated from the fourteenth moon of the first month to the twentieth day of the same month.

At that time Catholic baptism is also to be celebrated; and, if necessity requires it, anyone coming from the nations may be baptized under Christian confession, whether in a river, the sea, or springs.

### XVI. Zephyrinus

Zephyrinus, a Roman by nation, son of Habundius, served for eighteen years and seven months until the consulship of Praesens and Extricatus—that is, the sixth year of Antoninus Caracalla; according to the Chronicle of Eusebius, until the second year of Aurelian. He died on the seventh day before the Kalends of September.

He established three canons:

1. That the ordination of clerics should be celebrated in the presence of clerics and laypeople, and at a fixed time.
2. How and on what testimony a judgment against a bishop should be conducted.
3. That persons driven from their sees are not to be compelled to answer.

### XVII. Calixtus

Calixtus, martyr, a Roman by nation, son of Domitius, from the district of the Ravennates in the City, served for five years and two months; according to the Chronicle of Eusebius, until the third year of Alexander.

At Alexander’s command, because he healed Privatus [Note: [Col. 0993D] Read: *Privatus*.], he was thrown from the window of a house and, with a stone tied to his neck, drowned in a well. Fourteen days later the priest Asterius, together with clerics, buried his body in the cemetery of Calepodius. He died on the second day before the Ides of October.

He established fourteen canons. Writing one concerning the four Ember seasons:

> Greetings to the blessed brother and fellow bishop. The fast which you have learned is celebrated among us three times a year, we now decree should more fittingly be observed during the four seasons, so that, as the year turns through four seasons, we too may keep a fourfold and solemn fast in the four seasons of the year.

### XVIII. Urban

Urban, martyr, a Roman by nation, son of Pontianus, served for eight years and ten months; according to the Chronicle of Eusebius, until the twelfth [Note: [Col. 0993D] Above this number an equally ancient hand notes “X.”] year of Alexander. Through his teaching many were converted and suffered under Alexander and Blessed Cecilia. He died on the eighth day before the Kalends of June.

He established canons in five chapters:

1. Among whom the common life ought to flourish.
2. How the property of the Church ought not to be applied to secular uses.
3. That the sentence of a bishop is to be feared.
4. That the vow of common life is not to be broken.
5. On the laying on of hands.

[Note: [Col. 0994D] A fifteenth-century hand inserted this into our old history.] Cyriacus, martyr, a native of Britain, suffered at Cologne with eleven thousand virgins.

### XIX. Pontianus

Pontianus, martyr, a Roman by nation, son of Calpurnius, served for six years and five months; according to the Chronicle of Eusebius, until the third year of Maximinus. Under Maximinus he was deported with the priest Hippolytus to the island of Buccina in Sardinia, where he was beaten with clubs and brought to his end. He died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December.

His body was later brought back by Pope Fabian and buried in the cemetery of Calixtus, formerly called that of Calepodius. He established one canon: those who are not of good conduct; or who are suspect, enemies, easily quarrelsome, of blameworthy life, or who neither hold nor teach the true faith, ought not to be accusers.

### XX. Antherius

Antherius, martyr, a Greek by nation, son of Romulus, served for one year, until the last year of Maximinus. He diligently investigated the acts of the martyrs. He suffered under Emperor Maximinus, died on the third day before the Nones of January, and was buried in the cemetery of Calixtus on the Appian Way.

He established two canons:

1. On what grounds the transfer of bishops is to be permitted.
2. That a corrupt teacher is made such through the fault of the people.

XXI. Fabian, martyr, a Roman by nationality, son of Fabius. He held office for nearly fifteen years. The Holy Spirit, [Col. 0994C] descending from heaven upon him in the form of a dove and remaining above his head, caused him thereafter to be judged worthy of the episcopate and consecrated. He apportioned deacons and notaries among the districts, so that they might collect in full the acts of the martyrs. Having suffered, he died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February [20 January], and was buried in the cemetery of Callixtus. He established canons in twelve chapters, one of which is: Chrism must be prepared every year, renewed each year, and the old chrism burned in the holy churches.

Origen, as is found in a certain letter of Jerome, confessed to him his errors concerning the faith and was corrected by him; this, they say, Didymus affirms. They relate, moreover, that after Antherus’s death Fabian, returning from the countryside with his friends, found the entire people of the Church gathered together to elect a bishop. One person, as commonly happens in such matters, was loudly proposing one candidate and another another, yet the opinion of the crowd settled upon nothing. Fabian himself, desiring to know what the outcome would be, stood among the rest. Then, by God’s providence, a dove suddenly fell from heaven—bearing the likeness of that dove which descended upon Jesus at the Jordan in the image of the Holy Spirit—and stood above Fabian’s head. At this sight the mouths and eyes of all were turned toward him; all, as though moved by one spirit, decided that by God’s judgment he was worthy of the episcopate. Immediately he was placed in the chair and confirmed in the lawful priesthood. [Col. 0995A] Some relate that this occurred in connection with Fabian’s name, others with that of Zephyrinus.

XXII. Cornelius, martyr, a Roman by nationality, son of Castinus. He held office for two years and two months. Against him Novatus, a Roman presbyter, attempted to seize the episcopal chair. This heretic Novatus, denying hope of salvation to idolaters, to those worthily doing penance, and to those fallen into sin, was expelled from the Church and condemned by a council of sixty bishops and an equal number of presbyters.

Concerning Cornelius’s election, Blessed Cyprian says in the letter he writes to Antonianus:

> Cornelius was made bishop by the judgment of God and Christ, by the testimony of almost all the clergy, by the vote of the people then present, and by the assembly of venerable priests and good men, when no one had been made before him, when the place of Fabian—that is, the place of Peter—and the rank of the episcopal chair were vacant. Once this place had been occupied and confirmed by God’s judgment and by the agreement of us all, anyone who should thereafter wish to become bishop must necessarily be outside the Church; nor can one possess ecclesiastical ordination who does not hold the unity of the Church.

Again, in the same work concerning Novatus, from which that entire letter is composed:

> I am amazed that some are so obstinate as to think that penance ought not be granted to the lapsed, or that pardon ought to be denied to penitents, although it is written: “Remember from where you have fallen, and repent.”

There are also other letters of his to various persons, and to Pope Cornelius, in which they mutually console one another concerning the persecution of the Church. In these he also maintains that those baptized by heretics ought to be baptized again. Under Valerian he was deported into exile at Centumcellae because of the faith and was beheaded on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October [14 September]. He established only three canons:

1. An oath is not to be sworn except for the faith.
2. No one is to commit his own case to another’s judgment.
3. A sentence against an absent person is void.

He also raised the bodies of the apostles from the catacombs. Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, also wrote to Novatus when the latter alleged that he had unwillingly been ordained bishop at Rome; this is the beginning of his letter:

> Dionysius to Novatian, brother, greetings. If, as you say, you were ordained unwillingly, you will prove it when you withdraw willingly.

XXIII. Lucius, martyr, a Roman by nationality, son of Porphyrius. He held office for three years, three months, and three days, [Col. 0995D] until the third consulship of Valerian and that of Gallienus—that is, the first year of Valerian. Banished in their persecution for the faith of Christ, he was later permitted by divine direction to return to his Church, and completed his martyrdom by beheading. He was laid on the Appian Way near Saint Sixtus. He established three canons:

1. Those who bring accusations of crimes may accuse.
2. Concerning ecclesiastical property.
3. Whoever takes away the property of the Church commits sacrilege.

He commanded that two presbyters and three deacons should never leave the bishop, because of ecclesiastical testimony.

XXIV. Stephen, martyr, a Roman by nationality, [Col. 0996A] son of Lobius. He held office for six years and five months, until the third consulship of Valerian and the second of Gallienus; according to the Chronicle of Eusebius, only three months. After many good deeds, by command of the emperors Valerius [Note: [Col. 0995D] Thus this manuscript.] and Gallienus, he was seized before the holy altar while offering sacrifice to God; when he had finished, he was beheaded on the fourth day before the Nones of August [2 August].

He decreed that priests and Levites should not wear sacred vestments in ordinary daily use, but only in church. He ordained three presbyters, seven deacons, and ten clerics, with whom he constantly taught concerning the kingdom of God. He established seven canons:

1. Concerning infamous persons.
2. Concerning the vestments of the Church.
3. Concerning those despoiled.
4. What accusations ought to be received.
5. That no one is to be accused in writing.
6. That a bishop must be summoned by the primate before answering.
7. That the first hearing must take place within the province.

XXV. Sixtus II, martyr, a Greek by nationality and a philosopher. He held office for one year and nearly eleven months. After him presbyters presided until the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus. In Eusebius’s Chronicle, eleven years, until the thirteenth year of Gallienus. Under the emperor Decius and the prefect Valerian, he was beheaded on the ninth [Note: [Col. 0996D] Thus the manuscript incorrectly. Read: the eighth.] day before the Ides of August [5 August]; first a philosopher, afterward a disciple of Christ and teacher of the great martyr Lawrence. He established two canons:

1. Those unjustly condemned ought to be restored.
2. Concerning the reconsideration by the Apostolic See of a judgment made by a fellow-provincial court.

XXVI. Dionysius, formerly a monk and then presbyter of the Roman Church; his family origin is not known. [Col. 0996C] He held office for six years and two months, until the consulship of Claudius and Paternus—that is, the fifteenth year of Gallienus; according to Eusebius, eight years, until the first year of Probus. He was buried on the Appian Way in the cemetery of Callixtus. He was consecrated by Maximus, bishop of Ostia. He established two canons:

1. Concerning distinctions among ranks.
2. That individual parishes be assigned to individual presbyters.

According to Eusebius, Palmirienus succeeded Dionysius; according to others, Felix. But I think that, when the pontificate was interrupted through fear of persecution and priests presided, this Palmirienus—because he is not listed in the catalogue of pontiffs—was one of the presbyters who presided. Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, wrote two letters to him while he was still a private presbyter, and a third while he was pontiff, concerning Novatus.

XXVII. Felix, martyr, a Roman by nationality, son of Constantius. He held office for four years and nearly four months, until the consulship of Aurelian and Capitolinus—that is, the third year of Aurelian. In Eusebius’s Chronicles, five years, until the fifth year of Probus. He established seven canons:

1. Concerning uncertain judgments.
2. Where an inquiry ought to take place.
3. That the unjust condemnation of bishops must be reconsidered.
4. When primates must be approached.
5. How much time ought to be granted to one restored.
6. Concerning the examination of accusers.
7. That persons of ill repute are not to be barred from their own cases.

XXVIII. Euticianus, martyr, a Tuscan by nationality, [Col. 0997A] son of Marinus, from the city of Luna. He held office for one year and one month, in the consulship of Carus II and Carinus—that is, [up] to the fourth year of Aurelian; according to Eusebius’s Chronicle, only eight months, that is, in the fifth year of Probus. He was crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Aurelian and buried in the cemetery of Callixtus. He himself buried with his own hands 342 martyrs in various places. He decreed that only produce, beans, and grapes be blessed upon the altar. He established one canon concerning the bond of registration.

XXIX. Gaius, martyr, a Dalmatian by nationality, of the family of the emperor Diocletian, son of Gaius. He held office for eleven years, four months, and twelve days, until the fifth consulship of Diocletian and the second of Constantius—that is, the ninth year of Diocletian; according to Eusebius’s Chronicle, fifteen years, until the thirteenth year of Diocletian. Under Diocletian he was crowned with martyrdom [Col. 0997B] together with Gabinus, his brother and presbyter. He arranged the ecclesiastical orders so that anyone worthy of becoming a bishop should ascend through every rank: first porter, then reader, exorcist, subdeacon, deacon, and presbyter. He established two canons:

1. Whoever fails to prove what he has alleged is infamous.
2. Another [canon] concerning the order in which one must approach the orders.

I have found nowhere the decrees of Chrysogonus, who received the chair as the twenty-eighth successor from Blessed Peter, except that he wrote exhortatory letters to a certain virgin urging her to endure martyrdom. But why this occurred—whether he was overtaken by a swift death or something else happened to him—is not sufficiently clear. Hence he is not included in the catalogue of pontiffs.

[Col. 0997C] XXX. Marcellinus, martyr, a Roman by nationality, son of Praejectus. He held office for nine years, four months, and sixteen days, until the eighth consulship of Diocletian and the eighth of Maximian—that is, the seventeenth year of Diocletian. According to Eusebius’s Chronicle, until the twentieth year of Diocletian. Compelled by pagans, he offered incense to demons, but afterward became an eminent martyr.

For the council of bishops, declining to judge him as their master, said to him: “Judge your case by your own mouth, not by our judgment.” And again: “Do not be heard in our judgment, but gather your case into your own bosom.” And again: “For, they say, by yourself you shall be justified, or by your own mouth condemned.” Blessed Maurice, the great martyr, also received a blessing from him before setting out with the emperor Maximian against the enemies of the empire. [Col. 0997D] He established two canons:

1. Bishops may inflict no prejudice upon the pontiff by whom they were consecrated; and a cleric is not to be accused by a layperson.
2. No authority ought to do anything contrary to divine authority.

XXXI. Marcellus, martyr, a Roman by nationality, son of Benedict, from the district of the Via Lata. He held office for nearly five years and eight months. By command of Diocletian he was beheaded for the faith of Christ together with Claudius, Quirinus, and Antonius, and after thirty-five days was buried on the Salarian Way, in a chamber in the cemetery of Priscilla, by Marcellus the presbyter and the deacons, with hymns.

At that time there was a great persecution, so that within one month seventeen thousand persons of both sexes were crowned with martyrdom. [Col. 0998A] The episcopate then ceased for seven years, six months, and twenty-five days, while the emperor Diocletian persecuted Christians. He made cemeteries on the Salarian Way and established twenty-five titular churches in the city of Rome, for the baptism and penance of the many who were converting from paganism, and for the burial of martyrs. He established one canon: that the judgment of a provincial synod is not valid without the consent of the Apostolic See. He is not found in Eusebius’s Chronicle.

XXXII. Eusebius, a Greek by nationality, formerly a physician. He held office for six years and one month. In Eusebius’s Chronicles, eight months in the twentieth year of Diocletian. He found heretics in the city and reconciled them by laying on of hands. He instituted four canons:

1. Those whose conduct is not different ought not accuse one another.
2. One cannot be summoned as a despoiled person until all that belongs to him has been restored.
3. Who are infamous persons?
4. Concerning the finding of the Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, which has lately been found, while we hold the helm of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Nones of May [3 May]. We command you to celebrate solemnly, on the aforesaid calendar day of the Finding, the feast of the Finding. The Jew who showed it is baptized and named Cyriacus.

XXXIII. Miltiades, an African by nationality. He held office for six years, until the consulship of Volusianus and Anianus—that is, the fourth year of Constantine. He decreed that offerings from the consecration of a bishop should be sent throughout the churches. He established seven canons:

1. No one is to be judged suddenly.
2. What do baptism and confirmation confer?
3. One is not to fast on the Lord’s Day or Thursday; no one should observe a fast of the Lord’s Day or Thursday, so that a true and not false distinction may be maintained between the fasting of Christians and pagans, of those who truly believe and unbelievers, and of heretics. Hence Blessed Gregory, in arranging the offices, left Thursday in Lent vacant; afterward Gregory II assigned the offices of the Sundays to it and arranged the rest.
4. Concerning the primitive Church.
5. How did the Church grow among the gentiles?
6. The emperor ought not judge bishops.
7. Secular affairs are one thing; ecclesiastical affairs another.

XXXIV. Silvester, a Roman by nationality, son of Rufinus and Justa. He held office for twenty-three years and ten months, [Col. 0998D] until the consulship of Constantine and Volusianus. In Eusebius’s Chronicle, twenty-two years, until the twenty-fifth year of Constantine, whom he also instructed in the faith of Christ after he had been baptized.

Through his efforts the most distinguished synod of the whole world, of 318 Fathers, was held at Nicaea, a city of Bithynia, under the consulship of the emperors Constantine and Licinius, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July [19 June], though it was completed in the time of his successor. This synod was held against Arius, presbyter of Alexandria, who maintained three grades in the Trinity. Condemning this same blasphemy concerning the inequality of the Trinity, it defined through the Creed, still commonly used in the Church, that the Son of God is consubstantial with God the Father; and it established seventy canons.

[Col. 0999A] Likewise, at the counsel of the same emperor Constantine, he assembled 287 bishops in the city of Rome and again condemned Callistus, Arius, Photinus, and Sabellius alike. He also decreed that no one should receive an Arian presbyter who had come to his senses unless the bishop of that place reconciled him and confirmed him with the most sacred chrism by the laying on of hands, in the grace of the Holy Spirit—which cannot be given by heretics.

In this synod also, by the agreement and subscription of all, it was established that no layperson should dare bring an accusation against a cleric, not only against bishops but against persons of every clerical rank; nor should anyone of a lower rank bring any accusation against a superior. A bishop is not to be condemned except by seventy-two witnesses, nor is the supreme pontiff to be judged by anyone; a cardinal presbyter is not to be condemned except by forty-four witnesses; a cardinal deacon except by thirty-six; a subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, reader, or porter except by six witnesses. Witnesses and accusers must be free of any infamy, have wives and children, and openly profess Christ. No one may receive the testimony of a cleric against a layperson. No one may presume publicly to examine any cleric except in church. Nor may any cleric, deacon, or presbyter enter a court for any cause or presume to plead a case before a girded judge. If any cleric accusing a cleric enters a court, let him incur anathema.

Among other measures, in the aforesaid synod, with the counsel of all, he decreed that no one should presume to celebrate the sacrifice of the altar on a silk or dyed cloth, but on pure linen, consecrated by a bishop, produced from the earth from flax and woven, just as the body of our Lord Jesus Christ was buried in a clean linen shroud. He also decreed that the presbyter should anoint the baptized person. He performed ordinations on the sixth day [Note: [Col. 0999D] Thus the manuscript.], in the month of December: forty-two presbyters, twenty-five deacons, and eighty bishops in various places. He changed the sleeveless *colobia* formerly used by the apostles into dalmatics, adding sleeves. He died on the day before the Kalends of January [31 December] and was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way.

He also issued a decree showing which orders ought to be subject to which. He says that a presbyter must obey a bishop; a deacon, a presbyter; a subdeacon, a deacon; an acolyte, a subdeacon; a reader, an acolyte; an exorcist, a reader; a porter, an exorcist; an abbot, a porter; and a monk, an abbot.

XXXV. Mark, a Roman by nationality, son of Priscus. He held office for two years and nine months, until the twentieth year of Constantine. In Jerome’s Chronicle, nine months in the twenty-fifth year of Constantine. He established a canon that a bishop of a city, when consecrating the offerings, should use the *pallium*. He died on the Nones of October [7 October] and was buried in the cemetery of Balbina on the Ardeatine Way.

XXXVI. Julius, a Roman by nationality, son of Rusticus. He held office for fifteen years and two months. Although summoned by Constantine to the Nicene synod, [Col. 1000A] he was absent through the burden of old age; but the presbyters Vitus and Vincentius attended in his place. Under him Arius and his supporters, who disparaged the term “consubstantiality,” were completely condemned. Under Constantius, the Arian son of Constantine, he also endured troubles and exiles for ten months; after these, he returned to his see with great glory. Blessed Donatus was also consecrated bishop of Aricia by him. He established seven canons:

1. A bishop is not to be accused except in a lawful synod.
2. A bishop is not to be condemned without the judgment of the Apostolic See.
3. Concerning foreign judgments.
4. Concerning those who have confessed.
5. Those who bring accusations of crimes must accuse in person.
6. Concerning appeal.
7. Excommunicated persons are not to accuse.

He further decreed that no cleric should conduct any case publicly except in church; that notice should be faithfully recorded by notaries; and that securities, legal instruments, donations, exchanges, transfers, testaments, pleadings, and manumissions should be executed by clerics in church. According to Jerome’s Chronicle, fifteen years and nine months, until the twentieth year of Constantine.

XXXVII. Liberius, a Roman by nationality, son of Ligustus. He held office for six years and four months. In Jerome’s Chronicle, seventeen years, until the second year of Valentinian. He agreed with Constantius, son of Constantine, in persecuting Christians. Liberius returned from exile, at first Catholic, but afterward agreed in heresy. [Col. 1000C] He wrote a letter to all bishops in which he carefully warned them not to abandon the people entrusted to them, not to give themselves over to quiet because of the reproach of evil men, and not merely to save themselves: they should not leave their children orphaned. He also adorned the tomb of Blessed Agnes with marble.

XXXVIII. Felix II, martyr, a Roman by nationality, son of Anastasius. [Note: [Col. 0999D] Another hand, though scarcely later than the thirteenth century: this man is said to be Ursinus, who was secretly ordained in the Sicinian church [Col. 1000D].] He held office for one year and three months during the exile of Liberius, in the twentieth year of Constantine. He declared Constantius, son of Constantine, to be a heretic and to have been baptized a second time by Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia; and, by command of that same Constantius, he was beheaded. Liberius, returned from exile, was restored by Constantius.

Felix established four canons:

1. Concerning seeking delays: those who fear a place may choose a safe place for themselves.
2. Concerning the difference between an ecclesiastical and a secular case.
3. One lawfully accused ought to go to the council.
4. [Note: [Col. 1000D] Added by the aforesaid hand.] Who ought not be admitted to accuse bishops.

After Liberius, Damasus had received the priestly office in the city of Rome by succession. Unable to endure that Damasus was preferred to him, a certain Ursinus, deacon of the same Church, burst into such madness that, after persuading a certain bishop, very ignorant and rustic, he gathered a band of turbulent and seditious persons in the basilica called Sicinina and forcibly had himself made bishop, overturning laws, order, and tradition. From this event [Col. 1001A] arose such a riot—indeed such wars—as the opposing peoples defended one another, that places of prayer were filled with human blood. Through the faction of Maximinus, a cruel prefect, this affair was turned into an accusation against the good and innocent priest, so that the case proceeded even to the torture of clerics. But God, the defender of innocence, was present, and the punishment was turned upon the heads of those who devised deceit.

XXXIX. Damasus, a Spaniard by nationality, son of Antoninus. He held office for eighteen years and three months. In Prosper’s Chronicles, eighteen years, until the fifth year of Gratian. At a synod with twenty-eight bishops and twenty-five presbyters, he publicly condemned Liberius; and the persecution ceased, though not for long. Through his efforts also, a synod of 150 Fathers was assembled at Constantinople against [Col. 1001B] Macedonius, bishop of that city, who denied that the Holy Spirit is God; and against Sabellius, who maintained that he who is the Son is himself the Father, that he who is the Father is the Son, and that whenever he wills he is Father, whenever he wills Son, and whenever he wills Holy Spirit.

Having condemned the aforesaid heresies, they established three canons against Macedonius’s error, showing the Holy Spirit to be consubstantial with God the Father and the Son, and establishing the form of the Creed which the entire confession of Greeks and Latins proclaims in the churches. The principal author of these canons was Blessed Nectarius, bishop of Constantinople. He sought out and found many bodies of saints, and also set forth their memorials in verse. Though maliciously accused of adultery, he was cleared by forty-four bishops. He established four canons:

1. Concerning persons not to be joined together in a case.
2. Concerning summons to a synod.
3. Concerning the manner of accusing.
4. Again, concerning the same matter.

Blessed Jerome wrote many things to him.

XL. Siricius, a Roman by nationality, son of Tiburcius. He held office for fifteen years, or according to Prosper fourteen years, until the third year of Arcadius. In Prosper’s Chronicles Ursinus is mentioned, who above is said to have been elected and removed together with Damasus. He wrote to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, who had earlier written to his predecessor Damasus concerning these matters, an epistle containing fifteen decretal chapters; and through him he sent them to all the bishops of Carthage, Baetica, Lusitania, Gaul, and the other neighboring provinces:

1. Arians are not to be rebaptized.
2. Baptism is not to be celebrated except at Easter and Pentecost.
3. Concerning apostates.
4. It is not lawful to enter into the rights of marriage with another man’s betrothed.
5. Concerning those who have not maintained penance.
6. Concerning monks and virgins who do not keep their profession.
7. Concerning incontinent clerics.
8. What kind of clerics ought to be promoted.
9. Concerning the conduct of clerics.
10. Concerning the aged.
11. A cleric who has taken a second wife is to be deposed.
12. What women may live with clerics.
13. Concerning the promotion of monks.
14. A penitent is not to become a cleric.
15. If through ignorance a penitent who is twice married, or the husband of a widow, has been made a cleric, he is not to be promoted.

[Col. 1002A] He also commanded that viaticum not be denied to penitents at the end, which Novatus had forbidden.

XLI. Anastasius I, a Roman by nationality, son of Maximus. He held office for three years. In Prosper’s Chronicles, four years, until the seventh year of Arcadius. Finding Manichaeans in the city, he condemned them. He decreed that no overseas person should be admitted to the clergy unless designated by the signed documents of five bishops. He died on the fifth day before the Kalends of May [27 April]. He decreed that, when the Gospels are read, priests and all others present should not sit, but should all stand reverently bowed in the presence of the Gospel, attentively hear the words of the Lord, and faithfully worship.

XLII. Innocent, an Alban by nationality, son of Innocent. He held office for nearly fifteen years and four months. In Prosper’s Chronicles, fourteen years, [Col. 1002B] until the eighth year of Honorius. He persecuted the Novatians. He wrote letters to bishops of different provinces, containing fifty-six decretal chapters.

Writing first to Decentius concerning the kiss of peace, to be given after the mysteries have been completed, he says:

> You maintain that some command the people, or exchange the peace among priests, before the mysteries have been completed; whereas peace must necessarily be proclaimed after all those things which I ought not disclose, so that it may be evident that the people have given their consent to everything done in the mysteries and celebrated in the Church, and that these things have been concluded by the seal of the peace which brings them to an end.

And elsewhere, concerning the names not to be recited by the priest before the peace:

> How superfluous it is to announce beforehand the name of one whose offering you have not yet offered to God! Therefore the offerings must first be commended, and then the names of those whose offerings they are must be declared, so that they may be named amid the sacred mysteries, not among the other things which we set forth beforehand, in order that by the mysteries themselves we may open the way for the prayers to come.

One letter among these, addressed to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, and Augustine, bishop of Hippo, is full of affection and commendation. Again, to Bishop Aurelius concerning Easter:

> I have written this letter concerning the calculation of Easter for the next, that is, the coming year. For since on the fortieth day before the Kalends of April the moon is almost in its sixteenth day, and likewise reaches its fourteenth day on the fourth day before the same Kalends [29 March], [Note: [Col. 1001D] The reading is uncertain: XIV or XXIII.] I judged that the feast of Easter ought to be celebrated on the eleventh day before the aforesaid Kalends [22 March], since we know that Easter has never previously been celebrated on the twenty-third lunar day. I have set forth the tenor of my opinion. It will now be for your prudence, my brother, united with me in mind, and for our fellow priests, to reconsider this matter in a most devout synod; so that, if nothing opposes our arrangement, you may write back to us fully, in order that we may prescribe beforehand by letter, as is customary, the established day of Easter to be observed at its proper time.

We omit the rest of the necessary regulations concerning the many institutions of the Church which he established.

XLIII. Zosimus, a Greek by nationality, son of Abraham. He held office for three years and nearly five months, until the eleventh year of Honorius. He decreed that a deacon should cover his left side with pallia, [Col. 1003A] and that no cleric should offer a cup publicly except only in the private rooms of the faithful.

Under him the Carthaginian synod of 217 bishops assembled against Pelagius. Pelagius, a Briton and monk, and his disciple Caelestius [Note: [Col. 1003D] Thus the manuscript.], from whom his followers were afterward called Caelestians, were such enemies of the grace of God—by which we have been predestined for adoption as sons of God through Jesus Christ in himself, and by which we are delivered from the power of darkness so that we may believe in him—that they believed a human being able, without this grace, to fulfil all the divine commandments.

Finally, reproved by the brethren because he attributed nothing to the help of God’s grace, he yielded to their correction only so far that he did not set grace before free choice, but subordinated it with unbelieving cunning. He said that grace is given to people so that what they are commanded to do by free choice they may more easily fulfil through grace. By saying “more easily,” he wished it to be believed that, although more difficult, human beings nevertheless can fulfil the divine commands without divine grace. These and many other poisonous assertions he advanced; they were condemned in the same synod, in which Aurelius of Carthage and Augustine, bishop of Hippo, took part.

He wrote a decretal epistle, marked with three chapters, to Hesychius, bishop of Salona; and another to the presbyters of the church of Ravenna. He also instituted the blessing of the Paschal candle; but Blessed Ambrose composed the blessing, although some maintain that Gelasius made it, which is not so.

[Col. 1003C] XLIV. Boniface, a Roman by nationality, son of the presbyter Jocundus. He held office for three years and eight months, until the fifteenth year of Honorius. As clergy and people disagreed, he is said to have been ordained on one day along with Eulalius; but once the rulers had learned the case, they ordered both expelled from the City. Yet, recalling Boniface, they established him in the see in the time of Honorius and Valentinian.

He decreed that no slave or person liable to civic curial obligations should become a cleric. He wrote to the same emperor Honorius, asking him to establish that a pontiff should never be ordained by canvassing in the city of Rome. The emperor replied and decreed that, if two bishops should be ordained at Rome, both should be expelled from the city.

He likewise wrote another letter to the bishops of Gaul concerning Bishop Maximus, accused of various crimes, in which he set down one decretal chapter:

> We decree that your judgment ought to take place within the province and that you are to assemble a synod before the Kalends of November [1 November], so that, if he wishes to be present and has confidence, he may answer the charges in person. But if he neglects to be present, he shall not gain a postponement of judgment because of his absence. For it is evident that he is convicted of crime who, when granted and repeatedly assigned the opportunity of clearing himself in court, does not use it.

Likewise, to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne: “In each province no one is to be ordained bishop in contempt of the metropolitan.” He was buried on the Salarian Way.

XLV. Celestine, a Campanian by nationality, son of [Col. 1004A] Priscus. He held office for eight years and ten months, until the ninth year of Theodosius. Under him the Ephesian synod of 200 bishops assembled against Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, who maintained that a mere human being was born from the Virgin Mary, so as to make one part flesh and another divinity. He did not understand Christ to be one in the Word of God and flesh, but separately proclaimed one as Son of Man and called another the Son of God.

This synod met under the thirteenth consulship of the younger Theodosius and the third consulship of Valentinian. Cyril, patriarch of Alexandria, presided over it in the place of Pope Saint Celestine. By apostolic authority it also composed twelve chapters, anathematizing an equal number of Nestorius’s blasphemies. This synod showed that the one person of our Lord Jesus Christ remains in two natures. It decreed that the angelic hymn, “Holy, holy, holy,” should be sung during the celebration of Mass. It also decreed that the Davidic psalms should be sung antiphonally before the sacrifice; for previously only the Epistles and the holy Gospel were read. It likewise decreed that sacred mysteries should be handled only by sacred ministers, and that any bishop summoned to the Apostolic See, on returning to his parish, should not be received unless he brought back to the people letters of greeting—that is, letters of authorization.

He died on the seventh day before the Ides of April [7 April]. He wrote a letter to Venerius and the other bishops of Gaul, in which [Note: [Col. 1004D] Read: *which*.] twenty-two chapters are contained:

1. Concerning Prosper and Hilary, who accuse certain presbyters of Gaul of being followers of Pelagius.
2. A remarkable defense in praise of Saint Augustine, bishop.

[Col. 1004C] The authorities of past bishops of the Apostolic See concerning the grace of God, free choice, and other matters of various kinds.

XLVI. Sixtus III, a Roman by nationality, son of Sixtus. He held office for eight years, until the year of the Lord 440. Concerning the same matter as his predecessor, he sent the judgment of the westerners to Nestorius himself and to all the bishops of the East. After one year and eight months, accused by a certain Bassus, he cleared himself before fifty-six bishops; Bassus was condemned, as his letter which he himself sent to all the easterners testifies. Its opening is: “Thanks to your …” For he says:

> As [God?] is witness for us in heaven and witness in the heart [the text is uncertain], let us allow fools outside to say what they wish. Know that I am accused by a certain Bassus and unjustly persecuted. When the most august Valentinian heard this, by our authority he ordered a synod to be assembled; and, when a council had been held with a thorough investigation, satisfying everyone—although I could otherwise have escaped adequately—nevertheless, avoiding suspicion, I cleared myself before all of suspicion and freed myself from hostility. Yet we do not establish a rule and example that this must be done by others who do not wish it or have not voluntarily chosen it.

Again:

> The aforesaid Bassus was condemned by the already mentioned synod, yet so that viaticum should not be denied him on his last day, because of the Church’s humble mercy.

The emperor Valentinian likewise condemned him in writing together with his mother, the Augusta Placidia, and preserved for the Catholic Church all the estates of his property, thereby giving a precedent for similar action against such men in the future. This Bassus himself, after he had died by divine will, Sixtus later handled with his own hands, together with linen cloths and spices, and buried near Blessed Peter on the fifth day before the Kalends of April [28 March]. He established four canons:

1. Who are not to be received as accusers of priests.
2. Concerning the prohibition of foreign judgments.
3. Concerning appeal.
4. Concerning those under attack.

Accordingly, when the synod had said that it was not lawful to pronounce judgment against the pontiff, the emperor immediately rose and entrusted to the discretion of the aforesaid pontiff the judgment of his own case.

XLVII. Leo, a doctor, a Tuscan by nationality, son of Quintianus. Twenty-one years, nearly two months, until the year of the Lord 462. Through his exertions the Council of Chalcedon was held under the emperor Marcian, with 618 priests [bishops]; in it Eutyches, the abbot of Constantinople, who declared that the Word of God and the flesh had one nature, and his defender Dioscorus, formerly bishop of Alexandria, and likewise Nestorius himself again, with the remaining heretics who were their accomplices, were beforehand condemned by the unanimous judgment of the Fathers. The same council proclaimed that Christ God was so born of the Virgin that he must be confessed as one person, possessing both a divine and a human nature.

At this council were Juvenal of Jerusalem and Anatolius of Constantinople, who, after the authority of Saint Leo had condemned the heresy, established twenty-seven canons. Anatolius maintained that Dioscorus had been condemned not only on account of the faith, but because he had pronounced excommunication upon the most holy Pope Leo, the council saying: “Since the second offence surpasses and exceeds the former iniquity.”

He decreed that in the action [of the liturgy] there should be said: “the holy sacrifice, the spotless victim”; and: “We humbly beseech thee, Almighty [God].” Very many Manichaeans were detected by him in the city of Rome, and he compelled them publicly to profess in church, and to subscribe in their own hand, that they condemned Mani. Others, lest by their obstinacy they should pollute the holy flock of the Lord with their contagion, were, under laws established according to the ordinances of Christian rulers, banished permanently through public judges. Everything profane or shameful that they possessed in writings and in their secret traditions was proved by clear disclosure, so that even the man called their bishop, when seized, revealed their disgraceful practices and the things they held in their mysteries.

[Note: Col. 1005D: Supply “lest.”]

This man indeed, the hammer of heretics and destroyer of all heretical perversity, composed many outstanding writings for the instruction of the faithful: very many homilies, sermons, and letters excellently written against Eutyches and Nestorius. Like an angelic trumpet, he sounded forth for the salvation of the Church against pestilential doctrines. He issued decrees in forty-nine chapters, which may be known to all for their elegance.

Moreover, how greatly he set himself like a wall for the house of God against the persecution of tyrants is clear from what follows. When Attila, halting near the river Mincio where it flows into the Po, began to hesitate whether he should go to Rome or desist—not sparing or considering the city against which he was hostile, but fearing the example of Alaric, who did not long survive the city he had captured—most holy Pope Leo met him. Having entered before the barbarian king, he obtained all that he desired and secured the safety not only of Rome but of all Italy. For Attila had been terrified by the will of God and could say nothing to Christ’s priest except what the latter himself preferred.

It is reported that after the pontiff’s departure Attila was asked why, contrary to his usual manner, he had shown such great reverence to the Roman pope and obeyed all that he had commanded. The king replied that he had not feared the person of the man who had come, but had seen another man standing beside him in priestly dress, of more majestic appearance and venerable grey hair, who, with a drawn sword, terribly threatened him with death unless he fulfilled all that Leo required. Thus Attila, restrained from his cruelty, left Italy and returned to Pannonia.

Likewise, after the death of Valentinian and the killing of Maximus, the usurper of the empire, while most blessed Leo was still exercising the pontificate of the Roman Church, Geiseric, supported by a very powerful army of his people and, in addition, by Moorish auxiliaries, struck the Romans. The nobles and common people alike fled from the city; Geiseric occupied the City, empty of every defence, Saint Leo the bishop meeting him outside the gate. By God’s help Leo’s supplication so softened him that, although the city was delivered into his power, he nevertheless refrained from fire, slaughter, and tortures. For fourteen days Rome was emptied of all its possessions by a secure and unrestricted search.

Among his other decrees he did not omit this: a nun was not to receive the veil from a bishop unless her virginity had first been proved. He also wrote to the Augustus Marcian concerning the observance of Easter, so that, through Marcian’s admonition, all the Eastern Churches might agree in its celebration. By his letters he exhorted the Augusti Theodosius, Marcian, and Leo to strengthen the faith, and warned them to extirpate the Eutychian poison. These letters are thought by some to have been dictated by Prosper of Aquitaine, as Gennadius asserts in his book *On Illustrious Men*.

[Note: Col. 1006D: “For Equitanian” should read “Aquitanian.”]

XLVIII. Hilary, a Sardinian by nationality, son of Crispinus. Six years, three months, until the year of the Lord 477. He issued letters concerning the Catholic faith throughout the Eastern world, confirmed the three councils—Nicaea, Ephesus, and Chalcedon—and condemned Julian, bishop of Athilena, a Pelagian. At his command Victorinus also composed the Paschal Cycle, though it was faulty.

He held a synod at Rome in the basilica of Saint Mary, attended by forty-six bishops and priests, when Flavius, Basiliscus, and Hermenricus were consuls, in the time of the emperor Leo. He established six synodal chapters, of which I shall give only one: that matters unlawfully ordained by a bishop or his predecessor should be corrected by the bishop who survives [succeeds].

Blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, composed: “Glory to God in the highest.”

[Note: Col. 1007D: The author himself substitutes this line for words somewhat carelessly placed and partly erased shortly before in the eulogy of Pope Hilary: “He is said to have made ‘Glory to God in the highest’”; yet it is clear that the angels had said it first.]

XLIX. Simplicius, a native of Tibur, son of Castorius. Fifteen years, one month, until the year of the Lord 482. He condemned Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, and Peter, bishop of Alexandria, as Eutychian heretics. He established two canons.

1. No bishop shall choose his own successor.

Likewise, to John of Ravenna: No one unwilling is to be made bishop, priest, or deacon.

L. Felix III, a Roman by nationality, son of Felix the priest, of the title of Fasciola. Nine years, until the year of the Lord 491, from the time of Odoacer to that of King Theodoric. He condemned the bishop of Miseno and deprived him of his see. He held a synod in the Constantinian basilica, with Flavius Boethius, *vir clarissimus*, as consul, on the third day before the Ides of March, in the presence of eighty-one bishops and priests. There he established twenty-four canonical chapters concerning bishops, priests, and deacons rebaptized in Africa.

LI. Gelasius, an African by nationality, son of Valerius the bishop. Four years, seven months, twenty-eight days, until the year of the Lord 496. He delivered the city of Rome from danger and famine. He also recalled Misenus, whom his predecessor Felix had condemned, and restored him to communion and to his own Church. He wrote treatises in the manner of Ambrose, and likewise two books against Arius. He also composed prefaces and prayers for the sacraments in guarded language, and many letters concerning the faith in polished language.

He wrote to all bishops of every province an epistle with twenty-eight decretal chapters concerning ecclesiastical institutions, of which I shall give only one: that in every church governed by a bishop, four portions should be made both from revenues and from the offerings of the faithful—one for the bishop, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and a fourth assigned to the buildings of the church. He also wrote to the Augustus Anastasius, admonishing him concerning the faith; among other things he says: “Far be it, I beg, from a Roman ruler to consider truth brought to his ears an injury!”

LII. Anastasius II, a Roman by nationality, son of Peter. Nearly two years, until the year of the Lord 498, to the time of the emperor Anastasius, who was struck by lightning. He sent to that emperor, in an epistle addressed to him, eight decretal chapters concerning various ecclesiastical causes. At its beginning, rejoicing in the concord of the name Augustus, he hoped without doubt for aid from this; of these I give some and pass over others.

1. Sacraments conferred by heretics are not to be annulled.
2. Divine benefits conferred through Acacius are not void.
3. He asks that Acacius’s name be specifically kept silent in the Church—though Anastasius himself tried to defend him, because both were Eutychians.
4. The emperor should admonish the Alexandrians to return to sincere faith and Catholic peace.
5. The emperor should obey apostolic constitutions.

Pope Anastasius II too was struck by divine judgment because, with the favour of the emperor Anastasius, he communicated with Photinus, deacon of Thessalonica, who communicated with Acacius, the Eutychian bishop of Constantinople; Pope Anastasius II had wished secretly to recall Acacius but could not. And because, through the emperor’s favour, he decreed that clerics ordained by Acacius after sentence had been pronounced against Acacius should duly perform their offices once received, saying: “According to the custom of the Church,” etc. Therefore he is rejected by the Church, and in the *Acts of the Roman Pontiffs* is said to have been struck by God.

LIII. Symmachus, a Sardinian by nationality, son of Fortunatus. Fifteen years, eight months, until the year of the Lord 514. He lived in the time of King Theodoric, who, when Symmachus was competing for the see with Laurentius, bishop of Milan, summoned a synod, confirmed Symmachus in the chair, and made Laurentius bishop settled in the city of Lucera. Later, when Laurentius stirred up disorder, he banished him. This disagreement caused such persecution at Rome that countless Romans were killed because of their election. Yet Paschasius the deacon, a man of extraordinary holiness, supported Laurentius.

He held several synods at Rome for various affairs of the Church. The last, the Synod of the Palm Grove, was held by command of King Theodoric, under the consuls Rufius Magnus and Faustus Avienus, *viri clarissimi*, on the tenth day before the Kalends of November. This pope, accused by his adversaries, was prepared to clear himself before the king and all present. The council decided that everything which he had lost through the accusations of his enemies should first be restored to him by the council; that the bishop of so great a see should legally be restored to his former status; and that then he should come to trial and, if it seemed right to the accusers, answer the charges.

He refused on that occasion to recover these things. But while the synod was meeting in the Jerusalem basilica, it seemed good to the priests that the petition prepared by the accusers should be received by the synod. In it there were two matters either hostile to truth or, as it appeared to the assembly, contrary to ecclesiastical purpose.

[Note: Col. 1008D: The codex reads *repugnare*, “to be contrary.”]

First, they said that Symmachus’s crimes had come to the knowledge of the royal court. This was shown to be false: he would not have entrusted himself to a hearing as though it were a new case if he knew that his conscience, convicted of wrongdoing, awaited sentence alone. Secondly, they said they could convict him through slaves; this was so contrary to the canons and to public laws themselves that persons whom secular laws do not admit to make an accusation could not be granted licence to speak for the purpose of bringing disgrace or obtaining anything.

Meanwhile, as they discussed what should be done, the pope was summoned to plead his case. He was so attacked by the rushing mobs of his rivals that many priests who had gone with him met the occasion of death through that assault. When the distinguished Count Algerinus and the eminent men Gudila and Vadeulfus, chief officers of the royal household, saw the still-fresh traces of his wounds, they advised him to return to the enclosure of Blessed Peter the Apostle, from which he had come forth.

After the assault, however, the pope made known to the council through bishops that he had pleaded his case, and humbly expressed his desire for vindication. But the king, placing the matter in the discretion of the synod and declaring that nothing concerning ecclesiastical affairs belonged to him except reverence, entrusted it to the authority of the pontiffs, that they should decide what they thought more beneficial, provided that peace should be restored to all Christians in the city of Rome.

Therefore, when both the synod and the king saw that all the people adhered inseparably to his communion, they universally decreed, with an adjuration of God, and enacted that the adversaries should abandon the purpose they had undertaken:

“Pope Symmachus, bishop of the Apostolic See, having been assailed by such accusations as concern human matters, is manifestly, for the causes set out above, committed to divine judgment. Let him be immune and free, and let him dispense the divine mysteries to the Christian people, without any imputation of the matters alleged against him, in all churches belonging by right to his see; for we have recognized that, owing to the causes set out above, he could not be bound by the petition of his assailants.

“Therefore, in accordance with the principal commands which grant this authority to us, we restore to him whatever ecclesiastical right exists within the sacred city of Rome or outside it, reserving the whole cause to the judgment of God. We exhort all to receive holy communion from him, as the matter requires. Whoever, contrary to our instruction—which we do not expect—either does not accept this or thinks it can be reconsidered, should know that at the divine judgment he will render an account of his contempt, as we trust in God.

“As for his clerics who departed from their bishop contrary to the rules before the proper time and made a schism, we decree that, once they have made satisfaction to their bishop, mercy shall follow them and they shall rejoice to be restored to ecclesiastical offices. But if, after this decision issued by us, any cleric should presume, without the knowledge of Pope Symmachus while he lives, to celebrate Mass in any place consecrated to God in the Roman Church, he shall be struck by canonical penalties as a schismatic.”

[Marginal note, Col. 1009D–1010D: The author adds: “At the same synod, attended by Theodoric, Laurentius said: ‘It has not pleased us that a layman should have any authority to make enactments in the Church; he has the necessity of obedience, not authority to command.’”]

[Note: Col. 1010D: The codex reads *perficiant*, “perform/accomplish,” in place of *percipiant*, “receive.”]

He supplied money and clothing to thirty bishops in Sardinia whom Thrasamund, king of the Vandals, had sent into exile and shut up in churches. He also decreed that “Glory to God in the highest” should be sung on Sundays and on the feasts of saints. Together with 135 bishops, priests, and deacons, he established five synodal chapters; likewise, in his second decretal, seven synodal chapters. He gave the pallium to Theodore, archbishop of the Church of Lauriacum in the province of the Pannonias.

LIV. Hormisdas, a Campanian by nationality, son of Justus, from the city of Frusino. Nine years, from the consulship of Senator to the consulship of Symmachus and Boethius, until the year of the Lord 513. He organized the clergy and instructed them in the psalms.

While the Augustus Anastasius persisted in the heresy into which he had fallen, following Eutyches the heresiarch in denying the two natures in Christ, namely divinity and humanity, Pope Hormisdas, successor of Symmachus, sent Ennodius, bishop of Ticinum, and others with him as legates to Constantinople with a statement of the Catholic faith, in order that they might bring Anastasius back to the bosom of the Church. He not only spurned their salutary warnings, but also expelled them from his presence with insults, put them on a frail vessel, and commanded that nowhere throughout Greece should they approach any city. Divine vengeance followed this rashness: in the twenty-seventh year of his reign he perished by a stroke of lightning.

Germanus, bishop of Capua, a man distinguished in holiness, was sent by the same Pope Hormisdas to Anastasius’s successor Justin; he was received with honour and strengthened many in the faith. Justin wrote the pope a letter, and the pope sent him a most salutary letter instructing him in the faith against the doctrine of Eutyches, as well as another to the archimandrites. He also wrote to the bishops of Spain an epistle with two chapters:

1. He to whom the governance of the Church is entrusted ought to show his worth through a long testing of his life.
2. A blessing by the laying on of hands must not be purchased for money.

Likewise, he wrote another letter to Bishop John concerning what a legate of the Apostolic See ought to do; it begins: “The privileges being preserved.” He died on the eighth day before the Ides of August and was buried in the church of Blessed Peter.

LV. John, martyr, a Tuscan by nationality, son of Constantius. Two years, nine months, from the consulship of Maximus to the consulship of Olybrius. He died in the year of the Lord 526, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June. He was sent by Theodoric to the emperor Justin to recover Justin’s favour for Theodoric. Justin received and treated him honourably. On his return he was killed by the hardship of imprisonment inflicted by Theodoric himself at Ravenna, where he also died. His body was brought away and buried in the basilica of Blessed Peter.

At the Golden Gate, as he entered Constantinople, he restored sight before all present to a blind man asking for light. Gregory also mentions him in the *Dialogues*. On the ninety-eighth day after Pope John died, Theodoric suddenly perished. A certain hermit on the island of Lipari saw his soul led between the hands of Pope John and the patrician Symmachus, whom Theodoric had also killed, and cast down into the cauldron of Mount Vulcan.

He wrote an epistle to the bishops of Italy, in which he says: “Wherever you find Arian churches, consecrate them without any delay as Catholic churches by divine prayers and rites; for when we were in Constantinople, we consecrated as Catholic all that we could find in those regions.” He also wrote another letter to Zacharias the archbishop.

LVI. Felix IV, a Samnite by nationality, son of Castorius. Four years, two months, from the consulship of Maburcius to that of Lampadius and Orestes, that is, to the year of the Lord 530. He was ordained in a time of peace. He gave one very necessary canon: it is better not to sing or hear Mass than, except in extreme necessity, to celebrate Masses or offer sacrifices to the Lord in places where it is not proper. And three others:

1. Concerning the dedication of churches.
2. Concerning their consecration.
3. Those who are not consecrated ought not to perform exorcisms.

LVII. Boniface II, a Roman by nationality, son of Sigibald. Two years, one month, until the year of the Lord 532. He and Dioscorus were ordained amid rivalry; but after Dioscorus died, Boniface held the episcopal see. He assembled a synod in the basilica of Saint Peter and enacted that he should ordain his own successor. By this enactment, supported by the handwritten subscriptions of priests, he appointed the deacon Vigilius before the confession [shrine] of Blessed Peter the Apostle. But when everyone censured this action as contrary to the canons, and because his conscience reproached him for appointing his own successor, the pope publicly acknowledged himself guilty before the confession of Blessed Peter and burned the enactment in the presence of all.

He wrote to Eulalius, bishop of Alexandria, concerning those who had raised themselves against the Roman Church.

A copy of the prayers of himself and Prince Justin: “The first means of salvation is to preserve the rule of right faith and in no way depart from the decrees of the Fathers. Since we by no means wish to be separated from this hope and faith, and follow the decrees of the Fathers, we anathematize those who, in pride against the Roman Church, raise their necks.”

LVIII. John II, a Roman by nationality, son of Projectus of the Caelian Hill, also called Mercurius. Two years, four months, until the year of the Lord 533. His canons or writings are found nowhere.

LIX. Agapetus, a Roman by nationality, son of Gordianus, priest and bishop. One year, until the year of the Lord 534. He died at Constantinople and was brought back to Rome. He had been sent by Theodahad to regain the favour of the emperor Justinian, because Theodahad had killed the daughter of King Theodoric, who, after the death of her son Athalaric—her husband’s successor—had made Theodahad partner in the kingdom.

This pope, perceiving Eutychian error in the Augustus, rebuked him, saying: “I came to the most Christian emperor, but, as I see, I have found Diocletian.” The emperor yielded to his admonitions, so much so that he deposed Anthimus, bishop of Constantinople and defender of the aforesaid heresy, and, having persuaded the ruler, consecrated the Catholic Mennas in his place. He established this canon: churches concerning which there is doubt must be consecrated.

LX. Silverius II, confessor, a Campanian by nationality, son of Hormisdas, bishop of Rome. One year, five months. He was unjustly deposed and died in exile on 12 July, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord 536. While he was remaining in exile, Bishop Amator sent him consolation and wrote among other things:

“Most beloved Father, we have heard from some persons that you have been unjustly driven from the see of Saint Peter and condemned to exile. Grieving greatly at this, we have sent you thirty pounds of silver for the support of yourself and your people.”

The pope, explaining the cause of his deposition, replied:

“Before all else, the patrician lady was hostile to me because I would not restore Anthimus, formerly patriarch of Constantinople, whom my predecessor Agapetus had condemned for his deserts. At her pressing command false witnesses came forward, alleging crimes against me in which I never had any share. But while many persisted in that persecution, our patrician Belisarius became afraid and ordered me to come peacefully to him in the imperial palace for certain ecclesiastical arrangements. At the first and second curtain he detained all the clergy and people who came with me, permitting no one to enter except me alone and Vigilius our deacon. I was forcibly detained and brought before the aforesaid patrician lady; in exile I am sustained with the bread of tribulation and the water of distress.

“Nevertheless, on that account I have not relinquished, and do not relinquish, my office. With the bishops whom I could gather, I anathematized those who had done such things against me; and together with them, by apostolic and synodal authority, I decreed that no one should ever be deceived as I was deceived, and that if anyone henceforth should ever deceive any bishop in this way, he should be anathema maranatha in the sight of God and the holy angels.”

Nevertheless, the emperor Justinian consented in this matter to his wife Theodora. He established one canon, concerning invasion [of a see], which we shall give in the letter that he wrote to Vigilius, his successor.

LXI. Vigilius, a Roman by nationality, son of John the consul. Seventeen years, seven months. He was long exiled at Constantinople on the same account as his predecessor, namely on account of the anger of the empress Theodora concerning Bishop Anthimus; he was expelled from the see. At length released and recalled to the favour of the Roman people, he died at Syracuse, while returning, from the pain of a stone, in the year of the Lord 554. His body was brought thence to Rome and buried at Saint Marcellus on the Via Salaria.

Under him the Fifth Synod was held at Constantinople against Theodore of Mopsuestia and all heretics. Theodore said that God the Word was one person and Christ another, and, like Nestorius, denied that holy Mary was the Mother of God. In the time of Emperor Justinian, Domnus of Antioch and Eutychius of Constantinople wrote fourteen chapters anathematizing the blasphemies of Theodore himself and his associates.

Silverius, his predecessor, while in exile accused Vigilius of invasion [of the see] and pronounced a sentence of condemnation against him, writing as follows:

“Because, contrary to canonical law, in the time of Pope Boniface, while he was still living, you tried to have yourself designated his successor, and had not the justice of the most noble senate opposed you, the abominable beginnings of your pastoral office should then already have been cut short. But since the small wound in you was neglected, an incurable abscess has grown, which cannot feel the remedy of poultices unless it is more deeply cut away by iron.

“For the audacity of a most wicked spirit, conceiving the frenzy of ambition, turns into an insult against that apostle and physician to whom the power of binding and loosing souls has been granted. You strive once more to introduce a new crime of error into the Apostolic See; after the manner of Simon—whose disciple you show yourself to be by your deeds—you have given money and seek, by tearing me away, to evade my term of office, though, by the Lord’s favour, I have now presided over it through three complete periods.

“Therefore receive, together with those who agree with you, the sentence of full condemnation. Recognize that the name and office of priestly ministry have been taken from you: by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by apostolic authority, we condemn you. For thus the faith of the holy Fathers ought to be preserved in the Catholic Church: he who, with blameworthy rashness, has assumed what he did not receive must lose what he had.”

[Note: Col. 1013D: The codex reads *quae*, “which [feminine],” rather than *quod*.]

He established a canon concerning the rebuilding of a church if it has been destroyed, and whether the solemnity of consecration ought to be repeated in a place in which sanctuaries no longer remain. To his brother Eutherius he wrote an epistle with four chapters.

Gregory to Secundinus, a recluse and servant of God: “Your charity asks whether, after the most blessed Hormisdas, anything was added concerning the ordinations of pontiffs of the Apostolic See; but know that accounts of the ordinations of bishops have been set forth down to the time of Pope Vigilius.”

LXII. Pelagius, a Roman by nationality, son of John Vicarianus. Eleven years, ten months, until the year of the Lord 576. He was ordained by two bishops and one priest.
