He also began the church of the Apostles Philip and James, but his successor completed it. He established this canon: the Roman Church alone possesses fullness of authority in deciding cases.

LXIII. John III, a Roman by nationality, son of Anastasius. Three years, until the year of the Lord 578. He loved and restored the cemetery of the saints and decreed that offerings should be made there every Sunday. He asserts the succession of Clement to Blessed Peter, mentioned in the Prologue.

LXIV. Benedict, a Roman by nationality, son of Boniface. Four years, two months, until the year of the Lord 582. He established a canon concerning the restoration of things taken away. He died in the first year of Maurice.

LXV. Pelagius II, a Roman by nationality, son of Unigeld. Ten years, two months. He died in the ninth indiction, in the year of the Lord 595, of the groin-plague which had invaded the whole City. This pontiff was consecrated without the emperor’s command because the Lombards were besieging Rome on every side and no one could leave it.

He also sent a very useful letter to Elias, bishop of Aquileia, who was unwilling to accept the Three Chapters of the Council of Chalcedon. Blessed Gregory, still a deacon, dictated it; in that rank Pelagius sent him to Constantinople, where Gregory refuted before Tiberius a certain Eutyches who erred concerning faith in the resurrection. Pelagius made thirty canons concerning various ecclesiastical causes, among which one is that only nine prefaces are to be received:

1. At the Paschal *in albis*.
2. Another concerning the Ascension of the Lord.
3. Concerning Pentecost.
4. Concerning the Nativity of the Lord.
5. Concerning the Epiphany.
6. Concerning the Apostles.
7. Concerning the Holy Trinity.
8. Concerning the Holy Cross.
9. Concerning Lent.

The second is: A general synod is not to be convened without the pope’s command. You will find the rest in their proper place.

LXVI. Gregory Dialogus, doctor, a Roman by nationality, son of Gordianus. Thirteen years, six months, until the second year of the emperor Phocas. He died in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord 602, the see having been vacant five months. In the time of the Augustus Maurice, he wrote six synodal chapters with twenty-four bishops. Likewise, at Augustine’s request, he wrote eleven highly necessary chapters to Augustine in Britain. He was the apostle of the English, whom he converted to the faith of Christ through Augustine, Mellitus, and John.

For the edification of the Church he wrote many useful works: the Antiphonary, the Diurnal, the Nocturnal, the book of Divine Offices, the *Morals on Job*, homilies, sermons, letters, the Register, and many other works. He also added to the Canon: “Order our days in thy peace,” etc., and likewise the Lord’s Prayer. For, as he himself says in the letter he sent to John, bishop of Syracuse:

“Therefore we say the Lord’s Prayer immediately after the peace, because it was the custom of the apostles to consecrate the sacrificial offering by that prayer alone. It seemed very unsuitable to me that we should say over the offering a prayer composed by a scholastic, but should not say over Christ’s sacred body and blood the very tradition which our Redeemer composed.”

He also composed a preface concerning one apostle in honour of Blessed Andrew, for whom he built a monastery in the City.

LXVII. Sabinianus, a Tuscan by nationality, from the city of Blera, son of Bonus. One year, five months, until the year of the Lord 607, the see having been vacant nearly one year. He added lamps in the church of Blessed Peter.

LXVIII. Boniface III, a Roman by nationality, son of John. Nearly nine months, until the year of the Lord 609. From Phocas, then ruler of the Roman Empire, he obtained that the Roman Church should be called head of all Churches, because the Church of Constantinople had previously written that it was first.

Therefore Blessed Gregory, rebuking John of Constantinople, who wished to be called universal bishop, wrote to Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria:

“As your Holiness knows, through the holy Council of Chalcedon this title of universality was offered to the pontiff of the Apostolic See; yet none of my predecessors ever consented to use so profane a title. For if one patriarch is called universal, the name of patriarch is diminished for the rest.”

Likewise: “Therefore let your Holiness never call anyone universal in its letters, lest, while offering another an honour not due to him, it withdraw what is due to itself.”

Likewise, to John of Constantinople: “You who confessed yourself unworthy to be called bishop have been brought to the point of desiring, in contempt of your brethren, to be called bishop alone. Do not consent to be called by a foolish and proud title.”

LXIX. Boniface IV, a Marsian by nationality, from the city of Valeria, son of John the physician. Six years, eight months, until the year of the Lord 617, the see having been vacant seven months. He decreed that another should be elected while he himself lived, and was buried in the basilica of Blessed Peter on the third day after his deposition. From the same Phocas he obtained the dedication, in honour of all saints, of the Pantheon built by Domitian. He gave monks everywhere permission to minister in priestly office.

LXX. Deusdedit, a Roman by nationality, son of Stephen the subdeacon. Three years, one month, until the year of the Lord 620. During his time there was an earthquake, in the seventh indiction, the see having been vacant one and a half months. He loved the clergy and priests with fatherly affection and increased their support. In his time Jerusalem, among other cities of Palestine, was captured by Chosroes, king of the Persians, and the Lord’s Cross was carried into Persia.

LXXI. Boniface V, a Campanian by nationality, from the city of Naples, son of John. Five years, until the year of the Lord 625. A gentle and very pious man. He decreed and forbade under anathema that no one should be dragged out of a church.

LXXII. Honorius I, a Campanian by nationality, son of Petronius the consul. Thirteen years, until the year of the Lord 638, the see having been vacant one year and seven months. In his time, after the tyrant Chosroes had been killed by the emperor Heraclius, the Lord’s Cross was returned to Jerusalem. The Roman pontiff himself established that day as a feast for the whole Church in honour of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, namely the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October.

In the third year of his pontificate Dagobert, son of Lothar, the strong and religious king of the Franks, obtained the kingdom, in the year 628 of the Lord’s Incarnation. He also built and adorned many churches at Rome in honour of the Lord and his saints: Saint Agnes, Saint Apollinaris, the Four Crowned Saints, Severinus, Pancratius, Lucy, Adrian, and many other praiseworthy works he performed.

LXXIII. Severianus, a Roman by nationality, son of Abienus. Two years. In the year 640 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the see was vacant five months. He was a holy, gentle, and pious man.

LXXIV. John IV, a Dalmatian by nationality, son of Venantius Scholasticus. One year, eight months, and eighteen days, until the year of the Lord 642. The see was vacant one and a half months. With money sent out, he ransomed Christian captives from barbarians in Istria and Dalmatia.

LXXV. Theodore, a Greek by nationality, son of Theodore, bishop from the city of Jerusalem. Nearly six years, six months, until the year of the Lord 649. The see was vacant nearly two years. In the fourth year of his pontificate, Pyrrhus, patriarch of Constantinople, successor of Sergius both in the see and in heresy, came from Africa to Rome. Though long before condemned by this pope, he feigned repentance, was kindly received, and reconciled by him. Afterwards, however, having returned to error, he was again condemned and anathematized by the same pope.

[Col. 1016A] LXXVI. Martin, holy confessor, from the city of Todi in the province of Tuscany. Six years and two months, until the year of the Lord 655. He convened a synod in the city of Rome with 105 Fathers, in which he condemned Cyrus and his associates—the heretics Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul—together with Emperor Constans and their followers, who maintained that there was one operation and only one nature in the Son of God. Having copied out its acts, he sent them through orthodox men into East and West, and confirmed the fourth synod. In his time Paul, bishop of Constantinople, having led Emperor Constans astray, afflicted with imprisonment, exile, and diverse punishments the envoys of the Apostolic See who reproved him for heresy; and wherever he could, he stirred up no slight persecution against other Catholics.

[Col. 1016B] But the pope, by command of the heretical emperor, was seized at Rome in the basilica of the Holy Saviour, called the Constantinian basilica, by Theodore the Exarch, who had been sent for this purpose. Taken to Constantinople and utterly unable to be bent, he was banished to Cherson in the province of Lycia, where he ended his life, still shining there to this day through many signs. He wrote a letter to Amandus, with one decretal chapter: “Whoever, after his ordination, has once fallen into a lapse shall henceforth be deposed and shall be able to attain no rank of the priesthood.”

LXXVII. Eugenius I, a Roman by nation, from the first Aventine district, a cleric from the cradle, son of Rufinianus. Two years and almost ten months, until the year of the Lord 658. The see was vacant for two months. A kindly man,

[Col. 1016C] gentle and devout, and most attentive in preserving the traditions of his predecessors.

LXXVIII. Vitalian, a native of Segni in the province of Campania, son of Anastasius. Fourteen years and six months. He died in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord 672, in the second month. He entirely preserved the rule and vigour of the Church, as was customary. Under him Constantine, or Constans, son of Constantine, son of Heraclius, convened a synod and renounced heresy; afterward he notably exalted the Roman Church, sending the pope Gospel-books of gold from St Peter, adorned around their circumference with white gems of marvellous size. Moreover, he himself offered a pallium woven with gold, while the whole army entered the church.

LXXIX. Adeodatus, a Roman by nation, from Monchi,

[Col. 1016D] son of Jovinianus. Four years and two months. In the year of the Lord 677, in the second month. The see was vacant for four and a half months. A very gentle and devout man, so much so that he gladly received every person, from the greatest to the least, and showed compassion to the sick.

LXXX. Donus, or Donatus, a Roman by nation, son of Mauritius. One year and five months, until the year of the Lord 678. The see was vacant for two months. Among his other good works, he paved St Peter’s portico with marble. While he was a deacon, in the month of August, an immense star appeared for three months, rising at cockcrow.

LXXXI. Agatho, a Sicilian by birth. Two years and six months, until the year of the Lord 681, in the ninth indiction. The see was vacant for one year and seven months. Under him the sixth universal synod,

[Col. 1017A] of 150 Fathers, was written in Greek, in the time of Emperor Constantine, against Macarius, bishop of Antioch, and his associates, who falsely asserted one will and one operation in Christ; and against George of Constantinople, who was likewise in the same error but was corrected. Among them were also two legates of the Roman Church, John of Porto and John the deacon. Having condemned the aforesaid heresy by anathema, they set down nine chapters. It established this canon: “All enactments of the Apostolic See are to be received as though established by the public utterance of the divine command itself.”

LXXXII. Leo II, a Sicilian by nation [Note: [Col. 1017D] Thus the manuscript.], son of Paul. Almost eleven months. In the year of the Lord 683. In this eleventh indiction, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, on Good Friday,

[Col. 1017B] the moon suffered a total eclipse. The see was vacant for two and a half months. This man, most eloquent and sufficiently learned in the divine Scriptures, and highly skilled in Greek and Latin, restored, arranged, and dedicated churches. He also made a decree that anyone ordained archbishop should pay nothing from the church treasury, by any custom, either for the use of the pallium or for the various offices of the Church.

LXXXIII. Benedict II, a Roman by nation, son of John. Ten months; he died after Easter in the year of the Lord 685. A learned and devout man, restoring churches through very many benefactions; he was buried at St Peter’s during the reign of Constantine.

LXXXIV. John V, a Syrian by nation, from the province of Antioch, son of Cyriacus. One year, until

[Col. 1017C] the year of the Lord 686, and almost three months. While he was a deacon, Agatho sent him to Constantinople with others for the confirmation of the sixth synod, which he rendered secure by an edict of Emperor Constantine. A learned and discerning man.

LXXXV. Conon, descended from Trazeceus his father, eleven months, until the year of the Lord 687. The see was vacant for almost three months. A man of advanced age, of the highest innocence and holy simplicity; he ordained St Kilian and sent him into eastern Francia. He too was elected as a third candidate together with two others, one of whom was Theodore and the other Paschal [Note: [Col. 1017D] The remainder has been erased.]. [lacuna]

LXXXVI. Sergius, a Syrian by nation, son of Tiberius, at Palermo in Sicily. Fourteen years and nine months. He died in the fourteenth indiction, under Emperor Tiberius, in the year of the Lord

[Col. 1017D] 701. The see was vacant for almost two months. When factions disagreed in the election of two men, he too was chosen third by God’s will. One of those men, named Paschal, was convicted by the judgment of the Church for incantations and confined in a monastery; there, unrepentant, he died after five years because of the hardness of his heart. Under him the Synod of Aquileia assembled. Through ignorance of the faith it had hesitated to accept the fifth universal council, until, instructed by the salutary admonitions of blessed Pope Sergius [Note: [Col. 1017D] The manuscript has *instructi*, “having been instructed.”], it too consented to agree with the other Churches of Christ in this matter

[Col. 1018A] and accepted the synod. Because he refused to subscribe to the heretical synod held in the imperial city by Justinian, son of the heretic Constantine—in which the legates of the Apostolic See, having been deceived, subscribed—the pope himself did not assent, since certain chapters had been appended contrary to ecclesiastical rite. Justinian ordered Zacharias the protospatharius, whom he had sent, to bring him captive before him. The people of Ravenna rescued him and expelled Zacharias from the city. He decreed that the breaking be made in the undivided body of Christ and that, after the breaking, the *Agnus Dei* be sung by the Church. He also explained the meaning of the three portions as follows: “The Lord’s body is threefold. The portion offered and put into the chalice signifies the body of Christ that has already risen; the portion eaten, that which still walks upon the earth; the portion remaining upon the altar

[Col. 1018B] until the end of Mass, the body in the tomb, because until the end of the age the bodies of the saints will be in tombs” [Note: [Col. 1018D] These words were appended to Sergius’s notice, in a hand equally ancient and perhaps the same as that in which the rest was written.]. “The portion immersed in the blood signifies the martyrs in tribulation; the remainder placed upon the paten, that part of the Church which is in eternal peace; the third, those who live in rest.” He established many canons. He found in the treasury of St Peter a portion of Christ’s cross of marvellous size. He also ordained St Willibrord and sent him to preach in Germany. He baptized at Rome King Ceadwalla of the West Saxons and buried him there when he died in white baptismal garments. He further decreed that, on the feasts of blessed Mary, litanies should proceed from St Adrian’s and the people should assemble at St Mary’s.

[Col. 1018C] LXXXVII. John VI, a Greek by nation. Three years and two months, until the year of the Lord 705. The see was vacant for one and a half months. He sent priests and many gifts to Duke Gisulf of the Lombards, who had devastated Beneventan Campania with fire, sword, and captivity. Since there was no one able to resist his attack, John redeemed all the captives and caused the enemy to return home.

LXXXVIII. John VII, likewise a Greek by nation, son of Plato. Two years and almost eight months, until the year of the Lord 708. The see was vacant for three months. Among many splendid works, he made within the church of the blessed Apostle Peter an oratory of the Holy Mother of God, of most beautiful workmanship. He voluntarily relinquished the governance of the apostolate and became a monk.

[Col. 1018D] LXXXIX. Sisinnius, a Syrian by nation, son of John. Twenty days. Afflicted by gout, he suddenly died in the year of the Lord 708 mentioned above. The see was vacant for two months.

XC. Constantine, a Syrian by nation, son of John. Seven years, until the year of the Lord 715. He went to Greece to the emperor in the ninth indiction and returned in the tenth. Philippicus sent him letters containing a perverse doctrine, which he rejected; for this reason he had made in the portico of St Peter paintings containing the acts of the six holy synods, which Philippicus had ordered removed at Constantinople. He absolved Emperor Justinian,

[Col. 1019A] when penitent, for having blinded Patriarch Callinicus and given the bishopric to Cyrus, who had been abbot in Pontus and who had maintained Justinian in exile when he had been driven from the kingdom. Emperor Anastasius sent letters to Pope Constantine at Rome through Scholasticus, patrician and exarch of Italy, declaring himself a supporter of the Catholic faith and a promoter of the six holy councils.

XCI. Gregory II, a Roman by nation, son of Marcellus. Fifteen years and almost nine months; he died in the fourteenth indiction. This chaste man, learned in the divine Scriptures, decreed that on Thursday in Lent there should be fasting and the solemnity of Masses, whereas Pope St Miltiades had forbidden fasting on Thursday and Sunday. He lived in the time of Emperors Leo and Constantine,

[Col. 1019B] and through Archbishop Boniface, whom he ordained, he preached the word of salvation in Germany. He ordained Wivilo archbishop of Lorch. In his time also a certain deceiver, Tibertus surnamed Petasius, attempted to usurp for himself the sovereignty of the Roman Empire; he ordered the images both of the Saviour and of his Mother and of the saints to be burnt with fire and painted images to be whitewashed. Because of this many suffered, and Germanus, bishop of the Church of Constantinople, was deprived of his pontificate. He died on the third day before the Kalends of December. With thirty-three Fathers he wrote nineteen chapters to be observed by the whole Church and bound them under anathema. At this time, Greek aid having ceased and Lombard oppression increasing, the Roman

[Col. 1019C] Empire passed to the Franks.

XCII. Gregory III, a Syrian by nation, son of John. Ten years and almost eight months. He was suddenly found standing before his predecessor’s bier at the funeral, seized by force, and elected pope. He too lived during the reign and persecution of Emperors Leo and Constantine. As the persecution stirred up by them for the destruction of holy images continued, he admonished them to repent and sent them written remonstrances, as his predecessor had done; but he achieved nothing. Moved therefore by a greater zeal for the faith, he enacted a synodal decree, with Archbishop Antoninus of Grado, John of Ravenna, and the other bishops of the western region seated with him—ninety-three bishops,

[Col. 1019D] priests, and also deacons—that anyone thereafter found to be a blasphemer of holy images should be excluded from the body and blood of the Lord. All confirmed this by their subscriptions, and he caused holy images to be erected. He also added to the canon that the words “Within whose fellowship, etc.” should be said, and had this enactment inscribed on stone tablets. At that time Campania was plundered by the accursed Lombards and King Liutprand. Coming to Rome in the Field of Nero, he had many Roman nobles tonsured and clothed in Lombard fashion. Grieved by this, the man of God sent by sea the keys from the confession of St Peter to Charles, first king of the Franks,

[Col. 1020A] through Anastasius, a most holy bishop, and Sergius, a priest, asking the aforesaid Charles to free them from such Lombard oppression. He also cut Emperor Leo off from communion with the Church and turned all Italy, together with Rome, away from him. Learned in Greek and Latin, he held all the psalms in order by heart and was refined through most subtle exercise in their meanings. He established a canon. He died on the third day before the Kalends of December.

XCIII. Zacharias, a Greek by nation, son of Polochronius. Ten years and three months. He died in the fifth indiction, on the Ides of March, in the year of the Lord 752. A gentle and gracious man, adorned with every goodness, loved by all, slow to anger and swift to show mercy, repaying evil to no one for evil

[Col. 1020B] and granting no vengeance according to deserts, but devout and merciful. He found all Italy disturbed and the Roman duchy troubled by Liutprand, king of the Lombards. He decreed that on the fourth weekday before Lent ashes should be blessed and sprinkled upon the heads of the faithful, to display the humility of true contrition that is begun through fasting. He also translated St Gregory’s *Dialogue* from Latin into Greek, found the head of the martyr St George enclosed in a casket, and brought it to the city of Rome. He ordered Pippin to be made king. He wrote many useful things to Archbishop Boniface, whom Gregory had consecrated and sent into Germany.

XCIV. Stephen II, a Roman by nation, son of Constantine. Five years and almost one month, until

[Col. 1020C] the year of the Lord 757. At his request King Pippin marched against Aistulf, king of the Lombards. Having slain many Lombards, received forty hostages, and exacted an oath that Aistulf would no longer attack the Roman Church, Pippin raised the siege. For he had besieged Pavia, where the king himself was. In his time Duke Humald of Aquitaine [Note: [Col. 1019D] Thus the manuscript, for “Aquitania.”] came to the thresholds of the apostles and promised there to be their servant. Later, deceived by diabolical fraud, he broke his vow and wickedly joined the Lombard expedition; as he deserved, he ended his life by stones in a death worthy of him. At this time the Roman Church suffered great persecution from the kings of Italy. By Stephen’s authority, King Childeric was deposed and tonsured—or rather,

[Col. 1020D] sent into a monastery—and Pippin, son of Charles I, was elected king of the Franks and consecrated at Soissons to the kingship by St Boniface, archbishop of Mainz.

XCV. Paul, a Roman by nation, son of Constantine. Ten years and one month, until the year of the Lord 767. He is called Constantine by others.

XCVI. Stephen III, a Roman by nation, son of Olivius. Four years and almost six months, until the year of the Lord 772.

XCVII. Adrian I, a Roman by nation, son of Theodore. Twenty-four years and ten months, until the year of the Lord 796. He asked Charles to come to Rome to defend

[Col. 1021A] [Note: [Col. 1021D] Thus the manuscript; perhaps “to protect.”] the possessions of the Church. King Charles therefore came to Rome, besieged Pavia, and, leaving his army there, was honourably received at Rome by the pope on the holy feast of the Resurrection. After the holy Resurrection he returned to Pavia and captured Desiderius. Then, returning to Rome, he convened a synod there with the pope, in the Lateran patriarchium, in the church of the Holy Saviour, with 154 devout bishops and abbots. The pope and the whole synod granted Charles the right and power to choose the pontiff and appoint the Apostolic See. They also granted him the dignity of the patriciate. Further, they decreed that archbishops and bishops in each province should receive investiture from him and that no bishop should be consecrated by anyone unless he were approved and invested by the king. And he bound with the bond of anathema

[Col. 1021B] anyone who opposed this decree, and ordered that, unless he repented, his goods should be confiscated. On holy Easter Day, in the presence of Emperor Charles, the pope anathematized Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, unless he obeyed that emperor, his sons, and the Frankish people in all things, as he had sworn to Charles’s father Pippin and to Charles himself. If he refused and bloodshed or some other evil resulted, this should rest upon that duke and those agreeing with him, while the king and his followers should be free from blame.

XCVIII. Leo III, a Roman by nation, son of Azuppius. Twenty years and ten months, until the year of the Lord 816. In the Greater Litany he was blinded by the Romans and partly deprived of his tongue; but he was rescued through Abbot Wirimund and Duke Winigis of Spoleto, and brought into Saxony to King Charles. In the following year he was returned to Rome and restored by that prince. In the church of St Peter, carrying the Gospel-book before the king and all the people, he ascended the ambo; and, having invoked the name of the Holy Trinity, he cleared himself by oath of the crimes imputed to him in this manner: “*Luditum est* [reading uncertain; perhaps “it has been made clear” or “it has been judged”] [Note: [Col. 1021D] Perhaps *lucidum*, ‘clear,’ or *judicatum*, ‘judged.’],

[Col. 1021C] dearest brothers, and spread abroad in many places, how evil men rose against me, sought to disable me, and brought grave accusations against me. For this reason this most clement and serene lord Charles has come to this city with his priests and nobles. Therefore I, Leo, pontiff of the Roman Church, judged by no one

[Col. 1021D] and compelled by no one, but of my own free will, clear myself in your sight before God and his angels, who know my conscience, and before St Peter, prince of the apostles, in whose presence we stand: I have neither committed nor ordered to be committed these criminal and wicked acts which they allege against me. God is my witness, in whose presence we stand and to whose judgment we shall come. I do this of my own free will in order to remove evil suspicions, not as though I were imposing this custom or decree in the holy Church upon my successors, nor upon our brothers and fellow bishops,

[Col. 1022A] but so that you may the more readily cut off rebellious thoughts.” After this satisfaction, in which he had twelve bishops as supporters, the king took vengeance upon his opponents, killing some and sending others into exile. He established a canon.

XCIX. Stephen IV, a Roman by nation, son of Marinus. Seven months. He was a deacon of Pope Leo. He died in the year of the Lord 817; under him Louis, son of the great Charles, became emperor.

C. Paschal, a Roman by nation, son of Bonosus. Seven years and almost one month, until the year of the Lord 824. When he died, although two men had been elected to his place through popular faction, Eugenius, archpriest of the title of St Sabina, was nevertheless substituted and ordained when the party of the nobles prevailed [Note: [Col. 1022D] Thus the manuscript; the passage is corrupt.]. From him the election of the Roman pontiff was granted by Louis I to himself and the Romans.

[Col. 1022B] CI. Eugenius II, a Roman by nation. Four years and almost eight months, until the year of the Lord 818. He wrote to Ratfrid of Faviana, Methodius of Julium Forum—also called of Ougutura—Alcuin of Nitra, and Anno of Vetuar, bishops of the holy Churches; he sent and entrusted to them Urolf, archbishop of Lorch, as their ruler, and by privilege confirmed upon him the right of a metropolitan.

CII. Valentine, a Roman by nation, son of Peter. Forty days, in the year of the Lord mentioned above. Because of the brevity of his time, he did nothing worthy of remembrance.

CIII. Gregory IV, a Roman by nation, son of John. Sixteen years, until the year of the Lord 844.

[Col. 1022C] He consecrated Theodosius, whom Pope Eugenius had earlier deprived of the honour of the priesthood, bishop of the holy Church of Segni.

CIV. Sergius II, a Roman by nation, son of Sergius. Three years, until the year of the Lord 847.

CV. Leo IV, a Roman by nation, son of Rodoald. Nine years and three months, until the year of the Lord 856. He gave Archbishop Adalwin of Salzburg the blessed martyr Hermes, to bring with him to his own see. He wrote a canon to the bishops of Britain: “The enactments of the Roman pontiffs are to be held before others”; and many other things to Augustus Lothair concerning the observance of imperial capitularies. Likewise another to the same man: “As Roman law has hitherto prevailed and has been corrupted for no man, so now also may it retain its force.” He admonished Lothair and Louis concerning the canonical and just election and consecration of the Roman pontiff.

[Col. 1022D] CVI. Benedict III, a Roman by nation, son of Peter. Two years and six months, until the year of the Lord 859. After he had been elected by the harmonious acclamation of the whole City, the clergy, people, and nobles confirmed the decree with their own hands and sent it to the rulers Lothair and Louis. Approved by them, he was consecrated in the presence and with the approval of the envoys whom they had sent on this matter.

CVII. Nicholas, a Roman by nation, son of Theodore.

[Col. 1023A] Nine years and nine months, until the year of the Lord 868. He deprived Lothair of communion because of Queen Theutberga, whom Lothair had repudiated after taking Waldrada, with the support of certain bishops, despite repeated admonitions. He wrote to Archbishop Adalwin of Salzburg concerning a woman who, by putting on a veil, pretended to be a nun and afterward returned to marriage: she was to do penance for the deception and return to what she had promised.

CVIII. Adrian II, a Roman by nation, son of Bishop Jalaris. Five years, until the year of the Lord 873. Lothair, excommunicated by Nicholas, returned to Rome and was received. When he wished to clear himself of the charges laid against him, the pope proposed this judgment: if he were innocent, he should approach

[Col. 1023B] communion confidently. Rashly he approached and received judgment upon himself and his accomplices from the hand of the Apostolic See. For not long afterward, he and his supporters perished by sudden death; and so great a disaster followed this presumption by divine action that throughout Lothair’s kingdom all strength and nobility seemed to have been destroyed at once—not by plague, but as though by an enemy’s sword. For Lothair was first asked by the pope whether he had complied, concerning Queen Theutberga, with the admonitions of his predecessor, Lord Nicholas. While he falsely claimed that he had observed the injunctions laid upon him, he received the body of the Lord, as stated above, and paid the penalty on the journey.

CIX. John VIII, a Roman by nation, son of

[Col. 1023C] Gundo. Ten years, until the year of the Lord 883. He absolved Emperor Louis from the oath which he had made under compulsion to Duke Adelgis in order to preserve his life. He himself died after poison had been administered to him by one of his relatives, and he was then struck in the head with a hammer. He also restored Photius, patriarch of Constantinople, whom Nicholas had deposed, through the intervention of the emperors Basil, Leo, and Alexander. Various enactments made by him are found in the book of Gothic law. Concerning sacrilege: it is committed by carrying off anything from the area within thirty paces around a church, or from houses situated within those paces; likewise, if anyone has inflicted evil or injury upon clerics, monks, or ecclesiastical persons. Chapels situated within the circuit of the walls of fortified places are not included in this observance.

[Col. 1023D] Likewise, concerning the compensation for sacrilege: whereas Justinian fixed it at five pounds of gold, he decreed that it should be made in thirty pounds of refined silver—that is, a sum of six hundred solidi of the purest silver—to those to whom the complaint of sacrilege rightly belonged. And to Michael, king of the Bulgarians: “If you receive sacraments from excommunicated persons, it is certain that you have committed idolatry, so as to become schismatics.” And many other things: that those in positions of rank ought to hear the complaints of churches more attentively.

CX. Martin, a Gallician by nation, son of the priest Palumbus. One year and seven months, until the year of the Lord 885. He had been archdeacon of his predecessor.

[Col. 1024A] CXI. Adrian III, a Roman by nation, son of Benedict. One year and four months, until the year of the Lord 886.

CXII. Stephen V, a Roman by nation, son of Adrian. A little more than six years, until the year of the Lord 892. He established one canon: that witnesses are not to be sought in a matter manifest and known to many. He wrote this to Leo, bishop of Ziano.

CXIII. Formosus, formerly bishop of Porto, son of Leo. Four years and seven months, until the year of the Lord 896. With his consent Arnulf, king and son of Carloman, took Rome by arms. The king was also received by him with great honour and, before the confession of St Peter, was crowned emperor by him. Therefore Formosus was severely afflicted by them.

[Col. 1024B] In entering to avenge the pope’s injury, Arnulf ordered many leading Romans who hastened to meet him to be beheaded. The cause of the hostility between Pope Formosus and the Romans was this. When Formosus’s predecessor had died, a certain Stephen, deacon of the Roman Church, had been chosen pope by one party of the Romans. Another party, and no insignificant one, eagerly desired that the aforesaid Formosus, bishop of the city of Porto, should be made their pope because of his true religion and knowledge of divine teachings. For when Stephen was about to be ordained vicar of the apostles, the party favouring Formosus expelled Stephen from the altar with no small tumult and violence and made Formosus pope. Stephen went down into Tuscany in order that he might be aided by

[Col. 1024C] Adalbert, the most powerful margrave; and this came to pass. For after Formosus died, Arnulf the emperor had returned to his own lands and died from the affliction of lice, called *ptiriasis*, the man who had been appointed after Formosus’s death was expelled, and Stephen was made pope through Adalbert. Once appointed, being impious and ignorant of holy teaching, he ordered Formosus to be drawn from the tomb and placed upon the throne of the Roman pontificate, clothed in priestly vestments. He said to him: “When you were bishop of Porto, why did you usurp the universal Roman See in a spirit of ambition?” When these matters had been carried out, he ordered him immediately stripped of the sacred vestments, three fingers cut off, and thrown into the Tiber;

[Col. 1024D] and he deposed from their rank all whom Formosus had ordained and ordained them again. We can infer how great Pope Formosus’s authority and holiness were from this: when fishermen afterward found his body and brought it to the church of St Peter, certain images of saints reverently greeted him as he lay in his coffin.

CXIV. Boniface VI, a Roman by nation, son of Bishop Adrian. Fifteen days. He died of gout in that same year. He had been expelled by Stephen after Formosus’s death.

CXV. Stephen VI, a Roman by nation, son of the priest John, formerly bishop of Campania. One year and one month. He perished, deservedly expelled because he had exhumed

[Col. 1025A] Formosus. For, supporting the tyrants Berengar and Lambert and hating Emperor Arnulf, he had Formosus, as stated above, dug up eight months after his death, placed in his chair, accused—with a deacon speaking for him—and, as though convicted, deprived of rank. He ordered him dragged by the legs out of the church and cast into the Tiber. But the Roman citizens, frightened by divine miracles through Formosus’s merits, not long afterward expelled Stephen, after he had been suitably tortured, and restored Formosus to his tomb. He is said by others to have been Sergius, a Roman deacon.

CXVI. Romanus, a Gallician by nation, son of Constantine. Almost five months, in the year of the Lord 898.

CXVII. Theodore II, a Roman by nation, son of

[Col. 1025B] Photius. Twenty days, in the year of the Lord mentioned above.

CXVIII. John IX, a native of Tivoli, son of Rampoald. Two years, until the year of the Lord 900.

CXIX. Benedict IV, a Roman by nation, son of Mammolus. Three years and five months, until the year of the Lord 904.

CXX. Leo V, a native of Ardea, of Lompampi. Two months. In the year of the Lord mentioned above. He had been a priest from outside the city.

CXXI. Christopher, a Roman by nation, son of Leo, formerly cardinal of the title of Damasus. Four months. He was deposed and made a monk, in the year of the Lord mentioned above.

[Col. 1025C] CXXII. Sergius III, a Roman by nation, son of Benedict. Seven years and three months, until the year of the Lord 912.

CXXIII. Anastasius III, a Roman by nation, son of Lucian. Two years and two months, until the year of the Lord 914.

CXXIV. Lando, a Sabine by nation, son of Tainu. Five months, in the year of the Lord 915.

CXXV. Leo VI, a Roman by nation, son of Christopher the *primicerius*. Almost three months, in the year of the Lord mentioned above.

CXXVI. John X, a native of Ravenna, son of John. Fourteen years and two months, until the year of the Lord 929. It is said that he was made pope through a certain prostitute, Theodora.

[Col. 1025D] CXXVII. Stephen VII, a Roman by nation, son of Teudemund. Three years and one month, until the year of the Lord 931.

CXXVIII. John XI, a Roman by nation, son of Pope Sergius. Four years, until the year of the Lord 915.

CXXIX. Leo VII, a Roman by nation. Three years and six months, until the year of the Lord 938. He sent the pallium to Gerhard, archbishop of Lorch, and approved his confession of faith, though written briefly; nevertheless, he said that Gerhard ought to have expounded it more fully. He also wrote to Egelolf, archbishop of Salzburg, and to the bishops of Regensburg, Freising, and Säben, that they should be obedient to him and assist him in all ecclesiastical affairs,

[Col. 1026A] as one to whom he had entrusted his own office.

CXXX. Stephen VIII, a Roman by nation. Three years and almost four months, until the year of the Lord 942.

CXXXI. Marinus II, a Roman by nation. Three years and six months, until the year of the Lord 945.

CXXXII. Agapetus II, a Roman by nation. Almost ten years, until the year of the Lord 955. In his time the Synod of Ingelheim assembled in the presence of Kings Otto and Louis concerning Adalbero, nephew of St Ulrich. Bishop Marinus presided at that synod in place of Pope Agapetus and subscribed with thirty bishops of Germany. He also raised Gerhard, pastor of the Church of Lorch, to metropolitan rank, and settled through arbiters from both dioceses the dispute between him and Herold of Salzburg regarding the dignity of the archbishopric:

[Col. 1026B] he entrusted the care of western Pannonia to Herold, and that of eastern Pannonia to Gerhard, together with the land of the Avars, the Moravians, and the Slavs, whether already Christian or still to be won for Christ. He granted him the Apostolic office in those regions—to preach, establish bishops, and order all things as if he himself were present.

CXXXIII. John XII, also called Octavian, a Roman by nation, son of Alberic. Eight years and four months. He is blamed by some, who say that he spent his whole life in adultery and dissipation.

[Col. 1026C] In his time Emperor Otto, the first of that name, son of King Henry, came to Rome and was honourably received by him. The aforesaid emperor contended with him greatly, but could never remove him from his wickedness. Having taken counsel, he came again to Rome in order to recall that criminal from such great depravity. When John heard of his arrival, he fled to Campania and hid there in the mountains. Then all the Romans, clergy and laity alike, with one agreement and one will, asked the emperor to provide the holy Church with a worthy pontiff and devout ruler. He said to them: “Choose one who is worthy, and I shall most willingly grant him to you.” All, clergy and laity alike, chose Lord Leo, a venerable *protoscriniarius* of the supreme Apostolic See.

[Col. 1026D] When the emperor departed and Leo remained in the see, the Romans expelled Leo and restored that criminal John to the see. Consequently famine, severe persecution, and tribulation came upon the city. Lord Leo departed the city unharmed and came to the emperor at Spoleto. Honourably received by him, he prepared measures against the Romans. When he was approaching, Roman envoys came to the city of Rieti before his arrival, announced John’s death, and requested the election and consecration of Benedict the deacon. They obtained nothing, but received this response from him: “When I lay aside my sword, then I shall allow Lord Pope Leo not to be restored to the chair of St Peter.” The envoys returned and, against the emperor’s will, elected the aforesaid Benedict.

[Col. 1027A] When the emperor heard this, he blazed forth in greater anger, surrounded the city on every side, and afflicted its people in diverse ways all around. He reduced it to such straits that a modius of bran was bought for thirty silver coins. Unable to endure this scourge, the citizens handed Benedict, though innocent, over to the emperor and received Lord Leo, after taking an oath upon the body of St Peter. The emperor forgave them their offence and departed for Gaul.

CXXXIV. Leo, a Roman by birth, son of John the protoscriniarius, from the district called the Clivus Argentarii, [reigned] one year and three months; a man distinguished by every kind of integrity. After the wicked John had been expelled by Emperor Otto, [Col. 1027B] as is said, he was chosen by the common election of both clergy and people and consecrated Roman pontiff during the month of December in the Lateran patriarchal residence. In that same month he held ordinations: seven priests and two deacons. Having assembled a synod at Rome in the church of St. Saviour, following the example of Adrian, bishop of the Apostolic See, who granted to Lord Charles, most invincible king of the Franks and Lombards, the dignity of patriciate, the ordering of the Apostolic See, and the investiture of bishops, he decreed as follows:

“I, Leo, servant of the servants of God, bishop, together with all the clergy and people of Rome, establish, confirm, and strengthen; and by our apostolic authority grant and bestow upon Lord Otto the First, king of the Germans, and upon his successors [Col. 1027C] in this kingdom of Italy for ever, both the power of choosing his successor and that of appointing the pontiff of the supreme Apostolic See. Accordingly, archbishops and bishops are to receive investiture from him, but consecration from those from whom they ought to receive it, excepting those whom the emperor has granted to the pontiff and archbishops. Furthermore, henceforth no one, of whatever rank or religious profession, is to possess the power of choosing or appointing either a patrician or the pontiff of the supreme Apostolic See, or any bishop whatsoever, without the consent of that emperor; this, however, shall take place without any payment, and he himself shall be patrician and king. If anyone is chosen as bishop by God and the people, he is not to be consecrated unless he is approved and invested by the aforesaid king. If anyone should contrive anything against [Col. 1027D] this apostolic authority, we decree that he is subject to excommunication; and unless he repents, that he is to be punished by irrevocable exile or struck with the ultimate penalties.”

This Otto is called the first king of the Germans, not because he was the first to reign among them, but because he was the first from among them to restore the empire to the German Franks.

CXXXV. Benedict V, a Roman by birth, son of John. He reigned two months. When he was expelled, as has been stated, the emperor restored Leo and sent Benedict into Saxony, where he ended his life in exile in the archbishopric of Bremen. By order of Otto III his bones were brought back to Rome and honourably buried. Leo, however, endured many evils from the Romans a second time.

[Col. 1028A] CXXXVI. John XIII, a Roman by birth, son of John the bishop, formerly bishop of Narni. He [reigned] seven years, until the year of the Lord 902, and sat in the see by the common election of all. This man was learned and honourably educated in divine and canonical books. Remaining in clerical orders from his cradle, he was ordained in successive grades in the same Roman Church: doorkeeper, psalmist, reader, exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, and deacon in the Lateran palace; and thus, by God’s will, he was lawfully and canonically ordained pontiff. After he had reigned for two months and sixteen days, he was seized by Count Rofred and Prefect Peter with the Roman people, and they sent him into exile in Campania. He remained in that exile ten months and twenty-eight days. After Rofred’s death [Col. 1028B] he returned to Rome; and when Emperor Otto came, he exacted severe vengeance upon the Roman people, hanging some on the gallows and sending others into exile.

CXXXVII. Benedict VI, a Roman by birth, son of Hiltibrand. [He reigned] one year and ten months. Accused by the Romans, he was confined by Crescentius in the Castle of St. Angelo and strangled. While he was still alive Boniface was ordained; but he was immediately driven out and fled to Constantinople, while Otto I was still emperor, in the year of the Lord 974. According to some, Donus; according to others, Boniface. Donus [reigned] one year and six months.

CXXXVIII. Boniface VII, a Roman by birth, son of Ferrutius. He was immediately driven out and fled to Constantinople, [Col. 1028C] and Benedict, formerly bishop of Sutri, was substituted. This Boniface—or rather Maleface—had first been wrongly ordained and expelled; then, having wickedly returned, he finally died most miserably. He reigned nearly one year.

CXXXIX. Benedict VII, a Roman by birth, son of David, likewise bishop of Sutri. [He reigned] nine years, until the year of the Lord 983. He wrote to Emperor Otto II, to Duke Henry of Bavaria, and to the German archbishops; he restored metropolitan honour to the Church of Lorch and assigned Pilgrim six suffragan bishops there, namely, so that the Church of Salzburg should have the bishops of Upper Pannonia, while that church should have those of Lower Pannonia. Pilgrim also [Col. 1028D] clearly set forth his allegiance to him in a letter sent to him and requested that a pallium be sent.

CXL. John XIV, also called Peter, born at Pavia. He reigned eight months. Boniface mentioned above, having returned from Constantinople, where he had fled, seized him and ordered him to be worn down by starvation in custody for four months in the Castle of St. Angelo and killed. Boniface then usurped the see for eleven months; overtaken by sudden death, after his death he was cut and stabbed out of hatred by his own people, and, his body stripped naked, was thrown into the field before Constantine’s horse. In the morning he was buried by clerics who came upon him.

CXLI. John XV, a Roman by birth, son of Leo the priest. He reigned ten years and seven months, and decorated with painting the oratory [Col. 1029A] of St. Mary on the Steps. He died in the year of the Lord 996.

CXLII. Gregory V, also called Bruno, a Frank by birth, son of Duke Otto and Judith his mother. He reigned three years and nine months, until the year of the Lord 999. Crescentius, rebelling against him, was captured in the Castle of St. Angelo, mutilated, and hanged by his feet. John the Greek, surnamed Philagathos, bishop of Piacenza, usurped his see; but Otto’s vassal, named Birthilo, seized him, cut off his nose and tongue, gouged out his eyes, and dragged him by an ass’s tail throughout Rome. He was the first German to preside over the Apostolic See. William bishop of Strasbourg, Hezil, and Chuno were likewise four brothers, sons of Duke Otto of East Francia. From [Col. 1029B] Chuno and Hezil were born two brothers named Chuno, of whom the elder, called Conrad, became Roman emperor, although the election among the princes of the empire had been made only between these two.

CXLIII. Sylvester II, also called Gerbert the Musician, an Aquitanian by birth [Note: [Col. 1029D] “Aquitanian.”], from the monastery of St. Gerald; first archbishop of Rheims, then of Ravenna, and finally raised to the papacy. He reigned five years, until the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1004. Of him it was written:

Gerbert passes from R[heims] to R[avenna], then, flourishing as pope, to R[ome].

He was excessively devoted to secular learning and was therefore beloved by the intellectually curious Emperor Otto III, the Younger.

EPITAPH OF POPE SYLVESTER, ALSO CALLED GERBERT

[Col. 1029C]

This place shall give up the limbs of buried Sylvester  
At the sound of the coming Lord.

The most learned Virgin had made him renowned in the world  
And [had given him] the Roman heights, the head of the world.

Gerbert, born among the Franks, first deserved the see,  
The metropolitan church of the people of Rheims, his native land;

Then, noble and powerful, he deserved to ascend  
The supreme governance of the Church of Ravenna.

After a year he assumed Rome, his name changed,  
That he might become a new shepherd throughout the whole world.

Otto Caesar the Third greatly desired to join himself to him  
In loyal friendship, and offered him this [office].

Each adorned his own age; each was illustrious in wisdom;  
[Col. 1029D] every age rejoices, and every guilty thing is broken.

He was like the bearer of the keys, having attained the heavenly seat;  
Clothed in its covering, he was shepherd in place of the sheep.

After he had assumed Peter’s office, he drove away  
The ages by the lustral course of his death.

The world grew cold when peace was shattered; the wavering triumph  
Of the Church forgot repose.

Out of devotion, the priest Sergius altered this tomb;  
His successor adorned it out of love for him.

Whoever, bending down, turns your eyes toward this tomb,  
Say: “Almighty Lord, have mercy upon him.”

He composed a sequence in praise of the angels: “For the celebrated ones.”

[Col. 1030A] CXLIV. Sica, called John by others, [reigned] one year.

CXLV. John XVI, [reigned] one year.

CXLVI. John XVII, also called Fasanus, son of Urso and Stephania. After five and a half years he departed as a monk at St. Paul’s.

CXLVII. Sergius IV, also called Peter, surnamed “Pig’s Mouth,” formerly bishop of Albano, son of Peter and Stephania, “Pig’s Mouth.” He reigned five years and adorned the tomb of Sylvester, also called Gerbert.

CXLVIII. Benedict VIII, a Tusculan by birth, son of Gregory and the noblewoman Maria. He reigned eleven years and almost one month, until the year of the Lord 1024. He crowned Duke Henry of Bavaria, through the mediation of [Col. 1030B] Walter, bishop of Speyer, with an assurance of loyalty given on both sides; and he dedicated the cathedral church which Henry himself founded at Bamberg. The same Henry, second of that name but the first as emperor, was also crowned and exalted with the imperial blessing by him.

CXLIX. John XVIII. He reigned nine years, until the year of the Lord 1033. The brother of the preceding pope was made pope from the laity. He consecrated Emperor Conrad and Empress Gisela at Rome on holy Easter Day, in the presence of King Rudolf of Burgundy and King Cnut [Note: [Col. 1030D] “Canute.”] of England, who had come there with him.

CL. Benedict IX, also called Theophylact. [He reigned] twelve years. Driven out because of his crimes, he returned; then, given over to vices, he voluntarily withdrew from the papacy [Col. 1030C] in the year of the Lord 1046. Though unworthy in character of such great honour, he occupied the see for more than twelve years. When he had been expelled, the Romans set up in his place a certain Sylvester, whom Benedict himself, after returning, expelled as excommunicated. Restored to his see, he later deprived himself of it and, out of avarice, appointed in his place, contrary to the canons, another named Gratian. The Romans placed this man in the see and made him pope. For this reason King Henry III—second emperor of that name—seeing that the Church was troubled by schism, carefully examined the matter in a synod at Sutri, deprived Gratian of the pastoral staff, and placed Swidiger, bishop of Bamberg, called Clement, over the Apostolic See, which he governed only eight [Col. 1030D] months. The king himself and Queen Agnes, his wife, having received the imperial blessing, returned amid the highest rejoicing and honour during the most solemn days of Christ’s Nativity. And when Eberhard, bishop of Constance, died there and was buried at the thresholds of the apostles, Theoderic was immediately appointed there in his place.

CLI. Sylvester III. Having been ordained after Benedict’s expulsion, as stated above, he was immediately driven out in the year of the Lord 1044.

CLII. Gratian, a Roman by birth, also called Gregory. [He reigned] three years. Benedict, unjustly depriving himself, appointed him pope in his place in the year of the Lord 1047. Rich in inherited and movable property, he had compassion on the Church of God and wished to remove the schism that consisted in the rivalry of two men. He met each of them secretly and, offering and giving them his own goods, withdrew them both from their ambition for the see. Hence some assert that the Romans elected him against his will and installed him in their place. Yet, because it is not established by human judgment with what intention things capable of an indifferent construction are done, others accused him of simony, and he is said to have been lawfully deposed.

CLIII. Clement II, also called Swidiger, a Saxon by birth, bishop of Bamberg. After Pope Gratian had been deposed, as stated above, he was elected by the bishops and King Henry and reigned nine months [Note: [Col. 1031D] “Shortly before: eight.”]. He died in the very month of his appointment and was carried back to his bishopric and buried there in the year of the Incarnation [Col. 1031B] of the Lord 1047. Others judge that he deserved to be called mad rather than Clement, since they maintain that Gratian had been removed by force and that Clement was intruded.

CLIV. Damasus II, also called Poppo, a German by birth, bishop of Brixen, was sent by King Henry and elevated to the papacy. In the year of the Lord 1049 he survived less than a full month. The see was vacant for seven months.

CLV. Leo IX, also called Bruno, bishop of the Leuci, or Toul, which is the same thing; a German by birth, son of Count Hugh. Chosen by the aforesaid Emperor Henry and by the bishops and raised to the papacy, he reigned five years, two months, and six days, beginning in the year of the Lord 1049. While travelling through Gaul after assuming the papal purple, he came to Cluny, where, at the admonition of Hildebrand, [Col. 1031C] who administered the priory of that place, and persuaded that he was not permitted to ascend to the government of the whole Church through a lay hand, he laid aside the purple, took Hildebrand with him to Rome, and was elected pope by the Roman clergy and people. Thus the Roman Church was instructed in making an election. He held a synod at Mainz with the emperor and entered Pannonia in arms with him. When he wished to restrain Robert Guiscard, duke of the Norman people, who was invading the borders of Apulia, the Church, and the empire, battle was joined; many were slain, and he was compelled to flee to Benevento. He died the following year, was buried in the church of St. Peter at Rome, and is held to be illustrious for miracles. He established many canons.

One was directed against the rapacity of monks: “Since there are many who teach, not from zeal for charity but from zeal for rapacity, and deceive secular persons into giving their goods, during life or at death, to their monasteries, while leaving nothing of their property to the churches to which they appear subject and from which they receive baptism, penance, the Eucharist, and indeed the nourishment of life with the milk of the flesh, we altogether forbid this to happen any longer. Rather, we order that they leave half of all their possessions to the church to which they are known to belong; and thus they may have permission to convert and depart thence.”

He also made several chants of sweet melody: namely, the Office of St. Nicholas and [Col. 1032A] St. Gregory, the solemn “Glory to God in the highest,” the responsory “He led the just man,” and the responsory “Visit those, O Lord.”

HIS EPITAPH

Victorious Rome, mourn, bereft of Leo the Ninth,  
For among many you shall not have his equal.

CLVI. Victor II, also called Gebehard, bishop of Eichstätt, a German by birth. He reigned two years, two months, and seven days.

CLVII. Stephen, a Belgian by birth, son of Duke Godfrey. Formerly Frederick, archchaplain of Pope Leo, he became a monk from being a cleric and was abbot of Monte Cassino. He presided over the Apostolic See seven months and twenty-nine days. He also had a brother, Duke Godfrey.

[Col. 1032B] CLVIII. Benedict IX, a Burgundian by birth. [He reigned] nine months and twenty days. Formerly called John, he was advanced, through the private favour of certain Romans and contrary to the canons, and sat without consecration. Therefore he was expelled by Duke Godfrey, and Gebehard, bishop of the city of Florence, was ordained in his place and called Nicholas.

CLIX. Nicholas II, also called Gebehard, bishop of Florence. He reigned two years, six months, and twenty-five days; having presided nearly three years at the summit of the supreme pontificate, he was suddenly seized by death on the sixth day before the Kalends of August in the bishopric of Perugia, was carried to Perugia, and buried there in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1061. In the basilica of the Lateran patriarchal residence, called the Constantinian, sitting together with archbishops, [Col. 1032C] bishops, abbots, venerable priests, and deacons, he established many measures useful to the Church, especially concerning the election of the supreme pontiff.

When Pope Nicholas died, the Romans sent the crown and other gifts to King Henry IV of that name and appealed to him concerning the election of a supreme pontiff. He summoned most of the bishops of Italy; when a general council had been held at Basel, he put on the crown which the Romans had sent and was called Patrician of the Romans. Then, by the common counsel of all and with the Roman legates electing, Cadalus, bishop of Parma, was declared pope on the seventh day before the Kalends of November and, his name changed, was called Honorius. While this was taking place, the Normans, having enlisted some Romans, installed Anselm, bishop of the Tuscan city of Lucca, upon the Apostolic See, having given him the name Alexander, on the Kalends of October, twenty-six days before the bishop of Parma was raised to the papacy.

CLX. Alexander II. He reigned twelve years; he was also Anselm, first bishop of Lucca. He most steadfastly repelled Cadalus, bishop of Parma, when he sought to seize the Roman See by armed force. With the support of the Normans and certain Romans, he defeated and rejected Cadalus and reigned twelve years. Therefore it is written of him in the Lateran palace:

Alexander reigns; Cadalus falls and is defeated.

[Col. 1033A] CLXI. Gregory VII, also called Hildebrand, first prior of Cluny and afterwards archbishop of Ravenna; a Roman by birth, son of Bonico. He reigned twelve years, one month, and five days. This teacher of impossibilities decreed that no layman should attend the office of a priest whose wife he knew. He commanded deacons and subdeacons to put away their wives. He commanded bishops not to advance to sacred orders anyone born from the marriage of priests. Hence a criminal disturbance of both sexes increased. In the seventh year of his pontificate, in the year of the Lord 1080, he held a synod at Rome. There, among other decrees, he ordained that if any emperor, duke, or any secular power presumed to confer the office of any ecclesiastical dignity, he should be subject to the bond of anathema.

At this time Emperor Henry, whom he had specially marked by this decree of anathema, besieged Rome, expelled Hildebrand, and installed Wibert, archbishop of Ravenna, also called Clement, as pope. Hildebrand is reported to have said when dying at Salerno: “I have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore I die in exile.” The Church being placed in the utmost danger because Wibert had occupied the Roman See and city, a few Romans dragged the unwilling Abbot Desiderius of Cassino, a cardinal and also called Victor, to the papacy; having bribed the guards of the Leonine City, they brought him by night into the church of St. Peter for consecration, out of fear of schism. A synod was held at Quedlinburg under him against Wezilo, [Col. 1033C] archbishop of Mainz, over which Otto, bishop of Ostia, presided in the pope’s place. The archbishop of Mainz maintained that any person stripped of his possessions should go unpunished for whatever he might meanwhile commit, since he could neither be summoned to a synod nor judged under canon law. The same pope, having excommunicated the emperor, crowned Rudolf, duke of Alemannia, with these words:

Rome gave Peter; Peter gave the diadem to Rudolf.

CLXII. Victor III, also called Desiderius, abbot of Cassino and cardinal. He reigned four months and seven days. As stated above, he was consecrated by night, out of fear of schism, after the guards of the Leonine City had been bribed; [Col. 1033D] there he died of diarrhoea. Departing both from the City and from the world, he left the governance of the Church to Urban, bishop of Ostia, formerly called Otto. Wibert, however, whom Emperor Henry had installed, harassed the Church for seven years. On his account, in his presence, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1085, a synod was held at Mainz by order of the excommunicated ruler, assembled only from bishops also excluded from communion. It decreed that two archbishops and twelve bishops should be deposed because, unwilling to communicate with the excommunicated, they had obeyed the Roman See. It was judged to be a sister of the synod of Rimini held by the Arian Constantius.

CLXIII. Urban II, formerly called Otto, bishop of Ostia. He reigned eleven years, five months, and eighteen days. Returning from the Council of Clermont, which he had held in Gaul, [Col. 1034A] he expelled Wibert from the City, except for Crescentius’s fortress, with the help of those whom he had stirred up for the journey to Jerusalem, and recovered his own see. Then, travelling through Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, which the Normans then inhabited, he collected a great sum of money. With this he bribed those guarding Crescentius’s fortress, expelled Wibert from both fortress and City, and freely possessed all Rome. Not long thereafter he departed this life and left the see to Paschal. He established canons for Genebald, bishop of Constance, concerning those who communicate with excommunicated persons willingly or in ignorance. At the Synod of Piacenza he instituted and composed the preface to be said of Holy Mary: “And thee in veneration,” etc.

CLXIV. Paschal II. He reigned eighteen years, five months, and eighteen days. In the twelfth year of his pontificate he was seized by King Henry the Younger because an agreement, said to have been made and confirmed by hostages between him and the king, required the king to surrender investitures of bishops and the pope to resign the regalia to him. Since he could not fulfil this because the bishops objected, he was captured and entrusted for safekeeping to Ulric, patriarch of Aquileia; from him, however, Henry later received the imperial blessing.

CLXV. Gelasius, also called John of Gaeta. He reigned one year and five days. Emperor Henry expelled him from Rome and installed as pope Gregory—also called Burdinus by the Normans—archbishop of Braga, who [Col. 1034C] had previously been excommunicated at Benevento by Lord Paschal.

CLXVI. Calixtus, called Guy, bishop of Vienne. He reigned five years, ten months, and thirteen days. He excommunicated Henry and his pope Burdinus, and even thrust Burdinus into a cage. Therefore it is written of him:

Behold Calixtus, his country’s honour, the empire’s glory,  
Condemns wicked Burdinus and restores peace.

For fear of anathema Emperor Henry, through Honorius, his legate and later successor, resigned the investitures of bishoprics to him in this form:

“I, Henry, by the grace of God Augustus, emperor of the Romans, for the love of God and of the holy Roman Church and of Lord Pope Calixtus, and for the remedy of my soul, surrender to God, to God’s holy apostles Peter and Paul, and to the holy Catholic Church every investiture by ring and staff. I grant free election and canonical consecration in all churches within my kingdom or empire. The possessions and regalia of blessed Peter which have been taken away from the beginning of this dispute until the present day, whether in my father’s time or mine, and which I possess, I restore to that same holy Roman Church; those which I do not possess, I shall faithfully aid in restoring. I shall also restore the possessions of all other churches, princes, and other persons, clerical as well as lay, which I possess, according to the counsel and justice of the princes; and I shall faithfully aid in restoring those which I do not possess. And [Col. 1035A] I grant true peace to Lord Pope Calixtus, to the holy Roman Church, and to all who are or have been on its side; and in all matters in which the holy Roman Church asks, I shall faithfully give aid.”

The letter of Pope Calixtus, in which he in turn remitted to him the elections of bishops of the German kingdom, runs as follows:

“I, Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, grant to my beloved son Henry, by the grace of God Augustus, emperor of the Romans, that elections of bishops and abbots of the German kingdom, who belong to your realm, shall take place in your presence without simony or any violence; so that, if any disagreement arises between the parties, you shall give assent and assistance to the sounder party, by the counsel and judgment of the metropolitan and provincial bishops. The person elected shall receive the regalia from you by the sceptre without exaction, excepting [Col. 1035B] all things known to belong to the Roman Church, and shall perform what is rightfully due therefrom. In the other parts of the empire, those consecrated shall receive the regalia from you by the sceptre within four months. In matters concerning which you complain to me and request aid, I shall offer you aid according to the obligation of my office. I grant true peace to you and to all who are or have been on your side during this dispute.”

Thus under him the Church was fully restored to its liberty and peace was re-established.

CLXVII. Honorius II, also called Lambert. He reigned eight years. As stated above, he was mediator and legate between Pope Calixtus and Emperor Henry, through whom Henry also surrendered investitures. He deposed the bishop of Milan because [Col. 1035C] he had consecrated Conrad, nephew of Emperor Henry, whom his own citizens had elected king; [Note: [Col. 1035D] Corrected: “he deposed.”] and he afterwards excommunicated Conrad himself, when he had become king of the Romans.

CLXVIII. Innocent II, formerly called Gregory, a Roman by birth, cardinal deacon of St. Angelo. He reigned thirteen years, seven months, and eight days. Although canonically elected, Peter, son of Peter Leo, also called Anacletus, was intruded through the violence of his friends. Favoured by Roger, king of Sicily, he occupied the city and see. Since Innocent could not resist, he withdrew from the city and appealed for the aid of King Lothar. Lothar brought him to Rome; in the church of St. Saviour, also called the Constantinian [Col. 1035D] church, he was crowned by Innocent and attained the title Augustus. Under and through him a synod was also held at Rome in the Lateran during Lent, where two hundred [Note: [Col. 1035D] “Thus I read: dti.”] and more bishops and other prelates assembled. There he established many useful measures for the Church; among other things, he decreed that ordinations performed by Peter or by those ordained by him should be invalid, and that Peter and his followers should be subject to excommunication.

CLXIX. Celestine II. Six months.

CLXX. Lucius II, also called Gerhard. One year. He suffered severe persecution from the Roman citizens and urged and invited King Conrad [Col. 1036A] by letter to protect the Roman Church, as follows:

“Lucius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Conrad, illustrious king of the Romans: greeting and apostolic blessing. ‘Every good gift and every perfect present is from above,’ etc. (James 1).”

For the Roman people, unwilling to set bounds to their madness, added a Patrician to the senators whom they had previously established. Choosing Jordan, son of Peter Leo, for this dignity, they all subjected themselves to him as to a prince. Then they approached their pontiff and demanded for the right of their Patrician all his regalia, both in the City and outside it, declaring that their pontiff ought, after the manner of ancient priests, to be supported only by tithes and offerings. Thus from day [Col. 1036B] to day they did not fear to afflict the soul of the righteous man, etc.

CLXXI. Eugenius III, born at Pisa, a monk. He reigned eight years, four months, and twenty-one days, a man conspicuous for religion and holiness. Because of the violence of persecution he withdrew from the City with the bishops and cardinals, changed his manner of life and was consecrated in the monastery of Farfa. Removing himself to fortified places, he excommunicated Jordan and his accomplices. Later he made peace with the Romans, on the condition that they should renounce the dignity of the patriciate and restore the prefect to his former dignity, while retaining senators. Returning thus to the City, he celebrated Christ’s Nativity there in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1146; there he was again pressed regarding the destruction of the people of Tivoli. He also held a synod at Reims, at the prompting of the abbot of Clairvaux, against Master Gilbert, bishop of Poitiers [Note: [Col. 1035D] “Here the following two verses were erased.”]. [lacuna]

CLXXII. Anastasius IV reigned one year, four months, and twenty-four days.

CLXXIII. Adrian IV, an Englishman by birth, reigned four years, eight months, and six days. At his death a most serious schism disturbed the whole Church. It began in the year of the Lord 1159 and lasted until the year of the Lord 1177, some electing Roland, also called Alexander, and others Octavian, also called Victor. When Victor died, Guy, also called Paschal, was substituted. When he died, Calixtus, also called John, abbot of Struma, was put in his place. The whole Church, however, except for a few induced by fear or affection for Emperor Frederick, [Col. 1036D] approved Alexander. This Adrian raised King Frederick to imperial rank at Rome with the imperial blessing, although the citizens resisted. [Note: [Col. 1036D] These words were inserted by another hand, no older than the fourteenth century.] In the time of this pope, namely the aforesaid Adrian, the mystery of the Virgin Mary was consecrated at Czwetl. May God keep us therein and defend us from every evil; and may the blessed Virgin lead us to eternal life.

CLXXIV. Alexander III, a Sienese by birth, also called Roland, reigned nearly twenty-three years. In 1157 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the tenth indiction, with five in the concurrents and twenty-eight in the epacts, the nineteen-year cycle having been completed, on the ninth day before the Kalends of August, the schism which had long disturbed the whole [Col. 1037A] Church was ended and laid to rest in Alexander, Roman pontiff. That is: a dispensation having been made between kingship and priesthood, Pope Alexander and Emperor Frederick, long at variance with one another and mutually disparaging one another’s right, met at Venice with the kiss of peace and with oaths sworn and ratified on both sides. Many dispensations were introduced there, which, for the necessity and peace of the long-afflicted Church, were universally approved, through the mediation of princes who loved the unity of the Church: Christian, archbishop of Mainz; Wichmann, archbishop of Magdeburg; and Conrad of Worms.

In the following year, during Lent, having summoned countless bishops and prelates from different peoples and regions in order to restrain the insolences and enormities which had increased during the schism, he held a synod at Rome. In it he established nineteen synodal chapters:

1. A priest who dissipates the Church’s dowry or tithes belonging to another is to be deprived of office and benefice. [Note: [Col. 1037D] Supply “dissipating,” or something similar.]
2. No cleric or priest may have more than one church or canonry in different places.
3. A cleric or priest openly cohabiting in fornication is to be deprived of office and benefice.
4. No bishop may ordain a cleric except to a definite title.
5. No bishop or archdeacon may demand an exaction or levy collections from his clerics.
6. Masters of schoolboys must demand nothing from those to whom they preach the word of God.
7. When a bishop visits his diocese, he may not have more than [Col. 1037C] thirty-five mounts, or only thirty; an archbishop, not more than forty; and likewise for the others.
8. Schismatics who have sworn [an oath], and not under harsh compulsion, are not to be promoted.
9. Usurers are to be excommunicated and, if they come to religious life, are not to be received unless, where possible, they restore ill-gotten gains.
10. Heretics, such as Cathars, or those called by another name Patarines, are to be excommunicated and denied burial.
11. Laypersons are not to possess tithes.
12. No cleric may receive investiture from a layperson.
13. No one may be made priest unless he is legitimate-born.

Chapters concerning Black Monks:

1. They must demand nothing from those converting to religious life.
2. They must possess nothing as private property.
3. No appeal made by them is binding upon [Col. 1037D] the abbot.
4. An abbot cannot remove a canonically appointed prior without the pope’s consent, unless the cause has been investigated.

Among other things he decreed one measure concerning schismatics, that they should be deprived of orders and benefices, as follows:

“Renewing what was done by our predecessor Pope Innocent of happy memory, we decree invalid the ordinations performed by the heresiarchs Octavian and Guy, and likewise by John of Struma, who followed them, and by those ordained by them. We further add that those who have received ecclesiastical dignities or benefices through the aforesaid schismatics shall lose what they have obtained. [Col. 1038A] Alienations or usurpations of ecclesiastical property made by those same schismatics or by laypersons shall have no force whatever and shall return to the Church without any honour. If anyone presumes to act against this, let him know that he is subject to excommunication. But those who voluntarily swore an oath to maintain [Note: [Col. 1037D] The manuscript has *tinendo*, “holding.”] the schism, we decree to be especially suspended from sacred orders and dignities.”

Alexander died in the year of the Lord 1181.

HIS EPITAPH

Light of the clergy, glory of the Church, father of City and world,  
Bishop Alexander is enclosed in this tomb.

Of the extinguished light [Note: [Col. 1037D] The remainder has been obscured from sight by a stain which long ago disfigured this page.] [lacuna]

And with him the City mourns . . . a man.

Yet he is not believed guilty . . . of the misfortune

. . . [of] the man.

[Col. 1038B] [lacuna] care for the flock, gracious modesty, integrity,

[lacuna] obtained a place.

[lacuna] who and whence was he? His former name

was Roland; Tuscany his homeland; Siena his home.

[lacuna] fortunate and enlarged by his own people.

[lacuna] by those through whom he was made fortunate and enlarged.

CLXXV. Lucius III, also called Hubald, bishop of Ostia, a native of Lucca, reigned four years and two months. He and the emperor met at Verona; that sweet conversations might be exchanged between spiritual father and son [Note: [Col. 1038D] Perhaps *miscerentur*, “might be exchanged.”], and as though one commonwealth had been made from two principal courts and two heads of the world, ecclesiastical and secular affairs were discussed together between them. There also, mutually delighted by each other’s presence and strengthened by its vigour, by the common counsel [Col. 1038C] of all the archbishops, bishops, and other princes who had gathered there, they rose up against various heresies and their authors, whose various names professed various falsehoods: Cathars, Patarines, those who falsely call themselves “the Humiliated” or “the Poor of Lyons,” as much by a false name as they boastfully lie; Passagians, Josephites, Arnoldists, and Publicans. They condemned them according to their right. There he afterwards died in the year of the Lord 1185, concerning whom it was written:

Lucca gave you birth, Ostia the pontificate, Rome the papacy, Verona death.

CLXXVI. Urban III, also called Hubert, archbishop of Milan and likewise born there, sat for one year and a half. He died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November [17 October], [Col. 1038D] in the year of the Lord 1177. [Note: [Col. 1038D] This, as also everything that follows until the end of the work, was added by another hand, though a contemporary one.] He died on the Kalends of November [1 November]. Twenty days before his death Jerusalem was taken by the Turks.

CLXXVII. Gregory VIII, also called Albert, formerly chancellor of the Roman Church, died in the very year in which he was elected, namely, in the year of the Lord 1188. For in the preceding year of the Lord’s Incarnation Jerusalem was taken by the Turks. Therefore, at the beginning of his election, he sent a letter to the bishops of Germany both concerning his election and exhorting the princes to aid the Eastern Church; and, because of the correspondence of the dates, he judged a copy of it worthy to be inserted.

[Col. 1039A] Gregory, to the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and prelates of churches in Germany.
