Among the hidden things of the divine dispensation, which God works among human beings, there is for us great cause for wonder and astonishment: that He so orders the positions of superiority and subjection among men that he who ought to be placed lowest seems to be set highest, and conversely. Solomon himself marvelled at this, saying: “I saw servants upon horses, and masters walking on the earth like servants” (Eccles. 10). Would that it had been granted to us merely to marvel at and see this, rather than also to experience it! For though we had been called by the Lord to a lesser position, and had never acted therein as faithfully as we ought, [Note: [Col. 1039D] Read: *egissemus* (“we had acted”).] we were suddenly raised to the eminence of a more distinguished office; and so great a burden has been laid upon our weak shoulders [Col. 1039B] that, as far as heaven is distant from earth, so far do our powers appear to fall short of the burden.

For when our predecessor Urban, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November [20 October], had entered, in a good confession, upon the way of all flesh and had solemnly been committed to burial, we assembled together on the following day. After Mass had been celebrated in honour of the Holy Spirit, as is customary, we bishops, priests, and deacons withdrew together to one place, canonically [Note: [Col. 1040D] Perhaps: *canonice* (“canonically”).] setting aside the various ecclesiastical affairs and, especially, the calamity of the Eastern Church, which had been heard of in those days. It seemed necessary to proceed to the election of a pope, lest, if it should perhaps be delayed, harm should come to the Christian people in various regions through tardiness.

When the wishes of the citizens had been sought, it pleased all to lay the burden of providing for the Church upon our mediocrity [Col. 1039C] and to press the matter so insistently that not one of my excuses—though many were available to me—was heard. I did not sufficiently know what to do, since freedom was safe neither in resisting nor in consenting: on the one hand, I was held back by my great deficiency in virtue and learning; on the other, I was urged by the united will and insistence of the brethren. Yet at last, considering that a man’s ways are not his own, nor is it in him, as he walks, to direct his steps; and that “Christ died for us, so that those who live might live no longer for themselves, but for him who died for us and rose again” (2 Cor. 5), we entrusted ourselves to divine mercy and yielded to the will of the brethren. This was not because we believed ourselves suitable ministers, or believed that so great a burden could be well borne by us, but [Col. 1039D] lest we should seem to abound too much in our own judgment and to have too little trust in the mercy of the Lord our God.

Since, therefore, it is fitting for us to remain in reverence toward the Roman Church, we believe that your whole body should be admonished by this notice, so that you may persist in devotion to that Church, as is just and expedient for your salvation. Concerning the matter and the ruin of the Eastern Church, we render you watchful and attentive by apostolic letters, beseeching, warning, and exhorting you [Col. 1040A] in the Lord to direct yourselves, as you recognize to be expedient, toward the liberation of that land. Take care also to warn and exhort more diligently our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, the illustrious emperor of the Romans, ever Augustus, together with the magnates and all the people of the German kingdom, that they may so attend to the pious service of the Almighty that the recompense of eternal life may thereby be increased for you and for them by the Giver to all who hope in Him.

For this purpose we send the bearers of these presents, our beloved sons P., our subdeacon, and the prior of Pontid.; learned, prudent, and honourable men, whom we dispatch to announce our elevation and whom we commend most earnestly to your charity.

Given on Friday, the sixth day before the Kalends of November [27 October], indiction 6. He also wrote [Col. 1040B] another letter to all the faithful of the Church for the same exhortation, in which he lamented more fully the destruction of the land beyond the sea and its wretched fate; this letter is possessed by many.

CLXXVIII. Clement, formerly called Paul, bishop of Palestrina, sat for two and a half years, until the year of the Lord 1191. When William, king of Sicily, died, and a lawful heir and successor to the kingdom failed in him, he commanded, at the request of the archbishop of Palermo, that a certain Tancred, usurper of that royal dignity, be anointed and consecrated. Whether this was out of hostility to the Roman imperial majesty, over which the glorious emperor Frederick then presided—who was then undertaking the journey to Jerusalem and had left the kingdom to his son H.—or in hope of recovering Apulia, [Col. 1040C] which they had long asserted to be the dowry of the Roman Church, I do not know. Yet previously, in the marriage contract between the aforesaid son of the emperor, who immediately afterward succeeded his father in the name of Augustus and emperor, and the sister of King William, it had been stipulated and approved by all the princes of the land that, if the aforesaid brother of hers should die without an heir, the kingdom would pass to this man. The Romans believed, indeed, that through the same Tancred they had found an opportunity to recover the land more easily for as long as they aspired to it.

CLXXIX. Celestine III, also called Hyacinth, cardinal deacon. In 1191 he crowned King Henry, son of Emperor Frederick, who had come into Apulia to obtain the kingdom [Col. 1040D] which belonged to him through his wife, whom he had previously married—namely, the sister of William, who had recently died—and on the day after Easter elevated both him and her by the imperial blessing. For in the same year, after Clement’s death, he was elected about the middle of Lent; made priest on the Saturday before the Lord’s Passion; and on Easter Day and the following day consecrated both himself and the emperor and his wife.

[Col. 1041]

LETTER OF AN ANONYMOUS EYEWITNESS CONCERNING THE CAPTURE OF THE CITY OF CONSTANTINOPLE.  
(Year 1204.)

[MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 784, from a manuscript of Dunes.]

[Col. 1041A] Know that Alexius Barisiacus [perhaps Isaac’s son], as I previously informed you with some uncertainty, came to us at Corfu. There, bending his knees and shedding tears, he humbly entreated us in person to come with him to Constantinople and give him aid, so that by our assistance he might drive from the imperial throne his father’s brother. His father had freed this man from imprisonment among the heathen; but, once freed and redeemed by his brother, he repaid him with such a return that, through ambition for the empire, he wickedly blinded his brother and seized and unjustly held the imperial throne at the prompting of avarice.

A very great disagreement and tumult consequently arose in the army. All cried out that we should go to Ascalon, and few approved the road to Constantinople. Among the latter were the count of Flanders, Louis, marquis of Montferrat, Count Matthew of Montmorency, marshal of Champagne, Conon of Béthune, M. of Brabant, John of Fusiens, [Col. 1041B] John of Trie, Peter of Bracieux, Anselm of Cayeux, R. of Trie, Macarius of Sainte-Menehould, M. of Lille, the bishop of Halberstadt, the bishop of Troyes, and John Facete. We all plainly showed the whole army that the Jerusalem route, since they were poor and short of provisions, and since there was no one among them able to retain knights in paid service, to have mangonels drawn along, or other engines of war conveyed, was useless and ruinous for all.

At length they scarcely agreed with us on this condition: that they would remain at Constantinople no longer than one month. It was answered that it was not necessary for us to announce a short stay publicly, because the Greeks would fear us less if they knew beforehand the duration of our brief stay. Nevertheless, they demanded that we publicly assure them that the stay would be only one month. And so it was done.

When this had been done, the young emperor pledged to us that he would provide provisions for the whole army for an entire year, and that he would maintain at his own expense ten thousand horsemen for a year in aid of the Holy Land. He also promised that, for as long as he lived, he would maintain at his own pay five hundred knights in the Holy Land, and that he would give ten marks of silver to the doge of Venice and the same amount to our army. When these terms had been set forth and granted by common consent, we boarded our ships.

On the eighth day thereafter, we safely reached the harbour of Ducaeavia; from that place Constantinople is reckoned to be one hundred leagues away. From that harbour to Constantinople there is passage through a narrow and swiftly flowing sea. Sailing through that strait, we passed through the Arm of Saint George and took harbour on the mainland toward Iconium, a harbour one league distant from Constantinople. There we wondered greatly that none of the young man’s friends or relatives who were with us, nor any messenger of theirs, came to him to explain the state of Constantinople. Without delay, the emperor who held the empire sent gifts to the doge of Venice, [Col. 1042A] the marquis, the count of Flanders, the count of Ludes, and ourselves.

We then entered into secret counsel among ourselves, deciding that we would by no means listen to the emperor’s envoys unless he first stepped down from the imperial throne of majesty; otherwise, we would hear neither him nor his envoys. For we did not wish the Greeks to test us with their deceitful gifts or soften us with their promises.

Meanwhile the emperor’s army stood ready on the shore opposite us to prevent our crossing, displaying the appearance of boldness in fighting us. Seeing this, we resorted to confession of our sins, trusting solely in the merciful power of God. Afterward we drew up our battle-lines and then, all armed, set our ships in order. When, under God’s guidance, we had landed on the far side, all the Greeks had assembled to hinder our crossing. But by God’s grace they withdrew so far from us that we could not reach any one of them even with the flight of an arrow.

Then we advanced to a very strong tower called Galata, to which was fastened an immense iron chain, exceedingly thick. Placed upon transverse timbers, it stretched across the sea, reaching from land to the city walls. This chain held the harbour shut; beside it the city’s ships and galleys, joined side by side with barges, prevented our entrance. On the aforesaid land were serjeants, Pisans, Genoese, Danes, and others appointed to guard and protect it. They went out of and entered the tower as they pleased in order to shoot at our men.

On that tower we spoke with the doge of Venice, a most prudent man, saying that it could by no means be taken unless miners and stone-throwing engines, with their various military devices, were placed upon ships. We too caused our engines to be raised, so that, with the tower besieged on every side, it might be taken with God’s aid and our own. While these measures were being proposed, [Col. 1042C] the serjeants of the aforesaid tower made frequent and troublesome attacks upon our men with arrows. Yet never did they make an assault upon us without being briskly driven back, and they suffered many kinds of losses among their own men.

On the third day after our tents had been pitched there, they came out from within and attacked our knights and foot-soldiers from behind. But Peter of Branicol, coming upon them armed with certain knights and serjeants, attacked them with such swift and terrible violence that they could neither resist nor return to the refuge of the tower. Indeed, as our men pressed them, some had to leap into the sea and were drowned; some were cut down; others were captured. Immediately, by God’s marvellous working, the tower was taken without a military engine, and the iron chain was broken. As the city’s ships at once withdrew, our ships had free access to the harbour, and they captured some of them together with galleys, small vessels, and barges.

Then, arranging our ships and ourselves for battle, we advanced as far as a certain stone bridge, [Col. 1043A] more than one league distant from the aforesaid land. This bridge was stronger than the Petit-Pont at Paris and so narrow that scarcely three horsemen, riding side by side, could cross it at once. Since the ford was deep, we could not cross without making a circuit of three leagues. Had we been so far from our ships, we might perhaps have incurred great danger and loss.

When we reached the bridge itself, by God’s forbearance and with no one opposing us, we crossed it. Proceeding onward, we pitched our tents between the emperor’s palace, which is called Blachernae, and the palace of Bohemond. Thus we drew so near to Blachernae that our arrows fell upon the emperor’s palace and entered through its windows, while Greek arrows fell upon our tents. Having done this, we enclosed our army with thick stakes and cords. Then we raised our engines of war, with stone-throwing machines, before the walls.

The doge of Venice erected upon every ship a very high bridge made from masts, one hundred feet high, and four armed knights could go upon each bridge. Moreover, one of his *ussarii* had a raised mangonel.

While these things were taking place, the Greeks made many attacks on foot and horseback. Yet in this they always came off worse than we did. One day a great multitude of knights, pouring out in ranks from a certain gate—the gate which opens high up on the right—rushed forth and challenged us to arms. Our men drove them back with such great and bold violence that many of them, one pressing upon another, fell into the ditches. Among them was killed the son of the duke of Dyrrachium, who was said to be the noblest and handsomest among the people of Constantinople, together with several others.

On the following day a troop of the city’s knights rushed out through the gate of Blachernae, on the side where we had caused our engines of war to be set up. But, with God’s help, they were driven back inside disgracefully and forcefully. [Col. 1043C] Then a certain man was killed who was more powerful and better in knightly service than all others in the city, and was the emperor’s counsellor.

On Wednesday it was ordered and determined that an assault upon the city should be made on the following day: the doge of Venice was to attack by sea, and the marquis and count of Flanders by land. I, Count Matthew of Montmorency, marshal of Champagne, and A. of Saint-Cyr were to guard the army outside the rampart and across the fields while the assault was made; and so we did.

When the arrangement had been made and the appointed time fixed, the doge and the Venetians, with some of our men who were vigorously pressing forward by sea in ships, brought the vessels near the walls, leaned ladders against the walls, and entered the city with valiant force. They gained twenty-five towers and burned no small part of the city, equal in size to Arras. Our men also, making their assaults by land, placed ladders against the walls and set their banners and standards upon the walls. The miners, undermining the wall below, brought down one tower.

Then the emperor, hemmed in on every side by the burning of the city, our ambushes, and our repeated assaults, stationed companies of no small number of knights at every gate leading out into the fields, so that they might attack and cut us down from all sides. In response, we drew up our battle-lines: the count of Flanders with his men and I with mine, each standing, that is, in his own wedge before the guard. We rode in order; and, formed together, we came so near the battle-line opposite us that their archers and crossbowmen shot at us, and ours at them.

[Col. 1044A] When they saw us advancing in good order, bravely and steadfastly, rank by rank, and saw that they could not easily defeat us, greatly frightened and confused, they yielded to us and did not dare to engage us in battle. You should know that in our army we had no more than two hundred knights and an equal number of other mounted men; we had no more than two thousand foot-soldiers, for the greater part had been assigned to guard the engines. Seeing them flee, we did not wish to pursue them, lest perhaps, through their tricks, harm should be done to our army, our siege-machines, and the towers which the Venetians had captured.

The emperor returned to his palace and declared that he would fight us on the next day; but at midnight he secretly fled. On Thursday we ought, as he had promised, to have fought together. But on the following day, by God’s working, the city was surrendered to us; and eight days from the beginning of the siege of the city had been completed.

Then Emperor Karisacus and his empress, his wife—namely, [Col. 1044B] the sister of the king of Hungary—who had long been held and shut up in terror, gave us many thanks. They announced that through God’s grace and our aid they had been freed from prison, had regained the dignity of the empire, and wished us to come on the following day to the palace as though to our own, together with his long-desired son. And so we did, and we ate in the palace with great rejoicing and solemn honour.

I wish you to know that R. of Parke and R. of Montmirail, A. of Boue, who were seeking Jerusalem, together with J. of Boue, S. of Montfort, R. Malvoisin, and the abbot of Vaux, caused a great division in the fleet. Hastening to the king of Hungary and abandoning our army, they left us in peril of death.

As for the doge of Venice, we praise him highly as a most prudent man and one trained in difficult counsels. But something much better and more glorious than the foregoing has been added, [Col. 1044C] and it is principally on account of this that we took care to come to the imperial city; I strive to explain it to you. The matter of the Saviour has advanced so far that the Eastern Church, whose head was Constantinople, together with the emperor and his whole empire, acknowledges itself to be the son of its head, the Roman pontiff, and henceforth wishes to obey him more devotedly, with captive humility, according to the customary manner.

The patriarch himself also, supporting and applauding this undertaking, will seek the Roman see hereafter in order to receive the pallium of his dignity from the supreme pontiff; and concerning this he has given a pledge upon oath with the emperor. Moreover, after our emperor had fully and entirely discharged all that he had promised, he bound himself to us by oath to cross the sea with us in the middle of the coming March with ten thousand fighting men; to supply provisions to the entire army of the Lord for a year; and to extend the Venetian fleet’s service for us for a year.

Having also sent envoys on his own part and ours to the sultan of Babylon, the holder of the Holy Land, [Col. 1044D] he announces that the sultan will shortly behold the devotion of the Christian people displayed against his unbelieving nation, and will await the power and mercy of God for the overthrow of unbelief. Therefore, moved by benefits so many and so great and sustained by the holy hope of future goods, we propose to winter at the aforesaid city. We have also taken care to notify our brethren who await our arrival in the regions beyond the sea, so that, when they hear the reports of our joys—of which we most earnestly desire them to be participants—they may, strengthened by the support of holy hope, wait more steadfastly.
